en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I bow to that Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the syllable Om, the Lord who is not touched by these three— dharma and adharma, their fruition, and the five afflictions— which extend over all living beings.

The Dharmaśāstra spoken by the sage Yājñavalkya, which was extensively elaborated through the formidable explanations of Viśvarūpa, is now analyzed with straightforward and concise words for the sake of awakening the understanding of beginners.

A certain disciple of Yājñavalkya, having abridged the treatise on Dharma composed by the sage Yājñavalkya in the form of questions and answers—just as Bhṛgu [abridged] that composed by Manu—spoke it.
And this is its first verse:
"Having honored Yājñavalkya, the Lord of Yogins, the sages spoke."
"Tell us, without omission, the duties of those belonging to the castes (varṇa), the stages of life (āśrama), and others.

Having honored that Yājñavalkya—the supreme lord of Yogins such as Sanaka and others—by means of mental, vocal, and physical actions, the sages, beginning with Sāmaśravas, who were capable of hearing and retaining [the teachings], spoke, saying: "Tell us the duties."
How?
Completely and in its entirety.
Of what things?
Of the castes, stages of life, and others:
the castes (varṇa) are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; the stages of life (āśrama) are the student (brahmacārin) and so forth.
The others— those born of inverse and non-inverse unions, such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and so forth— are designated by the word "others" (*itara*).
According to Pāṇini 1.1.31 (*dvandve ca*), there is a prohibition of the technical designation of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) for this word when it occurs in a *dvandva* compound.
And here, the word "dharma" refers to the sixfold dharma prescribed in the Smṛtis. Namely:

the dharma of caste (varṇadharma), the dharma of the stage of life (āśramadharma), the dharma of both caste and stage of life (varṇāśramadharma), the dharma of specific qualities (guṇadharma), the dharma of specific occasions (nimittadharma), and the common dharma (sādhāraṇadharma). Among these, the dharma of caste is exemplified by such rules as: "A Brāhmaṇa shall always avoid liquor," and so forth.

The duty of the stage of life (*āśramadharma*) consists of tending the sacred fires, gathering fuel, begging for alms, and so forth. The duty pertaining to both caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) consists of such rules as "the staff of a Brāhmaṇa must be made of *pālāśa* wood," and so on. The duty based on specific qualities (*guṇadharma*) consists of the protection of subjects and other such duties incumbent upon a king who possesses the quality of having undergone the scriptural consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
The *nimittadharma* (contingent duty) is the penance prescribed as a consequence of performing what is enjoined or engaging in what is prohibited.
The *sādhāraṇadharma* (common duty) consists of non-violence and so forth; for instance, "one should not harm any living beings" is a common duty that applies to everyone down to the *caṇḍāla*.

Since the study of the Dharmaśāstra is enjoined by the rule for becoming a teacher— namely, "and he should teach him the rules of purification and conduct" (YDh 1.15)— the statement of its purpose and so forth is not particularly useful.
In that regard, this is the sequence:
Before initiation, one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire;
after initiation, until the commencement of Vedic study, one should study the Dharmaśāstras.
Then, for one endowed with the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras,
there is the study of the Vedas; thereafter, the desire to know their meaning.
Then follows the performance of those goals.
In this regard, although dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are all expounded by this treatise, nevertheless, because dharma is paramount, only "dharma" is mentioned.
And [the former] has primacy because the others have their root in the Dharma.
Nor should it be said that there is no distinction between "wealth has its root in the Dharma" and "the Dharma has its root in wealth."
Since the accomplishment of Dharma occurs even without wealth through means such as recitation, austerity, and pilgrimage, there is not even a trace of wealth without Dharma;
likewise, this applies to desire and liberation as well. // 1.1 //
Being thus questioned, what did he say? He says:
"That lord of yogis, staying in Mithilā, having meditated for a moment, spoke to the sages:
'In whatever place there is a black antelope, learn the laws (dharmas) from that place. (YDh 1.2)

In the city named Mithilā resided that lord of yogis, Yājñavalkya; having meditated for a moment and composed his mind for some time, he thought, "Since these people, who are qualified to hear [the truth], ask with humility, it is proper to speak to them," and thus he spoke to the sages. What did he say?
"In whatever region the black antelope (*kṛṣṇamṛga*) dwells, in that region learn the laws (*dharmān*).

The intention is that in whatever region the black-spotted antelope roams at will, in that region the laws whose characteristics are about to be described are to be practiced, and not elsewhere. (1.2)

"One should teach the rules of purification and conduct" (YDh 1.15): this is the rule for the teacher regarding the instruction of the Dharmaśāstra. But from where [is it established] that the student must perform that study?
To show that this is understood [from scripture], he says:
"The Vedas, together with the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the Aṅgas, are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma. (YDh 1.3)
The Purāṇas are those beginning with the Brāhma;
Nyāya is the science of logic;
Mīmāṃsā is the investigation of Vedic statements.
The Dharmaśāstras are those beginning with the Mānava; the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) are the six beginning with grammar (vyākaraṇa);
the four Vedas are accompanied by these.
The sciences (vidyā) are the means for accomplishing the goals of human life;
their fields are fourteen.
Furthermore, there are fourteen fields that are the causes of dharma.
These [Vedas] are to be studied by those belonging to the three higher castes;
since the Dharmaśāstra is included within them, it too must be studied.
In this regard, these [sciences] are to be mastered by a Brāhmaṇa for the acquisition of knowledge and for the performance of dharma;
by a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, they are to be mastered solely for the performance of dharma. And so it was said by Śaṅkha, after introducing the branches of learning:
"A Brāhmaṇa is authorized for these [duties], and he shows the means of livelihood to the others.
Manu also demonstrates that while the twice-born have the right to study the Dharmaśāstras, the authority to expound them belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, and not to anyone else:
"He for whom the rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground are prescribed by means of mantras..."
It should be understood that he alone has the qualification for this treatise, and never anyone else.
This should be studied with diligence by a learned Brahmin and correctly expounded to his disciples; it must not be taught by anyone else.
Thus [it is said] (MDh 2.16, 1.103). //1.3//
Granted that the treatise on Dharma should be studied, one might ask: what relevance does this particular treatise composed by Yājñavalkya have? To this, he says:
"Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras..."
Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara,
Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa,
and Vasiṣṭha are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
The compound ending with the word *uśanas* is treated as a singular collective (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*).
The intended meaning is that this Dharmaśāstra composed by Yājñavalkya is to be studied.
This is not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), but rather—
This is stated for the sake of illustration;
therefore, it is not contradictory that the works of Baudhāyana and others are also Dharmaśāstras.
Although each of these is authoritative in its own right, those that are incomplete fulfill their mutual requirements through mutual expectancy.
It is performed from another [source]; in case of conflict, there is an option. 1.4–1.5.
Now he states the causal factors for the performance of dharma:

"That which is given at the proper place, at the proper time, by the proper means, as a substance accompanied by faith, and to a worthy recipient—all that constitutes the complete definition of dharma. (YDh 1.6)
The place is that region characterized by the statement, "In which country the deer is black" (YDh 1.2);
the time is [the period] beginning with the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti).
"Means" (upāya) refers to the collection of procedures prescribed in the scriptures.

"Substance" (dravya) refers to cows and the like obtained through acceptance of gifts and other such means. "Faith" (śraddhā) is the conviction in the existence of the afterlife; [it is performed] in such a way that it is accompanied by that faith.
"A worthy recipient is not [found] by mere learning" (YDh 1.200)—such is the definition that will be stated hereafter.
It is given in such a way that it does not return; thus, it is relinquished with the finality of transferring ownership to another.
This is the producer of the Dharma.
Is it only this much? No, he says:
"entire."
Furthermore, whatever else is prescribed in the scriptures—such as [sacrifices] by birth, quality, oblation, or ritual—that entire range is a producer of *dharma*.
It has been stated that the producer of *dharma* is fourfold, consisting of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), substance (*dravya*), and action (*kriyā*).
And all of that, whether taken collectively or individually, is to be understood according to the scriptures.
Faith indeed persists everywhere. (1.6)
Now he states the means of knowing Dharma:

"Revelation (śruti), tradition (smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), and what is pleasing to oneself—that desire which arises from right resolve (samyaksaṃkalpa)—this is remembered as the root of Dharma. (YDh 1.7)
Śruti is the Veda;
smṛti is the Dharmaśāstra. And so says Manu:

"The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Smṛti is indeed the Dharmaśāstra" (MDh 2.10). "Sadācāra" is the conduct or practice of the virtuous and refined (sats and śiṣṭas); and "one's own preference" refers to what is dear to oneself.
In matters that are optional, such as "in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year" (YDh 1.14), one's own will alone is the determining factor.
A desire born of right resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) is not contrary to the scriptures, such as: "I shall not drink water except with food."
These are the sources of authority for Dharma;
in case of conflict among them, each preceding one is more powerful than the following. // 1.7 //
He states an exception to the causes consisting of [the merit of] place and so forth:
"But among the acts of sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study, this is the supreme dharma: that one perceives the Self through yoga. (YDh 1.8)
This alone is the supreme duty among rites such as sacrifice: the vision of the Self, which is knowledge according to reality, through yoga—that is, by the cessation of external mental fluctuations.
The meaning is that there is no restriction regarding place or other factors for the knowledge of the Self attained through yoga.
As it has been said: "Wherever there is one-pointedness [of mind], there [it may be practiced], because there is no distinction" (Brahma Sūtra 4.1.11).
Thus [it is stated] in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra], 1.8.
When there is doubt regarding either the causal grounds (*kārakahetu*) or the evidentiary grounds (*jñāpakahetu*), he states the ground for resolution:

"A council (*parṣad*) consisting of four who know the Veda and the Dharma, or even those possessing the threefold knowledge (*traividya*), shall declare that which is Dharma; or [the decision of] a single person who is the most excellent among those who know the inner self (*adhyātma*). (YDh 1.9)

The assembly consists of four Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras. Those who study the three branches of knowledge are called *traividyas*; the collection of such persons is termed *traividyam*.
The quality of being an expert in the Dharmaśāstras continues to apply here as well;
or else, that [body] is the assembly (parṣad).
That assembly previously mentioned is what constitutes the assembly, and whatever it declares is the Dharma.
Even if he is alone, that which one who is most skilled in inner knowledge and learned in the treatises on Dharma declares is also Dharma. 1.9.
Thus ends the section on the introduction.
Now begins the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*);
having stated the introduction to the entire treatise with these nine verses, [the author proceeds].
Now, in order to explain the characteristics of the castes and so forth, he first states the castes:
"The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are the castes; however, the first three are the twice-born."
For them, the rites beginning with conception and ending with the cremation ground are indeed to be performed with mantras.
The four castes (*varṇas*)—Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—are to be defined by their characteristics as they will be described;
among them, the first three—the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya—are the twice-born (*dvijas*).
Those who are born twice are the *dvijas*.
This [initiation] is indeed for those *dvijas*, and not for the *śūdra*.
By this, it is stated that the rites of a *śūdra* are performed without mantras.
"Even a Śūdra of such a kind should be consecrated with the rites, though without the mantras," according to the statement of Yama.
"Niṣekādyāḥ" means those for which *niṣeka*— that is, *garbhādhāna* (the rite of conception)— is the first.
The cremation ground is the cemetery; those rites related to it, which constitute its conclusion, are performed with mantras. // 1.10 //
Now he enumerates those rites:

Conception should take place during the fertile period; the *puṃsavana* rite before the fetus moves; the *sīmantonnayana* in the sixth or eighth month; and these [two], along with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), upon the birth of the child. (YDh 1.11)
On the eleventh day [after birth], the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month, the rite of going forth from the house;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be performed according to family custom.
"Garbhadhāna" (conception) is the name of the rite, as its meaning follows the literal sense of the word.
The same applies to the rites to be described hereafter.

That *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) is performed during the *ṛtu*, that is, at the time of the fertile period characterized by the features to be described; the rite called *puṃsavana* (the male-making rite) is performed before the movement of the fetus.

The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) takes place in the sixth or eighth month. Since these two rites—the *puṃsavana* and the *sīmantonnayana*—are rituals for the purification of the womb (*kṣetra-saṃskāra-karman*), they are to be performed only once, not for every subsequent conception.
As Devala has said:
"A woman who has been consecrated once is considered consecrated for all subsequent pregnancies;

whatever child she gives birth to, that child shall be consecrated. Or else, *jātakarman* refers to the rite performed when these two have come—that is, when the child has emerged from the womb and the boy has been born.
On the eleventh day, the naming ceremony is performed;
and that name should be connected with the grandfather, the maternal grandfather, and so forth, or connected with the family deity.
As Śaṅkha says (2.14):
The father should give a name connected with the family deity.
In the fourth month, the rite of looking at the sun, characterized by the first outing, is performed.
In the sixth month, the rite of the first feeding of solid food is performed.
"The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa), however, should be performed according to family custom"—this [phrase] is to be connected with each [of the preceding items]. 1.11–12.
He states the incidental benefit even though these [rites] are obligatory:
"In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb is pacified" (YDh 1.13ab).
In the manner thus described, when the purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*) such as *garbhādhāna* and the rest have been performed, the sin (*enaḥ*), which is evil, attains pacification.
Of what nature is it?

It arises from the seed and the embryo, being bound together by semen and blood, and is characterized by the transmission of bodily diseases; it is not, however, produced by falling [from a tree] and so forth.
He states the specific rule for women:
"These rites for women are silent, but their marriage is accompanied by mantras" (YDh 1.13cd).
These rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and so forth, must be performed for women at the appropriate times silently, that is, without mantras.
Furthermore, the marriage ceremony must be performed with the recitation of mantras. // 1.13 //
He states the time for the initiation ceremony:

"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth]; for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh; for Vaiśyas, in the twelfth; or according to family custom. (YDh 1.14)
Beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), birth occurs; then, in the eighth year, there is the initiation (upanayana) for a Brāhmaṇa.
The term *upanāyana* is simply *upanayana*; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the base word itself, following the requirements of the meter and to avoid breaking the metrical cadence.
Or the lengthening may be archaic (ārṣa); here there is an option according to one's preference. For kings, [the initiation] is on the eleventh [year].
For the *viśas*, that is, the Vaiśyas, it is in the eleventh year—
meaning the twelfth— counting from conception; the inclusion of "conception" (*garbha*) applies throughout all cases.
Even though the word *garbha* is subordinate within the compound, it must be mentally separated and applied to both [the preceding and following terms].
For it is said: "In the eleventh year from conception for a king, and in the twelfth year from conception for a Vaiśya" (Śaṅkha 2.17).
This is because of the observation of another traditional text (smṛti):
"Now begins the instruction on words; of which words? and so forth.
"Of the worldly and the Vedic.
Here too, the word "should be performed" (kāryam) is understood from the previous context.
Some desire the initiation ceremony (upanayana) according to family custom. 1.14.
He states the duties of the teacher:
Having initiated the student, the teacher should teach him the Veda preceded by the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) and should instruct him in the rules of purification and conduct. (YDh 1.15)
Having performed the initiation ceremony according to the rules prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the teacher should teach the Veda to the pupil preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
The *mahāvyāhṛtis* are seven, beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *satyam*;
or they are five, according to the opinion of Gautama (GDh 1.51).
Furthermore, one should teach the rules of purification and conduct whose characteristics will be described hereafter.

By the statement "having initiated him, one should teach the rules of purification and conduct," it is shown that prior to initiation there is freedom of action, with the exception of those duties pertaining to the social classes (*varṇadharma*).
This same [rule] applies equally to women before marriage, since marriage stands in the place of the initiation ceremony (upanayana). 1.15.

He states the rules for purification and conduct: "During the day and at the two twilights, with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) placed over the ear, one should void urine and feces facing north; if it is at night, facing south. (YDh 1.16)
"One whose sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) rests on the ear" is so described; and the ear meant here is the right one. Having placed the purifier on the right ear, one should void excrement and urine.

From this indicative mark [of the scripture]: during the day and at the two twilights, one should void urine and feces facing north; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that the place must be free from ashes and the like.
At night, however, one should face south. (1.16)
Furthermore:
Having risen with his penis still held [in the hand], he should, with unwearied effort, perform purification using earth and drawn-up water so as to remove both odor and residue. (YDh 1.17)

Immediately thereafter, having taken hold of his penis and stood up, he should perform the purification that removes both odor and stain by means of water drawn from [the source] and earth of the characteristics to be described hereafter;
being untiring and not lazy.
By the phrase "with water drawn [from the source]," bathing within the water itself is prohibited.
In this context, the rule "that which removes the odor and the smear" refers to this purification common to members of all stages of life (*āśrama*);
however, the restriction on the number of applications of earth serves an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. (1.17)
Seated in a clean place with his knees joined, facing either north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha. "In a clean place" means in a location untouched by impure substances.
By the mention of "place" (deśa), there is a prohibition against using shoes, beds, seats, and the like;
[it specifies that one should recite] while seated, not standing, nor lying down, nor bent over, nor walking;
and by specifying "facing north or east," there is an exclusion of other directions.
From the phrase "in a clean place," the washing of the feet is obtained.
[He should do so] with the *brāhma* *tīrtha*, whose characteristics will be described later; a "twice-born" (*dvija*) means one who is not a *śūdra* or similar.
He should always, at all times— even when situated in another stage of life—
perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet), that is, perform the ācamana. How?
With the hands placed between the knees, that is, with the hands inside the knees, using the right hand. // 1.18 //
He states the sacred sites (tīrtha) beginning with that of Prajāpati:

"The base of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand, are, in their respective order, the sacred sites of Prajāpati, the ancestors, Brahmā, and the gods. (YDh 1.19)
The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand, should be known respectively as the *prajāpati*, *pitṛ*, *brahman*, and *daivata* tīrthas. // 1.19 //
The manner of sipping water (ācamana):
Having sipped water three times and wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the cavities of the head with water—water that is in its natural state and free from foam and bubbles. (YDh 1.20)

Having drunk water three times and having wiped the mouth twice with the base of the thumb, one should touch with water the apertures— the openings located in the upper body, such as the nostrils and so forth—
using water that is unmixed with other substances.
The repetition of the word "water" (adbhiḥ) after "again" (punar) is for the purpose of indicating that water must be touched for each individual aperture.
From another Smṛti:
One should touch the nose and the mouth with the thumb and the index finger;
and the eyes and ears again and again with the thumb and the ring finger.
"One should touch the navel with the little finger and the thumb, the heart with the palm, the head with all [the fingers], and afterwards the arms with the tips. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, he specifies those very [fingers]: "in their natural state," meaning they have not reached another odor, form, taste, or touch, and are free from foam or bubbles.
By the word "tu" (but), there is a prohibition of water coming from rain-showers and that which has been rejected by Śūdras and others.
(1.20) However, the twice-born are purified respectively by [water] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate;
a woman and a Śūdra are purified by water touched once at the extremity [of the mouth]. (1.21)
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively;
a woman and a Śūdra are purified even by water that has merely touched the interior of the palate.
The word "once" indicates a distinction from the Vaiśya.
By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that even one who has not been initiated [is included]. 1.21.

Bathing with mantras addressed to the waters, sprinkling [the body] (mārjana), restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma), worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra. YDh 1.22: Morning bathing according to the scriptures with mantras addressed to the waters, such as "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and others; sprinkling [the body].
Prāṇasaṃyama is breath control (prāṇāyāma), characterized as will be described hereafter.

Following that, one should perform the worship of the Sun with a solar mantra. Furthermore, the daily recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī, beginning with "tat savitur vareṇyam," must be performed every day.
The word "kārya" (effect) is connected with each [of the preceding terms] according to its respective gender. (1.22)
Consideration of Prāṇāyāma:

One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras, preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with the Praṇava at each [syllable], three times; this is the regulation of breath (prāṇasaṃyama). (YDh 1.23)

One should mentally recite the previously mentioned Gāyatrī, conjoined with its head beginning with "āpo jyotiḥ," preceded by the aforementioned Vyāhṛtis, and joined with the Praṇava for each Vyāhṛti—namely, *oṃ bhuḥ*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ*, *oṃ svaḥ*—three times while restraining the breath moving through the mouth and nose; this is the Prāṇāyāma in all cases. 1.23.
The method for the recitation of the Sāvitrī:

Having restrained the breaths and sprinkled himself with water while reciting the three verses addressed to the Waters (the Āpohiṣṭhīya), he should sit facing west and recite the Sāvitrī until the appearance of the stars. (YDh 1.24)
In this same manner, one should stand during the morning twilight until the appearance of the sun (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.25ab).

Having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) as previously described, and having sprinkled oneself with water while reciting the previously mentioned three-verse hymn addressed to the Waters (adbhidaivata), one should sit for the evening twilight facing west, muttering the Sāvitrī; by implication, it is understood that one faces west.
Until the rising of the stars— that is, up to the time of the stars' appearance—
one should perform the aforementioned ritual during the morning twilight while facing east, remaining thus until sunrise.
That which occurs at the junction of day and night...
That [time] during which the ritual action is prescribed is the *saṃdhyā*. In that context, "the day having been completed" refers to the time when the solar disc is no longer visible;
its opposite is the night.
The time at which the perception of the horizon (khaṇḍamaṇḍala) occurs is the juncture (saṃdhi).

One should then perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) during both junctures. Following that, after the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), one should perform the fire-rite—consisting of the throwing of fuel-sticks and other acts into the fire—in accordance with the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra. (YDh 1.25cd)
Then he should salute the elders, saying, "I am so-and-so.
Immediately after that, he should salute the elders, beginning with his gurus.
How? [As follows:]
Proclaiming his own name, "I am this Devadattaśarman," he should say:
One should also attend upon the teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study (svādhyāya).
When summoned, one should study; whatever is obtained should be offered to him.
One should always act for his welfare through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (YDh 1.26cd–27)
Likewise, he should attend upon the Guru, whose characteristics will be described hereafter; intent on his service, he should remain dependent upon him.

For the sake of *svādhyāya*—that is, for the accomplishment of study—he should be concentrated, with an undistracted mind. And when called, he should study; that is, he should study only when summoned by the Guru, and he should not himself urge the Guru to teach.
And whatever has been obtained, all that he should offer to the guru;
likewise, he should always— constantly— perform what is beneficial for that guru.
One should not act in opposition [to the teacher] through actions of mind, speech, or body.
By the use of the word "api" (also), one should avoid covering the neck and so forth when in the presence of the guru, as stated by Gautama (GDh 2.14). 1.26–1.27.
He states those who should be taught: "Those who are grateful, free from malice, intelligent, pure, virtuous, and not envious;
and those who are righteous, good, capable, trustworthy, and givers of knowledge and wealth—these are to be taught according to the Dharma. (YDh 1.28)
One who does not forget a favor received is grateful (*kṛtajña*).
One who is free from malice is compassionate (*dayāvān*).
One who is intelligent (*medhāvī*) is capable of grasping and retaining the texts.
Pure, meaning possessing external and internal purity; healthy, meaning free from mental anguish and physical disease;
and free from envy, meaning one whose nature is to manifest virtues rather than exposing faults.
He is virtuous, of good conduct, capable of service, and a trusted kinsman.
The giver of knowledge is one who bestows learning;
the giver of wealth is one who bestows riches without prior bargaining.
These qualities are to be understood as existing either collectively or individually, according to the circumstances.
And these should be taught according to their true nature, following the instructions of the Teacher. (1.28)
He states the carrying of the staff and so forth:
"One should carry the staff, the deerskin, the sacred thread, and the girdle" (YDh 1.29ab).
Likewise, there is the staff made of *pālāśa* wood and others, as established in other Smṛtis.
The antelope skin is that of a black antelope and the like; the sacred thread is made of cotton and the like;
and the girdle as well.
A student of the Brahmin and other castes should wear [a girdle] made of muñja grass and so forth. (1.29ab) This is the manner of practicing the mendicant life.

He should go for alms among blameless Brāhmaṇas for his own subsistence. The practice of begging for alms among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is characterized by the word *bhavat* (sir) placed at the beginning, middle, and end respectively. (YDh 1.29cd–30)

Endowed with the previously mentioned staff and other requirements, the religious student (brahmacārī) shall beg for alms among blameless Brāhmaṇas—excluding those who have been accused of crimes and the like—who are devoted to their own duties.
This is for his own subsistence, that is, for his own livelihood, and not for the sake of others; and he shall do so except from his teacher, the teacher’s wife, or the teacher’s son.
Having informed the teacher, he should proceed with the teacher’s permission.

One should eat [from it]; in its absence, from the son of that [brāhmaṇa] and so forth—such is the rule. And here, the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) when such a person is available.
As for that which pertains to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*),...
The practice of wandering for alms refers to the domain of the three higher castes;
as for the statement that one may wander for alms among all four castes, that refers to times of distress.
How should this practice of begging for alms be performed?
In the beginning, middle, and end, it is characterized by the word *bhavat* [vocative]:
"Give alms, O lady" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*) or "O lady, give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*).
"Give alms, O lady," thus should the practice of begging for alms be performed according to the order of castes. 1.29–1.30.
The manner of eating:

Having performed his fire-rituals, restrained in speech, and with the permission of his guru, he should eat after first performing the *apośana* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it. (YDh 1.31)

Having collected alms according to the previously mentioned rule and having presented them to the teacher, he should— upon the teacher’s permission, having performed the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), remaining silent and restrained in speech, and having honored and worshipped the food— eat it without disparaging or criticizing it,
after first performing the *apośana* rite with the mantra "Thou art the under-layer of immortality" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and so forth.

The repetition of the term "fire-ritual" (*agnikārya*) here is for the purpose of prescribing an alternative time for one who has somehow failed to perform the fire-ritual at the time of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
But not for the sake of attaining a third [fruit]. (1.31)
One established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) shall not eat the food of a single person except in times of distress;
however, a Brahmin may eat at a *śrāddha* feast at his pleasure, provided he does not violate his vow.
Established in celibacy, one should not eat the food of a single person when there is no distress—that is, in the absence of illness or other such conditions.
Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa, being invited to a Śrāddha, may eat at his pleasure,
provided he does not violate his vows by avoiding honey and meat.
Here, the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of excluding Kṣatriyas and others from eating at the Śrāddha.
"And this duty is not prescribed for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya," according to the traditional law (smṛti). (1.32)
He states what is to be avoided, such as honey, meat, and so forth:
"One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food leavings, fermented acids, women, injury to living beings, gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and the like. (YDh 1.33)
"Madhu" refers to honey, not liquor, because of the prohibition: "A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid liquor. "Māṃsa" (meat) refers even to that of goats and other such animals.
Anointing the body with substances such as clarified butter, and applying collyrium and the like to the eyes;
"ucchiṣṭa" refers to [the use of] non-agaru incense; "śukta" refers to harsh speech, not to fermented food.
Because of its prohibition in the section concerning forbidden foods (*abhakṣya*);
"woman" refers to sexual enjoyment;
and "injury to living beings" means the killing of living creatures.
Beholding the rising and setting of the sun;
*aślīla* is the speaking of untruth;
and *parivāda* is the proclaiming of another's faults, whether real or unreal.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), perfumes, garlands, and so forth mentioned in other Smṛtis are included. A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should avoid these. 1.33.
He states the characteristics of the Guru, the Ācārya, and others:
"He is the Guru who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him;
he who initiates him and gives him the Veda is declared to be the Ācārya. (YDh 1.34)
He who, having performed the rites beginning with the conception ceremony and ending with the initiation according to the rules, imparts the Veda to this student is the *guru*.
On the other hand, he who merely performs the initiation and imparts the Veda is the *ācārya*. (1.34)

The definition of the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the officiating priest (ṛtvij): A preceptor is said to be one who teaches a portion [of the Veda], while an officiating priest is one who performs a sacrifice.
These are to be honored according to their precedence; yet among them all, the mother is the most venerable. (YDh 1.35)
One who teaches a single portion of the Veda— either a part of the Mantras or the Brāhmaṇas— or the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), is an Upādhyāya.
Furthermore, he who performs the *pākayajña* and other such sacrifices when chosen [for the purpose] is an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

These—namely the preceptor (*guru*), the teacher (*ācārya*), the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), and the officiating priest—are to be honored and revered according to their precedence and respective order.
Among all of these, however, the mother is the most venerable and the most worthy of worship. (1.35)
He states the limit for the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) for the purpose of learning the Vedas: "The period of studentship for each Veda is twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until the completion of the study, and the tonsure ceremony (*keśānta*) occurs at the sixteenth year. (YDh 1.36)

When, due to the impossibility of marriage, one proceeds according to the rule, "Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda" (MDh 3.2), then for each Veda, the previously mentioned period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) of twelve years must be observed;
in case of inability, five years.

Some explain that [the period of studentship] lasts until the time of initiation (*grahaṇāntika*). Furthermore, the *keśānta*—the rite known as *godāna*—should be performed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year from conception;
this is to be understood as applying when the Vedic vow (*vedavrata*) lasts twelve years, whereas in the other case...
In each case, it should be understood according to what is possible.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, however, it should be understood as being at the twenty-second or the twenty-fourth year, just like the time for their initiation (upanayana). 1.36.
He states the ultimate limit of the time for initiation:
"The period for the initiation of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya extends, respectively, until the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth year. (YDh 1.37)
Beyond this, these people, excluded from all religious duties,
fall [from their caste] as outcasts (vrātyas) who have lost their right to the Sāvitrī, unless they perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.
For the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, [the period of eligibility for initiation lasts] until the sixteenth year, the twenty-second year, and the twenty-fourth year respectively.
The "later time" refers to the period subsequent to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Beyond this point, there is no further time for initiation; rather, from this point onward, these individuals fall [from their status] and become excluded from all religious duties (*dharma*), becoming ineligible for any such duties.

Those who have fallen from the *sāvitrī* become ones for whom the *sāvitrī* has been lost; they are no longer fit for the imparting of the *sāvitrī*. They are *vrātyas*, devoid of sacramental rites, unless [they perform] the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice.
But once that has been performed, they become eligible for the initiation ceremony (upanayana). 1.37–1.38.
It has been stated that "the first three are twice-born";
therein he states the reason:
"Because they are born first from the mother, and secondly from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass."
Therefore, these—the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—are remembered as the twice-born (dvijas).

Since they are born for the first time from their mother and for a second time through the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, therefore these Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are called twice-born. (1.39)

He states the fruit of receiving and studying the Veda: "For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good (niḥśreyasa) through sacrifices, austerities, and auspicious rites. (YDh 1.40)

Among sacrifices—both those prescribed by the Śruti and those by the Smṛti—among austerities consisting of bodily mortification such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and others, and among auspicious rites such as the initiatory ceremonies (saṃskāras) beginning with the Upanayana, the Veda alone, by virtue of being the means of knowledge for them, is the supreme bringer of the highest good (niḥśreyasa) for the twice-born, and nothing else.
The phrase "the Veda alone" is intended to include the Smṛti as well, since the latter is rooted in the former. (1.40)

Having stated the fruit of learning and reciting [the Veda] for the sake of formal acquisition, he now declares the fruit of reciting the Brahma-yajña for the sake of specific desires: "The twice-born who studies the Ṛg-veda daily indeed gratifies the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. (YDh 1.41)
He who studies the Yajus mantras daily according to his ability gratifies the gods with ghee and nectar, and likewise the ancestors with clarified butter and honey. Furthermore,
he who recites them daily shall satisfy the gods with Soma and ghee.
And one should satisfy the ancestors with honey and clarified butter by means of the Sāman hymns.
He who daily studies the Ṛgvedic verses satisfies the gods and the ancestors with honey and milk;
furthermore, he who daily studies the Yajurvedic formulas according to his ability satisfies the gods and the ancestors with clarified butter and nectar, as well as with honey and clarified butter.
But he who studies the Sāman daily gratifies the gods with Soma and clarified butter, and the ancestors with honey and ghee.
The mention of the *Ṛk* and so forth is for the purpose of including the *Ṛk* and other Vedas in general. 1.41, 1.42, 1.43.
Reciting the Atharva-Angirasas, the twice-born man should satisfy the gods with fat,
and the ancestors daily with honey and clarified butter, according to his ability. He should also recite the Vakovakya, the Puranas, the Narashamsis, and the Gathikas.

For he who daily studies the Itihāsas and the sciences according to his ability brings satisfaction to the gods with offerings of meat, milk-rice, honey, and clarified butter; and he likewise provides for the ancestors with honey and ghee. (YDh 1.45–46)
Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires.

Furthermore, he who daily studies the *Aṅgirasas* according to his ability satisfies the gods with fat and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. As for the *Vākovākya*, which consists of Vedic statements in the form of questions and answers—
The Purāṇas beginning with the Brahma-purāṇa; by the word "and" (ca), the Dharmaśāstras such as that of Manu; and the Nārāśaṃsīs, which are mantras dedicated to Rudra.
The *gāthās*, such as the *Yajñagāthā* and *Indragāthā*; the *itihāsas*, such as the *Mahābhārata* and others;
and the *vidyās*, such as the *Vāruṇī* and others.
He who studies daily according to his ability satisfies the gods and the ancestors with meat, milk-rice, honey, and ghee; he satisfies them with honey and ghee. (1.44–1.46)

Furthermore, those gods and ancestors, being themselves satisfied, gratify this practitioner of sacred study with the auspicious fruits of all his desires, which are characterized by not being harmful to others. (1.47ab)
For the sake of praise, he says:
"Whatever season he studies during, he shall obtain the fruit of that very season;
he enjoys the fruit of giving away the earth filled with wealth three times over. (YDh 1.47cd)
And here, a twice-born man who is constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda attains the highest ascetic merit.
Whatever portion of the Veda elucidates a particular sacrifice, by studying that daily, he obtains the fruit of that very sacrifice.
Likewise, he obtains the supreme fruit of giving away the earth filled with wealth three times over.
Furthermore, one who constantly engages in the study of the Veda (svādhyāya) obtains even that fruit which belongs to ascetic practices such as the Cāndrāyaṇa.

The inclusion of the word "constant" (nitya) is for the purpose of making known that even though it may be performed for specific desires (kāmya), it possesses the quality of being obligatory (nitya). 1.47–1.48.
Having thus described the duties of a religious student (brahmacārin) in general,
he now states the specific rule for the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika): "But the lifelong student shall dwell in the presence of his teacher."
In the absence of these, he may do so for his son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire (vaiśvānara).
By purifying his body through this rule, having conquered his senses, he attains the world of Brahmā and is not born again in this world. (YDh 1.49–50)
One who leads himself to the final goal at the time of departure in the manner described is a *naiṣṭhika*;
he should dwell near his teacher for as long as he lives. He should not become independent after the completion of Vedic study. In the absence of such a teacher—
In the absence of that [son], near his son; in the absence of him, near his wife; and in the absence of her, even in the sacrificial fire (vaiśvānara).

Purifying and consuming the body by this prescribed method, with senses conquered—exerting special effort in the mastery of the senses—and remaining a celibate student (brahmacārī), he attains the world of Brahman and immortality.
He is never again born here.
Thus ends the section on the religious student (brahmacārin).
Now begins the section on marriage (vivāha).
Furthermore, regarding one who is about to marry, he describes the ceremonial bath for the purpose of that marriage.
Having given a gift to the teacher and with his permission, he should perform the ceremonial bath; this after having mastered either the Veda—
consisting of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas— as previously described by the stated rule, or the religious observances (vratas) which are the duties of the student (brahmacārin), or indeed both.

Or, having led [the student] to both shores and completed [the instruction], he should give a desired boon (*vara*) to the aforementioned teacher according to his ability and then bathe; if he lacks the means, he may do so even without giving a boon, with the teacher's permission. Among these alternatives, one should act in consideration of one's capacity, the time, and other such factors.
Establishment. 1.51.
To answer the question of what one should do after bathing, he says:

Having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—one who has not belonged to another before, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself. (YDh 1.52)
One whose celibacy is unviolated and whose celibacy is unerring [should marry] a woman endowed with auspicious marks, both external and internal;
the external ones being such as having fine hair on the body, fine hair on the head, fine teeth, and so forth (MDh 3.10).
The rites spoken of by Manu,
beginning with "having formed eight internal balls of food" (ĀśGṛ 1.5.5), are to be understood according to the procedure prescribed by Āśvalāyana.
A woman who has been examined as female in order to exclude the possibility of being a eunuch,
who has not belonged to another previously—
meaning she has not been taken by another man— either through gift or through enjoyment.
"Beloved" means desirable, bringing delight to the mind and eyes of the groom;
for according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba (ĀpGṛ 1.3.21; BGṛ 2.3.9), "that [girl] in whom the mind and eyes find their fixed attachment is the one who brings prosperity.
And this applies provided there is an absence of external defects such as missing or excessive limbs.
*Asapiṇḍām*: she whose *piṇḍa*—that is, body—is not common (*samāna*) or single (*eka*) is a *sapiṇḍā*; one who is not a *sapiṇḍā* is an *asapiṇḍā*, her [the bride].
And *sapiṇḍatā* arises through the connection with parts of a single body.
For instance, a son is [connected] with his father through the continuity of the father's bodily constituents;
likewise, he is connected with his grandfather and others as well, by way of the father, through the continuity of their bodily constituents.
In this way, one is related to the mother through the continuity of the mother's bodily parts;
likewise, one is related to the maternal grandfather and others through the medium of the mother.
Likewise, there is [a connection] with maternal aunts, maternal uncles, and so forth, due to the continuity of parts of the same body;
likewise with paternal uncles, paternal aunts, and so forth;
and likewise with the husband, because the wife is a co-originator of the same body.
In this same way, it applies to brothers and wives as well, through their mutual relationship as initiators of a single body together with those who have already been initiated into a single body.
Thus, wherever the term *sapiṇḍa* occurs, [it refers to this].
In this regard, it should be understood that there is a connection through the constituent parts of a single body, either directly or indirectly;
if this is so, then [the same would apply] even to maternal grandfathers and others.
"Ten days of impurity on account of a death is prescribed for sapindas" (MDh 5.59);
this rule applies without distinction.
This would be so if, in that case, others were to perform [the rites] for those women who have been given away in marriage (VaDh 4.19).
Otherwise, specific statements such as these would not exist.
Therefore, in cases among sapindas where no specific statement is found, the rule that "the impurity due to death lasts ten days" remains applicable.
Furthermore, sapinda-relationship must necessarily be described as being based on the connection with parts of a single body.
For according to such scriptural passages as "The self is indeed the sacrifice of the self," and likewise,
"Thou art born again following thy offspring" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.5.6), this very same [self] is perceived directly as having grown forth (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.24.2).
And because of the statement of Āpastamba:

likewise, in the Garbhopaniṣad, this body consisting of six sheaths is described as having three parts from the father and three from the mother—"bones, sinews, and marrow from the father; skin, flesh, and blood from the mother"—thus establishing the connection of the constituent parts in various places.
If *sāpiṇḍya* were accepted on the basis of the lineage of the *piṇḍa*-offerings (*nirvāpyapiṇḍānvaya*),
there would be no *sāpiṇḍya* in the maternal line, nor among brothers, paternal uncles, and so forth; this is because,
by accepting the collective power [of the word], one would be adopting its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).
The power of the suffix *va* (*vaya-vaśakti*), which is understood in various instances, would have to be abandoned.
When a word is used in a sense other than its constituent meanings, the collective whole becomes established there by virtue of having no other possible application.
We shall explain later how, through the connection of bodily parts in a lineage, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding *sāpiṇḍya*.
He should marry—that is, take as his wife—a younger girl, one who is inferior in both age and physical stature, according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. (1.52)
He states further specific qualifications:
"One who is free from disease, has brothers, and is not born of the same ṛṣi or gotra" (YDh 1.53ab).
"Free from disease" means not afflicted by an incurable illness.
By the mention of "one who has brothers," the apprehension that she might be made a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) is removed;
from this it is understood that even one not explicitly designated as such becomes a *putrikā*. "Born of a different *ṛṣi* and *gotra*"—that which belongs to an *ṛṣi* is the *ārṣa*.
"Name" means the most excellent [designation];
"clan" (gotra) refers to what is well-known through the succession of lineages;
"sage-clan" (ārṣagotra) refers to both the sage and the clan.
"One who has the same *ṛṣi* and *gotra* is a *samānārṣagotra*; born from such a person is a *samānārṣagotrajā*. One who is not so born is an *asamānārṣagotrajā*—her [the bride].
Both the *gotra* and the *pravara* are separately the grounds for exclusion."
Therefore, [one should marry] a woman who is not of the same *ṛṣi* lineage and not of the same *gotra*;
likewise, marriage is with those who have different *pravara*s (GDh 4.2).

Thus says Gautama. Likewise: "She who is not a sapinda of the mother and she who is not a sapinda of the father—she is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union" (MDh 3.5).
Thus says Manu. Likewise, some maintain that even a girl of the mother’s lineage (mātṛgotra) is not to be married; for it is said:
"Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one of the mother’s lineage, or one who shares the same *pravara*, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
This is because of the traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) on expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

In this context, by the phrase "not a *sapiṇḍa*," there is a prohibition against the daughters of one's father’s sister, mother’s sister, and so forth. Likewise, by the phrase "not of the same lineage" (*asagotrā*), there is a prohibition against a woman who, even if not a *sapiṇḍa*, belongs to the same lineage (*samānagotra*) though born of a different family line (*bhinnasantāna*).

Likewise, by the phrase "one who does not share the same *pravara*," there is a prohibition against a woman who, though not a *sapiṇḍa* and not of the same *gotra*, nevertheless shares the same *pravara*. And thus, the rule "one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*" applies to all castes (*sārvavarṇika*), because *sāpiṇḍya* exists everywhere.
The rule "one who is not of the same *ṛṣi* and *gotra*" pertains to those belonging to the three *varṇas*.
Although Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas lack individual *gotras* and consequently lack *pravara*s, nevertheless, the *gotra* and *pravara* of their domestic priest (*purohita*) are to be understood as theirs.

And likewise, having stated, "One should choose the ancestral seers (*ārṣeya*) of the sacrificer," Āśvalāyana says, "For Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, one chooses those of the family priest (*paurohitya*)" (ĀśŚr 1.3.1, 3). Marriage is simply not produced with women who are *sapiṇḍas*, nor those of the same *gotra*, nor those of the same *pravara*.
But in the case of those who are ill and so forth, even if the status of wife has arisen, there is indeed a contradiction with what is observed.
Regarding the phrase "not a sapinda" (asapiṇḍām), sapinda-relationship was stated there by way of the connection with parts of a single body, whether directly or through lineage;

however, since such a relationship could occur in every case for everyone somehow or other within the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Therefore, he says:
"Beyond the fifth and the seventh [generation] from the mother and likewise from the father. (YDh 1.53cd)

The remainder [of the statement] is that *sāpiṇḍya* ceases beyond the fifth degree on the mother’s side— that is, in the lineage of the mother— and beyond the seventh degree on the father’s side— that is, in the lineage of the father. Therefore,
although this word *sapiṇḍa* occurs everywhere by virtue of its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*), [it applies here in its technical sense].
Like the words *nirmanthya* (fire produced by friction) and *paṅkaja* (lotus), it refers to a restricted object alone.

Thus, there are six sapinda ancestors beginning with the father, six descendants beginning with the son, and oneself as the seventh; for even though there is a difference in the lineage, one should count up to that point by taking the lineage as a single unit despite its internal divisions.
The term "seventh" is to be applied in every case.

Thus, when counting from the mother through her father, grandfather, and so forth, she who exists within the fifth generation from the mother is figuratively designated as the "fifth from the mother."
Thus, by starting from the father and counting his ancestors and so forth,

one who exists within the lineage of the seventh generation from the father is called "the seventh from the father. Likewise, this applies to two sisters, a sister and a brother, a brother's daughter and a paternal uncle, and so on.
In the case of marriage, because it has become a conventional practice, the difference between Vedic schools (śākhā) is disregarded.
Although it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha: "The fifth and the seventh [generations] from the mother's side, and likewise from the father's side"— meaning,
having passed three generations from the mother's side and five from the father's side—

And thus, according to Paiṭhīnasi, that [statement] is for the purpose of prohibiting [the practice] in the present time, and not for the purpose of enjoining it; therefore, there is no contradiction among all the Smṛtis.
And this should be understood to apply to those of the same caste.
But there is a distinction in the case of different castes,
as Śaṅkha has said:
"If many persons born of the same caste have separate fields and are separate individuals..."
They share a single funeral cake but have separate purifications; however, the cake itself extends through three generations.
Those born from a single [man], such as a Brāhmaṇa, are "of one birth" (*ekajāta*).

Those born in separate fields—that is, born of women of different castes and different classes—are "separate persons" (*pṛthagjana*). Those born of women who are of the same caste but different individuals are "of one funeral cake" (*ekapiṇḍa*), yet they have separate purifications (*pṛthakśauca*).
We shall explain the separate rules for purification in the section on impurity (*āśauca*).
As for the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), it recurs among three [generations]; thus, *sāpiṇḍya* extends precisely to three ancestors. (1.53)
"From a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations":
the word *puruṣa* here refers to men;
it means renowned through ten generations—five on the mother's side and five on the father's side.
From that family;
[the term] "śrotriyas" refers to those who have studied the Vedas. The mention of "study" (adhyayana) is illustrative, implying those who are perfected in both learning and hearing.

And that family is great, hence it is a "great family" (mahākula), being prosperous with sons, grandsons, cattle, female slaves, villages, and so forth; therefore, it is ordained that a girl should be taken from such a family.
Thus, when it is possible to obtain [food] from all sources, he states an exception: "Nor even from an abundant [place], if it is afflicted by the defect of a contagious disease. (YDh 1.54cd)

Contagious diseases such as vitiligo, leprosy, epilepsy, and so forth, as well as the defects mentioned by Manu—namely, deficiency in ritual acts, lack of virility, and so on (MDh 3.7)—are the impurities that enter through the gateways of semen and blood.
A girl endowed with these defects must not be taken in marriage, even if she comes from a prosperous family or a previously mentioned great lineage. 1.54.
Having thus stated the rules regarding the acceptance of a bride, he now declares the requirements for the groom in the giving away of the bride:
"The groom should be endowed with these very same qualities, of the same caste, and learned in the Vedas."
One who has been carefully examined for virility, who is young, wise, and beloved by the people—
endowed with these very qualities previously mentioned and free from defects— he is a suitable groom.
This is another [qualification] for him.
The distinction is as follows: he must be of the same caste or of a higher caste, but never of a lower caste;
he must be a *śrotriya*, being himself perfected in sacred learning and Vedic study; and he must have been carefully examined with diligence regarding his virility.
And the means for examination was shown by Nārada:
"If his seed floats in water and his urine is pleasant-smelling and frothy, he shall be a man by these characteristics; but with the opposite traits, he is a eunuch."
[Additional verses in manuscript *ka*: One whose urine is pleasant, frothy, heavy, and has the sound of bull semen shall be a man;
otherwise, there is a vagina in the mouth, which is pale and difficult to treat.
"In a field possessing auspicious seeds, sons increase the lineage; the completion of the marriage mantras for those women occurs at the seventh step. (cf. NSm 12.10).
[The bridegroom] should be young, not old.
The wise one is skilled in both worldly and Vedic conventions;
he is beloved by the people, winning them over through gentle speech preceded by a smile and other such qualities. (1.55)
Marriage is of three kinds, according to the goals of pleasure, progeny, and dharma.

Among these, that for the sake of progeny is twofold: obligatory and optional. Regarding the obligatory for the sake of offspring, by the rule "the bridegroom should be of the same caste and learned in the Vedas," a woman of the same caste is shown to be the primary choice.
Now, since the secondary alternative (anukalpa) must be stated regarding both optional rites and the obligatory union with a wife,
he says:
"As for that which is said concerning the taking of a wife from a Śūdra by the twice-born..."
This is not my opinion, because in that case he is born of his own accord.
As it is said:
"For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage. (YDh 1.56)
Having begun with the statement, "But for those who proceed out of desire, these [wives] shall be inferior in the following order" (MDh 3.12), [it continues]:
"A Brāhmaṇa may have four wives, a Kṣatriya three, and a Vaiśya two" (MDh 3.13).
Regarding the phrase "the taking of a Śūdra wife by the twice-born," this is not the opinion of Yājñavalkya;
for in that case, this twice-born man himself is born [from her].

"Because he is born again from her, she is called *jāyā* (wife)"—so says the Śruti (AitB 7.13). And here, by stating the reason "he is born from her himself," [the text] prohibits the marriage of a *śūdrā* for one engaged in either the obligatory procreation of a son (*naityaka-putra*) or the optional procreation of a son (*kāmya-putra*).
Thus, regarding the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) for the obligatory procreation of a son and regarding the optional procreation of a son, for a Brāhmaṇa, [the wife] is a Kṣatriyā or a Vaiśyā...
And for a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya woman is permitted as a wife. // 1.56 //

Now, he describes the procedure for marriage for one who desires pleasure, or one who has fathered a son, or one whose wife has died— persons who are not eligible for other stages of life (*āśrama*) but merely desire to remain in the state of a householder:
"Three [wives] in the order of the castes, likewise two, and one, respectively."
The wife of one born as a Śūdra is his own [caste].
According to the order of the castes, there are three wives for a Brāhmaṇa and two for a Kṣatriya.
A Vaiśya has one wife,
while for a Śūdra,
his own [woman] alone becomes his wife.
Furthermore, for all [castes], a wife of the same caste (savarṇā) remains the primary option;
in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one becomes permissible.
And this very same sequence applies to the secondary rule for obligatory rites (*naityaka-anukalpa*) and to the procedure for procreating a son for the sake of a desired result (*kāmya*).

Consequently, the inclusion of the Śūdra’s son among the sons and the mention of his share in the partition—as in the verse, "From Brāhmaṇas, indeed, the Mūrdhāvasikta... (YDh 1.91)—is likewise explained.
Having begun thus,
and concluding with "This rule is ordained for women" (YDh 1.92),
[this applies] to one who desires sexual pleasure, or to one who merely desires the [other] stages of life (*āśrama*), when [the act] has arisen as an unavoidable necessity. 1.57.
He now describes the forms of marriage:
"In the Brāhma marriage, having invited [the bridegroom], a girl adorned according to one's means is given;
the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides. (YDh 1.58)

That marriage is called *brahma* in which, having invited a bridegroom who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, the daughter is given adorned according to one's ability with water as the formal precursor;
the son born of such a union [purifies] ten ancestors on both sides, beginning with the father, and ten descendants, beginning with the son.
And he purifies himself as the twenty-first, provided he is of virtuous conduct.
The Daiva and Ārṣa forms of marriage:
in the Daiva rite, [the bridegroom] receives her from the officiating priest at a sacrifice; in the Ārṣa, however, he receives two cows.
The son born of the first [form] purifies fourteen generations, and the son born of the latter purifies six. (YDh 1.59)

That is the *daiva* marriage in which, when a sacrifice has been commenced, a maiden adorned according to one's means is given to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, where a maiden is given after receiving a pair of cattle, that is the *ārṣa* marriage.
The son born of the first [type] and the son born of the *daiva* marriage are fourteen-fold [in merit].
One born of the *ārṣa* marriage purifies seven descendants and seven ancestors;
one born of the *uttara* (higher) marriages purifies six descendants and three ancestors.
Having stated the definition of the Prājāpatya marriage, [the text continues]: "That which is given to a suitor by those practicing their religious duty together is the Kāya marriage;
one born of that [union] purifies six ancestors on each side, along with himself. (YDh 1.60)
Having declared, "May you both practice dharma together," the giving away of the girl is the Prājāpatya rite;
the son born of that rite purifies thirteen generations—six preceding, six succeeding, and himself as the thirteenth. (1.60)
The characteristics of the Āsura, Gāndharva, and other forms of marriage are as follows:
the Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden. (YDh 1.61)
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth;
the Gāndharva, however, occurs through mutual affection;
and the Rākṣasa [form] results from abduction by means of battle.
The Paiśāca [form of marriage], however, occurs through deception—by means of trickery or guile—due to the abduction of a maiden while she is in states such as sleep. (1.61)
He states a specific rule regarding marriage with women of the same class and others:
"The hand should be grasped in the case of women of the same class; a Kṣatriya woman should grasp an arrow;
a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad when marrying a man of a higher birth. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.62)
In a marriage with women of the same caste, the hand alone shall be taken according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra; however,
a Kṣatriya girl should grasp an arrow,
and a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad.
In the case of marrying a woman of superior caste, a Śūdra woman, however, [must hold] the hem of the garment;
as Manu has said:
"The hem of the garment is to be grasped by a Śūdra woman when marrying one of superior caste" (MDh 3.44). 1.62.
He states the order of those who may give the daughter in marriage:

"The father, the paternal grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother; in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person who is of sound mind is the giver of the maiden. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.63)
By not giving her away, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo at every menstrual cycle.
However, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among those who are suitable.
Among these [givers], beginning with the father, each subsequent person is the giver of the daughter in the absence of each preceding one, provided that person is of sound mind.
If he is not afflicted by defects such as insanity and the like,
then he who has the authority [to procreate] incurs the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā) at every fertile season (ṛtu) by failing to grant [the opportunity].
And this should be understood as applicable when a bridegroom possessing the aforementioned excellent characteristics is available.
However, when there is an absence of givers [of the girl], then the maiden herself should choose as her husband a suitor who possesses the stated characteristics and is fit for approach. 1.63–1.64.
The punishment for abducting a maiden:
"A maiden is given only once; he who carries her away incurs the punishment of a thief.
(YDh 1.65ab) It is a scriptural rule that a maiden is given in marriage only once.
Therefore, having given her away, one who takes her back should be punished like a thief.
Since this would result in a universal prohibition, he states an exception:
"Even one already given away he may take back, if a more excellent groom should arrive.

(YDh 1.65cd) If a groom who is more excellent than the previous one— endowed with superior learning, lineage, and so forth— arrives, and the previous groom is tainted by sin or is of wicked conduct, then [the bride] may be taken back even though she has been given away.
And this should be understood as occurring prior to the seventh step. (1.65)
One who gives away a girl without disclosing a defect shall be punished with the highest fine;
but one who abandons a girl who is faultless shall be fined, while one who falsely accuses her of a defect shall be fined one hundred [paṇas].
Furthermore, he who bestows a girl upon another without disclosing a defect that is perceptible to the eye... [is subject to punishment].
He shall be punished with the highest fine (uttamasāhasa), and the nature of the highest fine will be explained later. Furthermore,
having accepted a woman who is not corrupt, he who abandons her shall likewise be punished with the highest fine.

Furthermore, he who, even before the marriage, defames the girl with false defects such as long-term illness and the like out of malice or other motives, shall be fined one hundred *paṇas* of the characteristics to be described hereafter. // 1.66 //
Regarding the phrase "one who has not belonged to another before," it is stated that one who has not belonged to another is to be married; therein, he explains what kind of woman belongs to another:
"One who is unblemished, one who is blemished, and a remarried woman who has been consecrated again."
A *svairiṇī* is she who, having abandoned her husband of equal caste, resorts to another out of desire. Furthermore, a *punarbhū* is of two kinds: the *svairiṇī* and the *punarbhū*;
and the *punarbhū* is also of two kinds: the deflowered (*kṣatā*) and the undeflowered (*akṣatā*).
And therein, the "defiled" (kṣatā) is one who has been corrupted even before the sacramental rite through her connection with a man;
the "undefiled" (akṣatā), on the other hand, is one who has been corrupted by the sacramental rite itself.
Furthermore, she who, having abandoned her husband during maidenhood, takes refuge with a man of the same caste out of lust, is a wanton woman (svairiṇī). 1.67.

Thus, when it might follow that all other forms of marriage are excluded, he states the specific exception: "Authorized by his elders, a brother-in-law, a sapinda, or one of the same gotra, having anointed himself with clarified butter and desiring a son, may approach [the widow] during her fertile period. (YDh 1.68)
He may approach her until the conception of the embryo; otherwise, he would become fallen.
A son born according to this rule shall be the *kṣetraja* (field-born) son of that man. [Regarding the *niyoga*:

when a woman is childless—that is, has not obtained a son—the brother-in-law, being the younger brother of the husband, having been authorized by the father and others for the sake of obtaining a son...]
A sapinda, as previously defined, or one of the same lineage (sagotra)—
in the absence of each preceding one among these, the succeeding one, with all his limbs anointed with clarified butter,
shall approach her only during the fertile period characterized as will be described below, until conception occurs.
Furthermore, if he departs again by another means, he then becomes a fallen man;
born according to this rule, he is the *kṣetraja* son of the original husband.

This would apply to the case of one betrothed by word, according to the teachers: "If the husband of a maiden should die after a verbal agreement has been made true, her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule" (MDh 9.69).
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu. (1.68) (1.69)
Regarding the unfaithful wife, he says:
"One should cause the unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground. (YDh 1.70)
She who commits adultery—stripped of her authority, meaning deprived of the right to maintain servants and other such duties;
soiled, being destitute of collyrium, ointments, bright garments, and ornaments;
and subsisting on mere alms, eating only enough food for the bare maintenance of life.
One should have her reside in one's own house even while she is being humiliated by reproaches and the like and lying on the ground;
this is for the purpose of generating world-weariness (*vairāgya*), and not for the sake of purification.
"Whatever [penance] is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others, he should cause her to perform that same vow," because of this instruction for a separate penance. (MDh 11.176) // 1.70 //
He states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the purpose of [prescribing] a light penance for her:
"Soma gave them purity, and Gandharva gave them beautiful speech; Pāvaka [gave] their fitness for all sacrificial rites; therefore, women are indeed pure. (YDh 1.71)
Prior to marriage, Soma, Gandharva, and Agni enjoyed women in succession; they bestowed upon them, respectively, purity, sweet speech, and complete sanctity.
Therefore, women are traditionally held to be pure and clean in all matters, such as touching and embracing. (1.71)

Nor should it be suspected that she is therefore free from fault; thus he says: "Purification is prescribed after her menses if there has been infidelity; abandonment is ordained if a fetus is conceived, or in cases such as the killing of the fetus or the husband, and likewise for other great crimes. (YDh 1.72)

The impurity resulting from unmanifested mental transgressions—such as the intention to enjoy another man—is purified by the appearance of menses during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). However, if a fetus is produced by a Śūdra, there is abandonment;
for the wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have united with a Śūdra [are to be abandoned].
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Those who have not yet given birth are purified by penance, but others are not.
Likewise, this applies to the killing of an embryo, the murder of one's husband, and other mortal sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there is also abandonment [of intercourse] when going to a female disciple and so forth;
however, four must be abandoned: she who goes to a disciple, she who goes to a teacher, and the other two.
And she who is particularly hostile, and she who has approached a degraded man.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa:
"A *juṅgita* is one born from a reverse-order union (*pratiloma*), such as a leather-worker (*carmakāra*) and others;
and 'abandonment' refers to the abandonment of both enjoyment and religious duties."
For there is the rule: "She should be expelled from the house, or she should be confined to a single room" (MDh 11.176). // 1.72 //
He states the grounds for a second marriage:

"A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, one who is deceitful, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly, one who bears only daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband—such a wife may be superseded. (YDh 1.73)
Because of the general prohibition: "One who drinks *surā* is a *surāpī*; even a Śūdra woman causes him to fall, half of whose body has a wife who drinks *surā*" (VaDh 21.15).
"Afflicted" means seized by a chronic disease;
"deceitful" means one who is untrustworthy; "barren" means fruitless; "wasting wealth" means one who destroys one's resources.
She speaks unpleasantly and speaks harshly;
she gives birth to daughters and is the mother of female children;
she hates men and causes harm everywhere.
The term "to be taken as a wife" (adhivettavyā) is connected with each [of the preceding cases]. "Taking another wife" (adhivedana) means the formal acceptance of a second spouse. (1.73)
Furthermore:
A woman who has been formally accepted must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish. (YDh 1.74)
She, having been taken in marriage, must be maintained with gifts, honors, and hospitality just as before;
otherwise, in failing to maintain her, there will be great demerit and the punishment that is about to be described.
Moreover, when there is support [of the wife], it is not merely the avoidance of demerit;
for where there is harmony between husband and wife and unity of mind, there is the daily increase of dharma, artha, and kāma. (1.74)
Regarding women, he says:
"She who does not approach another man, whether her husband is dead or alive, attains fame in this world and rejoices together with him in the hereafter. (YDh 1.75)
Whether her husband is living or dead, she who does not approach another man out of fickleness attains vast renown in this world; and by the power of her merit, she sports together with Umā. (1.75)
Regarding one who takes another wife in the absence of grounds for supersession, the author says to that superseder:

"Abandoning a wife who is obedient, skillful, the mother of heroic sons, and sweet-spoken, he shall be made to pay a third part [of his estate]; if he is without property, he must provide maintenance for her. (YDh 1.76)
One who carries out commands, one who follows instructions, one who is skillful, one who acts quickly,
one who gives birth to heroes, and one who has sons.

He who abandons a wife who speaks kindly and speaks sweetly shall be compelled by the king to pay a third part of his own wealth; if he is destitute of wealth, however, he shall be compelled to provide maintenance, such as food and clothing. (1.76)
He states the duties of women:
"The word of the husband must be carried out by women; this is the supreme duty of a woman."
For one who is defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must indeed undergo initiation until purification.
Women must always carry out the word of their husband,
because this alone is the supreme, most excellent duty for women.
Because it is a cause for attaining heaven;
however, when he is defiled by a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), then he must be awaited until his purification.
That is not a state of dependence.
But at a later time, its dependence [on causes] remains exactly as before. (1.77)
He states the fruit of taking a wife according to the scriptures:
"Through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, there is infinity of worlds and the attainment of heaven;
therefore, women should be enjoyed and should be well-protected. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.78)

The purpose of taking a wife is the infinity of one's lineage in this world—meaning its non-interruption—as well as the attainment of heaven.
