To the question "How so?", he says: the sequence is that through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons one achieves infinity in the world, and through the *agnihotra* and other rites one attains heaven. Since these two results arise from women, therefore women are to be served and enjoyed for the sake of progeny.
And they must be protected for the sake of *dharma*.

Accordingly, Āpastamba has stated that the purpose of taking a wife is the fulfillment of *dharma* and progeny, saying: "One should not take another wife while one's current wives are endowed with *dharma* and progeny" (ĀpDh 2.11.12).
As for the fruit of sexual pleasure (*rati*), however, it is merely worldly. (1.78)
It has been stated that women should be approached for the purpose of procreating a son;
regarding this, he states a qualification:
"The nights of women during their fertile period are sixteen; among those, one should approach them on the even nights."
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should indeed avoid sexual intercourse on the festival days and during the first four [days] of the menstrual period.
The *ṛtu* is the time characterized by the woman’s state of being fit for conception;
it begins from the day the menses appear.
A period of sixteen days and nights.
During that season, on the nights of the even years;
by the mention of "nights," the prohibition of the days is implied.
He should lie down with her or approach her for the sake of a son.
The plural number in the word *yugmāsu* (on even nights) is intended to express a cumulative sense;
therefore, [the practice applies] even in a single [instance].
Even during the fertile period, he may approach her on all nights that are not forbidden, provided they are even-numbered;
approaching her in this manner, he remains truly a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).

Therefore, there is no fault of violating celibacy even for one who goes where celibacy is enjoined, such as at ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and the like. Furthermore, "one should avoid the festival days (*parvan*); however, one should avoid the first four," because of the use of the plural *parvāṇi*, the meaning "the first" is understood.
The eighth and fourteenth days are included;
as Manu has said:
"The new moon, the eighth day, the full moon, and the fourteenth day..."
"A twice-born man who has completed his studies (snātaka) should always remain a celibate student (brahmacārī), even during the fertile period. (MDh 4.155).
Therefore, from the onset of menstruation, he should avoid the new moon day and the following four nights. 1.79.
Furthermore:
proceeding in this manner, he should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the Maghā and Mūla constellations;
when the moon is auspicious, a man shall once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks. (YDh 1.80)

In the manner thus described, when approaching his wife, he should approach her when she is emaciated (*kṣāmā*). Her state of emaciation at that time arises precisely through the observance of the rules for a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā-vrata*). If, however, this is not the case, then emaciation must be induced for the sake of producing a son by means of eating little, avoiding oily foods, and so forth.

"From a man, when the semen is in excess, a male is born; when that of the woman is in excess, a female is born. Because of this statement, even when conception occurs on an even night, if there is an excess of blood, then a female alone is born, though possessing a male form.
Even on an odd day, if there is an excess of semen, the offspring will be a male with a female form,
because time is merely a contributing condition for the semen and the blood.
Because it is more powerful due to its being the substantial cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*),
one should therefore perform the *kṣāma* rite;
however, one should avoid the lunar mansions of Maghā and Mūla.

And when the Moon has entered an auspicious position such as the eleventh, and by the use of the word "ca" (and), when there is the perfection of male constellations, auspicious yogas, the ascendant, and so forth— occurring once in a single night, not twice or thrice—
one then gives birth to a son endowed with the [auspicious] marks.
A man whose virility is unimpeded. // 1.80 //
Having thus stated the rule regarding the fertile period (*ṛtu*), he now states the rule for other times:
"Or he may act according to his desire, remembering the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, since women are declared to be protected. (YDh 1.81)
One should be "acting according to her desire" (yathākāmī), meaning one whose conduct proceeds without overstepping the wishes of his wife.
The word "or" (vā) is intended to include another restrictive rule; it does not signify the cessation of the previous restriction.
Recalling the boon granted to women by Indra— that he who obstructs their desire shall be a sinner—
he said, "As they spoke, 'We choose this boon: let us obtain offspring according to the season, and let us unite at will until childbirth.'"
Therefore, women who approach their husbands during their fertile seasons obtain offspring; they may engage in sexual union at will until delivery, for this is the chosen vow of theirs.
Moreover, he should be devoted solely to his own wife, being intensely delighted with her and focused entirely on her.
The word "should be" (*bhavet*) is supplied [from the previous context].
By means of the particle *eva*, he excludes intercourse with another woman, because such is prescribed as the penance (*prāyaścitta*) in the legal codes (*smṛti*).
This applies in both cases.
He states the visible purpose [of this rule] with the words, "since women are declared to be protected" (*striyo rakṣyā yataḥ smṛtāḥ*).
Because it has been stated and prescribed that "women are to be protected and well-guarded" (YDh 1.78),
and because that state of being well-guarded occurs through [the husband's] acting according to her desires and by not approaching other women.
Regarding this, it is said: "In that regard, he should approach her on even nights" (YDh 1.79).
Is this an injunction (*vidhi*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*), or an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)? It is replied: [it is a restrictive rule].
It cannot be an injunction (*vidhi*), because its purpose is already established;
nor can it be an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), because that would entail the threefold fault.
Therefore, those learned in logic have determined it to be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Which one?
Furthermore, there is a distinction between these:
an injunction (*vidhi*) is that which brings about the attainment of what has not been attained at all,
such as "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice."

"The Aṣṭakās must be performed. Restriction (niyama) is the prescription of an alternative not previously established for that which is already established as an option, such as: "One should sacrifice on level ground."

By the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," the sacrifice is prescribed as something to be performed. Since that cannot be performed without a location, a location is obtained by implication (*arthāt*). And that is of two kinds: level and uneven (as stated in the NSP edition: "it is of two kinds, level and uneven").
When the sacrificer intends to sacrifice on level ground, the injunction "one should sacrifice on level ground" remains indifferent,
because its own purpose is already established.
But when he intends to sacrifice on uneven ground, then the injunction "one should sacrifice on level ground" prescribes its own purpose.
Because at that time one's own purpose has not yet been attained; however, the cessation from an improper place is implied,
since the sacrifice is accomplished precisely by means of the enjoined location.
If one were to adopt a location not prescribed [by scripture], the sacrifice would not be performed according to the śāstra;
likewise, "one should eat food facing the east"—
this example from the Smṛti is explained by the preceding [argument].
*Parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is the restatement of something that has already been established in multiple places, for the purpose of excluding it from other instances.

For example, regarding the mantra "They took up this rein of immortality," which is used when taking up the horse's bridle: by its own inherent power (*svasāmarthya*), this mantra would apply to the grasping of both the horse's bridle and the donkey's bridle.
Having been enjoined [elsewhere],

when one takes up the horse's halter again, by this very act of being enjoined to the horse's halter, [the injunction] is excluded from the donkey's halter. Just as in the case of "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," where eating [all five-nailed animals] would have occurred by default, the mention of the hare and so forth [again] excludes dogs and the like.
[The rule] "śvādibhyaṣṭhak" [is applied]. In the Pāṇḍeya Chowkhamba edition, it says "nivartate" (it is excluded). What, then, is appropriate here?
He says: it is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
For instance, since one who has taken a wife is already entitled to approach her during her season by his own will, this is not the subject matter of an injunction (*vidhi*),
nor is it the subject matter of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

Because it contradicts the Gṛhya-smṛtis; for the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras record as follows: "After taking a wife, one should remain a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) for three nights, twelve nights, or a year."

In that case, because of the restrictive rule that one must indeed approach [one's wife] during her season when the season occurs even before twelve nights or a year have passed, the traditional teaching on celibacy (*brahmacarya*) would be contradicted. Furthermore, since the basic action (*bhāvārtha*) is already established, the statement is intended to specify a particular qualification.

It is logical and appropriate that approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) occurs solely by her own desire; therefore, the interpretation of the statement as "if he should approach her, only during her fertile period" is correct. Furthermore, since approaching her during her fertile period is already established as a constant obligation by the very injunction for the procreation of a son, it follows that [the rule applies] during the fertile period.
The restriction that "one must go" would be purposeless; furthermore, if there were such a restriction, an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated.
Moreover, one should go [only] during the fertile period (*ṛtu*).

If there were such a restriction (*niyama*) [that one must always speak the truth], then an impossible matter would be taught for one who is absent, one who is incapable due to illness or other causes, or one who lacks the desire [to speak]. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) in the case of a restriction;
for a single word, when uttered once, [cannot simultaneously enjoin and restate] that very same meaning.
"He speaks in accordance with [the husband's will] at one time, and he acts in accordance with it at another.

Therefore, a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) alone is appropriate, meaning that one should go only during the proper season and not otherwise. This view is not accepted by Bhāruci, Viśvarūpa, and others.
Therefore, a restrictive rule alone is logical, because the injunction for one's own purpose is possible in that case,
and because a fault is heard [in scripture] regarding non-attendance.

"And he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of foeticide; there is no doubt in this matter. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.79)
Nor is there a contradiction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), because there is an absence of restatement and because the statement serves the purpose of an injunction;
for it is in that case that a contradiction between injunction and restatement occurs.

In a case where something must be restated as the limit (avadhi) for that which is to be enjoined, it must be restated because it is already established, while the other [element] must be enjoined with reference to that [restated element] because it is not yet established.

For example, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section on the Vājapeya sacrifice, in the injunction "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," the sacrifice must be restated as the limit for the injunction of the accessory characterized as the Vājapeya.
That very [meditation] must be enjoined with a view toward the fruit characterized by self-sovereignty (svārājya);
furthermore, there is no purpose here for a mere restatement (anuvāda).
As for the statement that "an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) must be postulated when there is a restrictive rule (niyama)," that applies equally to an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā),
because a fault is postulated for one who engages in sexual intercourse outside the prescribed season.
As for the claim that because the obligatory rule for procreating a son necessarily entails the requirement to approach one's wife during her fertile period, there can be no further restriction—
that is incorrect.

This very same is the rule for the regular procreation of a son. It might be thought that, according to the statement, "By approaching a woman who is emaciated and possessed of auspicious marks, one shall beget a son" (YDh 1.80), there exists a rule for procreating a son that is distinct from the mere act of sexual intercourse with a woman.
That is not so;
for it is precisely the cultivation characterized by the act of going that is observed to have the production of a son as its objective.
Thus, by the statement "one should produce a son endowed with auspicious marks," it is just as [in the case of] "while offering the Agnihotra, one should effect heaven.
Nor does this entail the absurdity of enjoining an impossible task, such as [begetting a son] from one who is not present and so forth.
Because the instruction applies only to those whose capacity is present:
"But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is in his presence" (PSm 4.15);
"He who, being healthy, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses."
This is because of the mention of a specific [restriction];
however, the exclusion of those who do not desire [the result] follows simply from the injunction of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*).
Nor is there a focus on the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Since the injunction regarding the meaning of the action is possible within that alternative,
there is no contradiction with the Gṛhya-smṛtis;
for if one enters into union before the completion of a year upon the appearance of menses, there is no fault of violating the vow of celibacy.
Just as in the case of faith and the other [faculties],

therefore, enumeration (parisaṃkhyā) is not tenable, as it possesses the threefold defect characterized by the abandonment of its own meaning, the assumption of another meaning, and the contradiction of what has been established.

Thus, regarding the statement "five five-nailed animals are edible," although both restriction (*niyama*)—since eating is optionally established for rabbits and others—and exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)—since eating is established for rabbits and others as well as dogs and others—are possible, nevertheless, in the case of restriction, the non-eating of rabbits and others would entail a fault, while the eating of dogs and others would entail no fault; this would contradict the Smṛti texts on expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Therefore, exclusion alone is accepted. By this [same reasoning]...

"Twice-born men have their meals at morning and evening, as ordained by the Smṛtis"— here too, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is explained. Furthermore, if this were an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), the statement "one should not eat in between" would be redundant.

And since such a restriction exists, the distributive repetition "in every season" (*ṛtāv ṛtau*) is obtained, according to the principle that when the occasion recurs, the contingent duty also recurs.
Furthermore, the phrase "he may act according to his desire" is itself a restriction.
"Even outside the fertile period, if there is a desire for a woman, one should certainly please her; however,
one should approach her during the fertile period, or at all times except when forbidden"—
this pair of sūtras from Gautama is likewise intended solely as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
One should approach one's wife during her fertile period; however, if there is a desire for sexual union, one may approach her even outside that period, provided it is not a forbidden time.
Enough of this digression. (1.81)
Furthermore:
"Women are to be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, paternal kinsmen, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and relatives, with ornaments, clothing, and food. (YDh 1.82)
Virtuous women, such as those previously mentioned by Bhartṛ and others, should be honored according to one's ability with ornaments, garments, food, flowers, and so forth;
for when they are thus honored, they cause the increase of dharma, artha, and kāma. (1.82)
Furthermore, as for how she who has been entrusted with the management of the household should conduct herself, he says:
"With utensils kept in order, skillful, cheerful, averse to wasteful expenditure, and devoted to her husband, she should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law. (YDh 1.83)
She is described as such because her household utensils— the collection of domestic implements— are kept restrained and placed in their proper locations;
for instance, the mortar, pestle, winnowing basket, and so forth,
are kept in the place for threshing.
"In the place of grinding, by virtue of the non-separation of the two stones," and so forth. "Dakṣā" means skillful in domestic affairs; "hṛṣṭā" means always having a smiling face.
"Averse to expenditure" means one who does not have a habit of spending;
the phrase "she should be" is to be supplied in all instances. Furthermore, "mother-in-law and father-in-law" form the dual compound *śvaśurau*.
By the rule *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā* (Pāṇini 1.2.71), there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*). One should constantly perform the salutation of their feet.
The mention of the father-in-law is intended to include other venerable persons;
being devoted to her husband and remaining under his authority, she should perform what was previously described. // 1.83 //
It was stated [previously] regarding the presence of the husband; now, as to what she should do when the husband is away on a journey, he says:
"Amusement, bodily adornment, and witnessing social gatherings and festivals..."

A woman whose husband is away on a journey should avoid laughter, traveling to the houses of others, playing with balls and such, the adornment of the body with ointments and the like, and social gatherings. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.84) A woman whose husband has gone to another country [should likewise avoid these]. [She should also avoid] playing with balls and other such games, the refinement of the body through massage and similar treatments, and social assemblies.
A multitude of people, a festival such as a wedding and so forth,
and the sight of these two.
Laughing and yawning, and going to another's house—one should abandon each of these; thus "one should abandon" is connected with each item. (1.84)
Furthermore:
"The father shall protect the maiden; the husband, when she is married; and the sons in old age. In their absence, her kinsmen [shall protect her]; a woman never has independence. (YDh 1.85)
Before the taking of the hand in marriage, the father shall protect the maiden from the performance of improper acts;
after that, the husband; and in his absence, the sons, [protecting her] during her old age.
In the absence of those mentioned, the kinsmen (jñātis) [are entitled];
in the absence of kinsmen, the king (rajā), because of the scriptural statement: "At the conclusion of both sides [of the family], the king is the lord and master of the woman."
Therefore, women never possess independence in any circumstance whatsoever. // 1.85 //
Furthermore:

She should not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles while her husband is absent; otherwise, she would become subject to reproach. (YDh 1.86)
She should not be without a husband— meaning either husbandless or deprived of her father and other guardians—
because being deprived of them she would become censurable and blameworthy; and this applies to the view that she remains in a state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
For the Smṛti of Viṣṇu states: "When the husband has died, [the wife shall observe] celibacy or follow him in death" (ViDh 25.14).
By following him in death, there is great spiritual exaltation.
And so Vyāsa demonstrated this by means of the narrative of the female dove:
"The devoted wife entered the blazing fire;
there she was reunited with her husband, who wore variegated armlets."
"Then the bird, having gone to heaven and reunited with his wife, was honored there for his deeds and rejoiced together with his wife. Thus [it is said].
And likewise, Śaṅkha and Aṅgiras [state]:
As many hairs as there are on a human being— three and a half crores—
for that long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven.
Having thus established this, [the author] demonstrates their inseparability:
"Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
even so that woman, having rescued him, rejoices together with him."
There, devoted supremely to her husband and being praised by hosts of apsarases, she sports with her lord for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras. Thus it is said. Furthermore:
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or a slayer of a friend,
an unmarried woman purifies him by following him in death.
The woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral pyre,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world.
"As long as a woman does not cause herself to be cremated when her husband has died in the fire, she is by no means released from her female body. Thus says Hārīta as well.
"She purifies three lineages—the maternal, the paternal, and that into which she is given—she who follows her husband.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"When her husband is distressed she is distressed; when he is joyful she is joyful; when he has gone abroad she is soiled and emaciated;
and when he dies she dies—such a woman is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
And this entire rule is common to all women, from those who are not pregnant and whose children are no longer infants, down to the *caṇḍālas*.
Because it is stated without qualification that "Dharma follows the husband," as well as those scriptural passages which aim at prohibiting the following [of the husband] by a Brahmin woman.
According to the teaching of Brahman, there is no following in death for a Brāhmaṇī;
however, among the other castes, asceticism is said to be supreme.
A woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who follows her deceased husband [to death] would incur the sin of self-destruction; therefore, while still alive, she should perform that act beneficial to him.
By taking her own life, she would lead neither herself nor her husband to heaven.
Statements such as these concern the subject of ascending separate funeral pyres;
for there is a specific traditional injunction (smṛti) stating: "Having ascended separate pyres, the Brahmins must not depart [together]."
By this, it is understood that separate funeral pyres are permitted for women of the Kṣatriya and other castes.

As for what has been stated by some— that because suicide is prohibited for women just as it is for men, the scriptural prohibition applies to a woman who possesses an excessive desire for heaven— [that is incorrect].
"This instruction regarding following [the husband] by one who is passing away is like the *śyena* sacrifice.

Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the *śyena* when practicing malevolent magic," this is an instruction on the *śyena* for one whose mind is overcome by intense anger and who thus transgresses the prohibitive scripture—so it is said.

That is incorrect; for, insofar as there is no contact with an injunction regarding the harm (*hiṃsā*) which serves as the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) where the *śyena* is the instrument (*karaṇa*), [it cannot be compared].

They describe the Śyena sacrifice as being harmful by way of its result because it involves contact with a prohibition; however, in their view, since the scriptural injunction for following [the husband] in death prescribes that very act of killing for the sake of attaining heaven, it lacks contact with a prohibition. Thus, like the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, the clear disparity between following in death and the Śyena is evident.
As for the view that violence (*hiṃsā*) is an activity conducive to death,
and that the *śyena* sacrifice is indeed violence because it consists of an activity conducive to the death of another,
[it is argued] that in the context of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya-adhikāra*), [the performance] occurs through passion (*rāga*) regarding the instrumental factor.

Because an injunction does not incite action when the possibility of such activity already exists, and because the Śyena sacrifice is of the nature of violence prompted by passion, it is prohibited; thus,
it is harmful by its very nature.

In that case as well, since the scripture concerning "following" (anugamana) prescribes death itself as the means for attaining heaven, although one's engagement in dying may proceed from passion (rāga), nevertheless, regarding the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of activities conducive to death—such as entering the fire—one's engagement proceeds solely from scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), just as in the case of the rule: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu. Thus, there is no room for a prohibition [to apply].

Therefore, the disparity between the *anugamana* (following the husband in death) and the *śyena* sacrifice is indeed clear. As for the argument that following the husband is improper because it contradicts the Vedic injunction, "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his natural lifespan," and the further point that "one desiring heaven should not depart before the end of his lifespan"— meaning that a seeker of liberation (*mokṣārthin*) should not waste his life before its natural term for the sake of attaining the fruit of heaven— [these are addressed as follows].

Because, when there is a remainder of life, for one whose internal organ has had its stains removed by the performance of obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), liberation— characterized by the attainment of Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss— is possible through self-knowledge once the perfection of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) has been achieved.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should not squander one's life for the sake of heaven, which consists of impermanent and meager pleasure;
and thus, for one who does not desire liberation but desires heaven consisting of impermanent and meager pleasure—
Following [the deceased] is appropriate, just like the performance of other desired rites; thus, everything is beyond reproach. // 1.86 //
Furthermore:
A woman who is devoted to her husband’s pleasure and welfare, who conducts herself well, and has her senses subdued, attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death. (YDh 1.87)
"Priya" means agreeable because it is blameless and conforms to the mind; "hita" refers to that which produces welfare in the future. That which is both "priya" and "hita" is "priyahita."
"Devoted to her husband's pleasure and welfare" means she is intent upon that which is pleasing and beneficial to her husband. "Of good conduct" means she whose conduct is beautiful;
such beautiful conduct has been demonstrated by Śaṅkha:
She should not go out from her home without having spoken [to those present]; she should not walk without an upper garment, nor should she walk hurriedly;
she should not address a stranger, except [in cases of necessity].
Like a merchant, a renunciant, an elder, or a physician,
one should not expose the navel;
one should wear the lower garment reaching down to the ankles.
She should not expose her breasts;
she should not laugh uncovered;
and she should not harbor ill will toward her husband or his relatives.

One should not stay in the same place with courtesans, rogues, women who go to meet lovers, female renunciants, female performers, those who practice illusion, root-charms, or sorcery, nor with those of immoral conduct and the like;
for through such association, the character of noble women is corrupted.
Thus: she by whom the senses— the ears and so forth, as well as the speech and so forth together with the mind— have been conquered, that is, restrained,
attains fame and renown in this world, and in the next world, the supreme state.
And all this duty of women is to be understood as applying from marriage onwards; prior to initiation, they may act, speak, and eat according to their desire. (GDh 2.1)
Because of this traditional teaching, and because it is stated: "The marriage rite is declared to be the initiation ceremony for women" (Manu Smṛti 2.67). [1.87]
Regarding one who has many wives, he says:
"When another wife of the same class exists, one should not have religious duties performed by her;
among wives of the same class, according to the rule of dharma, no other may act without the eldest. (YDh 1.88)
While a wife of the same caste exists, one must never have another wife of a different caste perform religious duties.
Even when there are many wives of the same caste,
in accordance with the righteous rule for the performance of dharma, one must not— setting aside the eldest— employ any other, such as the middlemost or the youngest.
Or she should not be employed [in such tasks]. // 1.88 //
Having stated the rule for a woman whose husband has died, he now speaks concerning a man whose wife has died:
"The husband, having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire..."

He should take a wife and establish the sacred fires according to the prescribed rules without delay. Having cremated a deceased wife— who possessed the conduct previously described and was observant of proper behavior— with the Śrauta fire used for the Agnihotra, or in its absence with the Smārta fire, the husband— provided he has not yet procreated a son or performed the required sacrifices, and is thus ineligible for other stages of life (āśramas)— should proceed.
Or, in the absence of a wife or a son, he should again take a wife and establish the sacred fires according to the rules;
without delay, indeed very quickly,
a twice-born man who has not entered an āśrama should not remain even for a single day.

Thus, according to the recollection of Dakṣa, this applies only to a wife who was authorized for the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) together with her husband, and not to any other. As for the statement: "And he who should cremate a second wife with the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika-agni*)," [this refers to a different case].
"For while the first wife is alive, that [act] is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor.
Likewise:
"But when the second wife has died, he who should abandon the *agnihotra*..."
One should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin who would abandon [his wife] out of lust.

Such passages as these are to be understood as referring to the giving of fire to one who is not authorized [to perform the rite] together with the *ādhāna* (the formal establishment of the sacred fires). 1.89.
Thus ends the section on marriage. Now begins the fourth section, the distinction between castes and classes: A Brāhmaṇa has four wives, a Kṣatriya has three, a Vaiśya has two, and a Śūdra has one.
Having stated that sons are to be produced among them,
it is now explained by way of distinction which son arises from whom and in whom.
To distinguish them, he says: "From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage (sajātayaḥ);
through blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the progeny. (YDh 1.90)

From Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, when they marry women of their own caste—Brāhmaṇīs and so forth—the sons are of the same lineage (*sajātayaḥ*), meaning they belong to the same caste as their mother and father.
This rule is prescribed for those who have been duly married (*vinnāsu*). (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.92)
Since this is a concluding summary applying to all [the preceding cases], it is connected with the phrase "among wives of the same caste" (*savarṇāsu*).
Because the word *vinā* is a relative term,
it is understood that [the husbands] must be of the same caste as those who wed them (*vettṛbhyaḥ savarṇebhyaḥ*).
The word *savarṇa* (of the same class) is clear in meaning; therefore, this is the resulting sense:
those born from a woman of the same class (*savarṇā*) who has been wedded according to the prescribed rule are [the sons] of the husband from that woman of the same class.
They belong to the same caste;
and for this reason, it is stated that those born of a *kuṇḍa*, *golaka*, *kānīna*, *sahoḍha*, and so forth, are of a different caste (*asavarṇa*).
And they, being distinguished from those of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and from those born in the direct (*anuloma*) and inverse (*pratiloma*) orders, [are defined] by common characteristics.

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "They are authorized [to perform rites] through violence and so forth; however, all those born of transgression are recorded as having the same dharma as Śūdras" (MDh 10.41).
Those born of *apadhvaṃsa* (debased unions), being born of illicit intercourse, are entitled even to the duties of Śūdras, such as service to the twice-born (*dvija*).
Now, since the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are not Brāhmaṇas, their exclusion from the *śrāddha* rite would be illogical, and it would contradict established reasoning:
that whatever is produced from a man of a certain caste by a woman of a certain caste, that offspring belongs to that very same caste.
Just as from a bull and a cow a cow is born, and from a stallion and a mare a horse is born,
so too it is not contradictory that one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is a Brāhmaṇa.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the statement to be cited later: "Thus, having enumerated the son born of an unmarried girl, the son of a remarried woman, and the others, I have declared this rule regarding sons of the same caste" (YDh 2.133).
This is not the essential point.
The prohibition regarding the *śrāddha* is for the purpose of removing the misconception that one born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Brāhmaṇī woman is necessarily a Brāhmaṇa;
it is just as there is a prohibition against an outcast (*patita*) at a *śrāddha*, even though such a person is absolutely ineligible [for other reasons].
Nor is there any contradiction with logic; for where a genus (*jāti*) is perceivable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is so [established].
But the caste (*jāti*) of Brāhmaṇas and the like is characterized by traditional scripture (*smṛti*), and is established according to that tradition.

It occurs as follows: just as, despite the commonality of Brahminhood, there are lineages (*gotra*) characterized by tradition such as Kuṇḍina, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Gautama; so too, despite the commonality of being human, there are castes (*jāti*) such as Brahminhood and others characterized by tradition.
And this [distinction] belongs to the mother and father.
Such is the definition of a universal;
nor does it lead to an infinite regress,
because cyclic existence is beginningless, like the conventional usage of words and their referents.
"This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste" (YDh 2.133);
since this is a restatement of what was already said, it will be explained according to the circumstances.
However, the *kṣetraja* son belongs to the same caste as the mother, because of the traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) concerning *niyoga*.
And because this is the practice of the learned;
for example, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura, though born of others' fields (kṣetraja), were of the same caste as their mothers— enough of this digression.
Moreover, sons born from blameless marriages such as the Brāhma and others increase the lineage; they are free from disease, long-lived, and endowed with righteousness and progeny. // 1.90 //
Having spoken of those of equal caste, he now describes those born in the direct order (anuloma): "From a Brāhmaṇa, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born from a Kṣatriya woman; from a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha;
and from a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava. (YDh 1.91)
A son born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a married Kṣatriya woman is called a Mūrdhāvasikta;
one born from a married Vaiśya girl is called an Ambaṣṭha.

When a Śūdra woman is married [to a Brāhmaṇa], a son named Niṣāda is born. Lest this Niṣāda—a certain person born in the inverse order (pratiloma) who lives by killing fish—be confused with the other, this one is designated as a Pāraśava; thus there is an alternative designation of "Niṣāda."
The word "from a Brāhmaṇa" (viprāt) applies everywhere.
However, one begotten by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Kṣatriya woman becomes a Kṣatriya himself; likewise, one begotten by a Kṣatriya upon a Vaiśya woman...
The Smṛti of Śaṅkha states that one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother becomes a Vaiśya, and one born from a Śūdra father and a Śūdra mother becomes a Śūdra;

this is intended for the purpose of attaining the duties (dharma) of the Kṣatriya and other castes, and not for the purpose of negating the existence of specific mixed castes such as the Mūrdhāvasikta.
Or [it is for the sake of attaining] the status of a Kṣatriya and other castes.

Therefore, for those such as the Mūrdhāvasikta, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) and so forth must be performed using the very same staff, deerskin, sacred thread, and other implements prescribed for the Kṣatriya and others.
Prior to initiation, his freedom of action and so forth should be understood to be exactly as before. (1.91)
From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya or Śūdra mother who has been wedded, the sons Māhiṣya and Ugra are declared;

from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra wife, the son is Karaṇa. This is the rule prescribed for women who have been married. From a Kṣatriya father and a wedded Vaiśya or Śūdra woman, the sons Māhiṣya and Ugra respectively are born. By a Vaiśya...

From a Śūdra woman who has been married [by a man of a higher caste], a son named Karaṇa is born. This rule regarding the designations of the Mūrdhāvasikta and others for women who have been married [by men of higher castes] should be understood as having been declared and recorded in the Smṛti.
And these six—Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, Niṣāda, Māhiṣya, Ugra, and Karaṇa—are to be known as the sons born in the inverse order. 1.92.
He speaks of those born in the inverse order:
"From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
but from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties. (YDh 1.93)
Sons begotten by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras upon a Brāhmaṇa woman are respectively known as Sūtas, Vaidehakas, and Caṇḍālas;
among them, the Caṇḍāla is excluded from all religious duties. (1.93)
A Kṣatriya woman from a Vaiśya father gives birth to a Māgadha, and from a Śūdra father she gives birth to a Kṣattṛ;
a Vaiśya woman indeed gives birth to an Āyogava son from a Śūdra father. Furthermore, a Kṣatriya woman gives birth to a son named Māgadha from a Vaiśya man.
She herself, from a Śūdra, gives birth to a son who is a Kṣattṛ;
and the wife of a Vaiśya, from a Śūdra, gives birth to a son who is an Āyogava.
And these six—the Sūta, Vaidehaka, Caṇḍāla, Māgadha, Kṣattri, and Āyogava—are born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
Their occupations are to be found in the works of Uśanas and Manu. 1.94.
He now describes another distinct mixed caste born from a mixture of castes: "From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
those born from the inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) orders are to be known as 'unrighteous' (asat) and 'righteous' (sat) respectively. (YDh 1.95)
A Māhiṣya is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother;
a Karaṇī is born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother; and from that Karaṇī, a Rathakāra is produced by a Māhiṣya, who exists as a distinct caste.
And for him, all rites beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*) must be performed because of the scriptural injunction; as Śaṅkha says:

"The chariot-maker (*rathakāra*), who is born from a *kṣatriya* father and a *vaiśya* mother in the order of natural conformity (*ānuloma*), is entitled to the performance of the purificatory rites of sacrifice, giving, and initiation, as well as the study of the treatises on horses, the establishment of chariots, and architecture, and his livelihood [is therein]."

And so it is said: "ca" (and). In this way, it should be understood that for the Mūrdhāvasikta born from a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, and for the Māhiṣya and others born from the *anuloma* rites, there is a distinct caste status (*jātyantaratā*) as well as the attainment of initiation (*upanayana*) and other sacraments, because those two possess the status of the twice-born (*dvijāti*).
The specific designations, however, should be understood from other works of memory (smṛti);
this has been stated merely as an illustration,
because the mixed and further-mixed castes are infinite in number.
Because it is impossible to describe [them fully],
therefore this much alone is intended here:
those born in the inverse order (pratilomaja) are non-existent, while those born in the direct order (anulomaja) are existent.
These are to be known. // 1.95 //
By the verse beginning with "They are born from all [men] by all [women]" (YDh 1.90), the cause for attaining the status of a caste has been stated;
now, he states another cause.
The elevation of caste (jātyutkarṣa) is to be understood as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation;
upon the reversal of [forbidden] actions, there is equality [of status], and as before, there is the distinction of higher and lower.

(YDh 1.96) The "castes" refer to the Mūrdhāvasikta and others; their "elevation" (utkarṣa) is the attainment of a caste such as Brāhmaṇa-hood; this "elevation of caste" occurs within a "yuga," meaning in a birth.

It should be understood that [the offspring] is [born] in the seventh, the fifth, or—due to the word "api"—the sixth generation; and this alternative is fixed. The rule is as follows: a Niṣādī is one begotten by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Śūdra woman.

She, having been married by a Brāhmaṇa, gives birth to a daughter; she too, having been married by a Brāhmaṇa, gives birth to another. In this manner, the sixth generation produces a seventh Brāhmaṇa.
An Ambaṣṭha is one produced by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Vaiśya woman.
She too, in this manner, gives birth to a fifth [son] who is a sixth Brahmin. Likewise, a Mūrdhāvasiktā woman, in this manner, gives birth to a fourth [son] who is indeed a fifth Brahmin.
Similarly, an Ugrā woman wedded by a Kṣatriya, and a Māhiṣyā woman, produce respectively a sixth and a fifth Kṣatriya.
Likewise, a Vaiśya woman married by a Kṣatriya bears a fifth [son] who is a Vaiśya; in this manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well.

Furthermore, regarding the "reversal of occupations"—that is, the inversion of occupations for the sake of livelihood—just as a Brāhmaṇa, unable to subsist by his primary occupation, [subsists] by the Kṣatriya [occupation].

"One should live by one's own duty" is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). If one cannot subsist even by that, one may subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya; if one cannot subsist even by that, one may subsist by the occupation of a Śūdra.
A Kṣatriya also, if unable to subsist for the sake of livelihood by his own duty, may subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya or the occupation of a Śūdra. The same applies to a Vaiśya as well.
Not living by one's own occupation, one lives by the occupation of a Śūdra; this is the transposition of duties (*karmavyatyaya*).

When that transposition has occurred, if one does not abandon that occupation even upon liberation from the distress, then in the seventh, sixth, or fifth birth, one attains equality with that [lower caste].
One who lives by the work of a low-caste person comes to belong to that same caste;
for example, a Brāhmaṇa [living] by the occupation of a Śūdra.

If, while living and not abandoning her, he begets a son, and that son likewise lives by that same occupation and begets another son— thus continuing in this lineage— he produces one who is a Śūdra in the seventh birth.
If he lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, [he produces a Śūdra] in the sixth.
A Vaiśya living by the occupation of a Kṣatriya becomes a Kṣatriya in the fifth [generation];
a Kṣatriya also living by the occupation of a Śūdra becomes a Śūdra in the sixth [generation].
Living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, he produces a Vaiśya in the fifth generation;
likewise, a Vaiśya living by the occupation of a Śūdra,
without abandoning it, produces a Śūdra in the fifth birth through the succession of sons.
As before, there is the lower and the higher.

Its meaning is as follows: among the mixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) have been shown; now, those born from the mixture of mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇasaṃkaraja*) [will be discussed].
And these have been shown by the illustration of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*).
Now, those born from the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkīrṇa-saṃkarajāta*) are being demonstrated.
Regarding "lower and higher" (*adharottara*): for example, in the case of a *mūrdhāvasikta*, one produced by a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra [from a Brāhmaṇa woman].
Likewise, those born from a Vaiśya and a Śūdra father on an Ambaṣṭhā mother, and from a Śūdra father on a Niṣādī mother, are lower-born (adharāḥ) and born in the reverse order (pratilomaja).
Similarly, those born from a Brāhmaṇa father on Mūrdhāvasiktā, Ambaṣṭhā, and Niṣādī mothers,
and from a Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya father on a Māhiṣyā or Ugrā mother [are likewise classified].
Those begotten on a *karaṇī* by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya are the higher *anuloma*-born [classes].
In this same manner, it should be inferred for other cases as well.
This inversion of the superior and the inferior should be understood as "non-existent" and "existent," respectively, as previously explained. // 1.96 //
Thus ends the section on the distinction between social classes and castes.
Now begins the section on the duties of the householder.
Intending to demonstrate those rites prescribed by revelation and tradition that are to be accomplished with fire, [the author] states in which fire each rite should be performed.
A householder should perform every day the *smārta* rites in the nuptial fire,
or those performed at the time of inheritance, as well as the *śrauta* rites in the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika-agni*).
The *smārta* rites mentioned in the *Smṛtis*, such as the *vaiśvadeva* and others, as well as worldly activities like daily cooking— these too the householder [should perform].
One should perform [the rite] in the marriage fire, which has been consecrated by the marriage sacrament;

or, at the time of inheritance— that is, at the time of partition— one should bring fire from a Vaiśya household and [perform the rite] in that fire which has been consecrated by the sacraments mentioned in such passages as "having brought fire" (GoGṛ 1.1.15).
By virtue of the word "api" (also), [the rule applies] even when the householder has died or when [the food] has been brought and prepared;
consequently, one incurs the penance upon the lapse of these three periods of time.
One should perform the rites prescribed by the Vedas, such as the Agnihotra and others, in the sacrificial fires, namely the Āhavanīya and the rest. // 1.97 //
He states the duties of the householder:

Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rules of purification, the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsaṃdhyā), preceded by the cleansing of the teeth. (YDh 1.98)

Having performed the bodily care, such as the necessary duties (*āvaśyaka*), during the daytime and at the twilights according to the prescribed rule beginning with "with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) placed over the ear, facing north" (YDh 1.16), and having completed the rules for purification according to the procedure stated in "that which removes odor and stain" (YDh 1.17), the twice-born (*dvija*) should perform the morning twilight devotions (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*) preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
One should perform worship. And now, the procedure for cleaning the teeth:
[the twig] should be produced from a thorny or milky tree, twelve finger-breadths in length, as thick as the tip of the little finger, with its end trimmed into a brush-like shape at half a joint.
"The cleaning of the teeth is prescribed, as well as the tongue-scraper.
In this context, by the phrase "produced from a tree," the use of grass, clods of earth, fingers, and so forth is prohibited;
furthermore, the prohibition of using *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and other such trees should be understood as stated in other *smṛti* texts.
And the mantra for cleaning the teeth is:
"O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us long life, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence. Thus it is said.

The repetition of the *saṃdhyāvandana*, although already mentioned in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), is for the purpose of establishing that it must be preceded by the cleaning of the teeth;
for there is a prohibition stating, "A religious student should avoid cleaning the teeth, dancing, singing, and so forth. (1.98)
Having offered oblations into the fires dedicated to the Sun, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras;
he should also master the meanings of the Vedas and various treatises.

(YDh 1.99) After the morning twilight worship, having offered oblations into the Āhavanīya and other fires according to the prescribed rule, [he should likewise offer into] the domestic fire (aupāsana).
Or, immediately after that, being composed and with an undistracted mind, he should mutter the mantras dedicated to the Sun, beginning with *ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam* (RV 1.50.1).
In the interval between those, one should master and understand the meanings of the Vedas as well as Nirukta, grammar, and so forth by means of hearing;
and by the use of the word "ca" (and), one should also practice what has already been studied.
And he should master various treatises, such as the Mīmāṃsā and others, which establish the principles of dharma, worldly prosperity, and health. 1.99.
And one should also approach the Lord for the sake of accomplishing security and well-being.

Having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship the gods and the ancestors. Immediately thereafter, for the sake of securing his welfare (yogakṣema), he should visit the Lord endowed with qualities such as consecration, or another illustrious person who is beyond reproach. Yoga is the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained; kṣema is the preservation of what has been acquired.
The preservation of what has been attained is security;
for that purpose, one should approach and attend upon [the teacher]. By the word "should approach," he prohibits mere service.
Service consists in carrying out orders for the sake of receiving wages;
it is prohibited because it is the "livelihood of a dog," according to the traditional teaching of Manu: "Service is declared to be the livelihood of a dog; therefore, one should avoid it."

Then, at midday, having bathed in a river or similar body of water according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods, the ancestors, and— indicated by the word "and"— the sages (*ṛṣis*), using the *tīrtha* (specific parts of the hand) associated with the gods and so forth.
Following that, [one should worship] Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

One should worship any one [deity] according to their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*), by means of *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, or *Sāman* mantras that reveal them, or by using their own names in the dative case accompanied by salutations, according to the prescribed ritual procedure. 1.100.

To the best of one's ability, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite the Vedas, the Atharva, the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, as well as spiritual knowledge (ādhyātmikī vidyā). Immediately thereafter, one should recite the Vedas, the Atharva, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas— either collectively or individually— as well as spiritual knowledge.
For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should perform the recitation according to one's ability, following the prescribed rule. // 1.101 //
The offering of oblations (*balikarma*), the *svadhā* sacrifice, Vedic study, and the hospitable reception of guests are the great sacrifices to the spirits (*bhūta*),
the ancestors (*pitṛ*), the gods (*amara*), Brahman, and human beings.
The offering of oblations (*balikarma*) is the sacrifice to the spirits (*bhūtayajña*).
The ancestral sacrifice is the offering of *svadhā*;
the fire-oblation is the sacrifice to the gods; the private recitation of the Veda is the sacrifice to Brahman.
The hospitable reception of guests is the sacrifice to human beings.
These five great sacrifices must be performed day after day because they are obligatory (*nitya*).
Furthermore, the mention of their rewards is intended to demonstrate their purifying power, not to establish that they are optional rites (*kāmya*). (1.102)
From the food remaining after the oblation has been offered to the gods, one should present the *balī* offering to the spirits (*bhūta*).

One should place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows. Having performed the *vaiśvadeva* homa according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*, one should offer the *balī* to the spirits with the food that remains from it.

The mention of "food" (*anna*) is for the purpose of excluding uncooked [grains]. Immediately thereafter, one should place food on the ground according to one's ability for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also for worms, those afflicted with sinful diseases, and the fallen (*patita*).
As Manu has said:
"One should slowly place [the food] on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms" (MDh 3.92).
And this must be performed both evening and morning,
because of the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana: "Then, one should offer oblations of prepared sacrificial food (haviṣya) in the evening and in the morning" (ĀśGṛ 1.2.1).

In this regard, some maintain that the rite called Vaiśvadeva serves both as a rite for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and as a rite for the consecration of food (*annasaṃskārakarma*). For they perceive its status as a rite for the consecration of food from the rule: "Then, one should offer in the evening and morning cooked sacrificial food" (*Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra* 1.2.1).

Furthermore, beginning with "Now, therefore, the five sacrifices" (ĀśGṛ 3.1.1) and concluding with "One should perform these sacrifices day after day" (ĀśGṛ 3.1.4), their obligatory nature is stated; from this, it is understood that they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
That is incorrect; for if it were for the sake of the person, it would be impossible for it to be an action that prepares food.
For instance, under the view that it is a substance-preparation rite (*dravyasaṃskārakarma*), the Vaiśvadeva rite would have food as its purpose;

whereas, if it were for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the substance would have the Vaiśvadeva rite as its purpose. Due to this mutual contradiction, it is more logical that it is indeed for the sake of the person.
"By means of the great sacrifices and the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman.
Likewise:
"But when the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been completed, if another guest should arrive..."

Therefore, one should give food according to one's ability, but one should not offer the *bali* [offering]. This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "Thus, the rite known as Vaiśvadeva, being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), need not be repeated with every cooking. Therefore...
Now, by the passage beginning with "In the evening and in the morning," the procedures for the origin [of the rites] are shown;
and since the rule "One should perform these sacrifices day after day" (ĀśG 3.1.4) is the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), everything is faultless. // 1.103 //
Food and water should be given daily to the ancestors and to human beings;
one should constantly perform the private recitation of the Vedas (svādhyāya), and one should not cook food for oneself alone.
(YDh 1.104) Every day, food should be offered to the ancestors and to men according to one's ability.
In the absence of food, [one may offer] roots, tubers, fruits, and so forth;
in the absence of those as well, water should be given—this being understood from the word "api" (also).
One should constantly perform the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) for the purpose of not forgetting it.
One should not cook food for one’s own sake.
The mention of "food" (anna) is intended to indicate all substances that are to be consumed. How then? Only by dedicating it to the deities and others. 1.1.04.

Having first fed the children, the daughters living in the father's house, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, young maidens, guests, and servants, the husband and wife may eat what remains. A "svavāsinī" is a married woman who resides in her father's house.
The remaining terms are well known.
Having fed the children and others, as well as the guests and dependents— that is, having caused them to eat— the husband and wife should partake of the remaining food.
In times of non-distress, one should eat food according to the procedure for the Prāṇāgnihotra;
it is ordained that what has been cooked and prepared should be consumed with a sense of joy. (1.105)

By a twice-born person eating food, the food must be made "not naked" and "immortal" by means of the ritual known as *āpośana* performed both before and after. By the twice-born person while eating, the food is rendered "not naked" and "immortal" through the rite called *āpośana* at the beginning and at the end.
And this is the duty. The mention of "twice-born" applies to all stages of life (āśrama) beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana). 1.106.
To those who have arrived as guests, one should give according to one's ability and in the proper order of the social classes (varṇas).
A guest must not be turned away even in the evening, at least with kind words, a place to sit, grass, and water.
Following the Vaiśvadeva rite, when members of the various classes—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—arrive simultaneously as guests, they should be honored in the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇas.
One should give according to one's ability.
Even if a guest arrives in the evening, he must not be turned away nor refused;
even if there is nothing edible to offer, one should still show him hospitality with kind words, a seat of grass, and water.
As Manu said:
"Grass for a seat, ground, water, and fourthly, pleasant speech—these are never lacking in the house of the virtuous" (MDh 3.101). 1.107.
O monks, alms should be given with respect to one who observes good vows;
and one should feed friends, relations, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time.
(YDh 1.108) Alms should be given to a monk in general.

Alms should be given according to this rule: "Having honored one who is firm in his vows, a celibate student, and an ascetic, and having pronounced a blessing, the gift of alms is unprecedented" (GDh 5.18).
Almsfood is measured by mouthfuls;
a mouthful is the size of a peacock’s egg.
Almsfood should consist of a single mouthful, and four times that amount is called *puṣkala*.
Now, from those four [fingers], the "haṃta" [measure] is formed; that [measure] should be tripled to become the "agra."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Śātātapa,
one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen who have arrived at the time of the meal;
"friends" (sakhāyaḥ) refers to companions (mitrāṇi).
Relatives are those from whom a daughter has been taken [in marriage] or given [in marriage]; they are the kinsmen related through the mother and the father. (1.108)
One should provide a great bull or a great goat to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya),
along with hospitable treatment, a seat, delicious food, and pleasant, truthful speech.
(YDh 1.109) One should provide a large bull capable of bearing a yoke, or a great goat, for the sake of the recipient who possesses the aforementioned characteristics of a learned Brahmin.
"This has been imagined by us for the sake of pleasing him, not for the purpose of giving or for the purpose of killing;
just as [one might say], 'All this is yours.'"

And because of the prohibition: "One should not practice even that which is dharma if it results in the slaughter of a bull for every Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), if it does not lead to heaven, and if it is despised by the world" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.156).
Therefore, one must indeed perform hospitable treatment (*satkriyā*).
Hospitable treatment consists of welcoming words, the offering of a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth.
Once he has sat down, sitting down after him is "sitting alongside" (*anvāsana*).
"Delicious food" means sweet eating; "pleasant speech" refers to such words as, "We are fortunate today because of your arrival," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), [the rule is]: "The water-offering and the seat for one who is not learned in the Vedas" (GDh 5.31).
Thus it should be understood as stated by Gautama. 1.109.

Every year, however, those worthy of the *arghya* offering are the *snātaka*, the teacher (*ācārya*), the king, a dear friend, one for whom one is performing a marriage, and likewise the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at a sacrifice.
(YDh 1.110) A *snātaka* is one who has "bathed" [after completing] his studies, one who has "bathed" after his vows, and one who has "bathed" after both his studies and his vows.
He who returns home after completing the Veda but without completing his vows is a *vidyā-snātaka*;
he who returns home after completing his vows but without completing the Veda [is likewise a *vidyā-snātaka*].
He is a *vratasnātaka*.
He who returns home after completing both [the Vedic study and the vows] is a *vidyāvratasnātaka*.
(Note: Some manuscripts omit this.)
Having completed [the vow], the *vratasnātaka* is one whose characteristics have been described by the Teacher;
the *pārthiva* is one whose characteristics will be described hereafter;
and the *priya* is a friend.
A son-in-law is one to be welcomed;
by the word "and," the inclusion of the father-in-law, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, and others is intended.

Having chosen the officiating priests, one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to a *snātaka* who has arrived, as well as to a king, and to an *ācārya*, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle.
And because of the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana (*ĀśGṛ* 1.24.1):
"These [persons], such as the *snātaka* and others, having come to the house every year, are worthy of the *arghya* offering; they are to be honored with the *madhuparka* and saluted.
The word *argha* here indicates the *madhuparka*.

And the officiating priests (ṛtvij), possessing the characteristics already described, must be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) at every sacrifice, even if it occurs within a year [of their previous appointment]. // 1.110 //
A traveler on the road should be known as a guest (*atithi*), as well as one who is learned in the Vedas and has mastered them;
these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman.
A traveler on the road is to be understood as a guest.
Two śrotriyas who have mastered the Vedas and are traveling on a road should be known as guests to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman;
even one who is merely a śrotriya by virtue of his study [is such].
Nevertheless, one who is endowed with learning and study is here designated as a *śrotriya*;
he is one capable of teaching a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) and has mastered the Veda. (1.111)
One should not have a taste for food prepared by others, except when invited by those beyond reproach; one should also avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating.
(YDh 1.112) One who has a "taste for another's cooking" (*parapākaruci*) is so described.

One should not have a desire for food cooked by others; for there is a traditional legal maxim (smṛti) stating: "One should not depart when invited by one who is beyond reproach, unless that invitation was made without being censurable."

One should avoid the restlessness of speech, hands, and feet—namely, speech, hands, and feet (*vāk-pāṇi-pāda*), and their restlessness. Restlessness of speech is the utterance of vulgar, false, and so forth;
restlessness of the hands is such things as leaping and clapping.
Fickleness of the feet refers to leaping,
jumping, and so forth;
by the word "and" (ca), one should also avoid fickleness of the eyes and other senses.
"One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, the eyes, or speech," according to the traditional teaching of Gautama (GDh 9.50);
likewise, one should avoid overeating.
Because it is the cause of ill health. // 1.112 //
One should follow a guest who is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) until he is satisfied and has reached the boundary of the village;
for the remainder of the day, one should sit together with cultured men, beloved friends, and kinsmen.

[Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.113] One should follow as far as the boundary that guest previously mentioned—a learned Vedic scholar who has mastered the Vedas—once he is satisfied with food and other hospitality.

Then, after the meal, he should spend the remainder of the day in the company of learned men who know the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, beloved friends who are skilled in the elaborate details of poetry and storytelling, and kinsmen who are adept at agreeable conversation. (1.113)
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), having offered oblations into those fires and attended to them,
and having eaten with his dependents until he is moderately satisfied, he should then go to sleep. Thus,
having performed the evening twilight devotion according to the previously stated rule, [he should proceed].
Having offered oblations into the Āhavanīya and other fires, or into a single fire,
and having attended upon and worshipped them,
he should eat without over-satiating himself, surrounded by his aforementioned dependents, such as those living in his own household.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), having completed the consideration of income, expenditure, and other household matters, he should thereafter retire and sleep. 1.114.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate what is beneficial for oneself;
one should not neglect virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times, according to one's ability.
Thus, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*—that is, having awakened in the final half-watch of the night—
One should reflect upon one's own welfare— both what has been accomplished and what is yet to be done— as well as upon doubts regarding the meaning of the Vedas;
for at that time, due to the mind’s lack of agitation, it is fit for the discernment of reality.
Therefore, one should not abandon dharma, artha, and kāma at the appropriate times according to one's capacity; rather,
one should pursue them as far as possible, because they constitute the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
As Gautama said: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly;

among dharma, artha, and kāma, one should give precedence to dharma" (GDh 9.46–47). Although the pursuit of these [three goals] is mentioned here in general terms, nevertheless, desire (*kāma*) and wealth (*artha*) should be practiced only in a manner that does not conflict with dharma.
Since these two are rooted in dharma, they must be performed in this manner every day. // 1.115 //
They are to be honored according to their sequence by virtue of learning, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, when possessed of an abundance of these, deserves honor in old age.
"Learning" is as previously described.
Ritual action consists of that prescribed by the Vedas (śrauta) and that prescribed by the Smṛtis (smārta);
age is that which exceeds seventy years of one's own life;
and kinship is the prosperity of one's own relatives.
Wealth consists of villages, jewels, and so forth;
those endowed with these are to be honored and worshipped in due order.
One who is endowed with these—knowledge, action, kinship, and wealth—whether they be abundant, increased, or all of them combined or individually, [is worthy of respect].
Even a Śūdra deserves honor when he has reached old age beyond eighty, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "A Śūdra who is eighty years of age is excellent" (GDh 6.10). // 1.116 //

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath (*snātaka*), women, the sick, ascetics, and those who possess a wheel; among these, O King, the *snātaka* is to be honored even by the monarch.
(YDh 1.117) "Elderly" (*vṛddha*) is well known as one whose hair has turned grey.
"Burdened" means oppressed by a heavy burden;
"king" means a sovereign ruler, not merely a member of the kṣatriya caste; "bathed" refers to one who has completed the threefold graduation (snātaka) in both sacred learning and religious vows.
A woman is well known; a sick person is one afflicted by disease; a suitor is one intent on marriage.

The word *cakrī* means a cartwright. By the use of the particle *ca*, those who are intoxicated, insane, and so forth are included, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "From children, the elderly, the intoxicated, the insane, those whose bodies are afflicted, those burdened by loads, women, those who have completed their Vedic studies (*snātaka*), and renunciants."
The way must be yielded to these;
when they approach from the opposite direction, one should step aside from the path oneself.
When there is a meeting on the road between the king and those such as the elderly, the king is to be honored, and therefore the way must be yielded to him. [This applies] to the lord of the earth.
Even a *snātaka* is worthy of honor.
The mention of the *snātaka* is intended to include any *snātaka* whatsoever, and not specifically a Brāhmaṇa,
because the latter is always [automatically] venerable by virtue of his status.
As Śaṅkha says:
"Now, some say that the path should first be given to a Brāhmaṇa, [and] to the king;
but that is undesirable, for a Brāhmaṇa is both a guru and the elder."
"He surpasses the king; [therefore] the way belongs to him.
When elders and others meet one another on a path, the distinction should be understood as being based on those even more advanced in age, or by means of learning and other such qualities. (1.117)
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are for the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
for the Brāhmaṇa, however, there is additionally the receiving of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
(YDh 1.118) For the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya—and by the word "and" (ca), for the Brāhmaṇa and the twice-born anulomas—there are sacrificing, studying, and giving.
These are the common occupations.
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are additional ones: receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and teaching.
The phrase "likewise" includes the means of livelihood mentioned in other Smṛtis.
As Gautama said: "Agriculture and trade, when performed by oneself, as well as usury" (GDh 10.5–6).
However, teaching for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas occurs only when prompted by a Brāhmaṇa, not by their own will.

"In times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may acquire knowledge from a non-Brāhmaṇa; [the latter] shall follow him and serve him, but once it is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes the teacher"— so states the traditional teaching of Gautama (GDh 7.1–3).
These are the six duties of a Brāhmaṇa when there is no distress. Among them, three—sacrifice and the rest—are for the sake of dharma;
three—receiving gifts and the rest—are for the sake of livelihood.
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood: officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts. (MDh 10.76)
Therefore, sacrifices and the like must necessarily be performed, but not the acceptance of gifts and the like.
For the twice-born, there are study, sacrifice, and giving;
for the Brāhmaṇa, in addition, there are teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and the acceptance of gifts.
This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "In the case of the former [offenses], there is a restrictive rule" (GDh 10.1–2). 1.118.
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
for a Vaiśya, it is traditionally held to be moneylending, agriculture, trade, and animal husbandry.
(YDh 1.119) For a Kṣatriya, the protection of the subjects is the primary duty, both for the sake of dharma and for the sake of livelihood.
For a Vaiśya, the occupations for the sake of livelihood are moneylending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
Moneylending is the lending of goods for the purpose of interest.
Trade consists of buying and selling for the sake of profit; the rest is well known:
the bearing of weapons and missiles is for the Kṣatriya, while trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are for the Vaiśya.
"For the sake of livelihood, however, the Dharma consists of giving, study, and sacrifice," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 10.79). 1.119.

The service of the twice-born is the duty of a Śūdra; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. For a Śūdra, the service of the twice-born is the primary duty, both for the sake of dharma and for the sake of livelihood.
In that regard, service to Brahmins is the supreme duty; indeed, the specific occupation of a Śūdra is proclaimed to be the service of Brahmins alone. (MDh 10.123)

Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*. Furthermore, when one is unable to subsist through service to the twice-born (*dvija*), then one may live by the occupation of a merchant (*vaṇig-vṛtti*) through various means.
Or by performing crafts that are beneficial for the twice-born;
the meaning is: performing such works by which he does not become unfit for the service of the twice-born.

And those duties spoken of by the gods for the Śūdra are: service to the twice-born, avoidance of sin, the nourishment of one's wife and others, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying loads, trade in merchandise, painting, and playing the dance, song, flute, lute, *muraja*, and *mṛdaṅga* drums;
furthermore, delighting in his wife, being pure, supporting his dependents, and being devoted to the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
One should not omit the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation (namaskāra).
He whose pleasure and approach are directed toward his own wife alone, and not toward common women or the wives of others, is so described.
Being pure, he is endowed with both external and internal purity like a twice-born.
He is the supporter of servants and others;
he is devoted to the performance of *śrāddha* rites,
which are the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) offerings.
Devoted to those ritual acts and the vows of a *snātaka* that are not contradictory [to his status],
he should not neglect, but should perform day after day, the five great sacrifices previously mentioned, using the mantra "Namaḥ" (Salutation).
And some [recite] the Namaskāra mantra:
"To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis."
Homage to Svāhā and to Svadhā; always, indeed, homage, homage!
Thus they describe it;
others say "namaḥ.
Regarding this, the teachers maintain that the Vaiśvadeva offering should be performed in the common (laukika) fire, not in the nuptial fire. 1.121.
Now he states the common duties:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, charity, self-control, compassion, and patience are the means for the practice of dharma for all. (YDh 1.122)

Himsā is the infliction of pain upon living beings; its non-performance is ahiṃsā. Satya is truthful speech that does not cause pain to living beings. Asteya is the non-appropriation of what has not been given.
Purity is both external and internal. Restraint of the senses consists in the sense organs—both those of cognition and those of action—functioning only within their prescribed domains.
Charity consists in the removal of the suffering of living beings by giving food, water, and so forth, according to one's ability.
Self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Compassion (*dayā*) is the protection of those in distress. Forbearance (*kṣānti*) is the absence of mental fluctuation even when harm is inflicted.
Thus, all these are the means for accomplishing dharma for all persons, from the Brāhmaṇa down to the Caṇḍāla. (1.122)
One should likewise adopt a conduct that is appropriate to one's age, intellect, wealth, speech, dress, learning, birth, and actions— conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit.
(YDh 1.123) "Age" refers to childhood, youth, and so forth.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is innate [capacity] regarding worldly and Vedic activities;
wealth (*artha*) refers to property such as houses and fields;
and speech (*vāk*) is discourse.
Dress (*veṣa*) is the arrangement of garments, garlands, and so forth; learning (*śruta*) is the hearing of treatises on the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*);
and lineage (*abhijana*) is one's family.
"Occupation for the sake of livelihood" refers to receiving gifts and so forth.
One should practice—that is, adopt—a livelihood appropriate and suitable to these [stages of life] beginning with age;
