for example, as an elder should adopt what is appropriate for his own stage, not what is appropriate for youth.
The same should be applied to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties as well.
It is straight (*ajihmā*), not crooked (*avakrā*); it is not deceitful (*aśaṭhā*) and not envious (*amatsarā*). (1.123)
Having thus enumerated the Smṛti rites in sequence, he now enumerates the Śruti rites:
"A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of food may drink the Soma;
he whose food supply lasts for a year should perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice. (YDh 1.124)

Only he who possesses food sufficient for three years, or more than that, which is adequate for the livelihood of the three aims of life, should perform the drinking of Soma; one with less wealth than that should not.
Therefore, the twice-born who drinks Soma when his resources are very meager [commits a fault].
"Even one who has previously drunk Soma does not obtain its fruit [if he fails in this]," because such a fault is heard in the scriptures;
and this refers to optional rites (*kāmya*).
And because that which is eternal must necessarily be performed, it is not a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

For one who possesses enough food for a year's livelihood, those [rites] prior to the *Soma* sacrifice— meaning those occurring before the *Soma*, prior to the state of being *Soma*, or preceding the *Soma*—
are the "pre-*Soma*" rites (*prāksaumikyaḥ*).

Which are they? These rites—the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Āgrayaṇa, the animal sacrifice, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, as well as their modifications—are the actions to be performed by the Kriyas. 1.124.
Having thus described the optional rites prescribed by the Śruti, he now states the obligatory ones:
"The Soma sacrifice is to be performed every year, as well as the Animal sacrifice at each solstice; likewise, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed. (YDh 1.125)
A Soma sacrifice should be performed every year;
an animal sacrifice should be performed at each solstice, known as the southern and northern courses, specifically the Nirūḍhapaśuyāga.
Likewise, according to the statement of Baudhāyana— "Or [one may sacrifice] every year with an animal; one should sacrifice every year, or every six months"—
some maintain that the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi must be performed whenever grain ripens.
And the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are to be performed every year. // 1.125 //
In the absence of these, the twice-born should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a rite with deficient procedures when the necessary materials are available, for such a rite yields no fruit.

(YDh 1.126) "In the absence of these"—meaning if, by some circumstance, the previously mentioned obligatory rites beginning with the Soma sacrifice cannot be performed at their proper time—he [should perform] the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.

One should perform the *iṣṭi*. Furthermore, this deficient rite (*hīnakalpa*) that has been described must not be performed when the necessary materials are available. Moreover, one should not perform—that is, it must not be performed—a desired (*kāmya*) rite that yields fruit if it is deficient in its ritual procedure. Thus reads the NSP edition. (1.126)
One becomes a Caṇḍāla by performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra;
if one does not give what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one may become a vulture or even a crow.
By begging for the wealth of a Śūdra for the purpose of a sacrifice, one is born as a Caṇḍāla in another birth.

Furthermore, he who does not give everything requested for the sake of a sacrifice, nor renounces it, shall become either a vulture or a crow for a hundred years; as Manu said (11.25): [text follows].
"He who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not give it all away—
that Brahmin goes to the state of a *bhāsa* bird or a crow for a hundred years" (MDh 11.25).
*Bhāsa* is a type of bird.
The crow is well known. // 1.127 //
Or one who possesses grain in a granary or a jar, or one who has enough for three days, or even one who does not have enough for tomorrow;
"kuśūla" means a storehouse,
and "kumbhī" means a small jar.
A *kuśūla* and a *kumbhī* are "the granary and the jar"; he whose grain is measured by those two is thus called a *kuśūladhānya*.
Or one who has grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*).
In that regard, one who possesses grain sufficient for the nourishment of his own family for only twelve days is one who has grain in a granary (*kuśūladhānya*).
One who has grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*) is one who possesses grain sufficient for the nourishment of his own family for only six days.
One who has grain sufficient for three days is a *tryāhika*. One who has [grain] for tomorrow is...
One who possesses grain for tomorrow is called *śvastana*; one for whom there is no provision for tomorrow is *aśvastana*.
He states the means for accumulating grain in a granary and so forth:
"Or he may live by gleaning ears of corn (śila) and picking up individual grains (uñcha); each subsequent mode among these is superior.
Gleaning (śila) is the gathering of stalks of rice and other crops that have fallen and been abandoned.

The gathering of each individual grain that has been discarded is *uñcha*; *śila* and *uñcha* together constitute *śiloñcha*. By means of that *śila* or *uñcha*, there are four kinds [of livelihood], beginning with the one who possesses grain in a granary (*kuśūladhānya*).
A householder may live [by these means].
Among these four types of Brahmin householders— beginning with those who possess a granary of grain (*kuśūladhānya*) and so forth— the one mentioned later and later is superior and more praiseworthy.
And although the term "twice-born" (dvija) is the subject under discussion here,
it nevertheless ought to refer specifically to the Brāhmaṇa, because of his connection with learning, tranquility,
and so forth; and likewise by Manu:
"Having adopted that mode of livelihood which is entirely free from injury to living beings, or at least involving minimal injury, a Brahmin should live in times of non-distress"—
thus [the text] introduces the Brahmin specifically.
Because it has been stated [in the *Manusmṛti*]: "He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or even grain sufficient for a single jar" (MDh 4.7), and so forth;
and this is said with reference to the *yāyāvara* who is not excessively restrained, not with the intention of referring to a *vipra* in general.
If that were the case,
there would be a contradiction with the following [verse]: "That twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may indeed drink the Soma" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.124).
And thus, the twofold nature of householders has been stated in various places. As Devala says: "The householder is of two kinds: the *yāyāvara* and the *śālīna*.
Of these two, the *yāyāvara* is superior because he avoids officiating at sacrifices, teaching, accepting gifts, and the accumulation of inherited wealth."
"One who is established in the six duties, possessed of servants, quadrupeds, a house, a village, wealth, and grain, and who conforms to worldly ways, is called a *śālīna*.
Furthermore, the *śālīna* is of four kinds: one lives by means of the six [occupations], namely, officiating at sacrifices, teaching, receiving gifts, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
One [type of Brahmin] is supported by the three [means] beginning with officiating at sacrifices;
another by officiating at sacrifices and teaching; but the fourth is supported by teaching alone.
Thus Manu says:
"Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the Brahmasattra. (MDh 4.9)
And here, by the statement beginning with "acceptance of gifts is additional for a Brahmin," the modes of livelihood for the *śālīna* are shown;
likewise, for the *yāyāvara*, it is by means of "gleaning and picking" (*śiloñcha*). (1.128)
Thus ends the section on the duties of the householder;
now begins the section on the duties of the *snātaka*.
Having thus described the rites pertaining to the Śruti and the Smṛti, [the author proceeds].

Now, beginning with the bath, he states the observances (*vrata*) of a *snātaka*— which consist of mental resolves (*saṃkalpa*) regarding injunctions and prohibitions— that must necessarily be performed by a householder who is a Brāhmaṇa:
"He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from whatever source [it may come]."
And he should never be satisfied by resorting to prohibited means.
(YDh 1.129) The means for a Brāhmaṇa to acquire wealth, such as receiving gifts and so forth, have been shown; therein, a specific rule is now stated:
One should not pursue, nor seek after, a matter that obstructs one's private Vedic study, even if it is not formally forbidden;
nor from here and there— that is, not from any source whatsoever whose conduct is unknown.
"Through the occurrence of the prohibited and the occasioning of the forbidden": "the prohibited" refers to such acts as officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate;
"the occasioning" refers to dancing, singing, and so forth. "The prohibited and the occasioning" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*); [it means] by means of that.
"It should not seek an object" is how it is connected;
the repetition of the negative particle (nañ) serves for the purpose of exclusion (paryudāsa) with each [term].

In this entire section concerning the *snātaka*, the word "nañ" (the negative particle) is used in each instance solely for the purpose of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Furthermore, even when wealth is not obtained, he should be content and fully satisfied; and by the use of the word "ca" (and), he should also be self-controlled.
"Seeking happiness, one who is self-restrained should rely upon supreme contentment," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 4.12). // 1.129 //
From whom, then, should he seek wealth? To this he says:
"One who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from kings, pupils, and patrons;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, sophists, heretics, and those who act like herons. (YDh 1.130)

A Snātaka, sinking and oppressed by hunger, may take wealth from a king who has learned of his situation, from a pupil possessing the characteristics to be described, and from a sacrificer worthy of being officiated for.

By the phrase "suffering from hunger," it is understood that one who possesses sufficient wealth to maintain his family— having obtained it through partition and other means— should not seek wealth from any source whatsoever.
Furthermore, he should avoid hypocrites, sophists, and the like in all undertakings, whether worldly, Vedic, or scriptural.
By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), those who persist in improper actions, those who follow the "vow of the cat," and the deceitful are included,
as Manu has said: "Heretics, those who persist in improper actions, those who follow the 'vow of the cat,' and the deceitful..."

"One should not honor, even with mere words, those who rely on logic (*haituka*) and those who act like herons (*bakavṛtti*). (MDh 4.30). A hypocrite (*dambhin*) is one who performs ritual acts solely for the purpose of pleasing the world. A logician (*haituka*) is one who raises doubts everywhere by means of reasoning.
Those who have embraced a stage of life (āśrama) that contradicts the three Vedas are heretics (pākhaṇḍins). "Bakavṛtti" refers to one whose conduct is like that of a crane (baka);
as Manu says:
"One who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own self-interest, dishonest, and falsely humble, is declared to be one who acts like a heron. (MDh 4.196).
Those who practice what is forbidden are those established in improper occupations.
A *biḍāla* is a cat; one whose vow (*vrata*) or nature (*svabhāva*) is that of a cat is a *baiḍālavratika*.
Manu states its defining characteristic:
"One who makes a banner of dharma, ever covetous, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world..."
"One who is violent and intent on deceiving everyone is to be known as a 'cat-vowed' person" (MDh 4.195).
A "shameless" person is crooked in all matters.
Since association with such individuals is prohibited, it follows that one should not become like this oneself.
It is understood. // 1.130 //
Furthermore:

Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails clipped short, and being pure, he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing. (YDh 1.131)
One who wears two garments made of white, washed cloth is called *śuklāmbaradhara*.
One whose hair, beard,
and nails (*keśa-śmaśru-nakha*) have been cut short or clipped is described as such.
He should be pure both internally and externally, and fragrant through bathing, anointing, incense, garlands, and so forth;
as Gautama has said:
"A Snātaka is always pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing" (GDh 9.2). Since fragrance is thus enjoined, the use of scentless garlands is thereby prohibited. And so says Gobhila:
"He should not wear a garland that lacks fragrance, except for a garland of gold or jewels.
Thus should a *snātaka* always be;
and this applies provided it is possible [to obtain such materials].
For there is a traditional teaching (smṛti): "One should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes when wealth is available" (MDh 4.34).
Furthermore, one should not eat while looking at one's wife when she is standing before him, out of fear that it will result in the birth of weak offspring.
And so says the Śruti:
"One should not eat at the end of [the meal with] his wife; otherwise, the offspring will be lacking in vigor. Therefore, eating together with her is rejected from afar.
And he should not eat wearing only one garment; this is connected with the statement that he should not eat while standing or rising. 1.131.
Furthermore: One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
neither what is harmful nor what is untrue; one should not be a thief, nor a usurer. (YDh 1.132)
At no time whatsoever should one enter into or perform an action that brings about doubt or the risk of loss of life— such as, for example,
entering a region infested by tigers, thieves, and the like. Nor should one, without cause or reason, [address] any man or woman...
One should not speak words that are unpleasant or cause agitation;

nor should one speak what is harmful or untrue, even if it is pleasant. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is connected that one should not, without cause, speak what is vulgar, uncivilized, or loathsome.
And this [laughter] is to be performed except in cases such as jesting; for there is a traditional legal text (smṛti) stating: "One may even laugh with one's teacher, provided it is not crooked."
Nor shall he be a thief— that is, one who takes what belongs to another without it being given—
nor shall he be a usurer,
meaning one who lives by prohibited interest.
Usury. 1.132.
Furthermore:
"Wearing a girdle of muñja grass, the sacred thread, a bamboo staff, and carrying a water-pot, one should circumambulate clockwise the gods, clay, cows, Brahmins, and trees. (YDh 1.133)

One who possesses gold in the form of the *dākṣāyaṇa* ornament is called *dākṣāyaṇī*; one who possesses the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), also known as the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), is called *brahmasūtrī*.
"Carrying a bamboo staff," "carrying a water-pot"—
the phrase "he should be" is to be connected with each instance throughout.
And here, the mention again of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), although already stated in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), is for the purpose of obtaining a second one.
As Vasiṣṭha says:
"For those who have completed their studies (*snātaka*s), there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper garment."
"Two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water. (VaDh 12.14).
And here, although there is the general designation "dākṣāyaṇī," one should indeed wear earrings; [as it is said:
"One should carry the Vaiṣṇava staff and a water-pot with water."
For it is stated in the traditional law of Manu: "The sacred thread, the Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings" (MDh 4.36).
Likewise, "the deity" refers to the image of a divinity.
One should circumambulate clockwise earth taken from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, and trees such as the Aśvattha and others.
The meaning is that one should go forth [into homelessness] having kept these to one's right;
likewise for crossroads and so forth,
as well as clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, and a crossroads.
"One should perform circumambulations [of sacred sites] and well-known trees," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 4.39). 1.133.
But one should not urinate on a river, in a shadow, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one urinate facing fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or twice-born men.
(YDh 1.134) One should not urinate on rivers and the like, nor should one discharge urine or feces there.
The same applies to cremation grounds and other such places.
As Śaṅkha says:
"One should not urinate on cow-dung, ploughed land, sown fields, grassy plots, funeral pyres, cremation grounds, anthills, paths, threshing floors, cow-pens, holes, mountains, or river banks."
"Because it is the support of living beings":
likewise, one should not urinate facing fire and so forth,
nor while looking at them, as it has been said:

Gautama says: "One should not discharge urine, feces, or impurities while looking at wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows, nor should one extend one's feet toward them" (GDh 9.13–14).
Apart from these locations, one should void urine and feces after covering the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice.
Thus it is said; as Vasiṣṭha stated:
"Having covered his head and having spread over the ground grasses unfit for sacrifice, he should void urine and feces" (VaDh 12.13). 1.134.

One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor at urine or feces, nor at the impure moon or stars. Although it is stated here in general terms that "one should not look at the sun," this specifically refers to [the sun] when it is rising, setting, eclipsed by Rāhu, reflected in water, or situated at midday.
Thus, looking at the sun is prohibited, but not at all times;
as it has been stated by Manu:
"One should never look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun."
"Neither when it is obscured, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
(MDh 4.37) One should not look at a naked woman except for the purpose of sexual intercourse;
"One should not look at a naked woman except during coitus" (ĀśGṛ 3.9.9).
Thus says Āśvalāyana:

One should not look at a woman who has engaged in sexual intercourse, even if she has already finished her enjoyment; nor should one look at her while she is still naked at the conclusion of that enjoyment.
By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that she is performing such acts as eating; and thus Manu says:
"One should not eat together with one's wife, nor should one look at her while she is eating."
Nor [should one study] when she is sneezing or yawning, nor while she is seated at her ease.

"A twice-born man who desires his own welfare should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one giving birth. (MDh 4.43–44).
And he should not look at urine or feces.
Likewise, being impure, one would not see Rāhu or the stars;
and by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that one would not see one's own reflection in water.
"One should not look at one's own reflection in water," according to the traditional rule (dhāraṇā) stated in [Manu Smṛti] 4.38. 1.135.
One should recite the entire mantra: "This is my thunderbolt; may it strike away my evil. When it rains, one should go about uncovered, and one should not sleep with the head facing west.
When it rains, [one should recite]: "This is my thunderbolt; may it strike away my evil" (PārG 2.7.7).
Thus he should recite the mantra:
"While it rains, one should not go out uncovered or unsheltered, nor should one run; while it rains, one should not rush about" (MDh 4.38).
Because of this prohibition,
one should not sleep with one's head toward the west; and because of the word "and" (ca), one should not sleep naked, nor alone.
For it is stated in the legal tradition of Manu: "One should not lie down naked in an empty house," and "One should not sleep alone in an empty house" (MDh 4.57). // 1.136 //
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
nor should one warm one's feet over a fire, nor step over it.
(YDh 1.137) "Spitting" means ejecting [saliva] from the mouth.
Blood is *asṛj*,
feces is *śakṛt*, and the remainder is well known.
One should not throw these into water, nor likewise husks and so forth;
as Śaṅkha has said:
"One should not throw husks, hair, feces, ashes, bones, phlegm, nails, or body hair into water, nor should one strike the water with the foot or the hand;
and one should not warm one's feet over a fire."
Nor should one leap over fire; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that one should not cast spittle or other such things into the fire.
One should not blow upon a fire with the mouth,
and likewise Manu says:
"One should not blow on a fire with the mouth, nor should one look at a naked woman."
One should not throw impure substances into the fire, nor should one warm one's feet over it.
"One should not place it underneath, nor should one step over it; one should not treat it as if it were beneath one's feet, nor should one commit the killing of living beings. (MDh 4.53–54) 1.137.
One should not drink water with cupped hands; one should not wake a sleeping person;

one should not play with dice or with those who destroy dharma; nor should one lie down to sleep with those who are diseased. (YDh 1.138) One should not drink water with cupped hands—that is, with the two hands joined together.
The mention of "water" is an illustration for any drinkable substance.
One should not awaken—that is, one should not rouse from sleep—a person who is superior to oneself in learning and other qualities;
one should not awaken a superior person (MDh 4.57).
Thus, because of this specific traditional injunction,
one should not play with dice and the like;
nor should one play with those things destructive to dharma, such as the immolation of animals and so forth.
One should not sit down or lie down in one place together with those who are diseased or overcome by fever and other ailments. (1.138)
One should avoid prohibited actions, such as [inhaling] the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [at improper times],
and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, charcoal, or a skull.
One should avoid any action that is contrary to the customs of the country, the village, or the family.
It is connected [to the previous rule] that one should avoid the smoke of a corpse and crossing a river with one's arms;
one should also avoid staying among hair and such things.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), [the rule applies] also to bones, cotton, and impure substances. (1.139)
One should not point out a cow suckling [her calf], nor should one ever enter a place by a forbidden path;
one should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures. (YDh 1.140) One should not inform another that a cow is drinking the milk of another, nor should one turn her away.
One should not enter any city, village, or temple by way other than the gate or by a wrong path; nor [should one associate] with a miserly person who transgresses the scriptures.
One may accept [gifts] from the presence of the king. // 1.140 //
In the matter of receiving gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the dyer, the prostitute,

and the king are more wicked than each preceding one, respectively, by tenfold. When a gift is to be accepted, these five— beginning with the butcher— are each ten times more blameworthy than the one mentioned before.
A *sūnī* is one who possesses a slaughterhouse (*sūnā*), meaning one intent on the injury of living beings.
A *cakrī* is an oil-presser. A *dhvajī* is a seller of liquor.
A prostitute is a woman for sale; the ruler of men has been mentioned immediately above. // 1.141 //
Now he states the rules for Vedic study:

"The commencement of the annual course of study (upākarma) shall take place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa, or under the asterism Hasta when the medicinal herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. (YDh 1.142)

The term *adhyāya* refers to those things that are studied, namely the Vedas; their *upākarma* is the commencement [of study] when the appearance of herbs occurs, on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
or on a day joined with the lunar mansion Śravaṇa.
One should perform [the ceremony] on the fifth day of the month of Hasta, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.

However, when the medicinal herbs do not appear in the month of Śrāvaṇa, then one should perform it in the month of Bhādrapada under the asterism of Śravaṇā. Thereafter, for four and a half months, one should study the Vedas.
And so Manu says:
"Having performed the *upākarma* according to the rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months" (MDh 4.95).
The time for the ritual suspension [of Vedic study] is as follows:

under the asterism Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa, or on the Aṣṭakā day, one should perform the formal suspension of the Vedas outside [the village] near water, according to the prescribed rule. (YDh 1.143)

On the day of the Rohiṇī asterism in the month of Pauṣa, or on the Aṣṭakā day, one should perform the Utsarga (the ritual suspension) of the Vedas outside the village near water, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.

However, when the Upākarma is performed in the month of Bhādrapada, then one should perform the Utsarga on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, as stated by Manu: "Having performed the Upākarma rite according to the rule, the Veda-students should study the Vedas for four months and a half."

"In the month of Pauṣa, a twice-born man should perform the formal suspension (*utsarjana*) of the Vedas outside [the village], or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon. (MDh 4.96).

Following that, having observed a period of rest for either two days with the intervening night (*pakṣiṇī*) or a full day and night, he should study the Vedas during the bright fortnights and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) during the dark fortnights.
One should study [the Veda]. As Manu has said:

"Having thus performed the ritual dismissal (utsarga) of the Vedas outside [the village] according to the scripture, one should cease [studying] for a night with its two flanking days (pakṣiṇī rātri), or even for a single day and night."

"From this point forward, however, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights, and one should recite all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅgas*) during the dark fortnights. (MDh 4.97–98) 1.143.

He states the occasions when study is prohibited: "There is a three-day suspension of study upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative; likewise at the commencement (upākarma) and conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedic term, and when a master of one's own Vedic branch has died. (YDh 1.144)
For a twice-born man studying according to the prescribed rule, when his pupils, officiating priests, teachers, or kinsmen have died, there is a three-day suspension of study;
he should avoid recitation for three days and nights.
Likewise, when the rites of *upākarma* and *utsarga* have been performed, there is a three-day suspension.
There is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).

However, regarding the *utsarga* (the ritual of casting away the Veda), there is an option between this [one-day suspension] and the *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) mentioned by Manu, along with the day and night itself (MDh 4.97).
Furthermore, when a member of one's own *śākhā* who is learned in the Veda (*śrotriya*) or a student of one's own *śākhā* has died, there is a three-day suspension of study. 1.144.
In the event of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor;
and after completing the Veda, as well as having studied the Āraṇyaka for a full day and night; [one should remain silent].
(YDh 1.145) Regarding the sound of clouds at twilight:
In the case of a thunderclap, a portentous sound in the sky, an earthquake,
or the falling of a meteor, [the recitation] of the mantra [is suspended].
Furthermore, there is no study for a Brāhmaṇa for a day and night—both day and night—upon the completion [of a text] or during the study of the Āraṇyaka. (1.145)

On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during an eclipse of Rāhu, at the junctions of the seasons, after eating, or after accepting food offered at a Śrāddha ceremony; on the fifteenth day—
meaning the new moon (Amāvāsyā) or the full moon (Paurṇamāsī)— on the fourteenth day, the eighth day, and during an eclipse of Rāhu, that is, an eclipse of the moon or the sun.

And there is no study day or night [on such occasions]. As for the statement, "One should not recite the Veda for three days during the birth-impurity of a king or during Rāhu’s birth-impurity" (MDh 4.110), that refers to the case when [the moon] sets while being eclipsed. (Pāṇḍeya and Setlur read: [End of quotation]
When the forest regions are seized [by enemies],

and during the first days of the lunar fortnights occurring at the junctions of the seasons (ṛtusaṃdhi), there is a suspension of Vedic study for a day and a night upon eating at a Śrāddha feast or accepting a gift from it;
and this applies to cases other than the Ekoddiṣṭa rite.
In that case, however, having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three nights. (MDh 4.110)
Thus it is from the Smṛti. 1.146.
If an interval is created by cattle, frogs, mongooses, dogs, snakes, cats, or mice, there is an interruption for a day and night; likewise when the banner of Indra is lowered or raised.

(YDh 1.147) This means that if cattle and other such animals pass between [the teacher and the students] while they are studying, or on the day the banner of Indra is taken down, or on the day it is raised.

There is no study for a day and a night (*ahorātra*). Although "day and night" was already established by the context, the explicit mention of *ahorātra* again is for the purpose of indicating that [the suspension of study] lasts until the same time the next day in the event of thunder at twilight, a atmospheric crash (*nirghāta*), an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor (*ulkā*).
Based on the statement of Gautama, "Immediate thunderclaps, earthquakes, the appearance of Rāhu, and meteors" (GDh 16.22),
the period beginning from the time of the omen until the same time on the following day is called *akāla* (inappropriate time). During that interval, [the recitation of the Veda is suspended].
Existence itself is a time for which there is no suspension of study;
this applies when there is thunder during the morning twilight,
whereas when there is thunder during the evening twilight, the suspension lasts for the night.

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Hārīta, "if there is thunder at the evening twilight, [the impurity lasts for] a night; if there is thunder at the morning twilight, it lasts for a day and a night.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Gautama—"If a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat passes between [the teacher and pupil], there shall be a three-day fast and staying away from home" (GDh 1.59)—that refers specifically to the first lesson of study. 1.147.
In the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, or arrows;
in the vicinity of impure substances, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste (*antyaja*), a cremation ground, or one who has fallen [from his caste]—[in these cases, one should not study].
Here, "dog" (*śvan*) means a canine (*kukkura*).
The jackal is the *sṛgāla*;
the donkey is the *rāsabha*;
the owl is the *ghūka*.
Sāman is the Sāmans;
Bāṇa is the flute;
Ārtha is one who is suffering.
There is a suspension of study for as long as the sound of these, such as dogs and the like, lasts; likewise when there is the sound of lutes and so forth;
and during the sounds of flutes, lutes, kettledrums, clay drums, carts, and cries of distress. (GDh 16.7)
According to this statement of Gautama, "gantrī" refers to a cart; when there is the proximity of impure substances and the like, there is a temporary suspension of Vedic study. (1.148)
In an impure place, when one is oneself impure, during a flash of lightning or a clap of thunder,
after eating while the hands are still wet, within water, at midnight, or during an excessive windstorm;
[in these cases] one should not study in an impure place or when one is oneself impure.
Likewise, during a flash of lightning, when lightning flashes repeatedly,
and during a peal of thunder, when the roar of clouds continues for two *praharas*, there is a temporary suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).
Also, after eating while one's hands are still wet.
One should not study in the midst of water;
nor during the midnight hour known as *mahāniśā*—that is, during the two middle watches of the night; nor when there is an excessive wind, even during the day, for that same duration. // 1.149 //
When there is a dust-storm, a conflagration of the quarters, fear of a carriage or mist,
when running, when there is a foul odor, when a learned man has arrived at the house, and during an ominous rain of dust. (YDh 1.150) [This refers to] an ominous rain of dust.
When at the two twilights the quarters of the sky appear as if ablaze during a conflagration, or when there is mist and fog;

In times of fear caused by thieves, kings, and the like, there is a suspension of study for that duration. There is a suspension of study for one who is running or moving with haste. There is a suspension of study when there is a foul odor, such as the smell of impure substances, liquor, and so forth.
Furthermore, when a learned person such as a master of the Vedas arrives at one's house, there is a suspension of study until he has given his permission to depart. (1.150)

When riding on a donkey, a camel, a carriage, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; or when climbing a tree or ascending a mountain—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study (*anadhyāya*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to chariots and the like.
A barren wasteland, saline soil, or a desert is what is meant by "irīṇa," "ūpara," or "marubhūmi.
When these are ascended by donkeys and the like, there is a temporary suspension of study for that duration.
Likewise, starting from this point with the words "dogs, jackals, donkeys," these thirty-seven types of temporary suspensions of study are to be understood.
Those who know the rules regarding the suspension of Vedic study (anadhyāya) understand these [occasions] to be simultaneous with the appearance of the signs;
by the word "understand," he includes other [cases] mentioned in other Smṛtis,
as Manu has said:
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food provided by those in a state of birth-impurity. (MDh 4.12) 1.151.
And so forth.

Having thus stated the occasions when study is prohibited, he now declares the established observances of a Snātaka: "One should not step upon the shadow of the gods, officiating priests, Snātakas, teachers, or kings; nor upon another's wife, nor upon blood, excrement, urine, spittle, ointments, and the like. (YDh 1.152)

One should not intentionally step upon, stand upon, or cross over the shadow of gods, of images of gods, of officiating priests, of those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), of teachers, of kings, or of another man’s wife. As Manu has said:
"One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a guru, a king, a *snātaka*, a teacher, a brown (*babhru*) animal, or one who has been consecrated for sacrifice" (MDh 4.130).
"Brown" refers to one of the color of a mongoose, or any other such animal like a cow or a dark-colored beast.
Because of the use of the neuter gender in the word *babhruṇi*,
one should not stand upon red substances and so forth;
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), bathing water and similar items are included.
"One should not intentionally step upon a body-scrub, water used for bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit. (MDh 4.132) 1.152.

Brahmins and those whose nature is that of Kṣatriyas should never be treated with contempt. Until death one should desire prosperity; one should not touch anyone at their vital points. (YDh 1.153) A *vipra* is a Brāhmaṇa who is deeply learned in the scriptures.
A snake, a serpent, and a Kṣatriya king— these must never be despised.
One should not disparage oneself;
until death, as long as one lives, one should desire prosperity,
and not [despise] anyone at all.
One should touch a person only at their vital points; one should not disclose the hidden faults or misconduct of anyone. // 1.153 //
One should discard remnants of food, excrement, urine, and water used for washing the feet at a distance;
one should always properly practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
(YDh 1.154) One should discard at a distance from the house the remnants of food and the like, as well as excrement, urine, and the water used for washing the feet. [The Śrauta...]
And he should always properly observe the conduct prescribed by the Smṛtis. // 1.154 //
One who is impure shall not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food—especially cooked food—with his feet; nor shall he revile or strike them.

However, he may strike his son and his pupil. One who is impure shall not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food—especially that which is fit to be eaten, particularly cooked food. He shall not revile or strike them; yet he may strike his son and his pupil.
However, even if one is not rendered impure by the foot, when one touches it through negligence, then after the subsequent sipping of water (ācamana),
one who has touched these [impure things] and is impure must always touch the vital breaths (prāṇas) with water.
And one should touch all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand; this act prescribed by Manu (MDh 4.143) should be performed.
In this manner, one should touch the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the others.
One should not practice reviling or striking anyone at all; and this applies even to one who has done no harm:
"If one causes blood to flow from the body of a Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting..."
"A man, through lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death" (MDh 4.167).
One should strike a son or a pupil solely for the purpose of instruction;
by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), slaves and others are also included.

And the beating must be performed with a rope or similar instrument, excluding the head; for the statement of Gautama says: "The correction of a pupil is without corporal punishment; if that is impossible, it may be done with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane; one who strikes him with anything else is punished by the king" (GDh 2.42–44).
For it is stated in the words of Manu: "But [the blow] shall be on the back of the body, and never on the head" (MDh 8.300). // 1.155 //
One should diligently practice dharma through action, mind, and speech;
however, one should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world.
Through action—that is, with the body—one should perform dharma according to one's ability; one should contemplate that very same dharma with the mind and speak it with speech.

One should not perform acts such as the slaughter of a cow during the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*), even if they are prescribed by the Dharma, provided they are detested by the world and cause public censure;
for such acts do not lead to heaven, unlike the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice which is a means to attain heaven. (1.156)

With mother, father, guests, brothers, paternal and maternal kinsmen, maternal uncles, the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, relatives, officiating priests, family chaplains,
offspring, wives, servants, and uterine siblings; (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.157)
But by avoiding dispute, a householder shall conquer all the worlds;
"mother" means the biological mother,
and "father" means the biological father.
A guest is one who has traveled on a journey;
brothers are those born of different wombs; and female relatives (jāmi) are women whose husbands are living.
Relatives by marriage are those connected through matrimony. A maternal uncle is the brother of one's mother. An elder is one who is seventy years of age or more.
A child is one up to sixteen years of age;
a sick person is one afflicted by disease;
a teacher is an initiator; a physician is a healer.
A learned physician; one who has sought refuge or depends on him for livelihood;
kinsmen belonging to the father’s side and the mother’s side; and [the relatives] of the maternal uncle.
They are mentioned separately for the sake of emphasis. An *ṛtvij* is a sacrificial priest;
a *purohita* is one who performs rites for pacification and so forth.
Offspring refers to sons and the like;
the wife is the partner in the practice of dharma;
and the servant is the laborer.
The separate mention of "those with the same navel" (sanābhayaḥ) and "uterine" (sodarāḥ) brothers is for the purpose of including sisters who are not uterine.
Having abandoned verbal quarrels with these [relatives], beginning with one's mother... all of them.
One attains the worlds of Prajāpati and the others. 1.157–1.158.
One should not bathe in the waters belonging to others without having removed five lumps of earth;

however, one may bathe in rivers, natural reservoirs, lakes, and springs. Regarding "the waters belonging to others," this refers to tanks and similar bodies of water that belong to another and have not been relinquished for the use of all living beings. Without removing five lumps of earth from such places, one must not bathe.
One should not bathe [in these]. By this, bathing even between the extraction of the *piṇḍas* is permitted for one's own [water], for that which has been discarded, or for that which is authorized.
To the question "How then regarding rivers and the like?", he says: "One may bathe in a river.
Rivers are those streams flowing toward the ocean, whether directly or indirectly.
A "devakhāta" (divine excavation) refers to Puṣkara and similar sites created by the gods. A "hrada" (lake) is a large, deep depression filled with water, formed by the impact of flowing water.
[A "tīrtha"] is a place on high ground such as a mountain.
A spring is flowing water.
In these [cases], one should bathe simply by removing five lumps of earth.
And this refers to the context of the daily obligatory bath (*nityasnāna*).
When possible, one should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs. (MDh 4.203)
This is because of the mention of "always" [in the preceding rule].
However, for the purpose of purification, there is no prohibition against extracting five lumps of earth from other waters as far as possible, nor even when drawing water from a well. (1.159)
One should avoid another's bed, seat, garden, house, and vehicle;
one should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress.
(YDh 1.160) "Bed" refers to a mattress or bedding.
A seat refers to a stool and the like; a garden refers to a grove of mango trees and the like;
a house is well known.
"Vehicles" refers to chariots and the like.
One should avoid—that is, not make use of—those things belonging to others that have not been given or authorized;
these are foods that should not be eaten.
He said: "Of one who has abandoned the sacred fires.

One should not eat the food, nor accept as a gift in times of non-distress, the food of one who has abandoned the sacred fires—meaning one who is devoid of the right to maintain the Śrauta and Smārta fires—whether that person be a Śūdra or one born of an inverse (pratiloma) union, even if such a person possesses the requisite eligibility.
Therefore, based on the statement of Gautama: "A Brāhmaṇa should eat from and accept gifts from those who are praiseworthy and of pure birth through their own actions" (GDh 17.1–2). 1.160.
Of misers, bound thieves, eunuchs, actors, flute-players, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a group;
(YDh 1.161) — a miser (*kadarya*) is one who is greedy (*lubdha*).
He who, out of greed, causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, his children, his wife,
and his parents and servants, is known as a miser (kadarya).
Thus it is said: "Bound" means fettered with shackles and the like; "restrained by speech" means silenced.
A "thief" is one who steals the property of others, excluding the gold of Brahmins. A "eunuch" is a neuter person (*napuṃsaka*).
An actor is one who enters the stage, such as a dancer, bard, wrestler, and so forth.
A flute-player is one who lives by cutting bamboo.
An accused person is one who has been formally charged.
One who is engaged in actions leading to defeat;
a usurer, one who lives by forbidden interest;
and a courtesan, a woman for sale.
"One initiated into a *gaṇa*," "one who sacrifices for many"—the phrase "one should not eat the food of these" is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. 1.161.
[One should not eat the food] of physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and enemies;
nor of the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātya, the hypocritical, or those who eat leavings.
(YDh 1.162) A physician is one who subsists by the profession of medicine.
"The afflicted one is one seized by a great disease.
Wind-disorders, urinary stones, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal dropsy, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and dysentery—these eight are proclaimed as the great diseases. Thus it is said.
"Kruddhaḥ" means angry;
"puṃścalī" means an unchaste woman;
"mattaḥ" means one who is arrogant due to knowledge and the like.
A *vidviṣ* is an enemy;
a *krūra* is one whose internal anger is firm;
an *ugra* is one who causes agitation through the activity of speech and body.
An outcaste is one who has killed a Brahmin and the like;
a Vrātya is one whose Sāvitrī initiation has lapsed;
a hypocrite is a deceiver.
One who eats the leavings of another, one who eats what has been discarded by another after being eaten—these, including physicians and others, are those whose food one should not eat. 1.162.
[The food] of a woman without a protector, of a goldsmith, of a woman who has conquered her village [by her charms],
of one who sacrifices for a village, of a seller of weapons, of a blacksmith, of a weaver, and of one who subsists by keeping dogs [is forbidden].
(YDh 1.163) A "woman without a protector" is an independent woman, even if she does not commit adultery.
Others say [the term] means "one who is devoid of sons and grandsons";
a goldsmith (*svarṇakāra*) is one who produces various transformations of gold.
"Conquered by women" means being under the control of women in all respects.
"Village-priest" refers to one who performs rites for the peace of a village and so forth, or who initiates many people.
A seller of weapons is one who subsists by the sale of weapons; a blacksmith is a maker of worldly objects, as are carpenters and the like.
A weaver is one who subsists by the craft of the needle.
A "dog-liver" (śvavṛtti) is one whose livelihood, maintenance, or means of living depends on dogs. One should not eat the food of these people. 1.163.

[One becomes an outcaste] by associating with a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter, a washerman, a vintner, a paramour living in the same house, a slanderer, a liar, a wheelwright, and a bard. (YDh 1.164)
One must not eat the food of these, nor likewise that of a seller of Soma;
a *nṛśaṃsa* is one who is merciless,
and a *rājan* is a lord of the earth.
And by association with that, the food of a domestic priest (*purohita*) is also forbidden.
As Śaṅkha says:
"The food of those who are afraid, censured, weeping, wailing, shouting, hungry, having just finished eating, astonished, insane, despised, and of kings and domestic priests [is not to be eaten]."
"One should avoid" means:
a dyer is one who applies colors such as indigo to garments and the like;
an ungrateful person is one who destroys what has been done for them; a butcher is one who lives by killing.
A *vartaka* is one who subsists by the slaughter of living beings;
a *celadhāva* is a washerman who cleans clothes;
a *surājīva* is one who lives by the sale of liquor.
An *upapati* is a paramour.
One whose house is with a paramour is "one whose house is with a paramour" (*sahopapativeśma*).
A slanderer (*piśuna*) is one who [speaks] of another's faults.
A proclaimer; a liar, a speaker of falsehood;
some say [these are] a wheelwright, an oil-presser, and a cartwright.
Because they are mentioned separately as "the accused," "the outcast," "the wheelwright," and "the oil-presser";
"bandhins" are flatterers;
and the "seller of soma" is one who sells the *soma* plant—of these [it is said].

One must not eat the food [of these]. All these individuals, beginning with the miserly, are indeed twice-born (dvija) who, being defiled by faults such as miserliness, are those whose food is unfit to be eaten; for there is no possibility of their food being consumed otherwise, and because a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility. 1.165–1.166.
In the verse, "One should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress" (YDh 1.160), it was stated that the food of a Śūdra is unfit to be eaten;
regarding that, he states an exception.

Among Śūdras, the food of slaves, cowherds, family friends, and those who till half the field [with the owner] may be eaten, as well as that of barbers and of one who offers himself [as a servant]. (YDh 1.166) Slaves include those born in the house and others.
A *gopāla* is one who lives by tending cattle;

a *kulamitra* is a family friend descended through the lineage of fathers and grandfathers and so forth; an *ardhasīrī* is one who takes a share of the fruit of agriculture, characterized by the plough (*sīra*), which is synonymous with the plow (*hala*).
The barber who performs household chores is also a barber. Furthermore, he who offers himself through the actions of speech, mind, and body, saying "I am yours"—
these are the slaves and so forth.

Among Śūdras, those whose food may be eaten [are as follows]: by the use of the word "and" (ca), the potter is also included, according to the statement: "The family friend of a cowherd, a barber, and a potter, one who shares half the crop, and one who has offered himself—all these have food that may be eaten. (1.166)
Thus ends the section on the duties of a Snātaka;
now begins the section on what may and may not be eaten.
[One should not seek wealth] that is contrary to Vedic study (YDh 1.129).
Beginning from this point,
after having set forth the observances of the bath-graduate (*snātaka*) for the Brāhmaṇa,
he now declares the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*).

One should avoid meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, meat containing hair or insects, food that has turned sour, stale food, the leavings of another, food touched by a dog, food looked upon by an outcaste, food touched by a woman in her courses, food proclaimed [for public sale], and food intended for a group. Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.167.
That which has been smelled by a cow, that which is the leavings of a bird, or that which has been intentionally touched with the foot;
that which is given without respect to one worthy of honor out of contempt;
and "vṛthāmāṃsa" (meat not for a purpose), except in cases such as the loss of life which will be described later.
That which remains after the worship of the gods and others, that which has been prepared solely for one's own sake,
and that which is infested with hair, insects, and the like.

That which is not sour by itself but becomes sour solely through the passage of time with crows present, or through the passage of time due to contact with other substances—excluding curd and the like—is called *śukta*.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "One should not eat food that is spoiled, nor what has been cooked twice, nor what is *śukta*, nor what has turned stale, except for *rāga-khaṇḍava*, *cukra*, curd, molasses, and preparations made from wheat or barley flour."
"Paryuṣita" means that which has been left overnight. "Ucchiṣṭa" means that which has been abandoned after eating. "Śvaspṛṣṭa" means that which has been touched by a dog.
"Viewed by outcasts" means looked upon by those who are outcasts and the like. "Udakyā" refers to a woman in her menses; it has been touched by her.
The mention of the *udakyā* [is made]...

This is for the purpose of including *caṇḍālas* and others by way of illustration, according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Śaṅkha: "One should avoid food touched by those who are impure, those who have fallen [from caste], *caṇḍālas*, *pulkasas*, women in their menses, those with deformed nails, and those suffering from leprosy.
That which is given after it has been publicly proclaimed, "Who will eat?", is called *saṃghuṣṭānna*.
When food belonging to one person is given under the designation of another, that is "food by way of substitution" (*paryāyānna*); for example:
"A Śūdra giving the food of a Brāhmaṇa, or a Brāhmaṇa giving the food of a Śūdra."
"Both of these are persons whose food should not be eaten; having eaten [the food of] either, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Regarding the reading *paryācāntam*, it means that which is "surrounded by ācamana," i.e., that in which the taking of mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*) has occurred all around;
such food must not be eaten.
This is what is meant:
one should not eat from the time of taking the mouthful of water (gaṇḍūṣa) until after the ritual sipping (ācamana).

Regarding the reading "pārśvācāntam," it means that if someone sitting at one's side in the same row has performed the sipping, one should not eat until there is a separation created by ashes, water, or the like.
The word "vinā" (without) and "varjayet" (one should avoid) are to be connected with each [term]. Likewise, "goghrāta" means smelled by a cow;
"śakunocchiṣṭa" means the leavings of birds.
One should avoid food that has been eaten or tasted by a bird such as a crow, or that has been intentionally touched with the foot. 1.167–1.168.
He states an exception regarding stale food:
"Stale food that has been cooked for a long time may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or ghee;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk are edible even if they are not mixed with oil. (YDh 1.169)
Food that is fit to be eaten, even if it has become stale, provided it is mixed with oily substances such as ghee, may be consumed even if it has been kept for a long time.

Likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk— such as *maṇḍaka*, *saktu*, *kilāṭa*, *kūrcikā*, and so forth— even if they are not mixed with oil, may be eaten if they have been kept for a long time.

If they have not undergone any transformation, one should avoid cakes, parched grain, *karambha*, barley-meal, barley-gruel, oil, milk-rice, vegetables, and fermented liquids, according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "One should avoid cakes, parched grain, *karambha*, barley-meal, barley-gruel, oil, milk-rice, vegetables, and fermented liquids" (VaDh 14.37). // 1.169 //

One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat (*saṃdhinī*), of one whose calf is less than ten days old (*anirdaśāvatsā*), of a goat, of a camel, of one-hoofed animals, of a woman, of wild animals, and likewise of a sheep.
A *gauḥ* (cow) is that which is joined with a bull; she is a *saṃdhinī*.
"One should know that a *vaśā* is a barren cow, and a *saṃdhinī* is one that has been mounted by a bull," according to the recollection of the *Trikāṇḍī*;
furthermore, this also includes a cow that is milked after one [milk] time has passed, or one that is joined with another calf.
A cow in heat; one that has recently calved and whose ten-day period has not yet passed is called *anirdaśā*; one whose calf is dead is *avatsā*;
and [the term] *saṃdhinī* [also applies to her].

One should avoid the milk of cows that have not passed ten days [since calving], as well as those that are "saṃdhinī" (in heat), and those whose calves have not passed ten days; these are the cows whose milk has been exhausted.
The mention of *saṃdhinī* is intended to include both the cow in heat and one that miscarries.
As Gautama says:
Regarding the terms *syandinī*, *yamalasū*, and *saṃdhinī*: NSP reads *yamalasū ca* (GDh 17.25). A cow whose udder flows milk is called *syandinī*; one that gives birth to twins is *yamalasū*.
In this same way, one should avoid the milk of goats and buffaloes within ten days of calving; [as stated in VaDh 14.35]: "The milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats within ten days of calving..."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha; by the mention of "milk," its derivatives such as curd and the like are also prohibited. For indeed, when meat is prohibited...
It is logical that there is no prohibition of its modifications;
however, when the modification is prohibited, the primary substance is not prohibited,
as in the case of the prohibition of milk.
There is no prohibition against [using] excrement, urine, and so forth.
"Austrian" (*auṣṭra*) refers to milk, urine, and so on produced by a camel.
"Single-hoofed animals" (*ekaśapha*) refers to mares and the like.
That which originates from them is *aikaśapha* (single-hoofed).
That which originates from women is *straiṇa*.
The mention of "women" includes all two-teated animals other than goats and sheep.
This is for the purpose of illustration, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "The milk of all animals with two teats is unfit for consumption, with the exception of goats.
Those born in the forest are *āraṇyakas*; their milk is *āraṇyaka*, except for that of the buffalo.
Because of the statement: "And of all wild animals, except for the buffalo" (MDh 5.9),
[the term] *āvikam* refers to that which is born from a sheep (*avi*).
The word "should avoid" (*varjayet*) is connected to each [term].

Because of the use of the suffix indicating a derivative (*vikāra-pratyaya*) in "camel's milk" (*auṣṭram*) and so forth, there is a perpetual prohibition of all derivatives, such as milk, urine, and the like.
This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "The milk of sheep, of camels, and of one-hoofed animals is always unfit for drinking. (GDh 17.25). 1.170.
For the sake of the deities, sacrificial oblation (havis), the śigru plant, red exudations from incisions,
meat that has not been consecrated by ritual slaughter, substances produced in dung, and mushrooms [are forbidden].
"For the sake of the deities" means prepared for the purpose of offerings and oblations to the gods.

The *havis* is prepared for the purpose of offering prior to the oblation. *Śigru* is the *sobhāñjana*. "Red" refers to red exudations from trees; "produced by cutting" means those arising from the felling of trees, provided they are not red.
Furthermore, as Manu says:
"Red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions" (MDh 5.6).
Because of the mention of "red," there is no prohibition regarding asafoetida, camphor, and the like.
Meat not prepared for sacrifice refers to the flesh of an animal that has not been offered in a ritual.
"Born of dung" refers to plants such as *tandulīyaka* and others produced from the excrement of humans and other creatures upon which seeds have been eaten. "Mushrooms" refers to fungi (*chatrāka*).
The word "should avoid" is to be connected with each [item] individually. // 1.171 //
One should avoid carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, pecking birds, the ṭiṭṭibha,
the sārasa crane, one-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds.
Carnivorous birds are those whose habit is to eat raw flesh.
"Birds" refers to vultures and the like;
"dātyūha" refers to the cātaka bird; "śuka" refers to the parrot (kīra).
The *pratuda* birds, such as the hawk (*śyenādi*), are so called because they feed by pecking with their beaks (*cañcvā pratudya bhakṣayanti*).
The *ṭiṭṭibha* is named after its imitative sound;
the *sārasa* is also known as the *lakṣmaṇa*.
Single-hoofed animals are horses and the like;
swans are well known;
village-dwellers are pigeons and so forth.
One should avoid these, such as carnivorous animals and the like. // 1.172 //
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, baka, and viṣkira birds;
as well as kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī prepared in vain (without being offered).
YDh 1.173. The koyaṣṭi is the krauñca bird.
The *plava* is the water-hen;
the *cakrāhva* is the ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*);
the *balākā* and the crane (*baka*) are well known.
The term *viṣkira* refers specifically to birds such as the *cakora* and others, understood as those that scatter [food] with their claws and then eat;
for birds such as the quail (*lāvaka*) and the peacock (*mayūra*) are [also] fit to be eaten.

Because the village cock is already prohibited by virtue of its being a village-dweller, one should avoid these [other birds] such as the *koyaṣṭi* and so forth. One should avoid *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, *apūpa*, and *śaṣkulī* when they are prepared "in vain," that is, without being dedicated to a deity or for some other sacred purpose.
*Kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame and mung beans.
*Saṃyāva* is a specific kind of baked preparation known as *utkarikā*, made from milk, jaggery, ghee, and so forth.
*Pāyasa* is food boiled in milk.
*Apūpa* is a wheat product baked without oil;
*śaṣkulī* is a wheat product baked with oil.

Since the prohibition of *kṛsara* and similar dishes is already established by the rule "one shall not cook food for oneself" (YDh 1.104), the restatement here is for the purpose of increasing the severity of the penance. // 1.173 //
The *kalaviṅka*, the *kākola*, the *kurara*, the *rajjudālaka*,
web-footed birds, the *khañjarīṭa*, and wild animals and birds that are unknown [should not be eaten].
(YDh 1.174) The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*).
Since the prohibition is already established by the fact that they dwell in villages, the repetition is made because they frequent both [types of places].
*Kākola* is the *droṇakāka* (the raven);
*kurara* is the *utkrośa* (the osprey).
*Rajjudālaka* means one who cuts down trees.
*Jālapāda* means having feet with a web-like pattern.
Although there are swans that do not have webbed feet, the term "swans" is mentioned again for the sake of emphasis.
The *khañjarīṭa* is the *khañjana* (the wagtail). Those wild animals and birds that are not known [by name]—one should avoid these, such as the *kalaviṅka* and others. 1.174.
Having eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, dried meat, or fish out of desire, one shall dwell for three days observing a fast.
(Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.175) Blue jays are *kikīdivi* birds; red-footed birds include the *kādamba* and others.
Meat from a slaughterhouse abandoned by the butcher, even if it comes from an animal fit for consumption,
as well as dried meat (*vallūra*), which is dried flesh; these are [permissible].
"Matsya" means fish; one should avoid these, beginning with the *cāpa*,
and by the use of "and" (*ca*), [one should also avoid] the *nālikā*, *śaṇa*, *chatrāka*, *kusumbha*, and so forth.
"One should avoid *nālikā*, hemp, mushrooms, safflower, bottle-gourd, and products of *viḍ* salt; as well as *kumbhī*, *kanduka*, eggplant, and *kovidāra*.
Likewise:
One should diligently avoid flowers and fruits that have blossomed out of season, as well as anything that appears abnormal.
Likewise, because of the traditional law (smṛti) stating that one should avoid the fruits of the *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *kapittha*, *nīpa*, and *mātuliṅga* trees,

having intentionally consumed these aforementioned items— beginning with the milk of a cow in heat— one should fast for three nights; however, if unintentionally, one should fast for a day and a night.
"One should fast for a day for the remaining [permitted birds]," according to the recitation of Manu (MDh 5.20).

Furthermore, as stated by Śaṅkha regarding the eating of the following: the balāka crane, haṃsa goose, plava duck, cakravāka ruddy sheldrake, kāraṇḍava water-fowl, domestic sparrow, pigeon, dove, white parrot, sārikā starling, sārasa crane, ṭiṭṭibha lapwing, owl, kaṅka heron, raktapād bird, cāṣa blue jay, bhāsa vulture, crow, cuckoo, śāḍvalika, cock, and hārīta bird: [the penance is as follows].

"One should drink barley-gruel with cow's urine for twelve nights while abstaining from food"—this is to be understood as applying to cases of intentional consumption of the entire substance over a long period of practice. (1.175)
Having eaten onions, village pigs, mushrooms, village cocks,
garlic, or leeks, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
An onion (palāṇḍu) is a thick-stemmed bulb that resembles garlic.
The village pig is the *viḍvarāha* (filth-pig). The mushroom is the *sarpacchatra*.
The village cock is well known.
Garlic (*laśuna*), onion (*rasona*), the small white bulbous root, and the *gṛñjana*—
which resembles garlic and has a small red bulb—
if one eats these six intentionally even once, one shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, the characteristics of which will be described hereafter.

The mention here of the village cock and the *chatrāka* mushroom, which were previously prohibited, is for the purpose of establishing that they share the same penance as the onion (*palāṇḍu*) and other such items. However, in the case of intentional and long-term habitual consumption, [the rule is]:
"The *chatrāka*, the village pig, garlic, and the village cock..."
"Having intentionally eaten onions or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]," as stated by Manu (MDh 5.19).
Regarding repeated practice performed unintentionally:
Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra;
or else, as will be described in the third chapter, the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa. (MDh 5.20)
Thus it should be understood.

However, in the case of unintentional habitual practice, that which was stated by Śaṅkha applies: "Upon eating garlic, onion, leeks, village-pig, village-cock, or kumbhīka, one should drink milk for twelve nights. (1.176)

Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, and the pangolin may be eaten; likewise, the rabbit, and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka, the rohita, the pāṭhīna, the rājīva, and those with scales may be eaten by the twice-born. (YDh 1.177–178ab)
The *sedhā* is the porcupine;
the *godhā* is a large lizard that resembles a chameleon;
and the *kacchapa* is the tortoise.
The *śallaka* is the porcupine;
the *śaśa* is well known [as the rabbit].
Among the five-nailed animals, such as dogs, cats, monkeys, and others, these—namely the *sedha* and so forth—are edible.
Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the rhinoceros is also included;
as Gautama stated:
"The five-clawed animals [permitted] are the rabbit, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise" (GDh 17.27).

As Manu also said: "The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare— they say these are edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel" (MDh 5.18).

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"But regarding the rhinoceros, they dispute"—and thus its inedibility [was declared], that refers to occasions other than a *śrāddha* ceremony; for it is said:
"An offering made with the meat of a rhinoceros in a rite for the ancestors becomes inexhaustible."
Thus, because the declaration of rewards is seen in the context of the *śrāddha* rite;
likewise, among fish, those such as the *siṃhatuṇḍa* and others are edible.
A *siṃhatuṇḍa* is one that has the face of a lion.
The *rohita* is red in color;
the *pāṭhīna* is known as the *candraka*;
the *rājīva* has the color of a lotus.
It is called "with scales" (saśalka) because it exists together with scales that have the shape of oyster shells;
and these, such as the lion-mouthed fish and others, are indeed edible only when prepared [as prescribed].

For it is stated in the traditional law of Manu: "The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are the first [permitted] for use in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*); likewise, those with stripes, those with lion-like mouths, and those with scales are permitted in all respects. (MDh 5.16).
The mention of the "twice-born" (dvijāti) is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra. // 1.177 //
Having stated the duties of the twice-born, beginning with the verse "Meat that is not honored is meat in vain" (YDh 1.167), he now declares the duties of the four castes.

Therefore, listen to the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat (YDh 1.178cd). O sages, Sāmaśravas and others—listen to the rule concerning the eating of meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling (*prokṣita*) and so forth, and the avoidance of that which is otherwise forbidden; specifically, the rule consists of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the form: "I shall not eat meat except for that which has been consecrated by sprinkling and the like. 1.178.
In that regard, he shows the rule for eating:

"In a life-threatening emergency, at a Śrāddha ceremony, when it has been consecrated by sprinkling (prokṣita), or at the desire of a twice-born, one who eats meat after having duly honored the gods and the ancestors incurs no fault. (YDh 1.179)
When there is danger to life due to lack of food or being overcome by disease, and it cannot be avoided without eating meat,
then one may eat meat as a rule; one must protect oneself at all costs (GDh 9.34).

Thus, because of the injunction for the protection of the self, and because of the prohibition against death— expressed as "therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his lifespan"—
likewise, one invited to a *śrāddha* must eat meat according to the rule; in the case of not eating it, [there is a fault].
Because of the hearing of [this] defect:
"But that man who, when enjoined according to the rule, does not eat meat,
goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births" (MDh 5.35).
According to this recollection of Manu,

one should eat the consecrated meat (*prokṣita*)— that is, the meat remaining after the oblation of an animal such as the *agnīṣomīya*, which has been purified by the Vedic sacramental rite known as *prokṣaṇa* and intended for sacrifice.
Because the sacrifice cannot be accomplished without eating;
one who eats what has been prepared for the purpose of feeding Brahmins,
for the sake of the gods, or for the ancestors, after having honored them with that food, incurs no fault.
Likewise, even what remains after supporting one's dependents [may be used].
Praised wild animals and birds may be killed by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice and for the maintenance of their dependents; for in ancient times, Agastya did so. (MDh 5.22)
Because of this recollection from Manu,

the statement "one does not partake in the fault" indicates merely the absence of fault; it shows that there is simply permission for what remains after honoring guests and others, and not a restrictive rule like that regarding *prokṣita* meat and so forth.

Thus, since it is understood that even for animals such as the hare—which are not specifically prohibited—it is forbidden to eat them except when life is at stake, it follows that a Śūdra also possesses the entitlement to all injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to meat. (1.179)

Now, he states a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding the eating of meat that is not consecrated by sprinkling (*prokṣita*)—that is, meat prohibited by the term "meat for no purpose" (*vṛthāmāṃsa*): That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal’s body. (YDh 1.180)

He who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule— that is, without dedicating them to a deity or other such purpose— shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on that animal.
By the word "kills," all eight types of slaughterers are included.
As Manu has said:

"The one who consents, the one who dissects, the one who kills, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it—these are all slayers" (MDh 5.51). 1.180.
Now he states the rule for avoidance:
"Even while dwelling at home, a Brahmin becomes a sage through the total renunciation of meat; he obtains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice. (YDh 1.181)

He who possesses the resolve of truth, thinking "I shall not eat meat except that which has been consecrated by sprinkling and the like," attains all his desires without obstacle when engaged in their accomplishment, because of the purity of his intention.
As Manu said:
"Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and toward whatever one forms an attachment—that one obtains without obstacle, provided one harms nothing. (MDh 5.47)
And this is a secondary result;
he states the primary result:
"likewise, the fruit of the horse-sacrifice."
And this refers to the annual vow:
"The merit of one who performs the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years is equal to that of one who does not eat meat; the fruit of their merit is the same" (MDh 5.53).
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu,
even while living at home, a member of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa becomes worthy of honor like a sage by virtue of renouncing meat.

And this [prohibition] does not concern meat that is forbidden, nor does it concern meat that has been consecrated (*prokṣita*) and so forth; rather, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it concerns meat permitted as what remains after honoring guests and others. (1.181)
Thus ends the section on what may and may not be eaten;
now begins the section on the purification of substances.
He now declares the purification of substances.
The purification of vessels made of gold or silver, of lotuses, of upper cups, and of stones;
of vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and leather;
and of bowls and ladles, is prescribed to be by means of water. (YDh 1.182)
The *caru* vessel, the *sruc*, the *sruva*, and vessels for oily substances should be cleansed with hot water.
"Golden" means made of gold;
"silver" means made of silver.
The "lotus-born" (abja) refers to pearls, conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and so forth;
the "upward-facing vessel" (ūrdhvapātra) refers to sacrificial mortars and the like, because of their association with the *graha* vessels and other such items.
The *grahas* are those beginning with the *ṣoḍaśin*.
The stone (*aśman*) refers to the grinding-stone (*dṛṣad*) and so forth. The *śākta* refers to the *vāstuka* and so forth. The rope (*rajju*) is made from *balvaja* grass and similar materials.
Roots are ginger and so forth;
fruits are mangoes and so forth;
clothing is garments.
*Vidala* refers to bamboo and the like;
*carma* refers to the skins of goats and so forth. The mention of *vidala* and *carma* includes their derivatives, such as umbrellas, leather thongs, and the like.
This is for the purpose of illustration.
"Vessels" refers to the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and others;
"bowls" refers to the *hotṛcamasa* and so forth. Of these...

Objects made of gold and other such materials, when free from stains, are purified by washing with water upon mere contact with food remnants. *Caru* refers to the sacrificial oblation; *carusthālī* is the vessel for that oblation;
*sruk* and *sruva* are well-known sacrificial ladles.
Vessels that contain oily substances, such as the *prāśitra-haraṇa* and others,
are purified with hot water provided they are free of residue;
a golden vessel that is free of residue is purified by water alone.
"An earthen vessel, one made of stone, and one made of silver, provided it is unadorned," according to the traditional teaching of Manu;
"unadorned" means not filled with a hole [or, in the case of a vessel, not repaired by being filled in].
For vessels made of metal, gems, and all stone products,
purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth. (MDh 5.111)
Thus, that which was stated by Manu is to be understood.
Since earth and ash serve the same purpose, there is an option between them;
however, water is to be used in combination with both.
However, in the case of defilement by the mouth of a crow or similar bird, one should scrape out the vessel that has been touched by the mouth of a black bird;
it should be understood that a vessel touched by the mouth of a beast of prey must not be used at all.
And this [impurity] applies except in the case of a cat; for the Smṛti of Manu states: "The cat, the ladle, and the wind are always pure" (ViDh 23.52). 1.182–1.183.
The purification of sacrificial vessels and the like is by sprinkling;

likewise for the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the skin (ajina), grain, the pestle (musala), the mortar (ulūkhala), the nose-rope (anaḥ), and for many solid objects such as grain and garments, purification is by sprinkling. (YDh 1.184)
The *sphya* is a vajra, a component of the sacrifice;
the *anaḥ* is a cart;
the remainder is well known.
Their purification is by means of hot water.
The repetition of the word "antelope skin" (ajina) is for the purpose of including skins that are parts of a sacrifice.
As for composite objects, which are wholes composed of impure substances:
[This applies] to many kinds of grain and garments.
The mention of "garments" is intended as an illustration for those things whose purification has already been stated.
[It refers to] those things whose purification has already been stated.
For many items such as grain, clothing, and the like, when they are heaped in a pile, purification is achieved by sprinkling alone;
and "many" is relative to what has been touched.

This is what is meant: when grains, clothes, or similar items are piled in a heap, and among them a few have been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or others while many remain untouched, the purification for those that were touched is as already stated, while for the others it is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
And likewise, another Smṛti states:
