"In the case of a heap of clothes, grain, or similar items, if one portion is defiled, one should remove only that much; the remainder deserves purification by sprinkling."
Furthermore, when there is a multiplicity of touched items and a scarcity of untouched ones, then all of them must be washed. As Manu says:
"The purification of many grains and garments, however, is by sprinkling with water."
"But for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed" (MDh 5.118).
Even when there is equality between those touched and those untouched, sprinkling alone is required;
for while sprinkling is prescribed for large quantities, it applies to small quantities as well.
Since washing is already established, the mention of washing again for small amounts is intended to exclude washing when the amounts are equal. However,
when there is no distinction as to how much has been touched and how much has not been touched, washing must indeed be performed,
because even a partial defect must be avoided.

Regarding grains, clothing, and other such items being carried by many men, whether they have been touched or untouched, the authors of the legal digests (Nibandhakṛtaḥ) maintain that sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) alone is the required purification. 1.184.
Having stated the purification for items that are unsmeared and merely defiled by contact, he now states the purification for those that are smeared:
"The scraping of wood, horn, and bone; with cow-hair for those produced from fruit."
In the performance of a sacrifice, the cleansing of sacrificial vessels is done with the hand;
[this applies to] those made of wood, the horns of rams, buffaloes, and so forth, and the bones of elephants, boars, conchs, and the like—
the mention of "bones" includes teeth as well.
Regarding the taking up [of earth]: for objects smeared with food-leavings, oil, and so forth, where the smear has not been removed by means of earth, ash, water, and the like—Manu says:
"As long as the odor and the smear caused by it do not depart from an object defiled by impurity, so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances" (MDh 5.126).
Thus, because purification is prescribed in general terms,
*takṣaṇa* (scraping) is the removal of just that much portion [of the impurity];
this applies to those [vessels] produced from fruit.
Vessels made from fruits such as the *bilva*, the gourd (*alābu*), and the coconut are purified by scrubbing with cow-hair.
Sacrificial vessels, such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, when employed during a sacrifice, [are purified] with the right hand using *darbha* grass and the *daśāpavitra*.
Or rather, the cleansing (mārjana) should be performed as an auxiliary to the ritual act according to the scriptures;

and this is a Vedic example intended to show that other vessels as well— such as those made of gold and so forth— possess the status of being auxiliaries only when they have been purified according to the Smṛtis in the case of both scriptural and worldly rites.

Furthermore, for the components of the sacrifice that have already been purified, this cleansing with the *daśāpavitra* and other implements is for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*); this is the implied meaning. (1.185)
Woolen cloth (*āvikakauśika*) is purified by alkaline water, cow's urine, or water;
silk cloth (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) with *śrīphala* (bilva fruit); and likewise, *kutapa* wool with *ariṣṭa* (myrobalan).
[This refers to] application [of the substances] with cow's urine mixed with alkaline earth or with water, depending on the degree of staining.

"Woolen" means made of sheep's wool. "Silk" refers to what originates from cocoons, such as *tasarī* cloth, silk bands, and so forth; these become pure when washed with water and cow urine—the plural number being used [to indicate various types of liquids].
Later, for the sake of obtaining water,
[he used] a cloth made of strips of bark-fiber,
together with *śrīphala* fruits— that is, accompanied by *bilva* fruits.
A *kutapa* is a blanket made from the hair of mountain-dwelling goats;
it is purified by water mixed with cow’s urine and *ariṣṭa*, as the preceding rule continues to apply.
And this should be understood to apply when there is contact with residual oil and the like;
however, in the case of minor defilement, sprinkling and similar rites are prescribed, because [the object] cannot withstand washing.
Because it is accepted that purification occurs everywhere simply through the non-destruction of the substance;
and thus Devala says:
"Those [garments] produced from wool, silk, *kutapa* wool, bark-cloth, linen, and fine cotton..."
These [beings] possess little purity, due to such means as drying and sprinkling.
Having said this, he continued:
"One should wash those very [vessels] that are defiled by impurities with their respective purifying agents—
namely, with pastes of grains, with juices derived from fruits, or even with alkaline substances."
The case of hemp-cloth is exactly like that of linen, because they share the same origin.
The mention of wool and so forth is for the purpose of including items such as mattresses made from them.
Therefore, when there is only slight defilement of such items, no washing at all should be performed.
Except when smeared with impurities,
one should dry a mattress, a pillow, or likewise a flower-colored garment in the sun for a short while and repeatedly wipe them with the hands.
And afterwards, having sprinkled them with water, one should employ them in ritual action; even those that are extremely defiled, one should purify according to the rule.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Devala:
"Red with flowers" means dyed with saffron, safflower, and so forth; the mention of "red with flowers" includes other [dyes] as well, such as turmeric and the like.
This is for the purpose of obtaining [the status of] that which cannot withstand washing;
it does not apply to madder and the like, because those can withstand washing.
It has also been stated by Śaṅkha: "Dyeing substances are pure when they have been sprinkled with water. (1.186)
Linens are purified by white mustard seeds; earthenware by re-firing;
the hand of an artisan, merchandise, alms-food, and likewise the mouth of a woman, are pure.
(YDh 1.187) Linen—meaning cloth and the like made from *atasī* fibers—is purified by water mixed with white mustard seeds and cow’s urine.
An earthen vessel, such as a jar and the like, is purified by re-firing; this should be understood to apply when it has been smeared with the residue of oil. Manu says:
[It is defiled] by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood...
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "An earthen vessel that has been touched [by an impure substance] is not purified by re-firing";
however, in the case of defilement by a Caṇḍāla or similar persons, there must be total abandonment.
As Parāśara has said: "Grain or even clothing that has been touched by Caṇḍālas and others is purified by washing; however, an object made of earth is purified by discarding it."
Artisans— such as dyers, washermen, cooks, and so forth— their hands are always pure; that is,
they possess purity with respect to the work they perform, such as washing clothes and the like, even when there is the occurrence of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and other such conditions.
And likewise, another Smṛti states:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female slaves, male slaves, as well as kings and royal servants, are declared to be immediately pure. (YDh 3.20)
Merchandise, which is worthy of barter and fit for sale— such as barley, rice, and so forth—
does not become impure even when handled by many buyers or by the hands of others;
nor does it become so for merchants on account of childbirth or other such occasions.

Alms (bhaikṣa) is a collection of begged food; that which has come into the hands of a celibate student (brahmacārin) and others is not defiled even by such causes as being given by a woman who has not sipped water for purification, or by its passage through an impure street.
The same applies to the face of a woman.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "He is pure at the time of sexual enjoyment, as are women during the act of passion" (VaDh 28.8). // 1.187 //
Now he describes the purification of the ground:
"The purification of the ground is by sweeping, by burning, by time, and likewise by the treading of cows;
[it is also] by sprinkling, by scraping, and by smearing; and a house [is purified] by sweeping and smearing. (YDh 1.188ab–cd)
Sweeping (*mārjana*) is the clearing away of dust, grass, and the like by means of a broom (*mārjanī*).
Burning (*dāha*) is [the destruction] by means of grass, wood, and so forth.
Time (*kāla*) is that which lasts for as long as...
In due time, there occurs the depletion of the smearings and so forth to that extent;
"the treading by cows" means the trampling by the hooves of cattle;
and "sprinkling" means with milk, cow urine, cow dung, and water.
Or it may be by raining;
or by scraping, planing, or digging;
or by smearing with cow dung and the like.
By means of these— cats and so forth— either collectively or individually, ground that is defiled by impurities and the like, as well as that which is merely soiled, becomes purified.
And thus says Devala:
Where a woman gives birth, where one dies or is cremated,
where a Caṇḍāla dwells, or where there is a heap of excrement and the like;
Thus, the earth is proclaimed to be impure when it abounds in filth;
it becomes defiled when touched by dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, and the like.
It becomes defiled by charcoal, husks, hair, bones, ashes, and other such things.
Having thus stated the threefold classification of ground to be purified—namely, as impure (*amedhya*), defiled (*duṣṭa*), and soiled (*malinā*)—he demonstrates the division of purification:
"Ground, even when impure, is purified in five ways or four;
when possessed of defilement, in three or two ways; and when merely soiled, in one way. Thus [he says].

Where humans are cremated, and where Caṇḍālas dwell, purification occurs there through five means: burning, the passage of a cow at the time of death, sprinkling with water, and scraping. Where humans are born, where they die, and where there is an excessive accumulation of excrement and the like, purification occurs through those same four means, excluding burning.

For ground that has been inhabited for a long time by dogs, pigs, or donkeys, purification is achieved through the three methods of treading by cattle, sprinkling, and scraping. For ground that has been occupied for a long time by camels, village fowl, and the like, purification is through sprinkling and scraping.
For ground that has been occupied for a long time by charcoal, chaff, hair, and so forth, purification is by means of scraping alone.
However, sweeping and smearing are to be combined in all cases;
thus, a house is purified by both sweeping and smearing.
The house is mentioned separately so that sweeping and smearing may be performed every day. (1.188)

When food has been smelled by a cow, or is defiled by hair, flies, or insects, water, ashes, or even earth should be thrown into it for the sake of purification. (YDh 1.189) "Smelled by a cow" means food that has been defiled by the breath of a cow; this applies to all types of edible food.
Likewise, when [food] is defiled by hair, flies, or insects;
the mention of "hair" is intended to include body hair and the like.
Insects such as ants and the like,
water, ashes, or earth— whichever is available— should be thrown in for the sake of purification.

As for that which was stated by Gautama: "That which is constantly fallen into by hair or insects is unfit to be eaten" (GDh 17.8–9), that refers to food that has been cooked together with hair, insects, and the like. // 1.189 //
The purification of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, water, and earth; that of bell-metal and iron is by means of ashes and water; but for liquids, it is by immersion.
Tin and the others are well known.
For those [vessels], purification should be performed— either collectively or individually— with alkaline water, sour water, or plain water, depending on the degree of defilement;
for bronze and iron vessels, it is with ash-water.
By the mention of copper (*tāmra*), brass (*rītikā*) and bell-metal (*pittala*) are also included, because they share a common origin.
Furthermore, this prescription regarding the purification of copper and other metals with acidic liquids and the like is not intended as a restrictive rule.
That which arises from contact with impurity and is produced by it, and by whatever means that [impurity] is removed,
that is declared to be the general purification for making substances clean.
Because of this general injunction for recollection,

one need not invariably perform purification with sour liquids and the like whenever the stains of leftover water and so forth on copper and other metals can be removed by some other means. For this very reason, it was stated generally by Manu:
"The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water. (MDh 5.114).
As for that which [is stated]:
"Brass is purified by ashes; copper is purified by acid"—this [verse] is intended to establish the ultimate limit of purification for copper and the like, not to prohibit other methods. When...
In cases of excessive defilement, there is the repeated immersion of sour liquids and the like;
bronze vessels smelled by a cow, those left over by a Śūdra,
and those defiled by dogs or crows are purified by ten applications of alkaline substances.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
An additional passage from the NSP manuscript *ka* states:
"He mentions ten [types of] saline substances."
Of sesame, muṣkaka, śigru, kokilākṣa, palāśa, as well as kākajaṅghā, avajñā, ciñcā, aśvattha, and vaṭa.
However, by means of these ten purifying agents, purification occurs for bell-metal.

Regarding the statement "the purification of a liquid, however, is by overflowing": for a liquid substance such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) exceeding one *prastha* in measure, which has been defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, or touched by impure substances (*amedhya*), "overflowing" (*plāva*)—that is, filling the vessel with a liquid of the same kind until it overflows—is the purification;
the term "purification" (*śuddhiḥ*) is understood to follow from the context.
From that, there is the relinquishing of what is small;
and whether something is large or small should be understood in relation to factors such as place and time.
As Baudhāyana said:
"Having understood the place, the time, as well as the quantity, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the circumstances, and the state, one should determine the purification. (cf. BDh 1.8.53)
However, for that which has been defiled by insects and the like, purification is by straining;
as Manu said:
"The purification of all liquid substances is traditionally held to be by straining" (MDh 5.115).
In this context, "purifying by winnowing" (utpavana) means placing [the liquid] into a vessel separated by a cloth;
otherwise, it would be impossible to remove insects and other impurities. Honey, water, and the like contained in a Śūdra’s vessel are purified by transferring them into another vessel.
According to the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "Honey, water, milk, and their derivatives are pure when transferred from one vessel to another" (BDh 1.14.16).
Therefore, honey, ghee, and the like, even if obtained from the hand of a person of a low caste, become pure by being transferred to another vessel and then strained again.

And it must be purified; as Śaṅkha says: "The purification of edible foods that have been sprinkled with ghee is by means of blowing [upon them]; likewise for oily substances, and similarly for liquids. (1.190)

Having thus stated the purification for all items such as gold and silver mentioned in this section when they are defiled by food-leavings, oil, and so forth, he now states the purification for those same items when they are defiled by impure substances (amedhya).
The purification of that which is smeared with impurities is by means of earth and water, through the removal of odor and the like;
that which is commended by word, that which is washed with water, and that which is unknown [to be defiled] are always pure.
Impurities born of the body are the unclean substances such as fat, semen, and so forth.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nails, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
Likewise: [MDh 5.136] Thus:
"Human bone, a corpse, feces, semen, urine, menstrual blood, fat, sweat, tears, eye-secretion, phlegm, and wine are called impure (*amedhya*). Thus,
the impurities such as *amedhya* and others have been set forth by Manu, Devala, and other authorities.
That which is smeared with fat and other such things, stained with blood, or defiled by impurities,
must be purified with earth and water by removing the odor.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the application of ointment (*lepa*) is also included,
as Gautama stated:
"The purification of that which is smeared with impurity is by means of removing the stain and the odor" (GDh 1.42).
In all acts of purification, first the removal of stains and odors must be performed with earth and water alone;
if the odor and so forth do not depart by means of earth and water, then it should be done by other means.
In the event of inability [to bathe], one may use earth and water; for there is a traditional teaching of Gautama stating, "First with earth, and then with water" (GDh 1.43).

Furthermore, the mention of *vasā* (fat) and the other substances is intended to establish the impurity (*amedhya*) of all of them, and not to indicate that they cause an equal degree of defilement; for it is said:
"By liquors, by urine and feces, by phlegm, pus, tears, and blood..."

"An earthen vessel that has been touched [by impurity] is not purified even by re-firing," because of this specific statement regarding defilement; and their impurity is thus established by the rule: "And these excretions fall from the body as impurities. (MDh 5.132)
According to this statement,
[the result accrues] only for those who have departed from the body, and not for those remaining in their own place;
[it concerns] the part of the person above the navel.
For body parts other than the hands, bathing is required upon contact with other impure substances.
As Devala says:
"Human bone, fat, feces, menstrual blood, urine, and semen..."
"Having touched marrow or blood belonging to another, one should perform a bath.
And: "Having touched those very same [substances] belonging to oneself, one becomes pure by washing them, rinsing the mouth, and sipping water.
Likewise:
"Whatever limb, excluding the two hands, is defiled above the navel, one becomes pure there by bathing; however, for what is below that, one becomes pure by washing it and performing *ācamana*.

Even when purification has been performed as prescribed, if the mind is not satisfied and a doubt regarding purity arises, that [impurity] is removed by the declaration of purity by word (*vākśasta*).
The meaning is that it becomes pure by the words of a Brāhmaṇa, "May this be pure; let it be purified.
That which is washed with water is purified by washing when there is no specific rule for its purification stated.

That which cannot withstand washing is purified by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Furthermore, that which is "unknown" is always pure—that is, when it has been defiled by crows and the like, yet its use is never known;
it remains pure because of such usage.
The meaning is that there is no fault if it has not been seen. But is this not contradicted by the statement:
"The best of the twice-born should perform at least one *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of a year"?
For the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly, but especially for that which was known [to be impure].
This is not so, because although a penance is prescribed even for what is not seen to be defective,
that penance pertains specifically to the act of eating,
whereas the absence of defect pertains to its use for other purposes. (1.191)

Water on the ground that is sufficient to satisfy a single cow, being in its natural state and untouched by Caṇḍālas or the like, is pure; likewise is meat fallen from a dog, a Caṇḍāla, a carnivorous beast, or similar creatures. (YDh 1.192) Water situated on the ground (*mahīgata*) which is capable of producing satisfaction for one cow, if untouched by Caṇḍālas and others, is in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*).
Water that has not undergone a change in its color, taste, smell, or touch remains pure and fit for ritual sipping (ācamana) and other uses.
The phrase "situated on the earth" is intended to exclude water located on the ground that has become impure; it does not, however, exclude the purity of water from the atmosphere.
Nor [is purification] for that which has been drawn out;
even those waters that have been drawn out are purified when taken up in pure vessels,
yet water that has stood for one night must be discarded, even if it is pure in itself.
Thus, according to the statement of Devala:

"Likewise, there is no fault regarding water from tanks and the like made by Caṇḍālas and others; the same applies to wells, embankments, ponds, and so forth, even when constructed by those of the lowest castes."
Having bathed and drunk there, no expiation is required.
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śātātapa;
likewise, meat killed by dogs, Caṇḍālas, carnivorous beasts, and the like is pure.
By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (ādi), there is also the inclusion of Pulkasas and others.
The inclusion of the term "struck down" (nipātita) is for the purpose of excluding that which has been eaten. 1.192.
Rays, fire, dust, shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, the wind,
droplets, flies, and a calf during suckling are pure to the touch.
(YDh 1.193) "Rays" refers to the light-emitting substances of the sun and so forth.
Fire is well known;
"dust" refers to that which exists apart from its connection with goats and the like.
In that regard:
"Through contact with the dust of dogs, crows, camels, donkeys, owls, pigs, domestic birds, goats, sheep, and deer, one's lifespan and fortune decline.
Because this defect is heard [in the scriptures], one must perform sweeping and other purificatory acts upon touching them.
The shadow of a tree and so forth;
a cow; a horse; the earth.
The earth; the wind, meaning air;
droplets, meaning drops of dew (since those produced from the mouth will be mentioned later); and flies.
And these, even when touched by Caṇḍālas and others, are pure upon contact.
A calf is pure during the flow of milk—that is, while drawing out the milk descending from the udder. The mention of "calf" is intended as an illustration for any young animal.
That which is frequented by children, that which is practiced by women,
and whatever else is unknown— this is the established rule that it is always pure.
Because of this statement. 1.193.
The mouths of goats and horses are pure; the impurities found on the mouths of cows and humans are not [pure].
And roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.
(YDh 1.194) The mouths of goats and horses are pure.
Not [the stains] of a cow;
nor the impurities born of man.
The word "man" (nara) denotes the body by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
The impurities produced from those, such as fat and so forth, do not become pure. Paths or roads, even when touched by dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and the like,
are purified at night by the rays of the moon and by the wind.
But by day, [it is purified] by the rays of the sun and by the wind.
"Spittle produced from the mouth is pure, as are drops from sipping water;
likewise, beard [hair] that has entered the mouth and what is stuck between the teeth—having removed these, one becomes pure.
(YDh 1.195) "Produced from the mouth" means originating in the mouth; drops of phlegm are pure and do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa* (defiled by remnants).
For there is the statement of Gautama: "If they do not fall upon the limbs, drops from the mouth do not make one impure by leavings, provided they do not fall upon the limbs. (GDh 1.41)
And likewise, those drops of water from the ritual rinsing (ācamana) which touch the feet are pure;
and the beard located in the mouth does not cause impurity (ucchiṣṭa) once it has entered the mouth.
Food and such that have become stuck between the teeth becomes pure once it has fallen out by itself;
that which does not fall out is considered equal to the teeth.
And so Gautama says: "That which adheres to the teeth is like [food on] the teeth, except when touched by the tongue;
some say it is until it falls away, while others say that once it has fallen away, it is like saliva."
"One should swallow that [food] while reciting the Vidyās; thus it is pure" (GDh 1.38–40).
Furthermore, this "swallowing" is presented as an alternative to the "relinquishment" mentioned by Yājñavalkya.
The particle *eva* in the phrase "while swallowing indeed" (*nigirann eva*) [serves to exclude other actions].
One should always perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) after chewing [food], except when chewing betel;
likewise, after touching the lips when they are covered in hair, and after changing one's garment.
Thus, this is the meaning of Viṣṇu’s prohibition regarding the sipping of water (ācamana).
The mention of betel (tāmbūla) is intended as an illustration for fruits and the like.
As Śātātapa has said:
"When betel, fruit, or the residue of oily substances has been consumed, or when there is contact with a particle stuck to the teeth, a twice-born man does not become impure by leavings. (1.195)

Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, walked upon a road, or changed one's garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again. (YDh 1.196) Having performed bathing, drinking, sneezing, sleeping, eating, walking upon a road, or changing garments, one who has already sipped water should sip water once more.
The meaning is that one should sip water twice;
the word "and" (ca) includes weeping, beginning Vedic study, restlessness, speaking falsehoods, and so forth.
And thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again. So says [Vasiṣṭha] (VaDh 3.38). Manu also says:
"Having slept, sneezed, eaten, spat, or spoken a false word..."
"Having drunk water, one who is about to study should sip water even if he is already pure. (MDh 5.145).
Regarding eating, however, there is sipping twice even at the beginning:
"But one who is about to eat, though already pure, should sip water twice" (ĀpDh 1.16.9).
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba:
[the sipping of water] is performed once at the beginning of bathing and drinking,
but twice at the commencement of Vedic study.
In the remaining cases, the twice-repeated sipping of water (ācamana) is performed only at the end, as previously described.
The mud and water in a street that have been touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks. "Rathyā" means merely a path.
Mud is *kardama* and water is *toya*. Mud and water situated on a road,
when touched by outcasts such as *caṇḍālas*, or by dogs and crows, become pure— that is, they attain purification— by the wind alone.
The plural number is used for the purpose of including cow-dung, gravel, and so forth contained therein.
Temples, white palaces, and the like, which are constructed with baked bricks and such materials,
are purified by wind alone even when touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others.
And this sprinkling is for the purpose of prohibiting the previously mentioned sprinkling of solid objects;
however, for those made of grass, wood, leaves, and so forth, sprinkling is indeed required. (1.197)
Thus ends the section on the purification of substances.
Now begins the section on giving (*dāna*).

Desiring now to expound the duty of self-restraint (*dāntadharma*), [the author] speaks in praise of the recipient (*pātra*) for the purpose of establishing that [recipient], which is an ancillary part of that [duty].

Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of Dharma. (YDh 1.198) Brahmā, that is Hiraṇyagarbha, having performed austerities—that is, having engaged in meditation—at the beginning of the Kalpa, first [considered] "Which shall I create? and [then created] the Brāhmaṇas.
He created [them]. For what purpose? For the protection of the Vedas—that is, for the sake of preserving the Vedas—and for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the deities.
And for the sake of preserving the Dharma by means of instructing [others] in its practice;
therefore, the intention is that what is given to them yields inexhaustible fruit. (1.198)
The Brahmins who are devoted to sacred learning and study are the source of all;

among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and even more excellent than them are those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self. (YDh 1.199) All [castes], such as the Kṣatriyas and others, have the Brahmins as their source and are inferior to them in both birth and action.

Among the brahmins as well, those who possess learning and study and are disciplined in their conduct are superior; even among them, those devoted to ritual action and habituated to the performance of prescribed duties are superior to them. Among those...

"Even those who are the best among the knowers of the inner self (adhyātmavittama)—meaning those who are devoted to the knowledge of the reality of the Self through the yoga of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, according to the path that will be described—are the most excellent; this is to be supplied [to the verse]. (1.199)

Thus, having described the state of being a worthy recipient through each individual factor— namely birth, learning, ritual practice, and austerity— by way of praise, he now states that perfect worthiness arises from their combination:
"Worthiness does not come through learning alone, nor even through austerity."
Where both conduct and these two [learning and austerity] exist, that indeed is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient (pātra).
One does not attain the state of a complete recipient through learning alone— that is, through the perfection of what has been heard and studied—
nor even through austerity alone.
By means of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth;
for, by the word "also," it is implied that neither by mere practice nor by mere birth alone is there full qualification as a worthy recipient.
How then?
That person in whom conduct— that is, practice— and these two, namely knowledge and austerity, as well as the Brahmin caste (indicated by the word "ca"),
exist, is proclaimed by Manu and others to be a "full vessel."
For indeed, there is no recipient more excellent than this.
Here, one should observe the gradation of results according to the increasing excellence of the combination of birth, learning, ritual practice, and austerity. (1.200)
A gift of cows and other such things should be given to a worthy recipient (satpātra).
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be bestowed upon a worthy recipient with due honor;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise man desiring his own welfare. (YDh 1.201)

The aforementioned gift, such as a cow and so forth, should be given to a worthy recipient (pātra) along with the prescribed ritual procedures, including the offering of water as enjoined by the scriptures. However, regarding an unworthy recipient (apātra)— such as a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa who is fallen (patita)— a wise person, knowing the specific differences in results according to the specific nature of the recipient and desiring the highest good or the full fruit of the merit, should not give even the slightest thing.
By the mention of "the better" (śreyas), it is indicated that even in giving to an unworthy recipient, there is some kind of tamasic fruit;
as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has said:
"Gifts given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients, which are offered disrespectfully and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness" (BhG 17.22).

By stating that one should not give to an unworthy recipient, [it is implied that] when a worthy recipient is absent despite the presence of a distinguished place, time, and material, [the gift is of the nature of darkness].
Or, having made a renunciation for that purpose or having given a promise to him, one should hand it over;
however, it is indicated that it must not be given to an unworthy recipient (*apātra*).

Likewise, even what has been promised should not be given later if it is known to be associated with a sin or similar transgression; for there is a prohibition stating, "Even after promising, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness" (GDh 5.23). // 1.201 //
Having stated the prohibition against giving to an unworthy recipient, he now speaks concerning the recipient:
"A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward. (YDh 1.202)
One who is deficient in learning and austerity should not accept gifts such as gold and the like;
for one lacking in learning and other virtues, by accepting a gift, leads both the donor and himself downward, causing them to reach hell. (1.202)
It has been stated that [gifts] such as cows should be given to a worthy recipient; regarding this, he states a specific rule:
"One should give every day to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions."
Even when requested, one should give what is purified by faith according to one's own capacity.

Every day, in accordance with one's ability and following the prescribed rule, one should give cows and other gifts to a worthy recipient without detriment to one's own family. On specific occasions, such as lunar eclipses and the like, one should especially give more with great effort.
Even when requested, one should give according to one's ability that which is purified by faith and sanctified by freedom from envy;
by saying "it should be given even when requested," [the author] indicates the aforementioned worthy recipient.
It is said that a gift given after having gone there in person or having summoned [the recipient] yields great fruit. And thus it is remembered:
"The gift which is given after going there is remembered as having infinite fruit."
"If summoned, he shall pay a thousandfold; but if asked, only half of that. (1.203)
It has been stated that "cows and so forth are to be given. Regarding that, he states a specific detail concerning the gift of a cow:
"A well-behaved cow with horns tipped in gold, hooves of silver, and accompanied by a garment."
A milch cow, accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given away.
That cow whose horns are made of gold is called *hemaśṛṅgī*;
she should be provided with silver hooves (*śaphaiḥ*) and covered with a cloth.
And a cow that is well-tempered, accompanied by a bronze vessel, yielding much milk, should be given according to one's capacity along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). // 1.204 //
He states the fruit of the gift of a cow:
"The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is tawny (kapilā), she further delivers his family up to the seventh generation. (YDh 1.205)
The donor of this cow attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs upon her;
if she is tawny (kapilā),
then she not only delivers the donor but also his lineage, extending up to the seventh generation, including his ancestors.
The six [elements] and the self as the seventh; the word "bhūyas" (furthermore) has the sense of "also. 1.205.
The fruit of the gift of a cow with her calf facing both ways:

by giving a cow with her calf facing both ways according to the previously mentioned rite, the giver attains heaven for as many ages (yugas) as there are hairs on the bodies of the cow and her calf. (YDh 1.206)

One who gives a cow with its calf and its "two-faced" (ubhayatomukhī) status attains and experiences heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on the body of that cow together with its calf— namely, the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages— provided the giver follows the previously mentioned ritual procedure. (1.206)
What, then, is the "two-faced" [cow], and how is that gift of such great fruit? To this he says:
"As long as both the calf's two feet and its face are seen in the womb, for that long the cow is to be known as the earth, until she releases the fetus. (YDh 1.207)

As long as both feet and the face of the calf emerging from the womb are visible within the birth canal, for that duration she is called "ubhayatomukhī" (two-faced), because she possesses faces on both sides;
she remains so until the time she releases the fetus.
It should be understood as being equal to the earth;
therefore, a superior fruit is appropriate. // 1.207 //
The fruit of the general gift of a cow:

"By giving a cow in any manner whatsoever—whether it be a milch cow or even one that is not, provided it is healthy and free from affliction—the donor is glorified in heaven. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.208)

In any case, even in the absence of golden horns and so forth, by giving a cow— whether one that yields milk or not, but one that is not barren, free from disease, not afflicted, and not exceedingly weak— according to the previously mentioned procedure as far as possible, the donor is honored and exalted in heaven. 1.208.

He states that these are equal to the gift of a cow: massaging one who is fatigued, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away their leavings are equal to the gift of a cow. (YDh 1.209)
Relieving the fatigue of the weary by providing seats, beds, and so forth, is "consoling the weary.
Attending to the sick consists of serving them according to one's ability by providing medicine and other necessities.
Worship of the gods is the propitiation of Hari, Hara, Hiranyagarbha, and others with perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
washing the feet of Brahmins who are equal or superior;
and the clearing away of their leftovers—these [are the duties].
These are equal to the gift of a cow mentioned immediately above. 1.209.
By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a house, gold, and a draft animal,
one is glorified in heaven.
"Land" refers to that which yields fruit.
Lamps [are for use] in temples and similar places;
a shelter is a dwelling place for travelers,
intended for habitation.
That which is given for the sake of the household life is the *naiveśika* (marriage gift);
*svarṇa* means gold; *dhurya* means capable of bearing a burden.
A bull;
the rest is well known.
Having given these—the earth, the islands, and so forth—one is exalted and honored in the heavenly world.
Furthermore, the mention of heaven as the fruit of gifts of land and so forth is not intended to exclude other fruits; for it is said:
"Whatever sin one commits, whether knowingly or unknowingly, one is purified by a gift of land even as small as a cow-hide."
Likewise, Manu says:
"The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision."

Because other fruits are heard [in scripture], such as: "The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins; the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun. (MDh 4.229, 231).
And the definition of a *gocarma* was shown by Bṛhaspati:
"A *nivartana* consists of thirty rods measured by a staff of seven cubits; ten of those indeed constitute a *gocarma*. By giving [this much land], one is glorified in heaven. (1.210)
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella, garlands, ointments, a vehicle, a tree, a beloved object, or a bed, one becomes supremely happy. (YDh 1.211) A "house" is well known.
Grains such as rice, wheat, and so forth;
fearlessness, which is protection for those who are afraid; sandals; and an umbrella.
Garlands refer to jasmine and the like;
ointments refer to saffron, sandalwood, and so forth;
and vehicles refer to chariots and the like.
Having given a tree to be used for livelihood, such as a mango tree or the like; that which is dear to someone, such as their beloved dharma and so forth;
and having given a bed, most exceedingly—that is, with the highest degree of excellence.
One becomes happy. Nor is there an impossibility of giving the Dharma because it cannot be placed in the hand like gold and other such things, for the same applies to the gift of land and so forth.
In another *Smṛti* as well, the gift of Dharma is heard:
"Merit should be diligently bestowed upon the deities, the gurus, and likewise upon one's mother and father; it is nowhere enjoined that demerit should be given."
In the case of giving what is non-meritorious, that very [demerit] increases for the recipient as well, who proceeds out of greed and other such motives;
for the evil-minded one who accepts [the gift] knowing it to be a source of sin,
so much sin shall cling to him because of his reprehensible conduct.
Among givers, [the merit] increases twofold at each stage up to a thousandfold, and it becomes infinite.
Thus it is remembered in the Smṛti:

"And here, in every case, because of the distinction of place, time, and recipient; because of the distinction of the gift; and because of the distinction of the giver, I have indeed declared that the fruit in giving is exactly like that in injury."
Thus, one should observe the gradation of results for both the giver and the recipient based on the specific conduct of the recipient. 1.211.
The fruit of giving has been explained;
now he states the causes for obtaining the fruit of giving even apart from the act of giving itself:
"Since Brahman, which consists of all dharmas, is superior to all gifts," [it is the highest gift].

By giving that, one attains the imperishable world of Brahman (YDh 1.212). Since Brahman consists of all dharmas by virtue of being the means of awakening [to them], the gift of it is superior even to all other gifts.
Therefore, by giving that—through the medium of teaching and so forth—one attains the world of Brahman.

"Unfallen" means that there is no falling away; the meaning is that one remains in the Brahma-world until the dissolution of the elements (*bhūtasaṃplava*). And in this regard, [it refers to] the gift of Brahman.
Giving consists merely in the transfer of ownership to another, because it is impossible to effect the cessation of one's own ownership. (1.212)
The fruit for the giver has been explained.
Now, he states the reason for obtaining the fruit of giving even apart from the act of giving itself:
"He who, though capable of receiving, does not accept a gift..."
He who, though being a worthy recipient (*pātrabhūta*),

does not accept— that is, does not take possession of— gold or other gifts that have come to him, yet does not take what has not been offered, attains all those abundant worlds belonging to those whose nature is charity (*dānaśīla*). (YDh 1.213)
Now, in the context of the prohibition against accepting all gifts, he states the exception:
"Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water—these are not to be refused. (YDh 1.214)
*Dhānāḥ* are roasted barley;
*kṣitiḥ* is earth;
the rest is well known.
And this [offering] such as *kuśa* grass and so forth, when brought by oneself,
must not be refused;
by the word "and" (*ca*), [the inclusion of] houses and other such things is intended.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, *kuśa* grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables. (MDh 4.250).
Likewise:
"Fuel, water, roots, fruits, and food that is offered spontaneously—
one may accept these from anyone, as well as honey and the gift of safety," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 4.247). 1.214.
To the question "Why should it not be refused?", he says:
"A twice-born man may accept even that which is brought unasked from one of evil deeds, except from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, or an outcast. (YDh 1.215)
Since this grass and so forth, brought unasked, may be accepted even from one who has committed evil deeds— how much more so from one who acts as prescribed— it should not be refused;
except in the case of unchaste women, eunuchs, the fallen, and enemies.
A *kulaṭā* is one who wanders from family to family, such as an unchaste woman;
a *ṣaṇḍha* is the third gender. // 1.215 //
He states another exception to the prohibition against accepting gifts:

"For the sake of honoring gods and guests, or for the purpose of maintaining one's teachers and dependents, and also for the sake of one's own subsistence, one may accept gifts from anyone. (YDh 1.216)

Because the worship of the gods and guests and so forth is mandatory, one should accept gifts from all sources for that purpose— even from those who lack self-restraint— provided they exclude those who are outcastes or otherwise utterly despicable.
"Gurus" refers to parents and others of similar status.
Dependents are those who must be supported, such as wives, sons, and so forth. 1.216.
Thus ends the section on giving;
now begins the section on the ancestral rites (śrāddha). At this point, the section on the ancestral rites is commenced.
Śrāddha is the renunciation, with devotion, of food or of a substance serving as its substitute, intended for a deceased person (preta).
It is of two kinds: pārvaṇa and ekoddiṣṭa.
In that context, that which is performed with reference to three ancestors is the *pārvaṇa* rite;
that which is performed with reference to a single ancestor is the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Furthermore, it is threefold:
obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Among these, the obligatory is that which is enjoined for every day under the condition of a fixed occasion.
[The obligatory] is that which is enjoined on specific occasions such as the new moon (amāvāsyā) or the eighth day (aṣṭakā);
the occasional (naimittika) is that enjoined under the condition of an indefinite cause, such as the birth of a son;

and the optional (kāmya) is that prescribed under the condition of a desire for a result, such as when one desires heaven and so forth, [performed] under specific lunar mansions (nakṣatra) like Kṛttikā or on specific lunar days (tithi).
Furthermore, it is of five kinds:
the daily *śrāddha*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the *ekoddiṣṭa*, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
Among these, the daily *śrāddha* consists of food [offered] to the ancestors and human beings (YDh 1.104).
Thus it has been stated,
and likewise Manu says:
"One should offer the Śrāddha daily with food and the like, or even with water."
"Or even with water, roots, and fruits, one brings inexhaustible satisfaction to the ancestors. (MDh 3.82).
Now, intending to demonstrate the *pārvaṇa* and *vṛddhi-śrāddha* rites, he states their times:
"The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the *aṣṭakās*, the *vṛddhi* [occasion], the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), and the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*)."
The presence of a Brahmin, the Viṣuvat day, the sun’s passage into a new zodiacal sign (saṃkrānti),
the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Gajacchāyā, eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the proper times for a Śrāddha.

The day on which the moon is not seen is the new moon (amāvāsyā); when that [new moon] spans two days, the one falling within the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is to be taken, because of the scriptural statement: "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors."
And the afternoon is the fourth part of the day divided into five parts, consisting of three *muhūrtas*.
There are four *aṣṭakās*,
which, as stated by Āśvalāyana (*ĀśGṛ* 2.4.1), are the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons.
*Vṛddhi* refers to occasions such as the birth of a son;
the *kṛṣṇapakṣa* is the latter fortnight;
and the two solstices are those designated as southern and northern.
The substance consists of *kṛsara*, mung beans, and so forth.
The excellence of the Brahmins will be described later.
The two equinoxes occur at the [transits] of Aries and Libra.
The movement of the sun;
the sun’s transit (*saṃkrama*) is the sun’s passage from one zodiac sign (*rāśi*) to another. Regarding the transits at the solstices (*ayana*) and the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*):
Even though [the term] is already established, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of demonstrating a superior result.
*Vyatīpāta* is a specific astronomical conjunction (*yoga*). *Gajacchāyā*,...
When the moon is in the constellation sacred to the ancestors (Maghā) and the sun is situated in Hasta,
on whichever lunar day that occurs, it is indeed proclaimed as Gajacchāyā.
Thus she was addressed.
Some say it means "the shadow of an elephant," but that is not accepted here because the context concerns time.
An eclipse is the seizing (grahaṇa) of the moon and the sun;
and also when there is a desire on the part of the performer regarding the śrāddha—
by the word "and" (ca), the beginnings of the yugas and so forth are included.

These are the times for the *śrāddha*. Although there is a prohibition against eating during an eclipse—expressed in the rule "one should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun"—nevertheless, while the eater incurs fault, the giver gains merit. (1.217–1.218)
He now describes the excellence of the Brāhmaṇas required for the four types of Śrāddhas to be mentioned hereafter, excluding the daily (aharahaḥ) Śrāddha:

"Those foremost in all the Vedas, a learned scholar of the Veda (śrotriya), one who knows Brahman, a youth, one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, one who knows the Trimadhu, and one who knows the Trisuparṇa. (YDh 1.219)
Those who are capable of constant and unerring study of all the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, even with undivided attention, are the foremost.
A *śrotriya* is one perfected in learning and Vedic study.
One who knows the Brahman that is about to be described is a *brahmavid*. [He should be] young.
Of middle age;
this qualifies every [term].
One who knows the meaning of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is a "knower of the meaning of the Veda" (vedārthavid).
The *jyeṣṭhasāman* is a specific *sāman* chant and the vow that is an auxiliary to its study; one who studies it by performing that vow is a *jyeṣṭhasāmā*.
The *trimadhu* is a portion of the *Ṛgveda* and the vow associated with it; one who studies it by performing that vow [is a *trimadhu*].
The *trimadhu* and the *trisuparṇa*—the latter being a portion of the *Ṛgveda* and *Yajurveda* along with its specific vow—and he who studies it while observing that vow is called a *trisuparṇika*.
These [types of] Brāhmaṇas are connected to what will be stated later as "the perfection of the Śrāddha. (1.219)
A sister’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, one for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle,
one who has mastered the Triṇāciketa rite, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman;
[here] *svasrīya* means a sister’s son (*bhāgineya*).
The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is defined by the aforementioned characteristics;
the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) is the husband of one's daughter;
and the *triṇāciketa* is a specific portion of the Yajurveda.
He who studies that [text] by practicing its prescribed vows is one who has performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice;
the rest is well known.
And these [persons] are to be understood as being eligible in the absence of those previously mentioned, such as the foremost Śrotriya and others.
"This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
however, this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) has been declared by the virtuous as one that is never censured.
Having thus stated [this], [he continued]:
Because Manu has prescribed [the status of] the daughter's son and others. (1.220)

Brahmins who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong students, and those who are devoted to their father and mother, are the perfection of the Śrāddha. "Devoted to ritual action" means intent upon the performance of prescribed duties.
Those who are devoted to austerity and habituated to ascetic practice are "taponiṣṭhās tapaḥśīlāḥ.
One who possesses the *sabhya*, *āvasathya*, and the three sacrificial fires (*tretāgni*) is a "pañcāgni," as is one who studies the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
The student (brahmacārī) is of two kinds: the temporary student (upakurvāṇaka) and the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika).

They are devoted to their father and mother, intent upon honoring them; by the use of the word "and" (ca), qualities such as being established in knowledge (jñānaniṣṭhā) and so forth are also included.
Brahmins, not Kṣatriyas and the like, are the means for the perfection of the Śrāddha—that is, they are the causes for the attainment of imperishable fruit in Śrāddha rites. (1.221)

He states those who are to be avoided: "One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, a *kuṇḍa* and a *gola*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth. (YDh 1.222)

A "sick person" (rogī) is one afflicted by a major disease. One whose limb is deficient or redundant is "one with deficient or redundant limbs" (hīnātiriktāṅgaḥ). One who sees with only one eye is "one-eyed" (kāṇaḥ).

For this very reason, those who are blind, deaf, impotent, bald, afflicted with skin diseases, and so forth, are excluded. A *paunarbhava* is one born of a *punarbhū*, whose characteristics have been previously described.
An *avakīrṇin* is one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Thus, one whose celibacy has failed—
these two sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from the wives of others.
"One born when the husband is alive is a *kuṇḍa*, and one born when the husband is dead is a *golaka*";
these two have been defined by such characteristics.
A *kunakhī* is one who has deformed nails.
"Śyāvadantaka" is one who by nature has black teeth; these are to be connected with what will be stated later: "these are censured at a śrāddha. (1.222)

One who teaches for wages, a eunuch, one who defiles a maiden, one accused of a grievous sin, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother— [these are excluded]. (YDh 1.223) One who teaches by taking a fee is a "teacher for wages" (bhṛtakādhyāpaka).
He who studies for the sake of receiving wages is also [excluded];
a *klība* is a eunuch;
and he who defiles a maiden with false or true accusations of faults is a *kanyādūṣī*.
One who is accused of, or charged with, such acts as the killing of a Brahmin—whether falsely or truly—is called "abhiśasta" (one accused).
A "mitradhruk" is a betrayer of friends;
one whose habit is to proclaim the faults of others.
A slanderer; a seller of soma at a sacrifice, that is, one who sells the soma; a "parivindaka," that is, a younger brother who marries before his elder brother when the elder remains unmarried.
Or, when the elder brother has already taken possession of the sacred fires, he who—being the younger—takes a wife or takes possession of the sacred fires is the *parivettṛ*;
the elder brother, however, is the *parivitti*.
As Manu says:

"He who enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder), and the elder brother is a *parivitti*. Thus it is said (MDh 3.171).
The same applies to the giver [of the bride] and the officiating priest (*yājaka*).
"An elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who so marries,
she with whom he marries, as well as the giver and the officiating priest— the fifth— these all go to hell," according to the statement of Manu (MDh 3.172). 1.223.

One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala* (low-caste woman); the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.
[Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.224] He who abandons his mother, father, or teacher without a valid reason is "one who abandons his mother, father, or teacher."
Likewise, even one who has renounced wife and son [is not at fault],
as are those who have aged parents, a virtuous wife, or an infant son.
"Even after committing a hundred improper acts, [the husband] must support her," so Manu has declared;
because of this identical reference,
one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* is called a *kuṇḍāśin*.
The same applies to the *golaka* as well,
according to the statement: "He who eats the food of those two [the *kānīna* and the *golaka*] is proclaimed a *kuṇḍāśin*."
A *vṛṣala* is one devoid of dharma; his son is a *vṛṣalātmaja*.
A woman who has had another husband before is a *punarbhū*; her husband is an *adattādāyin* (one who takes what is not given).
A thief; those whose actions are corrupt, meaning those who act in contradiction to the scriptures;
and by the use of the word "and" (ca), gamblers, temple-priests (devalakas), and so forth are included.
These are censured and prohibited from being invited to a śrāddha.

Although the unfitness of those other than the ones described is already established by the very definition of the Brāhmaṇas worthy of the *śrāddha*— beginning with the words "the foremost among all Vedas"— the explicit prohibition of certain individuals such as those afflicted by disease is stated for the purpose of permitting those who lack the aforementioned characteristics provided they are free from the specific prohibitions. (1.224)
Having thus described the times for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the Brahmins [to be invited], he now states the procedure for the Pārvaṇa rite:
"On the day before [the rite], one who is self-controlled and pure should invite the Brahmins;
they too must remain restrained in their actions of mind, speech, and body. (YDh 1.225)

On the day before [the rite], or on the following day, or when the śrāddha ceremony is at hand— whether on the previous day, the next day, or both— one should invite the previously mentioned Brāhmaṇas with the words, "May a moment be granted for the śrāddha," and by means of this request, one should cause them to accept the invitation.
For it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*: "One should properly invite at least three Brahmins as described above" (MDh 3.187).
Thus, being self-possessed—meaning free from grief, madness, and so forth—one does not become possessed of fault.
Or rather, one should be self-possessed, with restrained senses, pure, and disciplined;
and even when invited by those Brahmins, one should act through the operations of mind, speech, and body [in such a manner].
One must be self-controlled and disciplined. 1.225
Having honored those invited Brāhmaṇas with a welcome in the afternoon, as previously defined, he—
having sipped water (ācānta) and holding the purifier (pavitra) in his hand— should cause them to sit upon their seats.
(YDh 1.226) Having summoned those invited Brāhmaṇas and honored them with words of welcome in the afternoon, as described.

Having performed the worship, and having had their feet washed and sipped water (ācamana), he— himself with *pavitra* grass in hand— should cause those who also have *pavitra* grass in their hands to sit upon the prepared seats.

Although it is stated here in general terms that this should be done in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), nevertheless, it is most auspicious to begin during the *kutapa* hour and complete the rite within the subsequent five *muhūrtas*.
The muhūrtas of the day are always known to be fifteen;
among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called kutapa.
Since the sun always becomes less intense at midday,
therefore an undertaking begun at that time is distinguished as yielding infinite fruit.
"Because of the scriptural statement: 'The four muhūrtas that follow the Kutapa muhūrta—this group of five muhūrtas is indeed desired as the abode of Svadhā. (Matsya Purāṇa 22.84–85, 88).
Likewise, another set of items useful for the *śrāddha* rite, known by the name *kutapa*, has been mentioned: midday, a sword, a vessel, as well as a Nepalese woolen blanket,
silver, *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth.
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because these eight cause torment (saṃtāpa) to such a person, they are therefore renowned as "kutapa."
Thus (1.226). (Matsya Purāṇa 22.86–87):

One should invite an even number of Brahmins for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors, on a purified spot that has been strewn [with grass] and slopes toward the south. YDh 1.227.
At a śrāddha for the gods or one performed on auspicious occasions, he should seat an even number of Brāhmaṇas of equal status;
how? according to his ability, without exceeding his capacity.

In that Vaiśvadeva rite, there are two [balls] for each of the three beginning with the mother—either two for each of the three individually, or two for all three together; likewise, two for each of the three beginning with the father—either two for each of the three individually, or two for all three together;
and likewise for the maternal grandfather and the others.
And in the three groups [of ancestors], the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed either separately or as a single common procedure (*tantra*).
In the ancestral *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, one should seat an odd number—that is, an unequal number—[of Brahmins]; this is how the text is to be connected.

And this should be performed on a site that is strewn all around, covered, pure, smeared with cow dung and other such substances, and sloping toward the south—that is, inclined toward the south. (1.227)

The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or else, the ritual procedure for the Vaiśvadeva rite [is performed]. Regarding the divine Vaiśvadeva rite, two Brāhmaṇas should be seated facing east;
regarding the ancestral rite, since there is no specific rule stated as "an odd number," [the general rule applies].
The specific rule is stated: "Three at the rite for the ancestors.
At the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), which is the station of the ancestors and so forth, three [brāhmaṇas] should be seated facing north.
He states another alternative: "Or even one by one."
In the Vaiśvadeva rite and the Pitrya rite, one should seat one [representative] for each;
there is an option according to what is possible.
The same applies to the invitation and other procedures for the maternal grandfathers in the Śrāddha.
"Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each"—this is the view; [the rite] should be performed like the ancestral śrāddha.
In both the ancestral śrāddha and the maternal grandfather's śrāddha, the Vaiśvadevika portion should be performed either separately or by a single ritual procedure (tantra).
The word *tantra* denotes a collective performance.
However, when only two Brahmins are obtained, then one should prepare a single vessel for the Vaiśvadeva offering and appoint one Brahmin for each of the two [offerings]. As it has been said:
Vasiṣṭha says:
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the portion for the gods (daiva) be prepared?
Having set aside from the vessel some of all the food that has been prepared, [one should offer it].
"Having performed [the rites] in a temple of the gods, one should then proceed with the *śrāddha*.
One should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). (VaDh 11.30–31) 1.227.
Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke the Viśvedevas with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas...
(RV 2.41.13). Immediately thereafter, having given water into the hands of the Brahmins intended for the Vaiśvadeva rite, [he gives] an even number of *kuśas* for the purpose of the seats.

Having placed double the number of seats on the right side and having asked the Brāhmaṇas, "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas," and being permitted by them with the words, "Invoke them," he should invoke them with the Ṛgvedic verse, "O Viśvedevas, come hither," and with the Smārta mantra, "May the highly fortunate ones come. This should be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin) and moving clockwise.

"Then, having performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should proceed counter-clockwise for the ancestors," because of this specific traditional injunction regarding rites for the ancestors. (YDh 1.232) // 1.229 //

Then, having scattered barley grains over a vessel containing a purifier (pavitra), and having poured water with the verse *śaṃ no devīḥ*, he should likewise pour barley grains with the formula *yavo 'si*.
With the mantra *yā divyāḥ*, he should distribute the *arghya* water into their hands. (YDh 1.230–231ab)
Then, having strewn barley-grains around the ground in a clockwise direction near the Brāhmaṇas invited for the Vaiśvadeva rite,

he should next pour water into a vessel made of metal or another material that contains a *pavitra* and is covered with a pair of *kuśa* blades, reciting the verse "śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye. Then, having poured barley-grains while reciting the mantra beginning with "yavo 'si dhānyarājo vā," and subsequently having scattered perfumes and flowers, [he should place them] within the *pavitra* of the *arghya* vessels.
With the mantra beginning with "The divine waters on the earth," he should pour the *arghya* water into the hands of the Brahmins, saying, "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*. (1.230)
Having offered water, fragrance, garlands, incense, and lamps,
as well as a gift of clothing and water for the purpose of cleansing the hands;
then, having given water for the purpose of cleansing the hands, one should offer fragrance, flowers, incense, and lamps in due order, as well as a gift of clothing.

And regarding perfumes and so forth, the specific distinctions mentioned in another Smṛti should be observed. Viṣṇu has stated: "Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka are for the purpose of anointing," as well as flowers.
At a śrāddha ceremony, jasmine, white yūthikā, all water-born flowers, and the campaka are praised as being of noble birth.
Thus have been stated those [flowers] that are to be avoided:
those with a pungent odor, those without fragrance, those growing from trees near a *caitya*, and those which are red in color. These flowers are to be rejected.
It should not be produced from thorny plants;
however, even if it is produced from thorny plants, one should offer that which is white and fragrant.
One should not offer that which is red.
One should also offer red substances, such as those derived from saffron and lotus; these and other such items are to be understood [as appropriate].
Furthermore, Viṣṇu has stated a specific rule regarding incense:
one should not offer any part of a living being for the purpose of incense.
"One should offer [incense] such as guggulu, śīkhaṇḍa, agaru, devadāru, sarala, and so forth, combined with ghee and honey" (cf. ViDh 79.9–10).
Regarding the lamp, a specific rule has been stated by Śaṅkha:
"A lamp should be offered with ghee or, alternatively, with sesame oil;
one should carefully avoid a lamp produced from fat or marrow. Thus it is said. And one should give a covering that is bright, new, unwashed, and complete with its fringe.
And one should perform this entire section on the Vaiśvadeva rites facing north;
the section pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya) facing south.
As Vṛddha-Śātātapa has said:
"Facing north for the gods and facing south for the ancestors, one should offer everything according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the rites for the gods in the Pārvaṇa ceremony. (1.231)
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and circumambulating the ancestors counter-clockwise,
he should offer double-folded kuśa grass and, having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," he should, being permitted by them, recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ."
Then, immediately after the Vaiśvadeva section,
having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) so that it becomes the prācīnāvīta;
by using the word "then" (tataḥ) here, the sequential performance according to sections (kāṇḍānusamaya) is indicated.

Having given an odd number of *kuśa* blades, doubled over, to the three ancestors beginning with the father, turning them from right to left (counter-clockwise) for the purpose of a seat upon the seats preceded by water, he should again give water; having given water, having given the doubled *darbha* blades as a seat, and having given water again— (ĀśG 4.7.7–8).
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Āśvalāyana.
Furthermore, this offering of water at the beginning and the end should be understood as being for the purpose of establishing each individual ritual item in both the Vaiśvadeva and the Pitrya rites.

Then, having asked the Brahmins, "Shall I invite the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers? and being permitted by them with the words, "Invite them," he should invoke the ancestors and others with this verse, "uśantas tvā nidhīmahi," and then worship them with the mantra beginning with, "āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ. (1.232–1.233)

Having scattered sesame seeds all around with the mantra "apahatāḥ," one should perform the functions usually served by barley using sesame seeds; then, as before, one should offer the *arghya* and other rites.
Having offered the *arghya*, one should place the remnants of those offerings into a vessel according to the prescribed rule.
With the words, "Thou art the place for the ancestors," he places the vessel face down on the ground.
The rites accomplished with barley—such as the scattering [of grains] and so forth—should be performed with sesame seeds.
Then follows the procedure from the placing of the arghya vessels up to their covering.
One should perform [the rite] as before;

however, there is this distinction: having scattered sesame seeds around the Brāhmaṇas in a counter-clockwise direction with the mantra beginning "The Asuras and Rākṣasas have been struck down," one should pour water into three vessels made of silver or other materials, each containing a *kūrca* (bundle) of an odd number of *kuśa* grasses, with the mantra "May the goddesses be auspicious to us. Then, having thrown sesame seeds and fragrant flowers with the mantra beginning "Thou art sesame, Soma is thy deity," one should [recite] "Svadhā-arghyāḥ."

Having thus placed the *arghya* vessels before the Brahmins, at the conclusion of the mantra "yā divyā," he should offer the *arghya* into the hands of the Brahmins, saying: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*.
According to the alternative view that there may be one vessel for each [deity] in both cases, there should likewise be three vessels.

The ritual action: Having thus offered the *arghya*, one should take the remnants of those *arghyas*—the water from the *arghya* offerings that has flowed from the hands of the Brahmins—and place them into the *pitṛ-pātra*.

Then, having placed a bundle of *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing southward upon the ground, one should turn that vessel face down (*nyubja*) over it with the mantra, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*).
Upon that, one places the *pavitra* strainers from the *arghya* vessels.

One should set them down. Immediately thereafter, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and coverings using the formula: "O Father, this is your perfume; O Father, this is your flower," and so forth. (1.234–1.235) He describes the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) in two verses:
intending to perform the *agnaukaraṇa*, one takes food soaked in ghee and asks [the ancestors for permission].
Having been authorized with the words "Do so," and having offered oblations into the fire according to the ritual for the ancestors (pitṛyajña),
he should, with a concentrated mind, place the remnants of the offering into the vessels—
using whatever are available, and especially those made of silver. (YDh 1.236–237)
Immediately thereafter, intending to offer it into the fire, he should take food soaked in ghee and smeared with ghee, and ask the Brahmins, "I shall perform the offering in the fire.
The mention of ghee is for the purpose of excluding soup, vegetables, and the like.

Then, having been authorized by them with the words "Do so," wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should prepare pure food, take a portion with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon, and offer it according to the requirements for a sacrificial oblation (*avadāna*) with the formulas: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage!

and "To Agni, the bearer of the *kavya*, *svadhā*! Homage! Having offered into the fire according to the ritual procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, and having thrown the *mekṣaṇa* into the fire, [he should place] the remainder of the offering—excluding that which is in earthenware—[into the vessels].

One should offer [the food] specifically into vessels made of silver or other materials obtained as available—such as those belonging to one's father and ancestors—and not into the vessels used for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. One should do so with composure, with an undistracted mind.
Although it is stated here without qualification that "into the fire," this nevertheless refers to one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni).

In the view that all fires are maintained, since the *aupāsana* fire is absent, the oblation in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*—which occurs immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—is performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
This is because we observe an exception to the rule "Smārta rites are performed in the marriage fire," namely: "The oblation is in the *dakṣiṇāgni* due to its proximity.
As Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"One who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), being composed, should offer the oblation in the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni);
one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), however, [should offer] in the domestic fire (aupāsana), or in the absence of fire, in a Brahmin or in water.

Thus, according to the view that maintains only half of the sacred fires (ardhādhāna-pakṣa), because the domestic fire (aupāsana) is present, the fire-oblation (agnīkaraṇa-homa) for one who has maintained the sacred fires is performed in the domestic fire itself, just as it is for one who has not maintained the sacred fires.
Thus, because the ritual procedure for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is extended to the three [occasions] beginning with the Anvaṣṭakā,
in the four [rites] beginning with those performed for specific desires (kāmya), the oblation is offered directly into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa. As the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have said:
The Anvaṣṭakya on the day before, the monthly rite performed month by month,
the Pārvaṇa, the Kāmya, that on the Aṣṭamī of a festival, and the Ekoddiṣṭa as the eighth.
In the first four [rites], the oblation is prescribed to be offered into the fire for those who maintain the sacred fires;
in the latter four, it should be placed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors.

The meaning of this is as follows: The *aṣṭakās* are prescribed by the rule, "The *aṣṭakās* [occur] on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons" (*Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra* 2.4.1). Among these, that which is performed on the ninth day is called the *anvaṣṭakya*.

That which is to be performed on the seventh [lunar day] is done on the preceding day; and that which is prescribed by extension from the *anvaṣṭakya* rite for any lunar day from the fifth onwards in the dark fortnight of every month.
That which is prescribed for the new moon day (amāvāsyā) after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is the Pārvaṇa rite.
That which is prescribed under asterisms such as Kṛttikā when there is a desire for heaven and other rewards is the Kāmya rite.
That which is prescribed for occasions of prosperity— such as the birth of a son and so forth, as well as the consecration of tanks, gardens, and deities— is the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity rite).
On the eighth lunar day, the *aṣṭakā* rites are prescribed.
Regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa*: here, by the term *ekoddiṣṭa*,
one indicates the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
In that regard, because the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite also exists there [in the *pārvaṇa*],

whereas it is absent in the direct *ekoddiṣṭa*; or else, according to the view of the author of the *Gṛhyabhāṣya*, because the *pāṇi-homa* (offering into the hand) exists even in the direct *ekoddiṣṭa*, it is the direct *ekoddiṣṭa* itself [that is intended].
Of these eight [offerings],
in the first four, the oblation is made into the fire by one who maintains a sacred fire; in the latter four, it is made into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors.

For a twice-born man who has lost his father, even if he is not maintaining the sacred fires (*niragnika*), the *pārvaṇa* rite is obligatory; therefore, for him as well, the oblation is offered directly into the hand.
"That twice-born man who has lost his father and does not perform the *śrāddha*... [is censured].
But he who [eats] at the end of the month [during the period of impurity] must perform an expiation every month.
Because of this statement:
"In the same way, in the case of optional rites, those for prosperity, the Aṣṭakā offerings, and the Ekoddiṣṭa, the oblation is offered in the hand alone;
indeed, in the absence of the sacred fire, one should present it in the hand of the Brahmin" (MDh 3.212).
Thus, according to the *Manusmṛti*,
it is stated that there is a prohibition against taking a separate mouthful from what has been placed in the hand;
as the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* have said:
The unintelligent eat the food given in the palm of the hand separately;
by that, the ancestors are satisfied, yet they do not receive the remaining food.
Whatever has been placed in the palm of the hand and whatever else has been prepared should be enjoyed as one; no distinction exists between them.
Thus [ends the section]. 1.236 // 1.237 //
Having offered food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra, "The earth is the vessel";
then, having recited "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should place the thumb of the twice-born guest into the food. (YDh 1.238)
