Having placed food—such as boiled rice, soup, milk-rice, and ghee—into the vessels, one should consecrate the vessels with the mantra beginning "The earth is your bowl" (*pṛthivī te pātram*). Then, with the verse "Viṣṇu strode across this" (*idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame*), one should place the thumb of the twice-born guest into the food. And in that regard, for the Vaiśvadeva rite, [the performer] should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). O Viṣṇu...

At the rite for the gods, one should say, "O Viṣṇu, protect the *havya*"; at the rite for the ancestors, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the *kavya*. One should indeed say, "Protect the *havya* and the *kavya*" in their respective order.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu (1.238).

Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyahṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhuvātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as necessary for their comfort. Immediately thereafter, having offered the food to the Viśvedevas in the divine rite with barley-water, saying: "This food, already served and yet to be served, is offered to the Viśvedevas until satiety."

Likewise, having informed the father by offering water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*), saying: "O Father, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarman*), this food has been served and will continue to be served until you are satisfied," and having similarly informed the grandfather and great-grandfather, he should then give the *āpośana* water. Following this, he should recite the *Gāyatrī* together with the previously mentioned *Vyāhṛtis*, the three-verse hymn beginning with "The winds are honey" (*madhu vātā*), and the word "Honey, honey, honey" (*madhu madhu madhu*) three times.
One should say, "Enjoy [the food] as you please. Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the ancestors and the gods, one should recite the Sāvitrī and the Madhumatī verses.
After announcing the Śrāddha, one should perform the *apośāna* rite, give the command to enjoy the meal (*juṣapraiṣa*), and then the feeding begins.
Likewise, one should recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the Vyāhṛtis either three times or once; and likewise the triplet beginning with "madhu vātā" and that group of three beginning with "madhu."

Thus, according to the statement of Pāraskara and others: "They too should eat while restraining their speech. Those Brāhmaṇas also, restraining their speech—that is, observing silence—should eat. (1.239)
Free from anger and without haste, one should give the desired food until [the guests] are satisfied;
likewise, having recited the purificatory mantras and the previously mentioned prayers.
"Food" consists of five kinds—eatable, chewable, lickable, suckable, and drinkable—and it should be that which is desired for the Brāhmaṇa, the deceased, and the performer of the rite.

Or whatever is pleasing [to the ancestors]. "Havisya" refers to food fit for the *śrāddha* oblation; it should be understood as comprising rice (*vrīhi*), *śāli* rice, barley (*yava*), wheat (*godhūma*), mung beans (*mudga*), black gram (*māṣa*), the food of sages (*munyanna*), black nightshade (*kālaśāka*), large-scaled fish (*mahāśalka*), cardamom (*elā*), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), black pepper (*marīca*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), jaggery (*guḍa*), sugar (*śarkarā*), camphor (*karpūra*), rock salt (*saindhava*), *sāṃbhara* salt, *panasa* fruit, coconut (*nālikera*), plantain (*kadalī*), jujube (*badara*), products of the cow such as milk, curd, ghee, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), honey, meat, and so forth, as established in other *smṛtis*.

By the term "fit for oblation" (*haviṣya*), there is the exclusion of that which is unfit—prohibited by other Smṛtis—such as *kodrava*, *masūra*, *caṇaka*, *kulattha*, *pulāka*, *niṣpāva*, *rājamāṣa*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *vārtāka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *upodikā*, bamboo shoots, long pepper (*pippalī*), *vacā*, *śatapuṣpā*, herbs, biḍa salt, buffalo milk, camel milk, curd, ghee, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and so forth. He should be free from anger even when causes for anger arise; he should be unhurried and composed.
The connection is that one should give until satiety; by the word "but" (tu), it is indicated that one should give in such a way that something remains as a remnant.
Because the remains of the meal are the allotted portion for the class of servants,

they declare that the leavings which have fallen upon the ground belong as their share to the class of servants at a rite for the ancestors, provided the giver is straightforward and free from deceit. (MDh 3.246)
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu;

likewise, having muttered purificatory texts such as the Puruṣasūkta and the Pāvamānī verses until satiety, and having recognized them as satiated, one should mutter the previously mentioned recitation along with the Vyāhṛtis, as it has been stated. (1.240)

Having taken up the food and asked them, "Are you satisfied? and having received their consent regarding the remainder, one should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once for each [guest]. Immediately thereafter, having taken all the food and asked them, "Are you satisfied?", and being told by them, "We are satisfied," [one should dispose of] the remainder...

Having asked, "Is there anything [else] to be done?", and having accepted the reply, "Let it be enjoyed together with those you desire," he should place that food on the ground in front of the Brahmin representing the ancestors, near the leavings, upon which Darbha grass with its tips pointing south has been spread;
after first pouring water mixed with sesame seeds while reciting the verse beginning with "ye agnidagdhāḥ," he should then pour more water mixed with sesame seeds.
Immediately after that, one should give water once into the hands of each Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of rinsing the mouth. // 1.241 //
Prior to this, the NSP adds: "The offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍapradāna):
taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing the south."
One should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) in the vicinity of the leavings, according to the ritual of the Pitṛyajña.

By the extension of the procedure of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, when there is the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru), one should take all the food together with the remains of the caru left over from the fire-offering (agnaukaraṇa) and offer the rice-balls in the vicinity of the fire.

In the absence of such [Brahmins], one should take all the food prepared for the sake of Brahmins, mix it with sesame seeds— that is, with *tila*— and, facing south, offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) near the remains of the meal according to the ritual procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. 1.242.
Before this, NSP and Pāṇḍeya add:
"The offering of imperishable water;
one should likewise give it for the maternal grandfathers, and then the water for sipping (ācamana)."
Then one should perform the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana) and the offering of inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka).

The ritual for the maternal grandfathers (mātāmaha), beginning with the invocation of the Viśvedevas and ending with the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), must be performed in exactly this same manner. Immediately thereafter, one should provide the Brahmins with water for sipping (ācamana).

Then one should perform the recitation of the benediction (*svastivācana*): one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce the blessing by saying, "Pronounce the *svasti*. When they have said "Svasti," one should offer water into the hands of the Brahmins, saying, "Say, 'May it be inexhaustible' (*akṣayyam astu*). They, in turn, should say, "May it be inexhaustible. (1.243)
Before this NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: "The recitation of *svadhā* / Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, one should utter the word *svadhā*."
"Let it be spoken," being thus permitted, [he should say] "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for those present.

Immediately thereafter, having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) such as gold, silver, and so forth according to his ability, and having said, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be spoken," and being permitted by those Brahmins with the words "Let it be spoken," he should utter the *svadhā*-formula: "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for those present—the ancestors beginning with the father, and the maternal ancestors beginning with the maternal grandfather. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.244)
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should then pour water on the ground;
and when the Brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should mutter this:
"May those Brahmins say, 'Let there be *svadhā*.'"
When they have spoken thus, he should immediately sprinkle water on the ground from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Then he should say, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased.
And when the Brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should mutter what is stated immediately hereafter. 1.245.
Before this NSP and Pāṇḍeya add:
*brāhmaṇaprārthanā* / *dātāro no'bhivardhantāṃ vedāḥ saṃtatir eva ca*.
"May our faith not depart, and may we have much to give. [This means:
"May givers of gold and other gifts increase in our family; may they be numerous;
and may the Vedas flourish."
[May it continue] by means of study, teaching, knowledge of its meaning, and the performance [of its rites];
and may our lineage— through the succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth— and our faith— that is, our steadfast devotion toward ancestral rites— not go away, let it not depart from us.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74).
The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] with the thought: "May there be for us much and boundless gold and other such wealth to be given. // 1.246 //

Having spoken thus and having uttered affectionate words, one should prostrate and dismiss [the guests] with the mantra "vāje vāje," being joyful; the dismissal is performed starting with the ancestors (pitṛpūrva).
Thus, having recited the previously mentioned prayer-mantra, [one should proceed].

And having spoken affectionate words such as, "We are blessed; our home has been purified by the dust of your two feet; disregarding the hardship of eating only vegetables and the like, we have been graced by you," he should bid them farewell after prostrating, performing a circumambulation, and offering salutations.

As for how one should perform the dismissal, he says: with this verse, "O winners of the prize, come to us for every prize," one should perform the dismissal with a pleased and well-pleased mind, beginning with the ancestors—starting from the great-grandfather and ending with the Viśvedevas—while holding on to the *darbha* grass, saying, "May the ancestors rise. (NSP reads: "May the ancestors rise. // 1.247 //
But on that vessel into which the remnants were previously poured,
having turned the Pitṛ-vessel face upwards, he should dismiss the Brahmins.

(YDh 1.248) "In which" means in that Arghya-vessel into which the remnants— the water from the Arghya offerings that had flowed from the hands of the Brahmins— were previously deposited at the conclusion of the Arghya-giving.
Having placed that arghya vessel face down, he should turn it face up—upward-facing—and then dismiss the Brahmins.
This [act] should be understood as occurring after the recitation of the benedictory mantras (*āśīr-mantra*) but before the verse beginning with "vāje vāje";
for this is indicated by the hearing of the suffix *ktvā* in the expression "having done, he should dismiss" (*kṛtvā visarjayet*). (1.248)
Having circumambulated [the Brahmins] from left to right, he should eat what has been served to the ancestors;
he should observe celibacy for that night together with the Brahmins.
Immediately thereafter, having followed the Brahmins as far as the boundary, they should depart.

Having been granted permission with the words "Be seated," he should circumambulate them and return; then, together with his loved ones, he should eat the remnants of the *śrāddha* meal enjoyed by his ancestors.
This is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Regarding the phrase "meat according to one's desire" (YDh 1.179), it was stated there that this is "at the wish of the twice-born.
On the night connected to the day on which the Śrāddha was performed, [the meat] should be eaten by the partakers.
The performer, together with the Brahmins, should be a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
By the use of the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that he should also be free from eating a second meal and so forth;
[specifically avoiding] brushing the teeth, betel, oil-massage, bathing, and [excessive] fasting.
One who performs a śrāddha ceremony should avoid these seven things: sexual pleasure, medicine, food given by others, and the remaining four.

Furthermore, one who has eaten at a funeral feast (śrāddha) should avoid these eight things: eating again, traveling on a journey, carrying a load, Vedic study, sexual intercourse, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and performing fire-offerings (homa).
Because of this statement. 1.249.
Having thus described the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, he now speaks of the *vṛddhi* śrāddha:
"In this manner, proceeding in a clockwise direction, [one should worship] the Nāndīmukha ancestors at a rite of prosperity (*vṛddhi*)."
One should sacrifice balls of food mixed with curd and jujube fruits, and perform the rites with barley.

Regarding the *vṛddhi* [śrāddha] performed on occasions such as the birth of a son, one should worship—that is, honor—the ancestors in the manner thus described. In this regard, he states a specific rule:

Regarding the term *pradakṣiṇāvṛtka*: one whose mode of proceeding (*āvṛt*) or method of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-paddhati*) is clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*) is called *pradakṣiṇāvṛtka*, which means, in short, one whose movement is clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa-pracāra*).
"Of the Nāndīmukhas" is an epithet for the ancestors (pitṛs).
Consequently, in the invocation and other rites, one should observe the following usage: "I shall invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors," "the Nāndīmukha grandfathers," and so forth.
To the question "How should he sacrifice? he says:
Mixed with curd and jujube;
*karkandhū* is the fruit of the *badarī* tree.
The connection is that one should worship after offering balls of food mixed with curd and jujube fruits (*badarīphala*).
All rites that are accomplished with sesame seeds should be performed with barley.
Furthermore, the number of Brahmins is already indicated here by the statement: "An even number for the gods, according to one's ability" (YDh 1.227).
The enumeration of "proceeding clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇāvṛt*) and so forth is for the purpose of illustrating other specific rules mentioned in other *smṛtis*.
As Āśvalāyana says:

"Now, in the case of an *abhyudayika* (rite for prosperity), the Brahmins are even in number, the *darbha* grasses are rootless, one should face the east, wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), and proceed clockwise."

The ritual procedure consists of using barley in place of sesame seeds and the offering of perfumes and other items twice each; one should provide straight *darbha* grass for the seat, [reciting]: "You are barley, having Soma as your deity, fashioned by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice;
offered by the ancients for the sake of prosperity, [I offer you] to these *Nāndīmukha* ancestors."
"Gladden the worlds for us, svāhā"—with these words, the barley is sown.
"O Viśvedevas, this is your arghya; O Nāndīmukha ancestors, this is your arghya"—with these words, the arghya is offered according to the respective gender of the deities.
The oblation in the hand [is made] with: "Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana! Svāhā to Soma Pitṛmat!
In place of the triplet beginning with "The winds blow sweet for the one who follows the Ṛta," [he recites] "Sing unto him."
Thus he should cause them to hear the five *madhumatī* verses; the sixth verse, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," is recited when they have sipped water and their stomachs are full.

"Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, one should offer two *piṇḍas* for each [ancestor] using the remnants of the meal mixed with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)," and so forth (*ĀśGṛParśiṣṭa* 2.19).
Although it is stated in general terms that "one should sacrifice to the ancestors," [the specific procedure follows].
Nevertheless, the three types of *śrāddha* and their sequence should be understood from another *smṛti*,
as Śātātapa has said:
"The *śrāddha* for the mother should come first, and that for the fathers immediately after."
"Therefore, on the anniversary of the death of maternal grandfathers, three Śrāddhas are prescribed. (1.250)
He speaks of the *ekoddiṣṭa*:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the gods; it has one *arghya* offering and one *pavitraka*;
it is indeed without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa*, and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). (YDh 1.251)
The term *ekoddiṣṭa* is the name of the rite, meaning that śrāddha in which a single person is designated (*uddiṣṭa*).
This is because of the concluding statement: "One should perform the rest as previously described" (YDh 1.254).
When the full dharma of the *pārvaṇa* rite is applicable, the specific details are now stated:

it is "devoid of gods," meaning it is without the Viśvedevas; it consists of a single *arghya* vessel with a single *darbha* blade as a purifier; and it is devoid of both the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇahoma*).
"Apasavyavat" means like one who wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
By this, he indicates that in the *ābhyudayika* rite mentioned immediately prior, the *yajñopavīta* (wearing of the thread over the left shoulder) applies. // 1.251 //
Furthermore:

At the dismissal of the Brahmins, while they are standing in the place of imperishability (akṣayya-sthāna), he should say, "May you be delighted," and they should reply, "We are delighted. (YDh 1.252)
Regarding what was stated:
"Then one should recite the benediction (*svastivācana*) and likewise offer the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*)" (YDh 1.242),
in that context, one should say "may [it] attend [the ancestors]" (*upatiṣṭhatām*) in place of the word "inexhaustible" (*akṣayya*).
When the dismissal of the Brahmins is to be performed, at the conclusion of the recitation of "vāje vāje," he should say, "May you be pleased," while touching darbha grass;
they, for their part, should say, "We are pleased. Thus it is said.
This is well known;
the rest is as before—this being the meaning.
And this should be performed at midday.
As Devala has said:
"Rites for the gods are performed in the forenoon, those for the ancestors in the afternoon;
the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity is in the morning."
Regarding the rule "one should eat what was consumed by the ancestors" (YDh 1.249), a prohibition is observed for a specific type of *ekoddiṣṭa* rite:
"In the case of *navaśrāddha* rites, that which remains [in the house], and that which has been kept overnight in the home..."
"And one should never eat what remains after the husband and wife have eaten. Thus [it is said]. And the *navaśrāddha* (the nine-day funeral rite) is also shown:
on the first day, the third day, the fifth, and likewise the seventh.
On the ninth and the eleventh [days] as well, that is called the *navaśrāddha*. Thus [ends verse 1.252].
He now describes the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite:

"One should prepare four vessels joined with scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of the *arghya* offering; one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (YDh 1.253)
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," one should perform the remainder as previously prescribed.
This Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for a woman is also performed as an Ekoddiṣṭa.
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of the Arghya offering, according to the procedure previously stated.
By stating that "there are four bowls joined with sesame seeds," it is shown that there are four Brahmins for the group of ancestors (pitṛvarge),
while two remain established for the Vaiśvadeva rite.

In this rite, one should divide the water remaining in the vessel for the *preta* into three parts and pour it into the vessels for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) with the two mantras beginning with "ye samānāḥ samanasaḥ.
The remainder of the ritual, from the invocation of the Viśvedevas until the final dismissal, is to be performed as before, according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure.

One should perform [the rite] as follows: having offered arghya with the water remaining in the arghya-vessel intended for the deceased into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa seated at the place of the deceased, one should complete the remainder according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure;
for the three [Brāhmaṇas] representing the ancestors, it is according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure.
This *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* just mentioned,

as well as the *ekoddiṣṭa* mentioned prior to it, must be performed for a woman— that is, for one's mother as well. By stating this, [the author implies that] in the case of the *pārvaṇa* [rite, it is not required].
It is thus stated that the śrāddha for the mother must be performed separately.
In this context, some explain the word "preta" as referring to the great-grandfather of the father.
Because it is included within those three, it is logical that the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) and other rites cease after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony;

however, for one who has died immediately [before the anniversary], since the offering of rice balls and water continues thereafter, its inclusion [within the three] is not appropriate. For this very reason, Yama said:
"He who joins a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed to a separate *piṇḍa* becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his ancestors.
Since the term "preta" (deceased) is applicable even to the fourth [generation]— as one has departed (*ita*) far away (*prakṛṣṭam*)— [this rule applies there as well].
Furthermore, because we observe the practical application [of the rule] stating, "One should offer [the oblation] specifically to the *preta*s," and also:
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha preceded by the gods; one should feed the ancestors (*pitṛ*s) there, but one should not designate the *preta* again."

Thus, a prohibition of the *śrāddha* and other rites for the deceased is observed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony; however, that [prohibition] is not possible for one who has died immediately [prior].
Because the performance of *śrāddha* is prescribed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions;

furthermore, this statement—"Sapiṇḍatā ceases with the seventh person" (MDh 5.60)—is only consistent if the fourth ancestor is indeed included within the [three] [ancestors]. For the fourth ancestor pervades three *piṇḍas*, the fifth pervades two *piṇḍas*, and the sixth pervades one *piṇḍa*.
Regarding the statement "cessation at the seventh," the phrase "in the vessels for the ancestors" also applies only to this position because the father is the primary [ancestor], and not otherwise,
since the great-grandfather is the primary [ancestor] in other cases.

Therefore, the claim that "one should pour that vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors" means that one should pour the vessel of the great-grandfather into the vessels of the father and the others, is incorrect.
For in this context, the joining of the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) does not serve the purpose of precluding the offering of further funeral balls and so forth hereafter;
rather, it is for the sake of the deceased father’s cessation of the state of being a *preta* and his attainment of the status of a *pitṛ*.
And the state of being a *preta* is a condition of experiencing extreme suffering produced by hunger and thirst.
As Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O descendant of Bhṛgu, it is proclaimed that the residence of men in the world of the departed lasts for one year; there, hunger and thirst shall prevail every day."
And the attainment of the status of a *pitṛ* (ancestor) consists in a connection with the deities of the *śrāddha*, such as the Vasus;

it is understood that one attains the status of a *pitṛ* through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, performed together with the previous *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, by means of the cessation of the state of being a *preta*.
"For him to whom these sixteen *preta-śrāddhas* have not been offered, his state as a *preta* remains firmly established even if hundreds of other *śrāddhas* are performed.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
One should offer four rice-balls; into these, one should first place [the portion] for him.
From that point on, the deceased indeed partakes in the commonality of the ancestors.

Because of such statements as these, and because by the phrase "the deceased for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed," the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is prohibited through the separate procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*,
the offering of the rice-ball is instead performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure along with [the other ancestors].
It is understood that this is set aside by the procedure for the annual, fortnightly, and ekoddiṣṭa rites;
furthermore, regarding the statement "one should not designate a deceased person [as a specific recipient],"...
This is for the purpose that one should not even utter the word "preta" (departed spirit) there, but rather only the word "pitṛ" (father/ancestor);
nor is the word "preta" applied there solely because of having gone to a superior state.

For it has been stated that the state of experiencing distinguished suffering is designated by the word *preta* through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Even the application of the word *preta* to one who has merely died is based on its previous state [of being a living being].
Furthermore, regarding the rule "the sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person" (MDh 5.60), [this refers to the living lineage].
And because the first *piṇḍa* pervades the fourth, the second pervades the fifth, and the third pervades the sixth.
It is likewise logical that [the sapinda relationship] ceases at the seventh [generation];
moreover, sapinda-relationship does not extend through the lineage of those who have offered the funeral cakes (nirvāpyapiṇḍa), because such a definition would be too narrow.
However, it has been stated that [the relationship] is through the continuity of the constituent parts of a single body.

Furthermore, the word "father" (pitṛ) applies to those who have attained the status of deities of the śrāddha by means of the cessation of their state as *preta*s; thus, the expression "in the vessels for the fathers" (pitṛpātreṣu) is not contradictory.
Therefore, the meaning is that the immediate teacher has presented the opponent's view by way of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[This concerns] the water in the vessel for the deceased and the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) for him.
It is established that the *saṃsarga* (merging) takes place with the *piṇḍas* in the vessels of the ancestors;
however, the Teacher has merely presented the opinion of others.
And this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father is to be understood as occurring when the three ancestors beginning with the grandfather have all died.

If the father has died while the grandfather is still living, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite does not take place at all; and for those who have died out of the natural order of succession, the *sapiṇḍatā* should never be performed.
Because of this statement; as for the verse of Manu: "He whose father has passed away, or even if his grandfather should still be living..."
"Having proclaimed the name of his father, he should proclaim the name of his great-grandfather" (MDh 3.221).
This rule, too, is intended to regulate the application of the word "father" [in the invocation], not for the purpose of offering two funeral cakes (piṇḍas). How so?
"But while the father is living, one should offer [the cakes] to those who precede him."
But if one's father has passed away while the grandfather is still living, [he should perform the śrāddha for the father].
The syntactical connection is that he too should offer [the cakes] to the ancestors alone.
To explain how he should offer them in both cases, [the text] says:
"Having pronounced the name of his father, he should mention the great-grandfather" (MDh 3.221).

By taking the beginning and the end in this manner, the formula "to the fathers, to the grandfathers, to the great-grandfathers" is to be used everywhere; never, however, should the grandfather or great-grandfather be placed at the beginning, nor the great-great-grandfather or his father at the end. And thus, because words such as "father" and so forth denote a relationship, even while the father is still living, [the offering is made] to the father’s [father].
"To the fathers, to the grandfathers, to the great-grandfathers. If the grandfather is still living, [the formula is]: "To the fathers, to the grandfathers, to the great-grandfathers."
Consequently, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the mantras beginning with "May the fathers be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*) in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

As for the statement of Viṣṇu: "He whose father is deceased should, having offered the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his father, offer to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather" (ViDh 75.4), its meaning is as follows:
While the grandfather is still living, or when the father has died, one should offer a single pinda for the father according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure; then,

one should offer [pindas] for the two ancestors beyond the father’s grandfather— that is, for the father’s grandfather and the one after him— while the grandfather himself remains as the representative of one's own self.
Since the great-grandfather remains as the recipient, one should then give to the great-grandfather and to the two who follow him;
however, the rule regarding the employment of words is exactly as previously stated.
In this same way, it should be understood that there is likewise an absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for one killed by a cow, a Brahmin, or similar causes;
as Kātyāyana has said:

"When one's father has been killed by a Brāhmaṇa or others, has fallen [from his caste], is devoid of social ties, or has died through a transgression of the rules, the offering should be given to those very persons to whom he himself would give.

Thus, when the father has been killed by a cow or a Brāhmaṇa, if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is possible, one should bypass him and perform the *pārvaṇa* ritual for the grandfather and the other ancestors.
By the statement "it is not possible," the absence of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is understood.
Also in another *smṛti*:
"For those men whose lineage is severed, there is no *sapiṇḍatā*."

"And the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites should not be performed together with these. Thus, regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the mother and so forth, there is a disagreement concerning the lineage (*gotra*):
should they be offered by the husband's lineage or by the father's lineage?
Because statements are seen in both [texts]:
"A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step of the marriage ceremony;
the offering of rice-balls and water for her must be performed by the lineage of her husband."
This statement concerns the husband's lineage and so forth:
"One should not abandon the father's lineage and act according to the husband's lineage;
for women, the paternal family remains [the primary one] both at birth and in times of misfortune."
This refers to the paternal lineage (*pitṛgotra*) and so forth.

Thus, in cases of disagreement regarding the lineage— such as in *āsura* and other types of marriage, or in the case of making a daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*)— the paternal lineage alone applies, because of specific statements in each instance and because the act of giving [the girl away] has not been rescinded.
In the *brāhma* and other forms of marriage, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*), just as between rice and barley, or as between the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* sāmans. And in that regard:
"By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone..."
Because of the statement, "One should travel by that path of the virtuous; traveling by it, one does not incur fault" (MDh 4.178),
there is a settled rule based on the practice handed down through family lineage.
Because there is no other subject matter for this statement apart from such topics as these;
however, where there is neither a settled rule from the scriptures nor established custom, in that case, "one's own satisfaction alone" [is the authority] (MDh 2.6).
From this statement, it follows that one's own satisfaction alone is the determining authority, as in the rule:
"in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [after birth]" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.14).
Regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a mother as well, contradictory statements are observed; therein, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with the paternal grandmother and others is recorded in the Smṛtis.
Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi states that the husband must also perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his wife together with his own mother and others:
"When a woman dies without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍatā*;
her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* shall take place together with [his] mother-in-law and the others."
Yama has stated that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a woman must be performed with her husband alone: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even after death, she has attained oneness with him through mantras, oblations, and vows."
But Uśanas has declared that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed together with the maternal grandfather:
"Just as the sons perform the *sapiṇḍatā* for the father's paternal grandfather when a full year has elapsed,
so too should this *sapiṇḍatā* be performed for the mother's maternal grandfather."
Likewise,
the Lord Śiva has declared: "When a full year has passed, sons should join their father with the grandfather, and likewise their mother with the maternal grandfather."
Thus, while there are various such statements, when a wife dies without a son, the husband should perform the sapindana for her with his own mother;
however, in the case of *anvārohaṇa* (following the husband in death), the son should perform the sapindana for his mother with his own father.
A son born of an Āsura or other such marriage belongs to the maternal grandfather alone;
whereas a son born of a Brāhma or other such marriage belongs to the father, the maternal grandfather, or the paternal grandmother.
One may act according to one's own discretion.
Even in this case, if there is a fixed family tradition, then one should act accordingly. Family tradition—
If it is also indefinite, then one may act according to one's own inclination, following the principle that "one's own satisfaction alone [is the authority].
In that regard, even when there is *sāpiṇḍya* with the mother, in cases such as the *anvaṣṭakā* rites where a separate *śrāddha* for the mother is specifically prescribed;

"On the Anvaṣṭakā days, on occasions of prosperity (vṛddhi), at Gayā, and on the anniversary of death, one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; elsewhere, it is performed together with the husband.
In that case, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha must be performed specifically with the maternal grandmother and the other female ancestors.

"In other cases, it is with the husband," because she shares in his portion through *sapiṇḍya* with the husband; "with the maternal grandfather," because she shares in his portion through *sapiṇḍya* with the maternal grandfather, and therefore [the offering is] with him alone.
As Śātātapa has said:
"Upon the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, she attains a single form with her husband's ancestors; therefore, the wife is a sharer in their portion.

This being so, when the mother’s *sapiṇḍya* is performed with the maternal grandfather, the śrāddha for the maternal grandfather must be performed as a regular (*nitya*) rite, just like the śrāddha for the paternal ancestors, together with the husband.
In the case of *sāpiṇḍya* with one's paternal grandmother or mother, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is not obligatory;
the settled conclusion is that if it is performed there is prosperity, but if it is not performed there is no transgression. (1.253–1.254)
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite occurs before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year.
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the end of the year, [one should offer] on his behalf every day or every month...
Or, for up to a year, he should give food along with a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa according to his ability.
By stating "prior to a year," it is shown that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* may take place either when the year is complete or before it;
as Āśvalāyana says: "Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* [is performed] at the end of the year or on the twelfth day" (ĀśGṛPar 3.11).

Kātyāyana also said: "Then, when a year has been completed, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* [should be performed]; or after three fortnights; or whenever an occasion for prosperity (*vṛddhi*) occurs before that time" (PārGṛPariśiṣṭa, Śrāddhasūtra 5).
[The occasions are] on the twelfth day, after three fortnights, upon the occurrence of a *vṛddhi*, or at the end of a year.
Thus, four positions have been shown.
Among them, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father must be performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) on the twelfth day,
because the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* cannot be accomplished without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
But when the performer is one who maintains the sacred fires, or if the deceased father himself possesses the sacred fires,
then the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa for the father must be performed on the twelfth day.
According to this statement,
one who maintains no sacred fires (niragnika), however, should perform [the rite] when three fortnights have passed, or upon reaching a year,
or even before the year has elapsed.

There arises this doubt: should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* be performed after having first performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, or should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* be performed first and those [sixteen śrāddhas] be performed at their respective times?
Because both types of statements are observed:
"One should not perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite at all without having offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*;
having completed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana*."
And there are sixteen *śrāddhas*:
on the twelfth day, at the three-fortnight mark, at six months, monthly, and the annual;
these sixteen *śrāddhas* have been remembered by the wise.
Thus they have been shown. Likewise:
"Even for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs before a year has passed, the monthly rites and the water-pot offering must be performed by him for the duration of that year. Thus it is said.

In that regard, having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, these [rites] should be performed at their own proper time; this is the primary rule (*prathamaḥ kalpaḥ*), because prior to that, there is no entitlement due to the time not having arrived.
As for the statement that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed even before the completion of a year after having performed sixteen *śrāddhas*, this is a rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*).
However, when one performs the *preta-śrāddhas* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* by virtue of it being a time of distress, one should perform them according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

But when one performs [the rites] according to the primary method at their own proper time, then one should perform the monthly *śrāddhas* in the same manner as one performs the annual *śrāddha*— whether it be the *pārvaṇa* or the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
This applies to those performing the sixteen *śrāddhas* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
One should perform all of those rites according to the procedure for the Ekoddiṣṭa.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, whenever one performs [the annual rites] again,
one should perform those [rites] in the same manner as one performs them every year.
According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),

this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*— performed together with the *śrāddha* for the deceased— is sufficient when performed by even one person, even if there are many brothers who have divided the inheritance; it need not be performed by all of them.
The *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the sixteen *śrāddhas* should be performed by a single person alone, even among those whose wealth has been divided.
This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).

Furthermore, this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, together with the *śrāddha* for the deceased (*preta-śrāddha*), must necessarily be performed by sons and other relatives for those who have not renounced the world (*asaṃnyāsin*), since its purpose is to effect liberation from the state of being a *preta*; however, it need not be performed for one who has renounced the world (*saṃnyāsin*).
As Uśanas said:
"One should never perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* for ascetics (*yatins*);
when the eleventh day has arrived, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed."
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for them should not be performed by sons or others;

simply by the taking up of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the state of being a *preta* does not arise at all. Thus, in the absence of a son, the funeral rites for the deceased must be performed until the end of the tenth day by that very person of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or another who has carried out the cremation ceremony.
Whether one is of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether it be a woman or a man,
whoever offers [the water] on the first day shall complete it for ten days.
Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*):
"This [rite] must also be performed for Śūdras on the twelfth day without mantras;
likewise, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for Śūdras is to be performed on the twelfth day, excluding the mantras" (ViDh 21.19–20).
Thus, according to the recollection of Viṣṇu:
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the annual rites, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, and others must necessarily be performed by the son;
for others, they are not mandatory. (1.255)
He states the times for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite:
"On the day of death, it should be performed every month for a year;
likewise, annually thereafter; and the first [rite] on the eleventh day. (YDh 1.256)
On the anniversary of the day of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed every month for a year;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone should be performed annually.
The first *ekoddiṣṭa*, which serves as the archetype for all *ekoddiṣṭas*,
is performed on the eleventh day; if the day of death is unknown, it should be performed on the day the news is heard or on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
For there is a traditional legal authority (*smṛti*) stating: "If [the day of death] is unknown, it should be given on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or on the day of the Śravaṇa constellation.
Regarding the phrase "on the new moon day," this refers to the new moon day associated with the month of departure;
it should be given on the day of departure, or even on the waning of the moon in that same month.
Thus it is from the Smṛti.
Regarding the phrase "on the day of death," a specific rule for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) has been stated by Jātūkarṇya:
"The Śrāddha that occurs after three fortnights [of the death] should take place on the very day of death."
"But for a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni), one should perform [the rites] below [the cremation], starting from the day of cremation.

The meaning is this: regarding the funeral rites (pretakarma) that take place within three fortnights (tripakṣa), those should be performed by the āhitāgni starting from the day of cremation; whereas the śrāddha that occurs after three fortnights should be performed on the very day of death.

However, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), everything [is performed] on the day of death itself. Some maintain that the phrase "the first [rite] on the eleventh day" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the period of impurity (*āśauca*).
This is because purity is an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) since the ritual must be performed by one who is pure.
Furthermore, having introduced the subject generally for all social classes with the words "Now, upon the cessation of impurity," Viṣṇu has prescribed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite [as follows] (ViDh 22.1–4).
That is incorrect;
for the śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common to all four castes, whereas the period of impurity (sūtaka) is distinct for each.
Thus, because of this contradiction with the traditional teaching of Paiṭhīnasi:
"One should perform the first Śrāddha on the eleventh day even while impure;
for the performer there is purity for that specific occasion, yet he remains impure thereafter."

And because this contradicts the statement of Śaṅkha, it follows that the statement of Viṣṇu, which begins with a general rule, is applicable even to the subject of ten-day impurity (daśāhāśauca). Furthermore,
regarding the phrase "and thus every year," it refers to every year.
On the day of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite was taught by the Lord of Yogins;
likewise, another Smṛti states:
"The honoring of one's mother and father should be performed year after year."
"One should perform a *śrāddha* without an offering to the gods (*adaiva*) and offer a single funeral cake (*piṇḍa*).
Yama also said:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the sons should perform [the rite] every year."
"The Ekoddiṣṭa rite for the mother and father should be performed separately on the anniversary of their death.
Vyāsa, however, prohibits the Pārvaṇa rite:
"The man who performs the Pārvaṇa rite while abandoning the Ekoddiṣṭa..."
"One should know that to be unperformed; he would be a slayer of his father.
However, Jamadagni spoke of the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]:
"And having effected sapinda-relationship according to rule, the legitimate son..."
"One should perform the *śrāddha* for one's mother and father on the anniversary of their death just as in the case of the *darśa* [new moon] sacrifice. Śātātapa also said:
"Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should always perform it according to the *pārvaṇa* rite."
The wise man should perform this rite every year, according to the procedure taught by Chāgaleya.
Regarding this conflict of statements,
the Southerners indeed maintain this settled rule:

"On the anniversary of the death of the parents, the *pārvaṇa* rite alone must be performed by the biological son (*aurasa*) and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), whereas the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is to be performed by the adopted son (*dattaka*) and others."
According to the statement of Jātūkarṇya:
"The *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons should perform [the rite] every year by the *pārvaṇa* procedure alone;
the other ten types of sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
That is incorrect; for there is no mention here of the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), but rather of "every year" (pratyabdam),
and there certainly exist [rites] distinct from the anniversary of death.
The annual *śrāddhas* are performed on the Akṣayyatṛtīyā, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Vaiśākha, and so forth;
therefore, this does not suffice to establish a fixed rule regarding the *pārvaṇa* or *ekoddiṣṭa* rites for the anniversary of the day of death (*kṣayāha*).
As for the statement of Parāśara:
For a legitimate son whose father has attained divinity, the rite extends through three generations;
in all cases, even for those of various lineages, it is performed on the single anniversary of the death of that one person.
Thus, even that does not establish [the rule],
because its meaning is as follows:
for one who has attained the state of a deity and has undergone the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite...
In all cases, for one's own biological father, the *pārvaṇa* rite must be performed for three generations.

However, regarding the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) for maternal uncles and others who belong to different lineages (*bhinnagotra*), that is an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a single individual alone.
Furthermore, it has been stated by Paiṭhīnasi that even after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone must be performed even by the legitimate son (*aurasa*):
"For the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed by the legitimate son on the anniversary of the day of death."
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, there is no *pārvaṇa* śrāddha for one's mother and father. Thus it is said.
The Northerners, moreover, establish this rule:
on the new moon day, or on the anniversary of death during the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the *pārvaṇa* rite is performed; on other anniversaries of death, it is only the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
This applies whether one's death occurred on the new moon day or during the fortnight of the departed (*pretapakṣa*).
In that case, the pārvaṇa rite must be performed; the ekoddiṣṭa rite is never to be done.
Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),
the elders do not respect that [view] either;
for by means of this statement of uncertain origin, they override many statements of certain origin that pertain specifically to the *kṣayāha* and the *pārvaṇa* rites.
For it is improper to excessively restrict general statements to the specific context of the new moon day, the dark fortnight, or the anniversary of death,

and because such general statements would otherwise be rendered meaningless; for in those cases where a general statement is restricted by a specific one, it occurs through the cognition of a relationship between the general and the particular.
The two statements are purposeful;

for example, the statement "one should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," which is taught as a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*) and pertains only to modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), becomes purposeful by conveying a connection through the medium of the characteristic of the *sāmidhenīs*.

In the case of the seventeen statements recited in the section concerning Mitravindā and others, the conclusion is meaningful because they convey a connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) specific to the Mitravindā sacrifice;
however, in the present case, since both [statements] relate solely to the occasion of death (*mṛtāha*), they lack such meaningfulness.
Therefore, in this context, it is logical that the rule for the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed as having the result of precluding the optional *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
nor [is there a contradiction] because the statements regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* refer specifically to the occasion of the death of one's mother or father.
And it is appropriate to establish that the statements regarding the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] refer to occasions other than the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*),
because the mention of mother, father, and son is present in both cases.
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, every year on the anniversary of death, the sons must separately perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* for their mother and father.
Likewise:

"Having established the status of being of the same funeral rice-ball (*sahapiṇḍatva*), the legitimate son (*aurasa*) should perform the *śrāddha* for his mother and father on the anniversary of their death (*kṣayāha*) according to the rules, like the *darśa* [rite]. Furthermore, as for what some say— that one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*) should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary of the death of his parents, while one without fires (*niragni*) should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*— [this is not correct].

Every year, on the anniversary of their death, a wise twice-born son who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite for his parents; one who does not maintain the sacred fires should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Sumantu,
that [objection] too is to be disregarded due to being countered by an opposing argument:
"Those Brahmins who maintain many sacred fires, as well as those who maintain only a single fire..."
For them, after the sapindikarana rite, the ekoddista ceremony is performed, not the parvana.
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa),
the following is the settled conclusion:
on the anniversary of the death (kṣayāha) of renunciants (saṃnyāsins), the son must perform only the pārvaṇa rite.
For an ascetic (yati), there is no *ekoddiṣṭa* rite here because he has taken up the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*);
due to the absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, his [ancestral rite] is always the *pārvaṇa*.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Pracetas:
"On the anniversary of death occurring on the new moon day, and on the anniversary of death occurring during the fortnight of the ancestors (pretapakṣa), the pārvaṇa rite alone is prescribed:
'Whether the anniversary of death for someone occurs on the new moon day, or again during the fortnight of the ancestors...'"
Since such statements, according to the method explained above, are intended to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*),
elsewhere— on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*)— there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) between the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, just as there is between rice and barley.
Nevertheless, while there exists a fixed convention established by family tradition, the choice is determined; in its absence, it is arbitrary.
Enough of this excessive elaboration. (1.256)
This is stated as the remainder of all śrāddhas other than the daily (nitya) śrāddha:
"One should give the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or one may cast them into fire or water;
while Brahmins are present, one must not sweep away the remnants of the twice-born's meal. (YDh 1.257)
Regarding the disposal of the previously offered rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) or of a single rice-ball: one should give those rice-balls to a cow, a goat, or a Brāhmaṇa who seeks them;
or one may cast them into fire or into deep water.
Furthermore, while the Brahmins are present and seated at the place of eating, one should not sweep away nor remove the remnants of the twice-born's meal. (1.257)
He states the specific results obtained from specific foods:
"By means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) for a month, or by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
[the same result is obtained] by fish, deer, ram, birds, goat, or the meat of the spotted antelope. (YDh 1.258)

The ancestors (pitāmahas) here are satisfied for increasing periods of one month each by the offering of the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively. "Haviṣya" refers to sacrificial food suitable for oblation, such as sesame, rice, and so forth.
As Manu said:
"By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, or fruits according to the prescribed rule, the ancestors of men are satisfied for one month" (MDh 3.267).

That food is sacrificial food (haviṣya); by that, the ancestors are satisfied for a month—this is the syntactical connection with what follows. By milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared from cow's milk, they are satisfied for a year.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "But for one year [one should subsist] on cow's milk and milk-rice" (MDh 3.271).
Fish that may be eaten includes the *pāṭhīna* and others; that which pertains to this is "mātsya" (fish-eating).
The *hariṇa* is the copper-colored deer;
the *eṇa* is black— the *eṇa* should be known as the black deer, while the copper-colored one is called the *hariṇa*.
This is because of the traditional authority of Āyurveda;
this [meat] belongs to the deer (*hāriṇaka*),
while that belonging to the sheep (*aurabhra*) is connected to the ram (*avi*).
A *śakuni* is a partridge; that which pertains to it is *śākuna*. A *chāga* is a goat; that which belongs to it is *chāga*.

The spotted deer is the *pṛṣat*; its meat is *pārṣata*. The black deer is the *eṇa*; its flesh is *aiṇa*. The *ruru* is the *śambara*; that which originates from it is *raurava*. [The word for] boar is *varāha*.
That which comes from a wild boar is *vārāha*;
that which belongs to a hare is *śāśa*.
When these meats are offered to the ancestors, [they are satisfied].

Since it has been stated, "Indeed, [the ancestors are satisfied] for a month with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna)," thereafter, the ancestors are satisfied by increasing the duration by one month each in successive order. // 1.258 // 1.259 //
Moreover:
rhinoceros meat, large-scaled fish, honey, or even the food of sages;
iron-flesh, great potherbs, and the meat of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane. (YDh 1.260)
Whatever one gives while staying at Gayā, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
"Khaḍga" means a rhinoceros; its meat [is what is offered].
*Mahāśalka* is a species of fish;
*madhu* is honey; *munyanna* refers to all forest-grown grains such as *nīvāra* and the like.
*Lauha* is red; *chāga* is its meat, thus *lauhāmiṣa*. *Mahāśāka* is black spinach (*kālaśāka*). *Vārdhrīṇasa* is an old white goat.
But one who drinks from three vessels, whose senses are decayed, who is aged and white-haired, and is the lord of goats—
that they call a *vārdhrīṇasa* in the ritual of the *śrāddha* sacrifice.
Thus it is well known among the ritualists (*yājñika*).
A "tripiba" is one whose two ears and tongue touch the water as he drinks; because he drinks with these three, he is called a tripiba.
The meat of that *vārdhrīṇasa* [goat];
and whatever he who resides at Gayā gives, even if it be merely vegetables and the like.
And because of the word "ca" (and), [the merit accrues] at Gaṅgādvāra and other such places; for it is said:
"A Śrāddha performed at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Arbuda, Saṃnihati, or Gayā attains imperishability."
"He attains infinity" means he obtains the state of being the cause of infinite fruit;
the phrase "he attains infinity" is to be connected with each [item].
Likewise, on the thirteenth day of the rains—that is, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada—
The connection with what precedes is that whatever is given specifically when [the moon is] conjoined with the Maghā asterism, all that attains infinity. Although here,
items such as the food of hermits, meat, honey, and so forth are shown to be generally suitable for the *śrāddha* for all castes, nevertheless, the regulation stated by Pulastya is to be respected.
"Hermit's food is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; meat for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; the gift of honey for the Śūdra; and whatever is not contradictory [to the rules] for all.

This is its meaning: "Hermit's food" refers to wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other such items that have been declared suitable for the *śrāddha* ceremony; that is the primary offering for the Brāhmaṇa, which bestows the complete fruit [of the rite].
That which is called "meat" is the primary [offering] for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya;
that which is called "honey" is for the Śūdra.
Apart from these three, whatever is non-conflicting, whatever is not prohibited—such as house-plantains (*vāstuka*) and the like—and whatever is prescribed [as food], [is acceptable].
Havisya food, such as kālaśāka and other such items, bestows complete results for all [of these rites]. // 1.260 // 1.261 //
He states the specific results arising from specific lunar days:
"A daughter, those who seek a daughter, cattle, virtuous sons, as well as gambling, agriculture, commerce, and likewise animals with cloven and single hoofs. (YDh 1.262)
The giver of a Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desires—
provided he performs it on the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad), excluding only the fourteenth (caturdaśī). (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.263)
But that which is given there for those who have indeed been killed by a weapon;
[one should give] a maiden endowed with beauty, auspicious marks, and good character;
to the "seekers of a maiden," namely the sons-in-law, who are endowed with intelligence, beauty, and auspicious marks; and cattle.
The lowly are goats and the like;
the virtuous sons are those who abide on the path of truth;
gambling is victory at dice.
Agriculture is the fruit of agriculture;
commerce is the profit of commerce;
cloven-hoofed animals are cows and the like.
"One-hoofed animals" refers to horses and the like.

"Possessing the splendor of sacred knowledge" (brahmavarcasvin) means having sons endowed with that brilliance (tejas) produced by the study of the Vedas and the performance of their prescribed duties; this is brahmavarcasa.
Gold and silver refer to gold and silver; apart from those, lead, tin, and so forth are called base metals (kupyaka).
"Preeminence among kinsmen" means being superior among one's relatives. "All desires" refers to things desired, such as heaven, sons, cattle, and so forth.
These fourteen fruits, beginning with a daughter-in-law, [are thus enumerated].
On the fourteen lunar days beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight up to the new moon, excluding the fourteenth day itself,

the performer of the *śrāddha* obtains [the results] in due order for those who have been killed by weapons; for them, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [he should perform it] according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
If they were not killed by a Brāhmaṇa or other such [forbidden causes],
then even for a father who has attained equality [with the gods] but was slain by a weapon,
the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the fourteenth day; this is the *mahālaya*.

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), it is restricted that on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada during the *mahālaya*, a *śrāddha* is to be performed only for one who has attained equality [with the ancestors] through *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and was killed by a weapon, and not for anyone else; however, it is not restricted that the *śrāddha* for one killed by a weapon must be performed only on the fourteenth day. And this...
On the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) and other such occasions, even for one killed by weapons, the *śrāddha* rite is to be performed exactly as prescribed.
Furthermore, it should not be thought that this rule for the *śrāddha* applies only to the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
This is because of the traditional teaching of Śaunaka: "On the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, during the dark fortnight, and likewise month by month. (1.262, 1.263, 1.264)
He states the specific results according to the specific lunar mansions:
"Indeed, heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength, as well as a son, preeminence, good fortune, prosperity, and auspicious leadership. (YDh 1.265)
He obtains the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], as well as success in trade and other such pursuits,
freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, the supreme goal, wealth, the Vedas, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, and even goats and sheep.

He who duly offers a Śrāddha for horses and long life during the period beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī— being a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy— shall obtain these desires. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.267–268)
He who offers a *śrāddha* to each lunar mansion (nakṣatra), beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī,
obtains in due order all desires ranging from heaven to long life, provided he is a believer (*āstika*), full of faith, and free from pride and envy.
A believer is one who possesses conviction.
"Full of faith" means endowed with an excess of reverence. "Free from pride and envy":
pride is arrogance, while envy is jealousy; he is devoid of both.
Heaven is unsurpassed happiness;
offspring is without distinction;
vigor is the excellence of one's own power.
Valour is fearlessness;
the field is that which bears fruit;
strength is physical.
A virtuous son,
preeminence among kinsmen,
good fortune, and being beloved by the people.
Prosperity (*samṛddhi*) refers to wealth and so forth; preeminence (*mukhyatā*) refers to being foremost;
and auspiciousness (*śubha*) is taken in its general sense.
The state of having set the wheel in motion is the possession of unimpeded authority.
Trade and so forth refer to commerce, usury, agriculture, and cattle-rearing.
Health is the state of being free from illness;
fame is renown;
freedom from sorrow is the absence of grief.
The absence of suffering produced by separation from the beloved and so forth;
the supreme goal is the attainment of the Brahma-world;
wealth consists of gold and other such things.
The Vedas refer to the *Ṛgveda* and the others;
the success of medical practice is the attainment of the fruits of medicinal herbs;
base metals (*kupya*) are those other than gold and silver.
Copper and so forth; cows are well known; goats, sheep, and horses; and longevity, which is long life. 1.265 // 1.266 // 1.267 // 1.268 //
By the statement, "The ancestors are satisfied here by what is given with monthly increments" (YDh 1.259), it is asserted that satisfaction of the ancestors occurs through the *śrāddha*;
however, that is untenable.

Because for humans who have gone to realms such as heaven or hell by the power of their own individual virtuous or non-virtuous karma, satisfaction through food, drink, and so forth offered by sons and others is impossible;
and even if it were possible, since they themselves lack mastery over their own selves, how could they bestow the fruits of heaven and so on? To this, he says:
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the Śrāddha;
when satiated by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
[They bestow] longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness.
In that same way, the grandfathers (pitāmahas), being pleased, bestow sovereignty upon men.

For in this context, it is not merely Devadatta and others who are designated by the words "father" and so forth as the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of the śrāddha rite; rather, they are [the recipients] only when accompanied by their presiding deities, such as Vasu and the others.
Just as by words such as "Devadatta" neither the body alone nor the self alone is denoted, but rather the self as qualified by the body,
so too [the elements] are [denoted] only when accompanied by their presiding deities.

Devadatta and others are designated by such terms as "father" and so forth; therefore, the presiding deities, Vasu and the rest, being satisfied by the food, drink, and other offerings given by the sons and others, in turn satisfy both Devadatta and the rest, as well as the agents, the sons and others.

They connect [the child] with the fruit [of their actions]. Just as a mother, being satisfied by consuming for herself the food, drink, and other desired things given to her for the nourishment of the fetus— which were not given to anyone else— also satisfies the offspring within her own womb who provided that food and drink.
And just as he unites [the recipient] with the fruit of a reciprocal favor, so too the Vasus, the Rudras, the sons of Aditi— the Ādityas—

who are designated by the terms "fathers," "grandfathers," and "great-grandfathers," are not only individuals such as Devadatta and others who serve as the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) in the rite of *śrāddha*; rather, having themselves been gratified by the *śrāddha*, they gratify the human ancestors, such as Devadatta and the rest.
By virtue of their possession of an excellence of the power of knowledge;
moreover, they do not merely gratify the ancestors, but also bestow upon those who perform the *śrāddha* rites longevity, progeny, wealth, learning, heaven, liberation, happiness, and sovereignty.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that in each respective case, the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the Vasus and others, being themselves pleased, bestow other fruits as well as those declared in the scriptures. // 1.269 // 1.270 //
Thus ends the section on ancestral rites (śrāddha).
Now begins the section on the ritual manual for Gaṇapati.
Although the rites that accomplish both visible and invisible fruits have been described and will be described [further], the actual accomplishment of their essential nature [is now set forth].
Since the attainment of the fruit occurs without obstacles, the author, intending to prescribe rites for the purpose of removing obstacles, states the causes that produce and indicate obstacles:
"Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā to preside over the Gaṇas and to ensure the successful accomplishment of the obstacles to ritual acts. (YDh 1.271)

"Vināyaka [is worshipped] for the sake of accomplishing actions and removing obstacles," and so forth; thus, through the thorough knowledge of the causes of both types of obstacles, those who act with foresight proceed either to preserve against the prior occurrence of an obstacle or to destroy one that has already arisen—
just as one acts upon having thoroughly understood the two kinds of causes of a disease.

Vināyaka, the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), was appointed— that is, commissioned— by Rudra, Brahmā, and by Viṣṇu (indicated by the word "ca"), for the purpose of ensuring obstacles to those actions that are means for attaining the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), specifically to effect the obstruction of their inherent nature, results, and means, among the hosts of attendants (gaṇa) beginning with Puṣpadanta.
In the sense of sovereignty and ownership. // 1.271 //
Having thus stated the causal factor that produces obstacles, he speaks in order to demonstrate the indicative signs:
"Learn now the characteristics of one who is afflicted by it:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men. (YDh 1.272)
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he stands together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels.
Even while walking, he imagines himself followed by others. (YDh 1.273–274ab)

O sages, understand—know—the characteristics that indicate one who has been afflicted and seized by that leader; the repeated address to the sages is for the purpose of commencing the section on pacification.
[This occurs] in a dream, that is, during the state of dreaming.
He plunges excessively into water, is carried away by a current, or sinks;
he sees men with shaven heads,
and those wearing saffron robes or garments and coverings of red, blue, and other colors.
He mounts birds that eat raw flesh, such as vultures and the like, as well as beasts of prey, such as tigers and the like;
likewise, he mounts outcastes such as Caṇḍālas and donkeys.
Surrounded by donkeys, camels, and dromedaries, he stands;
while walking or moving along, he perceives himself as being pursued and overwhelmed from behind by enemies running after him. (1.272–1.273)
Having thus described the visions in dreams, he states the signs perceived through direct observation:
"Dejected, with his undertakings fruitless, he desponds without apparent cause;
one possessed by him does not obtain a kingdom, O prince. (YDh 1.274cd)
A maiden does not obtain a husband, nor does a woman obtain offspring or a fetus;
likewise, a learned Brahmin does not attain the status of a teacher, nor does a student obtain the study [of the Vedas];
a merchant does not obtain profit, nor does a farmer obtain a harvest. (YDh 1.275–276)
"Dejected" means one whose mind is distracted;
"one whose undertakings are fruitless" refers to one for whom undertakings have no result, meaning he obtains no fruit whatsoever.
He desponds without cause and becomes dejected in mind;
though born in a royal family and endowed with qualities such as learning, heroism, and fortitude, the prince does not obtain the kingdom.
A maiden, though endowed with beauty, auspicious marks, noble lineage, and other virtues, [obtains] a desired husband; a woman who is pregnant obtains offspring;
a woman in her menses obtains a conception.
Even when there is study and knowledge of its meaning, the teacher is a *śrotriya*;
likewise, even if he is endowed with discipline, conduct, and so forth, the student [is characterized by] study or listening. It is not [otherwise].

The word "obtains" (*labhate*) is connected to every instance. A merchant, one who lives by trade, even if skilled therein, does not obtain profit from the buying and selling of grain and such; a farmer, a cultivator, even if diligent therein, does not reap the fruit of agriculture.

Thus, if one who lives by a particular mode of livelihood finds their undertakings therein to be fruitless, they should be known as being afflicted by that [obstructive spirit]. // 1.274 // 1.275 // 1.276 //
Having thus explained the causal factors (kāraka) and the indicative causes (jñāpaka), he states the ritual procedure for the purpose of pacifying obstacles:
"His ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rules" (YDh 1.277ab).
"Of him" refers to one who is afflicted by Vināyaka.
Or for one who desires to avoid the calamities brought by future leaders [of the world],
a ritual bathing and consecration should be performed on an auspicious day joined with favorable constellations and other such factors.
During the day, not at night; according to rule, accompanied by the procedure as prescribed in the scriptures.
He states the procedure for the ritual bathing:

"For one who has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter, and likewise whose head is smeared with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances... (YDh 1.277cd).

For one seated upon an auspicious throne (bhadrāsana), virtuous Brahmins should pronounce blessings (svastivācana). Having been massaged with a paste of white mustard seeds (gaurasarṣapa) mixed with ground white mustard (siddhārtha) and combined with clarified butter (ghṛta), and likewise having his limbs rubbed with all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadha) such as priyaṅgu and nāgakeśara, and with all fragrant substances (sarvagandha) such as sandalwood, agallochum, and musk;

For a man whose head has been anointed and who is seated upon the *bhadrāsana* to be described hereafter, four auspicious twice-born Brāhmaṇas—endowed with learning, study, and good conduct, and possessing handsome forms—should be addressed with the words, "May you, sirs, pronounce a blessing (*svasti*) for him. At this moment, one should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*; such is the meaning. (1.277–1.278)
Furthermore: From a horse-stable, from an elephant-stable, from an anthill, from a confluence,
and from a lake, one should take earth, yellow pigment (rocanā), fragrant substances, and guggulu resin, and cast them into water.
Having brought water from a lake using four pitchers of a single color,
one should then place a *bhadrāsana* (auspicious seat) upon the hide of a red bull.
[One should also bring] five kinds of earth from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, and a lake that does not dry up, as well as *gorocana*.
One should cast fragrances— such as sandalwood, saffron, and agalloch— as well as guggulu resin,

into those waters which have been brought from a place where the ground is not parched, using four jars of uniform color, free from cracks, fissures, or discoloration, and filled from the heart of the site.
Or from a confluence [of rivers].

And then, upon the hide of an ox that is dyed red, crimson in color, with the hair facing upward and the neck toward the east, one should place an auspicious and pleasing seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood.

Then, having placed [the jars] in the four directions starting from the east—adorned with water, earth, fragrance, and so forth as previously described; their mouths beautified with mango sprouts and other foliage; their necks encircled with garlands; smeared with sandalwood paste; and decorated with new, unwashed cloths—one should establish them upon a pure, well-smeared sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) where a svastika of five colors has been drawn.
Having spread out the red hide of a bull with the hair on the upper side and the neck facing east, one should place upon it a seat covered with a white cloth; this is the *bhadrāsana*.
For him who is seated upon it, the twice-born should pronounce the benediction (*svastivācana*). (1.279–1.280)
Moreover:
"With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, made purifying by the seers—I sprinkle you with it; may the Pāvamānī verses purify you. (YDh 1.281)

Immediately after the recitation of the benediction (*svastivācana*), the preceptor (*guru*), having taken the pitcher situated in the eastern direction— which has been consecrated with auspicious rites by women whose husbands and sons are living, who are endowed with beauty and virtue, and who are well-attired— should sprinkle [the disciple] with this mantra:
"The thousand-eyed one, possessed of manifold powers..."

With this water—which has many streams, which was made purifying and sacred by the sages beginning with Manu and others, and which was produced—I sprinkle you for the sake of pacifying the affliction caused by Vināyaka. And may these waters, consisting of the Pāvamānī verses, purify you. 1.281.
"May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune; and may the Seven Sages grant you fortune.
(YDh 1.282) Immediately after that, taking the second pitcher situated in the southern region, one should consecrate [the person] with this mantra.

"May Bhaga grant you auspiciousness; may King Varuṇa grant you Bhaga; may Sūrya grant you Bhaga; may Bṛhaspati grant you Bhaga; may Indra and Vāyu grant you Bhaga; and may the Seven Seers grant you Bhaga. (1.282)
"Whatever misfortune is in your hair, at the parting of your hair, or on your head;
whatever is in your forehead, ears, or eyes—may the waters destroy it forever.
(YDh 1.283) Then, taking the third jar, he should sprinkle [the person] with this mantra.

"Whatever misfortune or ill-luck is in your hair, at the parting, on the crown of the head, on the forehead, or in the ears and eyes— may the divine waters destroy all of that and pacify it forever. (1.283)
Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood into the head, while grasping *kuśa* grass with the left hand. Then,
taking the fourth vessel, one should sprinkle [the person] with the three previously mentioned mantras.
"By all mantras, the fourth [is performed]"— this is according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.
Having conferred the empowerment in the manner described, [the preceptor places] upon the head of the initiate [grass] hidden beneath *kuśa* grass held in his left hand.
The preceptor should offer mustard oil with a ladle made from the wood of the udumbara tree, using the mantras to be described hereafter. // 1.284 //
With the names Mita, Sammita, Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa,
Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Rājaputra, accompanied at the end by "svāhā," and with the bali-mantras joined by salutations (namas), [one should offer the oblations]. YDh 1.285–286ab.
