The connection with what has preceded is that one should offer oblations to Vināyaka using names such as *mitasaṃmita* and others, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the utterance *svāhā*.
Because of the application of *svāhā*, the fourth case ending is used.
And therefore, there are six mantras: "Oṃ, to Mitā, svāhā! Oṃ, to Saṃmitā, svāhā! Oṃ, to Śālā, svāhā! Oṃ, to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, svāhā! Oṃ, to Kūṣmāṇḍa, svāhā! Oṃ, to Rājaputra, svāhā!"
Immediately thereafter, having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru) in a worldly fire according to the rules for cooking in a pot,

and having offered it into that same fire with these very six mantras, he should present the remainder as an offering (bali) to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Ananta, using their names in the dative case followed by "namaḥ. // 1.286 //
He states what one should do immediately thereafter:
"At a crossroads, having spread kusha grass everywhere upon a winnowing basket, one should offer both husked and unhusked rice, as well as rice mixed with meat. (YDh 1.286cd)
Cooked fish as well as raw fish, and meat in equal measure;
likewise, variegated and fragrant flowers, the three kinds of liquor, radishes, *pūrikā* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, and garlands of *uṇḍeraka*. (YDh 1.287–288)
Having gathered all these— curd-rice, milk-porridge, and flour-cakes with molasses along with water— and having placed them on the ground, he should then place his head there;
thereafter, he should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka.
Having presented the collection of offering substances, such as those prepared and unprepared, before Vināyaka and his mother, and having touched the ground with one's head, [one should recite]:
"We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon the Crooked-Tusked One."
"May he, the Tamer, impel us"—
with this mantra one [worships] Vināyaka; "We meditate upon Subhagā, we contemplate Kāmamālinī."
With this [verse], "May Gaurī impel us," one should pay homage to Ambikā. Then,
having placed the remains of the offering in a winnowing basket spread with kuśa grass at a crossroads, [one should proceed].
One should place [the offering],
saying: "May the gods— the Ādityas, the Vasus,
as well as the Maruts, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas— accept this bali."
Asuras, Yātudhānas, Piśācas, Uragas, Mātṛs,
Śākinīs, Yakṣas, Vetālas, Yoginīs, Pūtanās, and Śivās.
The Jṛmbhakas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, those skilled in illusion, Vidyādharas, humans, the guardians of the directions, the guardians of the worlds, and all those who are obstacles and impediments;
May Brahmā and the other great sages, who bring peace to the worlds,
grant that there be no obstacle for me, no sin, and may there be no adversaries.
May the bhūtas and pretas be gentle, satisfied, and bringers of happiness.
With these mantras.
Rice grains are "prepared" when they have been husked once.
*Palala* is crushed sesame; rice mixed with that is *palalaudana*.
Fish are both cooked and uncooked;
meat is likewise only of these two kinds, cooked and uncooked;
and flowers are variegated, possessing various colors such as red, yellow, and so forth.
Sandalwood and other such fragrant substances;
liquor is of three kinds: that made from molasses, that made from honey, and that made from flour.
*Mūlaka* is a specific kind of food shaped like a bulbous root;
*pūrikā* is well known;
and *apūpa* is a wheat product not cooked with oil.
*Uṇḍeraka* garlands are garlands strung together made of *uṇḍeraka*—that is, items such as flour-cakes (*piṣṭa*). *Dadhyanna* is food mixed with curd;
*pāyasa* is milk-rice (*kṣaireyī*).
*Guḍapiṣṭam* is flour of *śāli* rice and other grains mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*). *Modakāḥ* are sweetmeat balls (*laḍḍukas*).
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Vināyaka and his mother Ambikā with the mantra to be recited hereafter. (1.286–1.289)
Having done what? He says:

"Having offered a full handful (añjali) as the arghya of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers. Having first offered a handful of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers with water containing flowers as the arghya, one should perform the ritual worship (upatiṣṭhet).
The connection is with that which has gone. // 1.290 //
He states the mantra for the ritual service:
"O Blessed One, grant me form; grant me glory; grant me fortune.
Grant me sons; grant me wealth; and grant me all my desires. (YDh 1.291)

Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, he should feed the Brahmins and give a pair of garments to his preceptor as well. In the ritual of worshiping Ambikā, the modification is "O Blessed One" (bhagavati). Pāṇḍeya and Seltur read: [as above].
"O Blessed One, [the modification] is *vināyakopasthāne*. Then,
immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the patron (*yajamāna*), wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, should feed the Brahmins according to his capacity.
One should give a pair of garments to the preceptor, who is endowed with learning, Vedic study, and good conduct, and who is knowledgeable in the ritual procedure for the bathing of Vināyaka.

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that one should likewise give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability to the Brahmins, dedicated to Vināyaka. In this regard, the sequence of the performance is as follows:

Together with four Brahmins, the preceptor, possessing the aforementioned characteristics and conversant with the mantras, having prepared the *bhadrāsana* seat, worships Vināyaka and his mother in its vicinity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the prescribed mantras; then, having cooked the *caru* oblation and performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite for the patron seated upon the *bhadrāsana*, [he proceeds] with four water-pots.

Having sprinkled mustard oil upon the head and performed the oblation of *caru*, one should offer a sacrificial gift (*bali*) to the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, in the four directions within the consecration hall.
The patron (*yajamāna*), however, following the bath, shall wear white garlands and garments.

Accompanied by his preceptor, he should offer an oblation to Vināyaka and Ambikā, bow his head to the ground, present an *arghya* of flowers and water, and offer a handful of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers; then he should worship Vināyaka and Ambikā.
The preceptor [should take] the remainder of the oblation.
Having placed [the image] in a winnowing basket, one should set it down at a crossroads.
Immediately thereafter, one should give a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and provide a meal for a Brāhmaṇa. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the bathing of Vināyaka. 1.291–1.292.
In order to demonstrate another application by way of a concluding summary of this very ritual bathing of Vināyaka, he says:
"Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity. (YDh 1.293)
Having thus worshipped the Vināyaka in the manner described, one obtains the fruit of actions without obstacle; this is the conclusion of what was said.
He states another application:
"and one attains the most excellent prosperity."
The meaning is that one who desires prosperity (*śrī*) should worship Vināyaka according to this very procedure;

and for one who desires the pacification of afflictions caused by the planets such as the Sun, or who desires fortune (*lakṣmī*) and so forth, there is the ritual procedure for the worship of the planets and so on.
Introducing the worship of the planets (graha-pūjā), he says: "By worshipping the planets according to the rule...
Having fully worshipped the planets, beginning with the Sun, according to the procedure to be described, one attains the success of one's undertakings and obtains prosperity. (1.293)
He states the connection between the obligatory and the optional rites:
"By constantly performing the worship of the Sun, as well as the tilaka of his Lord (Śiva) and that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain perfection. (YDh 1.294)
By constantly performing worship every day of the Blessed Āditya with red sandalwood, saffron, flowers, and other offerings,
and by perpetually worshipping Skanda and Mahāgaṇapati,
one attains perfection and liberation through the gateway of self-knowledge.
Thus is the perpetual conjunction.
By fashioning a *tilaka*— made of gold or other materials, or made of silver— for any one of Āditya, Skanda, and Gaṇapati, or for all of them, one attains the desired accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Likewise, "and the two eyes" constitutes a connection with a desired object. 1.294.
Thus ends the Mahāgaṇapati-kalpa.
Now begins the section on the pacification of the planets (graha-śānti):
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].

By the verse, "One obtains the fruit of actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity" (YDh 1.293), it is stated that through the worship of the planets, there is the successful accomplishment of the fruits of actions without obstacle, and prosperity is also the fruit.
Now he states other results:

"One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, or likewise even one practicing malevolent magic, should perform the sacrifice to the planets. (YDh 1.295)
"Desirous of prosperity" (*śrīkāma*) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. "Desirous of peace" (*śāntikāma*) means one who desires the pacification of calamities;
[it is also] for the sake of the growth of crops and so forth.
"Pravarṣaṇa" means rain; "āyus" means long life through the conquest of untimely death;
"puṣṭi" means a faultless body.
One who desires these is called "vṛṣṭyāyuḥpuṣṭikāmaḥ."
These individuals—those desiring prosperity (śrī), and so forth—should perform the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña) and the worship of the planets (grahapūjā).

Likewise, even one practicing malevolent magic (abhicāra)—which is the infliction of suffering upon another by unseen means—one desiring that [result] should also perform the sacrifice to the planets. 1.295.
He mentions the planets:
"The Sun, the Moon, Mars (the son of the Earth), Mercury (the son of the Moon), Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—these are known as the planets. (YDh 1.296)
These are the nine grahas, beginning with Sūrya. // 1.296 //
It has been stated that the planets are to be worshipped.
Having done what? He says:
from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, and both [silver and iron].
The planetary deities (grahas) should be fashioned, respectively, from silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal;
or they may be drawn upon a cloth with pigments of their own respective colors, or within mandalas using fragrant pastes.
The images of the Sun and the other planets should be made, in due order, from copper and other such materials.
If those are unavailable, they should be drawn on a cloth using pigments of their respective colors,
or else upon mandalas using fragrant scents.
The grammatical connection is that they are to be painted with perfumes such as red sandalwood and others, according to their respective colors.
However, the specific details regarding their having two arms and so forth should be understood from the *Matsyapurāṇa*, as follows:

Ravi should always be depicted with two arms, seated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, sitting in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with hands in the lotus gesture (padmakara), and possessing a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus.
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and grants boons.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace,
the son of the Earth (Mars) has four arms, rides upon a ram, and bestows boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, with a luster like that of the Karṇikāra flower,
holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, and seated upon a lion, the planet Mercury bestows boons.
Likewise, the preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white respectively, each with four arms,
holding a staff, granting boons, and carrying a rosary and a water-pot.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted as having the luster of sapphire, holding a trident, granting boons, mounted upon a vulture, and bearing an arrow and a bow.
With a formidable face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident, the blue Rāhu is praised here as the bestower of boons while seated upon a lion-throne.
All smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having deformed faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be granters of boons.
"All the planets that bring welfare to the world should be depicted wearing crowns;
all of them should always be one hundred and eight [in number] and elevated by their own finger-breadths.
Thus [it is said]. The location for their installation is also stated in that very same place.
One should know Bhāskara (the Sun) to be in the center, Lohita (Mars) to the south,
Guru (Jupiter) to the north, and Budha (Mercury) to the northeast.
One should know Bhārgava to be in the east, Soma in the southeast;
one should know Śani in the west, and Rāhu in the southwest.
"One should indeed place the banner in the north-west with white rice grains.
Thus [it is said]. He states the procedure for the worship of the planets:
"Garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors" (YDh 1.298cd).
Fragrance, offerings, and incense made of guggulu should be presented;
and oblations (carus) accompanied by mantras should be prepared for each respective deity.
According to the color—whatever the color of a particular planet is, garments, fragrances, and flowers of that same color should be given as offerings. As for the bali-offerings:

And incense— guggulu should be offered to all— and sacrificial porridges (caru) for each deity; having first performed the establishment of the fire (agnipratiṣṭhāpana), the placing of fuel (anvādhāna), and so forth,
he pours out four handfuls [of grain] for each.
The offerings should be performed according to the injunction beginning with "I offer you, acceptable to such-and-such a deity.
Immediately thereafter, having performed the rites from the placing of fuel on the well-kindled fire up to the *āghāra* libations,
one should offer the aforementioned fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in the manner to be described and with the mantras to be cited, in due order, dedicated to Āditya and the other deities.
Having offered the oblations, the sacrificial porridges (caru) are to be offered. 1.298–1.299.
He states the planetary mantras: the verses "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed respectively [for the planets]. (YDh 1.300)
"Bṛhaspate atiyadaryas," "tathaivānnāt parisrutaḥ," "śaṃ no devīs," "tathā kāṇḍāt," and "ketuṃ kṛṇvann imāṃs tathā"—
these nine mantras, beginning with "ākṛṣṇena rajasā vartamānaḥ," are to be understood as pertaining respectively to Āditya and the other [planets]. (YDh 1.300–1.301)
Now he mentions the sacrificial fuel sticks:
the *arka*, the *palāśa*, the *khadira*, the *apāmārga*, and then the *pippala*;
the *udumbara*, the *śamī*, the *dūrvā*, and the *kuśa* grasses are the fuel sticks in their respective order. (YDh 1.302)
The *arka*, *palāśa*, and other such trees serve as sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) for the Sun and the other deities respectively.
These should be prepared fresh, unbroken, with their bark intact, and measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length. (1.302)
Furthermore: for each one here, there are either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight [recitations].
They should be offered with honey and clarified butter, or combined with curd or milk.

(YDh 1.303) For each deity beginning with Āditya, the aforementioned *arka* and other sacrificial fuels should be offered in a number of one hundred and eight or twenty-eight, as the case may allow, combined with honey, clarified butter, curd, or milk.
Now he describes the foods:
rice with molasses, milk-rice, sacrificial food (haviṣya), ṣaṣṭika rice with milk, rice with curd, sacrificial oblation, flour-meal, meat, and variegated rice. (YDh 1.304)
In this manner, the wise man should provide food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets,
honoring them according to his capacity or as available, in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
"Guḍaudana" refers to boiled rice mixed with molasses.
Milk-rice;
sacrificial food such as the grains of sages;
and *kṣīraṣāṣṭika*, which is rice mixed with milk.
Rice cooked with sixty-day grain; rice mixed with curd is *dadhyodana*;
sacrificial oblation is *ghṛtaudana* (rice with clarified butter).
Powder refers to rice mixed with sesame powder; meat refers to rice mixed with edible meat;
variegated rice refers to rice of various colors.
One should give these items, beginning with rice mixed with jaggery, in due order to Brahmins— twice-born men— for the purpose of a meal, dedicating them respectively to Āditya and the other deities.
This is the number of Brahmins.
This should be performed according to one's means.

However, in the absence of rice with molasses and other such items, one should provide whatever rice and so forth are available, having first performed the ritual of washing the feet and the like, offering it with respect and preceded by honor. (1.304–1.305)
He states the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās): "A cow, a conch, likewise a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, in due order;
a black cow, iron, and a goat—these are declared to be the sacrificial fees. (YDh 1.306)
A milch-cow is one that gives milk;
a conch is well-known;
an ox is a draft-animal bull capable of bearing a burden.
Gold is yellow;
clothing is yellow; a horse is pale-white.
A black cow;
iron implements such as weapons and the like;
a goat is well known.
These cows and other items are recorded and taught by Manu and others as the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for Brahmins, intended respectively for Āditya and the other deities;
and this applies when such items are available.
However, in the absence of these, one may give whatever else is obtained according to one's means.
It should be given. 1.306.

It has been stated that all the planets should be worshipped without distinction by one who desires peace; regarding this, he states the specific rule: "Whichever planet is unfavorable for whichever person at whatever time, that person should worship that [planet] with effort."
A boon was granted to them by Brahmā: "When you are worshipped, you shall worship [the person].
When a particular planet is situated in an unfavorable position, such as the eighth house, for a given person, he should then worship that planet with special effort.
For a boon was previously granted to these planets by Brahmā, saying: "When you are worshipped, you shall honor the worshipper by granting what is desired and removing what is undesired. (1.307)
Rites such as those for pacification and nourishment have been set forth generally with reference to the twice-born;
however, he states that a king endowed with the qualities of consecration has a special entitlement to them.
The rise and fall of kings, as well as the existence and non-existence of the world, are dependent upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
One should perform this hospitality for the planets even once a year.
"Endowed with health and strength, may he live for a hundred autumns.
Among the lords of men, the consecrated kṣatriyas, the planets are most worthy of worship;
by this it is understood that they are to be worshipped by others as well.
He states the reason for both cases: since the prosperity and misfortune of living beings depend upon the planets, they should be worshipped by those who hold authority. Furthermore:
The existence and non-existence—namely, the arising and cessation—of the world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, are dependent upon the planets.
In that regard, if these [planets] are worshipped, then their arising and cessation occur at their own proper time;
otherwise, at the time of their arising...
Because there is no arising at the improper time and no cessation [of their influence],

and because they act as the lords of the world and provide for its welfare and security, the planets are most worthy of worship; thus, they have a specific authority over rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*).
And likewise, Gautama, referring to the king, states: "The king has authority over all, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇas" (GDh 11.1).

Having stated certain duties such as, "He shall protect the social classes (*varṇa*) and the stages of life (*āśrama*) according to justice, and he shall establish those who stray from them in their own duty" (GDh 11.9–10), [the author proceeds].

"And one should heed whatever those who contemplate divine portents might declare, for some maintain that even one's acquisition and preservation of well-being (*yogakṣema*) depend upon them" (GDh 11.15–16).

Having thus stated the reason for performing rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), [he describes] those rites pertaining to prosperity (*ābhyudayika*) which are joined with pacificatory, auspicious-day, benedictory, longevity, and propitious ceremonies.

"One should perform rites for those who harbor enmity, as well as rites for paralyzing, malevolent magic, and the increase of enemies, in the hall-fire (śālāgni); thus are the propitiatory rites and others demonstrated. (1.308)
Thus ends the section on the pacification of planetary influences.
Now begins the section on the duties of a king (*rājadharmaprakaraṇa*).
Having described the general duties of a householder, he now states the specific duties of one endowed with qualities such as royal consecration.
One who possesses great energy, is liberal, grateful, a servant of the elders,
humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, pure,
not procrastinating, possessed of memory, and likewise neither mean nor harsh. (YDh 1.309)

A king should be righteous, free from vice, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets; he should protect his own vulnerabilities in the sciences of metaphysics (anvīkṣikī) and statecraft (daṇḍanīti), as well as being disciplined in the science of economics (vārtā) and the triple Vedas (trayī). (YDh 1.310–311)

*Utsāha* (perseverance) is the determination to undertake actions that accomplish the goals of human life; one who possesses great perseverance is *mahotsāha*. One who perceives many objects to be given is *sthūlalakṣa*.
One who does not forget benefits or harms done by others is *kṛtajña* (grateful).
One who serves those advanced in austerity, knowledge, and so forth is a "server of the aged" (*vṛddhasevaka*).
One who is endowed with discipline is "disciplined" (*vinīta*).
By the word "discipline" (*vinaya*), the previously mentioned collection of duties for a *snātaka* is denoted as being consistent with [proper conduct].
"One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause," as stated in such passages;
"endowed with goodness" means being free from joy and dejection regarding prosperity and adversity.
He is of noble birth and well-born on both his mother’s and father’s side;
he is truthful, being of a nature committed to speaking the truth;
and he is pure, endowed with both external and internal cleanliness.

One who does not delay in undertaking necessary tasks nor in completing those already begun is one who is not dilatory (*adīrghasūtra*). One whose nature is such that he does not forget what has been learned is one possessed of mindfulness (*smṛtimān*).
He is noble-minded, not hating the virtues of others; he is gentle, having the habit of not proclaiming the faults of others;
and he is righteous, being endowed with the duties of his social class and stage of life.
One who has no calamities is "without calamity" (*avyasana*).
And the calamities are eighteen,
as Manu says:
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the threefold symphony [of song, dance, and music], and idle wandering— this is the tenfold group born of desire.

"Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault with others' merits, and the corruption of wealth, along with harshness of speech and severity of punishment— this is the eightfold group born of anger" (MDh 8.47–48).
Among these, seven are the most grievous.
And so Manu says:
"Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— these four, in this order, one should know to be the most grievous in the group born of desire."
"One should know that these three—inflicting punishment, verbal abuse, and the seizure of property—are always difficult to endure, even among those groups born of anger. (MDh 8.50–51).
A wise person is one capable of discerning profound meanings.
A hero is one who is fearless.
A knower of secrets is one who is skillful in concealing matters that ought to be hidden.

A protector of his own vulnerabilities is one who guards his own "vulnerabilities"—that is, any looseness in the gates through which an enemy might enter his seven constituent elements of sovereignty.
He was a concealer [of his own faults] in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), in the knowledge of the self (ātmavidyā),
and in the science of government (daṇḍanīti) which is conducive to the acquisition and preservation of wealth.
In *vārttā*, which consists of agriculture, commerce, and cattle-rearing, and serves as the cause for the accumulation of wealth;
and in the *trayī* (the triple Veda), known as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas.
He was trained and brought to proficiency by those experts in their respective fields,
as Manu says:
"From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple knowledge and the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti)."
"Philosophical inquiry from those who know the Self, and the means of livelihood from the world"—thus [it is said].
The connection "the king, consecrated for the kingdom, should be [thus]" applies in every case. (MDh 9.43) 309–311.
Having thus described the internal qualities of one endowed with consecration, he now speaks of the external ones:
"He should appoint as ministers those who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
together with them, and then with a Brahmin, he should deliberate upon the kingdom himself. (YDh 1.312)
A king endowed with qualities such as great energy should appoint ministers;
of what kind?
Wise ones who are skilled in discerning between the beneficial and the harmful.
"Hereditary" means those descended through one's own lineage.
"Steadfast" means those who remain free from agitation even in the face of great occasions for joy or sorrow.
"Pure" means those who have been cleared of any fraud regarding dharma, artha, kāma, or fear.
And they should be seven or eight in number,
as Manu says:
"Those who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, and of noble birth..."
"He should appoint seven or eight ministers who have been thoroughly tested" (MDh 9.54).
Having thus first appointed his ministers, he should deliberate on the affairs of state— characterized by peace, war, and so forth— with them, both collectively and individually.
Immediately thereafter, having ascertained their intention and deliberated upon the matter together with the family priest— a brahmin skilled in investigating the meaning of all the śāstras—
he should then consider the course of action himself through his own intelligence.
He states what kind of person one should appoint as a domestic priest (purohita):
"One should appoint as a domestic priest an astrologer who is highly distinguished, skilled in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]. (YDh 1.313)

And one should make the domestic priest (purohita) connected with oneself through gifts, honor, and respect in all activities concerning both visible and invisible matters, keeping him in front. Of what nature is he?
He is a knower of the divine (daivajña), an expert who understands the planets, portents, and the means for pacifying them.
"Exalted" means increased by those things such as learning, noble lineage, and religious observances that are themselves exalted;
"prosperous" means flourishing according to what is taught in the scriptures;
and "skilled in the science of government" means proficient in the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*).
And for rites such as pacification (śānti) and others, one should use the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda]. // 1.313 //

For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, he should indeed choose officiating priests (ṛtvij) and should perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
For the purpose of successfully accomplishing the performance of rites such as the Śrauta Agnihotra and the Smārta Upāsana, he should choose officiating priests; [he should perform] sacrifices...
And he should perform the Rājasūya and other sacrifices according to the rules, in accordance with their injunctions, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees—that is, with many dakṣiṇās. // 1.314 //
Moreover:
He should give enjoyments and various kinds of wealth to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings. (YDh 1.315)
One should bestow enjoyments and pleasures upon the brahmins by means of granting them the instruments for attaining them,
as well as various riches such as gold, silver, land, and so forth, in manifold ways.

Because this which is given to the Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure and storehouse for kings; although the duty of giving is already established as a common obligation, it is stated again for the purpose of demonstrating the preeminence of giving among the duties of kings. (1.315)
Moreover:

An oblation offered here into the fire of a Brahmin from the presence of the [ordinary] fire is said to be superior—provided it is not spilled, free from distress, and untainted by expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). (YDh 1.316)
It is said here that what is offered into the fire of a Brahmin is superior even to the Rājasūya sacrifice and others accomplished through fire, which involve abundant sacrificial fees;
for this [offering] is unspilled, performed without delay, free from distress, devoid of injury to animals, and untainted by the need for expiatory rites. (1.316)
It has been stated that one should give wealth to the learned;
as to the manner in which one should give it, he says:
one should seek what has not yet been obtained through righteous means, and what has been obtained, one should protect with effort.
One should increase by means of prudent policy that which has been protected, and one should bestow what has increased upon worthy recipients.
One should strive with effort according to the Dharmaśāstras for the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained;
and what has been acquired with effort, one should personally preserve.
He should protect [the wealth] with circumspection;
having protected it through devotion, he should increase what has been preserved by means of policy, such as trade routes and the like;
and having increased it, he should bestow it—that is, deposit it—upon the three kinds of worthy recipients: those worthy of dharma, those worthy of artha, and those worthy of kāma. // 1.317 //

Having cast [the dispute] into the bowl, what should he do? To this he says: "Having granted land or having established a fixed tenure, the king should cause a deed to be executed for the information of future virtuous monarchs. (YDh 1.318)

Having given land according to the prescribed rule and having effected the cessation of his own ownership, he should cause a document to be executed after establishing a fixed endowment (*nibandha*)— either specifying that so many silver coins (*rūpaka*) are for one load of merchandise, or that so many leaves are for one load of leaf-vegetables— and for what purpose? It is given by this [grantor] for the sake of those future, virtuous, and noble kings who are yet to come.
This is for the purpose of full recognition that "it was accepted by him";
[the term] *pārthiva* means a king (*bhūpati*). This applies specifically to the gift of land by a king.
It has been shown that one does not have the authority to grant a permanent endowment (nibandha) merely as a lord of enjoyment (bhogapati). // 1.318 //
It has been stated that "one should have a document executed.
To the question of how one should have it executed, he says:
"On a cloth or on a copper plate, marked with one's own seal."
Having caused his own lineage and himself to be inscribed,

the lord of the earth should cause a permanent edict (śāsana) to be made, complete with the dimensions of the gift, a description of the boundaries of the grant, and furnished with his own hand and the date. (YDh 1.319–320)
On a cotton cloth, a copper plate, or a wooden board, one should inscribe one's own ancestors— the great-grandfather, grandfather, and father—

preceded by a description of their lineage, heroism, learning, and other virtues, so that the plural number may be meaningful; and by the use of the word "ca" (and), one should also inscribe oneself and the recipient.
Having recorded the measure of the gift and the description of the limits of the donation:
"pratigraha" means that which is received; it refers to the endowment (*nibandha*), and its measure consists of silver coins (*rūpaka*) and so forth.

That which is given is a gift (*dāna*), such as a field and so forth. Its "demarcation" (*cheda*)—so called because it is delimited by this—is the river-bounds, the enclosures, the *nivartana* (a specific measure of land), and its dimensions; its description is as follows:
"to the south of such-and-such a river," and so on.

Whether it be a village or a field, one must record its measurements in nivartanas, such as "to the east, it is this many nivartanas from such-and-such a village," and so forth; for in the case of a boundary— such as a river, a city, or a road— it is possible that the land may become deficient or excessive due to encroachment.
To prevent that [misunderstanding],
it is complete and appropriate by means of this [formula]: "This is my opinion, of one named so-and-so, son of so-and-so, as has been written above here," written with his own hand.

And by means of two kinds of time— the time characterized by the passing of King Śaka and the time characterized by the year— this edict, which is endowed with lunar and solar eclipses and so forth, marked externally above with its own seal in the form of Garuḍa, Varāha, and others, and being stable and firm, is caused to be taught (issued) by it to future kings.
The lord of the earth, not the master of enjoyments, should cause this teaching to be promulgated by the minister of peace and war: "The preservation [of the law] is better than giving."
It is not by anyone at random;
rather, he who acts as the minister for peace and war, being the king's scribe and personally commanded by the king himself, shall write the royal edict.

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), since the fruit of giving is accomplished by the mere act of giving itself, the performance of instruction is for the purpose of an excellence of fruit through the increase of enjoyment. (1.319–1.320)
Now he describes the king’s place of residence:

"He should settle in a region that is delightful, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and dry (jāṅgala); there he should construct fortresses for the protection of his people, treasury, and himself. (YDh 1.321)
Delightful and beautiful with *aśoka*, *campaka*, and other trees;

beneficial for cattle (*paśavya*), meaning conducive to the welfare of livestock and increasing their numbers; and providing a livelihood (*ājīvya*), meaning a source of subsistence through roots, tubers, flowers, fruits, and so forth.

Although the term *jāṅgala* refers to a region with little water, few trees, and few mountains, nevertheless, a region that possesses water, trees, and mountains is also designated by the word *jāṅgala*.
One should settle in— that is, dwell in— such a region.
In such a location, one should construct a fortress for the purpose of protecting the people, the treasury consisting of gold and other assets, and oneself. And that is of six kinds,
as Manu has said:
"Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, or even a forest fort, or a human fort, or a mountain fort, he should dwell in his city. (MDh 7.70) 1.321.
Furthermore:
In various matters concerning income, labor, and expenditure, he should appoint officials who are expert, unimpeachable, skillful, pure, and diligent. (YDh 1.322)
In each respective matter concerning dharma, artha, kāma, and so forth, he should appoint capable and qualified officials as supervisors. As it has been said:
"One should appoint those who know dharma to matters of dharma, the wise to matters of artha, eunuchs to women, and low-born men to contemptible tasks."
Of what kind? Proficient, meaning having no other occupation; skillful, meaning adept in their respective duties;
and pure, meaning purified by the fourfold test.

Those who are diligent and untiring in matters of income—namely, in places where gold and other materials are produced—and in matters of expenditure—namely, in places where gold and other goods are disbursed;
and by the use of the word "ca" (and), those endowed with qualities such as wisdom. As it has been said:
"Wisdom, purity in the face of tests, vigilance, and application."
Absence of addiction to worldly affairs, devotion to the master, and competence—thus [is the definition]. (1.322)
"Let him give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins" (YDh 1.315)— thus the giving of one's own property has been stated in general terms.
Now, he describes the excellence of the fruit resulting from the gift of what has been acquired through the prowess of kings.
There is no higher duty for kings than this:
that wealth acquired in battle is given to the Brahmins, and constant fearlessness is granted to the subjects.
There exists no duty more excellent for kings than this: that wealth earned in war is bestowed upon the Brahmins.
And that which is the granting of fearlessness to all creatures. 1.323.
It has been stated that what is acquired in battle must be given.

However, since even misfortune can occur for one engaged in battle for the sake of acquiring wealth—resulting in neither dharma nor artha—it is better to desist from it altogether; therefore, he says:
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land,
without turning their backs and with weapons free from deceit, go to heaven just like yogins.
Those who have engaged in battles for the sake of land and other such things, and are killed while facing the enemy without turning away, they go to heaven.
They proceed just like those devoted to the practice of yoga, provided they are warriors who fight with weapons that are not intended to kill and are not smeared with poison and the like. (1.324)
Furthermore:
"The words of those who do not retreat when their ranks are broken are equal to a sacrifice;
however, the king takes away the merit of those who are slain while fleeing. (YDh 1.325)

When one's own forces— elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— are broken, the steps taken by those who do not retreat but advance toward the enemy force are equal to sacrifices, equal to the Aśvamedha.
He states the fault in the opposite case:
The king takes away the merit of those who flee, those who turn their backs in retreat, and those who are slain. // 1.325 //
Moreover:

One should not strike one who proclaims "I am yours," one who is impotent, one who is weaponless, one who has joined another side, one who has retreated, or one who is merely looking on at the battle and so forth. (YDh 1.326)
"One who says 'I am yours'—that eunuch, that neuter person; one who is weaponless, one who is unarmed; one who has joined with another, one who is fighting with someone else;

one who has turned back from battle, one who has retreated from the fight; and one who is a spectator of battle, a watcher of the fray—one should not kill him. This is the connection to be made in every case.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), horsemen, charioteers, and others are included.

As Gautama has stated: "There is no fault in killing [an enemy] in battle, except for those who are without horses or charioteers, those who are unarmed, those with joined palms, those with disheveled hair, those with their backs turned, those who are seated, those standing on the ground, those mounted on trees, those who are insane, messengers, cows, Brahmins, and so forth" (GDh 10.17–18).
Śaṅkha also said:

"One should not [strike] one who is drinking water, nor one who is eating, nor one who is taking off his sandals, nor one who is without armor against one who has armor; nor a woman, nor an elephant, nor a horse, nor a charioteer, nor a herald, nor a messenger, nor a Brāhmaṇa, nor a king against one who is not a king."
"One should slay," [it says]. 1.326.
Having performed his protective rites, he should rise and personally inspect the income and expenditures;
then, having attended to legal affairs, he should bathe and eat as he pleases.

(YDh 1.327) Having performed his protective rites—having established the security of both the city and himself—he should rise every day at the time of dawn and personally [inspect] the income and expenditures.
He should look [into the cases]; then, having seen the legal proceedings, he should bathe at midday and eat at the proper time according to his desire. // 1.327 //
He should deposit the gold brought by the officials into the treasuries;
thereafter, having personally inspected it, he should, in consultation with his ministers, dispatch spies and envoys.
(YDh 1.328) Immediately after that, having himself examined the gold and other items brought by the officials appointed to fetch them...
He should deposit them in the treasuries;
thereafter, he should observe the spies and scouts who have returned,
who were sent to ascertain the circumstances within the territory of another king.
Having seen those spies sent out in the guise of wandering mendicants, ascetics, and so forth, he should station them in various places;
immediately thereafter, he should observe the envoys—
those who travel openly back and forth to other kings.
They act; and they are of three kinds:
those with delegated authority, those with entrusted authority, and those who carry a message.
Among these, those with delegated authority...
Those who are capable of reporting the king’s affairs themselves, as they pertain to the specific place and time,
and who communicate them to another the very moment they have been told, are called *saṃdiṣṭārtha* (those entrusted with a message).
The messengers carrying royal edicts are those who deliver the king's letters. He should see them when they arrive after having been previously dispatched, in the company of his ministers.
Having seen them and deliberated upon their report, he should dispatch them again and again. (1.328)

Then, having inspected his forces, he should either wander at his own pleasure or meet with his ministers; having done so, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief. Immediately thereafter, in the afternoon, he should remain alone at his leisure as he desires, moving within the inner apartments.
Surrounded by ministers who are trustworthy, skilled in the arts, and conversant with jests, as well as by women endowed with beauty, youth, and elegance,
he should eat and then enjoy himself in the company of the women within the inner apartments.
For it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*: "Having passed the time as appropriate, he should again consider his duties" (MDh 7.221).
Then, adorned with excellent garments, flowers, ointments, and ornaments, [he should inspect] the forces consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Having seen [the situation], the commander-in-chief, together with his general, should consider its protection and other matters as appropriate to the place and time. // 1.329 //
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he may also enjoy singing and dancing, and likewise recite his private Vedic study (svādhyāya).
Having thus performed the evening twilight devotion at that time of dusk—
Although this has been stated in general, it is mentioned again for the sake of ensuring it is not forgotten due to the complexity of the task.
Immediately thereafter, one should consider the secret communications of those spies who were previously observed and stationed in various places.
One should listen while holding a weapon in hand within the inner apartments;
and as it was said by Manu:
"Having performed the twilight devotions, one should listen within the inner apartments while bearing a weapon."
"And [he should learn] the conduct of those who report secrets and of spies" (MDh 7.223).
Then, having amused himself for some time with dancing, singing, and other such diversions, he should enter another chamber and eat,
after having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "And he may enter the inner apartments together with the women for the purpose of eating" (MDh 7.224).
Therefore, for the sake of not forgetting [the sacred texts], he should recite his daily study (svādhyāya) according to his ability. 1.330.
He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise wake up with that same sound;
he should then contemplate the scriptures with his intellect, as well as all his duties.
Immediately thereafter, he should go to sleep, or lie down, to the sound of musical instruments and conch shells.
In the same way, having been awakened by the sound of musical instruments and the like,
and having awakened, he should— either alone or together with trustworthy experts in the sciences— in the final watch of the night, contemplate the scriptures,
all his duties, and all his tasks.
And this is said with reference to one who is healthy;
however, one who is unwell should appoint another for all tasks.
As Manu has said:
"A healthy lord of the earth should carry out this conduct; when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his chief minister" (MDh 7.225). 1.331.
Then, having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and others;
and having seen the astrologers and physicians, he should give cows, gold, and land.
Then he should acquire houses and furnishings from those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).

Immediately thereafter, remaining right there, he should dispatch his own trusted spies— honored with gifts, honors, and hospitality— to his own neighboring chieftains and officials, as well as to other kings, in order to ascertain their intentions.

Then, having performed the morning twilight devotions and offered the *agnihotra* sacrifice, being greeted with blessings by the domestic priest, officiating priests, teachers, and others, he consulted the astrologers; having learned from them the positions of the planets and other celestial bodies, he instructed the domestic priests to perform propitiatory rites and the like, and visited the physicians.

And having informed them of the maintenance of his own body and having assigned the means for its support, he gave to the *śrotriyas*— to Brahmins who had studied the Vedas— a milch cow, gold, land, wedding requisites such as ornaments for the bride, and houses whitened with lime and so forth.
The word "should give" (dadyāt) is to be connected with each [of the preceding items]. 1.332 // 1.333 //
Furthermore:
A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward those who are affectionate, and wrathful toward his enemies;
he should behave toward his circle of servants and his subjects as a father does.
Even when Brahmins are insulting him, he is patient; toward those who are affectionate and loving, such as friends and others, he is straightforward and not crooked;
and toward enemies, he is wrathful.

"He should be compassionate, like a father, toward the circle of servants and toward the subjects by practicing what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful"— this [phrase] is to be connected with each [term]. (1.334)
He states the fruit of protecting the subjects:
"Protecting [them] according to justice, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for the protection of subjects is superior to all other gifts. (YDh 1.335)

Because, by protecting the subjects according to justice and the path taught in the scriptures, he takes a sixth part— that is, a one-sixth share— from the merit bestowed by those subjects whom he has protected;
and because, compared to all gifts such as land and the like, the protection of the subjects is superior.
This yields a superior result;
therefore, the connection with what precedes is that "he should be exactly like a father toward his subjects. (1.335)
He shall protect the subjects when they are being oppressed by rogues, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like, and especially from the scribes (kāyasthas).
Rogues (cāṭas) are deceivers who, having gained someone's trust, seize their wealth.
Secret thieves are those who steal in concealment;
the wicked are such as conjurers, gamblers, and the like;
*saha* means strength, and that which is done by *sahas*, by force, is *sāhasa*, and it is great.

That is violence and great violence; those who act by means of it are "great-violent-doers," meaning those who seize by force. From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [one should understand] base practitioners of sorcery and those of evil conduct.
The king should protect his subjects when they are being oppressed and afflicted by these.
Scribes, copyists,
and accountants— being especially oppressed by these [officials], she should protect them,
because of their favoritism with the king and their extreme deceitfulness.
Because it is difficult to prevent. // 1.336 //
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected,

half of that belongs to the king, because he receives taxes from them. (YDh 1.337) When the subjects, being unprotected, commit any sin such as theft or adultery, [the king incurs] a share of that evil.
Half belongs to the king, because that king collects taxes from the subjects for the purpose of protection. (1.337)
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed to oversee the kingdom,
the king should honor the virtuous and have those who act contrary to them executed.
He should banish those who live by bribery after depriving them of their wealth.
He should always provide lodging for those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) with gifts, honors, and hospitality.

Having thoroughly ascertained through spies of the aforementioned characteristics the conduct and behavior of those appointed to administrative offices within the kingdom, he should honor the virtuous and well-conducted by respecting them with gifts, honors, and hospitality.
Having correctly identified those who act perversely and wickedly, he should have them executed according to their offenses;
furthermore, those who live by bribery should be deprived of their wealth.
Having done so, he should banish them from his own kingdom;
but having provided for the Vedic scholars with gifts, honor, and respect, he should always cause them to dwell in his own kingdom and country. (1.338–1.339)
That king who, by unjust means, increases his own treasury at the expense of the kingdom,
shall soon lose his royal fortune and meet with destruction along with his kinsmen.
That king who, having taken wealth from his own realm unjustly, increases his own treasury, will very soon— without delay— [suffer this fate].
Thus, deprived of glory and with his fortune destroyed, he meets his destruction along with his kinsmen. // 1.340 //
The fire produced from the distress caused by the oppression of subjects does not cease until it has consumed the lineage, the fortune, and the very life-breaths of the king; for like a fire,
it causes intense suffering arising from the affliction of the people by thieves and others.
The mass of demerit is called by the term "fire. Without burning and bringing to destruction the king’s family, fortune, and life-force, it does not turn back nor is it extinguished. (1.341)
Whatever merit belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,

that same merit in its entirety he obtains when bringing another's kingdom under his control. Whatever dharma accrues to a king through the just protection of his own realm, all of that he attains by the method to be described when [subjugating] another's realm.
Bringing [them] under his control and making them his own, he obtains one-sixth share of their merit. // 1.342 //
Furthermore:
"In whatever region there is a particular custom, legal practice, or family tradition..."
In the same way, when it has come under one's control, it must be protected accordingly.

(YDh 1.343) When a foreign land has come under one's control, then no mixing of the customs and so forth of one's own country should be allowed; rather, whatever custom, family tradition, or legal practice existed in that land previously, that very thing must be maintained as it was, provided—
It does not contradict the treatise.
By the phrase "when he has come under control," it is shown that prior to coming under control, there is no fixed rule. As it has been said:
"He should remain besieging his enemy and harass his kingdom; he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (MDh 7.195) 1.343.
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, therefore counsel must be well-guarded.
He should act in such a way that others do not know his actions until the emergence of their results;

for since it has been stated that "he should deliberate on the kingdom together with them" (YDh 1.312), and since the kingdom is rooted in counsel (*mantra*), he should therefore protect his counsel with great effort so that [it remains secret].
Until the emergence of the fruits—that is, until the completion of the results—of the king’s actions such as peace and war, others do not know his counsel. (1.344)
Furthermore:
the enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, the one beyond that, and the one beyond him.
The circle [of states] should be considered gradually through means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest.
An "enemy" (*ari*) is a foe;
a "friend" (*mitra*) is a well-wisher.
It is characterized by both [extremes] and is indifferent;
and these three are of three kinds: innate, artificial, and natural.
In this context, a natural enemy is one such as a co-wife's son, a paternal uncle, or his son;
an artificial enemy is one by whom a wrong has been done or to whom a wrong has been done.
The natural enemy (*prākṛta*) is the ruler of an adjacent territory.

A natural friend (*sahaja-mitra*) includes one's sister's son, one's father's sister's son, one's mother's sister's son, and so forth. An acquired friend (*kṛtrima-mitra*) is one who has rendered assistance or to whom one has rendered assistance.

A natural friend is the ruler of a territory separated by one intervening state. Those lacking the characteristics of both natural and acquired friends or enemies are natural and acquired neutrals. A natural neutral is the ruler of a territory separated by two intervening states.

Furthermore, the enemy is of four kinds, distinguished as those to be marched against (*yātavya*), those to be uprooted (*ucchettavya*), those to be oppressed (*pīḍanīya*), and those to be weakened (*karśanīya*). Among these,
one who is to be marched against is a neighboring sovereign who is in distress, possesses inferior strength, and whose subjects are disaffected.
One who is ill-fortuned, devoid of allies, and weak should be exterminated;
one who lacks the power of counsel should be oppressed;
and one endowed with powerful counsel and strength should be weakened.
"By uprooting, one effects total eradication; by oppression, one effects the suppression of power;
furthermore, they say that emaciation results from the depletion of treasury and army.
Thus, an ally is of two kinds: one to be strengthened and one to be weakened.
One whose treasury and army are deficient should be strengthened;
one whose treasury and army are excessive should be weakened.
"Adjacent, next to that, and beyond"—this refers to the natural enemy, friend, and neutral party.
The "adjacent" one is the natural enemy; "next to that" is the natural friend.

Therefore, the one beyond [the immediate neighbor] is the natural neutral (*udāsīna*); the remaining ones, however, are not mentioned because they are well known. This circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) should be considered in sequence according to the order of the directions starting from the east, and their activities must be understood.
And having understood this, one should proceed by means of the methods to be described, such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth.
Thus, with three kings each in front, behind, and on the sides, plus the self as the one [central king], this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) consisting of thirteen kings is shaped like a lotus.

However, the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the ally of the rear-enemy (*ākranda*), the ally of the rear-enemy’s ally (*āsāra*), and so forth, are actually included within the categories of enemy, friend, and neutral;
since they are shown in other texts to be merely different designations, they were not mentioned separately by the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya). (1.345)
It was stated [previously] that one should act by means of conciliation and the other methods;
now he states those very means:
"The means are conciliation, gift-giving, sowing dissension, and likewise force."
When properly applied, these means lead to success; however, punishment is the last resort when no other way remains.
*Sāma* is pleasant speech;
*dāna* is the giving of gold and other valuables.
Sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the act of creating division by instilling mutual enmity among those such as neighboring kings and their ministers.
Punishment (*daṇḍa*) is the infliction of harm, ranging from the seizure of wealth to execution, carried out either secretly or openly.
These means, such as conciliation (sāma) and the rest, are the methods for accomplishing [one's goals] against adversaries and so forth;
and these, when properly employed according to the requirements of place, time, and other factors, will achieve success.
And among these, punishment is the resort of last resort;
it should not be employed when other means are possible.
And this is said with reference to those who are to be oppressed or weakened.
However, in the case of one who is to be marched against or one who is to be exterminated, force alone is primary.
These means, beginning with conciliation (sāma), pertain not only to the administration of the kingdom, but to all worldly affairs as well;
for example:
"Study, my dear son, study! I will give you sweetmeats;
otherwise, if I must give them to someone else, I shall tear out your own ears. Thus [he spoke]. 1.346.
Furthermore:
He should properly deliberate upon these strategic qualities—peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and duplicity. (YDh 1.347)
Peace (*saṃdhi*) is the establishment of an agreement;
war (*vigraha*) is the infliction of injury;
marching (*yāna*) is an expedition against an enemy.
*Āsana* is equanimity;
*saṃśraya* is seeking refuge with one who is more powerful;
*dvaidhībhāva* is the division of one's own forces into two parts.
One should appropriately employ these qualities, beginning with the alliances, in accordance with the influence of place, time, power, allies, and other factors. // 1.347 //
Regarding the time for marching, he says:
"One should march when the enemy's kingdom is endowed with the excellence of crops, while one's own side is weak, and when the enemy is joyful with his mounts and men. (YDh 1.348)

When the enemy's kingdom is endowed with crops such as rice and other grains, as well as qualities such as water, fuel, and grass—meaning it is prosperous—and the enemy is deficient in strength and other resources, while one's own self has joyful mounts and men; "mounts and men" (*vāhanapūruṣāḥ*) refers to elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as the men; he whose mounts and men are joyful is thus described.
Then he should march forth to bring another kingdom under his own control. // 1.348 //

Since the prosperity and downfall of living beings depend upon destiny, if destiny exists, then even foreign kingdoms and the like will come under one's control by themselves; if, however, it does not exist, then they will not be won despite human effort. Therefore, this exertion for a military expedition is entirely futile.
Therefore, he says:
"The accomplishment of action is established in both destiny (daiva) and human effort (puruṣakāra); therein, destiny is that which was manifested in a previous body. (YDh 1.349)
The accomplishment of karma— the attainment of results characterized as desirable or undesirable—
is not established in destiny alone; rather, it is also established in human effort.
Because such is observed in the world, and because treatises on medicine and other sciences would otherwise be rendered useless;
furthermore, in the absence of human effort...
Regarding the statement "there is no such thing as destiny," he says "destiny" in that context;
for what is called destiny is simply human effort acquired in a previous body,
which becomes manifest as the arising of a great fruit immediately after a small amount of human exertion.
Human effort is the action performed in a previous life;
therefore, since destiny does not exist in the absence of human effort, one must apply oneself with diligence to human exertion. (1.349)
Now he states other opinions:
"Some of virtuous intellect maintain that the fruit [of action] arises from destiny, or from inherent nature, or from time, or from human effort, or from the combination [of these]. (YDh 1.350)
Some maintain that the fruit, characterized as desirable or undesirable, arises solely from destiny; others hold it arises from inherent nature,
occurring by itself.
It does not depend on a cause;
some say it arises from time, while others say it arises solely from human effort.
He states his own view:
"The wise, such as Manu and others, believe that the fruit arises from the conjunction—that is, the combination—of fate and the other factors. (1.350)
Regarding the point that the result does not arise from either one alone, he provides an illustration:
"For just as there can be no movement of a chariot with only a single wheel, so too destiny is not accomplished without human effort. (YDh 1.351)
There is nothing hidden here. // 1.351 //
It has been stated that one should go to a foreign kingdom for the sake of gain;
and gain is threefold: the gain of gold, the gain of territory, and the gain of allies.
Among these, the acquisition of a friend is the most excellent;
therefore, one should apply effort toward the means of attaining that.
And the means for attaining that is truthful speech; thus he says:
Since the acquisition of a friend is superior to the acquisition of gold or land,
one should strive for its attainment and protect truth with a concentrated mind.
(YDh 1.352) Because the acquisition of a friend is superior— that is, more excellent— than the acquisition of gold or land, therefore one should strive, exerting effort, for its attainment.
One should employ means such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest;
and one should protect the truth with a concentrated and attentive mind, because the acquisition of friends has its root in truth. (1.352)
Now he states the constituent elements of sovereignty:
"The sovereign, the ministers, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; sovereignty is said to have seven limbs. (YDh 1.353)
The "lord of the earth" (mahīpati) is the sovereign whose characteristics have been described starting with "possessing great energy" (mahotsāha).
"Ministers" (amātyāḥ) refers to the counselors, domestic priests, and so forth. "People" (janaḥ) refers to the subjects, such as the Brahmins and others.
A fortress refers to a natural stronghold such as a desert fort and so forth;
a treasury is a heap of wealth consisting of gold and other valuables;
and an army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
The fourfold army;
friends—whether innate, acquired, or ordinary;
and these constituents of sovereignty, beginning with the ruler, are the *prakṛtis* (constituent elements) of the kingdom.
These are the primary causes;
thus, the kingdom is said to have seven constituent parts. 1.353
Having obtained that [kingdom], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times.
Having thus acquired such a kingdom, [he should act] toward the wicked—those who are deceivers, rogues, scoundrels, stealers of others' wives and property, and those who cause injury, and so forth.
The king should inflict and employ punishment;
for indeed, Dharma itself was fashioned by Brahmā in the form of punishment in the past. And "punishment" (daṇḍa) is its etymological designation.
For it is said that "punishment [is so called] because it subdues," based on the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued" (GDh 11.28). // 1.354 //

He cannot be led away by right means by one who is greedy, of unrefined intellect, impure, lacking good companions, or lacking wisdom. That aforementioned punishment [is applicable] by one who is greedy, miserly, and of unrefined intellect— that is, of fickle mind— in accordance with justice.
It cannot be employed to lead [one astray].
By what kind of person, then, can it be employed? He says:
by one who is true to his word, one who does not deceive.
By one who is pure, who has conquered the six internal enemies,
who possesses good companions— endowed with the aforementioned assistants— and who is wise, being skilled in discerning right and wrong policy.
That punishment can be administered justly, in accordance with the Dharma. // 1.355 //

When applied according to the scriptures, it shall bring joy to the entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it would provoke their wrath. That punishment, when administered according to the path prescribed by the scriptures, [brings joy] to this entire world together with its gods, asuras, and humans.
It should gladden and delight the world;
otherwise, if it is employed by transgressing the scriptures, it would provoke the world to anger. (1.356)
It is said that not only does the world become agitated by unjust punishment, but the administrator also suffers the loss of both visible and invisible merit:
"Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the worlds;
whereas just punishment brings a king heaven, fame, and victory. (YDh 1.357)
Furthermore, any punishment inflicted out of greed or other such motives by transgressing the scriptures destroys heaven, fame, and the worlds, because it is a cause of sin.
However, that which is inflicted according to the path prescribed in the scriptures becomes a cause for heaven, fame, and victory, because it is a cause of dharma. (1.357)
"Neither a brother, nor a son worthy of honor, nor a father-in-law, nor even a maternal uncle—
if they have deviated from their own duty— there is no one who is not subject to punishment by the king.
(YDh 1.358) "Worthy of honor" (*arghya*) means one deserving of the *argha* offering, such as a teacher (*ācārya*) and others.
The rest is well known.
Since even these— such as brothers' sons and others— are to be punished if they deviate from their own duty, how much more so others?
For there is no one whatsoever who, having deviated from their own duty (*svadharma*), is exempt from punishment by the king;
and this applies with the exception of one's mother, father, and so forth.
Thus, another *smṛti* states:

The mother and father are exempt from punishment; likewise, those who have completed their Vedic studies, the family priest, wandering mendicants, and forest-dwellers who possess learning, good character, purity, and proper conduct, for they are the authorities on dharma. (1.358)
Moreover:

"The king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those deserving of death to be executed properly, has performed sacrifices completed with the most excellent sacrificial fees. (YDh 1.359)

But that king who properly punishes those deserving of punishment— those worthy of punishment for deviating from their own dharma and so forth— by means of the methods prescribed in the scriptures, such as censures, fines, and the like, and who causes those deserving of death to be executed, by him a sacrifice has been performed with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
the meaning is that he obtains the fruit of sacrifices involving many sacrificial fees.
Nor should it be thought that the infliction of punishment is optional merely because a reward for its performance is heard of in scripture,
for there is a traditional legal injunction (smṛti) regarding expiation in the event of its non-performance.
As Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon the failure to inflict punishment, the king shall fast for one night,
and the domestic priest for three nights."
"The domestic priest incurs the *kṛcchra* penance for punishing one who should not be punished, and the king [incurs it] for three nights" (VaDh 19.40–43). // 1.359 //
It has been stated that punishment must be correctly applied to the wicked; however,

since the identification of the wicked does not occur without the examination of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*), he says that the king himself must personally conduct the examination of legal proceedings every day for the sake of identifying them.
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine the legal cases daily, each yielding a fruit equal to that of a sacrifice;
for in the manner described, the fruit equal to a sacrifice arises from the proper infliction and non-infliction of punishment.
Having thoroughly considered the destruction of heaven and other realms resulting from punishing those who do not deserve punishment,

the king himself should daily examine legal cases according to the method to be described, for the purpose of discerning the wicked from the virtuous, surrounded by courtiers (sabhyas) of the characteristics to be mentioned hereafter, acting in accordance with the order of the social classes (varṇas) and so forth. 1.360.
Having disciplined those families, castes, guilds, corporations, and even provincial communities that have deviated from their own dharma, the king shall establish them on the right path.
"Families" refers to those of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes.
The *jātis* are those beginning with the Mūrdhāvasiktas; the *śreṇīs* are those of betel-leaf sellers and the like;
the *gaṇas* are those of the Helāvuks and the like.
The provincial people include artisans and others;

having disciplined and punished these individuals according to their offenses once they have wavered from or fallen away from their own duty (*svadharma*), the king should establish them on the path of their own duty.
It has been stated that one should inflict punishment upon those of evil conduct. That punishment is of two kinds: corporeal and monetary.
As Nārada says:
Punishment is indeed recorded as being of two kinds: corporeal and monetary.
Corporeal punishment is proclaimed to range from flogging up to the point of death.
"However, fines in money range from one *kākiṇī* up to all one's possessions. (NSm 19.60–61).

Thus, although there are two types [of punishment], each becomes manifold according to the nature of the offense. As it was said: "Corporal punishment is declared to be tenfold, while fines in money are of many kinds. (NSm 19.60). 1.361.

In this context, fines for offenses should be expressed using terms such as *kṛṣṇala*, *māṣa*, *suvarṇa*, and *pala*. Since these terms denote different quantities depending on the region, there might otherwise be a discrepancy in the amount of the fine—either less or more—due to regional differences even when the offense is of the same nature. Therefore, the terms *kṛṣṇala* and so forth must refer to fixed, standardized measures.
To demonstrate the system of weights and measures, he says:
"The mote of dust seen in a sunbeam through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those are a *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*. (YDh 1.362)
Three *gaura* seeds are one *yava*; three *yava* are one *madhya*; five of those *madhya* are one *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇala* are one *māṣa*; sixteen of those *māṣa* are one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇa* are proclaimed to be one *pala*, or even five.
The particle of dust that rests in a sunbeam entering through a lattice window is called a *trasareṇu* by the lords of yogis and other seers of reality.
Eight of those *trasareṇus* constitute a *likṣā*, which is the egg of a sweat-born louse. Three of those *likṣās* constitute a *rājasarṣapa*, also known as a *rājikā*.
Three of those black mustard seeds make one white mustard seed (siddhārtha);
six white mustard seeds make one medium-sized barley grain.
The medium [atom] is neither gross nor subtle;
by this, it is understood that even the white mustard seeds are medium.

Similarly, from the very word "middling" (*madhyama*), it is understood that even the words *rājasarṣapa* ("king- mustard seed") and so forth do not merely denote a measure, but rather denote the substance measured by that [measure],
just as "barley-measured-by-a-prastha" (*prasthaparimitā yavāḥ*) denotes barley.
A *prastha* is thus spoken of;
likewise, substances measured by mustard seeds and so forth are referred to by the words "mustard seed" and so on.
[This applies to] the words "mustard seed" and so forth.

Furthermore, if it were merely a statement regarding measurement, since it would be impossible to measure by withdrawing [the constituent parts] down to the *trasareṇu*s, there could be no conventional usage of terms such as *kṛṣṇala* and so forth through that means. In that case, given that a difference in conventional usage exists in each region due to the distinctions in measurement— such as coarse, coarser, coarsest, subtle, subtler, subtlest, medium, mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), and so on— it is regulated that "medium" is the standard in legal proceedings.
Three of those middle-sized barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five of those *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*.
Sixteen of those māṣas constitute one suvarṇa;
four of those suvarṇas are designated as a pala— thus the designations are stated—
or alternatively, five [māṣas] are also proclaimed to be a pala.
According to Nārada and others:
in that system, when a *kṛṣṇala* is calculated by means of three gross *yava*s, a *kṛṣṇala* constitutes one sixteenth part of a conventional *niṣka*.
Five of those [rattikas] make one māṣa;
sixteen māṣas make one suvarṇa,
and that is according to the conventional standard.
Five *niṣkas* make one *suvarṇa*;
four of those [suvarṇas] make one *pala*. Twenty *niṣkas* [make one *pala*].
A *pala*. However, when a *kṛṣṇala* is calculated as three fine *yava*s, then a *kṛṣṇala* becomes the thirty-second part of a conventional *niṣka*;
in that case, a *suvarṇa* is two and a half *niṣkas*.
And ten *niṣkas* make one *pala*.
However, when the *kṛṣṇala* is calculated according to the medium-sized barley grains, then the *kṛṣṇala* is the twentieth part of a *niṣka*.
Four niṣkas are one suvarṇa; sixteen niṣkas are one pala.
Thus, five suvarṇas [are one pala].

Regarding the term *pala*: in the case of refined gold (*paka*), twenty *niṣkas* constitute a *pala*. In this manner, other measures should also be inferred from this very sūtra according to worldly convention: for instance, one-sixtieth of a *niṣka* is a *kṛṣṇala*; two *niṣkas* are a *suvarṇa*; eight *niṣkas* are a *pala*, and so forth. (1.362–1.363)
Having thus established the measurement of gold, he now states that for silver:
two *kṛṣṇalas* make one silver *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* make a *śatamāna*, and indeed ten *śatamānas* make a *pala*. (YDh 1.364cd–365ab)
A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*; two *kṛṣṇalas*—as previously mentioned—are a silver *māṣa*, that is, a *māṣa* related to silver;
sixteen of those silver *māṣas* constitute a *dharaṇa*.
"Purāṇa" is another name for this very same unit;
for the Smṛti of Manu states: "Sixteen of those silver *māṣas* shall be one *dharaṇa*, and that [silver] unit is indeed called a *purāṇa*. (MDh 8.136).
Ten *dharaṇas* are also called a *śatamāna* or a *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* as previously described constitute one silver *niṣka*. (1.364)
Now he states the weight of copper:
"A copper *karṣa* is a *paṇa*.
A *karṣa* is well known in the world as the fourth part of a *pala*.

That which is measured by a *karṣa* is called *kārṣika*; that which is a product of copper is *tāmrika*. A product of copper weighing one *karṣa* is designated as a *paṇa*, and it is also known by the name *kārṣāpaṇa*.
And because of the statement of Manu: "A kārṣāpaṇa should be understood as a copper coin weighing one kārṣika, [also called] a paṇa" (MDh 8.136).
In the case where five *suvarṇa-palas* constitute [one *niṣka*], twenty *māṣas* make one *paṇa*. This being so,
the common practice expressed in such statements as "a *māṣa* is proclaimed to be the twentieth part of a *paṇa*" becomes established.
In the view that four *suvarṇa-palas* constitute [one *niṣka*], however, sixteen *māṣas* make one *paṇa*.
And in this view, although the words *suvarṇa*, *kārṣāpaṇa*, and *paṇa* have the same meaning, the words *paṇa* and *kārṣāpaṇa* refer exclusively to copper coins.
Thus, first, the measurement of gold, silver, and copper has been stated, because they are employed in legal proceedings involving fines (*daṇḍa*).
The measurement of bell-metal, brass, and so forth, which likewise constitute parts of worldly transactions, should also be understood in the same way. (1.365)
He states the technical definitions of his own treatise:
"A fine of eighty-one thousand paṇas is the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa);
half of that is declared the middle amercement (madhyama), and half of that is recorded as the lowest amercement (adhama). (YDh 1.366)
A *paṇa-sahasra* is a thousand *paṇas*; that which has this as its measure is *paṇasāhasra*. That which exists together with eighty is *sāśīti*.
The fine amounting to one thousand and eighty paṇas should be understood as known by the name *uttamasāhasa* (the highest amercement).

Half of that is the middle [amercement]; half of those one thousand and eighty paṇas is five hundred and forty paṇas, and half of that is a fine amounting to two hundred and seventy paṇas, which is recorded and declared by Manu and others as known by the name *adhamasāhasa* (the lowest amercement). As for that which...
"Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest," thus it was stated by Manu (MDh 8.168).
