That alternative view should be understood as referring to cases where there has been no prior intentional transgression. (1.366)
He states the different types of punishment:

"The staff of reproach, the staff of speech, the staff of wealth, and likewise the staff of death—these are to be applied individually or collectively according to the nature of the offense. (YDh 1.367)
The punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*) consists of censuring with words such as "Fie! or "Shame!"; the punishment of speech (*vāk-daṇḍa*), however, consists of harsh words and curses;
the punishment of wealth (*dhana-daṇḍa*)...
The punishment consisting of the seizure of wealth;
the corporal punishment involving imprisonment and so forth, ending with death—
these are the four kinds of punishments.
They should be employed individually, one by one, or collectively, two, three, or four at a time, according to the nature of the offense.
Following the stated sequence,
each subsequent method should be applied when the preceding one has failed to achieve success.
As Manu has said:
"One should first apply the punishment of censure, then the punishment of verbal reprimand; thirdly, the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal penalty" (1.367).
He states the grounds for determining punishment:
"Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength, as well as age, occupation, and wealth, one should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (YDh 1.368)

Having ascertained the offense, one should impose punishment accordingly; that is, having ascertained the place, time, age, action, and wealth [of the offender], one should impose punishment upon those deserving of it among those subject to punishment,
in accordance with whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and whether it occurred once or repeatedly.

And: although this collection of royal duties (*rājadharmakalāpa*) has been taught with reference to the king, nevertheless, it should be understood that these duties apply to others as well who are authorized to protect the realm, the district, and so forth.

This is because, in the verse "I shall proclaim the royal duties, how a king should conduct himself," there is a separate mention of the "king" (*nṛpa*), and because the taking of taxes is for the purpose of protection, and protection depends upon the administration of punishment (*daṇḍapraṇayana*).
Thus [ends verse] 1.368.

Thus ends the first chapter, on Right Conduct (*sadācāra*), in the *Ṛjumitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Vijñāneśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, son of the venerable Padmanābha Bhaṭṭopādhyāya. This work is the composition of his own disciple, who bears the title "Uttama."
This is the commentary on the Dharmaśāstra by the yogi Vijñāneśvara.
The sections in this chapter are:
1. The Section on the Introduction;
2. The Section on the Religious Student.
3. The Section on Marriage;
4. The Section on the Discrimination of Castes;
5. The Section on the Duties of the Householder.
6. The section on the observances of a Snātaka;
7. The section on what may and may not be eaten;
8. The section on the purification of substances.
9. The Section on the Dharma of Giving; 10.
The Section on Śrāddha Rites;
11. The Section on the Ritual Manual of Gaṇapati.
12. The Chapter on the Pacification of Planets;
13. The Chapter on the Duties of Kings. Thus, there are thirteen chapters.
This commentary on the treatise of the sage Yājñavalkya is intended for no scholar who is not wise;
though its words are few, it is rich in meaning and sprinkles nectar upon the ears. (1)
The Chapter on Judicial Procedure: The Section on the General Framework of Judicial Procedure.
For a king endowed with qualities such as consecration and the like, the supreme duty is the protection of his subjects.
And that [restraint] is not possible without the suppression of the wicked;
furthermore, the thorough knowledge of the wicked is not possible without the examination of legal cases. Therefore...
It has been stated that the administration of justice must be carried out day by day:
"He himself should examine the legal cases every day, surrounded by his court assessors" (YDh 1.360).
However, the nature of such a legal proceeding, its various types, and the full range of procedural requirements have not yet been explained.
To explain that,
the second chapter is commenced with the words "The legal proceedings. The king shall examine the legal proceedings together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
In accordance with the Dharmaśāstras and free from anger and greed, [he should act]. Legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is the narration of a matter concerning oneself in relation to another,
such as when someone says, "This field and so forth..."
He says, "It is mine," while another, in opposition to him, also says, "It is mine";
he thus demonstrates its manifold nature.
By the use of the plural number,

[the author] shows that this duty does not belong to the Kṣatriya alone, but rather to anyone else who is appointed to protect the subjects; the word "should see" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, intended for the purpose of prescribing specific duties.
By "learned men" (*vidvadbhiḥ*) is meant those who are experts in the Veda, grammar, and the treatises on dharma (*dharmaśāstra*);
it does not refer to Kṣatriyas and the like.
Because of the use of the instrumental case in the expression "together with Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇaiḥ saha*), these [others] are shown to be non-primary.
This is because of the grammatical rule (Pāṇini 2.3.19): "When joined with a companion, that which is not the principal [takes the third case].
Therefore, whether there is a failure to see or a seeing otherwise, the fault lies with the king, not with the brahmins. As Manu has said:
"A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and goes to hell. (YDh 8.128).
How so? According to the *dharmaśāstra*, and not according to the *arthaśāstra*.
Since the dharma pertaining to regions and so forth, provided it is not in conflict with the *dharmaśāstra*, also falls within the scope of the *dharmaśāstra*, it is not mentioned separately;
and thus he will state:
"Furthermore, that which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own dharma,
as well as that dharma established by the king, must also be protected with effort. (YDh 2.186) [The king should be] "free from anger and greed."
Since it is already established that [the king should act] "in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras," the statement "free from anger and greed" is for the sake of emphasizing respect; here,
"anger" (krodha) means intolerance (amarṣa).
Greed is an excessive desire for acquisition. 2.1.

And he said to the members of the assembly: "The king should appoint as members of the court those who are accomplished in learning and Vedic study, knowers of dharma, speakers of truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend. (YDh 2.2)

Furthermore, they were endowed with learning and study; that is, they were perfected through "learning"—the hearing of Mīmāṃsā, grammar, and so forth—and through "study"—the study of the Vedas. They were knowers of Dharma, meaning they were experts in the treatises on Dharma.
They were speakers of truth, meaning their character was devoted to truthful speech.
Those who are impartial toward both enemy and friend, being free from passion, hatred, and the like—
such are the members of the assembly (sabhāsadaḥ) who sit within the assembly hall (sabhāyām), that is, in the council.
They sit down, and likewise they should be honored by the king with gifts, respect, and hospitality;
although it was stated without distinction that those "endowed with learning and study" [should be honored], nevertheless, these are specifically Brāhmaṇas.
As Kātyāyana has said:

"But he [the king] should be joined by steadfast assessors—wise, hereditary, and the best among the twice-born—who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras and proficient in the Arthaśāstra. (KSm 57)

And those three must be appointed, because the plural number is meaningful, and also because of the traditional law of Manu: "In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit down... (MDh 8.11).
Bṛhaspati, however, states that there should be seven, five, or three members of the assembly:
"Where Brahmins who know the world, the Vedas, and the Dharma are seated—whether they be seven, five, or even three—that assembly is equal to a sacrifice. (BṛSm 1.59)

Nor should it be thought that the Brahmins mentioned in the preceding verse— those characterized by such attributes as "endowed with Vedic learning and study"— are qualified by the phrase "together with Brahmins," because a relationship of qualifier and qualified cannot exist between terms expressed in the instrumental and nominative cases respectively.
Furthermore, because this would entail the fault of redundancy with the term "by the learned" (*vidvadbhiḥ*),
Kātyāyana has clearly shown the distinction between the Brāhmaṇas and the members of the court (*sabhāsadaḥ*):
"Accompanied by the judge, the ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic priest, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven through his adherence to dharma. (KSm 56).
In this context, the distinction is that the Brahmins are unappointed, whereas the members of the assembly (*sabhāsadaḥ*) are appointed.
Therefore it has been said:
"Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma ought to speak.
In that regard, even when those who have been appointed speak of the matter exactly as it is, if the king acts otherwise, he must be restrained.
Otherwise, there is a fault.
And it has been said by Kātyāyana:
"Those members of the court who follow one proceeding even by unjust means [share in the guilt]."
"They too share in that responsibility; therefore, that king must be informed by them.

(KSm 75) Furthermore, for those not appointed [as judges], there is a fault if they speak otherwise than the truth or fail to speak at all, but there is no fault for the king in failing to restrain them.
Alternatively, one should either not enter the court or speak what is just.
For it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*: "Whether one speaks falsely or remains silent, a man becomes guilty of sin" (MDh 8.13).

Furthermore, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "toward an enemy or a friend," it is understood that [the market] may also be presided over by a few merchants for the purpose of pleasing the public.
The assembly must be constituted.
As Kātyāyana said:
"By those who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, conduct, and wealth, and who are free from envy..."
It should be presided over by a few merchants who have become like members of a single family.
Thus ends [verse] 2.2. (KSm 58)
It has been stated that "the king shall examine legal cases.
Regarding this, he states the secondary rule:
"But when, due to the pressure of business, the king does not personally examine the legal cases," [he should appoint others].

A Brāhmaṇa who knows all duties (sarvadharmavid) should be appointed together with the members of the court (sabhyas). By the king, who— due to being preoccupied with other affairs— is unable to personally oversee legal proceedings, a Brāhmaṇa who knows all duties— one who knows and deliberates upon all the duties prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras as well as those established by convention— should be appointed along with the aforementioned members of the court.
A Kṣatriya or others should not be appointed to oversee legal proceedings;
rather, one should appoint someone distinguished by the qualities mentioned by Kātyāyana, as he said:
"One who is self-controlled, of noble birth, impartial, free from causing agitation, and steadfast."

"One who is fearless in the hereafter, most righteous, diligent, and free from anger. (KSm 64) In the absence of a Brāhmaṇa of such a nature, one should appoint a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, but not a Śūdra.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"But where there is no Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the Dharmaśāstras; one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.
Thus [it is said]. However, Nārada has shown this very person as the primary [authority].
Placing the *dharmaśāstra* foremost and abiding by the opinion of the judge (*prāḍvivāka*),
he does not abide by his own opinion—
just as a king perceives the enemy army through the eyes of his spies.
And this is its etymological designation: he is a *prāṭ* because he questions the plaintiff and the defendant;
he [evaluates] their statements, whether contradictory or non-contradictory.
One who discriminates or investigates together with the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*) is a *vivāka*.
One who is both a judge (*prāṭ*) and a *vivāka* is a *prāḍvivāka*.
And it has been said:

"Having diligently questioned the litigant who has come for a dispute, he deliberates together with the members of the court; because of this, he is therefore remembered as the *prāḍvivāka* (the chief judge). (2.3)
If the judges and other members of the court deliberate on a legal case in a manner contrary to the sacred law (smṛti) due to passion and so forth, what should the king do? To this, he says:
"Those who act contrary to the sacred law and so forth out of passion, greed, or even fear..."
The members of the court shall each be punished with double the fine [imposed on the litigants] for the dispute.

Furthermore, the aforementioned members of the court, being overwhelmed by passion due to the unrestrained nature of *rajas*, may— out of attachment (*rāga*), excessive affection, greed (*lobha*), excessive desire for gain, fear (*bhaya*), or terror— act contrary to the *smṛti* (i.e., against the sacred law), and by the force of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), act contrary to established custom (*ācāra*).

Each individual shall be fined double the penalty resulting from their defeat in the dispute, on account of the litigation itself; however, this is not to be calculated from the property that was the subject of the dispute.
For if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of no punishment being prescribed for acts such as adultery with women.

The mention of "passion, greed, and fear" is for the purpose of restriction, [indicating] that double the punishment applies only to those cases involving passion and so forth, and not to ignorance, delusion, and the like. Furthermore, one should not conclude from the statement of Gautama— "And the king has no power over all [offenses], except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 11.1)— that Brāhmaṇas are exempt from punishment.
Because that [statement] is for the purpose of praise; whereas it is said:
"One who is to be avoided by a king in six ways—though not to be killed, nor to be bound, nor to be punished, nor to be exiled, nor to be censured, nor to be shunned."

And furthermore, he is one who is "learned" (*bahuśruta*): one who knows the *Lokaveda*, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas; who is skilled in *vākovākya*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*; who relies upon them and lives according to them; who has been refined by the forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*); who is devoted to the three duties or well-trained in the six rules of conduct (*samayācārika*). This refers to the subject matter of the learned person as previously described, and not merely to the Brahmin caste. (2.4)

He states the subject matter of legal procedure: "When one who has been oppressed by others through a course of action contrary to tradition and custom brings it to the notice of the king, that indeed is the subject matter of legal procedure. (YDh 2.5)

When one who is oppressed or overcome by others through a path contrary to the legal codes (*dharmaśāstra*), traditional conventions (*samaya*), and established custom (*ācāra*) makes a formal complaint or representation to the king or the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), that which is thus complained about is the "subject-matter of litigation" (*vyavahārapada*). Litigation (*vyavahāra*) consists of the plaint (*pratijñā*), the reply (*uttara*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the grounds for consideration (*hetu-parāmarśa*), the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), the decision (*nirṇaya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*);
this is the subject-matter (*pada*) of that litigation, and this is its general definition.
That, moreover, is of two kinds:
accusation based on suspicion and accusation based on truth.
As Nārada said:

"A lawsuit should be understood as being of two kinds: based on suspicion (*śaṅkā*) and based on proof of fact (*tattva*). Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while proof of fact arises from the discovery of stolen goods (*hoḍha*) and the observation of signs. (NSm Mā 1.22)
*Hoḍhā* means stolen property;
that is to say, the *liṅga* (mark).
By means of that, "seeing" refers either to direct observation or to seeing the stolen property (*hoḍhābhidarśana*).
Therefore, that [charge] is also twofold:
consisting of a prohibition and consisting of an injunction. For example:
"Having taken gold and other goods from me, he does not return them."
And [the thought], "This person is seizing my field and so forth.
And it was said by Kātyāyana: "He who does not wish to act justly toward his own property, or who performs what is unjust... (KSm 139).
Furthermore, it is divided into eighteen types,
as Manu said:
"Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt (ṛṇādāna), followed by deposit (nikṣepa) and sale without ownership (asvāmivikraya)."
Joint undertaking, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen;
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
"The duties of women and men, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these eighteen are the titles in the administration of justice here.
(MDh 8.4–7) These also become numerous again through the differentiation of the matters to be proven (*sādhya*).
As Nārada said:
"There is another division of these very [categories] which consists of one hundred and eight; due to the diversity of human actions, it is said to have a hundred branches. (NSm Mā 1.20)
By the phrase "if he informs the king," it is shown that he comes and informs on his own initiative, and not because he has been sent by the king or instigated by the king's official. As Manu says:
"The king himself should not initiate a legal case, nor should his official."
"And one must never, under any circumstances, swallow up a matter that has been brought forward by another.

(MDh 8.43) By the word "by others" (*paraiḥ*), he shows that a legal proceeding may take place between one person and another, between one and two, or between one and many. Furthermore, as for [the verse]:
"An action involving one person against many, or involving women and servants, shall be deemed inadmissible as a legal claim; so it has been declared by those who know the Dharma.
This statement of Nārada refers to cases where there are two distinct objects of proof (*sādhyadvaya*).

If he reports to the king, then, having been questioned by the king himself, he should report while dressed in modest attire. Once reported, if it is appropriate, the summoning of the defendant by means of a seal or other such methods, as well as the non-summoning of those who are ineligible for summons and so forth, is established by the sense of the matter itself; therefore, it has not been explicitly stated.
In another Smṛti, however, it is stated for the sake of clarity:
"At the proper time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him speaking of his business:
'What is your business? What is your distress? Do not fear; speak, O man!'"
"By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason should one ask? Thus should he who is thus questioned speak together with the members of the assembly and the Brahmins."
Having deliberated on the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter summon [the defendant] for that purpose,
or else deposit a seal with him, or appoint a person to represent him.

A king should not summon servants who are immature, childish, or elderly; those distracted by improper or difficult tasks; those overwhelmed by the failure of business or by calamities; those preoccupied with royal duties or festivals; or those who are intoxicated, insane, heedless, or afflicted by pain.

A young woman born of noble family who has not yet reached her menses, as well as a maiden who is the best among all castes and has already given birth— these are traditionally held to have their kinsmen as their masters.
The summoning of those women who are dependent on others for their livelihood, those who are wanton, prostitutes, those of ruined families, and those who have fallen from their caste is prescribed.
Having ascertained the time, the place, and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually summon even those who are unfit for court by means of vehicles.

"Even those who have gone forth as forest-dwellers and the like, once their intent is known, the king should summon them for matters of great importance, provided he does not provoke their anger. Thus,
the rule regarding restraint (*āsedha*) has been stated by Nārada as being established by the very nature of the matter.
The plaintiff shall restrain one who fails to appear at the matter to be stated or who departs from that place,
until the appearance for the summons.
Confinement may be of four kinds: restricted to a place, restricted by time, restricted from travel, and restricted from work; one who is not confined must not violate such restrictions.
When the time for restraint has arrived and one is under restraint, he who violates that restraint should be disciplined; by acting otherwise, the restrainer shall not incur a fine.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering danger in an inaccessible region,
one who departs while his protection remains unestablished shall not be held at fault for that departure.
One who desires to settle a debt, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal service.
"Cowherds [are exempt] during the time cattle graze; farmers during the sowing of crops; artisans at their respective times; and those in arms during a conflict. (NSm Mā 1.41–46).
"Seizure" (*āsedha*) is confinement by royal command.
Those who are incapable and others like them may send their son or another friend; yet they are not speakers on behalf of another,
for he is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent.
"An advocate who speaks falsely in legal proceedings should be punished," according to the statement of Nārada (NSm Mā 2.23). // 2.5 //
When one of the means—seals, written documents, or witnesses—has been brought by the defendant, what should the judge do? To this he says:

The defendant shall write down before him the claim exactly as it was stated by the plaintiff, marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other identifying characteristics. (YDh 2.6)
That which is sought after is the *artha*, meaning that which is to be accomplished; one who possesses such an object is an *arthin* (plaintiff),
and his adversary is the *pratyarthin* (defendant).
In front of him,
before him, it should be written— that is, it must be inscribed—
in the same manner as it was previously stated at the time of the formal petition.
It cannot be otherwise,
for if one were to speak otherwise, it would entail the collapse of legal procedure;
such a person is a speaker of falsehood, a hater of action, one who does not appear [in court], and one who is without a reply.
"One who flees when summoned is considered a defeated party; thus, the defeated is said to be of five kinds" (NSm Mā 2.33).

Since the plaintiff's statement has already been recorded at the very time of the formal complaint (*āvedana*), recording it again would be redundant; therefore, he says "the year, month," and so forth—meaning by means of the year, month, fortnight, lunar day, weekday, and so on.
It is marked by the plaintiff and defendant, the caste of the non-Brahmins, and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the object, its number, place, time, capacity, gender, and other such signs are included. As it has been said:
It should be meaningful, conjoined with dharma, complete, and unconfused;
it should consist of expressive words that state what is to be established and are connected to the subject at hand.
It must be well-known, non-contradictory, certain, capable of proving the point,
concise, complete in its meaning, and not inconsistent with time or place.
It is endowed with the year, season, month, fortnight, day, time,
place, region, location, dwelling, the name of the task to be accomplished, caste, form, and age.
It was marked with the names of many kings— both his own and those of others— as well as his ancestors, just like the number of proofs for a thesis or the names of one's own and opposing disputants.
"That which, like an embrace of forgiveness despite personal suffering,
conveys what is to be taken away and what is to be given when it is reported to the king, is called *bhāṣā*.
*Bhāṣā*, *pratijñā*, and *pakṣa* are not different in meaning."
At the time of the formal plea (āvedana), only the matter of the case was written down; the distinction is that before the defendant, it is written down as specified by the year, month, and so forth.
Although this specification of the year is not useful in all legal transactions, it is nevertheless useful for the purpose of determining [the priority] in cases of mortgage, gift, and purchase:
"In the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, however, the earlier one is indeed more powerful."
According to this statement,
even in terms of worldly transaction (*arthavyavahāra*), whatever quantity of whatever substance was taken from whom by whom in one year,
and was returned, that same substance, in that same quantity, is again taken from that person by that same person in another year.
If, when being questioned, he should say,
"It is true that it was taken and returned," [the judge should consider] whether it was taken and returned at the end of the year.
The phrase "in this year" is employed [as a specification];
in the same way, [specifications] such as the month and so forth are also to be applied.
Furthermore, [specifications] such as the location and place are used in the case of immovable property.
Thus they are employed: the region, as well as the location, the configuration,
the genus, the designation, the dwelling, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should cause these ten items to be recorded: [the names of] the father and grandfather, and the proclamation of former kings.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
"Place" refers to the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) and so forth;
"location" refers to Vārāṇasī and so forth.
"Location" (*saṃniveśa*) refers to houses, fields, and so forth, situated properly and delimited by the divisions of the eastern and western directions.
"Class" (*jāti*) refers to the status of being a Brahmin and so forth, belonging to the plaintiff and the defendant. And "name" (*saṃjñā*)...
Devadatta and others;
*adhivāsa* refers to people living in the vicinity;
*pramāṇa* refers to the measurement of land, such as *nivartana* and so forth.
The names of the fields— such as a rice field, a betel-nut field, black soil, or white soil—
as well as the names of the father and grandfather of the plaintiff and the defendant.

And there is the mention of the names of the three preceding kings. The intended meaning is that in whatever legal proceeding the year, month, and so forth are required, they should be written down to that extent. Thus...

Since the definition of a thesis (pakṣa) has been established, it is already proven that those things which lack the characteristics of a thesis but appear as if they were theses are merely fallacious theses (pakṣābhāsa);
therefore, the Lord of Yogins did not state the fallacious theses separately.
However, others have stated them for the sake of clarity.
"One should avoid a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) that is unestablished, non-exceptable, purposeless, useless, impossible to prove, or contradictory. (KSm 140).
An "unestablished" [thesis] is, for example: "He does not give my rabbit's horn after having taken it," and so forth.
"Unobstructed" means, for example, "this person conducts his affairs in his own home by means of the light from the lamp in our house.
"Meaningless" refers to that which is devoid of a denotable object, such as "kacaṭatapagajaḍadaba" and so forth.
That which is purposeless (*niṣprayojana*) is, for example: "This Devadatta is reciting in a beautiful voice in the vicinity of our house," and so forth.
That which is impossible to accomplish (*asādhya*) is, for example: "I [was killed] by Devadatta."
"Laughing with a contraction of the eyebrows," and so forth—
this is not something to be proven because of the impossibility of its accomplishment;
nor [is it so] because of its brevity of duration.
When witnesses are available, written evidence is set aside from afar because of its relative insignificance, and divine proof is not admitted; this is contradictory,
as in the case of saying "I have been cursed by a mute person," and so forth, or when it contradicts the city, the kingdom, and the like.
He who is shunned by the king, he who causes opposition among the citizens,
or likewise among the entire kingdom and its constituent elements;
Or any others who create discord among cities, villages, or the great multitude—all such legal proceedings are declared to be inadmissible. Thus it is said.

As for the statement that "a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) muddled by multiple words is not established," if in that context it is said to be "muddled by multiple subjects (*vastu*)," then there is no fault.
Because there is no fault in a claim such as, "My gold, clothing, coins, or the like was taken by him," [if it is not supported by evidence],
it constitutes a fallacious plaint (*pakṣābhāsa*) due to its confusion with categories such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*).
If this is argued, that too is not correct;
for it is indeed accepted that such claims as "my coins were taken by him at interest," "gold was deposited in his hand," and "he is seizing my field" constitute a legal plaint (*pakṣa*).
However, due to the difference in actions,
the legal procedure occurs sequentially and not simultaneously;
as Kātyāyana has said:
"Even if a matter involves many assertions and is well-established in legal proceedings,
the king may certainly take it up out of a desire to ascertain the truth.
(KSm 137) Therefore, the meaning of this is that a plaint involving multiple points cannot be resolved all at once.
By the mention of "one who has a purpose," sons, fathers, and so forth are included, because they share a single purpose;
for even in the case of one who is appointed [to officiate], that same single purpose is implied by the very fact of the appointment.

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant, whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory or defeat belongs to those two [parties]. According to this, victory and defeat belong to the original owners themselves.
And this, having been written with chalk on the ground or a wooden board and refined by the process of addition and subtraction, should subsequently be entered upon a formal document;
the judge shall record the plaintiff's case exactly as it was stated.
"Then it is refined on a board with chalk and subsequently on paper," according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana.
Furthermore, this refinement must be carried out until the defendant's reply (*uttara*) is seen; it should not go beyond that point.
Because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress;
for this very reason, Nārada stated:
"One should examine the plaintiff's claim as long as the defendant's reply has not been seen."
For one who has been restrained by the subsequent [rule], the purification shall be accomplished by means of the latter.
Thus,

if the members of the court (*sabhyas*) deliver a verdict without having even examined the plaintiff's case, then, after punishing those members with the penalty prescribed for acting out of passion or greed (*rāga* or *lobha*), the legal proceeding must be initiated again, beginning from the plaintiff's formal statement (*pratijñā*).
"By the king," [it is said]. (2.6)
When the plaint has been thus purified and recorded on the document, what should be done? To this he says:
"The defendant, having heard the meaning of the claim, shall write his reply in the presence of the plaintiff" (YDh 2.7ab).
He by whom the meaning of the *bhāṣā* (plaint) has been heard is the "one who has heard the meaning" (*śrutārtha*); his reply (*uttara*) follows after the plaint.
The word "bhavati" (it occurs) indicates that the *uttara* (reply) is to be written;
it is to be inscribed in the presence (*saṃnidhau*) or vicinity of the plaintiff (*pūrvāvedaka*), who is the claimant (*arthin*).
Furthermore, that which constitutes a refutation of what was previously stated is called the *uttara*. As it has been said:
"Those who know [the subject] recognize a reply as one that pervades the position (*pakṣa*), is essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation.
Here, "pervading the position" means being capable of refuting it.
"Essential" means that which is right and not deviating from justice;
"unambiguous" means free from doubt.
"Unconfused" means not contradictory in its preceding and succeeding parts.
"Not to be understood through commentary" means that which requires explanation because it employs unfamiliar terminology,
or because it expresses its meaning through poorly joined inflections, compounds, or ellipses, or by using the language of another region.
That is not a valid rejoinder.
And that is of four kinds: admission, denial, counter-attack, and the application of a previous legal principle.
Thus Kātyāyana says: "The true reply, the false reply, likewise the counter-attack, and the plea of prior judgment—thus the reply is of four kinds. (KSm 165)
In that regard, an example of truthful speech is as follows: when it is said, "He owes me a hundred coins," one says, "Truly, he owes them.
As it has been said:
"The defendant's declaration of truth is declared to be *pratipatti*.
(KSm 168) But a false plea (*mithyottara*) is "I do not owe [the debt].
And so Kātyāyana says:
"If the defendant should deny the charge brought against him,
one should know that to be a false reply (*mithyottara*) according to legal procedure.
(KSm 167) And that false reply is of four kinds.
"This is false; I do not know it; I was not present there at that time;
and I was not born at that time"—thus is a fourfold perjury.
Regarding what is called *pratyavaskandana* (denial by contradiction), it refers to asserting that what was truly received, returned, or obtained through a gift [was not]. As it has been said:
Nārada says: "If the defendant, having admitted the matter exactly as it was written by the plaintiff, should state a legal justification, that is known as *pratyavaskandana* (counter-pleading)."
But the plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāyottara*) occurs where the defendant says: "I have been accused in this matter, and in that case, I was defeated according to the course of legal procedure.
And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"Even if one has been defeated by conduct (*ācāra*), if he is made to write [an admission] again, he is to be declared as having been previously defeated; that is called *prāṅnyāya*. (KSm 171).
Thus, the definition of a *uttara* being established, those which lack the characteristics of a *uttara* yet appear to be *uttaras* are considered *uttarābhāsas* (fallacious replies).

This is established by the sense of the matter and is clarified in another Smṛti: "Anything other than what is under discussion— whether it be doubtful, too little, or too much— is not [to be cited]."
Another [type of] response would likewise not be valid if it only pervades one part of the subject (pakṣa).

"A response that has disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is likewise confused, requires interpretation, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the achievement of one's own objective. (cf. KSm 175)
In that regard, there is doubt:
when it is said, "A hundred gold pieces were taken by him," one wonders whether it is true that a hundred gold pieces were taken,
or perhaps a hundred māṣas.
Something other than what was stated:
for example, when charged with a debt of one hundred gold pieces, saying, "I owe one hundred *paṇas*.
Something too little: when charged with a debt of one hundred gold pieces, saying, "I owe five hundred."
"Excessive": when, upon a claim for one hundred gold pieces, one says, "I owe two hundred.
"Pervading a portion of the case": [is when the evidence applies only to part of the claim].
In a lawsuit concerning gold, clothing, and so forth, [the defendant's reply] is: "Gold was received, nothing else. This is a *vyastapada* (separate-member) response;
for example, in a lawsuit for a debt of one hundred *suvarṇas*, the reply is given by means of another term [denying the specific item].
"I was struck by him":
this is non-pervasive; it is non-pervasive with respect to specific qualifiers such as place and location, as for example, "in the Middle Country, in Vārāṇasī."

When the plaintiff has written in the plaint, "The field in the eastern direction was taken away by him," and [the defendant replies], "The field was taken away"— this is a hidden meaning (*nigūḍhārtha*). For example, in a lawsuit for a debt of one hundred gold pieces, when [the defendant says], "Do I owe this to him alone?"— here, by implication (*dhvaninā*), [the meaning is conveyed].

If the judge, a court member, or the plaintiff suggests that the defendant owes money to someone else, this is a "hidden meaning" (*nigūḍhārtha*). It is "confused" (*ākula*) when it is contradictory from beginning to end;
for example, when an accusation of a hundred gold pieces has been made, [the defendant] says, "It is true I received them, but I do not owe them."
"Accessible through commentary" means that it is accessible through commentary by virtue of the employment of ill-formed case endings, compounds, and necessary ellipses,
as well as by the use of regional dialects.

Or: for example, in a legal claim regarding a debt of one hundred gold pieces, [the defendant] says "I do not know [anything about] my father's gold" because of the statement "one hundred was taken. Here, because of the statement of the father who took the hundred, [the meaning is] "I do not know that a hundred gold pieces were taken.
"Substanceless" (*asāra*) means contrary to logic (*nyāyaviruddha*), such as: "He took a hundred gold pieces with interest, but only the interest was paid."
In the case of a legal claim stating, "The principal has not been paid" or "Interest was paid,
but the principal was not received," the use of the singular number in the term *uttara* (reply) excludes the possibility of multiple concurrent replies.
As Kātyāyana said:

"That which is true regarding one part of the claim, and contains a reason regarding another part, and is false regarding yet another part—because of this confusion, it is not a valid defense. (KSm 189)
And the reason for its unsurpassed nature was stated by that very same [author]:
"In a single dispute, there should not be legal action for both litigants;
there can be no establishment of the matter for both, nor can there be two actions in one case. (KSm 190)

In the case of a confusion between a plea of denial (*mithyā*) and a plea of a special cause (*kāraṇa*), the burden of proof (*kriyā*) would accrue to both the plaintiff and the defendant; for it is stated in the legal tradition: "The burden of proof lies with the plaintiff in a plea of denial, and with the defendant in a plea of a special cause."
Both of these are contradictory within a single legal proceeding;
for example, in a charge that "he took both gold and a hundred silver coins," [the defendant might claim] "the gold was not taken, but the hundred silver coins were taken and have been returned."
But when there is a confusion between *kāraṇa* and *prāṅnyāya*, the defendant alone must provide two means of proof;
for it is said: "When both *prāṅnyāya* and *kāraṇa* are asserted, the defendant shall point out the proof."
For example, it is as when gold has been taken and then returned, yet one is defeated through the course of legal procedure on the grounds of a monetary debt;
in such a case of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), the matter must be established either by a document of victory (*jayapatra*) or by those who witnessed the prior judgment.
But in the case of a plea based on a specific reason (*kāraṇokti*), it must be established by witnesses, documents, and so forth.
"There must be cultivation" is a contradiction.
The same should be understood regarding the confusion of the [other] three subsequent [factors].
Just as by this [process], gold [is produced].

In a lawsuit where it is alleged, "A hundred *rūpakas* and garments were received," the defendant replies: "It is true that gold was received and returned, but the hundred *rūpakas* were not received; as for the matter of the garments, however, I am defeated according to the previous legal principle.
This same logic applies even in the case of a fourfold confusion (*catuḥsaṃkara*). Of these...
Furthermore, its unsurpassed nature consists in the fact that without each respective [element], that particular part cannot be established; thus, it possesses superiority through sequence.
And this sequence occurs according to the desire of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the members of the court.
However, where both [parties]...

In that case, there is a confusion (*saṃkara*): for that [plaint] which has a vast range of subject matter, legal procedure must first be set in motion by adopting its [corresponding] reply; subsequently, legal procedure should be observed by adopting a reply with a narrower scope.
And where there is agreement (*saṃpratipatti*), there is no other reply.

And there is no confusion in that case; rather, the conventional usage should be understood as occurring through the subsequent adoption of another [term], because in the case of consensus, there is an absence of [further] action.
As stated by Hārīta:
If both a false reply and a plea based on a special cause should occur in one case,
or if a true reply occurs along with another, which reply is to be accepted there?
Having said this, he further stated:
"That answer should be known as non-confused which has a broad range of meaning, or where the fruit of the action resides; otherwise, it is the opposite."
The ellipsis is "it becomes mixed.
The meaning is that, with respect to the remainder, the order is optional.
In that regard, [the following] is for the sake of the extensive meaning:
For example, in a lawsuit where the claim is that "he took gold, a hundred silver coins, and clothes," but [the defendant] replies, "He did not take the gold or the hundred silver coins,
but he did take the clothes and returned them"; in this case,
because the plea of denial (*mithyottara*) covers the majority of the subject matter, [it prevails].
Having first taken up the action of the plaintiff, the legal proceeding should be initiated; afterwards, the proceeding concerning the garment [should follow].

This same principle should be applied in cases of confusion between *mithyā* and *pūrvanyāya*, as well as in cases of confusion between *kāraṇa* and *pūrvanyāya*. Likewise, in that very same accusation...

If, regarding the claim "I received gold and a hundred coins, but I shall give them back," the defendant replies, "Clothes were not received, or if they were received, they have been returned," then even though the subject matter (the clothes) is extensive, since there is no proof (*kriyā*) required for that part, the legal proceeding must be carried forward based on the proof required for the other parts of the defense, such as denial (*mithyā*). Where...

However, the pervasion of the entire position occurs in the case of both the "false" (mithyā) and the "counter-plea" (kāraṇottara), as for example: someone points out a specific cow by name and says, "This cow is mine; it was lost at such-and-such a time, and today it was seen in his house."
But another says: "This is false;
she was staying in my house even before the time you indicated, and she was born in my house."
This, first of all, is not a non-answer because it is capable of refuting the opponent's position, nor is it merely false because a reason has been put forward.
Nor is it a valid reason, because not even a single part [of the claim] is admitted;
therefore, this is a false rejoinder based on a cause. And in this case, the burden of proof (kriyā) falls upon the defendant.
Because of the statement, "When the defendant is the one who asserts the cause," one might ask:
why does the burden of proof (kriyā) not fall upon the plaintiff in the case of a false claim?
It is because that [false claim] has as its object a mere falsehood.
As for the phrase "when the defendant [pleads] *kāraṇa*," why does this not also refer to the subject of a pure *kāraṇa* plea?
It is not so;
because every *kāraṇa* defense is by nature associated with a denial (*mithyā*), there is no such thing as a pure *kāraṇa* defense.

In a reply based on a well-known cause (*prasiddhakāraṇottara*), there is the falsity of one part of the asserted proposition (*pratijñātārtha*) by virtue of its own admission; for example: "It is true that a hundred coins were received, but I do not owe them because they have been returned. This is the illustration under discussion.
However, the distinction is that there is no acceptance even of a single part of the meaning of the proposition.
And this has been clearly stated by Hārīta:
"Between the two [defenses of] *mithyā* and *kāraṇa*, the *kāraṇa* (causal) reply is to be accepted.
This refers to cases where both *mithyā* and *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment) pervade the plaintiff's claim.

For example, in a legal suit where the charge is "he owes a hundred coins," if it is argued that "this is false because he was previously defeated in this same matter," here too the burden of proof (kriyā) rests solely upon the defendant.

Because of the statement, "But when a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a ground for defeat (*kāraṇa*) has been stated, the defendant shall point out the proof (*kriyā*)," it follows that a pure plea of prior judgment would lack a valid rejoinder (*anuttaratva*), as such a pure plea does not exist [as a formal category].

An admission (*saṃpratipatti*) is also a valid rejoinder precisely because it negates the status of being "that which is to be proven" (*sādhya*) by presenting as established that very thesis (*pakṣa*) which was taught as something to be proven.
However, when there is a confusion between a ground for defeat (*kāraṇa*) and a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), [it is not a valid rejoinder].

For example, when one accused of having received a hundred [coins] replies, "It is true that I received it, but it has been returned," the defendant is defeated on that very point by means of *prāṅnyāya*.
In that case, it is according to the pleasure of the defendant; thus, it does not apply anywhere else.
The decision is that there would be the consequence of two actions in a single legal proceeding for both the proponent and the opponent.

When the plaint has been thus entered on the subsequent leaf, since the establishment of the matter to be proven depends upon the means of proof, [the author], anticipating the question of who should provide the statement of those means of proof, says:
"Then the plaintiff shall cause to be written the proof for the matter he has asserted" (YDh 2.7cd).
Immediately thereafter, the petitioner, who possesses the matter to be proven, should have it written down at once, without delay.

"The matter asserted" (*pratijñātārtha*) refers to that which is both the matter asserted (*pratijñāta*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*). Its "proof" (*sādhana*)—that by which something is proven—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By stating here that "one should write immediately," it is understood that even a delay in time for the presentation of the reply is admitted;
this will be examined further below.

By stating that "the plaintiff shall cause the proof of the matter asserted to be written down," it is meant that whoever possesses the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven) must cause the proof of the matter asserted to be written down. Consequently, in the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya-uttara*), since the prior judgment itself is the *sādhya*, the defendant alone becomes the plaintiff; therefore, he alone must cause the proof to be written down. Likewise, in the case of a plea of a special defense (*kāraṇa-uttara*), since the special reason itself is the *sādhya*, the party asserting the reason is the plaintiff; thus, he alone must cause it to be written down.
But in the case of a false reply (*mithyottara*), the plaintiff alone is the claimant (*arthin*); he himself must set forth the proof (*sādhana*).
Thus, by stating that "the claimant shall cause the document to be written," it is declared that the claimant alone—and no one else—shall cause it to be written.

And therefore, since both the "admission" (*saṃpratipatti*) reply and the "confession" (*bhāṣottara*) reply lack the object of proof due to the absence of the probandum, there is no presentation of a means of proof at all; it is understood that the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is concluded by that alone.

This very point has been clearly stated by Hārīta: "But when the grounds for the prior claim have been stated, the defendant shall indicate the means of proof; however, in the case of a denial (*mithyā*), the plaintiff shall do so; but in the case of a confession (*pratipatti*), there shall be no such need. (2.7)

"Upon its establishment, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite. (YDh 2.8ab) Upon the establishment—that is, the completion—of that means of proof (*pramāṇa*), characterized as the documents, witnesses, and so forth to be described hereafter, one attains success, which is the victory of the party for whom the matter is to be proven.

Therefore, the connection is as follows: if, by means other than this method—that is, by another way—the proof is not established, one incurs the opposite, namely the non-establishment of the thesis, which is characterized as defeat.

Having thus described the nature of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), he concludes: "This four-footed legal procedure has been set forth for disputes" (YDh 2.8cd). "The king shall examine the legal procedures" (YDh 2.1).
Thus has judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) been described.

This very procedure, consisting of four feet and divided into four parts through conceptualization, has been demonstrated and explained in connection with legal disputes such as the non-payment of debts and the like.
Among these, the first is the "foot" of the plaint (*bhāṣāpāda*), which consists of the writing to be presented before the defendant.
"The answer to the matter heard [by the court] shall be written"—this is the second part, the *uttarapāda*.
"Then the plaintiff shall have it written immediately"—this is the third part, the *kriyāpāda*.
"Upon its establishment, he obtains success"—this is the fourth part, the *sādhyasiddhipāda*. As it has been said:
The settlement of disputes among people arising from conflicting claims regarding their respective interests,
established through the logic of verbal testimony, is declared to be judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*).
"It is called 'four-footed' (catuṣpād) because it implies four components through its successive stages consisting of the statement, the rejoinder, the proof,

and the establishment. However, in the case of the rejoinder of "agreement" (*saṃpratipatti*), it does not possess the characteristic of "establishment of the probandum" (*sādhyasiddhi*), because no means of proof (*sādhana*) is indicated and because the object of the statement is not something yet to be proven.

The statement "there is a foot" merely implies that there are two feet. Following the statement of the plaint, the *pratyākalita*—characterized by the deliberation among the members of the court as to which action should be taken by the plaintiff or the defendant—is not designated as a "foot of the lawsuit" by the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya). Furthermore, because it lacks a connection with the litigant, it does not constitute a foot of the lawsuit.
Thus it is established. // 2.8 //

Thus ends the section on the General Matrix of Legal Procedure (*sādhāraṇavyavahāramātṛkāprakaraṇa*). Having thus explained the matrix of legal procedure (*vyavahāramātṛkā*) which is applicable to all legal matters, [the author now addresses] a specific legal matter.
To demonstrate a certain distinction, he says:
"Without having fully resolved the charge, one should not bring a counter-charge against him" (YDh 2.9ab).
That which is charged against is the *abhiyoga*, meaning an offense.
Without having settled or resolved that charge, one should not counter-charge the accuser; one should not connect him with an offense,
even if a counter-attack takes the form of a counter-charge.
Nevertheless, because it consists in avoiding one's own offense, it does not fall within the scope of prohibition;
therefore, this is a prohibition against counter-accusation (*pratyabhiyoga*) in the form of not suppressing one's own prosecution.
This was stated with reference to the defendant;
now, regarding the plaintiff, he says:
"One should not cause a person who has been accused by another, nor one who has not spoken, to undergo a change of state. (YDh 2.9cd)
Another claimant shall not bring a suit against one who has already been charged with a non-dilatory accusation.
Furthermore,
it was stated at the time of the formal petition:
What has been stated should not be brought to, nor made to reach, a state of natural deviation or contradiction.
This is what is meant:
whatever object was reported at the time of its perception in a certain form, that very object must be recorded in exactly that same way at the time of speaking.
"Not otherwise."
[Objection: But was this not already stated in the rule, "The plaint must be written in the presence of the defendant exactly as it was presented by the plaintiff"?
For what purpose is it stated again that "one should not alter what has been stated"? [Response:

It is said: by the phrase "exactly as presented by the plaintiff," it is meant that whatever matter was reported at the time of the formal presentation (*āvedana*) must be written down in the same manner at the time of the formal statement (*bhāṣā*).

It has been stated that even in a single word, there is no other entity [than the word itself]. For example, when one declares at the time of filing a suit, "I borrowed a hundred pieces of gold as interest," but later, at the time of the formal statement (bhāṣā) in the presence of the defendant, says, "I borrowed a hundred garments as interest."
This should not be said;
for if that were the case, even when one moves to another word, because one has moved to a different entity, the inferior debater would be subject to punishment.
By the rule "one should not lead [the discussion] away from its stated nature," moving to another word is prohibited even when there is a single underlying entity.

For example, having stated at the time of the formal complaint that "this person has taken a hundred coins on interest but does not repay them," he says at the time of the trial, "He forcibly seized a hundred coins."
In that context, moving to another object was prohibited; here, however, moving to another word is prohibited, so there is no tautology.
This very point has been clarified by Nārada:
"He who, having abandoned his former position, takes up another again—by such shifting of his footing, that man should be known as a defeated litigant. (NSm Mā 2.24).
A defeated litigant is subject to punishment, but he does not lose the matter at hand.

Therefore, this instruction—that "one should not depart until the legal proceeding is concluded," and so forth—is intended solely for the purpose of preventing negligence on the part of both the defendant and the plaintiff; it does not concern the actual success or failure in achieving the matter at hand.
For this very reason, the author will state later: "Having set aside frivolous objections, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the truth" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.19).
And this should be understood as applying to legal proceedings concerning material wealth;
however, in a legal proceeding arising from anger, if one makes a statement through negligence, one is indeed defeated even in the original lawsuit itself.

As Nārada said: "In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail because of verbal deception; however, in cases involving another's wife, land, or the non-payment of debt, even if punished, one does not lose the legal claim. (NSm Mā 2.25)

The meaning of this is as follows: in all disputes concerning matters of fact—not those arising from anger—even if there is a verbal quibble or a statement made through inadvertence, one does not sink;
that is, one is not defeated.
The sense is that one is not deprived of the subject matter at hand.
An illustration of this is the case beginning with "another's wife" and so forth.
Just as one who is subject to punishment for seizing another's wife, land, or debts by falsely claiming ignorance does not fail in his purpose, so it is in all disputes concerning property.

From the inclusion of the term "dispute over property" (*arthavivāda*), it is understood that in disputes arising from anger, if one makes a statement based on negligence, one is defeated even regarding the matter at hand;
for example: "I was struck on the head by him with his foot."
If, having stated [the truth] at the time of the formal plea, one says at the time of testimony, "I was struck by hand or foot," he shall not only be punished but also lose the case. (2.9)
He states an exception to the rule that "one should not bring a counter-charge against another without having first resolved one's own charge":
"One may bring a counter-charge in cases of quarrels and acts of violence.

(YDh 2.10ab) In the case of quarrels consisting of verbal or physical abuse, and in acts of violence such as the destruction of life caused by poison, weapons, and the like—where a counter-charge is possible—one may indeed do so.
One may bring a counter-charge against the accuser even without having fully discharged one's own obligation.

But surely, in this case as well, since a counter-charge—being of the nature of not refuting the prior plea—is not a valid rejoinder, it constitutes a separate proposition; thus, the impossibility of conducting two lawsuits simultaneously remains the same.
True.

Here, the instruction for a counter-charge (*pratyabhiyoga*) is not for the sake of simultaneous legal proceedings, but rather for the purpose of obtaining a lesser punishment or avoiding a heavier one.
For instance, when a charge is made such as "I was struck or cursed by him," [the defendant may reply] "Previously, I was struck or cursed by him."
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates that the punishment shall be light in the case of a counter-accusation;
as Nārada says:
"He who first brings a false accusation shall certainly be the one to bear the guilt."
"Furthermore, he who acts with disrespect later [is at fault], whereas previously discipline was paramount. (NSm 15–16.10).
Moreover, when both parties simultaneously engage in such acts as striking one another, there is an exemption from the heavier punishment;
for in cases of verbal abuse or assault, when both have engaged in the act simultaneously:
"If no distinction can be found, the legal procedure should be the same for both.

Thus, even though simultaneous engagement in legal proceedings is impossible, a counter-plaint is meaningful in cases such as quarrels; however, in matters such as the non-payment of debts, it is entirely useless.
Having stated the procedure for the plaintiff and the defendant, he now declares the duty of the presiding judge together with the members of the court:

"A surety capable of determining the case must be accepted from both parties. (YDh 2.10cd) "From both" means from both the plaintiff and the defendant in all disputes. "The task of determination" (*kāryanirṇaya*) refers to the act of reaching a verdict.

Because the word *kārya* is listed in the group beginning with *āhitāgni*, it takes the preceding position [in the compound]. A *pratibhū* (surety) is one who is capable of performing the duty (*kārya*) of the decision—that is, the payment of the adjudicated debt and the imposition of punishment. He is called a *pratibhū* because he stands in for that duty; he becomes like that very duty itself.
He should be accepted by the presiding judge together with the members of the court;
in his absence, men should be appointed to protect the plaintiff and the defendant.
And they must be paid their wages daily by those two.
Thus says Kātyāyana: "Now, if there is no surety and the litigant has business to attend to..."
Having protected it until the end of the day, he should give the wage to the servant.
Thus [ends verse] 2.10.

(KSm 117) It has been stated that in the matter of reaching a decision regarding the plaintiff and the defendant, a surety (*pratibhū*) should be taken by the presiding judge together with the members of the court.
Anticipating the question—“What is that judicial proceeding in which a surety is taken?”—the author says:
If the defendant denies a claim that has been proven by the plaintiff through witnesses and other means, he shall pay the debt to the plaintiff and an equal amount to the king.
One who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim as a fine.
(YDh 2.11) When the defendant denies a charge that has been presented by the plaintiff, if it is subsequently proven by the plaintiff through witnesses and so forth—

If the defendant is made to admit [the claim], he shall then pay the principal sum to the plaintiff and an equal amount as a fine for denial to the king. If the plaintiff is unable to substantiate his case, then he becomes a false accuser; consequently, he shall pay double the amount of the claimed wealth to the king as a penalty for the accusation.

This same rule should be applied to a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) and to a plea of denial (*pratyavaskandana*). In that case, since the plaintiff alone is the one who denies the claim, once he has been proved wrong by the defendant, he shall pay the defendant a fine equal to the subject matter of the suit. If, however, the defendant is unable to prove either the prior judgment or the legal justification (*kāraṇa*), then he himself is the one who brought a false accusation.
He should pay double the amount to the king, and the original amount to the claimant; however,
this applies only in the case of a confession.
There is simply an absence of punishment;
and this applies specifically to the subject of non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), because punishments are prescribed for various other matters in their respective places.
Furthermore, because this [rule] is impossible in transactions concerning property other than money, it does not apply to all subjects.
Although the rule "the king shall compel the debtor to pay" pertains to the subject matter of the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*), we shall explain its specific distinction within that very context.
Alternatively, this very point may also be applied to the scope of all worldly transactions. How so?
When a defendant has denied an accusation made against him, if the accuser [proves it] by means of witnesses and other evidence...
When he has been thus cultivated and applied, then, in each respective case, exactly what was prescribed [should be done].
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
The statement "he shall give wealth as a fine to the king" is a restatement (anuvāda).

Now, if the plaintiff is unable to state his charge, he is declared a "false accuser" (*mithyābhiyogī*) and is enjoined to pay double the wealth [claimed] as a fine; this rule is explicitly stated. Here too, in the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) and a plea of denial (*pratyavaskandana*), it should be applied exactly as before. (2.11)
By stating that "therefore, the plaintiff should immediately have the proof of the matter asserted written down," it is shown that one must wait for the time to write the response (uttara).
Regarding this, he states the exception:
"In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations involving cattle, a calamity, or [an offense] against a woman..."
One should initiate a lawsuit immediately; in other cases, the time is said to depend on one's discretion.
*Sāhasa* refers to acts such as depriving life by means of poison, weapons, and the like.
*Steya* is theft.
Harshness consists of verbal and physical violence,
the characteristics of which will be explained below;
"cow" refers to one that yields milk.
*Abhiśāpaḥ* is an accusation of a sin; *atyayaḥ* is the loss of life or wealth. The singular number is used because it is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) treated as a single unit.
In a dispute concerning character between a woman and a woman of good family, or in a dispute concerning ownership between a woman of good family and a female slave,
one should cause the defendant to state his case and cause him to pay the fine.
One should not wait for time; rather, one should act immediately.
In other types of disputes, however, the time for giving a reply is prescribed according to the wish of the plaintiff, the defendant, the assessors, and the presiding judge. (2.12)
He states the characteristics of a wicked person:
"He moves from one place to another, licks the corners of his mouth, his forehead perspires, and his face becomes discolored. (YDh 2.13)
With parched mouth and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and likewise distorts his lips.
He undergoes a transformation from his natural state through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
"He is proclaimed to be corrupt in a legal accusation or in giving testimony.

(YDh 2.15) He who, by his very nature and not due to causes such as fear, undergoes or experiences a distortion— a change of state— through the actions of mind, speech, and body, is proclaimed to be corrupt in a legal accusation or in giving testimony.
He demonstrates that transformation by dividing it [into parts]: "It moves from one place to another and does not remain anywhere;
it licks the corners of the mouth—the edges of the lips—with the tip of the tongue."
"It touches" or "strikes" refers to a transformation of the action.
His forehead perspires, becoming marked with drops of sweat;
and his face undergoes a change of color—becoming pale, or turning black—which refers to the body.

"Distortion" (*vikṛtiḥ*): one whose speech is parched and faltering; that is to say, he is so described because his speech is parched, faltering, stammering, and incoherent. Furthermore, "distortion of speech" refers to speaking much that is contradictory, meaning inconsistent with what was said before or after.
Not honoring the words spoken by another by giving a reply, or not honoring their gaze by looking back,
is a sign of mental distortion;
likewise, distorting or curling the lips is also a distortion of the body.
And this is stated merely as a suspicion of a fault, not for the sake of a certain determination of a fault;
for it is difficult to discern the distinction between a natural modification and one that is adventitious.
Now, even if someone of keen intellect were to attain discernment (*viveka*), nevertheless, it would not constitute grounds for defeat;
for people do not perform the funeral rites for one who is about to die simply because they observe the physical signs of death.
Even though it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "in this way his defeat will occur," there is no entailment of performing the action caused by defeat. // 2.13 // 2.14 // 2.15 //
Furthermore:
"He who, being independent, attempts to prove a doubtful matter, he who absconds, or he who says nothing when summoned—he is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment. (YDh 2.16)

He who, being independent and regardless of proof, establishes through means such as seizure (*āsedha*) a disputed matter that has not even been admitted by the debtor, becomes defeated and is subject to punishment;
as is he who himself admits [the debt] or [admits it] through proof.

"One who, when asked for what has been proven, slips away or flees; and he who, being accused by the king and summoned to the court, says nothing—such a person is also declared defeated and liable to punishment. This is how it is connected. Since it was introduced that "he is proclaimed wicked in the case of a formal charge or in testimony," the mention of "liable to punishment" (daṇḍya) is used so that it should not be understood as merely defining who is defeated.

Since one who is liable to punishment or correction does not, by virtue of the matter, suffer a loss of wealth—given that this shows a lack of loss in terms of the object—one uses the term "defeated" (*hīna*) here so that such [a case] may not be included. (2.16)
Now, when two parties who are litigants regarding a legal matter arrive at the judge simultaneously—
as for example, someone who,
having acquired a field by means of a gift and having enjoyed it for some time, departs for another country with his family due to some business obligation—

[One] has gone away. Another person also, having acquired that very same field by means of a gift and having enjoyed it for some time, has gone to another country. Then both, having returned simultaneously and disputing with one another—saying "This field is mine" and "This field is mine"—approach the judicial authority. When the question arises as to whose legal action (kriyā) should prevail there, [the author] says:

When witnesses are available for both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff; when the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant. (YDh 2.17) When witnesses exist for both parties—that is, for both litigants—the witnesses belong to the plaintiff at the earlier stage.
He who says, "It was accepted by me and enjoyed by me," is the plaintiff (pūrvavādī); however, the witnesses of one who merely previously reported [the claim] are not to be questioned.
But when another speaks thus: "It is true that this [person] previously accepted it..."

"But as for what was enjoyed: this very field was acquired by the king through purchase from him and given to me; or it was acquired by him through a gift and given to me. In that case, the plaintiff's initial claim having been defeated due to its lack of proof, once that initial claim has been refuted, there appear witnesses for the defendant stating that [the field] was received as a gift and enjoyed at a later time.
They must be questioned;
however, the explanation that the witnesses belong to the defendant once the plaintiff has stated his legal grounds and his initial position has been defeated is incorrect.

Since this very point has already been stated by the verse, "Therefore, one who desires that object should have it written down immediately for the purpose of proving the claim" (YDh 2.7), there would otherwise be the fault of tautology;
thus, Nārada has merely clarified the previous explanation:
"Falsehood occurs when there is a prior claim, a cause, or a defendant;
but in the case of a decision based on a previous judgment, the document of victory shall be the proof.
Having said this, [the text continues].
By stating, "When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both,

the witnesses shall belong to the one whose case is the *pūrvapakṣa*," [the author] has presented this separately because it is distinct from the previously mentioned types of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). (2.17)
Moreover:
"If a dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine, his own wager, and the debt itself to the creditor. (YDh 2.18)

If a dispute is a legal proceeding involving a wager— where "paṇa" means a wager and "sapaṇa" means that which exists together with such a wager— then in that sapaṇa proceeding, the king shall cause the defeated party to pay the previously mentioned fine, his own pledged wager to the king, and the wealth at issue to the plaintiff.
Furthermore, where one person, under the influence of a fit of anger,
pledges, "If I am defeated here, I shall pay a hundred-fold stake," while the other pledges nothing at all, a legal proceeding (vyavahāra) nevertheless proceeds there as well.
And when that [trial] has commenced, if the party who made the wagered promise loses, then he alone shall be made to pay the penalty along with the wager;
but the other defeated party shall be made to pay the penalty, not the wager.
This is because of the specific mention of "one's own stake" (*svapaṇam*).
However, where one party pledges one hundred and the other pledges five hundred, even in that case, they should both be made to pay their own respective stakes upon defeat.
By stating, "If the dispute should be accompanied by a wager," it is shown that a dispute may also exist without a wager. (2.18)
Furthermore:
Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the truth; for even if the truth exists, one who fails to present it loses the case in the legal process. (YDh 2.19)

Having cast aside and abandoned deceit and negligence, the king should bring legal proceedings to their conclusion according to what has actually occurred— that is, in accordance with the true nature of the facts—
because even a fact that is real and the true nature of the matter is lost if it is not presented or stated.
One suffers loss through legal proceedings—that is, by means of the judicial process involving witnesses and so forth.
Therefore, one must pursue the truth;
the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, must strive to ensure that both the plaintiff and the defendant speak only the truth.
By means of methods such as conciliation (sāma) and so forth;
that being the case, a decision is reached even without dependence on witnesses and the like.
Now, in every respect...
It is not possible to pursue the actual facts; such being the case, a decision must be made by means of witnesses and other evidence—this is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*).
As it has been said:
"Because it follows both the actual facts and deception, the judicial process is declared to have two courses."
"Truth is that which is conjoined with the real meaning; a quibble is that which is stated through negligence. (NSm Mā 1.24).
In this regard, legal procedure following the truth is primary, while that following a quibble is secondary.
When a legal dispute is resolved by means of witnesses, documents, and so forth...
Sometimes there is a correspondence with the actual fact and sometimes there is not, because witnesses and other such means of proof are also subject to error. (2.19)
Regarding the principle that "even a fact, if not presented [in court], is lost in legal procedure," he provides an illustration:

"If a defendant denies a written document, but is proven [to have made a claim] regarding even one part of it, he must be made by the king to pay the entire amount; however, what was not declared [at the outset] shall not be accepted. (YDh 2.20)

If a defendant denies everything that has been written and asserted by a plaintiff— whether it be gold, silver, clothing, or other items— and thus disavows it all, then, once the defendant has been proven on one part regarding gold through witnesses and other means,
he must be compelled by the king to pay the entire amount previously written, including the silver and other items, to the plaintiff.

But that which was not previously declared is not to be accepted; if, at the time of the trial, it is declared by the plaintiff for the first time with the words "I forgot it before," it is not to be accepted and must not be granted by the king.
And this is not merely based on the scriptural statement;
for, in one instance, there is a certainty regarding the defendant's state of being a liar.
Because the possibility of false speech exists even regarding another part [of the claim],
and because the truthfulness of the claimant is ascertained only with respect to one part.

Since truthfulness is possible even in one part [of his testimony], the conclusion is that the king must cause the entire amount to be paid based on this very statement of the Lord of Yogis, which is supported by the conviction of probability— another name for logical reasoning (*tarka*).
And thus, when a decision is made in accordance with logical arguments (*tarka*),
there is no fault for those who observe legal procedure even if the actual state of the matter is otherwise.
And so says Gautama:

Having stated, "In the acquisition of justice, reasoning (*tarka*) is the means; having inferred by means of it, one should lead [the case] to its proper place" (GDh 11.23–24), he concludes with, "Therefore, the king and the teacher are beyond reproach" (GDh 11.32).
And it is not understood here that an opponent whose testimony is established in only one part is one whose word is not to be accepted;
for there is the statement: "One who is proved in one part must be made to pay everything by the king.
As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:

"Even when there is a lawsuit involving multiple claims, the creditor receives only as much wealth as he can prove by means of witnesses; that much alone is the debt recovered. (KSm 473) This refers to cases concerning debts owed by a son or others to a father or others.

For in that case, a son or other relative who has been charged with many matters and responds by saying "I do not know" is not a concealer; thus, even if he is proven on one part, he does not conceal himself by claiming to be a liar in any respect. Therefore, the legal maxim "what is written is not [admissible] as one [part]" does not apply there, because there is no concealment and a lack of the required presumption (*tarka*).
As for the statement of Kātyāyana, "even when there is a charge involving multiple matters," it refers to a general subject;
having set aside the specific scope of the particular rule— the plea of denial— it applies to the plea of ignorance.

Indeed, in disputes concerning debts and the like which are generally stable, once a decision has been reached, the matter to be proven is not established even if the amount stated is deficient or excessive. (KSm 396)
