By stating this, Kātyāyana has declared that when a lawsuit involves multiple charges and the witnesses have proven only one part— or even more than one part— the entire matter to be proved (*sādhya*) is not established.
This being so, how can there be a proof of the unproven parts once one part has been proven?
It is said:

the meaning is that when witnesses— adduced for the purpose of proving all matters set down in writing— state only a portion or state more than is required, the entire matter to be proven is not established.

In that case as well, because of the statement "it is not established with certainty," there remains only doubt as before; thus, there is indeed an occasion for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
according to the rule that one must eliminate quibbling (*chala*).

In cases such as *sāhasa* (violent crime), however, when witnesses who were designated as capable of proving the entirety of both the charge and the defense establish even a single part, there is indeed proof of the whole charge;
for by that much alone, the *sāhasa* and so forth are established.

And from the words of Kātyāyana: "Even when only a portion of the matter to be proven has been stated by the witnesses, it shall be considered as if the whole were stated; this applies to matters concerning sexual intercourse with women, violence, and theft, which have been declared as the objects to be proven. (KSm 397) 2.20.

Now, is it not the case that this Smṛti rule— "one does not deny a single written document"— is a Smṛti, and likewise, this other rule— "even when there is an accusation involving multiple matters" is also a Smṛti?
In that case, since there is a mutual contradiction between these two Smṛti rules, [which one prevails?]
"Why does mutual contradiction not result in invalidity, and why is the fixed determination of the subject matter (viṣayavyavasthā) resorted to? To this, he says:
"But in the case of a conflict between two Smṛtis, that which is supported by reason (nyāya) is stronger according to worldly practice. (YDh 2.21ab)

Where there is a mutual contradiction between two traditional authorities (*smṛti*), the principle characterized as the general rule and the exception (*utsargāpavāda*)— which establishes the respective domains for the sake of resolving that contradiction— is powerful and effective.
But from what source is that principle to be understood?
Therefore, he says "from common usage" (*vyavahārataḥ*).
It is understood from common usage—that is, from the linguistic practice of elders characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
And thus, in the example under discussion:
In this case too, it is logical that there is simply a fixed determination of the object (*viṣaya-vyavasthā*).
Likewise, in other instances as well, the determination of the object, its conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and so forth, should be applied according to what is possible.
Thus, in response to this universal objection, he states the exception:
"But the law-code is more powerful than the treatise on worldly affairs; such is the settled rule" (YDh 2.21cd).
This is because [the king] acts in accordance with the law-code (dharmaśāstra) (YDh 2.1).
Since the *Arthaśāstra* of Uśanas and others has already been refuted by this very [argument],
the *Arthaśāstra* intended here is that which is characterized as royal policy (*rājanīti*) and is included within the *Dharmaśāstra*.
When there is a conflict between the *Arthaśāstra* and the *Dharmaśāstra*, it is an established rule and boundary that the *Dharmaśāstra* prevails over the *Arthaśāstra*;
even though the two, the *Arthaśāstra* and the *Dharmaśāstra*, have a common author.

Although there is no distinction residing in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), the intention is that the *Dharmaśāstra* is more authoritative because the object of knowledge (*prameya*)— namely, Dharma— is primary, whereas the [physical] object (*artha*) is secondary.
Furthermore, the primacy of Dharma has been demonstrated at the beginning of the treatise.
Therefore, when there is a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra, it is the Arthaśāstra that is simply sublated; there is neither a restriction of scope nor an optionality.
What is an example of this? It is not, for instance:
One should indeed kill an assailant who approaches, without hesitation— even if he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brahmin learned in the scriptures.
"No fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), whether done in secret or openly; fury recoils upon that fury. Likewise:
"Even if he has mastered the Vedānta, one may kill an approaching *ātatāyin* in battle..."
"One who would kill one seeking to kill him does not thereby become a slayer of a Brahmin"—
this and other such passages constitute the *Arthaśāstra*.
This purification has been declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally.
"No expiation is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 11.89),
and so forth— this is the Dharmaśāstra.
When there is a conflict between these two, it is logical that the Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative.

Since these two cannot possibly have the same subject matter, there is no contradiction between them; thus, the question of their relative strength or weakness does not arise. For it is said: "The twice-born may take up arms when their dharma is obstructed" (MDh 8.348).
Having begun thus:
"In self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, and in the protection of women and Brahmins, one who kills according to the law incurs no punishment" (MDh 8.349).

Having stated that one who kills an assailant (*ātatāyin*) with a non-deceptive weapon incurs no punishment— whether for self-defense, for protecting sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other sacrificial implements, in battle, or in the case of harming women or Brahmins—
this [verse] beginning with "or a teacher, or a child, or an old man," etc., is spoken as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of that [rule].
One may kill even preceptors and others who are extremely offensive, let alone other *ātatāyin* aggressors; however,
because of the hearing of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even one who has gone to the end of the Vedas," there is no perception that preceptors and others are to be killed.
And because of the statement of Sumantu: "There is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin* (one who comes to kill), except in the case of killing a cow or a Brāhmaṇa," [and because of the verse]:
"The teacher, the expounder, the mother, the father, and the guru..."
And because of the statement of Manu: "One should not harm Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics" (MDh 4.162),
this verse is meaningful as a prohibition against harming even preceptors and others who are *ātatāyins* (aggressors), and not otherwise.

Since the prohibition of mere violence is already established by the general rule itself, the statement "no fault whatsoever accrues to the slayer for killing an *atatāyin*" refers exclusively to those other than Brāhmaṇas and the like; for it is said: "The arsonist, the poisoner, one with weapon in hand, the robber of wealth," [and so forth].
One who seizes land and one who abducts a wife—these six are indeed assassins (*ātatāyin*).
Likewise:
"One with a raised sword, one with poison or fire, and likewise one with a hand raised to cast a curse..."
And by means of the Atharvan [rite], one may kill both a slanderer and even a king.
"One who commits adultery with one's wife and one who is intent on seeking out one's vulnerabilities—
one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin*s.
Thus, the *ātatāyin*s have been shown in general.

Therefore, it is the settled conclusion that if Brahmins and others, as well as those who are aggressors (*ātatāyin*), should happen to perish through negligence while being warded off for the sake of protecting themselves and so forth, with no intention to cause harm, the penance is light and there is no royal punishment.
Therefore, another example must be stated here. It is said:
"The acquisition of a friend is better than the acquisition of gold or land, because..."
"Therefore, one should strive for its attainment" (YDh 1.351);
this is the *artha-śāstra*.
"In accordance with the *dharma-śāstra*, free from anger and greed" (YDh 2.1).
Such is the Dharmaśāstra.
In certain matters, a contradiction arises between the two;
for example, in the case of a four-footed legal proceeding (*catuṣpādvyavahāra*).

When the victory of one side is being determined while [the conflict] is proceeding, there is the acquisition of a friend, but the treatise on Dharma has not been followed; when the victory of the other side is being determined, the treatise on Dharma has been followed, but the acquisition of a friend is reversed. In that case, the treatise on Dharma is more authoritative than the treatise on Artha.

For this very reason, Āpastamba has demonstrated the severity of the penance in the rule: "In a conflict between dharma and artha, for one who chooses artha, this very [penance applies]" (ĀpDh 1.24.23).
By the phrase "this very," the twelve-year penance is referred to. (2.21)
Then, it is stated that "the claimant should immediately have the proof of the matter asserted written down.
When the question arises as to what that proof is, he says:
"Evidence is declared to be documentary proof, possession, and witnesses."
In the absence of any one of these, any one of the divine means is prescribed.
That by which something is measured or determined is called *pramāṇa* (proof);
and that is of two kinds: human and divine.
In that regard, human evidence is said by the great seers to be threefold: documentary evidence, possession, and witnesses.
Among these, documentary evidence is of two kinds: royal edicts (*śāsana*) and private deeds (*cīraka*).
The "title" (śāsana) has its characteristics already described; the "document" (cīraka), however, will have its characteristics explained later;
and "possession" (bhukti) means enjoyment.
Witnesses are of the nature and types that will be described hereafter.

Now, it may be argued: since written documents and witnesses are included within the category of "verbal testimony" (śabda) by way of manifesting words, their status as valid means of knowledge is appropriate;
but how can possession (bhukti) be a valid means of knowledge?

It is said: possession (*bhukti*) also, when conjoined with certain qualifications, either infers—due to its non-deviation—the actions and so forth that serve as the cause of ownership, or, being otherwise inexplicable, it leads to their postulation; thus, being included within inference (*anumāna*) or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In the absence of any one of these three, beginning with written documents (*likhita*), there are the ordeals (*divya*), whose various specific forms will be described hereafter.
One or another [means of knowledge] is called "authoritative" (pramāṇa) depending on factors such as the species, place, time, and substance [of the subject].
From this very statement, it is understood that divine [knowledge] possesses authority only in the absence of human [knowledge].
Since the nature and the authority of divine [proof] are to be understood through scripture (*āgama*),

therefore, when two parties arrive simultaneously before a judge of dharma in mutual dispute, and one resorts to human proof while the other resorts to divine proof, the human proof alone is to be accepted.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"If one [party] should propose human evidence and the other should propose divine evidence, the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure. (KSm 218)
Even where human means for proving a portion of the principal claim are possible, there too one must not rely on divine methods.

For example, in a case of denial of a lawsuit such as, "Having taken a hundred coins at this rate of interest, he does not repay it," if there are witnesses to the taking of the money, but none regarding the amount or the specific interest rate;

Therefore, when it is said, "I swear by the divine," there is no occasion for the divine oath, because even by the principle of partial manifestation (*ekadeśavibhāvitanyāya*), the specific increase in the number [of witnesses] is established.
And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:

"If even a human act of proof exists that pervades only a single part [of the matter], it should be accepted; however, for men speaking, a divine act of proof, even if complete, is not to be accepted.
As for that which was stated:
"But for those who commit secret acts of violence, examination by means of ordeals is prescribed"—
this [rule] also is intended to establish a restriction based on the impossibility of human evidence.
Furthermore, as stated by Nārada:
"In the forest, in a secluded place, at night, inside a house,
in cases of violence, and likewise in the denial of a deposit, divine means of proof are applicable"—
this [rule] also applies only when human evidence is impossible.
Therefore, the general rule is that a decision by divine means occurs only when human evidence is absent;
however, an exception to this is observed: "In cases of assault, verbal abuse, and threats involving physical punishment..."
"In matters arising from force, there shall be witnesses or even divine proof" (KSm 229).
Likewise, a restriction is observed in certain cases regarding documents and other means of proof, as follows:
"The established rule that has been proclaimed for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like..."
But for that [dispute], the means of proof is documentary evidence, not ordeal nor witnesses.
Likewise:
"In matters concerning doors, paths, construction, enjoyment, water-conduits, and so forth, legal action [is required]."
In such cases, possession alone shall be weighty; neither ordeal nor witnesses [are required].
Likewise:
"Now, when a dispute arises between masters and servants regarding what has been given or what has been taken back..."
In a transaction involving the sale and delivery of goods, if one has purchased wealth but does not wish to accept it;
In matters of gambling, dueling, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared the means of proof; neither divine ordeal nor documentary evidence is required.

Since there may be evidence for both sides and no distinction can be made regarding the relative strength of that evidence, one might wonder which of the two subsequent actions is stronger; therefore, he says:
"In all disputes concerning matters of fact, the subsequent legal action is stronger. (YDh 2.23ab)
In all disputes concerning wealth, such as debts and the like, the subsequent action is performed; thus, "action" (kriyā) refers to the legal proceeding, which is the stronger factor.
When the matter of the subsequent action is established, the proponent of that case becomes victorious.
Even when the initial claim has been established, the proponent of that [subsequent] argument is defeated. For example:

one person seeks to establish possession by means of receipt, while another seeks to establish non-possession by means of restitution; in this case, since both the proof of receipt and the proof of restitution are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), restitution is the stronger [proof], and thus the proponent of restitution is the victor.
Likewise, having previously accepted a debt of two hundred, one subsequently agreed to three hundred; although there is evidence for both amounts, the acceptance of three hundred is the stronger.
Because it arises later, it does not arise without subverting what precedes it; and it has been said: "For the arising of the subsequent will be established only by not subverting the preceding."
He states the exception to this:
"But in the case of a pledge, a gift, and a purchase, the prior [title] is more powerful" (YDh 2.23cd).
Among these three—pledge and the rest—the earlier [transaction] alone is stronger.

For example: having made a single field a pledge for one person and received something from him, and then having made that same field a pledge for another person and received something from them as well— in that case, it belongs to the former alone, not to the latter.
The same applies to receiving as a gift and to purchasing.
But surely, since that which has been offered does not at that time belong to one’s own property, a re-consecration (*punar-ādhāna*) is simply not possible;
the same holds for what has been given away or purchased.
Furthermore, giving and buying would not be possible.
Therefore, this statement is meaningless.
It is replied: even though [the object] is not one's own property, if someone—out of delusion or greed—performs such acts as re-establishing ownership, in that case, the prior [claim] is stronger.
Thus, this statement is indeed rooted in logic; therefore, it is not subject to objection. // 2.23 //
Desiring to demonstrate the validity of possession when it is accompanied by certain qualifications, [the author] states another legal consequence for a particular type of possession:
"The loss of land occurs after twenty years for one who sees it being enjoyed by another and says nothing;
for wealth, it occurs after ten years. (YDh 2.24)

When one sees land or wealth being enjoyed by another without any connection to oneself, and remains silent— failing to object by saying, "This land is mine; you must not enjoy it"— there occurs a loss of that land due to twenty years of unchallenged enjoyment,
caused by that twenty-year period of possession.
In the case of wealth such as elephants, horses, and so forth, however, the loss occurs after ten years.
But is this not untenable?
For ownership does not depart merely because there is no prohibition [against its use].
For it is not established in either worldly usage or the treatises that something which cannot be prohibited can cause the cessation of ownership, just as the acts of giving or selling do;
nor does ownership arise from twenty years of possession.
Because enjoyment is not a valid means of proof for ownership,
and because a means of proof does not produce its object of cognition [prior to its own establishment], as in the cases of inheritance, purchase, and so forth.
And because [the owner] is not mentioned among the causes that produce ownership;
for it is said: "Ownership arises from inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or discovery; for a Brāhmaṇa, what is obtained through alms is [legitimate]."
The property of a Kṣatriya is that which has been won by conquest;
that of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra is what has been acquired through their own labor. (GDh 10.39–42)
Thus Gautama enumerates only eight causes for the acquisition of ownership, and not possession (*bhoga*).
Nor is it correct to maintain that this very statement establishes twenty years of possession as a cause for the arising of ownership.
This is because ownership and the causes of ownership are well-known in the world and are not something to be understood solely through the scriptures;
this will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the section on partition (*vibhāga*).
As for the statement of Gautama, however, it is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Furthermore:
"But the king should punish that sinner who enjoys [property] without a title, even for many hundreds of years, with the punishment due to a thief.
This [statement] contradicts the view that possession without a title is a cause of ownership.
It is not reasonable to say that "he who enjoys [property] without title" refers to enjoyment in the absence of the owner's presence,
while "he who sees and does not speak" refers to enjoyment in the presence of the owner;
for the statement "he who enjoys [property] without title" is made without distinction.

And because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "The owner or his son who takes [animals] must not exert force regarding the use of cattle, women, men, and so forth; such is the established law. (KSm 316) Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the case of possession in the presence [of the owner], since there is no cause for loss, loss is impossible.
Nor should it be thought that this is an exception based on the superiority of the prior act in the cases of mortgage, acceptance as a gift, or purchase.
By this, it is stated that a subsequent legal act possesses greater force when it is accompanied by twenty years of possession in the case of land, or ten years of possession in the case of wealth;
for, in reality, such a subsequent act is not even possible in those cases.
For only that which is one's own can be pledged, given away, or sold;
and there is no ownership over what has been pledged, given, or sold.
Regarding the gift and the acceptance of a horse, a punishment is prescribed in the Smṛti:
"He who accepts what should not be given and he who gives what should not be given—both of them are to be punished like thieves and made to pay the highest fine. (MDh; cf. DhKo 796)

Likewise, if this verse were an exception (*apavāda*) to the three [cases] beginning with "mortgage" (*ādhi*), then an exception for "boundary disputes" (*adhisīmā*) and so forth in the subsequent verse would be untenable.
Therefore, the loss of land and other such properties is indeed impossible;
nor is there a loss of the legal proceeding itself. For:
"Of one who remains silent and indifferent while the aforementioned time has elapsed, the legal proceeding is not established" (NSm 1.71).
Thus, Nārada stated that the loss of the legal proceeding is caused by the absence of signs of indifference, and not by the non-existence of the object itself.
Likewise, Manu also says:
"If a person who is neither mentally incapacitated nor a minor enjoys his property, that [possession] is invalidated by legal procedure; the enjoyer deserves that wealth. (MDh 8.148)
Thus, the refutation has been shown from the perspective of conventional usage, not from the perspective of ultimate reality.
And the refutation of conventional usage is as follows:
"The enjoyer," it is said...

He says: "This man is not dull-witted, he is not a minor, and he is not a child; in his presence I have enjoyed this property for twenty years without opposition, and there are many witnesses to that.
If I am enjoying his property unjustly, then why does he [not object]?"
Thinking, "He remains indifferent for such a long time," he becomes speechless in that regard;

yet, even for one who is thus rendered speechless, the actual legal proceeding still takes place, according to the rule: "Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings based on the truth."
Now, it might be thought:

even if there is neither a loss of the real object (*vastu*) nor a loss of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), nevertheless, for one who observes [the object] but does not refute it, there arises a suspicion of a loss of conventional usage; therefore, to prevent that, one should not remain silent.
"It is taught [that possession is lost].

But that is not so, because enjoyment during the period of memory cannot be a cause for suspicion of loss; if the intention were merely to state that "one should not remain silent," the mention of "twenty years" would be unintended. Now, it might be argued:
The mention of "twenty" is for the purpose of precluding the raising of objections regarding defects in the document after that time.
As Kātyāyana said:
"When the wealth of one who is capable [of producing evidence] is enjoyed by another through a written document..."
"An instrument more than twenty years old is free from defects.

This too is not correct; for since the refutation of the raising of defects regarding a document after twenty years applies equally even to pledges (*ādhi*) and the like, it would be impossible to establish exceptions such as "pledges and boundaries" (*adhisīmā*).
As Kātyāyana said:
Furthermore: "If a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years with absolute certainty, its validity is established by that document, provided it is free from defects of the document.
(KSm 300) Likewise:
"When a boundary dispute has been settled, a boundary document is prescribed;
its defects must be declared for as long as twenty years.
By this, the rule that "for wealth [the period is] ten years" is also refuted.
Therefore, the true meaning of this verse must be stated.
It is said: what is intended here is the loss of the fruit of land and wealth, not the loss of the substance itself, nor the loss of legal title.
For instance, even if after twenty years of possession without protest, the owner [seeks to reclaim] the field according to justice—
Nevertheless, one does not obtain the recovery of the fruit [of the deposit],

because of one's own fault characterized by non-prohibition and because of this statement. However, in the case of an enjoyment that occurred out of sight, one certainly obtains the recovery of the fruit even after twenty years.
Because of the statement "he sees," and because of the statement "even when there is direct enjoyment, he does not speak [of it] even when there is abuse."
One obtains [the fruit] before twenty [years], provided there is no physical injury and no verbal abuse, because of the mention of "twenty."

[Objection: But surely, since ownership (*svatva*) belongs even to a fruit that has already been produced, its loss would be logically impossible. [Reply: Certainly. While that [ownership] remains exactly as it was without the destruction of its own nature—just as in the case of betel-nut, jackfruit, trees, and so forth, which have been produced from that [tree]—in the case of that [fruit] which has been destroyed through consumption, the destruction of ownership occurs precisely because of the destruction of its own nature.
"But the king shall punish that sinner who enjoys what has not been transferred, even for many hundreds of years, with the punishment due to a thief.

By this statement, it follows that after calculating [the value] as a form of ransom, one must give an amount of wealth equal to that [property], like a thief; thus, there is the loss [of ownership] after twenty years.
By this [verse], [the king's punishment] is set aside;
however, the royal punishment certainly remains even after twenty years, because there has been no possession and because there is no denial [of ownership].
Therefore, it is established that due to the owner's fault characterized by negligence and because of this statement, he does not recover the fruit [of his property] once twenty years have passed.
By this, the rule that "wealth [is purified] after ten years" is also explained. (2.24)
He states the exceptions to this rule:
"Except for property placed in deposit, boundary land, and the wealth of the mentally incapacitated or minors;
likewise, except for bailments (upanidhi) and the property of kings, women, and Vedic scholars. (YDh 2.25)
A pledge (*ādhi*), a boundary (*sīmā*), and a deposit (*upanikṣepa*) are "pledges, boundaries, and deposits" (*ādhisīmopanikṣepāḥ*).
An idiot (*jaḍa*) and a child (*bāla*) are "the idiot and the child" (*jaḍabālau*);

their wealth is "the wealth of the idiot and the child" (*jaḍabāladhane*). [The compound] "pledges, boundaries, and deposits, and the wealth of the idiot and the child" is *ādhisīmopanikṣepajaḍabāladhanāni*.
"Without those [witnesses]"—*upanikṣepa* (deposit) refers to property placed in the hand of another for the purpose of protection, by indicating its form and number. As Nārada said:
"Where one deposits one's own property with confidence and without hesitation..."
"That which is called *nikṣepa* has been declared by the wise to be a title of law (*vyavahārapada*). (NSm 2.1).
*Upanidhāna* is *upanidhi*.
Regarding deposits (*ādhi*) and the like, for one who observes [the deposit] but does not speak [of it], after twenty years, the property [is lost].
Furthermore, even beyond ten years, there is neither increase nor decrease [in the merit],
because no such human fault exists and because the causes for indifference are present here and there.
For instance: since the enjoyment of a pledge is conditioned solely by its status as a pledge, there is no fault on the part of the person even if he neglects it;
likewise, because a boundary is easily established through long-standing marks such as husks and charcoal, neglect [of it] occurs.
It is possible;
for the depositing and the entrusting [of goods] are prohibited, and [the offense occurs] when one consumes them in violation of that prohibition.
And because of obtaining the fruit together with its increase, equanimity arises;
due to their dullness and childishness, equanimity toward the dull and the childish is indeed appropriate.
Because the king is preoccupied with many affairs;
because women are ignorant and lacking in confidence;
and because the Vedic scholar is occupied with studying, teaching, investigating the meaning of those [Vedas], and performing their prescribed rites.
Equanimity is indeed appropriate.

Therefore, since the causes for equanimity exist in all cases—such as with wealth and so forth—there is never any loss of the fruit when one enjoys what is present or when there is no verbal abuse. (2.25)
In order to prescribe specific punishments for those who misappropriate deposits and the like, he says:
"One should cause the person who misappropriates deposits and so forth to pay the wealth to the owner, and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity. (YDh 2.26)

YaNSP omits the portion stating that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rule: "He who, by the force of long-term possession, takes away wealth that has become the subject of dispute—from property belonging to those such as the *ādhyāt* up to the property of a *śrotriya*—shall cause that wealth to be restored to the owner";
and [it omits] the rule regarding the fine, which is equal to that, meaning equal to the substance that was the subject of the dispute.
The injunction is that one should cause [the offender] to pay this to the king;
even though a penalty equal to that [stolen property] is not possible in the case of houses, fields, and the like, nevertheless,
[the rule applies] "in the case of breaking a boundary and likewise in the case of crossing a limit" (YDh 2.155).
The punishment to be described hereafter, beginning with these words, should be understood [as applicable].
Now, if the thief cannot be subdued by a penalty equal to the value of the property because he possesses great wealth, then one should cause him to pay a fine according to his capacity.
One should cause the fine to be paid to such an extent that his pride is subdued;
for they say, "A fine is so called because it subdues," and therefore one should subdue those who are unsubdued by means of it. (GDh 11.28)
Thus, since the taking of a staff has the purpose of subduing [the offender],
even one who does not possess property equal to that [fine] must be made to pay as much as causes him pain.
Furthermore, he who possesses no wealth whatsoever is to be subdued by means of the "reproach-punishment" (dhigdaṇḍa) and so forth. And thus says Manu:
"One should first apply the reproach-punishment, and immediately after that, the verbal punishment."
"The third is the fine of confiscation of property, and after that, the punishment of death" (MDh 8.129).
Furthermore, the corporal punishment of death for those other than Brāhmaṇas has been shown to be tenfold.
Thus says Manu:
Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
when these apply to the three social classes, a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt.
"The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and fifthly the feet;

the eyes, the nose, the ears, as well as wealth and the body. (MDh 8.124–25). It should be understood that when an offense is committed through any of these, the punishment must be inflicted specifically upon that organ, such as the genitals and so forth. This refers to the action (*karma*).
Or he should be made to perform labor, or he should be cast into prison;
as Kātyāyana has stated:
"Having ascertained that he is unable to pay the fine, one should compel him to perform work under one's own authority."
"If he is unable [to pay], he shall be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
(KSm 479) Furthermore, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa who lacks property, measures such as the suspension of ritual duties should be employed.
As Gautama says:
"Exile, branding, and so forth, as well as the proclamation of the separation from [one's] caste-status, are for those who do not reform" (GDh 12.47–48).
Nārada also says:
"Death, confiscation of all property, exile from the city, and branding."
In that case, the punishment prescribed is the cutting off of the limb, which constitutes the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
Having stated, "The rule for punishment is ordained for all without distinction" (NSm 14.7–8), it was further said:
"Except for execution, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death; a Brāhmaṇa is not subject to capital punishment."
"Shaving the head is his punishment; banishment from the city, branding on the forehead with the mark of his crime, and being made to travel upon a donkey. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the specific rules regarding branding have been shown:

"For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the footprint of a dog; and for killing a Brāhmaṇa, the figure of a headless man" (NSm 19.51).
As for the statement, "Blinding of the eyes for a Brāhmaṇa" (ĀpDh 2.27.17):
This statement of Āpastamba means that at the time of banishing a Brāhmaṇa from the city, his vision must be obstructed by means of a cloth or similar object;
its meaning is not the extraction of the eyes, for it is said:
"A Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt" (MDh 8.124).
This is because it would contradict the statements of Manu, Gautama, and others, such as "There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.46); enough of this digression. 2.26.
It has been stated that possession (*bhoga*) is authoritative regarding ownership (*svatva*) because it is invariably concomitant with it.
Since mere possession can deviate from ownership, [the author] asks what kind of possession is authoritative, and therefore says:
"Title is superior to possession, except in the case of that which has come down through a prior succession.
(YDh 2.27ab) Title (*āgama*) refers to the causes of ownership, such as acceptance of a gift (*pratigraha*), purchase (*kraya*), and so forth;
it is more powerful than, and indeed superior to, mere possession.
Because possession requires a title to establish ownership,
as Nārada has said:
Possession acquired through pure title attains the status of valid proof;
possession with impure title never attains validity.
Thus [it is said].
Nor can ownership be understood from possession alone, because enjoyment is possible even for that which belongs to another through means such as theft. For this very reason:
"But he who asserts possession alone and never cites any legal title,
should be known as a thief under the pretext of a fraudulent claim of possession"—
thus it is recorded in the Smṛti.

Therefore, it is stated that possession (*bhoga*) endowed with five specific qualifications— being accompanied by title (*sāgama*), long-standing (*dīrghakāla*), continuous (*nirantara*), free from protest (*nirākrośa*), and witnessed by the opponent (*pratyarthipratyakṣa*)— is authoritative. And so it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"Acquisition, long duration, continuity, non-abandonment by another, and possession in the presence of the opponent—possession is thus fivefold. (N, KSm: DhKo 406, 416).
And since in some cases possession is authoritative even without regard for prior acquisition, he says: "except for that which has come down through prior succession."

The "prior sequence" refers to the sequence of the three ancestors, beginning with the father; the connection is that possession which has come down through that sequence is outweighed by title (āgama) in its absence.
Furthermore, that [direct perception] is superior to scripture;
the meaning is that it is a valid means of knowledge independent of scripture.
In that case as well, scripture is independent of what is unknown, but not independent of existence;
it should be understood that existence itself is apprehended by that very [scripture].
The phrase "except for that which has come down through prior succession" is intended to demonstrate a period beyond the range of memory;
conversely, the principle that "title is superior to possession" pertains to a period within the range of memory.
Consequently, during a period suitable for recollection, the absence of title can be ascertained through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible.
The validity of possession (*bhoga*) depends precisely upon knowledge of scriptural tradition (*āgama*).

However, in a period beyond memory, since it is impossible to ascertain the absence of scriptural tradition due to the lack of non-perception of a competent [witness], continuous possession is authoritative even without dependence on knowledge of scriptural tradition.
This very point has been clarified by Kātyāyana:
"In the period of memory, the possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by title;
in the period beyond memory, due to the absence of such a trace, it is valid through succession extending over three generations. (KSm 321)
And the temporal limit according to the Smṛti extends to a hundred years, based on the Vedic revelation: "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years.

The phrase "due to the absence of following" means that there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of tradition because of the absence of a suitable non-perception (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Therefore...

Furthermore, possession that has continued for more than a hundred years— being uninterrupted, undisputed, and witnessed by the opponent— even in the absence of a title or when the title is not determined, leads to the inference of a title due to its non-deviation, and thus establishes ownership.
This holds true even in a period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārta*), provided there is no succession of recollection regarding the lack of a title.
In the case of a valid title, possession is not the sole authority. For this very reason:
"But he who enjoys property without a legal title, even for many hundreds of years, the lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief. (NSm 1.76*)

Thus it has been stated. Furthermore, one should not conclude from the singular designation in the phrase "he who enjoys [property] without title" (*anāgamam tu yo bhuṅkte*) and from the use of the word "even" (*api*) in the expression "even for many hundreds of years" (*bahūny abdaśatāny api*), that the prescription of punishment applies only to the first person (the original owner) even when there has been possession for a long time without title.

For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that enjoyment— even when devoid of traditional authority (*āgama*)— would be valid in the second or third generation; yet this is not accepted,
since it is held that "in the beginning the cause is the gift, but in the middle the enjoyment must be accompanied by tradition" (DhKo 409).

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada, in all cases of possession without a legal title (*anāgama*), this [verse]—“But he who enjoys what is without a title”—is to be understood as applicable. Furthermore, as for the statement:
“Even that which has been enjoyed by three preceding ancestors, though by unjust means... [it follows the same principle].
"Nor can that which has come down through three generations in succession be taken away"—
this [verse] should also be construed as meaning "together with the father and three preceding ancestors.
In that context as well, the phrase "come down through three generations in succession" characterizes possession by means of enjoyment during the period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārta-kāla*).

If there is an intention to refer to three generations, then since it is possible for three generations to pass even within a single year, it would follow that possession in the second year—even without a title—would be authoritative. This being the case, [the verse states]:
"In the period of the Smṛtis, the possession of land is accepted as authoritative when accompanied by a title" (KSm 321).
Thus, there is a contradiction with the Smṛti.

Regarding the phrase "even that which has been enjoyed through injustice," this must be explained as follows: since even what has been enjoyed through injustice cannot be taken away, how much more so when the injustice is not established?
This is because of the hearing of the word "api" (even).
And as it was stated by Hārīta:
"That which has been enjoyed for generations by three preceding ancestors,
even without a title deed, cannot be taken away, having come down through the succession of three persons."
Thus, even there, "entirely without scripture" (atyantam āgamam vinā) is to be explained as "without scripture being perceived at all," and not as "without the very nature of scripture."

It has been stated that in the absence of a formal title (*āgama*), ownership does not arise even through a hundred years of possession. The phrase "transmitted through three generations in succession" has already had its meaning explained.
Now, an objection is raised: is it not the case that during a period when [the title] is capable of being remembered, the validity of possession—which depends upon a title—is untenable?

For instance, if the title (āgama) has been ascertained by another means of knowledge, then since ownership is already ascertained by that very [means], possession (bhoga) has no authority regarding either ownership or the title.
On the other hand, if the title has not been ascertained by another means of knowledge, how can possession qualified by it be a means of knowledge?

It is said: possession (*bhoga*) that is continuous and accompanied by title (*āgama*) known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) brings about ownership (*svatva*) after a lapse of time. Even if title is known, it is not capable of bringing about ownership after a lapse of time if it is devoid of possession, because in the interim there may have been [acts such as] giving or selling.
Because the possibility of the departure of ownership exists;
thus, everything is irreproachable.
It has been stated that possession dependent upon title is a means of proof;
therefore, he says the following [to show] that title, on the other hand, is a means of proof even when independent of possession.
"Even in the case of a title-deed, there is no strength at all where there is not even a slight possession.
(YDh 2.27cd) In that title-deed where there is not even a small amount of possession—that is, enjoyment—there is no complete strength in that title-deed whatsoever.
This is the intended meaning.
Giving consists in the cessation of one's own ownership and the production of another's ownership.
And the production of another's ownership is accomplished only when the other person accepts it, not otherwise.
And acceptance is of three kinds:
mental, verbal, and physical.
In that regard, the mental [appropriation] consists of the form of the conceptualization "this is mine";
the verbal, however, is the determinate cognition characterized by the utterance of such expressions as "this is mine."
Furthermore, the physical [gift] is of many kinds, consisting of touching, stroking, and so forth.
Regarding this, a rule is recorded in the Smṛti:
"One should give a black antelope skin on the back, a cow at the tail, and an elephant at the trunk."
"In the same way, one should cause the horse to be placed upon the filaments and the female slave upon the head.
Āśvalāyana also says: "One should consecrate with mantras, touch the vital breaths, and [touch] the bride."
In that case, regarding gold, clothing, and the like, because the act of taking possession and so forth occurs immediately after the offering of water,
all three types of acceptance are accomplished.

Furthermore, since in the case of a field and the like, physical appropriation is impossible apart from the enjoyment of the fruit, there must be even a slight enjoyment; otherwise, the perfection of acts such as giving or buying would not occur. Thus, a transmission (āgama) that lacks physical appropriation characterized by the enjoyment of the fruit is weak compared to a transmission that possesses it.
And this applies when the prior and posterior times of the two are not known;
however, when the prior and posterior times are known, the arrival at the earlier time alone is stronger, even if it is defective.
Alternatively, it has been stated that "written evidence, witnesses, and possession inherited through three generations are means of proof.
Regarding the concurrence of these, where and which one possesses greater force, this [verse] applies:
"Title is superior to possession, except in the case of possession acquired through prior succession."
"Even a title-deed has no strength at all where there is not even the slightest possession" (YDh 2.27).
This is the meaning:
in the case of the first person [in the chain of possession], a title-deed proven by witnesses is stronger than even possession.
"Without [income] from property inherited through prior succession.
Furthermore, that "property inherited through prior succession" refers to income derived from a legal title (āgama) established by written document in the case of the fourth generation.
The stronger [title] is as follows: however, between two titles, even one accompanied by slight enjoyment is stronger than a title devoid of enjoyment. This very point has been clarified by Nārada:
"In the beginning, the cause is the gift; in the middle, possession accompanied by a title."
"The sole cause is possession alone, which is continuous and long-standing. (DhKo 409) 2.27.

In the verse "paśyato 'bruvataḥ" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.24), it is stated that after twenty years of possession for land and after ten years of possession for other property, there can be no recovery of the fruits [of such possession].

Anticipating the objection that, just as there would be no pursuit of the fruit [of the offense], there would likewise be no pursuit of the punishment, he says the following to demonstrate the determination of punishment based on the status of the person and the determination of authority:
"But he by whom the legal tradition (āgama) was established, when accused, must uphold it."
Neither he nor his son [has the right]; in that case, possession is more weighty.

(YDh 2.28) That person by whom the acquisition—that is, the taking possession—of land and so forth was made, when challenged as to "Whence do you have this field and so forth?", should establish and prove that acquisition, such as a gift, by means of written documents and other evidence.
By this, it is stated that there is a punishment for the first person who fails to produce the title-deed;
his son, the second, being accused, did not produce the title-deed.
However, one should uphold [the title] characterized by uninterrupted, undisputed, and open possession;

and by this it is established that while there is no punishment for a second party who fails to uphold the title (*āgama*), there is indeed punishment for one who fails to uphold such distinguished possession.
His son, as the third in line,
shall neither inherit the ancestral estate nor any distinguished property,
but only the mere means of subsistence passed down in succession.

By this [verse] as well, it is stated that for the third [type of possessor], there is a penalty for failing to produce possession acquired through succession, but not for failing to produce a title-deed, nor for failing to produce superior possession;
in that case, between those two— the second and the third— possession alone is more weighty.
Even in that case, it should be distinguished that the offense is more serious in the second instance and even more serious in the third;
for although the loss of merit is exactly the same in all three cases if one does not uphold the tradition, the punishment, however, [differs].
The intended meaning is that there is a distinction.
And it has been stated by Hārīta:
"He who has made a formal agreement but does not fulfill it shall be punished for failing to carry it out."
Neither his son nor the son of that son is liable for the loss of the property; for them as well, there is no forfeiture of what has been enjoyed. (2.28)
It has been stated that possession for a period not recorded in memory (asmārta-kāla), when independent of knowledge of title (āgama-jñāna), possesses validity;
however, regarding the phrase "excepting that which has come down through prior succession," he states an exception to that:
"If one who is accused should pass away, his heir shall clear [the charge] against him."
In that case, possession does not constitute proof of ownership without being supported by a legal title (āgama).
Furthermore, when the original acquirer or another party dies before a judicial decision has been reached in the lawsuit, his heir— such as a son or other successor— must then establish that title.
Because in that legal proceeding, possession— even if established by witnesses and other means— is not a valid proof when it is devoid of documentary title (*āgama*),
since such possession is subject to exception due to a prior claim.
Nārada also said: "The son must clear up that debt of his deceased father who was engaged in a lawsuit; possession shall not bar it. (NSm 1.80) 2.29.

It has been established that when a legal proceeding remains undecided and the litigant dies, the proceeding does not continue. However, even when a legal proceeding has been decided and the litigant is still alive, the proceeding may in some cases continue and in others it may not.
To establish this distinction, the author states the relative strength and weakness of those who oversee legal proceedings.

Guilds, corporations, and families appointed by the king—among these, each preceding one is to be known as more authoritative than the following in the legal procedure for men. "By the king" means by the monarch; "appointed" means authorized for the administration of justice.

The "associations" (pūga) or groups mentioned in the passage beginning with "the king shall appoint members of the assembly" refer to communities of people of diverse castes and diverse occupations who reside in a single location,
such as villages, cities, and so forth.

Guilds (*śreṇi*) are associations of people of various origins who subsist by a single type of craft, such as those of the *heḍābuka* workers and so forth, or the betel-vendors, weavers, leather-workers, and so on.
*Kulāni* refers to groups consisting of kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
Among these four— beginning with the king’s officials— it should be understood and known that whichever is mentioned earlier is more significant and possesses greater authority.
This is stated regarding the procedure for legal proceedings— that is, the work of presiding over lawsuits— for men who engage in litigation:
even if there is dissatisfaction on the part of the defeated party due to a perception based on false views once the lawsuit has been decided by the king’s officials.
Nevertheless, there is no further proceeding before a *pūga* or similar body; likewise, even when a case has been decided by a *pūga*, there is no recourse to a *śreṇi* or similar group.
Similarly, when a case has been decided by a *śreṇi*, there is no recourse to a *kula*.

When a decision has been reached by a family, there is recourse to a guild (śreṇi) and so forth; when a decision has been reached by a guild, there is recourse to a corporation (pūga) and so forth; and when a decision has been reached by a corporation, there is recourse to those authorized by the king.
Furthermore, Nārada has stated that even when a legal dispute has been decided by the judges appointed by the king, it may still come before the king:
"Families, guilds, assemblies, judges, and the king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one among these is more authoritative than the preceding. (NSm Mā 1.7)

And in that case, when the king has arrived and the legal proceeding is being decided by him along with the presiding judge and the former judges in a suit involving a wager, if that proponent of a false view is defeated, then he is to be punished;
but if he wins, then the authorized judges [are to be punished].
They are to be punished. // 2.30 //

It has been stated that a legal proceeding seen by weak judges may be overturned, but one seen by powerful ones does not cease; now, he says that even a proceeding seen by powerful ones may in some cases be set aside: "One should annul legal proceedings brought about through force or fraud."

He shall set aside legal proceedings that have been brought about by force, by coercion, by fraud, or by fear and the like; likewise those involving women, those conducted at night, those within the inner apartments, and those committed by external enemies. He shall thus annul such transactions.
Likewise [those involving] women.

At night, even during the night; "in the inner apartment" means inside the house; and "transactions entered into by enemies outside the village and so forth"—the connection is that he should cause such transactions to cease. (2.31)
Regarding those who do not engage in legal proceedings, [Yājñavalkya] says:
"A lawsuit brought by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified, as well as one that is inconsistent, is not established. (YDh 2.32)
Moreover: "intoxicated" means by means of an intoxicating substance;
"insane" means afflicted by the fivefold insanity arising from wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, or possession by a spirit; "afflicted" means by disease and so forth.

*Vyasana* is suffering produced by separation from the desired and the attainment of the undesired; one who possesses that is *vyasanī*. A *bāla* is one unfit for worldly transaction. One who is *bhīta* is afraid of enemies.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [the list includes] that which is contrary to the interests of cities or kingdoms.
A lawsuit that is contrary to the interests of cities or kingdoms, as well as one that has been dismissed by the king,
is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.
Because of this recollection from Manu,
a legal proceeding (vyavahāra) conducted or carried out by these [persons] does not succeed;
this applies even to one conducted by those who are unauthorized or unconnected [to the case].
The connection is that "legal proceedings would not be established.
As for the traditional legal maxim (*smaraṇa*): "Between teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, and master and servant..."
"But when they are mutually contradictory, their legal procedure is not established" (DhKo 114).
Even this [statement] does not intend to prohibit legal procedures between teachers, disciples, and so forth absolutely,
because some form of legal procedure among them is also accepted.
For it is said: "The instruction of a pupil should be carried out without corporal punishment;
if that is impossible, by means of thin cords or split bamboo; one who strikes him with anything else shall be punished by the king. (GDh 2.42–44)
This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama,
and also because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "In no way [should one strike] on the head" (MDh 8.300).
If the teacher, under the influence of a fit of anger, strikes him on the head with a severe punishment, and the student— unassailed by a path devoid of mindfulness— reports this to the king,
then it certainly constitutes a ground for legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*).
Likewise, because of such statements as "the land acquired by the grandfather" (YDh 2.121), when ownership over land and other property acquired by the grandfather is equal for both father and son,
if the father [disposes of it] through sale or other means—
If [the son] destroys land or other property acquired by the grandfather,
then if the son approaches a judicial authority, a legal dispute certainly arises between father and son as well. Likewise,
"During a famine, for religious duties, in illness, or when there is an obstruction [to livelihood],

a husband is not required to give up the wife's property against his will," according to this traditional law (Smṛti). Therefore, if— apart from such circumstances as famine— the husband, even while possessing wealth, has spent the wife's property and is being asked [for it back], [he need not pay].
If he does not grant it, then legal proceedings between the husband and wife are indeed desired;
likewise, [the author] will later describe the legal proceedings of a bonded servant with his master.
Even regarding a slave born in the house, with reference to such slaves as those born in the house and others:
"Whoever among them should liberate their master from a life-threatening danger, he shall be released from slavery and receive a share equal to that of a son. (NSm 5.28)

Since this was stated by Nārada, who can prevent a legal dispute with the master regarding the non-release of that [pupil] or the taking of his share of the inheritance? Therefore, engaging in litigation with teachers and others is not conducive to one's welfare, whether in visible or invisible matters; thus, pupils and others [should avoid it] first.

"Those [who act improperly] must be restrained by the king together with his court members"—this is the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "the teacher [should be treated like] a pupil," and so forth.

However, in the event of extreme persistence, legal proceedings may be initiated even against pupils and others according to the method already described. Furthermore, as for that which... [text continues]
"The lawsuit of a single individual against many people, or against women and servants,
shall not be accepted; so it has been declared by those who know the Dharma"—
this is the statement of Nārada.
In that regard: "He who takes even a single thing belonging to the community, and he who violates the agreement" (YDh 2.187);
likewise, "and [the punishment for] one who kills many" (YDh 2.221).

Based on such traditional authorities (*smaraṇa*), it is accepted that legal transactions (*vyavahāra*) may indeed take place with many individuals who share a single purpose; therefore, it should be understood that a simultaneous transaction with many individuals who have distinct purposes does not occur.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of women," this refers to the transactions of women such as cowherds' wives, liquor-sellers' wives, and so forth, because of their independence.

It must be explained that [the statement] "it indeed exists" means that while the husbands of all other women are alive, their legal transactions are inadmissible due to their dependence on him. Furthermore, the phrase "and of the servant class" also implies that because the servant class is dependent on their master, their legal transactions for their own purposes [are inadmissible].
It should be explained that even in this case, legal proceedings occur only with the master's permission and not otherwise. // 2.32 //
Having stated that legal proceedings may be reversed, he now speaks of the property that may be reversed:
"Lost property that has been found must be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to its value. (YDh 2.33)
Gold and other property that has been lost, found by customs officers, local guardians, or others, and surrendered to the king, must be returned by the king to the owner,
provided that the owner establishes his claim through characteristics such as appearance, quantity, and other identifying marks.
If he does not acknowledge it, then he should be punished with the same fine,
because of his falsehood.
Since realization is the cause of ownership, once ownership has been attained,
its reversal is stated by this [verse].
And here, he will state the temporal limit.

"Lost or stolen property that has been recovered by customs officers or local guardians, the owner may take it back within one year; after that, the king shall take it. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.173).
However, Manu has specified a period of three years as the limit:

"The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years; within three years the owner may take it, but after that, the king may take it. (MDh 8.30). In this regard, it must necessarily be protected for a period of three years.
In that case, if the owner arrives before the lapse of one year, he shall receive the whole;
but when he arrives after one year has passed, he shall receive a sixth part.
Having taken the fee for protection, he should give the remainder to the owner. As it is said:
"Then the king, remembering the duty of the virtuous, may take a sixth part, or even a tenth or a twelfth, of property lost and found" (MDh 8.33).
In that regard, one should give the whole [debt] in the first year,
a twelfth part in the second,
and a tenth part in the third.

In the case of the fourth and subsequent [categories], having taken a sixth part, one should give the remainder. A fourth part of the king’s share must be given to the finder. But when the owner does not appear, having given a fourth part of the entire property to the finder, the remainder—
The king should take it.
Thus says Gautama: "Having found property whose owner has disappeared, it must be guarded by the king for one year; after that, a fourth part belongs to the finder."
"Of this, one part belongs to the king; the remainder [is for the others]" (GDh 10.36–38).
In this context, the singular number in the word "year" (*saṃvatsaram*) is not intended to be restrictive, as [Manu states]:
"The king shall cause it to be deposited for three years" (MDh 8.30).
Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),
the statement "the king may take [it] from another" also refers to the permission to expend [the property] after three years have passed, provided the owner has not appeared;
beyond that point, [the king may take it].
But when the owner has arrived, even though the property has been expended, the king shall set aside his own share and give an amount equal to it. And this refers to gold and similar items;
regarding cattle and other such things, he will state later:
"One should give one paṇa for each hoofed animal," and so forth (YDh 2.174). // 2.33 //

Having stated the rule for the discovery of lost gold and other items that have fallen in a street, at a toll-house, or elsewhere, he now states the rule for the discovery of what is called a "treasure" (nidhi)—gold and other such things long buried in the earth:
"The king, having found a treasure, shall give half to the twice-born; the twice-born, however, [shall keep the whole]."
A learned man may take the entirety [of a treasure], since he is the master of all. When a treasure is found by anyone else, the king shall take a sixth part;
if it was discovered without being reported, he shall be made to pay that [sixth part] as well as a fine.
Having discovered a treasure-trove of the characteristics previously described, the king, having given half to the Brāhmaṇas, should deposit the remainder in the treasury.
However, if a learned Brāhmaṇa— one perfected in sacred learning and study and possessed of virtuous conduct— should discover a treasure-trove, then he may take the whole of it.

Because he is the lord of the entire world; however, when a treasure is found by anyone other than a king, a learned Brāhmaṇa, or a learned Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya— that is, by an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or others— the king, having given a sixth part to the finder, [retains] the remainder.
He himself shall take the treasure.

As Vasiṣṭha says: "Whatever wealth is found whose owner is unknown, the king shall take that; he shall give a sixth part to the finder" (VaDh 3.13). Gautama also states: "The discovery of a treasure-trove becomes the property of the king."
"Some say that for a handsome Brahmin, one who is not a Brahmin who explains [the text] shall receive a sixth part" (GDh 10.43–45).

The word *anivedita* is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the active sense (*kartari*). Thus, *aniveditavijñātaḥ* means "one who has discovered [a treasure] without having reported it to the king.
Anyone who, having found a treasure, neither reports it to the king nor is discovered by the king, shall [retain] that entire treasure.
And he should be made to pay a fine according to his capacity.

Now, if the owner of the treasure arrives and establishes his ownership through its form, number, and other characteristics, then the king, having given the treasure to him, should himself take a sixth or a twelfth part. As it has been said:
Manu says: "If a man should truthfully declare, 'This treasure belongs to me,' the king shall take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it. (MDh 8.35)
However, the distinction regarding portions should be understood as depending on factors such as caste, time, and so forth. (2.34–2.35)
Regarding property stolen by thieves, he says: "The king must restore to the subject property stolen by thieves;
for by not restoring it, he incurs the guilt of the one to whom it belongs. (YDh 2.36)

Property stolen by thieves, having been recovered from those thieves, must be given by the king to the person belonging to the local population residing in his own country to whom that property belongs;
for, if he does not give it— that is, if he fails to restore it— to the one whose property was stolen, [he incurs sin].
He incurs guilt,
as does that thief;
as Manu has said:
"Property stolen by thieves must be restored by the king to people of all castes;
if the king makes use of it himself, he incurs the guilt of the thief. (MDh 8.40).
That is to say, if he takes [the property] from the hands of the thief and enjoys it himself, then he incurs the guilt of the thief.
If he neglects what has been stolen by thieves, then the fault belongs to the local official;
however, if he is unable to recover what was stolen by thieves despite making an effort to do so, [he is not at fault].

In that case, he should give wealth from his own treasury to restore it; as Gautama says: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place, or he should give it from the treasury" (GDh 10.46–47).
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana also said:
"If wealth stolen by thieves cannot be recovered, it must indeed be paid from his own treasury by the king who is unable [to recover it]. (MBh 12.76.10) 2.36.
Thus ends the section on the General Table of Contents of Legal Procedure;

now begins the section on the Non-payment of Debt (*ṛṇādāna*), following the exposition of the table of contents of legal procedure in both its general and specific forms, concerning the eighteen titles of law (*vyavahārapada*).

He demonstrates the first title of law, *ṛṇādāna* (recovery of debts), with the passage beginning "The eightieth part shall be the interest" and ending with "the pledge must be released when the debt has become doubled through the profit derived from it" (YDh 2.37–64).
That *ṛṇādāna* is of seven kinds:
such a debt is payable, and such a debt is not payable.
By whom it is to be paid,
at what time it is to be paid,
and in what manner it is to be paid— thus, with respect to the debtor, there are five aspects.
The procedure regarding a creditor is twofold: the method of giving [a loan] and the method of taking [it back].
And this has been clarified by Nārada:

"Debt that is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner—through the rules of giving and receiving—it is traditionally known as 'Recovery of Debt' (*ṛṇādāna*). (NSm 1.1).
Regarding this, he first states the rule for the creditor's payment, because the others are preceded by it.
The interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month when there is a pledge;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month.
(YDh 2.37) "Month after month" means every month; "pledge" refers to that which is deposited as security for the sake of confidence.
"Ādhi" means a pledge;
"sabandhaka" refers to a transaction that occurs together with a pledge. In such a transaction involving a pledge, regarding the substance that has been lent out:
An interest rate of one-eightieth part [of the principal] is lawful.
Otherwise, in a transaction free from collateral, for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, two, three, four, and five percent per hundred respectively is lawful.

When a Brāhmaṇa is the debtor, two per hundred; when a Kṣatriya, three per hundred; when a Vaiśya, four per hundred; and when a Śūdra, five per hundred—this is to be paid month after month. Thus, "two, three, four, or five" refers to two, three, four, or five [per hundred]; since this interest is given on this hundred, it is called "two-three-four-five" (dvitricatuḥpañcaka).
Regarding "śatam": following the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22),
the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *tad asmin vṛddhyāyalābhaśulkopadādīyate* (Pāṇini 5.1.47).
Additional verse found in some manuscripts:
Interest upon interest is *cakravṛddhi*; that which is paid monthly is *kālikā*.
That which is made according to one's wish is *kāritā*; *kāyikā* arises from bodily action.
And this interest, being taken month by month, is termed *kālikā*;
this same interest, when divided by a calculation of days and taken day by day, becomes *kāyikā*.
And so it has been stated by Nārada: "In the legal treatises, his interest is of four kinds: corporeal, periodical, stipulated, and likewise compound interest. (NSm 1.87)
Having said this, it was stated:
"That interest which is not inconsistent with the principal, consisting of pennies, quarters, and so forth,
and which flows month by month, is considered *kālikā* (periodical)."
"That interest which is caused by the debtor himself is called *svayaṃkṛtā* (self-made). Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest). (NSm 1.88–89) 2.37.
He states another category based on the specific nature of the borrower:
"But those traveling through a wilderness [owe] ten, those by sea twenty, and [those from] the city one hundred" (YDh 2.38ab).
A *kāntāra* is a forest; those who go there are *kāntāragas*.
Those who, having taken money at interest, enter an extremely perilous place where there is a risk to their lives and wealth for the sake of greater profit, shall pay ten percent;
and those who go by sea shall pay twenty percent every month.
This is what is meant:
the creditor may take ten percent from those traveling through forests and twenty percent from those traveling by sea, because there is even the apprehension that the principal might be lost.
Now he speaks of stipulated interest:
"Or they may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves, in all cases and among all classes.
(YDh 2.38cd) This means that all [creditors], such as Brāhmaṇas and others, whether the debt be unsecured or secured, may receive the interest agreed upon by themselves.
They should pay interest on all types of loans;
in some cases, however, interest may not have been stipulated.
Thus says Nārada:

"There shall never be interest on gifts made out of affection if they were not requested; however, even if unrequested, [the debt] increases after half a year has passed. (NSm 1.96) Regarding one who, having taken a loan, has gone to another country, Kātyāyana has stated:

"Whoever, having taken something on loan, should depart for another region without returning it, that property shall accrue interest for him after the lapse of one year. Thus it is said; and regarding one who, having taken something on loan, departs for another country even when requested to return it, it has been stated by that same [author]:
"If one who has been asked for a loan and has taken it out should depart for another region without returning it,
that debt shall begin to accrue interest after three months have passed.
(KSm 503) Furthermore, regarding one who, while remaining in his own country, does not return a borrowed item when asked, [interest shall accrue] from the time of the request until it is returned.
The king shall cause interest to be paid. As it has been said:

"Even if he resides in his own country, if one does not pay when requested at any time, the king shall compel him to pay that interest which was not previously agreed upon, even if he is unwilling. (KSm 504)
An exception to the increase of interest has been stated by Nārada:
"The price of goods, wages, a deposit, a fine, and that which is stipulated as a gift, as well as stakes in gambling—these do not accrue interest unless they are intended to do so. (NSm 4.7)
"Unintended" means not being made manifest. // 2.38 //
Now he states the specific increase for particular types of property:
"But the offspring of cattle and women" (YDh 2.39ab).
For cattle and women, the offspring itself constitutes the interest.
The application [of this practice] is possible for one who is unable to nourish livestock or women, yet desires their nourishment and progeny;
and its adoption is for one seeking the service of milk.
Now, regarding a commodity that has been lent out and remains for a long time even without the taking of interest, he states what the maximum interest may be for which commodity:
"The maximum [interest] on liquids is eightfold" (YDh 2.39cd).
For clothes, grain, and gold, the maximum interest is four, three, and two times the principal respectively.

Regarding liquids such as oil and ghee, which have been kept for a long time and are increasing by interest accrued through one's own effort even without an explicit agreement for interest, the maximum interest is eightfold.
Beyond this, it does not increase further.
Likewise, for clothes, grain, and gold,
the maximum interest is fourfold, threefold, and twofold respectively.
Vasiṣṭha, however, has stated that there is a threefold increase for liquids: gold is twofold and grain is threefold;
by this very rule regarding grain, liquids are also explained.
"And flowers, roots, and fruits;
[the interest on] gold weighed on a scale is eightfold" (VaDh 2.44–47).
However, Manu has stated that for grain, flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth, the [interest] is fivefold:
"In grain, fodder, wool, or beasts of burden, it does not exceed fivefold [interest].
(MDh 8.151) "Fodder" (*śada*) refers to the produce of a field, such as flowers, roots, and fruits;
"wool" (*lava*) refers to the wool of sheep, the hair of the *ūrṇā* animal, the hair of the yak, and so forth.
External [property] refers to oxen, horses, and so forth.
Interest on objects such as grain, wool, and carried goods does not exceed fivefold;
in that case, it depends on the debtor's capacity.
Furthermore, the determination [of the offense] should be understood as depending on factors such as famine and the like;
and this is to be known to apply when there is a single application and a single taking.

When a different transaction is carried out by transferring it to another person, or when multiple subsequent transactions are made with the same person through repeated pouring or adding [of interest], gold and other such items increase as before, exceeding even the doubling [of the principal].
Even in the case of a single initial transaction, if interest is collected daily, monthly, or annually, the debt owed by the debtor [continues to grow].
Because doubling is possible, it continues to increase even after reaching double the principal, together with the interest previously collected. As Manu says:
"Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, does not exceed the double [of the principal]. (MDh 8.151)
The reading *sakṛdāhitā* also exists.
*Kusīda* is wealth employed for the purpose of accumulation; its interest is *kusīdavṛddhi*.
That [interest] does not exceed, that is, does not surpass, the point of doubling [the principal].
If it has been produced once— that is, employed once—
it exceeds its twofold limit when the performance is brought to a conclusion through such means as transferring it to another person.
However, in the reading "sakṛdāhṛtā" (once brought forth), [the meaning is as follows]:
It should be explained that [the debt] recovered from the debtor gradually—day by day, month by month, or year by year—exceeds the double [of the principal].
Likewise, it has been stated by Gautama as well: "In a long-standing loan, there is a doubling of the principal" (GDh 12.31).
By the use of the singular number in the word "prayogasya" (of the loan), the intention is to indicate that the doubling [of the principal] is exceeded when another loan is made;
by the use of the term "cirasthāne" (in a long-standing case), the exceeding of the doubling is shown to occur when interest is collected gradually over time. (2.39)

The rules regarding the lending of debt have been stated. Now, the rules for the recovery of the lent wealth are being declared: one who is recovering a debt that has been admitted shall not be censured by the king.

If he recovers [the debt] by means of righteous methods such as conciliation (*dharma*) while the case is being proved, he shall not be censured by the king; he is not to be restrained. [The verse continues: "While being pursued for recovery, he may go to the king; he is to be punished and made to pay that wealth. (YDh 2.40) When the creditor is recovering the wealth—which has been admitted by the debtor or established through witnesses and other means—and is returning it by means of *dharma* and other methods, he is not to be spoken against by the king; he is not to be prevented.
And the means, beginning with *dharma*, have been shown by Manu:
"By means of *dharma*, by legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), by artifice (*chala*), and by custom (*ācāra*)."
"He shall accomplish his purpose by means of the fifth power as well" (MDh 8.49).
[This refers to] by means of dharma accompanied by goodwill, by truthful speech,
and by legal procedure through means such as witnesses and written documents.
By means of a pretext, such as under the guise of a festival or the like, or by taking ornaments and so forth;
by conduct, such as fasting.
By the fifth means, namely force such as binding with fetters and so forth, one should appropriate for oneself the wealth employed for the purpose of accumulation through these methods.
By stating that "one who is pursuing a claim already admitted should not be spoken against," he shows that one who is pursuing a claim not yet admitted must be restrained by the king.
This very point has been clarified by Kātyāyana:
"If any creditor should oppress a debtor who is speaking justly..."
"Therefore, he shall lose that wealth and incur a fine equal to it" (KSm 589).

However, one who, while being approached through means such as dharma and so forth, or being exhorted regarding a matter to be accomplished, goes to the king— that is, having approached the king, he initiates a lawsuit against the one who was acting to settle the matter— is liable to punishment.
