And he should be made to pay that wealth to the creditor according to his capacity; furthermore, the methods for compelling payment by the king have been shown: "But the king should cause the debtor to give it to the owner by means of conciliation alone."
But others who are wicked, he should compel to pay by means of local custom after having oppressed them.

"Or one should cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of trickery. This should be understood as the counter-example to the rule "one who is being pressed for payment should go to the king," which refers to those who have deviated from the Smṛtis and established custom. 2.40.
When many creditors present themselves simultaneously, by what order should the debtor be made to pay? In response to this inquiry, [the author] says:
The debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they received the loans;
however, after paying the Brāhmaṇas, he must pay the king immediately thereafter. (YDh 2.41)

Among creditors of the same caste, the debtor shall be made to pay by the king according to the very order in which the wealth was received; however, among those of different castes, the order shall be according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. (2.41)
Furthermore, when the creditor is weak and, being unable to recover the admitted debt through means such as moral persuasion (*dharma*) and the like,
has the debt recovered by the king, [the law] prescribes a fine for the debtor and the payment of a fee to the creditor:
"The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent of the amount recovered."
And the creditor who has recovered his debt shall be made to pay five percent upon a hundred;
for the debtor, from the amount of the debt admitted and proven, ten percent shall be made to pay to the king.
This refers to the admitted portion of the proven debt.
The meaning is that the king shall take a tenth part from the debtor as a fine;
however, the creditor who has recovered his property shall be made to pay five percent as a fee.
The meaning is that the king should take a twentieth part of the recovered amount from the creditor for the purpose of maintaining his servants;
however, regarding the non-recovery of the claimed amount, the distribution of fines has already been shown.
"By means of [the rule] beginning with 'In case of denial, one who has been examined shall pay' (YDh 2.5), etc. // 2.42 //
The means of recovery regarding a solvent debtor has been explained.
Now, he speaks concerning a debtor who is destitute:
"One may compel a debtor of low caste who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt."
But a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually according to his income.

(YDh 2.43) A creditor who is a Brāhmaṇa or of a higher caste should, for the purpose of recovering a debt, cause a debtor of a lower caste— such as a Kṣatriya or others— who is impoverished and destitute, to perform labor appropriate to his own caste, provided it does not conflict with the maintenance of his family.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has become impoverished and destitute should be made to pay the debt gradually, according to his income and according to what is possible;
and in this context, the mention of a person of "low caste" (hīnajāti) [is intended to include all non-Brāhmaṇas].
This is also an indication for those of the same caste;

therefore, one should cause even a person of the same caste who has been fully exhausted [of his debt] to perform work as is appropriate. And the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is an indication for those of a superior caste.
And for this reason, even a Kṣatriya or others who have fallen into poverty should be made to pay to a Vaiśya or others gradually, according to his means;
this very point has been clarified by Manu.
"Even by means of labor, a debtor of lower caste who is equal [to the creditor] should make himself equal to the moneylender; however, one of superior caste should pay that gradually. (MDh 8.177).
By means of labor, the debtor should make himself equal to the creditor, such that the designations "creditor" and "debtor" cease to apply between them.
Such is the meaning. // 2.43 //
If one who employs his own wealth neither increases it when it has been deposited with a neutral third party,
nor takes possession of it while it is being used,
then if it remains deposited with that neutral party, it shall increase, but not beyond that amount. (YDh 2.44)
Furthermore, if the creditor, out of greed for interest, does not accept the wealth being paid by the debtor— which was lent for the purpose of accumulation—
and if that wealth has been deposited with a middleman by the debtor, [then the following applies].
Then, after that establishment, it does not increase. However,
if even though it has been established, he does not give when requested, then it increases as before.
Thus. 2.44.
Now he states when and by whom a debt is to be paid:
"A debt that has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided, the heirs shall pay it upon the death or departure abroad of the head of the household. (YDh 2.45)

A debt incurred for the sake of the family by many members who are undivided, or by even a single individual, must be paid by the head of the household. Upon his death or departure, all his heirs shall pay that debt. (2.45) He states here a counter-example to the rule "by whom it should be paid."

A wife shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband or son, nor shall a father pay one contracted by his son, except for the sake of the family; likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife.
A wife shall never pay a debt contracted by her husband.
O woman, a mother shall not pay what was done by her son;
likewise, a father shall not pay what was done by his son;
and likewise, a husband shall not pay what was done by his wife.
The phrase "on account of the family's needs" applies as a supplement to all [the preceding cases].
Consequently, whatever has been incurred for the sake of the family by anyone whatsoever must be paid by the head of the household.
It has already been stated that in his absence, those who inherit his property must pay it. (2.46)
He will state later that "a debt must be paid by sons and grandsons" (YDh 2.50); before that, he states an exception to this rule.
A son shall not have to pay a paternal debt incurred here through drinking liquor, gambling, fines, or taxes remaining unpaid, nor for gifts made in vain.

(YDh 2.47) That debt which was contracted by drinking liquor, that which was contracted out of lust, that caused by addiction to women, that resulting from defeat at dice, and that consisting of fines or taxes— [the son shall not pay these].
A gift given in vain is that which is promised to rogues, bards, wrestlers, and the like; for it is said:
"What is given to a rogue, a bard, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer, a wandering minstrel, or a thief, becomes fruitless. (DhKo 715)
According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),
a son or other descendant need not pay to liquor-sellers and the like this debt contracted by the father;
in this context, it refers to what remains after fines and taxes have been deducted.
One should not think that because of the mention of "the remainder" (*avaśiṣṭa*), everything must be paid; for it is said:
"Neither the fine nor the remainder of the fine, nor the toll nor its remainder, nor that which is not part of the legal transaction need be paid by the son. (DhKo 714)
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Uśanas;
and it has also been stated by Gautama: "The [penalties for] liquor, tolls, gambling, and lustful offenses shall not devolve upon the sons" (GDh 12.41).
The meaning is that they do not fall upon the son.
By this, the debt that is not to be recovered has been described. (2.47)
He states an exception to the rule that "a husband [is not held accountable] for what is done by a woman" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.46):
"[In the case] of the wives of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, and hunters..."
"The husband shall pay their debt, because their livelihood depends upon him. (YDh 2.48) "Gopa" means a cowherd;
"śauṇḍika" means a liquor-seller.
A *śailūṣa* is an actor;
a *rajaka* is a dyer of clothes; a *vyādha* is a hunter. Whatever debt has been contracted by the wives of these [men], it must be paid by their respective husbands.

Since their livelihood— that is, their subsistence— is dependent upon her, and since it is stated as a reason that "since the livelihood is dependent upon her," others as well whose lives are dependent on a woman shall pay the debt incurred by that woman.
It is understood. // 2.48 //
He states an exception to the rule "a wife shall not pay what was contracted by her husband" (YDh 2.46):
"What was promised by the woman, or what was contracted together with the husband, must be paid."
A woman is not entitled to pay any debt other than one contracted by herself.
When a husband is about to die or is departing on a long journey, whatever debt she has agreed to pay at his request must be paid as a debt contracted by the husband;
likewise, a debt contracted by the wife together with her husband must also be paid by the wife in the absence of the husband, provided she has no son.
It must be paid; furthermore, even that debt which was contracted by herself must be paid.
[Objection: It need not be stated that "the three types beginning with what is admitted (*pratipanna*) must be paid by a woman," because there is no possibility of doubt.
[Response: It is said:
Regarding the statement, "The wife, the son, and the slave— these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong" (MDh 8.416),
this [next verse] is stated to address the doubt that one might fail to give to those who have been accepted as such because they are considered destitute.
"Debt should be paid by a woman who has entered [into a contract]," and so forth.
This statement does not assert that women and others are devoid of wealth, for its purpose is merely to establish their state of dependence.
And this will be clarified in the section on partition (*vibhāga*).
In that case, it should not be stated that "no other woman is entitled to give [the property]," since the prohibition regarding others is already established by the very injunction.
It is said: [the rule] that "what is promised by a woman should be given, or what was done together with her husband" is stated for the purpose of setting aside those two cases.
Other things included under the mention of "liquor, lust, and so forth," even if promised, and even if done together with the husband, need not be paid. (2.49)
Furthermore, he states the triad of what debt must be paid, by whom it must be paid, and at what time it must be paid:
"When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; if he denies it, it is established by witnesses. (YDh 2.50)

If the father, having failed to pay a debt that was due, has died and gone to a distant land, or has been overcome by an incurable disease or similar affliction, then the son or grandson must necessarily pay that debt incurred by him upon being called to account— even in the absence of paternal wealth—
by virtue of being a son or a grandson.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
in the absence of the father, the son; and in the absence of the son, the grandson.
When a denial has been made by either the son or the grandson, the debt—having been established by the plaintiff through witnesses and other means—must be paid.
The grammatical connection is with the words "by sons and grandsons.
Here, although it is merely stated that "the father has gone abroad," the specific duration of time must be understood as that which was declared by Nārada:
"If the father has been abroad for less than twenty years, the son [shall not inherit]."

"One should pay the debt to the paternal uncle or even to the eldest brother. (NSm 1.11) Even when [the father] has died, one who has not yet reached the age of legal capacity (*aprāptavyavahārakāla*) shall not pay; however, one who has reached the age of legal capacity (*prāptavyavahārakāla*) shall pay. And he...
Time has been shown by that very [text]:
"The fetus is to be known as such; the child is from the eighth year onward;
the boy is until the sixteenth year, and he is called *paugaṇḍa*."
"One who knows legal procedure is independent, except for his parents" (NSm 1.31–32).
Although a minor becomes independent after the death of his parents, he nevertheless does not become liable for debt.
As it has been said:
"For even one who is independent, if he has not attained legal capacity, shall bear the debt;
for independence is traditionally held to belong to the eldest, based on qualities and age.
(NSm 1.27) Likewise, a prohibition against arrest and summons is observed.

"An envoy, one who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation—these should not be obstructed, nor should the king summon them. (NSm 1.47).
Therefore:

"Therefore, once a son has been born, he must diligently release his father from debt by renouncing his own self-interest, so that the father does not go to hell. (NSm 1.6) This should be explained as meaning "by a son who has been born," that is, one who has come into being through the completion of the legal transaction [of procreation].

However, even a child has the entitlement to perform the *śrāddha*, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "One should not cause a [child] to recite the Veda, except for the utterance of *svadhā*. (GDh 2.5).

By the use of the plural number in the expression "by sons and grandsons," it is indicated that if there are many sons, they should pay the debt according to their respective shares if they are divided;
if, however, they are undivided, they should pay by way of collective enterprise (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*) while existing in a relationship of subordinate and principal.
Or rather, it is understood that he alone who is the primary [beneficiary] should give;
as Nārada says:
"From this point forward, the sons shall pay their father's debt according to their respective shares."

"Whether undivided or divided, he who bears that burden. (NSm 1.2) And although it has been stated here without distinction that "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons," nevertheless, the son must pay it in exactly the same manner as the father gave it, namely, with interest.
However, it should be understood that the specific distinction is that the principal alone, and not the interest, must be paid by the great-grandson;
for "the debt of the father, even when divided, should be paid by the sons just as if it were their own."
"An ancestral debt is to be paid equally; however, it is not to be paid by the son of that [debtor]," according to the traditional teaching of Bṛhaspati.

Here, because the term "established" (*vibhāvita*) is used without qualification, the inclusion of the word "witnesses" (*sākṣi*) in the phrase "established by witnesses" (*sākṣivibhāvita*) is intended to specify that form of proof.
This is an illustration of the authoritative measure:
as much as was received, so much alone shall be given back, and no interest; it is not to be repaid by the son or the great-grandson of that [debtor].
This refers to one who has not yet received his wealth;
this will be clarified in the following verse. (2.50)
In the discharge of a debt, three agents—the debtor, his son, and his grandson—have been shown; their order of succession in case of their simultaneous presence has also been shown.
Now, he states the order of succession in the case of the simultaneous presence of other agents as well.

The heir to the estate shall be made to pay the debt, as shall the one who takes the wife; likewise, the son whose property does not depend on others shall pay for his father who has no other heirs. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.51) That which becomes one's own through means other than purchase and the like, belonging to another, is called *riktha* (heritage).
One who takes the inheritance by way of partition is called an *rikthagrāha*; he is to be made to pay the debt.
This is what is meant.
He who takes another's property in the form of an inheritance shall be made to pay the debt incurred by that person, but not a thief or the like;
this refers to one who takes a woman as a wife.
The one who seizes a woman shall likewise be made to pay her debt;

whoever takes a woman belonging to another shall be made to pay the debt incurred by her. She is mentioned separately because, as property that cannot be divided, she is unfit to be designated as an inheritance.
And a son whose property is not dependent on others shall be made to pay the debt.

"Dependent on others" (*anyāśrita*) means that which is supported by another; "one whose property is dependent on others" (*anyāśritadravyaḥ*) refers to one whose wealth consists of property related to his mother or father.
The syntactical connection is: "One who possesses property not dependent on another—not one whose property is dependent on another—should be made to pay the debt of one who has no son and is an heir.

Regarding the concurrence of these [categories], the order is precisely that of the textual sequence: the taker of the inheritance (rikthagrāha) should be made to pay the debt; in his absence, the taker of the wife (yoṣidgrāha); and in his absence, the son.
But surely, even their coexistence is not possible, because [Manu Smṛti 9.185] states:
"Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs of the father"; for when a son exists, it is impossible for anyone else to take the inheritance.
"Even the seizure of a woman is not permissible, for it is recorded in the Smṛti: 'A second husband is never ordained for virtuous women. (MDh 5.162) Thus says the tradition.
Likewise, the claim that "the son alone should be made to pay that debt" is also incorrect,
because it has been stated that "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.50).
The qualification "not depending on another substance" is also redundant,
because as long as the son exists, it is impossible for the substance to depend on anything else; and even if such dependence were possible, [it would be unnecessary].
Since this is already implied by the term "heir" (*rikthagrāha*) itself,
the phrase "of one who has no son, [but has] an heir" need not be stated;
for it is established that even when a son exists, the heir is to be made to pay the debt.

It is already established that in the absence of a son, one who inherits the estate (*rikthagrāha*) must be made to pay all the more; to this it is replied: even when a son exists, another person may also be an inheritor of the estate.
Because eunuchs, the blind, the deaf, and others do not inherit property even though they may have sons;
and thus, having enumerated the eunuchs and others, [the law states]: "They should be maintained, but without a share" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.140).
Thus he will state;
likewise, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama— "Even the son of a woman of the same caste does not receive [the inheritance] if he is of improper conduct" (GDh 28.40).

Consequently, when there are sons who are impotent and so forth, and when there exists a son of the same caste (savarṇa) who behaves unjustly, the one who takes the inheritance is the paternal uncle, his son, or others;
even though the taking of a woman as a wife is not possible without contradicting the scriptures, nevertheless, it occurs once the prohibition has been transgressed.
He indeed becomes entitled to the discharge of debts incurred by his former husband;
this applies to the "seizer of women" who takes the last of the four types of unchaste women.
Furthermore, regarding the first of the three types of remarried women (*punarbhu*),
as Nārada has said: "Other women who have had previous husbands are declared to be of seven kinds, in their respective order."
The *punarbhū* is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* is of four kinds.
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage,
is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) by virtue of the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
When a woman is given away by her elders after considering the local customs (*deśadharma*), [she is likewise considered a *punarbhū*].
The second [type of remarriage] is proclaimed as that which occurs when a transgression has arisen. "When a transgression has arisen" means when infidelity has occurred.
When there are no brothers-in-law, the woman is given away by her kinsmen.
That third [generation] is proclaimed as being for one of the same caste (savarṇa) who is a sapinda.
Whether she has borne children or not, if a woman, while her husband is still living,
resorts to another man out of desire, she is the first type of unchaste woman (*svairiṇī*). But she who, having abandoned her husband from her youth, has resorted to another man...
She who goes again to the house of her husband is proclaimed as the second [type].
But she who, when her husband has died, having rejected the brothers-in-law and others who have approached her,
approaches another out of lust, is proclaimed as the third.
She who has come from another country, purchased with wealth, and arrived saying "I am yours," though afflicted by hunger and thirst, is proclaimed as the fourth [type of wife].
She is the last among the *svairiṇīs* (women of loose conduct) and the first among the *punarbhūs* (remarried women).
"Whosoever has taken refuge with her shall pay the debt contracted by her husband.
Likewise, another person who takes charge of a woman is also authorized to discharge the debt, as shown by that same [author]:
"But a woman who possesses property, or one who has offspring, may take refuge with another."
He shall either pay her debt to her husband or release her in that same manner.
"Sapradhanā" means she who exists together with abundant wealth;
that is to say, one possessing much wealth. Likewise.

"For when a man dies without wealth and without a son, he who takes his wife incurs the debt; he becomes the bearer of that [debt], and she alone is declared to be his wealth. (NSm 19) Furthermore, the mention of the "son" is for the purpose of establishing the sequence.

The phrase "one whose substance is not dependent on another" is intended to mean that, even when there are many sons and no inheritance [to divide], only one who is capable of taking a share has the right to discharge the debts of the deceased, and not one who is incapable, such as a blind person or the like. Furthermore, the expression "the heir of one who is sonless" refers to the grandson and subsequent descendants of one who is devoid of both son and grandson.
This is for the purpose of establishing that if they take the inheritance, then they must be made to pay the debt, and not otherwise;
furthermore, it has been stated that even in the absence of taking the inheritance, the son and grandson are liable to be made to pay.

As Nārada said: "A debt that was incurred by the father and cleared by the sons in due order without interruption, the grandsons must repay; that [liability] ceases with the fourth generation. (NSm 1.4)
Thus, everything is irreproachable.
Or rather, it has been stated that in the absence of a woman-seizer (*yoṣidgrāha*), the son shall be made to pay;

and in the absence of a son, it is now stated that the woman-seizer shall be made to pay. By the word "heir" (*rikthin*) in the phrase "the heir of one who is sonless," it is the woman herself who is meant.
For it is stated in the legal tradition: "That [wife] alone is remembered as his wealth" (NSm 1.19);
and: "He who carries off another's wife carries off his wealth" (NSm 1.18*).
And thus it is said.
But is it not a mutual contradiction that "if there is no woman-creditor, the son shall be made to pay the debt; if there is no son, the woman-creditor [shall be made to pay]"?
And if both exist, neither would be made to pay.
This is not a fault.

In the absence of one who has taken a woman for the last time, one who has taken her as a remarried wife (*punarbhū*) for the first time, or one who has seized her along with her property, the son shall be made to pay;
but in the absence of a son, the one who has taken a woman who is both destitute and childless shall be made to pay. This is the rule.

Thus it was said by Nārada: "Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, the one who inherits the debt shall take the property. If there is neither a wife nor wealth, the son [inherits]; if there is neither a son nor wealth, the wife; and if there is neither wealth nor a son, the wife. (NSm 1.20)

In the case of a combination of one who has taken the wealth, one who has taken the wife, and a son, he who takes the wealth shall be liable for the debt. Regarding the phrase "the son [is liable] when the wife and the owner of the wealth are absent": "owner of the wealth" (*strīdhanin*) refers to those two who possess both the wife and the wealth; when those two owners of the wealth are absent, the son is liable. As for the phrase "and the wife [is liable] when the owner of the wealth is absent": this means that when the owner of the wealth is absent, the wife is liable. And regarding the phrase "and the wealth [is liable] when the owner of the wife is absent": this means that when the owner of the wife is absent, the wealth is liable. Thus, it is established that among these three—the wife, the wealth, and the son—each is liable for the debt in the absence of the others. Therefore, it is concluded that the liability for the debt belongs to whichever of these three is present. Furthermore, it is understood that even if all three are present, the one who took the wealth is primarily liable for the debt. This is because the taking of the wealth constitutes a form of theft, and since the taking of the wife and the son likewise constitute forms of theft, the one who committed the theft is the one primarily liable for the debt. Consequently, it is established that the liability for the debt belongs to the one who took the wealth. However, if the wealth was taken through a legal transaction such as a sale, then the liability for the debt belongs to the one who took the wife or the son. This is because, in that case, there is no fault of theft on the part of the one who took the wealth. Thus, it is established that the liability for the debt belongs to the one who took the wife or the son. Moreover, it is understood that even if the wife and the son are present, the liability for the debt belongs to the one who took the wealth. This is because the taking of the wealth is a more serious offense than the taking of the wife or the son. Therefore, it is established that the liability for the debt belongs to the one who took the wealth. The son alone becomes liable for the debt; in the absence of both the creditor and the son, the husband of the woman shall be liable for the debt; in the absence of the husband of the woman...
The apparent contradiction—that "the son inherits the debt" and "in the absence of a son, the wife takes [the property]"—is resolved as before.
There is another interpretation for the phrase "of one who is heirless (putrahīna) and has an inheritor (rikthin)": [it refers to the case where the wife is the heir].
When the question arises as to whose debt these—the taker of wealth, the taker of the wife, and the son—should be made to pay, [the answer is] that they should be made to pay it to the creditor;

in his absence, to his son and so forth. When the further question arises as to whose debt they should be made to pay in the absence of such a son and so forth, this [verse] applies: "to the heir of one who has no son."
The heirs— such as *sapiṇḍas* and others— who are eligible to inherit the estate of a creditor who lacks a lineage of sons and so forth, must be made to pay [the debt] to that heir.
And thus it has been stated by Nārada:

"But if there is no one to whom the inheritance of a Brahmin should be given—neither his own descendants nor anyone else—it should be offered to his *sakulyas*; in their absence, to his *bandhus*. Thus it has been stated. (NSm 1.99)

"But when there are no agnatic kinsmen, nor relatives by marriage or maternal kin, then one should give [the property] to the twice-born; if they too are absent, one should cast it into the water. (NSm 1.100) 2.51.
Now, while prohibiting the assumption of debt from specific persons, the author incidentally prohibits other matters as well:
"Suretyship, debt, and witness testimony between brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son are indeed declared by the Smṛti to be invalid when they are undivided. (YDh 2.52)
The state of being a surety is "suretship" (*prātibhāvya*).
Regarding brothers, husband and wife, and father and son, when their property is undivided— that is,
prior to the partition of assets— suretship, debt, and witness testimony are not prescribed by Manu and other authorities.
Moreover, it is prohibited because the wealth is held in common,
and because, in the cases of acting as a guarantor or a witness, it results ultimately in the expenditure of property.
And because a debt must necessarily be repaid;
and this [is required] except by mutual consent.
By mutual consent, however—
However, even for those who have not divided their property, acts such as standing surety certainly take place;
but after division, they occur even without mutual consent.
Now, it might be argued that the prohibition of acting as a surety and so forth prior to the partition of husband and wife is not logical,
because since no such partition exists between them, the qualification would be purposeless.
Furthermore, the absence of partition has been shown by Āpastamba:
"No partition exists between husband and wife" (ĀpDh 2.14.16).
This is true; however, having stated that a partition does exist regarding those rites to be accomplished by the Śrauta and Smārta fires, as well as their fruits, why [is this said]?

In response to the inquiry as to why [the wife] does not exist [as an independent agent], he stated the reason: "For from the taking of the hand, there is jointness in ritual acts as well as in the fruits of merit" (ĀpDh 2.14.17–18).
For because from the taking of the hand onwards, jointness in ritual acts is heard in the scripture: "The husband and wife should together establish the sacred fires."

Therefore, because there is joint entitlement regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), there is joint entitlement in those rites accomplished by the fires established through that *ādhāna*;
likewise, the *smārta* rite is performed in the marriage fire (*vivāhāgni*). (YDh 1.97)
On account of such traditional authorities (smṛti), there is indeed joint entitlement even in those rites performed with the fire established at marriage and so forth.
Consequently, in those acts of public utility (pūrta) which do not depend on either of the two kinds of fire, the entitlement of the wife and husband is established as being separate.
Likewise, regarding the fruits of meritorious deeds such as heaven and so forth, the joint status of husband and wife is heard in the Veda:
"May they both attain undecaying light in heaven," and so on.

It should be understood that joint participation exists in the fruits of those meritorious acts in which one has joint authority; however, this does not apply even to the fruits of *pūrta* acts performed with the husband's permission.
But surely, joint participation has also been stated regarding ownership of property?

And regarding the possession of property, [the text] states: "For they do not teach that there is theft when a gift is made on account of a specific occasion during the husband's absence" (ĀpDh 2.14.19–20).
This is true; by this, the wife's ownership of the property is demonstrated, but it does not mean there is an absence of partition.
Because, regarding the acceptance of material goods, the reason has been stated through reasoning:
namely, when the master is away on a journey, or when there is an occasional obligation that must necessarily be performed, such as giving gifts, feeding guests, or providing alms.
Since Manu and others do not teach that theft [is committed] against a wife, it follows that the wife also possesses ownership over property; otherwise, it would constitute theft.
Therefore, the division of property for the wife occurs only by the husband's consent, not by her own will.
As he will state:
"If he should divide [the estate] into equal shares, the wives are to be made sharers of equal portions. (YDh 2.115) 2.52.
Now, in order to define suretyship (*prātibhāvya*), he says:
"Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment;
however, in the case of the first two [types] being rendered void, the debt must be paid by [the sureties], and in the case of the other, even their sons. (YDh 2.53)
Surety (*prātibhāvya*) is an agreement made with another person for the sake of inspiring confidence;
and it is divided into three types according to the difference in its subject matter, as follows:

Regarding "in the matter of seeing," it means when there is a need for visual verification, thinking, "I shall show him this. Regarding "in the matter of trust," it means: "Give him wealth on my guarantee; he will not deceive you, because he is the son of so-and-so, and his land consists mostly of fertile soil."
The phrase "he has a choice of what may be taken" and "if he does not give it when it is time for the gift, then I myself will give it"—
these two [statements] regarding the provision of surety are to be connected respectively with each [of the preceding cases].
However, the first two— the sureties for appearance and for guarantee—
are to be made to pay the stipulated sum to the creditor by the king if they fail to appear or if there is a breach of trust;
the sons of the other, the surety for payment, are also to be made to pay.

By stating, "Even the sons of the other [debtor] [are liable] if the debtor does not repay due to deceit or poverty," it is declared that the sons of the two preceding [debtors] are not to be made to pay. "Vitatha" means "untrue" [in this context].

Thus, by saying that even the sons of the other are liable when the debtor fails to repay because of deceit or lack of wealth, it is stated that the sons of the first two [categories of debtors] are not to be compelled to pay.
By stating "the daughters," it is shown that the grandsons are not liable to be made to pay.
To clarify this very point, he says:

"Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, his sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) shall pay it. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.54)

But when a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for trust (*prātyayika-pratibhū*) has gone to heaven, their sons shall not pay the paternal debt incurred on account of that suretyship. However, the sons of one who was a surety standing for payment (*dānāya sthitaḥ pratibhūḥ*) [shall pay].
Grandsons shall not pay [the debt];
they shall pay only the principal, not the interest.
A grandson is liable for his grandfather's debt, and a son is liable for a debt incurred as a surety.
"He should pay [the debt] equally; however, his two sons are not to be made to pay—this is the settled rule.
This is because of the statement of Vyāsa:
"A grandson shall pay an ancestral debt incurred by his grandfather, excluding that which was for suretyship, equally, as much as was received."
In this manner, one should pay the debt without interest;

likewise, the son of that [debtor] shall also pay the paternal debt incurred through suretyship in its entirety. Furthermore, the sons of those two—the grandson and the son—as well as the great-grandson and the grandson, shall discharge the liability arising from suretyship even if it was not a personal suretyship of their own.

And according to the sequence, those who have not received the wealth [of the debtor] shall not be made to pay the debt. As for the traditional legal maxim: "If the consumer should be devoid of wealth, while the surety is possessed of wealth..."
"The principal alone shall be given to him; he ought not to pay interest"—
this also refers to the *lagnaka* as the surety (*pratibhū*) and the *khādaka* as the debtor (*adhamarṇa*).
If the guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) is wealthy but deceased,
then it should be explained that his son must pay only the principal (*mūla*) and not the interest (*vṛddhi*).
Where [the term] *darśana-pratibhū* occurs...
Or, if a guarantor for a contingency, having taken sufficient collateral, becomes a guarantor,
then his sons also must indeed pay the debt incurred through that guarantee from out of that very collateral.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"Where a pledge has been taken and [the father] remains liable for its appearance, the son shall be made to pay that debt from that wealth, even without his father. (KSm 534)
The mention of "seeing" (darśana) is an illustration for any [means of] cognition; as in the cases:
"without his father," "when the father has died," or "when he has gone to a distant land. (2.54)
Regarding how one should be made to pay when there is the possibility of many sureties, he says:

"If there should be many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to their respective shares; but among those who have relied upon a single liability, it shall be as the creditor pleases. (YDh 2.55)

If there are two or more sureties for a single transaction, they shall divide that debt and pay according to their respective shares. Regarding sureties who have "resorted to a single shadow" (*ekacchāyāśrita*): the "shadow" refers to the likeness or status [of the debtor]; those who have resorted to that are "those who have resorted to a single shadow.
Just as the debtor stands ready to deliver the entire property, so too each of the sureties stands ready to deliver the entire property upon payment.
While they remain thus as guarantees (pratibhū) based on their appearance and their character, and while they are all resting under a single shadow, the creditor— the lender—
may act according to his preference or desire. And for this reason, whatever person the creditor requests for his own sake, taking into account wealth and other factors, he [is the one who must pay].
Thus, he must be made to pay the whole amount, not just a portion.
Among those who share a single liability, if one has gone to another country and his son is present, then at the creditor's wish, the son must be made to pay the whole.
But when someone has died, his son shall be made to pay his father's share without interest;
as Kātyāyana says:

"Among those who have entered under a single roof, he who is seen there shall be made to pay; if the owner is absent, his son shall pay everything; but if the owner is dead, [the heirs] shall pay equally. (KSm 538) 2.55.
Having stated the rule for the payment of a debt by a surety, he now states the rule for the repayment of what was paid by the surety:
"Whatever property of the creditor the surety is compelled to pay publicly, that shall be repaid double by the debtors. (YDh 2.56)
When the collateral, or its son, has been pressured by the creditor and compelled by the king to pay the debt publicly in the presence of all people,
and not given voluntarily out of greed for the doubling of the interest—
as Nārada says:
"And whatever amount the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor, the debtor shall cause that amount to be paid to the surety doubled.
(NSm 1.107) That property must be returned by the debtors—the *adhamarṇas*—to that surety doubled. That...
And, regardless of any specific time limit, it must be paid back twofold immediately,
by virtue of the force of the commencement of the statement;
and this refers specifically to the case of gold.

Now, it may be argued that this statement "he is a surety" establishes only the doubling [of the debt], and that is consistent even without contradicting the previously mentioned sequence of time and calculation.
Just as the injunction for the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice does not contradict the requirement of purity;

furthermore, in the view that the payment must be made immediately along with interest, since there can be no immediate offspring from cattle or women, it follows that only the price [of the animal or woman] should be paid.

That is incorrect, because the doubling [of the debt] and so forth is already established by the rule: "In the case of debts for cloth, grain, and the like, the maximum [interest] is four, three, or two-fold" (YDh 2.39), according to the sequence of the time-periods;
this statement would only be necessary if it were intended to enjoin doubling alone.

It would be purposeless. However, in the case of cattle and women, even under the view that they follow the sequence of time, there is only the restoration of their actual form when there is an absence of offspring. When the surety also comes together with the debtor after some time following the payment of the property, then—
A lineage certainly does exist;
or rather, that women of the animal species will bestow [offspring] along with an already established lineage—
this is nothing at all [new].
Now, a suretyship (*prātibhāvya*) may be entered into out of affection;
therefore, what is given by the surety is indeed a gift made out of affection (*prītidatta*).
And as for that which is given out of affection...
Interest exists prior to the request for repayment; as it has been said: "Whatever is given out of affection does not increase if not requested;
however, if it is requested and not given, it increases by five percent per hundred."
Thus [it is said].

And for this reason, by this statement it is declared that even in the case of what is given without affection or what is not requested, interest accrues in the course of time until it becomes double, starting from the day of the gift.
That too is incorrect, because this meaning is not understood from these words;
here, only this much is understood: "twofold must be returned."
Since it must be repaid as double regardless of the passage of time, by virtue of the force of the statement's commencement, it is well said [in verse 2.56]: // 2.56 //
An exception to the rule that a debt guaranteed by a surety becomes doubled everywhere is stated:
"In the case of offspring and female animals, [the interest] is only of the same kind; grain is tripled;
clothing is declared to be fourfold; and likewise, liquids are eightfold. (YDh 2.57)

Just as with the doubling of gold, women, cattle, and other such items must be returned along with the interest already paid, regardless of the lapse of time; this verse has indeed already been explained. Whatever maximum interest has been declared for a particular commodity, that commodity, when delivered by a surety, [must be restored].
The essential meaning is that the debtor must pay immediately along with the interest, regardless of any specific time limit.

However, when the surety for appearance is unable to produce the debtor at the agreed-upon time, then three fortnights (pakṣatraya) should be granted to him for the purpose of searching for the debtor.
In that case, if he produces it, then it should be enjoyed;
otherwise, he must be made to pay the wealth under dispute.
However, for the purpose of searching for what has been lost, he should be made to pay at most for a period of three fortnights.
If he should produce him there, he must be released; otherwise, he shall be the surety.
"Once the time has elapsed, if the surety does not produce that person,
he shall be made to pay the deposit; this rule is declared to apply when [the debtor] has died," according to the statement of Kātyāyana.
And the specific prohibitions regarding the ascendant have been stated by that same author:
"Neither the owner, nor an enemy, nor one appointed by the owner,
nor one who is imprisoned, nor one who has been punished, nor one who is under suspicion— none of these should ever [be appointed as a witness]."
Neither an heir, nor a friend, nor those who reside permanently [with him],
nor those appointed to royal service, nor men who have gone forth as renunciants [are liable for the debt].
He who is unable to pay the debt to the creditor and an equal fine to the king,
or whose father is still living and acts according to his own will, [is not liable].
"A surety should not be accepted for his obligation if he is unknown. Here, "one who is suspected" refers to one accused of a crime;
"those who dwell for life" refers to perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*).
Thus ends the rule concerning sureties. 2.57.
In the lending of wealth, there are two causes for trust: the surety and the pledge.
As Nārada said:
"In this matter, there are two causes of confidence: the surety and the pledge. (NSm 1.103)
In that regard, the surety has been defined;
now the pledge (*ādhi*) is defined.
A pledge is [a security] placed over the property that has been received.
For the sake of creating confidence, the debtor pledges an object to the creditor; this is called *ādhi*.
It is of two kinds:
that for which a time limit has been set (*kṛtakāla*) and that for which no time limit has been set (*akṛtakāla*).
Furthermore, each one is of two kinds: the pledge for custody (*gopya*) and the pledge for use (*bhogya*).
As Nārada said:
"That by which one is authorized [to use] is known as a pledge (*ādhi*); it is understood to be of two types."
And it should be removed at the appointed time, as well as when the gift is ready to be bestowed.

Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: that which is to be hidden (*gopya*) and likewise that which is to be enjoyed (*bhogya*). Regarding the "fixed time" (*kṛtakāla*): at the very time of pledging, it is brought near—that is, led into one's presence—with the determination: "At such a time, such as the festival of lamps (*dīpotsava*), this pledge must be released by me; otherwise, it shall become yours alone. (NSm 1.108–09)
The meaning is "to be released. "To be given" (deyam) means a gift; "not exceeding what is to be given" means as much as should be given.

"Udyataḥ" means "fixed" or "established. "Yāvad-deyodyataḥ" means one who is committed to returning whatever was borrowed; the meaning is that the time limit has not been determined, with the repayment of the received wealth as the boundary. "Gopyaḥ" means that which is to be protected.
Thus he states the distinction regarding the four types of pledge:
"If it is not released when the debt has doubled, the pledge perishes;
that which is fixed for a time perishes at the end of that time, but that which is to be enjoyed for its produce does not perish. (YDh 2.58)
When the stipulated debt has doubled over time through the interest accrued by the creditor, if the pledge is not released by the debtor through the payment of the principal, then it is forfeited;
the property of the debtor becomes the property of the lender. This refers to a pledge for a fixed period.
Because the word *kāla* is listed among the group beginning with *āhitāgni* in the rule for compounds whose time is fixed (*kṛtakāla*), it is placed first;
however, once that time has been determined and reached,
the debt would be lost either before or after its doubling.
"Phalabhogya" means that for which the fruit is the object of enjoyment; such property, consisting of fields, gardens, and the like, never perishes.
This applies to both a deposit (nyāsa) and a bailment (upanihitaka) for a fixed period, as well as to a bailment for enjoyment (bhogya), provided that time has not elapsed.

It has been stated that destruction occurs at the [stipulated] time, meaning "it shall be destroyed by time. It has also been stated that for that which is not subject to a fixed time and is intended to be enjoyed, there is no destruction, as in "that which is to be enjoyed as its fruit does not perish.
By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the statement "the pledge (*ādhi*) shall be lost" remains applicable specifically to the case of a pledge where the period for custody is not fixed.
In the event of loss due to the doubling of the principal or the lapse of the stipulated time, an expectation of fourteen days must be observed,
according to the statement of Bṛhaspati: "When the gold has doubled and the fixed period has expired..."
The creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for two weeks.
"Having paid that amount in the interim, the debtor shall obtain his pledge. (BṛSm 1.10.48–49) Now, it might be argued that the statement "the pledge shall perish" is untenable,
because there is an absence of any act such as giving or selling— which would cause the cessation of the debtor's ownership.
Furthermore, the wealthy person lacks the grounds for ownership— such as acceptance as a gift or purchase—
and this contradicts the statement of Manu:
"There is neither alienation nor sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time" (MDh 8.143).

"Kālasaṃrodha" means confinement for a period of time; it is a state of remaining for a long duration. Because of that confinement for a long duration, there is no relinquishment of the pledge (ādhi); other than this, there is neither its re-pledging nor its sale.
Thus, by the prohibition of re-pledging and sale, [the pledge remains with the creditor].

It is argued that the absence of ownership on the part of the creditor is understood [from this]. It is replied: in common worldly usage, the act of pledging itself is the cause for the cessation of ownership subject to conditions;
and the acceptance of the pledge is the cause for the acquisition of ownership subject to conditions.
This is well-known.
In that regard, when the doubling of the debt has occurred and the stipulated time has arrived, because the giving of the substance ceases entirely,
by this statement there is the absolute cessation of ownership for the debtor and the absolute acquisition of ownership for the creditor.
This is so, and there is no contradiction with the words of Manu; for Manu says:
"But one shall never receive interest on a loan secured by a pledge that yields profit" (MDh 8.143).
Regarding the pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*),
this is stated:
"There is neither alienation nor sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time" (MDh 8.143).

Even if a pledge for use remains in possession for a long time, the creditor has no ownership over it because of the prohibition against its alienation through mortgage or sale. This point is also stated here: "A pledge to be used for its fruit is not lost. However, regarding a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), Manu has treated it separately (8.144): "A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest" (MDh 8.144).
In this context also it will be stated:
"There is no interest on a pledge that is kept in custody" (*gopyādhibhoge no vṛddhiḥ*).
However, the rule "the pledge shall be forfeited when [the debt] has doubled" (*ādhiḥ praṇaśyed dviguṇe*) refers specifically to a pledge kept in custody; thus, everything is consistent. (2.58)
Furthermore:
"In the case of the use of a pledge by deposit, there is no interest; nor is there interest when a pledge that provides a benefit is lost.
That which is destroyed or ruined—except through acts of God or the king—must be restored. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.59)
Interest accrues through the use of a pledge such as a copper cauldron;
even when the use is slight, a great interest must be relinquished.
Because of the lapse of time due to negligence;

likewise, in the case of a beneficial pledge—such as a bull, a copper cauldron, or the like—which serves as a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*) and carries interest, if it is "lost" (*hāpita*), meaning its value has been diminished to the point of being unfit for legal transaction, then there shall be no interest. This is the connection [of the text].

If a copper vessel or similar object has been lost or damaged, it should be restored to its former condition by repairing cracks and so forth, and then returned. In that regard, if a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) is lost, it must be restored to its former condition and returned;
even if it was used, the interest (*vṛddhi*) must also be waived.
If the pledge for use is lost, then it must be restored as before;
if interest has accrued, the interest must also be relinquished.
If it is destroyed—meaning it has reached total ruin—that too must be restored by means of its value or equivalent.
If he gives it, he receives the principal value along with interest;
when he does not give it, there is the loss of the principal.
"Upon its destruction, there shall be loss of the principal, except in cases caused by fate or the king," according to the statement of Nārada; "except in cases caused by fate or the king" means:
"Divine" refers to calamities such as fire, water, or the destruction of one's location;
"without destruction caused by divine agency" means likewise without [destruction] resulting from one's own fault.

[This applies] to destruction caused by the king. However, in the event of destruction caused by both fate and the king, the debtor must pay the value together with interest, or provide another pledge. As it has been said: "When a field is swept away by a flood or confiscated by the king..."
"Otherwise, another pledge must be made, or the debt must be paid to the creditor.
(DhKo 661) In this context, the phrase "carried away by a current" is an illustration for anything caused by fate. 2.59.
Moreover,
if the pledge, though being preserved, reaches a state of worthlessness due to the lapse of time,
another pledge may be taken, or the creditor shall become a sharer in the profits.
The establishment of a pledge (*ādhi*)—whether it be for enjoyment or otherwise—results from its acceptance and actual use; it does not occur by mere witness or by mere verbal designation.
As Nārada has said:
"Adhi is declared to be of two kinds: movable and likewise immovable; the realization of both of these occurs through possession, and not otherwise. (NSm 1.119) And the result of this is:
"In the case of a gift, a pledge, or a purchase, the prior act is indeed more powerful" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.23).

That action which culminates in formal acceptance (*svīkāra*) is the prior one that possesses greater force; however, an act lacking acceptance does not possess force, even if it occurred earlier. Thus [it is said].

If a pledge, even when carefully guarded, by the force of time comes to lose its value without being damaged—reaching a state where it is insufficient to cover the principal along with interest—then another pledge must be made to the creditor, or the money must be paid;
for it is said: "even while being guarded, it has become worthless."
By saying this, it is made known that a pledge must be protected with effort by the creditor. // 2.60 //
He states an exception to the rule that "the pledge shall be forfeited when [the debt] has doubled" (YDh 2.58):
"One should cause the debtor to pay the money, along with interest, for a pledge given as a token of good faith (*caritrabandhaka*)."
One should cause the person who has made a formal pledge (satyaṃkāra) to return the object twice its value.

Regarding "caritra": it means a beautiful deed; a pledge based on such conduct is a "caritrabandhaka. By means of that, whatever property has been made one's own or rendered dependent upon another is [referred to].
This is what is meant: because of his pure disposition, the creditor allowed the debtor to take possession of only a small amount of wealth, even though the object pledged was of great value.

If, however, because of the debtor's honest disposition, he has taken a pledge of little value and left a large amount of wealth under the debtor's control, that wealth [the king shall restore]. That king—
One should cause the debt to be paid together with the interest.
This is the intended meaning:
in this way, even when the principal has doubled, the pledge does not perish.
However, the actual substance itself must be given doubled;
likewise for that which is made by a *satyaṃkāra*.
*Karaṇa* means "making" (*kāra*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). *Satyakāraḥ* means "the making of truth" (*satyasya kāraḥ*).
According to Pāṇini 6.3.70, the augment *mum* is applied in the word *satyāgada-* when followed by *kāra-*. Thus, that which is performed by means of a "making of truth" is called *satyaṃkārakṛtam*.
The underlying intention is this:
at the very time of pledging the deposit,
it was stipulated as follows:

If [the debtor] says, "Even though the principal has doubled, I must pay only the double amount of the principal itself, not the loss of the pledge," then he should cause that double amount to be paid;
this is another interpretation.
"Character as collateral" (*caritrabandhaka*) means that character itself is the pledge.
By the word "character," the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by bathing in the Ganges, performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so forth, is meant;
it is with reference to that very thing [as the object] that [the term is used].
Whatever property has been made one's own [as a pledge], that very thing, having become doubled, must be returned; it is not subject to forfeiture as a pledge.
This follows from the context of pledges (*ādhi*).
Another thing is called "made under oath" (*satyaṃkārakṛta*).

When a finger-ring or similar object is placed in another's hand for the purpose of ensuring the fulfillment of an agreement regarding purchase, sale, or other transactions, that object must be returned twofold if the agreement is violated.
In that case as well, if the very person by whom the ring and so forth were offered violates the established rule, then he alone must return that very thing;
if, however, the other person violates the established rule, then [the former need not return it].
He shall cause that very ring or other object to be returned to him, doubled in value. (2.61)
Furthermore:
A pledge should be enjoyed by one who has it at hand; otherwise, he would become a thief. In the absence of the creditor, the debtor may obtain the money from another family as a pledge. (YDh 2.62)
When one who has come for the purpose of pledging property through the gift of wealth arrives, the pledge must be released by the owner; it should not be withheld out of greed for interest.
Otherwise, if it is not released, he would be punished like a thief or a robber. Furthermore, this applies when the lender is present; however, if the lender is absent from the family...
Having placed that money, along with the interest, into the hands of a trustworthy person, the debtor shall take back his own pledge. (2.62)
Now, if the borrower is not present and there are no trustworthy persons to receive the money,
or if the borrower is absent and the debtor wishes to give the money by selling the pledge, what should be done in that case? In anticipation of this inquiry, he says:
"Or it may remain there at its value fixed at that time, without interest.

(YDh 2.63ab) Having determined whatever the value of that pledge was at that time, one should leave that pledge with the creditor right there, free of interest; beyond that point, it does not increase.
Until the creditor takes his wealth and releases that pledge, or until he applies the value of that property toward the debt.

But when it has been determined at the very time of contracting the loan that, even though the debt has doubled, only the doubled amount of money itself is to be taken and not the forfeiture of the pledge, then, once the property has doubled and the debtor is absent, by the creditor—
To the question "What should be done?", he says:
"Or even without the debtor, he may sell [the pledge] in the presence of witnesses" (YDh 2.63cd).
That is, when the debtor—the one who owes—is absent, he may sell that pledge together with witnesses and his trusted associates.
The creditor may take that wealth after selling it; the word "or" (vā) signifies a fixed alternative. This applies at the time of receiving the debt.

If it was not considered that even when the debt has doubled, only the principal is to be recovered and not the forfeiture of the pledge, then there would be forfeiture of the pledge according to the rule: "The pledge is forfeited when [the debt] has doubled" (YDh 2.58).
But when this position is examined, it is as follows: // 2.63 //
He states the specific rule regarding objects for enjoyment and the like:
"But when the debt has doubled upon the pledge, then indeed the pledge must be released once twice the amount of the original debt has been realized from its produce. (YDh 2.64)

When the lent capital has doubled by means of the interest accrued by the creditor's own effort, then, once the pledge has been made and the value of the pledge or the property produced from it has doubled and entered into the creditor’s possession, the pledge must be released by the creditor;
or, if the pledge was delivered at the very outset.
By the stipulation that "the pledge must be released when the principal has doubled," or by some other cause,

when the debt has doubled due to the absence of enjoyment [of the pledge], then, once the pledge has been taken by the creditor for the purpose of enjoyment and the value derived from it has doubled, the pledge must be released.
Even in the case of excessive enjoyment, that [debt] must be returned;
this statement refers specifically to the case of enjoying property for the purpose of clearing a debt consisting of both principal and interest in every respect.
Ordinary people call that a pledge for consumption (*kṣayādhi*);

however, where the technical definition is that the enjoyment is solely for the purpose of interest, there one continues to enjoy the pledge as long as the principal remains unpaid, even after the doubling of the interest has been exceeded.
This very point has been clarified by Bṛhaspati:
"The debtor shall obtain his release upon returning the property,
provided that the full period has elapsed and he has paid the equivalent value of the usufruct of the fruit."
"If that [pledge] were to be exhausted [by use], then the creditor would not be entitled to the wealth, nor would the debtor incur a lien without the mutual consent of both. (BṛSm 1.10.125–26).
The meaning of this is: "phalabhogya" refers to a pledge (*bandha*) or mortgage (*ādhi*) whose fruit is to be enjoyed.
And that [debt] is of two kinds: for the purpose of repaying the principal along with interest, and for the purpose of repaying the interest alone.
Among these, the bond for the purpose of repaying the principal along with interest is one whose term has expired.
The meaning is that the debtor shall obtain the release of the pledge when the full time has elapsed;
that is, when the principal, together with interest, has entered the creditor's possession by way of the produce.
However, for the purpose of clearing away the mere excess of interest, the debtor may recover the pledge by paying the *sāmaka*;
"equal" (*sama*) refers to the principal, and "equal" (*sāmaka*) means exactly that same amount.
He states an exception to this: "If that [pledge] were of superior quality.

If that pledge were of superior quality—that is, excellent or even yielding a greater return than the interest itself—then the creditor does not receive his share of the wealth; that is, the creditor does not recover the principal.

The meaning is that a debtor shall forfeit his pledge even without having paid the principal. However, if that pledge is not of high value and is insufficient even for the interest, then the debtor shall not lose his pledge even after paying the full amount (sāmaka).
The meaning is that one may obtain [the debt] even after giving the remainder of the interest.

Again, he states an exception in both cases: "without mutual consent" means if there is an absence of mutual agreement between the creditor and the debtor regarding what was stated as "excessive" and so forth.

If there is mutual agreement, even a field that has been ploughed [as collateral] the creditor may enjoy as long as the principal is not repaid; likewise, even a lowly pledge the debtor recovers by the mere repayment of the principal. (2.64)
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of debt; now begins the section on deposits, wherein he speaks concerning the deposit:
The section on deposits (upanidhi-prakaraṇa) follows; regarding the deposit, he says:

When an object placed in a container is handed over to another person without being described, that is a sealed deposit (*aupanidhika*); it must be returned in exactly that same manner. A "container" (*vāsana*) is another substance that serves as a receptacle for the deposited object, such as a basket or the like; "placed in a container" (*vāsana-stha*) means situated within that [receptacle].

When a substance— without specifying its particular qualities such as form, number, and so forth— is handed over or deposited in the hand of another for safekeeping out of trust, and remains sealed, that substance is called *aupanidhika*. As Nārada says:
"That which is deposited as an uncounted and unrecognized ocean, one should know that as an *upanidhi*; the wise know a *nikṣepa* to be counted.
Thus it is; it must be returned in exactly the same manner.
Whatever has been deposited by someone, marked with a seal or other signs just as it was before, must be returned and restored to the depositor exactly in that same condition. // 2.65 //
He states an exception to the rule "it must be returned":
"But he shall not be made to pay for that which has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves" (YDh 2.66ab).
That deposit (*upanidhi*) which has been stolen or lost by the king, by fate such as water and the like, or by thieves—he who [received it] shall not be made to pay for it.
That property which has been deposited remains with the owner alone if it was not lost through the fault of the depositary;
as Nārada says:
"That which is lost along with the object itself is lost to the giver."
"Likewise, if it was caused by a king or a god, provided it was not done through deceit. (NSm 2.6).
He states an exception to this:
"If, when the loss has been investigated, [the debtor] does not pay, he shall be made to pay [the debt] and a fine equal to it. (YDh 2.66cd)

If, when sought and requested by the owner, the borrower does not return the item, then even if subsequently a loss or destruction of it occurs due to the king or others, the borrower must still pay the value of that object to the owner according to its estimated price, and he must also pay a fine equal to that amount to the king. (2.66)
Regarding the consumer, he states the penalty:
"One who lives at will [on the deposit] is to be punished and made to pay that [debt] along with interest" (YDh 2.67ab).

He who, by his own will and without the owner's permission, lives upon—that is, uses or transacts with—the deposited property through lending or other means, is subject to punishment and must restore the value together with the interest accrued.

If he uses it for the sake of profit, he should be punished according to the extent of the enjoyment and the profit gained; furthermore, that deposit must be returned to the creditor along with interest if it was enjoyed, or along with the profit if it was used in trade.
And the measure of interest has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"If, when requested, one does not return a deposit, the remainder of interest, or what was purchased or sold, it increases by five percent per month. (NSm 5.5–6).
And this should be understood to apply in the case where [the object] has been consumed.
But when [the loss] occurs through negligence (*upekṣā*) or ignorance (*ajñāna*), a distinction is shown by that same [author]:
"He shall be made to pay the value with interest if it was eaten; he shall be made to pay the full amount if it was neglected;
he shall be made to pay a small reduction if the property was destroyed through ignorance" (NSm 5.97).
"Less by something" means diminished by one-fourth.
He extends the rules for deposits (*upanidhi*) to items borrowed and so forth:
this same rule applies to things borrowed, those held in trust, deposits, pledges, and the like. (YDh 2.67cd)
That which is brought after being requested at festivals such as weddings, consisting of clothing, ornaments, and so forth, is called *yācita*.

When a certain object has been deposited in the hand of one person, and subsequently that same object is deposited in the hand of another with the instruction, "Give this to the owner," it is called *anvāhita*.

*Nyāsa* means the act of depositing an item into the hands of a householder's family members without showing it to the owner and in his absence, with the understanding that it is to be returned to the owner;
whereas *nikṣepa* is the delivery of an item in the presence of the owner himself.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the taking of a deposit— such as gold placed in the hands of a goldsmith or others for the purpose of fashioning a bracelet or the like— and the mutual dependence of the exchange, wherein [one says], "This which belongs to me must be guarded by you," and [the other says], "This which belongs to you is being guarded by me."
As Nārada has said:
"This same rule is seen to apply to things borrowed, those held as collateral, and so forth;
it applies likewise to craftsmen, to deposits, to bailments, and to counter-deposits" (NSm 2.7).

Regarding these items—such as those borrowed for use or those deposited as a pledge—the same rule that applies to a sealed deposit (upanidhi) concerning its restoration and so forth should be understood to apply here as well. (2.67)
Thus ends the section on deposits;
now begins the section on witnesses.
It has been stated that "the means of proof are declared to be documents, possession, and witnesses."
In that regard, enjoyment has been defined;
now the nature of the witness is being defined. A witness exists by virtue of having seen or heard directly.
As Manu said:
"Testimony is established by seeing in person and by hearing" (MDh 8.74).
And that [testimony] is of two kinds: formal (*kṛta*) and informal (*akṛta*).
He has been designated as a witness; he is "designated" (nirūpita) when appointed, and "undesignated" (anirūpita) when not appointed.
Among these, the designated is of five kinds and the undesignated is of six kinds, making eleven kinds in total.
As Nārada said:
"Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the treatises by the wise;
five kinds are to be known as appointed, and six kinds are said to be unappointed. (NSm 1.129)

And their classification has been shown by that same [author]: "The written, the reminded, the incidental, the cognizant, the secret, and the subsequent witness— witnesses are declared to be of five kinds" (NSm 1.130).

The nature of written witnesses (*likhita*) and others has been stated by Kātyāyana: "A witness who is personally brought by the plaintiff and recorded in the document is called a 'written witness' (*likhita*); one who is reminded [of his testimony] without a document is called a 'reminded witness' (*smārita*). (KSm 371)
The explanation of the term *smārita* ("one who has been reminded") as "one [who has been] recalled from a document" was provided by that same author:
"A witness who, for the sake of accomplishing the matter at hand, is repeatedly reminded of the case after having seen it by the plaintiff—that witness is called *smārita* here. (KSm 372)

But one who is made a witness by chance is a "casual witness" (*yadṛcchābhijña*). The distinction between these two, even though neither is recorded in writing, has been shown by that very same [author]:
"One who has been brought for a specific purpose and one who has arrived incidentally—these two witnesses, even if not recorded [in writing], are effective in proving the plaintiff's case. (KSm 373).
Likewise:
"He who, remaining hidden, is clearly informed by the plaintiff for the sake of establishing his own case regarding the statement of the defendant, is called a hidden witness.
Likewise: [KSm 374] Thus:

"He who gives testimony again and again, whether by hearing [the evidence] himself or by causing it to be heard, is called an *uttara-sākṣin* (subsequent witness). (KSm 375). Nārada has also shown the division of the six kinds of witnesses when they have not been formally appointed:
The village headman, the presiding judge, the king, whoever may be authorized in the affairs of litigants, and whoever has been dispatched by the plaintiff;
"In disputes between families, members of those families should also be known as witnesses. (NSm 1.131–32).
The mention of the *prāḍvivāka* (judge) is intended to include the scribe and the assessors (*sabhyas*). "The scribe, the judge, and the assessors, in their respective order... [NSm 1.133].
"When the king observes that matter, witnesses are declared [to be required].
(KSm 355). To the question of what kind of people these witnesses should be and how many they should be, he says:
"Ascetics, those of a charitable disposition, those of noble birth, and speakers of truth."
Those who prioritize righteousness, who are upright, who have sons, and who are endowed with wealth—

such men should be known as witnesses, provided they are at least three in number and devoted to the performance of Vedic (śrauta) and traditional (smārta) rites. Alternatively, it is recorded that witnesses may be all types of people for all cases, according to their respective caste (jāti) and class (varṇa).
Those who practice austerity are ascetic by nature;
those who practice giving are devoted to charity;
and those of noble birth are born of great lineages.
They are speakers of truth,
having the habit of speaking the truth;
they prioritize the Dharma rather than prioritizing wealth or pleasure.
"Upright" means not crooked;
"having sons" means having sons currently present.
Those endowed with wealth, meaning possessed of much gold and other riches;
devoted to Vedic and Smṛti rites, meaning intent on the performance of obligatory and occasional duties—
men of such a character, being at least three in number, serve as witnesses.
"Those for whom three are the minimum" (*tryavarāḥ*) means those who have at least three; they do not fall below three,
but beyond that, they may be as many as desired— this is the meaning.
Transgressing birth according to birth: births refer to those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others.
Among these, regarding the *mūrdhāvasikta*s:
Anointed kings (mūrdhāvasikta) serve as witnesses;
the same should be understood for the Ambaṣṭhas and others as well,
without overstepping their respective castes (varṇa).
"According to class":
the classes are the Brahmins and so forth.
Among them, for the Brahmins, only those possessing the aforementioned characteristics and the aforementioned number are mentioned.
They serve as witnesses.
In this same way, it should be understood for Kṣatriyas and others as well;
likewise, women shall give testimony for women.
They should act in this manner, as Manu has stated:

"Women shall serve as witnesses for women" (MDh 8.68). In the absence of those of the same caste and class, all—including the *mūrdhāvasikta*s and others, as well as the *brāhmaṇa*s and others—may serve as witnesses for all, including the *mūrdhāvasikta*s and others.
Furthermore, Brahmins and others may serve as witnesses according to their availability.

Since witnesses possessing the aforementioned characteristics might not always be available, it is necessary to specify those who are *asākṣins* (non-witnesses) in order to establish that others who are free from disqualification may also act as witnesses. And they [the non-witnesses] are as follows:

Nārada has shown that there are five kinds [of non-witnesses]: "For even one who is not a witness is seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the wise: through statement, through defect, through division, through self-accusation, and through death in the interval" (NSm 1.137).
Regarding the question of who are non-witnesses by virtue of their specific status, he says:
"Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those who have renounced the world and so forth—they are non-witnesses by virtue of their status; no further reason is cited here. (NSm 1.140)
"Ascetics" refers to forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who quarrel with their fathers and others are included.
As Śaṅkha has said:
"One who quarrels with his father, a resident of a teacher's house, a wandering mendicant, a forest-dweller, and a naked ascetic are non-witnesses.
Thus, non-witnesses have been shown on account of their defects:
"Thieves, violent assailants, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise deceivers..."
"They are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them. (NSm 1.141) "Caṇḍas" means those who are prone to anger;
"kitavas" means gamblers.
The nature of non-witnesses due to disagreement has been shown by that very same [author]:
"When witnesses, whether written down or specifically designated by the plaintiff, speak otherwise than one another, they are all not witnesses because of their disagreement. Thus it is said.
Likewise, the nature of a self-accuser has been stated:
"One who comes forward and speaks of his own accord, without being pointed out, is called a *sūcī* in the legal treatises; he is not fit to be a witness. (NSm 1.139, 1.143)
The definition of a "deceased intermediary" (*mṛtāntara*) has also been stated:
"When the matter that ought to be heard is absent, and there is no claimant, where could he exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who is a deceased intermediary is not a witness. (NSm 1.144)

When a plaintiff or a defendant has something to be communicated to the witnesses— namely, "you are witnesses in this matter"— if that plaintiff or defendant is absent, deceased, or if the matter itself has not been brought forward,
where and in what respect can the witness [be held accountable]?
A witness who has passed away cannot testify as to for whose sake or on what matter one should speak;
however, in a case where a dying person,
or one who is healthy, has informed his sons and others, saying, "In this matter, these are the witnesses," there the deceased may indeed serve as a witness.
He is also a witness; as Nārada says: "One who dies in the interval when the plaintiff has passed away, except for one who was informed [of the suit] while about to die" (NSm 1.139).
Likewise:

Even if one has not been informed by a person who is not ill, if a matter connected with dharma is stated, he shall be a witness even after death; and this applies in the case of the six types of transactions, such as deposits and the like.
Thus [ends the citation from NSm 1.84]. 2.68 // 2.69 //
He shows these to be incompetent witnesses:
women, children, the aged, gamblers, those intoxicated or insane, those accused of crimes, performers, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired senses. (YDh 2.70)
An outcast, a relative, one interested in the matter, an associate, an enemy, a thief, one who commits violence,
