and one whose fault has been observed— these, beginning with the "expelled" (nirdhūta), are not witnesses. A woman is well known [as such].
A "child" is one who has not attained legal capacity for transactions;
an "elder" is one aged eighty or more.
The mention of "elders" includes those whose speech is prohibited by law.
This is also for the purpose of indicating others, such as those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and so forth;
a gambler is one who plays with dice;
"intoxicated" means by drinking and the like; "insane" [is one whose mind is deranged].
One possessed by a planet;
one accused or charged with such acts as the killing of a Brahmin;
and a performer who enters the stage, namely a wandering actor.
Heretics are those such as the Nirgranthas and others;
a forger is one who produces fraudulent documents and the like.
One with impaired faculties is one lacking [a sense organ] such as the ear; one who has fallen is a killer of a Brahmin and so forth;
a trusted person is a friend.
One who is connected by wealth is one with whom there is a connection regarding material interests; an associate is one who shares a common purpose;
and an enemy is an adversary.
A *taskara* is a thief;
a *sāhasī* is one who acts by means of forceful intimidation; a *dṛṣṭadoṣa* is one whose speech is seen to be contradictory.

One who has been cast out by his kinsmen and abandoned; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is an inclusion of other non-witnesses mentioned in other Smṛtis due to their defects, such as those excluded because of partiality, those excluded because of self-contradiction, and those who have died in the interim. These persons—women, children, and the rest—are not to be witnesses. (2.70–2.71)
Regarding the rule that witnesses must be at least three in number, he states an exception:
"Even a single person who knows the Dharma may be a witness if he is agreed upon by both parties" (YDh 2.72ab).
One who performs obligatory and occasional rites preceded by knowledge is "one who knows the Dharma."
Even though he is alone, if he is approved by both parties,
he becomes a witness;
by the force of the word "even" (api), two may also [be witnesses].

Although the status of being "knowers of dharma" is common even to those consisting of fewer than three—as indicated by the rule "those devoted to Vedic and Smārta rites" (YDh 2.69)—nevertheless, their eligibility as witnesses occurs even in the absence of mutual consent from both parties.
However, the witness-status of one or two persons occurs only through the mutual consent of both; thus, the mention of "fewer than three" is purposeful.
He states an exception to the rule that "ascetics and those of a charitable disposition [are witnesses]" (YDh 2.68):
"Every person may be a witness in cases of adultery, theft, verbal assault, and violence" (YDh 2.72cd).

Regarding those acts such as adultery whose characteristics will be described later, all persons prohibited by scriptural injunctions and those devoid of virtues such as austerity (*tapas*) serve as witnesses in these cases.
Furthermore, in this context as well, there are non-witnesses due to defects (*doṣa*), non-witnesses due to dissension (*bheda*), and witnesses who testify of their own accord.
Because the reason—that [the offenses] exist due to the absence of truth—is present here as well:
"Killing a human, theft, violating another's wife, harshness, and both [types of slander] constitute the fourfold *sāhasa* (violent crime). (NSm 14.1*)

According to this statement, although sexual intercourse with women, theft, and verbal assault constitute acts of violence (*sāhasa*), they are nonetheless classified as *sāhasa* only when committed by relying on one's own strength in the presence of people.

However, acts committed in secret are designated by terms such as "seduction" (*saṃgrahaṇa*) and so forth; therefore, they are mentioned separately from the category of *sāhasa* (violent crimes). 2.72.
Regarding the summoning of witnesses, he says:
"He shall cause the witnesses to hear [the case] while they are in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant" (YDh 2.73ab).
Witnesses must speak when assembled in the presence of the claimant and the respondent; those who are not assembled together, even if questioned, should not testify (GDh 13.5).
According to this statement of Gautama, one should cause [the person] to hear what is about to be stated.
In that regard as well, Kātyāyana has shown a specific distinction:
Within the assembly, the judge, consoling them, shall appoint all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant by means of this procedure:
"In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, he shall ask the twice-born for truthful testimony."
In the forenoon, being himself pure, he should [seat] those who are pure, facing either northward or eastward.
"Having summoned the witnesses, he should question them individually after restraining them strictly with oaths—
provided they are all of known conduct and have knowledge of the matter.
Likewise, a rule regarding the proclamation [of the oath] to Brahmins and others has been shown by Manu:
"One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins" (MDh 8.113).
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa who speaks otherwise to swear: "May your truth perish."
To a Kṣatriya, [one says]: "Your vehicles and weapons will be fruitless. To a Vaiśya, [one says]: "Your cattle, seed-grain, gold, and so forth will become fruitless."
"If you speak otherwise regarding a Śūdra, may all sins accrue to you"— thus he should pronounce a curse.
And an exception to this has been shown by that very same [author]:
"One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers like Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas" (MDh 8.102).
The mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is intended as an illustration for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well.
"Kuśīlavas" refers to singers.
When an opponent has offered a challenge regarding the witnesses,
if the grounds for challenge— such as their being minors and so forth— are such that they can be verified through direct perception, the decision shall be made accordingly.

However, in the case of incompetent witnesses, the determination is made from their own statements and from worldly circumstances, rather than by means of other witnesses; thus, there is no infinite regress.
This applies if one, having exposed the defect of the witness, is able to prove it.
If the defendant is unable [to prove his case], then he should be punished according to the gravity of the matter;
but if he establishes it, then the witnesses are not required.
As it has been said:
"One who fails to prove his case should be compelled to pay the fine for suborning witnesses, provided that the corruption of the witnesses is clearly established.
Once this is proven, those witnesses are to be excluded, having been disqualified by the rules governing witnesses.
(DhKo 345) Furthermore, when all the witnesses specified have been found to be corrupt and the plaintiff has no other means of proof (*kriyāntara*) remaining, he is then defeated.

If the litigant is free from further desire and remains established in the truth of the witnesses, he has been defeated and shall be compelled to undergo disciplinary action according to the procedure prescribed in the treatises. (BṛSm 1.5.27)
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa);
the intention is that if there is an expectancy, one should resort to another action.
To explain how one should cause [the text] to be heard, he says:
"Those worlds which belong to those who commit minor sins (pātaka), as well as those belonging to the perpetrators of great crimes (mahāpātakin);
those worlds which belong to arsonists, and those belonging to the slayers of women and children. (YDh 2.73cd)

He who gives false testimony incurs all those sins. Whatever merit you have performed throughout hundreds of previous births, know that it all belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood. (YDh 2.74–75)

He who speaks falsehood as witness attains all those worlds belonging to those who commit minor offenses, secondary offenses, and great sins; to those who set fire to dwellings, and to those who kill women and children.
Likewise, whatever merit has been performed by him throughout hundreds of other births, that too [is lost].
The connection is that one should cause [the defeated party] to hear: "Everything belongs to him who has been defeated by you through false testimony.
And this should be understood as referring to the Śūdra, according to the rule:
"But a Śūdra [is to be punished] for all mortal sins" (MDh 8.123).
Thus, because it is prescribed that a Śūdra may be made to hear of all sins,
and because [the rule] concerning cowherds and other twice-born castes refers to those such as cowherds and merchants (MDh 8.102).
Because this has been stated,

and because it is impossible for another person to transfer the merit accumulated over many births or to incur the fruit of great sins merely by speaking a falsehood, this [rule] is spoken for the purpose of intimidating the witnesses.
As Nārada said:
"By means of ancient dharma-injunctions, by proclaiming the greatness of truth, and by censuring falsehood, he should thoroughly terrify these [witnesses]. (NSm 1.182)

But when the witnesses, having been summoned, somehow do not speak, what should be done? To this he says: "For if men fail to give testimony, the king shall cause them to pay the debt along with a tenth part as a fine on the forty-sixth day. (YDh 2.76)

He who, having accepted to give testimony and being summoned, somehow fails to speak, shall be compelled by the king to pay the entire debt along with interest to the creditor, as well as the pledge together with a tenth part;
and that tenth part belongs to the king.
Because it has been stated: "The king shall compel the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount recovered" (YDh 2.42),
this [fee] should be understood as being due on the forty-sixth day.
One who speaks before that time shall not be made to pay; and this applies to one who is free from afflictions such as disease,
as Manu has said:

"If a man, being healthy, does not give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights, he shall be liable for that entire debt and a tenth part as a fine in every case" (MDh 8.107).
The term "healthy" (*agada*) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for being free from afflictions caused by the king or by fate. (2.76)
But regarding one who, though knowing the facts, does not accept the role of a witness out of wickedness, [the author] says:
"For that lowest of men who, though knowing [the truth], does not give testimony, is indeed equal to false witnesses in his sin and in his punishment. (YDh 2.77)
Furthermore, that lowest of men who, knowing the matter to be contested in particular, does not give testimony nor accepts it, is equal to false witnesses in terms of his sins and his punishment.
And the author will state the punishment for false witnesses.
After punishing false witnesses, the legal proceeding must be conducted anew;
or, even if it has already been concluded, it must be set aside once the perjury is discovered.
As Manu says:

"In whatever lawsuit false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; what has been done shall be as if undone. (MDh 8.117). To the question of how a decision is reached when there is a conflict among witnesses, he says:
In a case of division, the testimony of the majority is to be accepted; likewise, when there is an equal number, that of those possessing superior qualities.

But when there is a division even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most excellent in virtue is to be adopted. (YDh 2.78) When witnesses are divided—that is, in a state of contradiction—the testimony of the majority is to be accepted.

When those who are equal and of equal number are divided in opinion, the testimony of those possessing superior qualities is authoritative; but when there is disagreement among those possessing superior qualities, then the testimony of those who possess the highest degree of excellence is authoritative.

The testimony of those endowed with qualities such as learning, study, the practice of its meaning, wealth, and sons should be accepted. However, where there are only a few virtuous persons and many others, even in that case, the testimony of the virtuous alone should be accepted;
for "even a single person who knows the Dharma may be a witness if he is acceptable to both parties" (YDh 2.72).
Thus, because the excellence of qualities is primary;
as for what was stated—that there are no witnesses due to difference—that refers to cases where no distinction is perceived by all parties. (2.78)
To address how victory or defeat is determined based on what the witnesses have stated, he says:
"He whose claim the witnesses declare to be true shall be the victor;
for him who speaks otherwise, his defeat is certain. (YDh 2.79)
The proponent whose proposition— characterized by substance, genus, number, and so forth— the witnesses declare to be true, saying, "We know it to be exactly so," is the victor;
whereas for the proponent whose proposition they state otherwise, as being the opposite...
They say that this is false; his defeat is certain and settled.

However, where the witnesses do not establish the existence or non-existence of the matter asserted due to forgetfulness or other causes, there the decision must be reached through other means of proof.
This must be done; and the king should not question the witnesses again and again.
Only the statement as it was spontaneously uttered should be accepted, as it has been said:
"Their testimony, when stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted;
once the witnesses have spoken, they should not be questioned again by the king. (2.79)
He states an exception to the rule: "The defeat of one who speaks otherwise than the truth is certain" (YDh 2.79):
"Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if there are others who are even more virtuous..."

Or, if they should state it otherwise, the former witnesses would be considered fraudulent. (YDh 2.80) When the testimony has been stated by the previously described witnesses in a manner consistent with their own intention and not contrary to the matter asserted in the plaint, if others—being more virtuous than the former or twice as many in number—should give testimony otherwise, i.e., inconsistent with the matter asserted in the plaint; [then the former witnesses are deemed false].

In that case, the witnesses previously [adduced] would be fraudulent and false speakers. But is this not untenable? For when witnesses—who have been examined by the plaintiff, the defendant, the members of the court, and the presiding judge, and who have become authoritative—are declared [to be reliable], there would result the fault of infinite regress in seeking further means of proof.
But when a lawsuit has been decided, even written evidence or witnesses become fruitless if they were not previously presented.

And from the statement of Nārada: "Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless for grain that has already ripened, so too is evidence useless for those whose legal proceedings have been finalized. (NSm Mā 1.53–54).

It is said: when a litigant, considering the testimony of witnesses— even those whose faults have not been revealed— to be unreliable because it does not correspond with the facts of the case they had pledged to prove, and thus suspects a fault even in the witnesses, who then can prevent him from seeking other means of proof?
And it has been said: "That cognition which has a defective instrument and yet lacks the conviction that it is false is itself incorrect.

Just as, even when one does not ascertain a defect in the instruments such as the eyes, one infers a defect in the instrument because the resulting cognition is non-concordant with the object—due to its lack of validity—so too is it here.
And because of the instruction to examine the testimony beyond the examination of the witnesses themselves:
"One should examine the statement spoken by the witnesses together with the members of the court" (KSm 340).
Kātyāyana has also stated:
"When the action is pure according to the rule, then there is the purification of that statement;
and he who is pure from a pure statement is pure regarding the matter—this is the settled principle. (KSm 409).
"Action" refers to the characteristics of witnesses, not to those connected with the subject matter or those who are authoritative (MDh 8.64).
According to this principle, when [the matter] is pure, then the purification of that statement— the purification of the witness's testimony— must be performed;
and the purification of the statement is achieved by establishing the truth of its meaning.
"Speech is purified by truth," according to the traditional legal text (*smṛti*).

Thus, when an object is understood as pure from a pure action and a pure statement, that object is established as being pure and existing exactly as it was perceived; such is the settled rule and the boundary of those who know the principles of logic.
The meaning is that when there is an absence of defects in the cause and of subverting cognitions, the object is indeed non-erroneous.
But [an objection may be raised]: having bypassed the witnesses who have been accepted as authoritative by the litigant himself, how can another means of proof be accepted as authoritative?
This is not a fault; for:
"He who, having abandoned a strong means of proof, relies upon a weak one, shall not regain that means of proof once his defeat has been determined by the court members. (KSm 221)

Thus, because Kātyāyana prohibits the adoption of another means of proof after the determination of victory, he indicates that the adoption of another means of proof occurs prior to the determination of victory. Nārada also states:
"But once the legal proceeding has been decided, the means of proof becomes fruitless" (NSm Mā 1.53).

By saying this, it is established that the prohibition of other means of proof (*pramāṇāntara*) occurs only after the determination of victory, and not even before. Therefore, it remains settled that if one is dissatisfied even when testimony has been given by witnesses, another means of proof must be accepted. This being the case, if there are witnesses previously designated who are more virtuous or twice as numerous as those who have already spoken, but who are currently absent;

When witnesses exist, they alone must be made the authority; for the rule, "Whatever they may say by their very nature is to be accepted as the legal [verdict]" (MDh 8.78), is a supplement to all legal procedures, since once a lawsuit has been adjudicated, further evidence would be fruitless.
And from the statement of Nārada: "Neither a written document nor witnesses [are valid] if they were not previously presented" (NSm Mā 1.53).
Therefore, in the absence of those previously designated, even those not so designated should be accepted as witnesses provided they possess the same qualifications.
It is not divine [evidence], for according to the traditional law (smṛti): "When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof" (KSm 217).

In the absence of these, divine means of proof (*divya*) must be made authoritative. Beyond this, even if the plaintiff is not satisfied, no other means of proof should be sought, as there is no scriptural injunction for it; thus, the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) should be brought to a conclusion.
But where the defendant,

considering the testimony of the witnesses to be unreliable because it contradicts his own conviction, is dissatisfied by attributing faults to the witnesses, then— since there is no opportunity for the defendant to present evidence (*kriyā*)— [the case proceeds] upon the occurrence of divine or royal calamities within a seven-day period.
An examination of the witnesses must be conducted;
and if faults are ascertained therein, the witnesses shall be made to pay the debt that is the subject of the dispute, and they shall also be punished according to the gravity of the offense.
Now, if there is no determination of the defects, then the defendant should be satisfied with that much;
as Manu says:
"Within seven days of the witness having given his testimony, if disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall him, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine. (MDh 8.108).
And this—

"He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor" (YDh 2.79)— this [rule] should be understood as an exception in the case of a defendant who is completely satisfied [with the testimony]. However, some maintain that this statement, "even when the witnesses have spoken their testimony," refers to a situation where, after the witnesses designated by the plaintiff have testified in favor of the plaintiff's case, the defendant...

If one explains that other witnesses—who are more virtuous or twice as numerous—corroborate [the claim] in a manner contrary to what was stated by the first party, then it is said that the witnesses of the first party are false.
That is incorrect, because it is not possible for the defendant (pratyarthin) to perform the legal act [of examination]. For instance:
The plaintiff (*arthin*) is defined as the proponent of the matter to be established;

the defendant (*pratyarthin*) is the proponent of its opposite or its non-existence. Since the establishment of existence depends upon the establishment of the absence of non-existence, whereas the establishment of existence does not depend upon the establishment of non-existence, it is the existence itself [that is primary].
It is logical that [non-existence] is the probandum (*sādhya*),
because non-existence, in its own nature, lacks the status of being an object of knowledge through direct perception and other means;
therefore, it belongs only to one who desires [it].
The action is connected [to the claim].
Moreover, according to the subsequent [rule], the action is prescribed as fixed in every case:
"But when the plaintiff has stated the ground for his legal action, the defendant shall point out the proof."

"But in the case of a false statement, the burden falls on the plaintiff; however, that [burden] does not exist when there is an admission. (BṛSm 1.3.13) Furthermore, there is no legal action against two parties in a single lawsuit;
indeed, in a single dispute, there cannot be legal action against both litigants. (KSm 190)
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.

Therefore, it is untenable that the witnesses of the defendant—being most virtuous or even twice as many—should state otherwise. Now, suppose the following view is held: where both parties are proponents of a positive claim (*bhāvapratijñāvādinau*), each asserting, "This property of mine has been obtained through inheritance."

When two litigants speak without distinguishing between their respective prior and subsequent times, and there are witnesses present for both, in the event of such a dispute, when there is a desire to know whose witnesses are to be accepted among the two sets of witnesses:
"In a matter where two parties are disputing and there are witnesses for both... [and so forth].

Since it is established by the statement, "He for whom there may be a plaintiff, for him there shall be witnesses" (NSm 1.145)—meaning that witnesses are to be accepted for the one who first presents his case—there follows this exception: "Even when the testimony has been given by the witnesses... (NSm 1.146).
Therefore, when the number and qualities of the witnesses for both the plaintiff and the defendant are equal,
the witnesses of the defendant— who are either more virtuous or twice as numerous— should be questioned; and in this way,
there is no deficiency [in the evidence].
The state of being the probandum [applies] to both as well, because both are proponents of existence and because they differ from the four types of responses; thus, in the present example,
there is no establishment of action.

"In a single legal proceeding, just as two actions for a single plaintiff are not contradictory according to the opponent's view, so too there is no contradiction in the two actions of both the proponent and the opponent.
This also the Master does not accept, [saying]: "Even when it has been stated..."

Regarding the phrase "by witnesses in testimony," because of the word "also" (api), the meaning [of the rule] is not understood either from the context or by implication; therefore, enough of this digression. // 2.80 //
False witnesses have been shown; now their punishment is stated:
"The forger and the false witnesses are each to be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, and a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished. (YDh 2.81)
He who makes witnesses false by means of bribery and other such methods is a "false-maker" (kūṭakṛt), and those witnesses who likewise act falsely—
these shall each be punished individually with double the fine that has been prescribed in various places for defeat in a lawsuit.
But a Brāhmaṇa is to be banished from the kingdom; he is to be exiled, not to be punished with a fine.
This should be understood to apply when the specific motive, such as greed, is unknown and there has been no habitual practice [of the offense].
However, when the specific motive such as greed is known...
And regarding repeated offenses, it is stated by Manu: "Out of greed, he should be fined one thousand; out of delusion, the first amercement;
out of fear, the two middle amercements; and out of friendship, four times the first."
"Ten times more [severe] than desire is the former [anger], but three times more than that is the latter [ignorance];
two full hundreds [of years] for ignorance, and exactly one hundred for childishness. (MDh 8.120–21).
In this context, *lobha* means the longing for wealth.
Delusion is erroneous cognition;
fear is terror;
loving-kindness is an excess of affection.
Desire is the longing for sexual union with women;
anger is intolerance;
ignorance is indistinct knowledge; and folly is...
The non-arising of knowledge.
In transactions involving a thousand [coins] and so forth, copper *paṇas* are accepted. Likewise: "A righteous king should punish the three castes who give false testimony."

"Having punished him, he should banish [the offender]; however, he should exile a Brāhmaṇa. (MDh 8.123). And this refers to the case of habitual practice, because of the use of the present participle "kurvāṇān" (those who are doing).
Having punished the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya as previously described, he should banish them or put them to death;
for in the *Arthaśāstra*, the word "banishment" (*pravāsa*) is used in the sense of execution.
And because this work is of the nature of a treatise on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*),

even therein, banishment, the cutting off of the lips, the cutting off of the tongue, and the taking of life should be understood according to the specific subject matter of the false testimony involved.
But having punished the Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him— that is, expel him from his own kingdom—
or alternatively, "vivāsayet" means one who is deprived of his clothing (vāsas), i.e., disrobes him.
The form [vivāsasam] is derived by applying the causative suffix *ṇic* to the root *vas*, and then eliding the final syllable according to the rule *ṇāviṣṭavad bhāva-karmaṇoḥ*;
thus, it means "one should make [her] naked. Alternatively, *vāsaḥ* (clothing) refers to a dwelling, in the sense that one dwells (*vasati*) within it.
"He should banish" means he should cause the house to be demolished.
Even in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, if no specific motive such as greed is known and it is not a habitual offense, the punishment prescribed for each respective case shall indeed apply.
In the case of repetition, however, there shall be a fine according to the nature of the object and banishment. Even therein,

one should observe the legal determination that banishment may take the form of being made naked, the demolition of one's house, or expulsion from the country, depending on factors such as caste, the nature of the substance, and the circumstances of the offense.

When the specific cause— such as greed— is not fully understood, or when there is no habitual practice [of lying], or when the matter at stake is minor, even for a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment shall be monetary alone, just as it is for a Kṣatriya or others. However, if the matter is major, exile from the country is the only penalty.
In this case as well, regarding repeated offenses, that which was stated by Manu should be observed for all [castes].
Nor should it be thought that there is no monetary fine for a Brāhmaṇa;
for in the absence of a monetary fine, there is corporal punishment.

Furthermore, if [the rule] were prohibited even for a very slight offense, it would follow that there would be either the punishment of being made naked, the destruction of the house, branding, banishment, or the absence of any punishment at all,
for members of any of the four castes who fail to perform penance.
And because of the traditional legal authority (smṛti) stating: "One should prescribe a lawful punishment involving both corporal and monetary fines" (MDh 9.236); likewise:
"A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]" (MDh 8.378).
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
As for the statement of Śaṅkha:
"For the three castes, [the punishments] are the seizure of property, corporal punishment, imprisonment, banishment, and branding; but for a Brāhmaṇa, [these do not apply]."

In that context, "seizure of wealth" is intended to mean the seizure of all one's property because it occurs in conjunction with corporal punishment; whereas corporal punishment is proclaimed to range from confinement to the end of life. Likewise, monetary fines range from a *kākiṇī* up to the total forfeiture of one's possessions. (NSm 19.61)
Thus, because execution and the confiscation of all property are recited together;
and as it has also been said:
"He should banish him from the kingdom, with all his wealth intact and unhurt" (MDh 8.380).
Thus, this refers to the case of a first-time offender and is not applicable to all cases;
however, corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa never occurs.
"One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in all manner of sins," because of this general traditional teaching of Manu;
likewise, Manu says:
"No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin; therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind. (MDh 8.381) 2.81.
Moreover, before "api ca," NSP and Pāṇḍeya add:
"He states [this] regarding the refusal of a witness by one who knows [the facts]."

He who, having been made to hear the testimony by others, denies it while shrouded in darkness, shall be compelled to pay an eightfold fine; however, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he should be banished. (YDh 2.82) But he who, having accepted the status of a witness, when being made to hear the testimony along with other witnesses, at the time of his deposition, is shrouded in darkness...
One whose mind is overcome by passion and other such afflictions denies his testimony before witnesses, saying, "I will not be a witness in this matter.
He shall be made to pay eight times the fine that is imposed for defeat in a lawsuit.
However, as for a Brāhmaṇa who is unable to pay a fine consisting of eightfold the value of the property, [he shall be punished otherwise].

He shall banish him. Banishment should be understood as characterized by making [the person] naked, destroying his house, branding him, and expulsion from the territory, according to the circumstances of the case.

For others, however, in the event that the imposition of a fine of eightfold the value of the property is impossible, there shall be the performance of labor appropriate to their caste, fettering with chains, confinement in prison, and so forth.
This should be observed;
and this should also be understood to apply to the preceding verse.
When all [the witnesses] deny the testimony, then...

All [witnesses] are equally at fault; however, when they have given testimony and then speak otherwise, they are to be punished in consideration of the consequences and other factors. As Kātyāyana has said:
"Those who speak otherwise after having testified, being possessed of verbal deception, shall be punished.
Nor should witnesses spoken to by one person be pursued in secret by another.
As Nārada says:
"One should not approach a witness in private at the instigation of another;
nor should one cause dissension by means of someone else. By acting in this way, one surely comes to grief. (NSm 1.147) 2.82.
The failure to testify and the speaking of falsehood by witnesses is prohibited in all cases.
To provide an exception to that, he says:
"For where the execution of those belonging to the [social] orders would otherwise occur, there a witness may speak untruth. (YDh 2.83ab)

Where the death of members of the castes—Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Brāhmaṇas—is likely to occur through the telling of the truth, there a witness should speak untruth; he should not speak the truth.
And by this prohibition of speaking the truth, the previous [obligation] of the witness is set aside.
Untruthful speech and silence are both permitted.

In cases such as when one is accused on suspicion, where the death of a member of the twice-born classes would result from speaking the truth, while no one’s death would result from speaking untruth, there untruthful speech is permitted.

But where, by speaking the truth, the death of one of the plaintiff or the defendant would result, and by speaking an untruth, the death of the other would result, in such a case silence is permitted provided the king consents.
If the king does not release him despite some effort at non-disclosure, then one should become a non-witness by means of creating a rift. If even that is impossible, one must speak the truth alone.
In the case of speaking untruth, there is the fault of killing a member of the twice-born class (*varṇin*).
"And there is the fault of speaking the truth;
however, in the case of speaking the truth, there is indeed the fault of killing a member of the [protected] classes (varṇin).
And in that regard, there is an expiation according to the scriptures."
It must be performed.

Since there is no transgression in speaking untruth or remaining silent because the scriptures permit such things, he says [in response]: "To purify that, the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī" (YDh 2.83cd). That is, for the sake of purification—meaning to avoid the transgression caused by either speaking falsehood or remaining silent—the twice-born should offer a *sārasvata-caru*.
It should be prepared by cooking it bit by bit.
It is called *sārasvata* because Sarasvatī is its deity.
It consists of boiled rice cooked with internal steam that has not been allowed to escape.
The word *caru* is well-known. Here, the intended meaning is as follows:
that which consists of false testimony and silence by witnesses.
That which has been prohibited is here permitted. However, as for the statements:
"One should not speak untruth" (MDh 8.93), and "Whether by not speaking or by speaking falsely, a man becomes guilty of sin" (MDh 8.13).
Thus, lying and non-speaking have been prohibited in general; this penance is for the occasion of transgressing that prohibition.

Nor should it be thought that, even though lying and non-speaking are permitted for witnesses, the injunction of permission is useless because the sin arising from the transgression of the general prohibition against lying and non-speaking remains as it was.

Since the transgression incurred by speaking or not speaking falsely as a witness is greater than that incurred by speaking or not speaking a falsehood in ordinary circumstances, the statement of permission is purposeful;
for although the cessation of the greater transgression necessarily entails the cessation of the incidental, lesser transgression.

Elsewhere, however, because of the statement of permission and the prescription of penance, it is understood that although the majority [of the sin] ceases, even a small incidental transgression does not cease.
This very point is addressed in other inquiries regarding the apprehension of killing a member of the [four] castes (*varṇin*).
It should be understood that for travelers and others, there is permission to speak untruths or to remain silent;
furthermore, no penance is required in such cases, because there is no other prohibition [against it].
From this very statement, it is understood that there is no punishment for witnesses or others even when the true nature of the matter is realized at a later time through other means. // 83 //
Thus ends the section on witnesses;
now begins the section on written documents.
Possession and witnesses have been defined.
Now, documentary evidence is being examined.
In that regard, documentary evidence is of two kinds: royal edicts (śāsana) and local documents (jānapada).
The royal edict has been defined; the local document is now described.
And that is of two kinds: one executed by one's own hand, and [the other]...
And "made by another":
therein, that which is made by one's own hand is without witnesses, while that which is made by another is with witnesses;
and of these two, [the validity] follows the local custom.

Regarding the authority [of documents], as Nārada has said: "A document should be known to be of two kinds: one executed by one's own hand and likewise one executed by another; it may be without witnesses or with witnesses. The validity of these two depends upon their established usage in the region. (NSm 1.115)
Regarding that, he states what is executed by others:
"Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement through their own consent, a document with witnesses should be prepared for it, beginning with the name of the creditor. (YDh 2.84)

When a matter concerning gold or other property between a creditor and a debtor has been settled by mutual agreement— stipulating that "this much shall be paid after such a time, and the interest shall be this much per month"— and if, at a later time, there arises a dispute regarding that matter, a document accompanied by witnesses (meaning one containing witnesses possessing the characteristics previously described) and preceded by the creditor must be prepared for the purpose of determining the true facts of the case. The creditor [is the one who initiates it].
That in which the creditor comes first is "preceded by the creditor";
that is to say, the legal document (kārya) must be executed with the writing of the creditor's name at the beginning.
Or witnesses possessing the characteristics already described should be appointed;
for whatever action has been performed by the doer, it is for the sake of its success that witnesses are engaged in legal disputes, or else a document executed by oneself [serves as proof].
Thus it is from the Smṛti. 2.84.
Moreover:

[A letter] should be marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, one's own lineage (gotra), fellow-students, one's own possessions, and the names of one's father and so forth. (YDh 2.85)
The year is equal [to twelve months];
the month begins with Caitra;
its half is a fortnight, either bright or dark.
The day is the lunar date beginning with the first (pratipad);
the name refers to the creditor and the debtor.
Birth refers to being a Brahmin and so forth;
one's own lineage refers to lineages such as Vasiṣṭha and others. It is marked by these and other such signs.
Likewise, the name of a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin) refers to names derived from the recitation of Vedic branches, such as "Bahvṛca" or "Kaṭha";
the name of one's own father; and the names of the fathers of a creditor or a debtor.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of substance, genus, number, conduct, and so forth. And the connection with what has preceded is that a document marked by these [characteristics] must be prepared. (2.85)
Furthermore:
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall sign it with his own hand, stating:
"This which is written above is my assent as the son of so-and-so. (YDh 2.86)

Regarding a matter settled by mutual agreement between a creditor and a debtor, once that matter has been concluded and recorded, the debtor, having written his own name, should enter upon the document with his own hand: "This which has been written above is the opinion and intention of me, the son of so-and-so," and he should thus inscribe it on the leaf. (2.86)
Likewise, the witnesses, being equal in number, should write with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers, "I, so-and-so, am a witness here. (YDh 2.87)

Those witnesses who are written in that document shall also, after first writing down their own names and those of their fathers, write with their own hands one by one: "In this matter, such-and-such Devadatta is a witness. And they should be equal in number and in quality.
And these [documents] must be executed.
If the debtor or the witness is not literate, then the debtor should have his own statement recorded by another person,
and the witness should have his recorded by another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses.
As Nārada said: "A debtor who is illiterate should record his own opinion, or a witness [should do so] through another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses. (DhKo 357) 2.87.
Moreover, at the end, the scribe should then write: "This has been written by me, the son of so-and-so, requested by both parties; it was written by [name]. (YDh 2.88)
Then, at the end, the scribe, requested by both the creditor and the debtor, shall write: "This document has been written by me, so-and-so Devadatta, son of Viṣṇumitra. (2.88)
Now he states the document executed by oneself:
"But that document which is written in one's own hand is considered valid even without witnesses, except for that which is produced by force or fraud. (YDh 2.89)
A document written in the debtor's own hand is declared by Manu and others to be valid evidence even without witnesses, provided it was not executed through force or fraud—
that is, excluding what is done by force (*bala*), which means compulsion, or fraud (*upadhi*), characterized by deception, greed, anger, fear, intoxication, and so forth.
Nārada also said: "A document executed under intoxication, by one who is accused, by a woman, a child, or through force, as well as one executed through fear or fraud, is invalid. (NSm 1.117)

Furthermore, this document— whether executed by one's own hand or by another's hand— should be written, in accordance with local custom, for transactions involving a pledge as well as those not involving a pledge, so as to be consistent with the sequence of the matter and free from errors in spelling or characters; it need not, however, consist exclusively of grammatically correct words.

It should also be written in the local dialect of the specific region. As Nārada said: "That which is not contrary to local custom, and which possesses the clear characteristics of the rules for [specifying] the property and so forth..."
"That document is considered authoritative when its sequence and letters are not omitted" (NSm 1.116).
*Vidhāna* means a rule (*vidhi*);
the rule regarding a pledge (*ādhi*) is *ādhividhi*, which is the act of pledging (*ādhīkaraṇa*).
Its definition is "the pledge for deposit, the pledge for use, the time-limit," and so forth;

that in which this is clear and distinct is "that whose characteristics and rules for pledges are manifest" (*vyaktādhividhilakṣaṇa*). It is "one in which the sequence and syllables are not lost" (*aviluptakramākṣara*), [referring] to the syllables...

"Krama" refers to the sequence and "akṣaras" to the syllables; "kramākṣaras" are the syllables in their unbroken sequence. That document in which the syllables and their sequence are thus unimpaired is "aviluptakramākṣara.
Such a document is authoritative.
The intention is that, unlike a royal edict, there is no requirement here for the use of grammatically correct words (sādhuśabda). (2.89)
In connection with the subject of written documents, he states that even a debt recorded in writing must be paid by only three persons:
"A debt contracted by means of a document must be paid by only three persons" (YDh 2.90ab).
Just as a debt created by witnesses and so forth must be paid by only three, so too a debt contracted by means of a document must be paid by the debtor, his son, and his grandson.
It is thus restricted that the debt must be paid by exactly three [generations] and not by a fourth or subsequent ones.

But is it not already established that "the debt is to be paid by sons and grandsons," since, without distinction regarding the mere fact of being a debt, it is necessarily restricted to three? Certainly; this is indeed so, but [this statement is made] in order to dispel any suspicion of an exception arising from another Smṛti text concerning debts recorded in a document (*patrārūḍha-ṛṇa*), which might contradict this general rule (*utsarga*).
This statement was undertaken;
for after defining the characteristics of a document (*patra*), Kātyāyana declared:
"In this manner, when the time has elapsed, the debt is made payable to the ancestors. (DhKo 709)
In this manner, a debt recorded on a document, even if the time for repayment has elapsed, is to be made payable by those related to the ancestors.

Here, because of the use of the plural "of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*) and the statement "the time has elapsed," it is understood that a fourth-generation descendant or later is the one to be made to pay.
Likewise, Hārīta also states:
"One should declare the gain to belong to him in whose hand the document (patra) may be.
In this case as well, [the rule applies] to him in whose hand the document...
Since the rule *asti tasyārṇalābhe* is stated in general terms, it would follow that the recovery of a debt exists even in the case of [debts] from the fourth [day] onwards;
therefore, it is said that this statement is intended to remove such a doubt.
And these two statements are to be applied in accordance with the words of the Lord of Yogins.
He states an exception to this:
"But a pledge (ādhi) is enjoyed as long as it is not returned" (YDh 2.90cd).

Since there is a rule that even in the case of a surety, the debt recorded in the document must be paid by those three alone, and since [the surety] lacks the authority to discharge the debt, he may take possession of the pledge.
Even regarding the case where no specific entitlement has been established, this is stated:

by saying that "the pledge is enjoyed only as long as the debt is not paid by the fourth or fifth [generation]," it is shown that the fourth generation and those following also possess the right [to enjoy the pledge] upon the repayment of the secured debt.
But has it not already been stated that "one who enjoys the fruit does not perish" (YDh 2.58)?
True; even that [statement], in the absence of this specific restrictive rule, would apply only to the case of three generations. Thus, everything is faultless. 2.90.
Having concluded the incidental matter, he follows the subject at hand:
"If the document is located in another country, difficult to read, lost, rubbed out, stolen, broken, burnt, or torn, one should have another document executed. (YDh 2.91)
It is ordained that one should execute another document when the existing document is unfit for legal proceedings.

And the unfitness for legal proceedings arises when the document is located in an extremely remote foreign land, or when its written characters, letters, or words are poorly inscribed, defective, ambiguous, or unintelligible.
When that illegible writing— in which it was written— has been lost through the power of time,
or has been wiped away due to the fading of the ink and so forth.
when the written characters have been rubbed away,
when they have been stolen by thieves and the like, or when they have been broken or split apart;
When it is burnt— that is, set ablaze— or when it is cut— that is, split in two— the leaf becomes double.
And this applies when there is mutual consent between the plaintiff and the defendant;

however, when a dispute has reached the stage of formal litigation and the document is located in another country, time must be granted in consideration of the distance for the purpose of bringing the document,
especially if it is situated in a remote region.
Or, if the document is lost, the determination of the legal dispute must be made by witnesses alone.
As Nārada says:
"When a document has been deposited in another country, or is decayed, poorly written, or stolen..."
"The setting of a time-limit for what exists, and the examination by witnesses for what does not exist" (NSm 1.122).
For a document that exists but is located in another place, a time-limit—a deadline—must be granted for its production.
However, for that which does not exist, the examination by those who were previously witnesses—that is, the conclusion of the legal proceeding—is required.

The legal proceeding must be carried out; however, when witnesses are not available, a decision must be made by means of divine proof, for the traditional law states: "In a legal dispute where there is neither documentary evidence nor witnesses, one should prescribe divine proof" (KSm 224).
And this is a local legal document;
even a royal legal document is of exactly the same kind.
However, there is this much distinction:
"A royal document is defined as one bearing the king's own hand, marked with his own seal, and containing witnesses for all matters. (KSm 258).
Furthermore, another type of royal document, the *jayapatra* (certificate of victory), has been described by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:

A document of victory (jayapatra) is held to be that which is joined with the matter to be proven as it was presented, which includes the subsequent action, and which contains a definitive conclusion.

"Once the matter is settled, one should give the *jayapatra* (document of victory) to the victorious litigant, marked with the hand of the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and sealed with the royal seal. Likewise, the members of the court (*sabhāsada*) should also provide their signatures by hand, stating: "This is my opinion," [followed by] the name of their father.

"And those members of the assembly who are present there, being experts in the treatises on law (*smṛti-śāstra*), should likewise provide their own signatures according to the rules for documentation," because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).
Furthermore, a legal proceeding does not become free from blemish without the mutual consent of the members of the assembly. As Nārada says:
"Where all the people in the assembly consider, 'This is right'..."
"That lawsuit shall be free from thorns; otherwise, it would be thorny.
(NSm Mā 3.16) This [definition] applies only to a lawsuit consisting of four parts:
"That which establishes the matter to be proven and is endowed with four parts..."
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "A document of victory is required to be accompanied by the royal seal" (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.6.28).
However, where there is a deficiency, as for example:

"One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance [of the legal act], one who does not appear, one who is without an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these five are recorded as defeated" (NSm Mā 2.33).
In that case, there is no document of victory (*jayapatra*), but rather only a document of defeat (*hīnapatra*).

And the distinction is that such a document serves the purpose of obtaining a penalty after a lapse of time, whereas a *jayapatra* (document of victory) serves the purpose of establishing the validity of a prior legal proceeding. 2.91.
He states the grounds for determination when there is doubt regarding a document:

"The purification of a doubtful document may be established by means of a writing in one's own hand and so forth, as well as by logic, acquisition, performance, marks, connection, and the cause of title. (YDh 2.92)
The authentication of a document that is suspected of being either genuine or forged shall be established by means such as a writing in one's own hand;
that is, by another document written in one's own hand,
provided that the characters are identical.

The meaning is that, in that case, there would be purity; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that purity results from corroboration with witnesses, a written document, one's own handwriting, or other internal consistencies.
Attainment through reasoning is *yuktiprāpti*. Attainment is the connection between place, time, and person with a substance;
it is *yuktiprāpti* when it is established that "in this place, at this time, this substance belongs to this person."
Action is the presentation of evidence for that;
a mark is a unique sign such as the syllable *śrī*;
and connection is the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant.
Previously, too, there was a relationship involving giving, receiving, and so forth, based on mutual trust;
"acquisition" (āgama) refers to the possible means for obtaining such a quantity of wealth.
These indeed are the grounds;
the logical connection is that by these grounds, the purification of a disputed document may occur.

But when, due to doubt regarding a document, a decision cannot be reached, then a decision must be made by means of witnesses. As Kātyāyana says: "When the document has been challenged, the plaintiff shall point out those who were present at its execution. (KSm 283)
This statement refers to a case where witnesses are available;
however, the statement of Hārīta refers to a case where witnesses are unavailable: "I did not write this document; it was forged by him."
"Having set aside that document, the decision shall then be made by means of divine proof. (DhKo 374) 2.92.
When the document has been thus cleared and the debt is due for payment,
if one is unable to pay the entire debt,
what should be done? To this, he says:
Having paid the debt, the debtor should write on the back of the document;

or the creditor, upon the debtor's arrival, should provide a receipt marked with his own hand. When the debtor is unable to pay the entire debt, he should then, having paid as much as he is capable of, [execute a new agreement] regarding what was previously written.

On the back of the document, one should write: "This much has been given by me. Or, the creditor, having received the money that was due, should give it and write upon the back of that very document: "This much has been received by me."
How?
It is marked with one's own hand, meaning it is characterized by letters written by one's own hand; or else, it is "accepted" (upagata).
The creditor shall give a deed of entry, marked with his own handwritten signature, to the debtor. (2.93)
Regarding the question of what should be done with the document once the entire debt has been paid, he says:
"Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or for the sake of purification, one should cause another [document] to be made. (YDh 2.94ab)
Having paid the entire debt either gradually or all at once, he should have the previously executed document torn up. However,

when the document is located in a difficult place or has been lost, then the debtor, for the sake of purification— that is, to terminate his status as a debtor— should have another document executed by the creditor.
The meaning is that, according to the sequence previously stated, the creditor shall give a document of discharge to the debtor.
When the entire debt is to be paid in the presence of witnesses, what should be done? To this he says:
"Or whatever [debt] may be accompanied by witnesses, that must be paid in the presence of witnesses" (YDh 2.94cd).
But that debt which was contracted in the presence of witnesses should be paid in the very same presence of those original witnesses. (2.94)
Thus ends the section on written documents; now begins the section on ordeals.
It has been stated that human evidence is of three kinds, characterized by written documents, witnesses, and possession.

Now, intending to describe the divine means of proof (*divya-pramāṇa*) as it has reached its proper occasion, he sets forth the summary of the divine ordeals (*divyamātṛkā*) with the first five verses beginning with "The balance, fire, water... and so on.
Among those, first, the divine ordeals...
He teaches:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred bowl are the ordeals here for the sake of purification" (YDh 2.95ab).

These five ordeals, beginning with the balance and ending with the sacred bowl, are prescribed here in the treatise on Dharma for the sake of purification—that is, for the removal of doubt regarding a contested matter.
"These should be given."
But surely there are other divine ordeals elsewhere as well:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, the [Kōśa] ordeal, rice grains, and likewise the seventh, the heated gold coin—these are the divine ordeals" (DhKo 462; cf. BṛSm 1.8.3).
Thus, because of the recollection of Pitāmaha, one might ask: "How is it that there are only these many? To this he says:
"These [ordeals] apply in cases of great accusation" (YDh 2.95c).
It is restricted that these [ordeals] apply only to major charges and not to others; however, it is not restricted that these alone are the divine ordeals.
Furthermore, he will state the limit of what constitutes "majority."

But is it not the case that the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) is also desired in a minor charge, according to the traditional law (smṛti): "One should cause the libation to be administered even in a minor [charge]"?

True; however, the inclusion of the *kośa* among the ordeals such as the balance (*tulā*) is not intended as a restrictive rule meaning it applies only to major charges, but rather to a charge made with firm confidence.
The word "also" (api) has the sense of inclusion.
Otherwise, it would apply only to charges based on suspicion;
for those accused on the basis of physical evidence, one should prescribe the ordeal by the balance and so forth.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Rice grains and a sheath [are used] specifically in cases of suspicion; of this there is no doubt. (PiSm 36; DhKo 462).
Regarding the fact that these [ordeals] apply without distinction in cases of great charges, suspected offenses, and those involving defiance, he states an exception:
"When the accuser has placed his head [as a stake]. (YDh 2.95d).
These ordeals, such as the balance and others, belong to the accused when the accuser has placed his head [in jeopardy].

The *śīrṣaka* is the fourth stage of the judicial proceeding, characterized by victory and defeat; by this, punishment is indicated. One who stands upon that is "standing on the head" (*śīrṣakastha*), meaning one who is subject to the punishment incurred thereby. (2.95)

Then, by the rule "therefore, the plaintiff shall immediately have written the proof of the matter asserted" (YDh 2.7), it is shown that this procedure applies specifically to one who asserts a positive claim (*bhāvapratijñāvādin*).
He states an exception to that:
"Or, by mutual consent, one may undergo the ordeal while the other accepts the head [fine].
(YDh 2.96ab) By mutual agreement between the accuser and the accused, either the accused or the accuser may undergo the ordeal;
the other—whether the accused or the accuser—shall accept the "head," meaning either corporal punishment or a monetary fine.
This is the intended meaning:
divine valid cognition is not like human valid cognition, which has only existent things as its object; rather, it takes as its object both existents and non-existents without distinction.

And therefore, in the case of a false plea, a plea of denial (*pratyavaskandana*), or a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), an ordeal may be administered at the wish of either the plaintiff or the defendant.

It has been stated that the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) applies without distinction to both minor charges and major charges, as well as to those involving suspicion (*śaṅkā*) and those involving defiance (*sāvaṣṭambha*); whereas a restriction has been shown that the ordeals beginning with the balance (*tulā*) and ending with poison (*viṣa*) apply only to major charges and only when there is defiance.
Among these, regarding charges involving defiance:
He states an exception to this [rule]:
"One may proceed even without the head-piece in cases of treason against the king or in the event of a mortal sin (pātaka). (YDh 2.96cd).

In the case of suspicion of treason against the king or suspicion of a mortal sin such as the killing of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā), one may employ the balance and other ordeals even without the head-piece.
And one should administer it in cases of suspicion of a great theft; as it is said:
"For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits, and for those intent on proving their own purity, the ordeal should be given, excluding the [ordeal of] the head."
Thus [says Nārada].
Furthermore, rice is used specifically when there is suspicion of a minor theft;
however, the settled rule is that rice is to be administered as the ordeal only in cases of theft, and not otherwise. (PiSm 163; DhKo 463)
Thus, according to the statement of Pitāmaha:
"The ordeal of the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*), however, is for suspicion of great theft alone;
the *taptamāṣa* is prescribed for those accused under suspicion of theft. (DhKo 463: Pitāmaha)
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Furthermore, other oaths concern matters of minor importance:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, and gold."
He should touch the heads of his sons, his wives, and likewise his friends, as well as the offerings made to the gods and ancestors and the fruits of his meritorious deeds;
or, in all legal disputes, he may undergo the ordeal of drinking from the *kośa* vessel.
"Thus these oaths have been declared by Manu for minor matters," according to the traditional teaching of Nārada.
Although oaths are also designated as *divya* (ordeals) by popular convention— since that which determines what cannot be determined by human means of knowledge is called *divya*—

nevertheless, because they serve as the cause for a determination at a later time, they are designated as distinct from the *divya* ordeals such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) and others, which cause an immediate determination; this is similar to the expression "the Brahmin and the wandering mendicant" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*).

Although the *kośa* is indeed a form of oath, its inclusion among the *dhaṭa* and other ordeals is due to its similarity to the *dhaṭa* and others in that it pertains to cases of great accusation (*mahābhiyoga*) and cases of accusation based on firm conviction (*avaṣṭambhābhiyoga*), and not because it serves as the immediate cause for a judicial decision.

Although the *taṇḍula* (rice) and *taptamāṣa* (heated gold) tests are also causes for immediate determination, they are not included among those [oaths] because they differ from the *dhaṭa* (balance) and others in having a limited scope and being subject to doubt; one should be content with this. Furthermore, these ordeals (*divya*) and oaths (*śapatha*) are to be employed in disputes such as those concerning debts as far as possible. As for that...
As for the statement of Pitāmaha:
"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals" (PiSm 39;
DhKo 232), that too should be interpreted to mean that one should avoid ordeals when documents, neighbors, and other such evidence are available.
But surely, even in other types of disputes where other means of proof (*pramāṇa*) are possible, there would be no occasion for divine ordeals (*divya*).

True. However, in disputes concerning debts and the like, even when the plaintiff has presented witnesses possessing the characteristics previously described, if the defendant, relying on the support of accepting punishment, resorts to a divine ordeal, then a divine ordeal may indeed take place.

Because witnesses may be subject to defects of intention, whereas divine ordeal (*divya*) is free from such defects and pertains to the actual reality of the matter— since *dharma* is characterized by that very reality—
as Nārada has said:

"In that case, the law rests upon truth, while legal procedure rests upon witnesses; when a matter is to be proven by divine means, one should not employ human evidence such as a document. (NSm Mā 1.11).
And in disputes concerning immovable property, even if the defendant, out of obstinacy, resorts to an ordeal, [the court] should proceed provided there exists visible evidence such as neighbors.

The statement of Pitāmaha, "In disputes concerning immovable property, divine ordeals are not to be accepted," is intended to exclude specific types of ordeals as conceptual constructs; it is not for the purpose of absolutely excluding all divine ordeals.
Otherwise, in the absence of written documents, neighbors, and other evidence, there would be the undesirable consequence of no decision being reached in disputes over immovable property. (2.96)
Furthermore: Before *kiṃ ca*, NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: "The general procedure for divine [ordeals]:
having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on..."

One should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king, the court members, and the Brāhmaṇas. On the day prior [to the trial], having fasted, when the sun has risen, the judge shall summon the person undergoing the ordeal who has bathed with his clothes on, and cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king, the court members, and the Brāhmaṇas.

"Divine [substances] should always be given to one who has fasted for three nights or for one night, provided he is pure and wears wet clothes. (PiSm 53; DhKo 468). This alternative regarding the fast mentioned by Pitāmaha should be understood as being regulated according to the relative strength or weakness of the person and the magnitude or smallness of the task at hand.
The observance of fasting applies to both the litigant and the judge;
in matters concerning ordeals, the judge shall conduct all the proceedings.
For, according to the statement of Pitāmaha: "Just as the Adhvaryu priest at sacrifices, he [the king] shall remain fasting by the king's command. (Viṣṇusmṛti 54; Dharmakośa 465).

In this regard, although it is stated without qualification that "at sunrise," nevertheless, according to the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), divine ordeals should be administered on Sundays. Furthermore,
the fire-ordeal should take place in the forenoon, and the balance-ordeal (*dhaṭa*) should likewise be in the forenoon.
At midday, however, water should be offered by one who desires to understand the true nature of Dharma.

"The purification by the [balance] vessel is prescribed for the forenoon of the day, but during the final watch of the night, cool poison should be administered"—this specific rule stated by Pitāmaha is to be observed. (PiSm 45–46; DhKo 465)
For those ordeals whose specific times are not mentioned, such as the *taṇḍula* (rice) and *taptamāṣa* (heated bean), they should be administered only in the forenoon;
indeed, the administration of all divine ordeals is proclaimed to be in the forenoon. (NSm 20.12*)

Thus, according to the general recollection of Nārada, the day is divided into three parts: the first part is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), the middle is midday (*madhyāhna*), and the latter is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Furthermore, another specific time has been shown by way of both injunction and prohibition.
First, regarding the positive method (*vidhimukha*):
it is proclaimed that for fire, the two seasons of late winter and early spring (*śiśira-hemanta*) as well as the rainy season (*varṣā*) are favorable;
water is [favorable] during autumn and summer (*śarad-grīṣma*), while poison is [favorable] in late winter and early spring.
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these months are common to all and are not incompatible with the gods.
The treasury, however, must always be given; the balance scale may be used at all times.
Thus [it is said].

The mention of the "taking of the ordeal" (*kośagrahaṇa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all oaths (*śapatha*). Furthermore, because no specific distinction is stated regarding the *taṇḍula* ordeal, it is applicable at all times.
There is also a prohibitive rule:
there should be no purification of water during the cold season, nor the purification by fire during the hot season;
one should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor likewise use a scale in a strong wind.
"Neither in the afternoon, nor at twilight, nor ever at midday.

(NSm, C 320) Regarding the statement "there shall be no purification by water in the cold," the word "cold" includes the winter (*hemanta*), the dewy season (*śiśira*), and the rainy season (*varṣā*).

Regarding the statement "there is no purification by fire in the hot season," the word "hot season" refers to the summer (*grīṣma*) and the autumn (*śarad*). Although [the prohibition] was already established by the rule, its restatement here is for the sake of emphasis.
But the purpose will be explained [later]. (2.97)
He states the rule regarding those authorized [to undergo the ordeals]:
"For women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick, [the ordeal shall be] fire or water; for a Śūdra, it shall be seven barley grains or poison. (YDh 2.98)
A "woman" refers to any woman whatsoever, regardless of distinctions of caste or stage of life; a "child" refers to one up to sixteen years of age, regardless of distinctions of caste;
and an "elder" refers to one from eighty years of age onwards.
A blind man is one deficient in sight;
a lame man is one deficient in feet;
a brahmin is one defined by birth alone.
The sick person is one afflicted by disease.
For the purpose of purifying these [guilty persons], it is ordained that there shall be only the balance;
[as well as] fire, the ploughshare, and the heated gold coin.
And for the Kṣatriya [the water is the same];
for the Vaiśya, it is water alone.
The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of restriction.
Seven *yava* grains of poison, of the previously mentioned measurement, are for the purification of a *śūdra*.
Since the scale (*tulā*) is prescribed for a *brāhmaṇa* and seven *yava* grains of poison are prescribed for a *śūdra*, it follows that fire or water is intended for the *kṣatriya* and the *vaiśya*.
This very point has been clarified by the Grandfather (Brahmā): "The balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, and fire to a Kṣatriya."
"Water is prescribed for the Vaiśya, and one should administer poison to the Śūdra.
As for the traditional rule regarding the absence of ordeals for women and others—
"For those observing vows, those who are severely afflicted, the sick, and ascetics..."— [it refers to specific circumstances].
And [it is said]: "If dharma is what is intended, the ordeal shall not take place for women" (PiSm 44).
This is for the purpose of precluding the option [allowed by the rule] that "either party may perform [the ordeal] according to their preference" (YDh 2.96).
This is what is meant:
in cases of assault and charges involving women and the like, when they are the accusers,
the ordeal must be administered to those who are the accused alone.
Even though these [categories of persons] are subject to being sued, the ordeal belongs only to the plaintiffs;
however, when there is a mutual accusation, there is indeed an option between them.
In that case as well, it is restricted by the statement of Kātyāyana that "the balance alone [is used]";

likewise, in cases of accusation involving suspicion of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like, the balance alone is for women and others. And this statement applies when all ordeals are available to women and others during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Caitra, and Vaiśākha, which are common to all ordeals.
It is purposeful by virtue of its restrictive function;
yet, it is not the case that for women the ordeal is always the balance alone, for it is said:
"Poison has not been prescribed for women, nor has water been ordained for them."
"One should examine their internal truth by means of the *dhaṭa*, the *kośa*, and so forth" (NSm 20.48*).
Since purification is thus prescribed by means of the *dhaṭa*, the *kośa*, fire, and others— excluding poison and water—
it should be applied in the same way for children and others as well.

Likewise, for Brahmins and others as well, there is no rule regarding the balance scale and so forth that applies at all times; rather, the purification by means of the *kośa* (ordeal by sacred libation) is prescribed for all castes. All these [ordeals] apply to everyone, except for the Brahmin, for whom the ordeal by poison is excluded. (PiSm 41)
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Pitāmaha,
this statement is intended solely as a restrictive rule for the balance and other ordeals when many such ordeals are available together during the common period;
however, at other times, all [ordeals] are prescribed according to their respective specific periods.
For thus, during the rainy season, the fire alone is for all;
but during the winter and the cool season, there is an option between the two fires for the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya.
For a Brāhmaṇa, however, fire alone is [the means of death] and never poison, because of the prohibition: "There is no poison for a Brāhmaṇa except [fire].
But during the summer and autumn, water alone [is the means].
However, for those with specific diseases, there is a prohibition against fire and other such means:
"One should avoid fire for those suffering from leprosy, water for those afflicted by asthma and coughing,
and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with an excess of bile and phlegm" (NSm B 5.118).
Thus, for them, even at the time of the fire-ordeal and others, the ordeal by the balance and so forth is common. Likewise, from the statement:

"Water, fire, and poison should be administered to men who are strong" (Pitāmaha, DhKo 464), because of the prohibition [of these] in every way for the weak, [the ordeals] based on caste, age, and condition are applied without transgressing the specific time prescribed by rule.
Divine gifts are to be given. // 2.98 //
It has been stated that "these [ordeals] are for great charges" (YDh 2.95).
Now, he explains what constitutes the greatness of a charge in that context:
"One should not employ the ploughshare ordeal, nor poison, nor the balance, for a claim of less than one thousand [paṇas]. (YDh 2.99ab)
One should not employ the ploughshare ordeal, the poison ordeal, or the balance ordeal for a value less than five thousand paṇas;
this applies even to water when it is used as an intermediate measure. As it has been said:
"One should cause ordeals beginning with the balance and ending with poison to be administered in cases involving significant matters. (DhKo 471)
In this context, the "balance" (kośa) is not included because it is remembered [in the legal codes] that one may cause the balance to be administered even in a minor case;
the meaning is that these four ordeals occur only for amounts exceeding one thousand paṇas, and not below that.
But is it not the case that even for lesser amounts, fire and the other ordeals were shown by Pitāmaha:
"One should administer the balance for a thousand [paṇas], likewise iron for half a thousand;
for half of that, water; and for half of that, poison is prescribed"? (Viśvarūpa on PiSm 47)
True; in this regard, the established rule is as follows:
the statement of Pitāmaha refers to the case of stealing property for which loss of caste (pātitya) occurs, whereas the statement of Yogīśvara refers to the case of other types of property.
And these two statements concern the subjects of theft and violence;
however, a specific distinction regarding denial has been shown by Kātyāyana:
Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should determine the proof;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value.
Having ascertained the measure of all the substances, one should fashion the gold;
once it is endowed with the correct measure of gold, one should then employ that divine [image].
Having ascertained the number of gold pieces, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
indeed, for the loss of eighty, one should offer oneself to the fire.
If [the debt] is lost at sixty, water should be administered; if at forty, indeed the balance;
but for loss at twenty or ten, the drinking of the oath (kośapāna) is prescribed.

Or, upon the loss of more than five [measures], one should touch the heads of one's sons and others after the rice has been reduced by half and then by half again; for indeed, when half of that half is lost, one should touch their heads.
"For when [the value] is reduced by half and half again, worldly transactions are prescribed; reflecting thus, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha. (KSm 416–21).
Regarding the phrase "having ascertained the number of *suvarṇas*," the word *suvarṇa* here refers to sixteen *māṣas*, according to Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.363: "Sixteen *māṣas* are a *suvarṇa*."
Thus, the aforementioned statement is the authoritative word;
and here, the word "nāśa" (destruction) signifies denial.
However, in the case of the rule "one shall not take a plowshare for less than a thousand," it should be understood as one thousand copper *paṇas*.
Now, since these ordeals are prescribed for the great sin of treason against the king, why does he say here that "one should not take up the ploughshare until [the fine] reaches a thousand"?
To this, he replies:

In matters concerning the king, in cases of false accusation, and in cases of treason against the king or charges involving mortal sins (mahāpātaka), they should always administer these ordeals while remaining pure, regardless of the amount of wealth at stake; being pure,
they should perform them after undertaking fasts and other such purificatory rites.
Likewise, a specific location has been stated by Nārada:
"It should be placed—immovable and worthy of worship with incense, garlands, and ointments—in an assembly hall, at the gate of the royal palace, in a temple, or at a crossroads. (NSm 20.12*)
The *dhaṭa* ordeal is to be administered;
and the rule has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"In the place of Indra, for men who are accused or who are great sinners (*mahāpātakin*)."
One should employ those engaged in treason against the king at the royal gate.
For those born of inverse unions (*prātilomya*), the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for others, the wise know that the ordeal should be administered in the midst of the assembly hall.
For those who are untouchable, low-caste slaves, barbarians (*mleccha*), and evildoers—
"For those born of inverse unions, there is no certainty regarding the king; in cases of doubt concerning them, one should prescribe the well-known divine ordeals. (KSm 433) 2.99.
Thus ends the Divyamātṛkā.
