Having thus described the divine *mātṛkā* (the alphabet) which is useful for all divine ordeals, he now states the procedure for the ordeals beginning with the balance (*dhata*): "Accompanied by experts in the weighing of balances, the accused, having mounted the balance and been made equal to the counterweight, is lowered after a mark has been made. (YDh 2.100)
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward.
If he is pure, he should consecrate the balance with the mantra: "Lead me upward on the scale.

Those who know how to hold and weigh the balance, such as goldsmiths and others, having made him equalized—that is, balanced—by means of a counterweight such as clay or other materials, the person undergoing the ordeal, whether the defendant or the plaintiff, having ascended and mounted the balance, [should mark] the line...

Having arranged it in such a position that, during the state of balancing the counterweight, it remains on the surface of the sand-tray, one should mark it with a pale chalk-line, remove it from the scale, and consecrate the scale while making this request with the following mantra:
"O Scale, you are the seat of truth."
In the past, at the beginning of creation, it was fashioned and produced by the gods, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore,
O auspicious and beautiful one, tell me the true nature of this doubtful matter, show it to me, and release me from this uncertainty.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil and a speaker of untruth, then lead me downward;
but if I am pure and a speaker of truth, then lead me upward."
The mantra for the consecration of the scale belongs to the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka) as stated in another Smṛti;
however, this one [is for] the person undergoing the ordeal.
Furthermore, the signs of victory and defeat are understood precisely from the indicative marks (liṅga) within the mantra itself.
It has not been mentioned separately;
furthermore, the fashioning of the sacrificial post (*dhaṭa*) is established by the very purpose of the mounting and so forth, as clarified by Pitāmaha, Nārada, and others. For example:
"Having cut down a tree fit for sacrifice, like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), preceded by mantras..."
Having paid homage to the guardians of the world, the wise should prepare the scale.
A gentle mantra dedicated to the Vanaspati must be recited when cutting [the wood];
furthermore, the balance-beam should be made square, sturdy, and likewise straight.
And rings should be provided at three places for practicality.
The scale-beam should be four cubits long, and the two supports above it should be equal to that.
The distance between those two [supports] should be exactly one and a half cubits.
Two cubits, however, should be dug for both feet as well.
And likewise, the two side-arches (toraṇas) should be made at both sides;
they should always be ten finger-breadths higher than the balance-beam (dhaṭa).
And two downward-facing supports should be made from clay,
attached by strings to the two arches, reaching as far as the top of the balance-beam.
The balance-beam should likewise be made motionless, facing east, in a clean place;
having then suspended two scales on both sides.
One should arrange darbha grass facing east on both sides of the two scales;
one should weigh the performers on the western scale and auspicious earth on the other.
One should fill that cavity with bricks, stones, earth, and sand;
here, there is an option among clay, bricks, stones, and sand. Expert examiners who are skilled in the measurement of weights must be appointed.
Merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers must always have the balance-beam of the scale made equal by expert examiners.
And water should be poured upon the balance by the wise;
that balance upon which the water does not float is to be known as even.
Having first weighed the man and then having lowered him,
one should always cause the balance-beam to be made, adorned with banners and flags.
Then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deities according to this rite,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Then the judge, facing eastward with palms joined in reverence, should say:
"Come, come, O Blessed Dharma; enter into this ordeal."
Having invoked Dharma into the balance along with the world-protectors, the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts, one should subsequently assign the limbs [of the deity].
Having first established Indra in the east, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south; Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north.
One should place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.
Kubera is golden-hued, and Agni is also golden-hued;
likewise, Nirṛti is dark-blue, and Vāyu is praised as smoke-colored.
Īśāna, however, should be red; thus the wise one should meditate upon these in sequence.
On the right side of Indra, the wise one should worship the Vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna, one should likewise place the group of Ādityas:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who, though born last, is not the least.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names;
they know that the abode of the Rudras is in the western part of Agni.
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Giriśa of great renown, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita;
Bhavanādhiśvara, Kapālī, Viśāmpati,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhava— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should arrange the station of the Mothers in the midst of the lords of the pretas and the rākṣasas:
namely Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā together with her attendants;
they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti.
To the north of Varuṇa’s region, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located;
[the names of the wind-gods are] Pavana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīva, and the eight Maruts are proclaimed [as the deities];
moreover, the wise man should invoke Durgā on the northern side of the balance.

The wise know that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names, ending with ornaments and garments; and having offered [these] to Dharma, one should then present the *arghya* and other offerings in due order.
"One should prepare the secondary rites beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the ornaments;
one should perform the service beginning with perfumes (*gandha*) and ending with the food offering (*naivedya*).
(PiSm 57–74). And here, having fashioned a scale adorned with banners and flags, one should invoke Dharma upon it with the mantra "Come, come" (*ehy ehi*).

Having offered [the items] beginning with the *arghya*— using the formula "I offer *arghya* to Dharma, obeisance" (*dharmāyārghyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*) and so forth— and continuing through the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, *madhuparka*, *ācamanīya*, *snāna*, *vastra*, *yajñopavīta*, *ācamanīya*, up to the ornaments such as the crown and bracelets, one should then offer the *arghya* and other items up to the ornaments to Indra and the others ending with Durgā, using their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), in the dative case, and ending with "obeisance" (*namaḥ*),

according to the sequence of individual substances (*padārthānusamaya*). Then, having offered scents, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth to Dharma, [one offers them] to Indra and the others.
One should offer perfumes and the other articles as previously described; furthermore, in the worship of the balance, the flowers and perfumes should be red. As Nārada has said:
"One should first worship the balance with red perfumes, garlands, curd, cakes, unbroken grains, and so forth; thereafter, one should worship the remaining [deities].
Since no specific [offerings] are mentioned for Indra and the others, the sequence of worship is that they are to be worshipped with whatever is available, whether red or otherwise.
And all this the judge (prāḍvivāka) shall perform, as has been stated:
"Then the judge shall be a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, tranquil in mind, and free from envy."
True to his promise, pure, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings,
he has fasted, is dressed in clean garments, and has performed the cleansing of his teeth.
And one should perform the worship of all the deities according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, an oblation (*homa*) should be performed by four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the four directions using the common fire (*laukikāgni*). As it is said:
"In the same way, the oblation should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas."
With clarified butter, sacrificial oblation, and fuel-sticks as the means for the fire-oblation.
One should perform the oblation with the *sāvitrī* and the *praṇava*, ending with *svāhā*.

(PiSm 75–76) The meaning is that one should recite the *gāyatrī* preceded by the *praṇava*, and then again recite the *praṇava* ending with the utterance of *svāhā*, and offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) one hundred and eight times for each.

Having thus performed the worship of the deity ending with the oblation, one should immediately write down the matter at hand together with the mantra to be recited on a leaf; having purified that leaf, one should place it upon the head. As it is said:
Whatever matter for which one may be prosecuted, that should be written down upon a leaf together with this mantra, and that document should be placed upon the head.
And this is the mantra: *Piṭaka-smṛti* 77: Whatever matter for which one may be prosecuted, having written that upon a leaf, together with this mantra, that document should be placed upon the head.
And this is the mantra:
"The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, and Yama;
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma know the conduct of a man.
(PiSm 78) And this section of the ritual procedure, beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head, is common to all ordeals.
As it has been said:
"One should apply this entire ritual procedure for mantras to all divine beings;
one should likewise arrange the invocation of the gods. (PiSm 58)
Immediately thereafter, the judge should address the balance;
for it is recorded in the legal treatises: "The knower of the scriptures should address the balance according to this very procedure" (PiSm 99, note; DhKo 482).
And the mantras were revealed:
"O Balance, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked;
from the letter *dha* you are the embodiment of Dharma, and from the letter *ṭa* [you judge] the crooked man."
Because you hold and examine [the truth], you are therefore called the Balance (Dhaṭa);
you know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings.
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not understand; this man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
"Therefore, you ought to deliver him from this doubt in accordance with dharma. Thus [it is said].
The person to be tested should address the balance with the previously mentioned mantra beginning with "O Balance, you are...
Immediately thereafter, the judge [should place] the document upon the head [of the accused].
Having placed the person to be cleared in their proper position, one causes them to mount the balance;

one should cause them to mount it again with the document placed upon their head, according to the traditional legal authority which states: "One should cause [the accused] to mount it with the document situated on the head. (DhKo 484).
One should maintain the five *vināḍīs* thus established for that duration,
and one skilled in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) should perform an examination of that time.

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "An eminent Brāhmaṇa who is an astrologer shall perform the examination of the time; five *vināḍīs* are to be understood as the duration for examination by those skilled in the science of testing time" (PiSm 104).
The time required to pronounce ten long syllables is one *prāṇa*.
Six *prāṇas* constitute one *vināḍī*. And it has been said:
"Ten long syllables are a *prāṇa*; six *prāṇas* shall be a *vināḍikā*."

"Sixty *ghaṭīs* make one *ghaṭī*; sixty *ghaṭīs* make one day; and by thirty-six days [of such measure] a month is formed. At that time, for the purpose of examining purity and impurity, pure men should be appointed by the king;
they then report the state of purity and impurity.
As it was said by the Grandfather:
"Wise, pure, and free from greed, Brāhmaṇas who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them are the best witnesses; they should indeed be appointed by the king."
"Then the preeminent witnesses declare purity or impurity before the king.
(Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.95–96) And the means for determining purity and impurity has been stated:
"If, when weighed, he should increase [in weight], he shall be pure; of this there is no doubt."
"Whether he is equal or inferior, that man shall not be considered pure. (NSm 20.12; PiSm 107).
As for the statement of Pitāmaha:
"One who is equal should be known as having little fault, but one who is inferior has much fault. (PiSm 108)
In that regard, although it may not be possible to determine through divine means whether the object of the offense is small or large,

nevertheless, its smallness is determined by its being committed for the first time, and its greatness by its being committed repeatedly; thus, the smallness or greatness of the punishment and penance is established.
Furthermore, when the cutting or breaking of the beam and other parts occurs even though no visible cause is perceived, there is likewise impurity; for it is said:
"In the case of the cutting of the beam, the breaking of the scale, and likewise of the *dhaṭa* and the *karkaṭa*..."
For it is stated in the legal tradition (*smṛti*): "One should likewise declare [the ordeal] impure if the rope is cut or the axle breaks" (NSm C–284).
*Kakṣa* refers to the surface of the scale-pan.
The two *karkaṭas* (crab-claws) are slightly curved iron pins at the ends of the balance beam, resembling the horns of a crab; they serve as the supports for the scale-pan.
The *akṣa* (axis) is the beam that rests upon the two pillar-posts.
However, when the visible cause [is present]...

"In the event of their breaking, one should then set it up again; in cases of breakage such as the snapping of the scale-pan strings and so forth, one should set the man up again," according to the traditional legal text (*smaraṇa*). And therefore:
He should satisfy the officiating priests, the domestic chaplain, and the teachers with sacrificial fees;
thus, as the king who has caused this to be performed, he shall enjoy delightful pleasures.
He attains great fame and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.

When he wishes to set up the balance (dhaṭa) according to the characteristics previously described, he should then construct a hall provided with doors and other such features, in order to prevent interference by crows and other birds.
One should have a large, elevated, and bright water-pot shed constructed,
situated where it cannot be defiled by dogs, outcastes, or crows.
In that very place, one should establish all the world-protectors and others in their respective directions;
one should worship them at the three junctions of the day with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
"According to the Smṛti: 'The king shall cause [the dwelling] to be kept non-empty, provided with doors and seeds, guarded by attendants, and supplied with earth, water, and fire. (PiSm 81–83).
Seeds are those such as barley, rice, and so forth. 2.100, 2.101, 2.102.
Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal by balance.
Now he describes the ordeal by fire, which follows in sequence:
"Having examined the hands after they have rubbed the rice grains, one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with thread. (YDh 2.103)

While the common rules stated in the *Divyamātṛkā* exist, and while the procedure beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head as prescribed in the *Tulāvidhāna* is being performed, there is this specific distinction in the fire-rite (*agnividhi*):
"of crushed rice" (*vimṛditavrīheḥ*) means that the rice grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) have been crushed, that is, rubbed together.

Having observed the hands of that person by whom the rice was crushed with both hands, and having marked them at the locations of moles, dark spots, scars, calluses, and so forth with lac juice and other substances;
as Nārada has said:
"In all cases of wounds from weapons, one should make 'swan's foot' marks.
(NSm C–301) Immediately thereafter, one should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree into the hands joined in the *añjali* gesture;
having filled the *añjali* with leaves, using seven equal *aśvattha* leaves. (DhKo 490: Nārada)
According to this traditional teaching,
one should wrap those [leaves], together with the hands,
with thread as many times as there are *aśvattha* leaves— seven times.
The meaning is that one should wrap [them].
And there are seven white threads;
one should wrap the two hands with seven strands of white thread. (DhKo 490)
Thus, according to the words of Nārada:
likewise, one should place seven *śamī* leaves, seven *dūrvā* blades, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) mixed with curd upon the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
One should place seven pippala leaves, śamī leaves, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as seven dūrvā blades and unbroken grains mixed with curd.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"Likewise, one should place flowers,
seven leaves of the Pippala tree, unbroken rice grains, jasmine, and curd."
"One should place [the offerings] there in the hands and likewise wrap them with thread," according to the statement of Pitāmaha;
"sumanas" refers to flowers.
Furthermore, as for the test of memory:
if one carries red-hot iron concealed by seven *arka* leaves held in both hands, he is pure if he is not burned by the time he reaches the seventh step. (DhKo 498: Hārīta)
Thus, in the absence of *aśvattha* leaves, it should be understood that this refers to *arka* leaves;
for the *aśvattha* leaves are recognized as primary by virtue of the statement praising the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"From the *pippala* tree fire is born; the *pippala* is remembered as the king of trees."
"Therefore, the wise man should place its petals upon his two hands. (PiSm 119) 2.103.
The author states the consecration of the fire by the performer:
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth regarding my merits and sins. (YDh 2.104)

O Agni, you move within the bodies of all beings— whether born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from a sprout— functioning as the digester of the food and drink they have consumed; O Purifier, O Cause of Purity, O Sage who perceives all, you are like a witness.
"Speak the truth regarding merits and demerits.
The ablative case in "puṇyapāpebhyaḥ" is used with the elision of a gerundive suffix (*lyap*),
meaning "having regard for merits and demerits."
"Speak the truth; show [it]," is the meaning.

When a ball of iron has been heated by three burnings and is brought forward with tongs, the practitioner, standing facing east in the western mandala, should consecrate the fire with this mantra, as it is said:
Nārada says:
"Having heated an iron ball, glowing like fire, emitting sparks, and well-polished, on the third heating, one should speak while placing truth at the forefront. (NSm–C 289, 290)

The meaning of this is as follows: for the purpose of purifying iron, one should heat a lump of iron until it is thoroughly red-hot and cast it into water; then, heating it again and casting it into water a second time, and heating it a third time, the performer, grasping it with tongs and bringing it forward, should recite the mantra beginning with "O Agni, you who are present before all beings," accompanied by the word "Truth" (satya).

The judge, however, having kindled the common fire in the southern part of the court precinct, shall offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni Pāvaka," and he shall offer clarified butter into the fire one hundred and eight times for the sake of pacification. (DhKo 496: Pitāmaha)
Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),

having offered oblations into that fire and cast an iron ball into it, while it is being heated, one should perform the previously mentioned procedure beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the final oblation; then, while the third heating is taking place, one should consecrate the iron ball with these mantras addressed to Agni:
O Agni, you are the four Vedas; you are invoked in the sacrifices.
You are the mouth of all the gods; you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman.
For, dwelling within the bellies of all beings, you know their good and evil;
since you indeed purify sin, you are therefore called Pāvaka.
Reveal yourself among the wicked, O Purifier; become radiant with flames. Or else, toward those of pure intent, become cool, O Consumer of Oblations.
O Agni, you move within all the gods like a witness;
you alone, O God, know those things which human beings do not know. This man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
"Therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with dharma. (PiSm 123–27) 2.104 //
Moreover,
for one who has spoken thus, a ball of iron weighing fifty palas and heated to the color of fire shall be placed upon both his hands. (YDh 2.105)

For that maker who has spoken thus and performed the consecration with the mantras beginning with "O Agni, [you are] of all beings," there is an iron ball— a wrought iron product weighing fifty palas,
equal (meaning free from irregularities), uniform on all sides, round, smooth, and likewise eight finger-breadths in length.

"Having made it smooth and free of flaws, one should heat a uniform iron ball weighing fifty palas to the depth of eight finger-breadths in the fire," according to the traditional teaching of Pitāmaha.
The judge shall place the fire—red-hot and resembling fire—within both hands, which have been separated by an aśvattha leaf, curd, dūrvā grass, and so forth. (2.105)
To the question, "What then should he do?", the author says:
"Taking that [ball], he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles" (YDh 2.106ab).
That man, having grasped that heated iron ball with his cupped hands (añjali), should walk slowly for seven circles. By the use of the particle *eva* (only/exactly), [it is emphasized].
It demonstrates both the placement of steps within the mandalas and the crossing over of the mandalas, as Pitāmaha has said:
"One should not cross over a mandala, nor should one place a step beyond it. (PiSm 129)
It has been stated that one should proceed slowly through exactly seven circles;
in this regard, what is the measure of each individual circle, and what is the measure of the interval between two circles? To answer this, he says:
The mandala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths in size, with an interval of that same measure.
That which has sixteen finger-breadths is called "sixteen-finger-breadth";
thus, the mandala should be understood to have a measurement of sixteen finger-breadths.
The interval between two mandalas and their center is likewise exactly sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula).
By stating that "one should traverse seven mandalas," the first mandala of standing is mentioned as one;
therefore, there are eight mandalas, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths.

The "intervals between the circles" (maṇḍalāntarāṇi) means their middles; these intervals between the circles are seven in number and of that same measure. This very point has been stated by Nārada after enumerating them.
They say that the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred and forty finger-breadths in measurement from the ground. (NSm–C 285–6; DhKo 489)
This is the meaning:

from the mandala of the resting place, another mandala sixteen finger-breadths away is the next mandala; each subsequent one from the second onwards is thirty-two finger-breadths including the intervening space. Thus, the mandala of the resting place is sixteen finger-breadths.
And seven circles, including the intermediate spaces, are to be traversed, measuring thirty-two finger-breadths each.

Thus, by means of eight circles, there are two hundred and forty finger-breadths of ground; "measured by finger-breadths" (*aṅgulamāna*) is formed with the suffix *tasi* used in all case-meanings (*sārvavibhaktikas tasi*). But in this [case]...

Having established a sixteen-finger-width circle for the [first] step, one should divide each of the seven sections of ground— including the intervening spaces— measuring thirty-two fingers in total, into two parts. Setting aside the intervening ground sections measuring sixteen fingers,
seven circles should be made upon the sixteen-finger-wide sections of ground, with a size corresponding to the step of the walker.
Thus it was said by him [the author of the Smṛti]:
"One should make the measurement of the mandala equal to that [forefinger] step.
As for that which was stated by Pitāmaha:
One should cause eight mandalas to be made, and likewise a ninth in front;
the first mandala is that of Agni, and the second is known as that of Varuṇa.
The third has Vāyu as its deity, the fourth has Yama as its deity;
the fifth has Indra as its deity, and the sixth is said to have Kubera as its deity.
Those who know the divine [sciences] understand that the seventh has Soma as its deity, the eighth likewise belongs to Savitṛ, and the ninth has all the gods as its deities.
They say the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
The measurement of the ground should be calculated as fifty-six [units] more;
the mandala should be made by the practitioner according to that same measure.
"Kuśa grasses, as enjoined by the scriptures, should be placed in each and every mandala" (PiSm 109–16).

In this regard, setting aside the ninth mandala—which belongs to all deities and measures an unlimited number of finger-breadths (aṅgulas)—there are eight mandalas and eight intervening spaces, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths; thus, the total is two hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths.
It is accomplished;
therein, too, there are exactly seven mandalas to be traversed,
since one abides in the first and [emerges] in the ninth.
Thus, it is not contradictory that [the atom] is said to "cast" [itself].
And as for the measurement of a finger: eight horizontal barley-grain cavities, or three vertical grains of rice, constitute one finger-breadth.
The measure of a finger has been stated; a span (vitasti) consists of twelve fingers.
A *hasta* is two *vitastis*; a *daṇḍa* is four *hastas*;
two thousand of those [daṇḍas] is a *krośa*; and four of those is a *yojana*. This is how it should be understood. (DhKo 534) // 2.106 //
Having traversed seven circles, as to what must be done next, he says:
"Having released the fire, having crushed the rice grains, and being unburnt, one attains purification" (YDh 2.107ab).
Having stood at the eighth circle and having left behind the iron ball heated by fire at the ninth circle, [he should crush] the rice grains with both hands.
If, after rubbing [the substance], his hand is not burned, he attains purification;
if his hand is burned, he is impure—this is the established meaning.
However, if, due to being startled, he stumbles and is burned elsewhere than on his hands, even then he does not become impure.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"If one who is accused stumbles [in the ordeal] and is burnt elsewhere than the designated spot, the gods know him to be unburnt; one should have him undergo the ordeal once more. (KSm 441)

"If the rice-ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, one should take it again. (YDh 2.107cd) This means that when the rice-ball falls while one is walking, even before reaching the eighth circle, or if there is uncertainty as to whether it has been burnt or not, then one should take it again; this is stated as a matter of course.

And therein, this is the sequence of performance: having performed the purification of the ground on the previous day, and having constructed the mandalas according to the scriptures on the following day, and having worshipped the presiding deities of the mandalas in their respective places with mantras, one should kindle the fire, perform the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma), and place an iron ball into the fire.

Having performed the worship of all the deities, beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the oblation (*havana*), the judge— having applied the ritual purification of the hands such as the rubbing of rice to the defendant who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes while standing in the western mandala, and having bound the written pledge together with the mantras to the head of the litigant— should consecrate the fire during the third heating and [take] the heated iron ball.
Having taken [the substance] with a mantra recited over the blade of grass, he should place it in the other's joined palms.
Having passed through seven mandalas, if that person remains unburnt upon casting it in the ninth mandala, he is purified. // 2.107 //
Thus ends the procedure for the fire sacrifice.
Now he states the procedure for the water ordeal:
"O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth," having thus invoked the water, one should enter the water after grasping the thighs of a person standing in water reaching up to the navel. (YDh 2.108)

Having consecrated and empowered water with the mantra, "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth," the person to be purified should enter the water— that is, immerse himself— while holding the thighs of another man who stands in water reaching up to his navel.
And this [is to be done] when the worship of Varuṇa is performed:
with fragrant perfumes and garlands, and with honey, milk, ghee, and so forth, one should first perform the worship of Varuṇa with a concentrated mind. (NSm 5.01)
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada;

likewise, when the common duties—including the invocation of Dharma, the worship of all deities, the oblation (homa), and the placement of the document of pledge upon the head accompanied by mantras—are completed; and furthermore—
O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings; you were created as the first of all things, and you are declared to be the cause of purity for both material substances and embodied beings.
"Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious" (PiSm 139–40).
When the presiding judge has thus performed the consecration of the water, the person undergoing purification should pray to the water, saying: "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth.
And the locations for the water have been described by Nārada.
"In rivers of slow current, in oceans, and in flowing streams;
in lakes, in natural pools, in ponds, and in reservoirs.
Thus [it was stated]; likewise also by Pitāmaha:
One should immerse oneself in water that is still, not turbid, and not shallow;
it should be free of grass and aquatic weeds, and devoid of leeches and fish.
One should perform purification using water found in natural reservoirs;
one should always avoid water that has been drawn up, as well as water from rivers with swift currents.
"One should always enter water that is free from waves and mud. (PiSm 134–36) "Brought water" refers to water drawn from ponds and other sources and placed in copper vessels and the like.
And [the practitioner] stands in water reaching up to the navel.
"He should stand facing east, leaning against a pillar of dharma made from a tree fit for sacrifice;
and he should stand in water facing east while grasping the pillar of dharma," according to the traditional legal text (Smṛti). (DhKo 505) // 2.108 //
To the question of what should be done after that, he says:

"If a swift man, having brought back an arrow shot simultaneously [with the immersion], should see the person with his limbs submerged when that man has departed, he shall obtain purification. (YDh 2.109)

At the very moment that one swift man has gone down [into the water], another swift man stationed at the place where the arrow fell retrieves the previously discharged arrow; if he sees the person with their limbs submerged in the water, then that person is pure. This is what is meant:
When three arrows have been discharged, one swift man goes to the place where the middle arrow fell, retrieves it, and stands right there;
another swift man stands at the foot of the archway, at the spot from which the arrows were released.
While they remain thus positioned, at the third clap of the hands, the one to be purified sinks;
at that very same moment, the other, though standing at the base of the archway, moves even more swiftly to the point where the middle arrow falls.
And when the arrow-taker has reached the base of the archway, he must proceed very quickly; if he does not see [the accused] within the water, then he becomes pure.
This very point has been clarified as follows:
The grandfather [declared]:
"The journey and the immersion shall be equal for both the one who goes and the one who performs [the rite].
A swift man should go from the base of the archway to the target station."
When he had gone, the second one also, taking up an arrow,
would go with speed to the foot of the archway where that man had departed.
"But when the arrow-retriever, having entered [the water], does not see [the bowl] clearly while it is submerged within the water, then one should declare him pure. (PiDh 142–44).
Furthermore, Nārada has established the selection of two swift men.
"Of the fifty washermen, those two who are superior in speed should be appointed there for the purpose of fetching the arrows. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, an archway (*toraṇa*) should be constructed in a level spot near the place of immersion, rising to the height of the ears of the person undergoing purification.
"Having gone to that body of water, one should erect an archway on the bank at a spot on level and pure ground measuring only a cubit," according to the traditional teaching of Nārada.
One should first worship the three arrows and the bamboo bow with auspicious substances such as white flowers and the like;
one should first worship the arrows and likewise the bamboo bow.
"Then one should perform the ritual with auspicious incense and flowers," according to the statement of Pitāmaha (Yājñavalkya).
The measurement of the bow and the location of the target have been stated by Nārada.
A cruel bow is known to be seven hundred [inches], a medium one six hundred, and a mild one five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for bows.
Moreover, with a bow of medium size,
the wise man, having set a target at one hundred and fifty cubits, should discharge three arrows.
"But there would be a fault in [the distance being] too short or too long, just as when one hurls arrows.
Thus, a bow of seven hundred finger-breadths is called "fierce" (*krūra*);
likewise, there are those of six hundred and five hundred.
Thus, the measure of a cruel bow is four cubits plus eleven finger-breadths;
that of a medium one is [four cubits] plus ten finger-breadths.
For one of dull intellect, it is said that [the length] should be nine fingers more;
and the arrows should indeed be made of bamboo with tips not of iron.

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "One should prepare arrows with tips not made of iron for the sake of purification; those made of bamboo stalks, moreover, the thrower should discharge very firmly. (KSm 442).
The one who casts [the lot] should be a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa following that profession; he must be appointed while fasting. As it is said:
"The caster is declared to be a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa following that profession;
being gentle-hearted and tranquil, he should cast [the lot] while fasting. (PiSm 141)
When three arrows have been discharged, the middle one is to be taken up;
for, according to the injunction of the treatises regarding those discharged arrows, the middle arrow must be seized by a strong man. (PiSm 134 note; DhKo 504)
According to this statement,
in that case as well, [the distance] must be taken from the point where it falls, not from the point where it glides;
one should take the arrow’s fall and avoid its gliding.
"Moving, moving, let the arrow go from afar to even further distance"—
according to this statement,
one must not discharge an arrow when the wind is blowing or in a place such as a village.
A wise man should not discharge an arrow when the wind is blowing violently,
nor on uneven ground, nor in a place crowded with trees and thickets.
"Even if [the body] is covered with grass, shrubs, creepers, vines, mud, or stones"—
according to this statement of Pitāmaha;
"if one sees the submerged limb, he shall attain purification" (YDh 2.109).
By saying this, the impurity of one whose limb has emerged [from the water] is shown.
Furthermore, Pitāmaha has stated that there is impurity in moving to another location;
otherwise, there would be no purification, because even a single limb might still be seen [in the water]. Thus it is said.
"Whether from its place or by going elsewhere, [it is perceived] in that [place] where it was previously deposited"—
and also because "even a single part is seen," this refers to the ears and so forth.
"However, if only the head should be seen, and neither the ears nor the nose,
one should declare that person pure even if they have entered the water," because of this specific statement [in the Pitāmaha-smṛti].
The procedure for this practice is as follows:

having constructed an archway of the described characteristics near a body of water possessing the aforementioned features, and having placed the target at the specified distance, one should worship the bow together with an arrow in the vicinity of the archway.
Having invoked Varuṇa into a body of water and worshipped him, and having performed the rites up to the oblation for the gods beginning with Dharma on its bank,

the judge shall bind the written confession upon the head of the person to be purified and consecrate the water with the mantra beginning, "O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings. Then the person to be purified, having consecrated the water with the mantra beginning, "By truth," shall enter the water up to his navel while standing before a strong man who has grasped a pillar.
He approaches the man.

Then, after three arrows have been discharged, the judge— having taken the middle arrow from the spot where it fell— stands with one swift man positioned at the place where the middle arrow landed and another standing at the base of the archway.
When three claps of the hands are given, there is simultaneous movement, immersion, and then the bringing of the arrows. // 2.109 //
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for water.
Now he states the procedure for the ordeal by poison:
"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in the law of truth;
protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar to me. (YDh 2.110ab)
2.110cd–111ab. Having spoken thus, he should consume the Śārṅga poison from the snowy mountains; if it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare him purified. YDh 2.111ab.
Having consecrated the poison with the mantra beginning "tvaṃ viṣa," the performer shall consume the poison produced from the Himalayan mountains, originating from a horn.
When that [poison] has been consumed and is digested without the onset of its toxic effects, he is considered pure. The so-called "onset of toxic effects" (viṣavega) is as follows:
"The attainment of another element from an element;
the attainment of another element from an element is known as the 'force of poison' (viṣavega)," according to this statement.
The bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) are seven: skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
In this way, there are exactly seven stages of the poison's intensity (*viṣavega*). Their respective characteristics have been described separately in the *Viṣatantra*:
The first stage of poison produces horripilation, followed by perspiration and parching of the mouth; thereafter, the next two stages bring about discoloration of the body and trembling.
That which is the fifth stage renders one helpless, causing convulsions of the throat and hiccups.
"The sixth [day] brings about fainting and exhaustion, and the seventh brings death to the eater.
And in this regard, worship of Mahādeva must be performed,
as Nārada said:
"Having fasted and having worshipped Maheśvara with incense, offerings, and mantras, one should administer the poison in the presence of the gods and Brahmins. Thus [it is said].
The judge, having observed a fast and worshipped Mahādeva, should place the poison before him and perform the worship of Dharma and the other deities.
Having performed the rites up to the oblation (*havana*) and having placed the written pledge upon the head of the person to be tested, he consecrates the poison with this mantra:
"O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked;
reveal yourself to the sinful, but be nectar to those who are pure."
"O Poison, you are indeed the embodiment of death, created by Brahmā;
protect this man from evil! By truth, become nectar for him!
Having thus consecrated it, he should give it to one standing facing the south.
"In the presence of the twice-born, while standing facing south,
[the judge], being composed, shall administer the poison while facing north or east," according to the statement of Nārada.

And "poison" refers to *vatsanābha* and other such types, as stated in the words of Pitāmaha: "Of the poison from a horned creature, from *vatsanābha*, or from that born of snow. (Yājñavalkyasmṛti, Vyavahārakāṇḍa 149).

And the things to be avoided have been stated by that same [author]: "One should completely avoid all poisons that are prepared, aged, artificial, and likewise those produced from the earth. (PiSm 150)
Likewise, Nārada also says: "One should carefully avoid that which is *bhraṣṭa*, *cārita*, *dhūpita*, *miśrita*, as well as *kālakūṭa* and *alābu* poison. (NSm 20.34)
And the proper time has been stated by Nārada: "Having weighed it, that which is desired should be given at the proper time, specifically at the onset of winter;
for one who knows the Dharma, it should not be given in the afternoon, nor at midday, nor at twilight. (DhKo 507)
However, at other times, one should give less than the stated measure:
"The dose is four barley-grains in the rainy season, five barley-grains in summer, it is recorded as seven barley-grains in winter, and in autumn it is even less than that. (DhKo 508)
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
"Small" means six barley grains.
By the mention of "winter" (hemanta), the "cool season" (śiśira) is also included.

Because of the scriptural statement, "The two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira are treated together," and because the spring season is common to all divine ordeals, even there seven barley grains and poison soaked in clarified butter should be administered,
according to the words of Nārada:

"From a *pala* of poison, one should take the twentieth part; from that, having reduced it by one-eighth, one should administer it soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to the person to be cleared of guilt. (NSm 20.37).
And here, a *pala* consists of four *suvarṇas*.
A sixth part of that amounts to ten *māṣas* and ten *yavas*.
However, three *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*, and five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; thus, one *māṣa* consists of fifteen *yavas*.
In this way, the *yavas* in ten *māṣas* amount to one hundred and fifty.
And "ten barley-corns [in] the east" refers to one hundred and sixty barley-corns, which is the sixth part of a *pala*;

the twentieth part of that is eight barley-corns; the eighth part of that is one barley-corn. One should add seven barley-corns—[that is,] the twentieth part diminished by that one barley-corn—to the substance to be purified, having soaked it in clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
And thirty times the amount of ghee should be taken;
the poison should be administered to embodied beings in the cool of the morning in a cool place, finely ground and mixed with ghee in a thirtyfold proportion. (KSm 450)
According to this statement of Kātyāyana,
the poison should be mixed with thirty times its amount of clarified butter; furthermore,
the person undergoing the ordeal must be protected from fraud and other such deceptions.
For three or five nights,
the king should have the person undergoing the ordeal guarded by his own men to protect him from fraudsters and others.

"One should examine medicinal herbs, mantra-applications, and gems that neutralize poison, as well as those residing within the body of the perpetrator, which have arisen in a concealed manner," according to the traditional teaching of Pitāmaha.

Likewise, poison must also be guarded: that which is from the Śārṅga mountain in the Himalayas, praised, endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste, unadulterated, not confused, and not affected by mantras. (DhKo 507; NSm–A34)
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Nārada;
likewise, when poison has been drunk, he should be waited for as long as five hundred hand-claps take, after which he should be treated.
As Nārada said:
"When one remains free from transformation for a period of five hundred tālas, then one becomes completely purified; thereafter, one should apply medical treatment. (DhKo 509)
But the grandfather [Vyāsa] has stated that the end of the day is the limit, applicable to cases of small quantities:
"When, after eating, one is healthy, free from fainting and vomiting, and shows no adverse symptoms at the end of the day, one should declare even him to be pure. (PiDh 156)

And here, the judge, having fasted and worshipped Mahādeva, having placed the poison before him, having offered oblations to Dharma and the other deities, and having placed the written declaration upon the head of the person to be purified, consecrates the poison with mantras and administers it to one standing facing the south.
And that person to be tested, having consecrated the poison with mantras, eats it; such is the procedure. (2.110–2.111)
Thus ends the section on the varieties of poison.
Now he states the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation: Having worshipped fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having poured it out, one should then cause the person to drink three handfuls (prasṛti) of that water. (YDh 2.112)

Having worshipped the fierce deities, such as Durgā and Āditya, by honoring them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having bathed them, one should take that bath-water. Having taken the water while reciting, "O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings," and so forth, the judge (prāḍvivāka) should bathe [the deity] and have the person to be purified place that water in another vessel; then, having consecrated it with the mantra, "By truth, O Varuṇa, protect me," he should have him drink three handfuls (prasṛti).

And this [ceremony] takes place when all the common ritual elements are present, beginning with the invocation of the deities (*dharmāvāhana*), including the worship of all the gods, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the placement of the document of oath upon the head.
In this regard, the rules concerning the deity to be bathed, the rules concerning the purpose of the act, and the rules concerning the qualified person have been stated by Pitāmaha and others:
"One should cause the water belonging to whichever deity a devotee is devoted to that [devotee] to drink."
But when there is equality between the gods and Āditya, one should cause [the patient] to drink it.
One should cause thieves and those who subsist by the use of weapons to drink the water of Durgā;
however, one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to drink that water which belongs to the Sun.
"One should bathe the trident of Durgā and the discus of Āditya;
likewise, one should bathe the weapons of other deities as well"—
this is the rule regarding the deities.
"In matters of confidence, in all types of suspicion, and likewise in the business of making peace—
in these cases, the treasury must always be provided for the sake of purity of mind.
(PiSm 37) Thus is the rule regarding the [specific] tasks.

In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes, who possesses a sense of shame, is free from vice, and is a believer, the drinking of the ordeal-substance (kośapāna) is prescribed.
(DhKo 517) "Possessing a sense of shame" means being a believer (*āstika*).
The treasury should not be given by the wise to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the ways of nihilists;
nor to one who has committed a great offense, one devoid of virtue, an ungrateful person, a eunuch, or one who is contemptible. (PiSm 43)
"One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the vessel (*kośapāna*) among atheists, outcasts (*vrātya*), and slaves.

(DhKo 464). A "great offender" is one who commits a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). An "unrighteous person" (*nirdharma*) is a heretic (*pākhaṇḍin*) who is devoid of the duties pertaining to caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*).
One born in the inverse order (pratiloma) is despised;
"dāśas" refers to fishermen.
This is the restriction regarding those entitled [to perform the rite].

Likewise, it should be understood from the statement of Nārada that, having prepared a circle with cow dung and having placed the person to be purified therein facing the sun, one should make him drink [the ordeal liquid]. As he says:
"Having summoned that accused person, one should place him within the circle..."
Having turned [the patient] toward the sun, one should have them drink three handfuls. (DhKo 513) 2.112.

Now, while in the cases of the balance and the others ending with poison, the determination of purity or impurity occurs immediately thereafter, how is it in the case of the *kośa* (ordeal by sacred libation)? To this he says: "If, within fourteen days, no terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone, he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt. (YDh 2.113)

If, prior to the fourteenth day, no terrible or great calamity— whether caused by the king, caused by the king's motives, or caused by the gods— should arise for embodied beings, even if it be slight, because such things are unavoidable, he should be known as pure;
however, after that limit, there is no fault.
As Nārada said: "If, after two weeks have passed, a great abnormality should occur, he should not be prosecuted by a wise man, because the appointed time has elapsed. (NSm C 331)
Thus, this has been stated as a matter of established meaning:

"within fourteen days" refers specifically to the subject of major charges (*mahābhiyoga*), because this was stated after introducing [the topic] with the words, "these [procedures apply] in cases of major charges."

The time-limits mentioned by the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) have a limited scope, because of the traditional legal maxim (smṛti): "One may cause the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) to be administered even in a minor case. And those [limits] are:
three nights, seven nights, twelve days, or fourteen days.

"He who exhibits a physical transformation is declared to be a wrongdoer. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 161) Regarding the objects mentioned in the context of "great charges," one should divide the object into three parts and establish a period of three fortnights, starting from three nights, even for objects of lesser value. (2.113)
Thus is the procedure for the treasury.
The five great ordeals, beginning with the balance and ending with the sacred chest, have been explained by the Lord of Yogins according to their respective designations.
However, in another Smṛti, other ordeals are also mentioned for those who are unable to undergo the strenuous ones;
as the Grandfather (Brahmā) has said:
I shall now declare the procedure for the consumption of rice as prescribed:
it is a settled rule that rice should be given to the thief, and to no one else.
One who is pure should have white rice prepared from the *śāli* variety and no other;
having placed it in an earthen vessel, he should do so before the Sun.
One should let them remain mixed with bathing water right there during the night;
[the subject] should have fasted, bathed, and had leaves placed upon his head while facing the east.
Having eaten rice grains, one should then spit them out into a leaf;
it should be from a *pippala* tree, or in its absence, from a *bhūrja* tree and no other.
"One whose blood is seen [in the mouth], whose jaw and palate are parched, and whose body trembles—one should declare him impure. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.109).
The judge, having placed a leaf upon the head [of the accused], should have him chew rice grains and spit them out.
The form "bhakṣayitvā" is derived from the root with the causative suffix (ṇic).
Furthermore, the invocation of Dharma and other rites common to all divine offerings should be performed here as well, just as before.
Thus ends the procedure for the rice grains.

The procedure for the heated ball (*taptamāṣa*) has been declared by Pitāmaha as follows: "A circular vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay, sixteen *aṅgulas* in length and four *aṅgulas* deep. (PiSm 170)
The meaning is that it should be circular.
One should fill it with twenty palas of ghee and oil;
then, once it is well-heated, one should cast a gold māṣaka into it.
By joining the thumb and the fingers, one should extract the heated ball of gold;
he whose fingertips do not tremble, nor does a blister arise,
is proven pure by the law, his fingers remaining unchanged.
Based on the statement "one should lift up," one should understand that merely lifting [the food] from the vessel is intended, not its casting outside.
Another ritual procedure:
having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
One should place therein a well-purified ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, having washed it once with water.
In that place rich with swirling ripples and waves, which is beyond the reach of touch by the fingernails,
one should examine it with a moist leaf, listening for the distinct "curu" sound.
Then, one should consecrate that once with this mantra.
O clarified butter, you are the supreme purifier, the nectar among sacrificial rites;
burn away our sin, O Purifier, and be cool as snow when it is time for purification.
Then, once he has fasted, bathed, and approached still wearing his wet clothes,
one should cause him to grasp that ring while it is likewise placed within clarified butter.
"Then the examiners should examine her ring finger;
he on whose [finger] there are no eruptions is pure, otherwise he is impure. (PiSm 174–80).
Here too, the invocation of Dharma and other preliminary rites are to be performed.
The consecration of the clarified butter belongs to the presiding judge.
"Thou, O Agni, of all beings... is the mantra for the person undergoing purification to consecrate the fire.
Because of the statement, "They should examine the forefinger," the extraction of the ring must be performed with the forefinger alone.
Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal of the heated gold ball.
And the divine procedure known as *dharmādharmā* was declared by the Grandfather (*Pitāmaha*). As it is said:
"Now I shall fully explain the examination of *dharma* and *adharma* for men who are murderers, those who are pleading [for mercy], and those seeking expiation. (PiSm 181)
The term "of the slayers" refers to cases of violent assault; "of those who beg" refers to cases involving property; and "of those seeking expiation" refers to [cases of] transgression.
"In cases of accusations involving mortal sins,
one should have the Dharma made of silver and Adharma of lead or iron"—
this is the rule for the manufacture of the images, using either lead or iron.
He states another alternative:

"One should draw Dharma and Adharma, white and black respectively, either on birch bark or on cloth; having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship them with perfumes and garlands."
Dharma shall be represented by a white flower, while Adharma shall hold a black flower;
having fashioned these in this manner and drawn them, one should place them within the two ritual balls (piṇḍas).
Two balls should be made from either cow dung or clay, perfectly symmetrical on all sides;
they should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel and remain unobserved.
In a clean place that has been smeared with unguents, in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
one should then invoke the deities and the world-protectors as before.
One should first perform the invocation of Dharma and then write out the document of the pledge.
Thereafter:
"If I am free from sin, may Dharma come into my hand."
"If my hand is impure, let sin come to it according to the law. Thus [he speaks].
The accused person recites the mantra:
"The one who is charged shall take up one of those two without delay."
When one adheres to the Dharma, one becomes pure; but by following what is not Dharma, one falls away.
Thus has the examination of dharma and adharma been briefly explained.
Thus ends the procedure for the divine tests of dharma and adharma.

Furthermore, other oaths concerning the smallness or greatness of an object, as well as those concerning specific castes, have been stated by Manu and others. They are as follows: "For one *niṣka*, there is the speaking of truth; for two *niṣkas*, touching the feet; for less than three, it is a meritorious act; beyond that, the drinking of the *kośa* [is required]. (DhKo 442: Hārīta)
"One should cause a Brahmin to swear by [the truth], a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [possible] sins" (MDh 8.113),
and so forth. And in this regard, the determination of purification has been stated by Manu:
"And he who does not quickly meet with misfortune is to be known as pure in his oath" (MDh 8.114).
As for "misfortune," it is precisely that which has been described [in Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.113]: "For whom a terrible calamity, whether caused by the king or by fate, does not arise... and so forth.
The restriction regarding time is as follows: beginning with one night up to three nights, and beginning with three nights up to five nights.
The fact that it starts from one night and so forth should be understood by considering the lightness or gravity of the task at hand.

Thus, regarding the determination of victory or defeat by means of divine ordeals, a specific fine has also been shown by Kātyāyana: "One who is pure should be made to pay fifty [paṇas]; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment. He states that punishment as follows:
One should prescribe the punishment in order for poison, water, fire, the balance, the holy water-vessel, rice grains, and the ordeal of the heated gold coin.
"One thousand, six hundred, five hundred, and likewise four, three, two, and one; in this manner, one should prescribe a reduction among those who are inferior. (KSm 460–61).
This penalty based on ordeal is to be combined with the penalty previously stated for denial when the case has been proven: "He who denies [the debt] shall pay [the fine]."
Thus ends the section on divine ordeals;
now begins the section on the partition of inheritance.
Proof has been described according to its division into human and divine means.
Now the division of inheritance is described by Yogamūrti.

In this context, by the word *dāya* (inheritance), that wealth which becomes the property of another solely on the basis of its connection with the owner is denoted. That [inheritance] is of two kinds: unobstructed (*apratibandha*) and obstructed (*sapratibandha*).
Among these, for sons and grandsons...

In the case of a son and a grandson, the paternal wealth and the ancestral wealth become one's own property; thus, this is an unobstructed inheritance (*apratibandha-dāya*). However, in the case of paternal uncles, brothers, and others, the property becomes one's own only upon the absence of a son and the absence of ownership [by the previous owner]; thus, this is an obstructed inheritance (*sapratibandha-dāya*). This same principle should be inferred for their sons and subsequent descendants as well.
Partition (vibhāga) is the formal allocation of portions of a collective property among multiple owners to their respective shares.
With this very meaning in mind, Nārada stated:
"Where the division of paternal property is determined by the sons, that is declared by the learned to be the legal head of dispute known as *dāyabhāga*. (NSm 13.1).
The term "paternal" (*pitrya*) is an indicator for any relationship that serves as the basis for ownership.
The phrase "by sons" (*tanayaiḥ*) is also an elliptical indication of those who are proximate.
This must be examined here:
at what time, for whom, in what manner, and by whom should the partition be performed?
Regarding that, as for when, how, and by whom [these were taught], this will be explained in the commentary on the respective verses;
here, only this much is considered: "Of what is there a division?"
Is ownership [established] through partition, or is it partition of that which already exists as one's own? In this regard, ownership itself must first be defined:
is ownership cognizable solely through the scriptures, or is it cognizable through other means of valid knowledge?
Thus it is said.
In this regard, it is first logical that [the ownership of property] is to be understood solely through the treatises (śāstra), according to the statement of Gautama:
"The owner [is established] in respect of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and acquisition."
What is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa is *adhika*; what is won by a Kṣatriya is *vijita*; and what is earned by labor belongs to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. (GDh 10.39–42)
Thus,
if ownership were cognizable through other means of knowledge, this statement would not be purposeful.
Likewise, Manu says regarding the extension [of the rule] to a thief:
"A Brahmin who seeks wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching—is exactly like a thief" (MDh 8.340). [Objection:
It is illogical to prescribe a punishment for those who acquire property from a thief even through such means as officiating at sacrifices.
This would be the case if ownership were worldly;
moreover,
if ownership were worldly, one might think, "My property has been stolen by him."
One should not say that it belongs to the thief alone because of his ownership; otherwise, since the property of another was taken by him, it would not be the thief's own.
If that were the case, then, just like the essential nature of gold, silver, and so forth, there would be no doubt as to whether it is his own or the property of another.
It might be argued that, therefore, ownership is to be understood solely through the treatises (*śāstra*).
To this it is replied: ownership is indeed worldly (*laukika*), because it serves as the means for worldly purposive action (*arthakriyā*), just like rice and other such things.
For [worldly things] such as the *āhavanīya* fire—
Those things which are accessible through the scriptures do not possess the quality of being means for accomplishing worldly actions.
[Objection: But surely even the *āhavanīya* fire and others do indeed serve as means for cooking and so forth.
[Reply: This is not so; for in those cases, they do not serve as means for cooking and so forth by virtue of their form as *āhavanīya* and the like.
What then? They serve as such by virtue of their form as fire and so forth, which is directly perceived through the senses.

In this case, however, gold and the like do not function as means for purchase and so forth by virtue of their form as gold and so on, but rather solely by virtue of being one's own property (*svatva*).
For that which is not someone's own property does not accomplish for them any purposeful action, such as purchase.
Moreover,
even among those living in border regions who have not seen the treatises on legal procedure, the practice of property ownership is observed.

Because we observe the acts of buying and selling, and furthermore, because those learned in logic (nyāyavidaḥ) consider it established in the world that ownership is determined by specific means; for instance,
in the third section of the *Lipsā-sūtra*, regarding the view that the rules for acquiring property serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvarthatva*).
Fearing that the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) might be untenable on the grounds that ownership itself would not exist because ownership is not established by worldly means,

the Teacher supported the prima facie position by asserting that it is well-known in the world that the acquisition of property— through such means as acceptance of gifts— is the instrument for establishing ownership.

But surely, if the acquisition of property were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), ownership itself would not come into being, and thus the sacrifice could not even take place; this has been prattled by someone who says that acquisition does not produce ownership, which is a contradiction. Likewise, even in the Siddhānta, the purpose of the inquiry was stated precisely by accepting the worldly nature of ownership, [concluding] that "the transgression of the rule belongs to the person, not to the sacrifice."
And its meaning is explained as follows:

when the rules regarding the acquisition of wealth have ritual purpose (*kratvarthatva*), then the accomplishment of the ritual is achieved only with wealth acquired in accordance with those rules, and not with wealth acquired by transgressing the rules; thus, there is no fault for the person in the transgression of the rules.

In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), however, since the rule regarding acquisition serves the purpose of the person, the accomplishment of the sacrifice occurs even with wealth acquired by transgressing that rule;
the fault lies solely in the person's transgression of the rule. Thus, it should be understood that ownership exists even for that which is acquired through the violation of a restrictive rule.
Because ownership is not established in that regard in the world, and because it would contradict worldly convention;
thus, when ownership based on worldly means such as acceptance of gifts is established, [the following applies].

The rules for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*) are as follows: for a Brāhmaṇa, [the means of livelihood] are receiving gifts and so forth; for a Kṣatriya, conquest and so forth; for a Vaiśya, agriculture and so forth; and for a Śūdra, service and so forth.
However, inheritance and the like are common to all, as it is stated: "One is an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding" (GDh 10.39).
In this context, "inheritance" refers to property received without restriction;
"purchase" is well known; and "partition" refers to that which is received with restriction.

Inheritance (*dāya*) is the acquisition of water, grass, wood, and so forth that have not previously belonged to another; possession (*parigraha*) is the taking as one's own of such things; and discovery (*adhigama*) is the finding of buried treasure and the like.
When these causes are present, one becomes the owner.
"The master is known among those who are known; that which is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa through acceptance [of gifts] and so forth is his additional [share]" (GDh 10.40).
This means that whatever is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa through receiving gifts and other such means is "additional," that is, unique to him.
Regarding the rule "the conquest of a Kṣatriya" (GDh 10.41), the word "additional" (adhika) is understood to carry over from the previous context.
What is obtained by a Kṣatriya through victory, punishment, and so forth, is his exclusive property.
In the rule "The *nirviṣṭa* of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra" (GDh 10.42), the word "more" (*adhika*) also carries over from the previous context.
The *nirviṣṭa* of the Vaiśya is that which is obtained through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth.
"Uncommon":
that which is obtained by a Śūdra through service to the twice-born and the like, in the form of wages, is "uncommon.

Likewise, among the causes of ownership well-known in the world for those born in the direct order (anuloma) and those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), whatever is "uncommon" [is to be understood].
That which was stated, such as "the charioteering of the *sūtas*," and so forth— all that is expressed by the word *nirviṣṭa*,
because everything [therein] takes the form of wages (*bhṛti*).
According to the recollection in the *Trikāṇḍī* that "nirveśa" means wages or enjoyment,
each of those [shares] should be understood as specific [to the individual].

Furthermore, regarding the recollection beginning with "the wife and the daughters," even though ownership is well-known in the world, there arises— due to the connection with the owner— the possibility of many becoming co-sharers of the inheritance.
The statement that "recollection is for the purpose of removing delusion" is entirely faultless.
As for the argument that one would not say "this was taken by him from my own property" because ownership is a worldly (conventional) matter—
that too is incorrect.
Because doubt regarding ownership arises from doubt concerning the purchase and other such causes of ownership,
the purpose of the inquiry is as follows:
"When Brahmins acquire wealth through a censurable act..."
They are purified by its renunciation, by recitation, and indeed by austerity.

Thus, since ownership is to be understood solely through the treatises (*śāstra*), that which is acquired by reprehensible means such as accepting gifts from the unworthy or trade does not constitute ownership at all; therefore, it is certainly not subject to partition among one's sons.

But when ownership is worldly (*laukika*), then because ownership exists even for what is acquired through improper acceptance (*asatpratigraha*) and so forth, it must indeed be partitioned by his sons.
"By its renunciation they are purified" refers to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the acquirer.
However, since the sons and others possess ownership by virtue of inheritance (*dāya*), they have no connection with that fault;
for there are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, investment, performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. (MDh 10.115)
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu;
now this is doubted:
does ownership arise from partition, or is it partition of that which already belongs to one?
In this regard, it is first of all logical that ownership arises from partition,
because the injunction for the *ādheya* (consecration) is prescribed for one whose son has been born.
If ownership were to exist by birth alone, then even for a son who has already been born, [the rite would be unnecessary].
If that [property] were common to all, there would be no authority for the father in rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) which must be accomplished with material wealth;
likewise, prior to partition, the prohibition of partition regarding what was obtained through the father’s favor would not be logical.
Because it has been given with the consent of all, there is no possibility of partition;
as it is said:
"Both the wealth acquired through valor and that of a wife, as well as whatever may be the wealth of learning..."
"These three are indivisible: a gift of favor and that which is inherited from the father.
Likewise:
"That which has been given by a husband who is pleased to his wife remains hers even when he has died."

"She may eat or give away [the property] as she wishes, except for immovable property" (NSm 1.24). Furthermore, the statement regarding a gift out of affection would not be tenable if ownership were established by birth alone; nor would the phrase "except for what is eaten from immovable property" be appropriate.
Thus, this connection is appropriate, as it avoids the fault of a disjointed construction. Furthermore:
"The father is the master of all gems, pearls, and corals; but of all immovable property, neither the father nor the grandfather is the master. (Dharmakośa 1219: Nārada)
Likewise:
"By the favor of the father, garments and ornaments are enjoyed;
yet immovable property is not enjoyed, even when paternal favor exists."
Thus [says Nārada]:
"The statement prohibiting the gift of immovable property refers to immovable property acquired by the grandfather.
When the grandfather has passed away, although that wealth is common to both father and son, gems, pearls, and the like belong to the father alone; [the same applies to] immovable property."
That it is common [to all] is understood from this very statement;
therefore, ownership does not arise by birth,
but rather ownership arises from the destruction of the owner or from partition.

For this very reason, there is no room for the objection that "because the father's ownership over the property has been relinquished prior to partition after his death, another person taking possession of it should not be prevented";
the same applies to a man who has only one son.
"From the very moment of the father's departure [from this world], the property belongs to the son; thus, he does not depend upon partition.

To this it is replied: It has been stated that ownership is indeed what is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*). And in the world, ownership for sons and others is even more well-established by the mere fact of birth.
It does not deserve to be denied;
furthermore, the word "division" (vibhāga) is well-known in the world as referring to the property of multiple owners, not to that which belongs to another, nor to that which has been relinquished.
Likewise, according to the statement of Gautama, "The teacher [holds that] one acquires ownership of the object by the very fact of its arising," and regarding gems, pearls, and corals... [DhKo 1219]
Statements such as these are logically consistent only with the position that ownership arises by birth;
nor is it correct to claim that they refer specifically to immovable property acquired by a grandfather, for [the text states]: "Neither the father nor the grandfather... (DhKo 1219).

Because of this statement: for there is a rule stating that even what was acquired by a grandfather himself must not be given away as long as his son and grandson exist; this statement implies that ownership arises through birth.

Just as, according to the opponent's view, ownership of gems, pearls, coral, garments, ornaments, and so forth— even those inherited from one's grandfather— belongs to the father alone by virtue of scriptural injunction,
so too, in our own view, the father has the authority to give away these items even when they were acquired by the father himself.
The phrase "by virtue of [his] word" is without qualification.

As for the statement of Viṣṇu beginning with "if [the father] is pleased," which indicates that immovable property may be given as a gift of affection, this must be explained as applying only to property acquired by oneself, and even then, only with the consent of the sons and others.

Because it has been determined by the previously cited statements regarding gems, pearls, and so forth, that only that which is distinct from immovable property (sthāvara) is fit for a gift made out of affection (*prītidāna*).

As for the claim that there is no entitlement (*anadhikāra*) to Vedic rites accomplished through wealth, in that case, entitlement is understood precisely by the force of the injunctions for those rites themselves. Therefore, ownership (*svatva*) over paternal and ancestral property arises by birth alone; nevertheless, [the son has authority] over the father’s necessary [expenses].

It is established that one has independence in matters of religious duty (*dharmakṛtya*), such as recitations, granting favors, supporting the family, and relieving distress, as well as in the disposal of property other than immovable assets.
However, regarding immovable property— whether self-acquired or inherited from a father or others— one is subject to the dependence of sons and other heirs.
Likewise,
even if immovable property or bipeds have been acquired by oneself,
there can be neither gift nor sale without having assembled all the sons.

For it is stated in the Smṛti, such as [the verse by] Vyāsa: "Those who are born, those yet unborn, and those situated in the womb—they all desire their livelihood; it is neither through giving nor through sale."
The exception to this rule is as follows:
Even a single person may perform giving, mortgaging,
or selling of immovable property in times of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma.
Thus [it is said]. (DhKo 1588:
Smṛtyantara) The meaning of this is: when sons or grandsons have not yet attained legal capacity, or when brothers are incapable of giving permission and so forth.

Thus, even when such [properties] are undivided, a single [coparcener] alone is empowered to perform the giving, mortgaging, or selling of immovable property in cases of a calamity affecting the entire family, or when the maintenance of that family necessitates it, as well as in rites such as the *śrāddha* for ancestors.
As for the statement:
"Whether undivided or divided, sapindas have equal rights over immovable property;

for one alone has no power anywhere in giving, mortgaging, or selling. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.14.8) This [rule] also applies to undivided [property], because the wealth remains common to all and one individual lacks independent authority; therefore, the consent of all is mandatory.

However, after they have been divided, for the sake of facilitating legal transactions by removing doubts as to whether they are divided or undivided, a general authorization should be granted; this is not, however, because one individual lacks authority.
Therefore, even in the absence of the consent of those who are divided, the transaction may proceed.
It should be explained that [the land] is indeed established [as his]. Furthermore:
"By the consent of one's own village, kinsmen, neighbors, and heirs, and by the offering of water and gold, one acquires ownership of the earth through these six means."
