Thus, even in that case, there is the approval of the village; the acceptance [of a gift] should be made public, especially in the case of immovable property. (YDh 2.176)

According to this traditional teaching, the neighbors are required solely for the purpose of clarifying the legal proceeding; however, the proceeding is not rendered invalid without the consent of the village. The consent of the neighbors, moreover, serves to eliminate disputes regarding the boundary.
However, the purpose for obtaining the consent of kinsmen and heirs has already been stated as being [the same] as that for the gift of gold and water (DhKo 901).
Regarding immovable property, there is no sale; one may, however, create a mortgage with their permission (DhKo 1589).
Thus, because the sale of immovable property is prohibited:
"He who accepts land and he who bestows land—
both of them are performers of meritorious deeds and are destined for heaven."
*Kṛtyakalpataru*, *Dāna* 10.13 (Brick’s edition),
attributed therein to Dāna-Bṛhaspati.
And because of this demonstration of the praise of giving,
the meaning is that even when a sale must be performed, one should effect the sale of immovable property in the form of a gift by giving water along with gold.
Although ownership over paternal and ancestral wealth arises by birth alone,
we shall explain the specific distinction regarding land acquired by a grandfather in the verse beginning with "But land acquired by a grandfather" (YDh 2.121). 2.113.
Now, showing at what time, by whom, and in what manner the partition should be made, he says:
"If the father should make a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will;
either he may give the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. (YDh 2.114)

When the father desires to make a partition, he may then divide his sons from himself according to his own will—[giving] one son, two sons, or many sons. Since will is unrestrained, there would otherwise be no fixed rule; therefore, to establish a rule, he says: "Or [he may divide] the eldest with the best share.
He should divide the eldest with the best share, the middlemost with the middle share, and the youngest with the smallest share.
This [phrase] continues [from the previous verse].

And the division into "best" (*śreṣṭha*) and so forth has been stated by Manu: "The eldest's additional share (*uddhāra*) shall be one-twentieth [of the estate], as well as the best of all the property."
"Then half [of that] would belong to the middle one, but a fourth to the youngest.
(MDh 9.112) The word "or" (*vā*) refers to the alternative view to be stated later:
"Or all [the sons] may have equal shares."

Alternatively, all [sons], beginning with the eldest, should be made sharers of equal portions. Furthermore, this unequal division pertains to property acquired by oneself; however, in the case of property inherited through the paternal line, since equal ownership will be stated hereafter, an unequal division by choice is not appropriate.
"If the father should make a partition"—this refers first to the time when the father has the desire for partition.

There is also another time: even while the father is living, when he is indifferent toward wealth, when his sexual desire has ceased, and when the mother's menstrual flow has ceased, [the partition may occur] solely by the sons' desire, even in the absence of the father's wish.
There is a division [of the estate], as stated by Nārada:
"From this point forward, the sons shall divide the father's wealth equally. (NSm 13.2 variant)
Having thus established the rule for partition after the death of both parents:
"When the mother's menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage, and when the father has ceased from sexual pleasure and his desire has passed away... (NSm 13.3).
Thus it has been shown.
Here, the phrase "the sons shall divide the wealth equally" is to be supplied. Gautama also states: "After the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance" (GDh 28.1).
Having said this, the second period is indicated by the words "and when the menses have ceased" (GDh 28.2);
the third period is indicated by the words "if he lives and desires [her]."

Likewise, even when the mother has reached menopause, when the father is unwilling, when he behaves unrighteously, or when he is afflicted by a chronic illness, partition occurs at the wish of the sons.
As Śaṅkha says:
"If the father is unwilling, there is no partition of the inheritance when he is aged, mentally deranged, or diseased. (DhKo 1148) // 2.114 //
The division [of the estate] by the father's will is shown to be of two kinds: equal and unequal. Regarding that, he states the specific rule for equal division:
"If he should make the shares equal, the wives are to be made sharers of equal portions."
"Nor [is it given] to those women whose woman's property (*strīdhana*) was not given by their husband or by their father-in-law.

(YDh 2.115) When the father, of his own will, makes all his sons equal sharers, then he must also make the wives sharers of a portion equal to that of the sons— provided that those wives whose woman's property was not given by their husband or by their father-in-law.
Regarding property given by a woman, he will state: "But in the case of what is given [by her], one should assign half" (YDh 2.148).

But when he divides the eldest and the others by means of the "best share" and so forth, then the wives do not receive those best and other shares; rather, from the total mass after the *uddhāra* (preferential shares) has been set aside, they receive equal portions as well as their own respective *uddhāra*.
As Āpastamba says:
"And the household utensils and the ornaments of the wife [belong to him]," so says Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.14.8–9. // 2.115 //
Regarding the two positions—that the eldest shall receive the best portion or that all shall have equal shares—the author states an exception to both:
"For one who is capable but does not desire [to share], a separation may be made by giving him something. (YDh 2.116ab)

Even for one who is himself capable of acquiring wealth, if he does not desire his father’s property and is unwilling [to take it], the father must nevertheless effect a separation by giving him something— however insignificant or worthless it may be;
this is so that there be no desire on the part of his sons and others to seize the inheritance.
The word "bhūt" [is used].
By the rule, "Or the eldest by the best portion" (YDh 2.114), a division that is either deficient or excessive is shown.
In this regard, in order to prohibit any other unequal division apart from the unequal divisions such as the "extra share" (*uddhāra*) prescribed by the scriptures, he says:

"For those who have been divided with unequal shares, that which was made by the father is declared to be lawful. (YDh 2.116cd) If this unequal division of sons who have been divided by means of unequal shares is lawful—that is, if it is prescribed by the scriptures—[then it is valid].
In that case, it is recorded by Manu and others that a debt contracted by a father is indeed settled and does not persist;
however, the intention is that otherwise, even a debt contracted by a father may be set aside.
As Nārada says:
"A father who is diseased, or angry, or whose mind is attached to sensual objects, or who acts contrary to the scriptures, is not competent to effect a partition. (NSm 13.15*) 2.116.
Now he states the time for partition, the other party entitled to it, and the rule regarding its manner:

"After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally. (YDh 2.117ab) By the phrase "after the death of both parents," the time is indicated as being after the passing away of both the mother and the father.
By the word "sons," the agents [of inheritance] are shown;
by "equally," the restriction of the mode [of division] is indicated;
and by "equally indeed," it is meant that they shall divide both the estate and the debt.
Now, having begun with the words, "After both the father and the mother" (MDh 9.104), it continues:
"The eldest alone, however, shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety."
"The remaining [sons] should depend upon him just as they would upon their father.
Having said this, it was further stated:
"The eldest shall receive an extra portion consisting of one-twentieth of the entire estate and whatever is the most excellent among all the goods."
"Half of that shall belong to the middle one, and a fourth to the youngest.
(MDh 9.112) From the entire collection of property, the twentieth part, as well as whatever is the best among all the goods,
must be given to the eldest.

Half of that—the fortieth part—is the middling property, which should be given to the middle son; and a fourth of that—the eightieth part—is the inferior property, which should be given to the youngest son. Thus, regarding the division after the death of the parents, the sage Manu has shown the rule for the preferential allotment (*uddhāra-vibhāga*). Likewise:
But if their shares have not been set aside, this distribution of portions shall apply:
the eldest son shall take one share in excess, and the next younger brother shall take one and a half.

"Each younger brother shall receive a share; such is the established law. (MDh 9.116–17). Thus, even apart from the *uddhāra* (preferential share), an unequal distribution is shown for those dividing after the death of the parents: two shares for the eldest, one and a half shares for the one born immediately after him, and one share each for those born subsequently.
Furthermore, in the case of a division during the father's lifetime, an unequal division is shown by the rule itself: "Or the eldest [shall take] the best portion" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114).
Therefore, since an unequal division exists even in every stage [of the father's life], how can it be enjoined that they must divide the property equally?
To this it is replied: True;

although this unequal distribution is seen in the scriptures, nevertheless, because it is loathed by the world, it should not be practiced, for "one should not practice that which leads away from heaven and is loathed by the world, even if it is prescribed by dharma" (YDh 1.156).
This is because of such prohibitions;

for example, even though there is an injunction stating, "One should present a large bull or a large goat to a learned Vedic scholar" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.109), it is not practiced due to being loathed by the world.

Or, for example, although there is an injunction to slaughter a cow as an animal to be bound at the sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa—stated thus: "One should sacrifice a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anubandhyā*"—it is not performed because it is loathed by the world.
And it has been said:
"Neither the duty of the *niyoga* nor even the slaughter of the *anubandhyā* [is to be practiced by us]."
Likewise, even the distribution of the inheritance no longer takes place at present.
Thus [ends the section]. NSP and Pāṇḍeya add a parenthetical statement here,
which was likely intended to...
Explain the citation:
"Without transgressing the injunction, according to the injunction" (*niyogam anatikramya yathāniyogam*);
[this refers to] that dharma which is dependent upon the injunction [and performed] through the brother-in-law (*devarāt*).

"And the birth of a son," and so forth— this does not happen for us. [The phrase] "without transgressing the injunction" (*niyogam anatikramya*) means "in accordance with the injunction" (*yathāniyoga*).
"The dharma dependent on *niyoga*— such as the procreation of a son by a brother-in-law and so forth—
does not exist for us.
Āpastamba also, having stated the equality [of sons] in the rule, "One who is living shall divide the inheritance among his sons,"...

Having presented the taking of the entire estate by the eldest as the opinion of some, saying "the eldest is the heir," and having shown the distribution of the *uddhāra* (preferential share) according to the opinion of others— namely, that in certain regions gold, black cows, black soil, a chariot for the eldest, the father's personal effects, ornaments in the house, the wife's property, and the wealth of paternal kinsmen belong to him— then [the author proceeds].
He rejected that [position] on the grounds that it is contradicted by the scriptures (*śāstra*), as stated in Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.14.1, 5, 6–10.
Manu himself pointed out this contradiction with the scriptures, saying: "It is heard in the sacred texts without qualification that 'one should divide the inheritance among one's sons.'"
Therefore, although an unequal division is seen in the scriptures, it must not be practiced because it contradicts worldly custom and contradicts the revealed texts;
thus, it is ordained that they shall divide [the estate] equally.
It has been stated that sons shall divide the wealth of their mother and father;
regarding that, he states an exception concerning the mother's property:
"The daughters [shall take] the remainder of the mother's [property] after the debt. (YDh 2.117c)

The daughters shall divide the mother’s property. This refers to the case where the daughters divide the mother’s wealth that remains after the discharge of debts— that is, the remainder left over from the clearing of debts incurred by the mother— whether that wealth be equal to or less than the debt.
This is what is meant: a debt incurred by the mother must be repaid by the sons alone, not by the daughters;
however, the daughters may take the wealth remaining after the debt has been cleared.
This is logical, for it is said:
"A male is born when the semen of the man predominates; a female when that of the woman predominates" (MDh 3.49);
thus, there is a greater abundance of female constituents in daughters.
The property of a woman goes to her daughters;
the property of a father goes to his sons,
because the paternal elements are more abundant in sons.
And in this regard, Gautama has shown a distinction:
"The woman's property belongs to the daughters who are unmarried and unsettled" (GDh 28.24).
The meaning of this is: when there is a coexistence of married and unmarried daughters, the woman's property belongs exclusively to those who are unmarried.

And among those who have been given in marriage, when there is no co-residence between those who are settled and those who are unsettled, it belongs to the unsettled alone; "unsettled" means those who are destitute.

To address the question of who should take the mother’s property remaining after the discharge of debts in the absence of daughters, he says: "In their absence, the lineage. (YDh 2.117d) In the absence of those daughters—that is, in the absence of daughters—the "lineage," meaning the son and others, shall take it.
And this, which is already established by the rule "the sons shall divide [the estate] after the parents" (YDh 2.117), has been stated for the sake of clarity. // 2.117 //
He states what is not subject to partition:
"That which is acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through friendship or received at marriage, shall not belong to the heirs. (YDh 2.118)

If one recovers property that was lost and subsequently found, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what is obtained through learning. Furthermore, [the following are not subject to partition]: what is acquired by oneself without depleting the estate of the mother and father, what is obtained from a friend (maitra), and what is received at marriage (audvāhika).

Whatever is obtained through marriage and the like shall not belong to the brothers who are heirs. However, if any property that has come down by succession from the paternal line has been seized by others and was not recovered by the father or other ancestors due to incapacity or similar reasons, whichever son recovers it with the consent of the others [shall have it].

One should not give that [share] to the heirs, such as brothers and others; rather, the restorer alone shall take it. In that case, the restorer receives a fourth part of the field, while the remainder is to be divided equally among all.
As Śaṅkha has said: "If one person recovers land that was previously lost, others shall receive their shares in due order after he has given them a fourth part. (DhKo 1207)
The phrase "arrived in due course" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Likewise, that which is obtained through learning— whether by the study of the Vedas, by teaching them, or by explaining the meaning of the Vedas—
one should not give even that to the heirs.
Arjaka alone shall take it;
and in this context, the phrase "whatever has been acquired by oneself" is to be understood as applying to everything, provided it does not conflict with the paternal estate.
Consequently, whatever has been acquired through friendship, provided it does not conflict with the paternal estate, [belongs to him].
That which is received as a wedding gift without detriment to the paternal estate, and that which has been extracted from the paternal estate by inheritance without detriment to it;
The phrase "what is obtained through learning without detriment to the paternal estate" is to be connected with each [of the preceding categories].
Likewise, that which is acquired through friendship without conflict with the paternal estate or by way of a return favor, as well as that which is obtained in marriages such as the Āsura and others;

Likewise, whatever has been acquired by means of paternal wealth that was inherited or extracted, as well as whatever has been obtained through learning acquired at the expense of paternal wealth— all that must be shared by all the brothers.
And it must be divided by the father; furthermore,
because the phrase "without conflict with the paternal estate" applies to everything, even what is obtained through a gift must be divided without conflict with the paternal estate.

Furthermore, if this [term "self-acquired"] did not apply to all remaining cases, then statements such as "that which is obtained from a friend" or "that which is obtained through marriage" would not need to be commenced.

Alternatively, these statements regarding friends and so forth may be intended to ensure that what is obtained from a friend and the like remains indivisible, even if it conflicts with the paternal estate.
It is stated that [the name] must have a meaning;
if that were so, there would be a contradiction with established practice,
as well as a contradiction with the statement of Nārada regarding what is obtained through learning.
"He who maintains the family of a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself is unlearned. (NSm 13.10).
Likewise, Kātyāyana has stated the definition of the wealth acquired through learning which is not subject to partition:
"Furthermore, whatever wealth is obtained through a science acquired from another by means of subsisting on the food of others—that is called 'wealth acquired through science'. (KSm 867).

Likewise, if the phrase "without detriment to the paternal estate" were a separate sentence [from the preceding rule], then the non-divisibility of what is obtained through a gift (*pratigraha*) would contradict established custom (*ācāra*).
This very point has been clarified by Manu:
"That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
as well as that obtained through learning, one need not give to the co-heirs" (MDh 9.208).

"By labor" means through service, warfare, and so forth. Now, it should not be said that "wealth obtained through friendship and the like, provided it does not conflict with the paternal estate, is indivisible," because there is no possibility of its being subject to partition [in the first place].
It is most well known that whatever is obtained by someone belongs to that person alone and not to another;
furthermore, negation is preceded by prior acquisition.
In this regard, someone states the following rule for acquisition:
"When the father has died, whatever wealth the eldest son acquires,
a share therein belongs to the younger brothers, provided they are observers of their studies" (MDh 9.204).

[The opponent argues: "Whether the eldest, the youngest, or the middlemost—whether the father has died or not—by the explanation that this applies to those younger and older [than the eldest], it follows that the property of Maitra and others is subject to partition both while the father is alive and when he is dead; thus, what was previously established is now being prohibited.
This is incorrect, for here there is no prohibition of something that had been established; rather, this is merely a restatement of what is already settled.
In this section, the statements are for the most part merely restatements of what is already established in the world. Or else:
"But whatever is obtained by those who have come together, all of them shall have equal shares therein" (BṛSm 1.26.18).
May you be satisfied that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously established.
Therefore, the notion that there is a general application (*prāpti*) to the statement "when the father has died" regardless of whether the eldest son or others are intended is mere delusion.
Consequently, by means of the statements regarding friendship and so forth...
It should be explained that the statement "whatever [property] of the father, whether acquired before or after [marriage]," is an exception to the rule regarding property designated as divisible.
Likewise, Manu has stated other things that are indivisible:
"Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, and women."

"Yoga and kṣema, as well as [items] currently in use, are declared to be indivisible. (MDh 9.219) Thus, regarding garments already worn, there is non-divisibility: whatever was worn by whom belongs to that person alone.
This applies to garments worn by the father.
But when dividing the estate after the father's death, these must be given to the recipient of the *śrāddha*:
as Bṛhaspati has said:
"The clothing, ornaments, bed, and so forth, as well as the vehicle and other belongings belonging to the father..."
"Having honored [the recipient] with perfumes and garlands, one should present them to the eater of the *śrāddha* meal.
(BṛSm 1.26.60) However, new garments must indeed be divided. As for vehicles—such as horses, palanquins, and so forth—that too [is to be divided], provided that it was ridden by [the deceased].
That [property] belongs to him alone;
however, ancestral property is just like clothing.
But in the case of a plurality of horses and so forth, it belongs to those who subsist on their sale.
It is indeed subject to partition;
however, regarding unequal partition, the eldest [son] shall never divide goats, sheep, or one-hoofed animals unequally.
For it is stated in the legal tradition of Manu: "Goats, sheep, and one-hoofed animals are ordained for the eldest alone" (MDh 9.119).
Likewise, whatever ornament was worn by whom belongs to that person alone.
That which was not worn [by the woman] is common property and must indeed be divided:
"The ornaments that may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide; those who do divide them fall" (MDh 9.200).
Because of the specific mention of the phrase "it should be worn as an ornament," it is understood that those items not so worn are subject to partition.
Cooked food—such as rice, sweetmeats, and the like—is also not to be divided; rather, it should be consumed as the circumstances permit.
Water refers to a reservoir of water such as a well and the like;
and that, being of uneven value, cannot be divided by means of its price, but must be used in turn.

Female slaves, even if they are of unequal value, are not to be divided by way of their price; they should be made to perform labor in turn. However, those kept by the father—such as unchaste women and others—even if they are of equal status [to the master], [are not to be divided].
For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Gautama: "They are not to be divided by sons; and there is no division among women who are united [in marriage]. (GDh 28.47).
"Yoga and kṣema" is "yogakṣema.

By the word *yoga*, there is indicated the performance of *iṣṭa* rites— actions accomplished through the fires prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis— which serve as the cause for the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained.
By the word "security" (*kṣema*), pure acts such as giving outside the sacrificial altar, constructing tanks, gardens, and so forth— which serve as the cause for protecting what has been acquired—
are indicated. Both of these, even if ancestral and even if acquired in opposition to the paternal estate, are indivisible.
As Laugākṣi said:
"Those who see reality declare that security, purity, yoga, and what is desired are indivisible; and they say that these, as well as bedding and seating, are likewise indivisible. (DhKo 1233)
Some say that by the term *yogakṣema* are meant the king, ministers, priests, and others who provide security and prosperity;
others say it refers to the royal umbrella, fly-whisks, weapons, sandals, and so forth. *Pracāra* is the path for entering and exiting houses, gardens, and other such places.
That too is indivisible. As for what was stated by Uśanas regarding the indivisibility of land:
"It is indivisible among those of the same lineage, even up to a thousand families."

"An object to be sacrificed for, a field, a vehicle, cooked food, water, and women"—this refers to the case of sons born to a Brāhmaṇa from wives of the Kṣatriya and other castes; [it does not apply to land received as a gift], for it is said:
"Land obtained through acceptance as a gift must certainly not be given to a son of the Kṣatriya or other castes."
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Even if their father should give [the property], the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife shall take it when he is deceased" (BṛSm 1.26.121).
*Yājyam* refers to that which is obtained through the act of officiating at sacrifices.
It will be stated that what is obtained through the favor of a father is indivisible;
meanwhile, the indivisibility resulting from the violation of a rule has just been refuted.
It is established that what is acquired in contradiction to the paternal estate is subject to partition;

in that regard, the acquirer receives two shares according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "And he among them by whom something has been acquired by himself shall receive two shares" (VaDh 17.51). // 2.118 // 2.119 //
He states an exception to this:
"But when there is a joint undertaking for a common purpose, an equal division is ordained" (YDh 2.120ab).
This refers to the case where undivided brothers, by means of agriculture, trade, and so forth, engage in a collective enterprise for the sake of a common property and cause it to increase properly.
When [the property] was acquired by someone else, the division is indeed equal; the acquirer does not receive two shares.
The partition of the paternal estate among sons has been shown;
now he states the specific rule regarding the partition of the grandfather’s estate among grandsons:
"But for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to their fathers. (YDh 2.120cd)

Although the grandsons possess ownership over ancestral property by virtue of birth no differently than their fathers, nevertheless, the allotment of that ancestral property for them occurs solely through the mediation of their fathers, not by reference to their own individual status.
This is what is meant.
When undivided brothers have fathered sons and then passed away— such that one has two sons, another three, and another four— in this inequality among the sons, the two take one paternal share each,
the other three also take one paternal share, and the four likewise take only one paternal share.
Likewise, when some sons are living while others have perished after being born, this same principle applies: those who are living receive their own shares,
and even for those who have perished, their sons receive the paternal shares.
Such is the rule established by scriptural injunction. 2.120.

Now, when the father has already divided his estate or is no longer present, there is no division of the grandfather's property for the grandson; for it has been stated that "while the father is not deceased, the allotment of shares is according to the father" (YDh 2.120).
Or, anticipating the objection that it might be like property acquired by oneself—occurring solely through the father's will—he says:
"Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, or a fixed deposit, or even wealth itself;
in that case, the ownership of the father and the son shall indeed be equal. (YDh 2.121)

Land refers to fields of rice and the like. A fixed deposit (*nibandha*) refers to specifying that in one bundle of leaves there are this many leaves, or likewise, in one bundle of betel nuts there are this many nuts.
Regarding "betel nuts" and so forth, the definition has already been stated.

As for property such as gold, silver, and the like, which was acquired by the grandfather through gifts, victory, or other means—since it is a matter of worldly renown that ownership over such property belongs to both the father and the son, there is a partition of it. Indeed.
Since that [share] is similar and equal, therefore the partition is not by the father's will alone, nor is there a double share for the father.
Consequently, the rule "the allotment of shares is according to the father" (YDh 2.120) is a mere textual prescription, even though ownership is equal.
The rule "If the father should make a division" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.114) refers to property acquired by himself; likewise:
"When dividing [the estate], the father shall take two shares for himself" (Nārada Smṛti 13.12).

This [rule] also concerns property acquired by oneself. Furthermore, the statement, "Even when his parents are alive, he shall be dependent, even if he is advanced in years" (NSm 1.32), refers to dependence regarding property acquired by the mother and father.
Likewise, this [verse] "for they have no authority while the parents are alive" (MDh 9.104) also applies;
as does the case where the mother has her menses and the father is desirous [of intercourse], even though he does not wish for the partition.
The division of ancestral property occurs according to the wish of the son;
likewise, when ancestral property is being given away or sold by an undivided father, the grandson has the right to object even if he is not yet divided from him.
However, there is no authority to prohibit [the use] of what was acquired by the father,
because it is dependent upon him;
nevertheless, his consent must be obtained.

For instance, although ownership in what belongs to one's father and grandfather arises by birth alone, nevertheless, in the case of what belongs to the father, it is subject to the father's authority;
and since the father is primary as the acquirer, [the ownership] is determined by the father.

When property acquired by oneself is being employed [for a purpose], the son must give his consent; however, in the case of ancestral property, the ownership of both is indistinguishable, and thus the distinction is that he has the authority to prohibit its use. Manu also says:
"But whatever paternal property a father may acquire which was previously unobtained, he need not share that with his sons unless he so desires, as it is self-acquired. (MDh 9.209).

This means that if a father recovers ancestral property that was acquired by his grandfather but seized by someone else and not reclaimed by the grandfather, that is considered self-acquired by the father.

By stating that "one should not divide [the estate] oneself against one's will even with the sons," this shows that even if one is unwilling, one may divide the property acquired by the grandfather together with the sons at the desire of the sons. (2.121)
To the question, "How can there be an allotment for a son born after the time of partition?", he says:
"A son born after partition from a wife of the same caste is a sharer in the partition" (YDh 2.122ab).
This means that a son born subsequently from a wife of the same caste when the sons have already been partitioned is entitled to a share in the partition.
"Vibhāga" means that which is divided (*vibhajyate*). One who partakes in the division of the parents is "an heir to the partition" (*vibhāgabhāk*).
[This refers to] their share after the death of the parents.
The meaning is that she receives [it]; and the mother's share [is hers] when there is no daughter,
because it has been stated that "the daughters of the mother [take] the remainder."
But one born of a woman of a different caste receives only his own share from the paternal estate,
while the entire maternal portion belongs to him;
this very point was stated by Manu.
"But one born after the partition shall take only the paternal wealth" (MDh 9.216).

This should be explained as "paternal" (*pitrya*) meaning "belonging to the parents. "The elder brother born before the partition has no authority over the share of his brother born after the partition" (BṛSm 1.26.55).
According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),

the meaning is that in the case of a partition between parents who have already divided their property, one born before the partition is not an owner [of the share], and one born after the partition is not an owner of the brother's share.

Likewise, whatever is acquired by the father after the time of partition belongs exclusively to the son born after partition— that which was acquired by the father himself while living separately from his sons.
For it is stated in the legal tradition (*smṛti*): "All that belongs to one born after partition; the earlier-born [brothers] are declared to have no authority over it.
And those who, having been separated by their father, have reunited with him—with them together shall the son born after partition divide the inheritance after the father's death.
As Manu has said:
"Or those who may have been touched by him, he shall divide [the property] with them" (MDh 9.216).
Since the sons have already divided the estate after the father's death, how is the distribution to be determined for one born subsequently? To this, he says:
Or rather, its division shall be from what is visible, after it has been cleared by income and expenditure.

When the father has died and the time for the brothers' partition has arrived, even for one born after the brothers' partition while the mother’s pregnancy was not yet apparent, there is a division [of the estate].
To the question "From what does that division [arise]?", he says:
from the visible wealth taken by the brothers; of what kind? From that which has been cleared of income and expenditure.
Income is that which arises every day, every month, or every year;
expenditure is the repayment of debts incurred by one's father.
Having set aside from that [total] what remains after being cleared by means of those two—income and expenditure—[one should perform the rites].
A share of that should be given.
This is what is meant:
from among their respective individual shares, the income arising therefrom [should be given].

Having caused [the son born after partition] to enter [the family], and having removed the debt incurred by the father, one should set aside a small portion from each of the shares belonging to the remaining brothers so that the share of the son born after partition is made equal to their own shares;
and this applies when he was without offspring at the time of the division.
It should be understood that this applies even to one born after the partition, provided his brother’s wife was not yet visibly pregnant; however,
if she was visibly pregnant, the partition must be made only after waiting for her delivery.
As Vasiṣṭha has said: "Now follows the partition of inheritance among brothers;
and as for those women who are childless, [the property of] theirs [is held] until the birth of a son" (VaDh 17.40–41).
It should be understood that for those who have conceived, the waiting period lasts until delivery. (2.122)
It has been stated that the son born after partition (vibhaktaja) inherits all the paternal and maternal wealth.
In that regard, if the father or mother, though already divided, gives ornaments or other gifts to a son out of affection, then by that [act], the son born after partition—
He states that one must neither prohibit a gift nor take back what has been given:
"Whatever was given by his parents shall remain the property of that [recipient] alone" (YDh 2.123ab).
This refers to ornaments and other such items given by the mother and father—whether they were previously divided or not—to a son who was already divided from them.
That very thing does not become the property of one born after partition;
by parity of reasoning, even prior to partition, whatever was given to whom belongs to that person alone.
Likewise, in the absence of partition, it should be understood that when the parents divide their shares after death,
whatever was given to whom belongs to that person alone and not to anyone else.
Regarding the division during the father's lifetime, it was stated that wives are entitled to shares equal to their own sons in such passages as, "If he should make the shares equal" (YDh 2.115).
To demonstrate that even in a division after the father’s death, wives have shares equal to their own sons, [the author] says:
"When they divide after the father’s death, the mother also shall take an equal share" (YDh 2.123cd).

After the father—that is, after the father's death—when they are dividing [the estate], the mother shall also take a share equal to that of her own sons, provided that her woman’s property (*strīdhana*) has not been given to her;
however, it will be stated later that if it has been given, she is entitled to half a share. (2.123)
If the father has died and there are brothers who have not yet been consecrated, then who is authorized to perform their consecration? To this he says:
"But those who are unconsecrated are to be consecrated by the brothers who have already been consecrated" (YDh 2.124ab).
When brothers divide the estate after the father's death, those brothers who have not yet undergone the sacramental rites must be consecrated by their brothers using the collective property.
Regarding sisters who have not been consecrated, he states a specific rule:
"And the sisters, having received a fourth part from their own share... (YDh 2.124cd).
The meaning of this is as follows: sisters who have not been consecrated must be consecrated by their brothers.
Having done what?
Having [taken] from their own shares.
Having given a fourth part;
by this it is understood that daughters also are entitled to a share after the father's death.
In this regard, the meaning is not that "from his own share" means that a fourth part should be given after setting aside [a portion] from each individually allotted share.
However, she should be made to receive a fourth part of the share belonging to a son of the same caste as herself. This is what is meant:
if that girl is a Brāhmaṇī, then she shall receive a fourth of whatever share belongs to a Brāhmaṇī son.
A fourth part belongs to her;
for example, if a certain Brahmin has one wife and a son.

If there is one son and one daughter, he should divide all the paternal property into two parts; having divided one of those parts into four, he should give a fourth part to the daughter, and the son shall take the remainder.
But when there are two...

Then, having divided all the paternal wealth into three parts, they divided one part into four and gave the fourth share to the daughter; the remainder was then divided between the two sons, who took it.

Now, if there is one son and two daughters, then the paternal wealth should be divided into three parts; having divided one part into four and given two shares from that to the two daughters, the son takes all the remainder— thus it is among those of the same caste.
This principle should be applied to brothers and sisters alike, whether they are equal or unequal [in status].

However, when there is one son of a Brāhmaṇa woman and one daughter of a Kṣatriya woman, the paternal estate shall be divided into seven parts; then, having divided the shares of the Kṣatriya son into four parts, [the daughter shall receive two of those parts].

Having given a fourth part to the daughter of a Kṣatriya, the son of the Brāhmaṇī takes the remainder. However, where there are two sons of Brāhmaṇīs and one daughter of a Kṣatriya, the paternal wealth is divided into eleven parts, and from among those, three shares are for the portion of the Kṣatriya’s daughter.
Having divided [the estate] into four parts and given a fourth part to the Kṣatriya daughter, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇī shall divide and take all the remainder.
In this way, regarding the inequality of birth among brothers and sisters— whether their numbers are equal or unequal— it should be inferred in all cases.

Nor is it appropriate to explain the phrase "having given a fourth part from his own share" as meaning that he gives only enough wealth for the sake of the sacraments, while disregarding the intended meaning of a fourth share.
Because it contradicts the words of Manu:
"The brothers shall give to their unmarried sisters portions from their own shares;
each shall give a fourth part of his own share, for those who refuse to give would become outcasts" (MDh 9.118).

The meaning of this is as follows: brothers who are Brāhmaṇas and others should give to their sisters—the Brāhmaṇī and so forth—from their own respective shares prescribed for their own castes, a fourth part from each of their own portions, according to what will be stated later, beginning with "the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares. They should thus give a fourth part from each of their individual allotments.

And it is not stated here that a fourth part should be given by taking [a portion] from one's own share; rather, from each individual share prescribed for one's own caste, a fourth part is to be given separately to each individual girl. Thus, the method of distribution has already been explained for cases where there is inequality of caste as well as inequality in number.
Since it is heard that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for failing to do so— expressed as "those who do not wish to give would become outcasts"— the necessity of giving is understood.

If it is argued here too that the mention of the "fourth part" is not intended, and that what is intended is merely the giving of whatever substance is required for the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), we say no.
Furthermore, there is no evidence to suggest that the giving of a fourth part is not intended in both Smṛtis, and it is heard in scripture that there is sin in failing to give it.

As for what some say— that if there is no intention to convey the distribution of portions, it would follow that a woman with many brothers would possess much wealth while a man with many sisters would be destitute—
that has already been refuted by the method previously stated.
For here it is not stated that a gift of a fourth part is to be made after setting aside a portion from one's own share, by which [the latter] would be the case;
therefore, the interpretation of Medhātithi and others, who hold that [the son] has no companion [in the inheritance], alone is correct, and not that of Bhāruci.

Therefore, after the father's death, even a daughter is entitled to a share; however, if she receives whatever her father gave her previously, she obtains that alone, as there is no specific statement to the contrary—thus all is faultless. (2.124)

By the continuous passage beginning with "If the father should thus make a division" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.114), the rule for the mutual division among brothers of the same caste, as well as the arrangement of division with the father,
has been stated. Now, he describes the division for those of different castes.
The sons of a Brāhmaṇa [father] shall have four, three, two, and one shares respectively according to their caste;
those born of a Kṣatriya [father] shall have three, two, and one shares; but those born of a Vaiśya [father] shall have two and one shares. (YDh 2.125) [This follows from the rule:
"Three [wives] in the order of the castes... (YDh 1.17).

Thus, four wives are shown for a Brāhmaṇa, three for a Kṣatriya, two for a Vaiśya, and one for a Śūdra. In this context, "born of a Brāhmaṇa" means born from a Brāhmaṇa; by the word *varṇa*, women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes are denoted. Furthermore, because the numeral is in the singular, it implies repetition according to Pāṇini 5.4.43 (*saṃkhyekavacanāc ca vīpsāyām*).
Thus, from the singular number of the substratum (adhikaraṇa) kāraka, the suffix *śas* is applied in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
Consequently, those born as Brāhmaṇas in each respective caste shall receive four, three, two, and one shares respectively.
This is what is meant:
those born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother each receive four shares per person.
From that same [Kṣatriya], those born of a Kṣatriya woman each produce three, those born of a Vaiśya woman two each, and those born of a Śūdra woman one each.
Those born of a Kṣatriya woman are produced by a Kṣatriya.
The phrase "according to caste" (varṇaśaḥ) carries over [from the previous rule], meaning they consist of three, two, and one parts respectively.
Those born from a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya mother each produce three [offspring] per category.
Two each from a Vaiśya woman,
and one each from a Śūdra woman;
these are the Viḍjas, born of a Vaiśya father.
In this case as well, the phrase "according to caste" (varṇaśaḥ) is understood to carry over; they receive two shares each in due order.
Those born from a Vaiśya father and a Vaiśya mother each receive two shares.
In the case of a Śūdra wife, there is one share each;
since for a Śūdra there is only one wife, there is an absence of sons from different castes, and therefore the division for his sons is exactly as previously stated.

Although it has been stated without qualification that [the shares] are four, three, two, and one parts respectively, this should nevertheless be understood as referring to lands other than those acquired through inheritance (*pratigraha*). For so they record in their legal tradition (*smṛti*):
"Land acquired through acceptance as a gift (pratigraha) must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if the father should give it, when he is dead, the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take it.
(Bṛhat-Smṛti 1.26.121) By the term "acceptance," land obtained by purchase and other means certainly belongs even to the sons of Kṣatriya wives and the like.
And because of the specific prohibition regarding the son of a Śūdra woman:
"One born of a Śūdra woman by twice-born men does not deserve a share of land" (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.26.122).

If land acquired through purchase and other such means were not available to the sons of Kṣatriyas and others, then the specific prohibition regarding the son of a Śūdra would be untenable. As for the further statement:
"The son of a Śūdra is not an heir to the property of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas."

"Whatever his father might give him, that alone shall be his wealth" (MDh 9.155). This also refers to the case where something has been given by the living father to the son of the Śūdra wife; however, when there is no such gift out of favor, it is not contradictory for [the son] to receive one share. 2.125.
Now, something remaining after all divisions is stated:
"If any property is seen that was previously concealed from one another, they shall divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule. (YDh 2.126)

The established rule and the limit of the scriptures is this: property belonging to the collective that was mutually misappropriated, or which was unknown at the time of partition but is discovered after the paternal wealth has been divided, shall be shared in equal shares;
by stating "in equal shares" here, the practice of unequal distribution (uddhāra-vibhāga) is prohibited.
By stating that "they should divide [the property]," it is shown that what is seen by one person must not be taken by that very same person.
Thus, since the statement possesses meaning in this way, it does not intend to convey the absence of fault in the misappropriation of collective property.

But surely, Manu has shown that the fault lies only with the eldest when he misappropriates the common property, and not with the younger brothers: "The eldest who, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers—let him not be considered the eldest and let him be deprived of his share; he must be restrained by the kings" (MDh 9.213).

This is not so, because by stating the fault even of an eldest brother who stands in the place of a father and possesses presumed independence, [the author] implies— by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpika)— that younger brothers who stand in the place of sons are dependent upon their elder.
See Jacob, *A Handful of Popular Maxims* (Bombay 1907), Part I, p. 29. The fault has indeed been demonstrated all the more clearly.
And likewise, a fault is heard [in the scriptures] without any distinction.
(NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: Gautama;
however, this citation is not from the GDh.)
"Not so," says Seltur. "He who deprives a sharer of his share, and excludes him from it—if he does not exclude him in this life, then he excludes his son, or else his grandson" (AitB 6.7;
DhKo 1570). He who deprives a sharer—one worthy of a share—of his share, who sets him aside from his portion, and does not grant him a share.
He, having been driven out by his share, ruins this [other co-heir]—that is, he destroys him and makes him guilty.
If he does not destroy him, then he destroys his son or grandson; thus, even without the distinction of being the eldest, one who misappropriates common property [is liable].
The fault has been heard. Now, it may be thought that common property, being one's own as well, does not entail a fault when it is taken with the notion that it belongs to oneself.

That is incorrect. Even when one perceives something by one's own cognition, because it is unavoidable that another's property is also perceived therein, the entry of a prohibition certainly brings about a fault.
For example, when a dish of mudge beans has been spoiled and māṣa beans are taken up because of their similarity, the prohibition—"Māṣa beans are indeed unfit for sacrifice"—does not apply.

When the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) stated, "Because it is apprehended by the cognition of the parts of a mung bean," the respondent (rāddhāntin) replied that when the parts of the mung bean are apprehended, the beans of black gram (māṣa) are also necessarily apprehended; thus, the prohibition indeed applies. Therefore, it is established that there is certainly a fault in the theft of a common substance, both according to the scriptural statement and according to reason. 2.126.

Showing the specific share of the son of two fathers (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), he describes his nature: "A son begotten by appointment (*niyoga*) in the field of another by one who has no son is, according to the law, the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both. (YDh 2.127)

"Authorized by his guru, [he shall procreate] for one who has no son" (YDh 1.68)— according to the rule stated in such passages, a son begotten upon the wife of another (the *parakṣetra*) by a brother-in-law or similar kinsman through the appointment of a guru is, according to dharma, the heir (*rikthin*), the taker of the inheritance (*rikthahārī*), and the giver of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍadātā*) to both the progenitor (*bījī*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). This is the meaning.

When that appointed man—such as a brother-in-law (*devarādi*)—himself being childless, engages in intercourse with the wife of one who is childless for the sake of producing a son either for himself or for another, the son whom he begets has two fathers; he belongs to both lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), and he is the heir to the estate and the offerer of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*) to both. But when the appointed man already has a son and exerts himself solely for the sake of a son for the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), then the son born from him belongs to the owner of the field alone.
Thus, he becomes the son of the woman and not of the seed-giver;
and he does not necessarily inherit the estate of the seed-giver, nor is he bound to offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for him,
as stated by Manu:

"Because of the acceptance of the [procreative] act, that field which is given for the sake of seed—of that, two are seen here as sharers: the owner of the seed and the owner of the field. (MDh 9.53).
Regarding the phrase "because of the acceptance of the act," this refers to the formal agreement: "Let the offspring born [from this union] belong to both of us."

When a field is given by the owner of the field to the sower for the purpose of sowing seed, the great seers have observed that both the sower and the owner of the field are the sharers and owners of the offspring produced in that field. Thus:
"But the fruit [is shared] by the owner of the field and the sower, provided no other intention has been formed."
"The visible wealth belongs to the owner of the field; the womb is stronger than the seed" (MDh 9.52).
Regarding the phrase "without intending [for] fruit":
this refers to that which is produced in another's field without such an intention as, "Let the offspring born here belong to both of us."
The offspring that is produced belongs to the owner of the soil alone,
because the womb is stronger than the seed, as is observed in the case of cattle, horses, and other such animals.
In this case as well, the practice of *niyoga* applies only to the woman who has been verbally betrothed (*vāgdattā*),
because *niyoga* for any other [widow] has been prohibited by Manu.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring.

Having thus introduced the practice of *niyoga* with the words: "But one appointed to a widow, anointed with clarified butter and restrained in speech, shall procreate a single son at night; by no means a second. (MDh 9.59–60).
Manu himself prohibits this:
"A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma."
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed anywhere in the ritual rules for wedding ceremonies.
Indeed, this practice of treating humans like cattle was censured by learned brahmins when Vena ruled the kingdom. It was declared [as such] even for human beings.
In former times, that preeminent royal sage, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social orders, his mind being struck down by lust.
"From that time forward, virtuous men indeed censure him who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of offspring. (MDh 9.64–68).
Nor should it be thought that this constitutes an option (*vikalpa*) because [the practice] is both prescribed and prohibited.
Because one hears of the censure of those who employ [women],
and because one hears of the many faults of infidelity among the duties of women.
And because self-restraint is highly praised,
as Manu himself has said:
"One may indeed emaciate the body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits."
"But she should not even take the name of another man once her husband has died" (MDh 5.157).
Having thus prohibited resorting to another man for the sake of livelihood, [the text continues]: "She should remain patient, self-restrained, and chaste until death."
That supreme Dharma which those women whose husbands are living yearn for.
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for the continuity of their lineage.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates.
"But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world" (MDh 5.158–61).
Thus, [the text] prohibits resorting to another man even for the sake of obtaining a son.
Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that there is an option (vikalpa) because [the action] is both prescribed and prohibited.
Since the practice of *niyoga* with women who have undergone the sacrament of marriage has thus been prohibited, [the author] asks: "What then is the lawful *niyoga*?
and answers: "If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true..."
Her brother-in-law shall take her for himself according to this procedure.

"Having approached her according to the prescribed rule—she who is clad in white garments and observes pure vows—he shall enjoy her in private once in each season until the birth of a child. (MDh 9.69–69).
From this very statement, it follows that he to whom a girl has been verbally betrothed is her husband even without a formal acceptance (*pratigraha*).
It is understood as follows:
when he has died, his uterine brother—whether the eldest or the youngest—should take [the widow] for himself, that is, marry her.
Having approached and married her according to the rule and according to the scripture, by this procedure involving anointing with ghee, verbal restraint, and so forth.

He should approach his wife in private during each season, once [per cycle], until conception, provided she is dressed in white garments, observes pure vows, and is restrained in mind, speech, and body. Furthermore, this marriage is scripturally enjoined as being part of the practice of approaching the wife according to the rule, just like the observances such as anointing with ghee.
Thus, it does not establish the status of being a wife for the brother-in-law;
therefore, the offspring born from her belongs only to the owner of the field (the husband), and not to the brother-in-law.
But by means of consciousness, [the cognition] belongs to both as well. // 2.127 //
The method for dividing the inheritance among sons of both similar and dissimilar castes has been stated.
Now, intending to demonstrate the rules regarding the inheritance of primary and secondary sons, he first describes their respective natures.
The *aurasa* (legitimate son) is born of the lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*).

The *kṣetraja* (son of the field) is one begotten on the wife by a kinsman of the same *gotra* or by another. The *aurasa* son is he who is born from the breast (*urasa*), and he is born of the lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). A "lawful wife" is one of the same caste (*savarṇā*) who has been wedded according to the religious rites (*dharma-vivāha*).

The son born of her is the primary *aurasa* (legitimate) son. Equal to him is the *putrikāsuta* (son of an appointed daughter); that is, equal to the *aurasa*, the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*). For this very reason, he is equal to the *aurasa*.
As Vasiṣṭha said:
"I shall give you this unbrothered maiden, adorned;
whatever son is born of her, let him be my son. (VaDh 17.17)

Alternatively, a "son of an appointed daughter" (*putrikāsuta*) is indeed a son; he is equal to a legitimate son (*aurasa*), because the paternal elements are few while the maternal elements are abundant.
As Vasiṣṭha says:

The third [reading], *dvitīyaḥ*, found in NSP and several manuscripts (see Seltur, p. 690), means "the son is indeed a daughter. See the previous note. The meaning is that the son is indeed a daughter.
But the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* is inferior to the biological son (*aurasa*) of the progenitor because he was born in the field of another.
As for the *kṣetraja*: "The *kṣetraja* is one born in the wife's field by a man of the same *gotra* or by another.
A son produced by another man who is a *sapiṇḍa*, or by the husband’s brother-in-law (*devara*), is a *kṣetraja*. (2.128)
A son born secretly in the house is known as the *gūḍhaja* (secret-born) son;
a son born of an unmarried girl is considered the *kānīna* (maiden-born) son, the son of the maternal grandfather.
The *gūḍhaja* son is one born in secret within the husband's house, avoiding the possibility of being fathered by a man of either lower or higher caste.

This should be understood as applying when there is certainty regarding being born of a woman of the same caste (*savarṇa*), even if there is no certainty regarding being born of a specific type of man. However, a *kānīna*— one born of an unmarried girl— is, as before, the son of the maternal grandfather among women of the same caste,
provided she remains unmarried.
Likewise, if she remains in her father's house,
then when she is married, the son belongs to the husband alone;
as Manu has said:

"A son whom a maiden bears in secret in her father's house, one should call by the name *kānīna* (maiden-born); he originates from the maiden, not from the husband. (MDh 9.172) A son born of a woman who has been remarried—whether she was previously virgin or not—is called *paunarbhava*.

Whomever the mother or the father may give away, that son becomes a *dattaka* (given son). A *paunarbhava* son, however, is one born from a woman who has been married again (*punarbhū*), whether she be one who was previously unwedded (*akṣatā*) or one who was wedded (*kṣatā*), by a man of the same caste,
with the permission of her husband or her mother.
When the husband has gone abroad or is deceased, he whom the father, or both [parents], bestow upon a man of the same caste is his *dattaka* son. As Manu says:
"In times of distress, the mother or the father may give away a son with a libation of water."
"One who is similar [in qualities] and endowed with affection is to be known as an adopted son" (MDh 9.168).
Because of the mention of "distress," he should not be given away when there is no distress;
this is a prohibition against the giver.
Likewise, an only son must not be given away;
for Vasiṣṭha has recorded: "One should never give away an only son, nor should one adopt him" (VaDh 15.3).

Likewise, even when there are many sons, the eldest should not be given away; for, as it is said: "By the mere birth of the eldest, a man becomes the father of a son" (MDh 9.106), he alone is primary in performing the duties of a son.

And regarding the method for adopting a son, Vasiṣṭha has stated: "One intending to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen, announce it to the king, and having offered oblations with the Vyāhṛtis in the middle of the house, he should adopt one who is not distant in kinship— that is, one closely related by blood" (VaDh 15.6).
The phrase "not having distant relatives" is a prohibition against one who is extremely remote in terms of locality or language;
this same principle should be applied to those who have been purchased, those given by themselves, and those who are artificial (kṛtrima).
Because the principle is the same. // 2.130 //
One who is purchased from those two [parents] is a "purchased" son; one who is sold by them, or made so by himself, is an "artificial" (kṛtrima) son.

One who gives himself away is a "self-given" (svayandatta) son; one conceived in the womb and taken along [at birth] is a "son received with the bride" (sahoḍhaja). A "purchased" son is one who has been bought from those two, the mother and father, or from the mother or the father alone, as previously described.
Excluding the eldest son, in times of distress, one may take even a son of equal caste (*savarṇa*).
As for that which was stated by Manu:
"But he who, for the sake of offspring, shall purchase [a son] from his mother and father..."
"He is his purchased son, whether similar or dissimilar [to him]" (MDh 9.174).
This should be explained as meaning "similar or dissimilar" in terms of his qualities (*guṇa*), not in terms of caste (*jāti*),
because it is stated that "this [rule] is declared regarding sons among those of the same caste" (YDh 2.133).
Because of this summary [of the categories],
the "artificial" (*kṛtrima*) would be one made by oneself:
the artificial son is one who has been adopted as a son by one desiring a son, solely through inducements such as the offering of wealth, land, and so forth.
One who is bereft of parents is so because he is dependent upon them for his very existence.

A son who has given himself, however, is one who is bereft of parents or abandoned by them, and who has come forward of his own accord, saying, "I shall be your son. This is what constitutes being self-given.
But the son born of a woman married while pregnant is the *sahoḍha*; he who is begotten by the husband after she has been married is the son of the one who wed her. (2.131)
But he who is taken up after having been abandoned shall be an *apaviddha* son.
An *apaviddha* is one who, having been cast off by both mother and father, is taken up; he becomes the son of the one who takes him up, provided he is of the same caste (*savarṇa*) in all cases.
Having thus enumerated the primary and secondary sons, he states the order of their inheritance:
"Among these, each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and takes the share in the absence of each preceding one.
(YDh 2.132cd). Among these twelve previously mentioned sons, in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is the performer of the śrāddha.
"He should be understood as the one who takes the portion and the one who takes the wealth.
Since it would follow that the legitimate son alone receives the wealth when he coexists with the *pautrikeya* (the son of an appointed daughter), Manu states this exception:
"But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed [as an heir], the division of the property shall be equal there, for there is no seniority for a woman. (MDh 9.134).
Likewise, even when the preceding ones exist, the subsequent sons have a right to a one-fourth share.
Vasiṣṭha has stated:
"If a legitimate son (aurasa) is born after that [adopted son] has been received, the adopted son (dattaka) shall be entitled to a fourth share.
The mention of the "adopted son" is intended to illustrate those such as the purchased (krīta), the made (kṛtrima), and others.
Because there is no distinction in the act of adoption;
and so Kātyāyana says:
"But when a legitimate son (aurasa) has been born, the [adopted] sons are entitled to a fourth part."
"But those of the same caste and those of different castes shall receive food, clothing, and a vessel.

(KSm 857) Those of the same caste—such as the *dattaka* (adopted son), the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife), and others—in the presence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*), are entitled to a fourth part of the inheritance.
Those of different castes are the *kānīna* (maiden-born), the *gūḍhotpanna* (secretly born), the *sahoḍha* (born with the mother), and the *paunarbhava* (son of a remarried woman).
However, when a legitimate son (aurasa) exists, they do not receive a fourth part of the inheritance, but rather are entitled only to food and clothing;
as for the statement of Viṣṇu:
"But those born of an unmarried girl, those born in secret, and those born of a pregnant bride are unworthy [of inheritance]."

"And these [sons], including the *paunarbhava*, do not at all share in the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) or the portion of the inheritance" (DhKo 1390)— this too is intended solely to prohibit the fourth share when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) exists; however, in the absence of the legitimate son and the others, the *kānīna* and the rest [are entitled to it].
Furthermore, there is indeed the entitlement to take the entire paternal estate, according to the scriptural statement: "In the absence of the preceding, each subsequent one [inherits]."
As for the statement of Manu: "The legitimate son alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide a livelihood. (MDh 9.163)
Thus, that [rule] also should be understood to apply when the adopted son (dattaka) and others are opposed to the legitimate son (aurasa) or lack good qualities;
in that regard, a specific rule concerning the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) has been shown by that same author.
"But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son of the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share. (MDh 9.164).
When both hostility and lack of virtue are combined, he shall receive a sixth share.
It should be discerned that the fifth [alternative] applies when either one [of the two conditions] exists. Furthermore,
although Manu presents two groups of six sons, he states that the first group of six consists of both heirs and kinsmen (*dāyādabāndhava*),
while the latter group of six consists of kinsmen who are not heirs (*adāyādabāndhava*).

It has been stated: "The legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the adopted son (datta), the made son (kṛtrima), the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna), and the cast-off son (apaviddha)— these six are both heirs and kinsmen."

"The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with a bride (*sahoḍha*), the purchased son (*krīta*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the self-given son (*svayaṃdatta*), and the son of a Śūdra woman (*śaudra*)— these six are non-heirs but kinsmen" (MDh 9.159–60).
This [text] also refers to the first group of six [sons] in cases where there is an absence of other nearer heirs who take the inheritance among one's own paternal *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*.
However, that inheritance-holding status does not belong to the latter group of six;

rather, it should be explained that kinship— consisting in the performance of duties such as the offering of water through common lineage (*gotra*) and *sapiṇḍa* relationship— is equal for both groups.
"In the lineage and inheritance of the progenitor, the adopted son shall not share;
the funeral cake follows the lineage and inheritance, and the *svadhā* offering ceases for one who gives [him away]. (MDh 9.142).
In this passage, the mention of the "adopted" (*datrima*) son is intended to illustrate the principle of a substitute for a son.
However, the right to inherit the father's wealth belongs to each preceding one in the absence of the preceding among all [heirs], for it is said:
"Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs to the estate of the father" (MDh 9.185).
This is because [the text] is intent on establishing that all substitutes for a son, with the exception of the *aurasa* (legitimate son), are entitled to inherit property;
whereas regarding the *aurasa*, it says:
"The *aurasa* son alone is the master of the paternal wealth" (MDh 9.163).

Because inheritance (*rikthabhāktva*) has been stated by this very [verse], and because the word *dāyāda* is well-known— based on such passages as "one should also cause the *dāyādas* to pay"— as referring to those who share in the inheritance other than the son;

furthermore, in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* and other texts, where there is a transposition of reading in both groups, it should be understood as referring to those who possess qualities and those who do not.
However, the enumeration of the *pautrikeya* as the tenth in the Gautama-dharma-sūtra (GDh 28.32–35) refers to the case of a different caste (*vijātīya*).
Therefore, it remains established that [the succession of heirs] occurs in the absence of each preceding one.
"The other [son] is a sharer of the highest portion. As for that which was said:
"If among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, Manu has declared that they are all possessed of a son by means of that son" (MDh 9.182).

Thus, even that [statement] is intended to prohibit the adoption of others when the adoption of a brother’s son is possible; it is not, however, for the purpose of establishing his status as a son, because that would contradict the rule: "His sons are kinsmen belonging to the same lineage. (2.132)
Now, under the guise of a conclusion to what has been said, he states a restriction regarding that very point:

"This rule has been declared by me for sons of the same caste; in the absence of the preceding, each subsequent one [is the heir]. This stated rule applies only to sons of the same caste, not to those of different castes. (YDh 2.133ab) This procedure—whereby each succeeding son inherits in the absence of the preceding—is prescribed for sons belonging to the same caste, and not for those of different castes.

And in that regard, the status of being of the same caste (*savarṇatva*) for those born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), those born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*), those born while the mother was pregnant (*sahoḍha*), and those born of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), is established by way of their progenitor (*janaka*) and not by their own nature;
for it has been stated that they lack the defining characteristics of caste and birth (*varṇajāti*).
Likewise, among the *aurasa* (legitimate) sons, this applies to those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others.

Since they are included therein, it should be understood that in their absence, the *kṣetraja* and other sons are entitled to inherit the estate; however, even if he is the legitimate (*aurasa*) son of a Śūdra woman,
he does not receive the entire share even in the absence of others.
As Manu said:
"Whether there be a legitimate son or even if there be no son at all, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman. (MDh 9.154)

Whether there be a legitimate son (satputra)— meaning a son of a twice-born woman— or whether he be sonless (aputra)— meaning no son of a twice-born woman exists— if such a person dies, then a *kṣetraja* son or any other *sapiṇḍa* shall not give more than a tenth part of that wealth to the son of a Śūdra woman;
from this very rule, it is understood that in the absence of a son of the same caste (*savarṇāputra*), the sons of Kṣatriya and Vaiśya mothers are entitled to take the entire estate.
Now he states the specific rule regarding the division of a Śūdra’s wealth:
"Even one born of a Śūdra’s slave woman shall, if born of desire, be a sharer of the inheritance;
when the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share. (YDh 2.133cd)

A son born of a Śūdra man to a female slave may, by the father's will and out of affection, receive a share; after the father's death, he shall take the entire estate in the absence of a brother, except for the sons of daughters. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.134)
But if there are sons born of wedded wives, then those brothers shall make that son of a slave-girl a recipient of half a share;
the meaning is that they shall give him half of their own shares.
However, if there are no sons born of wedded wives, then [the slave-son shall receive] the entire wealth.
The son of a female slave shall take [the property] if there are no daughters born of a wedded wife nor their sons; however,
when they do exist, the son of a female slave is entitled to only a one-half share.
And here, because of the mention of the Śūdra, one born to a twice-born man from a Śūdra slave-girl does not receive a share, nor even half, by the father's will,
much less the whole.
But if he is favorable, he receives merely his subsistence. 2.133–2.134.
It has been established that the primary and secondary sons inherit the estate;
in their absence, the order of succession for all heirs is now declared:
the wife, the daughters, the parents, and likewise the brothers.
His son, a kinsman of the same lineage (gotra), a relative, a pupil, and a fellow student—
on the absence of each preceding one among these, the succeeding one is the heir to the wealth.
This rule applies to all castes regarding one who has died without a son.

He who does not possess the twelve types of sons previously mentioned is "sonless" (*aputra*). When such a sonless man has departed this world and gone to the next, the one among these enumerated heirs— beginning with the wife— who is the first in the absence of each preceding one, is the inheritor and receiver of the wealth.
The connection is that "each subsequent one receives a greater share of the wealth.

This rule for the taking of inheritance, as well as the order of succession in taking inheritance, is to be understood as applying to all—among those born in the natural order (anuloma) such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, among those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and among the social classes (*varṇa*) such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth. In this regard:
First, the wife is an heir to the property;
for it is recorded in tradition that "the wife is one who has been consecrated by the marriage sacrament for the sake of her husband's connection with the sacrifice" (Pāṇini 4.1.33).
And the singular number is used with reference to the genus;
and if they are many— whether of the same kind or of different kinds— they take the wealth by dividing it according to their respective shares.

Vṛddha-Manu also declares the wife’s connection to the entirety of the wealth: "The wife alone, preserving the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows, shall offer his funeral cake and receive the whole share. (DhKo 1527)
Vṛddha-Viṣṇu also states: "The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to the wife;
in her absence, it goes to the daughter;
in her absence, it goes to the father; in his absence..."
Regarding the phrase "it goes to the mother," Kātyāyana also says:
"The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall be the taker of his wealth."
"But in his absence, if there should be a daughter who is unmarried, then [she shall inherit].
Likewise:
"In the case of one without a son, the wife born of a noble family, or even daughters..."
"In their absence, the father, mother, brother, and sons are declared [to be the heirs]. Bṛhaspati also says:
"While paternal kinsmen—fathers, brothers, and uterine relations—are present..."
"The wife of one who has died without issue shall take his share.
Sentences such as these appear to be contradictory:
"If among brothers someone should die without offspring, or should renounce the world..."
The remaining [sons] shall divide his property, excluding the woman's separate property (strīdhana).
"And they should provide for her maintenance until the end of her life;
if they preserve their husband’s bed, [they share], but otherwise, they may take [the property] from the others.
Thus, Nārada has stated that even when a wife exists, the brothers take the wealth while the wives receive only maintenance. However, by Manu:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves" (MDh 9.185);
thus it is shown that the wealth of one without a son belongs either to the father or the brother. Likewise:
"The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who is childless."
"Furthermore, when the mother has passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth. (MDh 9.217).
