Thus, the connection to the wealth of both the mother and the paternal grandmother is shown.
Śaṅkha also states:
"For the property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers;
in their absence, the parents shall take it, or the eldest wife.
Thus, the succession to the wealth is shown to proceed in order among the brothers, the parents, and the eldest wife.
Kātyāyana also says:
"When [the estate] has been divided and the [owner] has passed away, in the absence of a son, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the mother of that [father], in that order. (KSm 928)

Regarding such statements of contradictory meaning, Dhāreśvara has shown the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*): the collection of texts stating that "the wife shall take [the property]" refers to the case of the wife of a brother who has been partitioned;
and she may do so provided she is desirous of *niyoga*.
Whence is this [conclusion] derived— that the wife's taking of the wealth depends upon her being appointed (*niyoga*) and not when she is independent?
Since there are such scriptural injunctions as "the father shall take the property of one who has no son" (MDh 9.185), the grounds for establishing this distinction must be stated.

And because of the statement of Gautama: "There is no other cause for the determination [of inheritance]; those related by *piṇḍa*, *gotra*, or *ṛṣi* shall divide the estate of one who has no offspring, or the wife shall take the estate if she desires to provide seed" (GDh 29.5–6).

The meaning of this is: those related by *piṇḍa*, *gotra*, or *ṛṣi* shall divide the estate of one who has no offspring, or the wife shall take the estate if she desires to provide seed. Manu also says:
"Whoever shall maintain the wealth and the wife of his deceased brother,
having procreated offspring for that brother, shall give that very wealth to that [offspring]"—
by this [verse], he demonstrates the following:
Even when a brother has died after the property was divided, the wife's connection to the wealth occurs only through her offspring and not otherwise;
this applies even in the case of divided property.
"If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder, the division of property there shall be equal; such is the established law. Thus [says Manu 9.120].
Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also states: "There is no [practice of] *niyoga* out of greed for inheritance" (VaDh 17.65).

Thus, by prohibiting *niyoga* out of greed for inheritance, [the author] demonstrates that the wife's connection to her husband's property occurs only through *niyoga* and not otherwise. Even in the absence of *niyoga*, the wife is entitled to mere maintenance according to the statement of Nārada:
"They shall provide maintenance for her until the end of her life" (NSm 13.25).
Indeed, it is said by the Lord of Yogins:
"The childless wives of these [deceased brothers] who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained; likewise, those who are unchaste or hostile shall be banished. (YDh 2.142)

Moreover, because the wealth of the twice-born belongs to them in its true sense, and because women lack the entitlement to perform sacrifices, it is improper for them to take that wealth. Thus, it has been stated by someone: "As for the wealth produced for the sake of sacrifice, those who are not entitled to it therein..."
They all share in no inheritance; they are entitled only to food and clothing.
"Therefore, one should employ wealth ordained for the sake of sacrifice in places approved by dharma, and not among women, fools, or those who act contrary to dharma.
This [assertion] is untenable.
In the passage beginning "the wife, the daughters," there is no perception of *niyoga* (appointment for procreation), nor is it relevant to the context.
Furthermore, this must be stated here: is *niyoga* the cause for the wife's acquisition of wealth, or is it the offspring born from it?
In that case, if the appointment (niyoga) alone were the cause, it would follow that even a woman who has not yet given birth to a son would have a connection to the property;
whereas for a son who has already been born, there is a connection to the property [by virtue of his birth].
It does not obtain;
for if that offspring alone were the cause [of the inheritance],
then, because the wealth would belong to the son alone, [the father would receive nothing].
The objection that "the wife" should not be mentioned [in the rule] is incorrect.
If it is argued that the connection of women to wealth occurs only through the husband or through the son, and not otherwise—
that too is false.

This is because it would contradict such [scriptural] passages as: "That which is given before the fire, that which is given at the wedding procession, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is received from a brother, a mother, or a father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman" (MDh 9.194).
Furthermore, since the text begins with "In the total absence of sons, the wife, the daughters," etc.,
by stating that the woman appointed [for levirate] has a connection to the property, it follows that the connection to the property is stated for the *kṣetraja* son alone.
And since that has already been stated previously in the section on those without sons—namely, "the wife"—it need not be restated here.
Furthermore: "The sonless man's property shall be inherited by those connected by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), the lineage (gotra), or the ancestral sages (ṛṣi), or by his wife."
Based on the statement of Gautama, "Or she may seek [her husband's] seed" (GDh 28.21–22), it is argued that the woman appointed for procreation has a connection to the property;
however, that too is incorrect.
For this meaning is not understood from this [text]: "If she should desire to take up the seed (bīja), then the wife of one who has no offspring shall take the wealth.

Rather, the meaning is that the kinsmen related by the funeral cake (piṇḍa), the lineage (gotra), or the seer (ṛṣi) shall divide the wealth of one who has no offspring; or else, as for that wife, there is an instruction regarding another duty for her: "either she [the wife] shall desire to take up the seed, or she shall remain self-restrained (saṃyatā)."
Because the word "vā" (or) expresses an alternative position, the sense of "if" is not perceived [thereby].

Furthermore, it is only appropriate for a *saṃyatā* (a widow remaining faithful) to take possession of the wealth, and not for a *niyuktā* (one appointed for procreation), who is censured by the *smṛtis* and the world.
"A sonless woman, protecting the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vow..."
"The wife alone shall give that funeral cake and receive the entire share"—
thus, the taking of wealth by the *saṃyatā* alone has been stated.
Likewise, such an appointment was condemned by Manu:
"A widow must not be appointed to another [man] by members of the twice-born classes;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma" (MDh 9.64).

By such statements as these, the declaration of Vasiṣṭha—"There is no *niyoga* due to greed for inheritance" (VaDh 17.65)—is to be explained as follows: when the husband has died, whether he was undivided or reunited, she has no connection to his wealth; therefore, *niyoga* should not be performed for the sake of establishing a connection to the wealth for her offspring.
As for the statement of Nārada,
"And they should provide for his maintenance until the end of the women's livelihood" (NSm 13.25),
that too—
"But the share of those who are reunited is intended for them alone" (NSm 13.23); since those who are reunited are the subject under discussion,
this [verse] is intended solely to establish that women who have no offspring are entitled only to maintenance.

Nor should one suspect redundancy with the rule "and among brothers, he who dies without offspring" (NSm 12.24) on the grounds that it refers to the case of reunited coparceners, since the rule "but as for the share of those who are reunited" (NSm 13.23) already addresses that matter.
For, by the explanation of what was stated previously, it is ordained that the property of women is indivisible and that they are entitled only to maintenance; this is also expressed in the verse:
"And the childless wives of these... (YDh 2.140).
It will be stated that such statements refer to women who are eunuchs and the like;
as for the argument that it is improper for women to take wealth because the wealth of the twice-born is intended for sacrifice and women have no entitlement to sacrifice— that is incorrect.
If all types of wealth were intended solely for the purpose of sacrifice (*yajña*), then acts such as giving (*dāna*) and oblation (*homa*) would not be established.

If it is argued that the word "sacrifice" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of *dharma* in general, and therefore there is no contradiction in [wealth] being for that purpose since giving and oblation are also *dharma*, then in that case, wealth—which is the means for accomplishing *artha* (prosperity) and *kāma* (pleasure)—would simply never be accomplished. This being so, [the following applies]:
"One should not neglect dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability" (YDh 1.115).

Likewise: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, and afternoon pass fruitlessly, but should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability" (GDh 9.46). Similarly: "These [virtues] cannot be restrained in that way without practice" (MDh 2.96).
This contradicts such statements by Yājñavalkya, Gautama, and Manu.

Furthermore, since wealth is for the purpose of sacrifice, the statement that "gold must be worn" establishes its status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) by refuting its common sacrificial utility (kratvarthatā);
that [position] has now been overturned.

It might be so. Furthermore, if the word *yajña* is intended as an indicator for *dharma* in general, it is even more appropriate that women have the right to receive wealth, since they too possess the entitlement to perform *pūrta* (charitable) duties.
As for the statement regarding their dependence—namely, "A woman does not deserve independence" (MDh 9.5)—it refers to her lack of autonomy in worldly affairs.
Let such dependence as that be granted; however, what contradiction is there in accepting wealth?
How then is the statement "wealth has arisen for the sake of sacrifice" and so forth to be understood?
It is said:
that wealth which has been acquired specifically for the purpose of sacrifice must be employed for sacrifice even by one's sons and others; such is the intent of that [text].
For one who does not give what was obtained for the sake of sacrifice may become a vulture or even a crow. (YDh 1.127)
Thus, because the hearing of these defects applies without distinction to sons and others;
and as it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "The property for which there is no heir, the wife's property, the servants' property, and the funeral rites shall go to the king."
"Having set aside the property of a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), one should bestow that upon other learned Brahmins.
Thus, wealth that has no heir—that is, which is devoid of a claimant—goes to the king; likewise, the property of women, servants, and funeral rites [belongs to the king].

The connection is as follows: having set aside that which is used for the food and clothing of women, and having excluded the wealth intended for the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) of the deceased and that used for the *śrāddha* and other ceremonies of another, it goes to the king.
The exception to this is stated in the second half of the verse.

Regarding the rule that "one should bestow upon a learned Śrotriya the property of another Śrotriya, as well as the property of a woman, of a servant, or for funeral rites (aurdhvadehika)," this too refers specifically to the case of a woman who is under the protection [of others], because of the use of the term *yoṣit* (woman).
And the words of Nārada:
"Except for a Brahmin, however, a king devoted to dharma shall provide a livelihood for their wives; this is declared to be the rule for inheritance. (NSm 13.49)
Thus, [the previous rule] refers exclusively to women who have not been married, because of the use of the word "woman" (*strī*);
here, however, because of the word "wife" (*patnī*), it refers to one who has been wedded and is restrained.
The taking of the wealth is not contradictory;
therefore, the meaning established is that when a man who is divided and not reunited has died without a son, his wife takes the property first.
Because partition has already been discussed and because the case of reunited coparceners (saṃsṛṣṭin) will be explained later,
it should be understood that the claim by Śrīkara and others— that this rule concerns only cases involving small amounts of wealth— is thereby refuted.
For it is so even when legitimate sons (aurasa) exist during a lifetime partition.
Furthermore, regarding the division of the estate of one who has died, it is stated that the wife shall take a share equal to that of a son:
"If [the father] should make [the distribution], the wives are to be made sharers of equal portions" (YDh 2.115).
Likewise:
And [it is stated]: "When dividing [the estate] after the father's death, the mother shall also receive an equal share" (YDh 2.123).
This being so, the wife of one who has died without a son does not obtain more than what is necessary for her maintenance from his wealth.
This is merely a delusion. Now, regarding the passages "the wives shall receive equal shares" and "the mother also shall take an equal share," [it is as follows:]
The view that a woman takes only the wealth necessary for her maintenance is incorrect, because it would result in the word "share" (aṃśa) and the word "equal" (sama) being rendered meaningless.
It might be argued: "In the case of great wealth, she takes the wealth necessary for her maintenance, but when the wealth is small, she takes a share equal to that of a son."
And that is not so, because it would entail an inconsistency in the injunctions.

For instance, the statements "wives shall be made sharers of equal portions" and "the mother also shall take an equal share" establish [equal shares] with reference to another scriptural passage concerning the maintenance of life when there is abundant wealth; however, in the case of meager wealth, [they receive only what is necessary for subsistence].
[The opponent argues that] he bestows a share equal to that of a son’s portion.

Just as in the case of the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, regarding the statement "they lead forward [the fire] for two," the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) demonstrates a prohibition of the *uttaravedi* altar—stating "they do not scatter the *uttaravedi* in the *vaiśvadeva*, nor in the *śunāsīrīya*"—as the reason for the extension (*atideśa*) of the *saumika-praṇayana* (the leading forward of the fire from the *sadas*). Then, the partial proponent of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*) states that this [prohibition] does not apply to the *uttaravedi* obtained through the extension of the *saumika-praṇayana* during the first and last *parvan* festivals.
As for the prohibition:

when it has been stated that this is a prohibition of the *uttaravedi* (high altar) which was established by the contextual statement "they strew [the grass] here," the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) further objects that the statement "they strew here" prohibits [the altar] in the first and last *parvan*s.
It is shown that there is a discrepancy in the injunctions: in the case of the two outer [carts], one reaches the *uttaravedi* with reference to the partial [altar],
whereas for the two middle ones, one reaches the *uttaravedi* independently, as if it were a permanent rule (*nityavat*).

Even in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), out of fear of an inconsistency in the injunctions, it has been shown that the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* for the first and last *parvan*s is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*); rather, based on a consideration of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "they carry [the fire] forward for two," the rule "they strew [the grass] here" enjoins the *uttaravedi* specifically for the middle two *parvan*s, namely the Varuṇapraghāsa and Sākamedha.
Furthermore, it is held that this is because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves. (MDh 9.185)
Likewise, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "For when one has died without a son, the property goes to the brothers; in their absence, the parents shall take it, or the eldest wife."

It follows from the rule, "The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to his brothers," and from such statements as, "They shall provide maintenance for his wives until the end of their lives," that it is established that the wife receives the portion of wealth necessary for her maintenance.
This being the case,
when a wealthy man dies without a son, the wife takes what is necessary for her maintenance, and the brothers take the remainder; however,
when there is only enough wealth to cover the wife's maintenance, or even less than that, [the brothers take it all].

In that case, since there is a conflict as to whether only the wife inherits or whether the brothers do so as well, the passage beginning with "the wife, the daughters" was commenced to indicate that the preceding [rule] is stronger.
However, the venerable Teacher does not accept even this, because:

Because of the traditional legal text stating, "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves" (MDh 9.185), this statement is not intended to prescribe a specific order of succession; rather, it merely demonstrates the eligibility for the acquisition of wealth. That...
He explained that [the rule] applies even when the group consisting of the wife and others is absent;
furthermore, he maintained that the statement of Śaṅkha also refers to the case of reunited brothers (*saṃsṛṣṭabhrātṛ*).
Moreover, from this statement and from the context, it follows that its scope is limited.
Or rather, it is not understood;

and as for the statement "each subsequent one is the heir to the wealth," since it requires another sentence—"the wife, the daughters"—for its application to two distinct cases, it follows that it refers to small amounts of wealth, whereas in the case of the father and others, it refers to wealth in general. Thus, the previously mentioned discrepancy in the injunction remains exactly as stated.
This is of little consequence;
however, as for the statement of Hārīta:
"If a widow who has reached the prime of youth becomes harsh..."
"But then, for the sake of exhausting her lifespan, she should be given a means of subsistence"—
this [statement] also has the purpose of prohibiting the seizure of all her wealth in the case of a woman whose infidelity is suspected;
it is precisely from this very text [that this is understood].
The seizure of the entire property is understood to apply to a wife whose infidelity is not suspected;
it is with this very intention that Śaṅkha stated, "or the eldest wife. The "eldest" is one who is senior in virtue and whose infidelity is not suspected.
She takes all the wealth and protects even another [stepmother], though she be harsh, as if she were her own mother; thus, everything is irreproachable.
Therefore, for one who has died without a son, having been partitioned and not reunited with his brothers—
It is established that a wedded wife who is self-restrained takes the entire estate;
in her absence, the daughters [inherit].
The use of the plural number in "daughters" refers to those of both the same caste and different castes.
This is for the purpose of obtaining equal or unequal shares.
And so Kātyāyana says:
"The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall be the heir to his wealth."
"But in his absence, if there should be a daughter who is unmarried, then [she inherits]. Thus says Bṛhaspati as well:
"The wife is declared the heir to the husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is so declared."
From limb after limb of men, a daughter is produced just like a son.
"Therefore, how could another man take the father's wealth? (BṛSm 1.26.126–27).

In that regard, when there is a concurrence between a married and an unmarried daughter, the unmarried one alone takes it; but in her absence, if there is a daughter who is unmarried, then she [takes it]. (BṛSm 1.26.128)
Thus, because of this specific traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*):

"In the case of a combination of settled and unsettled daughters, the unsettled one alone [inherits]; in her absence, the settled one; the property of a woman belongs to the unmarried and the unsettled daughters" (GDh 28.24).

Since this statement of Gautama applies equally to the paternal estate as well, it should not be considered that this refers specifically to the case of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*); for in the section on sons, both the appointed daughter and her son are declared to be equal to the legitimate son (*aurasa*), in the passage: "The son of an appointed daughter is equal to him [the father]."
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that in the absence of a daughter, the daughter's son (dauhitra) is the heir to the wealth.
As Viṣṇu has stated:
"In the absence of a lineage of sons and grandsons, the daughter's sons shall obtain the wealth."

"But for the ancestors, at the utterance of *svadhā*, the sons of the grandson (*pautra*) and the daughter's son (*dauhitrika*) are considered [the ones who offer]. Thus [says the law]. Manu also says:
"Whether she has been formally appointed (*akṛtā*) or not, whichever son she bears from a man of equal status..."
"The grandson of the daughter shall offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his wealth" (MDh 9.136).
In his absence, both parents—the mother and father—are the sharers of the wealth;
even though, in the case of a simultaneous expression of the substratum (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), [the dual number might suggest otherwise].

Because of the recollection of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), and because the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation is an exception to that, the sequence of the parents is not understood when the term "wealth" (*dhana*) is employed.

Nevertheless, because the word *mātṛ* (mother) is placed first in the compound sentence (*vigrahavākya*), and because in the case where there is no *ekaśeṣa* (elision of one term), the form *mātāpitarau* (mother-and-father) is heard with the word *mātṛ* preceding it, the sequence of meaning is understood from the very sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). Thus, when there is a need for a sequence regarding the connection to the inheritance, it is understood that—in accordance with the perceived sequence—the mother first receives the wealth, and in her absence, the father. Furthermore:
Because the father is common to other sons as well, whereas the mother is not common, she possesses a superior degree of proximity;
therefore, according to the statement, "The nearest sapinda and so forth shall be the heir to the wealth of each respective [deceased]," [the mother inherits].
It is proper that the mother alone should first take the property.
Nor is proximity restricted solely to the *sapiṇḍas*;
rather, since the taking of the property would otherwise apply without distinction even to the *samānodakas* and others, it is precisely this proximity that serves as the regulating factor.
From this very statement it is understood that,
due to the mother's superior proximity to both parents, her taking of the property is more appropriate.
In his absence, the father is the inheritor of the wealth;
in the father's absence, the brothers are the inheritors of the wealth.
And so says Manu:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or the brothers themselves" (MDh 9.185).
Furthermore, as for what Dhāreśvara stated:
"The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who is childless."
Based on the statement of Manu: "And when the mother has passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth" (MDh 9.217),
even while the father is living, if the mother has passed away, the father’s mother— the paternal grandmother— shall take the wealth, not the father.

Since wealth inherited from the father goes to sons even of a different caste, whereas wealth inherited from the paternal grandmother goes only to those of the same caste, it is the paternal grandmother alone who takes it.
The Teacher also does not approve of that,
because it has been stated that even sons of a different caste are entitled to take the inheritance:
"They shall have four, three, two, and one shares" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.125).
Regarding the phrase "and so forth":

as for the traditional teaching of Manu which states, "The property of a Brahmin is never to be seized by the king; such is the established rule" (MDh 9.189), that refers to the intention of the king [to avoid taking it].
But it is not with the intention of referring to sons;
even among brothers, uterine brothers should take first, because those of different wombs are more remote from the mother.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "The wealth of each [deceased] shall belong to his nearest sapinda.
Thus, in the absence of uterine brothers, half-brothers are the heirs to the property.
In the absence of brothers as well, their sons are the heirs to the wealth according to the paternal order; however,
when there is a coexistence of brothers and nephews, the nephews have no right of inheritance.
Because it is stated that the brother's sons have the right [to inherit] in the absence of a brother; thus,
when a brother has died childless, there is a connection to the property for his brothers without distinction.

If, prior to the division of the brothers' wealth, one brother should die, then since the right of his sons arises by virtue of their father, it is logical that when they and the [surviving] brothers divide the property, the allotment of shares shall be according to the father (YDh 2.120). In the absence of even the sons of the brothers, the *gotraja*s (agnates) are the heirs to the wealth.
The agnates (gotrajāḥ), the paternal grandmother, the sapindas, and those related by water (samānodakas) [are entitled to inherit].
Among them, the paternal grandmother is the first to receive the wealth; for it is said: "And when the mother has passed away, the father's mother shall take [the inheritance]" (MDh 9.217).
When the mother’s death immediately follows [the father's], she becomes entitled to take the property;
since the succession of the father and the others, ending with the brother’s son, is fixed in its order, there is no room for their intervention in the interim.
Because the statement, "The mother shall take the wealth of the father" (MDh 9.217), is intended merely to establish her entitlement to receive the inheritance,
[the succession] follows immediately after her son in the case of an advancement in rank.
There is no contradiction in [the rule] that the paternal grandmother takes [the inheritance].
And in the absence of the paternal grandmother, the paternal grandfather and other sapinda relatives born of the same gotra are the sharers of the wealth.
Since those who belong to different *gotras* but are *sapiṇḍas* are included under the term "kinsmen" (*bandhu*),
in that case, in the absence of the paternal line,
the paternal grandmother, the paternal grandfather, the paternal uncles, and their sons shall inherit the property in succession.
In the absence of the grandfather’s lineage,

it should be understood that the inheritance of the property belongs to the great-grandmother, the great-grandfather, his sons, and their sons— in this manner, among those of the same gotra who are sapindas up to the seventh degree.

In their absence, the inheritance belongs to those who share the same water (samānodaka). They should be understood as seven generations beyond the sapindas, or until the limit where birth and name are no longer known.
As Bṛhan-Manu has said:
"Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the state of being Samānodaka ceases at the fourteenth."
"According to some, the lineage (*gotra*) beyond that is said to be the recollection of one's birth and name.
(DhKo 1527) In the absence of those born of the same lineage (*gotraja*), the kinsmen (*bandhu*) are the heirs to the property.
And these kinsmen are of three kinds:
Namely, kinsmen on the father's side, kinsmen on the mother's side, and kinsmen on one's own side. As it has been said:
"The sons of one's father's sister and the sons of one's mother's sister [are kinsmen]."
One's own maternal uncles' sons should also be known as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal relatives (pitṛbāndhava).

"The sons of one's mother's paternal aunts, the sons of one's mother's maternal aunts, and the sons of one's mother's maternal uncles are to be known as maternal relatives (*mātṛbāndhava*). (DhKo 1528–29).
And in that regard, because of their being more proximate (*antaraṅgatva*),...
First, the paternal kinsmen are the heirs to the wealth; in their absence, the maternal kinsmen; and in their absence, the maternal relatives—this sequence is to be understood.
In the absence of kinsmen, the teacher [performs the rite]; in his absence, the pupil;
in the absence of a son, the nearest sapinda; in his absence, the teacher;
and in the absence of the teacher, the resident student (ĀpDh 2.14.2–3).
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba.
In the absence of a disciple, a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārī) is the heir to the property.
A fellow religious student is one who, together with another, has obtained the initiation, the study, and the knowledge of its meaning from the same teacher.
In the absence of such [heirs], any learned Śrotriya may take the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
for there is a Smṛti text of Gautama stating: "The heirs of a childless Brāhmaṇa who is a Śrotriya shall divide his estate. (GDh 28.41).
In the absence of those, any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever [shall inherit].
As Manu has said:
"But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas shall be the sharers of the inheritance."
"Those who possess the threefold knowledge, who are pure and self-controlled—in this way, Dharma is not lost. (MDh 9.188) "The king shall never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
it is an established rule that the property of a Brāhmaṇa must always remain unseizable by the king. (MDh 9.189)
Thus, from the statement of Manu;
and it has also been said by Nārada:
"In the case of property belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, if there is no heir whatsoever upon its loss..."
"It must be given to a Brāhmaṇa alone; otherwise, the king would become guilty of sin. (DhKo 1512).

In the absence of [heirs] beginning with the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*) and ending with the Brāhmaṇa, the King shall take the property of a Kṣatriya or others, not a Brāhmaṇa. As it has been said:
Manu says:
"But in the absence of all others, the king shall take [the property] of the other castes" (MDh 9.189).
It has been stated that sons and grandsons take the inheritance, and in their absence, the wife and others do so;
now he states the exception to both of those rules:
"The heirs to the property of forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students [are as follows]."
In order: the teacher, the virtuous disciple,
the spiritual brother, and the fellow student of the forest-dweller, the ascetic, and the student, respectively— in this reverse order— are the heirs to the wealth of the estate.
The lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) [retains his property];
however, in the case of the temporary student (upakurvāṇa), his mother and other relatives take his wealth.

However, it is stated that the teacher takes the property of a *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate) as an exception to that rule; whereas the property of a *yati* (ascetic) is taken by a good disciple. Furthermore, a "good disciple" is one who is capable of hearing, retaining, and practicing the meaning of the scriptures on the inner self (*adhyātmaśāstra*).

Because even a teacher or similar authority who behaves wickedly is unworthy of a share; as for the property of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), his dharma-brother or a fellow student (ekatīrthin) takes it. A "dharma-brother" is one who has entered the same religious path as a brother.
One who shares the same sacred ford (*ekātīrthin*) and the same stage of life (*ekāśramin*);
and he is both a dharma-brother and one who shares the same sacred ford— thus, "a dharma-brother who shares the same sacred ford" (*dharmabhrātṛ-ekatīrthin*).
In the absence of these [relatives], such as the teacher and others, even if sons and so forth exist, one takes [the inheritance] from only those belonging to the same religious order (*ekatīrthya*).
Is it not said: "But those who have entered another stage of life (*āśrama*) are entitled to no share" (VaDh 17.52)?
According to this Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha, those who have entered other stages of life (āśrama) have no connection whatsoever with inheritance; how, then, could there be a partition of it?
Furthermore, it is not logical for a perpetual student (naiṣṭhika) to have a connection with wealth acquired by himself.
Because of the prohibition against accepting gifts and so forth,
and because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "A mendicant is one who possesses no accumulation" (GDh 3.11).
It is argued that even for a monk, the possibility of possessing wealth acquired by himself does not arise;
first, let us consider the case of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
"According to the statement, 'He should make a collection of wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year;
what has been accumulated should be relinquished in the month of Āśvayuja,' there is indeed a connection with wealth even for the ascetic."
Or he may wear even a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts; likewise, he may take up sandals and the various requisites for yoga practice.
From such statements as these,

there is indeed a connection with clothing and books; even for one who has taken the vow of perpetual celibacy (naiṣṭhika), there is a connection with clothing and so forth for the sake of maintaining the body.
Since it is indeed so, the statement regarding its division is entirely appropriate. // 2.137 //
Now, he states an exception to the rule that the wife and other heirs of a son who has gone abroad (svar-yāta) are the sharers of his wealth:
"But one who is reunited (saṃsṛṣṭin) [inherits] from one who is reunited" (YDh 2.138a).
"Reunited wealth" (saṃsṛṣṭa) refers to divided property that has been mixed together again; one who possesses such property is "reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭin).
And this state of being "commingled" (saṃsṛṣṭatva) does not mean with just anyone, but rather with a father, a brother, or a paternal uncle;
as Bṛhaspati has said:

"Furthermore, one who was previously separated from his father or brother, but later resides together with him— whether with a brother or an uncle— out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭa* (one reunited). Regarding such a *saṃsṛṣṭin* who has died, his share or portion [is to be taken] when his wife was not known to be pregnant at the time of partition, but subsequently...
Upon the birth of a son, the coparcener shall give [the share];
in the absence of a son, the coparcener alone shall take it—that is, he shall receive it—and not the wife or others.
He states an exception to the rule "an associate [inherits] from an associate":
"But a uterine brother [shall inherit] from a uterine brother;
he shall give and take the share of one who is born and of one who has died. (YDh 2.138b–d)
The term "one who has reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭin) is understood to follow from the previous rule.
Therefore, when a reunited uterine brother dies, his reunited uterine brother shall give that share to the son born after the reunion.
"In his absence, he shall take [the property]"—this is to be connected as before.

And thus, in a case of association between uterine and non-uterine brothers, the uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* alone takes the wealth of the uterine *saṃsṛṣṭin*, and not even a non-uterine *saṃsṛṣṭin*; this is an exception to what was stated previously. (2.138)

Now, when a man who lived in joint association has died without a son, and there exist both a uterine brother who was not in joint association and a non-uterine brother who was in joint association, the author states the reason for the divisional appropriation of the property by both of them, as the question arises as to which one should take it:
"But a non-uterine brother who is in joint association shall take the wealth; a non-uterine brother who is not in joint association shall not take it."
Even one who is not reunited may take [the inheritance], but one who is reunited and born of another mother shall not [take it from a brother born of the same mother].
A uterine brother born of a different womb (anyodarya), being reunited, shall take the wealth; however, a brother born of a different womb shall not take the wealth if he is not reunited.
By this positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is stated that for a brother born of a different womb, the state of being reunited is the cause for taking the wealth.
The term "not associated" (asaṃsṛṣṭin) also connects with what follows;
therefore, even one who is not associated may take the wealth of an associate. To the question "Who is that?", he says: "the associate" (saṃsṛṣṭa).
"Associated" means associated by the same womb;
that is to say, a uterine brother.
By this [term], even one who is not [otherwise] associated is included if he is a uterine brother.
The fact of being a brother is stated as the ground for the taking of property;
this [term] "saṃsṛṣṭa" is also connected with what follows. And in that context, "saṃsṛṣṭa" means "one who has reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭin).
He is not one born of another mother.
Here, the explanation should be made by supplying the word "only" (*eva*): even if he is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, if he is indeed born of another mother, he shall not receive the wealth of the *saṃsṛṣṭin*.

And because of the hearing of the word "also" in the phrase "and thus he may also take [the property] even from one not united," and because of the negation of the restriction that "one united [with the father] takes only from one born of another mother," [it follows that] the undivided uterine brother [is entitled to inherit].
It is stated that the property of one whose womb was shared but who is now separated must be divided; for the grounds for each of the two to receive wealth exist individually.
This very point has been clarified by Manu:

Having introduced the division of reunited coparceners with the verse, "Those who, having been divided, live together, should divide again," [the text continues]: "Among those [reunited], if the eldest or the youngest should die before the distribution of shares... (MDh 9.210).
Or even if one of them should die, his share is not lost.
By stating, "The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally;

as well as those brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters," [the author indicates that] among those brothers who are reunited, whether they be the eldest, the youngest, or the middle one, [the division proceeds] from the distribution of shares.
Regarding "at the time of the distribution of shares": the suffix *tasi* has the sense of all case endings; that is to say, it means "at the time of partition."

He would be diminished, falling away from his own share by taking up another stage of life, or he might die through such acts as the killing of a Brahmin; yet his share is not lost. Therefore, it must be set aside separately; the meaning is that the *saṃsṛṣṭins* (those who have reunited) alone shall not take it.
He states the application of that extracted share: "The uterine brothers shall divide it.
This means that the uterine brothers—the *sahodarās*—even if they are not reunited (*asaṃsṛṣṭas*), shall come together and divide that extracted portion, even if they have gone to another country.
Having come together and assembled, the sisters should divide [the property] collectively; having divided it equally, they should take [their shares]. This is the explicit meaning. (2.139)
He states an exception to what was said regarding the inheritance of those who are reunited with sons, wives, and others:

"The impotent, the outcast, his offspring, the lame, the insane, the idiotic, the blind, and those afflicted by incurable diseases and the like, shall be maintained but shall receive no share. (YDh 2.140)
A eunuch is one of the third gender;
an outcast is one who has killed a Brahmin and so forth; "born of such" means born from an outcast.
A cripple is one who is deficient in his feet.
A madman is one overcome by forms of insanity characterized by the afflictions of wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, or possession by spirits.
An idiot is one whose internal organ (mind) is impaired.
This means one who is incapable of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful; "blind" refers to one whose faculty of sight is impaired;
and "afflicted by an incurable disease" refers to one seized by diseases such as consumption (yakṣmā) that cannot be remedied.

By the word "first," there is the inclusion of those who have entered another stage of life (*āśrama*), those who hate their father, those guilty of minor offenses (*upapātakin*), the deaf, the mute, and those deprived of their senses.
As Vasiṣṭha says: "But those who have entered another stage of life are non-partakers [of the inheritance]" (VaDh 17.52). Nārada also says the same.

"One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these, though legitimate sons (*aurasa*), shall not receive a share; how much less so a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*)? (NSm 13.20).
Manu also says:
"Those who have no share [of the inheritance] are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.
(MDh 9.201) "Devoid of sense organs" (*nirindriya*) means one from whom the sense organ has departed due to disease or other causes; such a person is *nirindriya*.
These individuals, such as the impotent and others, are "without shares";
they do not become heirs to the inheritance.
They should merely be maintained by providing food and clothing; for if they are not maintained—
However, there is the fault of being an outcast;
yet, according to the rule, a wise man should give food and clothing to all [outcasts] to the best of his ability, for by not giving these, he himself would become an outcast. (MDh 9.202)
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Manu;
"absolutely" means for as long as one lives.
Since the fault is incurred even prior to the division of these [assets], there is a lack of entitlement to a share.
This applies to what has been produced, but not to that which has already been divided;
for even after the time of division, if the humors are expelled by means of medicine and so forth, there is indeed still the attainment of a portion.
Because of the application of the same legal principle to the verse: "A son born after partition from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share" (YDh 2.122),
the masculine gender used in reference to those such as outcasts (patita) is not intended to be restrictive.
And for this reason, it should be understood that wives, daughters, mothers, and others who are tainted by the aforementioned defects are likewise excluded from inheritance. (2.140)

Since those such as the impotent (klība) and others are excluded from inheritance, it might follow that their sons are likewise excluded; to this [objection], he says: "But their legitimate (aurasa) or soil-born (kṣetraja) sons, being free from defects, are entitled to shares.

(YDh 2.141ab) The sons of these [excluded individuals], such as the impotent and others—whether legitimate or soil-born—who are "free from defects," meaning devoid of defects such as impotence which would otherwise bar them from receiving a share.
They become sharers of the portion, that is, recipients of a share.

Among them, for a eunuch, a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) is possible, while for others, sons of the body (*aurasa*) are also possible. The mention of both the *aurasa* and the *kṣetraja* is for the purpose of excluding other types of sons.
He states the specific rule regarding the daughters of the impotent and others:

"And their daughters are to be maintained until they have been given away to husbands. (YDh 2.141cd) The daughters of these—the impotent and so forth—must be supported until they undergo the sacrament of marriage; this is indicated by the word "and" (ca).
And those who are to be refined. 2.141.
He states the specific rule regarding the wives of eunuchs and others:
"The childless wives of these [men] should be maintained if they are of virtuous conduct; likewise, those who are unchaste or hostile should be expelled. (YDh 2.142)

If the wives of these [categories], such as the impotent and others, are childless but of virtuous conduct and good character, they must be maintained—that is, supported. However, those who are unchaste are to be banished;
likewise, those who are hostile are also to be banished and are not to be supported.
And if they are not unfaithful, one must not fail to provide maintenance for them merely because of their hostility. (2.142)

Having briefly stated the division of the property of both women and men in the verse, "The sons shall divide the property of the parents" (YDh 2.117), the division of the male's property was explained in detail.
Now, intending to explain the division of a woman's property in detail, [the author] first states its nature.
That which is given by the father, the mother, the husband, or the brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire;
and that which is obtained upon supersession—these and others are proclaimed as a woman’s property (strīdhana).

[Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.143] That which is given by the father, the mother, the husband, or the brother, and that which is received at the time of marriage with reference to the sacred fire from maternal uncles and others;
That which is to be stated [later] as "he shall give the *ādhivedanika*— that given for the sake of taking a second wife— to the woman who has been superseded" (YDh 2.148),
and that which is obtained through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or discovery, is this woman's property (*strīdhana*), as indicated by the word "first" (*ādya*).
This was stated by Manu and others.

Furthermore, the term *strīdhana* (woman’s property) is etymological (*yaugika*) rather than technical (*pāribhāṣika*), because when an etymological derivation is possible, a technical definition does not apply.
Because it is illogical.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
"What was given by the teacher, what was received at the wedding, and what was given as a token of affection..."
"Women's property is declared to be of six kinds: that obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father.
(MDh 9.194). Thus, the sixfold nature of women's property is stated for the purpose of excluding a smaller number, not for the purpose of excluding a greater number.
The nature of *adhyagni* and the other forms has been declared by Kātyāyana:
"That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *strīdhana* (woman's property) made *adhyagni*."
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being led away from her father’s house is declared to be the woman’s property known as *adhyāvahanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given for the purpose of honoring one's feet— that is called "gift of affection" (*prītidatta*).
This applies whether it is given by a married woman or by an unmarried girl, even in the house of her husband’s father.
"That which is obtained from a brother or from one's parents is known as *saudāyika*," so it is recorded [in the law]. (KSm 901) // 2.143 //
Furthermore:
"What is given by relatives, as well as the nuptial fee (śulka), and even the subsequent gift (anvādheya)" (YDh 2.144ab).
That which is given by the relatives of the maiden—namely, by her maternal relatives and her paternal relatives.
*Śulka* is that which is given after receiving a bride-price;
*anvādheyaka* is that which is given subsequently, after the marriage ceremony.

And it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage, as well as that property obtained from her father's family, is known as *anvādheya*. (KSm 899)
The phrase "is declared to be women's property" is to be connected with what has preceded.
Thus the property of a woman has been described;
he now states its distribution:
"If she dies childless, her kinsmen shall obtain it. (YDh 2.144cd)

That aforementioned property of a woman, when she has passed away childless—meaning devoid of daughter, daughter’s daughter, daughter’s son, son, or grandson—is taken by her kinsmen, such as the husband and others who will be mentioned hereafter. (2.144)
The general heirs entitled to take the property have been shown; now he states the distinction of heirs according to the difference in forms of marriage:
"In the four [forms of marriage] beginning with Brāhma, the property of a childless woman belongs to the husband."

If she has borne daughters, then [the property] goes to the father among the remaining [sons]. Regarding women who have not borne children— referring to those previously mentioned who have attained the status of wife through the four forms of marriage, namely Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, and Prājāpatya— the aforementioned property belongs first to the husband upon her death.
In the absence of him, it belongs to the sapindas who are proximate to him;
in the remaining forms of marriage— namely the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca— the property of a childless woman [belongs to them].
It goes to the father (*pitṛgāmi*). Since it goes to both the mother and the father, who together are called "the parents" (*pitarau*), it is said to go to the father.
It has already been stated previously that the mother, even though she is mentioned by means of a *ekaśeṣa* compound, takes the property first.
In their absence, those closely related to them shall take the property.
In all forms of marriage, if she has given birth to offspring, that property belongs to her daughters;
here, by the word "daughters," [the following is meant].
The term "daughters' daughters" refers to the granddaughters of one's own daughters; for it has been stated here that the rest belongs to the daughters of the [mother's] mother.
Therefore, when the mother has passed away, the daughters take the mother's property first.
In that regard, when there is a conflict between an unmarried woman and a married woman, the unmarried one alone receives [the inheritance];
and in her absence, the married one.
Even in that case, when there is a conflict between one who is established [in her husband's family] and one who is not established, [the former receives].
She takes [the bride] while standing;
in the absence of that, while standing.
As Gautama said:
"The woman's property belongs to the daughters who are unmarried and unsettled" (GDh 28.24).
In this context, because of the word "and" (*ca*), it also includes those who are settled. "Unsettled" means those who are childless or without wealth. This...
And [this applies] apart from the *śulka*;
for the *śulka* belongs only to the uterine brothers, as it is said:
"The *śulka* of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's death" (GDh 28.25).
According to this statement of Gautama,
in the absence of all daughters, the daughters' daughters take [the inheritance],
based on the scriptural authority that "if the daughters have borne [sons]."

In the case of an assembly of those [widows] who have different mothers and are of unequal status, the allotment of shares is determined by way of their mothers; or, according to the Smṛti of Gautama: "Or, according to each mother, there shall be a specific share for her own group" (GDh 28.17).
In the case of a conflict between daughters and granddaughters, something small should be given to the granddaughters;
as Manu says:
"Those who may be their [the daughters'] daughters, to them also [something] should be given according to their merit."
"Something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth out of affection. (MDh 9.193).
In the absence of the daughters of the daughter as well, the sons of the daughter (dauhitrāḥ) are the heirs to the wealth;
as Nārada has said:
"In the absence of the mother, [the inheritance goes to] the daughters; in the absence of the daughters, their offspring.
Since the word "their" (*tat*) refers back to the daughters mentioned in proximity, in the absence of the daughters' sons (*dauhitrāṇām*), the sons take [the inheritance]. From them...
Because it has been stated that there is no inheritance [for others] in the absence [of these].
Manu also demonstrates the connection of daughters and sons with their mother’s wealth: "But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers [shall divide it] equally."
"Those born of the same womb [the brothers] and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother's inheritance. (MDh 9.192).
The connection of the words is as follows: "All uterine brothers shall divide the mother's inheritance equally, and the uterine sisters shall likewise divide it equally."
The connection is that "the uterine brothers shall not divide [the inheritance] equally, nor shall the uterine sisters divide it equally";
it does not mean that the uterine brothers and sisters together shall divide it, because that would imply a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
Because there is no non-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), [the meaning] is not perceived;
furthermore, the word "ca" (and) is justified even by its connection with the agency of the act of dividing,
as in the case of "Devadatta."
"Yajñadatta should perform agriculture"— here,
the mention of "all" is for the purpose of excluding the taking of a preferential share (*uddhāra*), and the mention of "uterine" [brothers] is for the same purpose.
This is for the purpose of excluding those born of different wombs.

However, the wealth of a woman who is childless or of low caste is taken by a daughter of a co-wife who is of a higher caste, even if she is born of a different womb; in her absence, it goes to that daughter's offspring.
As Manu said:
"Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; it shall belong to her daughter or to her offspring. (MDh 9.198)
The mention of the *brāhmaṇī* is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for women of the highest caste;

therefore, in the absence of offspring, a daughter of the Kṣatriya caste takes the wealth of a Vaiśya woman who has no children. In the absence of sons, the grandsons are the heirs to the grandmother's wealth.
"Those who inherit the estate shall discharge the debt," according to the traditional teaching of Gautama; and "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons," according to Yājñavalkya.
Thus, since even grandsons have the right to discharge the debt to their grandmother,
in the absence of even grandsons, the aforementioned kinsmen beginning with the husband (the father-in-law) are the heirs to the property. 2.145.
In connection with the subject of a woman’s property, he says something regarding the case of a girl betrothed by word alone:

"Having given away a maiden, one who takes her back shall be fined and shall pay the expenses along with interest. (YDh 2.146ab) Having verbally given a maiden, one who takes her back must be punished by the king in accordance with the nature of the wealth involved and other relevant circumstances.

And this applies when there is no cause for the abduction; however, if there is such a cause, he is not to be punished, because the taking away [of the girl] is authorized by the rule: "But if a more excellent groom should come forward, one may take back even a girl who has been given" (YDh 2.65).

And whatever wealth has been expended by the groom, for the sake of his own relatives or those related to the bride, on account of the betrothal, all of that the giver of the girl shall return to the groom with interest— that is, together with the principal and the accrued interest.
Now, if she who has been verbally betrothed dies before the formal rite of disposal (saṃskāra), what should be done? To this he says:
"If she has died, one should take back what was given, after deducting the expenses of both parties. (YDh 2.146cd)
If a betrothed girl dies before marriage, the groom shall take back the ring and other items previously given as a bride-price (*śulka*);
having settled both sets of expenses—
that is, having calculated and deducted the expenditures incurred by both himself and the giver of the girl— he shall take what remains.

He should take [the property]. However, as for that which was given to the maiden by her maternal grandfather and others—such as head-ornaments—or that which has come down by succession, the uterine brothers shall take it; they shall take the inheritance of the deceased maiden because of the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "The uterine brothers shall take it; in their absence, the mother; in her absence, the father. (Not in BDh or DhKo) // 2.146 //
It has been stated that the property of a woman whose children have died belongs to her husband;
now, he states that in certain cases, the husband is authorized to take the property even of a woman who is living and has children.
In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction [to livelihood],
a husband is not required to return to a woman the property she received from him as a wife. (YDh 2.147) "In times of famine" means for the purpose of maintaining the family.
In matters of dharma that must necessarily be performed,
and in the case of an obstructing illness.

When a husband, being destitute of other property, takes his wife's wealth for purposes such as imprisonment or confinement, he is not required to restore it; however, if he misappropriates it by any other means, he must give it back.
Furthermore, no one else may take the wealth of a woman who is still living apart from her husband.

The heirs shall not take [the property]; however, if their own kinsmen should seize it while those women are still living, the righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the penalty for theft. (MDh 8.29)

Thus, because of the prescription of punishment; likewise: "The ornaments that may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide; those who do divide them fall [from their caste]. (MDh 9.200)
And because of the hearing of these faults [in the sūtras]. 2.147.

The property of a woman called *ādhivedanika* (given upon supersession) has been mentioned; regarding that, he says: "One should give an equal amount as *ādhivedanika* to a wife who has been superseded. To her for whom no woman's property (*strīdhana*) has been given, one should assign half [of the amount]. (YDh 2.148)
She upon whom a remarriage has taken place is called *adhivinnā*; she who is such a woman is an *adhivinna-strī*.

To that *adhivinna-strī*, one should give the *ādhivedanika*—the wealth intended for the occasion of remarriage—equally, as much as was expended for the purpose of the remarriage. This applies to her whose *strīdhana* (woman’s property) had not been given by her husband or her father-in-law.
Furthermore, from that woman's property, he should give half of the *ādhivedanika* (marriage-settled) wealth;
and here, the word "half" (*ardha*) does not signify an equal division.
And therefore, the meaning is that as much as is necessary to make that previously given amount equal to the compensation for supersession (*ādhivedanika*), so much should be paid. (2.148)

Having thus stated the division [of property], he now states the means for resolving doubts regarding it: "In the event of a denial of partition, the proof of partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, written documents, and separate houses and fields. (YDh 2.149)

In the case of a denial or concealment of partition, the determination of partition— that is, the ascertainment of the division— should be understood through witnesses possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, such as paternal kinsmen, maternal kinsmen, and maternal uncles, as well as through a written document, namely a deed of partition,
and likewise by means of separate houses and fields that have been individually assigned.

Nārada has stated that the separate engagement in activities such as agriculture and the distinct performance of religious duties such as the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) are signs of partition;
and when there is doubt regarding the law of partition, the determination for the heirs [is made by these means].
Because kinsmen may carry out separate business by means of a written partition of shares.
"For brothers who have not divided their property, a single dharma prevails; when division has taken place, their dharma also becomes separate for each. (NSm 13.36–37).
Likewise, other signs of partition have been stated by that same author:
"Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, stand surety, give gifts, or receive them; those who have not divided may never do so under any circumstances. (NSm 13.39) 2.149.
Thus ends the section on the division of inheritance;
now begins the section on disputes concerning boundaries,
wherein the determination of boundary disputes is set forth.

In a dispute over the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders, and others, the cowherds, those who cultivate the borderlands, and all those who frequent the forests shall determine the boundary by means of mounds,
charcoal, husks, and trees.

In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field belonging to two villages, as well as in a dispute regarding the limits of a field situated within a single village, the neighbors and others [should determine] the boundary marked by previously established boundary-indicators such as embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines,
and so forth.
They should lead [the boundary] and determine it. "Boundary" (sīmā) refers to the limit of fields and so forth;
it is of four kinds.
They are the boundary of a country, the boundary of a village, the boundary of a field, and the boundary of a house;
and that [boundary] possesses five characteristics according to the circumstances.

Thus it was said by Nārada: "The boundary is recorded as being of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that marked by fish, that established by fire, that free from danger, and that determined by royal decree. (DhKo 944)
*Dhvajinī* is characterized by trees and the like, because trees and such are similar to banners (*dhvaja*) in their quality of providing illumination.
*Matsyinī* is possessed of water.
Because the word "fish" indicates its own substratum, water;
and because the *naidhānī* [fire] consists of husks, charcoal, and so forth that have been buried,
due to their being buried.
Because it is equal to a treasure-store;
it is free from fear, produced by the mutual agreement of the plaintiff and the defendant,
and brought about by the administration of royal law.
In the absence of identifying marks of the owner, [the boundary] is established by the king's will;
in such a case, a sixfold dispute may arise. As Kātyāyana has said:
"Excess, deficiency, and the existence or non-existence of a portion; non-enjoyment, possession, and boundary—these six are the grounds for a dispute over land. Thus it is said.
For instance, when someone says, "I have additional land here, measuring five nivartanas," [the following applies].
There is a dispute regarding the excess [of land],
as [the claimant] says, "My land is exactly five nivartanas and no more," while [the opponent] asserts that it is actually less than that.
Regarding deficiency:
when it is said, "My share consists of five [coins] to be returned," a dispute over existence and non-existence arises, as one might argue that there is no share at all.

When it is said, "My land is being enjoyed as if its possession were previously non-existent," the dispute concerns non-enjoyment and enjoyment, namely, "My possession has been continuous and indeed long-standing. And when it is said, "This is the boundary, or that is the boundary," it is a dispute concerning boundaries; thus, there are six types [of disputes].
Thus, this dispute arises.

Even though land-disputes are of six kinds, because the boundary is also determined through both scriptural authority and reasoning, it is included within the section on the determination of boundaries.
The *sāmantakas* are those states that exist on all sides;
these are the neighboring villages and so forth in the four directions, established according to their respective boundaries.
"A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village, a field the neighbor of a field,
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, embracing it on all sides"— thus says the statement of Kātyāyana.
By the word "village" and so forth, the persons residing therein are indicated,
just as in the expression "the village has fled. And the mention of "neighboring villages" (sāmantas) is for the purpose of including those closely connected to them and others.

And it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "The immediate neighbors, their neighbors, and likewise those beyond them, and the neighbors of those neighbors—these are proclaimed to be arranged in the form of a lotus. (KSm 738)
"Elders" (sthavira) means those who are aged.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), both the fundamental (maula) and the extracted (uddhṛta) [stages] are included.
And the definition of the aged and so forth has been stated by that very same [author]:
Those by whom that work was seen being accomplished while they were endowed with its qualities—
whether they be old or not old— are proclaimed as "elders" (*vṛddha*).
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country...
"Because they are rooted in that [original Veda], they are proclaimed by the sages as 'fundamental' (maula).
They are characterized by overhearing, enjoyment, performance, and narration;
and because they extract [the meaning] again from that source, they are therefore known as 'extracted' (uddhṛta). (KSm 743–745)
Cowherds are those who tend cattle;
boundary-farmers are those who cultivate fields situated near the boundaries;
and forest-dwellers are all those who roam in the woods.
These include hunters and the like;
they have been mentioned by Manu:
"Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, and root-diggers..."
"Snake-catchers, those who live by gleaning, and others who roam the forest. (MDh 8.260).
"Thicket" (*sthalam*) refers to an elevated region of the earth;
"charcoal" (*aṅgāraḥ*) is the residue of fire.
Husks are the outer coverings of grain; trees are such as the *nyagrodha* and others;
a dam is a barrier against the flow of water.
A *caitya* is a construction of stone and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), bamboo, sand, and other materials are included. These are of two types, distinguished as being either exposed or concealed.
As Manu has said:
"One should establish boundary trees— *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees, as well as *śālmalī*, *śāla*, and *tāla* trees, and indeed milky-sap trees."
By means of thickets, various bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and open spaces,
as well as reeds and groves of shrubs, the boundary is not lost.
"Reservoirs, wells, ponds, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
Thus [are] the manifest forms [of boundary markers].
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made concealed,
having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung,
bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand;
Furthermore, those of this kind which the earth would not consume due to their age,
he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at the joints and boundaries.
"By these marks the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties.
Thus [ends the section on] concealed marks.
By these marks, both manifest and unmanifest, as shown by the neighbors and others, [he shall determine] the boundary.
The king shall determine the boundary between two parties who are disputing it. (2.150–2.151)
But when there are no marks, or when existing marks are doubtful as to whether they are indicative or non-indicative, he states the means for reaching a decision:
"Or neighbors— either all the villagers, or four, eight, or even ten."
Wearing red garlands and garments, the boundary-markers should lead [the procession].
The "boundary-markers" (sāmantas) are those possessing the characteristics previously described;
they are villagers from neighboring villages, equal in number—either four, eight, or ten—as a complete group.
Wearing red garlands and clad in red garments, with clods of earth placed upon their heads, they should lead to and point out the boundary;
or "neighboring landowners" (*sāmantāḥ*) is mentioned as an alternative option, intended to include witnesses as described in other legal treatises (*smṛti*).
As Manu has said:
"The determination of a boundary dispute shall be based solely on the testimony of witnesses" (MDh 8.253).
And in that regard, the primary role of the witnesses is to act as the determiners.
In their absence, it belongs to the neighbors. As it has been said:
"But in the absence of witnesses, four villagers residing as neighbors, being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king. (MDh 8.258)
In their absence, those who are attached to them and so forth shall act as the adjudicators.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"When the neighboring landowners are found to be corrupt in achieving their own ends, [the decision is made] on account of the gravity of the matter."
However, those associated with that [sin] must perform the rite of deliverance; there is no doubt in this matter.
"But those who are attached to one who is attached to the same fault are declared to be 'associated' with him;
however, they should not be punished by a king who understands the Dharma.
Thus, in the absence of neighbors and others, the *maula* (hereditary) witnesses and the rest are to be accepted.

"In their absence, the neighbors, the principal members of the family, the elders, the excavators, and so forth [should act] even regarding the six types of immovable property; there is no doubt on this point," because Kātyāyana has thus prescribed the sequence.
And these, beginning with the *sāmanta*, exist in accordance with an increase in number and quality:
"The *sāmanta*s should first be faultless and endowed with qualities;
those further [in rank] are to be known as having double [the qualities], and others than those are considered to have triple [the qualities]. (KSm 746)
According to this traditional teaching, those witnesses— the neighbors and others— having been sworn by their respective oaths, shall lead forth the boundary;
wearing garlands and clad in red garments, they shall carry the earth upon their heads.
"Having been sworn by their respective good deeds, they shall lead [the case] correctly," according to the traditional law (smṛti).
The use of the plural number in "they shall lead" is for the purpose of excluding two or one person.
"If one person should mark the boundary, he should do so while fasting,
wearing red garlands and garments, and holding earth upon his head"— since Nārada has thus permitted a single individual [to perform this task]. This person who—

"A man, even if he is trustworthy, should not determine a boundary alone; because of the gravity of this matter, the procedure for these [matters] is established upon many. Thus is the prohibition against a single person.
There is no contradiction, as that [rule] refers to matters other than those where both parties agree upon the law.
Furthermore, even in the absence of marks such as mounds and the like, Nārada has stated a specific means for witnesses, neighbors, and others to determine the boundary.

"Regarding lands whose boundary marks have been swept away, abandoned, or destroyed by a river, [the boundary shall be determined] by inferring that region, by measurement, and by observing possession.
(NSm 11.6) "Swept away" means carried off by a river; "abandoned" means displaced from their original location; and "destroyed" refers to the boundary marks.

In those boundary regions, they should determine [the limits] either by inferring from the local area, by inferring the ancient site through signs that have been effaced or lost, or by such evidence as "starting from this village, a field measuring one thousand *daṇḍas* lies in the western part of this village," or by means of possession characterized by a period beyond the reach of memory, even when contested in the presence of the opposing party.
And Bṛhaspati has shown a specific distinction in this regard:
"Those who know the title-deed, the means of proof, the duration of possession, the name, and the characteristics of the portion of land—they are the witnesses in this matter. (BṛSm 1.19.28)
And these witnesses, neighbors, and others, having been made to hear the oaths, must be questioned by the king in the presence of the family and other relevant parties.
As Manu says:
"The witnesses regarding the boundary shall be questioned in the presence of the villagers and the families."
"The boundary markers of those two disputants must be questioned" (MDh 8.254).
When questioned, those witnesses and others, being unanimous as a whole, shall declare the decision regarding the boundary. By them, the [boundary] thus determined...
One should record the boundary, together with all the characteristics it displays and the names of the witnesses and others, in a document for the purpose of preventing forgetfulness.
And it has been stated by Manu:
"When they have been questioned, whatever decision they all unanimously declare regarding the boundary..."
"Thus one should demarcate the boundary, naming all of them [the witnesses and neighbors]. (MDh 8.261).

Regarding these individuals—beginning with the witnesses and neighbors—from the day the boundary is traversed until the end of three fortnights, if no calamity caused by the king or by fate occurs, then the determination of the boundary is made through their testimony.
And this limit for calamities caused by kings or fate was stated by Kātyāyana:
"In the case of traversing a boundary, in the case of a treasury [being lost], and likewise in the case of touching a foot."
A period of three fortnights, one fortnight, or seven days is prescribed for calamities caused by fate or the king.
Thus: (KSm 751) 2.152) But when, within three fortnights, these aforementioned witnesses are seen to suffer from disease and the like,
or when their testimony is found to be contradicted by other witnesses of superior number and quality designated by the defendant;
Then, they are to be punished for speaking falsely; regarding this, it is said:
"But in the case of falsehood, they shall each be separately punished by the king with the middle amercement" (YDh 2.153ab).
When falsehood—that is, speaking untruth—is the cause, all the neighbors shall each be fined with the middle amercement, which consists of forty [paṇas] more.
They are to be punished with a fine of five hundred paṇas.
That his domain extends to the neighboring territory is understood from the prescription of different punishments for witnesses, sureties, and others in another Smṛti;
as Manu says:
"Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. (MDh 8.257).
Nārada also says:
"Furthermore, if the neighbors should speak falsely in the determination of a boundary,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement" (NSm 11.7). Having thus prescribed the middle amercement as the punishment for the neighbors, [the text continues:]
"If the remaining persons appointed to the task of examining the land should speak falsely, they,
being the lowest [in rank], shall each be punished with the first amercement";
thus he has stated that the first *sāhasa* applies to those associated with the witnesses and others.
He states that the same punishment applies even to the primary witnesses and others:

"But other [witnesses], such as the primary, the aged, and so forth, being situated in falsehood, are each to be disciplined individually with the first *sāhasa* fine according to the scale of punishment. (DhKo 946; cf. NSm 11.8)
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of cowherds, bird-catchers, hunters, and forest-dwellers.

Although for bird-catchers and others—who are devoted to sinful acts—their utility lies solely in the observation of signs and not directly in the determination of boundaries, nevertheless, since the possibility of speaking falsely exists precisely in the observation of such signs, [they must be examined].
The prescription of punishment is indeed appropriate;
however, the rule that "those who speak falsely shall be punished individually" refers to a case of ignorance.
But when many have been apprehended, if not all of them reach a conclusion [regarding the truth], [the rule applies].

"Whether out of fear or greed, they should be punished with the highest fine" (KSm 750). Thus, because Kātyāyana has prescribed a different punishment for witnesses and others in cases involving specialized knowledge; likewise, this same punishment has been stated by that very author even in the case of a contradiction in the testimony of witnesses.
"If a discrepancy should arise after [the boundary] has been proclaimed, those [witnesses] should be punished with the highest fine.
Thus, having punished the witnesses and others for speaking falsely through ignorance or other causes, the investigation of the boundary must be undertaken again.
Having punished them for stating [the boundary] out of ignorance, one should investigate the boundary once more.

Having spoken thus, and having removed the wicked neighboring lords along with the hereditary officials and others, he should cause the boundary to be established; so those who know the Dharma understand. (KSm 742)
Thus, the method of determination has been stated by that very [author].
But when there are no witnesses, such as neighbors and so forth, nor any identifying marks, how then is a determination made?
To this, he says:
"In the absence of those who know [the boundary] and of the marks, the king himself is the establisher of the boundary.
