(YDh 2.153cd) In the absence of the "knowers"—namely the neighbors and others—and of the "marks"—namely the trees and others—the king alone is the "pravartitā," meaning the one who establishes (pravartayitā) the boundary.
Here, the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is contained within the word.

Having divided equally the land situated between two villages that has become the subject of dispute, and having assigned it to both with the words "this land is yours" and "that land is yours," he should establish boundary markers in the middle of it;
when an exceptional benefit from that land is seen for one of the two, then the entire [land] belongs to that very village.
The land must be surrendered.
As Manu has said:
"When a boundary is difficult to determine, the king himself, who knows the dharma, [shall decide it]."
"He should assign land to some on account of their services; such is the settled rule. (MDh 8.265) 2.153.
Even though there is no suspicion that this [text] might not be its own nature, he states an extended application (atideśa) to demonstrate that this Smṛti is rooted in reasoning (nyāyamūla):
"In groves, temples, villages, watering places, gardens, and houses;
this same rule is to be known to apply to rainwater, flowing streams, and the like. (YDh 2.154)
An *ārāma* is a plot of land that serves as the cause for the cultivation of flowers and fruits.
An *āyatana* is a dwelling, a portion of land demarcated for purposes such as a stack of straw and so forth.
A village is well known;
the mention of "village" is intended to include cities and the like by implication. A watering place (*nipāna*) is a location for drinking water, such as a pond, a well, and so forth.
A garden (*udyāna*) is a pleasure grove;
a residence (*veśma*) is a house. In these places, such as parks and the like—
This very rule characterized by neighbors, witnesses, and so forth, is to be understood;
likewise, in a dispute such as "Does a flood of water arising from heavy rain flow between these two houses or not?"— the phrase "and so forth" (ādi) being included.
The same ancient rule should be understood to apply even to palaces and similar structures;
and so says Kātyāyana:
"In the case of fields, wells, and tanks, as well as of cultivated plots and groves..."
And in houses, palaces, dwellings, and the abodes of kings and gods.
Thus [ends the verse]. (KSm 749) //2.154//
Having stated the determination of boundaries, he now prescribes the punishment for the violation of boundaries and the like as a related topic:
"For the breaking of a boundary-mark, for the transgression of a boundary, and likewise for the seizure of a field, there are punishments of the lowest, highest, and middle degrees. (YDh 2.155)
The common ground that demarcates many fields is the boundary (*maryādā*). For its excessive breaking— that is,
for crossing the boundary or plowing beyond it— and for seizing a field by displaying threats and the like, the fines of the lowest, highest, and middle *sāhasa* are to be understood respectively.
And here, the mention of "field" is intended to include houses, gardens, and so forth by way of illustration.
Furthermore, when one seizes a field or similar property through the delusion that it belongs to oneself, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] is to be understood as the penalty.
As Manu has said:
"One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field through intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done out of ignorance, the fine is two hundred. (MDh 8.264)
Considering the great extent of the fields and other properties being stolen, even the highest punishment may sometimes be applied.
Therefore, it is said:
"Death, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, and branding."
In that case, the punishment prescribed is the severing of the limb, which constitutes the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
Thus [it is said]. (NSm 14.7) // 2.155 //

Furthermore, regarding one who wishes to construct a bridge, a well, or the like on another's field—having obtained permission through request or by the gift of wealth—the punishment falls upon the owner of the field alone for prohibiting such construction; thus he says:
"A bridge that causes little harm and brings about welfare shall not be prohibited."
A well that takes [water] from another's land, though occupying little ground, is a source of much water.

Even if it encroaches upon or destroys another's land— meaning a dam or embankment for binding the flow of water— it shall not be prohibited by the owner of the field, provided that it causes only slight harm and yields great benefit.
A well, because it occupies little space, causes little obstruction, and—due to its abundance of water—is beneficial; therefore, one whose water is abundant should certainly not be obstructed.
Furthermore, the mention of a "well" (kūpa) is intended to include by implication tanks, lotus-pools, and the like.

Furthermore, when that [water] is a source of great harm because it flows through all the fields, or provides little benefit because it flows through fields near rivers and the like, then it is to be prohibited; this is what is meant by implication.
And the two-fold nature of a watercourse (setu) has been stated by Nārada:
"A dam is to be known as being of two kinds: one that is to be dug out (*kheya*) and likewise one that is to be bound (*bandhya*).
It is 'to be dug out' because water is made to flow [through it], and it is 'to be bound' because water is turned back [by it]. (NSm 11.15).
But when one repairs by oneself a dam constructed by another that has been destroyed through breaking or other means, then [one must compensate] the former owner...
One should perform the consecration only after having questioned the king belonging to that lineage;
as Nārada said:
"But he who [performs rites] for a site already occupied and then abandoned, without having questioned the owner..."
If someone should initiate the construction of a bridge, he would not partake in its fruit.
But when the owner has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is a human being,
one should first consult the king and then proceed with the construction of the embankment.
This was taught with respect to the owner of the field.
Now, he speaks with respect to the one who initiates the irrigation channel:
"He who should construct a channel in a field without having informed the owner..."
When [the crop] has grown, it belongs to the owner; in his absence, to the king.
(YDh 2.157) He who constructs an irrigation channel on another's field without having obtained the consent of the field-owner—or, in his absence, the king—does not partake of the fruit;
rather, when the fruit has grown, it belongs to the owner of the field, and in his absence, to the king.

Therefore, the essential meaning is that a water-channel should be constructed on another's field only after obtaining the permission of the owner of that field, or in his absence, the king—either by means of a request or by providing compensation for the benefit. (2.157)
It has been stated that the owner of the field must not prohibit the construction of an embankment;
now, following this topic as a secondary consequence, he states another rule regarding certain cases.

Even if a field has been ploughed, he who neither cultivates it himself nor causes it to be cultivated shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation; another person shall cause that field to be cultivated. Furthermore, he who, having promised before the owner of the field, "I will cultivate this field," subsequently abandons it—[he too shall be liable for the loss].

And if he causes it to be ploughed by another, even if that field has been struck by the plough and slightly torn by the share so that it is not yet fit for the sowing of seeds, nevertheless, that cultivator must be made to pay as much of the fruit of that ploughing as is appropriate for production there, as determined by the neighbors and others.
And that field, having been confiscated from the former cultivator, he should cause it to be worked by another. // 2.158 //
Thus ends the section on disputes concerning boundaries;
now begins the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen.
Because the titles of law stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect, the first among them is the non-payment of debt (MDh 8.4).
Since the sequence of the text beginning with these words is not intended [to be strictly followed], the dispute between the owner and the herdsman is stated out of order:
"A buffalo that causes damage to the crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that; and a goat or sheep, half of that again. (YDh 2.159)
A female buffalo that destroys another's standing crop shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that, four māṣas;
and goats and rams shall each be fined two māṣas.

Since the queen and others have no direct connection with wealth, the term refers by implication to the man who owns them. Furthermore, in this context, a *māṣa* is one-twentieth part of a copper *paṇa*;
for it is said: "A *māṣa* is proclaimed to be the twentieth part of a *paṇa*. (DhKo 532; NSm 21.58)
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada; and this refers to cases of ignorance. But in the case of intentional [action], however:
"Two quarters of a *paṇa* for a cow, but double that for a buffalo; likewise, two quarters of a *paṇa* is declared to be the fine for goats, sheep, and calves"—
this statement from another *Smṛti* should be observed.
Furthermore, as stated by Nārada: "One should cause a fine of one māṣa to be paid for a cow, two māṣas for a buffalo, and for goats, sheep, and calves, the fine shall be half a māṣa. (DhKo 917)
Thus, this [rule] again refers to the eating of that which has its roots remaining, provided they are capable of sprouting once more. (2.159)
He states that in certain cases, due to an excess of offense, the fine is doubled:

"For those who remain after having eaten [the crop], the punishment is double that which was prescribed" (YDh 2.160ab). If cattle, having eaten the grain in another's field, lie down right there without being restrained, then, compared to what was previously stated...
A double fine should be understood as the penalty for [cattle] that have merely grazed;
however, for those that have eaten and are sitting down with their calves, a fine four times the aforementioned amount should be understood as the penalty.
For those that have died [naturally], it is declared to be double; for those with their calves, it is fourfold—so says the scriptural statement.
He states an extension [of the rule] to other fields and other animals:
"Among these, [the fine for grazing] in a *vivīta* is the same; for donkeys and camels, it is equal to that for a buffalo.
A *vivīta* is a protected, enclosed area of land abounding in grass and wood.
One should know that even upon damaging such [a field], these animals— buffaloes and the rest— shall receive a fine equal to the penalty for other fields;
and donkeys and camels (the compound *kharoṣṭra*) shall be treated the same as buffaloes.
Wherever a buffalo is punished with a certain kind of penalty, there a donkey and a camel should each be punished with that very same penalty;
for, by virtue of their obstructing the crops, each of these two is equal to a buffalo.
Since punishment must correspond to the offense, the collective compound "donkey and camel" (*kharoṣṭra*) is not intended here. (2.160)
The punishment for the owner of a cow that destroys another's standing crop has been stated;
now, [the author] says that this person should also be made to pay the value of the crop to the owner of the field.
As long as the crop is destroyed, so long shall the fruit belong to the owner of the field;
the cowherd is to be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine.
The mention of "crop" is intended to indicate the loss of the field's produce.

In whatever field, to whatever extent straw, grain, and so forth have been destroyed by cattle and the like, the owner of that field must be made to pay the value of that field’s produce— determined as "in this much field there would have been this much" by the neighbors— to the owner of the cattle.
The cowherd, however, is merely to be beaten and should not be made to pay the fine; and the beating of the cowherd,
accompanied by the previously mentioned monetary fine, is to be understood as applicable when the destruction of the crops is due to the fault of the herdsman,
as in the case where a cow, having been lost through the fault of the herdsman, destroys the crops.
For there is the statement: "In that case, there is no fine for the owner; the keeper deserves that fine. (NSm 11.31; DhKo 917).
Furthermore, when the crop is destroyed through the owner's own negligence, the owner of the cow deserves only the previously mentioned fine and not corporal punishment;
however, the payment for the loss of the fruit belongs in all cases to the owner of the cow alone.
Because one shares in the fruit of that field by means of enjoying the milk of the buffaloes and other animals nourished by its produce; therefore,

the straw and other remains left over after the cows and other animals have been fed must be taken by the owner of the cattle alone, provided the payment of a middleman-determined price has been made.
Because it is essentially equivalent to what has been purchased;
for this very reason, Nārada says:
"If a man demands back the grain that has been eaten by cows..."
That grain which was sown there should be given with the consent of the neighbors.
Straw should be given to the owner of the cattle, but the grain belongs to the cultivator.
Thus [it is said]. (NSm 11.34) // 2.161 //
He states an exception regarding specific fields:
"There is no fault in a field located on a path or at the edge of a village pasture;
however, if one acts intentionally rather than unintentionally, he deserves punishment like that of a thief. (YDh 2.162)

If cattle have grazed unintentionally upon a field situated on a path near a village, or upon a field adjacent to a village pasture (*vivīta*), there is no fault for either the cowherd or the owner of the cattle.
This demonstration of the absence of fault is intended to establish the absence of punishment.
And for the purpose of prohibiting the payment of compensation for destroyed crops:

in the case of acting according to one's own will—that is, stealing intentionally—one deserves the same punishment as a thief; whatever punishment is prescribed for a thief, such is the punishment he deserves.
And this refers to the case of an uncultivated field;
if cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the guardians of the cattle. (MDh 8.238)
Thus, since Manu has stated that the absence of punishment applies to uncultivated fields,
there is indeed still a fault even in the case of cultivated fields such as those used for roads;
furthermore, the construction of a boundary wall has been prescribed by him alone.
"And one should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it; one must eliminate every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig could pass. (MDh 8.239) 2.162.
He states that there is no punishment even for specific types of animals:

"Bulls set at liberty, animals that have recently calved, those that are stray, and so forth—for those which have no keeper, and those overwhelmed by fate or the king, they shall not be made liable [for damage]. (YDh 2.163)
A "great bull" (*mahokṣa*) is a large ox, a stallion, or a stud-bull.

"Released animals" (*utsṛṣṭapaśavaḥ*) are those set free according to the ritual injunctions for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) or dedicated to a deity. A "woman who has recently given birth" (*sūtikā*) is one who has delivered a child within ten days.

A stray animal that has wandered away from its own herd and come from another region—these are to be released even if they have eaten another's crops; they are not to be punished. Furthermore, those for whom no keeper exists are also exempt, as they are overwhelmed by fate or royal authority.
Those struck by divine forces (daiva), such as those causing the destruction of crops, are not to be punished.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), elephants, horses, and so forth are understood;
these have been described by Uśanas.
Indeed, elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are recorded as the protectors of the people;
likewise, those who are one-eyed or humpbacked, and those who bear permanent marks, are exempt from punishment.
"A cow that is about to calve, one that has recently given birth, or one that is carrying a load is not to be punished;
likewise, cows are not to be punished during a festival or at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony. (DhKo 920).

In this context, because animals released for sacrifice (*utsṛṣṭapaśu*) lack an owner, it is impossible for them to be subject to punishment; therefore, they are cited here merely by way of illustration.
Just as animals that have been set free are not to be punished, so too are large bulls and the like. // 2.163 //
The Gosvāmin has said:
Now, instruction is given regarding the cowherd;
just as the cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening, so [should he act].
And having caused those lost through negligence to be made good, he who has received his wages [shall do so].

At the time of dawn, the cowherd, having counted the cattle, shall return them to the owner exactly as they were entrusted; likewise, at the time of evening, the cowherd, having counted the cattle, shall restore them to the owner.
A cowherd who has received a fixed wage must restore to his master the cattle that have died or been lost through negligence— that is, through his own fault.
The determination of such wages has been stated by Nārada:
"From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the cowherd's fee; from two hundred, the milk;
and every year, the entire milk-gathering on the eighth day. Thus [it is stated].
Furthermore, the loss due to negligence has been clarified by Manu:

"Whatever is lost, eaten by worms, killed by dogs, or died in a dangerous place, [the owner] shall deliver that which was deficient in human effort; the keeper alone [is liable]," so says Manu Smṛti 8.232.
Furthermore, one should not be made to pay for what has been forcibly carried off by thieves.
As Manu said:
"But if cattle have been stolen by thieves after an attack, the keeper is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his master at the proper place and time" (MDh 8.233).
Furthermore, for animals that have died by natural causes, the ears and so forth must be shown:
"The owner of dead animals should give the two ears, the hide, the tail-hairs, the bladder, the sinew, and the bile, showing these parts [to the authorities]. (MDh 8.234)
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu (2.164).
Furthermore:
"But when there is destruction due to the fault of the keeper, punishment is ordained for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself for the owner. (YDh 2.165)
If the animal is destroyed solely through the fault of the keeper, the keeper shall be made to pay a fine of thirteen and a half paṇas;
and the owner shall receive the value of the lost animal as determined by arbitrators.
The verse concerning the measurement of the punishment is as previously stated; the rest is exactly as explained before. (2.165)
In connection with the cow, he describes the pasture for cattle:
"The pasture for cattle may be according to the will of the villagers or by the authority of the king;
a twice-born man may take grass, fuel, and flowers from everywhere at all times. (YDh 2.166)

The pasture for cattle (gopracāra) should be established according to the desire of the villagers—that is, the desire of the common people—or according to the King’s wish, depending on whether the land is small or large. The meaning is that even a small portion of uncultivated land should be set aside for the grazing of cows and other animals.
Furthermore, in the absence of grass, fuel, and so forth, a twice-born man may take grass, wood, and flowers from anywhere as he pleases for the sake of his cows, the sacred fire, or the deities.
One may take [grain] from an unenclosed field without being forbidden; however, one should take fruits only from what is openly accessible.
For the sake of cattle or fire, one may take grass and fuel, as well as flowers from shrubs and trees and fruits from those that are not enclosed, as if they were one's own. (GDh 12.28)
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Gautama.
And this [rule] pertains to the case of what has been accepted;
however, in the case of what is not accepted, since there is acceptance even by those other than the twice-born (dvija), [the rule does not apply].
For in this very way, ownership is established.
Thus it has been stated by that same author: "One becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or discovery" (GDh 13.39).
Furthermore, as for what was said:

"Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—one who takes these without asking deserves the amputation of his hand. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.22.25). This [rule] refers to persons other than the twice-born, or to circumstances other than times of distress, or to objects other than cows and the like. 2.166.
Furthermore, this is stated for the sake of providing facilities for the standing and sitting of cattle and other animals:
"The distance between fields around a village should be one hundred bows;
it should be two hundred for a market town (kharvaṭa), and four hundred for a city. (YDh 2.167)

The distance between a village and its field shall be one hundred *dhanus* in circumference; it must be made such that no crops are sown in any direction [within that space]. For a *kharvaṭa*—a village with an abundance of thorny shrubs—the circumference shall be two hundred [bow-lengths]. As for a city...
In a place crowded with many people, the distance between bows should be four hundred [units]. // 2.167 //
Thus ends the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen; now begins the legal title known as "Sale by One Not the Owner" (*asvāmivikraya*). He now commences this section.
And its definition was stated by Nārada:
"When another's property— whether deposited, lost, found, or stolen—
is sold in the presence [of the owner], that is to be known as sale without ownership" (NSm 7.1).
Regarding that, what [says] Pāṇḍeya? He says:
"One may recover one's own property sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if it was not disclosed."

If one sees property belonging to oneself that has been sold by another without ownership—that is, sold by one who is not the owner—then he may recover it and take possession of it, because a sale by one who is not the owner lacks the capacity to create legal ownership. This applies when the sale was conducted in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time; otherwise, he is a thief. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.168)
The mention of "that which has been sold" is intended to include by implication that which has been given away or bestowed,
because it is equal [to the former] in being a sale by one who is not the owner.
For this very reason, it has been said:
"One should annul a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift and a pledge.
(KSm 612) Furthermore, a fault accrues to the purchaser if the purchase was made in secret or concealed.
Likewise, from a "low" person—one who lacks the proper means for the acquisition of that particular object—[the purchase is invalid].
And when a purchase is made in secret and in private, even for a commodity that could have been obtained at a higher value, but is bought for a much lower price and at an improper time—
this being "velāhīna," meaning a purchase made outside the proper time, such as at night or at the beginning of the night— the buyer becomes a thief; he is treated like a thief.
The meaning is that he becomes liable to punishment and so forth. As it has been said:
"Having acquired property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall recover it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made publicly, whereas it is theft if the purchase was made in secret."
Thus [it is said]. (NSm 7.2) // 2.168 //
Regarding the question of what must be done by the purchaser when he is accused by the owner,
[the author] says: "Having recovered property that has been lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended by the man [who took it]."
And in the event of the lapse of time or place, having seized [the property], he should himself restore it.

Having recovered another's lost or stolen property through purchase or other means, he should cause the thief or the seller to be apprehended by means of the "thief-catcher" (cauroddharaṇaka) and others, for the sake of his own purification and to avoid incurring royal punishment.

If, however, he has gone to another country unknown [to the owner] or has perished after some time, then, because it is impossible to recover the original object, he should himself hand over that property to the owner without even showing the seller.
The explanation given by Śrīkarācārya— that he becomes pure by that alone— is untenable,
because it would result in the fault of tautology with the rule: "Purification [occurs] upon seeing the seller" (YDh 2.170).
Therefore, it is explained otherwise:
the instruction "lost or stolen" is given as a means of proof to the owner of the lost property.
Having discovered his own lost or stolen property and learning that it is in the hand of a purchaser, he shall have the thief— that is, the purchaser— seized by the local guardians and others.
This applies even in cases of "excessive lapse of place or time," meaning when there has been a violation of the proper place or time [for the sale].

In the absence of the local guardians and others, if there is a fear that the person might flee before the time for reporting them has arrived, one should seize him oneself and hand him over to them. (2.169)
When the purchaser has been caught, what should be done? To this he says:

"Purification [from the charge] comes from producing the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the purchaser recovers the price from him who was his seller" (YDh 2.170).
If that purchaser, having been apprehended, declares, "This was not stolen by me; it was bought from another," then his purification occurs merely by the production of the seller;
he is not, however, to be prosecuted further. But rather—
There is a dispute between the original owner and the seller indicated by him;
as Bṛhaspati says:
"When the original source has been recovered, the purchaser is not to be prosecuted in any way."
"But a dispute with the original owner (*mūla*) is not prescribed for the one who has lost the property" (BṛSm 1.12.6).

In that dispute, if it is determined that there was a sale by one who was not the owner, then the owner—the one who has suffered the loss—recovers his own property from the seller, the one who sold the cow or other goods that were lost or stolen; and the king [punishes] him in accordance with the offense.
The purchaser incurs the penalty and the price.
If, however, he has gone to another country, then time must be granted for his return, calculated according to the number of *yojanas*.

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "One may either make a public sale or surrender the root [of the stolen property]; and the time for bringing the root must be granted there according to the number of stages of the journey. (KSm 615).
If, however, one is unable to produce the root source because its location is unknown, then one becomes pure only by purifying the purchase;
but one whose root source cannot be recovered must purify the purchase itself. (KSm 618)
Because of this statement.

Furthermore, when one does not clear the purchase through witnesses and the like, or by means of an ordeal, and does not produce the original source [of the goods], then that person alone becomes liable for punishment. Thus:
"Not producing the source, nor clearing the purchase..."
"According to the demand, he shall be made to pay the wealth to the creditor and a fine as well," because of this traditional teaching of Manu. (DhKo 760) [2.170]

It has been stated that "one may recover what was sold by another" (YDh 2.168). To address the question of what must be done by one who desires to recover that [property], he says: "The lost [property] shall be restored through title and possession; otherwise, [it is not]."
If that [owner] does not manifest his fivefold proof to the king,

he must prove it— by means of title such as inheritance or purchase, and by means of possession— that "this property is mine, and it was thus lost or stolen," and this must be established by its owner.
Otherwise, if that owner does not prove [the loss], a fine of five times the value— namely, a fifth part of the lost property— must be paid by the claimant to the king.
And in this matter, the following is the procedure:
The former owner shall recover his lost property;
thereafter, the purchaser [shall recover] the seller for the purpose of avoiding the charge of theft and for the recovery of the purchase price.
He should bring it back; if he is unable to bring it back, then, in order to avoid his own fault, he should clear the purchase price and restore the property to the owner. (2.171)
Regarding one who conceals a thief, he says:
"He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost, without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas. (YDh 2.172)

If one seizes, out of pride or similar motives, property that has been stolen or lost and is currently in the possession of a thief or another, merely informing the king that "my property has been taken by him," he shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*.
Because it is wicked due to its nature of concealing thieves. // 2.172 //
In response to those brought by the king's officers, he says:
"If property lost or stolen has been recovered by customs officials or local guardians, the owner may take it back within one year; after that, the king shall take it. (YDh 2.173)

But when property that was lost or stolen has been recovered from the side of the king by customs officials or guards of the place, if the owner of the loss appears within one year, he shall recover that property; however,
after that period...
After one year, the king may take possession;
however, property brought by his own agents must be proclaimed among the crowds of people and guarded by the king for the duration of that year.
As Gautama has said: "Having found property whose owner has disappeared, they should announce it to the king;
it should be guarded by the king for one year after being publicly proclaimed" (GDh 10.36–37).
Furthermore, as for another rule stated by Manu:
"Property whose owner has disappeared, the king shall cause to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that, the king may take it. (MDh 8.30).
This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and good conduct.

The taking of a sixth part and so forth for the purpose of protection has also been stated by that same [author]: "Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of what is lost and then found" (MDh 8.33).
In the third, second, and first years, respectively, the sixth and subsequent portions are to be understood; this has been explained in detail previously. (2.173)
He states an exception to the rule regarding the taking of a sixth part and so forth as declared by Manu (cf. MDh 8.33) with respect to specific types of property:
"In the case of a single-hoofed animal, one should pay four paṇas; in the case of a human, five."
For buffaloes, camels, and cows, [the fine is] two pādas each; for goats and sheep, one pāda each.
When a single-hoofed animal such as a horse is recovered after being lost, its owner shall pay four paṇas to the king for the purpose of its protection.
For a human being—that is, property consisting of a person of human birth—he shall pay five paṇas.
For the purpose of guarding buffaloes, camels, and cows, two *paṇas* each shall be paid; furthermore, for goats and sheep, one-quarter (*pāda*) each shall be paid.
The phrase "he shall pay" is to be supplied in all cases.

Even though "goats and sheep" (*ajāvikam*) is expressed as a compound, by the force of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) "foot by foot," it is understood that the connection applies to each individual member. (2.174)
Thus ends the section on Sale Without Ownership;
now begins the section on Non-Delivery of What Has Been Given.

This matter receives two designations: "the non-withdrawal of what has been given" (*dattānapakarma*) and "non-delivery of what has been given" (*dattāpradānika*), because it rests upon two paths—the prescribed and the prohibited.
The legal title known as "gift" (dāna) is now described;
its essential nature was stated by Nārada:
"He who, having given property improperly, desires to take it back..."
"That legal title is indeed called *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what has been given). (NSm 4.1).
In that legal dispute where, having given property by resorting to an improper or unauthorized path, one desires to take it back, that is *dattāpradānika*;
it is the non-delivery of what was given, the taking back again, in that which is termed "giving. Thus, it is *dattāpradānika*.
The term "name" refers to a conventional category of discourse.

By virtue of being based on the prescribed path, that very same conventional category which serves as its antidote is effectively referred to by the term "non-delivery of what was given. This is the meaning.
The non-reversal of what has been given (*dattānapakarma*), which is known as "non-recovery," occurs within the legal title of dispute called "giving" (*dāna*); that is *dattānapakarma*.
And it is fourfold, through the distinctions of what may be given, what may not be given, and so forth.
As Nārada said:

"Now, that which is to be given and that which is not to be given, as well as what has been given and what has not been given—this fourfold path of giving is to be understood in legal proceedings. (NSm 4.2)
In this context, "that which is to be given" refers to what is suitable for the act of giving because it is not prohibited;
"that which is not to be given" is that which is unfit for giving either because it does not belong to one or because it is prohibited.

Furthermore, that which is given by one who remains in their natural state is called "given" (datta), as it is not to be revoked; however, that which is to be taken back is called "not given" (adatta).
To explain this briefly, he says:
"One's own property may be given without detriment to one's family" (YDh 2.175a).
"One's own" means belonging to oneself; "without detriment to one's family" means without causing hardship to the family;
that is to say, what remains after providing for the maintenance of the family.
He should give that [wealth], because it is necessary to support them;
as Manu said:
"An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son..."
"Even after committing a hundred improper acts, [the wife] must be maintained," so Manu has declared (MDh 11.10).
By the phrase "one's own property without detriment to one's family," he shows one kind of thing that must not be given away;

and by the phrase "one should give one's own," he indicates that things which do not belong to oneself—such as a deposit for another, borrowed items, pledges, common property, and trusts—are likewise excluded.
The inadmissibility of even these five [types of property] has been shown by way of contrast.
Furthermore, Nārada has stated that there are eight kinds of things that cannot be given: "That which is deposited, that which is borrowed, a pledge, and that which is held in common;"

Teachers have declared that a deposit, sons, wives, and one's entire property—provided there is a lineage—must not be given away by an embodied being even when existing in dire straits; the same applies to whatever has been promised to another. (NSm 4.4–5)
Thus, this [statement] is intended merely to indicate that [the object] is not to be given, and not because of an absence of ownership,
since ownership exists in the cases of sons, wives, and all one's possessions when they have been promised.
The nature of anvāhita and the others has already been explained in detail previously.

By the statement "one should give one's own," since there is no distinction in ownership regarding one's wife, sons, and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence that these too must be given; therefore, he states a prohibition:
"Except for his wife and sons" (YDh 2.175b), "nor his entire estate while heirs exist, nor that which has been promised to another" (YDh 2.175cd).
The meaning is that one should give away one's own property excluding wife and children— that is, apart from wife and children—
and likewise, while a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth exists, one should not give away all of one's wealth.
"Having procreated sons and performed their sacraments, one should provide for their livelihood," according to the traditional law (smṛti).
Likewise, gold or other property promised to one person must not be given to another. (2.175)

Having thus described the objects of gift other than wives, sons, and so forth, [the author] states, as a relevant digression, that the acceptance of even prohibited wealth must be performed openly by the recipient:
"The acceptance of a gift should be public, especially in the case of immovable property" (YDh 2.176ab).
Acceptance is "pratigraha"; it must be made public for the purpose of preventing disputes. In the case of immovable property, acceptance must especially be made public;
for, unlike gold and other such items, it is impossible to display that which remains fixed within oneself.
Having thus spoken incidentally, following the main subject, he says:
"What is to be given and what has been promised must indeed be given; once given, one must not take it back again. (YDh 2.176cd)

That which is promised as a gift, and that which has been promised for the sake of dharma, must indeed be given to that person, provided he has not fallen away from dharma; if he has fallen away, it should not be given again. Even after promising, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness. (GDh 5.23)
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Gautama:
"Having given, one should not take it back again.
That which has been given in accordance with the path of justice—even if it is of seven kinds—must never be taken back.
However, it should be understood exactly as stated:
furthermore, that which is given unjustly is "not given," and even in its sixteen forms, it must indeed be reclaimed; this is what is meant by implication.
And by Nārada,
having established that "what is given is said to be of seven kinds, while what is not given is of sixteen types" (NSm 4.3), [he continues]:

The nature of what has been given and what has not been given has been explained. Those who know the rules of giving recognize as "given" that which is offered for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return favor, or for the sake of a bride-price and for the purpose of showing favor.
But what is taken without it being given may be so through the force of fear, anger, or grief,
or likewise through bribery, jesting, a mistake, or by means of deception.
Furthermore, [that which is performed] by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane;
or that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking "I am the doer of this action."

"If what is called 'a worthy recipient' is actually an unworthy one, or if an act connected with Dharma is performed for a worldly purpose, that which is given through ignorance is declared to be as if not given. (NSm 4.7–10).
This is the meaning:
The price paid for merchandise or purchased goods; wages or salary given for work performed; and that which is given out of satisfaction to bards, wandering singers, and the like.
That which is given out of affection to one's daughters, sons, and so forth;
and that which is given by way of a return favor to one who has rendered assistance.
The "bride-price" (strīśulka)— that which is given to the kinsmen of the maiden for the purpose of marriage—
and that which is given for the sake of favor or for a transcendental purpose (adṛṣṭārtha): all this, being sevenfold, is indeed "given" and must not be reclaimed.
That which is given out of fear to kidnappers and the like;
that which is given out of anger to one's own children and others for the sake of avenging a grudge;
and that which is given while overcome by grief caused by the separation from a child or similar circumstances.
That which is given to officials for the purpose of removing obstacles to a task through bribery,
or that which is given in jest or derision.
One person gives his own property to another, and that other person also gives [something] to him; this is the exchange of giving (*dānavyatyāsa*).
Through the application of deception, having intended to give a hundred, one gives a thousand.
Having thus instructed, he gives [it] to one who is immature, not having reached sixteen years of age;
who is foolish, being unacquainted with worldly conventions.
By one who is not independent, such as a son or a slave;
by one who is afflicted, being overcome by disease.
"By one who is intoxicated" means by one intoxicated with liquor; "or by one who is insane" means by one seized by madness such as epilepsy and the like;
"given" means bestowed.

Just as [a gift] given with the desire to entice someone, thinking, "He will perform this work for me," or given to one who does not know the four Vedas after he has said, "I am a knower of the four Vedas," or having obtained wealth [thinking], "I shall perform a sacrifice."
That which is given for the purpose of gambling and the like— even though it consists of sixteen types— is said to be "not given," because it must be recovered.
The status of being "not given" regarding what is given out of distress applies to matters other than those pertaining to religious duties (*dharmakārya*).
"Whether given by one who is healthy or by one who is afflicted, if it was promised for the sake of dharma,
then upon death, the son must be made to pay it even if he did not give it himself; there is no doubt in this matter," according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana.

Likewise, this is another statement summarizing the meaning, applicable to all disputes: "Whatever is mortgaged or sold through fraud, or given or received through fraud, or where one perceives deceit—let him annul all that. (MDh 8.165)
The meaning is this: "Yoga" refers to a condition (*upādhi*).

By whatever specific condition a purchase, sale, gift, or acceptance was performed, upon the cessation of that condition, one should rescind those transactions such as the purchase; this is the sense.
Furthermore, regarding him who takes what has not been given in any of its sixteen forms, and him who gives what should not be given, the punishment for both has been stated by Nārada:
"He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who gives what should not be given..."
One who gives what should not be given is to be punished, as is one who accepts what has been given [in such a manner].
Thus [it is said]. (NSm 4.11) //2.176//
Thus ends the section titled "Non-delivery of what has been given.
Now begins the section on rescission of purchase;
next, the rescission of purchase is explained.
The nature of this [legal matter] was stated by Nārada:

"When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, does not regard it as highly [as expected], this is called the legal head of dispute known as *krītānuśaya* (repentance after purchase). (NSm 9.1)
And in that regard, it was stated by him [the author] that on the very day the merchandise is purchased, it must be returned in its unchanged state:
"When a buyer, having purchased merchandise for a price, considers it a bad purchase..."

"The seller must return that [article] on that very day, provided it is undamaged. (NSm 9.2) However, regarding its return on the second day or subsequent days, a specific rule has been stated by that same author:
"If the buyer returns it on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price as compensation."

"But on the third day it is double; beyond that, it belongs to the purchaser alone" (NSm 9.3). The meaning is that after that time, no rescission may be made. And this refers to perishable objects such as seeds, other than [perishable] enjoyments and the like.
Furthermore, regarding the purchase of seeds and other such items, there is a different procedure for their return; thus he says:

"The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month, respectively. (YDh 2.177)
The seed is the seed of rice and so forth;
iron is metal;
the draught animal is the ox and so forth.
Jewels refer to pearls, coral, and so forth; women refers to female slaves; milkable animals refers to buffaloes and the like;
and males refers to male slaves.

The period for examining these items, such as seeds and so forth, should be understood as ten days and so on, respectively. Furthermore, the purpose of this instruction is that if, while examining the seeds and so forth, a latent doubt arises regarding their lack of integrity, then the purchase must be rescinded within those ten days or other specified period, and not thereafter.
As for the statement of Manu:
"If, after having bought or sold anything here, one should have regret, he may return that object or take it back within ten days" (MDh 8.222).

Thus, this refers to perishable objects such as houses, fields, vehicles, beds, seats, and so forth, which are distinct from the aforementioned metals and other [durable goods]. Furthermore, all of this concerns items purchased without prior inspection;
for regarding that which has been inspected, there is an agreement that it shall not be returned.
Once it has been purchased, it need not be returned to the seller. As it has been said:
"The buyer should personally examine the merchandise beforehand for its merits and defects;
once it has been examined and accepted, what has been purchased shall not be subject to return to the seller."
In connection with the examination of milk and other substances, he describes the examination of gold and the like as well:
"Gold remains undiminished in fire; in silver, two palas [are lost] per hundred;
eight in tin and lead; five in copper; and ten in iron. (YDh 2.178)
Gold being heated in fire does not diminish;
therefore, for the purpose of fashioning bracelets and other ornaments, as much gold as has been placed in the hands of the goldsmith must be weighed out and returned by them.
Otherwise, they shall be made to pay for the loss and be punished.
In the case of silver, however, when one hundred *pala* are being smelted, a loss of two *pala* occurs;
in the case of tin and lead, the loss is eight [per hundred].
This continues [from the previous rule]:
when one hundred *pala* of tin and lead are heated, eight *pala* are lost;
in the case of copper and iron, five *pala* are lost from one hundred *pala* of copper.
In iron, ten palas are lost;
here too, it is simply "one hundred. However, since bell-metal (kāṃsya) originates from tin and copper, its loss should be calculated accordingly.
Artisans who cause greater loss than that shall be punished. (2.178)
In some cases, such as with blankets and the like, he states the interest:
"On woolen cloth, cotton, and silk, the interest on a hundred [units] is ten palas;
on medium quality, it is five palas, while on fine quality, three palas is considered the interest. (YDh 2.179)

In the case of a woolen blanket or similar item made with thick woolen thread, an increase of ten palas should be understood for every hundred palas [of the base material]. The same should be understood for cloth and other items made from cotton thread.
This applies to medium-quality cloth and other items made from thread that is not excessively fine.
The increase is five palas.
In the case of a hundred [threads] woven from very fine yarn, the increase should be known as three palas. And this refers to unwashed cloth. (2.179)
He states the specific rule regarding other materials:
"In the case of woven silk and woolen cloth, a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized;
however, there is neither loss nor increase in the case of silk and bark garments. (YDh 2.180)
The *kārmika* is that which is fashioned by various artistic works.
When a painting has been completed on a cloth, the subsequent application of designs such as wheels or svastikas with colored threads is called *kārmika*.
Where the hair is attached, as in the case of *prāvāra* and similar fabrics, that is called "hair-attached" (*romabaddha*);

in such cases, the thirtytieth part should be understood as the loss (*kṣaya*). This applies to silk (*kauśeya*), which originates from cocoons, and to bark-garments (*vālkala*), which are made from the bark of trees.
In the case of garments, there is neither increase nor decrease; rather, only as much as was given to the weavers and others for the purpose of weaving shall be reclaimed. (2.180)
Because it is impossible to demonstrate the loss and increase for every single commodity due to their infinite variety, he states the means for knowing decrease and increase in general:

"Having ascertained the place, the time, and the usage, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the commodities when they have been lost, those who are skilled should declare what must undoubtedly be paid. (YDh 2.181)

When goods such as hemp or linen have been lost or have deteriorated, those skilled in the increase and decrease of commodities—being experts in the valuation of goods—shall, having examined the place, the time, the usage, as well as the strength or weakness of the lost article and its quality or lack thereof, determine what is to be paid; of this there is no doubt, and the artisans shall be made to pay that amount. (2.181)
Thus ends the section on rescission of purchase;
now begins the section on the failure to serve after having agreed to do so, as he proceeds to describe another head of dispute known as *abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*.
And its nature was stated by Nārada:
"But he who, having undertaken service, does not perform it..."

"Having agreed to this, failure to serve is called the title of law known as 'non-performance after agreement' (abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā). (NSm 5.1) Service consists of carrying out orders; when one, having accepted it, subsequently fails to perform it, that is the title of law termed non-performance after agreement. And the servant is of five kinds.
A student, a resident pupil, a hired laborer, a supervisor, and a slave— among these,
the first four are called "manual laborers," and they are performers of auspicious work.
Furthermore, slaves are of fifteen types, such as those born in the household and so forth;
they perform inauspicious tasks such as cleaning the house, the door, impure places, the streets, and the refuse heaps.
This has been clarified by Nārada:
"In the treatise, five kinds of servants have been observed by the wise;
four kinds are laborers, and among them, fifteen are slaves."
Disciples, resident pupils, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer for extra work—these are to be known as laborers; slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth.

The wise have stated that their common characteristic is dependence; however, the distinction between them, as well as their specific functions, is said to be determined by their genus and their actions.
Action, too, should be known to be of two kinds: indeed, the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The inauspicious is said to be the work of a servant; the auspicious is remembered as the work of those who perform [right] action.
Cleaning the house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; touching private parts, and the taking up and discarding of food remnants, feces, and urine.

"Furthermore, the attendance upon a master who desires it with one's own limbs should be understood as impure action; other than that, it is pure. (NSm 5.2–7). In this context, the *śiṣya* is one who seeks the knowledge of the Vedas.
An *antevāsī* is one who seeks training in a craft; one who performs work for wages is a *bhṛtaka*;
and one who supervises those performing work is an *adhikarmakṛt*.
*Aśucisthāna* refers to a pit or similar place intended for the disposal of leftovers;
*avaskara* is the place where the dust and other refuse swept from a house are piled up.
"Ujjhana" means abandonment. Furthermore, the hired laborer here is of three kinds; as it has been said: "In this context, the one with weapons is the highest, while the farmer is the middling."
"One who carries a burden for the lowest wage—thus is the hired servant of three kinds.
(NSm 5.21) Furthermore, slaves are: one born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an inheritance, and one who has come of his own accord; |||
Likewise, one who was maintained out of season, as well as one who has been abandoned by his master.
I was liberated from great bondage; won at stake in battle;
approached you saying "I am yours"; and made to renounce my life as a wandering ascetic.
One who is a slave by inheritance, as well as one acquired through a female slave,
and one who has sold himself— these are recorded in the treatise as the fifteen types of slaves.
One born of a female slave in the house is known as "born in the house" (*gṛhaja*).

One acquired for a price is one obtained through payment; one received as a gift is one obtained by means of a donation or similar act; one who has come from inheritance is a slave belonging to a father or other relative.
One who was maintained during a famine at an improper time; one who was saved from death by being made a slave;
and one who was pledged by his master through the receipt of wealth, having been reduced to the state of a pawn.
A debt-slave is one who has entered into servitude by means of the discharge of a debt. One captured in battle is one seized after being defeated in combat.
"Having made a wager, saying, 'If I am defeated in this dispute, then I shall become your slave,' he was defeated;
having approached [the master], saying 'I am yours,' he has himself admitted, 'I am your slave.'"

"One who has abandoned the going-forth" means one who has fallen away from the religious life; "one who has been made [a slave]" means one who has been accepted [as such] with the agreement, "For this much time you are my slave."
A *bhaktadāsa* is one who has entered into servitude at all times, having accepted slavery solely for the sake of food.
A *vaḍavāhṛta* is one brought by a mare.
A house-servant was carried off by her; out of greed for her, he married her and entered into servitude.
He who sells himself is an "ātma-vikretṛ" (seller of self); thus there are fifteen types [of slaves].
As for that which was stated by Manu:

"One captured under a banner, one who serves for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given, one inherited from a father, and one enslaved as a penalty— these seven are the sources of slaves" (MDh 8.415).
Thus, the sevenfold nature has been stated;
that is for the purpose of demonstrating their status as slaves, and not for the purpose of an exhaustive enumeration.

Among these—namely, the student (*śiṣya*), the apprentice (*antevāsin*), the hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*), the assistant laborer (*adhikarmakṛt*), and the slave (*dāsa*)—the conduct of the student has already been explained previously.

"One should study when summoned, and one should report whatever has been obtained to him" (YDh 1.27), and so forth. Regarding the laborer who performs additional work, his wages will be discussed in the section on the payment of wages:
"The wage for him shall be proportional to the amount of work he performs" (YDh 2.196).
By such [statements] as these.
To state the specific rule regarding slaves and apprentices, he says:

"One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, or even one who has been sold, is released [from slavery] by saving the life of his master, by abandoning his food, or by the payment of his ransom. (YDh 2.182)
One who has been made a slave by force— that is, by means of physical compulsion—
and one who has been seized and sold by thieves;
by the use of the word "api" (also), one who has been pledged [is included].
And once it has been given, he is released;
if the owner does not release him, then he must be released by the king. And it has been said by Nārada:
"Those who have been stolen by thieves, sold, or forcibly made into slaves must be released by the king; for slavery is not permitted in their case. (NSm 5.36).
Furthermore, he who gives his life or protects the life of a master who has been seized by thieves, tigers, or the like, must also be released.
This is the common cause for the cessation of slavery for all types of slaves:
whoever shall liberate any of them from their master when their life is in danger, he is released from servitude and shall receive a share equal to that of a son. (NSm 5.28)
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada.
The means of liberation for each of the categories beginning with the *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food) is also stated:
the *anākālabhṛta* and the *bhaktadāsa* are liberated by giving back everything they have consumed, starting from their status as a slave due to the provision of food, up to the master’s property.

But regarding the pledged debtor (*āhitarnadāsa*)— that is, one who has been pledged by his master after receiving a loan, or one who has been liberated from creditors by the wealthy lender after giving [property]— he is released by the repayment of that debt along with interest.
A specific rule has also been stated by Nārada:

One who was maintained [as a slave] during a time of famine is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle; however, that which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by such an act. (NSm 5.29) By the relinquishing of food, a *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food) is immediately released. (NSm 5.34)
"Even if he has been pledged, if the master releases him after giving him wealth;
but by paying the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery. (NSm 5.30–31) Thus it is said.
Likewise, he stated the specific reasons for the release of those who have come saying "I am yours," those captured in battle, those won at a wager, and those brought in by fraud:
"One who has come saying 'I am yours,' one captured in battle, or one won at a wager..."
"They may be released by the giving of a substitute head through an equal act" (NSm 5.32).
"One who has made a formal agreement is also released upon the lapse of the stipulated time" (NSm 5.31).
"But one who was seized by a *vaḍavā* is released from the restraint of the *vaḍavā*" (NSm 5.34). Thus it is said.
The meaning is that [liberation is impossible] because of the cessation of enjoyment together with the slave.

Thus, for those born in the house, bought, obtained as a gift, acquired through inheritance, or who have sold themselves, there is no liberation except through the common causes consisting of saving the master’s life or gaining his favor.
Because no specific cause [for non-liberation] has been stated,
the emancipation of a slave must be performed according to this sequence:
"A master who, with a joyful heart, desires to make his own slave a non-slave..."
Taking [a clod of earth] from a heap, he would break that jar along with its water.
"He should sprinkle water with rice grains and flowers upon his head;
then, having said 'Thou art no slave,' he should release him three times while facing eastward.
Thus it was stated by that very same author. (NSm 5.40–41) [2.182]

But he says that for one who has fallen from the life of renunciation, there is no liberation: "One who has fallen from the life of renunciation is the king's slave until the end of his life" (YDh 2.183ab). Renunciation (*pravrajyā*) means *saṃnyāsa*; one who has fallen (*avasitaḥ*) from that is one who has lapsed from it.
If he does not accept the penance, he becomes the slave of the king alone; death is the only end to that slavery, for there is no release at any other time.
He states the regulation regarding servitude with respect to the social classes:
"Servitude exists among the classes in the direct order, not in the inverse order. (YDh 2.183cd) Servitude belongs to the classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa in the direct order [of caste].
The Kṣatriya and others for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Vaiśya and Śūdra for a Kṣatriya.

For a Vaiśya, a Śūdra may become a slave in this manner according to the natural order (ānulomya), but not in the inverse order (prātilomya). However, for a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) who has abandoned his own duty (svadharma), slavery is indeed permitted even in the inverse order; as Nārada has said:
Slavery by means of the inverse order of castes is not ordained;
except in the case of one who has abandoned his own duty, slavery is considered to be like marriage.
Thus [it is said]. (NSm 5.37) //2.183//
He states the duties of a resident pupil: "Even after he has mastered the craft, the resident pupil shall remain in the teacher's house for the prescribed period;
having received his food from the teacher, he shall offer the fruits thereof [to him]. (YDh 2.184)
A pupil, having agreed that he would reside in the house of his teacher for a fixed period of four years for the purpose of learning crafts such as Āyurveda, may live there for that duration;
even if he has acquired the required knowledge of the craft before the end of the four years,
how should he dwell [thereafter]?

"One who has obtained food from the guru" means one by whom food has been received from the presence of the guru. "One who offers its fruit" means one who gives the fruit of that craft to the teacher; such a person should reside [there]. Nārada has also shown a specific rule regarding this: "He shall give the teacher the best of his earnings, as well as ornaments and clothing. Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his relatives,
he should live with a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teachers should instruct him in their own home, providing him with food;
they should not make him perform any other work, and they should treat him like a son.
If one who is being instructed should abandon an uncorrupted teacher, he should be forced to stay by means of confinement; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even if he has been trained, the pupil shall receive his fee once the time [of training] is completed;
and whatever work he performs therein, the fruit of that belongs solely to the teacher.
"Having mastered the craft, and having circumambulated the teacher at the proper time, the pupil, once instructed, should take leave of him and depart. (NSm 5.15–19).
Here, the word *vadha* means "beating," because the offense is minor. (2.184)
Having thus concluded the section on disputes known as non-service,
now follows the section on the breach of agreement;
the breach of agreement is now being discussed.
And its definition has been shown by Nārada through the method of exclusion:
"The established practice of heretics, guilds, and others is called a *samaya* (convention); the non-abandonment of that convention is recorded as that title of dispute. (NSm 10.1)
The meaning is as follows: "Convention" (samaya) is the establishment [of rules] by means of technical terminology;
its non-abandonment is its non-transgression, which is its observance.
When that is being transgressed, it becomes a ground for legal dispute.
To introduce that subject, he says something:

"Having established a residence in the city and appointed Brāhmaṇas there who are learned in the three Vedas and provided with a livelihood, the king should tell them: 'Let your own duty be protected. (YDh 2.185)

The king, having constructed fortresses and other structures such as white palaces within his own city and stationed Brāhmaṇas there, established that community of Brāhmaṇas as *traividya*—endowed with knowledge of the three Vedas—and provided them with a livelihood consisting of land, gold, and other resources; he then instructed them, saying: "Let the *svadharma* pertaining to your caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), as ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti, be practiced by you."
He should speak to the Brahmins. Regarding the duty that must be performed by those thus appointed, he says:
"But he who is bound by agreement, provided it does not conflict with his own dharma," [should be honored].
That dharma which is established by the king must also be protected with effort. Even that dharma—

which is produced by convention (samaya) without contradicting the dharma prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis, and which takes the form of protecting pasture lands for cattle, preserving water sources, maintaining temples, and so forth—
must also be diligently upheld.

Likewise, whatever conventional duty has been established by the king—provided it does not conflict with his own dharma—such as the rule that food must be given to every traveler, or that horses and other resources must not be dispatched to the territories of our enemies, that too must be protected. (2.186)

Having stated that the rules of the community (samayadharma) must be observed in this manner, he now declares the punishment for their violation and so forth: "But he who misappropriates the property of the community, and he who transgresses the agreement—having confiscated all his possessions, the king shall banish him from the kingdom. (YDh 2.187)

Furthermore, whoever steals property belonging to a *gaṇa*— that is, a common asset belonging to a collective such as a village community— or whoever violates a *saṃvit*, which is a compact established by the group or by the king, having confiscated all of that person's wealth, the king shall banish him from his realm.
And this punishment is to be understood as applying when there is an excess in the consequences (*anubandha*) and so forth;
however, when the consequences are slight, [it is said]:
"He who, having made a covenant by truth with villages, districts, or assemblies..."
If a man should deceive out of greed, the king should banish him from the kingdom.

"Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the compact to pay four *suvarṇas*, six *niṣkas*, and one hundred *mānas* of silver"— thus, among the four punishments prescribed by Manu— banishment, four *suvarṇas*, six *niṣkas*, and one hundred *mānas* of silver— one or another should be applied depending on the caste, capacity, and other relevant factors of the offender.
It is to be inferred. // 2.187 //
And he states what must be done by them:

"The word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all. (YDh 2.188ab) Among the members of a group, the speech of those whose habit is to speak for the welfare of the community must be adhered to by others who belong within that group.
Otherwise, he states that there shall be punishment:
"He who therein acts contrary [to the decision] shall be made to pay the first fine" (YDh 2.188cd).
He who, among the members of an assembly, obstructs the speech of one who speaks for the benefit of the collective, shall be fined the first *sāhasa* by the king.
He is liable to punishment. // 2.188 //
The king should conduct himself toward the members of the guilds in this manner; so it is said:
"The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the community with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business is concluded. (YDh 2.189)

Having satisfied with gifts, honors, and respectful treatment those heads of monastic communities who have come to his side to accomplish the business of the collective and have completed their own purposes, that king should dismiss them. (2.189)
Regarding one who misappropriates what was given for a collective purpose, [the law] says:
"That which a person sent on behalf of a collective body may obtain, he shall hand over;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times the amount. (YDh 2.190)

Whatever gold, clothing, or other goods a person receives from the king on behalf of a collective undertaking when dispatched by the public, he shall report that to the public even without being asked;
otherwise, he shall be compelled to pay a fine eleven times the amount received. (2.190)
And regarding those who must be appointed as deliberators of affairs, he says:
"Those who know the law, who are pure and free from greed, shall be the deliberators of affairs;
the word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out. (YDh 2.191)

Those who know the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, who possess external and internal purity, who are free from greed regarding material things, and who deliberate on what ought to be done, should be appointed [as assessors].
Their word must be acted upon by others; this repetition is for the sake of showing respect. (2.191)
Now, extending the dharma established for those learned in the three Vedas to guilds and other groups, he says:
"This same rule applies to guilds, merchant corporations, heretical sects, and assemblies;
the king shall protect their internal divisions and preserve their ancient customs. (YDh 2.192)
Guilds (*śreṇi*) are those who subsist through a single trade or craft;
*naigamas* are those such as the Pāśupatas and others who maintain that the Veda possesses authority because it was composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*).
Those heretics (*pākhaṇḍinaḥ*) who do not accept the authority of the Veda at all— namely the naked ones (*nagna*), the Buddhists (*saugata*),
and so forth; the guilds (*gaṇaḥ*), which are groups of those such as professional soldiers (*āyudhīya*) who subsist on a single occupation—
for all these four types of people, this very same rule applies.
That which has been established by the passage beginning with "he who does not violate his own dharma" (YDh 2.2.186),
and so forth— the king shall protect the distinctions and the legal regulations of these guilds and other such groups.
And one should maintain the livelihood previously acquired. // 2.192 //
Thus ends the section on the breach of agreements;
now begins the section on the non-payment of wages, which is a title of legal dispute known as *vetanasyānapākarma*.

The nature of this has been stated by Nārada: "The rule for the giving and receiving of wages for servants has been declared; the non-payment of such wages is recorded as that title of dispute. (NSm 6.1)

The meaning of this is as follows: that subject of dispute (*vivādapada*) wherein the procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for servants—as described in the forthcoming verses—is concerned, is called "Non-payment of Wages" (*vetanasyānapākarma*). Regarding that, he states the legal decision.
One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double;

if he has not received them, he shall be made to pay an equal amount. The tools must be protected by the servants. (YDh 2.193) He by whom wages have been received, abandoning—that is, failing to perform—the work he had undertaken, shall give double the wages to the employer.

Furthermore, when one abandons work that has been undertaken before the wages have been received, then he should be made to pay the full amount of the wages that were agreed upon, but not double; or else,
having paid the stipulated fee, he should be compelled to perform the work by force.
"Having promised to perform work, one who does not do it; or having given wages, one who takes them by force"— according to this statement of Nārada,
wages have also been defined by that same author.
"The master of the work shall give wages to the servant in due order—
at the beginning, middle, or end of the labor— as has been determined.
(NSm 6.2) And by those servants, "upaskara" means equipment— the traces, yokes, and so forth for ploughs and other implements— according to their ability.
It must be protected, for otherwise the production of crops and other such things would be impossible. (2.193)
Regarding one who causes work to be performed without having fixed the wages, the author says:
"But he who causes work to be done without determining the wages must be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, or grain. (YDh 2.194)
But if a master— whether a merchant, an owner of cattle, or a landowner— causes a servant to perform work for which no fixed wage has been determined,
the king, the ruler of the earth, must compel him to give to that servant the tenth part of whatever is obtained from that work consisting of trade, cattle, or crops. (2.194)
Regarding one who fails to carry out what was commanded, he says:
"He who exceeds the place and time, and he who effects the profit otherwise—therein the master’s will shall prevail; if more is done, more should be given. (YDh 2.195)

If a servant, out of pride or other such reasons, fails to carry out the sale of merchandise or similar tasks at the appropriate place and time, or if he performs them in that very same place and time but realizes a profit that is inferior due to excessive expenditure and the like, then regarding the payment of wages to that servant, the master’s *chanda*— that is, his will or discretion— shall prevail.
The meaning is that one may give as much as one wishes, but not the entire fee;
however, when there is an additional gain due to knowledge of the proper place and time, [one may give more].
In that case, the master must give even more wealth to the servant than the previously agreed-upon wage. (2.195)

He states the method for the payment of wages regarding work that must be accomplished by multiple servants: "Whatever amount of work one performs, his wage shall be commensurate with that; however, if the task is impossible for both together to accomplish, they should perform it according to their respective shares when it is possible. (YDh 2.196)

Furthermore, when a single task with a fixed wage is performed by both [parties], yet remains unaccomplished by both due to being overcome by illness or other such obstacles— and if, according to the word [of the employer], it has not been completed even by many—
then the wage for whichever laborer performs the work shall be determined by a neutral arbitrator in accordance with the amount of work actually done by him.
Wages must be paid, though not necessarily equally;
nor should it be thought that payment need not be made because the wages for each specific portion of the work were not previously stipulated.

But when the work is completed by both together, they must each give what has been prescribed or stipulated according to the agreement; neither should each pay the full wage individually, nor should it be given after calculating a share proportionate to the individual's labor. (2.196)
Regarding those who carry weapons or loads, he says:
"The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or providence;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages. (YDh 2.197)
That merchandise for which no loss caused by the king or by fate exists is described as such.
If that [merchandise] has been destroyed by the carrier through lack of care, then he must be made to pay for that merchandise according to the extent of the loss.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
"If the goods should meet with misfortune due to the fault of the carrier, he shall be made to pay for whatever is lost therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king. (NSm 6.10)

Furthermore, if one who has previously agreed to perform the rites necessary for the departure of someone setting out on an auspicious day for the purpose of marriage or similar events, then fails to do so by creating an obstacle to that departure, he shall be made to pay double wages.
Because of the cessation of karma, which is the cause of ultimate excellence. // 2.197 //
Furthermore:
If he abandons the laborer on the way after he has set out, he must pay one-seventh of the wage;
if he abandons him halfway, he must pay the full wage; and the deserter shall also be made to pay the same. (YDh 2.198)
If a person abandons work that has been undertaken once the journey has commenced and the departure is finalized, he shall be made to pay a seventh part of the wages.
But surely, regarding this very same subject, the payment of double the wages was previously stated in the rule beginning with "one who causes an obstacle to the departure," and so forth?
Now, there is a contradiction in saying it is "the seventh part. It is replied:

If a person abandons the work he has undertaken when an opportunity arises to take on another servant, his seventh part [of the wages] is forfeited. However, there is no contradiction in the rule that for one who abandons the work at the very moment of departure, double the wages must be paid.
Furthermore, if one abandons the work while the journey has already begun and is in progress, he [forfeits] a fourth part of the wages.
He shall be made to pay a portion [of the wages];
furthermore, if he abandons him halfway, he shall be made to pay the entire wage.
But as for the employer who abandons one who does not abandon the work—
The master causes him to relinquish [the wages] in the aforementioned places; he too must cause the previously mentioned seventh part and so forth to be given to the servant.
And this refers to the case of one who is not ill and so forth:
"A servant who, being unafflicted, does not perform his work as is appropriate out of pride..."
"He shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages for that period shall not be paid," according to the statement of Manu (MDh 8.215).
However, when he completes the work after counting and making up for the days lost due to illness once the illness has passed, then he receives [his wages].
In this very manner, one who is ill may perform the work; however, once he has recovered, he must perform it as originally stipulated from the beginning.
Even after a long period of time, he shall indeed receive his wages. (MDh 8.216)
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu.

However, for one who is free from illness and in good health, yet does not perform the work he himself undertook even if it is slightly incomplete due to laziness or the like, or does not complete it through another, wages should not be paid to him.
As Manu says:

As it has been said: "Whether he be distressed or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be paid, even for work that is only slightly incomplete. (MDh 8.217) 2.198.
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of wages; now begins the section on gambling and betting, which is the legal title of dispute known as *dyūta-samāhvaya*.
And its specific nature was described by Nārada:
