"Gambling (*dyūta*) consists of playing with dice, sticks, small pebbles, and the like, conducted in a deceitful manner; and betting (*samāhvaya*) consists of games involving stakes and animals. (NSm 17.1)
The *akṣas* are dice;
the *vadhra* is a leather strap;
the *śalākās* are long, square pieces made of ivory or similar materials.
And by the inclusion of the word "first" (ādi),
the means for games such as those involving horses— namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth— are understood; gambling with those inanimate objects is what is meant.
A game is played with stakes;
likewise, there is that game played with stakes involving birds and winged creatures such as cocks and pigeons, and also involving living beings such as wrestlers, rams, and buffaloes.
Both of these, in their respective order, constitute the title of dispute known as *dyūta-samāhvaya*.
*Dyūta* (gambling) and *samāhvaya* (challenging to a match) together form *dyūta-samāhvaya*. Thus it has been said:
Manu says:
"That which is performed with inanimate objects is called 'dyūta' (gambling) in the world;
but that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as 'samāhvaya' (betting). (MDh 9.223)
Regarding that, he states the livelihood of the superintendent of the gambling house:
"The keeper of the gambling house (sabhika) shall take five percent from a gambler who stakes a hundred, and ten percent from any other [gambler]. (YDh 2.199)
A stake (glaha) is that which is established as a wager by mutual agreement among gamblers;

in that context, "bearing interest at the rate of one hundred" (śatikavṛddhi) refers to a gambler from whom one receives interest—whether amounting to one hundred or exceeding that—based upon that stake. From such a rogue gambler [one must not borrow].
A keeper of a gambling hall (*sabhika*) may take five percent for his own livelihood.
That hundred in which there is an income of five *paṇas* is called "five-percent" (*pañcakaṃ śatam*). This is according to the rule: *tad asmin vṛddhyāyalābha-* (Pāṇini 5.1.47).
By the word "ityādi," the suffix *kan* is applied;
the meaning is that one should take the twentieth part of the winnings.
A *sabhā* is a place for the residence of gamblers.
He who possesses these is the *sabhika*.
One who has prepared all the gaming implements such as dice and so forth, and subsists on the wealth accumulated therefrom, is called the master of the gambling house (*sabhāpati*).

Furthermore, from the other [the debtor], even when the interest has increased to a full hundred percent, one should take ten per cent—that is, the tenth part—of the wealth won from the gambler. (2.199)
Regarding what must be done by the master of the gambling house who has thus established his conduct, he says:
"Being properly protected, he shall pay the king the share as determined;
he shall cause the winner to receive what was won, and being patient, he shall speak the truth. (YDh 2.200)
The superintendent of gambling who has thus established his livelihood and is protected by the king from rogue gamblers shall pay the king the share as agreed upon;
likewise, he shall cause the won property to be recovered through the seizure of pledges, by means of restraint, and so forth.
And he should recover [the stake] from the one who has been defeated;
having recovered that wealth, the keeper of the gambling hall should give it to the winner, the victor.
Likewise, being patient, he should provide truthful speech for the sake of inspiring confidence among the gamblers.
Thus it was said by the Son of Nara:
"The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game, and he shall pay what is owed for what has been done therein. (NSm 17.2) 2.200.
Furthermore, when the keeper of the gambling house is unable to make the payment, then the king shall cause it to be paid; so it is said:
"When the king has received his share and the circle of gamblers is well-known, he should cause the winner to pay at that place where the keeper is present, but not otherwise. (YDh 2.201)

In a public, uncovered gambling hall attended by royal officials and presided over by a *sabhika* (the master of the game), once the *sabhika* has paid the king’s share, the king shall compel the deceitful gambler who has not contested the loss to pay the won stake. Otherwise, in a secret gambling match held without a *sabhika* and where the king’s share has not been paid, he shall not compel the winner to give the won stake to the loser. (2.201)
He states the means of decision when there is a dispute regarding victory or defeat:
"For they alone are the observers of the legal proceedings and the witnesses.
(YDh 2.202ab) The observers of gambling disputes—the members of the court—must be appointed by the king as those very same gamblers; it is not otherwise in that case.
There is a rule stating that [witnesses] must be endowed with learning and study, and so forth;
furthermore, in the case of gambling, only those who are gamblers themselves should be made witnesses.
In that regard, there is no prohibition against women, children, the elderly, gamblers, and the like.
In some cases, he prescribes punishment to prohibit gambling: "Those who play with false dice or by means of fraud should be banished by the king, marked with a brand.

Those who gamble using false dice and the like, or by means of fraud—that is, by means of gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, which serve as causes for deceiving the mind—[should be punished].
Having branded them with the mark of a dog's foot or similar signs, the king shall banish them from his kingdom.
However, Nārada has stated a specific rule regarding banishment:
"The king shall banish from the realm those wicked persons who play with fraudulent dice."
"Placing a rosary around the neck—this indeed is declared to be their discipline. (NSm 17.6) And as for those statements of Manu intended to prohibit gambling:
"Whoever engages in gambling or betting, or causes them to be done..."

"The king shall cause all those to be executed, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born" (MDh 9.224)— these and similar passages are also to be applied to the context of fraudulent gambling with dice and to the context of gambling supervised by royal officials or professional gamblers. 2.202.
Furthermore:

"Gambling should be conducted with a single face for the purpose of identifying thieves. (YDh 2.203ab) That gambling which was mentioned previously is said to be "with a single face," meaning that gambling of which one face—the primary side—is singular.

The term *kāryam* means that the work must be carried out by the king under the supervision of an official, for the purpose of identifying thieves. Having considered the objective— which is the identification of thieves— it is generally observed that gamblers are precisely those who have acquired wealth through theft.
Therefore, for the purpose of identifying the thief, it should be made with a single opening.
Applying the rules of gambling to a formal challenge, he says: "This very same rule is to be understood as applicable to a challenge involving living beings. (YDh 2.203cd) [As previously stated:
"In a wager, the interest shall be one hundredfold" (YDh 2.199).

The rules for gambling that have been stated by these and other such verses are to be understood as applying equally to "animal gambling" (prāṇidyūta), which is known as *samāhvaya* and is carried out with wrestlers, rams, buffaloes, and so forth. (2.203)
Thus concludes the section titled "Gambling and Betting";
now begins the section on "Verbal Abuse.
Verbal abuse is introduced here.
And the definition of that has been stated by Nārada:

"Speech that is contrary in meaning, consisting of abuse directed at one's country, caste, family, and so forth, and joined with personal insults—that is called verbal assault (*vākpāruṣya*). (NSm 15–16.1)
Abusive speech toward others concerning their country and so forth, joined with censure (*nyaṅga*):
"abusive speech" (*ākrośa*) is speaking aloud; "censure" (*nyaṅga*) is that which is blameworthy; it is [speech] joined with both of these.
Speech that is contrary in meaning or intended to produce agitation is called verbal harshness (*vākpāruṣya*).
Among these, to say "the Gaudas are indeed fond of quarreling" is an insult directed at a region.
"Brahmins are indeed excessively greedy" is an insult to the caste;
"The descendants of Viśvāmitra are surely of cruel conduct" is an insult to the family.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the harsh verbal abuse directed at learned men, artisans, and others by disparaging their own knowledge, crafts, and so forth, is included. And, having stated that this [abuse] is of three kinds—namely, the distinction between "harsh" (niṣṭhura) and so on—in order to determine the gradations of punishment, its definition was stated by that very same author: "A harsh word is one that causes pain to the heart; a cruel word is one that causes physical injury; and a word that is both harsh and cruel is called 'exceedingly severe'. ||| (Manu Smṛti 8.267) ||| Thus, having described the threefold nature of verbal abuse through the distinctions of "harsh" and so forth, he has also provided its definition.
That [abuse] is also recorded as being threefold, due to its being harsh, vulgar, or extreme;
and the punishment for it should likewise be progressively heavier according to that sequence of gravity.

"Harsh speech is to be understood as that which is accompanied by reproach; the wise say that speech joined with censure of a person's physical defects and involving accusations of acts leading to loss of caste is 'severe' (tīvra). (NSm 15–16.2–3).
Among these, "Fie on you, fool! You scoundrel! and so forth, is reproachful.
In this context, "nyaṅga" refers to that which is indecent; "avadya" refers to sexual intercourse with a sister or similar persons; and that which is associated with such acts is "aślīla."
Harsh speech is that which is joined with insults such as "you are a drinker of surā" and so forth, concerning the great sins (mahāpātaka) and the like.
Regarding that, he states the punishment for harsh abuse directed toward those of the same caste:
"If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, in sense organs, or afflicted by disease, by means of true, false, or distorted praise, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas. (YDh 2.204)
Those with deficient limbs are those lacking hands, feet, and so forth; those with deficient sense organs are those deprived of eyes, ears, and so forth;
and the diseased are those suffering from skin diseases and the like.
By their truth, by their falsehood, and by their praise that is otherwise or intended as censure—
wherein one who lacks a pair of eyes is called "blind," that is the truth.
Furthermore, where one who possesses sight is called "blind," that is untrue;
where one of deformed appearance is called "handsome," that is a praise based on something else.
By such [means...]

He who insults or reviles another shall be fined thirteen and a half paṇas. Even if one speaks the truth, saying that another is one-eyed, lame, or otherwise deformed, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa. (MDh 8.274)
Thus, that statement of Manu refers to those of extremely wicked character;
however, when sons and others swear against their mothers and so forth, it has been stated by that same author that they are to be fined one hundred [paṇas].

"One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, father-in-law, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher" (MDh 8.275).
This should be understood to apply to the mother and other elders when they have committed an offense, and to the wife when she is without fault. (2.204)
Regarding the punishment for using indecent insults, [Yājñavalkya] says:
"If one swears, 'I shall violate your sister or your mother,' the king should cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]. (YDh 2.205)

If a man swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," or swears, "I shall violate another wife of yours," the king shall cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five paṇas—that is, a punishment consisting of twenty-five coins. (2.205)
Having thus declared the punishment for Brahmins of equal qualities, he speaks in order to establish the punishment for those of unequal qualities:

"Half [the fine] for those of inferior [qualities], double for women who are the wives of others, and [double] for those of superior [qualities]. (YDh 2.206ab) For those of inferior qualities—meaning those whose conduct and other attributes are lower than that of the accuser—the fine is half.
Since twenty-five was the subject of the preceding statement, the "half" in relation to that should be understood as consisting of twelve and a half paṇas.
Furthermore, regarding the wives of others...
Without distinction, the double amount— namely fifty paṇas— should be understood as being in relation to twenty-five alone;
likewise, in the case of the highest class, where learning and conduct are superior relative to oneself, the fine shall consist of exactly fifty paṇas.
He states the determination of punishment when there is mutual insult among the castes (*varṇas*) and those such as the *mūrdhāvasikta*:
"The infliction of punishment must be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the caste and birth" (YDh 2.206cd).
The "castes" (*varṇas*) refer to the Brāhmaṇas and so forth.
The castes (jāti) are those beginning with the consecrated kings (mūrdhāvasikta) and so forth; the social classes (varṇa) and the castes are "classes and castes" (varṇajāti);
and the higher and the lower are "the higher and the lower" (uttarādharāḥ).
The castes and classes are "superior and inferior" (uttarādharāḥ) by virtue of their respective status;

when mutual insults are exchanged by those of superior and inferior caste and class, it should be understood that there is the "infliction of punishment," which means its application, leading forth, or determination.

And since that imposition of punishment is specified by the terms "superior" and "inferior," it is understood that it must be performed specifically with regard to the relationship of superiority and inferiority;
for example, [the punishment for] a *mūrdhāvasikta* [offending] a Brāhmaṇa.

A Brāhmaṇa, having reviled a Kṣatriya who is inferior to him and superior [to himself], deserves a fine of seventy-five paṇas— slightly more than the fifty-paṇa fine occasioned by insulting a Kṣatriya;
likewise, a Kṣatriya, having reviled that [Brāhmaṇa], [deserves a fine] occasioned by insulting a Brāhmaṇa.
One who reviles a *chatradaṇḍa* deserves a fine of exactly seventy-five [paṇas];
even a *mūrdhāvasikta*, having reviled him,
deserves that same fine.
When a Mūrdhāvasikta and an Ambaṣṭha mutually insult each other, the fines occasioned by the mutual abuse of a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should be understood to apply respectively.
In this same manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well. (2.206)
Having thus stated the punishment regarding those of equal caste, he now declares the punishment for the censure of castes in the inverse and natural orders:
"In cases of censure involving the inverse order, the fines for the castes are double and triple [respectively];
in the natural order, they decrease by half and half again from that. (YDh 2.207)

*Apavāda*s are insults; *prātilomyāpavāda*s are insults directed in the reverse order [of the social classes]. In the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa, the fines are double those mentioned in the preceding statement—namely, double the fifty *paṇas* prescribed in sequence for those two classes.

The fines should be understood as follows: for a Śūdra who reviles a Brāhmaṇa, the fines are threefold, amounting to one hundred and fifty paṇas; furthermore, there shall be either flogging or the cutting off of the tongue.
As Manu has said:
"A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred; a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. (MDh 8.267)

By the same logic, it should be understood that when a Vaiśya or a Śūdra reviles a Kṣatriya— one who is either immediately adjacent or separated by one degree— the fine is one hundred and one hundred and fifty respectively;
and when a Śūdra reviles a Vaiśya, the fine is one hundred.

But in the case of the *varṇas* in the direct order— namely, when a *brāhmaṇa* utters an insult against a *kṣatriya*, a *vaiśya*, or a *śūdra*— one should reduce by half the fine for each successive *varṇa* from the hundred *paṇas* prescribed for insulting a *brāhmaṇa*; thus, the remaining fines shall consist of fifty, twenty-five, and twelve and a half *paṇas* respectively.
A Brahmin is to be punished according to the sequence [of offenses].
As it was stated by Manu:
"A Brahmin is to be fined fifty [paṇas] for making a false accusation against a Kṣatriya."
"In the case of a Vaiśya, it shall be forty-five; for a Śūdra, the fine is twelve.
(MDh 8.268) When a Kṣatriya is reviled by a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the fines are fifty and twenty-five [paṇas] respectively.
It should be inferred that when a Vaiśya reviles a Śūdra, the fine is fifty [paṇas].
According to the traditional teaching of Gautama, "As it is for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, so it is for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas" (GDh 12.14),
and according to Manu: "For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is exactly the same regarding their own respective castes in truth" (MDh 8.277).
And because of this recollection from Manu [2.207].
Furthermore, with reference to harsh insults, he says:
"For verbal threats of destroying the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred;
for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that. (YDh 2.208)

When the destruction of each limb, such as the arms and so forth, is verbally expressed—such as in the form of the statement "I shall cut off your arms"—the fine should be understood as one hundred [paṇas]. In the case of verbal threats regarding the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth—the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi) referring to the buttocks and other parts—the fine is half of that; that is, half of those one hundred paṇas is "half-of-that" (tadardhika), and that which possesses this amount is [the offender].
Half of that, a fine of fifty paṇas, should be understood as the penalty. // 2.208 //
Furthermore: "But one who is unable [to pay] and speaks thus should be punished with a fine of ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is able should be made to provide a surety for his security. (YDh 2.209)
Furthermore, he who, being weakened in strength by fever or other ailments, utters an oath such as "I shall break your arm or other limb," is to be fined ten paṇas.

On the other hand, he who, though capable, assails one who is weakened in strength as before, shall, after the aforementioned fine of a hundred or more paṇas, be compelled to provide a surety for the safety of that incapacitated person. (2.209)
Regarding severe verbal abuse, he states the punishment:
"For an insult involving a cause for expulsion (pātitya), the punishment is the middle amercement;
but for one involving a minor offense (upapātaka), the offender shall be made to pay the first amercement. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.210)

When an accusation is made against members of the [first three] castes using grounds for loss of caste (*pātityahetu*), such as killing a Brahmin and so forth, the punishment is the middle amercement (*madhyamasāhasa*).

Furthermore, when an accusation is made involving a minor offense (*upapātaka*), such as "you are a cow-killer" and the like, he is to be punished with the first amercement (*prathamasāhasa*). (2.210)
Furthermore:
For the expulsion of those learned in the three Vedas, kings, or gods, the fine is the highest amercement;
for castes and guilds, it is the middle amercement; and for villages or districts, it is the first amercement. (YDh 2.211)
For the defamation of those kings and gods who are "Traividyas"—that is, those perfected in the three Vedas—the punishment is the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa).
Furthermore, for the defamation of corporations or assemblies (*pūga*) consisting of Brāhmaṇas, Mūrdhāvasiktas, and other such castes, the punishment is the middle amercement (madhyama-sāhasa).
It should be understood that for the defamation of a village or a district individually, the punishment is the first amercement (prathama-sāhasa). (2.211)
Thus ends the section on the title of dispute known as verbal assault;
now follows the section on physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
Physical assault is now introduced.

And its nature was described by Nārada: "Assaulting the limbs of another with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth, or injuring them with ashes and the like, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault). (NSm 15–16.4)

Assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) consists of both: (1) the infliction of injury, harm, or the production of pain through the hands, feet, weapons, or—as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—stones and other such means against the limbs of another, that is, against objects consisting of both the stationary and the moving; and (2) the causing of mental distress by contact, such as by means of ash—as indicated by "and so forth"—or by dust, mud, excrement, and the like. Both of these constitute assault. One is punished (*daṇḍyate*).

"One strikes," thus [it is said]; a punishment (daṇḍa) is to be given for that. That which is violence (pāruṣya), an act of hostility toward movable property such as living beings, is "violence involving a blow" (daṇḍapāruṣya).

Having stated its threefold nature according to the distinction of causes such as threatening with a weapon and so forth, it was further stated by that same author to be threefold again according to the threefold nature of the action consisting of inferior, middling, or superior objects.
The threefold [condition] of that [victim] is also observed through the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior,
by means of the sight of threatening, falling without hesitation, and injury.

"Because of the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior objects, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (violent crimes); therein lies the purification of the thorns. (NSm 15–16.5–6).
"Niḥsaṅgapātana" means causing a fall without hesitation; "niḥśaṅkapraharaṇa" means striking without fear.
There are exactly three thousand, and they are of three kinds;
the meaning is that these are acts of physical violence committed impulsively.
Likewise, between two who have engaged in both verbal and physical violence during a quarrel, he who remains patient not only incurs no punishment, but is indeed worthy of honor.
Thus, regarding the prior quarrel...
For one who initiates an assault, the punishment is severe;
and in a quarrel, only he who pursues a settled enmity incurs the penalty. Likewise, when the specific nature of the offense by either of the two cannot be determined, the punishment shall be equal.
Likewise, when an offense has been committed against noble persons by outcastes (śvapaca) and others, only virtuous men are authorized to inflict punishment;
if they are unable to do so, the king himself must surely execute them, but not [merely] seize their property.
"One should accept"— thus have these five types of rules been stated by him.
Indeed, a fivefold rule has been declared for both of these cases when verbal abuse arises from agitation between two people who are angry with one another.
He thinks thus: "He who forgives escapes the punishment;
but he who first initiates the abuse will certainly be the one to bear the guilt."
Even he who is the first of the five is one who acts without respect; however, discipline is paramount.
Furthermore, when two have fallen into offense equally, he who pursues [the matter] again [is at fault].
He incurs punishment for both of them, whether he was the first or the other,
if they both simultaneously engaged in verbal abuse while being shrouded by the fault of harshness.
If no distinction is perceived, then discipline would apply equally to both [the high and the low],
including outcastes, eunuchs, Cāṇḍālas, the deformed, and those who live by killing.
In the case of transgressing established boundaries by an elephant-driver, an outcaste, or a slave, or toward a teacher, a preceptor, or a king, immediate execution is the only prescribed punishment.
For if these [ministers] should transgress against a virtuous person among men, that king alone shall impose discipline; indeed, the king is the one who possesses the power of discipline.
"For these are indeed the stains of men; their wealth is of the nature of stain.
Therefore, the king should have them executed; he should not punish them with a monetary fine. (NSm 15–16.7–15).
Since the imposition of punishment is preceded by a determination regarding such severity of assault, [the author] states the grounds for determination when there is doubt as to its specific nature:
"But when a person has been killed without witnesses, the legal proceeding must be investigated through physical marks, logical reasoning, and scriptural tradition,
for [a crime] may have been committed with forged marks out of fear.

(YDh 2.212) When someone reports to the king in secret, "I have been killed by this man," then [the truth] must be determined by means of physical marks pertaining to the nature of the victim's body, such as caste and so forth.

An examination should be conducted by means of indicative signs, through reasoning consisting of the deliberation upon causes and purposes, through scripture, and through popular report; and, as indicated by the word "ca," also by means of divine [knowledge], out of fear of the suspicion that the marks might have been forged. // 2.212 //
When the specific nature of the offense has been thus determined, he states the specific punishment for each means of contact:
"For touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
for touching [him] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, it is double that. (YDh 2.213)
In the case of other men's wives who are of equal status, the fine is the same; however, it is double for those of superior status.
For women of lower status, the punishment is half; there is no punishment when the act is committed through delusion, intoxication, and so forth.
He who causes another to be touched by ashes, mud, or dust shall be made to pay a fine of ten paṇas. [The same applies for] impure substances.
By this, tears, phlegm, nails, hair, earwax, rheum of the eyes, food remnants, and so forth are included;
*pārṣṇi* is the rear part of the foot.
"Niṣṭhyūtam" refers to water expelled from the mouth.
If one touches [another] with such [water], then a fine of twenty paṇas— double the previous ten paṇas— is to be understood as the penalty.
Furthermore, regarding contact with feces and the like, a specific rule has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"If [the body] is defiled by vomit, urine, feces, and so forth, the penance is fourfold;
it is sixfold if it occurs on the middle part of the body, and it is traditionally held to be eightfold if it occurs on the head. (KSm 784)
By the inclusion of the word "first," fat, semen, blood, and marrow are understood.
Such a previously mentioned punishment is to be regarded as applying to the case of those of the same caste (savarṇa).
The same applies without distinction to the wives of others;
likewise, in the case of superior persons— those whose learning and conduct exceed one's own— the fines previously mentioned of ten paṇas and twenty paṇas should be understood as being doubled.
In the case of those who are inferior—meaning those whose conduct, learning, and so forth are lesser than one's own—the previously mentioned half-fine should be understood as five paṇas or ten paṇas.
*Moha* is mental derangement; *mada* is intoxication.
It is a particular state produced by the drinking of intoxicants;
by the inclusion of "etcetera," possession by spirits and so forth are meant.
When one is possessed by these, [it refers to] touching ashes and the like.
Even when [an offense] has been committed, punishment should not be inflicted. (2.213–2.214)
He states the punishment for offenses committed in the reverse order [of castes]:
"But for a non-Brāhmaṇa who causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa, the offending limb shall be cut off;
if he merely raised his hand, the first amercement is the penalty, but if there was actual contact, it is half of that. (YDh 2.215)

If a non-Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others, causes pain to Brāhmaṇas, his limb—such as a hand or a foot—must be cut off. Even for a Śūdra who inflicts pain upon a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, there shall be the amputation of a limb.
Indeed, if an outcaste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, [that limb must be severed].
"That very thing which ought to be cut off must be cut off from him; such is the instruction for that man. (MDh 8.279).

Since the cutting off of limbs is prescribed for a Śūdra in the case of an offense against any member of the twice-born classes, this same punishment applies to a Vaiśya as well who has harmed a Kṣatriya, because the underlying principle is the same.
When a weapon or similar object is raised for the purpose of killing, the first amercement is to be understood as the punishment;
however, in the case of a Śūdra, even when [a weapon] is merely raised, there shall be the cutting off of the hand and so forth.
For, according to the traditional law of Manu: "Having raised his hand or a staff, he deserves the amputation of his hand" (MDh 8.280).
But for touching weapons or similar objects for the purpose of brandishing them, it should be understood that the punishment is half of the first *sāhasa* fine.

Furthermore, regarding contact with ashes and the like, as well as insults involving the reverse order of castes for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, one should determine the fines as double or triple according to the principle stated in the section on verbal abuse (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.207). In those cases, however, for a Śūdra, there shall be the amputation of the hand itself.
"Out of pride, the king shall cause the two lips of one who spits upon him to be cut off;
the penis of one who urinates upon him; and the anus of one who passes wind upon him. Thus it is stated in the *Smṛti* of Manu (MDh 8.282). [2.214]
Having thus stated the punishment for an offense committed against the inverse order of castes, he speaks again concerning one's own caste:
"But when [the hand or foot] is merely raised, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively."

But for all [offenses] involving weapons against one another, the middle amercement applies. When the hand or foot is raised for the purpose of striking, the fine should be understood as ten paṇas and twenty paṇas respectively;
when a weapon is raised for the purpose of killing one another, the middle amercement is the punishment for all castes. (YDh 2.216)
Furthermore: For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing them by the hand, the fine is ten paṇas;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a garment, or placing the foot [upon another], the punishment is one hundred [paṇas].

If one seizes any one of another's feet, hair, clothes, or hands and pulls it away abruptly, he shall be fined ten paṇas. If there is a combination of causing pain, pulling, wrapping with a cloth, and placing the foot [upon the other], then for that aggregate of "pain-pulling-cloth-wrapping-foot-placement," he shall be fined one hundred [paṇas].
This is what is meant:
he who, having wrapped [the foot] with a cloth, presses it firmly, pulls it, and strikes with his foot, shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred paṇas. (2.217)
Furthermore:
A man who causes pain with wood or other materials without shedding blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine is double. (YDh 2.218)
Furthermore, he who inflicts a mild beating with wood, clods of earth, or other such objects in such a way that blood is not visible,
shall be fined thirty-two paṇas.

Furthermore, when blood is seen due to severe beating, he should be punished with sixty-four paṇas, which is double the amount for thirty-two. Moreover, a specific distinction regarding the piercing of the skin, flesh, and bone has been shown by Manu.
"One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished. (MDh 8.284) 2.218.
Furthermore:
For breaking a hand, foot, or tooth; for cutting off the ears or the nose;
for piercing through the skin; and likewise for striking someone who is nearly dead, the middle amercement is the punishment. (YDh 2.219)

In the case of breaking each of the hands, feet, or teeth, or cutting off each of the ears or nose, or piercing a healed wound, if one strikes or beats another so that they become as if dead, it should be understood as the middle amercement (madhyama-sāhasa),
depending on the circumstances such as the motive and so forth.
In this case, equanimity toward the object must be brought about. // 2.219 //
Furthermore:
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed. (YDh 2.220)

In the case of obstructing the movement, eating, or speaking of the eyes— and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [obstructing] the tongue as well— as well as in the case of breaking the neck (the cervical vertebrae),
the arm (which is well known), or the thigh (the leg), the punishment for each of these is the middle amercement. (2.220)
Moreover:

"For many who strike one person together, the punishment shall be double that which has been prescribed. (YDh 2.221ab) Furthermore, when many people acting in concert cause the breaking of a limb or similar injury to a single individual, then for whichever specific offense [the punishment applies]...
Whatever punishment has been prescribed in each case, from that a double fine is to be understood for each [of these],
because of their extreme cruelty;
this applies even to offenses committed in the inverse or natural order of castes, within the scope of the same categories of punishment already mentioned for those of equal caste.
One should determine the loss and gain according to the sequence stated for verbal abuse;

whatever punishment was prescribed for verbal abuse in the order of inverse and direct [caste relations], that same punishment shall be imposed by the king in cases of physical assault, respectively. (KSm 786)
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa).
Furthermore:
"That which was seized during a quarrel must be returned, and a fine double that amount shall be imposed.
(YDh 2.221cd) When a quarrel is taking place, whatever has been seized by one person must be restored by him.
A fine equal to twice the value of the stolen property, imposed on account of the theft, shall be paid. (2.221)
Furthermore:
He who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for recovery, as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel. (YDh 2.222)
Whoever causes pain to another by beating them shall pay for whatever expenses are incurred for the purpose of healing the wound, such as medicine and a nutritious diet;
"samutthāna" refers to the healing of the wound.
In whatever quarrel a fine is prescribed, that alone shall be paid, and not merely the expenses incurred for its settlement. 2.222.
Having stated the punishment for injuring the limbs of another, he next declares the punishment for the destruction of external property:
"In cases of striking, cutting, breaking, or causing a wall to fall, one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of repair. (YDh 2.223)
When a wall is struck with a mallet or similar object, torn apart, or split in two, the fines should be understood as five paṇas, ten paṇas, and twenty paṇas respectively;
furthermore, when a wall is brought down, these three fines are to be combined.
They should be seized; furthermore, he should pay the owner the cost for the construction of a wall. // 2.223 //
Moreover:

"Property in the home that causes suffering, as well as that which is life-threatening—one who throws such things [at another] shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas for the first offense, and double that amount for the second. (YDh 2.224)
One who throws an object such as a thorn into another's house, causing pain, shall be fined sixteen paṇas;
however, one who throws a life-threatening substance such as poison or a venomous snake shall be punished with the middle amercement. (2.224)
Regarding the punishment for injuring domestic animals, he says:
"In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise cutting off a limb or a member [of the body], the fine for small animals shall start from two paṇas and increase progressively. (YDh 2.225)
Regarding small animals— those consisting primarily of goats, sheep, and deer— if one causes them pain by beating them, draws their blood, or cuts off their branches and limbs;
here, by the word "branches" (śākhā), horns and the like devoid of the movement of life-force are indicated,
while "limbs" (aṅga) refers to the hands, feet, and so forth.
A branch and a limb constitute "branch-and-limb"; for cutting that, the fine begins at two paṇas— that is,
a fine consisting of two paṇas.
"Two-pana" refers to the fine;
that group of fines which has two panas as its starting point—that is, its first—is called "beginning with two panas.
And that group of fines consists of two panas, four panas, six panas, eight panas, and so forth; it does not mean merely two panas.
"A fine of three paṇas, four paṇas, or five paṇas.
If one asks how this is so, it is said:
first, because of the gravity of the offense.
It is understood that the three subsequent punishments are more severe than the first punishment;

in that case, rather than resorting to the unmentioned number three and so forth, it is faultless to achieve greater severity by resorting to the repetition of the mentioned number two itself. (2.224)
Furthermore:
"In the case of cutting off the male organ or killing [the animal], the middle amercement shall be paid, as well as its value;
for these great animals, in these circumstances, the fine is double. (YDh 2.226)
For the mutilation of the genitals or the killing of these small animals, the punishment is the middle amercement;

and one shall also pay the value of the animal to its owner. Furthermore, for large animals such as cows, elephants, horses, and so forth, in these same circumstances—such as beating them or causing them to bleed—the same applies.
In the case of signs, it should be understood that the fine is double the previously mentioned penalty. // 2.226 //
Regarding the punishment for injuring stationary beings, he says:
"For the cutting of branches, trunks, or the entire destruction of trees that bear shoots, as well as for trees that provide livelihood, the fine is double twenty [paṇas]. (YDh 2.227)

"Prarohas" refers to sprouts; "prarohiṇyaḥ śākhāḥ" are branches possessing such sprouts—those branches which, when cut and replanted, grow again from each joint. Those trees such as the banyan (*vaṭa*) and others that possess such branches are "prarohiśākhins. Regarding them, [the penance applies] for cutting their branches, for cutting the trunk (*skandha*) from which the root-branches emerge, and for cutting the tree together with its roots, respectively.
Starting from a fine of twenty paṇas, each subsequent fine is double the preceding one. This is what is meant:
fines of twenty paṇas, forty paṇas, and eighty paṇas—these three fines apply respectively to offenses such as cutting branches and so forth.

Even for trees such as mangoes that do not produce shoots but are nonetheless useful, the same fines previously mentioned for those places apply; however, for trees that do not produce shoots and are not useful, other [proportional] fines should be determined. (2.227)
Regarding specific types of trees, he says:

"In the case of trees that have grown at a shrine (caitya), a cremation ground, a boundary, a holy place (puṇyasthāna), or a temple, as well as for a tree renowned [for its sanctity], the fine is double. (YDh 2.228)

For the cutting of branches and so forth from trees growing near shrines (*caitya*) and the like, the fine is double that previously mentioned; and for well-known trees such as the *pippala* and *palāśa*, the fine is likewise double. (2.228)
Regarding shrubs and the like, he says:

"For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines, the fine is half of that prescribed previously for the places already mentioned. (YDh 2.229)
*Gulmas* are *mālatī* and other such plants characterized by dense, though not excessively long, creepers;
*gucchās* are those that are not of a vine-like nature and are mostly non-erect, such as *kuraṇṭaka* and others;
*kṣupas* are mostly erect, such as *karavīra* and others.
Climbers (*latā*) are those that grow for long distances, such as grapes (*drākṣā*) and *atimuktā*.
Creepers (*pratāna*) are those that grow straight without producing aerial shoots (*kāṇḍapraroha*), such as *sārivā* and others.
Medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) are those whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit.
Grains such as *śāli* rice;
creepers (*vīrudhaḥ*) are those which, even when cut, grow back in various ways, such as *guḍūcī* and others.
For cutting or lopping these in the aforementioned places, it should be understood that the penalty is half of the previously mentioned fine. (2.229)
Thus ends the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). Now follows the section on violence (*sāhasa*).
Desiring now to explain the title of dispute known as violence, [the author] first states its definition:
Sāhasa (violence) is defined as the forcible seizure of common property.

(YDh 2.230ab) The seizure of common—that is, shared—property, or of another's property, because there is no distinction in its being unfit for disposal according to one's own whim, is sāhasa. Why? Because...
"By forceful seizure" means by taking [it] away violently;
that is to say, by taking it away through the exercise of physical power.
This is what is meant.

The definition of *sāhasa* (violence) is as follows: whatever act—such as killing, theft, or the violation of another's wife—is committed in the presence of both royal officials and other people, transgressing both royal punishment and public outcry, all that is *sāhasa*.
Therefore, even the seizure of common property or the property of others constitutes *sāhasa*, because it is performed by relying upon physical force.
Thus [it is said]. Nārada also has explained the nature of *sāhasa*:
"Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength, that is declared to be *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength. (NSm 14.1)

This act of violence (*sāhasa*), although included within the categories of theft, verbal abuse, physical assault, and adultery, is distinguished by the factor of relying on force and arrogance; thus, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of prescribing a more severe punishment. Furthermore, it is mentioned [separately] in order to demonstrate the variety of punishments applicable to it.
Having designated the three types of knowledge according to their divisions as first and so forth, its definition was explained by that very [author]:
"Furthermore, it should be known as threefold— namely, the first, the middle, and likewise the highest— and its specific definitions have been stated separately in the treatises."
The first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is declared to consist of the breaking, throwing away, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and other such things that serve as field-supplies.
Regarding clothing, cattle, food, drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Malice, the use of poison, weapons, and the like; the violation of another's wife; and whatever else obstructs life—these are declared to be the highest form of violence (uttama-sāhasa).
For that first [offense], the punishment depends on the action performed and shall not be less than one hundred;
for the middle [offense], however, it is seen by those learned in the treatises as being not less than five hundred.

"In the case of the highest violence (*uttama-sāhasa*), the fine is prescribed as being at least one thousand [paṇas]. For such acts, the punishments are declared to be death, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of that specific limb. (NSm 14.2–7)
Furthermore, acts such as killing and the like should be applied—either collectively or individually—in cases of the highest violence (uttamasāhasa), according to the degree of the offense.
In that regard, he states the punishment for violence (*sāhasa*) consisting of the seizure of another's property:
"The fine is double its value; but in case of denial, it is fourfold" (YDh 2.230cd).
The fine is double the value of that stolen property.
Furthermore, he who, having committed a rash act, denies it by saying "I did not do it," shall be subject to a fine four times the value of the object;
this is because of the specific prescription of this particular penalty.
The general prescription of punishment, such as the first amercement and so forth, is understood to apply to cases other than theft. (2.230)
Regarding the instigator of a violent act, he says: "He who causes a violent act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said 'I will give,' causes it to be done, shall pay four times [the fine]. (YDh 2.231)

But he who, having said "Commit this act of violence," causes it to be done, shall be made to pay double the fine for such violence. Furthermore, he who, having said "I will give you wealth; you do it," causes an act of violence to be committed [is likewise liable].
He shall be made to pay a fine fourfold, due to the excessive nature of the consequences.

Regarding specific types of perpetrators of violence, he says: "One who throws away or transgresses the *arghya* offering, one who strikes his brother's wife, one who fails to give what has been promised, and one who breaks down a house situated by the sea. (YDh 2.232)
The settled rule is that for those who cause harm to neighbors, kinsmen, and others,
the fine shall be fifty paṇas. He who insults or disregards the commands of those worthy of honor, such as teachers and the like, [is subject to this].
He who beats his brother’s wife; he who fails to give the promised wealth as agreed upon; he who opens a sealed house;
and likewise, he who [harms] the *kulikas*—the masters of houses and fields attached to one's own house or field—who are born of one's own lineage.
Those who do harm to those who have been accepted as one's own kin or fellow countrymen shall all be punished with a fine of fifty paṇas. (2.232–233)
Furthermore:

one who approaches a widow of his own accord, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help, one who cries out falsely, and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the highest castes; YDh 2.234.
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors;
one who makes an improper oath; one who is unfit yet performs the duties of the fit;
and one who destroys the virility of bulls or small animals.
One who denies a common property, one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus,

and one who abandons any of these— father, son, sister, brother, husband and wife, teacher, or pupil— when they have not fallen from their caste, shall each be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (YDh 2.236–237)

He who approaches a widow of his own will without her husband’s authorization; he who, though capable, does not run to the rescue when others are crying out in terror due to fear of thieves and the like; and he who utters groundless abuse.
Furthermore, he who touches a Brāhmaṇa or others who are outcastes (caṇḍāla);
he who feeds at rites for the gods or ancestors those who have renounced the world from the Śūdra caste, such as the Digambaras and others;
and he who makes an improper oath, saying, "I shall go to my mother"—[all these are equal].
Likewise, he who performs the study of scriptures and other such acts which are appropriate only for the *śūdra* and others despite being unfit for them;
or one who destroys the virility—the procreative power—of bulls (*vṛṣa*, meaning oxen) and small animals such as goats and the like;
or, according to the reading "of trees and small animals," one who causes the falling of fruits and flowers from trees and so forth by the application of medicinal herbs such as *hiṅgu*.

One who denies common property, one who deceives regarding joint assets, one who causes the miscarriage of a female slave's fetus, and those such as fathers and so forth who, while not themselves outcastes, abandon one another; [these are excluded from inheritance].
Each of them shall be liable to a fine of one hundred paṇas. // 2.234-237 //
Thus ends the section on acts of violence.
Because of the context of rash acts, the author now states the punishment for washermen and others in cases of similar offenses:
"A washerman who wears another's garment shall be fined three paṇas;
however, in cases of selling, hiring out, pledging, or borrowing [another's garment], he shall be fined ten paṇas. (YDh 2.238)
A washerman who, having been entrusted with clothes for the purpose of cleaning, uses them himself for his own clothing,
shall be fined three paṇas.

Furthermore, he who sells them, or gives them on hire— meaning one who gives a garment for the purpose of enjoyment for such a period of time, saying "so much money must be given to me"— or lends them as a pledge, or gives them having requested them from his own friends;
For each offense, he shall be fined ten paṇas.
Furthermore, those garments must be washed on a smooth board made of śālmalī wood, not on stone; they must not be worn in reverse order, nor should they be kept at home.
Otherwise, he shall be punished.
A washerman shall wash clothes on a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood;
he shall not exchange clothes for clothes, nor shall he allow them to be worn [by others]. (MDh 8.396)
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu.
Furthermore, when one destroys them through negligence, then that which was spoken by Nārada should be observed:
"One-eighth of the value is lost for a garment washed once; for the second time, a half is lost; for the third time, a third part; and for the fourth washing, exactly half [the value] is lost."

"But beyond half-decay, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter [of the value] until it reaches the state of being worn out; for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its depreciation. (NSm 9.8–9).
For a garment purchased for eight *paṇas* that has been washed once and is destroyed, the price to be paid shall be the original value minus one-eighth of a *paṇa*.

For a garment washed twice, however, one-quarter less [of the price] is to be given; for one washed three times, two paṇas less; furthermore, for one washed four times, one-third less; and for one washed five times, half—namely, four paṇas—is to be paid.
After that, the remaining value of the cleansing materials shall be paid by reducing the price by one-quarter for each quarter [of the cloth's life].
As long as the cloth is not worn out or destroyed, the determination of the payment of its value may be made according to the owner's wish. (2.238)
In a dispute between father and son, the fine for witnesses is three *paṇas*;
however, for anyone who stands between them, the fine shall be eightfold.
When there is a quarrel between father and son, he who accepts the role of a witness but does not prevent the quarrel must pay a fine of three *paṇas*.

He is to be fined. Furthermore, he who acts as a surety for the payment of the wager in a dispute between those two involving a wager, and—by virtue of the word "and" (ca)—he who increases their quarrel, is also to be punished with twenty-four paṇas, which is eight times the three paṇas [of the wager].
This rule applies to couples and others as well.
In this manner, the punishment should be applied. (2.239)

One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins, as well as anyone who trades with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.240) "Scale" refers to a weighing rod.
"Teaching" refers to what was previously mentioned.
"Measure" refers to the *prastha*, *droṇa*, and so forth. "Coinage" refers to that which is marked with seals and the like.
Regarding coins such as the *dramma* and *niṣka*:

whoever forges these—by making them otherwise than their established local weight, whether by reducing or increasing the amount of *dramma* and so forth—or renders them non-standard by means of improper minting, or fills them with copper and other base metals; and whoever [uses] those forged [coins].
Even if he knows [the truth], if he engages in such legal proceedings, both of them shall be punished with the highest amercement. (2.240)
Regarding the examiner of coins, he says:
"He who declares a genuine coin to be counterfeit, or a counterfeit one to be genuine—that examiner of coins shall be made to pay the highest fine. (YDh 2.241)

Furthermore, whoever who examines coins declares a dramma or similar currency containing copper or other base metals to be genuine, or conversely, declares a genuine coin to be counterfeit, shall be punished with the highest amercement. (2.241)
He says in response to the physician:
"A physician who practices falsely shall be punished with the first amercement for treating animals, the middle amercement for humans, and the highest amercement for royal officers. (YDh 2.242)

Furthermore, any physician who, being ignorant of Āyurveda and practicing medicine falsely for the sake of livelihood, claims "I am a knower of medical treatment" and administers medical care to animals, humans, or royal servants, shall be punished with the first, middle, or highest fines respectively. Even in those cases involving animals and so forth, the degree of severity of the punishment shall vary according to the specific value of the subject, the specific caste, and the specific proximity to the king.
It is to be inferred. // 2.242 //
He who binds one who does not deserve to be bound, and he who releases one who has been bound,

as well as one who has not attained the age for legal capacity, shall be made to pay the highest fine. Furthermore, he who binds an innocent person who does not deserve imprisonment, without the king's command, [is liable for this penalty].
And he who abandons a prisoner who has been summoned for the purpose of legal proceedings and whose case has not yet been concluded, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.243)

He who takes an eighth part [of the goods] by means of false weights or measures shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this is ordained for both increase and decrease. Furthermore, whatever merchant otherwise embezzles an eighth part of merchandise such as rice, cotton, and so forth, by means of false weights or false measures—
He shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*. Furthermore, the increase or decrease of the fine should be determined according to the increase or decrease in the value of the stolen property. (2.244)
If one adulterates medicinal substances, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses,
and other such commodities with inferior materials, he shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen *paṇas*.
"Medicinal substance" (*bheṣaja*) refers to medicinal drugs.
Oiliness refers to ghee and the like;
salt is well known;
fragrant substances refer to uśīra and so forth.
Grain and molasses are well known;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), ginger, black pepper, and so forth are included.
Among these, one sells substance that is without essence for the purpose of trade.
For one who adulterates [the grain], the fine is sixteen paṇas. (2.245)
Furthermore:
For those who attribute a false origin to clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth,
the fine for selling such items shall be eightfold.
That which has no high value by nature— such as clay, leather, and so forth— is called "non-noble" (*ajāti*). Regarding such things,

one performs the act of making them appear noble by infusing them with different fragrances, colors, and tastes, thereby producing a resemblance to items of high value for the purpose of selling them.
Just as, by the diffusion of the fragrance of jasmine,
clay is called "fragrant myrobalan," and by the production of an excellence of color on cat skin, it is called "tiger skin."
Just as a crystal gem becomes a ruby by having its color changed,
and as cotton thread becomes silk thread by the application of superior qualities.
By imparting an excellence of color to black iron, one calls it "silver";
by infusing the scent of sandalwood into wood from the *bilva* tree, one calls it "sandalwood."

In the case of *kaṅkola*, it is called "bark" (*tvak*); in the case of *lavaṅga*, it is called "cloves. In the case of cotton cloth (*kārpāsika*), it is called "silk" (*kauśeya*) due to its excellence of quality.
The fine for merchandise such as clay or leather that has been made to resemble a sellable commodity should be understood as eightfold.
(YDh 2.246) Furthermore, the determination of punishment applies to one who brings about the exchange of a casket, the sale of high-quality goods, or the pawning of counterfeit items. (YDh 2.247)

For breaking a vessel worth five *paṇas*, the fine is declared to be fifty; for one worth ten *paṇas*, it is one hundred; for one worth twenty *paṇas*, the fine is two hundred; and as the value increases, the fine increases accordingly. A *samudga* is a covered box, so called because it exists together with its lid (*mudga*); *parivartana* means exchange or substitution.

For one who, having shown a completely full casket of pearls, hands over another casket full of crystals through sleight of hand; and for one who, having manufactured artificial goods such as musk and the like, brings them for sale or as a pledge— the determination of punishment for such a person is to be understood as that which will be described below.
When the *paṇa*— the price equivalent of artificial musk and the like—
is broken or deficient;
that is to say, when it is of less than the value of one *paṇa*.
When that counterfeit [coin] is sold, the fine is fifty paṇas; when its value is one paṇa, the fine is one hundred;
when its value is two paṇas, the fine is two hundred—thus the fines increase in proportion to the value.
The increase of the fine is to be inferred from [the preceding rules]. 2.247–2.248.

He says in reply to the merchants: "For those who, acting in concert, cause distress to artisans and craftsmen by manipulating the price—whether by knowing how to cause a decrease or an increase in the price—the punishment is the highest amercement. (YDh 2.249)
Even though they know the decrease or increase in the price fixed by the king, merchants who, having banded together in a combination,
out of greed for profit establish a different price that is oppressive and harmful to artisans such as washermen and craftsmen such as painters,
shall be fined one thousand *paṇas*. (2.249)
Furthermore:
For merchants who, acting in concert, withhold merchandise by fixing an improper price, or who sell it [at such a price], the prescribed punishment is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa). (YDh 2.250)

Furthermore, for those merchants who, having assembled together, obstruct merchandise brought from another country by demanding a low price when it is worth more, or sell it at a high price, the punishment of the highest fine (uttamasāhasa) has been ordained by Manu and others. (2.250)
But at what price should it be sold? To this he says: "The price that is established for the king, by that daily sale or purchase [is made];
from that, the profit of merchants is traditionally declared. (YDh 2.251)
When the king is present, whatever price is established or determined by him, trade— whether purchase or sale— must be conducted daily according to that price.
"Niḥsrava" refers to a specific deduction (nirgataḥ sravaḥ) from that price determined by the king.
That alone brings profit to merchants, and not what is merely imagined according to one's own whim. Moreover, Manu has shown a specific rule for determining the market price:
"Every five nights, or when a fortnight or a month has passed..."
"And the king shall publicly establish the standard value for these [commodities]. (MDh 8.402) 2.251.
Furthermore:
A merchant who buys and sells immediately may take five percent on goods from his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land. (YDh 2.252)

One who, having acquired merchandise obtained in his own country, sells it, shall take a profit of five per cent— that is, five *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas*. However, in the case of merchandise obtained from a foreign land, he shall take a profit of ten *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas* of its value.
In the case of a transaction where the sale is finalized on the very day the price is received,
it is otherwise for one who sells at a later time; for such a person, an increase in profit must be calculated based on the lapse of that interval of time.

And thus, having determined the price in such a way that there is a profit of five paṇas on a hundred paṇas, the king should establish that very price for goods produced within his own country. (2.252)
He states the method for determining the price of foreign merchandise:
"Having added the expenses arising from the merchandise to its cost, a price that provides favor to both the buyer and the seller should be established. (YDh 2.253)

When merchandise arrives from another country, the king, having calculated the amount of wealth expended at the various stages— such as the journey to and from that foreign land, the taking up of goods, and the payment of duties— and having combined that with the cost price of the merchandise, should establish a market price for the benefit of both buyer and seller, such that a profit of ten per cent (ten paṇas on a hundred) is realized. (2.253)
Thus ends the incidental section on violence;
now begins the section on the non-delivery of what has been sold, having concluded the incidental matter. Now, the topic of the non-delivery of what has been sold is commenced.
And its nature was described by Nārada:
"When, after selling a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer, that is called the legal head of dispute known as *vikrīyāsaṃpradāna* (non-delivery after sale). (NSm 8.1)
Having first stated that the goods for sale are of two kinds—distinguished as mobile and immobile—he further established their sixfold nature by the same authority:
"In this world, merchandise is of two kinds: moving and stationary;
however, the wise have prescribed a sixfold rule for its giving and receiving."
"Calculated, weighed, measured, [determined] by action, by appearance, and by quality.
(NSm 8.2–3) "Calculated" refers to betel nuts and the like;
"weighed" refers to gold, musk, saffron, and the like.
This refers to rice and the like; or, as characterized by activity such as carrying or milking, it refers to horses, buffaloes, and so forth;
or, by way of form, it refers to courtesans and the like.
By "splendor" (śrī) and "radiance" (dīpti), [the text refers to] emeralds, rubies, and so forth.
He states the penalty for one who sells these six kinds of merchandise but does not deliver it:
"If a person, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made to pay it with interest;
or, if the buyer has come from another region, he shall be made to pay the profit derived from that region. (YDh 2.254)

If the seller does not deliver to a buyer from his own country who has requested it that merchandise for which the price was received— that is, "the price-received" (gṛhītamūlya)— then [he is at fault].
And if that merchandise, having been of high value at the time of purchase, is later obtained for a low price,
then the increase or profit (*udaya*) of the merchandise— whether immovable or movable— which results from the decrease in its value;
The seller shall be compelled to deliver the goods along with their full value to the buyer.

When there is no increase in the value of the goods resulting from a decrease in price, but rather at the time of purchase it was agreed that for such a price these many goods were being sold— then [the seller must deliver exactly that].

Taking that merchandise and selling it in that region, he should be made to pay the profit together with the interest— whether in the form of the gain realized from the sale or in the form of the stipulated interest such as two-fold or three-fold— as determined by the buyer's wish. As Nārada says:
"If the price should fall, one shall bring back the merchandise with interest;
this is the rule for local traders, while for those traveling in various directions, it concerns the profit of their region" (NSm 8.5).
When, however, due to a high price the merchandise becomes deficient [in value], then regarding that merchandise, such as clothing or houses, whatever benefit [accrues]—
In that case, he must cause the seller to deliver the merchandise along with its covering, comfortable dwelling, and so forth;
as Nārada says:
"He who, having sold merchandise for its price, does not deliver it to the buyer..."
"He shall be made to pay for the loss of immovable property, and for movable property, the fruit of its use" (NSm 8.4).
The "loss" (*kṣaya*) of the seller is said to be his enjoyment [of the property],
because it is being depleted by virtue of its connection with the buyer.
It is not, however, of the nature of the collapse of a wall or the destruction of crops;
for in that case,
the merchandise might be damaged, burnt, or stolen.
For it has been stated therein: "That loss belongs to the seller alone who, having sold, does not deliver" (NSm 8.6).
However, when that buyer has come from another country for the purpose of acquiring merchandise, then, having taken that merchandise...
The seller must cause the commodity, together with whatever profit was made by selling it in another country, to be delivered to the buyer;
and this rule regarding the delivery of the purchased commodity is to be understood as applying in the absence of any rescission.
But when a latent disposition remains, one should understand that which was stated by Manu, beginning with "Having purchased or sold something... (MDh 8.222). // 2.254 //
Furthermore:
Even if a commodity has been sold, it may be resold if the original purchaser does not take delivery;
for if the loss occurs due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed belong to the buyer alone. (YDh 2.255)

Furthermore, when the buyer, having conceived a latent desire for it, does not wish to take possession of the commodity, then even though it has been sold, the commodity may be sold elsewhere. However, if the buyer does not accept the commodity when it is being offered by the seller, and that commodity is subsequently destroyed by the king or by an act of God,
then this loss shall belong to the buyer alone.
Because it was destroyed by the fault of the purchaser, in the form of his failure to take possession of the merchandise. // 2.255 //
Moreover:
"If a defect arises in the merchandise due to injury caused by the king or by fate, the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked, does not deliver it. (YDh 2.256)

Furthermore, when the seller does not deliver the merchandise even though it is requested by the buyer, yet— despite having no subsequent change of heart— the item is destroyed by the king or by fate, then that loss belongs solely to the seller.
Anything other than this is not considered defective.
If the merchandise is destroyed, something of a similar nature must be given to the purchaser. (2.256)
Furthermore: If,
having sold an item into the hand of another, one sells it again— whether it be defective or as if non-defective—
the fine in that case shall be double the price.

Furthermore, if one sells again into another's hand what was already sold into the first's hand without any underlying defect, or if one sells a defective commodity while concealing its defects, then a fine double the value of that commodity should be understood as the penalty.
Nārada has also shown a specific distinction in this regard:
He who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another,
shall be made to pay double the value of that property, and the fine for his misconduct shall be the same amount.
"But he who, having shown a faultless [article], delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double the price and an equal amount as a fine. (NSm 8.7–8) And this entire rule is to be understood as applying when the price has already been paid for the commodity.

Furthermore, regarding goods for which no price has been paid, if there is a transaction— whether proceeding or ceasing— based solely on the word of the buyer and seller through a mutual agreement (*samaya*), there is no fault whatsoever; as Nārada says:
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if it is not delivered, except by mutual agreement, there is no non-delivery on the part of the seller.
Thus [it is said]. (NSm 8.10) // 2.257 //
The rescission of sale has been explained;
the nature of the rescission of purchase, however, was already detailed previously.
Now, that which is common to both is [to be discussed].

He states the law: A merchant who, being ignorant of the decline or increase in value of his merchandise, has no right to repent after having purchased it; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth. (YDh 2.258)

After the purchase of goods that have been examined, a buyer who did not perceive an increase in value resulting from the price fixed at the time of purchase shall not exercise the right of rescission; nor shall a seller, failing to perceive a loss of value in the goods due to the high price set, be subject to rescission.

Furthermore, it is stated by way of contrast that a lingering regret (*anuśaya*) arises for both the buyer and the seller when there is a full understanding of the increase or decrease [in value]. However, the time limit for such lingering regret has been stated by Nārada:
"If, after purchasing a commodity for its price, the buyer considers it a bad purchase..."
That [article] must be returned by the seller to the buyer on that very same day, provided it is undamaged.
"On the second day, the purchaser, by returning it, shall incur a thirtieth part of the price;
on the third day, however, double that amount; beyond that, it belongs to the purchaser alone. (NSm 9.2–3).
Furthermore, regarding sales and purchases made without due examination, the limit for rescission based on defects in the commodity is ten, one, five, or seven days, as stated in YDh 2.177.
This has indeed been shown by such passages as these. Thus,
by this line of reasoning, it is understood that the thorough knowledge of increase and decrease is the cause for the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Just as, by the force of the rules for examining merchandise, defects in goods become a cause for subsequent loss (*anuśaya*), therefore, even within the period for such loss, if one causes a loss when the three causes— the defect of the merchandise, its increase, and its decrease— are absent, he shall be fined one-sixth of the value of the merchandise;
[but] if the cause of loss is present, [he is not liable].

Even for one who, by exceeding the period for [the payment of] interest, causes the interest to accrue further, this same punishment applies. For one who, through enjoyment, causes interest to accrue further on items that are imperishable and of stable value, the punishment prescribed by Manu is to be understood as applicable.
But after ten days, one should neither give [the object] nor cause it to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
Thus [ends the verse]. (MDh 8.223) // 2.258 //
Thus ends the section titled "Non-delivery after Sale.
Now begins the section on Partnership;
the title of this legal dispute, "Partnership," is now being set forth.

Regarding those merchants who perform work for the sake of profit through association (*samavāya*), the profit and loss shall be according to their respective capital or as determined by their agreement. "Association" (*samavāya*) is a mutual understanding of the form: "We all, having come together, shall perform this work."
Therefore, regarding those such as merchants, actors, and dancers who, desiring profit,

perform their respective occupations— their gains and losses, or increases and decreases— should be determined according to the substance, that is, in accordance with the amount of wealth given by each for the purpose of purchasing merchandise and so forth.

Alternatively, they are to be understood as having agreed upon them through a convention (*samaya*) consisting of a cognition of the form "this is one part" and "this is the other part," based on a consideration of their primary and secondary status. (2.259)
Furthermore:

"Whatever has been prohibited, whatever was not specifically assigned, and whatever has been destroyed through negligence—he shall restore that; and from what is recovered after being lost, he shall receive a tenth part as his reward. (YDh 2.260)
Among those who are engaged in business together, if someone practices what has been forbidden— namely, that "this merchandise must not be traded in this manner"—

and thereby causes loss; or if someone, acting without being instructed or without authorization, causes loss through negligence or lack of wisdom, he shall give that lost merchandise back to the merchants.
Furthermore, he who among them protects the merchandise from calamities caused by thieves, kings, and the like, receives a tenth share of that merchandise protected [from such dangers]. (2.260)
The king shall take a twentieth part as duty from the offering of the *argha*;
that which is established by custom (*vyāsiddha*), what is fit for the king, and what is sold [as such], belongs to the king.
*Argha* is the price determined by "for this amount of merchandise, this is the value."
Because of its being presented for examination by the king, he should take a twentieth part of its value as a tax;
furthermore, that which is "prohibited" (*vyāsiddha*)— meaning it is forbidden by the king from being sold elsewhere— is also subject to this.

Furthermore, whatever is fit for a king—such as gems, rubies, and so forth—even if not specifically prohibited—if it is sold out of greed for profit without first being reported to the king, then all that merchandise shall go to the king; the meaning is that the king shall confiscate it regardless of whether the seller has paid its value. (2.261)
One who speaks falsely regarding the quantity [of goods] while departing from the customs station,
as well as one who practices deceptive buying and selling, shall be made to pay eight times [the value].
Furthermore, that merchant who conceals the measure of his merchandise for the sake of defrauding the customs duty, or who slips away from the place where duties are collected—

And whoever buys or sells merchandise that has become the subject of such a dispute, saying "this belongs to him" or "that belongs to him," all of them shall be fined eight times the value of the merchandise. (2.262)
Moreover:
A ferryman taking toll for land transport shall be made to pay ten paṇas;
this same penalty applies for not inviting Brāhmaṇas who are one's neighbors.
For toll is of two kinds: land-based and water-based.
Among these, the king shall take a twentieth part as land-based toll from the addition of the market price (YDh 2.261).
Thus it has been stated here;
however, regarding water-crossings, it is declared in the *Mānava* [Smṛti]:
"A vehicle should be made to pay one *paṇa* at a ferry, and a person half a *paṇa*."
An animal and a woman [pay] one quarter; a man who is empty-handed [pays] half a quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they possess.

"A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a renunciant, a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks—these persons are not to be made to pay the ferry-toll. (MDh 8.404–5, 407).
Regarding both types of tolls, there is this further distinction:

"There is no toll for a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor for one engaged in a craft, nor for a child, nor for a messenger; nor for what is obtained as alms, nor for what remains after being plundered, nor for a *śrotriya*, nor for a renunciant, nor at a sacrifice. (VaDh 19.37).
A "crossing" (*tari*) is that by which one crosses over, such as a boat and the like.
The ferryman is the official authorized to collect the toll for crossing;
when he collects a toll for goods originating on land, he should be fined ten paṇas.

*Veśa* means a house; *prativeśa* refers to that which faces one's own house or stands adjacent to it. Those who reside there are *prātiveśyās*; and those who are both Brahmins and *prātiveśyās* are "Brahmin neighbors."
And the same applies to Brahmins who are neighbors.

For those who are endowed with learning and good conduct, even if they are not invited to śrāddha ceremonies and the like when wealth is available, this very fine of ten paṇas is to be understood as the penalty. (2.263)
Regarding the inheritance of a merchant who has died in a foreign land, [Yājñavalkya] says:
"When one has died while gone to another country, his heirs, kinsmen, or cognates shall take that property upon arriving there; in their absence, the king shall take it. (YDh 2.264)

When, among those who have entered into a partnership, anyone has gone to another country or died, then his share shall be taken by his heirs—consisting of the group of offspring such as sons and so forth; or by his kinsmen from the mother’s side, such as maternal uncles and others; or by his cognates (*jñāti*), meaning *sapiṇḍas* other than the group of offspring;
or by those who have come from another country and are joint partners in the business. They shall take it collectively.
In their absence, and in the absence of heirs and so forth, the king shall take [the property];
by the word "or" (vā), he indicates that the heirs and others have an optional right [to it].
And the rule regarding the sequence of priority,
established by the passage beginning with "the wife, the daughters" (YDh 2.135), is to be understood here as well.
The purpose of the statement is to exclude disciples, fellow celibates, and Brahmins, and to ensure that a merchant obtains [the property].
Even among merchants, he who is capable of providing funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*) and repaying debts and so forth should take it.
Furthermore, if there is no difference in their capacity [to manage the property], all the merchants who were partners should divide and take it.
