In the absence of those as well, the king should wait for ten years for the arrival of the heirs; if they do not arrive, the king himself should take it. This is the rule.

Nārada has clarified this: "If one of them should die, his heir shall receive that [property]; or, in the absence of an heir, all of them [the others] shall receive it, provided they are capable. (NSm 3.7)
In the absence of such [an owner], however, one should cause it to be kept in secret for ten years;
thereafter, that which has remained for ten years shall be ownerless and without an heir.
The king should indeed appropriate that for himself; in this way, dharma is not lost. (NSm 3.16) Thus [ends verse 2.264].
Furthermore:

"They should exclude the dishonest one who has lost his profit; one who is incapable should have the work done by another. (YDh 2.265ab) "The dishonest one" (*jihma*) means a deceiver; they should exclude him—that is, having deprived him of his profit, they should cast him out once he is stripped of gain.

And he who among those acting in partnership is unable to perform tasks such as the inspection of merchandise should have his own work— namely, the carrying of the load of goods and the examination of income, expenditure, and so forth— performed by another.
He extends the duties of merchants previously taught to priests and others:

"By this, the rule for priests, farmers, and laborers is declared" (YDh 2.265cd). By this—namely, the exposition of the merchant's duties beginning with "profits and losses according to the goods"—the rule is stated for priests such as the *hotṛ* and others, for farmers, and for actors, dancers, wrestlers, and so forth.
The rule regarding the mode of subsistence for those who live by their craft has been declared;
and in that regard, a specific distinction concerning the division of wealth among officiating priests has been shown by Manu.

"All [of these] are entitled to shares; the principal ones are entitled to half [the estate], others are entitled to half of that [quarter], the third-class are entitled to a third part, and those entitled to a fourth are entitled to a fourth part. (MDh 8.210).
This is its meaning:

By the statement, "They consecrate him with a hundred [cows] by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma," a hundred cows are enjoined for the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the form of the hiring of priests (*ṛtvij*). The priests are sixteen, beginning with the Hotṛ. In this regard, when there arises the expectation as to which priest receives what portion, this [text] is stated.

Among all the sixteen officiating priests, beginning with the *hotṛ*, those four who are principal— the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, *brahman*, and *udgātṛ*— are entitled to half of the hundred cows; by virtue of the logical necessity of completing the shares of all, they are sharers of a half in the form of forty-eight [cows].
Others—the Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ—are sharers of half; that is, by half of that principal share, they possess twenty-four forms as their half-share.
Furthermore, those who are entitled to a third share—
The *acchāvāka*, *neṣṭṛ*, *agnīdhra*, and *pratihartr̥* are the "thirders" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*); they receive one-third of the principal share by way of a third portion consisting of sixteen cows.
As for those who are "quarterers" (*pādinaḥ*)—namely the *grāvastut*, *unnetr̥*, *potr̥*, and *subrahmaṇya*—they [receive] of the principal share...
Those who possess a fourth part consisting of twelve cows are entitled to that share.

Now, how is this restriction of shares possible? For there is neither an agreement here, nor an inherence in a substance, nor a scriptural statement by virtue of which such a restriction of portions would exist.

Therefore, according to the principle that "it should be equal because it is not heard otherwise," it is logical that all [heirs] should receive equal shares, or that they should receive shares in proportion to their labor.

To this it is replied: In the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, which has the *jyotiṣṭoma* as its archetype, the descriptive reference—"those who receive half, those who receive a third, and those who receive a fourth"—as if it were already established, would not be possible if the Maitrāvaruṇa and others did not possess the status of receiving a half, a third, and a fourth part in that archetype, the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, by the force of the Vedic designations such as "half" (*ardhin*) and so forth, the previously mentioned rule regarding the shares is rendered consistent.
It is irreproachable. 2.265.
Thus ends the section on partnerships;
now begins the section on theft.
Theft is now introduced.
And the definition of *sāhasa* was stated by Manu:
"That act which is committed violently with an accomplice is *sāhasa*;
that which is done without an accomplice, as well as that which is denied after being committed, is *steya* (theft). (MDh 8.332)

*Sāhasa* (violence) is that which is committed by force, through the application of physical power, such as the seizure of another's property and so forth, in the presence of witnesses, including relatives, the owner of the property, the king, and officials.
Theft, however, is defined as the taking of another's property by means of deception, in the absence of the owner of the goods or others, and being contrary to that [act of appropriation].
Furthermore, it is also that which, even if committed in their presence, is denied out of fear, saying, "I did not do this."
To deny that [theft] as well constitutes theft.
Nārada also said: "The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] by deceiving them through various means, from those who are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless. (NSm 14.16)
In that regard, since punishment is preceded by the apprehension of the thief, and apprehension is preceded by knowledge,
[one should seek] the means of knowledge.
To this he replies:
"A thief is apprehended by his captors either through stolen goods or through his tracks;
likewise, one who has committed a prior offense and resides in an impure dwelling [is apprehended]. (YDh 2.266)
He who is proclaimed by the people as "this is a thief" is to be seized by the pursuers— the king’s officers, local guards, and others—
either by means of stolen goods such as vessels and the like, which serve as signs of theft, or by following the trail of the crime starting from the day of the disappearance.
Or he may be one who has committed an offense through prior actions and whose thievery was previously notorious;
or he may be one whose place of residence is impure or unknown—he too is to be apprehended. (2.266)
Furthermore:

Others also should be apprehended with suspicion on account of their concealing their caste, name, and so forth, as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and liquor, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered. (YDh 2.267)

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others, those who move about in secret, those who have no income yet spend lavishly, and those who sell goods that do not exist— these, as well as those previously mentioned, are to be apprehended on suspicion by means of the signs to be described hereafter. Not only those previously mentioned are to be seized, but others also are to be apprehended on suspicion through the following indicators.

Those characterized by the concealment of their birth— such as saying "I am not a Śūdra"— or the concealment of their name— such as saying "I am not Lapittha"— and, by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," by the denial of their own country, village, family, and so forth, are to be apprehended.
Those who are excessively addicted to vices such as gambling, prostitutes, and the drinking of liquor, as well as one who,
when questioned by thieves' catchers as to where he has come from, has a parched mouth or a broken voice—
such a person also should be apprehended.
By the use of the plural, those with perspiring foreheads and so forth are included;
likewise, those who, without cause, ask "How much is his wealth? or "What is his house? [are also included].
And those who wander about having concealed themselves by assuming different guises, and those who spend lavishly even when they have no income;

Furthermore, those who sell items whose substance has been destroyed— such as worn-out clothes, broken vessels, and the like— and whose owners are unknown, all of them should be apprehended on suspicion of being thieves.
In this manner, [one should identify] men by their various signs of thievery.
Having apprehended these, one should examine them thoroughly to determine whether they are thieves or virtuous men;
one should not, however, reach a conclusion regarding their thievery based merely on observing outward signs.
For even one who is not a thief may come into possession of stolen goods such as a pickpocket's pouch through a connection with the signs of theft; as Nārada says:
"That which has fallen from another's hand and has been picked up on the ground unintentionally..."
One should carefully examine whether the stolen property has been cast down by a thief;
likewise:
"The false appear as true, and the true appear as false."
"Various states of being are observed; therefore, examination has been prescribed. (NSm Mā 1.62).
And thus, he says that one who is seized on suspicion of theft must purify himself:
"If one seized on suspicion of theft does not purify himself..."

Having caused the stolen property to be restored, he should be punished with the punishment prescribed for a thief. If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft does not clear himself by means of an ordeal to prove his innocence, then he shall be subject to the punishments to be described hereafter, such as the payment of a fine or corporal punishment. Therefore, he must clear himself through human evidence or, in its absence, through a divine test.
[Objection: But how can there be any possibility of proof (*pramāṇa*) in a false plea such as "I am not a thief," since that [plea] consists of a non-existence (*abhāva*)?
[Response: It is said: first, divine proof (*divya*) has for its object both existence and non-existence; or else, either party may perform it by choice (*rucyā*). (YDh 2.96)
This has been established here.

Furthermore, although *mānuṣa* (human evidence) cannot directly constitute a pure *mithyottara* (denial), nevertheless, by means of establishing a cause that is of the nature of a "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭabhāva*) *mithyākāraṇa*, it indeed takes non-existence as its object.

Just as when, at the time of a theft, one who is accused establishes that he was in another country, his innocence is indeed established by implication through the absence of the act of stealing. (2.269)
Regarding the punishment for a thief, [the author] says:
"Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, one should have him executed by various methods of killing. (YDh 2.270ab)

But one who, through the aforementioned investigation, is determined to be a thief regardless of that [investigation], the king, having made him restore the stolen property to the owner either in its actual form or by calculating its value, shall have him executed by various means of death and torture;
and this applies to cases involving superior goods where the penalty of the highest amercement is appropriate.
But this does not apply to the theft of minor, middling, or superior items such as flowers, clothing, and the like;
for "whatever punishment has been declared by the wise for the three degrees of violence, that same punishment applies respectively to the three degrees of property in cases of theft. (NSm 14.20)

Thus, by the statement of Nārada, since the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*), which consists of corporal punishment, has been established for the case of high-value property; as for the further statement of Vṛddha-Manu:
"Because their wealth is acquired through unjust means, their riches are of the nature of impurity;
therefore, the king should have them executed, rather than punishing them with a monetary fine"—
this [statement] also refers to the case of a grave offense (*mahāparādha*).
He states an exception regarding a specific type of thief:
"Having branded the Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him from his own kingdom" (YDh 2.270cd).
Furthermore, even for a grave offense, one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa who is a thief to be executed.
Rather, having branded him on the forehead, he should banish him from his own country;
and the branding should be made in the shape of a dog's foot.
And so Manu says:

"For violating the Guru's bed, the mark of a vulva shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern-flag; for theft, the foot of a dog shall be made; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man. (MDh 9.237)
And this expiation is to be understood as applying to one who does not wish to perform it after the punishment has been imposed.
As Manu says:
"But all castes performing the prescribed expiation..."
"But they shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine. (MDh 9.240) 2.270.
He states the means for recovering stolen property when the thief is not seen:
"If [the theft] occurs within the village boundary and the thief has not departed, the blame lies with the village headman;
but on the road, it lies with the superintendent of the pasture-lands (vivīta), and in a non-pasture area, with the one who apprehends the thief. (YDh 2.271)
If the killing of a human being or other living creature, or the theft of property, occurs within a village, then the fault of negligence regarding the thief belongs solely to the village head;
to avoid that liability, he himself must apprehend the thief and hand him over to the king.
If he is unable to do so,
he shall restore the stolen property to the owner,
provided that he does not produce the thief's tracks as they have departed from his own village.
Furthermore, when [the thief] is pointed out, the lord of that district where he enters shall hand over the thief or the stolen property.
And so says Nārada:
"If [property] is lost within the range of a person's jurisdiction, he must diligently pursue the thief."
Or else, the remainder shall be made to pay if the foot [of the animal] has not yet emerged.

"But if it has gone out from this [enclosure] and has not fallen elsewhere, he shall cause the neighbors, the guardians of the road, and the guardians of the quarters to pay [the fine]. (NSm 19.23–24).
However, in the case of theft from a pasture (*vivīta*), the fault lies solely with the owner of the pasture.

But when that [stolen property] is found on the very road, or in an enclosure, or in a field other than the enclosure, then the fault lies with the thief-catcher, the road-guard, or the guardian of the region. (2.271)
Moreover:
A village shall provide a path within its own boundaries, or wherever it happens to go;
or else, five villages beyond the *krośa*, or ten villages. (YDh 2.272)

Furthermore, when theft or similar offenses occur in a field on the outskirts of a village, at the boundary limit, then the inhabitants of that very village shall pay [the fine], provided that the tracks of the thieves have not gone beyond the boundary. However, if the tracks have gone beyond, then [the responsibility falls upon] whichever village or location they [reach].
He who enters the trail of the thieves shall perform the delivery of the thieves and so forth;

however, when someone is killed or robbed in a place more than a *krośa* outside the midst of several villages, and the trail of the thieves has been lost due to a crowd of people and the like, [the responsibility does not fall on the village].
Then, he would give either a *pañcagrāmī*, which is a collection of five villages, or a *daśagrāmī*, which is a collection of ten villages;
this is a statement of an alternative.

But this is for the purpose of ensuring that he should perform such acts as the restoration of property seized through close association with the thief. However, when he is unable to cause the stolen goods to be returned from another source, then the king himself should give them from his own treasury;
having recovered what was taken by thieves, he should restore it to its rightful place.
For there is the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Or he may give from his own treasury" (GDh 10.46–47).
When there is doubt as to whether [the property] was stolen or not stolen, a determination must be made by means of human evidence or divine ordeal.
"If, while that [stolen property] is being claimed, there should be doubt regarding the theft,
the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to take an oath, or he may prove it through his kinsmen," according to the traditional teaching of Vṛddha-Manu. (DhKo 1766) // 2.272 //
He states the specific punishment according to the specific offense:
"Those who capture prisoners, as well as those who carry off horses and elephants, and those who kill by force—these men he shall impale upon stakes. (YDh 2.273)
One should impale upon stakes those who seize robbers and other men who commit violence by means of forceful oppression. This is an instruction regarding a specific mode of execution.
[Likewise, one should execute] those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples.

And one should slay without hesitation those who carry off elephants, horses, and chariots, according to the traditional teaching of Manu: "One should slay without hesitation those who carry off elephants, horses, and chariots" (MDh 9.280). 2.273.
Furthermore:
For those who commit the offenses of forcibly lifting [a monk's bowl] and breaking a knot [of his robe], their hands shall be cut off;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot.
One who throws up or carries away garments and such things is an *utkṣepaka*.
One who steals gold and the like that is tied within garments by untying or cutting it loose is a *granthibheda*.
Those two should be deprived of their hands in sequence— one by means of a hand resembling a pair of tongs, and the other by means of the thumb and forefinger.
Furthermore, for a second offense, both the hand and the foot— this being "hand-and-foot"— should be deprived of together as a single unit.
And "lacking one hand and one foot" means that those two [offenders] should be made deficient by one hand and one foot respectively;
the meaning is that one should cut off one hand and one foot each for the one who extorts and the one who breaks open a knot.

This also refers to property that merits the penalty of the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*), because of the statement of Nārada: "In such a case, the limb shall be cut off; the punishment prescribed is the highest amercement" (NSm 14.7).
But for a third offense, there shall indeed be execution;
and so Manu says:
"In the first seizure, one should have the fingers of a finger-knot-breaker cut off."
"In the second [offense], the hands and feet; in the third, he deserves execution. (MDh 9.277).
Thus, the punishment is to be determined according to the species, the quantity of the goods, and the value, and so forth. // 2.274 //

Since there is an infinity of causes for determining the gravity or lightness of a punishment— such as the species, the substance, the quantity, the appropriation, the purpose, the age, the capacity, the quality, the place, the time, and so forth—
and because it is impossible to state the penalty for every individual case, he states the method for determining the punishment in general terms:
"In the seizure of small, middling, or large property, the fine shall be proportional to its value."
In the matter of punishment, one must deliberate upon the place, time, age, and capacity [of the offender].
In cases of the theft of minor, middling, or superior goods, the punishment should be determined according to their value and other relevant factors.
The nature of "minor" (kṣudra) and other types of property has been stated by Nārada:
"Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, skins, grass, and the like,
as well as leguminous grains and prepared food— this is declared to be minor property."
Clothing other than silk, cattle other than cows,
metals other than gold, as well as iron, rice, and barley— these constitute the middling [gifts].
Gold, jewels, silk garments, excellent women, bulls, elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, Brahmins, and kings, should be understood as the highest category of goods.
Regarding these three types of goods, the general rule for punishment consists of the first, middle, and highest amercements.
This very point has been shown by him [Nārada]:

"The same punishment that has been declared by the wise for the three types of violent acts (sāhasa) applies likewise to theft (steya), according to the sequence of the three categories of property. (NSm 14.20)

Since there exists a gradation of value among earthenware items such as water-jars and flower-pots, among domestic animals other than cows and horses— such as buffaloes, rams, and the like— and among gold, grain, and so forth belonging to Brāhmaṇas, when there is a requirement for specific punishments ranging from high to low, the punishment must be determined in accordance with the value and other relevant factors.
And in that matter of inflicting punishment and determining the appropriate penalty, the place, time, age, and capacity—which serve as its causes—must be properly considered.
This is also an illustration for [the consideration of] caste, substance, quantity, possession, and so forth; for instance:
The guilt of theft for a Śūdra consists of eightfold fines; for the other castes, the fines increase twofold respectively. This applies when there is transgression by one who knows the law.
Regarding the phrase "an increase in punishment" (GDh 12.15–17),
this is the meaning:
here, by the word *kilbiṣa*, punishment (*daṇḍa*) is indicated.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular theft must be imposed eightfold when that theft is committed by a learned Śūdra;
however, for others— such as Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and so forth— the same applies.

For learned persons, the offenses for theft are doubled; punishments of sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four-fold [of the base rate] are to be imposed, because there is an increase in punishment for thefts committed by learned Śūdras and others. This very point has also been demonstrated by Manu.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
"For a Brahmin, it shall be sixty-four, or even a full hundred,
or double the sixty-four, for one who recognizes both the fault and the merit [of the case]" (MDh 8.337–38).
Likewise, an increase in the severity of the punishment based on the quantity [of the object] is also observed.
As Manu has said:
"For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for lesser amounts, he should be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property must be returned to its owner" (MDh 8.320).

A *kumbha* consists of twenty *droṇas*. Depending on the qualities of the owner of the property being stolen, and depending on whether the time is one of plenty or famine, punishments consisting of beating, amputation of limbs, or execution should be applied to the thief.
Likewise, there is a specific punishment based on the specific quantity in the case of gems and so forth;
for gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments and all kinds of gems, if the value exceeds one hundred, the penalty is death.
"But for an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remaining cases, one should determine a fine eleven times the value of the property. (MDh 8.321–22).
Likewise, [the punishment varies] according to the specific nature of the object (8.323):
For the theft of men of noble birth, and especially of women,
as well as of all kinds of gems, one deserves the death penalty.
However, for those of low birth, there is another punishment.
"The punishment for one who abducts a man is declared to be the highest amercement;
but for an offense involving a woman, the penalty is the forfeiture of all property, while for one who abducts a maiden, it is death.
(NSm 19.35) However, for small articles valued at less than a *māṣa*, the fine is five times their value.
Likewise, for wooden vessels, grass, and so forth, as well as for those made of clay.
In the case of stealing bamboo, articles made of bamboo, sinews, bones, hides, fresh roots, vegetables, fruits, and roots, as well as dairy products, sugarcane derivatives, salt, and oil;
"Regarding cooked grains, prepared foods, fish, and meat—
indeed, for all things that have a price— the fine shall be five times their value," according to the traditional teaching of Nārada (NSm 19.29–31).

Furthermore, that which is the first amercement, ranging from one hundred to five hundred [paṇas] for minor articles, shall be determined as appropriate for an object worth one māṣa or more than that.

Furthermore, as for the statement by Manu, "In the case of minor articles, the fine shall be double their value" (MDh 8.329), that refers to objects such as shallow bowls (*śarāva*) which serve little purpose.
Likewise, the severity of the punishment also depends on the gravity of the offense; as for example:
"Those thieves who, having broken through a wall, commit robbery at night—the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake. (MDh 9.276).

Thus, because all [offenses] are infinite and it is impossible to state [the penalty] for every individual substance, [the law applies] by means of causes such as genus (*jāti*), quantity (*parimāṇa*), and so forth.
The relative gravity or lightness of the punishment must be determined;
furthermore, for travelers and others, there is no punishment for a minor offense. As Manu said:
"A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane and two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished.
Likewise:
Those staying on the road may take a single handful of chickpeas, rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, or black gram, provided these items are not otherwise forbidden.
Likewise, one who has fasted for six meals may partake of food at the seventh mealtime.
"One should take from one who neglects his duties according to the rule of 'no provision for tomorrow. (MDh 11.16). 2.275.
He states the punishment for one who, though not a thief himself, assists a thief:
"Having provided food, shelter, fire, water, counsel, implements, or funds to a thief or a murderer, if he is aware [of their intent], the highest fine shall be imposed. (YDh 2.276)
Food is sustenance;
shelter is a place of residence;
fire is for the sake of removing the cold and so forth for the thief; water [is likewise].
"Thirsty" refers to one who desires [theft]. "Mantra" is the instruction on the methods of stealing.
"Apparatus" is the means for accomplishing theft. "Expenditure" is for the purpose of embezzlement.
Provisions for one traveling to another country:
if anyone provides these to a thief or a murderer even while knowing their wickedness, he shall be punished with the highest amercement.
There is also fault for those who remain indifferent;
for according to the traditional teaching of Nārada: "Those who, though capable, remain indifferent, are also partakers of that fault" (NSm 14.18). // 2.276 //
Furthermore:
"In the case of striking with a weapon or causing an abortion, the highest fine is prescribed;
likewise, for the killing of a man or a woman, the highest or the lowest fine may be imposed. (YDh 2.277)

For causing a weapon to fall upon the limbs of another, and for causing an abortion— except in the case of a slave woman or a Brāhmaṇa’s embryo— the highest fine is the punishment. However, in the case of causing the miscarriage of a slave woman’s embryo, [the rule is] "one who causes the destruction of a slave woman’s embryo" (YDh 2.236).
By such statements as these, a fine of one hundred [paṇas] is prescribed.
However, regarding the destruction of a Brahmin embryo, an extension of the penalty for killing a Brahmin will be stated in the verse: "But having killed an unknown embryo... (MDh 11.87).

In the case of killing a man or a woman, it should be understood that the punishment is established as either the highest or the lowest, depending on their character, conduct, and other such factors. (2.277)
Moreover:
Having bound a stone to a woman who is extremely corrupt, a female murderer, one who has not been pregnant, or one who destroys a dam, he shall cause her to be cast into the waters. (YDh 2.278)
Especially those who are corrupted, severely corrupted, who have killed an embryo, who have caused an abortion, who have been the slayer of a man,
and who have breached embankments— these women who are devoid of offspring, having tied a stone to their necks, one should cause them to enter the water, so that...
They do not float. // 2.278 //
Furthermore:
One who administers poison or sets fire [to a dwelling], or who causes the death of her husband, her elders, or her own children,
should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by cattle.
The phrase "one who is not pregnant" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Furthermore, she who, for the sake of killing another, puts poison into food, drink, and so forth, or casts it [therein];
she who sets fire to villages and the like for the purpose of burning; and likewise, she who causes the death of her own husband, teacher, or children.
Having cut off her ears, hands, nose, and lips, one should cause her to be killed by being driven along by unrestrained, wicked oxen.
It should be understood that this prescription of punishment for a perpetrator of violence mentioned in the section on theft is incidental. (2.279)
Regarding a killing where the perpetrator is unknown, he states the means for identifying the killer:
"The sons and kinsmen of one who has been killed while unobserved should be questioned immediately regarding the quarrel;
and his women, who were devoted to other men, should be interrogated separately. (YDh 2.280)
The sons and close relatives of one killed by an unknown person must be quickly questioned regarding the quarrel that occurred with him, asking, "With whom did he have a dispute?
Likewise, the female relatives of the deceased [must be questioned].
And those women who are devoted to other men and are unfaithful must also be questioned. (2.280)
How should he question them? To this he says:
"Or desiring information regarding a woman, property, or conduct, or with whom did he go? He should also slowly question people near the place of death. (YDh 2.281)
"Is he desirous of women, desirous of wealth, or desirous of a livelihood? Likewise, toward what woman, or toward whose relative, did he have an attachment;

in what wealth did he find pleasure; from where did his desire for a livelihood arise; or with whom did he go to another land?"—in these various ways, unchaste women should be questioned individually after having gained their confidence. Likewise:
Those people who live near the place where death occurred, such as cowherds and forest-dwellers, should also be questioned with trust.
Having thus identified the perpetrator through various forms of questioning, the appropriate punishment must be inflicted upon him. (2.281)
Furthermore:
Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of a king, shall be burned by a fire of straw mats (kaṭāgni).
A field endowed with ripened fruit and crops;
a dwelling, meaning a house;
a forest, meaning a wilderness or a pleasure grove; and a village.

Those who burn a pasture (*vivīta*)—whose characteristics have been previously described—or a threshing floor (*khala*), as well as those who approach the king's wife, all of them shall be wrapped in mats made of *vīraṇa* grass and burned.
This prescription of punishment is given because, in the case of those who set fire to fields and the like, there would otherwise follow the penalty of death. (2.282)
Thus ends the section on theft;
now begins the section on sexual intercourse with women (strīsaṃgrahaṇa).
The title of the legal dispute known as "sexual intercourse with women" is here explained.
In order to establish the application of these fines, Vyāsa has explained their nature in three ways:
that [fine] is declared to be of three kinds— the first, the middle, and the highest.
By means of improper place, time, or speech, and in a secluded location, [one commits adultery] with another's wife.
A sidelong glance, a look, a smile, and the first act of boldness; the sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments—these are recorded as the initial stages.
Enticement with food and drink is recorded as the middle form of violence;
so too is sitting together in secluded places and mutual physical contact.
Seizing each other by the hair is indeed considered a formal act of seduction (*saṃgrahaṇa*).
Seduction is the sexual union of a man and a woman.
Since the infliction of punishment upon the perpetrator of adultery is preceded by knowledge of that act, [the author] first states the means for obtaining such knowledge:
"In an act of adultery, a man is to be apprehended by seizing each other's hair;
or immediately by signs born of passion, as well as when there is mutual admission by both parties. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.283)
A man engaged in sexual intercourse should be identified by signs such as "hair-to-hair" (*keśākeśi*) and so forth.
*Keśākeśi* refers to a game involving mutual grasping of each other's hair.

In that context, when there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound [formed] by the rule *tatra tenedam* (Pāṇini 2.2.27), provided the members are of the same form (*sarūpa*), the suffix *ic* is applied by the rule *ic karmavyatihāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.127).
Thus, the suffix *ic* is applied as a compound-final affix (*samāsānta*). Because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the third case ending is elided.
Consequently, this is the meaning:

He should be apprehended when he has engaged in adultery, having been identified either by the signs of passion— such as fresh wounds inflicted by fingernails and teeth resulting from hair-to-hair grappling with another's wife— or by the mutual consent of the two parties.
The mention of "another's wife" [is intended to exclude one's own wife].
This is for the purpose of excluding those who are appointed [as wives] or those who are kept [in confinement], and so forth. // 2.283 //
Furthermore:
touching the knot of the lower garment, the breasts, the thighs, or the hair;
conversing at an improper place or time; and sitting together on the same seat. (YDh 2.284)
Furthermore, he who acts as if with desire by touching another's wife’s garments, the area of her knots, her breasts, her upper robes, her hips, her hair, and so forth; or likewise,
engaging in conversation at an improper place— whether in a secluded spot, a crowded public area, or in the midst of darkness— at an improper time.

He who acts [with another's wife], or who remains with another's wife on a single bed or similar place as if desiring to sport with her— he too, being engaged in sexual misconduct (*saṃgrahaṇa*), is to be apprehended.
And this refers to a person whose guilt is suspected.
But for the other, there is no fault; as Manu says: "But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks [against another] on account of a cause..."
"He shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is indeed no transgression on his part" (MDh 8.355).
By that same [author], it has been stated that he who, having been touched by another's wife, remains patient, is also to be apprehended:
"He who touches a woman in an improper place, or likewise he who, being touched, endures it."
"Everything is considered adultery when done with mutual consent" (MDh 8.358).
Furthermore, he who proclaims before a crowd of libertines, out of pride, "I have repeatedly enjoyed this clever woman," he too is to be apprehended; thus it has been stated by that same [author].
"Whether out of pride, or through delusion, or out of self-praise, he should say of himself: 'This woman was previously my wife'; that is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction). Thus it is said.
He now states the punishment for a man and a woman who, though both forbidden [from such contact], engage again in conversation and the like.

In the case of a prohibition, a woman shall pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], while a man shall pay two hundred; in the case of their transgressing such a prohibition, the punishment shall be the same as that for adultery (saṃgrahaṇa). "Prohibition" (pratiṣedha) refers to that by which conversation and other interactions with a particular person are forbidden by her husband, father, or other guardians.
In that case, a woman who persists in such conduct shall pay a fine of one hundred paṇas; a man, however, persisting despite being thus forbidden, shall pay two hundred paṇas.

However, when a man and a woman engage in sexual intercourse in violation of the prohibition, the same punishment that will be declared according to their respective castes (*varṇa*) for the offense of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual union) is to be understood here;
and this applies with the exception of the wives of performers (*cāraṇa*) and others. (8.362)
"This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers (*cāraṇa*) nor to those who live off their own labor,
for they entice women and keep them hidden," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 8.362). 2.285.
Now, regarding the punishment for sexual intercourse, he says:
"In the case of one of the same caste, the highest fine; in the case of a woman of a lower caste (ānulomya), the middle fine;
in the case of a man of a higher caste (prātilomya), death for the male, and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the female. (YDh 2.286)
If a man of any of the four castes, by force, has intercourse with the protected wife of another of his own caste, he shall be fined one thousand and eighty paṇas.
But when he approaches a woman of a lower caste who is unprotected, in the direct order of castes, then the middle amercement applies.
He is subject to punishment.

Furthermore, when one approaches a woman of the same caste who is unprotected, or one who is protected through a marriage in the direct order of castes (*ānulomya*), a specific rule is stated in the *Mānava* [Code]:
"A Brāhmaṇa approaching a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]."
He who has sexual intercourse with a willing [woman] shall be fined five hundred [paṇas].
Likewise,
a Brāhmaṇa approaching those [women] when they are guarded shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas].
"For [intercourse] with a Śūdra woman by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the fine shall be one thousand [paṇas]. (MDh 8.383).
And this should be understood as applying to cases other than those involving the wives of teachers or friends; [the following are protected]:
the mother, the mother's sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle's wife, and the father's sister.
The wife of a paternal uncle, a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, the wife of a teacher, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and she who is of the highest caste.
"Going to any one of these [women] is called violating the Guru's bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained," according to the traditional teaching of Nārada (NSm 12.72–74).

In the case of the reverse order, when a man of the Kṣatriya or other lower varṇas has sexual intercourse with a woman of a superior varṇa, his punishment is death; and this applies specifically to the case of a protected woman. In other cases, however, there is a monetary fine.
But both of them, having violated a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
shall be punished like Śūdras or burned in a fire of straw. If, however, a Vaiśya or a King should have intercourse with an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman, [he shall be punished as follows].
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "One should impose a fine of five hundred on a Vaiśya, but one thousand on a Kṣatriya" (MDh 8.376).
Furthermore, for a Śūdra who approaches an unprotected woman of a higher caste, the punishment is the excision of his organ and the confiscation of all his property.

"A Śūdra who dwells with a member of the twice-born caste, whether she be guarded or unguarded, is deprived of his limbs and all his property if she was unguarded, but of everything if she was guarded. (MDh 8.374).
Furthermore, for a woman who goes to a man of a lower caste, there shall be the cutting off of her ears and—by the inclusion of the word "and so forth"—her nose as well.
A punishment shall be prescribed for a woman who goes [with a man] either in the direct order of castes or with one of her own caste;
and this instruction regarding execution and other penalties applies to the king alone.
Because the authority to protect belongs not to every twice-born person merely by virtue of being so;
for there is a prohibition against taking up weapons, stating: "A Brāhmaṇa should not take up a weapon even for the sake of testing it" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.20.9).
But when, due to the king’s notification or delay, there is a fear that the execution of justice will be hindered, then he himself may slay adulterers and others;
for the twice-born may take up arms whenever dharma is obstructed. (MDh 8.348)
Likewise:
"In the killing of an *ātātāyin*, no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer, whether done openly or in secret; it is simply fury meeting fury. (MDh 8.351)
This is also because of the permission granted for taking up weapons;
likewise, it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya having sexual intercourse with each other's wives, the fines shall be one thousand and five hundred paṇas respectively.
Regarding this, Manu says:

"If a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a protected Vaiśya woman, both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman. (MDh 8.382) 2.286.
Following from the discussion on adultery, he now states the punishment for abducting a maiden:

"For abducting an adorned maiden, one should pay the highest fine; otherwise, the lowest. In the case of maidens of the same caste, the fine is prescribed; in the case of abduction against the natural order (prātilomya), death is ordained. (YDh 2.287)

One who abducts a maiden of equal caste who is adorned and ready for marriage shall be punished with the highest amercement; one who abducts a maiden of equal caste who is not so inclined shall be punished with the first amercement;
and one who abducts a maiden born of a superior caste [shall be punished with death].

Furthermore, the punishment for a Kṣatriya or others is indeed death; and from the prescription of this penalty, it is understood that the stolen property shall be taken away from the thief and restored to the other person. (2.287)
He states the punishment for abduction according to the order of castes:

"There is no fault in the case of women of the same caste who are willing; otherwise, there is a fine" (YDh 2.288ab). If one abducts a maiden of lower caste who is full of affection, then because there is an absence of fault, there is no punishment. But otherwise...
For one who abducts a woman against her will, the punishment is the first amercement.
He states the punishment for defiling a maiden:
"But for defilement, there shall be the cutting off of the hand; likewise, in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there is death.
The phrase "in the case of those born in the direct order" (anulomāsu) is understood to carry over from the preceding verse.
If one defiles an unwilling maiden by force through means such as scratching with the fingernails, then his hand shall be cut off;
but when he causes a wound in her vulva by inserting a finger, [the punishment is different].

"In that case, the cutting off of a finger, as prescribed by Manu, is added [to the fine]. But if a man, out of arrogance, should violate a maiden by force, his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. (MDh 8.367)
Furthermore, when he defiles a maiden who is already in love with him, as previously mentioned, a specific rule has been stated by that same [author]:
"One who defiles a willing maiden does not deserve the amputation of his fingers;
however, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] in order to prevent a recurrence. (MDh 8.368)
But when a maiden defiles another maiden, or a learned woman does so, a specific rule for that case has been stated by him [Manu]:
"A maiden who defiles a maiden shall be fined two hundred;
but a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head."
"Or else, he shall suffer the cutting off of his two fingers, or likewise be made to carry [the corpse] upon a donkey. (MDh 8.369–70).
"He shall defile the maiden" means that he shall cause her to have a wound in her vulva.

Furthermore, when one approaches a maiden of superior caste—whether she is willing or unwilling—without distinction, then for the inferior man, such as a Kṣatriya and so forth, there is indeed death; for the lowborn man who violates a woman of the highest rank deserves death. (MDh 8.366)
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu.
When he approaches a woman of his own caste who is willing, he shall give a pair of cattle as a bride-price (*śulka*) to her father, if the father so desires;
but if the father does not desire the bride-price, he shall pay that same amount to the king as a fine. [This applies to] a woman of his own caste.
But for one who approaches her against her will, there is indeed death;
as Manu says:
"If the father so desires, he who enjoys a maiden of equal status shall pay the nuptial fee. (MDh 8.366)
"He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal [in status], shall not suffer execution. (MDh 8.364)
Furthermore:

"One should pay a hundred [paṇas] for defiling a woman; but two hundred for making a false accusation. One who has sexual intercourse with a female animal should be made to pay a hundred; for having intercourse with a low-caste woman or a cow, the middle amercement. (YDh 2.289)

Here, by the word "woman" (*strī*), the maiden is referred to because she is the subject under discussion. If someone, having disclosed her existing defects— such as her being afflicted with chronic or loathsome diseases like epilepsy or pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), or her having engaged in sexual intercourse— defames her by saying "she is not a virgin," he shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
Furthermore, for false accusation— that is, for defaming by exposing a fault that does not exist— one should be made to pay two hundred [paṇas]; however,
for sexual intercourse with an animal other than a cow, one should be made to pay one hundred.
Furthermore, he who approaches a low-caste woman of the *antyāvasāyin* class— whether she be willing or unwilling— and likewise a cow, shall be punished with the middle amercement. (2.289)
He states the punishment for sexual intercourse with a common woman:

"In the case of women kept [in the household], female slaves, and likewise those who are free, even though they are women with whom one may have intercourse, a man shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas. (YDh 2.290)

The word "going" (gacchan) is understood to carry over from the previous context. Women of the [four] castes possessing the characteristics already described, who are female slaves, are those very persons who, for the purpose of preventing the neglect of service by their master, are restricted to staying only within the house; thus, being barred from enjoyment by other men, they are called *avaruddhāḥ* (confined women).

Female slaves are those who have been acquired through the exclusive possession of a man; when female slaves or female servants become *avaruddhā* (confined) or *bhujiṣyā* (at the disposal of another), then [the rule applies] to them as well.
By the word "and" (*ca*), [it includes] courtesans and unchaste women.
This includes the taking of common women and female slaves;
and even if one approaches those among them who are accessible because they are common to all men, he shall be fined fifty paṇas.
Because they are possessed by others, they are equivalent to the wives of others;
and this has been clearly stated by Nārada:
"A wanton woman, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who is cast out [from her family]..."
Women may be approached in the direct order of castes, but not in the inverse order.
"But in the case of these very female slaves, there would be a fault similar to that regarding the wives of others;

for even though they are approachable, one should not have intercourse with them, since they are the property of another. (NSm 12.77–78) A *niṣkāsinī* is a female slave who has not been appropriated by her master.
But has it not been stated that women such as wanton women (*svairiṇī*) and others are to be approached because they are common property?
For indeed, in the world, no women whatsoever are found to be common property either by birth or according to the scriptures.
For instance, courtesans and female slaves are indeed women of the [same] social classes.
"An independent woman who, having abandoned her husband of equal caste, resorts to another out of desire [is a svairiṇī];
according to the Smṛti, 'for the castes, service is permitted in the direct order, not in the inverse order. (YDh 1.67; YDh 2.183). NSP and Pāṇḍeya read as follows:
"Because of the recollection of Manu. This is likely an error;

Setlur notes that one manuscript contains that reading. Furthermore, it is not possible for women of the [upper] castes to enjoy the company of another man while their husband is either living or deceased.
Whether he is of immoral conduct, addicted to sensual pleasures, or devoid of virtues,
a husband must always be served like a god by a virtuous wife.

For there is a traditional prohibition stating: "She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits; but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died" (Manu Dharmaśāstra 5.154, 157).
Nor is the state of being a maiden common [to all women],
for it is taught that only a maiden protected by her father and others is to be given in marriage;
and even in the absence of a giver, it is taught that only such a woman may choose her own husband (*svayaṃvara*).
Nor does one fall away from the entitlement to one's own duties (*svadharma*) merely by becoming a slave;
for slavery consists in dependence upon another, not in the abandonment of one's own duty.
Nor is a courtesan common [to all], except in cases other than those born in the direct order of castes (*varṇānuloma*).
Because another class of women suitable for sexual intercourse is impossible;
and even if she were included within that [class], her unapproachability would remain exactly as before. This applies also in the case of those born from a *pratiloma* union.

However, they are absolutely unfit for such [sexual] intercourse. Therefore, because their loss of caste (*pātitya*) results from the repeated practice of a censurable act through enjoyment by another man,
and because association with the fallen is prohibited, they are not fit for enjoyment by any man whatsoever.
This is true;

however, in this case, the expression "she may be approached" (*gamya*) regarding the enjoyment of unchaste women and the like is used because of the absence of visible defects (*dṛṣṭadoṣa*), such as the fear of punishment by the king or the protection afforded by a father or other guardians.

Furthermore, the absence of punishment applies to enslaved women who are not restricted to a specific man, since the prescription of punishment is contingent upon the condition of being under the exclusive possession of a particular person; thus, it does not apply to those who lack that condition.
It is understood from the context that, however, for wanton women and the like, there is an absence of punishment because no specific injunction exists; as it is said:
"One should not cause even the slightest fine to be paid to a man who approaches a maiden of superior status who has been unchaste" (MDh 8.365).
This is understood from the indication of the gender [in the scriptural texts];

however, an expiation (prāyaścitta) indeed occurs for both those who have sexual intercourse with women who should not be approached and those who do approach them, as there is no distinction between them when it is caused by a lapse in one's own duty (svadharma).
Furthermore, as for the claim that courtesans (veśyās) are included within the [four] social classes (varṇas) because no other caste (jātyantara) is possible,

which was stated through inference: "Courtesans are included within the anuloma and other categories of the varṇas, because they are based on the human species (manuṣyajāti), just like Brāhmaṇas and others."
That is not so, because [the argument] is inconclusive due to the case of the Kuṇḍa, Golaka, and others.

Therefore, there exists a certain caste called "veśyā" (prostitute), which is beginningless; a woman born from a man of superior or equal caste within the class of prostitutes, whose livelihood consists of sexual union with men, is a "veśyā," just like a Brāhmaṇī and so forth.
This must be accepted on the strength of what is well-known in the world; nor is this common consensus without foundation, for it is recorded in the Skanda Purāṇa:

The golden *apsarases* named Pañcacūḍās have a lineage known as courtesans, which is the fifth caste. Therefore, because they are devoid of the rule regarding marriage with a fixed husband, there is neither spiritual fault (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*) nor punishment in their approaching men of equal or superior caste.
And although there is no legal punishment for men who approach women who are not married to them,
nevertheless, there is indeed a spiritual fault, because of the restrictive rule: "One should always be devoted to one's own wife" (MDh 3.45).

"Upon approaching a female animal or a prostitute, the Prājāpatya penance is prescribed" (ViDh 53.7); because of this traditional teaching on expiation (*prāyaścitta*), [the view] is beyond reproach. // 2.290 //

By the phrase "in the case of female slaves who are confined," the author prescribes a punishment for approaching female slaves such as those who are independent (svairiṇī) or others; by doing so, he implies that there is no punishment for approaching those who are not slaves.
He now states an exception to that rule.
For one who approaches a female slave by force when she is unwilling, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
if many men do so, the fine is twenty-four paṇas for each individually.

This applies to those who live off the sexual enjoyment of men—such as female slaves, wanton women, and the like—in the absence of any payment of a bride-price (śulka), when one approaches them through forceful compulsion.
The fine shall be ten paṇas.
If many men approach a single woman who does not desire it by force, then each of them shall be punished with a fine of twenty-four paṇas.
Furthermore, when they have given a fee according to her wish and subsequently depart by force even though she is unwilling, there is no fault on their part,
provided they are overcome by illness or similar circumstances.
If she does not come when invited because she is ill, exhausted, distracted, or occupied with royal business,
it is declared that the mare is exempt from punishment. (BṛSm 1.16.13)

Thus, from the words of Nārada: "A courtesan who has accepted her fee, if she refuses [to perform], shall pay double; if the fee was not accepted, she shall be made to pay an equal amount. A man likewise shall be dealt with in exactly the same manner. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.292)
But when, having received the fee (*śulka*), a healthy man does not wish to have intercourse, he shall pay double the fee.
Likewise, for a healthy man who, having paid the fee, himself does not wish to have intercourse, there is simply a forfeiture of the fee.
A courtesan who, having received the fee, does not wish to have intercourse, shall bear double the fee.
"Even one who has not desired [the marriage] shall suffer the loss of the nuptial fee if the fee has already been paid," so it was stated by that very same author.
Likewise, another specific detail has also been shown by him:

Likewise, a man who does not pay the bride-price after having enjoyed the woman, or who has intercourse in a manner contrary to the proper order, or who approaches her with his feet, teeth, nails, and so forth,
or who approaches her in a non-vaginal opening, or who causes her to dwell with many men; (NSm 6.20) [he is liable for punishment].
"He shall be made to pay eightfold the toll, and an equal amount as a fine.

"Those who are headed by courtesans and who dwell in their houses for the sake of lovers are known to provide the decision in cases of doubt regarding matters arising from them. (NSm 6.21; DhKo 851). Thus ends [verse] 2.292.
Furthermore:
For one who approaches a woman in a non-vaginal passage, or who urinates upon a man, as well as for one who approaches a female ascetic, the fine is twenty-four [paṇas]. (YDh 2.293)
But he who approaches his own wife by the mouth or other such parts, or urinates facing a man, or has intercourse with a female ascetic, shall be punished with a fine of twenty-four paṇas. (2.293)
Furthermore:
"In the case of approaching a woman of the lowest caste (antyajā), however, one should brand him with the mark of a dog's foot and banish him;

likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the lowest caste shall become an outcaste himself, and for the approach of an Ārya woman by one of the lowest caste, there is death. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.294)

And regarding the *antyajā* woman, namely the *caṇḍālī*, for approaching her, one should fine a member of the three higher castes who is unwilling to undergo penance one thousand *paṇas*, based on the statement of Manu: "But a thousand [paṇas] for approaching an *antyaja* woman" (MDh 8.385); and having branded him with a "bad bond," that is, with a loathsome mark in the shape of a vulva.
He should banish him from his own kingdom;
however, for one who is intent upon performing penance, there shall be punishment alone.
Furthermore, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste becomes an Antya— that is, a Caṇḍāla himself.
Moreover, when an Antya, such as a Caṇḍāla and so forth, approaches a woman of a superior caste:
It is indeed death. 2.294.
Thus ends the section on adultery with women;
now begins the section on miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka*).
Within the section on the types of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-prakaraṇa*), another head of litigation called "the union of man and woman" has been explained by both Manu and Nārada.
Regarding this, Nārada states:
"That title of dispute in which the rules for marriage and so forth of women and men are proclaimed is called Strīpuṃsayoga (the Union of Woman and Man). (NSm 12.1)
Manu also said:

"Women must be kept under dependence by their own men day and night; for when they become attached to sensual objects, they must be firmly established under one's own control," and so forth. (MDh 9.2)

Although a legal proceeding between a husband and wife before the king in the capacity of plaintiff and defendant is prohibited, nevertheless, when their mutual transgression is known either through direct observation or by hearsay, the king must establish the couple on the path of their own duty by means of punishment and other such measures.
Otherwise, one incurs fault; for this teaching concerning the various duties of men and women occurs within the section on royal duties in the context of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).
And this has already been explained in detail precisely in the section on marriage (*vivāha*).
Thus it has been stated by the Lord of Yogins, and not otherwise here.
Now the title of legal procedure known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters) is introduced.
Its definition has been stated by Nārada:
"In the *prakīrṇakas*, those legal proceedings which are not included [in the other titles] should be understood as being under the king's authority."
Obstructing the commands of kings and likewise performing their work [in opposition].
The offering of precedence, the sowing of dissension among the subjects, as well as the subversion of the laws of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies;
Disputes between father and son, the transference of penance,
the failure to accept gifts, and even the anger of those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas).

"The fault of the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), as well as the restriction of their occupations, and whatever was not seen among the previous [titles of law]—all that shall be *prakīrṇaka*. (NSm 18.1–4).
Regarding the title of law *prakīrṇaka*, those disputes concerning the transgression of the king’s commands, the carrying out of his commands, and so forth, are dependent upon the sovereign.

In that case, the king alone, adopting a stance of opposition toward those who proceed along a path devoid of the conduct prescribed by tradition (smṛti), should carry out the decision of the legal dispute. By stating this, it is implied as a matter of course that a legal proceeding which relies upon the king is termed *prakīrṇaka*.
Regarding that, he states the specific punishment according to the specific nature of the offense:
"He who writes a royal edict as deficient or excessive, or he who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment. (YDh 2.295)
He who records a royal edict while declaring a deficiency or an excess in the measurement of land granted by the king or its recorded assessment (nibandha),
and he who, having apprehended an adulterer or a thief, releases them without delivering them to the king— those two [shall be punished].
Both shall be punished with the highest amercement. // 2.295 //
In this context, he also states the punishment for legal matters other than those involving the king:
"If one defiles a twice-born man with something unfit to be eaten, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that. (YDh 2.296)

Having defiled a Brāhmaṇa with inedible substances such as urine or feces— substances unfit for consumption— either by mixing them into food and drink or by contaminating his person, and having caused him to eat it, he shall be punished with the highest amercement. Furthermore, having defiled a Kṣatriya in this same manner...
The connection is as follows: having defiled a Vaiśya, one incurs the first [amercement];
having defiled a Śūdra, one is to be punished with half of the first sāhasa.
But in the case of defiling [food] with garlic and other forbidden items, the gradation of the punishment should be inferred according to the gradation of the offense. // 2.296 //
Furthermore:
"One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall have three limbs maimed and be made to pay the highest fine. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.297)
One who habitually deals in counterfeit gold—such as goldsmiths and others—who have achieved an excellence of color through processes such as chemical infusion (rasavedha);

and one who habitually sells "bad meat" (vimāṃsa), meaning contemptible meat associated with dogs and the like, such as butchers and others; and by the word "and" (ca), one who deals in counterfeit silver and so forth.

All of them should be made individually deprived of three limbs—namely the nose, the ears, and the hands. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they shall be made to pay the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*) as a cumulative penalty for the cutting off of these three limbs. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:

"The king shall cause a goldsmith who is most wicked among all thorns and who practices injustice to be cut into pieces with razors. This [rule] refers specifically to the gold belonging to the gods, Brahmins, and kings. (MDh 9.292) 2.297.
He states the absence of punishment in specific cases:
"There is no penalty for a fault committed by a quadruped that cries out 'Do not go away,' nor for one caused by wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, the arms, or a yoke. (YDh 2.298)
The fault consisting of the killing of a human being or similar acts, which is committed by four-footed animals such as cows or elephants, does not belong to the owner of the cow and so forth,
provided he is shouting loudly, "Get out! Likewise,
[it does not belong to him] when [the animal acts] with the throwing of a club, a clod, an arrow, or a stone by its foreleg.

Furthermore, the previously mentioned fault regarding one who drives a yoked animal, such as a horse, is also not applicable to one who throws wood and other materials while shouting "there is no space to move.
This statement that there is no fault in injury caused by the throwing of wood and such is intended to establish the absence of punishment.
Furthermore, there certainly exists an expiation (prāyaścitta) occasioned by acting unintentionally;
and the mention of "wood" and so forth is intended as an illustration for [other weapons] such as spears, javelins, and the like. (2.298)
Furthermore:
When injury is caused by a vehicle with its nose-rope severed, or by one whose yoke-pole and so forth are broken, or which retreats backward, the owner does not incur guilt. (YDh 2.299)

The nose-string of your oxen has not been cut—that is, the nose-string of the oxen yoked to a cart or similar vehicle; [the phrase] "by that which has its nose-string cut" refers to such a cart or vehicle.
Likewise, [it refers to one] with a broken yoke, and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," also to one with a broken axle, wheel, or the like.

When injury is caused to humans or other beings by a vehicle that is moving backward or from behind, or by one that veers off to the side, or by one coming head-on, neither the owner nor the driver incurs fault,
because the injury was not produced by their intentional effort.
And so Manu says: "When the nose-string is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction,
when there is a breakage of the axle of the vehicle, and likewise when there is a breakage of the wheel;"
"Manu has declared that there is no punishment in cases of the breaking of the mechanical devices [of the cart], as well as the yoke or the reins, or when one cries out, 'Get away! (MDh 8.291–92).
He now states the punishment for the owner in the event of negligence:

Even if capable of doing so, a master who fails to rescue [his dependents] from fanged or horned animals shall pay the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, if [the victim] cries out for help, he shall pay double. When one is being attacked by fanged animals such as elephants or by horned animals such as cattle, driven by an unskilled driver, the capable [master]—
If the owner of that [animal], even though capable of doing so, neglects it and does not set it free, he shall pay the first *sāhasa* fine on account of employing an unskilled driver.
But when he does not release it even after it has been cried out, "I am being killed!", then the fine shall be double.
But when he drives the chariot while it is already skilled [in operation], then the driver alone is to be punished, not the owner. As Manu says:
"If the driver is experienced, the driver deserves the punishment" (MDh 8.294).

The driver is the controller; he must be trustworthy and diligent. Furthermore, a specific punishment should be determined according to the specific nature of the living being [injured], as it has been said:
Manu says: "In the case of killing a human being, the sinner shall quickly become as guilty as a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, the guilt is half [that of a human]."
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
"For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣakas; for the killing of dogs and pigs, the fine shall be one māṣaka. (MDh 8.296–98).
Furthermore:
One who addresses a paramour as a thief shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;

but if he releases him after having lived off his wealth, he shall be made to pay eight times that amount. (YDh 2.301) Out of fear of staining his own lineage, one who addresses a paramour or an adulterer as "thief, get out! shall be fined five hundred *paṇas*.
He who releases a paramour after receiving money from his hand in the form of a bribe, having lived off that wealth, shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred [paṇas] for that act; furthermore,
he who releases the paramour by taking money as a bribe shall be fined eight times as much as what was received.
He shall be made to pay. 2.301.
Furthermore:
Having cut off the tongue of one who speaks what is undesirable to the king, of one who reviles him, and of one who divulges his secret counsel, he shall banish them. (YDh 2.302)
Having cut out the tongue of one who excessively and repeatedly speaks what is undesirable and disagreeable to the king— such as praise of his enemies—

and who is habitually abusive and censorious toward that very king, or who betrays his secret counsel intended for the prosperity of his own kingdom or the ruin of another's kingdom, whispering it into the ears of his enemies; having cut out his tongue...
He should banish them from his own kingdom;
however, in cases such as the embezzlement of the treasury, there shall be death alone for those who steal the king's treasury and for those who persist in hostile acts.
For there is a traditional teaching of Manu stating: "One should have those who instigate enemies punished with various forms of punishment" (MDh 9.275).
The meaning of "various" is that they consist of the confiscation of all property, the amputation of limbs, and execution.
Even when all one's property is being confiscated, that which is a means of subsistence for someone must not be seized, except for implements used for theft;
as Nārada has said:
The weapons of those who live by arms, the outer garments and so forth of those who live by such external means,
the ornaments of courtesans, and the musical instruments and the like of those skilled in them.
"And whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live—even if all their property is to be confiscated, the king ought not to seize these. (NSm 18.11–12).
Furthermore, regarding a Brāhmaṇa: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.46).

Because of this prohibition, in place of execution, shaving the head and other such punishments must be performed; for a Brāhmaṇa, execution is [replaced by] shaving the head, banishment from the city, and branding.
"And on the forehead shall be the mark of one accused, and his departure [from the city] shall be by donkey," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 9.237). 2.302.
Furthermore:
For one who sells a corpse or a limb from it, for one who strikes his teacher,
and likewise for one who mounts the vehicle or the throne of a king, the punishment is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).

The highest amercement is the punishment for one who sells clothing, flowers, or other items belonging to a dead body; for one who strikes a guru, such as a father or preceptor; and likewise for one who mounts, without the king's permission, the vehicles of others—such as elephants or horses—or their thrones and the like. (2.303)
Furthermore:
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king,
and likewise for a Śūdra living as a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.

Furthermore, he who, out of anger or other such motives, pierces the two eyes of another; and he who, being an expert in the science of astrology, apart from wishing for the welfare of his teacher and others,
gives a prediction of an undesirable misfortune to a king— such as, "At the end of the year, your fall from the throne will occur"— and so forth.
Likewise, for a Śūdra who displays the marks of a Brāhmaṇa, such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth, for the sake of obtaining food,
the fine is eight hundred;
that fine in which there are eight hundred *paṇas* is described as such.

Furthermore, it should be understood from another Smṛti that if a Śūdra, wearing the dress of a Brāhmaṇa, comes for the purpose of eating at a Śrāddha feast, one should mark his body with a heated iron pin in the shape of a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
However, in the case of one who wears the marks of a Brāhmaṇa, such as the sacred thread, for the sake of livelihood, his execution alone is prescribed.
For there is a traditional legal text (smṛti) stating: "One should cause those Śūdras who bear the marks of the twice-born to be executed."
(These could not be traced) 2.304 //
Regarding the punishment for seeing legal proceedings otherwise due to passion, greed, and so forth, [the author] says:
"But having seen legal proceedings wrongly decided by the king, the members of the court, together with the judge, shall be fined double the amount of the dispute. (YDh 2.305)

If the judges, having failed to properly deliberate due to passion, greed, and so forth, and by transgressing the law established by tradition and custom, have wrongly decided cases that should have been suspected,

the king himself must re-examine them; then, once the fault has been determined, the former judges shall be made to pay double the fine imposed on the defeated party in each case of litigation, along with their associates.
Because the statement is intended to prescribe the punishment for one who has not yet been caught,
there is no tautology with the verse beginning with "out of passion, out of greed," and so forth.

Furthermore, when it is known that a legal proceeding was wrongly decided due to the fault of the witnesses, then only the witnesses are to be punished, neither the winner nor the members of the court. However, when the wrongful decision of the proceeding occurs with the king's consent, [the king alone is to be punished].

Then it was understood that all the court members and others, together with the king, were liable to punishment, according to the verse: "One quarter of the guilt falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king. (Manu Dharmaśāstra 8.18)
Because of this statement,

this [text] is intended to demonstrate the faults of each individual— such as the king and others— and not for the purpose of dividing a single non-manifest karmic potential (*pāpāpūrva*). As it has been said:
Because the *apūrva* has the nature of producing a result that inheres in the agent. // 2.305 //
Regarding the punishment for one who reverses a legal proceeding that has been decided according to justice, [the author] says:
"If one who has been defeated even by justice should think, 'I am not defeated,' and returns, having defeated him again, the judge shall cause him to pay double the fine. (YDh 2.306)

Furthermore, if one who has been defeated according to the path of justice, out of arrogance, thinks "I am not defeated" and approaches the court again, presenting forged documents and the like, the judge should, by means of legal procedure, bring about his defeat once more and cause him to pay double the fine.
Nārada also said: "If anyone considers a case to have been decided or adjudicated contrary to the law, he should impose double the fine and have that matter retried. (NSm Mā 1.56)
*Tīrita* refers to a case settled by means of witnesses, documents, and so forth, wherein the punishment has not yet been extracted;
*anuśiṣṭa* refers to one wherein the punishment has been extracted— that is,
up to the point of the infliction of punishment.
That is to say, it has been decided.
Furthermore, as for the statement of Manu:
"Wherever a case may be found to have been adjudicated and instructed..."

"That which has been done is to be known as lawful; a wise man should not reverse it" (MDh 9.233). Thus, when there is a suspicion that a legal proceeding has proceeded unrighteously due to the testimony of either the plaintiff or the defendant, one should initiate the lawsuit again after first declaring a double fine; however, this is not the case when there is certainty that it proceeded righteously.
This is intended to mean that even [in such cases], the king should not proceed out of greed or other such motives;
furthermore, even when a matter has been wrongly decided by another king, that too must be restored to the path of righteousness through thorough investigation.

For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Whatever has been decided by another king through ignorance, even if that was established unjustly, one should bring it back into accordance with justice" (NSm 18.9). [2.306]
He states the course of action for one who has received fines or wealth unjustly:
"The king shall offer to Varuṇa that fine which was taken unjustly, and he himself shall give it to the Brahmins, having multiplied it thirtyfold. (YDh 2.307)
Whatever fine has been unjustly taken by a king out of greed or other such motives, he himself should give that thirtyfold amount to Brahmins, resolving: "This is an offering to Varuṇa.
For whatever has been taken unjustly in the form of a fine, that much must be restored to him.
Otherwise, the fault of theft would follow; furthermore, if punishment were taken unjustly, there would be no severance of the previous owner's ownership. (2.307)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Legal Procedure" (*vyavahāra*), in the *Ṛjumitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Vijñāneśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, son of the venerable Padmanābha Bhaṭṭopādhyāya.
Now begins the chapter on expiation (Prāyaścitta).
Now, the section on impurity (Āśauca):
the obligatory and occasional duties of those in the householder stage of life have been declared.
The virtuous duties of a specific type of householder, who is endowed with qualities such as initiation (abhiṣeka) and so forth, have been demonstrated; now,
by means of explaining impurity (āśauca), which serves as the cause for the restriction of that [householder's] entitlement, [the author proceeds].
An objection to these [views] is now set forth.

By the word *āśauca* (impurity), there is described a certain extraordinary state (*atiśaya*) residing in the person, which is to be removed by bathing at the proper time and so forth, and which serves as the cause for the injunctions regarding the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*), as well as for the prohibition of Vedic study (*adhyayana*) and other such acts; it is not, however, [the mere absence of purity].
It is merely a lack of eligibility for ritual acts,
because of the designation of "impurity" in such passages as, "all [such] kinsmen are impure" (MDh 5.58).
