Furthermore, in the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), the term *aśuddha* is never employed for those who are merely ineligible, such as one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) or one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*);
and because the comprehension of word-meanings is based upon the linguistic usage of the elders.
Furthermore, if it is postulated that the meaning denoted by the word *āśauca* is "unfitness" because one observes prohibitions against giving gifts and so forth for those in a state of impurity,
then, since one also observes injunctions regarding the offering of water and so forth, "fitness" would likewise have to be the meaning denoted by the word *āśauca*.
In that case, there would follow the fault of postulating multiple meanings for a single term.
Thus, this position is to be disregarded.
In that regard, he first states what must be performed by those impure, such as the sapindas and others:
"One should bury a child less than two years of age and should not offer water for them thereafter;
the other [child], followed to the cemetery by his kinsmen, should be accompanied by them. (YDh 3.1)

He should be cremated with the worldly fire by those reciting the *Yamasūkta* and the Gāthās, provided he was initiated (*upeta*) and maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), according to the ritual procedure for such a person. One whose two years are incomplete—that is, one who is less than two years old—should be buried; having made a pit in the earth, one should inter that deceased child there.

The meaning is that one should place [the body] down and not burn it again. Furthermore, one should perform the funeral rites for the deceased, such as the offering of water, which are prescribed with reference to the dead by such rules as "and they do not pour water once" (YDh 3.5).

And this [body], having been adorned with perfumes, garlands, ointments, and so forth, should be buried outside the village on pure ground— other than in a cremation ground and free from heaps of bones—
as Manu has said:
Relatives should place a deceased child less than two years old outside the village,
having adorned it, on pure ground, except for the collection of bones.
"No cremation with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-rite be performed;
having abandoned him like a log in the forest, they should simply cast him away for three days. (MDh 5.68–69).
The meaning of "having abandoned him like a log in the forest" is as follows:

Just as people become indifferent toward wood once it has been abandoned in the forest, so too, having abandoned even a child less than two years old in the ground after digging, one must remain indifferent regarding that child in matters such as the *śrāddha* and other funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*).
By this illustration, the absence of the *śrāddha* and other rites— though required by custom and other authorities— is indicated.
And having anointed that [corpse] with ghee, it should be deposited while those reciting the Yama-gāthās are present;
one should bury a deceased child less than two years old in the ground after anointing it with ghee.
Singing the Yamagāthā while recollecting the Yamasūkta.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama.

Then, other than that child who has not yet reached two years of age, when another who has completed two years dies, he [the deceased] should be carried as far as the cremation ground by the kinsmen—the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*—preceded by the eldest.
(Note: I follow Seltur; the compound is the only grammatically correct reading.)
[He is] to be followed; *anuvrajya* means "to be pursued.
From this very statement, it is understood that following one who is less than two years old is not mandatory.
And having followed him who has departed... (*pareyivāṃsam*, RV 10.14.1).
Reciting such hymns as the *Yamasūkta* and verses dedicated to Yama as deities, he should be cremated with a worldly, unconsecrated fire if a fire-drill (*araṇi*) has not been produced;
however, if one exists, he should be cremated with fire produced by churning that drill, and not with a worldly fire.

Because its production is solely for the purpose of performing rites accomplished by fire, one should employ a worldly fire that is distinct from those of outcasts and the like; for it is said: "The fire of an outcast, the fire of impurity, and the fire of a woman who has recently given birth [must never be used]."
The fire from which one has fallen [by neglecting the daily rites] and the funeral pyre fire are not fit to be accepted by the learned.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Devala. And Laugākṣi has stated a specific rule regarding this:
"One should perform the water-libation silently, and likewise the funeral rite (saṃskāra) silently."
"For all those whose tonsure has been performed, [the offering of fire and water] is required, except by choice in other cases.
This is the meaning:
immediately after the time of the *caula* rite, the offering of fire and water must be performed as a rule.

Elsewhere as well, after the naming ceremony— even for one whose tonsure has not yet been performed— one may, by choice and out of a desire for the deceased's welfare, perform the two rites consisting of the offering of fire and water silently; however, this is not mandatory, and thus there is an option.
Manu has also shown a specific rule in this regard:
"The water-rite should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it for one whose teeth have emerged, or once a name has been given" (MDh 5.70).
The mention of "water" (udaka) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the ritual of fire (*agni-saṃskāra*) as well, due to their association;
this is because of the statement that [this applies] only to those who have not reached the age of three years.

Furthermore, even if the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) is performed later than usual in consideration of family custom, the rule regarding the offering of water, fire, and so forth remains fixed after the third year.

This is understood from the statement of Laugākṣi: it must be discerned that for one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed, even before the completion of three years, there is a restrictive rule regarding those two [funeral rites].

If he is *upeta*, that is, if he is initiated (*upanīta*), then he should be cremated with the very fire of the household, according to the procedure for cremation prescribed for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) as established in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and other texts;
this is "purposeful," meaning it serves a specific objective.
The meaning is this:

if for this [fire] there exists a possible purpose in the form of an effect, such as the selection of ground, sprinkling, and so forth, which serves as the means for its burning, then that [purpose] is to be adopted.
Furthermore, those [rites] such as the preparation of the sacrificial vessels whose purpose has been lost are discontinued.

Likewise, because their purpose has been superseded by the injunction for cremation with the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*)— as opposed to the consecrated fires (*āhitāgni*)— there is also the discontinuation of the *āhavanīya* and other such fires which were brought forward according to the rules for worldly fires.
And the rule regarding other fires has been stated by Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:
"A person who has maintained the sacred fires (Āhitāgni) should be cremated according to the rule with the three fires;
one who has not maintained the sacred fires (Anāhitāgni) with one [fire], and any other person with a common (laukika) fire."
Furthermore, a Śūdra must not perform the task of bringing firewood, fuel, and so forth to the cremation ground;
for he whose Śūdra brings the fire, the grass, the wood,
and the sacrificial offerings shall remain eternally in the state of a ghost, and he too becomes defiled by unrighteousness.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama.

Likewise, the cremation should be performed immediately after the ritual bathing, because of the traditional legal text (smṛti): "One should cremate the deceased after he has been bathed with auspicious fragrances and adorned with garlands."
Pracetas has also said:
"The sons and others should perform the bathing of the deceased as well as the worship with garments and other offerings;
one must never burn the body naked, and one should not abandon anything that ought to be given."
The meaning is that one should give away and discard a portion of the shroud as "something to be given" for the sake of those who dwell in the cremation ground.
Likewise, Manu has shown a specific rule regarding the removal of a corpse:
"One should not have a dead Brahmin carried away by a Śūdra while his own kinsmen are present."
"For that oblation would not lead to heaven, being defiled by contact with a Śūdra" (MDh 5.104).
And here, the phrase "while his own [kinsmen] are present" is not intended to be emphasized,
because of the scriptural mention of defects such as the failure to attain heaven.
"One should carry out a deceased Śūdra by the southern gate;
however, the twice-born [castes] should be carried out by the western, northern, and eastern gates respectively.
Likewise, Hārīta also states: "They should not carry the corpse facing toward the village."
But when the body of one who has died while abroad cannot be found, then one should perform the funeral rites after fashioning a substitute image from bones;
or, if even those are unavailable, after fashioning a substitute image from leaf-shafts (*parṇaśara*) according to the procedure taught in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of Śaunaka and others.
And in this case, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for ten days and so forth.

For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die while away from home, the period of impurity is the same as for a corpse after performing the cremation rites again. (VaDh 4.37)

But one who has not maintained the sacred fires shall be cremated with well-ground [grains] mixed with water by his kinsmen using fire, while they say: "He, for the sake of the heavenly world, svāhā! and this for three nights.
Having thus burned the leaf-weapon, one shall remain impure for three nights.
Because of this statement, the meaning is as follows:
prior to the naming ceremony, there is only burial, and not the offering of water and so forth.
Thereafter, for up to three years, the offering of fire and water is optional;
beyond that, until the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the offering of fire and water is performed silently.
It is certain that for one who has undergone the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), even before three years have passed,

the cremation should be performed according to the ritual procedure for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) once the initiation (*upanayana*) has taken place; thereafter, the entire post-mortem rite (*aurdhvadehika*) must be performed.
But this is the distinction:
for one who has been initiated, cremation must be performed with a worldly fire.
For one who has not maintained the sacred fires, cremation with the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni) and the joining of the ritual vessels (pātrayojana) should be performed as far as possible. 3.1, 3.2.
Regarding what should be done after the funeral rites (saṃskāra), he says:

"On the seventh or even the tenth day, the relatives approach the water facing the direction of the ancestors (the north), reciting: 'May the sin burn away from us with this [water]' (RV 10.9.8). (YDh 3.3)

Within seven days, or at the latest by the tenth day, the kinsmen— those of the same lineage (*samānagotra*), those who share the funeral cake (*sapiṇḍa*), and those connected by water (*samānodaka*)—
pour water toward the south while reciting the mantra: "May the evil be cleansed away from us" (*apa naḥ śośucad agham*, RV 1.97.1–8).
By the act of formal acceptance (*abhyupagamanena*), that acceptance which is distinguished by the offering of water— which serves as its purpose—
is indicated; for immediately thereafter, in the case of maternal grandfathers and teachers, there is seen an extension (*atideśa*) of the offering of water.
And this should be performed on odd lunar days, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "The water-rite [is performed] on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth [days]" (GDh 14.40).
And this should be performed immediately after the ritual bath, because of the traditional teaching of Śātātapa: "Having cast the body into the fire, they enter the water without looking back.
Likewise, a specific detail has been shown here by Pracetas as well:

The relatives of the deceased, having entered the water in order of seniority, should not splash it about, but should pour it out at the edge of the water; wearing their sacrificial threads and garments over the right shoulder (apassavya), facing south for a Brāhmaṇa, facing north for a Kṣatriya, and facing west for a Vaiśya.
However, in another Smṛti, it is stated that the offering of water should be repeated for as many days as there are days of impurity.
As Viṣṇu has said:
"For as long as the period of impurity lasts, so long should they offer water and rice-balls for the deceased" (ViDh 19.13).
And likewise it has been stated by Pracetas:
"Day after day, one should offer full handfuls of water for the sake of the deceased;
the increase [of offerings] should be performed until the final rice-ball (piṇḍa) is completed."

The meaning is that every day the number of *añjali*s (handfuls) must be increased until the tenth *piṇḍa* is completed. Although the purpose of the scripture is accomplished by performing either of these two procedures—the heavy or the light—nevertheless, since it is impossible for one to engage in the heavier procedure because it entails great hardship, it should be inferred that this will result in a superior benefit for the deceased; otherwise, [the practice would be futile].
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of the traditional teaching of the more weighty ritual manuals being rendered meaningless.
Vasiṣṭha also has stated a specific rule:
"They should perform the water-rite with both hands, the left and the right" (VaDh 4.12). 3.3.

He states the extension [of the rule] to maternal grandfathers and others who do not belong to the same lineage (gotra), regarding the offering of water characterized by the qualities of name, lineage, and so forth, as will be described in the "single sprinkling" (sakṛt-praseka):
"In this manner, the water-rite for deceased maternal grandfathers and teachers [is performed]."
Water for the deceased should be offered to lovers, to those given by a friend, to a sister’s son, to a father-in-law, and to officiating priests.

Just as water is offered for the deceased who are of the same lineage (sagotra) or sapinda relationship, so too must the perpetual rite of water-offering be performed for deceased maternal grandfathers and teachers.
A friend is a companion; a given [relative] refers to a daughter, sister, or others who have been bestowed in marriage; a *svastrīya* is a sister’s son (*bhāgineya*).
The father-in-law is well-known;

the officiating priests are the *ṛtvijas*. For these deceased persons, such as friends and others, the offering of water according to one's desire (*kāmodaka*) should be performed. "Desire" (*kāma*) means wish.

Regarding "kāmodakam" (water given out of desire): this means that water should be offered when there is a desire for the prosperity of the deceased ancestors, but it need not be offered when such a desire is absent; thus, the meaning is that there is no transgression in failing to perform it [in the latter case]. 3.4.
He states the rule regarding the merit of the water offering:
"Restraining their speech, they should pour water once, [pronouncing] the name and lineage. (YDh 3.5ab) And that water offering is to be performed in this manner.

The sapindas and the samānodakas, having become silent, should pronounce the name and lineage of the deceased and pour water once— or thrice— saying, "May the deceased named so-and-so of such-and-such a lineage be satisfied," for they should perform the pouring three times according to the traditional teaching of Pracetas: "May the deceased be satisfied."
The daily increase of the *añjali* measure has indeed already been established;
likewise, this specific detail was also stated by that same [author]:
"Then, having gone to the riverbank and performed purification according to the rule..."
One should first thoroughly clean one's garment, and thereafter perform the ritual bath.
Then, having bathed with his clothes on, being pure and with a restrained mind,
he should take a stone and offer ten handfuls of water to the brahmins.
One should give twelve [mouthfuls] to a Kṣatriya; for a Vaiśya, fifteen are prescribed;
thirty should be given to a Śūdra. Then one should enter the house.
Thereafter, bathing must be performed again, and one should cause the purification of the house to be carried out. Thus it is said.
Among the sapindas, he states the prohibition of offering water for certain individuals:
"Students and likewise those who are outcastes (patita) shall not perform the water-rite.

Even though they possess the status of kinsmen, students [are excluded] until their formal return home (samāvartana), and outcastes are those who have fallen away from the entitlement to the rites of the twice-born.
They should not perform the offering of water and other rites.
However, after the period of celibacy has passed, one must indeed perform the offering of water and the observance of impurity for the sapinda relatives and others who died previously.
As Manu said:
"One who has been initiated [for a vow] shall not offer water libations until the completion of the vow;
but when it is completed, having offered the water libation, he shall remain impure for three nights. (MDh 5.88)

The term *brahmacārī* refers to one who has been given an injunction (*ādiṣṭī*). Because he is joined with the assignment of vows (*vratādeśa*) such as, "Eat this water, perform your duties, do not sleep during the day" (ĀśGṛ 1.22.2), he is called a *brahmacārī*.
And he will state that this [prohibition] applies to those other than the father and so forth, in the passage:

"the teacher, the father, and the preceptor" (YDh 3.15). Furthermore, the teacher here holds this view: the term *ādiṣṭī* refers to one who has commenced a penance; it is for such a person alone that this prohibition of offering water and so forth applies, because his vow constitutes a form of penance (*prāyaścitta*).
The rule for the offering of water and the period of impurity follows after the conclusion [of the funeral rites]. Likewise, the duty of offering water is prohibited for eunuchs and others;
"eunuchs and the like, thieves, those who have not undergone initiation (vrātyas), and those who act contrary to dharma shall not offer water."
Women who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor, [are likewise excluded].
Thus, from the recollection of Vṛddha Manu. (3.5)
Having thus stated the prohibition regarding specific types of donors in the offering of water, he now states the prohibition based on specific types of recipients:

"Heretics, those who have not taken refuge [in the Triple Gem], thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who commit adultery, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide—these are not entitled to the impurity rites or the offering of water. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.6)
"Pākhaṇḍa" refers to the wearing of sectarian marks outside of the Vedic tradition, such as human skulls and the like;
those who possess these are "pākhaṇḍins. "Anāśritas" are those who, despite being eligible for religious duties, have not undertaken any specific stage of life (āśrama).

Thieves are those who steal superior goods such as gold and the like; "slayers of their husbands" are those who harbor malice toward them; and "those who go according to their lust" are unchaste women.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," those who kill their own embryos or Brahmins are included.
"Drinkers of spirituous liquor" refers to those for whom the drinking of a particular type of liquor is prohibited, yet they are addicted to its consumption.
"Those who abandon themselves" refers to those who [seek death] by means of poison, fire, water, hanging, and so forth.
Those who abandon their own selves—

such as heretics and the like— are not entitled to the impurity prescribed for three nights or ten nights (as will be stated in YDh 3.18), nor to the funeral rites such as the offering of water and other post-mortem ceremonies.
Those who "divide" (bhājayanti) are called "dividers" (bhājanāḥ); they do not become the cause for impurity (āśauca) and so forth for their *sapiṇḍa* relatives and others.
Therefore, upon their death, by the *sapiṇḍas*...
This statement is intended to establish that acts such as the offering of water and so forth should not be performed;
and in this context, the gender [of the word] in expressions such as "surāpī" (wine-drinker) is not intended to be significant.

number, location, time, and this fruit of the action—
those skilled in Mīmāṃsā declare these to be the pentad of non-essential factors (anupādeya).
This is because it pertains to what is not to be adopted.
And this refers to the domain of intentional action,
as Gautama said:

"Generally, for those who desire [to die], [death occurs] by fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice]" (GDh 14.12). "Prāya" refers to the Great Journey (mahāprasthāna);
"anāśaka" refers to fasting (anaśana).
"Throwing oneself from a mountain peak" means falling down.
Here, because of the inclusion of the qualification "if they so desire," it should be understood that there is no fault in an act committed through negligence;
for instance, if someone were to die through negligence by means of fire, water, or the like.
Impurity must be observed for her, and the water-libation rites must be performed.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Aṅgiras.
Likewise, there is a prohibition against impurity and other rites even in the case of specific types of death:
"Death at the hands of a Cāṇḍāla, by water, by a snake, by a Brāhmaṇa, by lightning, or from fanged animals or beasts, [is the lot] of evildoers."
Whatever water and offerings of rice balls are given to the departed spirits, none of that remains; it perishes in mid-air.

Thus, this [text] also concerns suicide preceded by intention, because Gautama’s statement establishes that impurity and other restrictions are prohibited only for one who has intentionally killed oneself with water;
and here too, because of the observation of its association with "from a Caṇḍāla, from water, or from a snake," it is certain that the subject matter concerns intentional acts.

Therefore, for one who goes out with pride or the like to kill Caṇḍālas and others, and is killed by them, this prohibition of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth— based on the transgression of the injunction "one should protect oneself from all [harm]"—
applies. Likewise, it applies to one who goes forward with pride for the purpose of seizing wicked fanged beasts and the like.
It should be understood that this prohibition applies even in the case of death.
Furthermore, this prohibition regarding impurity (*āśauca*) pertains to that which is delimited by periods such as ten days, as stated:
"For those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for suicides, [impurity ceases] immediately" (YDh 3.21).
Thus, since immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) will be described [later],
likewise, cremation and other rites should not be performed for them; there is no impurity, no water libation, no shedding of tears, nor any funeral rites such as cremation.
And one should not perform the carrying of the funeral bier for those who have been struck down by the *brahmadaṇḍa* (the curse of a Brahmin).
This is because of the traditional teaching of Yama. "Slain by the staff of Brahmā" means slain by the staff of a Brāhmaṇa.
The word *kaṭa* refers to items such as a cot (*khaṭvā*) used as a means for carrying a corpse.

One should not suspect that this Smṛti prohibition of cremation and so forth does not apply to an *āhitāgni* (one who has maintained the sacred fires) killed by a Brahmin or similar causes, on the grounds that it would result in the omission of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fires and sacrificial vessels prescribed by Śruti— namely, "They burn the *āhitāgni* with his fires and his sacrificial vessels.
For in another Smṛti, a different method of disposal is ordained for the fires and sacrificial vessels belonging to an *āhitāgni* killed by a Caṇḍāla or others.
"One should cast the *vaitāna* fire into the water and the *āvasathya* fire at a crossroads;
however, one should burn the sacrificial vessels in the fire if the sacrificer has died an untimely death.
Likewise, another method for the disposal of his body is also stated:
For those who have abandoned their own lives and likewise for those who have fallen [from their caste], there is no [prescribed] ritual act;
yet even for them, immersion in the waters of the Gaṅgā is beneficial.
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa),
there is therefore a prohibition against burning [the body] and so forth for all [deceased persons] without distinction.
Consequently, when one transgresses this prohibition out of affection or other such motives, an expiation (prāyaścitta) is required.
Having performed the cremation, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance after having carried out the fire, water, bathing, touching, carrying, conversation,
the cutting of the ropes, and the shedding of tears.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
And this should be understood to apply to each case when there is intentional action; however, in the case of unintentional action, [the following applies]:
Whoever carries or cremates any one of these deceased persons,
having performed the rites of the funeral mat and the water libation, shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Saṃvarta: "Furthermore,
if that corpse is merely touched, or if a tear is shed [upon it],
and if one has not performed the previously mentioned rites, there shall be a fast for one night."

Thus, fasting has been prescribed for touching [a corpse] or shedding tears. For one who is unable to perform the *kṛcchra* penances, Sumantu has stated that one should subsist on alms for a month and perform the three daily ablutions; this subsistence on alms is likewise intended only for the incapable. In this same manner, other Smṛti passages concerning those same subjects should be properly applied according to the individual's capacity.
Furthermore, this prohibition of cremation and other rites refers to those other than aged forest-dwellers and others who are incapable of performing obligatory duties (*nityakarman*),
since permission for them is observed [in scripture]:
"An old man whose mindfulness of purity has failed and whose medical treatment has been abandoned..."
He who would cause his own death by means of a precipice, fire, fasting, or water—
For him, the period of impurity lasts three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones takes place;
on the third day, having offered water, one should perform the Śrāddha on the fourth day.

Thus, according to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), when self-slaughter is permitted by the scriptures under specific conditions (*upādhi*), and the performance of funeral rites (*śrāddha*) and other post-mortem ceremonies (*aurdhvadehika*) are prohibited for those who have committed suicide by any such means, there arises the inquiry: "What, then, should be done for them? In response to this expectation, Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya and Chāgaleya have stated:
"Out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇabalih;
thus shall their purification come to pass, and not otherwise—so said Yama.
Therefore, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given even to them. Thus [it is stated].
Vyāsa has also said:
"Whatever is offered with intent for Nārāyaṇa or Śiva, that act shall be purifying; it cannot be otherwise."

Thus, the Nārāyaṇabali produces the fitness for the deceased to become a recipient of the śrāddha and other rites by means of effecting their purification; therefore, all post-mortem (aurdhvadehika) ceremonies must indeed be performed.
For this very reason, the permission for the aurdhvadehika rites is also seen in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
"And for those killed by cows or Brahmins, as well as for those who have fallen [from their caste],
one should perform all the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) after a year has passed.
Thus, having performed the Nārāyaṇabali exactly after a year, the funeral rites should be carried out.
The Nārāyaṇabali should be performed in this manner:

on a certain eleventh day of the bright fortnight, having duly worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, one should place near them ten rice-balls mixed with sesame seeds and soaked in honey and ghee, representing the form of Viṣṇu.

Recalling the deceased and pronouncing his name and lineage, he should face south and, having offered [the oblation] upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, having honored it with perfumes and other offerings, and having performed the rites up to the offering of the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa-pravāhaṇa*), he should cast it into a river; he should not give it to the wife or others.
Then, on that very night, having invited an odd number of Brahmins and observed a fast, at noon on the following day, he should perform the worship of Viṣṇu.

Having performed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite according to the prescribed rules—from the washing of the Brahmins' feet up to the inquiry regarding their satisfaction—and having silently performed the sequence from the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*) to the sprinkling of water (*avanejana*) as in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, he should offer four *piṇḍas* to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, and Yama along with their retinues.
Then, recollecting the deceased by mentioning his name and lineage, and chanting the name of Viṣṇu, he should offer the fifth *piṇḍa*. Thereafter...

Having gratified the Brahmins who have sipped water with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and having especially gratified one among them who is most virtuous by giving cows, land, gold, and so forth while remembering him as the deceased (preta), he should then, after the Brahmins— whose hands hold sacred grass (pavitra)— have caused water mixed with sesame seeds and other items to be offered to the deceased, eat together with his kinsmen.
But in the case of one killed by a snake, there is this distinction:

for the duration of a year, having performed the worship of the Nāgas on the fifth lunar day according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas, and having performed the Nārāyaṇa-bali at the completion of the year, one should give a golden Nāga and a living cow.
Thereafter, one should perform all the funeral rites for the deceased.
And the nature of the Nārāyaṇa-bali is declared in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa] as follows:
"Having reached the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight,
one should worship the god Viṣṇu as well as Yama Vaivasvata."
Restrained and facing south, one should indeed offer ten balls of food anointed with ghee, mixed with sesame seeds, upon blades of darbha grass while reciting the names of the Manus.
Having invoked Viṣṇu in one's mind, one should then cast [the offering] into the river water;
therein, one should perform the recitation of the name and lineage, as well as worship with flowers.
One should offer incense, lamps, and various kinds of food, both solid and soft; one should indeed invite five, seven, or even nine Brahmins.
When another day had arrived, having fasted and being composed, he [approached] those who were endowed with knowledge and austerity, born of noble lineage, and concentrated in mind, at midday.
Having performed the worship of Viṣṇu, he should seat those Brahmins facing north, according to seniority, while recollecting them as being of the nature of the ancestors.
Having fixed the mind on Viṣṇu, one should indeed perform everything without weariness;
whatever has been prescribed beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, one should perform that preceded by the deity.
Then, having ascertained that the Brahmins were satisfied and having asked them about their satisfaction according to the prescribed rule,
[he should offer] sacrificial food (haviṣya) with its side-dishes, accompanied by sesame seeds and other ingredients.
One should offer five morsels of food while recollecting the forms of the gods;
one should first give to Viṣṇu, and then to Brahmā and Śiva.

One should offer the fourth ball of rice to Yama along with his attendants, having mentally mentioned the deceased by name preceded by their lineage (gotra). After this, [the following should be done].
Having thus uttered the name of Viṣṇu, one should cast the fifth [offering] as before;
then, having caused the Brahmins to sip water according to the rule, one should honor them with sacrificial fees.
One should honor a most venerable Brahmin with gold,
a cow, a garment, and land, while mentally recollecting that deceased person.
Then the Brahmins, with *darbha* grass in their hands, should scatter sesame-water while keeping the name preceded by the *gotra* in mind.
With a concentrated mind, they should offer him oblations of fragrant sesame seeds and water;
thereafter, restraining his speech, he should eat together with his friends and servants.
Thus, standing in accordance with the doctrine of Viṣṇu, whoever gives [the gift] to one who has committed suicide quickly rescues that person; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Regarding the occasion of being bitten by a snake, Sumantu has declared in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* that the gift of a golden serpent serves as a remedy:
"Having fashioned a serpent out of a *bhāra* of gold, and likewise a cow, and having given them to Vyāsa according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain freedom from debt to one's father. (3.6)
Having thus stated the offering of water along with its prohibitions, [the author] next states what should be done thereafter:
"When they have finished the water-rite, emerged from the water, and are standing upon soft grass, once they have bathed, one should address them with ancient historical narratives. (YDh 3.7)

To those sons and others who have performed the water-libation (*kṛtodaka*), who have bathed, and who have properly emerged from the water and are standing firmly upon a soft grassy plot of ground covered with a fresh growth of young shoots, the family elders should console them— meaning they should awaken them— with words capable of dispelling grief, using ancient historical narratives (*itihāsa*) which are about to be described. // 7 //
He describes the nature of history (itihāsa), which is capable of dispelling sorrow:
"He who seeks the essence in human existence—which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble of water—is utterly deluded. (YDh 3.8)
By the word "human" (manuṣya), the fourfold class of beings—those born from a womb, from an egg, and so forth—is indicated; the state of being that is "humanity.

In this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is characterized by wandering like the trunk of a plantain tree and is devoid of internal essence, perishing as quickly as a bubble of water, he who seeks—that is, searches for—a stable essence is utterly deluded, his mind completely ruined.
Therefore, you who understand the true nature of saṃsāra should not act in this manner. (3.8)
Moreover:
If this body, which was composed of the five elements, has returned to the state of the five elements due to the actions arising from its own body, what cause is there for lamentation? (YDh 3.9)

If this body— which was produced and fashioned in five ways as consisting of the five elements, earth and so forth, for the sake of experiencing its own fruits from the seeds of karma generated by one's own bodies in other births— has returned to the state of the five [elements] upon the cessation of the experience of those fruits and has once again attained the nature of earth and the rest, what purpose does your lamentation serve in that regard?
Because it serves no purpose,
one should not grieve;
for such is the nature of reality.
For no one is able to transcend the established nature of reality. (3.9)
Moreover:
The earth, which supports all things, goes to destruction; so do the oceans and the gods.
How then will the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction? (YDh 3.10)
Death is not a marvel,
since even the great elements such as earth and the rest undergo destruction;
likewise, even the oceans are not exempt from old age and death.
Even the immortals reach their end at the time of universal dissolution;
how then could the multitude of beings, subject to death and as unstable as foam, not go to destruction? For it is indeed fitting that those whose nature is mortal should depart.
Therefore, the onset of grief is purposeless. 3.10.
He states that one should not indulge in lamentation even because it leads to undesirable consequences:

"Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, therefore one should not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability. (YDh 3.11)

Since the deceased, being powerless and even against his will, must consume the phlegm and tears shed from the faces and eyes by the mourning relatives, therefore one should not weep; rather, those desiring the welfare of the deceased should perform the *śrāddha* and other rites according to their own capacity. (3.11)
Having heard this, they should go home preceded by children;
having chewed neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water, they should touch fire and other elements, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds.
Having touched [the ground] and having placed their feet slowly upon a stone, they should enter.

Thus, having properly heard the words of the elders of the family, having abandoned their grief, and having placed the children in front, they should go to the house. Having arrived and standing at the door of the dwelling, being self-controlled and with restrained minds, they should chew nimba leaves.
Having bitten [the food] with their teeth, having eaten it, and having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), they should touch fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds;

and because of the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the statement of Śaṅkha—"dūrvā sprouts, fire, or a bull"—they should also touch dūrvā shoots and a bull, and placing their foot upon a stone, they should slowly enter the house without stumbling. (3.12–3.13)
He states an extension [of the rule]:
"Even for those who touch the deceased during the rites of entry and so forth, if they so desire, purification occurs instantly; for others, it results from bathing and self-restraint. (YDh 3.14)

This aforementioned ritual, beginning with the biting of neem leaves and ending with the entry into the house, applies not only to one's own kinsmen but also to others who, for the sake of dharma, perform the decoration and removal of the deceased and so forth;
such as the entry [into the village] and other rites.

In this context, the word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to indicate a reverse order because it is inauspicious. Furthermore, for those who are not *sapiṇḍas* and who have engaged in carrying [the corpse] or similar acts for the sake of dharma, desiring purification at that very moment, purification occurs through bathing and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) alone.
As Parāśara said:
"Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain, step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in successive order."
"For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin; for them, purification is ordained immediately by immersion in water. (PSm 3.39–40).
However, regarding the carrying out of the funeral rites out of affection or other motives, there is a specific rule stated by Manu.

Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda relative, as if he were a kinsman, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights; the same applies for the maternal relatives of his mother.
"If one eats their food, one is purified in ten days; if one does not eat their food, one is purified in a single day, provided one does not dwell in that house. (MDh 5.101–02).
Herein lies the established rule:
He who, out of affection or other motives, performs the removal of the corpse and eats that person's food and dwells in his house,
attains purification after ten days alone;
whereas he who merely dwells in that house but does not eat that food [attains purification after three days].
For one who eats [the food] of such a person, the impurity lasts for three nights;
however, for one who merely performs the removal of the corpse, but does not dwell in that house nor eat that food, it lasts for one day.
This refers to cases involving those of the same class;
however, regarding those of a different class, one must observe the period of impurity prescribed for the specific class of the deceased whom one carries out.

As Gautama said: "If a lower caste person touches a higher caste person, or a higher caste person touches a lower one, the impurity in that case is declared to be the same as that prescribed for a corpse" (GDh 14.29).
Here, *upasparśana* means carrying out [the corpse].
For a Brāhmaṇa who carries out a Śūdra, there is impurity for one month; for a Śūdra, [the same applies].
But regarding the removal of the corpse, the meaning is that the impurity should be observed for ten nights, just as in the case of a dead body. (3.14)
He says in response to the religious student (brahmacārin):
"Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or preceptor, the one observing the vow remains a practitioner of the vow;
he should not eat food from a difficult situation, nor should he dwell together with them. (YDh 3.15)

The teacher (ācārya) is one whose characteristics have been described; "parents" refers to the mother and father; and the "sub-teacher" (upādhyāya) is the one previously mentioned. Even after carrying out the funeral rites for these, the student remains a *vratī*, that is, a religious student (*brahmacārī*), and there is no lapse of his vow.
By the word *kaṭa*, impurity (*aśauca*) is indicated.

A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) shall not eat food that has been cooked in the same vessel as that [impure substance], nor shall he dwell together with those who are impure due to death. By stating this, it follows by implication that there is a violation of the vow for a student when he carries out the funeral procession of a deceased person other than his teacher or similar superiors.
This is what is meant.

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha has stated: "For a student who performs the funeral rites for [his own] parents, there is a cessation of his vows, except in the case of [the death of] his mother and father" (VaDh 23.7–8). 3.15.
He states the specific rules for those in a state of impurity: "They shall eat what is purchased or obtained and sleep separately on the ground;
food should be offered to the deceased for three days according to the procedure of the Piṇḍayajña. (YDh 3.16)
Those for whom food is obtained either by purchase or by being asked for are "those whose food is purchased or obtained"; the word "should be" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence],
because of the rule regarding food obtained by purchase or acquisition.
In the absence of that [food], fasting becomes established by implication.

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states: "Having gone to their houses, they should remain for three days without eating on a bed of grass spread on the ground, subsisting on what is purchased or obtained [by others]. A *adhaḥprastara* is a mat made of grass intended for the sleeping and seating of those observing impurity.
And those sapindas should sleep separately on the ground itself, not on beds or similar furniture;
a specific rule regarding this has also been shown by Manu.

"They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves [in water] for three days, they should not consume meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground" (MDh 5.73).
Likewise, a specific rule was stated by Gautama as well: "Those performing the funeral rites for a corpse must sleep on the ground, remain celibate, and observe the vow of chastity" (GDh 14.37).

Likewise, according to the procedure of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, characterized by wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīti) and so forth, food in the form of rice-balls (piṇḍa) should be offered silently upon the ground for the deceased for three days.
As Marīci has said:
Having bathed and with a restrained mind, one should prepare the *caru* oblation in the northeast and offer the *piṇḍa* for the *pretas* outside, devoid of *darbha* grass and mantras.
Thus [it is said].

The exclusion of *darbha* grass and mantras applies to those who have not been initiated (*anupanīta*), because of the traditional teaching of Pracetas: "One should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) on the ground for those who are uninitiated, but on *kuśa* grass for those who are initiated."
Likewise, the restriction regarding the performer is to be understood from the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Whether he be of a different lineage (*asagotra*) or of the same lineage (*sagotra*), whether a woman or a man—
whoever offers [the water] on the first day, he shall complete it for ten days."
Likewise, the restriction regarding the material has been shown by Śunaḥpuccha:
"Whether with rice, or with barley-meal, or even with vegetables,
whatever material is used on the first day, that same material shall be used for the ten-day period."
"One should silently offer the mouthful of water, flowers, a lamp, and likewise incense.

And the funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be offered upon a stone, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "They should offer the garland, the funeral ball, and the water either on the ground or upon a stone."
One should not infer from the plural verb "they should give" that the offering of the *piṇḍas* must be performed by all [relatives] together, as is the case with the offering of water;

rather, it must be performed by the son alone. In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, and the disciples should offer them; in their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). (GDh 15.13–14)
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama:
"When there are many sons, however, it must be performed by the eldest alone; for whatever has been done by the eldest alone, after having obtained the consent of all," [is valid].
And by means of property that has not been divided, it would be as if it were performed by all [the heirs] together.
Thus it is from the *Marīci-smṛti*;
and the rule regarding the number of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is as follows: ten rice-balls for a Brāhmaṇa, and twelve indeed for a Kṣatriya.

Thus, the number of days for impurity has been declared by Viṣṇu: "As long as the period of impurity lasts, they shall offer water and one funeral cake for the deceased" (ViDh 19.7). Likewise, in another Smṛti:
With a concentrated mind, one should offer nine funeral cakes over nine days;
having offered the tenth cake, one shall become pure at the end of the night.
This statement regarding purity is intended for the purpose of inviting Brahmins for the *śrāddha* to be performed on the following day;
however, the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) has prescribed the offering of three *piṇḍas*.
Regarding these two options—the more elaborate and the simpler—the established rule concerning the offering of water has been stated.
This is how it should be understood. Here, there is another specific rule from Śātātapa:
"Even when the period of impurity is shortened, one should nevertheless offer exactly ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Furthermore, Pāraskara has shown a specific rule regarding those for whom the impurity lasts three nights:
On the first day, three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered by those who are composed;
on the second day, one should offer four, as well as the collection of the bones.
"But on the third day, one should give three [gifts] such as clothing and so forth; likewise, one should wash them. (3.16)
Furthermore:

"Water and milk should be placed for one day in the open air in earthen vessels" (YDh 3.17ab). Water and milk must each be kept separately for one day in two earthen vessels, suspended in the open air on a swing or similar support.
Since no specific distinction is mentioned here, the rite should be performed on the first day;
likewise, according to the statement of Pāraskara: "Having set out water with the words, 'O deceased one, bathe here,' and milk with the words, 'Drink this.'"
Likewise, the collection of the bones should be performed on the first day and so forth.
Thus says Saṃvarta:
"On the first day, or the third, or likewise the seventh or the ninth."
"The collection of bones should be performed on that day together with those belonging to his lineage.

In some places, however, it is stated that the collection of bones occurs on the second day. But in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], it says: "On the fourth day, one should perform the collection of bones, and their casting into the waters of the Gaṅgā" (ViDh 19.10–11).
Therefore, on one of those days, the collection of the bones (asthisaṃcayana) should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
A specific rule regarding this has been shown by Aṅgiras:
"In the collection of the bones, a sacrifice to the gods is proclaimed."
If one who is pure does not perform the sacrifice to the deities intended for that deceased person,
then the deities curse him.
And here, the deities dwelling in the cremation ground are those previously mentioned;
the gods residing in the cremation ground are proclaimed to be the guardians of the corpses.
Thus it was said by him [the Lord].

Therefore, it is stated that one should perform worship there for those gods and for the deceased who has recently passed away, using incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as food in the form of ritual balls (piṇḍa).
Likewise, the shaving of the hair should be performed on the tenth day;
when the tenth day has arrived, the bath shall take place outside the village,
and there the garments, as well as the hair, beard, and nails, are to be discarded.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Devala.
Likewise, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"On the second day, the rite of shaving (kṣurakarma) should be performed with diligence;
or on the third, the fifth, or even the seventh day, provided the offerings have been made."
The phrase "until the offering of the *śrāddha*" means that there is no fixed rule [regarding shaving] prior to that point.
Furthermore, when the question arises as to whose hair should be shaved, Āpastamba has stated:
"And there is the shaving of those who follow [the deceased]" (*anubhāvināṃ ca parivāpanam*, ĀpDh 1.10.6).
The meaning is as follows:

"experiencers" (*anubhāvinaḥ*) are those sapindas who experience the suffering of a corpse; and when there arises the expectation—whether shaving applies to them without distinction, or only to those of young age—this very rule presents itself: "and for the experiencers, there is the shaving."
They are called *anubhāvinaḥ* because they come after [the parents]; they are those of tender age, and their shaving [of the head] is what is meant.
Some, however, consider that the *anubhāvinaḥ* are the sons.

Shaving the head is prescribed in seven instances: at the Gaṅgā, in the field of Bhāskara, upon the death of one's mother, father, or guru, at the time of the *ādhāna* rite, and during the *Soma* sacrifice.
Thus, because of the observation of such a rule.
Since it might follow that all eligibility for rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti ceases due to impurity, he says the following for the purpose of permitting certain acts:
"The Vaitāna and Aupāsana rites and ceremonies must be performed because of the injunctions of the Śruti" (YDh 3.17cd).

*Vitāna* is the expansion of the sacred fires; those rites occurring therein are *vaitāna*, such as the Agnihotra, Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, and others, which are accomplished by means of the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*).
Ritual acts (*kriyā*) are being described:

that which is attended to daily is called *aupāsana*, referring to the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*); the ritual acts performed therein, namely the evening and morning oblations (*sāyaṃprātar-homa*), are called *aupāsanāḥ*.
These Vedic rituals, both those pertaining to the sacrificial fires (*vaitāna*) and the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), are to be performed.
If it is asked how these possess the status of being Vedic,
it is because they are enjoined by the Śruti.
For instance, the injunction of the Agnihotra and other rites is quite explicit in such Śruti passages as, "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," and so forth.
Likewise, the Śruti prescribes the *aupāsana* oblation as well, stating: "Day after day one should offer the *svāhā*, even in the absence of food, [using] anything up to wood.
And here, because of the inclusion of the qualification "Vedic" (*śrauta*), it is understood that the performance of Smārta rites such as giving gifts and so forth is not required.
For this very reason, it was stated by Vaiyāghrapāda:
"In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), there is no abandonment of Smārta rites except for the eclipse of Rāhu;
however, regarding Śrauta rites, one attains purity by bathing at that specific time."

Thus, the statement that Śrauta rites are to be performed is intended with reference to obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. As Paiṭhīnasi says: "Obligatory rites may be omitted, except for those pertaining to the Vaitāna fires; some say this also applies to the Śālāgni. Since there is a risk of the omission of all necessary obligatory and occasional rites due to the general statement "obligatory rites may be omitted," the phrase "except for those pertaining to the Vaitāna fires" [is added].
There is an exclusion of those necessary rites that are to be accomplished by the three sacred fires.
Furthermore, by the rule "some [say] in the domestic fire," an optional exclusion is stated even for those necessary rites performed in the domestic (gṛhya) fire;
therefore, there is impurity regarding them.
It does not exist at all. Furthermore, because there is an absence of purification (*śauca*) regarding optional rites (*kāmya*), they are not performed.
With this very intention, Manu also stated:
"One should not interrupt the rites in the sacred fires" (MDh 5.84).

"One should not interrupt the rites performed in the fires"—this implies the suspension of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and other such rites that are not accomplished by means of fire. For this very reason, Saṃvarta states:
"In that situation, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) with dry food or with fruit."
One should not perform the ritual of the five sacrifices during death or birth.
Thus,
although the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is normally accomplished by means of fire, its omission occurs due to a specific scriptural injunction,
for it has been stated by that very same authority: "A Brahmin should remain for ten days excluded from the Vaiśvadeva."

Although it is heard that the suspension of the *saṃdhyā* and other rites is prescribed during *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) by the rule, "The abandonment of rituals [is enjoined] during *sūtaka*," nevertheless, one should perform the casting of the *añjali* and so forth;
for the Smṛti of Paiṭhīnasi states: "During *sūtaka*, having cast an *añjali* with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, having circumambulated, and meditating upon the Sun, one should pay obeisance."

Although it has been stated in general that "the domestic (aupāsana) rites should be performed [by oneself]," nevertheless, they must be caused to be performed by another, because of the traditional teaching of Paiṭhīnasi: "Others should perform these.
Bṛhaspati has also stated this.
"In cases of birth-impurity or death-impurity, when unable to eat at a *śrāddha*, or due to causes such as being on a journey, one should perform the oblation (*hāvayet*) but never omit it. Likewise,

even though they belong to the *smārta* (tradition-based) category, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *śravaṇākarma*, the *āśvayujī* sacrifice, and other such obligatory fire-oblations (*nityahoma*) must certainly be performed.
When birth-impurity (sūtaka) has arisen, how should the Smārta rite be performed?
One should have the Piṇḍayajña and the Caruhoma performed by a person who does not belong to the same gotra.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Jātūkarṇya:
even though another person may act as the agent in a ritual performed in association, one should nevertheless personally perform the primary act consisting of the renunciation of one's own property.
Because that [result] cannot be accomplished by anything else;
for this very reason it has been said: "In the case of a rite prescribed in the Śruti, one who has bathed at that time shall attain purity."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "giving, receiving, burnt offerings (homa), and Vedic recitation (svādhyāya) cease," this prohibition of *homa* must be established as referring either to optional (*kāmya*) rites or to the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Likewise, one must not eat food from a house in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*); for according to the traditional law of Yama, "in both cases, the food of the family is not eaten for ten days," where "both" refers to birth and death.
"Ten days" is an indicative term for the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*).
The food belonging to a family affected by birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) must not be eaten by those who are not agnates (*asakulya*).

Furthermore, there is no fault regarding those who belong to the same lineage (*sakulya*). For Manu himself has stated: "But during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the food of the family is without fault. And this prohibition is to be understood as applying when either the giver or the eater becomes aware of a birth or a death.
If neither of the two has full knowledge [of the impurity], the birth-impurity (sūtaka) does not constitute a fault;
however, if even one of them has full knowledge, it brings about fault for the eater.
Thus, according to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*,
in marriages and similar occasions, food set aside specifically for Brahmins must indeed be eaten even before the onset of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*).

For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati: "In the case of marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interim, no fault is proclaimed regarding matters previously intended. (cf. PSm 3.38).
Furthermore, another distinction is shown in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In the case of marriages, festivals, or sacrifices, if a death-impurity (*mṛta-sūtaka*) should occur in the interim,
food should be provided by others and may be eaten by the best of the twice-born."
"But while the Brahmins are eating, if a death or birth occurs in the interval,
they are all considered pure once they have rinsed their mouths with water from another house.
Thus, even when under the influence of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), there is no fault regarding certain substances.
As Marīci has said:
"In the case of salt, honey, meat, flowers, roots, and fruits; in vegetables, wood, grass, water, curd, clarified butter, and milk."
"Regarding sesame, medicinal herbs, and skins, as well as cooked and uncooked food,

and indeed all commodities for sale— there is no impurity during death or birth [in these cases]. Here, "cooked" refers to varieties of edible food such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like, while "uncooked" refers to rice and similar grains.
"Taking by oneself" (svayaṃgraha) means that one may take [the food] oneself, having been authorized by the owner;
the permission regarding cooked and uncooked food pertains to the context of one engaged in a food-distribution festival (anna-satra).
Raw grain is not censured for those who have begun a food-distribution hall (*annaśālā*);
however, having eaten their cooked food, one should drink milk for three nights.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Aṅgiras,
the word "cooked" (pakva) refers here to boiled rice and the like, as distinct from food that is to be chewed.
Regarding impurity caused by contact with a corpse, a specific rule has been stated by Aṅgiras:
"If impurity should befall a householder through contact with someone else..."
"His ritual acts are not interrupted, nor would that [impurity] belong to those living in his household.
The meaning is this: that impurity pertains solely to the householder himself, and not to his wife and others living in his house, nor to his property.
This same point is also shown in another Smṛti regarding impurity that has already elapsed:
"If, after the ten-day period has passed, the householder later becomes aware [of the birth], his impurity lasts for three nights, but never that of the object. (3.17)
Having thus stated the duties consisting of injunctions and prohibitions for those in a state of impurity (āśauca), he now declares the cause of that impurity and the regulation of its duration:
"Impurity on account of a death (śāva) is prescribed as lasting either three nights or ten nights."
If [the child] is less than two years old, the impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs to both; however, the impurity caused by death (*śāva*) belongs to the mother alone.
Here, *śāva* refers to that which is caused by a corpse;
and by the word *sūtaka*, which denotes birth, the impurity caused by that [birth] is indicated.
By speaking in this manner, it is stated that birth and death are the causes for impurity (*āśauca*);
and that birth and death serve as the cause only when they have actually occurred and been known.

Because of the observation of such indicative marks as, "Having heard of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son when ten days have passed" (MDh 5.77), and likewise: "But he who hears that one staying in a foreign land has died within the ten-day period... [and so forth].
One shall remain impure for exactly as long as remains of that ten-night period.
This is also because of the force of the commencement of such statements as these.

For if impurity depended solely upon the occurrence [of death], then the fixed periods of impurity—such as ten days and so forth—would begin precisely from those respective points; consequently, upon hearing of the death of a relative who has not yet reached ten days, the impurity would logically consist only of the remainder of the ten-night period.
If it were established that "whatever remains of the ten-night period" [is to be observed], then there would be no commencement [of the rite].
Therefore, birth and death are indeed known to be the causal conditions;
and both of these are the causal conditions.
Even regarding impurity (*āśauca*), a period of three nights or ten nights is prescribed by Manu and others.

In this section on impurity, the mention of "days" (*ahar*) and "nights" (*rātri*) is intended as an indication of a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*). The statement "is prescribed by Manu and others" is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between the different subjects mentioned by them, namely *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*. For instance:
"Ten days' impurity on account of death is prescribed for sapindas;

(MDh 5.59) the same applies in the case of birth for those who desire complete purification. (MDh 5.61) But in the case of a birth, purification for those related by the offering of water (ekodaka) is held to occur after three nights. (MDh 5.71)"

"Those who touch a corpse are purified after three days, but those who offer water [are purified] after ten days" (MDh 5.64)— by these statements, a distinction is established between the periods of three nights and ten nights, pertaining respectively to the *samānodaka* (distant sapinda) and the *sapinda* (near sapinda).
Therefore, for *sapindas* up to the seventh generation, the period of impurity is ten nights without exception.
"For those who share the same water [for libations], it is three nights.
Furthermore, as for the statement in another Smṛti:
"In the fourth generation, there should be ten nights; in the fifth, six nights, when [the deceased] is male."
In the sixth [case], purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, it is on the very day itself.
Thus, because it is contradicted [by other authorities], it is not to be respected;
and even that which is not contradicted, it should nevertheless not be practiced because it is loathed by the world, like the slaughter of an animal as part of the *madhuparka* ritual.
For it is stated in the *Smṛti* of Manu: "One should not practice even that which is consistent with Dharma if it does not lead to heaven and is loathed by the world.

Furthermore, when a Sapiṇḍa relative is nearby—such as one within the seventh degree—the period of impurity is one day; however, for Samānodaka relatives who are more distant, such as those from the eighth degree onwards, it is different.
The phrase "for three days" is appropriate.
Thus, when impurity (āśauca) for sapinda relatives has been established without distinction, he states the following as a restrictive rule for certain cases:
"When one under two years of age has died, the impurity lasts for ten nights for both the mother and the father alone, not for all the sapinda relatives."
But for them, he will say [later]: "For one whose birth has not yet occurred, it is immediate. And likewise Paiṅgya says: "If a person dies while in the womb, it is ten days for the mother."
"Born for both," and "after the naming of the uterine brothers";
or rather, this is the meaning:
If one dies before reaching two years of age, the impurity characterized by untouchability belongs only to both parents, and not to the *sapiṇḍas*.
Likewise, it is stated in another *Smṛti*:

When a child dies before reaching two years of age, the impurity characterized by untouchability applies only to the mother and father, and not to others; however, regarding the other type of impurity— characterized by disqualification from religious rites— it is ordained even for sapinda relatives by such rules as "until the eruption of teeth, [the purification] is immediate," and so forth.

Here is the illustration: "For the impurity of birth belongs only to the mother. Just as the impurity (*āśauca*) characterized by untouchability caused by birth belongs solely to the mother, so too, in the case of a child under two years of age who dies, the untouchability belongs only to the mother and the father.
By prohibiting the impurity of the *sapiṇḍas* regarding one who is less than two years old, it is implied that impurity exists in other cases;
and so Devala says:

"The touching [of the corpse] is to be understood as occurring after one-third of their respective periods of impurity have passed for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas, as prescribed by the scriptures.
This should be understood to apply to cases where death occurs before initiation (*anupanīta*) or when the period of impurity has already elapsed, such as in the case of the three-night period.
Regarding the subject of cremation,
he (Yājñavalkya) has stated:
"When the collection [of the bones] has been performed in sequence by means of a threefold division of the ten-day period and so forth..."
Those who perceive the truth desire the touching of the limbs of the castes.
"The castes are to be touched by three, four, five, and ten [days] respectively;
a Brahmin’s food may be eaten after ten days, while for the remaining [castes], it is after twelve, eighteen, and twenty-one days.
This should be understood as: "after twelve" (ten plus two), "after eighteen" (ten plus eight), and "after twenty-one" (ten plus eleven).
He now describes the impurity characterized by untouchability caused by birth:

"But regarding the parents, the *sūtaka* (impurity) belongs to the mother; it is certain because of the appearance of that [menstrual] blood. That day is not defiled for the ancestors, because it is the cause of their birth. (YDh 3.19)
*Sūtaka*—the impurity characterized by untouchability caused by birth—belongs only to the parents, that is, the mother and father, and not to all *sapiṇḍas*.
And that untouchability for the mother is "certain" (*dhruva*), meaning it remains fixed for ten days. Why?
Because of the sight of her blood— that is, because of seeing blood as belonging to her—
for this very reason Vasiṣṭha says:
"No impurity exists for a man, provided he does not enter into physical contact."
"In that context, the *rajas* (menstrual flow) is to be known as impure, and it does not exist in the male. (VaDh 4.23).
For the father, however, [impurity] certainly does not occur; his state of untouchability ceases by mere bathing.
As Saṃvarta says:
"When a son is born, bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may touch her immediately upon bathing.
This statement that "the mother becomes pure after ten days" refers merely to her fitness for ordinary social intercourse.
Furthermore, regarding rites whose purpose is invisible (adṛṣṭārtha), Paiṭhīnasi has stated a specific rule:
"One may have a woman who has given birth to a son perform ritual acts after twenty nights;
one may have a woman who has given birth to a daughter do so after a month."
Furthermore, the absence of untouchability among sapinda relatives during the period of impurity (aṅgarasa) has been made clear:
"During the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), contact with those other than the woman who has given birth is not prohibited;
however, regarding contact with the woman who has given birth, bathing alone is prescribed. Thus it is said.
On the day of the prince’s birth, that day shall not be defiled;
the meaning is that it does not cause the forfeiture of the entitlement to perform acts such as giving gifts on account of that occasion.
Since on that day there is the birth, or manifestation, of the ancestors— the fathers and so forth— in the form of sons, therefore that day should not be considered defiled.
And thus it has been stated by Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:
On the day of the prince’s birth, Brahmins should receive gifts of gold, land, cattle, horses, goats, clothing, beds, seats, and so forth.
"In that regard, one should accept all kinds of food, but one must not eat cooked food [if it is forbidden].
However, if a twice-born man should eat it out of delusion, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus [it is said].
Vyāsa has also stated a specific rule in this regard:
"The deities named Janmadās reside in the lying-in chamber;
for the purpose of sacrificing to them at birth, one is declared to be pure."
On the first, sixth, and tenth days respectively,
one should never observe the birth-impurity (sūtaka) upon the birth of a son on these three occasions.
Mārkaṇḍeya also said:
"The sixth night must be protected with special care; they should perform a vigil at night, and likewise on the tenth day during the period of birth-impurity. (3.19)

If another birth or death occurs during a period of impurity (āśauca), then according to the maxim that "for every cause, the corresponding effect recurs," there would arise again a period of ten days or more of impurity; [the author] states an exception to that:
"Between [two periods of impurity], if a birth or death occurs, one becomes pure by the remaining days.

(YDh 3.20ab) This means that for whichever person there is a certain duration of impurity—whether determined by caste (varṇa) or by age and stage of life (vayovasthā)—if a similar event occurs within that interval, [one is purified] by the remainder of that [original] period.
When a birth or death occurs that constitutes the cause for a shorter period of impurity, one becomes purified by the very same days remaining from the previous period of impurity;
one need not, however, observe a separate and distinct period of impurity for each subsequent cause such as a birth.
Furthermore, when a long period of impurity falls in the midst of a short period of current impurity, purification does not occur through the remainder of the former. As Uśanas said:
"But if a long period of impurity should occur in the midst of a short period of impurity..."
"Purification shall not occur by means of the preceding [rite]; one is purified only by its own time.
Yama also said: "One should conclude the impurity, which involves an increase in sin, with the latter [rite]."

And here, although it is stated without distinction that "in the interval between birth and death," nevertheless, there is no purification of a *śāva* (impurity due to death) occurring within a *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) by means of the remainder of the preceding impurity. As Aṅgiras has said:
"If a death should occur during a birth-impurity, or if a birth should occur during a death-impurity..."
"In that case, one should perform purification with respect to the death-impurity (mṛtaka), not the birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When birth-impurity occurs while death-impurity has already arisen..."
"Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity does not purify birth-impurity.
Therefore, death-impurity occurring within the period of birth-impurity is not purified by the remainder of the former;
rather, it is [purified] by that which occurs within the period of death-impurity.

In the same way, although impurity due to death (*śāva*) is included within the category of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), an exception to purification by the remainder of the previous [period] has been shown in another Smṛti in certain cases.

"If the mother dies first and the father dies during the period of impurity, his purification shall be by the remainder of the father's [period]; however, he should observe a *pakṣiṇī* [day-and-night] for the mother.
This is the meaning:

If, after the mother has previously died, the father should pass away during the period of impurity caused by her death, then purification does not occur through the remainder of the former period; rather,
purification must be performed according to the duration of the period of impurity occasioned by the father's passing.
Likewise, even if the mother passes away during the period of impurity caused by the father's death, purification does not occur merely through the remainder of the prior period;
rather, one must complete the previous period of impurity and then add a *pakṣiṇī* (a period of two days with an intervening night).

Likewise, an exception based on the specific timing of the concurrence of impurities has been stated by Gautama: "If [the second impurity] occurs when one night remains, [it lasts for] two days; if it occurs at dawn, [it lasts for] three days" (GDh 14.7–8).
The meaning is this:
if another period of impurity should coincide when only one night remains of the previous impurity, then,
upon the completion of the previous impurity, purification occurs after two nights.

Furthermore, if at dawn, during the final watch of that night, another impurity such as birth occurs, purification is achieved after three nights, and not merely by the remainder of the first period alone.
Śātātapa has also stated: "If [the period] remains for one night, purification occurs after two days; if it remains for one watch (yāma), one is pure after three days.
Furthermore, he stated that the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*) are not suspended even when there is a concurrence with the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
If death should occur within ten days after birth,
the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) must be performed for the deceased by one's own kinsmen.
"If, however, after the *pretapiṇḍa* has been commenced, a birth should occur in the interim,
one should likewise offer the remaining *āśaucapiṇḍas* according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, even when there is a coincidence (*sannipāta*) of impurity due to death and impurity due to birth, the rites for the deceased must be performed.
Because the same principle applies,
even rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*),
which are occasioned by the birth of a son, must indeed be performed even when there is the occurrence of another period of impurity (*āśauca*).
Likewise, Prajāpati [stated]:
"But when the birth of a son occurs while a period of impurity has arisen, the performer attains immediate purification; he is purified by the preceding impurity. Thus.
Having described the impurity resulting from birth at the full term of pregnancy, he now states the impurity caused by the premature discharge of the fetus:
"In the case of a miscarriage, the nights equal to the number of months are the cause of purification" (YDh 3.20cd).
Although the root *sravati* is used in common parlance for the flowing of liquid substances, [it is here applied to the discharge of the fetus].
Nevertheless, it occurs here in the form of falling downward, which is common to both liquid and non-liquid substances.
Why? Because fluidity (dravatva) is possible only during the first month, and since there are nights equal in number to that month, the use of the plural "nights" would otherwise be untenable.
In the case of a miscarriage, the number of nights equal to the months of gestation are the cause of purification;
and this applies only to the woman.
Regarding miscarriage, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha’s traditional teaching states: "For women, the nights are equal in number to the months [of pregnancy]; for a man, it is merely a bath.
As for the three-night period mentioned by Gautama—"and three days" (GDh 14.18)—[it refers to a different case].
That should be understood as occurring within three months; in the case of a miscarriage, it is according to the number of months, but for a very recent one, [the impurity lasts] three days.
For a Kṣatriya, however, it is four nights, and for a Vaiśya, it is exactly five days.
But for a Śūdra, this purification is proclaimed to take eight days.
Thus, according to the recollection of Marīci:

"In the case of a miscarriage within three months, for one born of the highest Brāhmaṇa caste, the period is three nights"—this is the meaning. And this should be understood to apply up until the end of the sixth month.

Furthermore, in the case of [conceptions] from the seventh month onwards, the full period of impurity due to childbirth must be observed; for there, the emergence of a living fetus with complete limbs is seen,
and the term "birth" (prasava) is used in common worldly parlance in that context.
As long as a miscarriage occurs within six months,
purification for those women is held to be achieved in days equal to the number of months [of pregnancy].
From this point forward, the impurity for those women is held to be as prescribed for their own caste;
however, when there is a miscarriage, the sapindas attain immediate purification.
Because of this traditional teaching.
