And this provision for immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for *sapiṇḍas* should be understood to apply to the miscarriage of a fetus that has become liquid.

As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "In the case of the death of one less than two years old and in the case of a miscarriage, there is a three-night [period of impurity] for the *sapiṇḍas*" (VaDh 4.34), that refers to the context of a miscarriage of a solidified fetus during the fifth or sixth month.
Up to the fourth month, there may be a flow; in the fifth and sixth months, it is a miscarriage (pāta);
beyond that, it is a birth (prasūti), and for ten days there shall be impurity (sūtaka).
In the case of a miscarriage, there shall be impurity for the mother for three nights, excluding the impurity of the sapinda relatives;
in the case of a full-term birth, the mother's impurity lasts according to the month of pregnancy, while that of the father and others lasts for three days.
Thus, according to the recollection of Marīci.

From the seventh month onwards, if a birth occurs that results in the death [of the child], or if the child dies after being born, the full period of impurity (āśauca) occasioned by birth applies to the sapinda relatives; for there is the traditional teaching of Hārīta stating, "Whether the child dies after being born or is born dead, the impurity for the sapindas lasts ten days. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement of Pāraskara: "If there is an impurity due to birth during the period of birth-impurity itself, it shall be like the birth-impurity."

"Until the rising" means until the mother rises from childbed, that is, for ten days; "as in the case of birth-impurity" (sūtakavat) means it is devoid of the water-libation offered on account of the death of an infant. Bṛhan-Manu also says:
"If a child dies within ten days, its relatives shall not observe the impurity of death (śāvāśauca); rather, the impurity of birth (sūtyāśauca) is prescribed.
Likewise, another Smṛti text also states: "For one who has died within ten days, the impurity lasts for the same number of days as those of a birth-impurity."
By reflecting on this collection of statements beginning with these, it is understood that there is no restriction of the impurity caused by birth for those who share the funeral oblation (sapiṇḍas).

As for the statement of Bṛhad-Viṣṇu, "If a child is born and then dies, or if one dies after being born, there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) for the family," that is intended to establish purification through bathing for the impurity caused by the death of an infant, not for the impurity caused by childbirth.
And likewise Pāraskara states: "If death should occur in the womb, there shall be impurity for ten days, because the cause of birth exists for the sapinda relatives;
if one born alive should die, one becomes pure immediately"—this refers to the impurity pertaining to the deceased.
And so it has been stated by Śaṅkha: "Before the naming ceremony, there is immediate purification.
Furthermore, as for the statement of Kātyāyana: "But if death occurs while the ten-day period has not yet elapsed..."
Purification occurs immediately; there is neither a funeral rite nor the water libation.
Thus, that [text] also has the same meaning as the Vaiṣṇava [text].

However, when the reading is "na pretaṃ naiva sūtakam" (neither impurity from death nor impurity from birth), then the meaning is that there is no impurity (*sūtaka*)—that is, no state of untouchability—for the father and the others. Alternatively, this is the meaning: if the death of an infant occurs within ten days, then there is no impurity due to death (*preta-āśauca*).

If a birth among the sapinda relatives occurs during that period, then even the *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) need not be observed; rather, purification occurs through the previous period of impurity alone.
As for the statement of Bṛhan-Manu:
If one born alive should then die, there is indeed birth-impurity (sūtaka);
the mother’s impurity lasts for the full duration, while that of the father and others lasts for three nights.
Thus, there is also the statement of Bṛhatpracetā:
"If a child dies within a muhūrta of being born,
the mother's purification occurs after ten days, but the agnates are purified immediately."

Thus, in this regard, the established rule is as follows: if death occurs after birth but before the naming ceremony (*nābhivardhana*), the impurity of the father and others caused by birth lasts for three days.

Immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), however, applies for the sake of the *agnihotra* and other such rites, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "For the sake of the *agnihotra*, purity is attained at that very moment through bathing and ritual touching. But after the naming ceremony (*nābhivardhana*), even upon the death of an infant, the full period of impurity occasioned by birth must be observed.
For sapindas,
as long as the umbilical cord is not severed, they do not incur the state of birth-impurity (sūtaka);
once the cord is severed, thereafter the impurity is prescribed.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Jaimini;
this same point has also been shown by Manu:
"In the case of a miscarriage, one is purified after as many nights as there were months [of pregnancy]."
"When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman made unclean by her menses becomes pure through bathing. (MDh 5.66).
The first half of this verse has been shown;
the meaning of the latter half, however, is as follows:

When the menstrual flow has ceased and the period of impurity has ended, a woman who was previously "rajasvalā" becomes pure through bathing; she is then fit for auspicious rites dedicated to the gods and other such activities,
including those involving physical contact.
Furthermore, even if the discharge has not ceased, she becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
Thus it was said by Vṛddha-Manu:
"On the fourth day she becomes completely pure for worldly transactions."
Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"A menstruating woman becomes pure for her husband by bathing on the fourth day;
however, she becomes pure for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors on the fifth day."
The phrase "on the fifth day" is intended as an indicator for the time when the menstrual flow has ceased.
When there is a manifestation of the menstrual flow again within seventeen days from the start of the previous flow, then there is no impurity at all.
In the eighteenth [day], purification occurs after one day;
in the nineteenth, after two days; and from those following, purification occurs after three days.
As Atri has said: "If a woman who has bathed after her menses becomes menstruating again within eighteen days, no state of impurity is recognized."
"Before nineteen days, it shall be one day; after that, two days;
from twenty onwards, among the subsequent [periods], one becomes impure for three nights.
Thus, another *smṛti* states that impurity does not exist before fourteen days; in that context, the intention is that [the period of impurity] begins from the time of bathing.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, this prohibition regarding impurity applies to the case where menstruation generally occurs only after twenty days have passed.
Furthermore, for a woman who has reached puberty and for whom the discharge of menses occurs profusely even before eighteen days have passed, the period of impurity lasts for only three nights;
and she must remain for those three nights without bathing or other such purification rites.

A woman in her courses remains impure for three nights; during that time, she should not apply collyrium, nor anoint herself with oil, nor bathe in water, nor sleep on the ground, nor sleep during the day,
nor look at the planets, nor touch fire, nor eat, nor spin thread, nor clean her teeth.

"One should rinse [the mouth], not laugh, and not perform any other action; one should drink from a vessel that is not small, or with the hollowed palms, or with a vessel made of copper or iron," according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha (VaDh 5.6–8).
There is also a specific rule from the Āṅgirasa:
"The consumer of sacrificial oblations (havirbhuk) should eat from his hand or from an earthen vessel;
sleeping on the ground, she who is in her courses shall attain purity by bathing on the fourth day."
In the *Pārāśara* as well, there is a specific rule:
"If a woman becomes menstruating when an occasional bath (*naimittika-snāna*) is required,
she should perform the bath by means of water transferred through another vessel and then observe her vow."
"One should somehow have one's limbs, along with the major and minor parts of the body, sprinkled with water;
one should not wring out the garment, nor should one wear another garment. Thus has Uśanas also shown a specific rule in this regard.
If a woman is overcome by fever and is also overwhelmed by her menses, how may she become pure? By what ritual act may she attain purification?
When the fourth day arrives, another woman should touch her;
having plunged into the water with her clothes on and bathed again and again, she should touch herself ten or twelve times and sip water repeatedly.
"And after the discarding of the garments, she shall then become pure;
thereafter, she should give a gift according to her capacity, and she is purified by a *puṇyāha* [ceremony].
This method of bathing is to be followed for a woman who has merely fallen ill.
When the time for bathing has arisen for one who is ill, a healthy person should bathe ten times and touch him after each bath; then that sick person shall become pure.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara:
"But when the death of a woman in her courses or a woman who has recently given birth occurs, this is the method of purification:
'When a woman who has recently given birth has died, how do the performers of sacrifices act?'"
Having taken water in a jar, and likewise the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),...
Then, having consecrated water with meritorious verses, one should obtain purification through speech;
having bathed [the body] with that very water, one should perform the cremation according to the prescribed rite.
But regarding a woman who has menstruated: "Having bathed the deceased woman who was menstruating with the five products of the cow,
and having covered her with another garment, one should cremate her according to the prescribed rule."
And regarding this— such as the appearance of menses or the birth of a son—

if it occurs after sunrise, then the calculation of the days of impurity must be made starting from that very day. However, when the appearance of menses, the birth of a son, or the like occurs during the night, then, if the birth or other event takes place before midnight:
One view is that even when the period of impurity (*āśauca*) covers only a portion of the preceding day, the counting must begin from that preceding day itself. Alternatively,
having divided the night into three parts, if birth or other such events occur during the first two parts, the preceding day is to be included.
Thus is the second [view]; another says "before sunrise," as Kaśyapa has stated.
But when the menses appear for women after the sun has risen,
that day is the night of either birth or death for him [the husband].
The time limit for impurity (sūtaka) and similar conditions is prescribed as ending at midnight;
one should divide the night into three parts, and the first two parts are considered part of the preceding day.
In the case of the birth-impurity (*ṛtusūtaka*), it is joined with the following day at dawn;
however, when death occurs, or during the impurity of menstruation (*rajasi sūtake*), it is joined with the night itself.
"The day should be taken as starting from before the sun rises.
Furthermore, the application of these rules should be understood according to local custom.
Moreover, this period of impurity (āśauca) for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) must be observed starting from the day of the cremation rite (saṃskāra).

However, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*) begins from the day of death; yet, according to the rule "for both [it begins] from the day of the consecration ritual (*saṃskāra*)," it must be discerned that for both types of persons, it begins from the day of the funeral rite.
As Aṅgiras said:

"For one without a sacred fire, purification [occurs] until the departure [of the breath]; for one with a sacred fire, it occurs from the purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarman*). The collection [of bones] and the cremation [are performed], and the day of death is according to the rule.
Because of the scriptural statement, "for one with a sacred fire, from the purificatory rite," [it is understood].

It should be understood that when a father who has maintained the sacred fires dies in another country, there is no lapse in the performance of duties such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) for his sons and others until the cremation (*saṃskāra*).
Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"For among the twice-born, impurity lasts until the departure [of the body] for one who maintains no sacred fire;
however, for one who maintains a sacred fire, one should know it begins from the cremation when he has died in a foreign land. (3.20)
Regarding the application of the ten-day period and others based on sapinda-relationship and so forth, he states an exception in certain specific cases of death:
"For those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for those who commit suicide, [the impurity lasts] immediately" (YDh 3.21ab).
A "king" (nṛpa) is an anointed Kshatriya or similar ruler.
The mention of "cow" is intended as an illustration for animals such as horned and tusked creatures;
the mention of "Brahmin" is an illustration for those of the lowest castes (*antyaja*).
This refers to the *sapiṇḍas* who are related to those killed by these [beings].
Those who intentionally bring about their own death by means of poison, hanging, and so forth, are "suicides" (ātmaghātinaḥ).

The mention of "suicides" is intended to indicate, by way of a single compound, those who have fallen [from their status] and those who have become outcasts, as well as those who have not taken refuge in the religious orders (pākhaṇḍins).
And for those related to him, *anvakṣam*— meaning following immediately after the eye (*akṣam*),

that is, immediately (*sadyaḥ*)— there is purification; and for those related to him, there is impurity (*āśauca*) lasting as long as the sight (*sānvakṣam*), i.e., until they are no longer within sight.
But it is not for ten days and so forth.

And thus Gautama says: "For those killed by cows or Brahmins, or by the king's wrath in a non-combat situation, or by suicide through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice], the impurity lasts until the news is seen" (GDh 14.9–12).
The mention of "killed in anger" (krodhagrahaṇa) is for the purpose of excluding those killed through negligence;
the mention of "not in battle" (ayuddhagrahaṇa) is for the purpose of making known that there is one day of impurity for one killed in battle.
For women who have perished for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or even during the seizure of cattle,
and for those killed in battle, the period of impurity lasts for one night.
Thus it is remembered [in the Smṛti]. And this applies specifically to one who dies after some interval due to a wound sustained during the time of battle,
as opposed to one killed on the very front line of the fray.
There is immediate purification.
As Manu has said:
"And for one slain in battle with uplifted weapons, according to the duty of the Kṣatriya..."
"The sacrifice is immediately completed, and so too is the period of impurity; such is the settled rule" (MDh 5.98).

Since birth and other such events become causes for impurity only when they are known, this verse provides an exception regarding the attainment of the ten-day period and so forth even when they are known at a time subsequent to the day of birth.
"When [the relative] has gone abroad, the remainder of the period [shall apply]; when it is complete, one becomes pure after offering water.

(YDh 3.21cd) When [the relative] has gone abroad—that is, resides in another country—and the news of the birth of a sapinda or other event is not known by the person staying at home on the very first day, then for that sapinda, whatever remains of the period limited to ten days or less, that remaining time alone is the cause of purification.
When the period of impurity, such as ten days or more, has been completed, purification occurs after offering water to the deceased.
Since the offering of water must be preceded by bathing, one becomes pure by bathing and then offering the water.

This has been stated by Manu: "Upon hearing of the death of a relative or the birth of a son after ten days have passed, a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes. (MDh 5.77)

Because of the injunction that "having offered water when [the period] is complete, one becomes pure," which establishes that the period of impurity associated with the offering of water for the deceased is the cause of purification, it is understood that in the case of a birth, there is no impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* once the [prescribed] time has elapsed.

However, for the father, there is indeed a ritual bath even before the ten-day period has elapsed following the birth, because of the scriptural statement: "And having heard of the birth of a son" (MDh 5.77).

And this mention of "the son" is an indicator that for sapindas, there is no impurity (āśauca) that has passed away at birth; otherwise, he would have simply said, "having heard of the death of a relative after ten days, and [of] a birth after ten days. But it was not so stated.
And so Devala says:
"There is no impurity during the period of birth-impurity, even when the days have already passed."
Therefore, it is established that the period of impurity is indeed transcended only in the case of misfortune.
Some read this verse differently:
"In the case of one who has gone abroad, the remainder of the time [shall apply]; but if no time remains, it shall be exactly three days."

"When a year has passed for all [classes], having offered water upon the death [of the deceased], one becomes pure. Thus, when one who was away has died, for all—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth—without distinction, the remainder of the period is the cause of purification. Furthermore, if that period has not been completed—that is, once the ten days and so forth have elapsed—for all, the impurity lasts for only three days.

If, upon the completion of a year, it should be learned that the deceased had departed on a journey while abroad, then everyone, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, shall become pure by bathing and offering water.
And so says Manu:

"But when a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by touching water" (MDh 5.76). This three-day period is to be understood as applying after ten days have elapsed but before three months; however, the aforementioned immediate purification applies [to shorter periods].
It should be understood as occurring after the ninth month and before one year has passed.
As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "Having heard [of it] after ten days, [the impurity lasts] for one night" (VaDh 4.36),
that refers to the period from after six months up until the ninth month.
As for the statement of Gautama, "Having heard [the news] after the tenth day, it is *pakṣiṇī*," that refers to the period after three months but before six months. And so says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:

"In the case of three months, there shall be a three-night period; likewise, for six months, a pakṣiṇī; but for less than nine months, a single day; beyond that, one is purified by bathing. And this refers to cases other than those involving the mother or father.
If both parents should die, even if the son is living far away,
from the moment he hears the news, he shall remain in a state of impurity for ten days.
Thus, from the Smṛti of Paiṭhīnasi;
and likewise in another Smṛti:
"But upon the death of a great guru, one should remain fasting and wearing wet clothes."
"One should perform the funeral rites according to the prescribed rule even in the year following [the death].

This means that even after a year has passed, the funeral rites—such as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) and the offering of water (*udakadāna*)—must still be performed; it does not mean that purification occurs merely through bathing.
Regarding the wife of one's father as well, a distinction is shown in another Smṛti text for those other than one's own mother:
"O best of the twice-born, even if a year has passed, one remains impure for three nights upon the death of the wife of one's father, with the exception of one's own mother."

However, if someone dies in another country separated by a river or other obstacles, for their *sapiṇḍas*, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) after ten days have passed, even if it is within three months; as it is said:
"Upon hearing that one has died in another country—whether it be a eunuch, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic—"
"Upon death, as well as in the case of a miscarriage, the kinsmen (gotriṇaḥ) are purified by bathing.
And the definition of "another country" (deśāntara) has been stated by Bṛhaspati:
"Where there is a great river between, or a mountain acting as a barrier..."
Where languages diverge, that is called a different country.
"Some say it extends to another country sixty yojanas in length;
others say forty, and others likewise thirty.
And this rule regarding impurity incurred by crossing [a distance] refers to the death of one who has been initiated (upanīta).
Furthermore, it does not refer to impurity based on specific stages of age;
for thus it has been said by Vyāgrapāda:
"For all [castes], [impurity] is equal during [the period of] youth, and likewise when that has passed."
"But when that [period] has been exceeded, it is irregular, arising from the lapse of time.
This is the meaning:
regarding the age consisting of three years and so forth, whatever impurity exists from birth until the eruption of teeth is immediate (*sadyas*). (YDh 3.23)
That which is ordained by such statements as these is equal and undifferentiated for all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas; and likewise,
when the ten-day period and so forth have elapsed, that impurity lasting three days or more is also undifferentiated for all.
Furthermore, when the death of one who has been initiated occurs, the impurity for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes lasts ten, twelve, fifteen, or thirty days; thus, the impurity is unequal.
This applies specifically to the case of the death of one who has been initiated.

Thus, it is only the impurity arising from excessive time that becomes "transgressed impurity" (*atikrāntāśauca*), and not the transgression of impurity based on the stage of life (*vayovasthā*). // 3.21 //
He states an exception to the ten-night period of impurity for sapinda relatives among Kṣatriyas and others:
"For a Kṣatriya it is twelve days; for a Vaiśya, fifteen;
for a Śūdra, thirty days; but half of that for one who lives according to the law. (YDh 3.22)

Upon the birth of a sapinda relative or upon their death, the period of impurity for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras is, respectively, twelve, fifteen, and thirty days. However, for a Śūdra who lives according to the law and is devoted to the *pākayajña* sacrifices and service to the twice-born, that period is half as long.

For that month, the period of impurity lasts for half a month, which is fifteen nights. And thus, by the principle of remainder (*pāriśeṣya*), the rule "three nights or ten nights" (YDh 3.18)— specifically this ten-night period of impurity— is established as applying to the case of a Brāhmaṇa.
In other Smṛtis, however, rules for impurity lasting ten days and so forth are also shown for Kṣatriyas and others.
As Parāśara says:
"But a Kṣatriya who is devoted to his own duty becomes pure after ten days."
In the same way, a Vaiśya shall attain purification in twelve days.
And so says Śātātapa:
"A Kṣatriya becomes pure after eleven days, a Vaiśya likewise after twelve,
and a Śūdra becomes pure after twenty nights in the case of death or birth impurity."
"Vasiṣṭha, however, says: 'A Kṣatriya [is purified] by fifteen nights, and a Vaiśya by twenty nights' (VaDh 4.28–29). Aṅgiras, on the other hand, says:
'For all castes alike, in the case of birth or death [impurity]...'"
"Śātātapa has declared that their purification occurs after ten days."
Thus, various high and low rules for impurity have been shown;
since there is no common practice of these in the world, demonstrating a fixed system of them is not particularly useful, and therefore no such system is presented here.
Furthermore, when Kṣatriyas and others become sapinda relatives of Brāhmaṇas and others, then the rules for impurity (āśauca) as stated by Hārīta and others should be followed:
"A Brāhmaṇa is purified after ten days upon the birth or death of those born of his own caste."

"By six, three, or one [day and night] for those born in the lineages of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. Viṣṇu also says: "For a Kṣatriya, purification occurs after six nights and three nights respectively among Sapiṇḍas who are Vaiśyas or Śūdras; for a Vaiśya, purification occurs after six nights when a Sapiṇḍa who is a Śūdra [dies]; but for those of lower varṇas, when births or deaths occur among Sapiṇḍas of a higher varṇa, purification occurs upon the expiration of that [latter's] period of impurity" (ViDh 22.23–24, 21).
Baudhāyana, however, has stated without distinction that purification takes ten days:
"If there are kinsmen of a Brāhmaṇa who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes,
the purification for the Brāhmaṇa in their case of impurity is held to occur after ten days."
And between these two positions, the distinction is established based on whether the context involves a time of distress or a time of no distress.
As for female slaves and others, their touchability is determined by the purity of their master; however, their lack of entitlement to perform religious rites lasts only until the end of one month.
Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:

"Whatever be the caste of the master, that same caste shall determine the purification for both the female and male slave; however, the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) for a female slave lasts one month."
However, for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), there is indeed an absence of ritual impurity (āśauca),
because of the traditional teaching of Manu that "those born in the inverse order are devoid of dharma.
There is only purification for the purpose of removing physical filth upon death or birth, similar to the purification after voiding urine or feces.
It indeed exists. // 3.22 //

He states an exception to the ten-day period of impurity based on specific stages of age: "Until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is declared to last one night;
until the initiation of vows (vratādeśa), it lasts three nights; and beyond that, ten nights. (YDh 3.23)

For as long as it takes for teeth to erupt, during that period, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) for the relatives of a deceased child. For one who dies before the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the impurity for the relatives lasts for a night—that is, an impurity lasting a full day and night. For one who dies after the tonsure but before the initiation (*vratādeśa*, i.e., *upanayana*), the impurity lasts for three days.

And although the expression "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) here is stated without qualification as being until the eruption of teeth, it should nevertheless be understood to apply specifically to the absence of the fire-rite (*agnisaṃskāra*); for when a child who has not yet erupted teeth dies, purification occurs immediately, as there is neither the fire-rite nor the rite of libation (*udakakriyā*). (ViDh 22.27–28)
Thus, according to the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], since immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed for one who has not undergone the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*),

whereas when the consecration by fire has occurred, there is a period of one day (*ekāha*), as will be stated later: "But in the case of unmarried girls and children, [purification takes] a day" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.24).
And likewise Yama says:
"In the case of a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, or a young child, or likewise one who has miscarried from the womb,
there is a period of impurity for all the sapinda relatives lasting one day and night."

Prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is indeed mandatory, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "Before the naming ceremony, there is immediate purity. Furthermore, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) is prescribed by tradition to take place in either the first or the third year.
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must, according to the Dharma,
be performed in accordance with Vedic injunctions either in the first or the third year.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Consequently, from the eruption of the teeth until the first annual *cūḍā* ceremony, the period of impurity lasts for one day;
however, in that case, for one whose *cūḍā* has not yet been performed...
Even when teeth have appeared, until the age of three years, it is only one day [of impurity];
and thus Viṣṇu says:
"Even when teeth have appeared, if the tonsure has not been performed, purification occurs after a day and a night" (ViDh 22.29).

After that, prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the impurity lasts for three days. As for the statement of Manu: "For men whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, the impurity is declared to last one night."
"However, for those whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, purification is held to occur after three nights"—
this same scope applies to that [rule] as well.
As for what was stated by that same author concerning a child less than two years old:
"Having abandoned [the body] like a log in the forest, they should dispose of it after only three days.
And as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha:
"When one dies before two years have passed, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity for the sapindas lasts three nights. (VaDh 4.34)
Thus [it is said], which refers to the intention that the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) should take place after one year;
as for the statement of Aṅgiras:
"Even if he has not had the tonsure performed, provided he has teethed and passed away..."
Nevertheless, having cremated him, one should observe impurity for three days.
Thus, this [period] is to be understood as applying when the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) is postponed beyond three years due to considerations of family custom;
for it has been stated by that same author: "But if a Brahmin dies before the completion of three years, purification occurs after one night."
Nor should it be suspected that this single day constitutes an absence of tooth eruption;
for it is impossible for teeth not to emerge in one who is less than three years old.

Likewise, even though teeth have emerged, a contradiction would be difficult to avoid with the statement of Viṣṇu (ViDh 22.29), which prescribes a single day for one whose tonsure has not yet been performed.
Therefore, the earlier explanation alone is more authoritative.
As for the statement of Kaśyapa that "for children who have not yet cut their teeth, purification occurs after three nights," that refers specifically to the mother and father.
Having discharged semen, however, a man becomes pure by touching water;
yet, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
Thus, because the Smṛti texts record a three-night period [of impurity] based on the limiting condition (upādhi) of the relationship between the born and the progenitor,
the following is the meaning:
prior to the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa), there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca).
After that, until the eruption of teeth, if the rite of cremation (agnisaṃskāra) has been performed, there is impurity for one day;
otherwise, there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca).
For one whose teeth have appeared, there is impurity for one day prior to the first-year *caula* ceremony;
from the end of the first year until the age of three, for one who has undergone the *caula*, it is three days.

But for the other [the child], it is one day; for one whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, even if more than three years have passed, it is three days; and after the initiation ceremony, it is as prescribed.
For all [the rites], beginning with the Brāhma, the period is ten nights and so forth. // 3.23 //

Now he states an exception regarding women according to their specific stage of life: "But for unmarried girls and for children, purification occurs after one day and night" (YDh 3.24ab). "Unmarried" refers to those girls who have not been wedded; for them, or for those who have undergone the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), before the formal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), one day and night is specifically the cause of purification.
The sapinda relationship among sapindas and among unmarried girls extends only to three generations,
because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "For unmarried women, [the sapinda relationship] is understood to extend to three generations" (VaDh 4.18).
In the case of children who have not yet cut their teeth, if cremation has taken place, purification lasts for one day;
however, in the case of a girl whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is immediate.
For, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "In the case of an unmarried girl, purification is ordained to be immediate.
However, after the verbal betrothal but before the sacramental rites, the period of impurity lasts for three days on both the husband's side and the father's side.
As Manu has said:
"In the case of women who have not been consecrated [by marriage], the kinsmen on the husband's side become pure after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) become pure according to the very rule already stated" (MDh 5.72).
Relatives on the husband’s side are purified in three nights; however,

uterine relatives on the father’s side who are *sapiṇḍas* are purified by the very rule already stated— namely, the three-night period mentioned in the passage beginning with "for those whose tonsure has been performed," and so forth— and not by the ten-night period.
Because that [gift] is improper prior to marriage;
for this very reason, Marīci says:
"But she who has been given with water, yet not formally bestowed..."
"But that [impurity] is to be known as unconditioned (asaṃskṛtā); it is prescribed for three nights for both.
"For both" means for both the husband's side and the father's side.
However, regarding the period after marriage, a specific rule has been shown by Viṣṇu:
"There is no impurity on the paternal side regarding women who have been refined [by marriage];
however, if their birth or death occurs in the father's house, then there shall be one night or three nights [of impurity]" (ViDh 22.33–34).
In that regard, the rule is that there is one day of impurity for a birth and three nights for a journey;
furthermore, this impurity based on age-stage is common to all social classes (varṇas).
Because [the rule] "for a Kṣatriya, twelve days" (YDh 3.22) is stated by specifying that particular caste,

it is for this very reason that Manu, while operating within the jurisdiction of all four castes, formulated his rules on impurity without specifying a particular caste in order to demonstrate their general applicability.
Furthermore, it has been stated: "Moreover, for all four castes, in due order and according to rule" (MDh 5.57). Likewise, it has also been stated by Aṅgiras:
"Without distinction among the castes, prior to the performance of the purificatory rites, purification shall occur after three nights; however, for girls, it is ordained to be by a single day.
And the statement of Vyāghrapāda, "for all [castes] it is the same regarding age," has been shown previously.

Therefore, just as the rule for the offering of funeral cakes and water— beginning with "the gift should be made according to the procedure of the piṇḍayajña" (YDh 3.16)— is common to all social classes,
so too is the rule regarding impurity for those related by water (samānodaka).

The rule regarding impurity due to a conjunction [of events] is stated as "between birth and death" (YDh 3.20), and the rule regarding impurity due to a miscarriage is stated as "in the case of a miscarriage, the nights are equal to the months [of gestation]" (YDh 3.20). Furthermore, regarding one who has gone abroad, it is said: "If the period [of impurity] remains, it shall be the remainder of that time; if none remains, it shall be three days only" (YDh 3.21).

Thus, just as the rules for impurity (āśauca) regarding those residing in a foreign land and the rules for impurity regarding teachers and others are common to all social classes (varṇas), so too the impurity caused by age or stage of life ought to be common to all classes. For this very reason, it is said: "When the tonsure ceremony (caula) has been performed at six years for a Kṣatriya, and at nine for a Vaiśya..."
But for a Śūdra who has passed three years [of age], a twelve-day period is prescribed.
Likewise:
"Where a three-night period of impurity is prescribed for Brahmins,
there it is twelve days for a Śūdra, and six or nine for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas."

The teachers Dhāreśvara, Viśvarūpa, Medhātithi, and others— who do not disregard such statements of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and others due to a perception of their being contradictory— hold this very common position: that these [contradictory] texts are to be explained as referring respectively to distressed and non-distressed Kṣatriyas and so forth.
He states an extension [of the rules] to the teacher and others:
"And in the case of the teacher's resident pupil, a learned scholar (anūcāna), and a maternal uncle...

(YDh 3.24cd). Here, "teacher" (guru) refers to the preceptor (upādhyāya); "resident pupil" (antevāsī) means a disciple; "learned scholar" (anūcāna) means one who expounds the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas); and by the mention of the "maternal uncle," one's own kinsmen are included.
Maternal and paternal kinsmen related by birth are indicated;
they have been shown in the verse beginning with "the wife and daughters" (YDh 3.135).
A *śrotriya* is one who studies a single branch (*śākhā*), for according to the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana, "having studied one branch, one is a *śrotriya*" (cf. ĀpDh 2.6.4).
When these [secondary gurus] have passed away, the period of impurity lasts for a day and night;
however, when the primary guru— the father— has passed away, it lasts for ten days because of the status of being a *sapiṇḍa*.

But for a father who, having procreated sons, performed their sacraments, taught them the Vedas, caused them to grasp the meaning of the Vedas, and provided them with a livelihood— for him, because of his status as a great preceptor (*mahāguru*), upon his death there is either a period of twelve nights; for regarding great preceptors, they should avoid giving gifts and Vedic study [for that duration] (ĀśGṛ 4.4.17).
This should be understood as stated by Āśvalāyana;
however, upon the death of the teacher, it lasts for exactly three nights,
as Manu has said:
"When a teacher has passed away, they declare the period of impurity to be three nights;
for his son and his wife, it is one day and night—this is the settled rule" (MDh 5.80).
However, when one performs the funeral rites for a teacher or similar person, the period of impurity is ten nights.

For it has been stated by that same author: "But the disciple of a deceased guru should undertake the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rites); he becomes purified there in ten days along with those who carry the corpse. (MDh 5.65).

However, this period of impurity applies to a *śrotriya* residing in the same village, because of the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana: "There is one day of impurity for a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) and for a *śrotriya* residing in the same village" (ĀśGṛ 4.4.26–27).
A fellow student initiated by the same teacher is [to be treated as such] when this [teacher] is not present; however, when he is present,
the period of impurity for a disciple and others lasts three nights and so forth.

As Manu has said: "Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya, one shall remain impure for three nights; for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one shall remain impure for a night with its two flanking days. (MDh 5.81)

"Upasaṃpanna" refers to one who is connected [to the donor] by being a neighbor through the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) or by other such ties, or one who is endowed with virtuous conduct (*śīla*). The mention of "maternal uncle" (*mātula*) is intended as an illustration for maternal aunts and others.
"Relatives" refers to one's own relatives, as well as the maternal relatives and paternal relatives;
and thus Bṛhaspati says:
"One shall remain impure for three days in the case of a maternal grandfather, a teacher, or a Śrotriya."
Likewise, Pracetas says:
"If the officiating priest (ṛtvij) or the patron (yājya) has died, one becomes pure after three nights.
And so too says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:

When a daughter's son has died, the impurity lasts for three nights; however, when he has been consecrated [as a Snātaka], it is established by dharma that the impurity lasts for three nights even if he dies after the completion of the period of mourning.
"When both parents have passed away, what should be the case for married women?
Purification occurs in exactly three nights; thus spoke the venerable Yama."
One should spend the night as a *pakṣiṇī* (a period of two days and the intervening night) with one's parents-in-law, a sister, a maternal aunt, a maternal uncle, and likewise with a paternal aunt.
Likewise,

there is impurity for one night with its two surrounding days (pakṣiṇī) upon the death of a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a friend, a teacher, or the wives of teachers; and also if a maternal grandmother has died.
And so says Gautama:
"For three nights [one observes impurity] for one who is not a sapinda, for a relative by birth, and for a fellow student" (GDh 14.19–20).
Those related by birth include the maternal uncle, the daughter of the mother's sister, the daughter of the father's sister, and others.
Likewise, Jābāla states:

"For those who share the same water (ekodaka), the impurity lasts for three days; for kinsmen of the same lineage (gotraja), it is remembered as one day; and likewise for a maternal relative, a guru, a friend, and a regional ruler."
Viṣṇu states: "If one dies in one's own house who is not a sapinda, [the impurity lasts] for one night. Likewise, Vṛddha [Yājñavalkya] says:
"But when a sister has been consecrated [by marriage], or when a brother has also been consecrated..."
Upon the death of a friend, a son-in-law, a daughter's son, a sister's son,
a maternal uncle, or his son, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.
When the lord of a village, the head of a family, a learned Vedic scholar, an ascetic,
or a pupil has met his death, one remains pure until the appearance of the stars.
As long as the corpse of anyone remains within the center of a village, that village shall remain impure; once it has departed, it shall attain purity.
Such Smṛti passages as these, which set forth specific rules regarding impurity (āśauca), are to be sought out;
they are not written here for fear of excessive length.
And this [present discussion], by virtue of setting forth heavy and light periods of impurity concerning a single subject, [is concluded].
In cases where [texts] are mutually contradictory, a systematic resolution must be sought by considering their proximity or distance. (3.24)
Moreover:

"In the case of sons other than those born of one's own body, when wives have gone over to another man, and when the king by whom one resides has died—that very day is the cause for purification. (YDh 3.25)
The word "day" (ahar) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
"Non-aurasa sons" refers to those such as the kṣetraja, dattaka, and others.
When they are born or when they have died, [the impurity lasts for] a day and a night.

Regarding impurity (*āśauca*): likewise, when one's own wives have gone to another man—provided that other is not of a lower caste (*pratiloma*)—or have died while residing with another, the impurity lasts for only one day and night; it does not last for ten nights even though *sāpiṇḍya* (lineal relationship) exists.
Furthermore, there is no impurity regarding wives who have resorted to those of a lower caste (*pratiloma*).
This is because of the prohibition stated in the verse, "Heretics, those who have no refuge, and thieves" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.6).
Furthermore, this is because the words *bhāryā* (wife) and *putra* (son) are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*), and thus that which is their correlative [is implied].

This period of impurity applies only to him [the deceased] in his capacity as a wife or a son; however, for the *sapiṇḍas*, there is indeed an absence of impurity. For this very reason, Prajāpati said:
"In the case of wives dependent on others, and the sons of another's wife,

the agnates (gotriṇaḥ) become pure by bathing, while their father becomes pure in three nights alone. Thus, for one who has taken as his support a woman who is unchaste (svairiṇī) or similar, the impurity lasts for exactly three nights.
As Viṣṇu has said:
"When non-legitimate sons have been born or have died;
and when wives who previously belonged to another have given birth or have died. (ViDh 22.43)
In this context, a period of three nights is prescribed.

Furthermore, the application of these two periods—the three nights and the one night—is determined by whether the relatives are nearby or living in a distant place. When the father’s impurity lasts for three nights, then that of the sapindas lasts for one night.
As Marīci said:
"In the case of birth or death, there is a three-night period of impurity for those who have previously been married to others;
however, for sapindas, it is one day, whereas for the father, it is indeed three nights."
Furthermore, "residence" (nivāsa) refers to one's own country, so called because one dwells therein;
the king who is its master, the lord of the realm, on whichever day he passes away, that very day is the cause of purification.
If [the king] has passed away during the night, then [the impurity lasts] for the duration of that night alone.
For this very reason, Manu says:
"When a king has died, he who resides within his domain remains impure as long as the light [of the sun or stars] endures" (MDh 5.82).
"Accompanied by light" (*sajyotis*) means that the period of impurity lasts as long as there is light;
the meaning is: if during the day, until the sun is no longer visible, and if at night, until the stars are no longer visible. (3.25)
He now states the rules regarding impurity resulting from following a corpse:
"A Śūdra must never be followed by a Brāhmaṇa, nor a twice-born man (Kṣatriya or Vaiśya) ever.
Having followed [a corpse], one becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (YDh 3.26)

A twice-born person, such as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, or a Śūdra, who is not a sapinda relative of the deceased, should not follow the corpse. If, out of affection or other reasons, he does follow it,
then he becomes pure by bathing in water from a pond or similar source, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter (ghṛta).
Furthermore, since there is no authoritative basis for prescribing the consumption of ghee as a substitute for the act of eating, there is no prohibition against eating;
this [rule] pertains to those of equal or superior caste.
As Manu said:
"If one follows a deceased relative or even a non-relative out of one's own desire,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter" (MDh 5.103).
"Kinsmen" refers to those who share the same sapinda lineage as the mother;
however, there is no fault in following others because it has been prescribed for them.
But regarding following someone of a lower caste, one should refer to what is stated in other Smṛtis.
Regarding following after a Śūdra:
"But that Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, follows a deceased Śūdra being carried away, becomes pure after three nights."
Then, having crossed [the period] in three nights and gone to a river that flows into the ocean,
one becomes purified by performing a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consuming clarified butter.
Thus it was stated by Parāśara:
"In the case of following a Kṣatriya [corpse], however, it is for one day and night;

having touched a human bone that is oily, there is impurity for three nights, but if it is not oily, for one day and night; and in the case of following a corpse, it is for one [day and night]. (VaDh 23.24–25)
Thus it was stated by Vasiṣṭha.
Furthermore, upon following after a Vaiśya woman, the penance lasts for two nights (pakṣiṇī).
Likewise, when a Kṣatriya follows after a Vaiśya woman of his own caste (anantara), the penance is one day and night.

In the case of following a Śūdra at one interval [of caste], it should be inferred that for a Vaiśya following a Śūdra, the period is "two nights" (pakṣiṇī), and for one day (ekāha) in the case of following a Śūdra;
as has been stated by Pāraskara even regarding weeping.
"Having performed lamentation together with the relatives of the deceased,
one should avoid giving gifts, performing *śrāddha* rites, and other such acts for that day and night.
Likewise, even the wearing of ornaments should not be performed.
If the decoration of a deceased person who is not a sapinda has been performed, one who has touched it must undergo the Kṛcchra-pāda penance;
if this was done through ignorance, there should be a fast, and in case of incapacity, a bath is prescribed.
Thus, because a penance has been prescribed by Śaṅkha. (3.26)
He states an exception regarding impurity for sapindas in certain cases:
"There is no impurity for kings when they are slain by lightning, or for those killed in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for one whom the ruler desires [to be pure]. (YDh 3.27)

Although the word *mahī* denotes the entire sphere of the earth, nevertheless, because it is impossible for the whole earth to have a single lord, and because of the requirement of the plural form *mahīpatīnām*, it here indicates the political circles (*maṇḍalas*) that constitute parts of it. There is no period of impurity for those consecrated Kṣatriyas and others who are authorized to protect those [circles].
The meaning is that they (the relatives) should not observe impurity;
likewise, this applies to the relatives of those struck by lightning or those who have perished while protecting cows or Brahmins.
Those who are sapindas should also not observe impurity;

nor should it be observed by a king’s ministers, priests, and others whom the king desires to be free from impurity for the sake of accomplishing rites such as secret counsel or malevolent magic that cannot be achieved by anyone else.

And in this context, regarding that protection of subjects which is prescribed as the unique duty of kings, there is an absence of impurity only in those specific activities— such as the distribution of gifts, honors, and respect, and the administration of justice— without which such protection would not be possible; it does not, however, apply to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and other such rites.
And so Manu says:
"Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high office;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting his subjects" (MDh 5.95).
Gautama also stated:
"And for the sake of ensuring that the king’s business is not obstructed" (GDh 14.45);
thus, even for the king's servants and others, there is no impurity (*āśauca*).
As Pracetas has said:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, male and female slaves,
as well as kings and royal servants, are declared to be immediately pure."
Artisans are those such as cooks and the like;
craftsmen are those such as painters, tailors, and washermen.
And this [refers to] the absence of impurity.

When the question arises as to what its object is, since the specific action of each [individual] is brought to mind by words that have action as their cause, it should be understood as referring to that very [action].
For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "Not for kings in their royal duties."
Not during the vow of those under a vow, not during the sacrificial session of those performing a *sattra*, and not during the work of artisans by those who are artisans. (ViDh 22.48–51)
Thus, he demonstrates that the absence of impurity applies specifically to restricted objects.
It is also stated in the Śātātapīya:
"Śūdras who work for wages, as well as female and male slaves," and so forth.
"In bathing, in personal purification, and in household work, they are not defiled.
It should be understood that this purification of slaves and others applies to instances where contact has occurred because it was unavoidable. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:
A slave born in the house becomes pure immediately upon being touched; a slave maintained on food becomes pure after three days.
Likewise:
whatever a physician performs cannot be accomplished by another.
Therefore, a physician is always pure in touch. Thus [ends verse 3.27].
Furthermore:

"As well as for officiating priests, those who have been consecrated, and those performing sacrificial rites; likewise for those observing the *sattra* vow, those under a religious vow (*vratī*), celibate students (*brahmacārins*), givers, and knowers of Brahman. (YDh 3.28)

Immediate purification is prescribed for giving gifts, at a wedding, during a sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity, and even in the face of dire distress. (YDh 3.29) The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are those specifically appointed for the performance of the *vaitāna* and *aupāsana* rites.

The term *dīkṣitāḥ* refers to those consecrated by initiation (*dīkṣā*). For them, while performing sacrificial acts (*yajñiya*) pertaining to a sacrifice, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained; this is to be supplied as a recurring rule in all instances.
"The Vaitāna and Aupāsana rites must be performed by the initiated" (YDh 3.17).

Although the qualification [to perform the rite] is already established by this [preceding rule], the repetition is for the purpose of enjoining the sacrificer's own agency and for the purpose of purification through immediate bathing.
By the inclusion of the word *satra*, those engaged in an *anna-satra* (food-distribution sacrifice) are included because of its similarity to continuous performance.
[These] are indicated, for as for the principal performers of sacrificial sessions (*satrin*), they are already established by the very mention of those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*);
whereas by the word "vow-observers" (*vratin*), those engaged in penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, as well as those engaged in the penances and expiations of a *snātaka*, are meant.
Likewise, by the mention of the *brahmacārin*, there is the inclusion of both the performer of the *śrāddha* and the eater who are engaged in vows such as celibacy;
so it is stated in another Smṛti.
Even for one who constantly gives food, when penances such as the *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* have been performed,
or when the *kṛcchra-homa* and other rites have been completed, [the feeding of] Brahmins and others [is required].
Even for one who has undertaken a religious vow, there shall be no [impurity] for anyone else when the Brahmins have been invited and the rite of Śrāddha has commenced.
For a Brahmin who has been invited and is devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas and other such duties,
there is never any impurity as long as his ancestors remain within his body.
"Likewise for those engaged in penance, as well as for givers and knowers of Brahman.

Thus, for those performing long sacrificial sessions (*satrin*) and those observing vows (*vratin*), purification applies during the session (*satra*) and the vow (*vrata*) respectively, but not merely regarding their ritual acts or social intercourse.
And so says Viṣṇu: "Not [is there impurity] for those observing a vow while they are in the state of the vow."
"Not at the sacrifice of those performing a sacrificial session" (ViDh 22.49–50).
A *brahmacārin* is both the *upakurvāṇaka* and the *naiṣṭhika*;
he who is always only a giver and never a recipient.
That Vaikhānasa is designated by the term "giver" (dātṛ);
he is a knower of Brahman (brahmavid) and an ascetic (yati). And among these three classes of āśramins, [this applies] everywhere.
Purity [is maintained], because there is no evidence for any distinction;
furthermore, regarding a gift, there is no impurity in the substance previously intended for donation,
for the substance already intended is not defiled when being given.
Thus it is because of the *Kratusmaraṇa*.
Furthermore, a specific rule regarding this matter is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"In the case of an interval between marriage, festivals, sacrifices, and so forth, occurring during a period of death or birth impurity..."
"The remaining food should be given by others; it should not touch the donors or the eaters.
This applies to sacrifices such as the *vṛṣotsarga*, and to marriages where the necessary provisions have been previously prepared.
And so another Smṛti states:
"In a sacrifice where the materials have been gathered, in a marriage, and in the performance of a Śrāddha rite...
Here, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is the subject under discussion.

The mention of "marriage" (*vivāha*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for previously commenced sacramental rites (*saṃskārakarma*) such as the tonsure (*caula*) and initiation (*upanayana*).

The mention of "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is likewise an elliptical expression for previously commenced festivals (*utsava*) such as the consecration of a deity (*devapratiṣṭhā*) or the dedication of a grove (*rāma*), and not merely for the installation of a deity, the ritual release (*utsarga*), or marriage.

As it is said: "There is no impurity (*āśauca*) during the installation of a deity, at a ritual release, or at a marriage; nor during a disturbance of the country, nor even in times of dire distress" (ViDh 22.53–55).
Thus, from the Smṛti of Viṣṇu:
"In battle, that is, in war;
'when battle has arisen, he should cause the king to put on his armor' (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.12.1)."

Thus, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśuddhi*) in the ritual of girding the sword as prescribed by Āśvalāyana and others, as well as in the propitiatory oblations (*śāntihoma*) performed at the time of departure. When a region is afflicted by an epidemic such as smallpox or by a calamity such as fear of a king, there is immediate purity for the sake of performing propitiatory rites (*śāntikarman*) to pacify those disturbances.
Even in the absence of such a calamity, Paiṭhīnasi has stated that purification occurs in certain specific regions.

"In marriages, during times of distress, at sacrifices, on journeys, and in rites for visiting sacred sites (tīrtha), there is no impurity (sūtaka) in those cases; one should likewise perform rites such as sacrifices.

Likewise, even in the midst of dire calamity, when one is overcome by disease and is in a state of being on the verge of death, there is [no impurity] regarding gifts given for the purpose of pacifying misfortune.

Likewise, for one whose conduct is contracted and who has a large family, such as parents exhausted by hunger, there is immediate purification regarding the acceptance of gifts intended for their maintenance.
And this purification applies to one for whom the alleviation of distress cannot occur without immediate purity.
It pertains to one who does not store for the morrow;
but for one who has accumulated wealth sufficient for one day, it pertains to one day,
and for one who accumulates what is necessary for three days, it pertains to three days.

For one who has acquired enough goods for four days, there is a period of three days; for one who possesses a jar of grain (*kumbhīdhānya*), there is a period of four days; and for one who possesses a granary of grain (*kusūladhānya*), there is a period of ten days. Thus, for as long as a person remains free from distress, for that long is their period of impurity (*āśauca*), since this status is conditioned by the presence of adversity.
Regarding the contraction of the period of impurity (āśauca),
for this very reason Manu stated:
"He may be one who possesses a granary full of grain, or indeed one who possesses a jar full of grain."
With reference to the four types of householders described here in the verse, "He may be one who eats only every third day, or even one who does not store for the morrow" (MDh 4.7),
the ten-day period of impurity following a death is prescribed for those who are *sapiṇḍas*.
"Until the collection of the bones, [the impurity lasts] for three days or even one day" (MDh 5.59);
thus, four alternative rules have been set forth.

And regarding those for whom one is a *samānodaka* (a sapinda relative), there are contracted rules for impurity consisting of a two-day period (*pakṣin*), one day (*ekāha*), or immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*).
Those [rules] seen in other Smṛtis should be applied only as being conditioned by the restriction of one's means of livelihood.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this restriction regarding impurity (āśauca) applies only to those cases where there is distress without [the acceptance of gifts] and so forth, and not in all instances.
(Objection: All editions read *manuḥ* here, but the cited text is attributed to another *smṛti*. Furthermore, the *Mitākṣarā* never introduces a verse by using the nominative *manuḥ* alone.
"Manu always says [this]. I believe the word here should be *nanu*,
introducing the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument), to which a response is given several lines below.
It is said: Manu [states], "A Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with both the sacred fires and the Vedas becomes pure after one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas, however, after three days; and one devoid of both, after ten days."

Why is it not accepted that, based on a consideration of such statements from other Smṛtis, those engaged in study, knowledge, and ritual performance attain complete purification through periods of three days, one day, and so forth? It is replied:
"An impurity of ten days is prescribed for sapindas upon a death" (MDh 5.59)—
this [rule] serves as the injunction that "a Brahmin becomes pure after one day," precisely by setting aside the previously obtained general rule of ten days;

and since the setting aside [of a rule] is based on the impossibility [of its application], it continues until the impossibility is resolved by not overriding [the general rule] to the extent possible.
It is not yet sublated;

therefore, when there arises the expectation as to how much of it is to be sublated, one observes the specific sentence "endowed with the knowledge of fire" (*agnivedasamanvitaḥ*), which is capable of providing the required qualification.
One is restricted to the rites such as the Agnihotra and to Vedic study within the domain of the Agni and Veda,
but not to acts such as giving gifts;
in this way, the words "Agni" and "Veda" possess a connection with the action.

Otherwise, the statement "one becomes pure after one day for him by whom the rites achievable through the Agni and Veda have been performed" would merely serve as a qualification of a specific person; and this is not tenable. This being the case, [the following applies]:
"One should not interrupt rites performed with the sacred fires" (MDh 5.84);
"The Vaitāna and domestic rites, as well as those enjoined by the Śruti, must be performed" (YDh 3.17).
Thus, there is consistency with the statements of Manu and others, such as: "Immediate purification is for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa's cessation of Vedic study and other such duties. And so it is.
"Food from the family is not to be eaten for ten days in both cases"—
by such statements of Yama and others which prohibit eating and other activities for a period extending up to ten days, a contradiction is also established;
therefore, this prescription for the contraction of impurity (*āśauca*) is merely occasional and not [universal].
It is the object of all conventional transactions and so forth; enough with this excessive elaboration.

And this rule for immediate purification regarding the study of the Veda should be understood to apply to one who possesses many Vedas when suffering from the distress caused by neglecting the Veda (*brahmōjjha*);
however, for another, [the following applies]:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended"—
this is indeed a prohibition. Thus, among Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, whoever has been declared to have impurity for a certain duration must, immediately after that [period], [resume these acts].
One becomes pure by bathing, not merely by the lapse of that time;
as Manu has said:
"A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water, and a Kṣatriya by touching his mount and weapons."
"A Vaiśya [should carry] a goad or reins, and a Śūdra who has performed his duties [should carry] a staff. (MDh 5.99).
The meaning of this is as follows:
the phrase "who has performed his duties" (*kṛtakriya*) is to be connected with each [of the preceding castes].
A Brahmin who has completed the period of impurity, having performed the required rites and bathed, becomes pure by touching water with his hand;
the word "having touched" (spṛṣṭvā) refers specifically to the act of touching and not to bathing.
Or it may refer to sipping water (ācamana),
because that [act] is invariably connected with riding vehicles and so forth;
or else, "one who has performed the rites" means one who has performed the rites of water-libation and so on for as long as the period of impurity lasts.

Immediately thereafter, it is stated that a Brāhmaṇa or others become pure by touching water and so forth, which is prescribed as a substitute for the bath that occurs at the end of the period of impurity;
likewise, a Kṣatriya or others may become pure by touching their vehicle and so forth. (3.28–3.29)
Having described the purification that extends to the entire family, he now, in this context, states the purification that extends to each individual:
"If touched by those who are menstruating or impure, one should bathe; if touched by them, one should sip water;
and one should mutter water-mantras and the Gāyatrī once mentally. (YDh 3.30)
A menstruating woman,

those who are impure— such as a corpse, a *caṇḍāla*, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, and others— and those under ritual impurity due to a death; one who is touched by these [is considered impure].
One should bathe. Furthermore, if one has been touched by those who have been touched by a woman in her courses, by the impure, or by similar persons, one should sip water—that is, perform *ācamana*.
Having sipped water, one should mutter three mantra-passages beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which are addressed to the waters (*ābliṅga*).
Because the plural number finds its purpose only in reference to these three [cases].
Likewise, one should recite the Gāyatrī once mentally.

Now, an objection is raised: since the rule "one who has been touched by a woman in her courses shall bathe" uses the singular form *udakyā-saṃspṛṣṭaḥ*, how can there be a reference by the plural *taiḥ* ("by them")?
This is true;

however, there is no contradiction here, because the use of the plural "by them" (*taiḥ*) is intended to prescribe sipping water (*ācamana*) upon touching anyone who merely requires bathing— excluding those such as a menstruating woman (*udakyā*) and others— who have been touched.
And those who are eligible for bathing should be understood from other Smṛtis;
as Parāśara says:
"In the case of a bad dream, sexual intercourse, vomiting, purging, or after the act of shaving..."
"One should perform a ritual bath upon touching a funeral pyre, pus, a cremation ground, or bones.
Likewise, Manu says:
"One who has vomited or been purged, however, should bathe and then consume clarified butter."
"One should indeed perform *ācamana* after eating food; bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse" (MDh 5.144).

The rule regarding bathing for one who has had sexual intercourse refers to the period of the woman's fertile season (*ṛtukāla*); however, when one approaches her outside that time, the purification is the same as for voiding urine or feces.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati;
furthermore, bathing even outside the fertile period has been prescribed in another Smṛti for specific times:
"Sexual intercourse on the eighth and fourteenth days, during the day, or on a festival day [is forbidden]."
"Having performed [the rite], one should bathe with one's clothes on and purify oneself with the Vāruṇī hymns.
Likewise, Yama says:
"In the case of indigestion, when the sun has risen, after vomiting, or likewise when the sun has set..."
"In the case of a bad dream or contact with a wicked person, mere bathing is prescribed.
And likewise Bṛhaspati says:
"In the case of sexual intercourse and exposure to the smoke from a funeral pyre, immediate bathing is prescribed."
This refers to cases involving contact with the naked;
however, when touching a funeral pyre (*cityā*) and the like while clothed, one must bathe while still wearing clothes. As Cyavana said:
"A dog, an outcaste (*śvapāka*), the smoke from a corpse, and one who subsists on the property of the gods..."

Having touched a village priest, a seller of *soma*, pus, a funeral pyre, wood for a funeral pyre, liquor, a liquor vessel, a human bone still moist with fat, one who has touched a corpse, a woman in her courses,
a great sinner (*mahāpātakin*), or a corpse— one should immerse oneself in water with one's clothes on, emerge, touch fire, and recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should recite [the mantra]; having consumed ghee and bathed again, one should sip water three times. And this applies to cases where the act was intentional;
in other cases, merely bathing [is required].
Having unintentionally touched one who has handled a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, a funeral pyre, pus, or a menstruating woman, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing.
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Bṛhaspati;
in the same way, the equalization of the subject matter should be inferred in other cases as well that will be mentioned hereafter.
As Kaśyapa has said: "Having emitted semen at sunrise or sunset, upon the twitching of an eye, upon the ringing in the ear, upon climbing onto a funeral pyre, or upon touching putrid matter..."
And having bathed with one's clothes on, one should mutter the mantra "punar mana" and offer seven oblations of clarified butter with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Likewise, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Having touched a Devalaka, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."
A Brahmin devoted to the worship of the gods, seeking wealth, [should do so] for three years.
This man, known as a *devalaka*, is censured in matters concerning offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Likewise, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Having touched Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Lokāyatas, Nāstikas,
twice-born men who follow improper occupations, or Śūdras, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."
And from the indicative mark (liṅga) in the passage, "For that oblation would not lead to heaven if it were defiled by contact with a Śūdra," there is a prohibition against touching a Śūdra.
Likewise, Aṅgiras says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa steps upon the shadow of a dog-cooker (śvapāka), he should perform a bath there; by consuming clarified butter, he becomes pure."
Likewise, Vyāghrapāda says:
"One should avoid a Caṇḍāla and one who has fallen from his caste from afar;
within the distance of a cow-tail whisk, one should enter the water wearing one's clothes."
This refers to a situation involving an extremely narrow space;
however, in other cases, Bṛhaspati has stated:
"One yoke, two yokes, three yokes, and four yokes."
"And for a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and an outcast, [the bath] is progressively lower [in status].
Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Upon touching a crow or an owl, one must bathe with one's clothes on; upon voiding urine or feces without water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis."
And: "In the case of voiding urine or excrement where there is no water"—this refers to the failure to perform purification from urine and excrement for a long period of time.
Likewise, Aṅgiras says:
[One should avoid] vultures, crows, cats, donkeys, camels, dogs, and pigs...

"And having touched impure things, one should enter the water with one's clothes on. This bath caused by touching a cat is to be understood as applying during the time of ritual impurity from eating and during the performance of religious rites, according to established custom;
however, at other times, [the rule is different].
"A cat, a ladle, and the wind are always pure"—
this refers to the absence of bathing [required for these]. However, upon contact with a dog, bathing above the navel should be understood as necessary.
But if one is defiled by a dog above the navel, excluding the hands, there is only washing.
In that case, if the bathing occurred below [the navel], one becomes pure by washing [the body] and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
For it has been stated by that very [author]:
likewise, Jātūkarṇya has stated a specific rule regarding contact with birds:
"If a bird should touch any part of the body above the navel, excluding the hands..."
"One should perform a bath there; by washing the remainder, one becomes pure.
Regarding contact with impure substances as well, Viṣṇu has shown a specific rule:
"If one is defiled below the navel or on the forearms by bodily impurities, by *surā*, or by intoxicants (*madya*), that limb [should be cleansed] with earth and water."

Having washed and sipped water, one becomes pure. If defiled by anything other than these [excretions], one should wash that limb with earth and water and bathe; but if defiled in the sense organs by those [excretions], one should fast, bathe, and [use] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), as well as if defiled by the lips. (ViDh 22.77–80).
And this refers to contact with the impurities of another;
however, in the case of contact with one's own bodily filth, there is only washing even above the navel.
As Devala has said: "If one should touch the bone of a human being, fat, excrement, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or even the blood of another person..."
"Having bathed, wiped away the [bodily] smears and so forth, and sipped water (ācamana), one becomes pure;
by touching those very same [limbs] of one's own and performing a wiping, one becomes purified.
And likewise, Śaṅkha says:

"A man who has been touched above the navel by the mud or water of a street, or likewise by spittle and the like, becomes pure immediately by bathing. Thus it is said; and Yama has also stated a specific rule regarding this matter:
"But having entered a muddy place mixed with village refuse during the rainy season, one should apply three applications of clay to the shanks and twice as many thereafter to the feet.
The meaning is: "having entered a muddy place mixed with village refuse" refers to entering a place where there is a flow of village water together with mud.
However, there is no fault when mud and the like have been dried by the wind; for it is said: "Roadway mud and water touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows [are pure]."
Because it has been stated previously [in verse 1.197]: "And those built with baked bricks are purified by the wind alone";
a specific rule regarding bones has been declared by Manu.
"Having touched a human bone that still has marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana), touching a cow, or looking at the sun. (MDh 5.87).
This refers to the bones of those belonging to the twice-born classes.
Elsewhere, however, Vasiṣṭha states:
"Upon touching a human bone that is oily, there is impurity for three nights; but if it is not oily, there is impurity for one day and night" (VaDh 23.24–25).
Regarding non-human [bones], Viṣṇu states:

"Having touched the carcass of a five-toed animal— excluding those [meant] for consumption— as well as its bone if it still contains fat, one shall bathe and wear the previously washed garment" (ViDh 22.70–71).
In this manner, others who are entitled to perform ritual bathing should also be understood from other Smṛti texts.

Thus, because those worthy of bathing are numerous, the use of the plural "by them" (tair) to express their intention is not contradictory. Furthermore, the rule "one should bathe [if touched] by a menstruating woman or the impure" should be understood to apply to contact mediated by an insentient object such as a staff; however, in the case of contact mediated by a sentient being, the rule of Manu applies.
"Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing. (MDh 5.85).
But for the third degree of contact, there is merely the sipping of water (ācamana).
If one should touch someone who has touched that [polluted object], bathing is prescribed for him;
for those [objects] above that, sipping water (ācamana) is declared, as well as the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of articles.
This is because of the traditional teaching of Saṃvarta;
and this refers to cases where the act was not preceded by conscious intent.
However, in the case of intentional action, even for the third degree of relationship, bathing alone is required. As it has been said:

Gautama states: "Upon touching one who has touched an outcaste, a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse—or even one who has touched someone who has touched them—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on.
However, for the fourth person in the chain, there is merely sipping water;
for a man who touches a third person who has touched an impure object, he must simply sip water.
Having washed both hands and feet with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), one becomes pure.

Thus, from the Smṛti of Devala. Furthermore, regarding those who are impure, Devala has stated a specific rule concerning contact with a woman in her courses and others: "A dog-eater (śvapāka), an outcast (patita), one with a physical deformity (vyaṅga), a madman, or a corpse-bearer—"
A woman who has recently given birth, one who is menstruating, and one who is drenched with menstrual blood.
