"A person who touches domestic dogs, chickens, or pigs becomes pure immediately by bathing with his clothes on and his head uncovered. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, if one who is himself impure should touch these [beings] which are already impure, [he must likewise bathe].
"One is purified by the *upavāsa* (fast) or again by the *kṛcchra* (penance). Thus it is said.

A woman who causes an abortion [is purified] by the *kṛcchra*; however, the rule is that for those such as dog-cookers (*śvapāka*), the *kṛcchra* applies, whereas for dogs and the like, it is the *upavāsa*. (3.30)

Now, as an illustration regarding the purification of time, he enumerates the causes of purification mentioned in the section on the purification of substances, as well as those that will be described in this present section:
"Time, fire, action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, and water."
Repentance, fasting, and all these are causes of purification.
Just as fire and the other elements are causes of purification within their respective domains, so too is time— such as the ten-day period and so forth— a cause of purification,
because it is understood through the scriptures.
Regarding the state of being a cause of purification: fire is indeed a cause of purification, as it was stated [in verse 1.187]: "An object made of earth [is purified] by re-firing."
And ritual action (*karman*) is a cause of purification, as he will state: "from the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*) of the horse sacrifice" (YDh 3.244).
Likewise, clay is also a cause of purification, as it has been said:
"Water, ashes, or even clay should be applied for the sake of purification" (YDh 1.189).

Air, too, is a cause of purification, as it has been stated: "By air alone they are purified" (YDh 1.197). The mind also is a means for the purification of speech, as it is taught in scripture: "Speech speaks as impelled by the mind," and so forth.
And spiritual knowledge is the primary cause for the purification of the intellect, as he will state: "From the knowledge of the Lord [comes the purity] of the Knower of the Field" (YDh 3.34).

And austerity (*tapas*) refers to the *kṛcchra* and other penances as he will state: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the *prājāpatya* or the *kṛcchra* for an equal [duration]," and so forth (YDh 3.260).
Likewise, water also refers to the body and such, as he will say: "Water for the body" (YDh 3.33).

Repentance (*paścāttāpa*) also produces purification, as it has been stated: "By confession and by remorse" (MDh 11.228). Abstaining from food (*nirāhāra*) is likewise a means of attaining purification, as he will declare: "Having fasted for three nights and having recited [the mantra]," and so forth (YDh 3.301). // 3.31 //
Furthermore:

"The gift [of property] by those who perform what should not be done, the current of a river, earth and water for that which is to be purified, and renunciation indeed [are the purifiers] for the twice-born. (YDh 3.32)
Austerity is said to be the purifier for those who know the Vedas, forbearance for the wise, water for the body, silent recitation for those whose conduct is hidden, and truth for the mind.
For the elemental self, austerity and sacred knowledge are the purifiers; for the intellect, wisdom is the purification. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.33)
The purification of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) through the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara*) is considered supreme (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.34).
For those who perform forbidden acts and indulge in prohibited things, giving alone is the primary cause of purification, as he will explain: "or by giving sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient.
Just as a river whose banks have been defiled by impurities during the summer due to its scant water becomes pure again through the force of the monsoon rains that erode its banks.

Purification: Clay and water are the purifiers of substances that require cleansing, as it has been stated here: "The purification of that which is smeared with impurity is by means of clay and water, through the removal of the odor" (YDh 1.191).

Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), that is, the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*), is the purifier for the mental transgressions of the twice-born. Vedic study is the purifier for those who know the Vedas.
The cause of purification:
however, practices such as the *kṛcchra* penance are common to all, not only to those who know the Vedas;
for the wise, patience is tranquility.
For those who know the meaning of the Vedas,
water is the supreme body;
for those whose sins are concealed and whose faults are not publicly known, the recitation of hymns such as the Aghamarṣaṇa is [the supreme body].
The cause of purification is the means for achieving purity.
The mind consists of both true and false volitions; since it is impure due to its false volitions, a true and virtuous volition is indeed its purifier.
By the word *bhūta*, the aggregate of the body and sense organs— which are its modifications— is indicated.
That Self which exists therein through the conceit "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am one-eyed," or "I am deaf," is the *bhūtātman*.
For him, austerity (*tapas*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) are the causes of purification.

By the word "austerity" is meant that continuity (*anvaya*) of the self— which persists through many births or even within a single birth across the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— that remains distinct from the body and so forth.
And that is called *vyatireka* (distinction/negation),
as in the sentence "Seek to know Brahman through austerity" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2.1), which is intent upon establishing the distinction from the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*).
And by the word "knowledge" (vidyā), [it refers to] the Upaniṣadic [teachings]: "neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long" (BṛU 3.9.26);
"for this Self is unattached" (BṛU 2.5.14).
This refers to the knowledge produced by the scriptural passages concerning the investigation of the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou").
By these two [means], its purification occurs;

for the cognition of the self's distinction from the body and so forth—which is impure due to being characterized by doubt and error—is purified by knowledge in the form of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Purification:

The supreme purification, characterized by liberation, arises from the knowledge of the Lord in the form of direct realization produced by such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), [referring] to the field that has been purified by austerity and knowledge, which constitutes the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou"). Just as these...

Purifications are the supreme human goals; likewise, purification of time is even more appropriate. Thus, the mention of the purification of the elemental self (bhūtātman) and so forth is for the purpose of praise. 3.32, 3.33, 3.34.
Thus ends the section on impurity; now begins the section on duties in times of distress: "And even in a most severe time of distress, immediate purification is ordained" (YDh 3.19).

Thus, having stated the secondary rule of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) and others because the primary rules for impurity (*āśauca*) cannot be practiced in times of distress, he now, in that same context, describes an alternative means of livelihood (*vṛttyantara*) since the primary occupations such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*)— as mentioned in the verse "In times of distress, the Brāhmaṇa has the additional [means] of receiving gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching" (YDh 1.118)— are impossible to perform.
In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even that of a Vaiśya;
having crossed over that distress and having purified himself, he should then settle upon his own path.
(YDh 3.35) A "twice-born" means a Brāhmaṇa who, due to having a large family, is unable to subsist by his own proper livelihood, may [live] by the work associated with a Kṣatriya.
In times of distress, he may live by taking up arms and other such means;
if he is unable to subsist even by that, he may live by the occupations associated with Vaiśyas, such as trade and the like.
Nor by the livelihood of a Śūdra.
And so Manu says:
"If one should ask how it would be if one cannot subsist by either of these two..."

"Resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing, he may live the livelihood of a Vaiśya" (MDh 10.82). Likewise, even in times of distress (*āpad*), a person of a lower caste must not adopt the occupation of a higher caste; rather, a Brāhmaṇa may resort to the occupation of a Kṣatriya, a Kṣatriya to one related to a Vaiśya, and a Vaiśya to that of a Śūdra—thus, one may only adopt the occupation of the caste immediately below one's own.
For the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "If they cannot subsist by their own dharma, they should resort to an intermediate, inferior mode of livelihood, but never to one that is superior" (VaDh 2.22–23);
and the Brāhmaṇical mode of livelihood is indeed superior.
And so another Smṛti says:
"Between those two, there is no such thing as superior or inferior karma;
for, having set aside middling karma, they are common to all."
For a Śūdra, there exists no superior Brāhmaṇical duty;
likewise, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is no inferior Śūdra duty.
Furthermore, the intermediate duties of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are common to all castes when they have fallen into times of distress.
A Śūdra who has fallen into distress may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya or by crafts;
if a Śūdra cannot subsist through service to the twice-born, he may become a merchant.
Because it was previously stated [by Yājñavalkya]: "Or he may live by various crafts, practicing what is beneficial for the twice-born" (YDh 1.129);
and Manu has also shown a specific rule in this regard:
"Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served—these are the duties of artisans. (MDh 10.100).
By this very principle, the occupation of those born in the *anuloma* order should also be inferred to be that of the caste immediately following their own.

Thus, having overcome the calamity by adopting a livelihood of lower status than his own immediate predecessor, and having purified himself through the performance of penance, he should place himself back upon the path—
that is, upon his own proper conduct.
The meaning is that he should set it aside; or rather, this is the meaning:
he should place on the road wealth acquired through a censurable livelihood.
"One should cast it off. And so Manu says:
"The sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitations and burnt offerings."
"But for the sake of receiving [gifts], it is purified by renunciation and by austerity alone. (MDh 10.111) 3.35.
He states what must not be sold by a Brāhmaṇa, even when living by the occupation of a Vaiśya:
fruits, stones, linen, Soma, humans, cakes, creepers, sesame, boiled rice, liquids, alkaline substances, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (YDh 3.36)
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, and the grass of the sacrificial altar;
earth, leather, flowers, blankets made of goat’s hair, hair, buttermilk, poison, and soil;
silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, and lead— [these are the items that must not be sold]. (YDh 3.37)

Likewise, even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one should never sell vegetables, fresh herbs, oil-cakes, or the scent of animals; the phrase "one should not sell" is to be connected with each of these items individually.
Fruits refer to those such as plantains and the like, excluding jujube (*badara*) and *iṅguda* fruits.
As Nārada has said:
"Leaves that have fallen of their own accord, and fruits of the jujube and *iṅguda*..."
"Rajju" refers to cotton thread, provided that it is unaltered.
"Upala" refers to any stone, such as a gem, ruby, or the like.
"Kṣauma" is a cloth made from flaxen thread.
The mention of "linen" (kṣauma) is an illustration for woven cloth and the like;
as Manu has said:
"And all woven cloth, whether dyed or not— including hemp, linen, and wool— as well as fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs" (MDh 10.87). *Soma* is a specific type of creeper.
By the term "human being" (manuṣya), women, men, and neuter persons are included without distinction;
"cake" (apūpa) refers to any edible food such as *maṇḍaka* and the like.
Climbers (*vīrudhaḥ*) are creepers such as the cane (*vetra*) and the *amṛtā* plant;
sesame seeds (*tilāḥ*) are well known;
and the mention of boiled rice (*odana*) is an indication for food in general.
Flavors include molasses, sugarcane juice, sugar, and so forth.
Likewise, Manu states:
"Milk, honey, curd, ghee, oil, honey [from bees], molasses, and *kuśa* grass... (MDh 10.88).
"Alkaline substances" refers to barley-ash (yavakṣāra) and the like.

The mention of curd and milk is an indicative illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for their derivatives, such as whey (*mastu*), solid curd (*piṇḍa*), inspissated milk (*kilāṭa*), and thickened milk (*kūrcikā*).
This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Milk along with its products" (GDh 7.11).
The mention of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is an illustration for all oily substances such as oil and the like.
Water is well known. "Weapon" refers to the sword and so forth. The mention of *āsava* is an elliptical expression for intoxicants in general.
*Madhūcchiṣṭa* is beeswax.
Madhu is honey;
lākṣā is lac; barhis is kuśa grass; mṛd is earth, as is well known.
A hide made of antelope skin;
"flower" is well known;
[it is] made from goat's wool.
A *kambala* is a woolen blanket;
*keśāḥ* are the hairs attached to yaks and similar animals;
*takram* is buttermilk.
Poison refers to *śṛṅgī* and the like. Earth means land; for Sumantu records in his Smṛti: "Some [hold that] land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and oxen are always [impure].
Silk refers to clothing produced from cocoons.
"Nīla" refers to indigo juice.
By the mention of "salt" alone, *viḍa*, *sauvarcala*, *saindhava*, *sāmudra*, *somaka*, and artificial salts are included without distinction.
Meat is well known.
"Single-hoofed animals" refers to horses and the like.
The mention of lead is an indicative mark for iron in general.
All vegetables [are permitted] because there is no distinction made;
"herbs" (oṣadhayaḥ) are those that end with the ripening of their fruit.
Since the qualification "fresh herbs" (ārdrauṣadhayaḥ) is employed, there is no fault regarding dried ones.
Oil-cake is well known. "Wild animals" refers to forest animals;
and all wild animals, as well as fanged beasts and birds. (MDh 10.89)
Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*.
"Fragrances" refers to sandalwood, agallochum, and so forth.
A Brāhmaṇa living by all these [means] through the occupation of a Vaiśya [is permitted].
One should never sell it;
however, there is no fault in the case of a Kṣatriya or others.
For this very reason, Nārada stated:
"In the occupation of a Vaiśya, milk and curd are not to be sold by a Brāhmaṇa"—thus the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" was made [in the preceding rule]. (NSm 1.57). [Verses 3.36, 3.37, 3.38]
He states an exception:
"For the sake of dharma, sesame seeds may be exchanged for grain of equal value" (YDh 3.39cd).
If necessary religious duties, such as the *pākayajña* sacrifices, cannot be accomplished due to a lack of the rice and other grains required for their performance, then [this exchange is permitted].
Sesame seeds should be exchanged for grain;
"equal to that" means one measure (*droṇa*) measured by another measure, such that they are equal in quantity to that grain.
And so Manu says:
"A farmer, having himself produced [sesame] through cultivation as he desires, may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long. (MDh 10.90)
The mention of "dharma" (religious duty) is an elliptical expression intended to include necessary medicine and so forth;
for this very reason, Nārada says:
"In cases of incapacity, for the sake of medicine, and likewise for the purpose of a sacrifice..."
"If sesame seeds must necessarily be sold, they should be exchanged for an equal amount of grain. (NSm 1.62) If one sells them otherwise, then there is a fault:
"Whatever he does with sesame seeds other than for food, for anointing the body, or for giving as a gift..."
"Having become a worm in a dog's excrement, one sinks down along with the ancestors," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 10.91).
Furthermore, one indeed undergoes rebirth among those of the same caste.
"Flavors may be exchanged for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;

prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal. (MDh 10.94) Prepared food means cooked food, and that should be bartered for other prepared food.
But in the reading *kṛtānnaṃ cākṛtānnena*, it means that prepared food (*siddham annam*) is to be exchanged for unprepared food (*akṛtānnena*), such as raw rice and the like. (3.39)
He states the fault incurred by transgressing the aforementioned prohibitions:
"Lac, salt, and meat, as well as ghee, curd, and liquor, are causes of downfall when sold; however, [the sale of] these [latter items] makes one low-caste. (YDh 3.40)
Lac, salt, and meat, when sold, cause immediate downfall and bring about the loss of the duties of the twice-born; however,
milk and similar items merely cause a degradation of caste, resulting in equality with a Śūdra.
In the sale of commodities other than these, one attains equality with a Vaiśya;
as Manu has said:
"One falls immediately through the sale of meat, lac, and salt."
A Brahmin becomes a Śūdra in three days by selling milk.
"By selling other goods that are not fit for sale here out of desire, a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights. (MDh 10.92–93) 3.40.
Moreover:
A Brahmin who, having fallen into distress, accepts or eats whatever may come his way, is not defiled by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.

But he who, being destitute due to the ruin of his family and fallen into distress, does not wish to enter upon the occupation of a Kṣatriya or the occupation of a Vaiśya— even if he accepts gifts from various sources, whether from those who are low, lower, or lowest, or even eats their food, he is not tainted by sin or evil.
Because in that state of calamity, he is authorized to accept gifts from improper persons and so forth, he is equal to fire and the sun;
just as fire and the sun are not defiled even when performing inferior purifications, so too this person, though fallen into calamity, is not defiled—
it is by this much alone that his similarity [to them] is established.
By speaking thus, it is shown that for one fallen into calamity, even though the practice of another's duty may be double [the effort], the performance of one's own duty alone is primary.
And so says Manu:
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another;
by resorting to the duty of another, a Brahmin falls immediately from his caste.
Thus [it is said]. (MDh 10.97) //3.41//
Furthermore:

agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, trade by cart, mountain-mining, service to others, marsh-land cultivation, and the king—these are the means of livelihood in times of distress, along with begging for alms. (YDh 3.42)

Because of the qualification "means of livelihood in times of distress" (*āpattau jīvanāni*), that specific occupation which was prohibited for anyone among those such as farmers and others during non-distress conditions is hereby permitted for them.
For example, in times of distress, agriculture performed by oneself— which is the occupation of a Vaiśya— is permitted for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
In this way, it is indeed permitted; likewise, crafts and so forth are also permitted for him. "Craft" refers to cooking and the like; "wages" refers to the state of being a servant.
"Learning" refers to teaching for wages and the like;
"usury" is the lending of goods for the sake of interest.
These are permitted when performed by oneself.
A cart is a means of livelihood by way of transporting grain and other goods for hire;
a mountain is a livelihood by way of its grass and fuel;
service is the following of another's will.
Anūpa is a region abounding in grass, trees, and water; likewise, there is the begging of kings,
and even for a *snātaka*, the practice of mendicancy.
These are the means of livelihood in times of distress.
And so Manu says:
"Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture."
Mountains, alms, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood.
Thus [ends the section]. (MDh 10.116) 3.42.
When even agriculture and other such means of livelihood are impossible, how then can one live? To this he says:
"Having fasted for three days while hungry, one may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa;
having received it, it must be reported according to dharma by the person so engaged. (YDh 3.43)

In the absence of grain, having remained hungry for three nights without eating, he may take from a non-Brāhmaṇa— a Śūdra— in his absence from a Vaiśya, and in his absence from a Kṣatriya of low occupation, an amount of grain sufficient for one day. As Manu has said:
"Likewise, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time, one may take [wealth] from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow. (MDh 11.16).
And thus, after the acceptance [of the gift], that which was taken away must be reported truthfully as it happened according to dharma, if...
"How indeed has this been stolen by you, an atheistic master?"—thus he is interrogated.
As Manu said:
"Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found..."
"But that [instruction] must be told to him who asks, provided he does indeed ask. (MDh 11.17) 3.43.
This other matter concerning association with trustworthy persons is prescribed for the king:
having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, study, austerity, and family, the king shall determine his righteous livelihood. (YDh 3.44)
For one who is sinking down, overwhelmed by hunger, [one should consider] his livelihood, his conduct, his family, his lineage, his character, and his personal qualities.

Having examined their learning— meaning the hearing of the scriptures— and their study— meaning the study of the Vedas— as well as their austerity, such as the *kṛcchra* penance and so forth, the king [should appoint them].
One should adopt a mode of livelihood that does not deviate from the Dharma;
otherwise, there is fault for him.
And so says Manu:
"But that king in whose realm a *śrotriya* perishes from hunger, his kingdom perishes as well, afflicted by famine and disease. (MDh 7.134) 3.44.
Thus ends the section on duties in times of distress;
now begins the section on the duties of forest-dwellers.
Among the four stages of life (*āśrama*), the duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) have been expounded.
Now, in order to set forth the duties of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) which have reached their proper occasion, he says:
"Having entrusted his wife to his son, or followed by her, [he should go] to the forest."
The forest-dweller, observing celibacy, shall go forth with his sacred fire and his domestic hearth.
One who stands or moves about in the forest with great persistence and according to restrictive rules is a *vanaprastha*;
such a person is indeed a *vānaprastha*.

The lengthening of the vowel in *saṃjñāyām* [is explained] by resorting to a future state of affairs; that is to say, "intending to depart for the forest. He is one by whom his wife has been entrusted to his son—that is, one by whom his wife has been placed or deposited with his son with the words, "She is to be supported by you."
He was addressed in that manner:
"If she herself also desires to go to the forest out of a longing to attend upon her husband, then he should be followed by her."

Or he may go accompanied [by his wife]. Likewise, a *brahmacārī*—one whose semen is drawn up (*ūrdhvaretas*)—may go to the forest either together with the *vaitāna* fires or together with the *aupāsana* fire, which is the domestic fire.
By stating "having entrusted his wife to his sons," it is shown that one who has fulfilled the stage of the householder (*gārhasthya*) is qualified for the forest-dweller's life (*vānaprastha*).
And this has been stated with reference to the position that there is a cumulative succession of the stages of life;
otherwise, [the rule would be] "one who has not violated his student discipline may enter whichever [stage] he desires" (VaDh 7.3).
Thus, even one who has not performed the duties of a householder is indeed entitled to dwell in the forest;
and this entry into the forest is for one whose body is worn out by old age or who has produced a grandson.
As Manu said:
"When a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair,
or even the offspring of his offspring, he should then take refuge in the forest" (MDh 6.2).
And this entrusting of the wife to the sons applies to one whose wife is living; for even in the case of one whose wife has died, Āpastamba and others prescribe forest-dwelling (ĀpDh 2.22.6–24).
Therefore, as for the injunction regarding the re-establishment of the sacred fires, namely, "having cremated [the wife] with the Agnihotra fire" (YDh 1.89), [this refers to that specific case].
That refers to the case where one's impurities (*kaṣāya*) regarding sense objects have not yet matured.

Regarding the rule "he who possesses the fire and the sacrificial hearth" (YDh 3.45), even there, when the *ardhādhāna* has been performed, he should go to the forest accompanied by both the Śrauta fires and the Gṛhya fire.
But in the case of the first establishment of the sacred fires (*sarvādhāna*), [the journey] is performed by means of the *śrauta* fires alone.

If, for some reason—such as the eldest brother not having established the fires—the *śrauta* fires have not been established, then one should distinguish the case thus: "He should go forth with only the domestic fire (*sopāsana*)."
And the bringing of the fire is for the purpose of accomplishing the rites such as the Agnihotra, which are to be performed after that [initiation];
therefore Manu says:
"And he should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the rule, not omitting the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices on their appointed days as far as his ability permits" (MDh 6.9).
Now, one might object: how can the performance of rites such as the Agnihotra be possible for one who has entrusted his wife to his son and is separated from her?
Because of the restrictive rule regarding joint entitlement, which states that "one must sacrifice together with one's wife," this is indeed true.
However, in this case, the entitlement is postulated as being independent of her [the wife] solely by virtue of the injunction for the depositing of the wife. Just as...

For, by the force of the injunction regarding exclusion— stating that "if on the day of the vow the wife is menstruating, one should perform the sacrifice after excluding her"— there is independence from her [in that context].
Alternatively, there is no contradiction because the wife gives her consent to the husband precisely as he is setting out for the forest.

Furthermore, one should not suspect that for one who has renounced his wife, there is likewise an absence of the *agnihotra* and other rites— as there is for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), a widower, or one who has departed for the forest—
because the scriptures declare this [obligation] to be non-optional (*apākṣika*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that even for one who has violated his vow of celibacy (*brahmacārin*) or for one who is impotent (*vidhura*), there is no entitlement to perform rites accomplished by fire;
for we observe that after the fifth month, one who has established the *śrāvaṇika* fire does have such entitlement.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha), with matted hair, clothed in rags or skins, must not tread upon land ploughed by the furrow;
he should gather roots and fruits that have not been cultivated,
remain chaste (ūrdhvaretas), be patient in disposition, give gifts but never accept them, and after five months, maintain the sacred fires according to the Śrāvaṇika rite.

For the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "Having established the sacred fires, one who dwells at the foot of a tree should make offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and men; he shall go to eternal heaven" (VaDh 9.112).
"Cīra" means a piece of cloth or bark.

He should stand upon land ploughed by a plough; he should not dwell upon a field that has been sown. This means [he should follow] the path prescribed by the Śruti and the Veda, and not the worldly one. (3.45)
It has been stated that the rule "he should go forth with the *agni* and the *upāsana*" (YDh 3.45) is for the purpose of performing the Śrauta and Smārta rites accomplished by means of fire;
regarding this, [the author] now states a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*).
Self-possessed, wearing a beard, matted hair, and body hair, he should satisfy the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents with food grown without the use of the plow.
The mention of the "plow" (phāla) is an illustration intended to include all implements used for cultivation.
One should satisfy the sacred fires with wild rice, bamboo seeds, śyāmāka, and the like, which grow in unplowed fields; one should perform those rites that are accomplished by means of the fire.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that the giving of alms should also be performed with those very same items.
He should perform [these rites]; likewise, by that very same means, he should satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and guests— the word "api" (also) implying living beings as well—
and likewise his dependents, the word "ca" (and) implying those who have arrived at his hermitage as well.
And so Manu says:
"Whatever his food may be, from that he should offer the bali-oblation and alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms. (MDh 6.7)

Having thus performed the five great sacrifices, he himself should eat only the remnants of that [offering], having offered to the deities the most pure sacrificial oblation of wild forest produce; he should consume the remainder for himself, as well as salt prepared by his own hand. (MDh 6.12)
This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu.
"Self-made" refers to saline soil and salt.
Thus, there is a restriction regarding the food of sages for the purpose of eating as well as for purposes such as medicinal application.
The abandonment of village food is established by implication;
for this very reason, Manu says:
"Having completely renounced village food and all personal belongings... (MDh 6.3).

But surely, since the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices require cultivated materials such as rice, how can there be a renunciation of them? Nor should it be said that [the rule applies] because of the statement: "and the fires with unploughed [grain]" (VaDh 9.3).
Thus, by the force of this specific statement, there would be a sublation of the *vrīhi* and other grains;
however, it is improper for even a *smṛti* concerning a specific case to sublate a *śruti*,
and because the injunction regarding what is not ploughed can also be understood as referring to rites accomplished by means of the *smārta* fires.
This is indeed true;
however, since even rice and other grains can be grown without being ploughed, there is no contradiction here.
For this very reason it was said:
Manu says:

"With pure forest grains fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons, he should separately prepare the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the cooked rice offerings (caru) according to the prescribed rules. (MDh 6.11)

Although it is already established that wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other such grains are inherently pure once produced, the term "pure" (*medhya*) is mentioned again for the purpose of including *vrīhi* and other grains suitable for sacrifice;
for "medha" means sacrifice, and that which is fit for it is "medhya.
Likewise, "beards" refers to the facial hairs, and "matted locks" refers to those grown in the form of matted hair.
And he should maintain his hair on the head as well as the hair in the armpits and other parts; the mention of "hair" (roma) is also an elliptical indication for the nails. Thus says Manu:
"He should always wear matted locks, as well as a beard, body hair, and nails. (MDh 6.6).
Likewise, being self-possessed, he should be devoted to the contemplation of the Self. (3.46)
He states the rule for the accumulation of the aforementioned materials:
"One should accumulate wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been accumulated, one should discard it in the month of Āśvayuja. (YDh 3.47)
One should accumulate a sufficient amount of wealth for the performance of visible and invisible rites, such as eating and sacrificing, pertaining to a single day;
or one may accumulate what is sufficient for the rites pertaining to a month, six months, or a year, but not more than that.
If, even when performed in this manner, it somehow exceeds [the required amount],
then one should abandon that excess in the month of Āśvayuja.
Moreover:
self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts, devoted to sacred study, disposed toward giving, and intent on the welfare of all beings; YDh 3.48.
He is self-controlled and free from pride;
he is habituated to bathing during the three ritual periods— morning, midday, and afternoon—
and likewise turns his face away from accepting gifts.
By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that he should also refrain from officiating at sacrifices and similar activities.
He should be devoted to his own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), delighting in the practice of the Vedas;
likewise, he should be habituated to giving fruits, roots, alms, and so forth, and intent upon acting for the welfare of all living beings. (3.48)
Furthermore:

One who uses his teeth as a mortar, one who eats only what is ripened by time, or one who grinds with a stone, may perform ritual acts and other rites using the oils obtained from fruits, whether they pertain to the Śruti or the Smṛti. (YDh 3.49)
The teeth themselves are the mortar; that which has teeth as its mortar is a "dantolūkhalika" (one who uses his teeth as a mortar).

That which is ripened by time alone is "kālapakva" (time-ripened), such as wild rice, bamboo seeds, śyāmāka grain, and so forth, as well as the fruits of the jujube, iṅguda, and others; one whose habit is to eat such things is a "kālapakvāśī" (eater of what is ripened by time). The word "vā" (or) [indicates an alternative].
"He may either eat food cooked by fire or eat only what is ripened by time"—
this is the intended meaning of Manu's statement regarding the practice of eating food cooked by fire;
or he may be one who grinds his food with a stone.
That which is crushed with a stone and pounded is described as such;
likewise, there are ritual acts prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as activities for visible purposes such as eating, anointing, and so forth.

One should prepare unctuous substances from the fruits of trees known for their purity, such as the *lakucha* and *madhūka*, and not from clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like. Thus says Manu: "One should eat unctuous substances produced from pure trees that originate from fruits" (MDh 6.13). 3.49.
To preclude the practice of eating twice a day which is prescribed for human purposes, he says:
"One should pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts or always subsist by Kṛcchra penances;
or one may eat when a fortnight has passed, or when a month has passed, or when a day has passed. (YDh 3.50)
He should pass his time with Cāndrāyaṇas, whose characteristics will be described below,
or he should spend his time with Kṛcchras such as the Prājāpatya; or else, he may eat only when a fortnight consisting of fifteen days has elapsed.
One should eat at night after a month or a day has passed; by the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that one may also follow the practice of eating only every fourth mealtime, and so forth,
as Manu has said:
"One should eat food at night or by day, having procured it according to one's ability; or one may eat at every fourth mealtime, or even at every eighth mealtime. (MDh 6.19).
Regarding these regulations of time, there is an option based on one's own capacity. (3.50)
Furthermore:

One should sleep on the ground at night, being pure; during the day, one should pass the time by standing on tiptoe, or by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or likewise by the practice of yoga. (YDh 3.51)
Except for the occasions of eating and walking about, one should sleep at night pure and self-restrained; one should neither sit nor stand [during that time].
Since sleeping during the day is prohibited because it serves only the purpose of a human being, this [injunction] is not intended merely to preclude that.
Likewise, he should sleep on the ground itself;
and that [sleeping] should be on the bare ground, not on a bed or similar object covered by bedding.
During the day, however, he should wander about on his tiptoes.
One should pass the day by means of standing, sitting, or various postures, movements, and transitions— alternating between standing for some time and sitting for some time—
or else by the practice of yoga.
And so Manu says:
"Various Upaniṣadic scriptures for the sake of the self's perfection" (MDh 6.29).
"For the sake of the self's perfection" means for the attainment of the state of Brahman.

From the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it may be understood that one should act according to the traditional law of Manu: "Or he should pass the day by trampling the earth, or by rolling about on the ground, or by standing on his tiptoes. (MDh 6.22).
With the forefeet, that is, the tips of the feet. // 3.51 //
Furthermore:

In the summer he should perform penance by standing amidst five fires; during the rainy season, he should sleep on the bare ground; and in the winter, he should wear wet clothes, or otherwise practice austerity according to his ability. (YDh 3.52)

Based on the observation that the year consists of three seasons—summer, the rainy season, and winter—one should stand in the midst of five fires: four fires in the four directions during the four months beginning with Caitra in summer, and the sun above. Thus, one should remain between these five fires.
Likewise, during the rainy season, in the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa,
he should sleep on the bare ground (sthaṇḍila), dwelling upon the earth without protection against the falling rain.
During the winter, in the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa...
One should wear wet clothes;
or, if one is unable to perform such ascetic practices, one should practice penance according to one's own capacity. One should strive in such a way that the body becomes emaciated.
For it is stated in the traditional law of Manu: "Practicing most rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body" (MDh 6.28). 3.52.
Furthermore:
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood—toward both of them, he remains equally free from anger and free from satisfaction. (YDh 3.53)

One should not become angry with whoever pricks one's various limbs or causes them pain with thorns and the like; nor should one feel gratified by whoever anoints one with sandalwood and the like to bring pleasure.
Rather, [one should maintain equanimity] toward both of them.
One should be equanimous; one should remain indifferent. // 3.53 //
Regarding one who is incapable of performing the service of the sacred fires, he says:

"Or, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, dwelling among trees and eating moderately, he should beg for alms only for the sake of sustenance from the houses of forest-dwellers. (YDh 3.54)
Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, he is one whose dwelling is in trees—that is, one whose hut is in a tree itself. He should eat sparingly, taking only a small amount of food;
by the use of the word "also," it is implied that he may subsist on fruits and roots as well.
As Manu has said:
"Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits" (MDh 6.25).
The sage, engaged in the vow of silence,
should practice begging for alms at the houses of forest-dwellers only to such an extent as is necessary to sustain life, in the event that fruits and roots are unavailable. (3.54)
But when that is impossible, or when he is overcome by disease, what should be done? To this he says:
"Or, having brought eight morsels from a village, he should eat while restrained in speech" (YDh 3.55ab).
Or, having brought alms from a village, being restrained in speech—that is, observing silence—he should eat eight morsels.
The restriction to the food of sages is rendered null by the rule for village alms;
this occurs when it is not possible to sustain life with only eight mouthfuls.
In that case, it should be understood as stated in another Smṛti: "The alms-food of a sage consists of eight mouthfuls; for a forest-dweller, sixteen."
Regarding one who is incapable of performing all [the prescribed rites], he says:
"Subsisting on air, he should go toward the north-east until the decay of his body" (YDh 3.55cd).
Alternatively, he whose food is air alone is a *vāyubhakṣa*; such a person should go toward the north-eastern direction, that is, the quarter of Īśāna, until—*ā*—[the end].
Until the exhaustion of his physical strength—*varṣman* meaning the body—he should proceed with a straight course until his fall. As Manu says:
"Or, having set out toward the unconquerable direction, he should go straight forward" (MDh 6.31).
If he is unable even to undertake the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*), he should perform such acts as leaping from a precipice;
for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating that a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should pursue the path of heroes (*vīrādhvāna*) by entering fire or water or leaping from a precipice.

Furthermore, the duties such as ritual bathing and sipping water (*ācamana*), which were prescribed in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and elsewhere, also apply to him provided they are not contradictory.
For there is the traditional teaching of Gautama: "And this is not inconsistent with the subsequent [stages]" (GDh 3.10).
Thus, one should practice everything previously mentioned, beginning with the *aindava* vow and ending with the *mahāprasthāna*, culminating in the abandonment of the body.
One attains veneration in the world of Brahmā.
As Manu said:
"Having cast off the body by means of one or another of these practices of the great seers..."
"Free from sorrow and fear, the Brahmin is glorified in the world of Brahmā" (MDh 6.31).
The "world of Brahmā" (brahmaloka) is a specific location and not the eternal Brahman,
because the word *loka* is not used [in that sense] there.

Furthermore, because liberation is not accepted as occurring apart from the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama), one should not suspect that the attainment of that state [of Brahman] occurs through the practice of yoga, on the grounds that the injunction for the meditation on Brahman would otherwise be untenable. This is because of the scriptural statement: "Or else, by the practice of yoga."
For that [liberation] is also logically possible as being for the sake of attaining *sālokya* and other states;
therefore, in the Śruti, after beginning with "There are three branches of dharma," [it continues].
Sacrifice, study, and giving constitute the first;
austerity alone constitutes the second; and the student of sacred knowledge who dwells in the teacher’s household [constitutes the third].

The third [section]: having described the nature of the householder, the forest-dweller, and the perpetual celibate by stating that "one who excessively degrades himself in the family of the teacher" [is so], and having stated that all these [three] attain worlds of merit— saying "he who is established in Brahman attains immortality" (ChU 2.23.1)— [it continues].

Thus, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is stated that the attainment of immortality characterized by liberation belongs exclusively to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) who is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*). As for the statement: "Even a householder who performs ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and speaks the truth is liberated" (YDh 3.205), [it refers to a specific qualification].
Thus, it should be understood that even the presentation of liberation for a householder refers to one who has experienced the life of a wandering mendicant in a previous existence. (3.55)
Thus ends the section on the duties of forest-dwellers;
now begins the section on the duties of ascetics.
Having set forth the duties of the *vaikhānasa*, he now introduces the duties of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), which follow in due order.

Having performed from the forest or from the home the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (sārvavedasadakṣiṇā), and having at its conclusion internalized those fires within himself; he who has studied the Vedas, who performs recitation, who has sons, who gives food, and who maintains the sacred fires— YDh 3.56.
And according to his capacity, the performer of sacrifices should set his mind on liberation, and not otherwise.

(YDh 3.57) For as long a time as it takes for the body to be withered by intense austerity such that the ripening of the impurities of the objects of the senses occurs, and furthermore, no suspicion of the arising of intoxication is raised—for that duration he should dwell in the forest; immediately thereafter, he should set his mind on liberation.
By the words "forest" (vana) and "house" (gṛha), the hermitages associated with them are indicated;
and by the word "liberation" (mokṣa), the fourth stage of life, which has liberation as its sole fruit, is indicated.

Alternatively, immediately after the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), one should direct the mind toward liberation (*mokṣa*). By this, it is indicated that the previously mentioned position of the combination of the four stages of life (*caturāśrama-samuccaya*) is merely optional (*pākṣika*). Accordingly, an alternative is heard in the Jābāla Śruti:

Having completed the life of a religious student, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; and having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce the world.
"Or otherwise, one may renounce even from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), or from the householder's life (*gṛha*), or from the forest-dweller's life (*vana*).
Likewise, Gautama has shown the sublation of the subsequent stages of life after the householder's stage:
"The teachers [maintain] that there is only one stage of life, because the householder's stage is explicitly prescribed" (GDh 3.36).
Since all these positions— whether of conjunction, option, or sublation— are rooted in Vedic scripture (*śruti*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) according to one's own inclination.

Therefore, that which has been stated by certain self-styled scholars— that because the states of perpetual celibacy (*naiṣṭhikatva*) and so forth are based on Smṛti, they are sublated by the Vedic state of the householder (*gārhasthya*), or else they apply only to those such as the blind or the impotent who are ineligible for the householder’s life— that should be disregarded as being based on a failure to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*).

Furthermore, just as the lame and others lack qualification for Vedic rites due to their inability to perform the Viṣṇukramaṇa steps, the inspection of the clarified butter (ājya), and so forth, so too they lack the capacity for Smṛti-prescribed duties such as carrying the water-pot and wandering for alms; how then can the maintenance of the lifelong stages of life (naiṣṭhika-āśrama) and the like be intended for the lame and others?
And in this stage of life, only the Brahmin has the entitlement; having internalized the sacred fires within himself, the Brahmin should go forth from his home into the wandering life. (MDh 6.25)
Likewise,

because Manu establishes the entitlement of the Brāhmaṇa through both the opening and the conclusion of the passage— "Thus has this fourfold dharma of the Brāhmaṇa been declared to you" (MDh 6.97)— it follows that [the rules apply specifically to him].

Based on the Vedic text, "Brahmins go forth [into the life of a wandering ascetic]," the entitlement belongs only to the *agrajanman* (the first-born, i.e., the Brāhmaṇa) and not to all twice-born (*dvijāti*) castes.

Others, however, maintain that the entitlement belongs to all twice-born castes because they are the subject under discussion and because of the author of the Sūtras' statement: "For the three castes, having studied the Veda, there are four stages of life (*āśrama*)."

When he goes forth from the forest or from the home, then— having performed that sacrifice (iṣṭi) dedicated to Prajāpati, which is called *sārvavedasī* because its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*)— and at the conclusion of that rite, having internalized those ritual fires (*vaitāna-agni*) within himself according to the procedure prescribed in the Śruti, [the word] "and" (*ca*) implies...

Having first performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) on the full moon day during the northern course of the sun, and having completed the preparatory rites and so forth as prescribed by Baudhāyana and others— such as offering eight or twelve *śrāddha* ceremonies with a purified body—
one who has studied the Vedas, is devoted to recitation (*japa*), has begotten a son, and has bestowed wealth upon the poor, the blind, and the wretched [should proceed].

Having become a giver of food according to his ability, and having— provided there is no obstacle such as being the eldest son or the like— performed the rites of establishing the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and performed the obligatory and occasional sacrifices (*nitya-naimittika-yajña*), he should set his mind on liberation and enter the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*); not otherwise.
By this, he shows that a householder who has not discharged the three debts lacks the qualification for renunciation;
as Manu said:
"Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation;
but by pursuing liberation without having discharged them, one goes downwards.
(MDh 6.35) However, when one renounces from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), then the rule regarding the procreation of offspring and so forth does not apply.
Because one who has not yet taken a wife has no authority there,
and because marriage is motivated by passion.
Nor should it be suspected that the injunction for the discharge of the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*) itself implies the acquisition of a wife; for,
just as with the rules regarding the acquisition of wealth through learning, that injunction does not imply [the taking of a wife] when a wife is available through other means.
But does not the passage, "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: to the sages through studentship, to the gods through sacrifice,
and to the ancestors through progeny" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5), show that even for one who has just been born, the production of offspring and so forth are mandatory?
Not so;
for one who has merely been born, and has not yet performed the taking of a wife and the consecration of the sacred fires, is not entitled to perform sacrifices and the like.
Therefore, it is one who is being born that becomes the qualified agent.
The meaning of this is that a Brāhmaṇa and others should perform sacrifices and other such rites;

therefore, for one who has been initiated, the study of the Veda is absolutely mandatory, and for one who has taken a wife and established the sacred fires, the procreation of offspring is also required—thus it is faultless. (3.56–3.57)
Having thus defined the qualified person, he states his duties:
"Beneficent toward all beings, tranquil, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot, delighting in solitude, having renounced the world, and seeking alms, he should resort to a village. (YDh 3.58)
He is beneficially indifferent toward all beings, whether they act kindly or unkindly;
he does not, however, practice active beneficence, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "He should abstain from both injury and favor" (GDh 3.24–25).
"Peaceful" means one whose external and internal faculties have ceased their activity.
He possesses three staffs, thus he is a "tridaṇḍī. And those staffs should be made of bamboo.
After the Prājāpatya sacrifice, he should hold three bamboo staffs reaching to his head in his right hand and a water-pot with water in his left, according to the observation of another Smṛti;
or he may hold a single staff.

According to the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana, "Whether he be a single-staffed ascetic or a triple-staffed ascetic," one devoted to the knowledge of Brahman should enter the fourth stage of life.
Whether carrying a single staff or a triple staff, he is free from all attachments.
And because it is seen thus in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Likewise, the wearing of the topknot (*śikhā*) is also optional;
he may be either shaven-headed (*muṇḍa*) or wear a topknot" (GDH 3.22).
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama,
and because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "Shaven-headed, free from the sense of 'mine,' without anger, and without possessions" (VaDh 10.6).

Likewise, the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is also merely optional, as seen in the Kaṭha Śruti: "Having shaved the hair, including the top-knot, and having discarded the sacred thread... (Kaṭha Śruti Upaniṣad 32).
Having abandoned his family, wife, and children, as well as the Vedāṅgas in their entirety,
his hair, and his sacred thread, the sage should wander in secret.

This is because of the *Bāṣkala-smṛti*, and also because of the observation in the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "Then he offers the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) into the water with the mantra 'bhūḥ svāhā'; then he takes up the staff (*daṇḍa*) with the words, 'O friend, protect me.
If there is an inability [to obtain these], then even a patched garment (*kanthā*) may be accepted.
For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Devala: "Clad in ochre robes, shaven-headed, carrying a triple staff, along with a water-pot, a purifier, sandals, a seat, and a patched garment.
He should possess a water-pot for the sake of purification and other such needs;
he should be devoted to solitude, being without companions among other renunciants.
And [it is so] with female renunciants (*saṃnyāsinī*) and women as well,
because Baudhāyana records the renunciation of women in the passage: "And some [say this applies] to women" (*strīṇāṃ caike*).
And so Dakṣa says: "A single monk as described, and two monks likewise, are considered a pair;
three are declared to be a village, and more than that acts like a city."
"But among them, talk of kings and the like, as well as talk of alms, will occur to one another;
moreover, slander and envy [will arise] from close association—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, the verb *vrajati* preceded by the prefix *pari-* functions in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāga*).

Therefore, one should renounce the conceit of "I" and "mine," as well as the collection of worldly actions produced by that [conceit], both Vedic— consisting of obligatory and optional rites— and non-Vedic.
This has been stated by Manu:
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the active and the renunciate.

Action performed with desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called *pravṛtta* (active); however, action free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as *nivṛtta* (withdrawn).
"Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, in tranquility, and in the study of the Veda. (MDh 12.88–89, 92).
Here, "study of the Veda" refers to the practice of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and he should be diligent in that.
One should resort to or enter a village for the purpose of seeking alms, and not for the sake of dwelling in comfort;
however, there is no fault during the rainy season.
For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Śaṅkha: "After the two months of the rainy season, one should not dwell in a single place.
However, in case of incapacity, one may remain for up to four months; otherwise, one should not dwell long in one place except during the rainy season.
Because of the traditional teaching of Devala that "the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa constitute the rainy season," [it is said]:
"One should dwell in a village for one night, and in a town for five nights;
except during the rains, one should dwell for four months during the rainy season."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Kāṇva. (3.58)
Regarding how the wandering for alms should be performed, he says:
"One should wander for alms with vigilance in the evening, unobserved, in a village secluded from other mendicants, seeking only what is necessary for sustenance and free from greed. (YDh 3.59)
Being vigilant—that is, free from the fickleness of speech, eyes, and so forth—one should go about for alms.
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha has shown a specific rule:
"One should go for alms to seven houses without prior intention" (VaDh 10.6).
In the evening, during the fifth part of the day;
and thus Manu says:
"When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, and when the people have finished eating."
"When the clashing of the alms-bowls has ceased, the ascetic should always go for alms.
Likewise:
"He should go for alms once a day; he should not be attached to abundance."
"For a mendicant who is intent on begging becomes attached even to sense-objects" (MDh 6.55).
"Unobserved" means not marked by the teaching of astrology and the like,
nor by portents or omens, nor by the science of stellar limbs (*nakṣatrāṅgavidyā*).
For it has been stated by him [Manu]: "One should never seek alms through instruction or by speaking. (MDh 6.50).

Furthermore, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "Or whatever he may obtain in a Brāhmaṇa family, that he should eat in the morning and evening, excluding meat" (VaDh 10.24), that refers to the case of one who is incapable [of begging].
[This applies] in a village avoided by mendicants, those habituated to begging, heretics, and the like.
Manu has stated a specific rule regarding this:
"He should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants" (MDh 6.51).
One should go for alms only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of life.
And so says Saṃvarta:
"A sage, having collected eight, seven, or five alms..."
"Having washed all of them with water, he should then eat while restraining his speech.
[The term] *alolupa* means one who is not greedy and is unattached to sweet foods, side dishes, and the like.
He speaks of the alms-bowl for the purpose of wandering for alms:
"The vessels of an ascetic are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair. (YDh 3.60)
The alms-bowls of ascetics should be made of materials such as clay;
for them, purification is achieved by washing with water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
This purification pertains to the implements used for activities such as wandering for alms, and does not concern objects defiled by impurities and the like.
In the event of its defilement, the rules for the purification of substances mentioned in the section on the purification of materials should be observed;
for this very reason, it was stated by Manu:
"His vessels shall be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as for the *camasa* cups in a sacrifice. (MDh 6.53).
By citing the example of the *camasa*, the practical method of purification is demonstrated.

In the absence of another vessel, the meal itself should be taken right there; for Devala records in his Smṛti: "Having received that alms-food, one should eat silently in a secluded place, using either that same vessel or another, only as much as is necessary to sustain life. (3.60)
Regarding such an ascetic, the author states the subject of the observances (niyama) as an auxiliary to the meditation on the Self:
"Having fully restrained the collection of senses, having abandoned passion and hatred, and having cast off fear toward all beings, the twice-born becomes immortal. (YDh 3.61)

Having properly restrained and turned back the collection of senses, such as the eyes, from their objects such as forms; having abandoned and cast off passion and hatred toward pleasant and unpleasant objects—and by the use of the word "and," likewise envy and other such traits; and not causing fear through harm to living beings—one whose internal organ is purified becomes immortal through the direct realization of non-duality, that is, one becomes liberated. // 3.61 //
Furthermore:
"But a mendicant, in particular, must purify his intention for action, because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence. (YDh 3.62)
The purification of the internal organ— the seat of intention— which is defiled by the faults born of desire for sense objects and aversion, must be accomplished through breath control (prāṇāyāma);
for that purification serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge in the form of the direct realization of the non-duality of the Self.

This being so, when the obstacles consisting of attachment to sense objects and the defects produced thereby have been destroyed, one becomes independent in the practice of meditation on the self, mental retention, and so forth. Therefore, this purification must be practiced especially by a mendicant.
Because that [knowledge] has liberation as its primary goal,
and because liberation is difficult to attain without a pure internal organ;
as Manu said:
"Just as the impurities of metals are burnt away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath. (MDh 6.71) 3.62.
He describes the nature of saṃsāra as a means for the cessation of the senses:
"One should contemplate the dwelling in the womb, as well as the destinies born of karma, mental anxieties, physical diseases, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of form. (YDh 3.63)

Throughout thousands of births, there is the reversal of the pleasant and the unpleasant. For the sake of achieving dispassion (*vairāgya*), one must observe and reflect upon the dwellings in various wombs filled with urine, feces, and so forth;
by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), the death and dissolution of people are also included.

Likewise, there are the destinies consisting of falling into hells such as Mahāraurava, produced by actions such as the performance of forbidden deeds; likewise, mental afflictions (ādhi) which are pangs of the mind,
and physical ailments (vyādhi) such as fever, dysentery, and so forth.

The afflictions (*kleśa*) are five: ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and clinging to existence (*abhiniveśa*). Old age (*jarā*) is the overcoming by wrinkles, gray hair, and so forth;
it is the transformation of form (*rūpa-viparyaya*) through such states as being lame or humpbacked, which alters one's previous appearance.
The alteration of form,
as well as birth— meaning arising— in various species such as dogs, pigs, donkeys, and snakes;
and the non-attainment of what is desired.

Having reflected upon the nature of saṃsāra—which brings about manifold afflictions such as the attainment of the undesirable—one should strive for the conquest of the senses, which is the means to self-knowledge, in order to abandon it. (3.63)
Having thus reflected, he states what should be done immediately thereafter:

"By means of the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the subtle Self abiding within the self. Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; meditation (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointedness of the self, which is the withdrawal of that very [mind] from external objects. By means of this yoga of meditation...

Through *nididhyāsana*— which is another term for [the practice of] discernment— one should correctly perceive, and thereby directly realize (*aparokṣīkuryāt*), the non-difference between the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, namely that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Self, which is distinct from the subtle body, the vital breaths, and so forth, is established within the Self, which is Brahman. For this very reason, the Śruti,
having referred to vision in the form of direct realization in the passage "The Self, my dear, is to be seen," [proceeds as follows:]
As the means to that [realization], it is ordained that "it should be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5);
thus, hearing, reflection, and meditation are prescribed.
Furthermore:
"Ascetic stage (āśrama) is not the cause for dharma; rather, it is that which is practiced [as dharma].
Therefore, one should not do to others that which is unwholesome for oneself. (YDh 3.65)

Regarding the dharma known as the meditation on the Self mentioned in the preceding verse, the specific stage of life (āśrama) or the carrying of the staff and water-pot (*daṇḍakamaṇḍalu*) is not the cause;
for that [meditation], when practiced, is certainly not very difficult.
Therefore, whatever is unwholesome to the Self and causes agitation, such as harsh speech and the like—
One should not practice that toward others.

Because the abandonment of passion and hatred is primary—since it brings about the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the cause for the arising of knowledge—and because it is thus an "inner" factor, the rejection of the [specific] stages of life (*āśrama*) is intended as praise; it is not, however, for the purpose of abandoning them altogether.
Because that too has been prescribed.
As it was said by Manu:
"Even if he is corrupted, one should practice dharma in whichever stage of life (āśrama) he is devoted to."
One should be equal toward all beings; outward signs are not the cause of dharma.
Moreover:
truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint, control of the senses, and learning—all this is declared to be Dharma. (YDh 3.66)
Truthfulness is speech that is factual and pleasant;
non-stealing is the non-appropriation of another's property; and freedom from anger is remaining free from wrath even toward one who causes harm.
The non-arising of anger;
*hrī* is a sense of shame;
*śauca* is purity regarding food and so forth.
Wisdom (*dhī*) is the discrimination between the beneficial and the harmful.

Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the re-establishment of the mind, which has been disturbed by the loss of the desired or the acquisition of the undesired, in its former state. Self-control (*dama*) is the abandonment of intoxication.
Control of the senses is the absence of excessive attachment even toward objects that are not forbidden.
Knowledge is self-knowledge. When these qualities, beginning with truthfulness, are practiced, every duty is thereby fulfilled.
By this, he demonstrates that qualities of the self such as truthfulness possess an internal character, as opposed to external characteristics such as the carrying of a staff or a water-pot.

Now, one might object that it is illogical to say "one should see the Self abiding in the self through the yoga of meditation," because there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme Self (paramātman); to this, he says:
"Just as sparks fly out from a heated mass of iron..."
"In the same way, individual selves indeed arise from the Self.

(YDh 3.67) Even though there is no ultimate difference between the individual self (*jīva*) and the supreme Self (*paramātman*), nevertheless, because they arise from the Self as distinct entities due to the differentiation created by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is entirely appropriate to designate a distinction between the individual self and the supreme Self.
Just as sparks, which are particles of fire, issue forth from a heated iron ball or a mass of glowing iron, and once issued, receive the designation of "sparks," so it is here.
Therefore, it is logically established that the Self is to be seen as abiding within the self.

Thus [it is said]. Or rather, this is the meaning: one might object that since at the time of deep sleep and during cosmic dissolution all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are merged into Brahman, for whom is this injunction for the meditation on the Self intended? To this, he says "emerging," and so forth.
Although they are dissolved in a subtle form at the time of dissolution, nevertheless, due to being differentiated by the limiting adjuncts of ignorance (*avidyopādhi*) originating from the Self,
the individual selves (*jīvātman*) emerge;
furthermore, under the influence of karma, they are born as those who identify with gross bodies.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the injunction for meditative worship;
the analogy of the iron ball is given because of the similarity in the separate existence of the fiery element. // 3.67 //

Now, one might object: since the conscious beings (*kṣetrajña*) whose bodies have not yet been assumed are devoid of movement, how can there be the assumption of the four types of bodies—womb-born, egg-born, and so forth—which are dependent upon that movement?
To this, he says:
"In that regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, and some [action] by its own nature."
"By means of practice, one performs something consisting of both dharma and adharma.
(YDh 3.68) Although in that state there is an absence of action consisting of physical movement, nevertheless, mental action consisting of the determination of dharma and adharma certainly exists.

And it indeed possesses the quality of being the cause for assuming a distinguished body, according to the traditional teaching of Manu: "By [evil] deeds of speech one becomes a bird or a beast; by those of the mind, one becomes a member of the lowest castes" (MDh 12.9).

Thus, having assumed a body, he himself— independently of [present] positive and negative concomitance— possesses an awareness of the effect arising from the force of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) produced by experiences in a previous life; this awareness is independent of such positive and negative concomitances as "when the drinking of breast milk and so forth is performed, satisfaction occurs, and when it is not performed, it does not occur," regarding some act such as the drinking of breast milk.

It performs some actions by its own nature through chance, such as the eating of ants and so forth, independent of any intention regarding a purpose; and it performs other actions, consisting of both merit and demerit, by the force of practice in previous existences.
And thus another Smṛti states:
"Whatever— be it generosity, study, or austerity— has been practiced throughout successive births,
by the very force of that habituation, one practices that same thing again."
Thus, the diversity of karma among living beings and the resulting diversity of bodies—such as those born from a womb and so forth—is indeed logical. (3.68)

Now, one might object: "If this is so, since the Brahmin himself is somehow designated as the 'living being' (jīva) and possesses attributes such as eternity, how can there be the common usage, 'Viṣṇumitra was born'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Unchanging (akṣara) is the efficient cause (nimitta), the agent, the knower, Brahman, the possessor of qualities, and the controller."

The unborn [Self], through the assumption of a body, is said to be "born. Indeed, the Self, by virtue of being permeated by ignorance (*avidyā*), manifests the entire phenomenal world (*jagat-prapañca*) and thus becomes, of its own accord, the threefold cause— namely, the material (*samavāyin*), the non-material (*asamavāyin*), and the instrumental (*nimitta*)— but it does not, however, fall within the category of the effect (*kārya*).
Because it is imperishable and indestructible;

for is it not observed that in the manifold world, which is an effect consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion— the transformations of the qualities such as *sattva*— there is the presence of those very qualities?
It is appropriate that agency over the world belongs to primordial nature (prakṛti) alone,
and not to the qualityless Brahman;
do not think thus.
The Self alone is the agent;
for it is that which is the cognizer of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, which serve as the causes of the pleasure and pain to be experienced by the individual soul (*jīva*).

Indeed, the construction of the manifold world (*jagat-prapañca*)—endowed with the various classes of enjoyers distinguished by name and form, and with the objects of enjoyment and the bodies suitable for their experience—could not belong to insentient primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
This is logical; therefore, the self alone is the agent.

Likewise, it is that very self which is *brahman*, the expander and the cause of expansion. Nor is it devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), because it possesses the power of the three *guṇas*—ignorance (*avidyā*), which has other synonyms such as *prakṛti* and *pradhāna*.
Therefore, although it is inherently devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), it is described as being endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and so forth by way of its powers (*śakti*).
Yet, this much does not constitute the causality of *prakṛti*.
Because the self alone is the controller and independent, whereas that which is called "prakṛti" is not an independent entity, as there is a lack of evidence for such a thing.
Nor should it be said that she herself, even in the form of power (śakti), is the agent; for:
The causal agent is that which possesses power, not the power itself;
therefore, the Self alone is the threefold cause of the world. Likewise, it is unborn (*aja*), meaning devoid of origination.

Therefore, although its direct production is not logically possible, it is nevertheless said to be "born" merely by virtue of taking up a body; this is because it arises through the acquisition of a different state, just as one says, "the householder is born. (3.69)
He describes the manner of assuming a body:

"Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, light, water, and earth, each possessing one additional quality [over the preceding], so too does he take them up when coming into existence. (YDh 3.70)

At the time of creation, that Supreme Self creates space and the other elements with their respective qualities in increasing order: the sky has the single quality of sound; the wind has the qualities of sound and touch;

fire has the qualities of sound, touch, and form; water has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; and the earth has the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus, He creates them with one additional quality each.
Likewise, the self, having attained the state of a living being (jīva) and coming into existence, also takes on [the body] as the initiator of its own physical form. (3.70)
How do earth and the other elements initiate the formation of the body? To this he says: "The sun is nourished by the oblation; from the sun comes rain, and from that, plants;
that food, in the form of essence, attains the state of semen. (YDh 3.71)
The sun is nourished by the essence of the sacrificial cakes and other offerings cast into it by the sacrificers;
and from the sun, through the power of time, rain arises from the ripened essence of the oblations such as clarified butter.

From that comes food in the form of rice and other plants; and when that food is consumed, it undergoes the process of becoming chyle, blood, and so forth, until it reaches the state of semen and ovum. (3.71)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"But when there is union of a woman and a man, and the semen and blood are pure, the Lord, being himself the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements. (YDh 3.72)

At the time of the season (*ṛtu*), during the union of a woman and a man, there is semen and blood; these two together constitute "semen-blood" (*śukra-śoṇita*). When these are conjoined with one another and are pure—being free from the defects mentioned in other Smṛtis, such as being corrupted by wind, bile, or phlegm, or being knotted, putrid, diminished, or smelling of urine and feces, which render them non-seeds (*abīja*)—then, having remained therein, [the self] itself [takes up] the five elements (*pañcadhātu*), the five great elements beginning with earth, for the purpose of initiating the body.

The sixth element, consciousness (*ciddhātu*), which is the self (*ātman*) and the lord (*prabhu*), being capable through its connection with the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭakarman*) that initiates the body, simultaneously takes up— that is, appropriates as the seat of yoga—
the semen mixed with the female menses in the womb at the very moment of union between man and woman, together with the elemental self (*bhūtātman*). Thus it is stated in the *Śārīraka*.
And impelled by the wind along with the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, it remains within the womb (*garbhāśaya*). (Suśruta 3.4) // 3.72 //
Furthermore:
the sense organs, the mind, the vital breath, cognition, life-span, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense; YDh 3.73.
Effort, form, color, likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—
all this is born of his self, as he desires a beginning for that which is without beginning.
(YDh 3.74) The sense organs are the organs of cognition and action, which will be described hereafter.
The mind is common to both. The bodily wind, distinguished by its fivefold functions—namely prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—is called prāṇa;
knowledge is comprehension.
Life (*āyus*) is existence delimited by a specific period of time;
happiness (*sukha*) is tranquility;
fortitude (*dhṛti*) is stability of mind; and retention (*dhāraṇā*) is [the faculty of] holding.
Wisdom and intelligence;
impulsion, which is the presiding over the organs of knowledge and action;
suffering, which is agitation; and desire.
Longing, egoism, the act of "I-making," effort, exertion, and form, appearance.
Complexion refers to whiteness and so forth; tone refers to the *ṣaḍja*, *gāndhāra*, and other musical notes;
and hatred refers to enmity.
"Bhava" is the manifestation of sons, cattle, and so forth; "abhava" is the opposite of that.
