For one who desires a beginning for this beginningless and eternal self—that is, for one wishing to assume a body—all of this, beginning with the sense organs, [comes into being].
The meaning is that it is produced by the self, namely, born from the seeds of karma belonging to a previous existence. // 3.74 //
He describes the sequence of the transformation of the combined semen and blood into the form of the effect:
"In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, coagulated with the elements;
in the second month, it is an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs. (YDh 3.75)
This conscious sixth element is "coalesced with the elements," meaning it has coalesced with the elements such as earth and so forth; that is to say, it has become unified, like milk and water.
In the first month of gestation, it becomes a state of moisture, taking on a liquid form.
Having reached that state, it remains as such and does not yet transform into hardness;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*, which is the form of a slightly hardened lump of flesh.
This is the intended meaning:

the collection of elements, which has attained a state of liquidity through contact with semen and is being gradually dried day by day by the abdominal fire produced from the internal wind, reaches solidity after thirty days.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the Suśruta [Saṃhitā], in the second [chapter]: "Being cooked by cold, heat, and wind, the aggregate of the elements becomes solid" (Śārīra 3.18).
But in the third month, it becomes endowed with limbs and sense organs. // 3.75 //
Furthermore: from space [he derives] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, strength, and so forth;
and from air, the sense of touch, movement, expansion, and even dryness. (YDh 3.76)
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, form, and luminosity;
from the essence (rasa), taste, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness;
and from earth, odor, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and material form.
"The unborn Self grasps everything; thereafter, it vibrates in the third [state].
The phrase "the Self grasps" is to be connected with every [instance].
[It grasps] from the ether the quality of lightness, which is useful for the action of leaping, as well as subtlety.
Subtle observation,
sound as the object,
and the ear as the faculty of hearing.
"Strength" means firmness;
by the inclusion of "and so forth," it refers to porosity and seclusion as well.
From space [comes] sound, the sense of hearing, distinctness, and the collection of all apertures, according to the vision of the Garbhopaniṣad;
from air [comes] the tactile organ,
and activity such as coming and going.
The various spreading out of the limbs is *vyūhana*;
and from the word "ca" (and), there is also roughness (*raukṣya*), which is hardness (*karkaśatva*), as well as touch (*sparśa*).
From bile (pitta) arises the vision of fire, which is the faculty of sight;
the digestion of consumed food, which is its cooking;
and the heat, which is the quality of warmth in the limbs.
Form refers to dark complexions and the like,
as well as manifest radiance.
Likewise, heat, indignation, and so forth [are fiery], for the *Garbhopaniṣad* shows that "courage, indignation, sharpness, digestion, heat, brilliance, color, form, and the sense organs are fiery.
Similarly, from the watery rasa, the gustatory organ [arises].
[It bestows] coolness of the limbs, smoothness accompanied by softness,
moisture, and dampness; likewise, the fragrance of the earth, the sense of smell, heaviness, and material form.
All this,
although the self is in reality devoid of birth, the self grasps [the body] in the third month;
thereafter, in the fourth month, it begins to throb.
It moves; likewise, in the *Śārīraka* (3.18):
"Therefore, in the fourth month, it forms an intention regarding movement and so forth. [3.76, 3.77, 3.78]
Furthermore:
By not granting her pregnancy-longings, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman. (YDh 3.79)
The fetus has one heart and the pregnant woman another; thus, that woman is "two-hearted" (*dvihṛdayā*). Whatever she desires is called "the two-hearts" (*dauhṛda*).
By not granting that desire, the fetus incurs a defect such as deformity or death. Therefore—
To avoid those defects and for the sake of nourishing the fetus, whatever is pleasing and desired by the pregnant woman should be provided.
And so it is stated in the Suśruta:
They call a woman with two hearts one who has pregnancy-longings;
one should grant her what she desires, so that [the child] may be vigorous and long-lived.
"She gives birth to a son" (Śārīra 3.18).
Accordingly, even physical exercise and such activities must be avoided by her from the time of conception;

from that point forward, she should avoid exercise, sexual intercourse, over-satiation, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, grief, fear, riding in vehicles, suppressing natural urges, squatting in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture, and bloodletting.
For it is stated in that very context [of the Śārīra-sūtra 3.16]: "One should avoid [these].
Furthermore, the conception of the embryo is to be understood through signs such as fatigue and so forth.

"Fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, weakness of the thighs, the retention of semen and blood, and throbbing of the vagina [occur] in one who has just conceived"— this and more is stated in that very same [text], Śārīra 3.13. 3.79.
Furthermore:
"In the fourth month there is stability of the limbs; in the fifth, the emergence of blood;
and in the sixth, the appearance of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair. (YDh 3.80)
In the fourth month, the mass of limbs that appeared in the third month attains stability and firmness; in the fifth, blood arises and originates;
likewise, in the sixth, strength, complexion, and the nails and body hair come into being.
Furthermore:
In the seventh and eighth [weeks], he is endowed with mind and consciousness, possessed of channels, sinews, and vessels, and also possesses skin, flesh, and memory. (YDh 3.81)

That aforementioned embryo, in the seventh month, becomes endowed with mind, consciousness, and volition; it is joined with channels for the transport of vital air, with sinews that bind the bones, and with vessels for the transport of wind, bile, and phlegm;
and likewise in the eighth month.
In the third month, he becomes endowed with skin, flesh, and memory.
Moreover,
his vital energy (ojas) repeatedly flows away from the nurse and back into the womb; consequently,
the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life.
In that eighth-month fetus, a certain vital energy— a specific quality— moves repeatedly and with extreme instability back and forth between the nurse and the fetus.
Therefore, a fetus born in the eighth month [is deprived] of its life-breaths.
It is separated [from the body]. By this, he shows that the very state of *ojas* (vital essence) is the cause of life. And the nature of *ojas* is shown in another Smṛti:
"That which resides in the heart, pure, slightly warm, and yellowish-white..."
Vitality is reckoned as being within the body; through its destruction, one meets with destruction. (3.82)
Furthermore:
In the ninth or even the tenth month, he is expelled by the powerful winds of labor like an arrow through the opening of a machine, while still possessed by fever. (YDh 3.83)

Thus, with hands, feet, eyes, and other limbs and sense organs fully developed in the ninth or tenth month— or even earlier, in the seventh or eighth month, as indicated by the word "api"— the fetus, whose body-machine is constructed of sinews, bones, skin, and so forth, is propelled by the powerful winds of labor characterized by excessive exertion and other defects; it is then expelled through the narrow opening of the birth canal, afflicted by unbearable suffering and accompanied by fever, like a puppet from a mechanical bow.
Like an arrow impelled by Sudhanvan, immediately upon exiting, it is touched by the external wind and its former memory is lost;
for the *Nirukta* (18.2) states: "Once born, being touched by the wind, it does not remember its previous birth, death, or its auspicious and inauspicious karma. (3.83)
Explaining the true nature of the body, he says:
"Its bodies are sixfold, and it possesses six layers of skin;
likewise, its limbs are six, and its bones number three hundred and sixty. (YDh 3.84)

Of that self, those bodies which are born from a womb or from an egg are each of six kinds, by virtue of being associated with six locations of fire that serve as the causes for the maturation of the six elements, beginning with blood.
For instance, the essence of food (*annarasa*), being cooked by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), attains the state of blood;
and the blood, in turn, [is cooked] by the fire residing in its own sheath.
The flesh being cooked becomes the state of flesh;
and the flesh, fully ripened by the fire of its own sheath, becomes the state of fat;
and the fat also [is ripened] by the fire of its own sheath.
When cooked, it becomes bone;
the bone also, being fully cooked by the fire within its own sheath, becomes marrow;
and the marrow too, being cooked by the fire within its own sheath...
It transforms into the final element;

however, since there is no further transformation of that final element, it constitutes the first sheath of the self. Thus, because of the connection with the fire of the six sheaths, bodies are of six kinds.
However, because the first element, which consists of the essence of food, is not fixed, it does not constitute a separate category by virtue of that;
and those bodies support six layers of skin.
The six elements known as blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen exist in both external and internal forms, like the layers of a plantain trunk;
because they act as coverings like a skin, these six skins sustain [the body].
This is well-known in the *Āyurveda*.

Likewise, the limbs are exactly six: the two hands, the pair of feet, the head, and the trunk. As for the bones, their number is three hundred and sixty, which should be understood as that which will be stated in the six verses following this one. (3.84)
Furthermore:
"The sixty-four teeth along with their sockets, the twenty nails, and the digits of the hands and feet—these constitute four groups of locations. (YDh 3.85)

The sockets are the bones located at the roots of the teeth; together with the thirty-two teeth, they constitute sixty-four. The nails are those growing on the hands and feet; there are exactly twenty such needle-shaped bones situated at the bases of the fingers and toes, located above the wrists and ankles.
Of those nails and the bones of the phalanges, there are four locations: the two feet and the two hands; thus, the total number of bones is one hundred and four. 3.85.
Furthermore:
there are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the heels; four in the ankles; four bones in the forearms; and exactly that many in the shanks. (YDh 3.86)
There are twenty fingers; since there are three bones for each of them, there are thus sixty bones connected to the fingers. Regarding the feet, the two rear portions are the heels (*pārṣṇī*);
there are two bones for those, one in each foot, [and] the ankles (*gulpha*).

"Two" refers thus to the four bones in the two ankles; there are four bones in the forearms, each measuring one cubit (aratni); and likewise, there are exactly four in the two shanks—thus, there are seventy-four. (3.86)
Furthermore,
one should designate two each as arising from the knees, the cheeks, the thighs,
the shoulder-blades, the elbows, the palms, the hips, and the buttocks. (YDh 3.87)
The joint of the lower leg and thigh is the knee;
the cheek is the *galla*;
the thigh is the *sakthi*, and its broad surface is the *phalaka*.
The shoulder is the head of the arm;
the axle is the region below the temple between the ear and the eye;
the palate is the uvula.
The hips are the "humped" [bones], and their two plates;
one should point out two bones for each of these, and thus there are fourteen bones in total. (3.87)
Furthermore:
There is one bone in the pubic region, forty-five in the back, fifteen bones in the neck, and likewise one each in the collarbones and the jaw. (YDh 3.88)
There is one bone in the secret region; on the back, in the posterior part, there are forty-five bones.
The neck, the cervical region, consists of fifteen bones.

The joint between the chest and the shoulders is the *jatru*; there is one for each *pratijatru*, one for the jaw (*hanu*), and one for the chin (*cibuka*). Including these, there are sixty-four bones. 3.88.
Furthermore:
At its base are the two [bones] of the forehead, the eyes, and the cheeks; the nose consists of solid bone;
and there are seventy-two ribs together with their sockets (sthālaka) and tubercles (arbuda). (YDh 3.89)
At the root of that jaw are two bones;
the forehead is the *lalāṭa*, the eye is the *akṣi*, and the cheek is the *gaṇḍa*—the region between the eye and the temple; the collective term for these is *lalāṭākṣigaṇḍa*.
In that regard, there is a pair of bones for each [toe];
the nose consists of bones known as *ghanas*;
the ribs are the bones connected to the region below the armpits, and the *sthālakas* are the bones that serve as their support; by means of these...
Together with the specific bones known as *sthālaka* and *arbuda*, there are seventy-two ribs;
when added to the nine previously mentioned, they total eighty-one. (3.89)
Furthermore:
"There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise seventeen bones in the chest; such is the collection of bones in a man. (YDh 3.90)
The two specific bones located in the region between the eyebrows and the ears are the *śaṅkhakas*.
There are four skull-bones (*kapāla*) belonging to the head.
The chest (*uraḥ*, *vakṣas*) consists of seventeen bones; thus, there are twenty-three [bones] in total.
Together with those previously mentioned, there are three hundred and sixty; thus has the collection of bones of a person been described. (3.90)
He states the sense organs along with their objects:
"Fragrance, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ear are the sense organs. (YDh 3.91)
These objects, such as fragrance and the rest, are the causes of bondage for the person (*puruṣa*),

because the word *viṣaya* is derived from the verbal root *ṣiñ*, meaning "to bind. Furthermore, by means of these objects— fragrance and the rest— which exist as things to be cognized, [the senses] are to be inferred through their function as the instruments for the cognition of their respective domains.
The five sense faculties, beginning with the olfactory faculty, come into being. (3.91)
To demonstrate the organs of action, he says:
"The two hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the two feet—these five one should know as the organs of action; and the mind is indeed of a dual nature. (YDh 3.92)
The two hands are well known; the anus is the rectum;
and the generative organ is the means for producing the pleasure resulting from sexual union.

The tongue is well-known, as are the two feet; one should understand that these five—the hands and so forth—are the organs of action (*karmendriya*), which serve as the means for the actions of grasping, excretion, sexual pleasure, speech, and locomotion.

The mind (*manas*) is the internal organ, known by the fact that cognitions do not arise simultaneously; and because it acts in conjunction with both the intellect and the organs of action, it possesses a dual nature. (3.92)
To show the seats of the vital breath (prāṇa), he says:
"The navel, the ojas, the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples, as well as the head, the shoulders, the throat, and the heart—these are indeed the seats of the prāṇa. (YDh 3.93)

The navel and so forth are the ten locations of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Although the wind named *samāna* circulates through all the limbs, the specific mention of its locations beginning with the navel is intended to indicate its predominance there. (3.93)

In order to elaborate upon the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*), he says: "The omentum, the liver, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the two kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces. (YDh 3.94)
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine,
the anus, the abdomen, and the two internal rectal folds— this is declared to be the extent [of the viscera].
The omentum is well known.
Fat is the oily substance of the flesh;
the *avahanana* is the lungs; the navel is well known.
The spleen (*plīhā*) is well-known in Āyurveda;
both of these are shaped like masses of flesh and are located in the left side of the abdomen.
The liver (*yakṛt*) is the *kālikā*.
The *kloma* is a mass of flesh, and those two are located in the right side of the abdomen;
the *kṣudrāntra* is the intestine situated at the heart.
The two kidneys are masses of flesh situated near the heart; the bladder is the receptacle for urine;
and the rectum is the receptacle for feces.
The stomach is the site where undigested food resides; the heart is the lotus of the heart;
and the large intestine, anus, and abdomen are well known.
From the outer anal circle, there are two inner anal circles; those two anus are abdominal, being located in the abdominal cavity in the region below the navel.
And this is the detailed exposition of the abodes of living beings (prāṇāyatana);
in the previous verse, however, it was presented in brief.
For this very reason, some of those mentioned in the previous verse are recited here [again]. (3.94–3.95)

Furthermore, for the purpose of elaborating upon the seats of the vital breaths (prāṇāyatana), he says: "The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-cavities, the two ear-flaps, the two ears, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins. (YDh 3.96)
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, and the breasts are produced from the accumulation of phlegm;
likewise are the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the calves, thighs, and the muscles of the shanks.
The palate, the abdomen, the top of the bladder, the chin, and the two tonsils [are also so produced].
And likewise, these cavities exist here in this body:
the two eyes, the four ears, and the feet, hands, and heart;
these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The *kanīnike* are the pupils of the eyes;
the *akṣikūṭe* are the sockets at the junctions of the eyes and the nose; the *śaṣkulī* is the auditory canal.
*Karṇapatraka* refers to the earlobes; *karṇa* refers to the well-known ears.
The gums are the *dantaveṣṭau*, the two rows of teeth are the *dantapālyau*, the lips are well known, and the hollows of the hips are the *kukundare*.
The groins are the junctions of the hips and thighs;
the kidneys have been mentioned previously; and the breasts are produced from a massification of phlegm (śleṣman).
The uvula is the *ghaṇṭikā*; the buttocks are the *kaṭiprothau*;
the arms are well known (*prasiddhau*).
The *piṇḍikās* on the calves and thighs refer to the fleshy portions of the calves and thighs;
the *galaśuṇḍike* are the joints at the base of the jaw and the cheeks.
*Śīrṣam* means the head; *avaṭaḥ* refers to any depressed region on the body, such as the base of the throat, the armpits, and so forth.
In the reading *avaṭuḥ*, it refers to the nape of the neck (*kṛkāṭikā*).
Likewise, there are four colors: the two white sides of each of the pupils of the eyes, or alternatively, the four eyelids;
the rest is well known.
Thus, these are the locations within this contemptible body;
likewise the pair of eyes and the pair of ears.
The two nostril apertures, the mouth, the anus, and the genitals—these aforementioned nine openings are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa). 3.96–99.
Furthermore:
there are exactly seven hundred veins, nine hundred sinews, two hundred arteries, and five hundred muscles. (YDh 3.100)
The vessels connected to the navel are forty in number; they carry wind, bile, and phlegm, pervade the entire body, and branching out in various ways, they become seven hundred in number.
Likewise, they serve as the binders of the joints of the limbs and their subdivisions.
There are nine hundred ligaments.

The vessels called *dhamanīs*, which originate from the navel and number twenty-four, become two hundred through their branching into various divisions, serving as the carriers of the vital winds such as *prāṇa* and the rest.
Furthermore, the muscles, which are fleshy in form and connect the major and minor limbs such as the thighs and calves, number five hundred. (3.100)
Furthermore, he states another number for these very vessels, such as the veins (*sirā*), due to the abundance of their branches:
"Know that there are twenty-nine hundred thousand, nine hundred, and fifty-six vessels designated as *sirā* and *dhamanī*. (YDh 3.101)

O Sāmaśravas and other sages, know that the veins and arteries, joined together through their divisions of branches and sub-branches, amount to twenty-nine hundred thousand nine hundred and fifty-six. 3.101.
Furthermore:
It should be known that embodied beings possess three hundred thousand hairs on their beard and head;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmans) and two hundred joints. (YDh 3.102)

The body hairs and facial hair of embodied beings, when combined, should be known as three hundred thousand. Their vital points (*marmāṇi*)— the locations that cause death and produce affliction— should be known as one hundred and seven.
There are two hundred bone joints, whereas the joints of the tendons, veins, and so forth are infinite. (3.102)
He states the number of the pores and other cavities of the entire body:
"There are fifty-four crores and sixty-seven and a half lakhs of hair-pores, along with the openings for sweat. (YDh 3.103)
The atoms, though divided, are counted by the winds; even if one person were to know their individual nature and their arrangement,
along with the head-hairs and other parts previously mentioned, the atoms of the body hairs— parts that are exceedingly subtle in form— are [dispersed] through the pores for the flow of sweat.
Together with fifty-four billion, sixty-seven million, and fifty-five thousand, they are divided by the aerial atoms— that is, separated by the atoms of wind— and thus enumerated;
this and this has been stated from the perspective of the treatise.
Because this object is not within the range of the sensory paths of the eyes and other organs,

O sages, whoever among you understands this exceedingly profound object— which exists in the form of the configuration of the head and other limbs— is indeed great and foremost among the intelligent. Therefore...
The established nature of existence must be understood with effort by one who possesses intelligence.
He states the quantities of the bodily fluids and other constituents:
"Nine añjalis of rasa are to be known; ten of water;
seven indeed of feces; and eight of blood are proclaimed. (YDh 3.105)
Phlegm is six [parts], bile five, and urine four;
muscle fat three, and fat two; marrow is one, while the brain is above that.
The essence of phlegm is of that same measure, and the semen is of that same measure as well.
Thus, this body is unstable; he who acts for the sake of liberation [should understand this].
For one whose food is properly digested, the essence is the *rasa* (nutritive fluid), the measure of which is nine handfuls (*añjali*s).
This [body] is caused by the conjunction of earthly atoms.
Ten handfuls (añjali) of water are to be known [as the measure];
seven of feces (purīṣa/varcaska);
and eight of blood—that is, of the essence of food (annarasa) rendered red by the digestion of the digestive fire (jāṭharānala).
The quantities are proclaimed in añjalis:
six añjalis for phlegm (śleṣman) or kapha,
and five for bile (pitta), which is of the nature of fire (tejas).
There are four [fingers] for urine and excrement;
three for fat, which is the grease of the flesh;
and [three] for marrow, which is the essence of the flesh.
There are two añjalis:
one añjali of marrow located within the hollows of the bones,
and another half-añjali in the head.
The marrow belongs to the essence of phlegm (*śleṣmau jasaḥ śleṣmasārasya*);

likewise, the semen, which is the final constituent element (*caramadhātu*), is exactly half an *añjali*. And this has been stated with reference to a person whose constituent elements (*dhātu*) are in equilibrium.
But for one with an unbalanced constitution, there is no fixed rule; because bodies differ in their characteristics and are unstable,
as well as because of the humors, tissues, and wastes, no definite measure exists.
Thus, according to the traditional authority of Āyurveda,

he who possesses the understanding that "this body is an unstable collection of impurities, composed of bones, sinews, and so forth," is a successful man, a wise person, and becomes capable of attaining liberation.
Because dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the discernment of the permanent and the impermanent (*nityānityaviveka*) are means to liberation,
and because the knowledge that [the body] abounds in bone, urine, feces, and so forth is the cause of dispassion;
for this very reason, Vyāsa said:
For the sake of even this wretched body— a storehouse of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable— the deluded commit sinful deeds.

"If what is inside this body were to be outside, people would take up sticks to ward off dogs and crows. Therefore, for the sake of the ultimate cessation of such a contemptible body, one should strive in the practice of the Self. (3.105–107)
He describes the nature of the Self that is to be meditated upon:
"Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā and Ahitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is [the space] with the luster of the moon. (YDh 3.108)
The mandala is situated within him, and the Self therein is immovable like a lamp;
that is what is to be known, for by knowing it here, one is not born again.
From the region of the heart, [the channels] have issued forth like the filaments of a kadamba flower, emerging on all sides according to whether they produce benefit or harm.
Regarding the notions of "beneficial" and "harmful," there are seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*).
Among them, there are three other channels; of these, two are named *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
These two channels reside on the left and right sides, are reversed at the heart, and are connected to the nostrils, serving as the abodes of *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
Furthermore, the third [channel] is called Suṣumṇā; it stands like a staff in the center and extends out to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
In the midst of those channels is a mandala with the luster of the moon, within which the Self (ātman) dwells, shining motionless like a lamp in a windless place.

He who has become such as this should be known as one who, because of the direct realization of that [Self], no longer wanders in this cycle of transmigration here and attains immortality. (3.108–109)
Furthermore:
"And that which I obtained from the Sun—the Aranyaka and the Yoga-shastra proclaimed by me—should be known by one who desires yoga. (YDh 3.110)

Yoga is the steadiness of the mental faculty within the Self by means of setting aside interest in other objects; for the sake of attaining that, one must understand what has been received by me from Āditya known as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, and likewise, the Yoga-śāstra which has been spoken by me must also be understood. (3.110)
But how is this Self to be meditated upon? To this he says:
"Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses free from other objects, the Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp—that Self is to be meditated upon. (YDh 3.111)
Having withdrawn the mind, intellect, memory, and senses from objects external to the Self and having made them focused solely on the Self,
the Self is to be meditated upon—
that Lord who, like a lamp in a windless place, remains unshakable and shining within the heart.

This alone is its state of being an object of meditation: that which is called the mind’s inclination toward itself by setting aside the appearance of external objects, like a lamp whose spreading radiance is confined within the hollow of two joined bowls and thus becomes fixed on a single point. (3.111)

Furthermore, for one whose mental fluctuations do not find delight in meditative concentration because they lack a formal object of focus, it is said that the worship of Śabdabrahman (the Brahman of Sound) should be performed; thus [the text says]:
"Reciting the Sāma-chant according to the prescribed rule, without any lapse..."
Being attentive, through the practice of that [Sāman], one attains the Supreme Brahman.
"Sāmagāna" means singing the Sāman without deviating from the path understood through the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya);
although the Sāman consists essentially of song, it is specified as "singing" (gāyam) for emphasis.
This qualification is for the purpose of excluding mantras that are sung to a melody (*pragīta*).

One who recites [the mantra] without deviation, without stumbling, and with vigilance—his mental activity being one-pointed and permeated by the sound of the *sāman*—becomes proficient therein through the power of such practice; by means of meditation (*upāsanā*) on that which is devoid of the form of sound, he attains the Supreme Brahman.
As it has been said:
"One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (3.112)
Furthermore, for one whose mind does not find delight in Vedic song, he says that one should practice the meditation on the Self as recollected through worldly songs:
"The Aparāntaka, the Ullopya, the Madraka, and likewise the Prakarī."
The Auveṇaka, the Sarobindu, the Uttara,
and the Gītakas; the Ṛggāthā, the Pāṇikā, the Dakṣavihitā, and the Brahmagītikā— this is the Geya (chanting), and through the practice of it, it is designated as liberation.
The *aparāntaka*, *kollopya*, *madraka*, *prakarya*, *oveṇaka*, together with the *sarovinda*, and the *uttara*— these seven songs are called *prakarās*.
By the word "and" (*ca*), the *āsārita*, *vardhamānaka*, and other *mahāgītās* are included.

The four songs beginning with the *ṛggāthā*—namely, this collection of songs such as the *aparāntaka* and others—are to be understood as being designated "liberation" (*mokṣa*) because they have superimposed upon them the nature of liberation due to their being means for achieving liberation; for, by way of producing one-pointedness through their practice, they are the cause for attaining one-pointedness of the self. (3.113–3.114)
Moreover:
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, who is proficient in the musical scales and modes, and who understands the rhythm, attains the path of liberation without effort. (YDh 3.115)
He is one who knows the reality of playing the lute as expounded by the sage Bharata and others.

*Śruti*—that which is heard—is of twenty-two kinds within the seven notes (*svara*). To explain: the notes Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama each possess four *śrutis*, while Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata each [possess three].
Gāndhāra and Niṣāda each have three śrutis, while [the remaining five] each have two śrutis.
As for the jātis, there are seven pure ones beginning with Ṣaḍja, and eleven mixed jātis; thus, they are of eighteen kinds.
He is skilled and proficient in them. "Tāla" refers to the rhythmic measure of song;
and because he knows its true nature and practices meditation on Brahman as permeated by it, he fears the breaking of the rhythm and so forth.
Because one-pointedness of the mind upon the Self is easily accomplished, one enters and attains the path to liberation with very little effort. // 3.115 //
He states another result for one who knows song but is struck by obstacles such as mental distraction:
"If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through yoga, having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices together with him. (YDh 3.116)
If one who knows song does not somehow attain the supreme state through yoga, then, having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices and plays together with him. // 3.116 //
He concludes what was stated previously:
"The self is said to be beginningless, but its beginning is the body;
the entire world originates from the self, and the self originates from the world. (YDh 3.117)

According to the manner previously stated, the self (*ātman*) is beginningless and is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*); its "origin" (*udbhava*) has been described as the very act of assuming a body, as in the passage: "The unborn [is so called] because of the assumption of a body" (YDh 3.69). Furthermore, from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is the origin of the entire world, beginning with the earth; therefore—

And it has been stated that at the beginning of creation, the emergence of living beings into the state of gross bodies occurs from the manifested aggregate of the elements, such as earth and the rest, in the passage beginning with "Just as [the Creator created] space" (YDh 3.70). // 3.117 //
He explains this very point by means of a question:
"How is it that we, along with the gods, asuras, and humans, are utterly bewildered?
Tell us how the world has arisen and how the Self exists within it. (YDh 3.118)

We are bewildered by this matter: how this entire world, together with all its gods, asuras, humans, and so forth, has arisen from the Self, and how the Self, within that world, comes to assume the bodies of animals, humans, reptiles, and the like.
Therefore, for the sake of dispelling our delusion, please explain this to us in detail. (3.118)
Thus questioned by the sages, he gave this reply:
"Indeed, that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion is the thousand-eyed one, possessing a thousand rays and the splendor of the sun. (YDh 3.119)
That very Self is the sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) of universal form;
as Virāj, he attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food.
Having cast aside that web of delusion in this world which consists of the conceit of selfhood regarding what is not-self, such as the gross body and so forth—
Distinct from that [body] is the Puruṣa who is seen with many hands, feet, and eyes, possessing the brilliance of the sun, with infinite rays, a thousandfold, and many heads;
and this is described as such by virtue of being the substratum for the respective capacities of those [senses].
Because there is no relation to direct perception and so forth for that [Self],
it alone is the sacrifice and Prajāpati,
since it is the universal form (viśvarūpa) and the essence of all.
If it is asked how this very multiformity [occurs],
it is because that Virāj attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food such as the *puroḍāśa* cake.
And from sacrifice, through the mediation of rain and so forth, there is the creation of living beings; such is its manifold nature (vaiśvarūpya). 2.119–2.120.
He elaborates upon this very point:
"That supreme essence which arises from the relinquishment of substance and deity, having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit. (YDh 3.121)
Having been joined with the wind, the Soma is then led by the rays;
it is brought to the solar abode prescribed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
From the sphere of the sky, that Sun emits the supreme nectar.
Since the birth of all beings— whether they are of the nature of eaters or non-eaters—
proceeds from food, from that food arises sacrifice again, from sacrifice food again, and from food the ritual again;
thus this wheel revolves without beginning or end.

From the substance— such as the sacrificial pap (caru) or the cake (puroḍāśa)— which is relinquished for the sake of a deity, there arises a "sap" (rasa) that is of the nature of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), a supreme transformation of the self, which is most excellent because it serves as the seed for the birth of the entire world;
this [sap] reaches the deities who constitute the recipient factor (saṃpradāna-kāraka).
Having properly gratified [the deities] and having united the sacrificer with his desired fruit, [he],
impelled by the wind, [reaches] the lunar orb.
It is led back from that lunar orb by means of the rays to the solar orb;
this indeed is the threefold knowledge itself.
Because it is designated as non-different by the statement "it shines," it is brought forward toward that which consists of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas];
and thus, from its own sphere...

That sun emits the supreme nectar-essence in the form of rain, which is the cause of birth for all beings— both moving and non-moving, and both animate and inanimate— who subsist on food or do not eat; therefore,
from that food consisting of herbs produced by rain, which is the cause of the origin of progeny, [the moon arises].
Furthermore, from sacrifice comes sacrifice again by the manner previously described, and from sacrifice comes food again, and from food comes ritual action again;
thus this entire wheel of worldly existence (saṃsāra-cakra) revolves perfectly in the form of a continuous flow, devoid of beginning or end.
In this sequence, the origin of the entire universe proceeds from the Self.
And therein, the self assumes a body in accordance with its own karma. (3.121–124)
Now, if the transmigratory wandering of the self is indeed without beginning or end, does it not follow that liberation is impossible? To this, he says:
"The self is beginningless; no origination exists for the inner self.
But the person (puruṣa) is a composite entity, born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma. (YDh 3.125)

Although no origination exists for the inner self (antarātman) because it is beginningless and pervades the body, nevertheless, the person (puruṣa) is inherently connected with the body; as the locus of experience, he enjoys the collection of objects of enjoyment consisting of pleasure and pain—
thus, by means of such a connection, he indeed becomes related [to the body].
And that inherence is produced by karma generated through delusion, desire, and hatred, rather than being innate;
since it is subject to destruction due to its being an effect, there is no lack of liberation. (3.125)
It has been stated that the birth of the world proceeds from the Self;
to elaborate upon that, he says:
"That primordial deity who was described by me as the thousandfold Self,"
From his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the social classes (varṇas) were produced in their respective order.
From his feet the earth was born; from his head the sky arose;
from his nose the vital breaths; from his ears the quarters of space; from his touch the wind; and from his mouth the fire.

From his mind the moon was born, from his eye the sun; from his loins came the intermediate space and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings. He who, as the soul of all living beings and as the essence of the phenomenal universe, is the thousandfold self of manifold forms, and likewise the cause of the entire world.
The Primordial God has been described by me to you; from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet were born, in due order, the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
Likewise, from his feet came the earth, from his head the abode of the gods, from his nose the vital breath, and from his ears—

From her touch came the wind, from her mouth the fire, from her mind the moon, from her eye the sun, and from her hips the sky and the entire world consisting of both the moving and the unmoving. (3.126–128)
Regarding this, they raise an objection:
"If it is so, O Brahmin, how is he born in evil wombs?
Being the Lord (Īśvara), how is he joined with undesirable states? (YDh 3.129)
O Brahmin, lord of yogis,
if the Self alone assumes the state of the individual soul and so forth, then how is it that it is born in sinful wombs among animals, birds, and the like?
Now, it might be argued that birth there is said to occur because [the soul] is defiled by faults such as delusion, attachment, and aversion;
but that is not so. For since the Lord is independent, how could he be joined with undesirable states such as delusion and attachment? (3.129)
Furthermore:
Why is there no prior knowledge [of the soul] even when it is endowed with the instruments [of perception]?
And why does the all-pervading [soul], though itself omnipresent, not perceive the sensation [of others]? (YDh 3.130)
Likewise, this is also a refutation here:
why does that self, even when accompanied by the means of cognition such as the mind and so forth, not produce a prior cognition whose object was experienced in another birth?
Likewise, why does he— who is himself all-pervading and present within every body— not perceive the sensations, such as pleasure and pain, belonging to all living beings?
Therefore, the Self alone is the Lord, assuming the state of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth.
To say "one should worship" is incorrect. 3.130.
Regarding this, he states the answer to the previous objection:

"By means of defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living soul goes to existence among the hundreds of wombs, including the final states of birds and stationary beings. (YDh 3.131)

Although the Lord is by nature characterized by truth, knowledge, and bliss, nevertheless, under the influence of the penetration of ignorance (avidyā), being overwhelmed by states such as delusion and passion, he performs a threefold accumulation of karma— mental and so forth— which is the means for birth in various low wombs;
and by that, he attains the state of low-born origins, such as those of outcastes.
The "lowest" refers to outcastes (caṇḍāla) and the like; the "birds" to crows and the like; and the "stationary" to trees and the like.

This individual soul (jīva), through the defects of actions initiated by mind, speech, and body, attains the state of being one of those lowest, birds, or stationary beings over the course of thousands of births, respectively. (3.131)
Moreover:
Just as the bodies of embodied beings within their physical forms are infinite,
so too are the forms of those possessing bodies here in all wombs.

Just as the dispositions—the specific intentions—of embodied living beings within their bodies are infinite due to the varying degrees of predominance of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, so too do their effects, such as physical forms like being hunchbacked or dwarfed, occur for embodied beings across all wombs. (3.132)
Now, one might object: "If conditions such as being hunchbacked are produced by karma, then they ought to occur immediately after that karma.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The ripening of some karmas occurs after death; for others, it arises in this very life."
"For some, the result [of their action] occurs either here or in the next world;
for others, the ripening—the fruit—of rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma occurs after death in another body;
and for some, [the fruit] of rites such as the Kārīrī..."
The fruit of [rites such as] rain-making occurs in this very life;
however, for certain [rites] such as the Citrā sacrifice, the fruit— such as cattle and so forth— is indefinite, occurring either in this life or in another body.

For it is not the meaning of the scripture that the fruit of action must necessarily follow immediately; rather, in this context, the state of being a sentient being (*sattva*) and so forth is the actual determinant for actions producing pure or impure fruits, because the gradation of those fruits depends upon that very state. (3.133)
It has been stated that one attains the final and other types of births through actions born of mind, speech, and body;
to elaborate upon that, he says:
"Coveting the property of others, and likewise thinking of what is undesirable..."
And one who is intent upon false attachments is born in the lowest wombs;
namely, one who meditates with direct intent, "How might I steal the wealth of others," as well as those who commit undesirable acts such as the killing of a Brahmin.

Thinking, "I shall perform acts of violence," one who possesses a persistent attachment— that is, a repeated mental resolve— toward an unreal and false object is born among the lowest wombs, such as those of dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and the like. (3.134)
Furthermore:
A man who speaks untruth, who is slanderous, harsh, or a speaker of idle chatter, is born among beasts and birds. (YDh 3.135)

But that man who is habitually a liar, a slanderer, a whisperer into the ear, one whose speech causes agitation to others, a babbler of incoherent talk, and a speaker of irrelevant matters, is born among inferior or superior beasts and birds, according to the degree of whether his actions were intentional or unintentional. (3.135)
Furthermore:
One who is devoted to taking what is not given, who courts the wives of others, and who is a violent injurer of immobile beings by improper means, is born among stationary things. (YDh 3.136)

One who delights in taking what is not given, being addicted to seizing the wealth of others that has not been given, who is intent on the wives of others, and who kills living beings by unrighteous means, is born among stationary beings such as trees, creepers, and spreading vines, according to the relative degree of gravity or lightness of their faults. (3.136)
He describes the ripening of the qualities such as *sattva*:

"One who knows the self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses, performs dharma, and is learned in the Vedas and sciences—such a person of *sattva* attains birth among the gods. (YDh 3.137)
One who knows the Self, free from pride regarding learning, wealth, lineage, and so forth; pure, endowed with both external and internal purity;

self-controlled, possessed of tranquility; ascetic, engaged in penances such as the *kṛcchra*; likewise unattached to the objects of the senses; devoted to the performance of obligatory and occasional duties;

and a knower of the meaning of the Vedas—such a person is *sāttvika*. And by virtue of the varying degrees of the predominance of *sattva*, he attains births among the gods that are progressively more and more exalted.
He attains it. // 3.137 //
Furthermore:
"One who delights in the non-existence of the effect, who is undisciplined, enterprising, and sensual—he, being of the nature of *rajas*, attains birth among humans after death. (YDh 3.138)

But he who is devoted to unreal activities such as instrumental music, dancing, and the like; who is thus lacking in fortitude, whose mind is distracted, who is enterprising yet always preoccupied with his undertakings, and who is excessively attached to sense objects—he is endowed with the quality of *rajas*. Due to the varying degrees of that quality, immediately after death, he attains birth among the inferior or superior classes of human beings. (3.138)
And likewise:
"One who is sleepy, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar, as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct—such a person characterized by *tamas* becomes among the animals. (YDh 3.139)

Furthermore, he who is habitually prone to sleep, who causes injury to living beings, who is possessed by greed, as well as one who is an atheist, a reviler of dharma and other virtues, one who is habitually begging, negligent, devoid of discrimination between what should and should not be done, and one of contrary conduct—he is endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas); according to the degree of that [quality], he is born in the wombs of lower and lower beings, such as animals and so forth. (3.139)
He summarizes what was previously stated:
"Thus, possessed by both passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), wandering here and joined with undesirable states, he enters into the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). (YDh 3.140)

Thus, this self, pierced by ignorance and thoroughly possessed by *rajas* and *tamas*, wandering here in *saṃsāra* and overwhelmed by various states that produce manifold sufferings, repeatedly undergoes *saṃsāra*, that is, the assumption of a body.
How then can he be the Lord (*īśvara*)?
Thus, there is no room for the objection that [the self] is joined with undesirable states. (3.140)
Regarding the second objection, namely that "even for one endowed with the instruments [of perception]," he states the answer:
"For just as a mirror that is soiled is not capable of reflecting forms."
Likewise, one whose faculties are unripened is not capable of self-knowledge.

Even if the self is endowed with the means of knowledge such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, it is nevertheless incapable of comprehending objects experienced in other births if its faculties are unripened— that is, because its mind is overwhelmed by impurities such as passion (rāga).
Just as a mirror covered with dust is not capable of producing the cognition of forms. // 3.141 //

An objection is raised: "Since even the knowledge belonging to a previous birth is manifested by the self, and since that [knowledge] is established intrinsically (*svataḥsiddhatva*), non-perception of it is not logical.
Anticipating this, he says:
"Just as in an unripe *kaṭvervāru* fruit, even though the taste is sweet, it is not perceived;"
For in the same way, knowledge is not attained within the self when the faculties are unripened.

Just as the sweet taste existing in an unripe bitter cucumber or a bitter karkaṭikā fruit is not perceived, so too, although the state of being a knower (jñātṛtā)—the capacity to have objects of previous births as its domain—exists within the self, it is not attained when the faculties are unripened. (YDh 3.142)
Regarding what was asked— "Why does the all-pervading soul not experience sensation, even though it is omnipresent?"— the answer is stated there:
"The embodied soul experiences sensation which has its locus in everything within its own body."

The yogi is liberated from all [sufferings] he who does not experience sensation. Furthermore, the embodied soul (*dehin*) who is possessed of the conceit of being the body experiences sensation—consisting of internal and other forms—which rests upon everything, only in that very body acquired through his own karma; he does not experience that which belongs to another body, precisely because of the distinctness of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that initiates the commencement of a new locus of experience. As for he who...

The yogin, being liberated and free from egoism and the like, becomes the knower of all experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth occurring within all fields, because his faculties have reached full maturity. // 3.143 //
Now, one might object that the perception of difference among the bodies of gods, humans, and others within a single Self is not tenable; anticipating this, he says:
"Just as the one space appears distinct within jars and other vessels..."
Likewise, the Self is indeed one and yet manifold, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.
Just as the single sky is perceived as many through the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as wells and jars,
or as the sun [is seen differently in different waters].
Just as even a single moon is perceived as many when reflected in various broken water-vessels such as jars, water-pots, and bowls,
so too the one Self is perceived as manifold through the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa).
The employment of the second example is for the purpose of illuminating that the distinction between selves is not ultimately real. // 3.144 //
Having summarized the meaning stated in such passages as "The Lord, being the sixth himself, simultaneously takes up the five elements" (YDh 3.72),
he says: "Brahman, ether, wind, fire, water, and earth— these are the elements."
These worlds and this Self, as well as all that is moving and unmoving, [proceed] from that. *Brahman* is the Self;
*kham* is the sky or ether.
Anila is wind,
tejas is fire,
and jala is well known.
Earth and the others—
these very elements, such as wind and so forth, are called "elements" (*dhātavaḥ*) because they pervade and sustain the body. Among them, [the first are] space and the rest.
The five elements are called "worlds" (lokas) because they are perceived or seen; that is to say, they are insentient. This conscious element is the Self, and from this [Self]—
From the aggregate of the insentient and the sentient, the world consisting of the stationary and the moving arises. // 3.145 //
He explains how this Self creates the world:
"Just as a potter makes a jar through the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood. (YDh 3.146)
Just as a goldsmith, taking mere gold,
[fashions] a vessel through its union with his own saliva, or as a silkworm [produces] a cocoon;
so too, having taken various causes, [the self enters] into those various wombs here in this world.
And the Self, having brought together the instruments, creates itself.
For just as a potter, taking up a collection of causes such as clay, the wheel, and a cloth, fashions various kinds of effects such as water-jars and bowls;
or just as a carpenter, by means of grass, clay, and wood which are mutually dependent, produces a single effect known as a house.
It acts as follows: just as a goldsmith, taking only gold as his material, produces effects such as bracelets, crowns, and earrings that are composed entirely of gold;
or just as a silkworm, a particular kind of insect, produces its own cocoon—called a "sheath"—which begins from its own dwelling and serves as its own confinement.

In the same way, the Self also initiates action; having taken up the means such as earth and so forth—which are mutually dependent—as well as the instruments such as the ear and so forth, the Self itself creates itself in bodily form within this cycle of existence, in various wombs such as those of gods and others, bound by the fetters of its own karma. (3.146–148)
Anticipating the objection, "What, then, is the proof for the existence of a self distinct from the sense organs that perceive objects? he says:
"Just as the great elements are real, so indeed is the self."
Who else, having seen with one eye, sees again with the other?
Or who recognizes speech once it has been heard again after being heard before?

For just as the great elements such as earth and the rest are real because they are accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too is the Self real; otherwise, [it would not be perceived].
If there were no permanent knower distinct from the sense organs and the intellect,

then who would recognize with another sense organ, such as the tactile organ, an object previously seen by the visual organ, thinking, "I touch that very thing which I saw"? Likewise, having previously heard the speech of a certain person, when that same person's speech is heard again, [who would recognize it as his?]
Who recognizes "this is that"?
Therefore, it is established that the knower is certainly distinct from the organs of cognition. // 3.149 //
Furthermore:
Whose is the memory of past objects, or who is the creator of a dream?
[It belongs to one] who is identified with the ego through birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth.

If the Self were not eternal, then whose would memory be— that memory which has as its object things previously experienced and which is based on the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience, [arising] from the exertion toward objects such as sound through action, mind, and speech? (YDh 3.151)
For it is not possible for one person to have a memory of an object seen by another;
likewise, what could be the cause of dream-cognition? Indeed, the sense-faculties, whose activity has ceased, cannot be its cause.
Likewise, for whom does such a connecting cognition arise as "I alone am endowed with noble birth and so forth," if there were no stable self distinct [from the body]?
Similarly, for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of objects such as sound and touch...
Who would exert effort through mind, speech, and body [if there were no self]?
Therefore, the self exists as distinct from the organs of cognition. (3.150–3.151)
Explaining the nature of saṃsāra for the purpose of prescribing specific forms of worship, he says:
"With a doubtful mind as to whether the fruit of action exists or not, one who is unaccomplished, being deluded, considers himself accomplished. (YDh 3.152)
That aforementioned self, which is ruined and corrupted by egoism, becomes one whose mind is doubtful as to whether or not there is fruit in all actions;
likewise, though unaccomplished and having failed to achieve his purpose, he perceives himself as truly accomplished and having achieved his purpose.
he thinks. // 3.152 //
Furthermore:
"My wife, my son, my ministers; I belong to them"—such is his state of mind, always possessing a perverted intellect regarding things that are beneficial or harmful. (YDh 3.153)
For me, whose mind is thus corrupted, there arises an extremely agitated state of possessiveness, thinking, "I am theirs" and "they are mine," regarding my wife, children, servants, and so forth.
Likewise, in matters concerning what is beneficial or harmful, that person of corrupted mind will always possess a perverted intellect. (3.153)
Furthermore:
"One who makes no distinction between the knower and the known, or between primordial nature and its transformation; one who exerts himself in fasting, fire, blows, or leaping into water; YDh 3.154.
One who behaves in this manner—undisciplined in self, possessed of false attachments—is bound by action, as well as by hatred, delusion, and desire.

He is called a "knower of the knowable" (jñeyajña) because he knows that which is to be known; [this applies] to that Self, to primordial nature (prakṛti), to the state of equilibrium of the qualities of the Self, and to its transformations (vikāra).
Furthermore, due to egoism and the like, one becomes indiscriminate and ignorant of the means of discrimination;
likewise, under the influence of delusion, one might exert effort toward such acts as fasting to death, entering fire, drowning in water, or consuming poison.

Thus, one who is engaged in various kinds of improper actions, whose self is undisciplined and unrestrained, and who is possessed by an attachment to what should not be done, becomes bound by the collection of karmas produced thereby, as well as by passion, hatred, and delusion. (3.154–3.155)
How, moreover, does confidence in that [knowledge] arise by means of the assumption of a body? To this he says:
"Service to the teacher, discrimination regarding the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures, the performance of those duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech. (YDh 3.156)
Abstaining from looking at or touching women, perceiving the Self as the essence of all beings,
renouncing possessions, wearing worn-out saffron robes,
restraining the senses from their objects, and abandoning drowsiness and laziness.
The enumeration of the body, perceiving evil in worldly activities,
the purification of *sattva* by being free from *rajas* and *tamas*, freedom from desire, and tranquility—
one who is thoroughly purified by these means becomes fit for *sattva* and attains immortality. (YDh 3.158–159)
Service to the teacher for the sake of knowledge,
discernment regarding the meanings of the Vedānta as well as the Yoga-śāstras of Patañjali and others,
and the practice of the meditations and rituals prescribed therein.
Association with virtuous persons, speaking words that are pleasant and beneficial, the renunciation of gazing at and touching women,
and the vision of all beings as oneself— this is the vision of equality.
The renunciation of possessions such as sons, fields, wives, and so forth,
and the wearing of worn-out saffron robes.
Likewise, it is the cessation of the activity of the sense organs, such as the ear, with respect to objects like sound and touch;
lassitude is that which resembles sleep.
Laziness is a lack of enthusiasm; the specific abandonment of these two,
as well as the thorough enumeration of the body— contemplating its defects such as instability, impurity, and so forth.
Likewise, there is reflection upon the faults such as the subtle killing of living beings in all activities like walking and so forth;
likewise, there is freedom from passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) through practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Purity of being,
freedom from longing, lack of desire for sense objects,
and tranquility, which is the restraint of the external and internal organs— by these [means].

One who has become thoroughly purified through means such as service to the teacher and is endowed with pure *sattva* alone shall become immortal— that is, liberated— through the meditation upon Brahman. (3.156–159)
To explain how the attainment of immortality occurs, he says:

"Through the presence of the mindfulness of reality, through the application of being, through the complete exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, union with the Real proceeds. (YDh 3.160)

Through the recollection of the reality called the Self, by the presence of the Self with unwavering steadiness, through the purification of the *sattva* quality, through the conjunction with pure *sattva* alone, through the complete destruction of the seeds of karma, and through association with virtuous persons, the yoga of the Self proceeds. (3.160)
Moreover:
"He whose mind, upon the dissolution of the body, is established in the Lord as pure being, with an undeluded intellect, shall truly attain the recollection of his former births. (YDh 3.161)

Furthermore, when a yogin of undeluded mind, at the time of the body's dissolution, directs his mind— endowed with sattva— toward the Lord with perfect one-pointedness, if he does not realize the Self due to a lack of proficiency in the practice of worship, then by the force of the intensity of his specific latent impressions (saṃskāra),
he will experience the recollection of the various sufferings arising from dwelling in wombs such as those of worms and insects, which were experienced in other births.
And through the anxiety born from recollecting that [suffering], one applies oneself toward liberation, which brings about its cessation. (3.161)

Regarding the question of what happens to one who, due to a lack of sharp mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), does not remember their previous birth, he says: "Just as an actor paints his own body with colors, assuming various forms, so too does the self [assume] bodies born of karma. (YDh 3.162)

Just as an actor, Bharata, assuming various forms such as Rāma or Rāvaṇa, fashions and colors his own body with white, black, yellow, and other hues, even so the Self assumes various bodies— such as those of the hunchbacked or the dwarf— caused by karma, for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of those respective actions. (3.162)
Furthermore:
"The deformity of the embryo at birth—such as being deficient in limbs—is seen to result from defects in time, karma, the self, and the seed, as well as those of the mother. (YDh 3.163)

Not only is karma alone the cause of conditions such as being hunchbacked or dwarfed; rather, in the case of time and karma, the defects of the father’s seed—which is its own cause—and the defects of the mother are also factors.
All of this constitutes the collection of auxiliary causes, consisting of both visible and invisible natures.
The impairment of the embryo, such as being born with missing limbs and so forth, is observed to occur at an indefinite time starting from birth. (3.163)

Now, one might object: "At the time of the natural dissolution (prākṛtapralaya), when all transformations beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) are destroyed, the karma [of the individual] is also destroyed; how then can the first assumption of a physical body, which is dependent upon that karma, occur?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
This self has never before been liberated from egoism, the mind, the course [of rebirth], the fruit of karma, and the body in any way whatsoever. (YDh 3.164) "Mind" and "egoism" are well known.
The "state" (gati) is the mass of defects that serves as the cause for transmigration;

the "fruit of action" (karmaphala) consists of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma); and the "body" (śarīra) is of the nature of the subtle body (liṅga). By means of these—beginning with egoism (ahaṃkāra)—this self (ātman) is never liberated at any time, so long as...
Liberation. // 3.164 //

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that for living beings with their specific karmas, cessation [of life] is only logical at a specific time, and not rather the simultaneous destruction of life at an improper time in battle and the like?
Anticipating this, he says:
Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the support, and the oil, so too is its transformation observed; likewise, the premature exhaustion of the life-force occurs.
For indeed, just as there is the simultaneous persistence of various flames upon many wicks soaked in oil, so it is with those [lives].

And just as for those standing there, a simultaneous cessation occurs due to the coincidence of various causes of calamity— such as being struck by violently shaking winds— in the very same way, it is not illogical that the destruction of the life-force of warriors, charioteers, horses, elephants, and others should occur even at an untimely moment due to the coincidence of causes known as battle.
This is what is meant:

there is an obstruction of the unseen cause (adṛṣṭa), which is the cause of a specific failure at a particular time, by the occurrence of a seen cause that produces an effect contrary to it. // 3.165 //
He describes the path to liberation:
"His rays are infinite, like those of a lamp situated in the heart;
they are white, black, variegated in form, tawny, blue, and red. (YDh 3.166)

Among them, one stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [path] he goes to the supreme goal. That individual soul (jīva) which resides in the heart like a lamp has infinite rays, which are the channels (nāḍīs) that serve as the causes of pleasure and pain.

Of those seventy-two thousand rays described by the phrase "seventy-two thousand," etc., which are white, black, variegated, and so forth and are situated everywhere, one ray is positioned upwards; that very ray, having pierced the orb of the sun and transcended the abode of Hiraṇyagarbha, exists, and by means of it, the individual soul attains the supreme goal characterized by non-return. (3.167)
That other hundred rays of his which are situated directed upwards,
by means of them he reaches the bodies of the gods together with their abodes.
Of this Self, that other hundred rays— which serve as the path to liberation— are established in an upward direction.

By that [merit], he attains divine bodies composed of light, which are the exclusive substrata for the enjoyment of happiness, together with their abodes—celestial cities fashioned from gold, silver, and jewels. (3.168)
He describes the path of transmigration:
"Those many-colored rays of his that shine below with gentle luster—by means of them, he transmigrates here helplessly for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his karma. (YDh 3.169)

Furthermore, those rays below it which are of mild radiance cause him to wander helplessly in saṃsāra for the sake of experiencing the fruits [of his actions], dependent upon the karma he himself has created. (3.169)
Desiring to refute the position of those who maintain that consciousness is inherent in the material elements (bhūtacaitanyavāda), he says:
"By means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge; by birth and death;
by affliction, departure, and likewise return; and indeed by truth and falsehood. (YDh 3.170)
[One should not judge] by means of prosperity, pleasure, or pain; nor by auspicious or inauspicious actions;
nor by the results arising from omens, the knowledge of birds, or planetary conjunctions; nor by the movements of stars and constellations, nor even by those born of wakefulness or dreams.
Likewise, through ether, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness;

through the periods of the Manvantaras and the arrival of the Yugas; and even through mantras, medicinal herbs, and fruits—one perceives the Self as the Knower and the Cause of the universe. (YDh 3.172–173)
By the Vedas it is said: "This Self is 'not this, not this'"; "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long";
and "without hands or feet."
By such [scriptures], by treatises such as Mīmāṃsā and Anvīkṣikī,
and by cognitions such as the experience of a self distinct from the body in the form "this is my body," etc.
Likewise, from birth and death—which are determined by the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) performed in other lives—there is an inference of a self distinct from the body;
from suffering (*ārati*), which is determined by the performer of actions in another life;
and similarly, from going and coming—which are determined by the substratum of knowledge, desire, and effort—there is also an inference of a self distinct from the material body.
For consciousness and such qualities cannot possibly belong to the body;
because, according to the sequence taught regarding the qualities of the cause, the production of specific qualities in an effect-substance [must proceed from the qualities of its cause].
It is observed [in the self], yet the inherence of consciousness and so forth in the earthly atoms and other elements that constitute its cause is impossible,
because such qualities are not perceived in the physical objects like pillars and jars produced from them.
Nor is it produced by contact with another substance, such as water, in the manner of the power of intoxication.
This must be stated, because power (śakti) is a common quality;
therefore, one must accept a substratum for consciousness and so forth that is distinct from the material body.
Truth and falsehood are well known.
Welfare is the attainment of what is beneficial.
Happiness and suffering pertain to the next world.
Likewise, there is the performance of auspicious actions and the abandonment of inauspicious actions;
and by these, which are invariably concomitant with knowledge, one infers a self distinct from the body.
"Omens" refers to earthquakes and the like.
"Knowledge of omens" (śākunajñāna) is knowledge characterized by the signs of the movements of birds such as the *piṅgalā*.
"Planets" refers to the sun and others; [the term denotes] the results arising from their conjunctions.
*Tārā* refers to the luminaries other than Aśvinī and the rest, namely the *nakṣatras* beginning with Aśvayuj; by means of their movements, which indicate auspicious and inauspicious results,
and by means of "waking states," that is, visions of the sun with holes and so forth produced during the waking state.

Likewise, by means of cognitions arising from dreams—such as mounting a chariot yoked with donkeys or boars—and likewise by means of space and so forth created for the sake of the individual soul's experience; likewise, because they are untenable within the body during the attainment of a *manvantara* or another *yuga*; and likewise by means of the powers of mantras and medicinal herbs, such as minor rites performed with deliberate intent, either directly or through a causal sequence.
Or, O sages, know—that is, understand—that which is being experienced as impossible within the body. 3.170–173.
Furthermore:
"Egoity, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude, the transition between different sense organs, desire, retention, and life. (YDh 3.174)

Heaven, dreaming, the impulse of entities, the movement of the mind, the winking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and the grasping of the five elements— since these signs of the Supreme Self are observed, [it exists]. (YDh 3.175)
Therefore, there exists a Self beyond the body, all-pervading and sovereign. *Ahaṃkṛtiḥ* is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāraḥ*);
*smṛtiḥ* (memory) is based on the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed by experiences in a previous birth, and has as its object the drinking of breast milk and so forth.
Happiness is pertaining to this world;
fortitude is steadfastness.

For when an object has been seen by one sense organ, the transition to another sense organ—consisting of the synthesis in the form "I touch that which I saw"—is what is meant by the transition between sense organs.
In this [verse], desire, effort, and consciousness possess the status of an inferential mark (*liṅga*) by their very nature; however,
in the preceding verse, they possess an implied inferential status as the causes for such acts as going and speaking the truth— thus there is no redundancy.
Likewise, "maintenance" refers to the body; "life" refers to the maintenance of the vital breaths;
and "heaven" is a specific kind of happiness to be experienced in another fixed body.
Dream is well known.
However, in the previous verse, the dream was mentioned as a sign for the purpose of indicating auspicious results, whereas here it is mentioned in its own nature; thus, there is no tautology.
Likewise, the impelling of entities such as the sense organs,
the movement of the mind, and the blinking of eyes are all pervaded by the presiding presence of consciousness; this is well known.
Likewise, there is the appropriation of the five elements.

Since these marks—whether directly or indirectly—are seen to be impossible within the elements and yet serve as indicators of the Supreme Self, it is therefore established that there exists a Self distinct from the body, the all-pervading Lord. // 3.174–176 //

He states the true nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña): "The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action, as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the elements beginning with earth. (YDh 3.177)

The Unmanifest is called the Self (ātman), the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this field; it is the Lord (īśvara) residing in all beings, who is both being and non-being, and that which is both existent and non-existent. The organs of perception, beginning with hearing, together with their objects such as sound; the mind; the organs of action, beginning with speech; likewise the ego (ahaṃkāra); the intellect (buddhi) consisting of determination; and the five elements, beginning with earth—[these constitute the field].

The unmanifest is called *prakṛti*; this is the field (*kṣetra*) of that Lord who is omnipresent and, for that very reason, of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), because he cannot be grasped by other means of valid cognition.
Because it lacks clear perceptibility, this Self, which consists of both existence and non-existence, is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field). (3.177–3.178)
He states the origin of the intellect (buddhi) and the rest:
"The origin of the intellect is from the Unmanifest; from that, the emergence of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
and from the ego-sense, the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the rest, possessing one additional quality each. (YDh 3.179)
The equilibrium of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

From that arises the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of the threefold nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and from that intellect arises the threefold ego (*ahaṃkāra*), namely the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*.

Therein, from the *ahaṃkāra* known as *bhūtādi*, which is characterized by *tamas*, the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) arise; by the inclusion of the word "first" (*ādi*), space and the other elements are meant, and these are produced with each successive quality added.
By virtue of the word "and" (ca), the sense organs of cognition and action arise from both the *vaikārika* and *taijasa* [aspects]. (3.179)
He states the nature of their qualities:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever among these emerges from which [element], that dissolves back into that very one. (YDh 3.180)
The five qualities, beginning with sound, should be understood to increase by one for each of those five elements, beginning with space.

And among these transformations such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, whichever arises from a particular source—such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—dissolves back into that very same source in its subtle form at the time of dissolution. (3.180)
Concluding the meaning of this section, he says:
"I have explained to you how the Self creates itself, even though it is the Lord, through the ripening of the three kinds of karma. (YDh 3.181)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed proclaimed to be his very qualities;
for when possessed by rajas and tamas, he is whirled around like a wheel.
He alone is the Supreme Person, both without beginning and possessing a beginning.
The form that is perceivable by the sense organs through their indicative marks (liṅga) is declared to be subject to modification.

It has been explained to you how the Self, though being the Lord, creates itself according to the ripening of the three types of karma— mental and so forth— and how the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest belong to that very Self when it is characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Likewise, it has also been stated that when that very same [Self] is possessed by rajas and tamas, it wanders here in this cycle of existence like a wheel;
he alone is the beginningless Supreme Person.

By the term "taking on a body," it is described as having a beginning, being subject to transformations such as being hunchbacked or dwarfed, likewise transformed into a gross form, and having a nature that is perceivable by the marks, that is, the sense organs. (3.181–183)
He describes the path to heaven:
"The space between the Path of the Fathers (pitṛyāna), the Aja-vīthī, and Agastya—by that do those who maintain the Agnihotra and desire heaven proceed toward the celestial realm. (YDh 3.184)

The path of the Aja-vīthī is the path of the immortals; that which lies between it and Agastya is the Pitṛyāna (the path of the ancestors). By that [latter path], those who maintain the sacred fire and desire heaven go to the sky; they attain heaven. // 3.184 //
Furthermore:
Those who are devoted to giving and endowed with the eight virtues correctly, they too, being dedicated to the vow of truth, proceed by that very same path. (YDh 3.185)

And those who are devoted to the traditional rites such as giving, being perfectly free from hypocrisy, and likewise endowed with the eight qualities of the self— compassion, patience, lack of envy, purity, lack of weariness, auspiciousness, generosity, and lack of greed— as set forth by Gautama and others;
and likewise those who are intent on speaking the truth— they too [proceed] by that very path of the ancestors.
They attain the abode of the gods. // 3.185 //

Now, one might object: "In the dissolution following the *pratisaṃcara* of the Naimittika and other types, since all teachers have perished, the people living above that level will not know the Vedas;
how then will they perform rituals such as the *agnihotra*, and how much less, being devoid of performed rites, will they ascend the path to heaven?
To this, he says:
There, eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders,
