subject to rebirth, the seeds [of future lineages], and promoters of the Dharma; there,
on the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), these eighty-eight thousand sages belong to the stage of the householder and are characterized by the law of returning again.

At the beginning of creation, by virtue of being the instructors of the Veda, they serve as the seeds for the manifestation of the tree of Dharma and are the initiators of duties such as the Agnihotra; therefore, the aforementioned defects do not apply here. // 3.186 //
Moreover:
Between the Seven Sages and the Nāgavīthī, they dwell in the world of the gods;
there are just as many sages, who have abandoned all undertakings. (YDh 3.187)
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings;
these are the well-known Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
The Nāgavīthi is the path of Airāvata;

within that interval, there are likewise eighty-four thousand sages who have abandoned all undertakings, are established in absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), are endowed with austerity and celibacy, and have renounced worldly attachment.

Residing in the world of the gods (devaloka), they remain until the dissolution of all beings—that is, until the end of the primordial dissolution (prākṛtapralaya). And remaining there, at the beginning of creation, they set in motion the internal phenomena (ādhyātmikadharma). 3.187–3.188.
To explain what kind of sages they were, he says:
"From whom the Vedas, Purāṇas, sciences, Upaniṣads, as well as verses, aphorisms, commentaries, and whatever else consists of speech [proceed]. (YDh 3.189)

Since from both types of assemblies of sages the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, the auxiliary sciences, and the Upaniṣads— which are eternal and have descended through a lineage of students— have proceeded; and likewise the verses consisting of historical narratives (itihāsa), the Sūtras concerning grammar and Mīmāṃsā,

the commentaries (bhāṣya) which take the form of explanations of those Sūtras, and whatever other body of literature there is, such as the science of medicine (āyurveda), [all have proceeded] from him.
Those sages who promulgated the Dharma proceeded in such a manner;
this being so, there is no consequence of the fault of impermanence even for the Veda. (3.189)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"The recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint, faith, fasting, and independence are the causes for the knowledge of the Self. (YDh 3.190)

Since the Veda is eternal, by virtue of its authority, the recitation of the Veda and other such practices become logically established as causes for the knowledge of the Self, by means of bringing about the purification of one's being. (3.190)
Moreover:
He is indeed to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
furthermore, he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard from by the twice-born.
Those twice-born who know him thus, and those who have resorted to the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), worship the Truth endowed with supreme faith.

Since the Veda is eternal and constitutes the authoritative means of knowledge for the Self, therefore it has been stated that he [the Truth] is to be worshipped in various ways by followers of all stages of life (āśrama) according to the prescribed path.
It is to be desired for inquiry.
He shows that very manner [of inquiry]: it is to be seen—that is, to be made directly perceived—by the twice-born.
He shows the means for that:
"It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon.
First, it must be determined through the hearing of the Vedānta;
immediately thereafter, it must be reflected upon by means of reasoning.
It should be investigated;
thereafter, it becomes directly perceived through meditation by those twice-born who are endowed with extraordinary faith.
The virtuous, having resorted to a secluded place, worship this Self—which is truth and the ultimate reality—in the manner described; they know it, they find it, and they attain it. 3.191–3.192.
He describes the path of attainment as the way of the gods:
"In due order, they arise [in the worlds of] light, day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice, the world of the gods, the sun, and lightning" (YDh 3.193).
Then a person born of the mind approaches them and leads them to the world of Brahmā;

for them, there is no return here again. Having realized the Self, they rest in succession in the abodes of the presiding deities of fire and the other elements—which constitute the path to liberation—and, being sent forth by them, they reach the supreme state.
They reach [the following]:
*arcis* is fire, *ahan* is the day.
The bright fortnight,
likewise the northern course [of the sun],
and the abode of the gods;
Savitṛ, Sūrya, and the lightning-splendor— these, situated in the stages beginning with light (arcis) in this sequence, the mental person (mānasaḥ puruṣaḥ) leads to the world of Brahman. For them,
there is no return again to this cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), but rather [only] at the time of the dissolution of primordial nature (prākṛtapratisaṃcara).
Having abandoned the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), they become one with the Supreme Self. // 3.193 // 3.194 //
He describes the path of the ancestors mentioned previously:
"Those men who have won heaven by means of sacrifice, austerity, and gifts, [travel] through smoke, the night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice. (YDh 3.195)

The self-possessed person who does not understand this twofold path— the way by which they sequentially arise here in this world from the world of the ancestors, the moon, the wind, rain, water, and the earth, and then return again— [is deluded]. (YDh 3.196)
Or they may become a venomous snake, a moth, an insect, or even a worm.

However, those who enjoy the fruit of heaven by means of prescribed paths—sacrifices, gifts, and austerities—reach, in due order, the deities presiding over the stages beginning with smoke and ending with the moon; then, having reached air, rain, water, and earth, and having attained the state of semen in the form of food such as rice and other grains, [they enter a womb].
Those wandering in saṃsāra go to their place of birth.
He who, being heedless, does not understand these two paths and does not practice the dharmas that serve as the means for those two paths— he is a biting serpent.
He may become a moth, a locust, a worm, or an insect. (3.195–197)
He describes the method of meditation:
"With the feet turned upward and placed upon the thighs, having laid the right hand upon the left, slightly raising the face and steadying it with the chest. (YDh 3.198)
With eyes closed, established in *sattva*, not touching tooth against tooth,
with the tongue fixed on the palate and the mouth closed, perfectly motionless;
having restrained the collection of the senses, he should sit on a seat that is neither too low nor too high.
One should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) for either double or triple [the duration].
Then, that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp should be meditated upon;
there the wise man, maintaining concentration (dhāraṇā), should fix the self.
He whose feet are placed upon his thighs with the soles upward is thus described as being in the *baddhapadmāsana* (bound lotus posture).
Likewise, having placed the right hand, palm upward, upon the left hand which is also turned upward, slightly raising the face, and supporting [the body] with the chest— having made it steady— thus.
With eyes closed, established in *sattva*, free from desire, anger, and the like, not touching the teeth with the teeth, and likewise one whose tongue is fixed immovably against the palate;
thus described, he has his mouth closed, his face covered, and is perfectly motionless and unshakable.

Likewise, having properly withdrawn the entire collection of sense faculties from their objects, seated in a posture that is neither too low nor too high so that no mental distraction occurs, one should undertake the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) twice or thrice. Then, by the yogi who has mastered the vital air (*pavana*), there arises in the heart that Lord who is unshakable like a lamp.
One should meditate upon him as he stands there;
and therein, one should hold oneself within the heart by making it the object of the mind,
maintaining that concentration.
And as for the nature of *dhāraṇā*: the time taken to snap the fingers while rotating the knees forward constitutes one *mātrā*. With fifteen such *mātrās*, there is the lowest form of *prāṇāyāma*.
With thirty [breaths] it is middling; with forty-five, it is superior. Thus, one *dhāraṇā* consists of three *prāṇāyāmas*.
Those three are designated by the term "yoga," and one should maintain them;
as it is said elsewhere:
"Having made a snapping sound, one should place the tips of the hands upon the kneecaps."
Prāṇāyāma consisting of fifteen mātrās is considered the lowest.
The middling [concentration] is double that, and the best is triple; likewise for *dhāraṇā*.
Each one is said to consist of three [units], and yoga is likewise composed of those. (3.198–201)
He states the purpose for practicing yoga characterized by concentration (dhāraṇā):
"Invisibility, memory, luster, vision, as well as knowledge through hearing, and the ability to enter another's body after casting off one's own. (YDh 3.202)
The creation of objects at will is indeed the characteristic mark of perfection in yoga;
for one who has attained yoga, upon casting off the body, he is fit for immortality.
Through the attainment of *aṇimā*, invisibility to others is concealment (*antardhāna*).
*Smṛti* is the recollection of objects beyond the reach of the senses, like that of Manu and others;
*kānti* is loveliness;
and *dṛṣṭi* is vision even regarding objects past and future.
Likewise, auditory knowledge is the state of being a knower of sounds that have not yet reached the path of the ear because they are manifested in an extremely distant location;
and it is the entry into another's body by means of relinquishing one's own body.
The creation of objects by the power of one's own will, independent of external causes, is the defining characteristic and sign of the perfection of yoga.
And this is not the only purpose; rather—
When yoga has been perfected, one who abandons the body is fit for immortality and becomes capable of attaining the state of Brahman. // 3.202 // 3.203 //
He states another means for the purification of the inner being when sacrifices, gifts, and the like are impossible:
"Alternatively, by practicing the Veda, having renounced ritual acts, dwelling in the forest, eating only what is unasked for, and eating sparingly, one may attain supreme perfection. (YDh 3.204)

Alternatively, one who has abandoned optional and forbidden actions, who studies any one of the Vedas, who is devoted to solitude, and whose purity of being is brought about by eating only what is unasked for and measured, attains through the meditation on the Self the supreme perfection characterized by liberation. // 3.204 //
Moreover:

"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites (śrāddha), and who speaks the truth—even such a householder is indeed liberated. (YDh 3.205)

Since even a householder— who has acquired wealth through righteous means such as receiving gifts, who is devoted to honoring guests, who is intent on the performance of obligatory and occasional *śrāddha* rites, who is habituated to speaking the truth, and who is absorbed in meditation on the reality of the Self— attains liberation, it follows that the adoption of the wandering life (*parivrājya*) alone in this world is not the sole means to liberation. (3.205)
Thus ends the section on the Inner Self;
now begins the section on Expiation:
"Tell us, without omission, the duties of those belonging to the castes, the stages of life, and others. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.1)

Thus, having explained five types of dharma among the sixfold dharma promised here as the subject matter to be established, and now desiring to undertake the remaining class of occasional dharma designated by the term *prāyaścitta*, [the author] first states the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*) in the form of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), for the purpose of generating interest therein and for the purpose of demonstrating the specific qualifications of the agent.

Having reached the terrible and dreadful hells born of great sins (*mahāpātaka*), those who have committed great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma. Regarding the designation "great sin" for the group of five beginning with the killing of a Brahmin, [the text states]: "The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor... (YDh 3.227).

To this it will be said here: those practitioners of yoga who are great sinners, having reached the Tamisra and other hells produced by their great sins—which are terrible because they cause exceedingly intense pain, most fearsome, dreadful, and are abodes solely for the experience of suffering—and which correspond to the evil deeds they themselves committed; then, upon the exhaustion of their karma—that is, after the exhaustion of the experience of hellish suffering born of that karma—due to the remainder of their karma, once again...
In this saṃsāra, they are born repeatedly and in abundance among the animal wombs of dogs, jackals, and so forth, which abound in suffering.
The mention of "those who commit the great sins" (mahāpātakins) is an elliptical indication that includes others as well, such as those who commit secondary offenses (upapātakins).
And because it will be explained later that they attain births such as those of animals and so forth. (3.206)
Having described the attainment of worldly existence by those who have committed the great sins, he speaks in order to specify their particular destinies:

"The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a deer, a dog, a pig, or a camel; the drinker of spirituous liquor [enters the womb] of a donkey, a Pulkasa, or a Venā; of this there is no doubt. (YDh 3.207)
A stealer of gold shall attain the state of worms, insects, and moths;
and one who violates the Guru’s bed shall gradually become grass, shrubs, and creepers.
(YDh 3.208) "Deer" refers to the *hariṇa* and other such animals.
Dogs, pigs, and camels are well known;
the killer of a Brahmin attains their state of birth as the residue of his own karma.
A "khara" is a donkey.
A Pulkasa is born from a Niṣāda of inverse birth upon a Śūdra woman;
a Veṇa is born from a Vaidehaka upon an Ambaṣ�ṭha woman; a drinker of spirituous liquor enters the womb of those [outcastes].
Worms (*kṛmi*) are produced from meat, excrement, cow dung, and so forth, being independent of the enjoyment of their own kind;
from them arise slightly larger insects (*kīṭa*) such as ants, which lack wings and bones;
and moths (*pataṅga*), that is, locusts—of these...
A Brahmin who steals gold shall enter the womb [of a lower species];
"grass" refers to *kāśa* and the like, while "shrubs and creepers" are as previously described.
One who violates the Guru’s bed gradually attains the state of being born as that [same species];
and this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.
But those who act out of their own will transmigrate even into other wombs abounding in suffering;
as Manu has said:
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; of a cow, a horse, a deer, or a bird; or of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.
A Brahmin who steals [the property of others] becomes, by the thousands, spiders, snakes, lizards, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas.
The spider,
the lizard,
the chameleon, and those that feed on raw flesh among the grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as those with fangs.
"And likewise for those who perform cruel deeds, and for one who violates the teacher's bed—[these] by the hundreds. (MDh 12.55–58) 3.207–8 //
Furthermore, in the NSP and Pāṇḍeya editions,
there is an introductory statement:
"And thus, for those who have emerged from the state of being animals..."

He says that in the human state, characteristics such as disease and so forth occur. Furthermore, the phrase *kiṃ ca* is provided as part of the commentary; since this is unusual, I believe Seltur is correct.
Taking this as the introduction, he notes that the longer sentence is found only in a single manuscript:
"A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; a drinker of spirituous liquor shall have black teeth."
One who steals gold becomes one with deformed nails; one who violates the teacher’s bed becomes one with a skin disease. Whosoever associates with any of these [sinners] is born with their same mark.
Having thus experienced terrible suffering in hells such as Raurava and in wombs such as those of dogs, pigs, and donkeys, immediately thereafter—
Due to the remainder of their evil deeds, even at the very moment of birth, they transmigrate through abundant human bodies afflicted with symptoms such as consumption and other diseases.
A killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with consumption and pulmonary tuberculosis;
one who has drunk forbidden liquor naturally has black teeth.
The stealer of a Brahmin’s gold is born with deformed nails;
the violator of the Guru’s bed is born with a skin disease such as leprosy.
Among these, including the slayer of a Brahmin and the others, whichever fallen person a man associates with, he is born bearing that same mark. (3.209)
Furthermore:
"The stealer of food shall suffer from chronic illness; the stealer of speech shall be mute;
one who adulterates grain shall have redundant limbs; and a slanderer shall have a putrid nose. (YDh 3.210cd)

A stealer of oil shall be one who drinks oil; a slanderer shall have a foul-smelling mouth. A stealer of food shall suffer from disease, and one whose food is not digested [shall be one who steals it].
One who steals speech, one who studies without permission, and a stealer of books [shall likewise suffer these fates].

One who steals grain becomes mute, that is, deficient in the faculty of speech. One who slanders—meaning one whose habit is to proclaim the existing faults of others—becomes one with redundant limbs, such as having six fingers and so forth. One who steals oil becomes one with a foul-smelling nose, while a stealer of oil becomes a *tailapāyin*, a specific kind of insect. A slanderer... [becomes... a *sūcaka* (a needle-worm).
One is born with a mouth that emits a foul odor, proclaiming its six defects;
and this is to be understood as occurring upon obtaining a human body after having attained the state of an animal.

"Whatever another's property it may be, having forcibly seized it, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal, as does one who has consumed an oblation that was not consecrated," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 12.68). 3.210–3.211.
Furthermore:
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest. (YDh 3.212)

In place of the actual commentary, the NSP edition erroneously inserts here a portion of the commentary on 3.213: "In a low caste called that of the goldsmiths, among the species of birds, one who steals the jewels and other property of others is born; in a waterless [place]..."
In that region, one is born as a *brahmarākṣasa*, a specific type of spirit,
who seizes the wives of others and steals the property of Brahmins, with the exception of gold.
In a waterless region of the forest, he is born as a *brahmarākṣasa*, a particular kind of spirit. (3.212)
Moreover: "One who steals the jewels of others will be born into a low caste;
by killing a peacock one becomes a leaf-eating bird, and by stealing auspicious perfumes one becomes a muskrat. (YDh 3.213)
In a low-born species known as that of the goldsmith, one who steals the jewels and other property of others is born as a bird;
and so too says Manu:
"A man who, out of greed, has stolen gems, pearls, and corals..."

"And various kinds of gems are produced from those who work with gold" (MDh 12.69). By stealing leafy vegetables, one becomes a peacock; by stealing auspicious perfumes, one becomes a muskrat known as the "king's daughter."
She is born as a mouse. 3.213.
Furthermore:
a rat [is the retribution for] stealing grain; a camel for a vehicle; a monkey for fruit;
a water-fowl for water; a crow for milk; and a house-builder (white ant) for household utensils. (YDh 3.214)

A honey-thief becomes a gadfly; a thief of meat, a vulture; a cow-thief, a monitor lizard; likewise, a fire-thief, a heron; a thief of clothing, one afflicted with leucoderma; a thief of liquids, a dog; a thief of salt, a cricket; and a thief of grain, a rat. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.215)
Having stolen a vehicle, one becomes a camel; having stolen fruit, a monkey; having stolen water, a water-fowl known as the *śakaṭavila*.

Having stolen milk (payaḥ), which is cow's milk, one becomes a crow (kāka); having stolen household utensils such as a pestle and so forth, one becomes a house-builder, a specific type of insect called a *caṭaka*;
and having stolen honey, one becomes an insect known as a *dāṃśa*.
Having taken a pala of meat, one becomes a bird called a vulture; having taken a cow, a specific creature called a monitor lizard;
and having taken fire, a bird called a heron.
By stealing clothing one becomes afflicted with vitiligo; by stealing the juice of sugarcane and the like, one becomes a dog.
One who steals salt becomes a cricket; one who steals firewood becomes a cricket with a loud cry. (3.214–3.215)

Having spoken thus for the sake of illustration, since it is impossible to speak of every single substance by means of exhaustive questioning, he says the following to demonstrate the ripening of karma through a single limiting condition (*upādhi*):
"But this which I have stated regarding the act of theft was said merely for the sake of illustration."
For just as there are various kinds of objects, so too are there various classes of living beings;

whatever the specific types of objects being stolen may be, the perpetrators of the act of theft become members of corresponding classes of living beings. For example, one who steals bell-metal becomes a swan.
Alternatively, one who steals the material substance that is the means for accomplishing a result becomes deprived of that very means, just as a horse-thief suffers lameness;
in this regard, Śaṅkha has shown a specific distinction in certain cases.
A killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with leprosy; a stealer of light becomes afflicted with circular skin spots;
one who reviles gods or Brahmins becomes bald.
One who administers poison or sets fire [to property] becomes insane; one who strikes back at his teacher suffers from epilepsy;
and a killer of a cow becomes blind.
A specific type of creature that pierces with sound, having abandoned its lawful wife, engages elsewhere; likewise,
one who eats from a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍāśī) is a consumer of the female organ (bhagabhakṣa).
One who steals the property of the gods or Brahmins suffers from jaundice;
one who misappropriates a deposit becomes one-eyed; and one who lives by trafficking women becomes a eunuch.
One who abandons his wife while she is still young becomes unfortunate; one who eats only sweets suffers from abdominal tumors caused by wind; and one who eats forbidden food suffers from scrofula.
One who approaches a Brahmin woman is seedless;
one of cruel deeds is a dwarf; and one who steals clothing [is such].
One who steals a cloth becomes a moth; one who steals a bed becomes a mendicant ascetic; one who steals a conch or a pearl-oyster shell becomes a skull-bearer;
and one who steals a lamp becomes an owl.
"One who betrays a friend becomes consumptive; one who reviles one's mother or father becomes lame.
Thus [it is said]. Gautama also states a specific distinction in certain places.
One who speaks untruth becomes weak; one whose speech is constantly faltering becomes a deserter of his wife;
one who gives false testimony becomes afflicted with elephantiasis, with his shanks and feet cut away.
One who creates obstacles to a marriage has his lips cut off; one who utters threats has his hands cut off;
a matricide is blind; and one who violates his daughter-in-law [is likewise punished].

One who emits semen through the anus suffers from wind-disorders; one who voids feces and urine at a crossroads suffers from dysuria; a defiler of virgins becomes impotent; and an envious person becomes jealous.
Maśaka, quarreling with his father, became afflicted with epilepsy; the embezzler of a deposit was childless;
and the stealer of jewels became utterly destitute.
One who sells knowledge is a "deer-man," one who sells the Vedas is a "leopard," and one who officiates at many sacrifices is a "water-fowl."
One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice becomes a boar; one who eats without being invited becomes a crow;
and one who eats only delicacies becomes a monkey.
The cat eats from here and there;
the firefly [shines] from the forest-fire in the thicket; the teacher of children has foul breath from his mouth.
One who eats stale food becomes a worm;
one who takes what is not given becomes an ox;
one who is envious becomes a bee.
One who extinguishes the sacred fire becomes afflicted with ringworm and leprosy;
one who acts as a teacher for a Śūdra becomes a dog-cooker (outcaste); and a stealer of cows becomes a serpent.
One who steals oil suffers from consumption; one who steals food suffers from indigestion;
one who steals knowledge becomes mute.

By having sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī or a Pulkasī, one becomes a python; by having intercourse with a female renunciant, a desert piśāca; and by having intercourse with a Śūdra woman, a long worm.
One who approaches a woman of his own caste becomes poor; one who carries water becomes a fish; one who carries milk becomes a crane;
and a usurer becomes deformed in limb.
One who sells what should not be sold becomes a vulture; one who has sexual intercourse with the king's queen becomes a eunuch.
One who reviles a king becomes a donkey; one who has sexual intercourse with a cow becomes a frog;
and one who studies on forbidden days becomes a jackal.
One who steals another's property becomes a servant of others;
by killing a cow, one dwells in a womb.
Thus, these are those who do not ascend further.
Women also, under these same circumstances, experience womanhood within the very same castes previously mentioned;
as Manu has said:
"Women also, by stealing according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives of these very same creatures.

(MDh 12.69) And this description of the characteristics such as wasting away is intended to produce a sense of dread in those who have committed the murder of a Brahmin and others, so that they may turn toward penance.
Nor, however, is it for the sake of attaining a twelve-year vow or similar observances, nor for the sake of ceasing social contact with those characterized by such traits as being subject to decay;
for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is intended for the destruction of sin,
and through expiation, there is no destruction of the unseen force (*apūrva*) of sins whose fruits have already begun to manifest.
There is no further purpose [served];
for an arrow released from a bow does not require any other state of existence for the piercing of the target, nor for the continued existence of the archer or his exertion.
Nor should one seek the destruction of a new unseen force (*apūrva*) for the purpose of destroying the fruit already initiated by that [action];

for the destruction of a pot or similar object initiated by a wheel, a loom, or other instrumental causes does not follow from the destruction of those instruments themselves. Furthermore, innate defects such as deformed nails cannot be restored.
Furthermore, for one who has experienced the succession of sufferings produced in the hells, the animal realm, and so forth,
the final fruit is indeed physical deformities such as having webbed fingers;
and by its mere arising, there is the destruction of the unseen force (*apūrva*) which is its own cause.
Just as the destruction of the fire-drill wood is produced by the fire generated through friction,
so too the practice of vows does not serve to destroy sin, nor is it for the sake of worldly transaction.
For the learned do not avoid association with those who have deformed nails and the like;

since their fitness for social intercourse is established through the destruction of past sins by means of [the prescribed] expiation, there is no need for the performance of a vow. As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One with deformed nails and one with black teeth shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights" (VaDh 20.6).

Thus, it should be understood that this is merely occasional (naimittika), like the *kṣāmavatī* sacrifice and others, and not for the purpose of destroying sin or for the sake of establishing fitness for social intercourse. // 3.216 //
Moreover:
Having obtained their fruit according to their karma, through the passage of time they are born as animals;
then, having fallen from their auspicious marks, they become impoverished and the lowest of men. (YDh 3.217)

Having obtained, in accordance with their own committed good and evil deeds and without escaping them, corresponding fruits such as rebirth in hell or the state of an animal, they are born among men as inferior beings—possessing deformed characteristics and being impoverished—once their karma has been exhausted over the course of time. (3.217)
Furthermore:
Then, having become free from blemish, they are born into a great family as enjoyers of wealth, endowed with knowledge, and possessed of riches and grain. (YDh 3.218)

Then, immediately after that birth as a human being with unfavorable marks, having become free from stain and having exhausted their sins through the experience of hell and other realms, they are born into great families endowed with enjoyments, wealth, and grain by virtue of the remainder of their previously acquired merit. (3.218)
Having thus described the ripening of karma for the purpose of encouraging [the performance of] expiations, he now speaks in order to define those who are entitled to them:
"By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the practice of what is censured, and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall. (YDh 3.219)
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become propitiated.

(YDh 3.220) That which is prescribed as mandatory—such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), and so forth—is obligatory; however, in cases such as contact with impurity, it becomes occasional (*naimittika*).

Both that which is enjoined, such as ritual bathing and so forth, and that which is prohibited are here referred to; by the non-performance of the former, by the performance of the latter— such as drinking liquor and other forbidden acts— and by the failure to restrain the senses, a person incurs or attains downfall (*patanam*).
The meaning is that one incurs sin.
Now, an objection is raised: "One should not indulge in any objects of the senses out of desire," for even indulgence of the senses has been prohibited.
Since the meaning is already understood by the very mention of "blameworthy" (*nindita*), for what purpose is the separate inclusion of the phrase "and from the non-restraint of the senses"?
To this it is replied: The prohibition of attachment to the senses does not have an exclusively negative form, because this is recited among the *snātaka* vows.

Furthermore, since there is the governing context of the word "vow" (*vrata*) in the injunction "one should maintain these vows," and because of the presence of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that prohibits attachment to the senses which is being enjoined.
And since that [non-performance] is of the nature of an entity (*bhāva*), it is mentioned separately.
Now, how is it determined that one incurs sin from the non-performance of what is enjoined?
For the injunction regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites does not, by its very nature, consist in the instigation of a person toward non-performance.
It implies that [the Veda] is not the cause of sin (pratyavāya).

For that [injunction], which culminates merely in the understanding that the performance of the object [of the rite] serves a human purpose, permits engagement by that much alone; it does not, however, state that non-performance is a cause of sin.
Because its power is exhausted, it is untenable.

Furthermore, if another entity were postulated for the sake of establishing the occurrence of the cessation of what is untenable, then even though the status of that avoidance as a human goal would be established simply by way of avoiding the demerit (*pratyavāya*) produced by the prohibited action, one would have to postulate yet another result.
And this is not accepted by anyone.

Now, just as in the case of prohibited acts, their status as human goals (puruṣārtha) is established solely for the sake of avoiding the transgression understood through the explanatory passages (arthavāda), so too [is it here].
Even in the case of prescribed acts, why should they not have the purpose of avoiding the sin (pratyavāya) produced by their non-performance, as understood from explanatory passages (arthavāda)?
Do not say so; for such explanatory passages do not exist in all cases, such as the Agnihotra and other rites.
Nor is it tenable to claim that the Smṛti rule—"By the non-performance of what is prescribed, a man incurs downfall"—itself stands in the place of an explanatory passage.
For an explanatory praise (arthavāda) by means of one sentence is not possible regarding an effect already established by another sentence.

Or, even if it were somehow an explanatory praise through syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), nevertheless, there is no non-existence [of the act] in the case of the non-performance of what has been enjoined.
It is capable of producing another effect.

Now, just as it is understood from the statement of Āyurveda that "fasting is the supreme medicine for fever and diarrhea," and thus fasting in the form of the absence of food produces the subsiding of fever, so let it be here as well.

It is not so; for even here, the subsiding of fever does not result from jumping itself. Rather, it should be understood that it occurs because of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-sāmya*) produced by the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala-paripāka*), provided there is an absence of food which would otherwise obstruct the destruction of the fever. Therefore, one must explain how the following traditional law (*smṛti*) applies: "By the non-performance of what is enjoined, a man incurs a fall."
It is said: there is no fault, for this is intended to refer to the transgression consisting in the failure to establish eligibility for rites such as the *agnihotra*.
[Objection:
"A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*) with a face like a flaming torch, eating what has been vomited."
And a Kṣatriya who eats impure things and corpses becomes a Kaṭapūtana.
"A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Maitrākṣajyotika who feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
How can these words of Manu, which concern the sin arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties, be reconciled?

It is said: Just as there is suffering for one who eats what has been vomited or whose mouth is burned by a firebrand, so too is there suffering for this person who does not perform what is enjoined because he fails to achieve the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*). Thus, the censure of non-performance is intended to encourage performance; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Alternatively, [the result] takes the form of being a hungry ghost (*preta*) with a mouth like a firebrand who eats vomit, produced by passion, laziness, and so forth, which obstruct the performance of enjoined duties that were triggered by the practice of prohibited acts in a previous life.
Thus, one should not think that non-existence (abhāva) ever functions as a cause.

Now, [one might object]: in cases such as being falsely accused by a prostitute, a monkey, a donkey, or a dog, or for failing to perform prescribed duties, even one of the various causes—such as the non-performance of what is enjoined—is present.
Since [the sin] does not exist, how can there be transgression, and how can there be an injunction for expiation in its absence?

It is said: Precisely from this injunction for expiation intended for the destruction of sin, it is understood that there exists a *pāpāpūrva* (sinful latent impression) produced by the performance of prohibited acts and so forth committed in other births.

"Cast off" (samākṣiptam) refers to such things as curses and the like, which are to be removed by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by them; it is inferred that these have been performed by this person.
This is because the arising of sin in the form of an effect is impossible without dependence on human effort, nor [is it possible] through the effort residing in an unchaste woman or others.
The production of demerit occurs in another person,
because merit and demerit are necessarily inherent in the agent;
therefore, this is indeed logical.
There is an enumeration of three causes for expiation;
and so Manu says:
"One who fails to perform prescribed duties and performs censurable acts..."
"And a man who is attached to the objects of the senses incurs the need for penance" (MDh 11.44).
The mention of "man" (*nara*) is intended to include those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), so that they may also obtain the entitlement to perform penance;
for even they are capable of transgressing common duties such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).

Since one incurs sin by performing prohibited acts and the like, therefore that person who has engaged in such prohibited conduct must perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the sake of purification in this world and the next.
Furthermore, this word *prāyaścitta*— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the complete portion supplied.]
It is conventionally established as a specific type of ritual action intended for the destruction of evil.
Thus, when the expiation has been performed, his inner self becomes serene through purity, and the world also becomes inclined to engage with him in social intercourse.
By saying this, the following is shown:
this section on penance is contingent upon specific circumstances.

And in that context, even the destruction of evil (durita) mentioned in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is accepted as something to be accomplished (sādhya) according to the logic of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice; yet,
one should not entertain the suspicion that this constitutes a mandate based on desire (*kāma-adhikāra*), merely because the rite is performed by one who wishes to avoid evil.
"Therefore, one must always perform penance for the sake of purification;
for those whose sins have not been expiated are born endowed with censurable physical marks. (MDh 11.54)
Thus, because the necessity [of this practice] is understood through the hearing of the faults incurred by its non-performance. // 3.219 // 3.220 //
He states the fault incurred by failing to perform expiation:
"Men who do not perform expiation, who are devoted to sinful acts, and who feel no remorse, go to terrible and dreadful hells. (YDh 3.221)

Men who are addicted to sins produced by the transgression of the meaning of the scriptures, who feel no remorse—thinking "a wicked deed has been done by me"—and who, being devoid of agitation, do not perform expiation, attain unbearable hells. (3.221)
Explaining the nature of the hells, he says:
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka. (YDh 3.222)
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃprapātana,
the great hell Kākola, Saṃjīvana, Mahāpatha, Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka.
The Asipatravana and the Tāpana are the twenty-first [hell].
Wicked men who have not performed penance go there, afflicted by the terrible consequences of both mortal sins (mahāpātaka) and minor offenses (upapātaka). (YDh 3.224–225)

Those lowest of men who have not performed expiation fall into twenty-one hells, beginning with Tāmisra and ending with Tapana; these hells possess intermediate subdivisions indicated by their literal names and are filled with the terrifying misfortunes produced by the great and minor sins (mahāpātaka and upapātaka). (3.222–225)
It has been stated that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose of destroying committed sins.
Regarding this, he states a specific distinction:
"Sin that may have been committed through ignorance is removed by expiations."
However, one becomes subject to legal proceedings here on account of intentional speech.

The sin or evil committed through ignorance is removed—that is, it departs—by means of the penances whose characteristics will be described hereafter; but that which is committed intentionally is not.

However, by the force of the scriptural injunctions prescribing expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in those cases, one becomes fit for social intercourse (*vyavahārya*) in this world. And here, since the opening statement says, "By expiations, the sin committed through ignorance departs," it would have been expected to say "through knowledge" (*jñānataḥ*) as its counterpart; yet, that "through desire" (*kāmataḥ*) was stated instead in order to demonstrate the equality between knowledge and desire. For instance:
That which is prescribed for those acting unintentionally shall be doubled when done intentionally;
likewise, in the case of an act committed without prior awareness, the penance is half. Similarly, if a Śūdra is somehow acquired by a Mleccha through ignorance...
One should perform three *kṛcchra* penances; however, if it was done intentionally, it shall be double.
From such statements as these, since an identical expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is seen for both knowledge and desire, their fruits are indeed equal.
Furthermore, independent activity is invariably preceded by either the knowledge of an object or the desire for it.
Since that [transgression] is impossible even upon the absence of either one of those two, it is therefore stated "intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*).
Even if it were stated "through knowledge or ignorance," intention would still follow because of their inseparable connection.
Furthermore, this does not apply to one who is being compelled by force by thieves and the like.
It should not be argued that there is no invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) because, even when there is knowledge of the object, there may be an absence of desire;
for in this case, even though the knowledge exists, it is equivalent to non-existence due to its lack of being a cause for purposeful action (pravṛtti).
As for the case where one falls into mud through delusion while desiring to fall on dry ground,
even there, due to the absence of knowledge of the reality and the absence of desire directed toward that [reality], there is indeed an absence of both ignorance and desire.
This is likewise the case with ignorance and lack of desire.
It is indeed non-deviation [from the rule].
But is it not improper to say "sin departs through penances," since karma is to be destroyed only by its fruit?
It is not so; for just as the arising of sin is known through the scriptures, so too is its destruction, and thus no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies here.
For this very reason, Gautama demonstrated this matter by way of a prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and a conclusive (*uttara-pakṣa*) argument:
"In that regard, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) or not."
"One should not perform [actions]," they say, "for action is never exhausted. Others say, "One should perform them."
It is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *Punaḥstoma*, they return to the *Savana*";

and, "He who sacrifices with the *Vrātyastoma* overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of an embryo; he who sacrifices with the *Aśvamedha* [attains the same]. Regarding the phrase "they return to the *Savana*," it means that one becomes fit for the duties of the twice-born, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others, which are accomplished through the *Savana*.
This is the meaning. Nor is this merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda);

for when there is a requirement for a qualification of the qualified person (adhikārin), it is logical to postulate the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage itself, according to the principle of the Rātrisatra sacrifice.
Therefore, it is logical that "sin departs through penances.

But [one might object]: since there is no penance for an act committed intentionally (*kāmakṛta*), how can there be eligibility for social interaction (*vyavahāryatva*)? And the absence of such a penance follows from the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "There is penance for an offense committed unintentionally" (VaDh 20.1).
This purification is declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
however, it is understood from the statement of Manu: "In the case of intentionally killing a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed. (MDh 11.90).
This is not so:
whatever great sin a man might commit through desire,
no atonement for it is seen except by leaping from a precipice or entering fire.

Thus it is ordained; and furthermore, because it is stated that "what is prescribed for those without desire shall be doubled for one who acts out of desire," a penance is seen to be required even when an act is committed intentionally.
As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha,

its intended meaning is that "an expiation brings about purification when the offense was committed unintentionally," and not that there is an absence of expiation when the offense was committed intentionally.

As for the statement of Manu beginning with "This purification has been declared," that too refers specifically to the performance of the twelve-year vow and so forth, as indicated by the pronoun "this" (*iyam*).
By the rule "No atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa," there is a prohibition [of the specific penance], but not of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in general.
Because expiations such as those ending in death have been shown [in the scriptures].

Now, if there is indeed an expiation even for an act committed intentionally, why should there not also be a destruction of the evil (pāpakṣaya), since there is no distinction [between the two cases]?
If even the destruction of evil does not occur, then how can there be eligibility for social interaction?

It is said in reply: although there is no difference in the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in both cases, a distinction in the result is understood from the scriptures. However, in the case of an act committed unknowingly...

In all cases, there is the destruction of evil; however, those who have killed a Brahmin, drunk liquor, violated the bed of their guru, or committed incest with a mother or paternal aunt; those connected by birth to such persons; thieves; atheists; those who habitually perform censurable acts; those who have abandoned an outcaste or one who has abandoned them; and those who associate with outcasts—these are the outcasts (patita), as well as those who join in their sinful acts. (GDh 21.1–2)

In the case of the great sins (mahāpātaka) and others mentioned by Gautama, the capacity for social intercourse (vyavahāryatva) is prohibited; when such an act leading to a fall (patanīya) is committed intentionally, there is merely the restoration of social standing, but no destruction of the sin.
Nor is it impossible for one to be fit for social interaction in the absence of the destruction of evil;
for evil has two powers: that which produces rebirth in hell and that which obstructs social interaction.

In that case, even though the other capacity remains unimpaired, the destruction of the capacity that obstructs social interaction is not logically untenable; therefore, it is not illogical for one to remain subject to social interaction even when sin has not been removed. As for the statement of Manu:
"The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
some say it is also [prescribed] for what is done intentionally, based on the evidence of the Śruti. (MDh 11.45).
Even this [statement] is intended to establish the attainment of expiation even for intentional acts, and not to demonstrate the destruction of the sin itself.
Furthermore, even in the case of an act that does not cause loss of caste, if it was committed intentionally, the destruction of the sin occurs through penance;
however, a sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas, whereas a sin committed intentionally out of delusion is purified by various kinds of penances. (MDh 11.46)
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu,
even in the case of an act causing loss of caste (patanīya) committed intentionally, the destruction of the taint (kalmaṣakṣaya) certainly occurs through penances ending in death,
because there is no other result [of such acts].
For there is a traditional teaching of Āpastamba stating: "In this world, no restoration [to caste] exists for him; rather, his taint is destroyed" (ĀpDh 1.24.25). // 3.226 //
It has been stated that the performance of prohibited acts and so forth constitutes the occasion for penance; to elaborate upon that, he says:

"The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru's bed—these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is he who associates with them. (YDh 3.227)
The term *hanti* (to kill) is conventionally established for an action that causes the separation of life;
it refers to that action after which the separation of life occurs, either immediately or at a later time, independently of any other cause.
A "brahmahā" is one who has killed a Brāhmaṇa;
a "madyapa" is a drinker of prohibited liquor;
a "stena" is a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa's gold.
According to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba, "the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold" constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*);
and "one who approaches the bed of his guru" (*gurutalpaga*) refers to one who goes to the wife of his guru—
the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, by association refers here to the wife.
It is observed that these, such as the slayer of a Brahmin and others, are "great sinners" (*mahāpātakinaḥ*).
They are called "sins" (*pātakāni*) because they cause one to fall; these are the [crimes] such as the killing of a Brahmin.
By the word "great" (*maha-*), their gravity is made known; thus, those who are associated with them are "great sinners."
The designation is made for the sake of brevity:
"He who indeed lives with each of those such as the slayer of a Brahmin individually,
but he who lives with these [five] for a year, he too is equal to them" (YDh 3.266).

Thus, by the logic to be explained hereafter, he too is a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). The word "tathā" (so/likewise) expresses a manner and is intended to include the abettor (*anugrāhaka*), the instigator (*prayojaka*), and other such agents. Furthermore, the abettor is one who obstructs an enemy fleeing or protects a slayer from others.
He who assists by instilling firmness in the killer is said to be an accessory;
for this very reason, Manu has shown that the one who aids is connected to the fruit of the violence:
"Among many who perform a single act, all of whom bear weapons..."
"If even one person should cause [another] to kill, they are all considered killers.

Likewise, Āpastamba has stated that the instigator and others are also connected to the fruit: "The instigator, the consenter, and the doer—in actions whose fruits are heaven or hell, the distinction in the fruit belongs to whichever of these exerts the greatest effort."
Thus, the instigator (*prayojaka*) is one who prompts someone who has not yet engaged in an action;
and that [instigator] is of three kinds:
the commander, the one who entreats, and...

Regarding the term "instructor" (*upadeṣṭṛ*): therein, one who is called a commander (*ājñāpayitṛ*) is he who, being himself superior, impels an inferior such as a servant, saying, "Kill my enemy. This is what is meant.
But he who, being himself incapable, incites another— through entreaties and the like— saying, "Kill my enemy," while making such a request, is called an instigator (*abhidhātṛ*).
And for both of these [the perpetrator and the instigator], it is for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose.
Thus is the state of being the agent [of action].
Furthermore, the instructor is described as one who impels [another] by means of instructions such as exposing their vital points, saying, "Kill the enemy in this manner."

In that regard, their distinction is that the fruit belongs only to the one who is employed [in the action]. The "consenter" (anumantṛ), however, is one who incites another who has already begun to act;
he is of two kinds:
One permits for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose, while another does so for the sake of another's purpose.
Now, how can inference be a cause of violence?
It cannot be by producing the separation of the vital breaths (*prāṇaviyoga*),
since that is produced directly by the operation of an agent.
Nor is it like an instigator,

because [the word] functions as an inciter by way of producing activity in the direct agent. Furthermore, one should not suspect that it merely approves of an activity already undertaken, as in the case of saying, "Well done, you have rightly resolved."
For such an authorization is neither a cause for the act of violence nor is it purposeful.

It is said in reply: where, due to dependence on a king or other authority, one might personally engage in the act through the mind, yet—out of fear of interrupting that engagement or fear of future punishment—[does not do so].
Or, if one whose effort is slackened requires the consent of a king or others, in that case, the consent— strengthening the agent's engagement—
becomes a cause with respect to the result of injury.
Likewise, even for one who [acts] by means of reviling, beating, the seizure of wealth, and so forth...
He who provokes others certainly becomes a cause of violence by way of generating anger, which is the cause of death;
for this very reason, Viṣṇu has said:
"Whether reviled, beaten, or even deprived of his wealth..."
"He who would give up his life for such a person, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
Likewise:
"For the sake of kinsmen, friends, and wife, and likewise for the sake of friends and fields..."
"He who, for whose sake one might give up one's life, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
Nor should it be suspected that [abusive speech and the like] are not causes because anger is not observed to arise in anyone even when such insults have been committed;
for there is a diversity in the inherent natures of men.
Since those who become incensed even by a slight cause do not deviate [from that state], there is no lack of causality.

Furthermore, regarding these [actors]— such as the benefactor, the instigator, and so forth— [the degree of responsibility] depends on proximity or distance, and on the relative weight or lightness of their respective activities.
Furthermore, the gravity or lightness of the expiation (prāyaścitta) should be understood from the gravity or lightness of the result;
for there is the statement: "In that case where one undertakes more [of an act], there is a distinction in the result.
Thus, first, regarding the instigator (anugrāhaka), since he has himself engaged in the act of violence, he possesses independent agency (svatantrakartṛtva).

Even though [the instigator] lacks the direct engagement in activities such as striking with a sword— which results in the immediate loss of life— and thus, unlike the direct perpetrator, does not initiate a greater degree of violence, his act yields a lesser fruit and entails a lesser expiation.
However, as for the instigator...
Because it is mediated by being the cause for the engagement of an independent agent, its fruit is less than that [of the actual performer].
Among instigators, the teacher’s fruit is less because of his engagement for the sake of another.

But surely, since the person being prompted (prayojya) stands in the position of one held by the hand of the prompter (prayojaka), it is not logical for him to have a connection with the fruit [of the action].
If, however, there were a connection even for one who acts under the prompting of another, then there would also be a connection for architects, diggers of tanks, and so forth, who act for wages.
[Objection: There would be the undesirable consequence [of the fruit] such as heaven being obtained [by anyone].
[Reply: It is said:
according to the principle that "the fruit taught in the scripture belongs to the performer," the construction of divine wells, tanks, and so forth generates a fruit for the qualified agent.
Furthermore, carpenters, those who dig tanks, and others are not qualified for the construction of temples, wells, and tanks because they do not desire heaven;
however, in this case [of non-violence], even those who act under the instigation of another are indeed qualified, and thus [the result] certainly occurs.
The fault arises from the transgression of that [prohibition].
As for the consenter, however, his fruit is even smaller than that of the instigator, because the act of consenting is external to the operation of the instigator and is therefore lighter.

Furthermore, for the instigator— such as one who reviles— the fruit is smaller than that of the approver because it is mediated by the production of anger in another person which serves as the cause for the latter's action, and because the instigator acts without directly intending the death.
Now, if even a mediated factor can be a cause, then would it not follow that the parents also possess the status of being the killers, by way of producing the person who becomes the killer?

It is said: mere priority in time does not constitute causality, for it is possible for that which is a cause to exist in such a manner [as a subsequent effect]. Indeed, that which possesses an operation conducive to the production of an effect distinct from its own nature is a cause. If [the *rathantara-sāman* were the cause],...

"One should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu when there is Soma"—this, like the *rathantara* melody, is the reason for the precedence of the Indra-Vāyu cup in the sacrifice (*kratu*).
For in that case, the Soma-sacrifice in its own form is not the cause, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
nor do the parents possess the characteristics of such a cause.
Thus, there is no over-extension [of the principle].

By this very same reasoning and with the same underlying intention regarding the Dharma, there is no fault for the one who has the well dug when a Brāhmaṇa or similar person falls into negligence and dies in a magically created well, pond, or the like.

For it is not as in the case of reviling and so forth, where one kills oneself thinking, "This well was dug by him; therefore, I shall destroy myself," such that the killing is caused by the digging of the well.
Consequently, even the maker of the well possesses the status of a causal cause.
Thus, there is no quality of being a cause for injury; rather, there is simply equality with one's mother and father.
Likewise, even when there is an association with a cause for injury in some cases, there is an absence of fault due to speech [or action] undertaken for the sake of benefiting others.
As Saṃvarta says:
"In the case of a cow's confinement, for the purpose of medical treatment, or for the release of a dead fetus—
if death occurs despite an effort having been made, no expiation is required."
One who provides medicine, oil, or food to cows, Brahmins, and others,
is not tainted by sin even if misfortune should occur while it is being given.
"For those who provide assistance through efforts such as cauterization, excision,
and venesection for the sake of achieving the preservation of life, no expiation is required.
This refers specifically to a physician who is skilled in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases.
However, regarding the other case, the fault has been shown in the verse: "But a physician practicing falsely shall be made to pay" (YDh 2.142).
In that situation, even for one who does not engage in abuse or the like caused by anger, [the fault arises] when he reveals himself through madness and so forth while uttering the [victim's] name.
Even if he causes death therein, there is no fault; however, if any twice-born man should abandon his life for no reason,
the fault lies with him alone, and not with the one whom he might have praised.
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa).

Likewise, even in a case where one who has been provoked to anger by an abuser strikes himself with a sword or similar weapon and, before dying, is appeased by the abuser through the giving of wealth or other means, and then proclaims aloud in the presence of people that "there is no fault here on the part of the abuser," there is still no offense because of that statement.
As Viṣṇu has said:
"If one strikes [an animal] in anger with it in mind, but afterwards, being appeased, causes the rite to be proclaimed again;
when that [animal] has died, there is no fault, provided the proclamation has been made for both [the initial and subsequent acts]."
And we shall explain the specific penances for these [offenses] by considering the relative gravity or lightness of the fault through the roles of the instigator and so forth. (3.227)
He states those acts equal to the killing of a Brahmin:
"Insulting one's gurus, reviling the Vedas, the murder of a friend, and the destruction of what has been studied—these should be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (YDh 3.228)

Excessive reviling of gurus and false accusation against them— specifically, "false accusation against a guru"— are equal to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "False accusation against a guru" [is a mortal sin] (GDh 21.10).
And this refers to cases of making false accusations regarding faults unknown to the world,

because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "Having recognized a fault, one should not be the first to announce it to others, and one should avoid such a person in social dealings" (ĀpDh 1.21.20).
Through the obsession with nihilism, one reviles the Vedas;
even the killing of a friend or a well-wisher [is a sin] for such a non-Brahmin.
Furthermore, the destruction or forgetting of the studied Veda—whether through diversion by false treatises or through indolence and the like—is likewise [a sin].
Each of these is equal to the murder of a Brahmin;
furthermore, there is the abandonment of Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's son. (YDh 3.239)

Thus, the inclusion of "abandoning what has been studied" among the minor offenses (upapātaka) should be understood as referring to forgetting [the Veda] due to being preoccupied with maintaining a family or distracted by listening to improper scriptures. 3.228.
He states those acts equal to drinking liquor:
eating forbidden food, deceitfulness, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses; these indeed are equal to drinking liquor. (YDh 3.229)
The intentional consumption of garlic and other such prohibited items is forbidden;
for this very reason, Manu says:
"Mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, and the village cock..."
"Having intentionally eaten onions or leeks, a man shall fall [from his caste]" (MDh 5.19).
However, for unintentional consumption, there is another penance:
"Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* *kṛcchra*."
For it has been stated by that same author [Yājñavalkya]: "Or one may perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*; for the remaining [offenses], one should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20).
*Jaihmaya* means crookedness; it consists of speaking otherwise or acting otherwise through the intent to deceive. In this context—

And although "crookedness" (*jaihmyam*) is stated in general terms, nevertheless, because the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is heavy, it is understood that the crookedness intended as the occasion for it must also concern a grave matter.
Furthermore, by reflecting upon the nature of the occasional rite (*naimittika*), there is [an understanding] of the gravity of the occasion.
It is the comprehension of a specific qualification (*viśeṣāvagati*).

For example, in the rule: "If for someone both fires should be extinguished, or become defective, or set while [the sun] is still above the horizon, there a re-establishment [of the fires] is the expiation," the word "both" (*ubhau*) functions as a qualification of the causal condition (*nimitta*), [and thus] the sacrificial oblation (*havir*)...

Just as, even though both [the fires] are not intended [to be established simultaneously], the occurrence of two fires is inferred as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) by virtue of the rule for re-establishment (*punarādheya*), which is a conditional injunction (*naimittika-vidhi*) for producing two fires, so too here it is logical to assume a heavy occasioning cause. Likewise, the occasioning cause for the displacement [of the *brahmaudana*] is the speaking of falsehood, such as saying "I am a master of the four Vedas" (*caturveda*) before a royal court or similar assembly, when one is actually not a master of the four Vedas.
Drinking the mouth-fluid of a menstruating woman out of lust—
these are equal to the drinking of liquor. 3.229
He states what is equal to the theft of gold:
"The seizure of a horse, a gem, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow, as well as that of a deposit—all these are indeed equal to the theft of gold. (YDh 3.230)

The theft of horses and other such animals belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as the misappropriation of a deposit consisting of anything other than gold—all this should be understood as equal to the theft of gold. (3.230)
He states those acts equal to violating the Guru’s bed:

"Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, with virgins, with women of one's own uterine kin, with women of the lowest castes, with women of the same lineage (sagotra), and with the wives of sons is recorded in tradition as equal to violating the Guru’s bed. (YDh 3.231)

A friend, a companion, his wife, a maiden, or a girl of the highest caste—among these, there is no offense if they are willing and of a lower social order; otherwise, there is punishment. But for defiling [a maiden], the hand shall be cut off; likewise, for defiling one of the highest caste, there is death. (YDh 2.288)
Thus, because a specific punishment is prescribed for that very case, the severity of the expiation is appropriate.
"Svayoni" means a sister;
"antyajā" means a Caṇḍālī.

A woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), meaning one of the same clan (*samānagotrā*); a daughter's wife (*sutastrī*), meaning a daughter-in-law (*snuṣā*): sexual intercourse with each of these is equal to violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpasama*).
And this should be understood as applying after the emission of semen; however,
if it occurs before that, it is not equal to violating the Guru's bed, but rather the penance is indeed slight.

"Emission of semen into one's own female relatives, into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, as well as into the wives of a friend or a son, they know to be equal to violating the Guru's bed"—
thus it is stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] (MDh 11.59), because of the inclusion of the qualification "emission of semen."

Since the matter would already be established by the mention of "one of the same lineage" (*sagotra*) alone, the further mention of "the wife of a son" (*sutastrī*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the gravity of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
And here, the statement regarding its equality with the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth refers to [offenses such as] reviling one's guru and the like.
This is for the purpose of instructing on the specific expiations (prāyaścitta) corresponding to those respective causes.
[Objection: But surely, since the fault in cases such as reviling the Vedas is slight, it is not appropriate to prescribe the heavier expiation for killing a Brahmin and so forth.
[Response: Not so; for the gravity of the fault is understood precisely through the force of the instruction regarding the heavy expiation.

Nor should it be suspected that this statement is intended solely for the purpose of extending the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta) such as those for killing a Brahmin, and not rather for the purpose of demonstrating the mere gravity of the offense.

For if the purpose were merely to establish that [the sin] is equal [to others], then the designation of equality through distinctions such as "this is equal to the killing of a Brahmin" or "equal to violating the Guru's bed" would be untenable;
and that expiation, being taught by means of the word "equal," [is distinct] from the expiations for the killing of a Brahmin and so forth.
It is taught as being only slightly less [than the former],

because in worldly expressions such as "the minister is equal to the king," we observe the use of the word *sama* (equal) to denote something that is somewhat inferior, and because it is illogical for a great sin and another [lesser] one to be truly identical.
And this being the case,

although Yājñavalkya has stated that abandoning the Veda (*brahmojjhatva*), reviling the Vedas (*vedanindā*), and killing a friend (*suhṛdvadha*) are equal to the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), Manu nevertheless equates them with the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*):
"Abandoning the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, and killing a friend..."
"Eating forbidden food and clarified butter [in certain quantities] are six acts equal to the drinking of liquor" (MDh 11.57).
This has been stated for the purpose of providing options regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*).
In this same manner, contradictions in other statements must also be resolved.

As for the light penance stated by Vasiṣṭha— namely, that "if one has falsely pressured a guru, one becomes purified through the guru’s grace after performing the twelve-night Kṛcchra and bathing with one's clothes on" (VaDh 21.28)— [this applies to a specific case].
This should be understood to apply when the act is performed once unintentionally. (3.231)
He states the enumeration of those who occupy the bed of the guru:
"The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife,
the daughter-in-law, the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter" (YDh 3.232).

One who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed; having had his penis cut off, he shall be put to death, as shall the woman if she was willing. Fathers’ sisters and others are well known; one who approaches them is a violator of the guru’s bed, and his penis shall be cut off by the king, followed by execution.
Punishment shall be imposed for the sake of deterrence, and the same penance [as prescribed] must be performed;
by the word "and" (ca), queens, female ascetics, and others are included.
As Nārada has said:
A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt,
the wife of a paternal uncle or a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her friend, and a daughter-in-law;
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
"Going to any one of these [wives] is called violating the Guru's bed; for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained. (NSm 12.72–74).
Here, "queen" (*rājñī*) refers to the wife of the one who rules the kingdom, not necessarily only a Kṣatriya.
Because a different expiation is prescribed for approaching her;
a *dhātrī* is one who nourishes [the child] by giving breast milk and so forth, distinct from the biological mother;
a *sādhvī* is one who observes religious vows.
A Brāhmaṇī woman is the highest among the castes; here, the mention of "mother" is for the sake of illustration.
Furthermore, this punishment consisting of the cutting off of the male organ and execution applies to anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa.
Because of the prohibition against killing him, as stated in the verse, "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in all manner of sins" (MDh 8.380),
since the act of killing itself constitutes the nature of the penance.
We shall elaborate upon its subject matter in the section concerning penance for violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpa*).
Here, the daughter-in-law and the sister, who were equated with the Guru’s bed in the preceding verse, are mentioned again.
This is for the purpose of providing an alternative penance.
However, when these women, being desirous, bring these very men under their control and enjoy them, then for them also, as for the men, the punishment is indeed death and the penance is likewise.

These [acts], beginning with reviling one's guru and ending with the study of forbidden scriptures, fall under the extension of the category of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*); they are called *pātaka*s because they cause immediate downfall (*sadyaḥ-patana*).
As Yama has said:

"A man who approaches his mother's sister, a mother's female friend, a daughter, a father's sister, a maternal uncle's wife, a sister, or a mother-in-law, shall fall [from his caste] immediately. Furthermore, Gautama has stated that other acts as well constitute mortal sins (*pātaka*).

"Those related by birth to a mother or father, a thief, an atheist, one who performs censurable acts, an outcast, one who abandons those who should not be abandoned, and one who abandons those who are not outcasts— these are outcasts, as are those who associate with outcasts" (GDh 21.12). And because they are listed between the *mahāpātakas* and the *upapātakas*, their status is inferior to the *mahāpātakas* yet superior to the *upapātakas*.
The gravity [of the offense] is understood. As it has been said:

"Those sins which have been declared equal to the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) are designated as 'transgressions' (pātaka); that which is less than those is a secondary transgression (upapātaka). Thus it is stated.
And likewise Aṅgiras says: "For minor sins, the stay in hell shall be for a thousand years; for major sins, twice that;
and for secondary sins, a quarter of that, according to the number of years."
Thus [ends verses 3.232 and 3.233].

Having thus enumerated the great sins (mahāpātakas) and the sins equal to them, he speaks in order to enumerate the minor sins (upapātakas): "Killing a cow, being a Vratya, theft, non-payment of debts, neglecting to maintain the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and gambling. (YDh 3.234)

Taking instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, the state of being a younger brother whose elder brother is unmarried, usury, the manufacture of salt, the killing of women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, or Kṣatriyas, and living by reprehensible means; YDh 3.235.
Atheism, the breaking of vows, and the sale of one's own sons; the theft of grain, base metals, and cattle; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice;
the abandonment of father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove. (YDh 3.236–237)
Defiling a maiden, officiating at a sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother,
giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, crookedness, the breaking of a vow,
undertaking actions for one's own sake, and consorting with women who drink liquor; YDh 3.238.
Neglecting one's Vedic study, neglecting the sacred fires and one's children, and likewise abandoning one's kinsmen;

cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, living by the sale of women, by causing injury, or by the sale of medicinal herbs; the construction of injurious machines, indulgence in vices, and the selling of oneself—[these are minor sins]. (YDh 3.239–240)
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth, likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), subsisting on the food of others,
studying false scriptures, and being entitled to [exploiting] mines; YDh 3.241.
And the sale of one's wife—each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).
Cow-slaughter is the killing of a cow;
being uninitiated at the proper time constitutes the state of a *vrātya*.

Theft (*steya*) consists of the misappropriation of another's property— whether it be gold, an object equal in value to gold, or something other than those— as well as the non-return of gold or similar items once received,
and the failure to repay debts.
Likewise, there is the non-discharge of debts pertaining to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
and the failure to establish the sacred fires when one is qualified to do so.

Now, it is a well-established tenet of the Mīmāṃsakas that the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites impel the performance of the fire-consecration (ādhāna) for the sake of producing the fires that constitute their own subsidiaries;
and therefore, whoever has a need for the fires will engage in the consecration as the means to attain them, just as one who desires rice and the like engages in the acquisition of wealth.
"But for one who has no need for the fires, there is no engagement [in the rite]; how then can there be the fault of not having established the fires (*anāhitāgnitā*)?

It is replied: From this very statement regarding the necessity of the fire-establishment (*ādhāna*), the intention of the authors of the *Smṛtis* is perceived to be that even the eternal scriptural injunctions (*nitya-śruti*) are motivators for the fire-establishment, since there is no difference in their status as possessing the requisite qualification (*adhikārin*). Thus, there is no fault.
Likewise, the sale of forbidden goods such as salt,
and "parivedana," which is the taking of a wife and the establishment of the sacred fires by a younger brother while his elder uterine brother remains [unmarried].
The undertaking of study from a teacher for a fee, and teaching for a fee.
Adultery with another's wife—excluding the case of the teacher’s wife or those equal to her;
*pārivittya*, which is the elder brother remaining unmarried while the younger brother has already married;
and usury, which is living off prohibited interest.
The manufacture of salt, the production of salt,
the killing of a woman— even one who is not a Brahmin— with the exception of an Ātreyī,
and the killing of a Śūdra.
The killing of an uninitiated Vaiśya or Kṣatriya;
