since its primary status is established everywhere by virtue of the qualifying condition (upādhi) of possessing the power to produce intoxication.
"The assumption of a secondary sense is improper"—
this is incorrect, because [the following are mentioned]:
"The juice of the *pānasa*, the *dākṣa*, the *mādhūka*, the *khārjūra*, the *tāla*, and the *aikṣava*."
That which is produced from honey, from sugar-cane juice, *ariṣṭa*, *maireya*, and that which comes from the coconut;
One should know that there are exactly eleven types of intoxicants that are equal;
however, the twelfth is the liquor of *surā*, which is recorded as the lowest of all.
Thus, because Pulastya has specified *surā* as a particular type of intoxicant (*madya*),

the application of the word *surā* to intoxicants in general is therefore figurative (*gauṇa*). Others, however, maintain that the word *surā* is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) specifically for the three types beginning with that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*).
For instance, although the use of the word *surā* is observed in many places, when a doubt arises as to where its beginninglessness lies, [it is stated]:
"Surā should be known to be of three kinds: that made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that made from honey (*mādhvī*), and that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*)" (MDh 11.95).

Thus, according to the statement of Manu, since it is determined that among products of molasses, honey, and flour there is no beginning, it is logical that the primary sense [of the term] applies precisely to those. Nor is there the fault of postulating multiple powers [for the word], for that can be easily avoided by resorting to the power of intoxication as a limiting condition (upādhi).

Nor is there an over-extension [of the term] to the juices of the palmyra tree and so forth, because the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is present there as well; for, like words such as "paṅkaja" (mud-born), we rely on the principle of etymological-technical convention (yogarūḍhi).
And therefore:

"Just as one [type of liquor] is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.95). This verse is intended to establish that the three types of *surā* are equal in their faultfulness; it does not, however, intend to establish the equality of these two—the *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*—with the *paiṣṭī* *surā*. The mention of "the best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the twice-born (*dvijāti*) in general.

This too is incorrect, because in the statement of Pulastya— "The twelfth, however, spirituous liquor (surāmadya), is remembered as the lowest for all"— it is observed that *surāmadya* is superior even to *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*. Likewise, [the text continues]:
"Surā is indeed the impurity of grains, and sin is called impurity" (MDh 11.93).
Since this passage specifies that *surā* is a derivative of grain,
and since the word "grain" (*anna*) in such expressions as "seasoning with grain" refers to derivatives of rice and other cereals, [it follows that *surā* is likewise a grain derivative].
Because such usage is observed,
and because molasses and honey consist of the nature of taste,
and likewise in the case of the Sautrāmaṇī cups which are modifications of food.
Since the word *surā* is heard [in the text] in this way, only the liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) is called *surā* in its primary sense;
however, the word *surā* is used figuratively for the other two types.
As for the claim that, based on the statement of Manu, "Gauḍī, Mādhvī... (MDh 11.94), the inherent nature of all three [liquors] is determined,
that too is incorrect.

For this [text] does not aim to establish the beginninglessness of the relationship between words and their meanings, as is the case with grammatical treatises (śabdānuśāsana); rather, it aims to establish [the nature of] the effect (kārya).
Therefore, because they serve as the occasion for a heavy penance, the application of the word *surā* to *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* is secondary (*gauṇa*).
In this way, there is neither the fault of postulating multiple denotative powers (*śakti*), nor is there recourse to a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
It has been established that the mention of the "best of the twice-born" here is not intended as a mere figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore:
"Wine is indeed the dregs of food, and it is called the dregs of sin;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink wine" (MDh 11.94).
Thus, the prohibition applies specifically to liquor made from flour (paiṣṭī) in relation to all three castes;
however, regarding liquors such as that made from molasses (gauḍī), the prohibition applies only in relation to Brāhmaṇas, and not to Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas.
"Alcohol, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation for the gods must not consume them.
Since the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] specifies "by a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena*), this restriction applies specifically to him.
Bṛhad-Viṣṇu also demonstrates that the prohibition of liquor applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa:
"The wine made from Madhūka flowers, from sugarcane, from Sairam, from Tāla, from dates, and from jackfruit;
as well as that produced from honey, Mādhvīka, Maireya, and that derived from coconut."
"These ten intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].

Bṛhadyājñavalkya also demonstrated the absence of fault for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas: "For even if a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should drink liquor or *surā* out of desire, under any circumstances whatsoever, he incurs no guilt."
Vyāsa also permitted the drinking of honey-wine for those two, saying:
"I have seen Keśava and Arjuna both intoxicated by honey-liquor, both anointed with sandalwood paste, riding together in a single chariot with a single seat."
Thus, although there is a general prohibition against all types of intoxicants for those connected with the Brahmin caste, it is specified:
"Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī—these three kinds of *surā* should be known.
Just as one is [forbidden], so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born. (MDh 11.95)
Thus, the separate prohibition of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* is intended to establish their equivalence to *surā* on account of the gravity of their faults.
Furthermore, this prohibition of *surā* applies indeed even to one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) and to an unmarried girl (*kanyā*);
therefore: "A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*" (MDh 11.94).

Thus, because the prohibition is made by way of delimitation based on caste alone (*jātimātra*), the mention of the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) in Manu’s injunction regarding penance— "Having drunk *surā* through delusion, a twice-born man... (MDh 11.91)— is intended as an indicator for all [members of] the social classes (*varṇa*).

Because the injunction regarding the contingent rite (*naimittika-vidhi*) depends upon the negation that serves as its occasion (*nimitta*), and because in that negation the mere class (*varṇa*) functions as the delimiting factor;

just as in the occasion-statement, "For whom the oblation has been set aside and the moon rises before [the sacrifice]," once it is understood that the rising of the moon over the oblation in general is the occasion, then in the contingent statement dependent upon that—

Even though it is stated that "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts," the mention of "rice-grains" (*taṇḍula*) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for sacrificial offerings (*havis*) consisting of rice and other such substances. However, there is this distinction: because of the statement, "A quarter [of the penance] should be given for minor offenses; this rule applies to all sins," even in the case of intentional (*kāmakāra*) commission, the penance does not end in death, but rather one must double the quarter-penance to make it a six-year penance.
For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Aṅgiras: "That which is prescribed for those who act unintentionally should be performed twofold when done intentionally."

The same should be applied to the elderly, the sick, and others as well. Likewise, because even liquor is prohibited by way of its restriction to the mere fact of caste—according to the rule: "That [liquor] must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the oblation for the gods" (MDh 11.96)—it follows that it is forbidden.
It should not be drunk even by one who has not been initiated.
But how can there be a fault for one who is uninitiated?
For prior to initiation, one may act as one pleases, speak as one pleases, and eat as one pleases (GDh 2.1).
According to the statement of Gautama, likewise:
"In the consumption of liquor, urine, or excrement, there is no fault whatsoever for one up to the fifth year; beyond that, however, [there is fault] toward the parents, friends, and teachers."
And because the absence of fault is understood from these words of the prince, it is said:

since the defining characteristic (*chedaka*) in the prohibitory statement regarding *surā* and *madya* is heard to be the mere genus (*jāti*), the application of the prohibition remains entirely unimpeded.
For this very reason, there is a prohibitory statement in another *Smṛti*:
"The prohibition against drinking liquor, however, is based on caste; such is the established rule.
Therefore:
"A quarter [of the penance] is to be given for offenses against children; this is the rule for all sins."
Because of the statement, "Even among all sins, such as the drinking of liquor," the penance for drinking liquor is indeed only one quarter [of the standard].
Likewise, Jātūkarṇya has also stated a penance even for the drinking of liquor:
"If an uninitiated boy should drink liquor through delusion,
his mother, brother, or father should perform three *kṛcchra* penances for him."
Therefore, the statement of Gautama refers to substances such as fermented gruel (*śukta*) and stale food that are distinct from *surā* and other [forbidden liquors].
The statement of Kumāra, however, is intended to indicate that the fault is minor.
For this very reason, Manu has stated that for one who commits a transgression prior to initiation (*upanayana*), initiation itself constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

"By means of domestic fire-sacrifices (*gārbha-homa*), the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the tonsure (*cauḍa*), and the tying of the girdle (*mauñjīnibandhana*), the taint (*enaḥ*) derived from the seed (*baijika*) and from the womb (*gārbhika*) is wiped away for the twice-born. (MDh 2.27).
This is the meaning here.
For members of the three higher castes, the prohibition against liquor made from flour applies from birth;
however, for a Brāhmaṇa,
the prohibition against all intoxicants likewise applies from birth.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, however, there is never a prohibition against liquor made from molasses (gauḍī) and the like.
For the Śūdra, there is neither a prohibition against *surā* nor a prohibition against *madya*. (3.253)
He states another expiation:
"Clad in hair-cloth or even wearing matted locks, he should perform the vow for killing a Brahmin;
or he should eat oil-cake or grain-particles at night for three years. (YDh 3.254)
One clothed in garments made from the hair of cows, goats, and so forth is "one dressed in hair" (*vālavāsas*).

The mention of "hair-cloth" (*vālavāsa*) is intended as an elliptical indication for rags (*cīra*) and bark (*valkala*), because of the traditional teaching of Pracetas: "The violator of a cow and the violator of the Guru's bed shall perform the penance for killing a Brahmin while wearing rags and bark."
The mention of "matted hair" (*jaṭi*) is for the purpose of excluding the state of being shaven-headed (*muṇḍitva*).

Since the performance of the penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyāvrata*) is already established by that very [rule], the specific mention of "wearing garments of hair" (*vālavasana*) and so forth is intended to exclude the possibility of using a skull or other items obtained from someone killed by oneself, which might otherwise be applicable elsewhere.
This [penance] refers to the case where one unintentionally drinks *surā* under the mistaken belief that it is water.
"This purification has been declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally" (MDh 11.90).
Because of this, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the twelve-year penance itself, which was prescribed under the condition of being unintentional.
And in this case, regarding the drinking of *surā*...

Because it is a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin), even though there is an extended application (*atideśika*) [of the penance], one should perform the twelve-year penance in its entirety and not reduced by a quarter.
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Hārīta states: "Those who have committed *mahāpātaka*s are purified in twelve years.
Alternatively, one may eat *piṇyāka* (oil-cake) in a solid mass for three years—that is, until the end of the third year—at night; [the same applies to] *kaṇās* (grains).
Or he may eat fragments of rice as before; and this [penance] should be performed only once. Alternatively, he may eat grain-particles for a year, or eat oil-cake once at night. (MDh 11.93)
This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu.

Furthermore, since this consumption of oil-cake and the like is prescribed for the purpose of eating, there is a total renunciation of other food. And this should be understood to apply at the time after vomiting when one has drunk *surā* under the impression that it was water.
A drinker of intoxicants who has vomited should perform this very same vow;
and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed for him daily as a purification of the body.

This is because of the statement of Vyāsa. Nor is it correct to claim that this [prohibition] refers to drinking water in which liquor has been mixed such that its smell and taste are only slightly perceptible; for even upon mixing, the nature of the liquor (surātva) does not depart.

Just as the term *ājya* (ghee) applies to *pṛṣadājya* (spotted ghee), for this very reason the Vedic citations (*nigama*) should be made as "the drinkers of ghee" (*ājyapāḥ*) and not "the drinkers of spotted ghee" (*pṛṣadājyapāḥ*); thus it has been stated by those who know the principles of logic.
As for the statement of Āpastamba, however:

"Having committed theft, having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru, or having committed the murder of a Brahmin, he who approaches the ritual baths at the fourth meal-time, eating sparingly, and passes his time by alternating between standing and sitting, removes that sin in three years" (ĀpDh 1.29.9–10).
As for the statement of Aṅgiras:
"Those joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) are purified in three years"—
both of these [statements] refer to the same subject as the rule "or oil-cake, or grain-particles."
Furthermore, regarding the two penances mentioned by Yama:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor, having performed the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, shall again attain equality with Brāhmaṇas; such is the Vedic revelation."
If an excellent twice-born man, having drunk liquor, should make a gift of land and never drink it again, he becomes purified once he has undergone the consecration ceremony.
Thus, both of these, together with the former, share the same subject matter;
or alternatively, by resorting to a ritual procedure involving additional sacrificial fees, they are treated as optional alternatives to the twelve-year penance.

In this case as well, one should make the following determination: for children, the elderly, and others, the period is one year and a half; however, for those who have not been initiated, it is nine months.
As for the statement of Manu:
"Or he may eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year, wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks, and carrying a banner, in order to remove the sin of drinking *surā*. (MDh 11.93).
This [penance] should be understood to apply when there is contact with *surā* only on the palate and it was done unintentionally.
But surely, the drinking of a liquid substance is called "drinking" (pāna);
and "swallowing" (abhyavaharaṇa) is the leading [of the substance] down from the throat, not merely contact with the palate and so forth.
Therefore, how can there be an expiation for drinking in that case?
It is said: that conjunction of the palate and other organs, without which the act of drinking cannot be accomplished, is also prohibited by the prohibition of the act of drinking itself.

Therefore, although there is no major offense (*mahāpātaka*) due to the absence of actual drinking, nevertheless, because the prohibition of that [act] also prohibits the contact with the palate and other parts— which is invariably concomitant with it— the fault remains present; thus, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed required.
"One should observe the vow even if he does not kill, provided he has come together for the purpose of killing" (YDh 3.252).
Just as by the prohibition against killing, the determination and other acts that constitute its constituent parts are also prohibited, so too is the prescription of penance [stated].

As for the rule of Baudhāyana: "In the case of drinking *surā* unintentionally, one should perform the three-month penance (*traimāsika*) and a quarter of a year's *kṛcchra*, and then undergo re-initiation" (BDh 2.1.19).

Thus it is said: "Having drunk liquor, having killed a twice-born man, having stolen gold from a twice-born man, or having entered into association with those who have fallen (patita), a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. This is what pertains to Yama.
Furthermore, regarding the teaching of Bṛhaspati:
"Having drunk liquor made from molasses, honey, or flour, a Brāhmaṇa shall perform the Taptakṛcchra,
the Parāka, and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances in that order."

All three of these [remedies] are to be understood as intended for drinking in order to pacify a disease that cannot be cured by any other medicine, because the penance is otherwise too slight. However, when one eats food that is mixed with *surā* but has become dry in taste, then there must be a renewed initiation (*punar-upanayana*). As it has been said:
Manu says:
"Having unknowingly consumed feces, urine, or even that which is contaminated by *surā* liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again. (MDh 11.151)

And when one drinks water contained in a dried liquor vessel, then one should perform what was declared by Śātātapa: "In the case of drinking water from a liquor vessel, there shall be vomiting, the consumption of clarified butter, and a fast for a day and night.
As for that which is stated by Baudhāyana:
"He who drinks water that has stood overnight in vessels used for drinking liquor..."

"One should drink milk or clarified butter boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three days" (BDh 2.1.22); this [penance] is more severe because [the act] was committed when the food had become stale. Furthermore, regarding repeated unintentional practice, Manu has stated (11.149):
"Water contained in a vessel for *surā* or likewise situated in a liquor jar—one who has drunk it should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights. (MDh 11.148).
As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu:

"Having drunk water contained in a vessel that held liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights"— this refers to drinking intentionally. However, regarding intentional habitual practice, Bṛhad-Yama says:
"If a twice-born man should drink water situated in a liquor vessel,
he should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* with milk for twelve days. Regarding the smelling of the breath from one who has drunk liquor, however, there is the rule of Manu:
"But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the odor of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes purified by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter"—
this [rule] applies only to one who has performed the Soma sacrifice, and only in cases of unintentional [contact].
But if it is done intentionally, the penance is double.
However, this should be prescribed for one who has not yet drunk Soma;

whereas for one who directly smells the scent of *surā*, since smelling the odors of *agheya* (forbidden) and *madya* (intoxicant) causes loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), [the penance is different].

"Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if unintentionally, the *prājāpatya* penance. This statement by Manu (MDh 11.125) should be observed. 3.254.
Having thus stated the penance for drinking the primary types of *surā*,
he now states the penance for drinking *madya*:
"But having drunk *surā* out of ignorance, as well as semen, feces, or urine..."
Furthermore, the three twice-born castes are eligible for re-consecration.
Moreover, if a Brāhmaṇa drinks *surā* or *madya* (intoxicating liquor) out of ignorance, thinking it to be water,
as well as those Brāhmaṇas and others who [consume] semen...
Those who consume feces and urine—
even those of the three twice-born castes— are required to perform the penance of re-initiation preceded by the *taptakṛcchra* austerity.
In this regard, this re-initiation following the drinking of liquor applies only to the Brāhmaṇa, since it has been shown that such permission is granted to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.

And here the word *surā* refers to intoxicating liquor (*madya*), because the expiation is extremely light, and because a twelve-year penance is prescribed for drinking the primary *surā* unintentionally.

For this very reason, Gautama employs the word *madya* here: "If one drinks liquor unintentionally, he should drink milk, clarified butter, or water, each heated, for three days; that is the *taptakṛcchra*. Thereafter, his purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is required, as is the case for consuming urine, feces, a corpse, or semen" (GDh 13.2).
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu regarding this very subject—
"Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite" (MDh 11.147)— that too must be preceded by the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
This is in accordance with the statement of Gautama.
Furthermore, "re-consecration" (punaḥsaṃskāra) refers to re-initiation (punarupanayana),
and that should be performed according to the sequence prescribed by Āśvalāyana and others.

As it has been stated: "Now, for one who has previously undergone initiation, there is the shaving of hair—both performed and not performed—the production of smoke, the unexpressed *paridāna*, and the time; [and] the *sāvitrī* beginning with 'We choose that of Savitṛ'. (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 1.22.24–29).
Regarding intentional drinking of liquor, that which was spoken by Vasiṣṭha should be observed:

Regarding the drinking of *madya* out of ignorance, [the Vaikhānasa Dharma Sūtra] states: "For drinking *asurā* or *surā* through ignorance, there shall be the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, followed by consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and undergoing the *punaḥsaṃskāra* (re-initiation)" (VaDh 20.19). Alternatively, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed by Śaṅkha:
"One who drinks *asurā* or *madya* shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa*."
Regarding the mere entry of liquor into the mouth, Āpastamba prescribes a six-night penance:
"If one consumes what is not to be eaten, what is not to be drunk, or what is not to be licked,
how should the expiation for semen, urine, or feces be performed?"
"Having drunk the water of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the palāśa, and the kuśa grass, one becomes pure in six nights.
This refers specifically to intoxicants such as those derived from the palm tree (*tāla*).
Furthermore, regarding the unintentional drinking of Gauḍī and Mādhvī liquors, as well as the unintentional drinking of Asurā and Surā liquors,
one should observe the re-initiation (punaḥsaṃskāra) accompanied by the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance and the consumption of clarified butter, as prescribed by Vasiṣṭha (VaDh 20.19).
In the case of intentional drinking of those two [Gauḍī and Mādhvī], however—

"Or [he should eat] oil-cake or grain-dust"—this refers to a three-year penance. However, regarding the habitual drinking of that [liquor] out of desire, the rule of Vasiṣṭha—"But in the case of repeated practice, one should drink liquor as hot as fire; through death he becomes purified" (VaDh 20.22)—is to be understood as a penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*).
In this context, the word "surā" does not refer to liquor made from flour (paiṣṭī),
because it has been shown that even a single drinking of that [flour-based liquor] entails a penance ending in death.
Regarding the unintentional drinking of water contained in a dry vessel that has been perfumed with liquor, the *Bṛhadyama* states:
"If any twice-born man should drink water situated in a liquor vessel,
he should subsist on milk for three days, having boiled it with the roots of *kuśa* grass."
Regarding practice [of drinking] out of ignorance, Vasiṣṭha has stated:
"If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor,
[he must fast for three days] upon lotus, udumbara, bilva, palāśa, and kuśa leaves."
"Having drunk their water, one becomes pure after three nights" (VaDh 20.21).

However, regarding drinking [such water] intentionally, Viṣṇu has stated: "Having drunk water situated in a vessel for intoxicants, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights" (ViDh 51.23–24).
But regarding repeated intentional practice, Śaṅkha has stated:
Having drunk water kept in a liquor vessel, one should drink cow’s urine and barley gruel for seven nights.
But regarding the case of absolute appearance (atyantābhāsa), that which was stated by Hārīta is as follows:
"If any twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel for liquor,
he shall drink the *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* plants with milk for twelve days."
Furthermore, it has been shown previously that in these statements the mention of "twice-born" (dvija) refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas, because there is no prohibition against Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
Moreover, this [prohibition] concerns the drinking of water contained in vessels that have held Gauḍī or Mādhvī liquor.
Because the expiation is so severe, however, one must determine the appropriate penance for drinking water from vessels used for palm wine and other such liquors. (3.255)
He says to the wife of a twice-born man:
"That Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband;
in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, and a sow. (YDh 3.256)

A wife of the twice-born who drinks liquor, even if she has performed meritorious deeds, does not go to the world of her husband; rather, in this very world, she successively attains the animal births characterized by dogs, vultures, and pigs.
And here, the mention of a "Brāhmaṇī" [is intended to include all wives of the twice-born].
By the principle stated in "three [wives] according to the order of the castes" (YDh 1.57), this is an indicative reference to however many wives a twice-born man may have;
for this very reason, Manu says:
"Half of the body falls [with the sin] of him whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed. (cf. PSm 10.26).
Because husband and wife have a joint entitlement in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, they constitute a single body; therefore, when the wife of a twice-born man...
He who drinks liquor has half his body, which is his wife's form, fall away;
and for that fallen half-body in the form of a wife,
no expiation is prescribed.
Therefore, liquor must not be drunk by the wife of a twice-born man, whether she be a Brāhmaṇī or otherwise;

hence, "a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor" (MDh 11.94). Since, in this prohibitory injunction, the gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), the prohibition is established as applying to the wives of all three castes as well.
The repetition [of the prohibition] is for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition of *surā* applies even to a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a twice-born man;
therefore, when wives of twice-born men drink *surā*, they must perform half of the penance.

But for a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a Śūdra, there is no prohibition [against drinking], as she is exactly like a Śūdra; however, regarding acts equal to drinking *surā*—such as eating forbidden food—it was stated previously that the penance is half of that for drinking *surā*. (3.256)
Thus ends the section on penance for drinking liquor.
Now, the penance for stealing gold, which follows in order, is stated:
"One who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall hand over a wooden mace to the king."

"Having proclaimed his own deed, he is purified whether he is killed by him or released. (YDh 3.257) He who steals gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa should offer a club to the king while proclaiming his own deed, saying, "I have committed the theft of gold. This is because the offering of the club serves a visible purpose.
The king shall strike him with that pestle;
whether struck by that king or released, he becomes pure by virtue of the term "seizure."
And "seizing" is defined as taking [something] either in the presence or absence [of the owner], whether by force or by theft, without any cause for ownership such as purchase and the like.

Although it is stated in general terms that "one should offer a club," nevertheless, because that [club] is intended for the purpose of striking, one should understand it to mean the taking of iron or other materials capable of such a blow.
For this very reason, it was said by Manu:
"Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood, or a double-edged sword, or even an iron rod. (MDh 8.315).
A specific detail regarding this has also been stated by Śaṅkha:
A thief of gold, with disheveled hair and wearing wet clothes, should approach the king taking an iron mace and say: "This evil has been committed by me; strike me with this mace.
Having been punished by the king, he becomes purified.
And because there is no injunction for repetition, the killing should be performed only once;
for this very reason, Manu has stated:
"Then, taking up a mace, he himself shall strike him once" (MDh 11.101).
Thus, by being struck once by the king, he who was killed would be purified;
or, having been released from death, even while living, he would be purified—this is the sense. And so it has been stated by Saṃvarta:
"Then, taking up a club, he himself shall strike him once;
if that thief survives, he is purified from the theft.
This is as it was stated regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa: "One who is afflicted by a blow and rendered near-death, even if still living, is purified."
Now, why is this meaning not accepted—that a thief would be purified even if he were released by the king without being struck?
It is said in reply: because in the text of Gautama, "A king who does not strike becomes a sinner" (GDh 12.45), the fault of the king is stated for one who fails to inflict a beating.

If it is argued: "Let there be fault on the part of the king; nevertheless, how could the thief not be purified when released by the king out of affection and the like, despite having transgressed the prohibition?
It is said in reply: If that were so, purification would result without any [necessary] cause.
Now, it might be argued that because purity is accepted through the performance of twelve-year penances and the like after liberation, [the state of being pure] is not without a cause.
That too is unsatisfactory,
because by stating "the liberated one is pure," it is precisely liberation itself that is declared to be the cause of purity.
Therefore, the former explanation alone is superior; that is to say, one who has been released from death—even while living—would be purified.
And this penance ending in death applies to a thief of any caste.
But it does not apply to the Brahmin alone,
because no such distinction is specified in the occasional injunction (naimittika-vākya) stating "one who steals the gold of a Brahmin," which applies to Kṣatriyas and others as well.
This is because there is no distinction in their status as perpetrators of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), and because no other expiation has been prescribed for them.
Furthermore, regarding the verse in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "A Brahmin who commits the theft of gold... (MDh 11.100).
Thus, the mention of the "brahmin" is an indicative reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to human beings in general,
because it is that very [human being] who is the subject under discussion in the statement, "the man undergoes penance" (MDh 11.44).
Furthermore, because no specific qualification is provided in the causal statement, "Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher's wife" (MDh 11.55),
the corresponding conditional statement dependent upon it— namely, "A Brahmin who commits the theft of gold" (MDh 11.100)— [refers to all such acts].

In this case, even though it is explicitly heard [in the text], it is proper to regard it as merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), just as in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, the mention of "rice" (*taṇḍula*) in the sentence "whose sacrificial offering... refers to sacrificial material in general.
And this killing by the king applies to anyone other than a Brahmin.
For it is stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he stands guilty of every possible sin" (MDh 8.380); thus, the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is prohibited.
Even if, by some chance, the prohibition is transgressed and he is killed by the king, nevertheless...
"He becomes pure;
a thief is purified by execution, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone" (MDh 11.101);
thus, because it is stated that even a Brāhmaṇa is purified by execution.
Nor does the prohibition of killing [the offender] follow from the word "or" (*eva*) in the phrase "nor by penance alone" (YDh 1.200),
because that [verse] is intended to state that purification occurs even through penance alone. If...
In that case, the statement of an alternative— that "killing is either forbidden or [permitted] by means of austerity itself"— is untenable;
nor can the statement of an alternative be intended to refer to punishment, because such punishment has not been specified.

Furthermore, according to the principle that "only those things which have the same purpose may be treated as alternatives," an alternative is possible only between items that serve a single purpose, such as rice and barley.
However, there is no single purpose for the staff and asceticism,
because the staff serves the purpose of subduing [the senses] while asceticism serves as the cause for the destruction of evil.

And since the rule "a thief is not purified by execution" (MDh 11.101) refers to execution in a general sense, it is logical that there should be an option between that execution and austerity, which refers to a specific case, namely for a Brāhmaṇa: "or [he is purified] by austerity alone.
For there can be no option such as "let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, or buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya"; therefore...
Both [of these] have as their object only the general category;
or rather, there is no prohibition even for a Kṣatriya, as [stated] by Manu: "A Brahmin who commits the theft of gold... (MDh 11.100).
Having said this,

[the verse] "the king, having taken up a club, should himself strike him once" (MDh 11.101) prescribes the act of killing by referring back to the previously mentioned Brāhmaṇa through the use of the pronoun "him" (tam).
This is because the rule "one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 8.380) is also logically consistent with referring to killing as a form of punishment distinct from penance;
and this [penance] is one that ends only with death.
Regarding the theft of gold committed intentionally,
that penance ending in death which has been proclaimed by the wise should be understood as applying to a sin committed through desire; there is no doubt in this matter.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Madhyama-Aṅgiras.

And here, the word *suvarṇa* refers to a substance of gold characterized by a specific measure, not merely the genus (*jāti*) itself; for it is traditionally taught that "the mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is called a *trasareṇu*."
Eight of those [yūkās] make one *likṣā*; three of those are said to be a *rājasarṣapa*.
"Three *gaura* [barley-corns] make one *yava*; three of those make one *māṣa*;
five of those make one *kṛṣṇala*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.362–63).
Thus, the term *suvarṇa* is technically defined as gold weighing sixteen *māṣas*.
Therefore, in applications such as "the theft of gold from a Brahmin is a mortal sin" (mahāpātaka), it is logical that only gold of a specified measure is intended,
since the act of defining a measure has been performed.
Because its purpose is perceptible;
for there is no recollection of a measurement whose purpose is unseen,
nor is it for the sake of worldly convention.
Because the activity of the authors of the *Smṛtis* is not directed toward that [end].

For this very reason, it has been stated by those who know the *Nyāya*: "At the time of the application [of a rule], both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and governing rules (*paribhāṣā*) present themselves."
Likewise, it has been stated in the context of the passage "there are fifteen *ājya* [hymns]" that names are meaningful through their connection to qualities and results;
and it has also been stated that there is no traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) regarding a measurement intended solely for the purpose of a staff.
This is logical, provided that the purpose is limited to that alone.
Because there is no evidence [to the contrary],
it is therefore logical that, due to the absence of distinction, it applies to all remaining cases.
Furthermore, because the staff is for the purpose of subduing.
Furthermore, since the [offense] is established even without a specific measurement of the *damanaka* flower, the recollection of its measure is not particularly useful.
However, in the case of matters such as being a perpetrator of a great sin (*mahāpātakin*), which can be understood solely through the word [of scripture], recollection is absolutely necessary.
Therefore, the theft of gold measured at sixteen *māṣas* of *suvarṇa*— [End of sentence fragment]

Thus, the status of being a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) and the prescription of penances such as those ending in death for that cause [apply only to stealing gold exceeding a certain weight];
however, it is logical that the theft of gold consisting of two or three *māṣas* is merely a minor offense (*upapātaka*), just like the theft of gold from a Kṣatriya or others.
Furthermore,

since a different penance is prescribed for stealing gold of a quantity less than one *suvarṇa*, it follows that the penances ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) and so forth apply only to the theft of gold of that specific measure.
This is appropriate; for it has been stated thus in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"If even a portion the size of a hair-tip is stolen, one should perform a breath-control exercise (*prāṇāyāma*);
likewise, if even a portion the size of a nit is stolen, a wise man should perform three breath-control exercises."
If [the sin] is the size of a black mustard seed, one should perform four breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times for the purification of sin.
If [the theft] is the size of a white mustard seed, one should indeed recite the Sāvitrī mantra for one day;
if it is the size of a barley grain of gold, the expiation lasts for two days.
Having stolen even a single *suvarṇakṛṣṇala* of gold, the best of the twice-born should perform the *sāntapana* penance for the removal of that sin.
Having stolen even a single *māṣa* of gold, the best of the twice-born is purified after three months by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel.
For the theft of gold, one shall subsist on barley gruel for a year; beyond that, the penance is known to be either ending in death or the vow prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin.
And this practice of subsisting on barley-gruel for one year pertains to the theft of gold slightly less than a *suvarṇa* in weight;
for regarding the theft of a full *suvarṇa*, the great legal codes (*smṛtis*) such as those of Manu prescribe a twelve-year penance.
Those lowest of men who seize their own property by force or through lustful intent [are subject to this].
But for those who steal strength, the penalty here is said to be the taking of life.
The intention is that this applies even for amounts less than the measure of a *suvarṇa*.
Furthermore, this expiation for theft must be performed only after the stolen wealth has been returned to its owner.
Furthermore, in the case of theft involving gold or other property belonging to a Brahmin,
the thief must restore the stolen goods to the owner along with an additional eleventh part.

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), and likewise because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "He who has paid that [debt] should perform the *sāntapana* penance for the purification of his self" (MDh 11.165).
It is also stated in the section on punishments (*daṇḍaprakaraṇa*):

"In the remaining cases, he should be made to pay eleven times [the value], and that property shall belong to him" (MDh 8.320). Alternatively, if the king is unable to kill [the offender] due to extreme incapacity, then the rule declared by Vasiṣṭha should be observed:
A thief, with his hair disheveled, should supplicate the king;
then the king should give him an udumbara weapon, with which he should take his own life.
"It is known from scripture that one becomes purified through death" (VaDh 20.41).
"Audumbara" means made of copper.

Furthermore, he has stated a second penance: "One who is naked and smeared with cow-ghee should cause himself to perish by means of a fire of cow-dung, starting from the feet; through death, he becomes purified."
Regarding the statement "it is known" (VaDh 20.42),

that too refers to the theft of the property of a Guru, a Śrotriya, or a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a sacrifice, or to a thief who is a Kṣatriya or of similar status. In that context, the term *niṣkālaka* denotes one whose hair, beard, and body hair have been removed.
Or likewise, by the performance of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites.
Thus, after describing penance ending in death, Pracetas stated: "Or, having sacrificed with the horse sacrifice or the *gosava*, one shall be purified."
And this refers to those who steal from Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and others. (3.257)
He states another expiation:
"Without having reported it to the king, one becomes purified by performing the vow for a liquor-drinker;
or one may give gold equal to one's own weight, or provide that which brings satisfaction to a Brahmin. (YDh 3.258)
Having failed to report one's own theft to the king, one becomes purified by performing the twelve-year vow prescribed for a liquor-drinker (*surāpa*).
It is stated that this "vow of the liquor-drinker" is intended to exclude the carrying of a skull-bowl, which is otherwise associated with the banner of a corpse-head.
And this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally,

because of the extension [of the rule] to the twelve-year penance prescribed for unintentional killing of a twice-born: "This purification has been declared for having killed a twice-born unintentionally" (MDh 11.90).
[Objection: But surely, theft cannot occur unintentionally; how then can it have that as its object?

[Response: It is said: when one steals gold or the like, which is tied within the hem of a garment, out of ignorance, or having stolen it with the notion that it is another substance such as silver, and then immediately gives it away to someone else or destroys it without returning it to the owner—then [it constitutes theft].
Theft committed unintentionally is indeed possible;
however, this expiation does not apply to the theft of copper or similar metals that have been transformed into the form of gold through processes such as chemical transmutation (rasavedha).
Because there is no inherence of the primary genus [in the secondary],
and because the properties of the primary do not belong to the secondary merely by virtue of a primary resemblance.
Even if one steals such a thing that is not gold under the mistaken belief that it is gold, nevertheless this expiation does not apply,
precisely because it is the theft of what is not gold.

Nor should it be argued that there is a fault here even without killing, as in the case of "if one has not killed [but] has attempted the murder of a Brahmin" (GDh 22.11), because in this instance the effort was directed toward something other than gold.
For this does not apply to one who was created as a non-Brāhmaṇa;
rather, having mentally contemplated a sin, one should recite the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava* with the mind.
"One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times with the vyāhṛtis;
in the case of [repeated] engagement [in such acts], one should perform the twelve-night kṛcchra penance" (VaDh 23.23)— that too refers to the context of engaging in such acts intentionally.

Therefore, such a theft of gold through ignorance is not the occasion for penance; rather, it is only the aforementioned theft of gold when committed with the notion that it is silver or the like. In this very case, when the thief is extremely wealthy, he should give gold equal to his own weight. Furthermore, if [he is not so wealthy]...

If he has no wealth and is incapable of performing austerities, then he should give wealth that causes satisfaction to the Brahmin—sufficient to maintain his family for as long as he lives. However, when one steals property belonging to a master who lacks merit, then this very vow should be performed by the thief reduced by one quarter; as stated by Vyāsa, this should be understood as a nine-year penance.

But when one steals for the sake of protecting a family emaciated by hunger, then one should perform a sacrifice such as the Svarjit or the Ṣaḍvārṣika prescribed by Atri, or undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites; or else,
the twice-born should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six years or sacrifice with a ritual.

"Or by wandering among sacred fords (*tīrtha*), a learned man is liberated from that theft. However, when immediately after the misappropriation he feels remorse, thinking "Alas, what a tragedy I have committed," and returns the object or abandons it, then the penance prescribed by Āpastamba— consisting of eating only at every fourth mealtime— for three years,
or the penance called *Vajra* lasting three years attributed to Aṅgiras, should be observed.

Now, if [the act] consists in returning or abandoning [the stolen object], since the meaning of the verbal root *apahṛ* (to steal) has already been accomplished, how can there be a small penance? On the other hand, if it is not accomplished, then there would simply be an absence of penance,
rather than a small penance.

Not so; because theft culminates in its fruit, which is enjoyment, and because when it ceases before enjoyment, the full purpose of the theft is absent, a lesser penance is indeed appropriate, just as in the case of one who has drunk and then vomited an undrinkable substance.

[Objection: But if this were so, then even in the case of seizing [gold] by force from the hand of a thief, since there would be an absence of the fruit characterized by its enjoyment, it would follow that the penance should be slight. [Reply:

Not so; because in the act of relinquishing [the property], he has no spontaneous inclination, whereas in the act of theft culminating in the fruit [of enjoyment], he does have a spontaneous inclination. Furthermore, for one who steals gold mixed with silver, copper, and so forth, this light penance does not apply.
For, even when in contact [with other substances], its nature as gold does not depart, just as its nature as clarified butter (ājya) does not depart in the case of speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).

Therefore, it is logical that in that case, the penance is indeed twelve years. Alternatively, if a different substance is intended for a light penance and so forth, then it is called a "light penance. In that case, however, there is no applicability of a three-year penance or similar durations precisely because the substance is not gold.
However, this refers specifically to the expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Furthermore, there is another rule stated by Āpastamba: "Having committed theft or having drunk liquor, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year."

Thus, this refers to an object whose weight exceeds one *māṣa* but is less than a *suvarṇa*. As for that which was stated by Sumantu: "A thief of gold should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Sāvitrī mantra for one month, fasting three nights each day."

Regarding the statement, "One becomes purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance," this is to be treated as an alternative (*vikalpyate*) to the previously mentioned expiation for stealing gold weighing one *māṣa*. Furthermore, another [penance] stated by that same author is: "A thief of gold becomes purified by subsisting on air for twelve nights."
This should be understood to apply to one who has set out to steal with the mind but whose desire to take has ceased of its own accord.
In this case as well, it should be understood that even for women, children, the elderly, and so forth, the penance is only half.

Furthermore, regarding those acts such as the theft of a horse, a jewel, a man, a woman, land, or a milch cow— which have been established as being equal to the theft of gold— it is only half [of the penalty] that should be applied. As for the statement from the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
Having stolen silver through delusion, a twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
for an amount exceeding ten gadyāṇas up to one hundred, he should perform double that penance.
But for gold exceeding one thousand [units], the procedure is remembered as being threefold;
however, for all other metallic ores, one should perform the Parāka penance.
For stealing grains, a Kṛcchra penance is prescribed; for stealing sesame seeds, an Aindava is traditionally taught.
"A Brahmin who steals gems shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow"—
this [text] also intends to establish that stealing silver exceeding one thousand gadyāṇas carries the same expiation as the theft of gold, and not to exclude it [from the category of theft].
Furthermore, that which has been stated regarding the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the theft of gems should be understood to apply to the theft of gems valued at less than a thousand gadyāṇas;
however, for a value exceeding that, it is equal to the theft of gold. (3.258)
Thus ends the section on penance for stealing gold;
now, following the order of enumeration, he states the penance for violating the Guru’s bed:
"He shall lie upon a heated iron bed together with an iron woman."
Having seized and cut off his testicles, he should cast off his body toward the southwest;
the term "one who violates the Guru’s bed" (*gurutalpagah*), which appears in the verse to be cited later as *samā vā gurutalpagaḥ* (YDh 3.260), is to be connected here.

Just as one becomes capable of death upon a heated iron bed, so too shall he who has violated the Guru’s bed lie down upon a heated bed made of black iron, glowing with the color of fire, together with a heated female effigy made of iron.
Having slept thus, one should cast off the body—
that is to say, one should die—
after having made manifest one's own deed by thinking, "I have committed this act of lying in bed with the wife of my teacher."
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "Having spoken with one who has violated the teacher's bed... (MDh 11.104). Likewise, [the penance] should be performed after embracing a woman.

For the Vṛddha-Hārīta Smṛti states: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed becomes purified by making an image of a woman out of clay or iron, heating it until it is red-hot, and embracing it upon a bed of black iron (or having made an iron image of a woman, embracing it)."
Likewise, it should be performed by one whose hair and beard have been shaved and who is anointed with ghee;
for it is known from tradition that "one who is naked and anointed with ghee, having embraced that heated iron image or one made of clay, becomes purified through death" (VaDh 20.14).
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha; and not [contradicted by]:
"The violator of the Guru’s bed, having confessed his sin, shall lie upon a heated iron bed; he shall embrace a blazing iron image of a woman and is purified by death" (MDh 11.104).
In accordance with this statement of Manu, one should not suspect that lying on a heated iron bed and embracing a heated iron woman are two independent penances; rather,
[the latter] means one should lie down with an iron woman.

When there is the expectation "Where?", because the understanding of oneness arises from mutual dependence in the phrase "on a bed of heated iron," it is logical that this constitutes a single ritual procedure (*ekakalpatva*).
Alternatively, having himself cut off his two testicles along with the penis and taken them in his joined palms (*añjali*), [he should proceed].
Having gone with a straight course in the south-western, southern, or western direction until the fall of the body, one should cast off the physical frame;
as Manu has said:
"Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms..."
"One should proceed toward the southwestern direction (nairṛtī) straight on until one falls" (MDh 11.105).
The journey must be performed without looking behind;
for the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha and Likhita states: "Having cut off the penis and testicles with a razor, he should go away without looking back."

Proceeding in this manner, wherever he is obstructed by a wall or other such barrier, there he shall remain until death; having cut off his penis along with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he should go facing south, and wherever he is stopped, there he shall remain until the dissolution of his body. (VaDh 20.13)
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha;
and the punishment here is also this very same one,
as Nārada has said:
One who approaches any one of these women is said to have violated the Guru’s bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.
Thus, even the excision of the penis and other organs intended as a punishment also serves to destroy sin;
it was with reference to this very punishment ending in death that Manu spoke.
"Men who have committed sins, once they have been punished by kings, go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. (MDh 8.318).
Furthermore, through a monetary fine, expiation (*prāyaścitta*) indeed still takes place.

For it has been stated by that very same author: "But all castes who perform penance as prescribed shall not have a mark branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine. (MDh 9.240).
And by performing either one of these two penances ending in death, the violator of the Guru's bed is purified;
and here, the word "Guru" refers primarily to the father.
"In accordance with the rule, he who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception ceremony), and who supports [the child] with food—he is called a *guru*, a Brahmin.
Since this statement by Manu, which is intent on establishing the status of a *guru*, designates the father—who performs the *niṣeka* and other rites—as the *guru* himself; [it follows that...]
And the Lord of Yogins (Yogīśvara), with reference to the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception), has stated:
"He is a guru who, having performed the [initiatory] rite, imparts the Veda to him" (YDh 1.34).
Now, it may be objected that the word *guru* is seen to be used in other senses as well:

"Having initiated the pupil... (MDh 2.69), and so forth; and [it is said]: "One should know him also as a guru here, who benefits another with even a small or great amount of sacred learning" (MDh 2.149).
Thus [it is said] regarding the preceptor. Vyāsa also has shown the application here:
"Teachers, mother, father, husband, one who imparts knowledge, an elder brother, officiating priests, a protector from fear, and a giver of food."

Nor is there the fault of postulating multiple meanings, because the quality of being worthy of honor— which serves as the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "guru"— is consistently present in all cases.

And its status as the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) has been demonstrated by the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*), who, beginning with the word "these are to be honored" (*mānyāḥ*) and concluding with "the mother is more venerable than these" (*ebhyo mātā garīyasī*;
YDh 1.35), establishes that "more venerable" (*garīyasī*) is the final point. Nor does this contradict the statement:
"An *ācārya* is ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*); a father is a hundred times more venerable than *ācāryas*. (MDh 2.145)

It should not be argued that the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is the primary [authority] because of the statement that he surpasses the teacher (*ācārya*) and the father; for this superiority applies equally to the *ācārya* as well, according to the verse:
"Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable" (MDh 2.146).

Gautama has also stated: "The teacher is the best among gurus" (GDh 2.50). Furthermore, if preeminence were asserted merely on the basis of being superior, then by virtue of the statement "a thousand [times more than all others]," the mother [would be the foremost].
In this way, [the status of] being a guru would be established.
Therefore, it is logical that all [elders] are gurus, and thus approaching their wives constitutes approaching the wife of a guru (gurvaṅganāgamana).

It is said: Manu’s statement, "beginning with the impregnation," is intended solely to establish the status of the progenitor as a guru in relation to the one who performs the rites beginning with impregnation, as it has no other purpose.
On the other hand, the statements of Vyāsa and Gautama are intended for another purpose, serving as praise by way of being supplementary to the rules concerning service, worship, and so forth.

Therefore, based on the statement of Manu that "the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* [are for the purpose] of establishing the status of a guru," it is established that the father alone possesses the primary status of a guru.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states: "And likewise in the case of the teacher's son, pupil, and wife" (VaDh 20.15).
Thus, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed has been stated by extension to apply to the wives of the teacher.
Likewise, it has also been stated by Jātūkarṇya and others:
"One should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed in relation to the wives of the teacher and others."

And so forth. If the teacher and others were the primary gurus, then since the vow would be obtained through their very instruction, the extended application (*atideśa*) would be entirely purposeless. Furthermore, Saṃvarta has explicitly mentioned the taking of one’s father’s wife: "The lowest of men, having ascended to his father’s wives, excluding his mother... and so on.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well, it is stated:
"But he who, having recognized his father's wife, approaches her when she is of the same caste [is guilty of a sin].
From this also, it follows that the father alone—who performs the rites such as the *niṣeka* (conception)—is the primary *guru*.
And that gravity is undifferentiated among all four castes,
because there is no distinction in their status as performers of the *niṣeka* (conception rite) and other ceremonies;
therefore, in the phrase "that Brahmin is called a guru," the mention of "Brahmin" is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, sexual intercourse with the wife of one's father alone constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). Furthermore, "intercourse" is defined as extending up to the emission of the final element; consequently, if one desists before that point, there is no status of being a mortal sinner.
In that regard, this pair of penances ending in death— beginning with "lying upon a bed of heated iron together with an iron [woman]," and so forth—
is prescribed for unintentional [killing] of one's mother or her co-wife.
But this should be understood to apply to cases of intentional [intercourse] with a woman of the same caste or one of a higher caste;
however, he who approaches his father's wife, knowing her to be of the same caste,
or approaches his own mother without knowing her to be so, shall not attain purification unless he dies.
This is because it is stated thus in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.

However, in the case of intentionally violating one's mother, the rule of Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "One who has committed [the act] intentionally shall remain naked, smeared with clarified butter, and burn himself from the feet upward by means of a fire of cow-dung" (*VaDh* 20.14).
Even in the case of repeated practice without desire, this same [penance] applies.
Now, one might object:
"The co-wife of one's mother, a sister, and likewise the daughter of one's teacher..."
"However, one who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed" (YDh 3.232–33).
Since this is stated as an extended application (*atideśa*), it would be improper to apply the specific (*aupadeśika*) penance for approaching a mother’s co-wife.

It is replied: because of the inclusion of the term "of the same caste" (*savarṇām*) in the very statement "the father’s wife of the same caste," this extended application refers specifically to a co-wife of a lower caste.
There is no contradiction;
this [designation] applies only to the primary son,
whereas for the others, there is merely the performance of the duties of a son.
It is not [the case that] they possess the status of a son, as Manu said: "These eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, who are born in the prescribed manner..."
"The wise declare that substitutes for a son are [meant] to prevent the omission of religious rites" (MDh 9.180).
In that regard, if one proceeds out of mutual desire, the first penance is "lying on a heated iron bed.
But if one incites him oneself, the second is "having seized and cut off the testicles."
For it has been stated that the gravity of the expiation increases when there is an excess in the persistence [of the offense].
However, for one who is incited by her,
the penance prescribed by Manu— either lying on a bed of heated iron or embracing a glowing iron image (sūrmī)— should be observed.
As for that twelve-year penance which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, he should eat only once a day; and when twelve years have passed..."
"The stealer of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru's bed—
these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.
This [text] should be understood as referring to the unintentional (*akāmakṛta*) sexual approach to the wives of one's father, or to women of equal or higher caste.
In that very case, for one who has engaged intentionally but desists before the emission of semen, the penance is six years;
however, if it was unintentional, it is three years.
However, for one who engages with his mother intentionally, the penance is twelve years if he desists before the emission of semen;
but if it is unintentional, it is six years.
This is to be considered as follows: whereas Saṃvarta has stated that for the mere act of mounting [another's wife], "the lowest of men who mounts the wives of his father,
excluding his mother," a *taptakṛcchra* penance is prescribed;
This [act] should be understood as occurring prior to the emission of semen upon women of lower caste or upon the wives of one's elders. (3.259)
He states another expiation:
"One who has violated the Guru's bed shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra for one year, or he shall practice the Vedic Saṃhitā for three months according to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (YDh 3.260)
Alternatively, one should perform for three years (*samāḥ*)—that is, for three years—the *prājāpatya* penance whose characteristics will be described below.
This should be understood to apply to the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who intentionally approaches the wife of his preceptor (*guru*) who belongs to the Śūdra caste.
However, when [he approaches] the wife of the preceptor...
If one approaches a woman of the same caste who is unchaste unintentionally,
then he should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances accompanied by the recitation of the Veda. Regarding intentional engagement in that very act, the Auśanasa [Smṛti] states:
"One who has approached the bed of his guru shall perform the vow of a Brahmin-slayer for one year, or the *taptakṛcchra* penance for six months.
However, regarding intentional sexual intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman, the rule of Yājñavalkya applies:
"The co-wife of one's mother, a sister, and likewise the daughter of one's teacher... (YDh 3.232).

Thus, by the extension (*atideśa*) of the penance for violating the Guru’s bed, there is a nine-year penance. However, this extended rule does not apply to the case of approaching the wife of a Guru of the same caste (*savarṇa*), because in that instance, a penance ending in death is prescribed for intentional acts, and a twelve-year penance for unintentional acts. Therefore...
It is logical that this refers specifically to the case of a Kṣatriya woman and others;
for in that very case, if there is repeated intentional practice, the penance ends in death:
"If a twice-born man, having intentionally approached his teacher's daughter who is a Kṣatriya woman, makes her his wife again..."
Having cut off the penis together with the testicles, he becomes pure upon death.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Kaṇva:
"In this very case, when he does not wish to perform an expiation, then his punishment is the cutting off of the organ; and the same applies to the woman who acted with desire. (YDh 3.233)
Thus, the corporal punishment prescribed by Yājñavalkya is to be understood as standing in place of penance;
however, for intentional sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru who is a Vaiśya woman,
the penance lasts for six years.

For this very reason, another Smṛti text states: "In the case of the son of a Brāhmaṇī woman approaching a Kṣatriya mother, the twelve-year penance is reduced by one quarter; the same applies to women of other castes as well. This is the meaning.

For a son of a Brāhmaṇa who has sexual intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman who is his mother’s co-wife, the penance lasts for twelve years minus one quarter (nine years); for that same man, if she is a Vaiśya woman in such a relationship, it is six years;
but if she is a Śūdra woman, the penance is three years.
Thus, for the son of a Kṣatriya, the penance is nine years if the mother is a Vaiśya,
but six years if she is a Śūdra;
the same applies to the son of a Vaiśya as well.
But in the case of repeated intentional intercourse with a Vaiśya woman, the penance ends only in death:
"He who intentionally approaches the wife of his guru, who is a Vaiśya woman, again and again,
shall be purified from that sin only after having the tip of his penis cut off."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Laugākṣi:
"But for intentional repeated practice with a Śūdra woman, the penance is twelve years;
furthermore, having intentionally approached a Guru’s Śūdra wife, a composed Brāhmaṇa [should perform this]."
With a pure soul, he should practice celibacy for twelve years.
Thus, according to the recollection of Upamanyu;

however, in the case of unintentionally approaching the wife of one's guru who is a Kṣatriya woman, the three-year penance prescribed by Yama—consisting of eating only at the eighth meal-time—should be observed:
"Eating only at the [proper] time or at the eighth meal-time, remaining celibate and always observant of the vow."
"By subsisting on standing and sitting postures, approaching water three times a day,
and sleeping on the ground, one may remove that sin after three years.
Regarding the repetition of this very act, Jātūkarṇya has stated:
"Having unintentionally approached the wife of a guru who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya, one shall be purified by cutting off only the testicles, whether living or even dead.
Regarding unintentional intercourse with a Vaiśya woman, however, one should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance. (YDh 3.260)
This is precisely the view of Yājñavalkya;
and likewise Vṛddha-Manu says:
"In approaching the wife of a guru, as well as in approaching the wife of one's father..."
"But for three years, one should constantly perform the *kṛcchra* penance unintentionally.
In that same context, regarding repeated practice, Hārīta has prescribed a life-long vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) ending only in death:
"If a Brahmin, deluded by ignorance, repeatedly cohabits with a Vaiśya woman [belonging to his teacher],..."
"And he should practice the six-limbed celibacy for as long as he lives.
Regarding unintentional intercourse with the wife of a guru who is a Śūdra woman, however, the rule of Manu applies:
"Bearing a staff of a bedstead, clad in bark, or with his beard unshorn, he shall dwell in a lonely forest."
"He should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind" (MDh 11.106).

Alternatively, he who has approached the wife of his guru becomes purified by embracing a thorny branch for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, and subsisting on alms— this is what one should do as prescribed by Sumantu.
In that same case, regarding repeated practice, the *Mānava* [Smṛti] states:
"Or, with his senses restrained, he should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance for three months.
For one who has intentionally engaged with a Kṣatriya woman but desists before the emission of semen, the rule stated by Vyāghra applies.
"A Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of his guru shall perform the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and likewise the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances for three months.
Regarding this, the following is the settled rule:
For one incited by her, there is the performance of the Prājāpatya penance for three months;
for one who proceeded out of mutual desire,
there is the performance of the Atikṛcchra penance for that same duration.
Furthermore, when one has been incited by oneself, the performance of the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances is likewise limited to that duration.
In that same case, for one who has proceeded intentionally, the rule stated by Kaṇva is to be observed prior to the emission of semen.
"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, has once approached the wife of his guru who is a Kṣatriya woman, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra.
For one who is incited by her [to commit the act], the penance is the Atikṛcchra.
For one who engages in it out of mutual desire, the penance is the Taptakṛcchra; but if she was incited by him,
the penance is the Cāndrāyaṇa.

Regarding one who has intentionally approached a Vaiśya woman but desists before the emission of semen, Kaṇva has stated: "Having intentionally approached his teacher’s Vaiśya wife once, a twice-born man should perform the Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and likewise the Sāntapana penances for one month."
In this case, if both parties engage in the act by mutual desire, the penance is the *taptakṛcchra*.
If she was incited by him, the penance for her is the *parāka*;
for him, if he was incited by her, [the penance is likewise the *parāka*].
Regarding the *sāntapana* penance,
Prajāpati has said for one who has engaged in it unintentionally:
"One should not eat for five nights, or likewise for seven or eight."
"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, approaches his guru’s Vaiśya wife even once [must perform penance for] five nights; but if he is incited by her,
[the penance is] seven nights, provided the act proceeds from the mutual desire of both."
If she has been incited by him herself, the penance lasts for eight nights.
However, regarding one who has intentionally engaged with a Śūdra woman but desists before the emission of semen, Jābāli says:
"A Brahmin who intentionally approaches the Śūdra wife of his guru once shall perform either the Atikṛcchra, the Taptakṛcchra, or likewise the Parāka penance. Thus it is said;
for one who is incited by her [to do so], the Atikṛcchra is prescribed.
If the act proceeds from the mutual desire of both, the Taptakṛcchra penance is prescribed; if she was incited by him, the Parāka;
and for one who engages in it there unintentionally, the Dairghatamasa penance applies.
"A Brahmin who, with a composed mind, has approached his Guru's Śūdra wife even once, shall perform the Prājāpatya penance and the Sāntapana penance, followed by a fast for seven nights.
Thus it is said; for one who is incited by her [to commit the act], the Prājāpatya is prescribed.
If the act proceeds from the mutual desire of both, it is the Sāntapana penance; if she was incited by him alone,
it is a fast for seven nights.
In this very manner, the determination of the scope of other Smṛti statements should also be inferred.
And just as in the case of men, for women as well, the status of being a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin) here is without distinction.
For thus says Kātyāyana:
"Thus have the fault and the purification for those who have fallen been declared;
this same rule is recorded as applicable even to women who have committed adultery.
Therefore, when she too engages in such an act intentionally, the penance ending in death is no different.
For this very reason, after stating that for a man [the penance] ends at death, the Lord of Yogins has shown that for a woman as well it ends at death:
"Having cut off the *liṅga*, there is execution for him; likewise for a woman who acts with desire" (YDh 3.233).
But regarding unintentional [offense], it has been stated by Manu:

"This very same vow must be performed even for women who have fallen [into sin]. (MDh 11.189) Thus, the twelve-year penance itself should be performed by applying the principle of reduction by one half.

Furthermore, those acts which are equal to violating the Guru’s bed are traditionally declared to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed when committed with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage, or the wives of sons. (YDh 3.231)
Thus have been set forth those who are the subjects of the extended application (atideśa):
the father’s sister, the mother’s maternal uncle’s wife, and even the daughter-in-law.
Likewise, one's mother's co-wife, a sister, or the daughter of one's teacher.

"Having approached the wife of his teacher or his own daughter, one is a violator of the Guru’s bed. Regarding those [offenses] thus established, if they are committed unintentionally after a single night has passed, the penance is six years in sequence.
And the penance for nine years should be understood [as applicable here]. In this very case, if there is excessive repetition committed intentionally, the penance ends only with death.
And so says Bṛhadyama:

"Having emitted semen into virgins, women of one's own kin, women of the lowest castes (antyajā), sapindas, children, or wives [of others], the abandonment of life is ordained. Regarding this, the "lowest castes" (antyajā) are as follows:
The Caṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, the Vaidehika, as well as the Māgadha and the Āyogava— these seven are the Antyāvasāyins.
Thus, those [lineages] shown by Madhyamāṅgiras are to be understood;
however, those set forth [in the list] beginning with "the washerman and the leather-worker" are not, because a light penance is prescribed for them. Likewise,
"By approaching, eating with, or accepting gifts from women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, a Brāhmaṇa falls [from his status] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them].
By this statement of Manu, which establishes equality with Caṇḍālas and others, it is shown that for intentional and excessive repetition, the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) is indicated.
For thus, through repeated practice of sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman out of ignorance, one falls; therefore, one should perform the twelve-year penance for the fallen (patita).
And in the case of extreme repetition out of intentional desire, [one falls] with the Caṇḍālas.
It attains equanimity;
therefore, one should perform the death-ending [fast] for more than twelve years.
And this refers to the domain of long-term practice.
But for practicing it for one night, [the penance lasts] three years. As Manu said:
"Whatever a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night..."
"By subsisting on alms and reciting [the mantra] constantly, one removes [that sin] in three years. (MDh 11.179).
Here, by the word *vṛṣalī*, the *caṇḍālī* is designated; for it is said:
"A *caṇḍālī*, an unchaste woman (*bandhakī*), a prostitute, a woman in her menses, and a maiden..."
And she who has been married into a family of the same lineage (sagotra); these are proclaimed as the five types of *vṛṣalīs*.
Thus, because the term *vṛṣalī* is seen used for a *caṇḍālī* in another Smṛti text,
[it follows that] *bandhakī* means a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*).
But how, then, is repetition understood here?

It is said: because of the observation of the third case ending in the phrase "that which one performs in a single night" (MDh 11.179), which expresses both absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) and completion (*apavarga*);
and because there is absolute connection with a single night.

Since going is not possible without practice, the practice of going is understood. For this very reason, what was previously mentioned regarding the practice lasting from one night up to a long period of time—
including the extension of the penance for violating the Guru's bed for twelve years and so forth, as well as that which ends only in death— is intended to apply to such cases.
Furthermore, when one approaches a Caṇḍālī or others even once, whether knowingly or unknowingly, then,
having eaten the food of Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas and having gone to their women—
If one does so intentionally, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year; if unintentionally, two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Thus, the performance of the *kṛcchra* penance for one year and two *cāndrāyaṇa*s mentioned by Yama and others should be understood according to their respective order.

Because they are mentioned in a single syntactical unit with the phrase "among those born of one's own womb and among the lowest castes (*antyajāḥ*"), this same rule is to be understood as applying even to [the case of] sisters and so forth.
[The penance ending in] death—
Furthermore, entering fire,
as well as sexual intercourse with one's mother, sister, daughter,
