or daughter-in-law, should be known as an *atipātaka* (a most heinous sin).
But those who have committed mortal sins should enter the fire.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana. It should be understood that entering the fire [is the penance] when one has approached one's mother once, or when one has approached a sister or others repeatedly; for approaching one's mother is a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), whereas approaching a sister or others falls under the category of a near-mortal sin (atipātaka), which is subject to that same extension of penance.
And because equality is untenable;
as for that which was stated by Bṛhad-Yama:
"A Caṇḍālī, a Pulkasī, a Mlecchī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, and a female friend..."
One's mother, father, sister, one who has been entrusted to one's care, and one who has come for refuge.
Having approached his maternal aunt, a female ascetic, a woman of his own lineage, a king's wife, a disciple’s wife, or a teacher’s wife, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, as for the statement of Aṅgiras:
"Having approached women who are outcasts or of the lowest castes, having eaten [their food], or having accepted [gifts from them],
one should perform a month-long fast or else the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

Thus, both of these [penances] are to be understood as applying to one who has intentionally engaged in acts that are subject to the extension of the rule regarding violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), provided he desists before the emission of semen.
As for the statement of Saṃvarta:
Having approached out of delusion these women— a mother’s sister, a close female relative, a sister born of another mother— one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Thus, this should be understood as applying to one who, having unintentionally engaged in the aforementioned act, desists before the emission of semen; however,

when he approaches these very women who are excessively promiscuous, then this same pair of penances— consisting of the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Taptakṛcchra— should be observed respectively for intentional and unintentional engagement.
However, in the case of common women,

even if they have been enjoyed by one's teacher, there is no fault of violating the teacher's bed (*gurutalpātva*) upon approaching them; likewise, there is no [sin of] adultery as defined by birth-status, nor the defilement of a maiden.
Furthermore, there is no offense of violating the Guru's bed in the case of a common woman.
Thus, according to the *Vyāghra-smṛti*;

in this manner, other Smṛti statements as well, which are intent upon establishing various penances for different circumstances, should be sought out and their application to specific cases inferred, lest the work become too voluminous.
They are not written down. // 3.260 //
Thus ends the section on penance for violating the Guru’s bed.

Having thus described the penances for those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka), such as killing a Brahmin, the author now states the penance for associating with them, as the occasion has arisen:
"But he who indeed associates with these for a year becomes equal to them. (YDh 3.261ab)
He who dwells together with or associates excessively for one full year with any of those previously mentioned persons, such as the slayer of a Brahmin and others, is also equal to them.
This is intended to extend the application of their specific penance, according to the principle that whoever associates with another must perform that very person's penance.

The inclusion of the word "with them" (*tatsama*) is not, however, for the purpose of extending the status of being an outcaste (*pātakitva*); for it has been stated: "And he who lives together with them... (YDh 3.223).
Because this is established by the direct instruction itself,
and because here, even though there is an extension [of the rule], the full twelve-year penance must be performed, since the associate is directly a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin).

By the use of the word "api" (also/even), it is shown that not only is one who associates with a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin) equal to him, but rather, among those who commit heinous sins (atipātakin), sins (pātakin), or secondary sins (upapātakin), whoever enters into association with another, he too becomes equal to that person and must perform the very same expiation as he.
For this very reason, after enumerating the entire range of penances, Manu declared:
"Whatever man enters into association with any one of those who have fallen,
he must perform that same vow for the sake of purification from that association" (MDh 11.182).
Viṣṇu also has shown, in general terms, that one who comes into contact with any sinner, even one guilty of a minor offense (*upapātaka*), must undergo the penance prescribed for that specific sin:

"Whosoever associates with a person of sinful soul, he shall perform the very same vow as that person" (ViDh 54.1). For this very reason, Manu has established a general prohibition against associating with any sinner whatsoever.
"One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins and have not been purified" (MDh 11.190);
likewise,
"one should not associate with the virtuous until the penance has been performed" (MDh 11.47).

And thus: "Furthermore, this penance for those who have fallen [from their caste], such as that lasting twelve years and so forth, applies to cases of intentional association. For it is said: 'A man who, knowing [the other] to be fallen, dwells together with him for one year, becomes fallen himself at the end of that year because of his association with him.'"
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Devala;
furthermore, regarding contact through ignorance, Vasiṣṭha has stated:
"In the case of association with outcasts—whether by means of the Brāhma, the Yauṇa, or the Srauva [connections]—whatever portions were received from them..."
"By renouncing them and not associating with them, having gone toward the northern direction and reciting the *Saṃhitā* while fasting, one becomes purified; so it is known. Likewise:
"A killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and likewise one who violates the teacher's bed..."

"These are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakins), as well as he who dwells with them. Since the word "by them" (*taiḥ*)— referring by means of the third-case pronoun to the previously mentioned four, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin— indicates that only one who associates with those four is declared to be a perpetrator of a mortal sin, it follows that one who associates with such a person [of the fourth degree] is not himself a perpetrator of a mortal sin.

Now, it might be argued that association with a great sinner (*mahāpātakin*) alone is the cause for becoming a great sinner, and not specifically association with a killer of a Brahmin (*brahmahan*) and so forth,

because such specific association is subject to deviation. Therefore, since even one who associates with someone who associates with a killer of a Brahmin and so forth possesses association with a great sinner, he too [is a great sinner].
There would be the status of a great sinner, yet there would be no prohibition.
It is said: this might indeed be so if the status of being a great sinner were cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
however, since it is to be understood solely through the Word (*śabda*), [it is not so].
It must apply to that very [case] alone,

because by the pronoun "by them" (taih), which refers back to the specific subjects under discussion, it is understood that the connection with specific individuals such as the slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā) and others is indeed the cause of being a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin).

This being the case, even the absence of a prohibition is not a reason [for the loss of caste], precisely because there is no acquisition [of a new status]. Therefore, for those who have come into contact with those associated [with sin], there is no loss of their twice-born status; however, there is indeed penance (*prāyaścitta*).
It certainly does occur.

Nor should it be argued that if there is no loss of caste for one who associates with another who has associated [with an outcaste], how can there be an expiation; for it is said: "One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified" (MDh 11.190).

Thus, since by this general prohibition against contact with anyone who has committed an offense, contact even with one who has associated with a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin) is also prohibited,
it is indeed appropriate that there be an expiation even in the absence of formal degradation (pātitya); and that [expiation] shall be reduced by one-quarter.
Whoever lives with another for a year shall attain equality with him;
that twice-born man must also perform the penance of the other, though reduced by one quarter.
Thus the statement of Vyāsa is to be understood.

Likewise, for those who associate with an outcast through desire in the fourth and fifth degrees, it should be understood that the penance is reduced by half and reduced by three-quarters respectively.

Therefore, it is established that the entitlement to perform the penance for those such as the slayer of a Brahmin belongs only to one who has direct contact with them, and not to one who has contact with the person who had contact with them.
And in this regard, although a penance ending in death is prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin and others when the act is intentional, nevertheless—
That [penance] is not extended to the associate,
because it is the vow itself that is extended by the rule "he shall perform the vow of that very person," and because death is not denotable by the word "vow."
Therefore, in this case, even when the association is committed intentionally, the penance is twelve years; however, if it is unintentional, it is half of that.
And "association" [is defined] according to the specific nature of the acts that constitute its basis.
It is divided into many ways,
as the elder Bṛhaspati said: "Sharing a bed, sharing a seat, sitting in the same row, sharing vessels, and mixing food [with those of lower caste]."
Sacrificing for others, teaching, sexual union, and likewise eating together [with those of lower status].
"Ninefold commingling has been declared; one should not engage in it with the base. Devala also says:
"From conversation, touch, breathing together, traveling together, sitting together, and eating together..."
"Sin is transmitted among men through officiating at sacrifices for them, teaching them, or [marrying] them through kinship.

Here, "sharing a bed or seat" means sleeping on the same bed; "eating in the same row" means eating in a single line; "cooking in the same vessel" means mixing food; and "association" (saṃsarga) means, in short, eating the food belonging to that person.
Performing sacrifices for oneself or for one who has fallen [from caste] by means of that [person];
teaching him or teaching through him.
Sexual union means giving a maiden to him or receiving a maiden from him;
eating together means eating from the same vessel;
and conversation means talking with one another.
Touching (*sparśa*) is physical contact with the body; breathing (*niḥśvāsa*) is contact with the breath exhaled from the mouth;
traveling together (*sahayāna*) is riding upon the same horse or other vehicle.

In response to the inquiry as to which of these acts causes loss of caste (pātitya) and after what duration of time, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu has stated: "One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for one year through sharing a vehicle, food, a seat, or a bed, or through sexual intercourse, officiating at sacrifices, or teaching."
"By these connections, one falls immediately.
Here, "eating together" means eating in the same row;
however, by eating from the same vessel, there is immediate loss of caste (*sadyaḥ-pātitya*). [The same applies to] officiating at a sacrifice...
By performing a marriage alliance, Vedic study,

or eating together with one who has fallen (patita), or by officiating at his sacrifice, contracting a marriage alliance, studying the Vedas, or eating together with him— one falls immediately; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Devala;
by the word *srauva* (pertaining to the sacrificial ladle), officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is denoted,
and by the word *mukhya* (principal), because it originates from the mouth, teaching (*adhyāpana*) is denoted.

Regarding the phrase "by means of sexual union, officiating at sacrifices, or [receiving] gifts," although they are mentioned in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), each one of them is individually a cause for immediate loss of caste;
for Sumantu records that whoever enters into any one of these relationships— sexual, officiating, or receiving gifts— with those who have fallen, for him too this very same penance applies.
However, the fourfold set beginning with the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) constitutes a cause for downfall only when taken collectively,
because they are specified as being mutually connected in the phrase "by means of eating, sitting, and lying down together in the single vehicle.
Although practicing them individually does not constitute a cause for downfall, it remains a cause for fault.
It is indeed so: from sitting together, from lying down together, from traveling in the same vehicle, from conversing, and from eating together,
sins indeed transfer like a drop of oil upon water.
Thus, from the statement of Parāśara, it is understood that even [acts] such as conversation, touch, and breathing are causes of sin when they are independent;

however, in the case of conversation, touch, and breathing, their status as causes of falling occurs only when they are combined with the fourfold set beginning with riding in a vehicle, as they are merely incidental, and not when they exist separately due to their insignificance.
Furthermore, the status of being a cause of sin certainly remains,
as the statement of Devala— “conversation, touch, and breath”— has already been shown. Therefore,
when the four acts such as traveling together are performed while devoid of conversation and so forth, [the penance] is reduced by one-fifth.
One should perform a twelve-year penance;
however, if one associates with such a person, the full [penalty] applies.

This being the case, the statement of the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya), "He who indeed associates with these for a year becomes equal to them," is appropriately understood as referring specifically to the four modes beginning with traveling together.
Since conversation and the like do not individually constitute a cause for falling [into loss of caste], for this very reason Manu stated:
"By associating with an outcast for one year, one falls."
"From officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and marriage, but not from [sharing] vehicles, seats, or food" (MDh 11.181).
Thus, it is stated that this quartet beginning with vehicles alone is the cause of loss of caste (*pātitya*) after one year;
here, the mention of "seats" includes "beds" as well.
This is an elliptical indication;
and here [the rule] "one falls by associating for a year with one who has fallen" (VaDh 1.22) [is understood], as well as "from [sharing] vehicles, food, and seats" (VaDh 1.22).
Thus there is a connection with the distant [term], in accordance with the statement of Viṣṇu shown previously; likewise:
"By associating with one who has fallen, one falls within a year."
While constantly performing such acts as eating, sitting, and lying down, he [should remain mindful].
And this is also because of the statement of Devala.
Nor is there the fault of lack of logical connection (*ananvaya*),
for the distinction is intended in the sense that one "practicing" means performing conduct (*ācāra*) by reason of [specific] vehicles, seats, food, and so forth.
Because the connection is established;
as in the case of "having sacrificed with this sacrifice which is commensurate with the re-establishment [of the fires]," or as in "practicing."
Because the sense of the causal agent (*hetu*) is already conveyed by the suffix *-trā*,
the ablative case in *yānāśanāsanāt* is used in the sense of the accusative;
[as in] *yājanādhyāpanāt*.

One does not fall [from caste] through sexual intercourse or eating together, but rather immediately upon the completion of a year; this is solely in accordance with the collection of ancient authoritative statements. Therefore...
One falls immediately through the four [acts] beginning with sexual intercourse (*yauna*),
whereas through the four beginning with riding [in a carriage] one becomes equal [to the outcaste] after a year of continuous practice;
this is because the accusative case in the phrase "for a year" (*vatsaraṃ*) indicates immediate connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*), and thus the counting of intervening days must be performed.

Just as the duration of the association extends over three hundred and sixty days, so too, when it is less than that, the penance for a fallen person does not apply; rather, it is something else entirely. As Parāśara said:
If a Brahmin unintentionally associates with those who have fallen (patita) and the like,
he shall observe a penance for five days, ten days, or even twelve days;
or for half a month, one month, or even three months.
It may last for half a year or one full year; beyond that, it is equal to the former.
In the first fortnight, one should observe a three-night fast; in the second, one should perform the *kṛcchra*;
in the third fortnight, however, one should perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*;
in the fourth, it should be ten nights; and thereafter, in the fifth, it is the *parāka*.
In the sixth [case], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; but in the seventh, two Aindavas.
"And likewise, in the eighth fortnight, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six months.
Furthermore, regarding intentional contact, a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti by Sumantu:
"In the case of five days, one should perform the Kṛcchra; in ten days, the Taptakṛcchra."
"For half a month, however, it shall be the Parāka; for a month, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa. Thus it is said.
For three months, one should perform the Kṛcchra followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa;
but for six months of association, one should perform the Kṛcchra for half a year.
"But in the case of association for a year, a man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a year.

In this regard, the phrase "in the case of association for a year" should be understood as meaning slightly less than a full year, because for a full year, Manu and others prescribe a twelve-year penance.
As for the statement of Bṛhaspati:
"In the case of contact lasting six months through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and so forth,
or by sharing a seat or bed in one place, one should perform half of the penance."

This statement regarding loss of caste (*pātitya*) after six months for officiating at sacrifices, teaching, traveling together, or eating from the same vessel should be understood as applying when these acts are performed unintentionally during extreme distress,

specifically in the case of officiating at sacrifices that primarily consist of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), teaching the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and forming a matrimonial alliance with anyone other than one's daughter or sister.

Since it has been stated that one becomes fallen immediately through such acts as officiating at sacrifices for those who are outcasted, by following this very principle, for those who intentionally associate with those who have committed the most heinous sins (atipātaka)— such as one who has violated his daughter, sister, or daughter-in-law— the penance is nine years; if unintentionally, it is four and a half years.
This must be considered:

for those who intentionally associate with outcasts (pātakins) who have sexual relations with female friends, paternal uncles' wives, and so forth, the penance is six years; if unintentionally, it is three years.

Now, it should be inferred that for those who associate with those guilty of secondary sins (upapātakin) and so forth, the penance is likewise three months if intentional, and half of that if unintentional.
Just as in the case of men, women also incur loss of caste (pātitya) equally through association with those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) and the like.
As Śaunaka said: "Whatever causes for downfall apply to a man, those same apply to women as well;
however, for a Brāhmaṇī woman, there is an additional [cause] in serving a man of lower caste."

[The sin] falls [upon them]. Therefore, among those such as the perpetrators of mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*), the very same penance belonging to whomever one has associated must be applied to them by performing half of it.
Likewise, for children, the elderly, and the sick, [the penance is] half if committed intentionally, and [less] if unintentionally.

One quarter [of the penance applies]; likewise, for a child who has not yet been initiated, one quarter is prescribed if done intentionally, and half of that if unintentionally—this is the general principle.
He states an exception in certain cases to the prohibition of matrimonial alliance, which was itself prohibited by the prohibition against associating with outcasts:
"One may marry a maiden of these [outcasts] who is fasting and possesses nothing.

(YDh 3.261cd) This means that one may marry a maiden of those outcasts who was born while they were in the state of being outcasts, provided she is fasting—that is, she has performed the penance appropriate for the period of association—and is "possessing nothing" (akiñcanā).

One should marry a girl who possesses nothing— that is, one who has not inherited her father’s wealth such as clothing, ornaments, and so forth. By stating "one should marry a girl," [the author] himself shows that one should marry a girl who has abandoned contact with the fallen, and not accept her from the hand of a fallen person.
And this being the case, the contradiction with the prohibition against sexual union with a fallen woman is also resolved.
And this meaning has been clarified by Bṛhaddhārīta:

"But for one who has fallen [from caste], he may marry a maiden who has fasted for a day and night, and in the morning, having been covered with a new, white garment, should declare three times aloud: 'I am not theirs, nor are they mine'; he may then take her as his wife at a sacred ford or in his own home.
Likewise, because of the statement: 'He may marry a maiden of these [outcastes]...'"
This shows that his offspring, excluding the woman herself, is unfit for social intercourse (*saṃsarga*).
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"One born of an outcast becomes an outcast, except in the case of a woman."
"For she goes to another; he shall marry her as one who does not inherit property" (VaDh 13.51–53). // 3.261 //
Thus ends the section on penances for prohibited association.
Following the discussion on prohibited association, [the author] now states the penance for killing those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) resulting from such prohibited association:
"Having killed all those of lower castes, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (YDh 3.262ab)
The *avakṛṣṭas* are those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as Sūtas, Māgadhas, and others; for the killing of each of them, there is a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Thus says Śaṅkha: "For the killing of all those born in the inverse order, there is a *cāndrāyaṇa* for each.
Or else, as stated by Aṅgiras:
"In approaching all outcastes, eating with them, or causing their death, purification is achieved through the Parāka penance; so says the discourse of Aṅgiras."
Thus one should perform the Parāka penance;
in that regard, for the intentional killing of a Sūta or similar castes, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed,
but for unintentional killing of a Sūta, [the Parāka is prescribed].
The Parāka penance; for killing a Vaidehaka, three-quarters of it;
for killing a Caṇḍāla, two-quarters; for killing a Māgadha, three-quarters of a Parāka.
For a Kṣattṛ, there are two feet;
for an Āyogava, likewise two feet.
By this same method, the proportional gradation of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is also determined.
This is to be considered as follows: as for the statement of Brahmagarbha—"For women born of inverse unions, the period is remembered as one month;
for those of intermediate origin, such as Sūtas and others, it is four, two, and six [months respectively]."
Thus, that [penance] refers to cases of repetition;
therein, the connection is made according to the fitness of the circumstances: six months for killing a Sūta, four for killing a Vaidehaka, and two for killing a Caṇḍāla.
Likewise, in the case of killing a Māgadha, the rule is a two-month penance for a Kṣattṛ and a two-month penance for an Ayogava.

Anticipating the objection that since occasional vows (naimittika-vrata) are accomplished through recitation (japa) and other such means, they would be impossible for Śūdras and others who lack Vedic knowledge—just as the blind have no entitlement to rites accomplished by gazing at clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa) and the like—the author says:
"Even though a Śūdra lacks the entitlement [to Vedic study], he is purified by this [prescribed] time. (YDh 3.262cd)

Although a Śūdra is devoid of the entitlement to perform recitations (*japa*) and other such rites, he nevertheless becomes purified by this vow (*vrata*) which is to be accomplished over a period of twelve years and so forth. The mention of the Śūdra is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for women and those born of inverse-caste unions (*pratiloma*). Even though it is impossible for him to perform the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and other mantras, [he may still be purified].
Nevertheless, the recitation of the *namaskāra* mantra takes place.
For this very reason, it is stated in another Smṛti: "His food may consist of leavings, and the *namaskāra* is prescribed as his mantra."
Or rather, by the force of the scriptural statement, one may perform the vow even without recitation (*japa*) and other such acts;
therefore, having approached a Śūdra who always stands on the path of dharma,
the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be administered devoid of recitation and burnt offerings (*homa*).
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras;
likewise, another [rule] has been stated by that same author:
"A Śūdra devoted to the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas shall become pure in time."
"Either by gifts, or by fasts, or likewise by service to the twice-born.
As for that which is from Manu:
"One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow for him" (MDh 4.80).

Thus, the statement regarding the prohibition of instructing a Śūdra in religious observances (vrata) refers to a Śūdra who has not approached [a teacher for initiation]. As for that other statement from another Smṛti:
These penances (kṛcchra) must always be performed by the three castes;
however, it is ordained that a Śūdra has no entitlement to these penances.
Thus, that [statement] refers to optional (kāmya) kṛcchra penances.
Therefore, it is established that women, Śūdras, and those born of inverse castes (pratiloma) possess the entitlement to perform vows just like the members of the three higher varṇas.

As for the statement of Gautama, "Those born in the reverse order are devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.25), that refers to those excluded from specific dharmas such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). 3.262.
Thus ends the section on penance for the five great sins (*pañcamahāpātaka*).
Having now explained the penances for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), the heinous sins (*atipātaka*), and the secondary sins (*anupātaka*) among the group of five beginning with the great sins,
the penances for the minor sins (*upapātaka*) are discussed hereafter.
Explaining the penance for cow-slaughter as it occurs in the order of the text, he says:

"The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for one month, remaining self-controlled, sleeping in a cow-pen, and following the cows; he is purified by the gift of a cow. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.263)
Or, being composed in mind, he should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and one bull. One who kills a cow is called a "cow-killer" (goghna).
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.
He remained in meditative concentration (*samāhita*) for one month.
What was he doing? He was consuming those five products of the cow (*gavya*)—cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter—mixed together according to the prescribed rule.
He should subsist on drinking [milk] alone, by abandoning all other types of food,
because that is prescribed for his meal;
likewise, he should sleep in a cow-pen.
Since the cow-pen is prescribed as a supplement to the mention of his having obtained a bed,
and since sleeping during the day is prohibited, he sleeps in the cow-shed at night and follows after the cows.

The term *go'nugāmī* means "one who follows the cows," based on the rule that the suffix *ṇini* is used after the word *vrata* (vow). Consequently, he sleeps in the cow-pen because of their proximity.
In the morning, he should follow those very cows as they roam through the forest;
from the expression "he should follow," it follows that he himself should go at the very moment they depart.
But when they stand or sit, since it would be impossible for her to follow them by walking behind at that time,
it is understood that she herself should also stand or sit;
this is because following them [is prescribed] specifically for the evening at the cow-pen.
Entering the cow-pen together with those who are departing is also established as the purpose.
Performing this at the end of the month, by giving one cow as a gift, one becomes purified from the sin of killing a cow through the fulfillment of the scriptural injunction; such is one vow.
The phrase "lying in a cow-pen for a month, following the cows" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

However, there is an exclusion of the practice of subsisting on the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), precisely because the *kṛcchra* penance has already been prescribed. And therefore, another [rule] states: "For a month, one should perform the *kṛcchra* continuously with a concentrated mind."
For this very reason, Jābāla has stated that the month-long *prājāpatya* is a distinct expiation:
"If a killer of a cow unintentionally performs the *prājāpatya* penance for a month, he should follow the cows for their benefit;
he becomes pure by the gift of a cow."
Alternatively, one may likewise perform the *atikṛcchra* penance;
the characteristics of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* will be explained later. Or else, having fasted for three nights, one should give cows with a bull as the eleventh among them.
Thus ends the set of four vows.
Among them, in the case of unintentionally killing a mere cow belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who is a mere member of the caste,
one should observe a three-night fast accompanied by the gift of eleven cows, including a bull, after having performed a single day’s fast.
For it will be stated that the penance for killing a woman who has a distinguished master and possesses distinguished virtues is heavy;
however, in the case of killing one related to a Kṣatriya under such circumstances...
Consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for one month is the first penance;
here, because the consumption of pañcagavya for a month is extremely meager, it is equivalent to a month-long fast.
Furthermore, by calculating each set of six fasts as equivalent to one *prājāpatya* penance,

there are five *kṛcchra* penances; through their substitution (*pratyāmnāya*), this results in six cows— five at the end of the month and one cow given at the conclusion— making it lighter than the three-night vow accompanied by the gift of eleven cows including a bull.
Furthermore, how is it that the cows of Brahmins possess such gravity?
It should be understood that among the Vedas, Brahmins, and kings, the property [of the first two] is the most excellent.
Thus, because Nārada (NSm 14.13) has declared that such property is of the highest quality,
[and] regarding cows belonging to Brāhmaṇas (NSm 19.40).
And because of this observation regarding the greater severity of the punishment,
in the case of killing one related to a Vaiśya, however, one should perform an Atikṛcchra penance for a month.
Regarding the *atikṛcchra*, it is prescribed that for the first three periods of three nights one eats a handful of food,
while during the final three nights there is fasting;
therefore, when the month-long vow is performed according to the rules of the *atikṛcchra*, there is fasting for six nights.
And for twenty-four days, there is the eating of a handful of food.

Thus, by calculating the substitution for the *kṛcchra* penance, it amounts to slightly less than five cows; therefore, because it is lighter than the two previous vows, its scope is the killing of a cow owned by a Vaiśya.
This is appropriate. For the very same offense—specifically, the killing of a cow belonging to a Śūdra—the second [penance] is the Prājāpatya vow for one month.

In that case, since the substitute (pratyāmnāya) consists of two and a half Prājāpatyas, it amounts to slightly more than two cows; because it is the lightest among the preceding [penances], it is fittingly intended for the subject of a Śūdra.

Now, these four expiations are to be applied to the same subject matter previously mentioned, with reference to the relative degree of gravity or lightness among the direct perpetrator, the abettor, the instigator, and the consenter.
As for the three Vaiṣṇava vows, however—
For one who has killed a cow, there shall be three palas of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) every day for one month,
or else a parāka penance, or even a cāndrāyaṇa.

Thus, the rule of Kāśyapa— "having killed a cow, one should remain clothed in its hide, sleeping in a cow-pen for a month, bathing at the three periods of the day, and constantly subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)"— and the rule of Śātātapa— "subsisting on pañcagavya for a month"— these five [rules] also share the same scope as the rule of Yājñavalkya regarding the consumption of pañcagavya.

And as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Pracetas— "A cow-killer, subsisting on the five products of the cow, shall fast for twenty-five nights; having shaved his head including the top-knot, clothed in a cow-hide, following the cows and sleeping in a cow-pen, he shall give a cow as a gift"—
this refers to the same subject matter as the *māsātikṛcchra* vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya.
Or, having fasted for three nights, he should give [the cow]; this should be understood as referring to a killer who possesses extreme virtues.
Within this very context, however, for one who is unable to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), Kāśyapa’s second rule—"for a month with the five products of the cow"—is established.

It should be understood that at the sixth meal-time he should subsist on milk alone; he should follow the cows when they go out, sit down when they sit comfortably, not swim too much, not lead them down by a very uneven path, and not let them drink where there is little water; and at the end, having fed the Brahmins, he should give a sesame-cow as a gift.

In this regard also, it should be understood that Paiṭhīnasi has stated: "A cow-killer who is incapable [of the aforementioned penances] becomes purified by eating for one month a gruel (yavāgū) prepared with a handful of rice, while doing what is pleasing to cows.

As for that which was stated by Saumanta—"The cow-killer [should perform] the gift of a cow, sleeping in a cow-pen for twelve nights, consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and following after the cows"—and that which was stated by Saṃvarta, [these apply to those capable of such observances].
Eating barley meal, barley gruel, and alms-food, and consuming milk, curd, and ghee once a day,
he should eat these in succession for half a month with a well-concentrated mind.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should give a cow for the sake of one's own purification.
Thus, both the twelve-night penance prescribed by Bṛhaspati— consisting of consuming the five products of the cow—
and that [penance] of Yājñavalkya, the Māsa-Prājāpatya, share the same scope,
or they apply specifically to the case of killing a cow that is nearly dead.
One should understand that this refers to death resulting from disease produced by fear of uneven terrain, or from other such circumstances;
all of this previously mentioned pertains to the domain of the involuntary. However, when...
If one intentionally causes the death of such an ordinary cow belonging to an ordinary Brahmin, then according to Manu, there is the drinking of barley-gruel for one month,
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) at every fourth mealtime for two months,
and for three months, the gift of eleven cows along with a bull.
Subsisting on vegetables and the like is prescribed as a triad of vows. As it has been said:
"One who has killed a cow, being afflicted by a minor offense (upapātaka), shall drink barley-gruel for a month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide."
He should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his ablutions using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served them and paid homage, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
One should stand when they stand, follow when they walk,
and likewise sit when they sit— self-controlled, free from envy, and disciplined.
Whether she is ill, or accursed, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers,
or fallen, or mired in the mud, one should rescue her by every possible means.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
One should not speak of a cow eating in one's own house, or in the field or threshing-floor of others, nor of a calf drinking.
He who, being a cow-killer, follows cows according to this rule,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
"One who has properly observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. (MDh 11.109–117).

This triad refers to the threefold set of vows prescribed by Yājñavalkya: the *māsa-prājāpatya*, the month-long consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the three-night fast accompanied by the gift of ten cows and a bull.
It should be understood according to the sequence [of the texts].
However, after Aṅgiras has described the three-month penance associated with the Mānava procedure, he further stated:
"His food shall be dry, free from pungent substances and salt, at the sixth meal-time."
Or one should recite the Gomatī-vidyā, the syllable Oṃ, or even the Veda itself.
One should carry a staff according to the vow, and likewise wear a girdle accompanied by its mantra.
Thus, this refers to a maiden;

in the same way, it should be understood to apply to one who possesses some excellence of qualities such as full development and youth, [but not] one who is too young, too emaciated, too old, or diseased.
Having killed [such a creature], the twice-born shall perform half of the vow according to the previously prescribed rule.

Thus, since it is observed that a half-penance applies to a cow devoid of nourishment, youth, and so forth; when, however, one intentionally kills a cow belonging to an unspecified owner— a cow characterized merely by its species— which serves as the occasion for the Māsātikṛcchra vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya,
then:

According to the principle that "what is prescribed for those acting unintentionally should be performed twofold when done intentionally," one should perform the previously mentioned month-long *atikṛcchra* vow— prescribed for unintentional acts— twofold. As for what was stated by Hārīta, after describing the procedure according to Manu beginning with "the cow-slayer, having clothed himself in its hide with the hair upwards," etc.:

"Having given eleven cows and a bull, one becomes purified in the thirteenth month"—this should be understood as referring to the unintentional killing of a cow belonging to a *śrotriya* engaged in a *savana*.
As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "If one should kill a cow, he shall remain wrapped in its raw hide for six months, performing the *kṛcchra* and *taptakṛcchra* penances."

By the statement, "One should give [the gift] at the killing of a bull or a cow" (VaDh 21.18, 22), the performance of the Kṛcchra and Taptakṛcchra penances for six months is prescribed; and furthermore, as stated by Devala: "The killer of a cow, clothed in its hide, dwelling in a cow-pen and moving together with the cows for six months, is liberated."
Both of those [texts] have the same scope as that of Hārīta. In that very context, regarding an act committed intentionally, the rule of Kātyāyana is for three years:
"The killer of a cow, clothed in its hide, shall dwell in a cow-pen."
He should constantly follow the cows, observing silence and maintaining postures such as the hero's posture (vīrāsana).
One who is afflicted by the fear of rain, cold, heat, suffering, fire, mud, and danger should strive with every effort to liberate [beings]; thus, one is purified in three years.
Thus it should be understood.
And as for the three-year penance prescribed by Śaṅkha:
"But one quarter [of the penance] is for killing a Śūdra, and likewise for approaching a woman in her courses."
One should likewise do so in the case of killing a cow, and likewise in the case of approaching another's wife.
Thus, that [penance] also has the same scope as the vow of Kātyāyana.
As for what Yama, after describing the procedure according to the Āṅgirasa tradition, states:
"One who has properly performed the vow should give a thousand cows or even a hundred."
If nothing else is available, one should offer all one's possessions to those learned in the Vedas.

Thus, two types of two-month vows have been described: one involving a thousand cows and one involving a hundred cows. In that regard, when a wealthy man devoid of merit, having made a vow, kills with a sword or similar weapon a Kapila cow belonging to a destitute Brāhmaṇa who is a learned priest (*śrotriya*) engaged in a sacrifice—provided the cow is an essential part of the ritual, pregnant, and endowed with qualities such as abundant milk and youth—then [the penance] involves a thousand cows.

One should perform a two-month penance for killing a pregnant cow, a tawny cow, a milch cow, a sacrificial cow, or one that is well-behaved; however, having killed such a cow with a sword or similar weapon, one should observe double the vow.
Thus, because a specific expiation is observed for the killing of a distinguished cow belonging to Bṛhaspati,

it is for this very reason that Pracetas, with reference to such a specific kind of cow-slaughter, extended the vow for the murder of a Brahmin to cases involving the killing of a woman, a pregnant woman, a child, or an elderly person, stating: "In these killings, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin."
The second, however,
which pertains to Yama and involves the gift of a hundred cows, is to be understood as applying to a wealthy person in the context of the Kātyāyanīya vow;
whereas Gautama, having prescribed for the killing of a Vaiśya a period of celibacy combined with the gift of one hundred and one bulls, extended that rule by analogy to the killing of a cow.

Regarding the rule "and having killed a cow, [one should perform penance] like a Vaiśya" (GDh 22.18), this refers to the previously mentioned case where the number of cows— consisting of one hundred and one bulls along with ninety cows that serve as substitutes for the three-year vow— is two hundred minus nine; thus, because it is less than the three-month vow involving a thousand cows, it applies to that specific context.
Or rather, it should be understood as referring specifically to the intentional killing of a woman who is not pregnant in that same context. Furthermore,
even for the unintentional killing of such a woman who is not pregnant, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana should be applied.
As for that which was stated by Yama:
"If cows are killed by pieces of wood, clods of earth, stones, or weapons—
how is expiation prescribed in such a case, whether by weapon or without weapon?"
One should perform the Sāntapana penance for striking with wood, the Prājāpatya for striking with a clod of earth,
the Taptakṛcchra for striking with a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for striking with a weapon.
Then, when the penance has been performed, he should provide a feast for Brahmins and give them thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee.

Thus, this [text] is intended to establish that the *sāntapana* and other penances are preceded by specific means of purification, such as wood and so forth, within the context of the previously mentioned gifts of a hundred thousand cows and the like, or the three-year vow and similar observances;
it does not, however, prescribe them independently, because the vow itself is light.

Likewise, regarding the matter of expiation, it has been stated that on account of differences in age as well: "Having killed a woman who is very old, very emaciated, very young, or diseased, a twice-born man shall perform half of the vow according to the previously prescribed rule."
One should feed Brahmins according to one's ability and likewise give gold and sesame seeds as gifts.
Thus, half of that which is prescribed for the killing of healthy animals and the like [is ordained here].
A specific rule regarding this has also been stated by Bṛhat-Pracetas:
"When a calf of one year is killed, a quarter of a Kṛcchra penance is prescribed."
"If it occurs unintentionally by a man, it shall be two pādas for a two-year-old [calf];
for a three-year-old, it shall be three pādas; beyond that, it shall be a Prājāpatya penance. Thus [it is said].

Likewise, regarding the killing of a pregnant woman, when the fetus is also killed, the rule that "the effect recurs for every cause" implies that the vow of penance would apply doubly without distinction. However, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, a specific qualification is stated: "One quarter [of the penance] applies when [the fetus] has merely been conceived; two quarters apply when it has reached firmness."
Having killed an insentient embryo, the vow is declared to be three-quarters deficient.
"When the fetus is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, one should perform a double cow-vow; this is the expiation for the killer of a cow.
Regarding a killing committed by many agents, Saṃvarta and Āpastamba state a specific rule:
"If a certain [cow] is killed by many people somewhere by chance,
they shall each perform a quarter of the penance for that killing individually.
According to this statement, whatever vow has been prescribed for a particular kind of cow-slaughter, they should each perform a quarter of it, because of the scriptural injunction.
The phrase "if [it is] one" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, when two or many people kill two or many [beings], two quarters or three-quarters [of a *pārājika* offense] should be assigned to each individual.
And this should be understood to apply to killing unintentionally, because of the inclusion of the qualification "by chance" (daivāt);
for in the case of intentional action, even if there are many [participants], the full fault attaches to each one individually.

The connection with the entire vow is appropriate, because— as in the case of those performing a sacrificial session (*satrin*)— the full performance of the ritual activity is combined for each individual;
however, for many who kill a single person, the fine shall be double that which has been stated.
And because a doubling of the punishment is seen for each individual case;
however, when many cows have been killed by a single act such as obstructing them, Saṃvarta and Āpastamba state a specific rule:
"But if many [animals] have perished due to confinement or even binding, or if a physician has administered improper treatment,
one should perform double the Gograta penance. Thus,
even when many have perished, the performance of the occasional rite is not repeated for each individual cause.
Nor is it doubled by way of compounding; rather, it is doubled solely by the force of the scriptural statement.
Likewise, a physician also incurs double [the penalty] for the unintentional killing of even a single person by administering contradictory medicine.
One should perform the cow-vow (govrata).
However, regarding the unintentional administration of a counter-indicated medicine by one who is not a physician but has engaged solely for the purpose of helping, Vyāsa says:
Medicine, salt, and even food for the sake of merit—these should not be given in excess; rather, one should cause them to be given in small quantities at the proper time.
"If there is misfortune when [the animal] has strayed further, a quarter-kṛcchra penance is prescribed.
As for that which was stated by Āpastamba: "One should perform one quarter [of the penance] for confining [the animal], and two quarters for binding it."
"In the case of [causing] a miscarriage, one should perform [the penance] reduced by one-quarter for every *yojana* [of distance];
this applies to the indirect agent who acts as the instrumental cause (*nimittakartṛ*), and not to the direct perpetrator (*sākṣāt-kartṛ*). For the direct perpetrator and the instrumental cause..."
And the distinction has been shown by that very [author]:
"Those who forcibly strike down cows with stones, clubs, weapons, or anything else, they must indeed perform the entire vow."
"Likewise, by twisting the arms, shanks, thighs, sides, neck, or feet.
This means that those who cause a cow to fall by means of stones, swords, and the like, or by twisting its neck and so forth, are [guilty] directly.
The entire expiation applies only to those [who directly commit the act];
however, those who are instrumental— being engaged in indirect activities such as obstructing or confining— are not connected to the full vow.

Rather, it is by means of its very parts— such as one foot, two feet, and so forth. And in that regard, although there is no difference in the fact that the functions of obstructing and so on are mediated [by these parts], it is logical that, according to the scriptural statement, in some cases it is "one foot," in some cases "two feet," and in some cases "one foot minus a quarter."
Regarding this, Parāśara says:
"If death should occur through the ropes or tethering-ropes used for cattle unintentionally,
one should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance for that sin committed unintentionally."
"Then, when the penance has been performed, one should provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin. Thus it is said.

And this Prājāpatya penance is to be understood as applicable when one, having committed an act such as confinement, remains watchful with the desire to avoid the negligence resulting therefrom; for the qualification "of one who has committed a sin unintentionally" is specifically employed.
But when one does not exercise vigilance to prevent it,
then one should perform one quarter of the penance for obstructing [the flow], two quarters for binding,
three-quarters for piercing, and the whole for killing.
Thus, one should perform the penance for killing a cow as seen by Aṅgiras: a quarter-penance lasting three months, or slightly more than twenty days.
Āpastamba has also stated a specific rule:
"In the case of excessive burning, excessive driving, or likewise the cutting of the nose," [the following applies].
"In the case of obstruction by a river or a mountain, one should perform three-quarters [of the penance] when [the body] has been carried away.
However, there is no fault in burning [the body] for the purpose of mere identification;
nor is there any fault in branding or marking it, or even in driving it [into the water] or releasing it.
And for the sake of protection at night, there is no fault in confinement or imprisonment.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara:
*aṅkana* is the making of a permanent mark, while *lakṣaṇa* is a temporary identification.

Even when binding [the animal] with coconut fibers and the like for the sake of protection while it is being transported according to the path prescribed by the scriptures, there is indeed a fault; for it is said:
"Not with coconut fiber, nor with hemp, nor even with muñja grass, nor with iron chains."
But the cows should not be tied up by these means; rather, having bound them, he should stand holding an axe.
One should bind it with kuśa and kāśa grass at a site free from defects.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Vyāsa.
Likewise, another distinction has been stated by that same author:

"Wherever the death of a cow should occur due to the fault of a bell or ornament, there [the penance] shall be half of a *kṛcchra*; for that is traditionally prescribed for the purpose of decoration."

In the case of death resulting from excessive milking, excessive taming, confinement, or being yoked, as well as from being bound with chains or nooses, one should perform a penance amounting to three-quarters of the prescribed rule.
Thus, regarding negligence through the failure to provide protection and so forth, a specific penance has been stated by that same author:
"Even if she is submerged in a flood or a pond, struck by lightning from a cloud, or suddenly fallen into a pit, or even devoured by a wild beast..."
The owner of the cow shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra, the highest vow,
even if the cow has been killed by cold or wind, or even if it has died by hanging.
"One should prescribe the *prājāpatya* penance for indifference in an empty dwelling.
This, however, should be understood to apply to indifference even when there is no other task [to be performed].
But in the case of indifference due to being preoccupied with another task, [the rule is different].
In the case of killing a deer, a water-bird, a tiger, a beast of prey, or similar animals,
or if one dies from falling into a pit, a precipice, or due to snakes and the like, one should perform half a Kṛcchra penance.
But due to the presence of a serpent, there would be hardship in an empty house during an eclipse.

Thus, according to the recollection of Viṣṇu; likewise, even when there is an intent to kill, in certain cases where one has engaged for the sake of providing assistance, there is an absence of fault due to scriptural authority. As Saṃvarta says:
"In the case of constriction, for the purpose of treating a cow, or for the extraction of a dead fetus—if death should occur despite an effort having been made, one is not tainted by sin.
Here, "constriction" refers to the insertion of forceps, hooks, and the like, for the purpose of relieving a disease or similar ailment. Likewise, [it is said]:
If a twice-born man gives medicine, oil, or food to a cow or a Brahmin,
he is not tainted by sin even if a misfortune occurs while it is being given.
For twice-born men who provide assistance during a village raid with a shower of arrows, during the collapse of a house,
or by means of applying fire, cutting, or piercing a vein,
and for those acting for the sake of the welfare of cows, no penance is prescribed.

On this point, Parāśara also says: "In the event of a village being destroyed by a shower of arrows, or when houses collapse [due to an earthquake], or for those killed by excessive rain, no penance is prescribed."
Likewise:
"In the case of one who dies while digging a well for the sake of dharma, or during a house fire,
or likewise in a terrible village fire, no penance is prescribed."
This, however, refers to the case of one who has died due to the accidental burning of his house and so forth while still unbound;
otherwise,
Āpastamba has stated as follows:
"Furthermore, in wildernesses, in difficult terrains, in house fires, and in quarrels—

if misfortune should occur there, one quarter [of the penance] is prescribed. Likewise, a penance has been stated in certain cases for the breaking of bones and so forth, even in the absence of death.
"Having caused the breaking of the bones of cows, as well as the cutting off of their tails,
or the splitting of their teeth and horns, one should drink barley-gruel for half a month.
As for that which is from Āṅgirasa:
Whether there is a breaking of a horn, a fracture of a bone, or even the shedding of its hide,
one should drink the *vajra* for ten nights, even if the cow remains healthy.
Thus, the practice involving milk and so forth, which is denoted by the term "vajra," has been described;
that refers to the case of one who is incapable [of the standard practice].
And this is the penance.
Having given to the owner a cow similar to the one that died, the duty is fulfilled;
as Parāśara said:
"In the case of killing living beings, one should give a substitute for it."
"Yama declared that one should pay a price commensurate with that [damage].
Manu also says:
'Whoever should damage another's goods, whether intentionally or even unintentionally...'"
"He should cause him satisfaction and give that same amount to the king.
(MDh 8.288) This aforementioned collection of penances, however, is to be understood as applying only to a Brāhmaṇa who is the slayer;
[not] to a Kṣatriya or others.
However, a distinction has been stated by Bṛhad-Viṣṇu regarding the slayer:
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the full amount must be given; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as one-quarter less;
for a Vaiśya, half; and for those of the Śūdra caste, one quarter is prescribed. Thus it is said.
As for the statement of Aṅgiras:
"The assembly for Brāhmaṇas is considered to consist of twelve; for Kṣatriyas, it is held to be double that;
for Vaiśyas, it is declared to be triple. And the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly."
Thus, that [penalty] applies in reverse order to cases involving verbal or physical cruelty and the like;
likewise, it should be understood as previously stated that for women, children, the elderly, and so forth, the penalty is half, and for an uninitiated child, it is a quarter.
A specific distinction regarding women has been stated by Parāśara:
"There is no shaving of the head for women, nor following [the deceased], nor the recitation of prayers and so forth;
they do not sleep in the cow-pen, nor shall they wear a cow-hide."
"Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut it [leaving] two finger-breadths;
for in all cases, this is remembered as the method for the shaving of the heads of women.
And a distinction regarding men has been shown by Saṃvarta:

"For a one-fourth offense, there is the shaving of the body hair; for a two-fourths offense, the beard as well; for a three-fourths offense, everything except the topknot; but for a complete (four-fourths) offense, including the topknot.
Thus, for one deserving a quarter-penance, there is the shaving of only the body hair below the neck.
However, for one deserving half the penance, even the beard [must be shaved];
for one deserving three-quarters of the penance, moreover, even the hair on the head must be shaved, with the exception of the topknot (*śikhā*).
"But for one who is worthy of the four-footed [tonsure], it refers to the entire mass of hair together with the *śikhā*.
In this manner, by following this direction, the scope of other statements from the *Smṛtis* should also be determined. (3.263–264)
Thus ends the section on penance for cow-slaughter;
now he states the penance for other minor offenses (upapātaka):
"Purification from a minor offense may be achieved in this manner, or by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa."

"Or else by milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance. (YDh 3.265) Thus, by the vow for killing a cow as described above—consisting of consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth for one month—there shall be purification from other minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as being a *vrātya* and the like. Alternatively, purification may be attained by the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, whose characteristics will be described later, or by a month-long vow of subsisting on milk, or by the *Parāka* penance.

Here, by the force of the extended application (*atideśa*), a deficiency is understood through certain factors not common to the killing of a cow— such as wearing a cow-hide garment or tending cows— which [otherwise] would apply.
And these four vows [are prescribed] for unintentional acts, depending on one's capacity.
This should be understood as an alternative view.
However, in the case of acting according to one's own will,
twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) should observe this very same vow.
"Or else, for the sake of purification, one may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, with the exception of the Avakīrṇin [rite]. This three-month penance mentioned by Manu should be understood as applicable here.
Precisely because of this statement, this extension of the penance applies to all those enumerated in the category of minor offenses (upapātaka).

This [rule] is to be understood as applying without distinction to those for whom a penance has been stated and to those for whom one has not been stated, with the exception of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy).

However, for the *avakīrṇin*, only that which is specifically prescribed applies. Now, it might be argued that extension (*atideśa*) is only logical when applied to cases where no penance has been stated.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to rely on the sublation of the specific expiations prescribed for each case.
Not so; for if that were the case, the inclusion of those aforementioned expiations within the list of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) would be purposeless.
At most, [they apply] among the minor offenses...
A different specific expiation is stated for what has been mentioned in general elsewhere;
for example, regarding "officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate," it is said:

"One who officiates for *vrātyas* should perform three *kṛcchra* penances, even if he does not otherwise wander [from his duties]. This very same subject is merely excluded [from the general rule], but it is not the case that what was specifically mentioned [in the general rule] is [excluded] elsewhere as well.

Likewise, where a penance is prescribed—such as "cutting down a tree for the sake of fuel" or "one hundred *ṛc*s must be recited for cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants"—the purification from minor sins (*upapātaka*) in cases such as being a *vrātya* should be understood through the application of the fourfold set of vows established by the phrase "in this manner" and so forth, whether found in this treatise or in another treatise; thus, there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on the assumption of a common scope (*samaviṣayatā*) for those [penances]. This constitutes the distribution of the respective domains.
It is to be adopted.
And we shall apply those penances seen in other Smṛtis to the cases of the *vrātyas* and others according to the order of their recitation.
Among them, regarding the state of being a *vrātya*, this has been stated by Manu:

"Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the prescribed limit— having made them perform three Kṛcchra penances, one should initiate them according to the rule. And as it was stated by Yama:
He for whom the Sāvitrī has fallen for fifteen years shall,
having shaved his head including the top-knot, perform the vow with a concentrated mind.
For twenty-one nights, one should drink a handful of barley gruel,
and one should feed seven or five Brahmins with sacrificial food (havis).
Then, for one who has been purified by the barley-meal penance, the initiation ceremony is prescribed.
Thus, both of these refer to the subject of the month-long milk-vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya;
as for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One whose Sāvitrī has fallen away shall perform the Uddālaka-vrata."

For two months he should subsist on barley-gruel, for one month on milk, for a fortnight on curdled milk (*āmikṣā*), for eight nights on clarified butter, for six nights on unsolicited food, for three nights on water, and for a day and night he should fast; then he should either go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice or perform the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice. (VaDh 11.76–78)
In this matter, the established rule is as follows:

for one who, due to the absence of an initiator (upanetr) or other such causes, suffers the lapse of the prescribed time, there shall be one of the vows prescribed by Yājñavalkya according to his capacity.
However, if the lapse occurs when no such distress exists, the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
In that very case, even after fifteen years have passed, if some further time elapses, there is either the Uddālakavratam or the Vrātyastoma.
However, for those whose fathers and ancestors likewise remained uninitiated, that which was stated by Āpastamba applies:
For one whose father and grandfather have not been initiated, his period of Vedic studentship (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of the three Vedas (*traividyaka*) shall last one year.
For one whose initiation (*upanayana*) is not remembered by his great-grandfather or ancestors further back, his period of Vedic studentship for the sake of the three Vedas shall last twelve years.
(Thus ends the section on *vrātyatā*.)
These endings are found only in the NSP and Pāṇḍeya editions and are omitted by Seltur. I have enclosed them in parentheses; they may have been inserted by the editors of the NSP.
Likewise, regarding theft as well, Manu has prescribed a penance that sets aside the four standard vows applicable to minor offenses (*upapātaka*):

"Having intentionally committed the theft of grain, food, or wealth from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the *kṛcchra* for one year" (MDh 11.163).
Since the "best of the twice-born" (dvijottama) is of the same caste as a Brāhmaṇa— namely, a Brāhmaṇa himself— this [penalty] applies to a Brāhmaṇa who steals from another Brāhmaṇa;
however, for a Kṣatriya or others, a lesser amount should be prescribed.
Now, the guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold; for the other castes, it is doubled successively for each,
provided they are learned and yet transgress.
Because it is observed that for a Kṣatriya or others who steal, there is a lesser punishment—as indicated by the rule "the punishment is greater [for the higher castes]" (GDh 12.15–17)—likewise:
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the full amount must be paid; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as one-quarter less."
Thus, since an expiation is seen to be reduced by a quarter for each successive quarter [of the caste hierarchy],
it should likewise be inferred that when a Kṣatriya or others are involved as the perpetrators, the expiation is proportionately diminished in accordance with the prescribed punishment.
Therefore, for theft involving the property of a Kṣatriya, the vow for cow-slaughter is to be observed for six months;
for property belonging to a Vaiśya,
it is to be observed for three months.
In the case of taking [grain] from a Śūdra who does not maintain a storehouse, a Cāndrāyaṇa penance should be prescribed;
the same should be inferred for subsequent cases as well.
And this refers to the theft of ten kumbhas of grain; but in the case of more than that, [the penance is different].

For one who steals grain from ten jars, the highest fine of ten [paṇas] is prescribed; for more than a thousand palas, death is ordained— such is the indication of the death penalty [found in Manu Smṛti 8.320–321].
And the *kumbha* measures five thousand *palas*;
by association with grain, it should be understood that food and wealth [measured] in this way are limited to the quantity of grain.
By the word "food" (anna), rice and the like are denoted;
by the word "wealth" (dhana),
copper, silver, and so forth.
But this expiation refers to the case of intentional action;
however, for unintentional [killing], the vow for cow-slaughter is to be observed for three months. Likewise:
"In the case of stealing humans, women, fields, houses,

or the water of wells and tanks, purification is indeed by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa" (MDh 11.164). Thus, even though this Cāndrāyaṇa applies to the theft of water obtainable for two hundred and fifty paṇas, it is prescribed here for the purpose of precluding the vow required for the killing of other cows.
It is ordained that for the theft of water or grass worth that amount,
the fine shall be double its value.
Thus, because of the prescription of a fine of five hundred [paṇas], and because fines of that many paṇas and cāndrāyaṇa penances are associated with the killing of a cow and similar offenses,
likewise:
Furthermore, because a fine of five hundred paṇas is prescribed for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance— according to the rule: "For the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and Indava [penances], five hundred paṇas likewise"—
this applies to the theft of property belonging to Kṣatriyas and others.
It should be observed:
"But in the case of misappropriating property belonging to a Brāhmaṇa,
as well as the theft of a deposit, a man, a horse, or silver..."

"And for stealing earth, gems, or gold, it is considered equal to stealing gold" (MDh 11.58)—thus it should be understood. Likewise: "Having committed theft from another's house of articles of little value..."
"By this [verse], *caret sāṃtapanaṃ kṛcchraṃ tan niryāty ātmaśuddhaye* (MDh 11.165),
there is an exception to the general penance for the minor sin of theft (*steya-sāmānya-upapātaka*) based on the specific theft of materials such as tin or lead which serve a minor purpose.
And this [penance] applies to the theft of half-a-tenth part— namely, half a *trapu* or *sīsa*— of the two hundred and fifty *mūlya* units that constitute the cause for the *Cāndrāyaṇa*."
The expiation [is determined] because it constitutes a fifteenth part of the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Likewise, there is an exception to the vow generally prescribed for minor offenses (upapātaka) based on the specific nature of the substance:

"In the case of stealing food that is chewed or eaten, as well as vehicles, beds, seats, and flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is the purification. (MDh 11.166).
This [penance] applies to the theft of edible food sufficient for a single meal.
For consuming an amount of food sufficient for two or three meals, the penance lasts for three nights;

as Paiṭhīnasi has said: "In the case of taking an amount of edible food that merely fills the stomach, the penance is three nights or one night, along with subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
Because of this association, even in the case of vehicles and the like, this expiation applies only when they are stolen for a value of this much.
In all cases, the lightness or heaviness of the expiation must be determined according to whether the stolen object is of lesser or greater value.
Likewise, [the same principle applies].
"And for [eating] grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses, oil, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights" (MDh 11.167).

Since this shows that for these items, such as grass and the rest, the penance consists of a three-night fast multiplied by three according to whether they are edible and so forth, [the rule applies].
This expiation applies to those [articles] whose value is threefold or half that amount;
likewise for gems, pearls, corals, copper, and silver.
"And for stealing iron, bronze, or stone, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days" (MDh 11.168).
Here too, because a twelvefold penance is observed— just as in the case of edible foods and the like—
it follows that the theft of gems, pearls, and so forth involves a fine equal to twelve times their value.
This should be understood as the expiation:
"Likewise, for cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed animals, single-hoofed animals, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must drink milk for three days" (MDh 11.169).

Since a threefold penance is seen here as well for the theft of foodstuffs and other such items, this penance should be understood to apply specifically to the theft of goods whose value is threefold that amount. Furthermore, the lesser or greater severity of the penance must be determined according to whether the stolen property is less or more than that value.
And this expiation for theft is to be understood as applying only after the stolen property has been returned to the owner;
as Viṣṇu says:
"Having indeed given back the stolen property to its owner, one should perform the vow."

(Thus ends the section on theft. Furthermore, regarding the non-payment of a debt for which it has been ordained that "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons" (YDh 2.50), as well as the failure to perform the sacrifices and other rites praised as debts in the Vedic statement, "A Brāhmaṇa is indeed born [with three debts]..."— in these cases, purification from minor sins (upapātaka) shall likewise occur.
By such statements as these, the fourfold set of vows prescribed generally for minor offenses (upapātaka) should be applied according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, another penance has been stated here by Manu:

"At the end of the year, one should indeed perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the sake of expiation for the animal and Soma sacrifices that have been omitted when they cannot be performed. (MDh 11.27).
"At the end of the year" means at the conclusion of the twelve-month period.
(Thus ends the section on the non-payment of debts.

Likewise, even for one who is authorized [to perform the rites] but has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), these same four vows are to be applied after a year in times of distress, according to his capacity; however, in the absence of distress, the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
However, Kārṣṇājini has stated a specific rule for the period prior to one year:
"A Brahmin, having established the sacred fires at the proper time, should perform the rites according to the injunctions;
if he fails to do so, he becomes purified month by month after three nights."
"If a son intends to perform a sacrifice while his father or other ancestors have not maintained the sacred fires,
he should indeed sacrifice with a *vrātya* animal as a means of expiation for that [neglect].
A specific rule regarding even a single-maintainer of the fire (*ekāgni*) has been stated by that same author:
The eldest son who has married and lives at home must maintain the *upāsana* fire;
if he does not do so, he should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for a year, or else for one day every month.
(Thus [the state of] not having established the sacred fires.
Prior to this, the NSP and Pāṇḍeya add a passage within parentheses which is found in one manuscript; it is likely an interpolation.
Whatever vow is prescribed for the sale [of certain items], it is indeed doubled for their theft.
For the sale of *surā* (liquor), the *somya* penance is required; for the sale of lac, salt, meat, honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and those used in *homa*, three *cāndrāyaṇas* are prescribed.
For milk, milk-rice, cakes, curd, sugarcane juice, molasses, sugar-candy, and other oily or cooked foods, the *parāka* penance is required.
For selling prepared food, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance; for selling a jackfruit, three days;
and for selling plantains, coconut, jambīra, bījapūraka, or nāraṅga, one must perform a quarter-kṛcchra.
For the sale of musk and other fragrances, the penance is a *kṛcchra*;
for camphor, it is half of that; and for the sale of asafoetida and similar substances, it is a day of fasting.
For the sale of white, black, or yellow garments, the penance lasts three days; for goats, it is the Aindava;
for donkeys, mules, and young camels, it is the Parāka.
For selling the Vedas, the penance is double that for dogs; for selling them on a single day, it is a Cāndrāyaṇa;
and for selling the auxiliary sciences (Aṅgas), it is a Parāka.
For the Smṛtis, the Kṛcchra penance;
for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Sāṃtapana penance; for the Rahasyas, the Kṛcchra penance.
[This refers to] a quarter-verse of the *Gāthās* concerning the science of the essence of the cold season.
Likewise, regarding the sale of items that should not be sold, a specific penance is stated in another Smṛti.
As Hārīta says:
For the sale of molasses, sesame, flowers, roots, fruits, or cooked food, the penance is the Somapāna Saumya Kṛcchra.
For the sale of any one of the following— lac, salt, honey, meat, oil, milk, curd, buttermilk, clarified butter, perfumes, skins, or garments— the penance is the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Likewise, for the sale of the *ūrṇā* hair, a lion, a cow, a house, a stone, or weapons;
and for the sale of edible meat, sinews, bones, horns, nails, or mother-of-pearl, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is prescribed.
For [stealing] asafoetida, guggulu, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, red ochre, alkali, salt, gems, pearls, coral, bamboo, or earthenware,
one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. For the sale of groves, ponds, wells, lotus-pools, or meritorious deeds, one must bathe at the three periods of the day and sleep on the ground.
"One who eats at the fourth mealtime while reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times becomes purified in one year;
this also applies to the sale of inferior weights and measures, or mixed and adulterated goods.

Thus, by other statements as well—such as those of Śaṅkha, Viṣṇu, and others—in cases where no specific penance has been prescribed, the three-month penance applicable to minor offenses (upapātaka) generally established by Manu is to be applied when no exception occurs.
In times of distress, however, the fourfold set of observances prescribed by Yājñavalkya should be applied according to one's capacity.
(Thus ends the section on the sale of forbidden goods.
Likewise, regarding the *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother), Vasiṣṭha has stated concerning the matter of penance:

"The *parivividāna* (the one who causes such a marriage), having performed the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances and having given [his bride] back to him, may marry again and wed that very same woman" (VaDh 20.8).
One who marries before his elder brother is called a *parivettṛ*;
his nature has already been explained previously.
He [must perform] the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances.
