Having performed [the penance] for that elder brother and having given his own wife to him—having offered her like alms obtained through celibacy (brahmacarya) in order to avoid the humiliation of the guru—he may marry again. To the question "Which woman? it is stated: "He should marry that very same one."
One should marry that very woman who has been carried off [by another], announced to the elder brother, and permitted by him.
As for what was stated by Hārīta:

"When the elder brother is not yet married, the younger brother who marries becomes a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder), the elder brother becomes a *parivitti* (the one superseded), and the woman becomes a *parivedanī* (one who is superseded)."

"The giver of a maiden, the one who receives her, the one who performs the sacrifice for her, and the officiating priest— all these shall become outcasts; they may purify themselves by performing the Prājāpatya penance for one year"—
this is also what was stated by Śaṅkha.
"The elder brother who has married before his younger brother and the younger brother who marries before his elder brother shall both subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for one year"—
this penance applies to both cases involving a marriage performed out of one's own will without the permission of the girl's father or other guardians.
Because of its gravity: when, however, one intentionally marries a maiden who has been given by her father or others, then the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.

The previously mentioned *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*, as well as the fourfold vow of Yājñavalkya, apply to cases where the act was committed unintentionally. A specific rule regarding this matter has also been stated by Yama:
"In the case of marrying two sisters, there are two *kṛcchra* penances; for the maiden herself, there is indeed a *kṛcchra*.
The giver should perform an *atikṛcchra*, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*.
This same rule applies equally to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*paryāhitāgni*) and others as well.
Because it is taught as a single yoga.
As Gautama said:

"For those who have superseded their younger brother in marriage, those who have been superseded, those for whom the marriage rites were performed by another, those who have performed the rites for another, those who marry a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, and those who marry an elder sister while the younger is already married—for these, the *prākṛta* penance lasts for one year."
Regarding the phrase "celibacy" (*brahmacarya*): for this very reason, Vasiṣṭha has prescribed this same penance for one who marries an *agredidhiṣū* woman and others:
"The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* woman, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may enter the household and marry her."
"The husband of a *didhiṣū* shall perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance and then marry her again if she was given to him" (VaDh 20.9–10).
The definitions of the *agredidhiṣū* and others are stated in another Smṛti:
"If a younger sister is married while an elder sister remains unmarried,
she is to be known as *agredidhiṣū*, while the elder is remembered as *didhiṣū*.
In that case, the husband of the *agredidhiṣū* should perform a *prājāpatya* penance and subsequently marry that same elder sister after she has been married by another.

But the husband of a *didhiṣū* (a younger sister married before her elder), having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, shall give his own wedded wife to the man who previously married the younger sister, and then marry another woman.
(Thus ends the section on supersession.)

Likewise, with reference to the one who teaches for a fee and the one taught by such a teacher, Viṣṇu has stated: "Having performed the teaching for a fee, as well as the one taught for a fee... [and so on, concluding with] "...one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā* with milk."
"By providing an inquiry (anuyoga), one should certainly drink [the water] for three fortnights.
Thus, "providing an inquiry" refers to questioning a student who is studying for the sake of excellence, saying, "What are you reading? You have ruined it!
For this very reason, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Manu has declared that those who study [the Veda] from those to whom instruction has been improperly given are fallen.
This has been stated. In this case as well, there is an option between this [penance] and the previously mentioned vows, depending on one's capacity.
Thus ends the section concerning the teacher for hire and the student taught for hire.

Likewise, regarding adultery (*pāradārya*), although the three-month penance prescribed by Manu—which applies generally to minor offenses (*upapātaka*)—and the fourfold vows prescribed by Yājñavalkya would otherwise apply, an exception has been stated for the case of the teacher’s wife and others.
Similarly, elsewhere exceptions have been stated by Gautama and others based on specific types of adultery.
As Gautama says:
"Two [years] for violating another's wife, three for a *śrotriya* [wife]" (GDh 22.29–30).
Likewise, having introduced the standard (*prākṛta*) vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) lasting one year, he stated this very same thing:
"And likewise in the case of minor offenses (*upapātaka*)" (GDh 22.34).

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: for intentionally approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman who is merely so by birth during her fertile period, one must observe the standard vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) for one year.
At that very time, for approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman who possesses qualities such as being the means for performing ritual acts, there is ordinary celibacy for two years;
for approaching the wife of a Śrotriya of the same description, there is ordinary [celibacy] for three years.
Or celibacy for three years toward a virtuous Brāhmaṇa wife who is learned in the Vedas; [the same applies] toward such a woman.
In this same manner, the rule is that for a Kṣatriya woman it is two years, and for a Vaiśya woman of the same status it is one year;
this is established by viewing them as equal.
In the case of a Śūdra woman, the standard period of celibacy (brahmacarya) should be calculated as six months.
For this very reason, Śaṅkha states: "One who has violated his vow with a Vaiśya woman shall observe celibacy for one year and perform the three daily ablutions;
with a Kṣatriya woman, for two years."

In the case of a year, [the penance] for a Brāhmaṇa woman is three years, and for a Śūdra woman married to a Brāhmaṇa it is like that of a Vaiśya; thus, a reduction is shown according to the order of the castes. Similarly, for a Kṣatriya as well, in the case of women of the Kṣatriya and other castes, the penances of two years, one year, and six months respectively should be applied to the same aforementioned subject matter.
For a Vaiśya, [the penance] is one year for a Vaiśya woman and six months for a Śūdra woman; for a Śūdra, it is likewise six months for a Śūdra woman who is the wife of another.

As for the rule of Āpastamba stating that there is a quarter-penance for a single union with a woman of the same caste who has not belonged to another man previously, [that refers to a different case].
"In this manner, with each repetition, one quarter [of the penance] falls away; at the fourth [repetition], it is all gone" (ĀpDh 2.27.11–13);
thus, this refers to the same subject matter as Gautama’s three-year penance.

However, since a twelve-year penance is prescribed for the fourth repetition of intercourse with a woman who has not belonged to another before, this penance does not apply to the repetition of intercourse with the same woman; rather, for each subsequent act, a penance reduced by one quarter should be assigned.
All of this refers to cases of intentional action (*kāmakāra*).

Furthermore, in the case of unintentional [intercourse] within the aforementioned scope, this very same rule should be applied by halving the penance. However, for intentional intercourse with a woman who is a Brāhmaṇī by birth alone during a period other than her fertile season (anṛtu), the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
In the case of women who are Kṣatriyas and so forth by birth alone, however, within this same scope, their respective penances—the two-month Cāndrāyaṇa and the one-month [Cāndrāyaṇa]—apply.
These [penances] are to be applied accordingly; and for Kṣatriyas and others, when they have intercourse with Kṣatriya women and so forth, the penances are likewise two months and so on.
Furthermore, in the case of unintentional [action]:

Among these [offenses], for members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), the penances prescribed by Yājñavalkya—namely, the gift of eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh (*ṛṣabhaikādaśagodāna*), subsisting on the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month, and the performance of the *prājāpatya* penance for one month—should be understood respectively.
However, in the case of sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman, the very same monthly vow (*māsavrata*) prescribed for intentional [intercourse] should be applied by reducing it by half.
For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"But a Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Śūdra woman should subsist on cow-urine and barley-gruel for one month or even half a month to be freed from that sin. By this,
it is intended that the penance lasts for half a month in the case of unintentional [action].

If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach the wife of another Brāhmaṇa, then for one who has not desisted from such unrighteous acts, the penance is a Kṛcchra; for one who has desisted, it is an Atikṛcchra. This should be understood to apply when the wife is a Śūdra woman, or when she is the wife of a twice-born man who has been adulterous two or three times.
Or [it applies] when one goes unintentionally;
and thus Saṃvarta says:
"Having gone to a Brahmin woman who is not his own kin, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance."
But if it is done intentionally,

one should perform two *kṛcchra* penances for approaching a queen, a female ascetic, a nurse, a virtuous woman, or even a woman of the highest caste, as well as for approaching a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*).
Thus, the two *kṛcchra* penances mentioned by Yama are to be understood.
However, in the case of repeated transgression with a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) or a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*),
one who has spilled his seed (*avakīrṇin*) shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa.
If [the offspring] is from a Vaiśya woman, he should eat only at the fourth mealtime, feed Brāhmaṇas, and give a load of fodder to the cows.
If it is from a Kṣatriya woman, having fasted for three nights, he should offer a vessel of clarified butter.
One should give [a gift]. For one who has violated a Brāhmaṇa woman, having fasted for six nights, he should give a cow; for one who has violated cows, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
For one who has violated an unmarried girl, he should give a load of straw and a *māṣaka* of lead—this is to be understood as stated by Śaṅkha.
And this applies to the case of repeated practice beginning with the fourth [offense].
"In the fourth [case] she is called *svairiṇī*, and in the fifth she is considered a *bandhakī*";
this is understood from another Smṛti.
On this very subject, it is also stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
Having approached an unchaste Brāhmaṇa woman, one should give something to a twice-born man;
if she is a Kṣatriya woman, one should give a bow; but having approached a Vaiśya woman, one should give a garment.

This is omitted by Seltur. The passage in question is likely an interpolation:
(in the case of intercourse in the natural order, [regarding] the fetus...)
If she is excessively defiled but not born of a lower caste (*pratiloma*),

then [the penance] is doubled; however, in the case of approaching a woman of another caste who is defiled by being of a lower caste, or in the case of women of the *antyāvasāyin* class, and as in the case of violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), there is a certain [penalty] regarding the womb of a *caṇḍāla* woman.
A lesser gradation [of penance] should be prescribed:
for sexual intercourse with a Cāṇḍālī woman, the penance lasts for one year;
likewise, if a fetus is conceived, it constitutes the sin of violating the Guru's bed.
This collection of expiations is to be understood as pertaining to cases where conception does not occur.
However, when conception does occur, one should perform double the specific expiation that has been prescribed for that particular case.
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Uśanas: "But whatever vow there may be for intercourse, one should perform that twofold during pregnancy.
Regarding one who causes conception in a Śūdra woman, a specific rule is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"But one born of a *vṛṣalī* shall eat only at night during the fourth meal-time for three years. As for the statement of Manu:
"A Brāhmaṇa who mounts the bed of a Śūdra woman goes to a low state."
"Having fathered a son upon her, he falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 3.17)—
this [verse] is intended solely to proclaim the gravity of the sin;
however, in the case of sexual intercourse in the reverse order (prātilomya), there is always only the death penalty for the man.
"Against the natural order, there shall be death for the man and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the woman"—
from such a statement; as for the statement of Vṛddhapracetas:
For a Śūdra who, out of delusion, approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman and desires purification,
this entire vow must be prescribed, because she is indeed his mother.
For one who approaches women of lower castes by degrees of inferiority, the penance is that prescribed for all castes.

Thus, this extension of the twelve-year penance is to be understood as applying to one who approaches [another man's wife] under the mistaken belief that she is his own wife, because of the inclusion of the qualification "through delusion."
As for the statement of Saṃvarta:
"If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should somehow have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman,
the penance for purification shall be either the Kṛcchra or the Sāntapana."
If a Śūdra, however, should somehow approach a Brāhmaṇa woman, being deluded by lust,
he becomes pure after one month by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (yāvaka).

That [penance] refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman who has completely strayed from her duty. Regarding sexual intercourse with an outcaste woman as well, a penance has been stated by Bṛhatsaṃvarta:
"In the case of washermen, hunters, actors, and those who subsist on bamboo or leather..."
"But having approached these [women], a Brāhmaṇa shall perform two Cāndrāyaṇas.
This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa approaching [these women] intentionally and only once;
however, for Kṣatriyas and others, the penance should be calculated as reduced by one-quarter for each successive class.

On this very point, Āpastamba has stated: "Having had sexual intercourse with a Mlecchī woman, a Naṭī, a leather-worker's wife, a washerwoman, or a Buruḍī woman, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances."

And the outcastes (antyajas) have been shown by that very same [author]: "The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker, the fisherman, the Meda, and the Milla—these seven are indeed remembered as the outcastes. Thus it is said.

As for those such as Cāṇḍālas who are outcasts (antyāvasāyins), a more severe penance for sexual intercourse with their women has been shown in the section on violating the Guru’s bed (gurutalpa). Among these women of the lowest castes, whatever penance is prescribed for intercourse with one applies to all of them.
Because all [of them] are equal;
as Uśanas said: "When that which is stated applies even to one among many things that share a common property..."
"That [penance] shall apply to all of them, for they are recorded as being of one form.
However, regarding unintentional intercourse with Caṇḍālas, Medas, Śvapacas, or those who observe the Kapalavrata:
Having approached women unintentionally, one should perform the Parāka vow.
Thus, that which was stated by Āpastamba is to be observed; and as for the statement of Saṃvarta:
"Of washermen, hunters, actors, and those who subsist on bamboo and leather..."
If a Brahmin should have sexual intercourse with women [of lower castes], he shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Thus, that [rule] also refers to cases where there is no desire involved;
as for what was stated by Śātātapa:
"A fisherwoman, a washerwoman, and one who subsists on bamboo and leather..."
One is purified by a single *kṛcchra* penance performed according to the rules for the *prājāpatya*.
Thus, this refers to the subject of abstention prior to the emission of semen;
as for that which was stated by Uśanas:
"For those who eat the food of Kapālikas, and likewise for those who have sexual intercourse with their women..."
If committed knowingly, it is prescribed as a year of kṛcchra penance; if unknowingly, two lunar penances (aindava).
Thus, that [act] is an object of repeated practice;
however, when a fetus is conceived from approaching a Caṇḍālī or similar women,
then, having caused conception in a Caṇḍālī, one should perform the vow for violating the Guru's bed.

This statement by Uśanas should be understood as referring to the twelve-year penance. As for the verse: "For one who has procreated with a woman of the lowest caste (antyajā), no expiation is prescribed;
he should undoubtedly be banished after having been branded."
This statement of Āpastamba refers to cases of intentional action;
for women as well, in the case of sexual intercourse with a man of the same caste or a lower caste, that which has been prescribed for the man applies.

That very [penance] lasting for three years and so forth applies here, because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "Whatever penance a man must perform for adultery with another's wife, that same penance he shall cause her to observe. (MDh 11.177)
The distinction in penance for a man and a woman of another caste occurs specifically when the intercourse is in the inverse order (*prātilomya*).
As Vasiṣṭha has stated:
"If a Śūdra approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire; as for the Brāhmaṇī..."
"Having caused her head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a donkey and cause her to be led along the high road;
thus she becomes purified—so it is known" (VaDh 21.1).
Likewise, if a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and cast him into the fire.

"Having caused the head of the Brāhmaṇī to be shaved, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a donkey, one should cause her to be led along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known" (VaDh 21.2).
Likewise, if a Rājanya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī, one should wrap the Rājanya in leaves of the Śara grass and cast him into the fire.

"Having caused the head of the Brāhmaṇī to be shaved, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a bull and a donkey, one should cause her to be led along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known" (VaDh 21.3).
In the same way, a Vaiśya [is purified] for adultery with a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śūdra for adultery with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman.

By the statement "he becomes purified," it is shown that the act of wandering through the royal street itself constitutes the form of the punishment, serving as a means of purification independently of any other expiatory rite.
Regarding sexual intercourse with members of the twice-born castes in the reverse order by a Brāhmaṇī woman, Saṃvarta has also stated another penance:
"If a Brāhmaṇī woman should approach a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya against her will,
she is purified after one month of consuming cow-urine and barley-gruel, or after half that time."
But if it is done intentionally, double that [penance] must be performed, according to the scriptural statement: "If done intentionally, it shall be double.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well, it is stated: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman serving a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, she should perform an Atikṛcchra and a Kṛcchrātikṛcchra."
For a Kṣatriya woman who has sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, the penance is half a Kṛcchra, a Prājāpatya, and an Atikṛcchra respectively.
For a Vaiśya woman who has sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya...
A quarter *kṛcchra*, half a *kṛcchra*, and a *prājāpatya* [are the penances].
For a Śūdra woman's service to a Śūdra, the penance is a *prājāpatya*;
for service to a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, [the penances are respectively]...
"One day and night, three nights, or half a *kṛcchra* [are the penances].
However, regarding service to a *śūdra*, a specific rule has been stated by Bṛhat-Pracetas:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman has sexual union with a *śūdra* but does not bear a child from him..."
The expiation prescribed for her is the Kṛcchra penance and three Cāndrāyaṇas.
This should be understood as applying when she is unwilling or when there is a mistake regarding her husband.
For a Brahmin woman’s service to a Vaiśya, two Cāndrāyaṇas and one Kṛcchra are prescribed;
for her union with a Kṣatriya, a Kṛcchra and a Cāndrāyaṇa should be performed.
A Kṣatriya woman, through contact with a Śūdra, shall perform a Kṛcchra penance and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
one who has had sexual union with a Vaiśya shall perform a Cāndrāyaṇa together with a Kṛcchra.

"Having approached a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman shall perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by a Cāndrāyaṇa; in the case of approaching [a man] in the direct order of castes (ānulomya), she should perform a Kṛcchra reduced by one quarter. Regarding a woman who has given birth, a rule is stated in the Viṣṇu-smṛti (Caturviṃśatimata): [text follows].
If a Brahmin embryo is miscarried, the penance shall be a Parāka; for a Kṣatriya, it is likewise an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa).
For a Vaiśya who acts unintentionally, the penance is both an Aindava and a Parāka.
"Abandonment [of the fetus] occurs in the womb of a Śūdra, whereby one is born as a Caṇḍāla;
therefore, in the case of a miscarriage due to defects of the bodily constituents (dhātu), one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

Because of the inclusion of the qualification "unintentionally" (*akāmakārataḥ*), in the case of intentional action (*kāmakāra*), one should instead perform double the Parāka and other such penances. When—
If she gives birth after having remained for ten months while the fetus has not yet emerged, then there is no expiation; for it is said:
"The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by expiation if they have not conceived, but not otherwise. (VaDh 21.12)
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha;

however, when a woman who has already conceived subsequently commits adultery with Śūdras and others, she should perform the penance only after delivery, due to the apprehension that the fetus might be miscarried.
But a woman who is pregnant, having been approached by a lustful man,
shall not perform penance as long as the fetus has not emerged.
Once the child is born, she should thereafter observe the vow of eating only barley-gruel for one month;
there is no defect in the fetus, and he should be consecrated according to the prescribed rite.
This is because of the observation of another Smṛti text. However,
it should be understood that when they do not perform the penance due to arrogance, then there shall be the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the women.
Even regarding sexual intercourse with those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*) and others, an expiation for women is shown in another *Smṛti*:
"When a Brāhmaṇa woman approaches these— a washerman, a hunter, an actor, or one who lives by bamboo or leather— whether intentionally or unintentionally, she must perform three *Aindava* penances."
Likewise, even regarding sexual intercourse with those of the lowest castes such as the Cāṇḍāla, it is said:
"A Brāhmaṇī woman who unintentionally approaches a Cāṇḍāla, a Pulkasa, a Mleccha, a Śvapāka, or one who has fallen from his caste, shall perform four Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
Because of the statement "if unintentionally," it should be understood that the penance is double if done intentionally. Likewise:
"If one should somehow come into contact with a Cāṇḍāla, he should have his hair shaved, including the top-knot, and should eat boiled barley."
One should fast for three nights and dwell for one night in water within a well that is equal in size to oneself, filled with cow-dung, water, and mud.
Having remained there without food for three nights,
she should then cast away [the previous substances] and drink milk mixed with gold after having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper.
Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
and she should dwell outside for as long as she performs that vow.
"Once the penance has been performed, one should then provide a feast for Brahmins;
Svāyambhuva declared that two cows should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of purification.
This [penance] also pertains exclusively to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.

Based on the statement, "If she should somehow go [to them]," even Ṛṣyaśṛṅga has prescribed another penance for sexual intercourse with an outcaste: "She who has become defiled by contact with outcastes should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year."
This [penance] applies when one has approached her once out of desire;
however, when she was already pregnant and subsequently had sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla or similar person, a specific rule for that case has been stated by him [the author].
But a young woman who is pregnant, even if she has had sexual intercourse with one of the lowest castes,
shall not perform penance until the fetus has been brought forth.
She should not frequent the house, nor should she adorn her limbs;
she should not sleep with her husband, nor should she eat together with her kinsmen.
"When the fetus has been lost, one should perform the penance of a Kṛcchra for one year;
or else, one should give gold or a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa.
But when one engages in excessive sexual intercourse intentionally, then:
But if she has engaged in contact with an outcaste— whether in eating or in sexual intercourse—
she is purified by death through entering a blazing fire.
Thus should the statement of Uśanas be understood. However, when one does not perform the prescribed penance, then she should be marked with the sign of a male organ or be put to death.
"Or she who has been enjoyed by one of inferior caste may be subjected to the *sāṅkhya* penance or even put to death," according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara.
(Thus ends the section on adultery.)

Likewise, the determination of the penances for the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (*parivitti*) should be understood to be analogous to those for the younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*).
However, there is this distinction: whereas for the *parivettṛ* the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance applies in a certain case, for the *parivitti* it is the *prājāpatya*.
For the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "The *parivitti*, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may marry again and take that very same woman as his wife."
(Thus ends the section on the elder brother whose younger brother marries first.

Regarding usury and the purchase of salt, however, the penances for general minor sins (*upapātaka*) as stated by Manu and Yājñavalkya should be applied according to considerations of caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth. 3.265.

Immediately after [the section on] the sale of salt, the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya is recited among the minor sins (upapātaka); regarding that, he states another penance as well:
"For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a man should give one thousand cows and one bull."
Or he may perform the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa for three years. A killer of a Vaiśya should perform this same penance for one year, or give one hundred and one cows;
a killer of a Śūdra should perform this for six months, or else give ten cows.
That in which there is one more than a thousand is "one-thousand-plus" (*ekasahasra*); that which completes it is "the one-thousand-plus," namely,
the bull (*ṛṣabha*).
One should give those cows, numbering one thousand with a single bull among them, upon killing a Kṣatriya; or else, one should perform the great penance,
the vow for the slaying of a Brāhmaṇa, for three years.
Furthermore, one who kills a Vaiśya shall perform this vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa for one year,
or he may give one hundred cows and one bull;
however, one who kills a Śūdra shall perform the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa for six months.
He should perform [the penance]; or else, he should give ten cows that have recently calved along with their calves.
This refers to the killing of a Kṣatriya or others by one who is merely a member of the caste and acts unintentionally; for it is said:
"But having unintentionally slain a Rājanya... (MDh 11.128).
Having introduced [the topic] in this manner, because these very penances are prescribed in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra],
the application of giving (*dāna*) and austerity (*tapas*) is determined according to one's capacity. However, in the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who are slightly established in their conduct—
"A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty; and it should be known that a sixteenth part applies to a Śūdra. Thus is the statement of Manu to be understood. (MDh 11.127)
But in the case of a Kṣatriya who abides by his conduct, a penance of four and a half years should be prescribed;
and here, by the word "conduct" (vṛtta), qualities and so forth are meant.
Worship of the guru, compassion, purity, truthfulness, restraint of the senses,
and the promotion of what is beneficial— all that is called proper conduct (vṛtta).
This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu; as for the statement of Vṛddha-Hārīta:
"A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a Kṣatriya, shall observe the vow for six years."
Having killed a Vaiśya, a twice-born man should likewise observe this vow for three years.
Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform penance for one year and give ten cows with a bull as the eleventh.
Thus, that [penance] refers to cases where one acts out of personal desire;
however, regarding the killing of a *śrotriya* Kṣatriya or others,
the vow for a Brahmin-killer is reduced by one-quarter in the case of killing a Kṣatriya.
One should perform half [the penance] for killing a Vaiśya, but a fourth part for a Śūdra.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Vṛddha-Hārīta.
As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a Kṣatriya, shall observe the vow for eight years."
"Six for a Vaiśya, three for a Śūdra" (VaDh 20.31–33);
that too refers to the same subject matter as the rule of Hārīta.
However, if the Kṣatriya is slightly deficient in qualities, that is the only distinction.

But when he is both learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in good conduct (vṛttastha), then the twelve-year penance prescribed by Āpastamba— namely, "having killed one who has studied the Veda" among the first two castes— should be observed.

However, in the case of killing a non-Vedic Kṣatriya or others who have already begun a ritual sacrifice, it should be understood that the rule applies: "One who kills a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall observe the vow prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa" (YDh 3.251).

Furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa kills a Kṣatriya or others who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and engaged in a sacrifice, he shall perform the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for six years and give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh; if he kills a Vaiśya, he shall perform it for three years and give one hundred cows with a bull as the eleventh;
if he kills a Śūdra, he shall perform it for one year.

The combination of giving and austerity mentioned by Gautama in the rule, "And one should give eleven *ṛbhu*-oxen" (GDh 22.14–16), is to be understood as applying to cases where the act was not intentional.
This refers to a situation involving unintentional [transgression].

As before, having killed [a Brahmin] unintentionally among the four castes, one should prescribe penances of twelve, six, three, and one year respectively; at the conclusion of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that, and half of that again, for all of them in due order—so says the Smṛti of Śaṅkha.
And this twelve-year penance is to be understood as applying specifically to a Kṣatriya who is slightly inferior in qualities, while it applies to a Vaiśya and a Śūdra who possess superior qualities.

Since the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya is specifically enumerated among the minor offenses (upapātaka), it does not fall within the scope of the maxim regarding general rules and exceptions; therefore, even those penances that apply generally to minor offenses must be applied here as well.

In that regard, when a Kṣatriya or others of evil conduct are killed intentionally, the penances prescribed by Manu— lasting three months, three years, two months, and the Cāndrāyaṇa— should be applied according to the order of the castes. However, if it is done unintentionally, the penances stated by Yājñavalkya— the gift of eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh accompanied by a three-night fast, subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for a month, and the milk-vow for a month— should be applied respectively.

And this collection of vows previously mentioned is to be understood as applying to the killing of a Kṣatriya or others when committed by a Brāhmaṇa; however, regarding unintentional killing: "But having slain a Rājanya unintentionally, the best of the twice-born... (MDh 11.128).

In the statements of Manu, Gautama, Hārīta, and Vasiṣṭha beginning with "A Brāhmaṇa having killed a Kṣatriya" (VaDh 20.31), because of the mention of the Brāhmaṇa [as the agent], it should be understood that when a Kṣatriya or others are the agents in the killing of a Kṣatriya or others, the penance is reduced by one quarter; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The full [penance] is to be given for a Brāhmaṇa, but one-quarter less is prescribed for a Kṣatriya."
For a Vaiśya, half [of that] is prescribed, while for those of the Śūdra caste, one quarter is recommended.

Thus it is from the Smṛti of Vṛddha-Viṣṇu. As for that which states: "The assembly for Brāhmaṇas is such; for Kṣatriyas, it is considered double; for Vaiśyas, it is declared to be triple; and the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly."
This is the statement of Aṅgiras;
it was stated in the section on cow-slaughter that this refers, in reverse order, to the subjects of verbal and physical cruelty regarding the Mūrdhāvasikta and the other [mixed castes].
This collection of expiations does not apply to killing [them],
because they lack the status of being Kṣatriyas and so forth;
therefore, it applies only according to the punishment.
In the case of killing such a person, the increase or decrease of the previously mentioned collection of penances (*vrata*) should be postulated.

Furthermore, the increase or decrease of the punishment has been shown in the passage: "The infliction of punishment should be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the caste and birth" (3.266–267).
(Thus ends the section on penance for killing Kṣatriyas and others.
He now states the penance for killing a woman:
"But having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly..."
For purification, one should give a water-skin, a bow, a goat, and a sheep in sequence.

Having killed unchaste wives of Brahmins and other castes who have led evil lives, one should give, respectively, for the sake of purification, a *dṛti* (a leather bag for holding water), a *dhanus* (a bow), a *bastam* (a goat), and an *avim* (a sheep).
And this [penance] refers to the unintentional killing of women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes born of the inverse order (prātilomyena); however,
regarding intentional killing, Brahmagarbha says:
"For women born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), a period of one month is prescribed;
for those of intermediate origin (*antaraprabhava*), such as the *sūta* and others, [the periods are] four, two, and six [months] respectively.
Thus, in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇī and so forth, the application is according to the actual facts: six months for a Kṣatriyā, four for a Vaiśyā, and two for a Śūdrā.

But when one kills a woman who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, then something must be given, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "In the case of a Vaiśya woman, nothing [need be paid]. (GDh 22.27).

If she who lives by the work of a Vaiśya— that is, by the occupation of a Vaiśya— is killed, only a small amount should be given as compensation; and that shall be water, a water-pot, or a well, which one should present to a Brāhmaṇa or a Brāhmaṇī.
For the killing of a Kṣatriya woman, a cow is prescribed; for the killing of a Vaiśya woman, a goat is traditionally ordained.
Having killed a sheep, a man should give water as an offering for killing one born of a Śūdra woman, and for killing one born of a Vaiśya woman.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Aṅgiras.

However, when Brāhmaṇas and others who have been violated by Kṣatriyas and others through inverse order (prātilomya) are killed, then the penances for killing a cow (govadha-prāyaścitta) should be applied as appropriate. 3.268.
He states a specific rule regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa woman or others who has committed only slight infidelity:
"Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra" (YDh 3.269ab).
This means when one kills a Brāhmaṇa woman or another of such status who is slightly corrupted—that is, one who has committed only minor infidelity—[then this applies].
Then one should perform the six-month vow for killing a Śūdra,
or alternatively, give ten cows as a gift.

And this six-month penance is to be understood as applying to the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇī woman; however, for the intentional killing of a Kṣatriya woman, it should be observed [as the standard penance].
For the intentional killing of a Vaiśya woman, one should give ten cows.

In the case of intentionally killing a Śūdra, one must consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for one month, as this is the general penance prescribed for minor offenses (upapātaka). However, when one intentionally kills a Brāhmaṇī woman, the penance lasts for twelve months.
As for the unintentional killing of Kṣatriyas and others, [the penances are as follows]:
Three months, one and a half months, or twenty-two and a half days;
as Pracetas said:
"Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who has not reached her menses, one shall perform a Kṛcchra for one year or for six months."
Having killed a Kṣatriya woman, [one must observe penance] for six months or three months; having killed a Vaiśya woman, for three months or one and a half months;
having killed a Śūdra woman, for one and a half months or twenty-two and a half days.
Or [as stated by others]:
"As for what was set forth by Hārīta—that for a Kṣatriya the common period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) is six years, three for a Vaiśya, and one and a half for a Śūdra—and then he said:

'In the case of Brāhmaṇa women, it is as for a Kṣatriya; in the case of a Kṣatriya woman, as for a Vaiśya; in the case of a Vaiśya woman, as for a Śūdra; having killed a Śūdra woman, [one observes penance] for nine months'—that is appropriate."

That [penalty] also should be understood to apply to the intentional killing of women who possess qualities such as being instrumental in the performance of rituals; however, in all cases of unintentional [killing], half [of the penalty] should be prescribed.
Regarding the killing of an Ātreyī woman, that which was stated previously applies.
(Thus ends the section on penance for killing a woman.

Following the context of penances for violence, he now states the penance even for the killing of living beings that constitutes a minor offense (*anupātaka*), which is designated by the term "miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*).
"Having killed a thousand vertebrate creatures,
such as lizards and others for whom no specific expiation has been mentioned,

and having killed a cartload— that is, a full cart— of boneless creatures, such as lice, bedbugs, gadflies, mosquitoes, and so forth, one must perform the vow prescribed for killing a Śūdra. (YDh 3.269cd)
One should observe the ordinary vow of celibacy for six months or give ten cows;
since there is a fixed rule regarding the quantity as "a thousand," a greater amount must be prescribed for killing more than that number.
On the other hand, regarding the killing of individual animals below that level,

he will state that "something" should be given for killing an animal with bones, whereas for one without bones, a breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is required; likewise, the rule "breath for boneless creatures" refers to very small insects.

Regarding the killing of very large insects, such as wood-boring beetles (*ghuṇa*) and the like, after the defiling acts have been enumerated beginning with "Having killed worms, insects, or birds" (MDh 11.71), one should observe the penance stated by Manu: "For those acts that cause defilement, one should subsist on *yāvaka* for three days" (MDh 11.126). // 3.269 //
Furthermore:
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or a bird,
one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
Having killed well-known animals such as cats and the like, or birds such as blue jays, crows, and owls, one should drink milk for three nights or perform a quarter-pāda-kṛcchra penance;
by the use of the word "or," one may also perform such acts as traveling a yojana, as Manu has said: [Manu 11.132].
"Or he may drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana*, or touch the waters of a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the Waters (*ab-daivata-sūkta*). (MDh 11.133).
And this [penance] refers to the case of killing each [of these creatures] individually.

But in the case of killing a group of animals, having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, and a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, and a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. (MDh 11.132)
Thus, that which was stated by Manu should be understood as referring to a six-month penance.
Furthermore, regarding that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a snake, a rat, or a mouse, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and give some small gift."
Regarding the injunction "he should give" (VaDh 21.24), that should be understood as referring to the case of intentional repetition.
A *dahara* is a small mouse or a *chuchundarī* (musk-rat). 3.270.
Furthermore:
For an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for a donkey, a goat, or a sheep, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull]. (YDh 3.271)
When an elephant is killed, five dark-colored bulls must be given;
for a parrot bird, a two-year-old calf;
and for a donkey, a goat, or a sheep [the same applies].
For each of those killed, one bull [is to be given];
for a *krauñca* bird, a three-year-old calf;
the phrase "is to be given" is to be supplied everywhere.
Manu has also stated a specific rule in this regard:
"Having killed a horse, one should give five dark-colored bulls as a gift; having killed an elephant, a goat, a sheep, or an ox, one should give a one-year-old calf. (MDh 11.137) 3.271.
Furthermore:
Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous beast, a water-fowl, a land-peacock, or a vulture, one should give a cow; however, for killing a non-carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
A "kravyāda" is a specific type of wild animal, such as a tiger or a jackal, that eats raw flesh (*kravya*, i.e., uncooked meat); this is understood from its association with the monkey.
Likewise, due to its mention alongside the *haṃsa* and the *śyena*, it also includes specific types of birds, such as the *kaṅka* and the vulture.
By the word "water," water-dwelling creatures such as cranes and the like are included;
by the word "land," land-dwelling creatures such as herons and the like are included.
Śikhaṇḍin is a peacock;
bhāsa is a specific kind of bird;
the remaining terms are well known.
For the killing of each of these, one should give a single cow;
however, having killed non-carnivorous deer such as the *hariṇa* and so forth, or specific birds such as the *khañjarīṭa* and so forth, one should give a heifer. And thus says Manu:
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, a peacock,
a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for a bull, five dark-colored oxen;
for an elephant, a goat and a sheep; and for having killed a donkey, a one-year-old ox.
"But having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow; for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; and having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold. (MDh 11.136–38) 3.272.
Furthermore: For a snake, an iron rod; for a eunuch, tin and lead;
for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; and for a horse, a fine cloth. (YDh 3.273)
When reptiles have been killed, an iron rod with a sharp point should be given as restitution;
when a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) or a neuter person has been killed,
one should give a *māṣa*-weight of tin and lead, or a load of straw.

For it is seen in another Smṛti text: "Having killed a *paṇḍaka*, one should give a load of straw, or tin, or lead. Although Devala states in general terms that "a *paṇḍaka* may be devoid of sexual organs, yet he is not at all fit for sacramental rites," thereby indicating anyone lacking the male or female organ, nevertheless, [the specific form of] a cow or a Brāhmaṇa is not intended here.

Regarding the intention [of the speaker]: since the prohibition against killing cows and Brahmins operates by way of delimitation through the genus (*jāti*), and because the inherence of that genus is no different in a eunuch who lacks sexual organs, it is stated that for him there is a light penance caused precisely by that [genus]. Therefore, [the rule applies] only to wild animals and birds.
They are intended [to be understood] from the mention alongside deer and birds; furthermore,
when a boar or a pig has been killed, a jar of ghee should be given.
A guñjā seed should be given for a camel;
when a horse has been killed, a fine silk garment (*aṃśuka*) should be given.
And so says Manu:
"Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade; for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead. (MDh 11.134) 3.273.
Furthermore:
"If one is unable to give a drona of sesame seeds for each of the tittiri birds, elephants, and so forth, as a gift, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for the purification of each. (YDh 3.274)
When a winged partridge has been killed, one should give a *droṇa* of sesame seeds;
and the word *droṇa* denotes a specific measure of capacity. Eight handfuls make a *kiṃcit*, and eight *kiṃcit*s make a *puṣkala*.
Four *puṣkala*s, moreover, are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas make one droṇa; this is the definition of measurement.
According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),

if one is unable to perform the gift of five blue bulls and so forth due to poverty upon killing the previously mentioned elephants and other animals, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each in order to achieve purification.
And here, the word *kṛcchra* should be understood by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring simply to ascetic practice (*tapas*) that is accomplished through hardship.
And those ascetic practices have been shown by Gautama:
Time consists of a year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, or a day and night.
In the absence of a specific instruction, these periods may be performed optionally, with longer durations for grave offenses and shorter ones for minor offenses.
Regarding the phrase "light [penances]" (GDh 19.17–19):
if the primary meaning of the word *kṛcchra* were taken, then in the case of an elephant or a parrot, there would specifically have to be a *prājāpatya*;
and that is not tenable.

If, however, asceticism were the sole criterion, then even within asceticism, a distinction between heavy and light would be appropriate based on the consideration of the gravity or lightness of the gift;
and thus, for an elephant, there would be a two-month fast of barley-gruel, whereas for a parrot, it would be a simple fast.
In this manner, even in other cases, the penance should be determined in accordance with the gift [received]. // 3.274 //
And what does it say?
"In the case of killing a living being produced from fruit, flower, food, or sap, one should consume ghee" (YDh 3.275ab).

This refers to fruit such as that of the *udumbara* tree, flowers such as those of the *madhūka*, food such as boiled rice or parched grain that has remained for a long time, and sap such as molasses and the like.

Furthermore, for the killing of those beings that are born as living creatures, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) is the means of purification; and this consumption of clarified butter is prescribed specifically for the purpose of eating,
because expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are of the nature of ascetic penance (*tapas*).
And the nature of austerity has been demonstrated under the guise of etymologically explaining the term *prāyaścitta* in the *Āṅgirasa*:
"Prāya" is said to be austerity (*tapas*), and "citta" is called determination (*niścaya*).
That which is joined with the resolve for austerity is called penance (prāyaścitta). Thus it is said.
Since there is an infinity of expiations for each individual living being, and because it would be impossible to state them even by questioning ten million times, he declares a general expiation:

"In the case of killing a vertebrate creature, something small should be given; however, for a boneless creature, a breath-control (prāṇāyāma) [is required]. For the killing of each of the vertebrate creatures such as lizards and others, numbering fewer than a thousand, "something" means a very small amount.
Grain, gold, and so forth are to be given as a gift;
however, for an animal without bones, there is one *prāṇāyāma*.
In that context, "something" refers to when [the gift] is gold.
In that case, only a *paṇa* is to be given, because of the traditional teaching of Sumantu: "Upon killing a creature possessing bones, a *paṇa* shall be paid.
However, when grain is to be given, then eight handfuls (*muṣṭi*) are to be given, because of the traditional teaching: "Eight handfuls shall constitute 'something' (*kiṃcit*)."
And this refers to the killing of animals for which no specific expiation has been mentioned;
however, where a particular expiation is prescribed, that alone shall apply.
As Parāśara has said: "One who kills a swan, a crane, a ruddy goose, a curlew, or a cock,
and having killed a peacock or a ram, becomes pure by eating only one meal [per day]."
Having killed a water-crow, a lapwing, a parrot, a pigeon,
an āḍikā, or a crane, one is indeed purified by eating only at night.
One who kills blue jays, crows, pigeons, sarīs,
or partridges is purified by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water at both twilights.
One who kills vultures, hawks, other birds, or owls,
and eats uncooked food, should remain standing during the day and subsist on air alone for two meal-times.
Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a water-snake,
one should feed Brahmins individually, and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee.
A killer of porcupines, tortoises, iguanas, rabbits,
and hedgehogs is purified in a day and night by eating eggplants and guñjā fruits.
One who kills deer, roe-deer, boars, sheep,
goats, wolves, jackals, bears, and hyenas [is born as a worm].
He should subsist on air for three days and give a prastha of sesame seeds as a gift for killing an elephant, a ram, a horse, a camel, or a gayal.
The expiation for one who kills a donkey, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger is a fast of one day and night, along with immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
"One attains purity after three nights and by feeding Brāhmaṇas. Thus it is said.
In this way, the determination of the scope of other scriptural statements concerning mindfulness should also be understood by taking into account factors such as place and time. (3.275)
(Thus ends the section on expiation for injury.
Regarding the cutting down of trees for the sake of fuel (YDh 3.240),
which was recited in the enumeration of minor offenses (upapātaka), it has been extracted here because it was listed out of order due to the context of injury.
Regarding that, he states the penance:
"For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
for the useless cutting of medicinal herbs, one should subsist on milk and follow after cows for a day. (YDh 3.276)

If one cuts fruit-bearing trees such as the mango or the jackfruit, or shrubs and the like, for any purpose other than a sacrifice or similar rites aimed at unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), one must recite the *gāyatrī* and other Vedic verses (*ṛc*) one hundred times.
However, if one cuts cultivated or wild herbs in vain, [the penance lasts] for a day.
Having followed the cows for the sake of their service throughout the entire day, one should drink their milk at the end, abandoning all other food;
however, there is no fault if it is for the purpose of the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña).
And this should be understood to apply to those things that are useful by way of fruits and the like.
For the cutting of fruit-bearing trees, one hundred *ṛc*s must be recited;
the same applies to shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs—
so states the traditional law of Manu (MDh 11.143).

Even though it serves a visible purpose, there is no fault in its being for the sake of the plow and other implements that are auxiliary to agriculture, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "One should not harm trees that bear fruit and flowers, yet one may cut them down for the purpose of performing cultivation. (VaDh 19.11–12).
However, where there is an increase in punishment due to a particular location, an increase in penance must also be prescribed there.
As it has been said:
"In the case of sacred trees, cremation grounds, boundaries, holy places, and temples..."

"For trees that have grown [wild], the fine is double; and for a tree of renown, likewise. (YDh 2.228) Furthermore, this recitation of a hundred Ṛgvedic verses pertains to the twice-born (dvijāti), and not to Śūdras and others, because they lack the qualification for such recitation.
Therefore, for them, a penance of two nights and so forth should be prescribed according to the severity of the punishment.
Furthermore, in order to avoid the redundancy of its specific mention among the minor offenses (upapātaka), the general penance applicable to all minor offenses also applies here.
And because of its gravity, that [object] is to be considered a subject for repeated practice. (3.276)
In connection with the penance for killing unchaste women, monkeys, and so forth, he now states the penance occasioned by being bitten by them:

"Having been bitten by an unchaste woman, a monkey, or a donkey, or by a dog, a camel, or a crow, one becomes pure by performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in water and consuming clarified butter. (YDh 3.277)
Prostitutes and the like are well known; a man bitten by these, having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water and having consumed clarified butter (ghṛta), becomes purified.
By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (ādi), jackals and other such animals are included.
As Manu has said:
"One bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals, as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma). (MDh 11.200)
And this consumption of ghee should be understood as a substitute for a meal,
because expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), being of the nature of austerity (tapas), are intended to cause emaciation of the body;
this [prescription] applies to one who is incapable [of the standard penance].

Regarding the statement of Sumantu— that for those bitten by a dog, jackal, deer, buffalo, goat, sheep, donkey, camel, mongoose, cat, mouse, water-fowl, crane, crow, or human, there shall be bathing with the hymns beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma)—
that refers to cases where the bite is merely slight and occurs below the navel.
As for the statement of Aṅgiras:
"A student (brahmacārī) bitten by a dog should drink milk in the evening for three days;
if he is a householder (gṛhastha), then for two nights; but one who maintains the sacred fires (agnihotrin) [should do so] for one day."
For one bitten above the navel, that same [penance] shall be doubled;
it shall be tripled for the mouth, but quadruple for the head.
Thus, that [penance] has as its object one who possesses right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
However, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, it should be calculated as reduced by one-quarter [of the full amount] respectively. But for a Śūdra, however—
For Śūdras, purification is achieved either by fasting or by giving a gift;
for the sake of complete purity, one should give a cow or a single bull to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus should the statement of Bṛhad-Aṅgiras be understood.
As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha:
"A Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean..."
"Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and consumed clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one becomes purified"—this [rule] refers to the case of a bite on the head. As for women, however:
"A Brāhmaṇī woman who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf..."
Upon seeing a planet or a lunar mansion that has risen, one becomes immediately pure.
Thus should the statement of Parāśara be understood.
Furthermore, a specific rule for a woman observing vows such as the Kṛcchra has been shown by that same author:
"A woman of virtuous vows who is bitten by a dog should fast for three nights."
"Having eaten barley-gruel with ghee, one should complete the remainder of the vow. A specific rule regarding a woman in her menses has also been shown by Pulastya:
"When a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey..."
By fasting for five nights, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
"But above the navel it is double; at the mouth it is likewise triple;
it is recorded as fourfold at the head. If bitten elsewhere, there shall be immersion.
"Elsewhere" refers to a state other than that of menstruation.
However, regarding one who is defiled by dogs and the like through smelling and so forth, a specific rule has been stated by Śātātapa:
"For one who has been smelled by a dog, or scratched with its claws,
purification consists of washing with water and heating with fire."
Scorching is [the penance of] heating.
However, when worms arise in a wound produced by the bite of a dog or the like, or by a blow from a weapon and so forth, then a specific rule has been stated by Manu:
If a worm should arise from the opening of a wound in a Brāhmaṇa where pus and blood have formed,
what expiation shall there be for him?
One should perform ablutions three times a day with the urine and dung of cows;
by consuming the five products of the cow for three nights, one who has defiled himself below the navel is purified.
And a worm shall arise in a wound produced between the navel and the throat;
it is traditionally taught that one should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for six nights or three days.
In that regard, regarding a wound from the bite of a dog or similar animal, this [penance] must be performed after the specific expiation for that particular bite has been completed.

In the case of a wound produced by weapons and the like, however, this same rule of consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth for three days applies; this is the remainder [of the rule].
But in the case of Kṣatriyas and the other castes, there is a reduction of one-quarter for each successive class.
It is to be inferred. // 3.277 //

In connection with the expiation for biting that causes the severance of the bodily skin-element (*tvag-dhātu*), he states the expiation for emission that causes the severance of the final bodily element (*carama-dhātu*):
"One should consecrate the emitted semen with these two [verses], *yan me 'dya retaḥ*..."
One should touch the space between the breasts and the middle of the eyebrows with that ring finger.

If, somehow even without sexual intercourse with a woman, the final element (semen) is emitted, then one should recite over that spilled semen: "That semen of mine which today has been spilled upon the earth... (Yajurveda 12.104).
One should consecrate [the semen] with these two mantras: "May my virility return to me" (TaitĀ 1.30.1).
With that consecrated semen, [one should apply it] to the breasts and the eyebrows.
And one should touch the middle [of the penis] with the ring finger (*upakaṇiṣṭhikā*).

Others, however, explain that because spilled semen is impure and thus unfit for the act of touching, the word "by it" (*tena*)— due to its association with the ring finger— refers by implication to the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) which is present in one's own mind.
The claim that "it" (tena) was specified [as the referent] because using the expression "the thumb and the ring finger" (aṅguṣṭhapada) would result in a metrical fault is incorrect,
because the thumb is not present in the mind [at that point].

Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with a meaning that exists only in the mind, by abandoning what is directly expressed by the word. As it has been said:
"And no qualification of a meaning that is merely being understood is ever seen, whether by other words or by case-endings, as in the case of saying 'this smoke is burning. (PV 3.259)
Nor is semen unfit for touch due to its impurity;
for it is understood from the injunction itself that it is fit for touch when intended for the purpose of expiation, just as liquor is fit for drinking when it takes the form of an expiatory rite.
And this expiation applies specifically to a householder who has unintentionally emitted [semen],
since more severe expiations are prescribed for a student (brahmacārin) in both the states of dreaming and waking.
As for that statement of Yama—
which the NSP reads as a statement of Manu:
"If a householder should intentionally cause the emission of semen upon the ground..."
One should recite the thousand [names] of the goddesses together with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Thus, that refers to the case of acting according to one's own will. (3.278)
Furthermore:
"When one sees one's own reflection in water, thinking 'there is fire in me,' one should mutter the Sāvitrī;
likewise when seeing something impure, or when acting with fickleness, or even when speaking an untruth. (YDh 3.279)
If one sees one's own reflection in water, then one should mutter this mantra: "The light-sense (teja-indriya) is in me.
Furthermore, upon seeing an impure substance, one should mutter the Sāvitrī verse dedicated to the deity Savitṛ, beginning with "tat savituḥ.
Likewise, in the event of engaging in restlessness of speech, hands, feet, and so forth, one should mutter that same verse.
And regarding false speech:
this should be understood as applying when done intentionally;
however, in the case of unintentional action, [the following applies].

One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), as prescribed by Manu: "Having slept, having eaten, having sneezed, having spat, having spoken untruths, and after drinking water—even if one is already pure—one who intends to study should sip water. (MDh 5.145). This is the manner of ācamana to be observed.
As for the statement of Saṃvarta:
"Upon sneezing, spitting, or when something is stuck between the teeth, as well as upon speaking an untruth or conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear."
Thus, this [penance] should be understood as applying when there is little purpose served or an absence of water.

Following the mention of the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, "living by reprehensible means" is recited; in that case, the penances for minor offenses (upapātaka) proclaimed by Manu and Yājñavalkya are to be understood in consideration of caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth.
Even in the case of atheism (nāstikya),
those same penances (prāyaścitta) are to be applied in the very same manner;
and by the word "atheism," the reviling of the Vedas is intended.
By that, it is called "living.
Regarding both of these cases, Vasiṣṭha has also stated another penance:
"An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should desist from atheism; but one who follows the conduct of an atheist [should perform] the *atikṛcchra*" (VaDh 21.29–30).
And this refers to the case of performing [the act] once;

whereas the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) refer to cases of repeated practice. Furthermore, as stated by Śaṅkha: "An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who brings false accusations—these [five], for five years..."
"They should go for alms at the houses of Brahmins," as it is said;

and that which was stated by Hārīta, beginning with "an atheist or one who follows the lifestyle of an atheist," [and continuing] that "they should perform the penance of the five fires, staying in the open air, and lying in water during the summer, the rainy season, and the winter respectively."
Both of these, moreover, concern objects of long-term cultivation through adherence to extremes. (3.279)
It was stated [previously] that "the violation of a vow follows immediately after atheism" (YDh 3.236).
Since the term *avakīrṇin* is not well-known there, he states the penance preceded by a definition of its characteristics:
"An *avakīrṇin* is a religious student (*brahmacārī*) who, having gone to a woman, has spilled his seed."
Having sacrificed an ass as an animal dedicated to Nirṛti, he becomes purified.
A religious student—whether a *upakurvāṇaka* or a *naiṣṭhika*—who approaches a woman becomes an *avakīrṇin*;
[this refers to] the emission of the final constituent.
*Visarga* means emission; he who has that is an *avakīrṇin*.
He [should perform] a sacrifice with a donkey as the victim, dedicated to the deity Nirṛti.
[The rite] becomes purified by performing [this].

Although the donkey's status as an animal (*paśu*) is already established, the word "animal" is mentioned again for the purpose of extending the ritual rules for animals prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Āśvalāyana and others, such as [the rule]: "Now follows the procedure for the animal sacrifice" (*atha paśukalpaḥ*).
And this should be performed in the forest at a crossroads in the common fire;
for if a student violates his vow with a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas in the forest at a crossroads in the common fire. (VaDh 23.1)
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha.
Likewise, at night, one who has violated his vow of celibacy (avakīrṇin) should perform the sacrifice with a one-eyed donkey at a crossroads;
so too says Manu:
"But the avakīrṇin [should sacrifice] with a one-eyed donkey at a crossroads."
"One should sacrifice to Nirṛti at night according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*. (MDh 11.119).
In the absence of an animal, one should sacrifice with an oblation (*caru*); or one should offer an oblation to Nirṛti.
One should offer oblations for him with the words: "To Desire, svāhā! To the one who desires desire, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā!
To the deities of the Rākṣasas, svāhā!"—according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha.
And this [penance] refers to one who is incapable;

however, for one who is capable, having committed the *avakīrṇin* offense with a donkey, he should sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads. Having put on its skin with the hair turned upward and carrying a red vessel, he should beg for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his deed.
The animal sacrifice or the *caru* oblation mentioned by Gautama in the rule, "He is purified in a year" (GDh 23.18–19), should be understood as being conjoined with the year-long austerity;
likewise, there is bathing at the three sessions of the day and eating only once a day.
And this should be observed:
when this offense has been committed, having put on the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his own deed.
"Subsisting on alms obtained from them, eating only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year"— so states the traditional law of Manu.

And this [penance] lasting for the rainy season is to be understood as applying to the case of discharging semen in a Vaiśya woman who is the wife of a non-Vedic (aśrotriya) Brāhmaṇa, and also in the case of the wife of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
However, when one discharges semen in a virtuous Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya woman who is the wife of a Vedic scholar, then—
The penances of three years and two years should be understood respectively.
As Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "One who has emitted semen in a guarded Vaiśya woman should perform the rite for one year, bathing at the three sessions of the day;
but for a Kṣatriya woman, for two [years]."

"In the case of a Brahmin woman, [the penance lasts] for three years. As for the statement of Aṅgiras: "On account of having spilled his seed, however, one should perform the vow prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa."
But one who wears rags for six months shall likewise be freed from sin.
Thus, this [penance] refers to a case of unintentional [intercourse] with a woman who has committed a minor transgression, or it pertains to the annual [observance] for a Mānava.

However, in the case of women who have completely strayed—such as a wanton woman (svairiṇī) or a Śūdra woman—one who has spilled his seed should bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa; in the case of a Vaiśya woman, having fasted for three nights, he should give a vessel of clarified butter.
Having had sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should fast for six nights and give a cow as a gift.
One who has discharged semen among cows should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
One who has discharged semen into a eunuch should carry a load of straw and [give] a māṣaka of lead.
"One should give [the gift]"—this is to be understood as stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita.
Furthermore, this expiation for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) is the same for a student (*brahmacārin*) belonging to any of the three twice-born classes; for it is said:
"A twice-born man who has broken his vow, whether he be a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya, [must perform the penance] with a donkey."
Having performed the sacrifice and always subsisting on alms, those who are composed become pure after one year.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Śāṇḍilya:
"When one intentionally emits the final element (semen) without sexual intercourse with a woman, whether during the day or in a dream,"
In that case, only the sacrifice to Nirṛti is to be observed,
because Vasiṣṭha has extended the application of the sacrifice alone to the cases of intentional emission of semen and sleeping during the day (VaDh 23.4).
If emission occurs during other vows—such as the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and others—in which celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has been extended by rule, this same sacrifice alone is required;
and it is the same regarding other vows. (VaDh 23.4)
Because this has been thus extended by that very [author],
however, in the case of emission during sleep, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:
"A twice-born student who, having emitted semen in sleep unintentionally..."
"Having bathed and worshipped the Sun, one should then mutter three times the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with 'mām'. (MDh 2.181).

For forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others, this same vow for a *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his celibacy) becomes increased by three *kṛcchra* penances in the event of a deliberate emission; for both the forest-dweller and the ascetic (*yati*), when such an emission occurs intentionally.
One should perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) conjoined with three *parāka* penances.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Śāṇḍilya:
when one has fallen from renunciation by taking up the life of a householder, then that which was stated by Saṃvarta should be observed:
"If some evil-minded person, having renounced, should return to the worldly state..."
"He should perform the *kṛcchra* penance without weariness for six months immediately thereafter.
Here, "restoration" (*pratyāpatti*) means the resumption of the householder's life.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"But he who, having become a renunciant, should again indulge in sexual intercourse,
is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Thus says Parāśara.
If a Brahmin who has fallen from his status, one who has turned back from the life of renunciation, or one who has desisted from fasting unto death, desires to enter the householder's state again;
"He shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances;
consecrated by all the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), he shall attain purity.
In that regard, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is a six-month *kṛcchra* penance and again the sacrament of re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃnyāsa*).
The settled rule is that for a Kṣatriya there are three Cāndrāyaṇas, and for a Vaiśya three Kṛcchras;
or alternatively, this applies to a Brāhmaṇa alone, depending on his capacity and whether the act was committed once or repeatedly.
The three types of penance should be understood as established [in this manner].
NSP and Pāṇḍeya add here a passage within parentheses: "(But that woman who, out of delusion, has fallen from the funeral pyre...)"
In some cases, however, one is purified by the Prājāpatya penance from that very same wrongful act.

It has been stated that in some cases [the practice occurs], because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba regarding following the husband when she has fallen from the funeral pyre (*citibhraṣṭā*). Likewise, Yama has also prescribed an expiation for those who renounce the world through death (*maraṇasaṃnyāsinaḥ*).

Those who have perished by water or fire, by hanging, or by falling; those who have died after entering the homeless life, through fasting, or by leaping from a precipice; and those who have died by poison, by falling, or by the stroke of a weapon.
"These nine, having fallen away and being excluded from all society,
are purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
This pair of expiations— the Cāndrāyaṇa and the two Taptakṛcchras— is established according to one's capacity and other such factors.

This is what must be understood. However, when the reading is *śastraghātahatāś ca* ("and those killed by the stroke of a weapon"), then this instruction for their sons and others should be seen as applying to one who has died through an unscriptural means such as suicide.

As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One who attempts suicide while still alive shall perform a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance and fast for three nights" (VaDh 23.19), that too should be understood as referring specifically to one who has resolved upon an unscriptural death but somehow remains alive, depending on his capacity.
Alternatively, the rule is that for one merely intent upon [the act], it is three nights, while for one wounded by a weapon or the like, it is twelve nights.
Furthermore, this penance for an *avakīrṇin* applies to the case of approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyā*) other than the wife of a guru or those equal to her;
for in those cases, there is a more severe penance.
Because it has already been demonstrated [that this is not the case],

and it is not appropriate that the minor penance for an *avakīrṇin* (a student who has broken his vow of celibacy) should suffice to remove the taint of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) such as that which must be expiated by a twelve-year penance; nor is it logical to maintain that the prescription of a light penance is conditioned solely by the fact that he was a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Because it has been shown in the section on the killing of a Brahmin that there is a doubling and so forth of the penance for each successive stage of life (*āśrama*),
and because no penance for approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*) is prescribed here.
It must be treated as distinct,
because for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), the failure of celibacy with respect to a woman is necessarily concomitant with approaching one who should not be approached (*agamyāgamanena*);
therefore, in any other case as well, whenever a certain cause is necessarily accompanied by another cause that is either equal or lesser, that [other cause] is distinct.
He prescribes specific penances for specific occasions:
"For threatening, one should perform the *kṛcchra*;
for striking, the *atikṛcchra*; for drawing blood, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and for internal injury [without external blood], the *kṛcchra*" (MDh 11.209).

Thus, in this case, regarding the occasion of causing bloodshed, the two causes characterized by threatening and striking do not necessarily bring about their respective effects—the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances—because they are not inevitable;
the same should be inferred in other cases as well. Where...

Furthermore, there is no fixed rule for the inclusion of the *nimittas* (causes/conditions) therein; rather, the *naimittikas* (consequent rites) are applied separately according to the specific *nimittas*. For example:
when one approaches another's wife on her menstrual period, being anointed with oil, during the day, or in water.

Now, it might be argued that for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), the lapse of celibacy with respect to a woman does not necessarily entail the offense of approaching a forbidden woman (*agamyāgamanāntarīyakatva*), because there is no fault of approaching a forbidden woman when one approaches a daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*).
