For instance, she was not a maiden, because her virginity was intact;
nor was she another's wife, because she had never been given away in marriage.
Nor can she be a courtesan, because that is not her occupation; nor can she be a widow, because there has been no death of a husband.
Therefore, [she must be] a putrikā.
Because it is not included anywhere else, it is not prohibited; therefore, for one who has transgressed only in that specific case, the vow of the *avakīrṇin* alone [is required].
However, for one who has transgressed elsewhere, because of the concurrence of other causes (*nimitta*), both the vow of the *avakīrṇin* and another occasional rite (*naimittika*) must be performed.
That is incorrect, because a daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) is included among the wives of others;

for even in the absence of a formal gift (*pradāna*), she is consecrated by the sacrament of marriage (*vivāhasaṃskāra*), just like one wedded through the *gāndharva* and other forms of marriage. Nor is it the case that...
Because of the prohibition: "A wise man should not marry her whose brother does not exist or whose father is unknown, for fear of the practice of *putrikā*," (MDh 3.11).
It should be stated that the status of wife does not arise with respect to those of the same lineage (*sagotrā*),
because the prohibition has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), just like the prohibition against marrying women who are physically deformed or have missing limbs.
And its purpose is seen to be for the sake of dharma, because of the mention of the reason [for marriage] as being out of fear regarding the duty toward a daughter.
Furthermore, marriage is not solely for the sake of obtaining a son,
but also for the sake of dharma.
Therefore, for one who has fathered a son but whose wife has died, what contradiction is there in marrying a *putrikā* for the sake of dharma?
This has already been explained at length above.
Thus, enough of this excessive elaboration.

Therefore, since for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) the failure of celibacy with a woman is invariably connected with approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyāgamanānantarīyakatva*), it is well said that a separate penance based on that specific occasion need not be applied. (3.280)
In connection with the penance for a religious student (brahmacārin), he states another penance for a minor offense (anupātaka):

"But having neglected the practice of begging alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill, one who has emitted semen through lust should offer two oblations with these two [verses] beginning with 'kāmāvakīrṇaḥ'. (YDh 3.281)

Then he should perform the ritual attendance with the mantra: "May they sprinkle me with this. However, that student who, while not being ill, continuously neglects begging for alms or the fire-ritual for seven nights, being one who has violated his vow through lust, should say: "I am one who has spilled [the seed], I have spilled it; svāhā to the one who desires lust! (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.282ab).
Having offered two oblations with these two mantras: "I have fallen into desire; I have fallen into desire; svāhā to the one who desires desire," [he continues]:
"May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me."
He should worship the fire with this mantra: "May this Agni sprinkle me with glory and with the splendor of sacred knowledge."
And this [exemption] is to be understood as applying when one fails to perform [the duties] due to being preoccupied with more weighty tasks, such as service to the guru;
however, when one is not so preoccupied and yet neglects both the begging for alms and the fire-ritual, then—
"Having failed to go out for alms and having failed to kindle the sacred fire,
one who is not ill shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights"— this is the rule of Manu that should be observed.
Regarding the destruction of the *yajñopavīta*, however, Hārīta has stated the following expiation:

having offered four oblations of clarified butter with the verses beginning "manovrata-patībhiḥ," one should resume one's duties as before; [this applies also] upon eating improper alms-food, at sunrise or sunset, after vomiting, during daytime sleep, upon seeing a naked woman, upon sleeping naked, or after treading upon a cremation ground.

Having mounted horses and other such animals, if one has transgressed against those worthy of worship, one should offer oblations with these very same [verses]. For the kindling of the fire, for the killing of stationary beings, reptiles, and the like, one should offer clarified butter with the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses beginning "Whatever offense against the gods... For the acceptance of jewels, garments, cows, and so forth, [one should likewise offer].

"One should recite the Sāvitrī eight thousand times. By "with those [verses] characterized by *manas* and *vrata*" is meant: with those verses containing the characteristic mark of *manas*, such as *mano jyotiḥ*, etc., and those containing the characteristic mark of *vrata*, such as *tvam agne vratapā asi*, etc. "One should understand according to the actual meaning" means [one should perform it] with the mantras according to the procedure stated for the initiation (*upanayana*).
The meaning is that one should take [it].
However, regarding the performance of eating and other acts without the *yajñopavīta*, [the text says]:
"If one eats or voids urine or excrement without the *brahmasūtra*..."
One is purified by eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī mantra accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus it should be understood as stated by Marīci. 3.281.
Furthermore:
"In the case of eating honey or meat, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance and the remaining vows.
Having acted in opposition to the Guru, one becomes pure only after propitiating him. (YDh 3.282cd–283ab)
If a student (brahmacārin) unintentionally consumes honey or meat, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance;

immediately thereafter, he should complete the remaining vows. This refers specifically to the consumption of the meat of animals such as the hare and others that are fit to be eaten by the learned (śiṣṭas).
For the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "If a religious student should eat meat, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then complete the remainder of his vow" (VaDh 23.11).
The mention of "twelve nights," however, is intended to include even the *atikṛcchra*, *parāka*, and other penances, with respect to intentional and habitual practice.
But when one is overcome by a disease that can only be cured by meat, then meat may be eaten after making it the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) of the teacher;
for if he is ill, he may at will eat all the leavings of the teacher for the sake of medicine (VaDh 23.9).
Because it has been stated by that very [author]:
"The inclusion of the word 'all' is for the purpose of encompassing all things unfit to be eaten, such as meat, garlic, and so forth;
and by eating those, one's disease is removed."
He should worship the sun.
And thus Baudhāyana says:
"But when one who desires to treat [a patient] becomes free from disease, then, having risen, he should worship the sun with the verse, 'The swan dwelling in purity' (BDh 2.1.28)."

There is no fault even in the consumption of honey when it occurs through ignorance, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "In the Vājasaneyaka, honey that comes unintentionally is not considered defiled" (VaDh 23.13).
The expiation for consuming food during the period of impurity caused by birth or death will be discussed in the section on expiations for eating forbidden food.
One who acts contrary to the teacher’s wishes through disobedience and the like becomes purified by propitiating the teacher with prostrations at his feet and other such means. (3.282)
In connection with the penances for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), the author now states the penance for a teacher (*guru*) as well:
"If one sent by the teacher dies, the teacher should perform three *kṛcchra* penances" (YDh 3.283cd).
This refers to a case where the teacher, having been dispatched to a region disturbed by dangers such as thieves, snakes, or tigers, at the time of midnight when it is shrouded in dense darkness...
If he urges a disciple for the sake of a ritual task, and that disciple dies by chance after being urged by the teacher,
then that teacher [must perform] the *kṛcchra* penances.
One should perform three [penances] beginning with the Prājāpatya;
however, it is not three separate Prājāpatyas, for if that were the case, they would reside separately.
The number would be untenable;
nor is it correct to argue that the number depends on repetition— as in the case of "he performs eleven *prayāja* offerings"—
since when the distinctness of the individual entities themselves is possible, there is no need for dependence on repetition.
Because it would be illogical;
for if this number were associated with what has already arisen, then perhaps there might be some dependence on repetition. However, this [number] pertains to the process of arising.

Therefore, as in the case of the injunction "he offers three oblations of clarified butter," it is logical that the number three is constituted solely with respect to the distinctness of their own forms. (3.283)
He states an exception to the general penance for all acts of violence:

"But when a Brahmin dies while being assisted, there is no sin; likewise in the case of bulls during the ripening of crops, or in the administration of medicine or fire-rituals. (YDh 3.284ab) [And also in the case of bulls during the ripening of crops, or in the administration of medicine or fire-rituals.]

If a Brahmin or anyone else, toward whom assistance has been rendered through medical treatment and the provision of medicine, wholesome food, and so forth, in accordance with the instructions of Āyurveda, should by some chance die due to fate, no sin whatsoever accrues [to the helper].
The mention of the "Brahmin" is [intended to be] illustrative.
This is for the purpose of indicating all living beings whatsoever. For this very reason, it is said:
"If death should occur despite an effort made for the purpose of restraining [an animal], for treating a cow's disease, or for dislodging a hidden fetus, one is not stained by sin."
Thus it was stated by Saṃvarta and others;
and this has already been explained in detail previously.
With the intention of explaining the expiation for one who makes a false accusation, [the author] first states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) relevant to that purpose:
"The fault of one who makes a false accusation is twice as great as that of one who speaks the truth;
furthermore, by speaking falsely, he takes upon himself the guilt of the person falsely accused. (YDh 3.284cd)

But he whose internal organ is defiled by anger born of envy toward the excellence of another, and who falsely imputes a charge such as the killing of a Brahmin against that person in the presence of the public, saying "this man has committed [such a deed]," for him that very sin becomes doubled.
However, he who [imputes] a fault that actually exists but is unknown to the world...
If one proclaims it in the presence of people,
that person also incurs a fault equal to that of the sinner;
and thus says Āpastamba:

"Having recognized the fault, one who was previously [acquainted with the sinner] shall not proclaim it to others regarding one who has fallen; rather, he should avoid him in religious duties" (ĀpDh 1.21.20). Not only does the false accuser incur double the fault, but he also incurs whatever other collection of evils belongs to the one falsely accused.
The statement "he takes that up as well" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) to be mentioned later;
it is not intended here to establish a doubling of the sin or similar consequences.

Because the cause is minor, because a light penance is about to be prescribed, and because it would otherwise entail the fallacy of the destruction of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done. (3.284)
Regarding this, he states the expiation:
"He who falsely accuses another of a great sin (mahāpātaka) or a minor sin (upapātaka) shall subsist on water for one month, reciting [the sacred texts] with his senses restrained. (YDh 3.285)

But he who falsely accuses another of a great sin such as the killing of a Brahmin, or of a minor sin such as the killing of a cow, shall for one month subsist on water, remain devoted to recitation (*japa*), and keep his senses under control;
and the recitation to be performed should be that of the *Śuddhavatī* verses.

For it is recorded in the tradition of Vasiṣṭha: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste or a minor offense, one should subsist on water for a month and recite the Śuddhavatī verses, or go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice" (VaDh 23.39–40).

The mention of "great sins" (mahāpātaka) and "minor sins" (upapātaka) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for others as well, such as the "most heinous crimes" (*atipātaka*) and so forth. And this should be understood to apply specifically when a Brāhmaṇa has been falsely accused by another Brāhmaṇa;
however, when a Brāhmaṇa [accuses] a Kṣatriya or the like...
If a Kṣatriya or others bring a false accusation against a Brāhmaṇa, then, in cases of insults involving the inverse order of castes, the fine shall be double or triple.
"Accordingly, for the castes in the direct order [of precedence], there is a reduction by half and half again.
(YDh 2.207). Following this principle regarding punishment, the increase or decrease of the penance should be determined.
However, for one who falsely accuses another of a grave offense, it should be determined in accordance with the explanatory passage (arthavāda) previously cited.
And that [penance] should be determined according to the severity of the punishment;

likewise, for one who falsely accuses another of an *atipātaka* (extremely grave sin), this very vow is reduced by one-quarter, while for one who falsely accuses another of a *pātaka* (grave sin), it is reduced by one-half.
"But for one who accuses [another] of a minor offense (upapātaka), [the penance is] one quarter;
for killing a Kṣatriya, a fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed" (MDh 11.126).
Since this shows that for killing a Kṣatriya or others—which constitutes a minor offense—the penance is a fourth part of that for a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), so it is likewise [in other cases].
Even for those who accuse others of miscellaneous offenses, a lesser penance than that for minor sins (*upapātaka*) should be prescribed;
for it is stated in the Smṛti: "One should determine the penance after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin" (MDh 11.210).

As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita as a heavy penance—"An atheist, an ungrateful person, one who engages in fraudulent transactions, one who destroys the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas, and one who brings false accusations—these six should subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for six years; they should eat only washed alms-food for one year, or they should follow cows for six months"— ... [the text continues] ... [this is the heavy penance].
This should be applied according to the degree of proficiency in that practice. // 3.285 //
In connection with the penance for one who falsely accuses another, the author states the penance for the one who has been falsely accused:
"One who is falsely accused shall perform a Kṛcchra penance, or specifically an Āgneya penance;
alternatively, he may offer a Puroḍāśa cake to Vāyu, or even a sacrificial animal to Vāyu. (YDh 3.286)
Furthermore, he who has been falsely accused shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance,
or he shall sacrifice with a *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni, or he shall sacrifice with a *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Vāyu.

Or [one may perform penance] with an animal dedicated to Vāyu; the application of these alternatives is determined by one's capacity and circumstances. As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"By this very [penance], the accused is explained" (VaDh 24.37)—[it refers to the same].
Thus, this [penalty] should be understood to apply to one who has been accused but has not yet performed penance for a short time;
for it is observed that there is an increase in punishment, as stated: "For a wicked person who has been accused for a year, the fine is double" (MDh 8.373).

As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi—"One who is falsely accused shall perform a Kṛcchra penance for one month, and for two months in the case of mortal sins (pātaka) or great mortal sins (mahāpātaka)"—that also refers to the same subject matter as the rule of Vasiṣṭha.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Baudhāyana—"For one who accuses another of a mortal sin, a Kṛcchra is prescribed; for the one accused, half of that."
That [penance] refers to the case of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and so forth, or to the case of one who is incapable [of performing the full penance].
In this same way, the determination of other various high and low penances intended for those accused of crimes should be understood as depending on factors such as time and capability.
As Manu has said:
"Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
and daily *Śākala* oblations— these are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals" (MDh 11.201).
Among those excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkta*), persons such as the falsely accused (*abhiśasta*) are enumerated.

Even though no actual performance of a prohibited act is observed in the case of the falsely accused here, nevertheless, it is based on the *apūrva* (unseen merit/demerit) resulting from the performance of a prohibited act in a previous birth, as inferred from the mark of being falsely accused.
This expiation is like that for those bitten by worms; thus, there is no contradiction. (3.286)
Furthermore:
"One who approaches the wife of his brother without being appointed shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance" (YDh 3.287ab).
He who, without a formal appointment (niyoga), approaches the wife of either his elder or younger brother, must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa.
He shall perform penance; and this should be understood to apply to a single instance committed unintentionally.

As for the statement of Śaṅkha—"The elder brother who has married before his younger brother and the younger brother who marries before his elder, as well as he who approaches the wife of an elder brother without authorization, and likewise he who approaches the wife of a younger brother—these two shall subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for one year"—that refers to a case of intentional action.
Furthermore, it says:
"Having consumed clarified butter at the end of three nights, one who has approached a woman in her courses is purified" (YDh 3.287cd).
Moreover, he who approaches a woman in her courses—even his own wife—is purified by fasting for three nights and consuming clarified butter at the conclusion.
One becomes pure by consuming [the substance].
This refers to the case of approaching her once unintentionally.
In that same context, regarding repeated intercourse with a woman in her menses, one should observe what was stated by Śātātapa: "for seven nights."
Even in the case of approaching [these women] once out of desire, this same penance applies.
As for that which was stated by Bṛhatsaṃvarta:
"He who approaches a woman during her menses, or one who is pregnant, or likewise one who is fallen (patita)..."
For the sake of purifying that sin, the *atikṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.

Thus, that refers to the case of intentional repetition; whereas as for what was stated by Śaṅkha regarding a three-year penance— "But a quarter [penance] is for killing a Śūdra, and likewise for approaching a woman in her courses"— it refers to a different context.
Thus, this refers to a case of intentional practice that is absolutely uninterrupted;
however, regarding the touch of a menstruating woman by one who is also menstruating, the penance prescribed in another Smṛti should be observed.
And likewise, Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha says:
"If two women who have reached their menses touch each other while having the same husband,
they are both purified immediately by bathing, whether it was intentional or unintentional."
However, for two women of the same caste who have no husband, there is merely bathing if it occurs unintentionally.
But if a woman in her courses should be touched by another woman in her courses who is of the same caste,
she attains purification without doubt by bathing on that very same day.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Mārkaṇḍeya. As for the statement of Kaśyapa:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman who is menstruating is touched by another Brāhmaṇa woman..."
Having fasted for one night, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus, that refers to the case of intentional action.
However, regarding the touch of a woman of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha has shown a specific rule:
"If a Brāhmaṇī woman and a Śūdra-born woman, both in their menses, should touch one another..."
A Śūdra woman from a previous birth is purified through austerities; she is purified by giving gifts.
"By means of a gift" means she is purified by giving a gift equal to one-fourth of a *niṣka*, which serves as a substitute for a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance.

Regarding the rule: "If two women—one a Brāhmaṇī and the other born of a Vaiśya—touch each other while in their menses, the former shall perform a three-quarter *kṛcchra*, and the latter likewise a quarter-*kṛcchra*."
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance, and the latter by half of that.
If two women— one a Kṣatriya and the other born of a Śūdra— touch each other while in their menses,
the former is purified by three fasts, and the latter by one day and night.
If a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman who have both reached their menses touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after one day and night.
If a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after two days.
"This is the ancient rule for purification when there is intentional contact between castes.

However, regarding unintentional contact, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu has stated that bathing alone suffices: "If a menstruating woman touches another menstruating woman of a lower caste, she shall not eat until she has become purified;
but having touched one of her own caste or of a higher caste, she becomes pure immediately after bathing."
Regarding contact with Caṇḍālas and others, however, a specific rule has been stated by Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha:
"If a woman in her menses is touched by an outcast, an Antya, or a dog-cooker,
she should perform the penance after those days have passed."
On the first day, there should be a three-night fast; on the second, a two-day fast;
on the third day, a single day and night; and thereafter, one should observe eating only at night.
"Having been touched by a Śūdra woman who has eaten leftovers, or by a dog, one should observe [this penance] for two days.
This means that having passed those days, one should spend them by fasting.
This refers to the case of intentional contact; in the case of unintentional [contact], [the penance is different].
But if a woman in her menses is touched by a Caṇḍāla, an Antya, a dog, or a crow,
she should remain without food for as long as it takes for her to become pure.
This is to be understood as stated by Baudhāyana. Furthermore, he [Baudhāyana] himself has said: "But a menstruating woman who has been touched by village cocks or pigs..."
Having bathed with dogs, one should throw [the substance] until the moon is visible.
Thus, that [rule] refers to a case where one lacks the capacity [to act otherwise].
However, when a woman who is menstruating is touched by a dog or other such beings while eating, a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti:
"If a menstruating woman, while eating, should be touched by a dog, an outcaste (antyaja), or the like..."
Subsisting on cow urine and barley gruel for six nights, one becomes purified.
"In the event of inability, one should give gold or even food to the Brahmins. Thus [it is said].
But when there is mutual contact between two persons who are both impure from food remnants, then:
"If a woman in her menses is ever touched by one who is impure from food remnants, the former is purified by a *kṛcchra* penance; a Śūdra woman is purified by gifts and fasting."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Atri.
But when a woman in her courses touches twice-born men who have food remnants [on their hands], then:
"If a woman in her courses should somehow touch twice-born men who have food remnants,
she should fast for one day and night if they were defiled below the navel, but for three days if they were defiled above the navel."
Thus it should be understood as spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya.
Thus, having explained certain penances for minor offenses (anupātaka) in connection with the topic of the penance for an *avakīrṇin*, we shall now follow the main subject at hand.
In that regard, it was stated [in verse 3.266]: "Immediately after [the sin of] *avakīrṇa* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy), there is likewise the sale of one's sons.

In this matter, the penances lasting three months and so forth, as declared by Manu and Yājñavalkya, are to be determined as before, depending on whether the act was intentional or unintentional, the caste of the person, their physical capacity, and other such factors.
As for the statement of Śaṅkha:

"Having sold a temple, a dwelling, a garden, a grove, an assembly hall, a water-booth, a pond, a meritorious bridge, or one's own son, one shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance"— and that which was stated by Parāśara: "Having sold a daughter or a cow, one shall perform the *sāntapana* penance."
Thus, both of these [acts] should be understood as applying when committed unintentionally; however, if done intentionally: "Having sold women, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
the wise say that for a man, the vow is double."
Thus, that which is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata should be observed.
As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi:
"In the case of selling a grove, a pond, a well, a lotus-pool, or a virtuous son, one should bathe at the three periods of the day, sleep on the ground, and eat only at every fourth meal-time."
"The statement that 'one becomes purified after a year' refers specifically to the case of stealing a single son;
immediately following that, the theft of grain, base metals, and cattle is mentioned, and the penances for those are detailed at length in the section on theft. (3.287)
Immediately following this, it was stated: "and officiating at the sacrifices of those for whom one should not sacrifice" (YDh 3.237).
Regarding that, he now declares the penance:
"One who performs sacrifices for Vratyas, even if performing malevolent rites, shall perform three Kṛcchra penances."
One who has submerged the Vedas and one who eats barley for a year [are purified] by abandoning one who has sought refuge.
However, he who performs sacrifices for those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī should perform three Kṛcchra penances beginning with the Prājāpatya.
And among these Kṛcchras, which vary in severity, the specific penance must be determined according to the gravity or lightness of the cause. Likewise...
Even one performing malevolent magic (abhicāra) should perform this very same expiation;

and this applies except in the case of an assailant who attempts to kill with fire and so forth, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "One does not fall [from his caste] by performing malevolent magic against the six [types of offenders]."
The word "api" (even/also) is intended to include both those who perform sacrifices for those of low caste (*hīnayājaka*) and those who perform funeral rites for such persons (*antyeṣṭiyājaka*).
For this very reason, it was stated by Manu:
"Having performed sacrifices for *vrātyas*, and having performed the funeral rites for others..."
"He removes [the sin of] sorcery and the Ahīna sacrifice by means of three Kṛcchra penances" (MDh 11.198).

Regarding the phrase "performing the funeral rites for others," this refers either to cases of extreme habitual practice or to the performance of funeral rites for Śūdras or outcastes; such is the scope of the expiation.
Because of its gravity: the *ahargaṇa-yāga* (sacrificial session consisting of a series of days) begins with the *dvirātra* and ends with the *dvādaśāha*.
As for that which was stated by Śātātapa:
"One should not initiate those whose *Sāvitrī* has lapsed, nor teach them, nor cause them to perform sacrifices."

The statement, "He who should initiate these [students], teach them, or perform sacrifices for them, must observe the Uddālaka-vow," refers to cases where such acts are performed out of personal desire.
The Uddālaka-vrata has already been shown previously.
And these three Kṛcchras constitute exceptions to the general expiation for minor offenses (upapātaka).
Therefore, the penance common for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is prescribed for officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, such as Śūdras;
in that case, if done intentionally, the penance lasts for three months.
However, if [the act was committed] unintentionally, one should perform the month-long vow and other penances prescribed by the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya).

As for that which was stated by Pracetas after enumerating those who officiate at sacrifices for Śūdras and others— "they should perform the five-fire austerity, sleeping in the open air, and lying in water,
respectively during the summer, the rainy season, and the winter, for one month"— [that refers to a different case].
"They should eat cow-urine and barley-gruel"— this refers to the case of intentional repetition;
as for that which was stated by Yama:
If the priest of Śūravarṇa acts [improperly],
whether out of affection or for the sake of material gain, a *kṛcchra* penance is the means of purification for him.
Thus, that [rule] refers to the case of one who is incapable [of performing the penance].
And as for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi— "One who officiates for a Śūdra becomes pure by the renunciation of all property after ten thousand repetitions of breath-control (prāṇāyāma)"—
that too refers to the case of repeated practice committed unintentionally.
As for that which was stated by Gautama— "In the case of employing forbidden mantras, one should perform the *sahasravāg* [penance]" (GDh 22.23)—

this prescribes the ordinary vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) when the employment of mantras consisting of officiating at sacrifices or teaching for outcasts (*patita*) and others who are forbidden has been practiced many times.
That refers to the scope of repeated practice out of desire; likewise, it applies to one who corrupts his own Veda, and to one who,
though capable of protecting, neglects a refugee other than a thief.
He too is purified by eating barley-rice for one year;
in that context, "viplava" refers to occasions when study is prohibited, such as on festival days, upon hearing the cry of a *caṇḍāla*, or during other times unfit for study.
Study:
for one studying for the sake of excellence, the act of subjecting him to such questioning as "What are you reading? or "Has it been ruined by you?
is called *viplāvana* (corruption).
For this very reason, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Manu declared those who do not study when questioned about what has been taught to be fallen.

As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Upon hearing of a fallen person, a Cāṇḍāla, or a corpse, they should remain silent and fasting for three nights, or practice the recitation [of the Veda] up to a maximum of one thousand times."
"It is known that they become purified" (VaDh 23.34–35);

by this very [statement], those who teach or officiate at sacrifices for those whose conduct is censured are explained; and "it is known that they become purified through the renunciation of the sacrificial fee" (VaDh 23.36), which refers to cases where the act was intentional.

As for that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*— "if one recites the Śruti or Smṛti within earshot of a Cāṇḍāla, there shall be fasting for one night"— that refers to cases where the act is unintentional.

When there is merely the passing of a snake or similar creature between [the teacher and student], and no further study takes place there, Yama has prescribed the following expiation even in that case:
Of the snake and the mongoose, of the goat and the cat,
as well as of the mouse, the camel, and the female frog.
Listen now to this immediate expiation for when a man has sexual intercourse with a woman who has come between him and a ram, a sheep, a dog, a horse, or a donkey.
"One shall fast for three nights and perform ablutions three times a day;
or else one must go to another village on one's knees—of this there is no doubt."

Regarding the abandonment of father, mother, or son, and the sale of tanks or groves, the penances common to minor offenses (*upapātaka*) as stated by Manu and Yājñavalkya should be applied as before, taking into account caste, capacity, qualities, and other factors. Among these, concerning the abandonment of father, mother, and so forth: "Those who abandon their mother, father, or guru without cause... [and so on].
Thus, because he is listed among those excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkteya*), there is also an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) necessitated by that reason.
As Manu says:
"Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation (*japa*) of the *Saṃhitā*..."
"And the Śākala oblations performed daily are the purification for those excluded from the company at meals" (MDh 11.201).
Those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkta*) are those indicated in the section on *śrāddha* by such statements as: "Theives, the fallen (*patita*), and eunuchs... (MDh 3.150).

Regarding the sale of tanks and groves, certain specific two-month penances along with their respective scopes were stated during the discussion on the penance for the sale of one's own son. Immediately following that is the defilement of a maiden (MDh 11.62).

Thus it has been stated; and in that regard, penances such as the three-month, two-month, and Cāndrāyaṇa fasts are to be applied for members of the [higher] castes in relation to women of their own caste.

Furthermore, in the case of *ānulomya* (intercourse with a woman of a lower caste), there is a month-long subsistence on milk or a Prājāpatya penance. However, there is no fault in the case of willing women of lower castes; otherwise, there is a fine. (YDh 2.288)
Thus, because a light punishment is observed [in this case],
as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha— "One who defiles a maiden and one who sells Soma shall perform the Kṛcchra penance while subsisting on water"—

and as for the statement of Hārīta: "One who defiles a maiden, a seller of Soma, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who abandons a wife married in youth, a drinker of *surā* or other intoxicants, a priest for a Śūdra, [one who neglects] the Guru..."

An obstructer, an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, one who destroys the livelihood of Brahmins, a false accuser, one who associates with outcasts, a betrayer of friends, a killer of those seeking refuge, and one who lives by counterfeiting—these shall perform the five-fold penance: remaining in the open air during the summer, under a rain-cloud during the rainy season, and lying in water during the winter; for one month they shall subsist on barley-gruel mixed with cow's urine.
Both of these [penalties] are to be applied for the defilement of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya by [a Śūdra] acting in the inverse order;
however, for a Śūdra, there is only corporal punishment.

For it is seen that death is prescribed [as punishment] for such acts as "in the case of defilement, however, there shall be the cutting off of the hand; likewise, in the case of the highest [offense], there shall be execution" (YDh 2.288).

This applies to officiating at a sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother (*parivindaka*), giving a daughter in marriage to such a person, practicing deceit, and violating a vow not prohibited by the learned.

In the case of undertaking the act of cooking for one's own sake and the consorting with a woman who drinks liquor, the common penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) should be established as before; however,

specific penances for the first two [acts] will be discussed in the context of explaining the penances for marrying before an elder brother and officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice.
These have been shown. Immediately following, it was stated: "The abandonment of one's own Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's son" (YDh 3.239).

In that context, regarding abandonment due to addiction or incapacity, it was stated: "And there is the destruction of what has been studied," for which a penance equal to that for killing a Brahmin was prescribed (YDh 3.228).

However, if one abandons [the Veda] due to distraction caused by listening to other treatises and the like, then the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as those lasting three months, should be applied in consideration of the individual's caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth.

As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One who has abandoned the Veda (*brahmojjha*), having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may again receive the Veda from a teacher" (VaDh 20.12).
Thus, that [rule] refers to a case of extreme distress.
Even regarding the abandonment of the fires, a specific distinction has been shown by that same [author]:
"He who abandons the sacred fires shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then have the fires re-established" (VaDh 21.27).
The mention of "twelve nights" is intended to include the *prājāpatya* and other *kṛcchra* penances—whether heavy or light—in consideration of the duration for which they have been neglected.
Among these, if [the period] has lapsed for two months, the *prājāpatya* is prescribed; if four months, the *atikṛcchra*;
if six months have elapsed, the *parāka*; and beyond six months...
Beyond this, the general expiations for minor offenses (upapātaka) declared by the Lord of Yogins should be applied according to the time and other relevant factors;
however, after one year,
the rule is that the three-month or two-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
And this refers to the abandonment [of the sacred fire] out of atheism; likewise, Vyāghra states:
"The twice-born who abandons the fire out of atheism should perform the Prājāpatya penance."
But when one neglects [the vow] through negligence, then a specific rule is stated in the Bhāradvāja-gṛhya:

"Up to three nights, there shall be a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas); up to twenty nights, there shall be fasting; beyond that, up to sixty nights, one should fast for three nights; and beyond that, up to a year, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance."
Beyond this, when a long period of time elapses, the gravity of the fault increases.
However, regarding the case where one abandons [the practice] due to laziness and so forth, a specific rule has been stated by that same [author]:
Upon the lapse of twelve days, there is a three-day fast; upon the lapse of a month, a twelve-day fast; and upon the lapse of a year, a month-long fast or subsisting on milk.
However, regarding the period beyond a year, a specific rule has been stated by Vṛddha-Hārīta:
If the *agnihotra* has been neglected for one year, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and then re-establish the fires.
If it has been neglected for two years, one should perform both the *cāndrāyaṇa* and the *somāyana*.
"If [the sacred fire] has been extinguished for three years, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year and then re-establish it.
The *Somāyana* will be explained in the section on *kṛcchra* penances.
A specific rule has also been stated by Śaṅkha:
"One who causes the extinction of the sacred fire shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year and give a cow as a gift."
For the intentional abandonment of one's Vedic study or the abandonment of a kinsman, the penance for killing a cow (*govadhavrata*) is to be observed for three months.
However, if it is unintentional, the fourfold set of vows (*vratacatuṣṭaya*) spoken by Yogīśvara should be applied according to one's capacity and other relevant factors.
Regarding the cutting down of trees, the penance has been stated previously.

For making a living through such acts as killing women or animals, subjugating others, and operating oil-presses or sugarcane-mills, those same penances are to be applied in that very same manner. And for vices such as gambling and hunting, those same vows are likewise to be applied in that very same manner.
As for that which Baudhāyana [states]: "Now, the causes of impurity are:

gambling, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), gleaning for one who has not established the sacred fires, the practice of begging for one who has returned home from his teacher, and his residence in the teacher's household beyond four months, as well as teaching him [beyond that period], and the pointing out of constellations."

And thus, [the text] states: "Twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, and three days and one day—this is the specification of the causes of impurity" (BDh 2.2.15–17).
Thus, the annual vow regarding gambling has been described.
That refers to the subject of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

As for that which was stated by Pracetas: "A liar, a thief, a king’s servant, one who subsists by planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, one who subsists by riding horses, chariots, or elephants, a stage-player, one who keeps packs of dogs, a teacher of Śūdras, the husband of a Śūdra woman, a maker of musical instruments, one who subsists by the stars, and one who lives like a dog [are all excluded]."

One who lives off Brahmanas, a physician, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, a gambler, a drunkard, a forger, one who sells his offspring, and one who sells human beings or cattle— these he shall redeem by assembling [the community] and acting according to justice through the established rules of the Brahmanas. Having renounced all their property, they shall eat only at every fourth mealtime, bathe three times a day for a year, and at the end of that period, perform libations to the gods and ancestors and provide daily maintenance for cows.
And thus they are to be treated [in this manner]; that also refers to the same subject matter as Baudhāyana.
A *śvāgaṇika* is one who lives by means of a pack of dogs.
A *bhāṇḍika* is one distinct from a bard (*bandin*), who awakens kings with the sounds of musical instruments and the like; he is mentioned separately because he is distinct from a bard.
One who lives like a dog is a servant;
one who lives by Brahman is a paid attendant at the ritual duties of Brahmins.

Even those penances for those excluded from the *paṅkti* (asat-pātra) mentioned by Manu—such as eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month and so forth—should be applied according to considerations of caste (*jāti*) and other factors;
for even among those he listed as excluded from the *paṅkti*, gamblers and others addicted to vices are specifically mentioned. This applies likewise to the sale of oneself and service to a Śūdra.
And the general expiations (sāmānyaprāyaścitta) should be applied exactly as before.

As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana: "Sea-voyage, the misappropriation of a Brāhmaṇa’s deposit, trading with all kinds of merchandise, falsehood regarding land, service to a Śūdra, and he who is born of a Śūdra woman—along with whatever offspring he may have—for these, the following is the instruction."
They should eat moderately at the fourth mealtime, partake of water according to the ritual procedure for the Soma-pressings,
and pass their time by alternating between standing and sitting.
"By three years they remove that sin"—
this refers to the case of long-term service; however,
in the case of friendship with those of lower caste, the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) apply.

As for that which was stated by Pracetas— "For causing a breach of friendship, one should fast for a day and night, perform an oblation, and drink milk"— that refers to the case of breaking a friendship that is not [otherwise] deficient.
Regarding the pursuit of those of inferior birth as well, the penances common to minor offenses (*upapātaka*) apply.

These [penances] are to be applied. As for that which was stated by Śātātapa: "A Brāhmaṇa who has previously married a Kṣatriya girl should perform a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance and then marry her;

if she was previously a Vaiśya girl, he should perform a *taptakṛcchra*; if she was previously a Śūdra girl, he should perform a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. If a Kṣatriya has previously married a Vaiśya girl, he should perform a twelve-night *kṛcchra* and then marry her; if she was previously a Śūdra girl, however, he should perform an *atikṛcchra*."

"If a Vaiśya has previously married a Śūdra woman, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then marry her"— in this context, "he should settle down and marry her" means that after the performance of the Kṛcchra and subsequent to marrying a woman of his own caste, he may then marry that Kṣatriya woman or others.

And this refers to the case of ignorance; however, in the case of knowledge, it should be understood that the general expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is indeed established. This applies to sexual intercourse with a common woman.
And regarding what was stated there concerning "resorting to low wombs," it is also said that for approaching cattle or a prostitute, a Prājāpatya penance is prescribed;
this statement by Saṃvarta should be understood as applying to cases where the act is committed unintentionally.

However, the statement made by Yama regarding intentional [offense] should be observed: "The twice-born remove the sin born of approaching a prostitute by drinking boiled water infused with *kuśa* grass once every day for seven nights. Thus it is said.
And the general expiations for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) are to be applied according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional and with regard to its repetition;
in that regard, however, when there is intentional repetition,
the rule applies that "the occasional rite (*naimittika*) recurs for every occasion" (*pratinimittaṃ*).
Regarding the contingency of applying the interest rate for each individual occasion when such occasions recur, Laugākṣi has stated a specific rule:
"In the case of repetition, an increase by the daily rate is prescribed until one month has passed;
thereafter, an increase by the monthly rate applies for as long as it takes to reach a year."
"Then he shall perform [the penance] for as many years as the number of years he has committed the sin.
This refers to cases where the act was intentional (*matipūrva*).
Regarding the repetition of an unintentional (*amatipūrva*) act, a specific rule is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
That which is prescribed for a single performance is said to be tripled over three days;
it is said to be fivefold after a month, and after six months, it becomes tenfold.
"From one year it becomes fifteenfold; from three years it becomes twentyfold; beyond that, it should be calculated in the same manner, according to the words of Śātātapa. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, as for the rule that "one should perform double [the penance] in the second instance compared to this first injunction," which prescribes repetition for every occasion, it has already been stated previously that this refers specifically to the case of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).
As for Yama’s extension of the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*) to the case of approaching a common woman:
"Some prescribe the vow of the Guru’s bed, and some the Cāndrāyaṇa vow."
Some, however, desire [this penance] for one who has killed a cow, while others [prescribe it] for one who has broken his vow of celibacy.
Thus, this refers to the subject of uninterrupted practice from birth onwards accompanied by its consequences.
Immediately thereafter, it was stated: "Likewise, dwelling in a non-ashrama" (YDh 3.241); regarding that, a specific detail has been stated by Hārīta:
One who has not entered an āśrama for a year should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and then enter an āśrama; for a second year, the Atikṛcchra;
for a third year, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra; and beyond that, the Cāndrāyaṇa.
This refers to cases where [the offense] is impossible; however,
when it is possible, the general penances for minor offenses (upapātaka) should be applied according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional.

And in the cases of taking pleasure in the food prepared by others, studying false scriptures, entering a mine, usurping authority, and selling one's wife, the general penances for minor offenses (upapātaka) prescribed by Manu and Yājñavalkya should be determined according to the caste, capacity, qualities, and other relevant factors. (3.289)

Regarding the phrase "and the sale of their wife" (YDh 3.242), it has been stated that the word "and" (*ca*) is intended as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the acceptance of improper gifts (*asatpratigraha*), the eating of forbidden food (*ninditānnādana*), and so forth, as mentioned by Manu and others. Among those, concerning the acceptance of improper gifts:
He states the specific expiation:
"Living in a cow-pen as a celibate student for one month, subsisting on milk and devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts. (YDh 3.289)

But he who accepts an improper gift— that is, a gift which is forbidden— becomes purified by living for one month in a cow-pen while engaged in celibacy, devoted to the recitation of the *gāyatrī*, habitually performing the *gāyatrī* recitation, and observing the milk-vow (*payovrata*).
As for the "impropriety" of the gift:
The [impurity] of the giver is based on birth and action, such as that of a Caṇḍāla or one who has fallen from his caste;

likewise, it is based on place and time, such as at Kurukṣetra or during an eclipse; and it is based on the object to be received, such as liquor, a ewe, a bed for the deceased, or a cow with two faces.
However, when one accepts a ewe or similar animal from an outcaste (patita) or the like, this heavy penance (guruprāyaścitta) should be observed,
because the cause is grave due to the observation of two transgressions.
In that regard, a specific number for the recitation of mantras has been stated by Manu:
"Having recited three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk milk in a cow-pen for a month, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts" (MDh 11.195).
Thus, it should be understood that the recitation of three thousand [verses] is to be performed every day.
By the use of the accusative case in the word "māsam" (for a month), it is understood that the recitation, numbering three thousand [times], must extend over each day; however,
when [the recitation is obtained] from a Brāhmaṇa or others who abide by the rules of conduct, even if it is prohibited [by other means].
If one accepts a ram or similar animal, or land and so forth from an outcaste or the like, provided it is not otherwise forbidden,
then that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* should be observed:
"All terrible types of acceptance are purified by the *pavitra-iṣṭi*."
"By means of the Aindava rite, the Mṛgāreṣṭi, or sometimes the Mitravindā sacrifice,
or simply by one hundred thousand recitations of the Devī [mantra], they are purified from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
As for the statement of Bṛhaddhārīta:
Having accepted a gift from a king, one should always dwell in water for a month;
subsisting on milk at every sixth mealtime, one becomes purified when the month is complete.
Having constantly gratified the twice-born with their desired objects, he remained steadfast in his observances.
Thus, this should be understood as referring to the practice mentioned previously;
or else, it refers to the acceptance of items such as a black antelope skin from outcasts and others on occasions such as at Kurukṣetra or during an eclipse.
Likewise, due to the smallness of the substance to be accepted, there is a smallness of the penance;
as Hārīta says:
"Upon accepting gems, garments, cows, and so forth, one should mutter the Sāvitrī eight thousand times."
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* it is said:
"When even a mere alms-meal has been received, one should recite the mantra;
in all acts of acceptance, one should assign a sixth part [to the deity]."
Thus, this entire collection of expiations is to be understood as applying to the time following the renunciation of wealth: "When Brāhmaṇas acquire wealth through a censurable act,
they become pure by relinquishing it, and by means of recitation and austerity alone" (MDh 11.194).
Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*.
In this manner, other Smṛti passages as well are to be applied to specific cases according to the smallness or greatness of the value of the substance involved.

Thus ends the section on expiations for minor offenses (upapātaka). Now, however, the multitude of vows taught by the Lord of Yogins [Yājñavalkya] regarding those who consume censurable food due to defects such as caste or source, and so forth, shall be set forth.

In that regard, if one intentionally consumes onions and other such substances defiled by their very nature (*jātiduṣṭa*) even once, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed by the verse beginning with "Onions, a village pig" (YDh 1.176). However,
in the case of intentional repeated practice, [the penance is] that for eating forbidden things or practicing deceit (YDh 3.229).
By these and other such statements, the penance equal to that for drinking liquor has been described.
For consuming [liquor] once unintentionally, the *sāntapana* penance is prescribed;
for repeated practice of that same act, the following applies.
Having unintentionally eaten these six [forbidden things], one should perform the Kṛcchra Sāṃtapana penance or the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa;
for the remaining cases, one should fast for a day. (MDh 5.20)
Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*. As for that which was stated by Vṛddha-Yama:
"And those originating from beds, eggplants, gourds, and the cutting of trees..."
Bhūtṛṇa, śigruka, khukhaṇḍa, and mushrooms as well.
Having consumed these, a twice-born man shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of intentional repetition;

for the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) has prescribed a three-day fast for eating fish intentionally even once, stating: "And having eaten fish intentionally, one should spend three days fasting" (YDh 1.175).
The bird called *khaṭvā*,
while others say it is *kusumbha*;
and *kavaka* is the vegetable known as *rājasarṣapa*.
The term *khukhaṇḍa* is specified as a particular variety of that [vegetable] according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull. As for that which was stated by Yama:
"Likewise, those originating from *taṇḍulīyaka*, *kumbhīka*, and *vraścana*..."
The nālikā, the coconut, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
Having consumed bhūtṛṇa, śigruka, that which is called khaṭvā, and likewise kavaka, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow.
Thus, that too refers to the object of intentional practice;
*nālikā* and *nārikelī* are specific types of vegetables,
as is that which is called a *khaṭvā*.
However, regarding eating [forbidden food] once unintentionally, one should observe the rule stated by Manu: "But for the remaining [offenses], one should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20).
In that same case, if there is repetition, a recurrence of the penance should be inferred.
But in the case of excessive repetition,
having unintentionally eaten food that is defiled by contact, defiled by its preparation,
or defiled by its inherent nature, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Thus should the statement of Pracetas be understood.
Regarding the unintentional single consumption of indigo, however, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed:
"If a Brāhmaṇa should ever consume indigo through negligence..."
"Purification shall come through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; thus the sage Āpastamba has declared."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Āpastamba;
and in the case of intentional repetition, a recurrence [of the penance] should be inferred.
Furthermore, that which has been stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
Having eaten hemp flowers, silk-cotton tree flowers, curd churned with the hand,
or the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered outside the altar, one shall not eat for a day and a night.
Thus, that [penance] also refers to an unintentional case.
As for what was stated by Sumantu— "Upon eating garlic, onion, *gṛñjanaka*, or mushrooms, one should pour eight thousand oblations of the Sāvitrī mantra over the head"—
that refers to a case of eating against one's will due to forceful compulsion.
This should be understood as referring to eating for the purpose of alleviating a specific disease that can be cured by it alone;
for this very reason, he stated immediately thereafter:
These very acts are not prohibited for a physician when treating a patient;
and there is no fault even in those other acts of a similar nature.
One should lead the drops to their convergence; that is, one should cast them in.

Now follows the expiation for drinking the milk of a cow that is naturally unfit, or of one in heat (*saṃdhinī*), and so forth. Regarding that, if one drinks it once unintentionally: "The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, camel's milk, and likewise the milk of one-hoofed animals..."
Milk from a sheep, milk from a cow in heat, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died; these are forbidden.
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo, the milk of females must be avoided; likewise, all substances that have turned sour are indeed to be shunned.

Having stated, "Curd is edible among sour substances, as is everything produced from curd" (MDh 5.8–10), the fast prescribed by Manu— "one should fast for a day regarding the remaining [forbidden foods]" (MDh 5.20)— is to be observed.
However, if done intentionally, one should observe the three-night fast prescribed by the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya).
As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi:
"Upon consuming the milk of a camel, a female donkey, or a human woman, there is the Taptakṛcchra penance and a second initiation."
Upon consuming the milk of a cow or a buffalo within ten days of calving,
there shall be fasting for six nights;
likewise, this same penance applies to drinking the milk of all animals that have only two teats, with the exception of the goat.
And as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"A wise man who eats the products of those milks that are unfit to be consumed should diligently perform the vow for seven nights with a concentrated mind."
Thus the barley-gruel vow has been described;
both of these refer to cases of intentional and repeated consumption.
As for the fortnightly vow prescribed by Śaṅkha regarding the drinking of milk from a cow that is either in heat or has eaten impure matter:
Regarding the statement, "Having eaten [the milk] of a cow in heat or of one that eats impure things, one should observe the vow for a fortnight," that too refers to the case of habitual practice;
however, if one drinks [milk] even once, having consumed all types of milk except those of cows, goats, and buffaloes, one should fast.

For Viṣṇu has stated that fasting is required even for these: milk from a cow within ten days of calving, the milk of a cow in heat, the milk of one whose calf has died, and the milk of those that eat impure food;
likewise, there is a prohibition based on caste.
Whether he be a Kṣatriya established in his duty, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra,
whoever drinks the milk of a Kapila cow— there is no other doer of such demerit than him.

In such cases as these, where no specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is seen to be prescribed for each individual act, one should observe the general expiation stated by Manu: "For the remaining [offenses], one should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20).
Now, the expiation for eating meat and other substances that are inherently impure has been stated:
"In that regard, if one eats [such things] intentionally even once, one should fast for a day regarding the remaining cases" (MDh 5.20).
Thus, the general expiation mentioned by Manu should be understood. However, for intentional consumption, [Manu says]:
"Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, dog-meat, dried meat, and fish, one shall dwell for three days while fasting."
Thus it should be understood as stated by the Lord of Yogins.
However, in the case of intentional and repeated practice, [Manu Smṛti 11.153 states]:
"Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights."
Thus, the statement of Manu is to be understood;
and this refers to cases other than the meat of village pigs and the like, specifically regarding the eating of carnivorous animals, wild boars, camels, and cocks.
"And for those who eat the excrement of hell-beings, crows, or donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* is the purification" (Manu Smṛti 11.157).
Since Manu has thus prescribed specific penances according to the particular species [of the offender],
this same [penance] applies even to the consumption of urine and feces.
As well as boars and single-hoofed animals, crows and roosters,
all carnivorous creatures, and those which have been declared inedible.
Having consumed meat, urine, or feces, as well as beef,
or the flesh of a dog, a jackal, or a monkey, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is prescribed.
Or, having fasted for twelve days, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
Thus, according to the *Bṛhadyama-smṛti*,
the settled rule is that for an intentional act there is a *taptakṛcchra* penance,
whereas in the case of repetition, it is a *parāka* accompanied by the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblations.

Likewise, Pracetas has also stated: "In the case of eating the flesh of a dog, jackal, crow, cock, leopard, monkey, leopard-cat, blue jay, carnivorous animal, donkey, camel, elephant, horse, village pig, cow, or human, one should prescribe the *taptakṛcchra* penance; however, for eating the urine or excrement of these, one should prescribe the *atikṛcchra*.
And this refers to cases of intentional action (*kāmakāra*).
As for the statement of Uśanas:
"Having eaten human flesh, dog flesh, cow flesh, or even horse flesh, as well as the flesh of five-toed animals, one should perform the Mahāsāntapana penance."
Thus, that [rule] refers to unintentional cases;
as for the statement of Aṅgiras: "A crane, a vulture, a hawk, a rat, a donkey, a monkey, and a pig..."
Having seen or touched their impurities, one becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana).
If twice-born men eat these impure substances intentionally, they should perform the Sāntapana penance;
if unintentionally, they should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra.
Thus, that refers to the case of having swallowed and then vomited [the substance]; and here,
by the word *sāntapana*, the *mahāsāntapana* is meant, because the *prājāpatya* penance is prescribed for unintentional [consumption].
Furthermore, as for the statement of Aṅgiras: "Having eaten the flesh of hell-beings, crows, donkeys, horses, and elephants,
and having consumed their urine and excrement, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Thus, as for that which was stated by Bṛhadyama— "A Brahmin who eats dried meat should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow"—
both of these [rules] refer to the case of intentional repetition.
Furthermore, as stated by Śaṅkha: "Having eaten animals with two rows of teeth, as well as those with uncloven hoofs,
and having consumed the flesh of camels or cattle, one should perform a vow for six months."
Thus, that refers to the case of intentional and extreme repetition;
however, as stated in another Smṛti:
"Having eaten the flesh of humans, village pigs, and likewise donkeys..."
One should observe the vow for one year regarding all five-toed animals— such as cows, horses, elephants, and camels— as well as carnivorous beasts, chickens, and domesticated animals.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of practice that is absolutely uninterrupted;
in this context, the mention of urine and feces is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for fat, semen, blood, and marrow.
In the case of the six impurities beginning with earwax, however, half [of the penance] should be prescribed.
Furthermore, regarding hair and so forth, a specific rule is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In the case of intentionally eating the raw flesh of goats, sheep, buffaloes, or deer, or consuming hair, nails, or blood, [the penance is] three nights."
"Fasting [is prescribed] due to ignorance.
As for that which was stated by Pracetas:
"In the case of eating nails, hair, earth, or clods of earth, purification comes from fasting for a day and a night."
That [penance] also applies to the case of consuming [such things] once unintentionally;
as for the statement from another Smṛti: "Having consumed hair, insects, or nail-clippings, and likewise fish-bones..."
Having drunk blood-heated ghee, one becomes pure at that very moment.
This refers to the case where [food] enters only the mouth;
however, when food contained in a vessel becomes defiled by hair or other such things, then—
But when food is defiled by flies or hair at the time of eating,
one should immediately touch water and then touch that food with ashes.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Pracetas.
This verse is incidental;
however, regarding the consumption of even very minute worms, insects, or bones, [the following applies].
Hārīta has stated a specific rule: "In the case of eating worms, insects, ants, leeches, moths, or bones, one becomes pure after three nights by subsisting on cow urine and cow dung.
Here, *jalauka* refers to fish and the like.

Thus, the penances for consuming the meat of cattle, birds, aquatic animals, humans, and so forth have been shown in brief; they are not written out for each individual case here for fear of excessive length.
Now, regarding the expiation for eating food touched by impure things, first the case of eating the leavings of those whose food is forbidden will be discussed. On this point, Manu says:
"Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose..."

"One should drink *brahmī* and *suvarcalā* [if] hair or insects have fallen into it" (MDh 11.160). Since no specific duration of time is mentioned here, it refers to one night; furthermore, this should be understood as applying to intentional consumption.

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "In the case of eating a large quantity of food or meat that has been devoured by birds or beasts of prey, even if it is not otherwise defiled, one must perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance."
Thus, that [rule] refers to cases of intentional action.

Furthermore, the purification of substances should be understood as stated in the section on the purification of materials in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], beginning with the rule regarding "the sacrificial shed of the gods" (*devadroṇī*).

As for what was stated by Śātātapa—"In the case of eating what has been licked by dogs, crows, and the like, or the leavings of a Śūdra, one must perform an *atikṛcchra* penance"—[that also applies to intentional acts].
That refers to the case of unintentional repetition.
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"Having eaten the leavings of dogs, one should observe a vow for one month."
Having eaten food left over by a crow or smelled by a cow, one should observe a vow for a fortnight.

Thus has the vow of barley-gruel been described; that refers to the case of intentional repetition. However, regarding the consumption of the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa or others, it has been stated by Bṛhad-Viṣṇu:
A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for seven nights;
for eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, for five nights;
and for eating the leavings of a Rājanya, for three nights.
As for the rule that "one [should fast] for one day for eating the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa," that refers to a case where the act was done intentionally;
however, as for the statement of Yama:
Having eaten together with a Brāhmaṇa of the Prājāpatya class, one is purified by [that] Prājāpatya penance;
having eaten food together with a king, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Having eaten food together with a Vaiśya, one is purified by the Atikṛcchra penance;
having eaten food together with a Śūdra, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of intentional repetition.
Furthermore, as for the statement of Śaṅkha: "Upon eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, one should drink water consecrated with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
upon eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, [one should drink water] boiled with the juice of the Brāhmī plant."
One should subsist on milk for three days;
having eaten the leavings of a Vaiśya, one should fast for three nights and drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*;
and having eaten the leavings of a Śūdra, there should be a fast for six nights.
That refers to cases where there was no intention [to cause death];
in those instances, a doubling or other increase of the penalty should be prescribed for repeated practice.
And this applies except in the case of [killing] one's father or others [for whom the penance is greater].
For there is the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "The leavings of the father and the eldest brother may be eaten" (ĀpDh 1.4.11).
As for the statement of Bṛhadvyāsa:
One should not eat together with one's mother, sister, wife, or other women; having so eaten, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, that [rule] refers to the matter of eating together.

However, regarding the eating of mere leavings, one should observe what was stated by Āpastamba: "In the case of eating the leavings of a Śūdra, there shall be a fast for seven nights, as well as for women" (ĀpDh 1.26.4–5).
As for the statement of Aṅgiras:
"If one should ever eat together with a Brāhmaṇī, or [eat her] leavings,
the wise consider that there is no fault in that at all."
Thus, this refers either to the context of marriage or to a state of distress;
however, regarding the consumption of the remnants of food from those of the lowest caste, [the rule is]:
"But having eaten the remains of the food of those of the lowest caste, the twice-born..."
The Cāndrāyaṇa penance and half of that [the Kṛcchra] are the prescribed rules for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas respectively.
Thus, that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed.
Here, "cāndra" refers to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
However, regarding the consumption of the leavings of an Antyāvasāyin:
Upon eating the remnants of food from Caṇḍālas, outcasts, and the like,
a Brāhmaṇa should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and a Kṣatriya should perform the Sāntapana penance.
And for six nights and three nights respectively for the two castes.

Thus, what was stated by the Aṅgirases regarding the *sāntapana* penance should here be understood as the *mahāsantapana*. However, in times of distress: "But if food has been eaten by a Brahmin in the house of a Śūdra during a time of distress, he shall be purified by mental anguish and by reciting the *drupadāḥ* one hundred times."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Parāśara.
As for that which was stated by Bṛhacchātātapa: "Whatever remains after being drunk, or whatever has been poured out from the mouth into a vessel..."
One should know that to be unfit for consumption; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of repeated practice,
because the cause is extremely slight;
furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa should ever drink water that has been left over after someone else has drunk from it.
Or alternatively, one should observe the vow for three nights using only the left hand.
This refers to cases where the act is intentional;
however, if it is done unintentionally, half [the penance] should be prescribed.
But in the case of a lamp-wick remnant, [the following applies]:
Oil remaining from a lamp, that which has been taken from a street at night,
and the residue remaining after an oil massage— one becomes pure by eating these as a nocturnal meal (nakta).
Thus, that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* should be observed.
Now, regarding the expiation for consuming food touched by impure substances,
Saṃvarta says on that matter:
"Food into which hair or insects have fallen, or that which has been defiled by indigo or lac..."
"Having eaten food touched by sinews, bones, or skin, one should fast for a day.

Likewise, Śātātapa says: [One must avoid] food fallen into which hair or insects have fallen; that touched by blood, meat, or an untouchable; that looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan); that licked by birds; that smelled by a dog, a pig, or a cow; that is sour, stale, or cooked for no sacred purpose; and the food of the gods (devānna) and sacrificial oblations (havis).
"Fasting from food and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)—both of these apply to cases where the act was unintentional. However, if done intentionally:
'Having consumed earth, water, flowers, and the like, as well as fruits, tubers, sugarcane, and roots that have been defiled by feces or urine, one should perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.'"
If [the offense] is proximate, it should be half; the Kṛcchra penance is the purification for such impurity.

Thus it should be understood as stated by Viṣṇu; the rule is that for minor contact, one quarter [of the penance] applies, while for major contact, half of a Kṛcchra applies. As for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
Having intentionally eaten food that is defiled by contact, defiled by the manner of its preparation,
or defiled by its very nature, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

Thus, this should be stated regarding the perception of the taste of mixed impure substances and the like. However, concerning contact with a woman in her menses and others, that which was spoken by Śaṅkha applies:

"Having eaten food touched by those who are impure, outcasts, Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, women in their menses, Avadhūtas, those with elephantiasis, lepers, or those with deformed nails, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance."
"He should wander. Thus [it is said]. A *kuṇi* is one whose hand is deformed.
This refers to the case of intentional action;
in the case of unintentional action, it is half [the penance].
Having eaten food defiled by those who are untouchable, or by impurities such as hair and insects,
one becomes purified by drinking a decoction of *kuśa*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, and other such leaves, as well as *panasa* and lotus petals, along with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *suvarcā*, and similar herbs.
Thus, that which was stated by Viṣṇu refers to cases involving those who are incapable [of purification] or those touched by washermen and the like; however,
in the case of defilement by Śūdras and others, that which was stated by Hārīta should be understood:
Food defiled by a Śūdra, or by insects that frequent impure substances, is unfit for consumption; likewise,
if a Śūdra touches those who are eating because he is unworthy, or if, while they are eating in a row, he stands up and gives them his leavings or sips water after having reviled them.
Or, where they might give food, the penance there is for one day and night.
This same [penance] applies even to eating from a row of leavings;
for whatever twice-born man should ever eat from a row that is defiled by leavings...
Having fasted for a day and night, one becomes purified by means of the five products of the cow.
Thus, according to the *Kratu-smṛti*:
"But he who eats from food released by the left hand, or he who eats from a vessel that has been set aside..."
Thus Vaivasvata has declared: having eaten [forbidden food], one should perform the Sāntapana penance.
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Likewise, Parāśara has also said here:
"When Brahmins seated in a single row eat together..."
If even one person should leave his bowl, one should not cause the remaining food to be eaten.
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, eats the leavings of food in that row, he shall perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Sāntapana penance. Thus it is said.

Regarding the drinking of water from wells or similar sources contaminated by corpses and the like, Viṣṇu says: "Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-nailed animal, or from one that is extremely defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three days, a Kṣatriya for two days, and a Vaiśya for one day."
"A Śūdra [should fast] for a night;

and all [those who have touched the corpse] should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at the end. By "or from something extremely defiled," it is intended to mean [defilement] by urine, feces, and so forth.
But when the corpse in that very place becomes bloated and bursts open, then Hārīta states a specific rule:
If one should drink water situated there in a corpse that is moist or decomposed,
for the sake of purification one should perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance.
"If any excellent twice-born man should happen to bathe there through negligence,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night while performing the recitation of mantras and bathing at the three periods of the day.
This *cāndrāyaṇa* penance refers to the case of intentionally drinking water from a well defiled by a human corpse.
But if [one sees] a corpse that is decomposed or broken, or one situated in a well, unintentionally, one should drink water for six nights;
if it is a human corpse, it is ordained that the period be doubled.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Devala.
And when one drinks water found in a well or other vessel belonging to a Cāṇḍāla, then that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed:
"If a man should intentionally drink water situated in the well or the vessel of a Cāṇḍāla..."
How should one prescribe the expiation in each respective caste?
"A Brahmin shall perform the Sāntapana penance, and a Kṣatriya the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya shall perform half of that, and for a Śūdra, one quarter is prescribed.
This [rule] refers to cases of intentional action.
But if one unintentionally drinks water from a well or a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance,
he shall be purified in three days; however, a Śūdra is purified in one day.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Devala:
