even in small reservoirs of water connected to outcasts (cāṇḍāla) and others, purification is like that of a well; [as it is said:
"In small reservoirs, in stagnant waters, and on the surface of the earth..."
"Regarding large [reservoirs], however, there is no defect; purification is declared to be like that of a well," according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu (ViDh 23.46).
Furthermore, regarding lotus ponds and the like:

Having drunk water from a well, a pond, or even a lake belonging to Mlecchas and others, it should be known as pure up to the depth of the knees; that which is below is traditionally held to be impure.
If a Brahmin drinks that water, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he should eat only at night for one day and night if unintentional, but for two days and nights if intentional.
Thus, that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed.
Regarding water contained in the vessels of washermen and others, [Āpastamba says]:
"If one should drink water, curd, or milk situated in the vessels of those of the lowest castes..."
A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and even a Śūdra, through negligence.
For the twice-born, however, expiation is achieved through the Brahmakūrca fast.
And for a Śūdra, it is likewise through fasting and by giving according to his ability.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Parāśara;
however, if done intentionally, the penance is double.
"Wells, tanks, or even ponds dug by those of the lowest castes..."
Having bathed in and drunk from these, one is purified by the Prājāpatya penance.
This statement by Āpastamba is to be understood as referring to the case of habitual practice.

However, regarding the drinking of water from wells, tanks, and so forth belonging to a Caṇḍāla or others, Āpastamba has prescribed the consumption of only the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); likewise for water from public water-stations (prapā), in the forest, from a small jar, from a vessel belonging to the Sun-god (saura), from a trough (droṇī), or water that has emerged from a leather bag (kośa).
Having drunk water from the vessels of dog-cookers or caṇḍālas, one should be purified by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus, that [rule] refers to a case where one lacks the capacity [to bathe].
He who, having gone to a water-shed (*prapā*), sprinkles his body without water,
shall perform a fast for one day and then bathe with his clothes on (*sacaila*).

"Having drunk water from a vessel containing liquor, or water from a watering-trough, or likewise water from a boat, one should fast for a day and night and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the expiation for consuming that which is defiled by intention (*bhāvaduṣṭa*):
that which is called "defiled by intention" is said to be that which, by its color or shape, is so dissimilar as to produce a sense of loathing or the impression of bodily impurities and the like.
Or when there is suspicion of poison administered by an enemy;
and regarding that, Parāśara says:
"That which is corrupted by speech, that which is corrupted by intention, and [that which is placed] in a vessel corrupted by intention..."

"Having eaten food, a Brāhmaṇa afterwards becomes purified after three nights. This refers to the case of intentional action. As for that which was stated by Gautama: "That which is defiled by intention alone... (GDh 17.13, 14).

Having recited the passage beginning with "thus, etc., prior to the five-toed animals" and stating the penance as "vomiting and the consumption of ghee [are required] for what precedes the five-toed animals" (GDh 23.26), that refers to an unintentional case;
however, in the case of suspicion, [the following applies]:
When a cause for doubt has arisen regarding what is considered unfit to be eaten or consumed, I shall explain the purification of food; listen to me as I speak.
A Brāhmaṇa should drink the dry *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*, free from alkaline salt, for three nights;
or he may drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* together with milk for three nights.
"One should drink the water after boiling it with leaves of the *palāśa* and *bilva*, *kuśa* grass, lotus, and *udumbara*; one becomes purified in three nights"—
this statement by Vasiṣṭha is to be observed.
Manu also stated regarding the suspicion of eating what is unfit for consumption:
"The best of the twice-born shall perform even a single Kṛcchra penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; but for that which is known, the penance is specifically greater. (MDh 5.21)

Now, regarding the expiation for consuming what is spoiled by time (*kāladuṣṭa*): that which is spoiled by time includes stale food, the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, and so forth. In that regard, [Manu Smṛti 5.20 states]: "If one has consumed these unintentionally, one should fast for a day."
It should be understood as stated by Manu:

"But intentionally, having eaten only fermented [grains], as well as anything that has turned sour, or what has been kept overnight, or food cooked in a vessel containing dregs, one shall observe the vow for three nights."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Śaṅkha;
these alone are declared to be without oil.
Regarding the milk of a cow within ten days of calving and similar cases, the penance has been demonstrated previously.
Upon drinking rainwater for the first time, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having drunk fresh rainwater from vessels made of horn, bone, or ivory, or from shells, mother-of-pearl, or cowrie-shells, one becomes pure by consuming pañcagavya.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhad-Yājñavalkya:
"But if [the drinking] was done intentionally, a fast must be observed;
for during that time, one should not drink fresh water for three days, as it is impure."
But if one drinks at an improper time, there shall be a ten-day period of impurity; having drunk, one must not eat for a day and a night.
This is because of the observation in another Smṛti text:

"But for eating at the time of receiving [the gift], the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed; likewise for eating the food of a Navaśrāddha, or the food of one who officiates as a village priest during an eclipse."
Having eaten during the first pregnancy of women, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śātātapa;
but when one eats at a prohibited time other than during an eclipse, then Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"O Bhārgava, on whichever day of the moon or the sun..."
However, there may be an acceptance of it [the food] after that, but not before the act of eating.
One should not eat during an eclipse, nor likewise when [the sun] has set;
one should not eat at all until its re-appearance.
Likewise,
the lunar eclipse may occur from the first watch of the night;
one should eat before the sun's turning [at midday] during the first [watch], and below the first [watch] during the first [eclipse].
Likewise:
"One should eat in the afternoon, not at midday; in the evening, but not during the *saṅgava* [period].
If one were to eat during the *saṅgava*, there would be no prior act of eating."
And as for that which was stated by Manu:
"One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor too early, nor too late," and so forth (MDh 4.55).
And that which was stated by Bṛhacchātātapa:
"One who desires prosperity should avoid at night parched grains, curd, and roasted flour; likewise, a wise man should avoid eating anything mixed with sesame seeds and bathing at night."
Regarding such cases where no specific penance has been prescribed:

"A hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) must be performed for the removal of all sins, indeed for those born of minor offenses (upapātakas) and for that which is specifically unenjoined. (YDh 3.305)

Thus, the hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) spoken by the Lord of Yogins (Yogīśvara) should be observed; however, for unintentional [acts], the fast prescribed by Manu— "But for the remaining [offenses], one should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20)— should be observed.
Now, regarding the expiation for consuming things spoiled by defects such as fermented acids:
on this matter, Manu says:
"Having drunk fermented acids, astringent decoctions, and even impure substances, a twice-born man..."
"One remains unrestrained only so long as that [sin] does not descend. (MDh 11.154).

In this regard, for unintentional acts, fasting for a day should be understood as prescribed by the rule: "In the case of the remaining [offenses], one should fast for a day" (MDh 5.20). But in the case of intentional acts, however:
Having eaten pure fermented liquids, as well as anything that has turned sour overnight, or food cooked in a vessel containing dregs, one must observe a vow for three nights.
Thus should the statement of Śaṅkha be understood.
And this is to be understood as referring to cases other than sour gruel (kāñjikā) and the like that contain fruits such as the āmalaka.
"In those houses where a water-pot (kuṇḍikā) together with its fruit is kept... [is the rule].
From that [cow], however, the sour gruel (kāñjikā) should be taken, and never from any other.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.

Regarding foods from which the oil has been extracted and so forth, after stating: "One should not eat those whose essence has been removed, such as oil-cakes from which the oil has been pressed out, molasses that has solidified, and products of churning," [the text continues]: "Before the five-toed animals, there is vomiting and the consumption of ghee" (GDh 23.26).
Thus it should be understood as stated by Gautama.
"Vilayana" refers to the impurity of ghee and other substances.
Regarding the eating of food that has not been offered in sacrifice and so forth, however, Likhita says:
That which is not offered into the fire and the first portion of which is not given away is not to be eaten by the twice-born; having eaten such food, one should fast for a day.
"A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, having eaten kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, or śaṣkulī in vain, shall perform the Prājāpatya penance. Thus it is said.

However, regarding the remnants of food from one who has not maintained the sacred fires, fasting for a day should be observed, as per Manu Smṛti 5.20; furthermore, regarding eating from broken vessels and the like, it has been stated by Saṃvarta:
"Having eaten from the vessel of Śūdras, or having eaten repeatedly from a broken vessel,
one becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus it is also stated in another Smṛti.

"Having eaten from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *arka*, and *aśvattha* trees, or from the leaves of the *kumbhī* and *tinduka* trees, or from the *kovidāra* and *kadamba* trees, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Likewise:
"A householder who eats from palāśa or lotus leaves shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, a forest-dweller and an ascetic incur the fruit of a Cāndrāyaṇa. Thus it is said.
Now follows the expiation for eating food that is unfit to be eaten due to defects in the act of giving by hand and so forth.
On this matter, Parāśara says:
"Honey, molasses, vegetables, milk products, salt, and ghee..."

"Having eaten food given by hand, one must fast for one day. However, if it is done intentionally, then for eating food given by hand, eating in the presence of a non-Brāhmaṇa, eating in a defiled row, eating at the head of a row,
voiding urine or excrement while anointed with oil, eating the food of a Śūdra during a period of death or birth impurity, or sleeping together with Śūdras, the penance is three nights.

"Abstaining from food" is to be understood as that which was stated by Hārīta. However, regarding the fault of giving food through an intermediary: "A Śūdra giving the food of a Brāhmaṇa, or a Brāhmaṇa giving the food of a Śūdra..."
These two are unfit to be eaten; however, having eaten them, one should fast for a day.
Thus should the statement of Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya be understood. Regarding eating from the hand of a Śūdra, however:
"He who eats from the hand of a Śūdra, or should ever drink water [from such a hand]..."
Having fasted for a day and night, one becomes purified by means of the five products of the cow.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Kratu.
Even in the case of one who is defiled by flatulence:
"Or one whose foot is placed upon his seat, or even one who is half-covered by a garment."
Having eaten food blown upon with the mouth, one should perform the Kṛcchra Sāntapana penance.
Thus it was said by that very [author]:
"But if one eats food offered with the intention of dedicating it to the ancestors and others during a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, one should perform six *prāṇāyāmas*."
The fast (upavāsa) is proclaimed to last from three months up to one year.
In the case of an increase [in the number of rites], three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) are prescribed; on the day of the sapindikarana, one day and night;
for a rite involving dissimilar [deceased relatives], a fast is prescribed; and likewise at the conclusion of a vow.
This [penance] is doubled for eating the food of a Kṣatriya, tripled for eating the food of a Vaiśya,
and it is recorded as being fourfold when eating the food of a Śūdra directly.
If twice-born men drink water while a guest stands at the door, that water becomes blood; having consumed it, they must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Bhāradvāja. Hārīta has also said:
"Having eaten food on the eleventh day, and likewise having eaten at the *saṃcayana* (the gathering of bones),"
"Having fasted and bathed according to the rules, one should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras.
Thus it was also stated by Viṣṇu:
"In the case of a *navaśrāddha*, the penance is a *prājāpatya*; in the first monthly *śrāddha*, it is three-quarters of that."
"In the case of the three-month [impurity], half of that; in the case of the two-month, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
This refers to a situation of distress (*āpad*). However, in the absence of distress:
"The *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance for a *navaśrāddha*, and the *Prājāpatya* for a *miśraka*."
In the Purāṇas, however, a single day's fast is prescribed as the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus, what was stated by Hārīta is to be understood.

As for the statement "the Prājāpatya [penance] is for the Miśraka," this should be understood as referring to the first monthly [impurity]. However, in the case of the second month and subsequent months:

For a *navaśrāddha*, the penance is a *prājāpatya*; for the first monthly *śrāddha*, it is three-quarters; for the third-fortnightly (*traipakṣika*), it is half; likewise, for the second-month, it is one-quarter. For the sixth-month and the annual *śrāddhas*, a *pādonakṛcchra* is prescribed.
In other months, it is for three nights; however, if [the event] occurs every day, it is prescribed for one day.
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Regarding the consumption of food at a *śrāddha* for Kṣatriyas and others, however, when not in a state of distress, it is stated in that very same work:
"A *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed for a *navaśrāddha*, while a *parāka* is remembered for a monthly (*māsika*) *śrāddha*."
For three fortnights, the Sāntapana penance is prescribed; for two months, the Kṛcchra is traditionally taught.
This vow has been declared for a Kṣatriya at a Navaśrāddha;
however, the wise have stated that for a Vaiśya it is half more than that of a Kṣatriya.
For a Śūdra, however, at a *nava-śrāddha* (funeral rite for the newly deceased), one should perform two *cāndrāyaṇas*;
at a monthly rite, one and a half *cāndrāyaṇas*; and at a three-fortnightly rite, an *aindava* (*cāndrāyaṇa*) is prescribed.
"In two months, it shall be a Parāka; beyond that, Sāntapana is prescribed.
As for the statement of Śaṅkha:
"Cāndrāyaṇa is prescribed for the Navaśrāddha; Parāka is prescribed for the monthly (māsika) rite."
For three fortnights it shall be the Atikṛcchra; for six months, however, it is simply the Kṛcchra.
For an annual [śrāddha], there shall be a quarter-pādakṛcchra; for a second annual one, a single day's penance.
Beyond that, there shall be no fault, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.

Thus, that [rule] refers to those killed by snakes and the like, or else it refers to those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkteya*), such as "those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs" (MDh 3.150).
Death from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning,
or from fanged beasts occurs for those of evil deeds.

"By those who have committed suicide by falling [from a cliff], by those who have perished [in fire], and likewise by those who have died through poison or hanging—a twice-born man, having eaten at their sixteen śrāddhas, should perform the Indu-vrata.
Thus it is said. And likewise:
"If a Brāhmaṇa eats food at a Śrāddha performed on the eleventh day for those excluded from the company (apāṅkteya), he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Likewise, having eaten at an Āma-śrāddha, he becomes pure by performing the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Likewise, having eaten at a meal intended for a specific purpose, there shall be a fast for three nights.
Thus, because Bharadvāja has stated that the penance is generally [the same] as for a teacher,
Bṛhadyama, however, states a specific rule regarding a religious student (brahmacārin):
"If a twice-born who has not completed his vow should eat at the monthly śrāddhas and other such occasions..."
A fast for three nights is prescribed as his expiation.
"Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consumed clarified butter, one becomes purified.
This refers to cases of ignorance.
Regarding intentional acts as well, he says the same:
"But he who should eat honey or meat at a śrāddha, or during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka),
shall perform the Prājāpatya penance and complete the remainder of his vow.
In the case of an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food), however, the penance is half [of the prescribed amount] in all instances.
"In the case of an *āmaśrāddha*, however, it is half of that; but in all cases, it is a *prājāpatya*," according to the statement in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*. As for that which was stated by Uśanas:
A twice-born man who has partaken in a śrāddha feast should drink water ten times while reciting the Gāyatrī;
thereafter he should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and immediately after that, he shall become pure.
Thus, that [rule] refers to the subject of *śrāddha* for which no expiation has been stated;
however, regarding the eating at a *śrāddha* that forms part of a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), a specific rule has been stated by Vyāsa:
"But in the case of one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) and fire-offering (*homa*) have been performed, as well as prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*)."
Indeed, having eaten at a birth ceremony, one should perform the Sāntapana penance.
"But for other refined foods, O best of the twice-born, after having eaten, one is purified from the consumption of censurable food by fasting at the command [of the teacher]. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, regarding the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) and other such rites, Dhaumya stated this specific rule: "In the case of the *brahmaudana* rite, the *soma* sacrifice, the parting of the hair,
as well as at a birth-śrāddha and a new-śrāddha, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
In this context, the rite called *brahmaudana* is an auxiliary part of the *ādhāna*, because of its association with the *soma*.
Now, regarding the expiation for eating food that is unfit to be eaten due to its ownership:
that which, though not forbidden by its very nature, is declared unfit to be eaten because it belongs to a specific person, is called "impure through ownership.
Concerning this, the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) states:

Beginning with the verse, "One should not eat the food of one who has not maintained the sacred fires unless in times of distress" (YDh 1.160), those whose food is unfit to be eaten have been set forth in five and a half verses (YDh 1.161–65).
Manu, as well, has set forth the same persons, with some additional ones.

A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one performed by a priest who officiates for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor the food of a group, nor the food of a courtesan, nor that which is despised by the wise.
The food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been consecrated for sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound in fetters— [these are not to be eaten].
[The food] of one who is falsely accused, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman,
of a hypocrite, of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, and of one who eats the remnants of another's meal.

The food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, that which has been tasted by another, that which is less than ten days old, food offered without honor, meat not intended for sacrifice, and the food of a woman who has no male relatives— [these one should avoid].
The food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of one who has fallen, that which is sneezed upon,
and likewise the food of a slanderer, a liar, and a seller of sacrifices.
The food of an actor, a tailor, an ungrateful person,
a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, and one who enters the stage [as a performer].
[The food] of a goldsmith, of a bamboo-worker, of a seller of weapons,
likewise of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, and of a washerman [is forbidden].
The washerman, the cruel man, he in whose house a paramour resides,
those who tolerate a paramour, and those entirely conquered by women— all these go to hell.
"And food offered to the deceased within ten days [of death], as well as that which causes dissatisfaction.
(MDh 4.205–17). Here, the items [prohibited] have been explained in the section on forbidden foods and the section on *śrāddha* rites. Regarding this, he states the penance:
"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. (MDh 4.222).
Paiṭhīnasi also stated that for unintentional [consumption], it is exactly three nights:

One who has cut off a limb, one with black teeth, one who quarrels with his father, one conquered by women, one afflicted with leprosy, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, a merchant, a village priest, one accused of a crime, one begotten on a Śūdra woman, a younger brother who marries before his elder, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, the husband of a *didhiṣū* woman, the son of a remarried woman, a thief, a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, and a servant—these are persons whose food should not be eaten; they are excluded from the row (*apāṅkteya*) and are unworthy of the *śrāddha*. Having eaten the food of these, or having given it to them...
"Until [the fact] is known, it lasts for three nights."
But Śaṅkha, having recited these very same [acts] with a slight addition, has prescribed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; that refers to the case of habitual practice.
Furthermore, Gautama, having enumerated those whose food is not to be eaten starting with "those who are impure, unchaste women, and those accused of crimes" (GDh 17.17),
states: "Up until the five-toed animals, [the penance is] vomiting and the consumption of clarified butter" (GDh 23.26).
Thus the expiation has been stated;
that refers to the case of distress.
But regarding one who is made to eat by force, a specific rule has been stated by Āpastamba:
But those who have been forcibly enslaved by barbarians, outcasts, or bandits,
and have been made to perform inauspicious deeds such as the killing of living beings like cows and others;
The wiping away of leavings, as well as eating what has been left over,
and the devouring of the flesh of donkeys, camels, and wild boars;
Likewise, association with their women and eating together with them—
when a twice-born man has lived thus for a month, the Prājāpatya penance is the means of purification.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, however, there shall be either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance;
or, having lived [in this manner] for a year, he should perform both the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Parāka.
A Śūdra who has lived [as a guest] for one year should drink barley-gruel for half a month;
a Śūdra who has lived for one full month is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
"After one year, an expiation (prāyaścitta) should be prescribed by the best of the twice-born;
after three years, he indeed attains the same state [as the deceased].
Regarding the eating of food taken from one who is under ritual impurity (āśauca), Chāgaleya says:
If Brahmins eat during a period of impurity due to birth or death out of ignorance,
they become pure by performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) when the impurity caused by a Śūdra's birth has passed.
For a Vaiśya it shall be sixty days, for a Kṣatriya twenty, and for a Brāhmaṇa ten;
[the penance consists of] fasting for one day, three days, five days, and seven nights respectively.
"Then their purification occurs; thereafter, they should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus, one-day, three-day, and other periods should be applied according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇas.
This refers to cases where the act was unintentional.
But Mārkaṇḍeya has stated regarding intentional acts:
"Having eaten during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a twice-born man shall perform the Sāntapana penance;
having eaten during the period of impurity of a Kṣatriya, a sevenfold Kṛcchra is prescribed."
Having eaten during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya, one should perform the Mahāsāntapana penance;
likewise, having eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, one should observe the vow for three months.
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha: "Having eaten during the period of impurity (sūtaka) of a Śūdra, one should perform a vow for six months;
likewise, having eaten during that of a Vaiśya, one should perform a vow for three months."
Likewise, having eaten [at the house] of a Kṣatriya, one should observe the vow for two months;
and having eaten during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, one should observe the vow for one month.
Thus, this refers to the subject of repeated practice.
And this expiation is to be understood as occurring after the period of impurity;
for one who eats food even once during the period of impurity of Brāhmaṇas and others, his own impurity lasts for as long as theirs.
For it is recorded by Viṣṇu: "Upon the cessation of the period of impurity, however, one should perform the penance" (ViDh 22.8–9).
Regarding the eating of food from those such as childless persons, Likhita says:
"Having eaten the food of a usurer, of one who does not observe vows,
of one who has no son, and likewise of a Śūdra, one shall fast for three nights."
Likewise:
"A twice-born man who eats the food of one who has ceased cooking for others, yet delights in cooking for others—that is, a non-cook—must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus it is said.
And this refers to the subject of practice;
the definition of one who has desisted from cooking for others and so forth was stated by that very same [author]:
"Having taken up the sacred fire and performed the ritual installation, one should not fail to perform the five sacrifices."
He is proclaimed by the sages as one who has desisted from the ripening of others' [offerings].
But he who, having performed the five sacrifices, subsists on the food of others,
is one who constantly rises early yet remains devoted to the cooking of others.
"He who gives [food] while avoiding the duties and conduct of a householder is proclaimed by the sages, who know the essence of Dharma, to be an *apaca* (one who does not cook).
As for what Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya said regarding the eating of food from a student (*brahmacārin*) and others:
"Both the ascetic (yati) and the student (brahmacārī) are the owners of cooked food;
one must not eat the food of these two, and having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the eating of the food of one who does not perform the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and other rites, Bharadvāja says: "If the deities do not eat from one's [offering] for a fortnight or even a month, a twice-born man who eats the food of that evil-minded person shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Thus, both of these refer to the subject of repeated practice; however,
regarding the eating of the food of those who are not included in the previous enumeration but are habitually inclined toward prohibited conduct:
Having eaten the food of a Brahmin who is devoid of proper conduct and who practices forbidden acts, a twice-born man should observe a fast for one day.
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Regarding the practice [of this penance] for one year, it is stated in that very same *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"For one who is guilty of a minor offense (*upapātaka*), [the penance lasts] for one continuous year."

"Having eaten [forbidden] food, a twice-born man should perform the Parāka penance as a means of purification. This collection of vows, which is stated without specific distinction in the section on penances for eating what should not be eaten, applies specifically to the foremost of the twice-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
For Kṣatriyas and the other castes, however, it is reduced by one-quarter at each successive stage.
To a Brahmin, however, the full amount should be given; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as one-quarter less;
for a Vaiśya, half; and for those of the Śūdra caste, a single quarter is prescribed.
Thus, according to the recollection of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the section on penance for consuming forbidden food.
At the time of enumerating the causes [of sin], those acts that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) and so forth were enumerated immediately after the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Regarding those, the penances are now stated.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra; if done unintentionally, one should perform the Prājāpatya."
"For acts causing mixture [of castes], for using an unworthy vessel, and for acts causing defilement, the Aindava penance is the purification for one month;
for acts causing impurity, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days. (MDh 11.125–26).
The word "anyatama" (one or another) is to be connected with every [clause].
Yama has also stated a specific rule in this regard:
"Having committed an act that causes the loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), one should eat barley-gruel for a month,
or else perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance as an expiation."
Having committed an act that renders one unworthy of receiving gifts, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
"Purification for acts causing impurity is achieved through the Śītakṛcchra or the Mahāsāntapana;
for acts causing defilement, the Taptakṛcchra is the means of purification. Thus it is said.
Bṛhaspati has also stated a specific rule regarding acts that cause loss of caste:
"Having inflicted a wound upon a Brāhmaṇa, having killed a donkey or similar animal,
or having accepted wealth from censurable persons, one should perform half of the Kṛcchra penance."

The scope of these penances for acts causing loss of caste and so forth, as prescribed by Manu and others, must be distinguished according to considerations such as the caste and capacity of the offender.
Thus, the penance for consuming forbidden food and similar acts, as held in the heart of Yogīndra, has been shown in brief. (3.289)
Now we shall follow the subject at hand.
Five types of sinful categories have been mentioned: mortal sin (mahāpātaka), heinous sin (atipātaka), secondary sin (anupātaka), minor sin (upapātaka), and miscellaneous sin (prakīrṇaka).
Having thus described the fourfold penance (*prāyaścitta*), he now states the penance for miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*) as they arise in due order:
"One who has traveled in a donkey-cart or a camel-cart shall bathe in water and perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*)."
Having bathed naked, having eaten, and having gone to a woman by day;
"kharayāna" means a vehicle yoked with donkeys;
"uṣṭrayāna" means a vehicle yoked with camels, such as a chariot or a cart—traveling on a road by means of these [incurs a penance].

Having gone naked, bathed, and eaten during the day, and having engaged in sexual intercourse with his own wife, he becomes pure by plunging into a pond, a river, or similar body of water and performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
And this refers to an act committed intentionally.

For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "Having intentionally mounted a camel vehicle or a donkey vehicle, one becomes pure by immersing oneself in water with one's clothes on and performing breath control (prāṇāyāma). (MDh 11.202).
If it is done unintentionally, a mere bath is prescribed.
However, in the case of actually riding a donkey, a double repetition [of the penance] should be prescribed, because of its greater gravity. (3.290)
Furthermore:

Having addressed a guru with "huṃ," or addressed a Brahmin as "thou," or having defeated him in debate, or having bound him with a garment, one must quickly propitiate him and fast for a day. (YDh 3.291)

Having addressed one's teacher, father, or others with the term "thou," and having reviled them by using the singular form of the pronoun *yuṣmad*— saying "you have spoken thus" or "this was done by you"—
whether toward a Brahmin, an elder, an equal, or a younger person.
Or, having rebuked him angrily with "Hūṃ! Sit silent, Hūṃ! Do not speak much," and having defeated the Brahmin through disputation and cavil, which have victory as their fruit;
Having bound him around the neck even with a cloth of soft touch,
and having quickly appeased him by prostrating at his feet and other such acts, one should cause him to abandon his anger for the duration of the day.
One should fast; one should spend the entire day without eating.
As for that which was stated by Yama: "Having defeated a Brāhmaṇa in debate, if one desires to perform an expiation..."
Having fasted for three nights and bathed, one should prostrate and seek his favor.
Thus, that refers to the object of practice. 3.291
Furthermore:
"In raising a staff against a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; in striking him down, an *atikṛcchra*;
in drawing blood, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and when there is internal bleeding, a *kṛcchra*. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.292)
If one raises a staff or similar weapon with the intent to kill, the *kṛcchra* penance is the means of purification;
if one strikes or causes a fall, it is the *atikṛcchra*;
and if blood is shed, causing the flow of blood, it is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
Even when the blood is internal, the *kṛcchra* penance is the cause of purification.
Bṛhaspati has also stated a specific rule in this regard:
"If one strikes [another] with wood or other objects but no wound is produced, one should perform the *kṛcchra*."

"If the bones are broken, it shall be an *atikṛcchra*; but if a limb is severed, it is a *parāka*. Regarding a kick with the foot, Yama says: "Having touched a Brāhmaṇa with one's foot, desiring to perform the penance..."
Having fasted for a day, bathed, and prostrated, one should seek his favor. Thus it is said.
Manu, however, has shown other penances for miscellaneous offenses:
"But one who, being distressed, has discharged semen without water or even in water, becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow" (MDh 11.203).
"Without water" means even when water is not available.
"Bodily [excretions]" refers to urine, feces, and so forth.
This refers to cases where there is no intentional desire [to discharge them].
But if one intentionally,
while in a state of distress, consumes human excrement when water is unavailable,
he shall fast for one day and enter the water together with his clothes.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Yama.
As for the statement of Sumantu, "For one who urinates in water or fire, [the penance is] the *taptakṛcchra*," that refers to a case where one is not afflicted or to a case of habitual practice.
Regarding the omission of daily obligatory rites such as the Śrauta sacrifices, Manu says:
"Upon the transgression of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda,
and upon the violation of the vows of a Snātaka, the penance is fasting" (MDh 11.204).

In the case of Śrauta rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and Smārta rites such as the occasional (anitya) homas, there is a combination of fasting with the specific expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) prescribed for each, such as the Iṣṭis;
this also applies to the observances of a Snātaka.
"One should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes when one has the means," and so forth; these were previously mentioned.
Regarding the observances of a *snātaka*, Kratu also stated:
For each one of these transgressions of the rules of conduct, one becomes purified by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.

Regarding the non-performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), Bṛhaspati says: "A householder who, while not being ill and possessing wealth, eats every day without having performed the great sacrifices, is purified by half a *kṛcchra* penance."
"He who, having established the sacred fires, does not perform the ritual attendance on them on the festival days (parvan),
or who does not approach his wife during her season (ṛtu), shall also perform half a *kṛcchra* penance.
Regarding the death of a second or subsequent wife, Devala says:

"If one should cremate a second wife with the sacrificial fires while the first is still living, that act is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor. Regarding the false accusation against one's own wife, Yama says:
If a man, out of anger, should call his own wife "unapproachable," a Brahmin must perform the Prājāpatya penance, and a Kṣatriya for nine days.
A Vaiśya, however, should perform it for six nights, while a Śūdra should perform it for three nights. Thus it is said.
Regarding not bathing before eating and similar matters, Hārīta says:
"Carrying an empty water-pot while not having bathed and while eating food,
purification shall occur after one day and night, as well as by means of daily recitation."
Regarding the unequal distribution of gifts and so forth out of affection or other motives among those seated in a single row, Yama said:
"One should not give unequally in the row, nor should one beg, nor should one cause others to beg;
the beggar, the one who causes begging, and the giver—none of these indeed go to heaven."
One is liberated from that karma by means of the *prājāpatya* penance;
this applies also to one who destroys a bridge over a river and to one who creates an obstacle to a maiden's marriage.

"And no atonement is possible for one who commits an equal or unequal offense against these three; yet, if they seek restoration, the twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, subsisting on food obtained through begging. Thus it is said.
A *saṃkrama* is a path for descending into water.
Regarding one who makes the level uneven during acts of worship and the like,
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said in reference to the sighting of a rainbow and similar occasions:
If one should point out the rainbow as the fire of the Palāśa tree to another person,
the penance is a fast for a day and night, and the sacrificial fee is a bow and a staff.
Regarding conversation with those who have fallen from their status and so forth, Gautama said:
"One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous; having conversed with them, one should meditate mentally upon those who perform meritorious deeds."
Or he may converse with a Brāhmaṇa.
For [the offenses of] violating the bed, stealing land or wealth, and killing, there shall be separate years [of penance] (GDh 9.16–18; 22.28).
For obstructing the acquisition of a wife, food, or wealth, or for causing their destruction, one must observe the standard vow of celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*) for one year in each case.
Likewise, another Smṛti text prescribes an expiation for voiding feces or urine and so forth without the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*):
"If a twice-born man becomes impure while lacking his sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), [he must perform penance]."
The expiation is either fasting for a day and night, or the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.

In that regard, the rule is that for one who has been defiled by food from above, there is a fast; for one defiled by food from below, there is the recitation of the Gāyatrī during the drinking of water and so forth.
However, in the case of unintentional acts:
"For one who drinks, urinates, or eats while not wearing the sacred thread..."
Three sets of three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), six [sets], and three nights, in sequence.
Thus, what is stated in another Smṛti should be observed:
"If one rises after eating without having performed purification and sipping water,
or if one rises from a fast without having sipped water..."
One should perform an immediate bath; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
This should be understood as stated in another Smṛti.
Regarding the release of a thief or similar offenders, Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon releasing one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night."
The domestic priest shall observe a three-night fast for punishing one who should not be punished;
the king shall observe a three-night fast for failing to punish one who deserves punishment.
"One with deformed nails and one with black teeth, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, should extract [them]" (VaDh 19.40–43;
20.6). "They should extract" means they should perform the extraction of the deformed teeth and nails.
Regarding the eating in a row [of diners] where a thief, an outcast, or others are present, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Any excellent twice-born man who eats in the row of one unworthy of the row becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Thus it is said.
Regarding the subject of indigo, Āpastamba says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa wears a garment dyed with indigo on his limbs,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
If the juice of indigo should enter anyone through the pores of the skin,
the common purification for all three castes is the Taptakṛcchra penance.
The keeping, the selling, and living by that trade as one's livelihood—by these acts a Brahmin incurs a fall; he removes it by three *kṛcchra* penances.
If one should pierce the body of a Brāhmaṇa with indigo wood,
and blood is seen there, the twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"In the case of women, there is no fault in using indigo on a bed for the purpose of pleasure and sexual enjoyment.
Thus it was also said by Bhṛgu:
"Indigo worn by a woman on a bed does not cause fault for a Brāhmaṇa."
"In the case of a king or a Vaiśya, wearing [blue-dyed cloth] is permitted except on festival days.
Likewise, there is an exception based on specific types of garments: "The use of indigo dye does not cause fault in the case of woolen blankets or silk thread."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Regarding the mounting of a bed, vehicle, seat, or sandals fashioned from the wood of the Brahma-tree, Śaṅkha says:
"Having placed upon them a bed, a vehicle, a seat, or likewise sandals..."
A twice-born man who has touched a Palāśa tree shall observe a vow for three nights.
But a Kṣatriya who, intent on saving his life, turns his back in battle,
or one who cuts down a fruit-bearing tree, shall perform a vow for one year.

If one should pass between two Brahmins, or between a Brahmin and the sacred fire, or between a husband and wife, or between a cow and an excellent twice-born man, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
"At the time of the fire-oblation, likewise during milking, during Vedic study, and at the taking of a wife—
if a twice-born man passes between [the husband and wife], he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Here,
"milking" refers to that which is an ancillary part of the Sānnāyya sacrifice and so forth.
And this [remedy] pertains to the subject of practice (*abhyāsa*).
Regarding the sight of ill omens (*ariṣṭa*) such as the sun with gaps and so forth, Śaṅkha says: "Upon seeing bad dreams, ill omens, and the like, one should give ghee and gold."
Regarding travel to certain specific regions, Devala says: "Having gone to Sindhu, Sauvīra, and Saurāṣṭra, as well as those dwelling in the borderlands,
and to Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and Āndhra, one deserves a purificatory rite."
And this should be understood as applying except during a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*).
Regarding the sight of one's own excrement and so forth, Yama says:
"One should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at one's own feces."
"Having seen [these], one should look at the sun, a cow, fire, and likewise a Brahmin.
Śaṅkha also says:
"Having placed his foot forward and having likewise placed the fire below..."
Having wiped his feet with *kuśa* grass, he shall observe a vow for one day. Thus it is said.

Regarding the reception of Kṣatriyas and others, Hārīta says: "Upon greeting a Kṣatriya, one should fast for a day and a night; upon greeting a Vaiśya, for two nights; and upon greeting a Śūdra, there is a fast for three nights."

Likewise, there shall be a fast for three nights for saluting one who is reclining on a bed, one whose feet are placed in sandals or shoes, one who is impure from food remnants, one situated in darkness, one performing a *śrāddha*, or one intent on recitation (*japa*) or the worship of gods; and likewise for three nights for eating elsewhere after having been invited elsewhere.
This same rule applies even when one who holds sacrificial fuel, flowers, and so forth in his hands offers a salutation:

"One should not salute a twice-born man who is holding sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, clarified butter, water, earth, food, or unbroken grains in his hands, nor one who is engaged in silent recitation (japa) or burnt offerings (homa)."
Thus, according to Āpastamba, because of its mention alongside recitations (*japa*) and other such acts, this same expiation applies even to one who offers a salutation; for it is said:

"One should not offer a salutation with a water-pot in hand, nor while wandering for alms, nor with flowers, clarified butter, or similar items in hand, nor while impure, nor while engaged in recitation."
"One should not do so while performing rites for the gods or ancestors, nor while lying down," for this too is prohibited by Śaṅkha.
Other such statements should likewise be sought from other Smṛtis; they are not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. (3.292)
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous penances (*prakīrṇaka-prāyaścitta*).

Since causes (*nimitta*) are infinite and it is impossible to state a penance for every single individual case, he says this in order to provide knowledge of specific penances regarding both those subjects already taught and those not yet taught, by way of general instruction.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin,
an expiation (prāyaścitta) should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been stated.

Whatever collection of expiations has been mentioned or will be mentioned hereafter, that should be applied after considering the place and other factors, so that there is no loss of life for the performer.

It does not exist in that way; rather, it must be conceived as being in relation to a specific object, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the cessation of the primary cause (pradhāna). And so he will state later.
"Subsisting on air, standing during the day, and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun. (YDh 3.311).

In this regard, if dwelling in water were prescribed for those living near the Himavat mountains, or during seasons such as the winter when it is afflicted by extreme cold, then loss of life might occur; therefore, one should arrange for dwelling in water by avoiding such places and times.

Likewise, even on account of a difference in age, if a twelve-year penance were prescribed for one who is ninety years old or for one who is less than twelve years of age, then their life-breaths would perish; therefore, that penance should be assigned to those of a different age.
For this very reason, it is stated in another Smṛti that there is a reduction of the penance for those who are elderly and so forth, such that in some cases it is half and in others a quarter;
this has already been explained in detail previously.
Likewise, [the penance varies] depending on one's capacity for giving wealth, performing austerities, and so forth.
Furthermore, for one who is destitute, it is not possible [to say] that "wealth or sufficient food exists in the vessel," and so forth;

likewise, for one whose bile and other humors are aggravated, [the performance of] *parāka* and similar penances is impossible, nor is *japa* and the like possible for women, *śūdras*, and others. For this very reason:
It has been stated: "Being unable to give elephants and the like as gifts, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for the purification of each [offense]. Likewise, [it is said]:

"Women and the sick deserve only half of the penance"— thus, in another Smṛti, a reduction of the penance is prescribed for one incapable of performing austerity. Likewise, sin [is categorized] by way of its form as a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth, and by way of its nature as being committed with full awareness (*sapratyaya*), without full awareness (*apratyaya*), once, or repeatedly (*sakṛd-abhyāsa*).
Having carefully examined this through a thorough investigation of all the treatises on Dharma, the penance should be determined;
therein,
whatever has been prescribed for an unintentional act, that very same penance is doubled when committed intentionally.
In the case of repeated intentional acts, it should be understood that the penance is fourfold, according to other Smṛti texts. Likewise,
he who falsely accuses another of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) or a minor sin (upapātaka) shall subsist on water alone for one month.

Thus it has been stated; in that regard, since it is improper for the same penance to apply to both a major sin (*mahāpātaka*) and a minor sin (*upapātaka*), a reduction of the month-long vow (*māsika-vrata*) must be conceived for the minor sin in comparison to the major sin.
And where [the act occurs] spontaneously through laughing, yawning, crying out, clapping, and so forth—
One should act accordingly;
one should not bathe in the waters of the ocean, nor should one have one's beard and so forth shaved.
A husband who performs these acts while his wife is pregnant will certainly become childless.
In such cases, no expiation has been prescribed;
even there, an expiation must be determined with due regard to the location and other relevant factors.
Now, is there not found any collection of occasions for which no atonement has been stated?
One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins,
indeed for those arising from minor offenses (upapātaka) and for that which is not specifically prescribed.
This is because an expiation is to be prescribed even for those cases where no specific atonement has been mentioned;

furthermore, Gautama has established that in cases where no instruction is given, these very [penances]—such as the one-day fast and others—should be performed optionally: "In the absence of a specific injunction, these very [penances] should be performed as alternatives" (GDh 19.18).

It is said: True, there is indeed a general instruction regarding expiation; nevertheless, because factors such as place and time must be taken into account in every case, there certainly remains occasion for specific determination.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to apply a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in every case of laughing and so forth,
because the cause is minor; therefore, a reduction should be conceived in accordance with the gravity of the sin, or another expiation (prāyaścitta) should be prescribed.
Now, how can there be lightness of sin such that a reduction in penance might be prescribed?
Nor should it be said that this is because the penance is small, for [the reduction] occurs precisely because no specific atonement has been stated.

True; however, the relative gravity or lightness of a fault is indeed easily understood through the mention of explanatory passages (arthavāda), as well as by considering factors such as whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and its attendant consequences.
Likewise, the relative gravity or lightness of the penance is determined by the corresponding decrease or increase in the punishment.
Just as it has been stated that for acts such as threatening a Brahmin and so forth when the object belongs to one's own caste, penances such as the Prājāpatya are prescribed;
in that regard, when such acts as threatening are performed either in the direct order (anuloma) or the inverse order (pratiloma), [the following applies].

Or, when [the offense is committed] by those such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, then, precisely because a gradation of punishment is observed, one understands the smallness or greatness of the fault; thus, the heavy or light nature of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must also be determined accordingly. And the heavy or light nature of the punishment has indeed been demonstrated.
"In cases of defamation involving the reverse order [of castes], the fine shall be double or triple," and so forth. (YDh 2.207) // 3.293 //

Thus, the expiation for one who has fallen due to great sins (mahāpātaka) and the like has been stated; however, as to what should be done for one who, out of arrogance, does not wish to perform this, he says:
The kinsmen of one who has fallen from his caste shall carry out a water-pot of a female slave outside the village;
they shall exclude him from all social functions.

(YDh 3.294) Those who are the kinsmen and relatives of the one who has fallen—those on the side of the father and the mother—shall all assemble together and have a female slave... [carry out the water-pot].
A female servant sent by her *sapiṇḍas* and others should carry out a jar or pot full of water from the village;
this should be done on the fourth, sixth, eighth, and other such lunar days (the *riktā-tithis*) during the fifth part of the day, in the presence of the teacher and other elders.
The water-rite for an outcaste must be performed outside by his *sapiṇḍas* and kinsmen.
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "On a censurable day, in the evening, in the presence of kinsmen, officiating priests, and gurus.
Alternatively, a female slave may herself pour out [the water] when directed by a sapinda or other relative.
As Manu has said:
"A female slave should kick over a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
[the relatives] should observe impurity together with their kinsmen for one day and night" (MDh 11.184).
The phrase "like a *preta*" is intended to establish that one should face south and keep the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*); furthermore,
that pouring of water should be understood as occurring after the *preta*-rites, such as the offering of water and rice balls (*piṇḍa*).
His preceptors of knowledge and his blood relations, having assembled, shall perform all the funeral rites beginning with the water libations;
they shall overturn his alms-bowl.
A slave or a laborer, having brought a bowl from the refuse heap and filled it from the pot of a female slave...
Facing south, he should step with his foot [upon the water], uttering the name [of the deceased]: "I make so-and-so free from water.
All those who are teachers of knowledge or blood relations should touch him, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) and with their topknots loosened.
And they should look [at them];
having touched water, they should enter the village— so from the traditional teaching of Gautama (GDh 20.2–7).
And this abandonment is to be understood as occurring if, even when urged by his kinsmen, he does not perform the penance.

Having publicly proclaimed his faults in the presence of that teacher’s relatives and the king, and having repeatedly exhorted him, "Obtain [proper] conduct," if he should nevertheless remain of unsettled mind, then one should overturn his vessel (deprive him of his status), according to the Smṛti of Śaṅkha.
Then, once he has received water and fallen [from his status], they should exclude him from all activities, such as conversation, sitting together, and so forth; that is, they should avoid him.
And so says Manu:
"And they shall desist from conversing with him, sitting together on the same seat,
giving him an inheritance, and even engaging in his worldly affairs" (MDh 11.185).
If one converses with him out of affection or similar motives, then a penance must be performed.

"Beyond this, having conversed with him, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī if it was done unintentionally; but if it was done intentionally, for three nights" (GDh 20.8–9). // 3.294 //
But when, through the abandonment of kinsmen or otherwise, detachment has arisen and penance has been performed,
then what should be done?
To this he says:
When he has completed his vow and returned, they should pour out a new jar [of water] for him;

they should not despise him, nor should they live with him in any way whatsoever. When he has performed the penance and returned to the presence of his kinsmen, his sapindas and others, together with him, [should offer] a new, unblemished [jar].
They should pour out a jar full of water.
This pouring out is to be understood as occurring after bathing in a meritorious pool or similar place;
however, when the penance has been performed, [one should give] a new jar full of water.
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "They should throw [the bones] into a sacred body of water together with that very person after bathing" (MDh 11.187).
However, a specific rule has been stated by Gautama:

But for one who is purified by means of a penance, once he is purified, they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most sacred pool or from flowing rivers, and then cause him to touch that water;
thereafter, they should give that vessel to him.

Having accepted that, he should mutter [the mantra]: "Peaceful is heaven, peaceful is earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; that which is the radiant realm, that I accept here. With these *yajus* verses, with the *pāvamānī*, *taratsamandī*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns, he should offer clarified butter into the fire and give gold as a gift.
And he should give a cow to the teacher.
However, he for whom the penance ends with death shall be purified upon dying; this very same water of pacification is prescribed for all minor offenses (upapātaka). (GDh 20.10–17)
Then, once he has performed the penance, they should not despise him;
likewise, in all affairs such as buying and selling, they should carry on transactions with him. (3.295)
He states an extension of the previously mentioned rule regarding the abandonment of outcasts and others:
"This very same rule for men who have become outcasts is proclaimed for women as well;
they should be given a dwelling near the house, food, clothing, and protection. (YDh 3.296)
The same rule regarding the abandonment of men— including the procedure for offering funeral cakes and water— and the procedure for readmitting those who have performed penance,
should be understood to apply to women who have fallen from their status as well;
however, there is this distinction.

To those women who have fallen [from their caste] and for whom the water-libation and other rites have been performed, a small hut made of grass and leaves should be provided near the main house; likewise,
food sufficient merely to sustain life and a soiled garment, along with the restriction against intercourse with another man, must be given.
It must be given. 3.296.

Now, one might ask: "Who are those women who have fallen such that this rule of abandonment applies to them? To this, he says: "Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming the husband—these also are certainly specific acts leading to loss of caste for women. (YDh 3.297)

"Approaching a man of inferior caste, causing an abortion, and the killing of a husband—even if he is not a Brāhmaṇa—or of a husband who is not a Brāhmaṇa: these are the causes of loss of caste (patananimitta) specific to women.
By the use of the word 'even' (api), it is implied that those which are causes of loss of caste for a man [are also applicable]."

Major sins (mahāpātaka), secondary major sins (atipātaka), minor sins (anupātaka), and repeated minor sins (upapātaka) and so forth— these too certainly and inevitably become causes for the downfall of women.
For this very reason, Śaunaka says:
Whatever causes for a man's downfall are the same for women as well; however, a Brāhmaṇī woman falls even more severely by serving a man of a lower caste. As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins of a woman in this world."
"Killing one's husband, killing an embryo, and causing the abortion of one's own fetus" (VaDh 28.7)—
thus the mention of "killing an embryo" (bhrūṇahatyā) is made for the sake of illustration, and not for the purpose of excluding other great sins (mahāpātaka) and so forth.
This is for the purpose of refuting the claim that [such conduct] is a cause of downfall. Furthermore, by that same [author], it was said:
"But four [types of women] are to be avoided: those who have gone to a disciple and those who have gone to a guru."
"Especially one who is hostile and one who has approached a degraded man" (VaDh 21.10).
Thus, it is stated that there is abandonment only of these four;
even in that case, among those women who do not wish to perform penance, [the rule applies].

The intention is that one should effect the abandonment of only the four types of female disciples—such as those who provide clothing, food, a house, or shelter—as a means of livelihood, by cutting off such support, and not of others.

Consequently, it is understood that for other women who have fallen from their status, even if they do not perform penance, one must still provide them with a dwelling near one's own house and so forth. (3.297)
"One should not despise him, nor should one associate with him in any way"—this states an exception to that rule:

"One should not, however, dwell with those who harm one who has sought refuge, children, or women, even if they have completed their vows, nor with these when they are joined by ungrateful persons. (YDh 3.298)

This prohibition is based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*): one should not engage in social intercourse even with those whose faults have been exhausted through penance, provided they include those who have committed murder against those who sought refuge and the ungrateful;
for why would [the scripture] not issue such a command?
For there is no excessive burden for a scriptural injunction;
and therefore, although the expiation for killing women who are unchaste is indeed very slight, nevertheless, this prohibition of social intercourse is based on a direct scriptural statement. (3.298)

Having thus explained the specific rule regarding women by way of digression, he now states the specific rule for the actual procedure of completing the vow: "When the water-pot has been discarded, he should, standing in the midst of his kinsmen, first give fodder to the cows; for this is the true honoring of one who has already been honored by the cows. (YDh 3.299)
When the jar has been removed from the lake and another full jar has been brought down, he who has completed his vow, standing in the midst of the sapindas and others, should give fodder to the cows;
for him who has first been honored— that is, worshipped— by them, there shall afterwards be an honoring by his kinsmen.
He should perform an act of hospitality toward the cows by feeding them the very fodder given by him;
if the cows do not accept the fodder given by him, then he should perform the penance once again.
As Hārīta says:
"Taking grass with his own head, he should give it to the cows; if they accept it, then they should let him go."
Otherwise, it is not so; this is the intended meaning. (3.299)
Having described the collection of specific penances for each of the five classes of sins beginning with the *mahāpātaka*s, [the author] now states the duty common to all penances:
"One whose fault is well-known shall perform a penance approved by an assembly (*parṣad*). (YDh 3.300ab)
He who possesses a fault known and recognized by others as being such that it must be remedied by a specific agent— that person should perform the vow prescribed by the assembly.
Even if he himself is clever in discerning the meaning of the entire treatise, he nevertheless [approaches] the presence of the assembly.
Having approached her and deliberated with her, he should do exactly what she approves. Regarding such an approach, a specific rule has been stated by Aṅgiras:
"When a sin has been committed that is beyond doubt, one should not eat without having confessed it."
One who eats increases their sin as long as they do not confess it before an assembly.
"Having bathed with his clothes on while restraining his speech, wearing wet garments and being composed, the man, having been authorized by the assembly, should confess the whole truth;
then, having taken up the vow once more, he should likewise perform the penance after bathing. Thus it is said.
And the public proclamation [of the penance] should be performed immediately after the presentation of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the assembly.
As Parāśara says:
"The sinner, having given a cow and likewise a bull, should proclaim his sin."
And this refers to the category of minor offenses (upapātaka);
for major sins (mahāpātaka) and the like, a greater penance should be prescribed. As for that which was stated:
"Therefore, a twice-born man who has incurred sin, having immersed himself once in the water..."
Having made his sin known to the assemblies and having given something as a gift, he should observe the vow.
Thus, that refers to the subject of miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka*).
And the nature of the assembly has been shown by Manu:
"One learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, and a reciter of the Dharma..."
And the three preceding stages of life—this assembly consists of at least ten members.
A *haituka* is one who knows the true principles of the meaning of the Mīmāṃsā and other sciences;
a *tarkī* is one skilled in the science of Nyāya.
Likewise, another two assemblies were also shown by him:
those who know the Ṛgveda, those who know the Yajurveda, and those who know the Sāmaveda.
"Another assembly should be understood as that which resolves doubts regarding the Dharma" (MDh 12.112).
Likewise:
"Even a single person who knows the Veda, if he is composed, may determine the Dharma."

"That should be known as the supreme dharma, not that which has arisen from tens of thousands of the ignorant. (MDh 12.113) And the application of these assemblies is determined either by their availability or by the gravity of the offense, such as a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*).
As for what is stated in another Smṛti:
For major sins, the assembly shall consist of one hundred members; for great sins and the like, one thousand;
for minor offenses, fifty; and for very slight offenses, it shall be correspondingly small.

Thus, that [statement] also aims at demonstrating the gravity or lightness of the assembly (parṣad) according to the severity of the fault, such as a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), and not for the purpose of fixing a numerical limit,
because that would result in a contradiction with the great legal codes (smṛti) of Manu and others.
Likewise, Devala has shown a distinction in this matter:
"In cases of minor offenses, the Brahmins themselves shall prescribe the expiation;
but in major cases, both the king and the Brahmins shall determine it after due investigation."
And by that assembly, the vow must certainly be prescribed for those twice-born ones who, though knowing the penances for those who are afflicted and seeking them,
do not grant them; they go to the same state as those [who refuse].
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Aṅgiras,
the assembly must instruct the vow only after having understood [the case];
for he who, without knowing the treatises on Dharma, bestows an expiation—
Having performed the penance, he becomes purified; he should then approach the assembly with his transgression.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha.
However, regarding the instruction in dharma for Kṣatriyas and others who have committed sins, a specific rule has been shown by Aṅgiras:
"A Brāhmaṇa should quickly [instruct] a Kṣatriya or other [caste] who has committed a sin in accordance with justice."
Having placed the Brāhmaṇa in between, one should prescribe the entire vow.
"Having approached a Śūdra, one should always grant expiation preceded by [instruction in] Dharma, excluding recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa).
In that context, for those whose habit is the performance of sacrifices and other rites, recitation and so forth must be prescribed.

But for others, there is austerity. Those devoted to ritual action and those devoted to austerity who have occasionally fallen into sin are given special instruction in recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth.
One should especially give the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances to those Brahmins who merely bear the name, being ignorant and destitute of wealth.
Thus concludes the section on public penances;
now, having explained the secret penances, [the author] shall describe the series of vows that destroy well-known sins.
The sage spoke, removing the multitude of sins committed in secret.
In this regard, he first states the dharma common to all secret vows:
"But one whose fault is not made known by others should perform a secret vow.
He whose fault is not disclosed (*anabhikhyāta*) by persons other than the perpetrator should practice a secret (*rahasya*), that is, non-public, expiation.
Therefore, since she too is an agent in such acts as sexual union with women, it should be understood that for one whose fault remains unknown to others, this is a secret vow (*rahasyavrata*).
In this regard, if the performer is himself proficient in the *dharmaśāstra*, then, having ascertained [the offense] from another, he should perform the penance appropriate to his own cause.

But one who is himself ignorant, having learned through some pretext from another that "a secret act such as the killing of a Brahmin was committed by someone in private," [should proceed accordingly].
One should observe the secret vow (*raho-vrata*).

For this very reason, even for women and *śūdras*, the qualification [for knowledge] is established through this same path, since the attainment of the knowledge of the secret vow is possible for them as well.

Nor should it be argued that women and Śūdras lack eligibility because secret vows (*rahasyavrata*) consist primarily of recitation (*japa*) and the like, and such [recitation] is impossible for those two who are unlearned;
for it is not the case that secret vows are exclusively [restricted to the learned].

The primacy of recitation and the like is established because giving and other such acts are also taught, and because breath control and other practices mentioned by Gautama are likewise possible. (GDh 24–25)
For others as well, merely knowing the deity, seer, and meter of a mantra is useful for their specific application, but not for other matters;
for indeed, a cognition concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is of no use in the construction of a tank or similar works.
This applies to the knowledge of the deity and so forth.
This must certainly be taken into account:
"He who teaches or even recites [the Veda] without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, and the application, becomes a sinner."

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Vyāsa; here too, since no specific food is mentioned, milk and the like are to be understood; since no specific time is mentioned, periods such as a year and so forth; and since no specific place is mentioned, mountains and the like—as set forth by Gautama and others—are to be sought out, just as in the case of the public penances (prakāśaprāyaścitta). (3.300)
Having thus stated the common rules for all secret penances, he now describes the secret penances for killing a Brahmin and other offenses, following the same sequence as the public penances:
"A killer of a Brahmin, having fasted for three nights, shall recite the Aghamarṣaṇa [hymn]."
One shall be purified within the water by giving a milch cow;

having fasted for three nights while remaining within the water, one should mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn— seen by the great seer, consisting of the triplet beginning with "Truth and Reality" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*), composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and having Bhāvavṛtta as its deity—
and at the end of the three nights, having given a milch cow.
A Brahmin is purified by recitation;
and the recitation must be performed three times while submerged within the water.
As Sumantu has said:
One who has killed a god, a twice-born man, or a teacher shall immerse himself in water and repeat the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* hymn three times.

Having approached his mother, a sister, a maternal aunt, a daughter-in-law, a female friend, or having committed any other forbidden sexual act, he shall likewise perform the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* while submerged within the water.
"By repeating that three times, one becomes purified from this"— this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally. As for that which was stated by Manu:

"Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), performed daily with the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava for a month, purify even the slayer of an embryo"— this [rule] also should be understood to apply to this very same case for one who is unable to perform the gift of a cow (godāna).

As for that which was stated by Gautama after prescribing the thirty-six-night vow— namely, "In the case of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, or violating the Guru’s bed, one should, while observing that very vow, bathe with breath-restraints and mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn" (GDh 24.10)— that refers to the case of a single instance of killing committed unintentionally. As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana:

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, bathed, pure, and wearing clean garments, he should smear a sacrificial mound at the water's edge; then, wearing a single wet garment, with hands purified by cow-dung, facing the sun, he should study the Aghamarṣaṇa for self-recitation. He should recite it one hundred times in the morning, one hundred times at midday, and one hundred times in the afternoon; and when the stars have risen, he should consume a handful of barley-gruel.

He should consume it. By doing so, he is freed from minor offenses (*upapātaka*) committed knowingly or unknowingly after seven nights; after twelve nights, he is freed from the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), with the exception of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, and stealing gold; and after twenty-one nights, he overcomes even those [three]. (BDh 3.9.4; 3.5.3–6)

Thus, this refers to the case of intentional action, or to the case of unintentionally killing a learned teacher (*śrotriya*) or one engaged in a sacrifice (*savanastha*). As for that which was stated by Manu:
"Or, having purified himself, he should recite the Vedic Saṃhitā three times in the forest..."
"One who has been purified by three *parāka* penances is released from all sins" (MDh 11.259).
This refers to the intentional killing of a *śrotriya* and others, or otherwise to the intentional repetition [of such acts]. As for that which was stated by Bṛhad-Viṣṇu:

"Having committed the murder of a Brahmin, one should go out from the village toward the east or the north, kindle a fire with abundant fuel, and offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter while reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn;
then one becomes purified from this."
That [penance] refers to the killing of one who is devoid of virtues, or it refers to the case of one who was a benefactor.
As for that which was stated by Yama:
"One should fast for three days, self-controlled, approaching water three times a day."
By reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa three times, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, that [penance] refers to a virtuous slayer who has killed one devoid of virtue, or it pertains to the instigator or the consenter.

As for what was stated by Hārīta— that when any one of the great sins (mahāpātaka), extreme sins (atipātaka), minor sins (anupātaka), or secondary sins (upapātaka) occurs, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times— [that applies to the same case].
The injunction "one should recite" refers to that which has the agent as its cause.

In this same manner, other Smṛti statements should also be investigated and divided according to their respective subjects; they are not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. This...

In these cases, the entire set of penances prescribed for the sacrifice must be performed less by one-fourth when the woman belongs to the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya castes, when she is an Ātreyī, when she is the wife of one who has maintained the sacred fires, when she is pregnant, or when the fetus was killed unintentionally. (3.301)
He states another expiation:
"Or else, subsisting on air for a day, standing in water, one should offer forty oblations of clarified butter with the mantra 'To the body-hairs, svāhā'. (YDh 3.302)

Alternatively, having fasted for a day and night and stayed in the water during the night, one should emerge from the water in the morning and offer forty oblations of clarified butter— five oblations for each of the eight mantras beginning with *lomabhyaḥ svāhā*— thus performing forty such offerings.
This [rite] also pertains to the same subject matter as previously mentioned.
Because of the great abundance of suffering in the rainy-season retreat (udavāsa). // 3.302 //
He now states the expiation for drinking liquor, which follows in sequence:
"Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses, one becomes pure. (YDh 3.303ab).
For a drinker of *surā*, the phrase "forty oblations of clarified butter" is understood to carry over.
