Having fasted for three nights, one becomes pure by offering forty oblations of clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses— beginning with "yad devā devaheḷanam"— which were seen by Kūṣmāṇḍa, composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and addressed to deities indicated by the mantras' internal signs (*mantraliṅga*).
Thus it has also been stated by Baudhāyana:

Now, one who considers himself impure should offer oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses; he is thereby released from whatever sin he has committed up to and including the murder of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā), as well as from the emission of semen in a place other than a womb, except in a dream. (Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 3.1–4)
As for that which was stated by Manu:

"By muttering the *apaḥ* hymn of Kautsa and the verse of Vasiṣṭha beginning with *pratīti*, as well as the *māhitra* and the *śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified" (MDh 11.250).

Thus, it is prescribed that for one month, sixteen times each day, one should mutter any one of these following [hymns]: *apanaḥ śośucad agham*, *prati stomebhir uṣasam vāsiṣṭham*, *mahitrīṇām avo 'stu*, or *etod indraṃ stavāma*;
this applies to one who is unable to perform a three-night fast or the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblations.
This should be understood to apply when one drinks *paiṣṭī* liquor once unintentionally; however,
it should be understood that for *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors, the same applies even upon repeated drinking.
And as for that which was stated by Manu:
"A twice-born man who, having offered clarified butter for a year with the Śākala-homa mantras,
recites the verse beginning with 'namaḥ', destroys even a heavy sin" (MDh 11.257).

Thus, for one year, the performance of oblations with the eight mantras beginning with "devakṛtasyainasaḥ" each day, or the recitation of the verse "nama id ugram nama āvivāse," has been prescribed; that refers to cases of intentional action. As for the rule:
"One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) should follow cows with a concentrated mind..."
By reciting the Pāvamānī verses for one year while subsisting on alms, one becomes purified.
Thus, this refers either to the case of repeated practice or to the case of the commission of all the great sins (mahāpātaka) together.
He states the penance for stealing gold:
"But one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, standing in water, [should] mutter the Rudra [hymn].

(YDh 3.303cd). Furthermore, one who has stolen the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted for three nights and remaining in the midst of water, becomes purified by performing the recitation of the Śatarudriya with the mantra "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, to your wrath" (namas te rudra manyave).
Regarding this, a specific rule has been stated by Śātātapa:
"Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of one's guru, having committed theft, and having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
one should be covered in ashes."
"Reclining on a bed of ashes while reciting the Rudrādhyāya, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, the recitation (japa) should be performed eleven times;
or else, the knower of dharma, having repeated the Rudras eleven times over, [is purified].
Even one touched by great sins is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Atri;
as for that which was stated by Manu:
"Having recited once the *Asyavāmīya* and the *Śivasankalpa*..."
"Even after stealing gold, one becomes stainless in an instant. (MDh 11.251).

Thus, [one should recite] the hymn (*sūkta*) "Of this lovely, unaging Hotṛ... (RV 1.164.1), which consists of fifty-two verses, as well as "That divine [light] of the waking one which rises far away... (VS 34.1).
Thus, the recitation once of this six-verse hymn seen in Śiva’s own mental resolve has been prescribed;
that [penance] is to be understood as applying to a virtuous thief who steals gold belonging to a master who is utterly devoid of merit.

This refers to a quantity of gold less than the prescribed measure, or to one who instigates the act for the sake of favor; however, in the case of repetition, one should refer to what was stated in the verse beginning with "one associated with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) should follow [the corpse]," and so forth. // 3.303 //
He now states the expiation for one who violates the Guru’s bed, which follows in the sequence:
"One who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated by reciting the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn];
at the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow must be given separately for each of these [offenses]. (YDh 3.304)

But one who has violated the teacher’s bed is liberated from that sin by reciting the sixteen-verse hymn beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā," which was seen by Nārāyaṇa, has Puruṣa as its deity, is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and ends in *triṣṭubh*.
Because of the suffix denoting habitual action (*tācchīlya*) in the phrase "one who habitually recites the *sahasraśīrṣā*," there must be repetition [of the recitation].
It is understood. For this very reason, Yama has stated:
"By reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, one is liberated from all sins.
And since a specific number is required for this recitation, the number forty, found in the preceding verse, is inferred here as well.
The phrase "having fasted for three nights," occurring in the preceding verse, is to be connected here.
For this very reason, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu states:
"One who has violated the Guru’s bed is purified by reciting and offering oblations with the Puruṣasūkta while fasting for three nights."
And by these three— the drinker of spirits, the thief of gold, and the violator of the Guru’s bed— separately at the conclusion of this three-night vow,
a cow yielding much milk must be given.
This refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.
As for that which was stated by Manu:
"By practicing the Haviṣyāntīya [Sāman] and by reciting 'na tamaḥ' and the Puruṣasūkta, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated" (MDh 11.252).
"Thus: 'The protector of the oblation, ageless, finding the light' (RV 10.88.1);
'Neither distress nor misfortune [reaches him]' (RV 2.23.5);
and 'Thus indeed is my mind' (RV 10.119.1)."
It is taught that one should recite any one of these [hymns], beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā* (RV 10.90.1), sixteen times every day for a month; this, moreover,
pertains to one who is free from desire.
Thus it is; however, one should refer to what was stated by Manu: "But intentionally, [one should perform penance] with the *śākalahoma* mantras" (MDh 11.257).
As for that which has been declared in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
A twice-born man should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds using the Mahāvyāhṛtis one thousand times for the sake of purification from minor offenses (upapātaka).
One who is joined with a great sin (mahāpātaka) is purified by a hundred-thousandfold oblation (lakṣahoma).
Thus, that refers to the subject of repetition;
however, as for what was stated by Yama:
"Or one may recite the Asyavāmīya hymn, or likewise the Pāvamānī verses."
The Kuntāpa, the Vālakhilyas, the Nivids and Praiṣas, and the Vṛṣākapi.
Having recited the Hotṛ Rudras once, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of approaching a woman who is an adulteress.

However, regarding those cases which fall under the extension of the rule for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), or those equal thereto, designated by the terms *atipātaka* (heinous sins) or *upapātaka* (minor sins), it should be understood that the penance is respectively reduced by one-fourth and by one-half.

Or, it should be understood that Hārīta’s statement—that one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times when any one, or a combination, of the minor sins (*pātaka*), secondary sins (*atipātaka*), sub-minor sins (*upapātaka*), or major sins (*mahāpātaka*) occurs—should be observed.
Furthermore, because of the scriptural injunction: "And one who associates with a perpetrator of a major sin shall perform the very same penance as that person" (MDh 11.182).
The penance for one who associates with such a person is that very same [penance] belonging to him;
nor should it be argued that, because association through teaching and so forth is accomplished by multiple agents, its status as a secret matter is untenable.
Since secrecy is maintained even when there are multiple agents— just as in the case of adultery with another's wife— merely by the lack of knowledge of a third party or others besides the agent,
secret penance (*rahasya-prāyaścitta*) is indeed applicable.
In this way, it should be understood that even for one who associates with those who have committed mortal sins (*atipātakin*) and the like, the same penance as theirs must be observed. (3.304)
Thus ends the section on secret penances for the great sins (mahāpātaka).
Now, following the sequence, he states the penances for the fifty-six minor sins (upapātaka), beginning with the killing of a cow:
"One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) should be performed for the removal of all sins."
Indeed, for those born of minor offenses (*upapātaka*), as well as for those not specifically prescribed,

one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be performed for the removal of all [sins], including the fifty-six minor offenses such as killing a cow, as well as the caste-degrading acts (*jātibhraṃśakara*) and others for which secret penances have not been specified.
Likewise, for the removal of all [sins], from the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) down to the miscellaneous ones (*prakīrṇaka*), breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be performed;
and among those, for the great transgressions, four hundred [are required].

In the case of secondary sins (anupātaka), the increase in the number [of repetitions] should be understood as three hundred for the most heinous sins (atipātaka) and two hundred for the secondary sins; likewise,
in the case of public penances, one-fourth of the penance for a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) applies to the secondary sins.
Because a specific rule is observed,
a reduction should be inferred for the miscellaneous cases;
for this very reason, it was stated by Yama:
"By four hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) joined with ten *praṇavas*, one is released even from the murder of a Brahmin; how much more so from the remaining sins.
A specific detail regarding this has also been stated by Baudhāyana:
Alternatively, one is purified by three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for transgressions involving speech, sight, hearing, touch, smell, and the mind.
For approaching a Śūdra woman or eating [the food of] a Śūdra, one should perform seven breath-restraints separately for each instance over the course of seven days.

In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten, consuming impure substances, or selling forbidden articles— with the exception of honey, meat, clarified butter, oil, lac, salt, liquids, and cooked food— and whatever else may be of a similar nature,
one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for each day during a half-month.

Except for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and those causing loss of caste (*patanīya*), whatever else may be of this nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) each month for twelve months;
except for other mortal sins (*pātaka*), whatever else may be of this nature, [one should perform] twelve breath-restraints for twelve half-months.
"One should perform [prāṇāyāmas]; furthermore, for mortal sins (pātaka), one should perform twelve prāṇāyāmas each for a year" (BDh 4.1.4–10).
Among these, the triad of prāṇāyāmas beginning with "speech, sight," and so forth, refers to miscellaneous offenses (prakīrṇaka);
whereas the forty-nine prāṇāyāmas mentioned in the passage beginning with "intercourse with a Śūdra woman or eating [her] food" refer to mortal sins.
These refer to specific minor offenses (*upapātaka*).

Likewise, the one hundred and forty-four breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "unfit food" (*abhakṣya-abhojya*) also refer specifically to particular minor offenses.

Now, the one hundred and eighty breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "excluding the major and minor sins" (*pātaka-upapātaka-varjyam*) are intended for those acts that cause loss of caste (*jāti-bhraṃśakara*) and the like.

Next, the three hundred and sixty breath-restraints mentioned in the passage beginning with "excluding the mortal and degrading sins" (*pātaka-patanīya-varjyam*) are intended for minor sins such as cow-slaughter (*govadha*) and the like.

Finally, the two thousand two hundred and sixty breath-restraints mentioned in the passage beginning with "excluding the mortal sins" (*pātaka-varjyam*) are intended for heinous crimes (*atipātaka*) and those that are not minor sins.

Now, the four thousand breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), consisting of three hundred and twenty [repetitions] as stated in the passage beginning with "In the case of mortal sins" (*atha pātakeṣu*) and so forth, pertain to the category of great sins (*mahāpātaka*).

Furthermore, this pentad of expiations (*prāyaścitta*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "Eating what is not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyabhojya*) and so forth pertains either to cases of extreme habitual practice or to cases where [the offenses] are accumulated. As for that which was stated by Manu:

Desiring to remove gross and subtle sins, one should mutter daily for a year the verse beginning with *ava*, or the verse beginning with *yat kiṃcedam*, or the verse beginning with *iti me manaḥ*, at times not inconsistent with other purposes. (MDh 11.253). Thus, for the duration of a year, one should perform the recitation every day at appropriate times, using either the verse *avate heḍo varuṇa*, the verse *yat kiṃcedam*, or the verse *iti me manaḥ*.
That too is an object of cultivation. (3.305)

He states an exception to the requirement of one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) which applies generally to minor offenses (upapātaka): "Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink the purifying Soma-liquid consecrated with the syllable Om. (YDh 3.306)

Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, a twice-born man should drink the juice of the *soma* creeper consecrated with the syllable *oṃ* as a means of purification; this applies to cases where the act was committed unintentionally. However, if it was done intentionally, that which was spoken by Sumantu is as follows:
Having consumed semen, feces, urine,
or having eaten garlic, onions, leeks, mushrooms, and other such forbidden foods;
And having consumed the flesh of swans, village fowls, dogs, jackals, and so forth,
one should then descend into water reaching up to the neck, perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Śuddhavatī* verses, and drink water from the chest with the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*.
"Therefore, by this [rite], one becomes purified.
Manu also stated another penance for consuming the seven kinds of forbidden food:
"Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten reprehensible food..."
"A man who recites the *Taratsamandīya* hymn is purified in three days" (MDh 11.254).
This refers to things that should not be accepted, such as poison, weapons, liquor, and so forth, as well as the property of outcasts and others.
Furthermore, when bodily waste such as semen, feces, or urine is discharged into water...
Even when he emits semen [other than during intercourse], it has been stated by that same [author]:
"But having performed an improper act, one should subsist on alms for a month while dwelling in water" (MDh 11.256). 3.306.
He states the penance for miscellaneous minor mental offenses committed through ignorance:
"Whether it occurs by night or by day, whatever has been done through ignorance—all that perishes by performing the twilight devotions at the three times of day. (YDh 3.307)

Whatever miscellaneous minor offense— whether mental or verbal— is committed through negligence during the night or the day, all of that is destroyed by the performance of the obligatory twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) prescribed for the three times of morning, midday, and so forth.
And thus says Yama:
"Whatever sin one commits during the day by deed, thought, or speech,
one destroys it while seated during the evening twilight through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). Thus it was also said by Śātātapa.
"The twilight worship performed outside purifies falsehood, the smell of liquor, sexual intercourse during the day, and the food of a *vṛṣala*. (3.307)

Now, he states the purificatory mantras common to all major sins and others: "The recitation of the Śukriya and the Āraṇyaka, and especially that of the Gāyatrī—these, as well as the eleven Rudras, are indeed removers of all sins. (YDh 3.308)
The *Śukriya*, a specific portion of the *Āraṇyaka*, beginning with "O God Savitṛ, all things... (*viśvāni deva savitaḥ*, VS 30.3), is recited in the *Vājasaneyaka*;
and the *Āraṇyaka* Yajus, beginning with "I take refuge in the Ṛc, the speech; I take refuge in the Yajus, the mind," is likewise recited in that very same place.
The recitation (*japa*) of these two removes all great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like;
likewise, for the *gāyatrī*,

[the number is] one hundred thousand for great sins, ten thousand for heinous sins (*atipātaka*) and secondary sins (*upapātaka*), one thousand for minor sins (*upapātaka*), and [one hundred] for miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇaka*).
Reciting [the Gāyatrī] specifically one hundred times is the remover of all sins;
and likewise, a verse concerning the Gāyatrī has been stated by Śaṅkha:
The Sāvitrī, when recited one hundred times, destroys great sins;
when recited one thousand times, it likewise liberates one from all transgressions.
By reciting it ten thousand times, she destroys all sins;
but when that Goddess is recited one hundred thousand times, she destroys even the greatest of transgressions.

"A Brahmin who has stolen gold, a killer of a Brahmin, one who has violated the Guru’s bed, and a drinker of liquor—all these are purified by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; of this there is no doubt. As for that which was stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
By reciting the Gāyatrī ten million times, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he who recites it eighty thousand times is liberated from the drinking of liquor.
Seventy lakhs of the Gāyatrī purify one who steals gold;
sixty lakhs of the Gāyatrī, however, release one who has violated the Guru’s bed.
Thus, because of its weightiness, that refers to the subject of illumination (*prakāśa*).
Likewise, *rudraikādaśinī* is the collection of the eleven Rudra-anuvākas; it is called *rudraikādaśinī* because it is a combination of eleven Rudras.
And when that [mantra] is recited specifically, it removes all sins. Or, by repeating the eleven Rudra hymns, the knower of dharma is liberated from great sins; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, since an elevenfold repetition is observed for the great sins (mahāpātaka), a reduction by one-fourth for each subsequent degree— such as the extreme sins (atipātaka) and so forth— should be applied. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the Aghamarṣaṇa and other such rites.
As Vasiṣṭha said:
"Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by the recitation and oblations of which people are purified; of this there is no doubt."
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍyas, the Pāvamānyas, and likewise the Durgā-sāvitrī;
The *abhīṣaṅgas*, the *padastomas*, the *sāmans*, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*;
the *bhāradaṇḍas* and *sāmans*, and likewise the *gāyatra* and *raivata*.
The Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa, as well as the Devavratas,
the Ārtvija, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and likewise the Madhvṛcas.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Trisuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans known as Indraśuddha;
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner Vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these songs purify living beings when sung.
He obtains the memory of his past births if he so desires. (VaDh 28.10–15) 3.308.
Furthermore:
"In whatever place a twice-born man considers himself defiled, in that very place he should perform an oblation with sesame seeds and likewise recite the Gāyatrī. (YDh 3.309)

In whatever case a twice-born person considers himself defiled or overcome by the mass of impurity produced by such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, in each such instance an oblation of sesame seeds with the Gāyatrī mantra must be performed;
in the case of the great sins (mahāpātaka), this is to be done one hundred thousand times.
A fire sacrifice (homa) must be performed;
for it is stated in the Smṛti of Yama: "By a hundred-thousand-fold homa with the Gāyatrī, one is liberated from all sins."
In cases such as the most heinous sins (*atipātaka*), a reduction of one-quarter for each [subsequent] degree should be calculated.
Likewise, the recitation and the gift should be performed with sesame seeds.
And so Vasiṣṭha says in the section on secret rites:
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should cause five or seven Brāhmaṇas to recite [mantras] while offering black sesame seeds mixed with honey, or otherwise [white sesame seeds].
"May the King of Dharma be pleased"—whatever [wish] dwells in one's mind [should be uttered];
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant. (VaDh 28.18–19).
Likewise, he has stated that a gift may also be given at an indefinite time.
"He who places sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter,
and gives them to a Brahmin, overcomes all evil deeds" (VaDh 28.22).
Likewise, it has been stated by Vyāsa as well:

"He who, with self-restraint, gives a sesame-cow to a twice-born man, is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this. Such a collection of gifts mentioned in the section on secret rites (rahasyakāṇḍa) is to be understood as applicable for ignorant twice-born men, as well as for women and Śūdras.
As for that which was stated by Yama:
"He who gives sesame seeds in the morning, touches sesame seeds, eats them,
bathes with sesame seeds, and offers sesame seeds as an oblation— such a person crosses over all evil deeds."
Likewise,
the two eighth days of the month, the two fourteenth days,
as well as the new moon day, the full moon day, the seventh day, and the two twelfth days.
One who abstains from food for a year, remaining constantly with senses subdued,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
Thus it is said; and as for that which was stated by Atri:
"Hari should recline upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, and he abandons sleep on the full moon of Kārttika; one should worship Hari during those two [periods]."
It swiftly dispels even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin.
All such passages as these are to be established as referring to the practice of those devoid of knowledge, whether performed with desire or without desire, and either repeatedly or not. (3.309)
Moreover:

"Neither sins nor even those born of the great crimes (mahāpātaka) touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and intent on the performance of the five sacrifices. (YDh 3.310)
First, the acquisition of the Veda; then reflection, practice, recitation, and its impartation to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold.

According to the sequence thus described, sins arising even from the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, endowed with forbearance, and intent on the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*);
how much less so, then, those arising from minor offenses (*prakīrṇaka*), or the secondary sins (*upapātaka*) produced by speech and mind? In this regard:
The intended meaning is also indicated by the word "api" (even). And this refers to cases where there is no intentional transgression; for this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Even if more than a hundred improper acts have been committed, if the Veda is retained,
the fire of that person's Veda burns them all away, just as fire consumes fuel"— having stated this with reference to miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*) and the like, it was further declared:
"One should not take delight in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Vedas;
for it is through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by karma, and not otherwise. (VaDh 27.4) 3.310.
Moreover:

Subsisting on air, standing during the day and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun, one is purified from all sins except the killing of a Brahmin by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times. (YDh 3.311)

Fasting during the day and remaining seated, having spent the night dwelling in water, one who recites the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times immediately after sunrise is liberated from the entire collection of sins, including all great crimes (mahāpātaka) with the exception of the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, this applies even to minor offenses (upapātaka) and the like.
This should be understood to apply either in the case of repetition or when there is a combination of multiple faults,
because it is unjust to treat unequal objects as equal.
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha has prescribed specific vows for major sins (mahāpātaka) and minor sins (upapātaka) according to the distinction of time.
As it is said: one should consecrate with the mantra "You are barley, the king of grains;
you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey;
you are the cleanser of all sins, declared as a purifier by the seers," either the handful or the double-handful of barley while it is being cooked or once it is cooked.
Or with this [mantra]: "Barley is ghee, barley is honey; barley is the purifier, barley is nectar. May they purify all my evil arising from speech, mind, and body."
One should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) with that [remnant], as well as the oblation to the spirits (bhūtaliṅga);
one should not discard the first portion, nor seek alms, nor attend to guests, nor leave behind any food remnants.

"May those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, and whose father is Dakṣa— may they protect us, may they favor us; obeisance to them, svāhā to them!"— with these words, one should offer oblations into oneself for three nights for the increase of intelligence and the destruction of sin, for three nights in cases such as the killing of a Brahmin, and for twelve nights in the case of one born of an outcaste.
In this manner, by following this general direction, other statements from the Smṛtis should also be analyzed. // 3.311 //
Thus ends the section on secret penances.
Now, since the specific distinctions among the various forms of vows and observances have been introduced, their definition— answering the question of what they are like— will be stated concisely.
In that regard, he first states the duties which constitute the limbs of the vow of the secret of all illumination:
"Celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity, truthfulness, freedom from guile, non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-control—these are known as the *yamas*. (YDh 3.312)
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas).
Celibacy (brahmacarya) consists of the restraint of all the senses. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.313)

The restraint of the attendants (*upastha*) is the restraint of the sexual organ (*liṅga*); this is indicated according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull. Freedom from guile (*akalkatā*) means freedom from crookedness.
The remainder is well known.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu:
"One should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness" (MDh 11.223),
that too is an illustration of these [virtues] rather than an exhaustive enumeration.

And here, although compassion, patience, and so forth are already established as ends of human life (*puruṣārtha*), they are enjoined again for the purpose of being auxiliary to the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
In some cases, there is also a specific distinction, as follows:
The injunction regarding truthfulness is intended to prevent the speaking of falsehood, even when permitted in contexts such as marriage ceremonies.
The injunction regarding non-violence is for the purpose of ensuring that even one's sons, disciples, and others are not to be beaten, and so forth. (3.312–3.313)
Regarding that, he first describes the vow known as Sāntapana:
"Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with Kuśa grass, one should fast on the following day while performing the Sāntapana Kṛcchra. (YDh 3.314)

On the previous day, having abandoned other food and having mixed and drunk the five substances of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)—namely cow urine and so forth—along with kuśa-water, one should fast on the following day; this is the two-night Sāntapana Kṛcchra. This is the method of mixing.
It is understood from its being mentioned separately in the subsequent verse;
furthermore, this is an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), since it consists of the nature of austerity (*tapas*).
Because it is to be accomplished through the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The measurement of the cow-urine and other substances will be explained.
Furthermore, when one has fasted on the previous day and [performs the rite] on the following day...
When the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are consumed together with their respective mantras, it is called the *brahmakūrca*.
As Pārāśara has said:
"Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass..."
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have been specified; each one individually purifies the body.
The urine of a copper-colored cow, the dung of a white cow,
the milk of a golden-colored cow, and likewise the curd of a blue cow.
The ghee for a woman of dark complexion should be from a Kapila cow;
this is the rule regarding the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) when cows of all colors are unavailable.
Cow's urine is eight māṣakas, cow dung sixteen,
milk is said to be twelve, and curd is proclaimed to be ten.
The quantity of ghee desired is like that of cow urine, while the water of *kuśa* grass is half of that;
having taken the cow urine with the *gāyatrī*, the cow dung with "gandhadvārā," the milk with "āpyāyasva," and the curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."

One should offer into the presence of the fire clarified butter with the mantra "tejo 'si śukram," water from *kuśa* grass with "devasya tvā," and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) purified by the *ṛc*.
And with those seven-leaved *darbha* grasses that have uncut tips and pure luster,
one should offer the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) after drawing it up, according to the prescribed rule.

With the verses beginning with "irāvatī," "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "mānastoke," and those that are auspicious, the twice-born should offer oblations; he should then drink the remainder of what has been offered.
Having stirred it with the *praṇava*, having consecrated it with the *praṇava*,
and having drawn it up with the *praṇava*, one should drink it indeed with the *praṇava*.
One should drink [the water] with a cup of medium size made of *palāśa* wood or a lotus leaf,
or again, with a vessel of gold or silver, using the *brāhma-tīrtha*.
"Whatever sin resides in the body of a human being, reaching even to the skin and bones,
the *brahmakūrca* fast burns it away like fire consumes fuel.
When this very same mixture of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is practiced for three nights, it is then designated as the *yatisāntapana*.
"One obtains [the merit];
this very same [practice] repeated for three days is known as the *yatisāntapana*," according to the Smṛti of Śaṅkha.
Jābāla, however, has described the Sāntapana penance as being accomplished in seven days:
having drunk each of these— cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass— one day at a time, one should then fast for a day and night.

"The penance called Sāntapana is difficult [to perform] and destroys all sins. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the application of these heavy and light *kṛcchra* penances should be understood as depending on one's capacity and other such factors;
the same applies hereafter.
The systematic arrangement is to be understood. (3.314)
He describes the penance known as the Mahāsāntapana:
"With separate Sāntapana substances for six days, followed by a day of fasting, this seven-day penance is remembered as the Mahāsāntapana. (YDh 3.315)
The penance known as the *mahāsāntapana* is to be understood as one completed in seven days.

To address the question of how this is done, it is stated that one should pass each of the first six days with each of the six substances— cow urine and the rest— individually, and the seventh day with fasting.
Yama, however, has prescribed the Mahāsāntapana penance, which is to be accomplished in fifteen days:
"One should drink cow's urine for three days, and indeed drink cow dung for three days;
[then] curd for three days, milk for three days, and clarified butter for three days—one becomes pure thereby."
"For this Mahāsāntapana indeed destroys all sins.
However, Jābāla has stated that the Mahāsāntapana is to be completed in twenty-one nights:
"One should employ each one of these six for three nights."
"One should fast for the final three days; this they know as the Mahāsāntapana.
When, however, each of the six substances of the Sāntapana is consumed for two days, then it is the Atisāntapana.
As Yama has said:
"These very [substances] should be drunk in that same manner, each for two days at a time; this is called the *atisāntapana*, which purifies even a dog-eater (*śvapāka*).
The phrase "it would purify even a dog-eater" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (3.315)
Thus he has described the vow known as *parṇakṛcchra*, which is more severe than the *mahāsāṃtapana* and *atisāṃtapana*.
[It is performed] with the leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, *rājīva*, and *bilva* trees, along with *kuśa* grass and water.

The *parṇakṛcchra* is declared to consist of drinking [these] individually every day. One should drink water boiled with each of the leaves of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aravinda*, and *śrīvṛkṣa* trees on successive days, and drink *kuśa* water on one day; thus, the *parṇakṛcchra* is accomplished in five days.
But when a decoction of the *parṇa* leaves and the other ingredients, combined together, is drunk at the end of three nights, that is the *parṇakūrca*;
as Yama has said:
"One who, being pure and having fasted for three nights, boils all of these [herbs] together and drinks them with water, is said to perform the *parṇakūrca*. However,
when the fruits of the *bilva* and others are each boiled separately and drunk for a month, then it receives the designation of *phalakṛcchra* and so forth.
They obtain [the results]. As Mārkaṇḍeya said: "The *phalakṛcchra* is described by the wise as boiled fruits for one month;
the *śrīkṛcchra* is proclaimed to be with *śrīphala* fruits, and another likewise with lotus seeds."
Likewise, another Śrīkṛcchra is prescribed with *māsa* and *āmalaka* fruits;
the Patrakṛcchra is considered to be performed with leaves, and that [same] kṛcchra is said to be performed with flowers.
"The Mūla-kṛcchra is prescribed as being with roots, while the Toya-kṛcchra is with water. (3.316)
Thus ends the elevenfold *parṇakṛcchra*.
Now he describes the *taptakṛcchra*:
one should drink each of these—boiled milk, boiled ghee, and boiled water—one per day.
And fasting for one night is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*.
Having consumed each of these—boiled milk, boiled ghee, and boiled water—on successive days, one should fast on the following day;
this [penance] is accomplished in four days.

The *mahātaptakṛcchra* is accomplished over two nights by performing all these [preceding penances] together with a fast, just like the *sāntapana*. The *taptakṛcchra* is performed in the same manner.

But by Manu, a twelve-night rite is prescribed: "A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days, bathing once and remaining composed" (MDh 11.215).
The specific quantities of milk and so forth should be understood as stated by Parāśara:
"One should drink three *palas* of water, two *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of clarified butter;
this is to be done for three nights while inhaling warm air."
The meaning is that during the completion of the *trirātramāruta* [penance], one should drink the steam of hot water;
however, when cold milk or similar substances are drunk, then it is the *śītakṛcchra*.
For three days one should drink cold water; for three days one should drink cold milk;
having drunk cold ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for the final three days.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama: (3.317)
Thus, the *taptakṛcchra* is of four kinds;
he now describes the *pādakṛcchra*:
by eating once a day, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked for.
And this is proclaimed as the *pādakṛcchra* (one-quarter penance) by means of fasting alone;
for [the term] "ekabhakta" refers to eating only once during the day, since "nakta" (eating at night) is mentioned separately.
And therefore, one should pass the entire day and night by eating only once during the daytime alone.
In that context, "during the day" (divā) serves to exclude the night; [the phrase] "once" (ekavāram) [serves to exclude multiple meals].
Thus, there is the exclusion of eating twice or more;
by the word "with food," there is the exclusion of fasting.
And this is because the *kṛcchra* and other penances are of the nature of a religious vow (*vrata*).
By means of the exclusion of eating for the sake of human ends, eating that constitutes a limb of the *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed.
And thus says Āpastamba: "For three days one should eat without anointing oneself and not during the day; then for another three days."
"For three days he observes the vow of not begging, and for three days he eats nothing at all.

Here, by means of the suffix *ṇini* prescribed as a vow (*vrata*) in the expression "one who does not eat at night" (*anaktāśī*), the author indicates a rule of eating during the day through the exclusion of eating at night. This very point has also been made clear by Gautama:
"Having eaten sacrificial food for the morning meal, one should not eat for three nights" (GDh 26.2).
The same applies to the rule regarding eating only at night (*naktabhojana*).
That meal in which no food is requested is called *ayācita* (unasked-for).
Since no specific time is prescribed therein, it may be performed once either by day or by night;
for since *kṛcchra* penances are of the nature of austerity, such a practice would be impossible if one were to eat a second time.

Regarding "without asking": this is not merely a prohibition against asking for the food of others; rather, one should not ask even for one's own food from servants, wives, and so forth, because the act of requesting is common to both sending and entreating.

Therefore, even in one's own home, if servants, a wife, or others offer food without being commanded, then it may be eaten, but not otherwise. With this very intention, Gautama stated: "Furthermore, for three days, one should not beg from anyone" (GDh 26.4).
And in this regard, Parāśara has shown the rule for the number of mouthfuls:
"Twelve mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening meal, fifteen for the morning; twenty-four are for those who do not beg; beyond that, fasting is prescribed. Thus it is said.

Āpastamba, however, has stated otherwise: "Twenty-two mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening meal, twenty-six for the morning; twenty-four are for the day when food is sought [from others]; beyond that, there are three days of fasting."
"Having the size of a hen's egg, it enters easily according to one's desire. Thus [it is said].
Regarding these two alternatives, there is an option depending on one's capacity.
Āpastamba, however, having divided the Prājāpatya penance into four parts and established them as four Pādakṛcchras, has shown their application according to the respective castes.

Three days without eating constitutes one quarter; likewise, three days of eating only what is unasked for is another quarter; three days of eating only in the evening is a quarter; and similarly, three days of eating only in the morning is a quarter.
"A Śūdra should perform [the penance] for one day at dawn; for a Vaiśya, he should cause it to be given at evening;
for a Kṣatriya, it is [to be done] without being asked; and for a Brāhmaṇa, it is prescribed as three nights.
When, however, there is the performance of two sets of three days consisting of fasting without asking, that is an *ardha-kṛcchra* (half-penance).
However, it should be understood that the performance of the other three sets of three days, excluding the evening [fast], constitutes "three-quarters" (pādona); for it is said:
"Without the morning and evening [fasts], it would be half; without the night [fast], it is three-quarters."
Since this was stated by that very same author,
another form of the *ardhakṛcchra* penance has also been shown by him:
"In the evening and in the morning, one should likewise eat [once] for two days, and for two days [eat] what is unasked."
"And one should not eat for two days; that is prescribed as half a *kṛcchra*. (3.318)
He describes the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra:
"This Prājāpatya is said to be threefold in whatever manner.
This very same [penance] is the Pādakṛcchra, performed either by repetition like a "measuring-stick" (daṇḍakalita) or by increasing the duration at its own place.
In that case as well, whether in direct order or reverse order, or even without the recitation to be described later, when practiced three times, it is called a *prājāpatya* penance. Regarding this,
Vasiṣṭha has demonstrated the method of repetition as being like the striking of a staff.
One day in the morning, one day at night, one day without begging,
and one day as a *parāka*— thus there are four days, and the next two are likewise.
"For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma,
has thus prescribed the Śiśukṛcchra for children, the elderly, and the sick" (VaDh 23.43). However,
the position that there is an increase in the duration according to the natural order of the castes has been shown by Manu.

"A twice-born man performing the Prājāpatya penance should eat [food obtained] unasked for three days in the morning, three days in the evening, and three days [unasked]; for the final three days, he should not eat at all" (MDh 11.212).
However, Vasiṣṭha has shown that the sequence may be reversed.
"A Brahmin should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa in the reverse order [of the castes]. (VaDh 21.13).
However, the alternative involving the omission of recitation (*japa*) and other such rites has been shown by Aṅgiras regarding women, Śūdras, and others:
"Therefore, having encountered a Śūdra who always stands upon the path of dharma..."

"An expiation (prāyaścitta) should be administered, excluding recitation (japa), burnt offerings (homa), and the like. The alternative involving japa and other such acts, however, by process of elimination and by virtue of its suitability, pertains to members of the three twice-born castes (traivarṇika). And that has been shown by Gautama and others:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Kṛcchra penances. Having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣya) for breakfast, one should not eat for three nights.
Then, for another three days, one should eat only at night.

Then for another three days he should not beg from anyone. Then for another three days, fasting, he should stand during the day and sit at night if he desires quick results. He should speak the truth. [He should avoid] ignoble people.
One should not converse with them;
one should constantly recite the *raurava* and *yodhā* mantras and perform the ritual touching of water at each of the three daily libations.
One should perform the purification with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, which contain the word *pavitra*, and with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*.
Then follows the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*):
"Homage to Ahamā, to Mohamā, to Mahamā, to Dhanvan, to Tāpasa, and to Punarvasu; homage!"
Homage to the one with the girdle of muñja grass, to the one born of the waters, to the finder of wealth, to the all-knowing!

Homage to the one who has gone across, to the one who has well crossed over, to the one who has greatly crossed over, to the giver of the further shore, to the one who has reached the beyond-shore, to the one who causes others to cross over!

Salutation to Rudra, the Lord of Creatures, the Great God, Tryambaka, the Solitary Wanderer, the Sovereign, Hara, Śarva, the Destroyer of Sin, the Fierce One, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, the Compassionate One, and the One with Matted Hair.
Salutation to Sūrya, the Āditya.
Homage to the blue-necked one, to the white-throated one; homage to the black one, to the tawny one;
to the eldest, to the most excellent, to the ancient, to Indra, to the golden-haired one, to the one whose vital energy flows upward.
Homage! Homage to the Truthful One, the Purifier, the one of purifying color, the one of singular color, to Kāma, who assumes forms at will;
homage to the Radiant One, whose form is radiant;
homage to the Sharp One, whose form is sharp.
Salutation to the gentle one, to the good man, to the great man, to the middle man, to the supreme man, to the celibate student;
salutation to him whose forehead is the moon, who is clothed in a hide.
Thus [ends the section]. This indeed is the worship of the Sun;
these are the offerings of clarified butter.
At the end of the twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial pap (caru),...
He should offer oblations to these deities:
"Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! To Agni and Soma! To Indra and Agni! To Indra! To the Viśvedevas! To Brahmā! To Prajāpati! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!"
"Before the feeding of the Brahmins" (GDh 26.1–17).
In that context, the meaning of the rule "one who desires speed should stand during the day and sit during the night" is as follows:
whereas one who [performs the rite] even for a great [purpose]...
Thinking, "May I be quickly released from sin by means of this single *kṛcchra*," he desires thus: during the day, he should stand during times not opposed to his duties; at night, he should sit.
In this manner, there is the chanting of the *Sāman* known as *Raurava-yodhā*, and libation (*tarpaṇa*) with [mantras] such as "namo hamāya" and so forth.

One who desires swift results should perform the worship of the Sun and other rites, as well as the cooking of the *caru* oblation and so forth, even if they were not mentioned by Yogīśvara and others.

Therefore, in place of the two *prājāpatya* penances mentioned by Yogīśvara and others, that which is prescribed by Gautama—accompanied by its various procedural details (*itikartavyatā*)—should be observed. In this same manner, other [penances] mentioned in different *smṛtis* should also be specifically sought out.
He describes the *atikṛcchra*:
"This very same [fast] would be the *atikṛcchra* when one eats a handful of food.
This very practice, when endowed with the rules of the *prājāpatya* such as eating only once a day and so forth, constitutes the *atikṛcchra*.
However, there is this distinction:
during each of the first three sets of three days, one should eat only as much food as fills the hand, and not twenty-two or more morsels.

And here, since the filling of the hands with food is prescribed as a restatement of the meal already obtained, the fasting— which is extended by analogy to the final three-day period— is indeed not set aside. In this case as well, the arrangement according to quarters should be understood to be exactly as before.

As for that which was stated by Manu: "A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat a single morsel for three periods of three days as before, and should fast for the final three days" (MDh 11.214).
Thus, because it is smaller than that which is measured by a handful of food, this [rule] pertains to those who are capable. 3.319.
He describes the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*:

"The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days" (YDh 3.320ab). It should be understood that the vow known as *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of living on milk for a period of twenty-one nights.

But Gautama has stated that subsisting on water for twelve nights is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra; "The third [type] is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra, consisting of consuming only water" (GDh 26.20). Therefore, the application of these two is determined according to one's capacity.
He states the *parāka*: "The *parāka* is proclaimed [to consist] in fasting for twelve days.
This half-verse has a straightforward meaning. (3.320)

He describes the Saumya-kṛcchra: "The daily consumption of oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, followed by a fast for one night—this is called the Saumya-kṛcchra. (YDh 3.321)

Having consumed each of these five daily—oil-cake from which the oil has been extracted, sesame-rice, the scum of boiled rice, whey, and water-gruel—one should fast on the sixth day; this is designated as the *kṛcchra* penance known as the *saumya*.
This is the quantity of the substances.
However, one should understand that [this practice] is restricted merely to sustaining life.
But Jābāla has described the *saumyakṛcchra* as lasting for four days:
oil-cake, barley meal, buttermilk, and fasting on the fourth day.
One should give a garment as the sacrificial fee; this is called the Saumya Kṛcchra. (3.321)
He describes the penance known as Tulāpuruṣa:
"By practicing each of these for three nights in succession, this [penance] lasting fifteen days is to be known as Tulāpuruṣa. (YDh 3.322)
It should be understood that by practicing each of these five— sesame paste and the others— in succession for three nights, there is a penance lasting fifteen days called the *tulāpuruṣa* *kṛcchra*.
And because the rule here specifies a duration of fifteen days, fasting (*upavāsa*) is excluded.
Yama, however, has prescribed the Tulāpuruṣa penance lasting twenty-one nights:
"Consuming gruel, then oil-cake, then buttermilk, and then water and barley-meal— practicing this for three days each, and subsisting on air for two days."
"The Tulāpuruṣa [vow] is said to last for twenty-one nights.
Here, the procedure (itikartavyatā) as stated by Hārīta and others is not written down for fear of making the book too voluminous. 3.322.
He describes the Cāndrāyaṇa penance:

"While performing the Cāndrāyaṇa, one should consume morsels of food equal in size to a peacock's egg, increasing them by one each day during the bright fortnight, and decreasing them by one each day during the dark fortnight. (YDh 3.323)

Performing the vow known as *cāndrāyaṇa*, one should consume morsels of food the size of a peacock’s egg during the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), increasing them according to the lunar days (*tithi*); that is,
just as there is an increase of one digit of the moon each day during the half-month starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
In the same manner, having taken up morsels of food, one should eat by increasing them one by one— one on the first day, two on the second, and so on—
until the full moon. Then, having eaten fifteen morsels on the fifteenth day, one should eat fourteen in the dark fortnight.
On the first lunar day (pratipad) and the second, he should eat thirteen mouthfuls, thus reducing the number of mouthfuls by one each day until the fourteenth.
Then, on the fourteenth day, having consumed a single mouthful, he should fast when the moon has waned; for that is the implied meaning. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

"One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight; one should not eat at all when the moon has waned. This is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa. (VaDh 27.21).
That ritual in which the course (*ayana*)—meaning the movement or practice—is like that of the moon, characterized by decrease and increase, is called *cāndrāyaṇa*.
In the case of *saṃjñā*, the vowel is long;
and because this [syllable] is finer at both ends like a barley grain (*yava*) and thicker in the middle, it is called "barley-middled" (*yavamadhya*).

When this very vow is undertaken on the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and performed according to the previously mentioned sequence, it is called "ant-shaped" (*pipīlikamadhyama*), because it becomes thinnest in the middle like an ant. For instance,
by eating fourteen morsels on the first day of the dark fortnight according to the aforementioned sequence, one should decrease the morsels by one each day until the fourteenth.
He should eat as much as he can;
then, having consumed a single morsel on the fourteenth day and fasted on the new moon day, he should consume only one morsel on the first day of the bright fortnight.

Then, as the remainder of the fortnight is completed by increasing the food intake by one morsel at a time, fifteen morsels are reached on the full moon day; thus, the "ant-middle" (pipīlikāmadhya) nature of the fast is indeed appropriate.
And so says Vasiṣṭha:
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
eating while gradually reducing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.

"In the same way, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, one should eat another mouthful; eating while increasing the number of mouthfuls, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight. (VaDh 23.45).
However, when in a single fortnight there are sixteen days or fourteen days due to the increase or decrease of lunar days (*tithi*), then:

The increase and decrease of the morsels (*grāsa*) should also be understood, according to the rule that "one should consume the portions of the *piṇḍas* in accordance with the increase of the lunar days.
A specific detail regarding this has been shown by Gautama:
Now, therefore, follows the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Its procedure has been explained in connection with the Kṛcchra; one should perform the shaving of the head and observe the vow. On the day following [the preparation], he should fast on the full moon day.

With these [verses], "āpyāyasva," "saṃ te payāṃsi," and "navo nava," one should perform the libation, the oblation of clarified butter, the consecration of the sacrificial food (*havis*), and the worship of the moon. One should offer clarified butter with the four verses beginning "yad devā devaheḍanam" and at the end with "devakṛtasya. Finally, one should offer with three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and the [syllables] "oṃ bhūḥ bhuvaḥ."

With these—*svaḥ*, *mahaḥ*, *janaḥ*, *tapaḥ*, *satyam*, *yaśaḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *ūrj*, *iṭ*, *ojaḥ*, *tejaḥ*, *puruṣaḥ*, *dharmaḥ*, *śivaḥ*—he should perform the consecration of each morsel with the respective mantra, or mentally recite "namas" and "svāhā" for all of them. He should eat all these morsels using these very [mantras]. The measure of a morsel is such that it does not distort the mouth; [the permitted foods are] sacrificial porridge, alms-food, barley-meal, grains, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curds, ghee, roots, fruits, and water.
The sacrificial offerings (havīṃṣi) are increasingly praiseworthy.
Having eaten fifteen mouthfuls on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing the amount by one at each meal;
having fasted on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the amount by one at each meal.

"For some, it is the reverse; this is the Cāndrāyaṇa month" (GDh 27.1–15). Regarding this, what was stated concerning the size of the morsels—that they should not exceed the capacity of the mouth—is intended for children, because they are incapable of consuming fifteen morsels the size of a peahen's egg.
In the case of sacrificial offerings such as milk and the like, the quantity measured by a cock's egg must be prepared using leaf-cups or similar vessels.

Likewise, other Smṛtis state that items such as chicken eggs, fresh Āmalaka fruits, and so forth, should be the size of a mouthful; these are intended for those who lack the capacity [to eat more], since they are smaller than the measure of a cock's egg.

Furthermore, regarding the statement here that "one should fast on the day after the full moon," which prescribes fasting on the fourteenth day and then eating fifteen morsels on the full moon day and so forth— thereby describing the Cāndrāyaṇa as consisting of thirty-two days— that is intended to show an alternative method and is not universal.
Because it has been shown, in accordance with the words of the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*), that [the *cāndrāyaṇa*] consists of thirty days;
if this were universal, then the performance of the *cāndrāyaṇa* continuously for a year would be impossible.
And there would be the impossibility of following the course of the moon. // 3.323 //
He states another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa:
"Alternatively, one may consume two hundred and forty morsels of food in a single month in any manner whatsoever; this is another Cāndrāyaṇa. (YDh 3.324)
One should consume two hundred and forty morsels of food in a month; that is,
in some manner, eight mouthfuls every day at midday.
Alternatively, one may perform four [repetitions] each during the day and night;
or else, four in one [period] and twelve in the other; or likewise, having fasted for one night, sixteen in the following [night], and so forth—by means of any one of such methods.
"One should eat according to one's capacity" refers to another form of Cāndrāyaṇa, distinct from the two previously mentioned types of Cāndrāyaṇa; therefore,
for those two [previous types], this rule regarding the number of mouthfuls does not apply,
but rather the number is fixed at exactly two hundred and twenty-five.
And these varieties were shown by Manu:
"With self-restraint, one should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food when the sun has reached midday; thus one should perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa."
A composed Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; thus he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"Just as one who, being composed, eats three hundred and eighty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in some manner over the course of a month, attains the same world as the Moon" (MDh 11.219–21).
Likewise, the inclusion of the word "others" (*para*) is for the purpose of encompassing even that [practice] which is accomplished by a number of morsels less than two hundred and forty.
As Yama has said: "One who is self-restrained and firm in his vow should eat three morsels at each meal for a month of sacrificial food; this is remembered as the Ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa."
And in these [penances] beginning with the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*, it is not necessary to follow the actual course of the moon; therefore,

when performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* continuously by means of a common month consisting of thirty days, if— due to the increase or decrease of lunar dates (*tithi*)— it should somehow occur on the fifth day or subsequent days, [the rule remains valid].
Even so, there is no fault in undertaking it.
Furthermore, regarding the monthly vow called Saumāyana which was taught by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"One should drink cow's milk from four teats for seven nights."
From three breasts for seven nights, and from two breasts for seven nights.
For six nights or three nights one should subsist on air alone, eating from only one breast;
this is the vow called Somāyana, which destroys all impurities.

Thus, in another Smṛti it is said: "And for seven days [one should consume] the entire udder of a cow; then one may consume three udders, two, or likewise one; and if there should be three fasts, then that constitutes a Soma-ayanam within a month."
That too is indeed a rite consisting of the *cāndrāyaṇa*,

because Hārīta, after describing the *cāndrāyaṇa* along with its procedural requirements (itikartavyatā) in the passage beginning "Now, therefore, we shall explain the *cāndrāyaṇa*," states by way of extension (*atideśa*) that "the *somāyana* is exactly like this. As for the *somāyana* mentioned by him as starting from the fourth day of the dark fortnight and ending on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight—
For three nights with four breasts beginning from the fourth [day];

for three nights with three breasts; for three nights with two breasts; for three nights with one breast. Thus, starting again from one breast up to four breasts: "O Soma, that which is your fourth body—with that protect us; obeisance to it, svāhā!"

Having praised the lunar-day oblations intended for sacrifice with the words, "O Soma, that which is your fifth, that which is your sixth," and so forth, one who is purified from sins attains equality, co-residence, and union with the Moon;
thus the *somāyana* consisting of twenty-four days has been described, and this refers to the case of those who are incapable [of the standard practice]. (3.324)
Now he states the procedure common to both the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances:
"One who bathes at the three periods of the day should perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Cāndrāyaṇa;
one should mutter purificatory mantras and consecrate the morsels of food with the Gāyatrī. (YDh 3.325)

One should perform the *kṛcchra* penance, such as the *prājāpatya* or the *cāndrāyaṇa*, accompanied by bathing at the three sessions of the day; and this applies except in the case of the *taptakṛcchra*, for in that instance it is prescribed: "Bathing once, with a concentrated mind" (MDh 11.215).
Thus, because of this specific statement by Manu;
furthermore, regarding the *kṛcchra* penances, Śaṅkha states:
"Three times during the day and three times at night, one should enter the water wearing one's clothes."
Thus, that [rule] refers to one who is incapable;
furthermore, as for what was stated by Vaiśampāyana— that bathing should be performed twice a day, or even three times a day for the twice-born— [that applies to those who are capable].
Thus, this should be understood as applying to one who is unable to perform the ritual bath at the three sessions of the day.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Gārgya— "One should wander for alms wearing a single garment, and after bathing, one should not wring out the garment"— [is also applicable].
Thus, that too applies only to one who is capable [of the vow],
because Śaṅkha has stated that wearing a single garment is optional: "Wearing a single garment, or wearing wet clothes, eating light food, or sleeping on the bare ground."
And regarding bathing, a specific rule has been stated by Hārīta:

"Having bathed at least three times with the *śuddhavatī* verses and having muttered the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn while submerged in water, one should put on a washed or unwashed garment and worship the Sun with the *saumya* Sāman."
After bathing, one should recite purificatory texts (*pavitra*).

These purificatory texts—namely the *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *devakṛta*, the *śuddhavatyaḥ*, the *taratsamāḥ*, and so forth—as well as any others prescribed by Vasiṣṭha and others, one should recite while submerged in water at times not incompatible with their purpose; or else, one may recite the *sāvitrī*.
For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "One should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to one's ability" (MDh 11.226).
As for that which was stated by Gautama:

Regarding the statement, "One should constantly employ the *raurava-yodhā* [mantra] in recitation" (GDh 26.9), that too was stated precisely because of its purificatory nature (*pavitratva*), and not as a restrictive injunction;
for were it so, it would entail the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a basis in another Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Therefore, one who has not studied the Sāmaveda should recite only the *gāyatrī* and other such mantras; even after reciting "Obeisance to Haṃma, to Mohamma," and so forth [as stated in GDh 26.12].
It has been stated that "these indeed are the offerings of clarified butter" (GDh 26.14); however, even that is not mandatory, but rather,
the oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis must be performed by oneself every day (MDh 11.223).
Thus, because the performance of the *homa* with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* has been prescribed by Manu;
likewise, it is also stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Whatever [penance] such as recitation (*japa*) or *homa* is prescribed for a *kṛcchra*, if it cannot be performed..."
"One should perform everything with the *vyāhṛtis*, with the *gāyatrī*, and with the *praṇava*.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*), the worship of the sun (*ādityopasthāna*), and so forth are included.
For this very reason, Vaiśampāyana says:
"Having bathed, one should worship the Sun with verses addressed to the Sun, with palms joined in reverence.
Thus, in other cases as well, an option (*vikalpa*) should be adopted regarding conflicting items,
while a combination (*samuccaya*) is to be applied for those that are non-conflicting.
Since ritual action is based on the cognition provided by all Smṛtis according to the principle of the section concerning different Vedic branches (Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa),
the specific rule regarding the number of recitations has been shown by that very same [principle].
One should recite the Ṛṣabha, the Viraja, and likewise the Aghamarṣaṇa,
or one should mutter the divine Gāyatrī, the purifier and mother of the Vedas.
One should satisfy the ancestors and deities either one hundred times, or one hundred and eight times, or a thousand times, or even more; this may be done either in a whisper or mentally.
"And having bowed one's head to humans and all beings," so it is said.
Likewise, one should consecrate each of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) with the *Gāyatrī* mantra;
as a specific rule has also been stated by Yama:
"Having consumed the morsel placed on the tip of the finger while it is consecrated with the Gāyatrī, and having sipped water, one should again perform the consecration of another [morsel].
And therefore: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" (GDh 27.8).
An alternative to this has been stated by means of the consecration mantras spoken by Gautama, beginning with these [verses].

Furthermore, the consecration of the sacrificial oblation prior to the forming of the *piṇḍas* has been prescribed by means of [mantras] such as "May you swell" (*āpyāyasva*) and "Your milks" (*saṃ te payāṃsi*).
Because they involve distinct physical acts, these are to be combined;
furthermore, when these observances such as the *kṛcchra* are performed for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), they must be undertaken preceded by the shaving of the hair and so forth.
For there is the traditional teaching of Gautama: "One should observe the vow of shaving" (GDh 27.3);
however, for the sake of an auspicious occasion (*abhyudaya*), there is no shaving at all.
Vasiṣṭha has also stated a specific rule in this regard: "In the case of penances consisting of vows, one should have the beard, hair, and so forth shaved,
with the exception of the hair on the belly and the topknot" (VaDh 24.4–5).
Regarding "of the *kṛcchras* in the form of vows":
the remainder [of the sentence] is that the constituent parts (*aṅgas*) in the form of vows, such as shaving the hair and so forth, will be described.
Furthermore, the undertaking of the vows as instructed by the assembly (*parṣad*) should be performed on the evening preceding the day of the vow's observance. As it has been said:
Vasiṣṭha says:
I shall now fully explain the formal undertaking of all vows according to the prescribed rule for all sins, when an expiation is intended to be performed.
At the end of the day, having removed the nails, body hair, and so forth, one should perform a bath prepared with ashes,
cow dung, earth, water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and other such substances.
The removal of impurities must be performed for the sake of achieving external purity,
preceded by the cleansing of the teeth and accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The vow should be undertaken at the beginning of night when the stars are visible outside;
thereafter, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should remain silent while meditating upon one's own misdeeds.
"He shall bear intense mental anguish and, in the end, grief.
Regarding the word "outside," having gone outside the village, even a woman must likewise undertake the observance of the vow;
[this includes] the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails.

But this [penance] does not apply; for, regarding the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such observances, there is the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "For a woman, this very same [penance] applies, with the exception of shaving the hair. (BDh 2.2.45).
But for one who does not desire shaving, a specific rule has been stated by Hārīta:
"Whether he be a king, a prince, or a learned Brāhmaṇa,
having performed the shaving of his hair, he should perform the penance."
"But for the sake of protecting the hair, one should observe a vow that is double [the usual duration];
when that double vow has been performed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be double.
This should be understood as referring specifically to particular faults such as the great sins (mahāpātaka).
The shaving of the hair is not prescribed for learned Brahmins, kings, or women;
nor for those who have committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), a cow-killer, or one who has violated his vow of celibacy (avakīrṇin).
Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*;
furthermore, a specific rule has been stated here by Jābāla:
"At the commencement of all *kṛcchra* penances, and especially at their conclusion..."
And with that very food, one should offer the Vyāhṛtis individually into the domestic fire.
"One should perform a *śrāddha* at the conclusion of the vow, with gifts such as cows and gold as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Yama has also stated a specific detail regarding this:
"Remorse, cessation [of the transgression], and bathing are declared to be constituent parts (*aṅga*) [of the rite]."
And likewise, there is the recitation of all the various omens.
Likewise:
"One observing a vow should avoid anointing the limbs, anointing the head, betel, ointments, and everything else that produces strength or passion."
This collection of duties and so forth is to be sought from other Smṛti texts.
Having thus undertaken the vow according to this rule, it must necessarily be brought to completion; otherwise, however, there is a transgression.
Having previously taken a vow, if one does not practice it while deluded by desire,
he becomes a Cāṇḍāla while alive and is born as a dog after death.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Chāgaleya; enough of this prolixity. (3.325)
Having thus described the nature of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances whose application has been stated, he now states their application to other effects as well, following the present context:
"In the case of sins for which no specific penance is prescribed, purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa."

He who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon. That which is prescribed is called *ādiṣṭa*; there is no other penance [required] for those sins for which a specific one has been ordained. For those sins, purification is achieved by means of the *Cāndrāyaṇa*.

By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that purification may also be attained through the *Prājāpatya* and other *Kṛcchra* penances, either in conjunction with the *Aindava* (Cāndrāyaṇa) or independently of it.
And so it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Whatever sins there may be, even those more grievous than the most grievous,
Manu declared that they are purified by the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
Thus, the combination of all three has been established;
however, Uśanas has stated the combination of two:
"Of misfortunes, of ill-performed rites, and of sins—even great ones."
"The *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances indeed destroy all sins. Here, *durita* refers to a minor offense (*upapātaka*), while *duriṣṭa* refers to a major transgression (*pātaka*).

By Gautama’s formulation, "The *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* are the universal expiation" (GDh 19.20), the use of a non-compound construction indicates that the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* are independent [of one another]. Furthermore, by the word "and" (*iti*) following the *cāndrāyaṇa*, the conjunction of all three is indicated.
However, regarding the *prājāpatya* alone, it is stated independently in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"But when a minor offense has not been specifically prescribed, one should perform a *prājāpatya*."
Gautama also stated the independence [of these penances] from the *prājāpatya* and others:
"Having performed the first, one becomes pure, purified, and fit for ritual action;
having performed the second, one is freed from other sins except for the great mortal offenses (*mahāpātaka*)."
"He commits evil, but from that he is released;
having performed the third [penance], he is released from all sin" (GDh 26.21–22); by this, it is intended that one is released even from a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*).
Manu has also said:
"This penance called Parāka is the remover of all sins" (MDh 11.216).
Hārīta has also said:
The Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal fast, the Tulāpuruṣa,
and likewise following after cows— these destroy all sins.
Likewise, cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water infused with *kuśa* grass,
and a fast for one night— these would purify even an outcaste dog-eater (*śvapāka*).
Likewise, with reference to the *taptakṛcchra* penance, he (Yājñavalkya) has stated:
"This *kṛcchra*, when practiced twice, shall liberate one from mortal sins (*pātaka*);
practiced three times according to the rule, it removes even the murder of a Śūdra. Thus.
And it has been said by Uśanas:
"Whether it be mentioned or not mentioned as a destroyer of great sins (mahāpātaka), one should purify oneself by means of the Prājāpatya penance; there is no doubt in this matter."

These penances, beginning with the *prājāpatya*, are to be applied— either individually or collectively— to the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and others that are not specifically prescribed, depending on whether they are committed once or repeatedly; likewise,
they are also to be applied to the major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and others that involve specific vows, depending on the degree of repetition.
For this very reason, Yama stated, "Where it has been declared," and so forth.
Gautama also employed the term "all penances" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) for the purpose of summarizing the various expiations.
Likewise, although he himself stated [the following]:

Having stated, "By performing the second [twelve-year penance], one is released from whatever sin other than the great sins (mahāpātaka) one may commit," and further stating, "By performing the third, one is released from all sin" (GDh 26.21–22), that too refers to the intention of [excluding] the great sins, and not the intention of minor sins (kṣudrapātaka).
Furthermore, it is impossible for a great sin (mahāpātaka) to exist without a prescribed expiation;
therefore, even in cases where specific expiations have been mentioned, penances such as the Prājāpatya should also be applied.
In that regard, regarding the twelve-year vow, if one calculates by assigning one *prājāpatya* penance for every twelve days,
then three hundred and sixty *prājāpatyas* constitute the optional practice to be performed during the twelve-year period. If one is unable to do so, that many cows must be given as gifts.
In the absence of that, three hundred and sixty niṣkas should be given. Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"If one is unable to perform the Prājāpatya penance, a wise person should give a cow."
In the absence of a cow, its equivalent value must undoubtedly be given.
"Or half the value, or a *niṣka*, or half of that, according to one's capacity;
in the absence of cows, it shall be a *niṣka*, or half of that, or even a quarter," so says the Smṛti.
If one is unable even to pay the prescribed fine, one should perform that many *udavāsas* (fasts).
If one is unable even for that, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* thirty-six lakh times.
The Kṛcchra penance, ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, likewise staying in water,
and the gift of a cow to a Brahmin— these four are equal in merit.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Parāśara.
As for that which has been stated in the Caturviṃśatimata: "By reciting the Gāyatrī ten million times, one removes the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa."
Whoever recites it eighty thousand times is liberated from the sin of drinking liquor.
Seventy lakhs of the Gāyatrī purify one who steals gold;
sixty lakhs of the Gāyatrī liberate one who has violated the Guru’s bed.
Thus, that [penance] is stated as having a procedure equal to that of the twelve-year penance;
it is not, however, intended for those who are incapable, so there is no contradiction.
The same applies to others as well.
A *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand recitations of the Goddess’s mantra, two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
a thousand oblations of sesame seeds, and likewise the complete recitation of the Vedas.

These and other such substitutes, as prescribed in the *Caturviṃśatimata* and other treatises, should be understood to amount to three hundred and sixty times [the standard penance] for mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).
For heinous sins (*atipātaka*), two hundred and seventy *prājāpatya* penances must be performed.
Or, there may be as many substitutes as there are cows and so forth;
however, for mortal sins (pātaka), there are one hundred and eighty Prājāpatya penances, and the substitutes such as cows and so forth are likewise that same number.
Likewise, it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Having committed many various sins from birth onwards,
even those falling short of the killing of a Brahmin, one should perform the vow for six years."
"In substitution for cows, one hundred and eighty [cows] should be given by the wealthy;
or the wise man should mutter the Gāyatrī eighteen lakhs.
This very statement serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for calculating each *prājāpatya* penance over twelve days within the twelve-year vow.
Thus, for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) that fall within the scope of the three-year penance, there are ninety *prājāpatya* penances and an equal number of substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*).
Furthermore, for those offenses within the scope of the three-month penance, there are seven and a half *prājāpatya*s, and the substitutes consist of cows, fasting, and so forth.
They are exactly that many.

Regarding those matters concerning the monthly vows (*māsika-vrata*), however, there is either two *prājāpatyas* and a half, or that same amount as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*). Furthermore, regarding those minor offenses (*upapātaka*) that fall within the scope of the *cāndrāyaṇa*, there are three *prājāpatyas*.
