For one who is unable [to perform the penance], the substitute (pratyāmnāya) is of exactly that same measure. Furthermore, as stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"In the rule for substitutes, eight [cows] are always to be given for a Cāndrāyaṇa."

Thus, that [penance] as well refers to the wealthy person regarding the substitutes for the *cāndrāyaṇa* such as the *pipīlikāmadhya*; however, in the case of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) which fall under the category of the *māsakṛcchra*,
there are seven and a half *prājāpatyas*, and the substitutes such as cows are likewise the same number.
In the Prājāpatya penance, one should give one cow; in the Sāntapana, two;
and likewise, in the Parāka, Taptakṛcchra, and Atikṛcchra, three cows each.

This is because it is stated thus in the *Caturviṃśatimata*. Furthermore, this [rule] regarding "he should eat each morsel" should be understood as referring to the alternative of eating morsels the size of an *āmalaka* fruit; however, according to the alternative of eating food that fills the hollow of the hands (*pāṇipūra*), two cows [are required].
Thus, because the *prājāpatya* penance is equivalent to six days of fasting, and the *atikṛcchra* is double that amount;
even though one eats a handful of food during nine days, nevertheless, due to the extreme hardship of performing it continuously for twelve days.
It is precisely the equality of two *prājāpatya* penances with a six-day fast;

and it is indeed logical that a single *prājāpatya* is equal to six days of fasting. For instance, when one abstains from the three evening meals during the first three days, the accomplishment of one full day of fasting is achieved.
During the second three-day period, for one intent on abstaining from the three morning meals;
likewise, during the next three days of not begging, for another who avoids the three evening meals—in this way, there are three fasts over nine days. Furthermore...
And since there is a three-day fast during the final three days, it is logical that this is equal to six fasts.

However, for the vow of cow-slaughter consisting of a three-night fast accompanied by the gift of eleven cows including a bull, the substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*) are eleven and a half *prājāpatya* penances, along with an equal number of water-fasts and so forth.
In the case of a month-long vow of subsisting on milk, it is equivalent to two and a half *prājāpatya*s; however,
for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) involving a *parāka* penance, three *prājāpatya*s are required in place of the *parāka*, *taptakṛcchra*, and *atikṛcchra*.
"One should perform three *kṛcchra* penances, or one and a half *sāntapana* penances; if unable [to do even that], one should observe the vow"—
so it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
The Cāndrāyaṇa, Parāka, Kṛcchra, and Atikṛcchra penances— each consisting of three Prājāpatyas— are to be performed in the place of the twelve-year vow in a number of one hundred and twenty.
However, their substitutes, such as cows and other gifts, are to be tripled.
For the ninety types of *atipātaka* (grave offenses), there are penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*;
furthermore, for those equal to them, which are designated by the term *pātaka*, there are sixty such penances.
Regarding the minor offenses (upapātaka) that require a three-year penance, there are thirty [subdivisions].
In place of the three-month vow for killing a cow, because of the abundance of duties such as bathing in cow-urine and so forth, there are three [variants] beginning with the Cāndrāyaṇa.

In the case of the monthly vow (*māsika-vrata*) described by the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*), there is only one *cāndrāyaṇa*; however, in all instances, the substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*) such as cows, water-dwellings, and so forth, are indeed threefold.

Furthermore, regarding miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*), a *prājāpatya* penance should be applied according to the specific expiation prescribed for each case, by calculating it as a quarter and so on. In the case of repetition, [the same applies].
Furthermore, regarding the statement "the Cāndrāyaṇa and so forth," one should apply this same principle to other cases as well.
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"Whatever sin or minor offense (upapātaka) has been committed from birth onwards..."
One should repeat the Kṛcchra penance until it has been performed sixty times.

Thus, this refers to the same subject matter as the two-year penance prescribed by Gautama for adultery with another's wife (*paradāra*), or else it concerns the repeated commission of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) that are the subject of three-month and other such penances.

Or, it refers to the case of a double repetition of approaching women such as Cāṇḍālas and others, who are designated by the term *pātaka* (sinners). In that regard: "If done intentionally, a year-long *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed; if done unintentionally, two *aindava* [penances].
(Ascribed to Uśanas at 3.265 under the section on adultery.)
Since a one-year *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed for going [to a forbidden woman] once intentionally,
it is indeed appropriate that a sixty *kṛcchras*— equivalent to two years— is prescribed for the repetition of that act. As for that which was stated by Sumantu:
Even that great sin which has been repeatedly committed intentionally is purified by a year-long *kṛcchra* penance, except in the case of a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*).
Thus, that [penance] also concerns the repetition of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like;
likewise, the statement "two *aindava* [fasts] for ignorance" refers either to the repetition of those sins which are the subject matter of the two *aindava* fasts prescribed by Yama,
or— [in the case of one who is unable to perform penance but is rich in grain]— it concerns that.
And he should fulfill the *kṛcchra* and other such vows by providing food and gifts for the foremost of the twice-born.
For thus says another *Smṛti*:
"In the *kṛcchra*, [one feeds] five; in the *atikṛcchra*, three times that; in the third [the *parāka*], thirty every day; and in the *tapta-kṛcchra*, forty."
In the *parāka* penance, there should be twenty multiplied by three;
in the *sāntāpana* *kṛcchra*, that same number becomes twenty-six;
and in the *cāndrāyaṇa* austerity, it would be that same number diminished by two. One whose strength is weakened by these ascetic practices should feed the most eminent Brahmins.
The phrase "day by day" (aharahar) is to be connected with every [penance].
The third is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
In this case, it is calculated by treating each day as equivalent to one day of the *prājāpatya* penance.
There is a feeding of sixty learned Brahmins.
As for that which is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata: "Twelve Brahmins should be fed, and likewise the Pāvakeṣṭi sacrifice."
Or whatever else is purifying, the wise say that all is equal.
Thus, the feeding of twelve Brahmins in place of a *prājāpatya* penance has been prescribed;
that refers to the case of one who is destitute.
Furthermore, regarding the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance as well, the corresponding substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*) and so forth have been stated in that very same context.
The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Mṛgāreṣṭi, the Pavitreṣṭi, as well as the Mitravindā, the animal sacrifice, and likewise the three-month Kṛcchra penance.
In the absence of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, as well as of *iṣṭi* sacrifices and animal sacrifices, *caru* offerings are prescribed.
Thus, that [penance] as well is for one incapable of performing the Cāndrāyaṇa;
as for the eight Kṛcchras prescribed as a substitute for "three months of Kṛcchra" in that same manner,
that too applies to the case of an elderly person or a fool.
Since it has been shown that "the Cāndrāyaṇa consists of three Kṛcchras," enough with this elaboration;
let us return to the subject at hand.

But he who, desiring prosperity, performs this Cāndrāyaṇa for the sake of dharma— in order to accomplish the rites prescribed for specific desires— and not for the sake of expiation, attains *candrasālokya*, a particular heaven characterized by co-residence with the Moon.
And this is with reference to the repetition for a year;
having attained one [year], he becomes free from evil, free from blemish, and destroys all sin;
having attained a second, he [purifies] ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself.

For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Gautama: "He purifies the twenty-first generation and the lineage, and having attained [the duration of] a year, he reaches the same world as the Moon" (GDh 27.16–18).
Moreover:
One who performs the Kṛcchra penance with a desire for dharma shall attain great prosperity;
being well-composed, he obtains the fruit of a major sacrifice. (YDh 3.327)
But he who, desiring worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), performs penances such as the *prājāpatya* and others, experiences great fortune and power characterized by sovereignty and the like;
just as the performer of major sacrifices such as the *rājasūya* experiences its fruit characterized by universal sovereignty (*svārājya*) and so forth.
One obtains a great fruit;
likewise, this [person] too, being well-concentrated, performs the entire collection of constituent parts without deficiency.
Thus, the mention of the analogy of the sacrifice is for the purpose of illuminating the majesty of the fruit.
By the phrase "well-concentrated," he indicates the unimpaired performance of the scripture;

by stating this, he shows that when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), the fruit is not attained because [the rite] is a *kāmyakarman* (an action performed for a specific desired result).
Therefore, in this case, it is not as in the case of expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
Since the performance of all possible constituent parts (aṅgas) must be accepted, the substitution of one rite for another (pratyāmnāya) is cast far aside.

However, regarding the repetition of the performance of penances such as the *kṛcchra*, the repetition of the result for the qualified performer is established as being obtained through logic—namely, that a ritual action (*karman*) is something to be accomplished through its commencement; thus, this [result] is certainly not unintended. (3.327)

Under the guise of summarizing all the matters previously stated, he speaks in order to set forth, along with their explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the injunctions regarding the memorization of the *Dharmaśāstra* and so forth, in the form of a request and the granting of a boon:
"Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya, the sages..."
They spoke thus to the high-souled lord of yogis, who possessed immeasurable splendor.

For here, the sixfold duties distinct from those pertaining to caste, stage of life, and so forth, have been expounded; having heard all these words spoken by the Lord of Yogis, the sages, their eyes wide with joy, addressed him—who was endowed with majesty and virtue—with the following words that are about to be related. (3.328)

Those who, unwearied, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and go to the third heaven. A seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and likewise, one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth.
Likewise, one who desires long life shall obtain long life, and one who desires prosperity shall obtain great prosperity.

Furthermore, for whoever shall cause even these three verses to be recited during a Śrāddha ceremony, there shall be inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt. (YDh 3.330–331)

"A Brāhmaṇa attains the state of a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth through the retention of this scripture. (YDh 3.332). In this manner, through verses of straightforward meaning, Sāmaśrava and others made their requests in many ways. (3.329–3.332).
He states another prayer as well:
"May you grant your approval for that wise man who shall cause the twice-born to hear this on every sacred festival day; let him obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. (YDh 3.333)

"He who shall cause the twice-born to hear this treatise on Dharma at every section (parvan) shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice"—this is the explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the injunction regarding its recitation.
Therefore, may you grant your approval everywhere for this matter which we have requested. (3.333)
Regarding the granting of the boon, [the text] says:
Having heard this speech of the sages, Yājñavalkya also, with a joyful soul, said, "So be it," after bowing to the Self-born One. (YDh 3.334)

Having heard this spoken by the sages, the Lord of Yogins, his lotus-face blossoming with the desire for the fruits of upholding the Dharma-śāstra composed by himself and other such acts, paid homage to the Self-born Brahmā; and having prostrated, the Blessed One indeed spoke thus: "May everything requested by you come to pass exactly so."

Thus ends the third chapter, on Expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in the *Ṛjumitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Vijñāneśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, son of the venerable Bhāradvāja Padmanābha Bhaṭṭopādhyāya.
Now, the table of contents for this chapter is written here:
therein, first is the section on birth-impurity (sūtaka), [chapter] 1;
then the section on duties in times of distress (āpaddharma).
2. The Section on Forest Hermitism; 3. The Section on Spiritual Knowledge; 4. Then, the Section on Expiation; 5. [The Section on Renunciation].
Therein, first: 6. The ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*);
7. An enumeration of the causes such as the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*);
[and] the expiations for the great transgressions (*mahāpātakaprāyaścitta*).
8. Expiations by extension (ātideśika); 9. Expiations for minor offenses (upapātaka);
10. The section on miscellaneous expiations (prakīrṇaka).
11. The procedure for abandoning those who have fallen [from their vows]; 12. The procedure for undertaking the observances;
13. The section on secret penances.
14. The characteristics of the *kṛcchra* and other penances. Thus end the chapters.
This commentary on the Dharmaśāstra is the work of the yogi Vijñāneśvara, a disciple of the one whose title is Uttamopapada. (1)

Thus, this commentary on the treatise of the sage Yājñavalkya is not for whom it is intended? Though its words are few, it is rich in vast meaning; it sprinkles nectar upon the ears of the learned. (2)
I have composed this commentary using words that are profound yet clear, concise in their syllables, and brief yet rich in meaning. (3)
There has not been, is not, nor will there ever be on the surface of the earth a city equal in excellence to ours, nor has a sovereign king like Śrī Vikramārka ever been seen or even heard of;
and as for the scholar Vijñāneśvara, he has no peer at all.
May this triad, which is like a wish-fulfilling creeper, be both small in measure and enduring.
May he who is the creator of words of sweet form that reach the limit of wonder for the learned, the giver of objects of exceeding excellence upon the petitions of the multitude of supplicants,
and the meditator upon the form of the conqueror of Mura, live as long as the sun and moon.
The Lord of the Knowledge of Reality is the conqueror of those enemies that are co-nascent with the body. // 5 //
From the bridge of Setu to the king of mountains,
from the western ocean with its high, surging waves and swarms of frolicking dolphins to the eastern sea, his fame spread, while his feet shone with the luster of the crest-jewels of bowing kings.
May King Vikramāditya protect this entire world as long as the moon and stars endure. // 6 //
If the sense-faculties are turned inward, what is the use of austerity?
If the sense-faculties are not turned inward, what is the use of austerity?
If Hari is both within and without, what is the use of austerity?
If Hari is neither within nor without, then what is the use of asceticism?
This Yājñavalkya-smṛti, known as the Samitākṣarā, is hereby completed.
